 You won’t see John and Monique Davidson at many fashion parties. They’ve been married (to one another) for 44 years. A stylish couple, they avoid showy events. Sartorial standards remain high, however. “Even on the plane, you can’t slob out,” says John, when I admire the silk handkerchief in his Brooks Brothers blazer. “You don’t know who you’ll bump into. We are our brand.” Leni bag in pink, £820, J&M Davidson; and Large carnival bag in burgundy, £595, J&M Davidson. I suspect they’re also immaculate when cooking up family dinners for their two daughters or their grandson Leni in their sprawling home in Chiswick, or visiting the factories in Spain, where their desirable bags are made, and Belgium, where their knitwear is produced. Yes, they design clothes, too. The small ready-to-wear collection is a reflection of Monique’s innate chic-simplicity: voluminous artist-shapes in glossy cotton and silk failles, it’s utility meets C Z Guest, the doyenne American socialite who exemplified functional, patrician style. This is the couple who put the knitted coat, now a staple of so many wardrobes (and other brands), on the map. If you weren’t aware that the coatigan began at J&M Davidson, that just goes to prove how under-flaunted they are. As for the discreet but glamorous bags, they’ve always been loved by those who appreciate class over logos. They’re also impeccably made, initially in Manchester, when there was once – hard to imagine now – a functioning leather crafts industry in the UK. When the last of those bag factories closed, J&M moved production to Andalucia, where they use the very best factories and achieve a quality that, in my opinion, is up there with the best of the bigger (and far more expensive brands). They’re big in Japan, too, where consistency is revered (“They order the same styles in new materials every year,” says John). Yet J&M remains an insiders’ secret. John is philosophical about their fringe status. “You can make the best bags in the world, but if you don’t advertise you can’t ever really compete with the big boys. We never really pushed ourselves forwards.” That’s the nub. Manolo Blahnik scarcely advertises in relation to the scale of his business, but he has a huge personality. The patronage of Sex and the City didn’t hurt, either. Fashion designer Martin Margiela, on the other hand, is so self-effacing that most people who work in the industry don’t know what he looks like – but that anonymity in itself became a clever talking point. Poncho, £455, J&M Davidson; Trouser, £580, J&M Davidson; and Greta bag, £1425, J&M Davidson.  The thing about being under the radar is that existing fans tend to love it. But businesses need regular growth spurts to keep investors smiling. J&M has the Japanese on board [it is backed by fashion conglomerate Yagi Tsusho, which also owns Mackintosh) – and the latter have been thinking big recently. So, three decades after they set up shop in the basement of Margaret Howell’s store (Diana, Princess of Wales, or Lady Dee, as they both call her, à la franglais, used to buy their belts by the armful), they opened in Mount Street in Mayfair, swankiest and most fashionable of London’s shopping drags. Here, their neighbours include Céline, Marni, Simone Rocha, Loewe and Christopher Kane. It’s a far cry from their last shop on the Golborne Road, on the gamier fringe of Notting Hill, where they were flanked by halal butchers and Portuguese cafés. The geographical shift has resulted in a perception shift – by the company ye keep shall ye be judged. They still have their studio on Golborne Road, however, and the contrast with Mount Street neatly encapsulates the label’s no-nonsense stealth-status. Medium carnival bag in brown, £550, J&M Davidson, and Gabby bag in lime, £580, J&M Davidson. “People kept asking if we would put up our prices, but zis we absolutely don’t want to do,” says Monique, in an accent so steeped in Brie that it’s perfectly possible, even after all her time in London, to misunderstand wildly what the French-born designer saying. No doubting the prices, though, which are roughly a third less than comparable products from flashier brands – the flip side of not spending millions of advertising. Jean jumper,  £235, J&M Davidson.  The other advantage is that J&M is poised to benefit from the consumer fatigue that is nibbling at the profits of more famous, over-exposed brands. It’s only taken J&M Davidson, 40 years to reach the glossiest shopping street in the UK. To those in a hurry, their progress might be at a discouraging pace. But perhaps it’s better to view it as the closest luxury leather comes to a morality tale: consistency trumps flash – eventually. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  For all the column inches that have been taken up dissecting the hemlines, paisley-print swirls and questionable wedges of the Duchess of Cambridge’s wardrobe on the Royal Tour of India and Bhutan this week, comparatively little has been said about Prince William’s choice of attire. Of course, it’s entirely gallant that Kate should be the one to shine (and no one wants a future king who’s a walking fashion plate – we had that back in the 1930s and it resulted in abdication), but it’s a damning insight into how unremarkable the Duke of Cambridge’s style choices are that they’ve been, well, so unremarked upon. There seems to be a whisper of invisibility about Prince William’s clothing, fading quietly into the background as much as possible in a series of nondescript khaki shirts and trousers, oddly stiff and formal tailoring, strangely shiny trousers that seem a tad too tight, and the same pair of scuffed desert boots. The suede boots seem to have become as world-weary as the Prince himself as the week has progressed. “Men’s style moves far more slowly that women’s fashions,” says Bill Prince, deputy editor of GQ magazine. “And it slows to a glacial pace when it comes to royal mens’ style – observe the bespoke navy suit, white shirt and tiny knotted tie for proof. William is not only channelling his father and maternal grandfather, he’s obeying traditional rules of formal dressing.” It’s certainly true that Prince William has built up a solid wardrobe of impeccably tailored pieces, following in his father’s discerning footsteps by patronising the Savile Row establishments of Gieves & Hawkes and Anderson & Sheppard, alongside Turnbull & Asser. But while that stands him in sartorial good stead opening a hospital in Chelsea or meeting school children in Yorkshire, it looks curiously at odds in 32 degree heat, or meeting the joyously attired King of Bhutan. Such is the quandary for many a man who might spend his life in solid suiting, only to find himself somewhat adrift in murky sartorial waters when the pinstriped armoury is off and it’s time to unbutton the cuffs and untuck the shirt. And yet, this is Prince William, a man who has access to the most impeccable tailoring, the most exceptional accessories and who carries a hefty sartorial legacy on his shoulders from both his mother and his father. Prince Charles, whose name lines the ledger books of some of Mayfair’s most august tailoring houses and who relies on decades-old classics to lend substance and precision to his wardrobe, has stellar form where foreign style is concerned. Pairing a light linen suit with perhaps a lavender shirt or a thoroughly elegant safari suit, and merrily throwing himself into proceedings with a garland here, a bindi there, Prince Charles should be providing sartorial inspiration for his son. “Prince William could certainly take a leaf out of his father’s book when visiting tropical and sub-tropical climes,” says Prince, whose magazine has positioned HRH as a fixture on its annual best-dressed list several times over. “Prince Charles has always struck the right note when travelling further afield, and seems in his element when wearing lightweight suits in a variety of tasteful, pastel hues. Topped with a panama, it’s stood him in very good stead for five decades, at least.” Prince Charles’s look, in essence, boils down to a sense of confidence in one’s style and the ability to toy with a classic formula while always remaining appropriate. Perhaps in this respect Prince William is still finding his desert boot-shod feet. It’s telling that, while we know every detail of Kate’s stylist and Kensington Palace release information of her outfits on formal engagements, there’s no equivalent for the Prince. Aside from his valet and an order from menswear online retailer Mr Porter, which was spotted arriving at Kensington Palace in the month leading up to this royal tour, Prince William seems rather isolated style-wise. So how should we expect our future king to dress, looking suitably regal while at the same time tackling rainforests and dusty terrain? “What William should avoid is the ‘gap-year chic’ favoured by the off-duty Harry,” advises Prince. “The heir’s role as menswear icon-apparent is too important to be reduced to a roomy polo shirt, Aztec belt and chinos.” Instead, the Duke of Cambridge would do well to look to the traditional tenets of tailoring, filtered through a more relaxed gaze – a lightweight seersucker suit with open-necked shirt, a veer towards linen suiting, accented with considered accessories and, should the photo call demand something more casual, experimenting with boat shoes and a preppy pair of chinos and crisp shirt. As for the specifics of this India trip, while no one wants the Prince drawn into embarrassing costume affairs, looking to a local designer such as Raghavendra Rathore of Jodhpur – a purveyor of sleek polo shirts and high-collared Bandhgala jackets, who has garnered attention from Hollywood stars – would demonstrate the kind of cultural experimentation his wife’s been applauded for. And not a down-at-heel desert boot in sight.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  With Sadie Frost and Jude Law for parents and supermodel Kate Moss as godmother, it was only a matter of time before Iris Law found herself in front of a camera lens.  And here she is, aged 15, making a rather edgy debut. The middle child of Sadie and Jude sports a directional plum lip and scraped-back hair to model the sleepwear collaboration between stylist Violetta Thalia Kassapi (who operates under the name Violetta Fancies You) and London label Illustrated People. Together the brands have created three pyjama sets and also called in Evangeline Ling, sister of fashion blogger Bip, to assist on the modelling front. Law has only been pictured a handful of times in public – once at Kate Moss’s wedding in 2011, where she was one of 13 bridesmaids, and in 2012 aged 11, when a dress she wore to Vivienne Westwood’s London Fashion Week show generated headlines due to its rude nature (despite being covered in prints of Love Heart sweets, the usually innocent messages had been replaced with ‘drink poison', 'eat sh*t' and 'blow me'). But her Instagram account, like many a teenager’s, features plenty of selfies. Of course, she’s not the first celebrity offspring to turn her hand at modelling (check out our gallery below for plenty of examples) but she is part of the second generation of the Primrose Hill Set coming through into the public eye. Meg Matthews and Noel Gallagher’s daughter Anais, also 15, recently modelled for Accessorize, while Law’s 19-year-old brother Rafferty, a musician, has posed for Tiger of Sweden and starred in a DKNY catwalk show. The term Primrose Hill Set was used to dub celebrities such as the Laws along with Moss and actors Jonny Lee Miller, Ryhs Ifans, Ewan McGregor and their friends as they all resided in the desirable north London neighbourhood and enjoyed hedonistic lifestyles. Frost and Law split in 2003 after seven years of marriage. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Actress Eleanor Tomlinson is certainly a star on the rise, as she is the leading lady in the cult BBC show Poldark, which returns for season two next weekend. Fashion ad campaigns are now something of a right of passage for actresses breaking through the industry, and so it's not at all surprising that Tomlinson has landed an AW16 campaign given the frenzy surrounding the Poldark series.   Tomlinson joins model Karolina Kurkova and American singer Judith Hill in Karen Millen's AW16 campaign, which sees the Poldark star wear chunky knitwear, autumnal hues and a leopard print coat in a Georgian terrace house. "Modelling is still new to me," Tomlinson says of her time on set, "but to work with Karolina Kurkova and Judith Hill was fab and we had a good laugh." Tomlinson explains why she will always be a red head, the unglamorous side of the costumes in Poldark and how we can expect Demelza's style to change in series two... "I work very closely with the costume and make-up team on Poldark in order to get Demelza's look just right," Tomlinson tells The Telegraph. "In series one when we first meet Demelza, she is mistaken for a boy. To create this look we bound my chest to flatten my bust and I wore shabby hand-me-down clothes with the idea that these could have been passed on from her brothers. As the series progressed, we started introducing corsets to create a more feminine and mature shape. I was adamant that all Demelza's outfits were practical and that she never becomes as ladylike as Elizabeth. There still has to be that class divide." Wearing corsets on set all day of course has its downsides, as Tomlinson says about her new film Alleycats: "It was great to do something modern, and not wearing a corset was a dream. It's very easy to be pigeon holed in this industry so I think for me to do something where my character was so different was really important." The second series of Poldark airs this weekend, and Tomlinson says her character's style has shifted: "Demelza has matured and settled in to her married life a little more. Ross and Demelza still have very little money so it was important to me that we kept everything low key. Demelza also supposedly makes a lot of her own clothes and we wanted each garment to have that real lived-in feel. " "A lot of the pieces we use in Poldark are original garments," reveals Tomlinson. "They are often very well worn but this all adds to the character and I think especially for Demelza, this works well. Sometimes you will hear a rip as you reach for a doughnut and you think 'Oh no'!" Tomlinson isn't new to the red carpet, as in her teens she starred in the films Angus, Thongs and Perfect Snogging and  Alice In Wonderland, and so started dressing for premieres at an early age. "I'm very lucky in that I have an amazing stylist - Nisha Grewal - who helps create my red carpet looks," she says. "It's great fun playing dress up for a night. I don't feel there is ever a need to show too much skin. The classier the better for me. Why wear something skimpy when you could steal the show like Claire Danes did at the Met Gala in that stunning dress by Zac Posen." "I think I will definitely stay a red head," Tomlinson says of her flame-red hair. "Over the years I have dyed my hair every colour under the sun but red seems to really fit my skin tone and I like to be a bit unusual. When reading the Poldark scripts I was creating this feisty, sexy heroin in my head and I felt that red would be kind of fabulous. She's untameable and in a sea of mainly brunettes, it was nice to have something that immediately packs a punch." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The last time I saw Jourdan Dunn was at the Topshop Unique catwalk show in London four days before our interview, so, naturally, I assume she has been hanging out in the city. No. ‘Straight after Topshop I had to dash to New York, where I was filming, and then I flew back yesterday,’ she says. ‘What is today?’ Thursday, I say. ‘Thursday…’ She looks confused. ‘So I flew back yesterday. No, I didn’t. And tonight I’m going to Milan. It’s never-ending. I actually don’t know what day it is.’ Would that the rest of us looked as beautiful when this exhausted. It takes a lot to draw the eye from Dunn, a model who, unusually, contrives to look yet more flawless in the flesh than she does on the cover of a magazine. Still, if you are to have your thunder stolen, it may as well be filched by your cute six-year-old son, a boy with a dazzling smile and a demeanour so placid that his mother can conduct an hour-long interview without him intervening until the 53rd minute – surely some sort of under-seven record. When Riley does eventually wander over (he has spied a jar of sweets – who can blame him?), he whispers shyly in his mother’s ear. ‘You’re starving?’ she asks, one eyebrow raised on account of the fact that 53 minutes ago they were both sitting in the studio eating a hearty post-photo shoot lunch. ‘So what snacks would you like? No, that’s not really a snack, though,’ she says when he points hopefully at the sweets. ‘How about a banana?’ Riley accepts defeat graciously. ‘I don’t really give him chocolates or sweets,’ Dunn says. ‘And then he goes to his dad’s on the weekend, and he’s like, “I had this! Daddy gave me that!” I’m like, you know what? That’s fine, because it’s on the weekend.’ We are here to talk about Dunn’s collaboration with Marks & Spencer, a 22-piece collection of childrenswear that will be manna for any parent who believes girls and boys should burst out of the pink and blue gender constraints so often placed on their clothes. That M&S approached Dunn, 25, she describes as ‘kind of mad. I’d never have thought they would want to do something with me – it’s such an iconic British brand.’ This from a woman born and bred in Greenford, and spotted, aged 15, in the Hammersmith branch of Primark. ‘I wasn’t really a girlie girl growing up,’ she says. ‘I liked the best of both worlds, because I had two younger brothers. I still enjoy wearing men’s oversized T-shirts or sneakers. That’s why the collection is unisex – for girls who don’t want to wear pink, look girlie or dress like a princess.’ It was also sparked by the fact that nice boys’ clothes are thin on the ground. ‘When I went shopping for Riley, either stuff was too babyish or there wasn’t anything cool. When you go into a shop, there’s a huge selection for girls, then a little corner at the back for the boys.’ She says Riley has strong opinions about what he wears. ‘It’s important that he has a way to express himself.’ Unless he wants to wear his Lego T-shirt. ‘That’s the only time we had a real battle. He’s like, “Mummy, how can you not like it? You’re the one who bought it for me!” ’ She has also started soliciting his opinion about her own clothing. ‘He’s quite a little charmer; he knows the right things to say. But whenever my boobs are out, he definitely covers them. He says, “Mummy, why are you being sexy?” I remember he once said, “Mummies are not supposed to be sexy.”’ She laughs. Dunn became a parent at 19, split from Riley’s father when their son was still a baby, and returned to work when he was nine months old – as many mothers do, but with the added pressures of world travel and having to look good in a bikini. That she took this in her stride and went on to become one of the highest-earning models in the industry (several international Vogue covers, cosmetics contracts with Maybelline and Burberry, starring with Kendall Jenner and Gigi Hadid in the Balmain x H&M campaign) is down to three things: her looks, her work ethic and her mother. ‘Thank God for my mum, because she’s amazing. She said to me, “Once you have Riley, I’m going to be here for you, 100 per cent. So do what you have to do.”’ When not in New York, where she has an apartment, Dunn lives with her mother, Dee, in the family home in Greenford. ‘My family are the realest people around me and will always have my back. That’s when I feel most comfortable, when I’m with them. I’ve always been really close with my mum and both my brothers.’ Her brother Antoine, a fitness instructor, recently had a child of his own. ‘It’s so weird to see my baby brother as a dad now,’ she says.  Dunn is also close to a coterie of models who started out with her, particularly Karlie Kloss and Cara Delevingne. ‘Karlie and I bonded straight away. Once we found out we had the same birthday, we were like, “OK, this was destined to be.” 'It’s difficult now because we’re both so busy, and we don’t do as many shows. But I was with her last night, and every time we do get together it’s as though we haven’t been apart. I love her dearly – she’s like my little sister. 'Cara, I also consider a sister. I was so heartbroken when she told me she was going to focus on acting and stop modelling. I said, “No, my partner in crime!” But I’m happy for her, because this is what she really wants. She’s in a great place and I love seeing her smile, love seeing her happy… I just miss being backstage with her. 'It didn’t seem to be work. It was easy, just chilling with a friend and then doing a show. When you’re away from your family, with long days of fittings and castings, she had a great, positive energy to be around.’ Me with no make-up, scraped-back hair, baggy jeans and a hoodie = wholly anonymous. Jourdan Dunn with no make-up, scraped-back hair, baggy jeans and a hoodie = famous international supermodel who gets pointed out and asked for selfies wherever she goes – so much so that she sometimes has to camouflage her appearance. Is a beanie with sunglasses the most fail-safe disguise? ‘Yeah, but then you don’t want to be that weirdo walking in the shop,’ she says, laughing. ‘You don’t want to be that person.’ With 1.6 million Instagram followers, a cookery programme on Jay Z’s YouTube channel, and cameos in Zoolander 2 and the forthcoming Ab Fab film, Dunn finds it increasingly hard to slip under the radar. ‘I totally understand why people want to take pictures of me, but I feel there is a time and a place. 'I don’t want to come off rude, though. I still stop if someone asks me for a picture, but there was a period when it got too much, so sometimes I will say so. ‘People forget that I’m also human. People put celebrities or models on such a high pedestal, and it’s really ridiculous.’ Therein lies the dilemma of this modern, access-all-areas, 24/7 type of celebrity: the pedestal that is your platform to do everything you want to do is one you can never jump off. ‘Modelling opens you up to so many opportunities, and it would be a shame not to take advantage of that,’ Dunn says. ‘It’s a good time right now. People are interested in the model, and social media means people get to understand who we are, so there’s much more we can do.’  Her easy humour means that Dunn is a natural on social media, even if her long-time followers (such as me) miss the time when she was less guarded. ‘I swear some people need to learn to do black hair/skin,’ she tweeted in 2011, during Paris Fashion Week. ‘I do love social media, but it’s now become part of work,’ she laments. ‘The reason I used social media was to get my point across and have control of the pictures I put up, and now I feel it’s kind of been taken away.’ Taken away? ‘You just have to be more, you know… There’s…I mean, I just don’t enjoy getting told what to do. So getting told to post this and I don’t want to post it. It misses the point. But I understand. I guess I just have to play along with it.’ One advantage afforded by her fame for which she is especially grateful is the platform to publicise sickle-cell anaemia, an inherited blood disorder with which Riley was diagnosed as a baby. When abnormal blood cells block the small blood vessels that supply the body’s tissues, it causes painful swelling, most noticeably in small children in the hands and feet. Dunn is an ambassador for the Sickle Cell Disease Association of America. ‘I’m happy I’m in a position to spread awareness. You can’t actually see it [sickle-cell anaemia], which means people don’t always understand it,’ she says. ‘I’ve spoken to sufferers, and they say the pain is the worst you can think of. I wish I could have taken away my son’s pain and put it on myself.’ She is equally vocal on the subject of diversity (or the lack of it) in the fashion industry. In 2008 she became the first black model (she has Jamaican heritage) to be cast in a Prada show in more than 10 years, and she is one of the few black models to have garnered cosmetics contracts. To be aware of your own fortune yet unafraid to speak out about the odds you have fought speaks of a bravery not every celebrity, black or otherwise, possesses. Last November, in a tweet widely construed as a criticism of Victoria’s Secret (in whose catwalk shows she walked from 2012 to 2014), she wrote, ‘Feeling so much better about not doing BS… sorry I mean VS now that Rihanna isn’t doing it also,’ though she swiftly deleted the post. You sense that there is a lot more that Dunn would love to say on the subject of diversity in the industry, but that she has been counselled not to bite the hand that feeds her. Does she feel the situation has improved? ‘I definitely feel I’m seeing a lot more girls on the runway. But I would like to see the same [racial diversity] when I look through magazines, or when I’m looking at [advertising] campaigns. 'I think people forget that it’s not just about the shows – it’s also about the editorial and the campaigns. So yes, during show season you might have three or five ethnic models, but then, OK, let’s see what happens afterwards. 'Young girls want to go through a magazine and see an image of a woman who represents them or looks like them. There’s a lot more to be done, but it’s getting there.’ Balmain designer Olivier Rousteing has said he ‘doesn’t see race’ and simply casts beautiful girls. ‘I love Olivier for that. And that’s how it should be. It shouldn’t be, “OK, now we should have a dark-skinned girl” – just cast beautiful women. And beautiful women come in different shades.’  It is important, I say, for women like Dunn to speak out about diversity, lest it fall off the fashion industry’s agenda. ‘I might as well use my mouth for something that people need to hear about and pay attention to,’ she says wryly. ‘All it takes is for people to speak up.’ Our attention is momentarily diverted by Riley, who has started dancing with enthusiasm. I ask whether he is into music, expecting Dunn to namecheck Kanye or Drake. ‘He just discovered U2,’ she says. ‘“Mummy, this is real music,” he said to me. So now he wants to be a rock star.’ If he has inherited his mother’s charm and drive, it’s a done deal.  Life before skinny jeans: remember it? It’s been a decade since spray-on jeans came on to the scene and began their rise to denim domination. The style’s popularity grew out of its ease and versatility – they suited everyone from the Kates  (Moss and Middleton) to mums on the school run. But skinnies became so trusty and ubiquitous that they crossed over into ‘basic’ territory, creating an opportunity for more individual styles to divert our attention. Today we’re in the midst of a denim renaissance, with skinnies just one option amid a panoply of styles. In autumn 2016, jeans come cropped (M.i.h Jeans, Rachel Comey), straight (3x1), embroidered (Bliss and Mischief) and kick-flared (J Brand). Even vintage jeans are subject to more choice: do you want them original (old-school Levi’s  are hot commodities); patchworked, with stepped hems, as at cult label Vêtements; or of a more modern pattern, as at Re/Done? As a true denim freak, I adore the pick’n’mix of denim on offer. In my tweens there were very few options – it was basically Levi’s, Wrangler or Lee, and you got the ones that did up. My dad was a mod and a denim connoisseur, so my first Wrangler jeans came with a matching denim shirt with mother-of-pearl poppers. I was hooked. There followed circulation-obstructing Moschino skinnies and big-ticket 7 For All Mankind bootcuts. (I sheared off the waistband and got a belly piercing, following in the fashion footsteps of noted denim icon Britney Spears.) At university in Edinburgh, it was all about Diesel. A pair of indigo flares gave me the best-looking bum I’ve ever had (probably something to do with being 19), while some Liz Hurley-inspired white bootcuts, which I wore with huge platforms, raised me out of the ‘petite’ height range for the first time in my life. I wore those jeans  on the first day of my first magazine internship after moving to London, and can still feel the blush of realisation at how passé I looked – the skinny was already beginning its inexorable rise. My bootcuts were over.  If jeans are the cornerstone of your wardrobe, as they are for me, it can be difficult to move on – it’s taken me some time to find a skinny alternative that works for my 5ft 2in stature. And jeans are much more than just cotton trousers: emotion and memory are stitched into their very seams. Here, in an attempt to unravel exactly what it is about jeans that keeps us coming back for more, five women delve into the very best denim of their lives. I grew up in Southsea, Portsmouth, and the whole family made the trip to London to buy my first pair of jeans – on the King’s Road. My parents were very bohemian, and  I can remember us all in rolled-up, rigid, indigo jeans. I’m not sure  how often they got washed. I wore that first pair of Levi’s for years, until they were like a second skin. Other than that, my very best jeans were always found in jumble sales – I bought the red dungarees I’m wearing here 20 years ago. Denim makes me think of music. Original or vintage jeans have that emotion that connects me to the soundtrack of when I was a kid or at art college. I’d say my style has never really changed. It’s always been about non-stretch, 100 per cent cotton jeans. When we started designing our first denim collection for Rockins this season,  I knew exactly what I wanted  them to look like.  I guess I’m a bit of denim  snob. I’ve definitely got some showstoppers in my wardrobe,  like a pair of Vivienne Westwood high-waisted flares with a built-in bum. One of my favourites was  a pair of 1970s flares from Lee – they had a beautiful high pocket. After I had kids I gave away a lot  of jeans, including those flares, thinking I wouldn’t get back  into them. I so regret it now.  From a really young age I knew exactly what I wanted to wear. I went to school in Ghana as well as in London, so I experimented a lot with my style. One moment it was raver pants with fabric inserted into the flares, the next it would be really skinny high-waisted jeans from Cimarron. We didn’t have any references aside from music, so we just pleased ourselves.  My high-end denim habit started with a Saturday job in Selfridges. I remember buying  a pair of Earl Jeans for £125, which seemed crazy at the time, but  they really were my gateway  jeans. Next up were the iconic pleat-waistband denim flares  by Phoebe Philo at Chloé, and Stella McCartney’s buckled ankle jeans. They were all so expensive that my sister and  I had to buy them together. We’ve shared them ever since.  Here, I’m wearing some vintage jeans that my friend at Lockhart Embroidery made for me. They’re covered in naked girls pole dancing. They’re entirely original — something that has become the most important factor to me. I used to hate the actual process of buying jeans – just the dread of standing in a changing room and looking at yourself while you try piles and piles on – it’s a nightmare. But I think the older you get, the more used to your body you become. You can look  at jeans on a hanger and just know if they will work on your shape.  The best pair of jeans I’ve ever had are by Donna Ida: they’re light blue, high-waisted and cut to the ankle. There’s really nothing like a pair of jeans that make you look good, whatever you wear them with. I also think there’s a big-time emotional connection. When I first moved to London, I bought a pair of Scandi-look skinnies from Denham. A year later they didn’t fit any more, but I’ve never thrown them away. Let’s call it nostalgia. Back in the day, jeans were seen as super-casual and you wouldn’t have gotten into a club wearing them. But now I can’t think of many occasions where I wouldn’t feel comfortable in denim. Still,  I’ve always found jeans shopping tricky. Sometimes they look  great from the front, but when  you turn around you get a real fright. I’ve got a generous behind but a small waist, and when I was younger I’d get the waist taken  in. Stretch jeans were an absolute godsend for me.  Since skinnies have fallen out  of fashion, I’ve been at a bit of  a loss. Last year, I ripped all the knees to give them a bit more  life, but now I’ve found the Levi’s Wedgie, which I love because they’re high-waisted, but  flattering on the bum. I also still rely on my trusty 501s, which  I’m wearing here: they’re ripped  at the knees, fit like a dream and are great for work. If you’re curvy it’s not easy to find your fit, but when you do, you stay loyal.  I’ll never forget my noughties, ultra-glam going-out jeans. I hit the Victoria Beckham for Rock & Republic moment hard, with a pair of indigo bootcut jeans that had two Rs in diamanté across the back pockets. At the time, your best jeans were always worn with heels and I can remember feeling like the bee’s knees in mine.   These days, my denim style is really functional. A pair of jeans has to get me through the whole day. I have to get my 10-year-old off to school, but, because I run a shop, I also have to look the part  – I can’t just turn up in gym gear. Since I spend the day shifting boxes, running to the bank and climbing stairs, comfort is now as big a factor for me as fit and colour.  In my shop, you really see  how denim can make or break  a look. Jeans can highlight your muffin top, belly, bum and thigh gap. When you’re looking for perfection and see your normal body looking back at you, it can be disheartening. But there’s a style to make the best of any figure.  These days I love Paige denim. The mistakes I’ve made over the years mean I’m good at picking out jeans that suit me now. I grew up just outside Boston, Massachusetts. When I was still  at high school, I would drive into the city to go to a gigantic second-hand store, where you paid a dollar per pound of clothing. Everything  was on the floor. They’d give you  a garbage bag and you’d get rummaging. One day I found the most amazing pair of pre-loved denims. They had holes in the knees and were completely frayed at the bottom, but with a big brown belt they hung just perfectly. They were the very best jeans. Since then, denim has been about the thrill of the chase. During my mid-20s in New York, I decided to go into fashion design and my denim taste got a lot quirkier. I’d always loved vintage, but I wore things that were awkward and dorky – it wasn’t about being attractive, it was about the vision. When I was younger I was an enigma to myself. I couldn’t discover what worked  for my body. I also lost weight when I moved to Europe, which changed things a lot – you don’t think about what looks good when you don’t feel anything is flattering. These days, I’m a lot more aware  – what suits me is the most important consideration. Now I’m a mother, there’s just not the time to go hunting from market to market. Even the idea of going into a fitting room and trying on a stack of jeans feels like a real luxury, but it’s important to set that kind of time aside. I just bought a pair of Paige jeans  that I’m living in — worth the investment in time and money.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  “The funny thing,” Maria Grazia Chiuri tells me over the phone from one of her two bookstrewn offices overlooking a fountain in the Rue Francois 7er in Paris, “is that I didn’t really discover feminism until I was about 48 (she’s now 53), largely thanks to my daughter Raquele.” This is not because Chiuri was some kind of surrendered wife. The opposite. “I came of age at a golden time in Italy. I was brought up to think a woman could do anything she wanted. That was pre Berlusconi. It was downhill for Italian women once he came into power. Total objectification. Honestly, I’m so happy my daughter is living in London. I just wish my son wasn’t living in Italy right now”. Grazia’s late awakening, (courtesy of Raquele and Chimamanda Ngochi Adichie’s short book We Should All be Feminists, a title Chiuri emblazoned onto a collection of sell-out t shirts in her first Dior show) explains why she only took up the metaphorical placards once she’d arrived at Dior, in late 2016. “For all those years I worked at Fendi, it never occurred to me to be vocal. It was such an amazing company - and entirely run by the five Fendi sisters. There didn’t seem any need to shout about feminism. I guess I had got very complacent, like a lot of my generation.”  When she became joint head designers at Valentino in 2008 with Pierpaolo Piccioli, they chose to fight the Berlusconi-fication of women not with fist-pumping declarations but with a dignified, romantic, depiction of womanhood that wouldn’t have looked out of place in paintings of Guinevere and Sir Lancelot. But times change. Trump’s election, the subsequent women’s marches , the unfolding Weinstein horrors and the concomitant sisterly solidarity of the #metoo campaign called for more explicit engagement in the debate. In September 2017, inspired by the art critic Linda Nochlin’s 1971 essay, Why Are There No Great Women Artists?, she waded into the conversation again, splattering the accusatory question across more t-shirts. Not everyone was appreciative, not understanding the implicit irony in the title. “Women are often their own worst enemies in this respect,” gurgles Chiuri, her voice ricocheting from husky to excitable squealing. “We’re so conditioned to think the most important thing is to please others, that we don’t always put ourselves forward. You have to keep challenging your thinking. That’s the only way to change anything.” That fact that feminism has proved such a hot seller for Dior irks some critics. In the fifteen months since her arrival, sales of Dior’s feminist and feminine accessories – Guevara-esque berets, bandolier cross- body bags that look like the kind of thing an upmarket revolutionary would sling across her body and all that luxuriously soft, 70s –in- spirit, eye wateringly expensive denim – have kept Dior at the forefront of luxury shoppers’ minds. A cavalcade of celebrities wearing her We Should All be Feminist T shirts on Instagram lead to accusations of a crass commercial take over of a nobel cause. “Honestly, this was not about making money,” says Chiuri. Getting Sydney Toledano (Dior’s CEO) to agree to doing a T shirt wasn’t easy,” she laughs. “‘Dior is not a t-shirt brand’, I was told. All the profits have gone to charity. “ She’s delighted if people buy high street versions.” It shows the message is more important than the label”. Having found her political voice, does she now feel the need to keep exercising it, especially given the award. Probably. It is quite a responsibility. But it’s not a thing I have to force. The more I read and learn about the world, the more there is to say.” As for those who contend that fashion should be above politics… "that’s like saying fashion should be above life. Since I’ve been researching Christian Dior, I’ve learned that understanding this house isn’t just about learning how he cut. It’s discovering how he thought. He was a gallerist before he worked in fashion. He had avant-garde tastes and a lot of views that for the times were quite progressive. Plus, I’ve realised that fashion is a very powerful medium.” It’s also, an industry that needs to clean up its own act, besides promoting awareness about inequalities in the outside world. “She's reinvented Dior's magic for the 21st Century, shone a light on feminist writers and sorted conversations around the globe about female empowerment,” says Nadja Swarovski, who sponsors the award.  As a mature woman working in a business that seems terrified of ageing, she's concerned about its narrow focus on youth and thinness, although as she explains, there are practical reasons why catwalk models tend to be the same size.  “You need a single prototype or production becomes impossible.”  Dior has signed up to the charter that is trying to safeguard against the use of underage and underweight models. As for all the allegations of sexual misconduct among a growing roster of photographers, she insisted on working mainly with women photographers since she arrived at Dior – although next season’s campaign has been shot by a man. She can’t yet say who. What about gender pay gaps? “At Dior it’s all about talent, not whether you’re a man or women”. We haven’t talked about her clothes at all, which are both lovely and women friendly – even the transparent ones. Her favourite uniform currently is Dior denim, which she’s wearing today. “But I grew up in a family where nudity was totally OK and natural. I never saw a contradiction between showing your body and being feminist…” One thing’s certain, Monday’s ceremony is gearing up to be interesting – and not just for students of cutting edge fashion design or red carpet junkies. From Cameron Russell, the whistle blowing, high fashion and Victoria’s Secret model, to Gucci’s ban on fur, this is the year that fashion fully got on board with that fact that it can’t always dodge politics, be they personal or universal. This may create tricky terrain for the British Fashion Council, which organises the glitzy event – one superstar photographer had to be retroactively airbrushed from a list of nominations because of serious allegations of misconduct . But the upshot is that rather than being a hermetically sealed incubus of air kisses and insideriness, the Fashion Awards could end up saying something about the wider world in 2017. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Finding an interesting pair of glasses has always been challenging: for everyday wear you need something flattering and dependable, veer off into anything too weird and you risk whispered Dame Edna references in your direction. It's all too easy to get into a spectacle rut, and to rely on the same stalwart pair to get you through day, night, parties, weddings and bar mitzvahs. However, latterly, there has been such a shift towards fashionable eyewear that even women with 20:20 vision have been spotted sporting glasses. Which is obviously idiotic, but as so often on the Telegraph fashion desk, we can but shake our heads and roll our eyes at their dedication to “A Look”. Said Look has originated, as with most things in the past two years, from Gucci, where spangly specs have been trotting down the catwalk ever since designer Alessandro Michele took over. Alongside this, a general mood for more interesting eyewear has taken shape. Which is handy, because come party season there is nothing that will kill your pretty dress dead in the water than shoving on your slightly wonky old favourite frames. Cat-eye acetate and rose gold tone opticals, £330, Cutler & Gross, Net-A-Porter; Round frame glitter glasses, £205, Saint Laurent, Matchesfashion.com; Embellished cat-eye opticals, £356, Miu Miu, Davidclulow;  Gold aviators, £125, RayBan, Davidclulow  I have become obsessed with aviator styles in a gold frame, a shot of luxe, and enough space to sort your eye make-up out. Sarah Rutson, Net-A-Porter’s vice global president of buying, was wearing her very chic re-worked vintage pair at the recent fashion weeks. But you can buy styles from Ray-Ban, Cubitts, Chloé and Tomas Maier, as well as through low-cost glasses store Toy Shades (from £40 for prescription pairs, toyshades.com). Rutson agrees that attitudes to glasses wearers have shifted. “People used to think glasses didn’t make them look attractive. Marilyn Monroe’s character in How to Marry a Millionaire takes her glasses off because she thinks she is not perceived to be attractive when she wears them. That’s not the case at all nowadays.” Caren Downie, founder of Finery, the online high street store, has recently started a sideline in statement eyewear called Byocular. Its striking and beautifully made-to-measure frames (which feature a half glass at the bottom of the frame – ideal for reading, but they can also be made to fit any prescription). The idea for the project came from a vintage pair. “I was fed up with taking my [reading] glasses on and off in meetings,” explains Downie. “These offered the perfect solution as well as looking interesting and stylish.”  If you are keen to take Downie and Rutson’s lead and find your own vintage pairs to get reconditioned, try klasik.org which has a very good selection. Wallace black matte glasses, £98, Bailey Nelson; Gold Cats eye, £365, Byocular;  Green Wayfarer, £365, Byocular;   Gold-peach aviators, £225, Chloe  Or let Downie do the hard work for you: Byocular’s cat-eye gold and coloured frames would make excellent partywear: plus each of the four styles are available in various acetate colours depending on your preference. Downie counsels that “striking eyewear is about being brave enough to make a statement. The first consideration has to be what suits your colouring. Then what works with your outfit. But there are no hard and fast rules – an all black outfit with green frames could be super chic, or go for more of a co-ordinated approach.” Natalie Kingham, buying director at matchesfashion.com, agrees that finding the right pair to go with an evening outfit can be challenging: “An aviator can be really good, but it does depend on your face shape,” she says. “They can be a difficult style on some as they really pull the face down.” In which case, she recommends “cats eyes, which can lift [up a face]”.  Kingham also cautions there’s no one-size-fits-all solution. “I think you need a couple of pairs depending on your mood. A signature pair can become your trademark, but I love playing around as well.”  As with all things worthwhile, a little effort goes a long way. And for those with partners keen to take very clear direction, why not propose that a new pair of snazzy specs would go down well this year under the tree?   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Abbey Clancy’s new lingerie campaign makes a case for sporting impeccable underwear under your ski pants this winter; forget thermal onesies - suspender belts and balcony bras should be part of your slope-side attire. We were being tongue-in-cheek, but Clancy says: “I always match my underwear and it always has to be sexy.” As the new face of Agent Provocateur, the 29-year-old Liverpudlian revels amid a faux-alpine backdrop for the luxury lingerie label. She follows in the model footsteps of previous  AP ambassadors Kate Moss, Rosie Huntington-Whiteley and most recently, Paloma Faith. “AP has always been one of my favourite lingerie brands,” she says, “They are the epitome of sexiness and I’m obsessed with lingerie so it was fantastic to work with the brand.” Clancy has plenty of lingerie modelling experience. Previously she was the face of Ultimo lingerie, and she admitted in 2014 that she didn’t wear a bra until she was 16 because she was so flat-chested. Is there anything she does to get camera-ready? “I make sure I eat as healthily as possible, with lots of juice drinks” she says. If you’ve already started to indulge in mince pies, it might be bad timing to mention that mother-of-two Clancy, who is married to Stoke City striker Peter Crouch, gave birth to her second child just five months ago. The couple have two daughters, four-year-old Sophia and baby Liberty. Last week she revealed her new collection in collaboration with high street retailer Matalan and stars in the brand’s charitable ‘Beanie vs Bobble’ Christmas campaign. Underwear fanatic Clancy's rules are quite simple: “There’s nothing worse than a white underwear set that’s gone grey from washing – time for the bin!” and she has some savvy advice for men who’d like to treat their other halves to new smalls this Christmas: “Firstly, you have to know your partner’s size – that’s key. And go to the AP store as the girls are fantastic at picking out the perfect gift and if you’re buying underwear as a gift, always go super sexy as it should be a gift your partner may not buy for themselves.” Agent Provocateur is a British success story that was founded in 1994 by Vivienne Westwood’s son, Joe Corré and his now ex-wife Serena Rees. Their first store was on Broadwick Street in Soho, London. The company was acquired by a private equity firm For £60m in 2007 and boasts a total of 104 stores worldwide.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge may not be celebrating Christmas at Sandringham with the rest of the royal family this year, but they nevertheless exhibited pitch perfect Christmas day style as they attended church in Englefield, Berkshire with Prince George, Princess Charlotte and the rest of the Middleton family this morning.  The Duchess chose one of her old favourite coats- a rich brown midi length coat from Hobbs which she has worn several times since 2013- for the occassion, the first time George and Charlotte have attended church on Christmas morning. She added a suitably wintry element to her ensemble with a burgundy faux-fur stole, a black polo neck and a pair of co-ordinating heels by Tod's which we first saw during the family's tour to Canada in the autumn.  Meanwhile, George and Charlotte were both wrapped up in suitably traditional coats which both bore an uncanny resemblance to styles worn by Prince William and Prince Harry in the 1980's. George's £120 grey coat is by Pepa and Co-  a  Spanish kidswear company to which the Duchess of Cambridge often turns for timeless pieces for her children.   With its navy Peter Pan collar,velvet pockets and buttons, the coat is remarkably similar to a style which William wore as he arrived at Balmoral in 1986. Some on social media were shocked to see the three year-old Prince sporting shorts on Christmas Day, but the long-socks-plus-shorts combination has been the customary formal dress for young upper class boys for several generations.  Meanwhile, Charlotte was dressed in an all-navy riding coat with burgundy tights, dress and a £2.50 hair bow from Amaia Kids which perfectly matched her Mother's outfit. In fact, the Cambridges' Christmas Day look seemed to have been orchestrated to be just on the right side of matchy-matchy; William's maroon tie was a nod to the colours of Kate and Charlotte's outfits while the navy accents of George's outfit matched his Dad and sister's looks. Clever.  "Matching what your daughter wore used to have really naff connotations but I think that's changed a lot recently as very stylish dressers have begun to do it in a tasteful and interesting way,” Eva Karayiannis, founder and creative director of Caramel- a brand which specialises in co-ordinating mother and daughter looks told The Telegraph earlier this month, alluding to the subtle way the Duchess has approached dressing her family. The Duchess of Cambridge is noted for her love of midi-length coats, always choosing the warm yet elegant options for her Christmas Day outings, often in opulent hues. Last year, she also turned to an old favourite Hobbs coat, that time in forest green while she has also previously chosen a tartan McQ coat and a brown tweed style by Moloh. But while this year's coat followed tradition, the Duchess swapped the knee-high boots she usually favours for sleek heels- a sign of the stylish tweaks which she has made to her look this year.  The 'Kate Effect' on fashion is well-documented, with the Duchess having the power to propel the brands she wears to higher sales; the specific items she chooses often sell-out within hours of her being seen in them. Some economists have estimated that Princess Charlotte will be worth £3.2 billion to the UK, as she becomes as much of a fashion influence as her mother. "We had a huge uplift in traffic to our website following the release of the Royal portraits," explained founder of Pepa & Co, Pepa Gonzalez earlier this year. "The royals have not only created demand in England for this traditional Spanish style, but around the world. I have received an order from South Korea!" Today's stylish Christmas outing will no doubt cause parents across the country to reconsider their children's winter coats.       © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Sixty-one is an unusual age to become a global style icon. But that’s exactly what has happened to Sarah Jane Adams, an Australian woman whose unique ability to mix Adidas sportswear with tropical prints and pieces she has collected on her travels has made her the star of Advanced Style: Older and Wiser, a new book celebrating older women’s style around the world.  The man behind Advanced Style: Older and Wiser is Ari Seth Cohen, who has spent the last eight years on a mission to bring women like Sarah Jane to the world’s attention. In 2008 he started a blog called Advanced Style, photographing and interviewing stylish older women he saw around his adopted hometown of New York. His posts about his admiration for them, their lives, approach to ageing and dedication to personal style gained him (and his subjects) a global following. Designer Marc Jacobs was so inspired by Cohen’s work that he dedicated his AW12 catwalk show to Advanced Style.  Perhaps inevitably a book followed, and then a documentary where Cohen followed some of his most popular and eccentric subjects around their daily lives in New York. Then Cohen decided to take his reputation as the go-to man for scouting inspiring OAPs to international level. “There’s a global problem with ageism and a lot of prejudice,” Cohen tells The Telegraph of what he discovered from meeting hundreds of stylish elderly men and women around the world. “It comes through in little comments like (he puts on a patronising voice) ‘Are you ok?’ or ‘I can’t believe you remember that’.” If there’s anyone who can banish stereotypes about senior citizens, it’s Cohen. He has amassed an astounding network of individuals whose approach to life and style would put most of us to shame. There’s Ruth Kobin, 104, who is a regular on Advanced Style and always impeccably turned out in elegant cashmere jumpers, chic above-the-knee dresses and perfectly tailored blazers - always with a scattering of statement jewellery. And she still does Pilates twice a week. Meanwhile Illona Royce-Smithkin, 96, has a striking auburn crop and a wardrobe full of vibrant prints and vivid turquoise, purple and scarlet. She insists on living on the third floor of her apartment building, forcing her to tackle the stairs every day, but also allows herself to luxuriate in a long bath each morning. In Montenegro, he met Tao Porchon-Lynch who, at 97, is the world’s oldest yoga instructor - “she has the most energy of anyone I’ve ever met,” says Cohen. It was in Australia that Cohen discovered Sarah Jane Adams, when one of her daughter tagged his hashtag in an Instagram picture of her. “I had hardly any time left in Sydney but I wrote back to her immediately and met her on my way to the airport,” he recalls. “She was wearing this amazing Adidas jacket with a red scarf.” Aside from her style, Cohen was impressed with her attitude. “My wrinkles do not scare me; they show me and therefore my experience,” she wrote on Cohen’s blog. “Hopefully there is a little wisdom which comes with these stripes.” Since then, Adams has amassed 54,000 followers on Instagram and this week modelled on the cover of American fashion publication, WWD. If you’re wondering how a 34-year-old man became such a powerful advocate for the older generation, Cohen traces it back to his close relationship with his grandmother, Bluma. After her death, he fulfilled a long-held dream and promise to her to move from San Diego to New York. A stranger in a new city, he called the only person he knew - a 90-something actress called Mimi Weddell he’d met previously at a film festival. He began working at a bookshop and soon met more older women with unique style and inspiring attitudes to life. “Gratitude and taking care of your health really allows you to have a very meaningful older age. Being active keeps your mind creative and sharp,” Cohen says. “I realised these women can change the way you look at life.” His global travels have only reiterated that view - showing him that there is still a huge job to be done to champion older women. “You might think it would be different in Japan but actually everyone I met there thanked me. They said they felt left out in their society. It’s ridiculous that we treat older people as if they invisible,” he says of the Asian leg of his journey. But perhaps things are changing. Designer brands have taken to casting older women in their advertising - think 80-year-old Joan Didion for Celine and 72-year-old Joni Mitchell for Saint Laurent - and the centenary issue of Vogue, released this week, includes the modelling debut of 100-year-old Bo Gilbert. So you might think that Cohen’s work is done. But he’s not giving up on his anti- age discrimination mission quite yet. Next on the agenda? Tackling the taboo of love in later life. We can’t help but wonder what Sarah Jane will have to say about that.  The next generation of online shopping destinations – powered by  women – have got our wardrobes all sewn up. Roberta Benteler, founder of avenue32.com
For the woman who wants to be surprised If homogenised designer fashion leaves you cold, Roberta Benteler’s curation of rarely-seen-anywhere-else clothes and accessories will be a treat. 'I wanted to bring that idea of treasure hunting to the online shopping experience, so that it wasn’t just about finding great fashion but also fostering that emotional connection when you come across something truly special.’  Unsurprisingly, Avenue 32 is a hit with design aficionados looking for something different. Front-row favourites include Vilshenko dresses, colourful Ainea faux-fur coats and architectural Annelise Michelson ear cuffs. Roberta scouts the globe for new talent – 'that’s the fun bit’. But alongside her finds from undiscovered designers, she also includes less commercial pieces from established designers that risk-adverse buyers do not usually pick up. Avenue 32’s gift section is also one of the best for 'the woman who has everything’-type friends in your life, with many bespoke and monogrammed items costing from £50. Always passionate about fashion, Roberta worked in finance before launching Avenue 32 when she was just 26, in 2011. She has since lured Stephen Ayres, previously fashion director at Liberty, to the label. Setting up the business hasn’t been without its trials. 'At first we wanted to create the idea of a shop within a shop, so we let the designers themselves decide what they sold. Except their edits didn’t necessarily relate to our customers, or they were just trying to get rid of old stock.’  Bestsellers include Kiini bikinis, which have sold out many times over, the colourful faux-fur coats from Shrimps and the uber- luxe structured tops and eveningwear by Australian designer Matičevski. shearling bomber jacket, £910, by Bartmans and Siegel, pinstripe trousers, £615, by Pedro del Hierro and gold, silver earrings, £345, Charlotte Chesnais all from Avenue 32 Caren Downie, founder of Finery
For women who want directional pieces without designer prices  Caren Downie is quietly one of the most influential women in British fashion. Formerly fashion director of Asos and buying director of Topshop, since February she has applied her expertise to the job of brand director at Finery, a website that caters to women who want considered quality and design but who don’t want to pay designer prices. 'Have you wondered why, despite all the apparent choice, so many things on the high street look the same?’ Caren asks. 'Possibly because retailers aren’t willing to take as many risks as they used to. We wanted to offer something that was innovative and exciting. We’ve tried to bring the process and culture of a design house to a high-street brand, with a real point of difference in original cut and colours.’  Finery has been described as the British version of & Other Stories or Cos, although Downie thinks Finery is a bit more feminine.  'I suppose it’s quite London in its outlook. It’s how women dress: with something pretty, toughened up with something harder. Finery is less about catwalk trends and more about favourite wardrobe pieces.’ As such, mannish tailoring sits happily next to organza dresses and architectural ruffle tops. Bestsellers include brogues and boots, which start at £59, as well as tops from £19 and trousers from £39. Caren has been pleasantly surprised that customers are happy to take a chance on items that traditionally they might want to try on. 'Who knows, perhaps that’s down to the quality of our photography,’ she says. 'Early on we decided to shoot all our products very large so that the finer details could be seen clearly and everyone could understand the cloth.’  shirt dress, £65, bracelet, £39 and boots, £125 all from Finery Debra Hepburn, founder of Young British Designers
For women who love discovering new home-grown talent Young British Designers’ showcasing of the best emerging UK talent means Debra Hepburn and her husband (who also run an ad agency together) were among the first to spot the potential in JW Anderson, Sophie Hulme, Bionda Castana and Eudon Choi. 'Back when we launched in 2010, people said we were crazy to invest in unknown brands and talent,’ says Debra. 'They said we would have late deliveries, poor quality and disappointed customers. Five years later, and everyone wants to create an individual style statement.’ Around 70 per cent of their stock is unique to YBD, so can’t be found elsewhere. It’s just so cool, so groundbreaking, so “chuck away the rule book”, and all with a British twinkle in the eye.’ Debra recalls that starting out was scary as hell. The site went live and its first order 'from a VIP’ didn’t go according plan.  The catwalk used to be the stage on which models won a 'super’ prefix and earned a fortune in the process. Now it’s an expensive, exhausting trial, says Ellie Pithers. Has modelling moved on? Or have we? You probably won’t have heard of Binx Walton, a nineteen-year-old model and the only person nicknamed after a Star Wars character to star in a Chanel campaign. A lithe, lean Tennessee native with a soupy drawl to match, Walton began her career on the catwalk for Marc Jacobs in 2013, and was soon booked for campaigns at Céline, Balmain and Coach. During fashion month last autumn, she  walked down the catwalks for Bottega Veneta, Roberto Cavalli, Versace, Loewe, Céline, Stella McCartney, Chanel, Valentino and Miu Miu. Binx, in other words, is at the top of her game. But it’s lonely up there. “Recently, designers have been hiring a lot of newer girls, so it’s not as fun because I’m not with as many of my friends,” she says when we catch up in Milan. “New girls – I feel sorry for them. My first and second seasons were my worst. It’s like being in a new school. There are cliques and I didn’t have many people I could trust.” Three years and six seasons in, Binx considers herself a veteran. “These new girls – they’re sixteen, they’ve just quit high school and they’re only going to be around for two seasons,” she says, animatedly. “A lot of them stop growing up. They get to twenty, twenty-four, and they’re still the same. They’re stunted.” The same can’t be said for Binx, currently quietly growing her profile via careful collaborations, the latest of which is a capsule range of sneakers for the Italian brand Superga. “The logo is on the sole because I wanted to stay away from putting my name everywhere,” she says, chucking me a style to peruse. “Even though I’m doing well, I’m not huge. People aren’t gonna buy a shoe just because it says Binx on it. So I wanted to make some cool shoes and focus on the little details – 3D mesh on the inside because in this industry you get a lot of blisters and mesh is more comfortable than canvas, little metal lace hoops that feel quite urban…”   As we continue to chat, Binx exudes the trademark keeping-it-real ethos that has led to her success, talking of her family – “my most expensive purchase? I bought my mom a car” – and her friends – “I live with a model, Lexi, in New York, in an apartment with a snake tank and a huge brown couch and that’s it. You don’t wanna live too fancy. It just makes your ego bigger”. She plays down her good fortune, but Binx is one in a million. Few girls make it big these days, and fewer still have the backing to convert a smash debut into longevity. For while the Kate Mosses and Gisele Bündchens amass millions, and command thousands for a catwalk appearance, most models work long hours with scant job security and earn very little. Part of that is due to the fact that the catwalk, once a breeding ground for supermodels, is no longer the springboard to a long and illustrious modelling career. Neither is it financially rewarding for the models themselves, many of whom actually find themselves in debt at the end of the season. Where twenty years ago Linda Evangelista and Christy Turlington could command £30,000 for a show, nowadays models can earn as little as £300 – or just get paid in clothes. According to Ashley Mears, a professor of sociology at Boston University, and a former model, between 2000 and 2010, 47% of models appearing on catwalks at one of the four major fashion weeks around the world appeared only once. She writes on the Boston University website: “At the agencies I studied, the median earnings were estimated by agents to be under $60,000 a year, but that’s a very uncertain sum which fluctuates over short periods of time, and agents expect models’ high-fashion careers to last less than five years. A sizeable share – 20% of the models at one agency I studied – were actually in debt to their agency for the costs of starting their career, such as pictures for their portfolios or even a place ticket to New York.” Now, more than ever, designers and casting directors are interested in new faces on the catwalk. Amanda Bretherton, the president of Next Models London, attributes that to the following: “Firstly, designers have decided to use their finances more wisely and not spend huge amounts on one-off fees for supermodels. Secondly, I think there is a true desire not to have the models detract from the actual collection by being too well-known and in turn stealing the show. If they can choose girls who look very similar, they create an image of uniformity which then means the clothes stand out within the show.” Karlie Kloss, one of the industry’s top models, confirmed the latter in an interview with Vanity Fair, claiming that designers have told her she’s “too famous” to walk in their shows and that her appearance on their catwalk would mean “no one will pay attention to the clothes”. That those models who do manage to forge a career are required to have “additional talents” is an added irony in an industry predicated on selling luxury while paying those whose images they are utilising very little. As Bretherton points out, today’s models “must dominate not only the runway but social media, campaigns and editorials. Whether they act, or design, or have a strong social media presence, they need to be more desirable for casting directors.” To that end Kloss, 23, who can only be booked for a catwalk show via “special arrangement”, has a line of gluten-free cookies, Karlie’s Kookies’, the proceeds of which go to the charity FEED, and promotes technology via her scholarship at the Flatiron School in New York, Kode with Karlie, which sponsors 20 girls between the ages of 13 and 18 to attend coding classes. In July she launched her own Youtube channel, Klossy, which documents her daily life, showing her backstage on a Glamour cover shoot or making “apple krisp”. It’s all part of the plan to become a “personality”. For increasingly, the most lucrative fashion campaigns and magazine covers are being won by actresses and reality TV personalities such as Gigi Hadid and Kendall Jenner. So-called “big” girls, the top models in the industry, are also competing for these gigs, and eschewing the exhausting merry-go-round of catwalk shows in the process. With over 40 million Instagram followers between Hadid and Jenner alone, it’s not hard to see their appeal – and model agents are reacting accordingly, now including specific Instagram-related clauses in contracts with clients to negotiate a fee for an Instagram post of the campaign pictures in which the model stars. But even that gets boring quickly: Cara Delevingne, arguably the closest thing this decade has seen to a supermodel, now eschews the catwalk and all but the most remunerative modelling campaigns in favour of her acting career.              Is the age of the supermodel over? Carole White, the CEO and founder of Premier model agency, which has looked after the careers of Naomi Campbell, Linda Evangelista and Christy Turlington, thinks so: “I don’t think there will ever be new supermodels like there were in the Nineties. There are girls who have a “name” in fashion whilst they are hot; but supermodels were names the man in the street knew.”    Back in Milan, Binx weighs in with a characteristically pragmatic view. “New girls, new girls, every season – you have to accept that,” she says. “You don’t believe in this industry? Well, then you’re not going to be in it. You’ll get thrown away like a toothpick. It’s that simple.” She sighs. “You don’t have to believe in everything, but fighting it? You have to remember: fashion is always bigger than you.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Style-wise, it’s been quite the week for the Duchess of Cambridge. She divided opinion in a ‘banana’ Roksanda dress while watching Elena Visnina take on Serena Williams in the Wimbledon semi-finals, and then furthered her mission to bring back the Alice band during a visit to the International Air Tattoo. Today, the Duchess is back at Wimbledon for the men’s finals, and, thankfully sans headband. Supporting Andy Murray on centre court, Kate chose a short-sleeved Alexander McQueen white midi dress, peppered with the brand’s ‘Obsession’ print. Look closely at the busy fabric and you’ll see a treasure trove of tiny trinkets, including butterflies, lipsticks, and the label's signature skull motif. This is quite the departure from the block colours and feminine embroidery Kate has established as her dress signatures over the years. The Duchess has a long-standing relationship with the brand Alexander McQueen, and it is perhaps this foundation of trust that swayed her towards a more experimental design. Kate selected creative director Sarah Burton to design her wedding dress because of the beauty of McQueen’s craftsmanship, its respect for traditional workmanship and the technical construction of its clothing. Burton’s ability to combine tradition and modernity is the reason that Kate has continued to commission her to design bespoke formalwear befitting her royal duties. Today’s ‘Obsession’ dress, though avant-garde in pattern, certainly chimes with McQueen’s elegant style, through its cut and proportions. Kate is known for using clothing to communicate a message when in public, and it’s no coincidence that this McQueen dress nods to the tennis whites associated with Wimbledon. It’s also no coincidence that the dress is by a British fashion house, as she is supporting Scottish player Andy Murray attempt to take the championship title for Britain in the men’s finals against Milos Raonic. The Duchess of Cambridge is an avid tennis fan and is expected to take over from the Duke of Kent as Patron of The All England Club next year. “It's a huge thing for tennis and for women's sport to have her in a high profile role," Judy Murray told to The Telegraph of her appointment. "I'm sure she'll be a very active patron because she's a regular attender. It's very clear she loves watching and playing and that can only be good for the sport.” Though Kate’s Obsession dress retails for upwards of £1,000 (a similar style on the brand’s website is on sale for £1,325), she is known for balancing high-end fashion with thrifty finds. This year’s Royal tour of India saw the Duchess turn to Topshop and Accessorize for a selection of summer-ready pieces, and she continues to shop in Zara. In our books, you can’t put a price on experimental style though, and we salute Kate’s bold move into McQueen’s world of unusual print.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This month marks the 20th anniversary of Princess Diana's death. There have been numerous events to mark the milestone, including last night's controversial Channel 4 documentary based on the video taped conversations between Diana and her voice coach Peter Settelen and 'Diana, Our Mother: Her Life and Legacy' which was aired in late July and saw William and Harry speak about their memories of their mother.  All this means that Princess Diana is well and truly back in the public consciousness, and it seems her status as an enduring style icon is as potent as ever.  Since 30th July, global fashion search platform Lyst has been monitoring search and sales patterns surrounding the perennial fashion muse's most iconic outfits. And the findings solidify her position as just that.  ''Every woman could do with more Diana in her wardrobe, and it’s no wonder her style continues to be iconic for women everywhere,''  Charlotte Austin, Lyst's editor, tells The Telegraph. From swimwear to tailoring, these are the pieces which Diana made her own, and that continue to captivate the nation's sartorial psyche... The leopard print swimsuit that Princess Diana was pictured in while on holiday with boyfriend Dodi in the South of France in 1997 continues to offer summer style inspiration to this day. Hers came from Israeli swimwear specialists Gottex, after her friend June Kenton- owner of Rigby and Peller- put her in touch with the label's founder. Following the announcement of Channel 4's documentary, Lyst has recorded a 39% increase in searches for 'leopard print swimsuit' and says that the resurfaced images of Diana wearing the piece are likely to have influenced this piqued interest.  Belrose swimwear swimsuit, £95, Ganni A style of jacket that Diana was frequently spotted wearing- the oversize, slightly mannish blazer with shoulder pads- has come full circle (as is often the case) with the likes of Saint Laurent, Balmain and Balenciaga propelling it back into favour.  It appears that Nineties pictures of Princess Diana have had a similar effect, with Lyst recording a 21% increase in searches for 'shoulder pad blazers'' -the most popular colour clicked on being black.  Joseph Hampstead tuxedo blazer with lightly padded shoulders, £545, Net-a-porter  While Little Black Dresses are forever in style, the 61% spike in searches over the last week is undoubtedly Princess Diana-inspired. Most famously, Diana appeared in an off-the-shoulder mini dress by Christina Stambolian at a charity dinner at the Serpentine Gallery in 1994 (main picture). It was the same evening that Prince Charles admitted his infidelities on national television; consequently the outfit has gone down in history as 'the revenge dress'.   ''Diana was the people’s princess, with a quirky and personable sense of style that provided enough subtext to keep us talking about each outfit to this day - case in point: the revenge dress,'' says Austin.   Crossover neckline dress, £12.99, Zara On the 26th July, the founder of fashion label Off-White,Virgil Abloh, Instagrammed a collage of Princess Diana photos, including a shot of her in her favourite blouson-style letterman jacket. Since then, the term 'varsity jacket' has been searched more than 20,000 times.  "Never has a royal wardrobe been so diverse as Diana’s,'' continues Austin. ''From pop-print knitwear to slinky little black dresses and sparkly gowns, the Royal’s wardrobe was so much more than a twin-set and pearls.''  Varsity jacket, £625, Coach    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
