 We might still be coming to the end of Paris Fashion Week, but for most women, even a cursory glance at the clothes on the catwalk may call to mind that Ancient Mariner quote: “water, water everywhere/nor any drop to drink.” Beautiful as they undoubtedly are, fashion’s hautest creations aren’t always useful for everyday life. However, while for cocktails, there is Givenchy, for smart work attire, happily, there is Goat. Set up by Jane Lewis, Goat has never staged a fashion show in its life, yet in the fifteen years since it  launched it has quietly become fashion’s secret weapon label, beloved by the fashion pack and the famous alike. The Duchess of Cambridge, Victoria Beckham, Kim Sears, Sienna Miller and Emilia Fox are all fans, although Goat’s simple dresses, elegant blouses and neatly tailored jackets are just as likely to crop up in the boardroom or on the BBC news.  “I’ve tried very hard to be very discreet,” says Lewis, 42, herself the quintessence of discretion in black trousers, black shirt (both Goat) and black Gucci mules. “We don’t show - we’re not a bells and whistles company. It’s much cooler and more chic to be under the radar. We’ve been dressing the great and good for a very long time.” Lewis is completely self-taught; her initial enthusiasm for a career as an art dealer derailed after a chance meeting with the designer Elspeth Gibson led to an assistant’s position. She worked with Gibson for two years, learning on the job before deciding to branch out on her own. “I started Goat not to become a maverick, but to address very real concerns, and provide those key basics which seem to be eternally elusive,” she says. “The things we take for granted are the most difficult to find.” Redgrave Coat, £590, Goat Indeed they are, which is why Goat’s loyal customer base adores its basic knits (Goat started as a cashmere brand - hence the name - but now provides a whole arsenal of wardrobe solutions), as well as its boxy tops and dresses, all of which can be relied upon not to crease, pull or in any way embarrass the wearer. That the quality is so high may be down to the fact that most of the manufacturing is done in Britain. “There are amazing resources here - wonderful craft, excellent heritage. It’s almost like a detective trail; you slowly uncover these gems of factories, and wonderful individuals who are tucked away and almost forgotten about.” Lola dress, £440, Goat To mark its fifteenth anniversary this month, Lewis is launching Goat 15 - an edit of the best-loved, best-selling pieces over the years, in a selection of signature colours including black, navy, cream and pink. Standouts include the Lola dress, the Binky blouse and the Redgrave coat - a favourite of the Duchess of Cambridge. All are sleek investment pieces, as opposed to trend-led items that will quickly date. “My motto is style over fashion, because style endures,” says Lewis. “If you are a stylish person, you are likely to invest in pieces and wear them in your own way.” She agrees that there is too much currency attached to the new. “The way we dress is changing. We want value. But what is value? What is luxury? Luxury is knowing you’ve bought something that is going to have a very long lifespan; that you’ve invested in something in a real sense. Expensive luxury is obsolete - I don’t like that concept. Goat 15 takes all of this on board. I want to make future classics. Nothing would make me prouder than if someone digs out something of mine from their wardrobe that they bought four years ago and says 'I’m still wearing it’.” Lewis is hesitant to offer specific wardrobe tips, believing every woman is different, with her own set of needs. But she does espouse the virtues of a tailored knit. Goat’s are cut neatly under the arm and snug enough to be worn under a jacket without bunching, as well as being smart enough to wear on their own. Likewise, her day dresses are cut above the knee but not frighteningly so, and hang loosely, ensuring they don’t ride up the thigh when the wearer sits down. Binky blouse, £290, Goat She is a firm believer in comfort, and that it doesn’t need to be sacrificed at the altar of looking smart. “I’m pro dressing for the life you live,” she says. “My aim with Goat is to provide a full collection but allow customers to then edit that for themselves. I believe in dressing for yourself - find your style, find your groove, dress accordingly.” Ava dress, £550, Goat Above all, Lewis believes in keeping things simple. “This is real fashion for real people,” she insists. “One part of our business has stayed true: we want to provide wardrobe essentials and basics that are the best they can be - really well-designed, simple. But to achieve simplicity is very complex.” Looking at the rail of crepe trousers, pristine blouses and perfect-for-the-office dresses hanging in her flagship London store, I’d say she’s cracked it.  It’s departure time at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, and Sara Blakely is in the thick of her standard pre-flight panic. Pulse frantic, chest tight, tears streaming, she presses ‘play’ on her ritual take-off track (What It Is by Mark Knopfler) and focuses on her breathing. And then the flight attendant flashes Sara her bra strap.  This happens more than you might think. ‘I get flashed all the time. People lift up their skirts or pant legs, or open up their tops,’ Sara says, smiling and composed on a London hotel sofa. Because she isn’t just any fearful flier. She’s the founder of Spanx, the company synonymous with its lump-and-bump-smoothing flagship products – elastane ‘shapers’ that women rely on when it comes to dressing for their most important social occasions. And big meetings. And christenings, hot nights out, red carpets and, as Sara discovered thanks to one conspiratorial stewardess, transatlantic flights. ‘My husband says it’s a perk of being married to me, because he’s constantly flashed too.’ At 45, Sara is America’s youngest self-made female billionaire. To women who buy her products, she’s just Sara from Spanx, a woman with a smile as sparkling and hair as blonde as Sunny, her cartoon doppelgänger from the original Spanx packaging. She has an ability to connect with her clients – fans, even – that can eclipse her status as one of the world’s most successful inventors. She’s also evangelical about her products. ‘Being in the butt business for as long as I have, I can’t help but notice people’s butts everywhere I go,’ she says, managing to come across as both playful and matter-of-fact. ‘If I see a woman wearing great clothing and the undergarments are distracting, that’s where I want to say something to her.’ The Spanx story is the stuff of corporate mythology. In 1998, Sara, then a 27-year-old door-to-door fax-machine saleswoman, wanted to wear white trousers to a summer party, but couldn’t find any VPL-free undergarments. ‘I wanted a smooth canvas, a smooth look,’ she says, and she found it by cutting the feet off a pair of control-top tights. Sara realised that these proto-Spanx represented an opportunity. ‘All of these things that I owned, I just kept staring at hanging up in my closet and thinking, you see the panty line, you see the thong, you see everything – there’s got to be other women who are feeling this way.’ She ploughed $5,000 of savings and two years of nights and weekends into developing a prototype. Then she pitched it – taking retail buyers into office toilets for before-and-after fashion shows and sending gift baskets and handwritten notes to potential celebrity ambassadors. One of those baskets made it to Oprah’s dressing room. Sara quit her sales job right after she got the call that the chat-show host and lifestyle guru would feature Spanx on-air as her favourite product of the year 2000.  Today, those problematic white trousers reside in a display case at Spanx HQ in Atlanta. Every day, 189 employees walk past them as they work on products such as the Slim Cognito high-waisted shaper, Boostie-Yay! bodysuit, and the Bra-llelujah! back-fat-blasting bra, beloved by the company founder and flight attendants alike. ‘All the women we tested it on started singing “Hallelujah,”’ Sara sings, raising her hands into the universal “praise be” pose, ‘and so it just became “Bra-llelujah.”’ Of all the products in the Spanx arsenal, Bra-llelujah is the one Sara says she’s most proud of. She wears one every day. Spanx are now sold in 60 countries, from the UAE to Sri Lanka and Peru, and have become red-carpet mainstays. Gwyneth Paltrow said she double-Spanxed after having children. (‘It’s not necessary,’ Sara says, ‘but I have a lot of respect for the women who go there.’) Spanx are the bedrock upon which most of the Kardashian-Jenner women’s skin-tight looks are based. The world’s most powerful trouser-suit aficionada is a fan. ‘I met Hillary Clinton at an event, and she specifically came over and told me how much she loves Spanx, which was awesome,’ Sara says. It’s not lost on Sara that the brand’s most vocal devotees include women whose bodies seem least in need of Spanx-style shaping. That applies in the civilian world, too – Selfridges’ bestselling size of core Spanx styles is small. ‘The bar for us is: “does everything, but feels like nothing”, no matter the size,’ she says. Creating a smooth canvas is good business. Sara retains full ownership of her company, and business magazine Forbes values her net worth at $1.07 billion. Money, to her, is a ‘magnifying glass’. ‘It makes you more of who you already were,’ she says, ‘whether that’s generous or kind or a jerk.’ She set up the Sara Blakely Foundation in 2006, aimed at helping women through educational scholarships and entrepreneurial training, and in 2013 she became the first woman to join the Giving Pledge, Bill Gates’ and Warren Buffett’s initiative in which billionaires commit to donating at least half their wealth to charity. She also relishes spending her earnings on property (including multimillion-dollar homes in Atlanta and on the Florida beachfront, among others), fashion and jewellery (today: a white top and blazer from Ann Demeulemeester, jeans, Maison Margiela heels and about five figures’ worth of diamonds) and leisure (she’s part-owner of the Atlanta Hawks basketball team). ‘I’ve never subscribed to the idea that money’s bad or that I shouldn’t have a lot of it, because I think it’s great. I think it’s fun to make, fun to spend and fun to give away.’  While she was working her way to billionaire status, Sara was single and dating: money and ambition ‘always seemed to bubble up as an issue or a problem’. She met Jesse Itzler, entrepreneur and former rapper, who would become her husband, at a charity poker tournament in Las Vegas. Initially he didn’t understand the extent of her success.  ‘Watching him struggle to explain Spanx to his friends was hilarious. At parties, I’d overhear him trying to talk through it, and then finally one day he said, “Guys, she’s like the Michael Jordan of undergarments,” and then all the men would get it.’ One month before their wedding, Sara took Jesse out for dinner and a ‘major talk’. ‘I was nervous. I said, “I think I make more money than you think I do.” He looked at me and smiled and said, “It couldn’t have happened to a nicer person.” And then he started eating his spaghetti and we never talked about it again. It didn’t change a thing, not a single dynamic in our relationship.’ The couple have been married for eight years and have four children: a seven-year- old son, two-year-old twin boys, and a baby daughter. They run their family like a relay. ‘We tag-team a lot. If he’s getting up in the middle of the night with the children, then I get up first thing in the morning.’ They use rock-paper-scissors to decide everything from where to send their son to school, to which movie to see at the cinema. ‘For some reason he always beats me.’ A few things have changed since Sara was the sole Spanx employee, including the reactions she perceives from her, mostly male, negotiating partners. ‘I think it went from, “Aw, isn’t she cute, with her idea,” in a way that people weren’t really taking seriously… to now. Results speak for themselves,’ she says. ‘Business is very masculine. There’s more male energy, and I approach this with a real feminine energy.’ She pauses, recrosses her legs. ‘I can tell you this: when I say things like, “Well, let me think about it – I’m going to ask the universe for a sign,” they don’t think I’m as crazy as they did 16 years ago.’  Blakely takes pride in the fact that most of her employees are women. She understands her symbolic importance as a female company founder and talks a lot about empowering women, particularly through her Leg Up initiative, aimed at helping female entrepreneurs, and her foundation. But even with a recent marketing pivot to emphasise comfort rather than compression, at the heart of Spanx remains the assumption that women everywhere want to ‘shape’ and ‘smooth’ – correct – their bodies, rather than accept them. Sara brushes off the idea that her wares might be problematic from a feminist perspective. ‘I make Spanx for all different women,’ she says. ‘For me, it’s about celebrating all different shapes and sizes, and it has been from the start.’ Between her work on Spanx product development, marketing and public-facing initiatives, and her busy family life, Sara calls ‘time alone to think’ her greatest luxury. She could have it, of course – many founders sell up, move on, retire. What keeps her going? ‘The idea that there’s another thing that women don’t know that they need, but can’t live without, that I can create for them,’ she says, eyes sparkling. ‘I’ve got pages and pages of ideas. The list is really long.’  What’s on it? ‘Oh my God, crutches! I broke my leg last year and those things are archaic – I don’t think they’ve changed apart from going from wood to metal since, like, the 1500s.’ I kind of hoped and expected that you would say swimwear, I tell her. ‘Really? Tell me what you want. What silhouette do you like? What complaints do you have with what’s out there?’ She smiles, leans in. ‘We put a man on the moon – certainly we can figure this out.’ © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.   ‘Rock chick’, ‘It girl’, ‘muse’… these are just a handful of the descriptions used to encapsulate the unique power of Anita Pallenberg, the model, actress and designer who died this week. Her friend Pam Hogg says it better though. “Anita was a force, not just an incredible beauty, she lived her life to the full.”   For most of us, Pallenberg’s inimitably eclectic style is filtered through in grainy, dreamy images of her hanging out with her boyfriend Keith Richards and the rest of The Rolling Stones (she is credited as being a highly influential, honourary member of the band), gallivanting through airports or breezing around Morocco in perfectly pitched and totally inventive looks. It arguably defined a whole new genre of louche, creative dressing. Fashion designer Bella Freud knows what it was like to witness Pallenberg’s appeal from afar. “She was the first woman that I registered as being dazzlingly, amazingly beautiful but who also had something undefinable that made me admire her and be intrigued by her,” Freud remembers. “That was when I was 11 or 12. It was like she personified all the happiness and satisfaction that music could give you. Listening to records made you feel lit up and happy and then there she was looking completely amazing and original.” Pallenberg’s earlier years may have been a haze of experimental adventure in which her innate style was a visually rich co-star but later she came to have a more tangible influence on fashion and the industry’s key players in London. “I was honoured to discover she championed my work and bought clothes from my shop in the 80s long before we became friends,” says Hogg. “Later on in 2000, she starred in my first fashion film playing Keith's guitar in a mock band with myself, Bobby Gillespie and her long-time friend Patti Palladin.”   For Freud, it was “a dream coming to life” when she became friends with Pallenberg. “I met her in the early 80s when I was living in Rome,” she remembers. “I was sitting in a cafe in the square by the Pantheon and somebody tapped me on the shoulder and said hello and it was her.” Pallenberg and Freud became close, forging a friendship she likens to that of school friends. She pinpoints Pallenberg’s idiosyncratic style philosophy as particularly inspiring. “Weirdly, we did discuss fashion, even though it’s something one doesn’t usually talk about but she had interesting observations about clothes and style, why things were good or not. It was as if by dissecting someone’s personality she would be able to see something. It was like when I used to listen to my Dad [the artist Lucian Freud] talk about painting and why something was good and I’d think, ‘Wow, that would never have come into my mind.’ She was like that about clothes.”   Her reputation as a fashion inspiration firmly cemented, Pallenberg became more intrinsically involved in the industry. She completed a fashion and textiles degree in 1994 and went on to make some select catwalk appearances, as well as rocking up to parties in looks which were just as effortlessly eclectic as those she wore back in her 60s and 70s heyday.    “I loved her, Anita was very special,” reflects Vivienne Westwood whose clothes Pallenberg adored. “A very strong character; philosophical, dry humour. She used to pop in out of nowhere, it was always great to work with her. She modelled in our shows, once in a beautiful silver dress that suited her no end.” Last year, Freud even created a t-shirt and knit dedicated to her friend, a gesture acknowledging her influence. “If I’m slightly lost about where I want to be with a collection, I think about her and there’s an immediate electricity which happens.”   Most recently, Pallenberg made a characteristically fabulous turn on Pam Hogg’s catwalk. “She called me up last season the day before my show and asked if she could walk. Incredibly only minutes before a model had called to say she had to cancel,” Hogg remembers.  “I knew by instinct the gold outfit now free would fit Anita perfectly; it was truly destined for her. When I told her it was gold she was like an excited kid asking if she could wear her gold Elvis sunglasses and walking stick. As a surprise the next day she arrived at the venue an hour before showtime wearing a gold fringed fake leopard coat she'd bought from my shop in the 80s. She was awesome, completely stole the show with a standing ovation and screams that could have taken the roof right off.”   That joyful moment is now imbued with extra meaning for Hogg. “I’m so glad she had her last moment of glory knowing the magnitude of love there was for her. It was an honour to be her friend.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Important news; The Duchess of Cambridge has been shopping. In the last few weeks, Kate has debuted a clutch of new items from designers that have scarcely appeared in her wardrobe before - think Prada, Simone Rocha, Oscar de la Renta and more. It likely all began with her fresh ‘Kob’ haircut - as many women will attest, going for the chop will often prompt a full wardrobe revamp too. Certain silhouettes work better with certain hair lengths, so it makes perfect sense that the Duchess and her stylist Natasha Archer have been experimenting with new colour combinations, new outfit proportions and even a new pair of staple shoes to rival those trusty courts... Kate hasn’t exactly thrown her faithful L.K. Bennett court shoes out, but she has invested in a more modern alternative to wear to evening receptions and on red carpet occasions. She wore Prada’s scalloped suede sandals, which are priced from £550, to three different events in the last two weeks, treating them as a versatile styling tool in exactly the same way that she has always done with her courts. These are just a more exciting, refreshed version. Simone Rocha’s crystal bead earrings were a fashion-savvy purchase as they have been shown on the runway a couple seasons in a row, making them something of a modern classic for the designer.  Ears proved themselves the new zone for denoting chic at any age. We’re now just as likely to spy school-run mums and empty-nesters sporting multiple pretty piercings as cool young starlets like Emma Watson. “We love that generational thing,” says Maria Tash, New York-based piercer to celebrities including actresses d’un certain age, such as Julianne Moore and Uma Thurman. “When Meg Ryan came in with her daughter, it was a really sweet bonding thing for them,” Tash remembers. With a multitude of holes snaking from lobe to cartilage and across to the tragus, it’s all about clashing twinkling Carolina Bucci studs with fabulous statement styles (try Marni). We think you read it on these pages first, back in December 2014.   Julianne Moore Gucci’s self-effacing new creative director Alessandro Michele, proved his intuitive skills in the first five minutes of his first show back in February when he put male and female models on his catwalk in interchangeable clothes. That may have set the bar unfeasibly high for gender-fluid dressing, but it proved prescient. 2015 may turn out to be a watershed year for sexual politics, and fashion – or Michele – was at the front of the bus. That’s not all. In a flurry of statement-making fur-lined loafers, floral suiting, pussy-bow blouses and glitz-edged glasses, he instantly brought the double G logo back to mouth-watering status and added another category to Instagram’s favourites – Kim Kardashian, avocados and shoe-fies (taking endless pictures of one’s shoes, ideally on exotic flooring).  If Michele killed off minimalism, Instagram has murdered nuance. In times past, you might have looked to a friend or cheerful onlooker for outfit validation. Now, if a thousand strangers haven’t paused to lightly yet forcefully tap “like” on your ensemble, perhaps you shouldn’t have bothered getting dressed at all.   Gucci SS16 Visiting Victoria Beckham for a pre-show catch up in New York, an extraordinary, rare sighting occurred: The Never Knowingly Under-Soled one appeared in a pair of Stan Smith trainers. Worn with a loose-cut black suit, she summed up the low key, low effort yet high chic we are currently very into. The proliferation of gamely designed versions mean that you can now wear trainers to the office (you have ours and Beckham’s approval on this – pass it on). An off-shoot of this, came the drearily titled 'athleisure’ hybrid category which offers a heightened approach to casual dressing: cashmere jogging bottoms for all your long haul flight and in-between-yoga-class needs. Its close relation the humble pyjama has also become a 'thing’, silk versions of which are designed to be worn for partying not napping. As a sartorial movement, it did make us question our lot in life, and approach to sitting on a sofa (quietly, without an outfit change).  Miroslava Duma wears trainers Early on in the summer, a rank outsider achieved blogger catnip status: the Ukrainian label Vita Kin, whose cheerily bright coloured, embroidered vyshyvanka dresses (maxi, with sleeves and nipped in at the waist, ergo, the dream) even with their £1000 plus price, the pieces take up to three weeks to hand craft and are delivered when they are ready, they sold out on Net-A-Porter within an hour. This laissez-faire approach to delivery didn’t however pull any weight with the online giant’s VP of global buying Sarah Ruston. Perturbed by a lack of product but insane demand, she searched, she hash-tagged and found an alternate source: March 11, which offers the same folkloric charm but with a keener take on retail margins. Fashion is sometimes a battlefield.     Leandra Medine wearing Vita Kin As Conservative MP Caroline Nokes chairs a parliamentary committee looking to regulate the size of women in the modelling industry, on the catwalks there is a marked line between the so called 'high fashion’ (read: very thin) girls and those whose Instagram reach is perhaps more useful to designers than their dress size: and neither seem to satisfy the baying crowds of onlookers. When Gigi Hadid (5ft 7, a healthy size 6-8, with 9.7 Instagram followers) appeared in Tommy Hilfiger, Versace, Balmain, DVF and Balmain’s shows, she was subjected to the social media mob’s nasty declarations that she was too big to model. On the flip side, when 17 year old Peyton Knight (5ft 9, size 4) appeared in Victoria Beckham’s show, she was castigated for being too thin. With vitriolic condemnation showering down on frankly, any woman who goes near a fashion show (Plus Size Fashion Week is equally lambasted for 'promoting obesity’), it does beg the question: just what shape women does the world want to see?  Gigi Hadid at Versace SS16 and Peyton Knight at Victoria Beckham SS16 It seems fitting that in the year the Queen became Britain’s longest ruling monarch – cue many a feature reminding us of her majestic style over seven decades – women of substance became a talking point. Beginning with Dolce & Gabbana’s charming campaign starring three nonne (grandmothers), fashion finally engaged with women of a certain age. And unlike previously, that certain age wasn’t 26, but 66, minimum. Linda Rodin, starred in several fashion shoots, Joan Didion (81) was centre front of Celine’s Spring ads. Joni Mitchell (72) became a mascot for Saint Laurent and in July, Iris Apfel (94) charmed this side of the Atlantic at the London premiere of her eponymous biopic. Come autumn, Dame Maggie Smith (80) dazzled critics and audiences in Lady In the Van and Monica Belluci made a brief but notable appearance as the first 50 year old Bond “Girl”. You can believe this is as transient as fashion’s mania for culottes, but like culottes, it will keep coming back.   HM the Queen While the film Suffragette somewhat worthily reminded us that pole-dancing isn’t the only road to female “empowerment”, it was business as usual for Beyonce, Kim Kardashian, and Rihanna. Boobs, backsides and barely there dresses are the weapons of choice here, even at The Met Ball – the annual red carpet marathon at which Anna Wintour allegedly bans black but is powerless in the face of industrial quantities of silicone. Beyonce wearing Givenchy at the Met Gala  However, in a sweet note on which to end the year, 2015’s most popular fashion hashtag had nothing to do with naked nipples and gynaecological crotch shots, but with a rather conventional blue and black dress. 'That' lace dress, £25, romanoriginals.co.uk Or was it white and gold? (or periwinkle and sand, as Lady Gaga described it). A week before the wedding of Grace and Keir Johnston in Scotland in February, a picture of the bride’s mother’s outfit was posted on Facebook and Tumblr then Twitter -and a relentless cycle of global media coverage. At one point the story generated more than half of Buzzfeed’s traffic. Not even Emmeline Pankhurst’s backside could do that.     Once upon a time, about 6 years ago, fashion designer was a career that would have been up there with chocolate tester. Nowadays they can’t give those creative director gigs away. This year Alexander Wang, Raf Simons and Alber Elbaz all left their top jobs at, respectively, Balenciaga, Dior and Lanvin. In London Jonathan Saunders closed his label. Alber Elbaz's last bow at Lanvin While specific reasons for departures continue to be vague, much has been said about the huge commercial demands placed upon designers in these roles and how perhaps they’d actually rather have time to go to the pub sometimes.  When a glamorous summer party pops into the calendar, most women in Amal Clooney's position would be straight into consultations with their stylist about which big-name designer's services to call upon. But Clooney has adopted a refreshingly different strategy for many of her most glamorous outings by opting for unique vintage pieces sourced from William Vintage, the Marylebone boutique and online store owned by 'King of Vintage', William Banks-Blaney.  A case in point came last night when Clooney opted for a white fringed dress for a Darfur fundraising party thrown near to the Clooney's own Como abode. With its delicate gold straps and tiers of tassels, Clooney's choice of gown had echoes of a look from an F.Scott Fitzgerald novel and might almost have been plucked from the wardrobe of The Great Gatsby's Daisy Buchanan. The white gown actually originates from the 1960s and comes from Banks-Blaney's 'The Great Unknown' offering which sources fabulous dresses by unknown designers. Writing on Instagram, the vintage impresario said:  "Proving that an amazing dress doesn't have to be haute couture nor by a legendary designer, Amal is looking AMAZING in a William Vintage 1960s Great Unknown." The dress still appears on Banks-Blaney's site with a cost price of £395, although it's not currently available (obviously!) It's not the first time that Clooney has turned to Banks-Blaney's for something suitably dazzling yet unique. Earlier in the summer, she chose a 70s silk printed Valentino maxi dress for another Como get-together, while for the Berlinale International Film Festival in February, Clooney eschewed the 2016 collections in favour of a handpicked a 1980s Yves Saint Laurent dress from William Vintage.  Earlier this year, Banks-Blaney described his Great Unknown collection as excellent choices for a night out. “A drunk dress doesn’t have to have a label,” he said, “they were made to have a good night out in, something that it would be impossible to have a row in.” Words which seem to fit perfectly with the joyous shots of Amal and her husband George having a royally good time as they arrived by boat at the festivities and then sipped champagne and enjoyed live tunes played by a group of musicians.  While Clooney's life of juggling high profile law work with her marriage to one of Hollywood's most famous actors might seem impossibly unrelatable, her love vintage is something we can (and should) all get on board with. "I love a rummage as much as the next person but we're removing that struggle for people who don't. This is the next stage of vintage shopping," Banks-Blaney explained to The Telegraph when he opened his online store earlier this year.  "The beauty of vintage is being able to find your own treasure and feeling a real sense of ownership," Banks-Blaney explains. "There's this thing now where you really desire something but there are 150,000 of them in the world so it seems like everyone has one and then you get sick of it within six months, and everyone recognises it as the last season thing."  Clooney's Twenties look comes just weeks before Woody Allen's latest film Cafe Society is released in cinemas. Centred around the glamour of 1930s Hollywood, starring Kristen Stewart and Blake Lively, the film promises to shine a light on all things decadently Art Deco- feathers, jewels and, yes, fringing.      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The first time singer Florence Welch tried to meet Alessandro Michele, the eccentric duo walked straight past one another in the street. “I saw this man with a Shakespearean beard and a lot of jewellery. I was wearing red flares and a pom-pom waistcoat, and we both checked out each other’s outfits. When we did manage to meet in the right place [Welch credits them both for having scatty minds], we were like, “Oh, it’s you – I saw your outfit!” Now longtime friends and admirers of each other’s creative work - Michele reportedly designed his debut Gucci collection to Florence and the Machine’s album How Big, How Blue, How Beautiful - Gucci has appointed the eccentric singer as the official ambassador of the watches and jewellery collections. Alessandro’s fascination with memento mori trinkets was not lost on Florence. “I love his use of nature and animals [in the new jewellery collection]. The bees I think are really interesting; they used to be seen as messengers between the living and the dead. Then there are the snakes, which are obviously temptation… and flowers, which are obviously pretty but there’s an idea of decay as well.” Sharing a vested interest in uncomfortable sources of inspiration forms the base of both Michele, and Welch’s, creative processes. “It’s about exposing yourself, in a way," the singer told us at the launch of Gucci’s latest timepiece collection. “Alessandro literally put cut-out loafers with fur in them on the runway. Even I, when I first saw them, was like ‘What the f***?!’ But then when you wear them, they go with everything and they look great. “In terms of music, if it makes you feel uncomfortable or if it feels exposing, it’s probably the right thing to do, because you’re really giving a part of yourself that you believe in, and you’re not sure how people are going to respond to it – but that jumping off point is actually where you have to go to.” After openly writing about heartbreak in her latest album, Florence credits Michele for bringing out her inner maximalist again. “With this record I really felt like I wanted to have less of a boundary between performer and person. I wanted to have clothes I would wear off stage and on, because with the record being so personal I didn’t feel like hiding behind a big dress or a stage persona.” Michele’s designs for her current tour “started very stripped back and streamlined, with a white suit – then these coloured shirts with big sleeves were introduced. It’s like I could only hold down my inner maximalist for so long! I think now that I’m finally ready to embrace brighter colour.” Welch is keen to emphasise Michele’s very “generous” way of working. “You really feel like he’s giving you a very personal view on clothes, fashion and the things that he loves. You feel like he is really giving you his heart, that there’s a story behind his clothes.” Whimsical and unconventional they both might be, but that’s a kind of creativity we can definitely get on board with.  "Along with her honey voice, her soulful sensibility, Diana exuded glamour and grace and filled stages that helped to shape the sound of Motown," said President Obama as he presented Diana Ross with America's highest civilian honour, the Medal of Freedom, yesterday. "Today, from the hip-hop that samples her to the young singers who've been inspired by her to the audiences that still cannot get enough of her, Diana Ross's influence is inescapable as ever." Of course we heartily agree with all of the above, but there's one other detail from yesterday's award ceremony which merits stylish consideration: the fact that Diana Ross chose to accept her medal wearing a pair of fabulous dangling earrings which co-ordinated perfectly with her gleaming medal and stood out marvellously next to her that other signature of hers, the full-bodied mane of hair.  Ross's choice of earrings was of course a glamorous nod to a styling trick which she's employed constantly since she burst onto the scene with The Supremes, bringing extra glitz to her stage and red carpet looks with a magpie-friendly array of statement ear attire. But it also serves as brilliant inspiration for one next Spring/Summer's easiest-to-adopt trends; the showstopper earring. Seen everywhere from Delpozo (extravagant glass chunks) , Proenza Schouler (sculptural shapes), Balenciaga (crystal studded) and Celine (delicately graphic), it's guaranteed to be on your jewellery radar early next year, but also happens to be an ideal way to transform yourself  for a Christmas drinks 'do in five minutes flat. It's no wonder that sales of 'statement earrings' are already up by 73% on last year according to luxury site Lyst, which which cites Delfina Delettrez's enamel eye mono-earring as one of the most popular takes and, in anticipation of the stellar rise the earring is set to enjoy in the coming months, freshly-founded Instagram account @earafterear now posts a constant stream of aural decoration ideas. Let's turn to Ross's exceptional earring archive for a few pointers... Just because you're keeping the look simple (yes, head-to-toe red jersey is fairly pared-back in the Diana Ross scheme of things) doesn't mean you can't add an earring which goes with the mood; these delicate spirals are simple but interesting.  This look is so 2016- just the right amount of bling set against a sumptuous velvet dress. Take note of Ross's combed back hair which offers the ideal frame for a pair of dazzlers which Pat Butcher would be proud of.  As this throwback shot of Ross proves, your oversized earrings need not always be long-length lobe stretchers, these glimmering discs offer just as much impact.  If you have short hair, play with proportion by choosing earrings that reach to your shoulders and beyond.  Every woman needs a perfect pair of hoops in her jewellery arsenal, but it's also worth using the new trend for major  earrings as an excuse to broaden your hoop horizons with something a little more artful.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. The park became a state of mind. The park became my strength. The park is what made me who I am. Where's your park?" "When I'm working and rehearsing I live in my work out clothes but I didn't feel there was an athletic brand that spoke to me," Beyoncé said in a release.  Hillary Clinton made one of her first public appearances since attending Donald Trump’s inauguration in January, speaking at the Professional Businesswomen of California conference on Tuesday night. Her messages on gender equality and fair pay - plus an attack on Donald Trump for his lack of female appointments - made the next day’s headlines, but Clinton also used the opportunity to debut her new, post-election sartorial stance. The former presidential candidate appears to have left the pantsuits that defined her campaigning days behind, in favour of a look that is somewhat edgier than we’ve seen her in before. The Oscar de la Renta and Ralph Lauren tailoring that became her go-to in 2016, has effectively been re-rendered in kick-ass leather - a statement of defiance, perhaps, as she begins the next chapter of her career. Clinton has repeatedly used her clothing to send messages in the past - think of the time that she wore “suffragette white” to accept the Democratic presidential nomination, or indeed the connotations of her pantsuit choices, as a woman taking on men in the running for the most powerful job in the world. The leather jacket, of course, is synonymous with rebellion. Its origins are all masculine (from the bikers of the 1920s, to the army uniforms of the 1930s, to the on-screen bad boys of the 1950s) and the women who first adopted the style were considered rulebreakers. On the spring 2017 catwalks, the leather jacket took many incarnations.  Hillary’s blazer-esque shape nods to a wider trend for supple, glossy outerwear, as designers have been thinking beyond the biker, exploring trench, duster and tuxedo jacket styles in both patent and matte finishes. Whether Hillary will now be adopting the leather jacket as her hero topper of choice for spring remains to be seen, but, in the meantime, it’s worth us celebrating the piece as a wardrobe staple for those wanting to nail transitional weather dressing.  Helen Mirren has indisputably become a national treasure; she’s our de facto stand-in for The Queen, a glossy but brilliantly British presence on the red carpet and an admirably honest and outspoken advocate for very modern issues like social media pressures which you might not expect a septuagenarian to become involved in.  Style-wise, the Calendar Girls star- who is celebrating her 72nd birthday today- has the knack of always looking polished with an inherent ease and joy to her look, whether it’s a sharp suit or full-skirted gown. Here, we break down the building blocks of her ageless, sophisticated look… If Mirren had to choose one designer to wear forever, then we feel confident in assuming that she would bundle up her wardrobe of glamorously flattering Dolce and Gabbana and skip off into the sunset. The Italian design duo’s cheerful florals and witty prints are rendered on dresses with cinched waist and romantic flared skirts which Mirren turns to for photocalls and premieres.  Exhibit 1. The black turban which Mirren topped her outfit with at the Power of Women awards in October last year. Exhibit 2. A patchwork pouch bag which Mirren slung over her shoulder for a party at Versailles.  Both these offbeat accessories were paired with quite polite looks- a black suit and a white lace dress respectively- but transformed them into something unique and memorable.  “There isn’t a tip or piece of advice that works for all. I think ‘fake it’ is a good one, but going to the gym isn’t bad either. Exercising is a very good way of controlling your mind. Yoga is all about meditative practices,” Mirren told The Telegraph earlier this year as she discussed mental health at a L’Oreal event. A quick glance at any shot of Mirren on the red carpet reveals this ‘Fake It’ (or maybe she’s made it already?) approach; she’s all dazzling smiles, jolly poses and perfect posture. It makes any outfit she wears look infinitely more fabulous.  When Mirren announced at the height of Christmas party season last year that she thought it might be time for us to begin going bare-faced, the statement did raise some eyebrows. "I think it would be wonderful if it became a fashion (to go barefaced),” she admitted. "Things are always cyclical, so I suspect we might've reached saturation with the whole selfie thing and maybe we're moving in another direction. It would be great if we are, without being puritanical, because I love make-up, dressing up, so I don't want to be 'Oh we've all got to go without make-up'." I think what she is saying here is that we shouldn’t consider a full-face of make-up the only option for looking and feeling good.  While feminine dresses are Mirren’s go-to look, she is also savvy enough to know that one cannot live on florals and frippery fabrics alone. So her other go-to look has become a sharply tailored suit which she teams with crisp shirts, slicked-back hair and sometimes a swipe of red lipstick. It’s a complete step change but works just as brilliantly.  On the whole Mirren toes the lines with her fashion choices, striking a sophisticatedly modern rather than daring tone. But she does sometimes remind us that mixing things up is rarely a bad idea. See the time she wore her beautifully embelllished floor-sweeping skirt with the most simple cashmere jumper.  Close analysis of Mirren’s style reveals that often the key to the effortlessly chic impressions of her looks doesn’t necessarily lie in the clothes (as well judged as they are) but how she wears her hair. Sometimes it is styled into a glossy blow dry, sometimes it’s tousled curls and others it’s glamorously swept back. But it’s always a style which would look as great on a 20 year-old as a 70 year-old.      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. There is, therefore, a degree of pressure to get it right.  For all the family jewels she has on offer and designers clamouring to dress her, The Duchess of Cambridge keeps it consistently simple when looking for neat workwear - relying on hard-working separates picked up on the high street. Today's outfit proved just that. On a visit to East Anglia’s Children’s Hospices in Quidenham, Norwich, Kate wore a boucle suit from one of her favourite shops, Hobbs.  It's the first time Kate has worn the elegantly-cut Sinead peplum jacket and pencil skirt, which cost £189 and £110 respectively, but intriguingly she must have bought her outfit some time ago. "The skirt and jacket are from a past season and came out in late August 2015 and would have sold out in the AW15 sale," a Hobbs representative told us of The Duchess's outfit.  That means that the latest Kate could have bought the green suit is December 2015 - implying the Duchess's wardrobe is planned meticulously and exceptionally well in advance. It's been suggested before that Kate buys clothes well in advance of wearing them to avoid being seen in the same outfit as other guests. And, of course, it dampens the impact of the so-called Copy Kate effect; fans of her look can't buy her exact item because it has long sold-out.  Why Kate felt that today's event, where she knew her role was to cheer up desperately ill children, was the perfect occasion to debut her Hobbs suit is perhaps down to it's vibrant forest green colour. The Queen famously often opts to wear pink - a flattering, traditional fairytale colour - on occasions where she's meeting children, according to her personal dresser Angela Kelly. And, when Princess Diana visited children she made sure to take off her gloves and wear lots of jewellery that kids could play with and touch.  Whatever the thought that went into The Duchess's look today, it makes sense that she is often spotted scouting out suitable attire in Hobbs. She has a number of coats and day-dresses from the British high street stalwart that she repeat-wears regularly. For last year's Christmas Day church service Kate pulled out a burgundy Hobbs coat she's worn three times since 2013, neatly updating it with a faux-fur stole.  Such Royal support has had a significant impact on the brand. Hobbs posted a 14.3pc sales rise over the 13 weeks to New Year’s Eve 2016 - one of a number of British brands loved by The Duchess to see such a surge in festive sales. No doubt today's outfit will only help those numbers increase for 2017, whilst also throwing light on a new label The Duchess is incorporating into her Royal wardrobe. Sitting elegantly over the zip up jacket's collar was a Peter Pan blouse by French label, Gerard Darel - another classic, workwear staple stocked in Kate's favourite shop Peter Jones.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. It’s a relief when the bell goes. Fast-forward to the disco, and half the room is wearing lace gloves, including one of the teachers.  Supermodel Kendall Jenner turns 21 today and she celebrated  in typically lavish Kardashian-Jenner style last night with a dinner and party hosted at Delilah in Hollywood. Of course, just one fabulous outfit was never going to be enough for Jenner's milestone coming-of-age and she was spotted in two looks during the evening.  For the dinner, she wore a black Julien Macdonald jumpsuit with a plunging lace-up neckline, a black body and sheer embellished trousers with a green stole nonchalantly thrown over one shoulder. For dancing she changed into an even more sensual look, opting for a backless party dress covered in sparkling Swarovski crystals, with a draped cowl neckline, chains around her neck and slits on the miniskirt. It was created for Jenner by Lebanese brand LaBourjoisie. According to People, the silver dress is thought to cost as much as $9,000. “I have a longstanding relationship with stylist Monica Rose,” the designer Antoine Salameh, who has worked with Nicole Scherzinger, Mariah Carey and Nicki Minaj, said to WWD of  working with Kendall on the look. “[Rose] reached out to our p.r. company requesting a custom look for Kendall. The dress took two weeks from inception to creation.”  He adds that it is “the perfect party dress because it’s very lightweight and easy to move in." According to The New York Post, Salameh's custom-made dresses start at $10,000.  According to WWD, Kendall Jenner sent over reference images for the dress, asking for a modern twist on 1920s flapper style. But one wonders if these inspiration pictures might have included an image of Paris Hilton, as her party look bears a striking resemblance to the glittering silver backless dress which LA-based heiress wore to her 21st birthday party fourteen years ago in 2002. Proving that whatever the decade when it comes to 21st birthday parties for the Hollywood set it's all about wearing as many shiny things- and showing as much skin- as possible.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  There is a modern obsession with “what fashion editors wear”. The notion may conjure visions of “crows” dressed mostly in black, resolute in their refusal to kowtow to the trends that they’re responsible for telling the world about. Or perhaps a “peacock” comes to mind, so overdressed that one couldn’t possibly trust their guidance on quotidian matters like how to look stylish at the office. Franca Sozzani, who was the trailblazing editor-in-chief of Vogue Italia until her death in December 2016, trod the line between these two extremes impeccably. In fact, she is probably the fashion editor whose style you are most likely to want – and be able – to emulate.  Jemima Kirke is the new face - or ‘head’ - of Maison Michel, the couture houses’ go-to milliner, in their new Karl Lagerfeld-lensed campaign. As part of a new direction for the historic French hat brand, the 30-year-old sports the brand’s autumn/winter 2016 offerings, instantly making us all wish we could be a ‘hat person’ too. In the images, the actress’ bohemian charm comes to the fore as she models a variety of headpieces, adding an irreverent take to the Edwardian-esque vignette framing. Karl Lagerfeld is a regular behind the camera for Maison Michel campaigns, which would be surprising if not for the fact that the hatmaker is part of the Chanel group. Famed for playing the wild child provocateur Jessa on Lena Dunham’s hit US TV series, Girls, the British-born actress and artist has some serious cool-girl credentials, being a painter by trade and also coming from creative stock: she’s the daughter of Simon Kirke, drummer in 80s band Bad Company, and her mother, Lorraine, is the owner of Geminola, a New York vintage destination that has supplied costumes for Sex and the City. Maison Michel is millinery’s answer to couture, having created headwear fantasies since 1936. Its expertise in shape and material mean that they have been tapped to create the hat counterparts to couture and ready-to-wear collections for a who’s who of illustrious designer names, starting with Pierre Cardin and Yves Saint Laurent in the late sixties, to Givenchy, Dior, Chanel, Nina Ricci and Christian Lacroix.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We may be in the midst of a heatwave but thanks to Fearless- ITV's new drama starring Helen McCrory- a conker-shiny leather jacket is currently top of the nation's  wish list. "Frantically googling where I can get Helen McCrory's fierce leather jacket," read one tweet during last week's kick-off episode. It might seem like madness  but it makes sense too. Not only is it one of those perfectly luxe-but-lived-in leather jackets which we all aspire to eventually own but find impossible to actually track down, but it helps to encapsulate the fiercely determined attitude of the character who inhabits it. McCrory plays Emma Banville, a determined human rights lawyer who follows in that modern TV tradition of female crime solvers whose style helps define their captivating narrative; think Stella Gibson in The Fall (silky shirts and sleek tailoring), Sarah Lund in The Killing (that homespun knit) or Saga Noren in The Bridge (spunky leather trousers). "We really wanted to keep Emma's look minimalist," explains Marianne Agertoft, Fearless's costume designer, adding that the idea of one key piece was always an important principle for the character "She needed to look accessible but also have a sense of individuality and simplicity." Research began with vintage pictures of Patti Smith and although Agertoft says that the focus soon turned away from that route, the reference doesn't seem a million miles from Banville's functional, cool and tomboy-ish look. Instead, it was a raid on McCrory's own wardrobe which uncovered a leather jacket as the piece which the rest of Banville's wardrobe would orbit around. "Helen is an amazing dresser, and her wardrobe is full of gems," Agertoft remembers. "We tried on so much stuff, she is no snob so had everything from amazing pieces by unique designers to great high street buys. Then we found this old black jacket from Topshop which proved to be brilliant inspiration." Having decided that black would be too harsh a colour for the look they were after, Agertoft sought out a ruby-hued kid leather which would complement McCrory's 'beautiful jewel eyes'. With its side zip and neatly cropped length, the leather jacket which Agertoft eventually created is distinctive but still a believably grab-and-go piece for a woman clearly spending more time interviewing criminals or ferociously following up leads than meticulously planning her every outfit, as evidenced by the muted khaki shirts, polo necks and  skinny jeans which make up the rest of her look.  Expect the jacket to be a regular feature in Fearless's first series, with events happening over a short time span. Besides, the ultimate proof that you've found the perfect leather jacket is when you can't stop wearing it- now Agertoft and her team just need to recreate it for the rest of us.   Fearless is on ITV at 9pm on Mondays     With its side zip and neatly cropped length, the leather jacket which Agertoft eventually created is distinctive but still a believably grab-and-go piece for a woman clearly spending more time interviewing criminals or ferociously following up leads than meticulously planning her every outfit, as evidenced by the muted khaki shirts, polo necks and  skinny jeans which make up the rest of her look.  Expect the jacket to be a regular feature in Fearless's first series, with events happening over a short time span.  Online brand Missguided is a teenage favourite, known for its affordable Kylie-Jenner esque bodycon dresses, overly distressed denim and crop tops and bodysuits. But instead of casting a twenty-something party girl to front its Christmas campaign, it has selected an 88-year-old great-grandmother as its new face.  It might sound like an unlikely choice, but it makes immediate sense when you see pictures of social media star Baddie Winkle. Her style is daringly madcap,  with her wardrobe featuring a rainbow of acid brights and blingtastic accessories. In the campaign, Baddie Winkle, whose real name is Helen Ruth Elam Van Winkle, wears a number of oversized pink and leopard print faux fur coats, sequin halter neck dresses, silver mini skirts, statement platform trainers and wacky accessories (including a gold necklace which says 'bitch'). In the images she parties in a London nightclub with her crystal-encrusted walking stick and throws pink dollar bills in the air.  Missguided explains in a release that the concept of the campaign is to pose the question - "who says you can't slay at any age?" The great-grandmother from Kentucky has built a huge following online with over 2 million followers on Instagram. Her trippy style caught the attention of singer Miley Cyrus, who shares the pensioner's love of emoji prints and tie-dye, and invited her to attend the 2015 MTV Video Music Awards as her guest, making Baddie Winkle a celebrity in her own right.  Dubbed the 'baddest granny around,' she shows that you don't have to wear boring 'old lady clothes', but can sport slogan beanies and chokers at any age (if you want to). Baddie's style shows her wicked sense of humour - which is demonstrated perfectly by her Instagram bio 'stealing your man since 1928'.   'Baddie Winkle' uses her online persona as a way to overcome her own personal tragedies. Her husband died on their 35th wedding anniversary and her son David died at the age of 46 after a short battle with cancer.  “I cried all the time because I couldn’t come to terms with it," Helen said to Refinery29 of her grief. "So I made myself over into Baddie Winkle. This new chapter in my life, I’m looking forward to it. It’s got more interesting as a matter of fact. But, right down deep, I don’t think I’ve changed all that much.” Her alter-ego 'Baddie Winkle' began when her great-granddaughter Kennedy posted a picture of Helen on Instagram and since then she has worked as her stylist, helping her to dress for her outfit posts. Although the brand is primarily worn by teens, Missguided has form when it comes to representing age diversity in its advertising. Earlier this year, 49-year-old Pamela Anderson fronted its SS16 campaign. There has been a growing pressure on brands to diversify their campaign castings beyond including only twenty-something, size six, white models, and one of the ways in which fashion brands are beginning to be more representative is by using older models. Earlier this year 60-year-old Scottish stylist Gillean McLeod modelled a black swimsuit for H&M and at J Crew's presentation at New York Fashion Week staff and friends of the brand between the ages of 13 and 70 wore the new collection instead of models. Although there are a number of positive signs, the overall figures still remain rather bleak as according to The Fashion Spot's diversity report only  1.2% of the models featured in SS16 advertising campaigns were over 50. Baddie Winkle is now leading the way for representing the over-80s demographic.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Kylie Jenner is only 18 years old, but is one of the most famous people on the planet with over 50 million followers on Instagram. The youngest Kardashian-Jenner daughter has opened up to Wonderland Magazine about how the heavily-filtered Kylie Jenner we think we know isn't really her, and that "Kylie Jenner is ready to retire" from the spotlight. Jenner, the younger sister of Kim Kardashian and Kylie Jenner, grew up in front of millions of viewers on the reality TV show Keeping Up With the Kardashians and her entire life has been documented in a constant stream of paparazzi pictures. Although it is assumed that she craves attention, she says in the interview that she doesn't like to always be in front of the camera like her Instagram persona. "It’s not that I don’t want to do it...Yeah, actually I kind of just don’t want to do it anymore. Honestly. But I’ve always been like that. I want to be a businesswoman and be behind-the-scenes. Kylie Jenner needs to retire.”  "I am not Kylie Jenner. That's my alter-ego," she explains. Identifying herself as just "Kylie". Although her entire life appears to be live-streamed via Snapchat, television, her app, Instagram and through paparazzi pictures, she says "nobody really knows who I am. People think that because we have a reality TV show that they know everything, but it’s like, I’m not filming right now. That’s maybe 5% out of my day.” When asked if she felt like she was playing a role, she says: “I don’t think I was dressing up to be Kylie, because everything that I do is all me. But I did feel a sense of Keeping Up With Myself — like, ‘Ooh I need to come up with a new hair colour or a new cool makeup trick.’”  Kylie wears a gold Rolex, drives a Range Rover, Ferrari, Mercedes and Rolls Royce and posts pictures of her designer pieces almost every day on her social platforms. But she says this wealth no longer makes her happy: “I was just so excited to get another car or get all these materialistic things and I realised that when I got them it didn’t make me happy. It didn’t fill the hole in my heart. People will be like, ‘Oh shut up, just go drive your [Mercedes] G-Wagen’ and I’m like, ‘That will not make anyone happy.’ That’s not real.” Jenner also touches on how she dealt with her father's very public transition from Bruce to Caityln Jenner last year. She tells Wonderland: “I mean, obviously I knew about it my whole life, but it was never admitted to and then when it was all said and done, I honestly just wanted to not be lied to.” As for her decision to still call him 'Dad', she says “I could call her mum, I’m not against it, I’m just saying it’s not correct.” Kylie  is barefaced in her Wonderland shoot, but we see many of the key ingredients of her iPhone persona: her car keys, gold Rolex and Cartier Love bracelet and her Italian greyhounds Norman and Bambi. In one image she yawns into an iPhone and in another she's behind the wheel of her white Ferrari (a shot that mirrors Caitlyn Jenner's Vanity Fair shoot where she is at the wheel of a red sports car.) She is rarely seen without her heavy make-up and has turned her trademark lip liner and eyeliner into her own beauty empire. But in the shoot she has a more bare-faced look: "I feel like I didn’t really appreciate that side of me; the very simple, no makeup Kylie. Honestly, it all started with me just getting so sick and tired of having to dress up everyday.” The interview ends with Kylie being asked if she'd miss it if she stopped being famous tomorrow. “See, I think about that sometimes. I don’t think so – I would miss a part of it, but I would enjoy that next chapter of my life. I’d enjoy being normal.” The images are from the 'Fame' issue of Wonderland magazine which is out this week Photographer: Richard Kern Fashion: Danielle Emerson © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Jourdan Dunn is celebrating tonight after being crowned Model of the Year at the British Fashion Awards for the second time. She first received the accolade in 2008. She was presented with the award by Olivier Rousteing, creative director of Balmain, for whom she has modelled many times. "I'm going to tell you a story about her," he said, "it was four or five years ago, a significant show - the Balmain show that would save my life - the difficulty was finding a leader who had a really strong personality. I realised she was an Amazon of our time. She worked all night in very high heels and a really, really short dress." Accepting the award, Dunn said: "To start the year with a British Vogue cover and to finish with this is amazing." Now 25, the Greenford-born beauty was spotted aged 15 while shopping in the Hammersmith branch of Primark with a friend. She made her catwalk debut at the Marc Jacobs autumn/winter 2007 show and has worked solidly since, taking only a brief break to give birth to her son, Riley, in 2009 when she was just 18. She has since scored a number of significant career highlights; in 2008 she became the first black model to appear in a Prada show in 13 years, and in January 2015 she was credited with ending British Vogue ‘ethnic diversity drought’ when she became the first black model to appear solo on the cover of the publication in 12 years. This year she was ranked the ninth highest-earning model in the world, with an estimated income of £2.2 million in 2014 - hardly surprising considering the countless campaigns she has under her 24-inch belt, from Balmain and Burberry to H&M and Next. She is known for her outspoken attitude towards the fashion industry’s inequalities and has often spoken of her experiences with racism. She once revealed that she has been turned away from castings because they "didn't want any more black girls", and that a white make-up artist once refused to do her make-up. She has also lent her support to Naomi Campbell and Iman's Balance Diversity campaign, which seeks to end racism in the modelling industry, saying "I want to talk about what goes on. A lot of people are scared to speak up." "The people who control the industry … say if you have a black face on a magazine cover it won't sell, but there's no real evidence for that. It's lazy," she told The Guardian in 2014. Motherhood brought more than just the challenge of bringing up her son alone. Riley, now six, suffers from Sickle Cell Disease and Dunn campaigns tirelessly to raise awareness of the illness.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Once upon a time, we knew where we were with Hillary Clinton and fashion: she didn’t really do it, and it didn’t really do her, and both parties were extremely happy with that situation, thank you.  In fact, her attitude to fashion could be neatly summed up by her refusal to pose for the cover of Vogue as a presidential candidate in 2008. It was a stance that prompted Anna Wintour, the magazine’s editor, to respond: “Imagine my amazement, when I learned Hillary Clinton…had decided to steer clear of our pages…for fear of looking too feminine. The notion that a woman must look mannish in order to be a seeker of power is frankly dismaying. This is America, not Saudi Arabia."  Clinton’s reluctance was understandable. Her appearance had traditionally been used as a stick to beat her with, witness the nickname “Cankles”; her sartorial choices deployed as a way of trivialising her. Female public figures have a long history of being examined with a scrutiny that speaks of sexism and misogyny. Men have their words reported, women their outfits. For a politician rather than a First Lady, little wonder fashion seemed a trap.  And, yet, flash forward eight years, and Clinton is the subject of a slick, ten-page profile in this month’s US Vogue, a panegyric accompanied by glamorous Mario Testino portraits. Wintour has been hosting fashion fundraisers for her heroine not only across the pond, but here in Blighty. The South Kensington effort was hosted last month at the home of Net-a-Porter founder and chairman of the British Fashion Council, Dame Natalie Massenet. Meanwhile, Wintour stole the show when she forsook her trademark dresses to don a Warhol-esque, Marc Jacobs Hillary T-shirt at the recent close of New York Fashion Week. Clinton, left, in the new issue of US Vogue Putting aside her po-faced stance of yesteryear, Clinton has become a delighted collaborator with Planet Fashion, signalling not merely a period of détente with its denizens, but a positive love in. Incorporating fashion as part of her political lexicon and personal iconography is a move that suggests a new ease about herself as a candidate, as a woman, and – most importantly - as herself. It is also nothing if not strategic. If talking about the world’s first female presidential candidate in terms of her choice of costume feels retrograde, none of this is to suggest that Clinton’s sartorial decisions are up there in importance with her views on abortion, or gun control. But as Jeremy Corbyn could have told her, people do care what politicians wear. And having finally recognised that fashion matters, Hillary is now mastering it is a tool in her armoury, like any other.  Much of this Machiavellian modishness can be laid at the door of Kristina Schake. A former aide to Michelle Obama, Schake joined Team Clinton in a communications capacity a year ago, shortly before Hillary’s candidacy was declared. As Mrs Obama’s guru, Schake encouraged the fashion-plate first lady to indulge in shopping trip to discount store Target and to make a cameo at the Oscars. And it is Schake who is now in charge of marketing Hillary’s softer side, lack of evidence of which was seen as her mistake in 2008. In a fabulously meta moment, Clinton’s make-up artist, Barbara Lacy, has not only served time on NBC’s The West Wing, but also worked on Veep, the HBO comedy about an image conscious, female Vice-President.  Meanwhile, her longtime hair stylist Isabelle Goetz appears to have warmed up once harsh, salt and pepper streaks with buttery caramels and golden highlights, a common hairdresser’s tactic for “softening up” a woman’s appearance. Last May, Hillary herself joked about her dedication to remaining blonde. “You’re not going to see me turn white in the White House,” she informed the crowd at the South Carolina Democratic Women’s Council. “I’m aware I might not be the youngest candidate in this race, but I have one big advantage: I’ve been colouring my hair for years.”   And that’s the most profound aspect of this impeccably groomed volte face: the indication that Hillary is at last letting her hair down – blonde or otherwise – and both enjoying and being herself.  At first, this enjoyment manifested in a period of zany jubilation. In February 2011, when Secretary of State, Clinton reflected on the life-enhancing properties of thinking pink: “I have this Ferragamo hot-pink bag that I adore. My view was that I would carry it around only in spring, but it makes me so happy, I’m even now lugging it around in January. I mean, how can you be unhappy if you pick up a big pink bag?”  At the same time, her whole wardrobe morphed into much-mocked coruscating hues, inspiring a rainbow-coloured pantsuit meme to spread like a rash over the Internet.  Since then, Team Hillary has encouraged our heroine to streamline the elements she adores - loud bags, bright tones, practical trouser combos - into something empowering, and that (in contemporary parlance) she can “own”.  Said owning occurs, not least, via moments of self-parody. When her book Hard Choices came out in spring 2014, Clinton joked that her favourite alternative title had been: The Scrunchie Chronicles, 112 Countries And It’s Still All About The Hair.  At the beginning of her campaign in June 2015, Clinton issued her first Instagram post: the legend “Hard Choices” attached to an image of a rail of red, white and blue trouser suits. Her twitter biography was edited to read: “Wife, mom, grandma, women+kids advocate, FLOTUS, Senator, SecState, hair icon, pantsuit aficionado, 2016 presidential candidate.” No longer does Clinton view fashion as a pitfall that might destabilise her, but as an asset that can anchor her to an image as everywoman. As such, it is no longer a trap, but a weapon to be wielded to her advantage, not least with female voters admiring of Wintour, Massenet and company, and no less buoyed by the prospect of a pink bag.  As in the case of Britain’s first female Prime Minister, Margaret Thatcher, she can accentuate feminine detail when she needs to be noticed - compare the royal blue Ralph Lauren pantsuit she wore for her first campaign rally in New York City in June with Baroness Thatcher’s power blue skirt suits. Or she can “drag up” in more masculine guise, again à la the late Baroness, donning dour darker clothes for January's televised debates, when she didn’t want her wardrobe to distract from the discussion. As the New York Times noted, afterwards, the ensuing coverage contained “barely a whisper about what she wore.” This may be, in part, because our obsession with image is becoming ever more unisex. We live in an age in which even former president Bill dishes out diet tips. Barack Obama shares his wardrobe of identikit suits, Marco Rubio’s stack-heeled cowboy boots make headlines, while YouTube features a satirical Donald Trump makeover tutorial, beginning with concealer in the shade ‘Veiled White Supremacy’.  After all, even if it was, once, all about Hillary's hair, it has been superseded by a male coiffure that appears to symbolise nothing short of incipient madness.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  After months of speculation, British Vogue has this morning announced its new Editor. Edward Enninful OBE, the British fashion stylist and current Creative and Fashion Director at America's W magazine, will replace outgoing editor Alexandra Shulman effective 1st August 2017,  and will be the first male Editor at the title. Enninful, 45, has a rich fashion CV, having been appointed Fashion Director at British title i-D in 1991 (at the age of just 19) and worked extensively with both American and Italian Vogues throughout the 2000s. Enninful has over 481,000 followers on Instagram and is an esteemed and well-connected personality within the industry, counting designers from Donatella Versace to Marc Jacobs, as well as countless photographers and models including Naomi Campbell and Kate Moss, as friends as well as peers. In an internal announcement issued to Condé Nast employees this morning, Jonathan Newhouse, Chairman and Chief Executive of Condé Nast International, described Enninful as "an influential figure in the communities of fashion, Hollywood and music which shape the cultural zeitgeist" and cited his work under the late Italian Vogue editor Franca Sozzani as having "attained landmark status in recent cultural history." "Edward is one of the most talented and accomplished fashion editors in the world," Newhouse said. "Since 2011 he has been Creative and Fashion Director of W, where he has worked with the finest photographers to produce ground-breaking, highly admired editorial work. He has more than 25 years of experience as a fashion director, starting in 1991 when he became the Fashion Director of i-D at age 19, a post he fulfilled for more than two decades." "In the years between 1998 and 2011 he contributed extensively to Italian Vogue and American Vogue. His work for Italian Vogue under the direction of its late editor, Franca Sozzani, encompassed features such as Makeover Madness, The Black Issue and The Curvy Issue, which have attained landmark status in recent cultural history." Having moved from Ghana to London as a child, Enninful's first contact with the fashion world was when the stylist Simon Foxton scouted him on the Tube, encouraging him to pursue modelling. His first shoot was with esteemed photographer Nick Knight, who introduced him to fashion director Beth Summers at i-D magazine and he quickly showed his smarts as a stylist. Enninful assisted summers whilst studying at Goldsmiths, University of London and, when she left her post, he was offered her role at just 19 - making him the youngest fashion director in the industry. Enninful was awarded his OBE in 2016 for services to diversity in the fashion industry. He took his family and close friend Naomi Campbell with him to Buckingham Palace and described the moment as "one of my proudest." "If you had told my 18 year old self that this would one day be possible, He wouldn't have believed you," he wrote on Instagram. ‘I’ve known Kate [Moss] since I was 16 and she was 14,’ he told The Telegraph last year of his relationships with some of fashion's greatest names. ‘I’ve known Naomi [Campbell], my gosh, forever. She’s like a sister to me. All the others I’ve seen since they started.' ‘When I first met him it was just like meeting family,' Campbell told us then, on the news that he had received an OBE. 'We connect on so many different levels. The sky’s the limit for Edward. He’s patiently waited for his time, and this is his time. He’s so respected by the greats. He’s worked his arse off to be where he is and I’m just so proud of him.’ The fashion rumour mill had been in a constant churn since Alexandra Shulman, who had been at the helm for 25 years, announced that she was leaving back in January. Dozens of names were put in the frame to take fashion’s top job, including LOVE magazine editor Katie Grand and Shulman’s current Vogue deputy Emily Sheffield. Enninful's appointment is slightly left-of-field, in that his successor was a more traditional writer-turned-editor, as opposed to a fashion stylist-turned-editor. Reaction from fashion communities has so far been extremely positive, though, with many approving of Enninful's extensive experience and excited at what he might do to promote diversity within the industry.  British high street stalwart Warehouse has today announced it will be getting a face lift in time for its 40th birthday next year. In the first of  a raft of new appointments, Alasdhair Willis has been appointed to the board as a brand consultant and will oversee the company’s new identity, from digital concepts and branding to new store experiences. Alongside his own successful furniture design business Established & Sons, Willis (who is married to Stella McCartney), will continue to hold the title of creative director at Hunter where he has been ushering the heritage boot brand into next phase of its more fashion-forward life since 2013, introducing new lines and staging a high profile bi-annual catwalk show during London Fashion Week. Alongside Willis, beloved British fashion designer Emma Cook has signed on as Warehouse’s new creative director. Cook, who graduated from Central Saint Martins in 1999, debuted her eponymous label at London Fashion Week in September 2001 to widespread acclaim and quickly established Emma Cook as one of the hottest tickets on the schedule. Since 2009 she has elected to show her collections away from the catwalk, and has combined work on her own label with consultancy for other high profile brands. She will present her first full collection for Warehouse in 2016, with her first designs hitting stores next autumn. “As a British designer I’m thrilled to be joining Warehouse at such an amazing time for the brand,” Cook said in a statement today. “I’m really looking forward to help establish the brand's new DNA and to champion a new vision for the British high-street.” Warehouse opened in 1976 and has been a treasure trove for fashion-loving twenty-somethings ever since. In recent years, however, it has been rather left behind by the global dominance of more powerful rivals including Zara and Topshop, making it ripe for re-invention. “This is going to be an incredibly exciting journey for Warehouse as we re-launch this iconic British brand, says Willis. “As a creative consultant I’m passionate about British brands so when one comes along that I see has the potential and an opportunity to do something inspiring, meaningful and relevant to today’s consumer then I get excited…Warehouse has these elements.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
