 One of fashion’s most powerful tools is it ability to transform our perspective in a matter of moments. Open a fashion magazine hating pie-crust blouses, put it down with the overwhelming urge to drop everything and hunt one down like your life depends upon it. There’s probably no better medium for challenging our perceptions of what looks good than fashion photography. A fact recognised by Sotheby’s who are auctioning off a selection of era-defining images today - including a shot of supermodels rejected by Anna Wintour, a portrait considered 'the most honest photograph ever taken of Marilyn Monroe' and more recent shots such as Miles Aldridge’s sumptuously colourful photographs.  The image that's perhaps most immediately recognisable to the public is probably Peter Lindbergh’s 1990 work  Models. Six great supermodels of the day - Linda Envangelista, Tatjana Patitz, Christy Turlington, Estella Lefebure, Karen Alexander and Rachel Williams are on a beach in LA. They all wear mannish white shirts and are laughing and joking like a group of old school friends. It’s a beautiful image but American Vogue, who had commissioned the shoot, ended up not using it because the editor Anna Wintour thought it was too controversially casual.  “They look so at ease and so themselves,” says Brandei Estes, Head of photographs at Sotheby’s London, of the models shot. "But in 1990 that was considered too avant-garde, they said it couldn’t be used.” Ironically, Lindbergh had already made waves at American Vogue - when his 1988 shot of model Michaela Bercu became the first time a cover star had worn jeans on the high fashion magazine. As he put it, “I want to free women, and finally everyone, from the terror of youth and perfection.” Lindbergh's sense of freedom through his work is one that runs through Sotheby's auction. Another of his images - Mathilde – shows the model Mathilde posing topless looking out across Paris from the bars of the Eiffel tower. It references an earlier work by esteemed mid-century photographer Erwin Blumenfeld who had shot Swedish model Lisa Fonassgrives in a similar pose. But Lindbergh relaxed things, saying his aim was “not to violate the model’s personality by transforming them with makeup and hair, but to find their personality.” While Lindbergh’s works are a great example of fashion photography’s role in changing perceptions, Estes points out that this tension is what unites the auction. “What’s really interesting about these images - and what ties them together despite  them being from different periods - is that each of the photographers was groundbreaking in their time,” she explains. “Helmut Newton’s work was sexualised and risqué, nobody shot fashion like that then.” For some it even took a while for their work to be acknowledged as trailblazing. The auction includes a startlingly honest portrait of Marilyn Monroe by Richard Avedon. “For hours she danced and sang and flirted and did this thing that’s—she did Marilyn Monroe," the photographer recalls. "And then there was the inevitable drop. And when the night was over and the white wine was over and the dancing was over, she sat in the corner like a child, with everything gone. I saw her sitting quietly without expression on her face, and I walked towards her but I wouldn’t photograph her without her knowledge of it. And as I came with the camera, I saw that she was not saying no.” While his portrait is one of the most honest ever taken of Marilyn, it's beauty wasn't immediately acknowledged. “It was really only in the 1980s that the market took off and the value of their work was truly realised,” says Estes. So how do you get all these iconic fashion images together in one auction?  “It’s involved a lot of blood, sweat and tears,” laughs Estes, who says that it’s mostly because the market is so strong that her contacts have been persuaded to sell. “I’ve known many collectors who would turn their nose up at fashion photography but that’s changing, you can really see the historical value now,” she says of the market which has taken off in the past ten years. “I mean in the 80s, no one would ever have heard of these image makers, but Mario Testino is a household name now.” For more information about Sotheby's Photography auction, visit the catalogue here   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Game of Thrones actress Maisie Williams might only be 18, but she is already one of the freshest new fashion stars on the red carpet. Remember, this is an actress who once went to an awards show in a dress covered in tiny wrestlers.  At last night's premiere of the The Devil and the Deep Blue Sea at the Tribeca Film Festival she wore a strapless blue gown by under-the-radar Manchester-based label Zeynep Kartal.  Earlier this week at the Game of Thrones season 6 Los Angeles premiere, Williams matched her GoT manicure to her Emilio de la Morena outfit - a classic example of the actor's tendency to champion of young, upcoming design talent. "I always keep an eye out on new designers. I'm not a brand snob; if a dress works, it works irrelevant of the brand. Often we get tagged on things on Instagram, and it'll be something I haven't noticed before, and so we'll go with that," her stylist Harriet Byczok explains to The Telegraph of how they choose their looks. "I stumbled upon Sadie Williams, which she wore to the Empire Awards, on Instagram, and I fell in love with the outfit. I am always looking to Instagram for my inspiration, and follow a lot of brands and designers, so it's a great source for style inspiration for Maisie." As for their approach to the red carpet, she says: "We always try to find something that reflects Maisie's personality. She's a really cool girl and I think she's never going to be a plain black dress kind of girl. With the red carpet, a lot of the dresses can look old or often celebrities play it quite safe." This week's Emilio de la Morena look was influenced by the the fact that the premiere took place in Los Angeles. "With LA you need to be very glamorous, and in London you can be cooler," she explains. "We wanted to stick to Maisie's cool personal style, but make sure she's in keeping with the glam LA look. With the crop top it looks a lot more fun, and the colours make it look a lot more young and quirky. But with the length and shape and hair and makeup it fits in with the LA requirements." "We decided to have her hair down because it's quite fleshy, and wanted the makeup to add a bit of colour," she continues. "I like to use a lot of accessories, because they can stop a dress being just a dress and make it an outfit. But with this dress being a statement on its own we didn't over accessorise, so used the makeup so it didn't look plain." Although you might assume that you have to be careful to remain age-appropriate when styling a teenager, Byczok says that her age actually makes it a little easier as Maisie is more willing to take a risk. "When she was 16 she did have her own personal style and it's developed," she tells The Telegraph. "With 16-year-old's it's easier, because they know what they want to look like. When you're older sometimes you're a little more scared." Being in a cult TV show such as Game of Thrones means that there is a huge fanbase watching - and commenting - on Maisie's every move. But they don't let her 2 million followers on Instagram influence her decisions, or stop her from wearing something divisive.  "Everybody is going to have an opinion," says Byczok. "So the most important thing is that Maisie feels like herself. For me, comments that people say on Instagram are irrelevant." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The annual reception held for the Diplomatic Corps at Buckingham Palace is always a dazzling occassion on the royal calendar, with the Queen and her closest family members donning their finest regalia as a show of regal glamour for the assembled dignitaries. Usually, images from the event are scarce but Buckingham Palace last night released a portrait of the Queen, Prince Phillip, Prince Charles, the Duchess of Cornwall, Prince William and the Duchess of Cambridge, showing their gowns, tiaras, jewels, medals and sashes in their full glory.  The Duchess of Cambridge chose the same Cambridge Lover's Knot tiara, which she also wore to last year's event. First created for Queen Mary by E. Wollf & co for Garrard's in 1914, the tiara has been worn by royals including the Queen and Princess Augusta of Cambridge; Her Majesty wore it often during the early years of her reign. The design features 19 diamond arches from which hang 19 baroque pearl pendants. It was a favourite of Princess Diana's who was loaned it by the Queen after her marriage. Although she is said to have complained about its heaviness, it became one of her go-tos and she often wore it for evening receptions, including on a visit to Hong Kong in 1989 with her iconic 'Elvis' outfit- a raised collar bolero jacket and matching dress created for her by Catherine Walker.  Kate showed once again last night that Jenny Packham has become her favoured designers for these grand evening engagements, when only full-length gowns, often delicately embellished and created in bold colours will do. Yesterday, the Duchess re-wore a scarlett design first seen last October when she was seated beside President Xi of China during the state banquet which the Queen hosted as part of his visit to London. The red hue was a cleverly diplomatic nod to China's favourite colour for that event, but last night it seemed to imbue festive cheer.  With its elegantly capped shoulders, sequinned bodice and flowing chiffon skirt, the Packham gown has a timeless look which means that we can likely expect the Duchess to wear it for years to come. It's also a quality which is key for these events; the evening gowns which Jenny Packham creates aren't about fashion, like many of the Duchess's other looks this year, but hitting a note which chimes with the grandeur of an event. For the royal tour to India and Bhutan in April, Packham was enlisted to dress the Duchess for a gala celebrating Bollywood. She created a cobalt blue dress in a similar design to the red style worn last night, but with a matching shawl which gave a sari-like effect. And in June, the Duchess re-wore an old favourite blush pink and heavily beaded gown by Jenny Packham for a gala at Houghton Hall in Norfolk.  The Queen and the Duchess of Cornwall both wore white for last night's diplomatic reception. Camilla's beaded silk gown was by Bruce Oldfield, the British couturier also favoured by Sophie, Countess of Wessex, for his elegant, occassion-befitting designs. Her look was finished with a Boucheron tiara, pearl choker and diamond earrings and The Royal Family Order and Dame Grand Cross of the Royal Victorian Order.  Meanwhile, Angela Kelly was responsible for  the white dress overlaid with beaded tulle worn by the Queen. A sapphire and diamond tiara, a sapphire necklace and earrings and the Garter sash completed the ensemble.  While we revel in the glamour and glitz of this portrait, it's worth remembering that the jewels and regalia worn by the six most senior members of the royal family are a carefully calibrated show of power and pomp, created to impress the assembled diplomats.        © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.   If by the end of the day your eyes feel dry and scratchy, and you’re having trouble nodding off, then you could be in need of some sci-fi sounding, but thankfully not looking, blue-light blocking glasses. Blue light, also known as high-energy visible light, naturally occurs in sunlight, but it appears in digital devices including smartphones, computer screens and even some LED televisions. Similar to UV light, long periods of exposure are increasingly becoming linked to a reduction in the body’s production of melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy, as well as damage to the eye tissue itself. Valentino’s pale embellished designs tantalisingly reveal a little flesh without actually revealing anything at all. Such exquisite craftsmanship would create an element of allure, while maintaining Jane's poise. Not an easy line to toe. Admittedly, adjustments would need to be made for hiding weapons and such, but we're sure the Valentino design team could whip up a discreet custom belt? Jane would never be caught on camera in just her smalls, but would certainly allow herself to play the seductress in an elegant McQueen gown that plays with the concept of conceal and reveal. Whether on private jet or the Orient Express, Bond needs to look pulled together at all times. A catalogue of classic Chanel suits would do just the trick. Tilda Swinton in A Bigger Splash will be Bond’s style muse for ventures to warmer climes. Think structured, airy shirt dresses and choice, architectural accessories.  Last night, King Felipe and Queen Letizia of Spain attended the second glittering banquet of their three-day state visit to the UK. It was the turn of the Lord Mayor to host the royal couple last night at London's Guildhall, with Princess Anne in attendance to represent the Queen.  Letizia continued to uphold her reputation as one of the world's most stylish royals, showcasing a look which offered a modern spin on the classic tropes of regal elegance. The centrepiece of her look was  the Spanish Floral tiara, which was a gift to Letizia's mother-in-law, Queen Sofia, when she married Juan Carlos of Spain in 1962. The ornately delicate diamond tiara was worn with a pair of chunky sapphire and diamond earrings which Letizia debuted for the first time. The dazzling jewellery display was finished with Letizia's favourite diamond cuff bracelets which come from the 'Joyas de Pasar' collection, the closest which the Spanish royal family have to a collection of crown jewels and which translates as 'passing along jewels'. Despite their vintage provenance, Letizia's way of wearing the bracelets stacked together makes them look of-the-moment.  It was also the pairing of the sweetly antique tiara with the bolder look of the earrings- thought to have been a recent gift from a Middle Eastern royal family- which confirmed Letizia's ability to make an offbeat statement with seemingly traditional pieces.  She enhanced the effect of the look by selecting a deep blue, one-shouldered gown with softly draped  details by Armani as a strikingly simple antidote to all those jewels.  The tiara did cause some controversy when it was first worn by Letizia in 2013, as it had been given to Queen Sofia by General Franco, who was Spain's dictatorial ruler at the time of her marriage. He eventually restored the monarchy by naming Juan Carlos as his successor. However, the tiara's history actually goes back to 1879 when it was created by British jewellers J.P. Collins for King Alfonso XII as a gift for his second wife. It fell out of the royal family's ownership in the 1930s but was bought back by Franco. If Queen Letizia was making the case for a modern interpretation of royal style, then Princess Anne's look was a glittering reminder of a classically romantic take on banquetting attire. She wore a daintily embellished, pale silver dress with floral embroidery and puff sleeves which looked as it if it could have been borrowed from her mother's 1950s collection of  couture Norman Hartnell dresses. Her refined diamond tiara is one of her favourite pieces and was given to her in 1973 by the World Wide Shipping group after she christened one of their ships.  What does your back to school look say about you? For the children, it’s likely ‘my uniform is the cleanest it’ll be all year’, or ‘look, my parents have replaced the jumper that was too small for me with one that’s now a bit too big’. But does anyone care about what the adults are wearing at the school gates as the new term kicks off? For mums on the run, time is of the essence, and fast fashion and beauty solutions are essential for anyone who wants to look remotely like themselves at the crack of dawn. “My top tip for showing off your new season style at the school gates is not to try too hard, says Erica Davies, a fashion editor, mother-of-two, and founder of The Edited. “Pick a couple of statement pieces that are useful enough to be practical and will elevate a relatively simple jeans and jumper uniform.” Erica Davies in another classic coat with statement boots Davies recommends that a strong outerwear option will lift any outfit with minimal effort and at maximum speed. “A new coat is always a great investment,” she says. “This year it’s all about the leopard - although to be honest, it never goes out of fashion for me.” Leopard print coat, £235, Ganni at Net-A-Porter.com Lucy Felton, a mother-of-one, fashion journalist and blogger at The Lucy Edit, agrees and suggests finding a smart blazer in one of this season’s hero check prints, for the months before ‘coat weather’ properly kicks in. “It can be thrown on over your trusty sweater/hoodie/pyjama top while hunting for the car keys and grabbing the packed lunches from the fridge,” she says. “The perfect blend of smart and relaxed, and you won’t even need to look in the mirror before heading out the front door.” The potential to wear it with everything from jeans to party frocks adds to the appeal. “Be sure to buy a size bigger for maximum layering potential,” she advises. When it comes to makeup, beauty director of This Is Mothership Sam Silver recommends nailing the search for a multi-tasking product. "It's 7:06am and you have four minutes to get yourself and/or the kids out the door, find your keys and get everyone into a coat,” she says, “I drop my son at nursery each morning and then head straight into town for work, so I keep the Bobbi Brown Essentials 5 in 1 Face Palette in my handbag. Designed to be applied on-the-go, it has everything you need and the addition of a bronzer makes me look human.” Essentials 5 in 1 Face Palette, £40, from Bobbi Brown Meanwhile her This Is Mothership co-founder, the stylist Gemma Rose Breger, applies the same logic to her choice of handbag. A cross-body style, she says, is the most practical and easily accessible choice, with the added benefit of tying the rest of your outfit together in one fell swoop. “Even when I still needed to use a changing bag, which was always a backpack on my back, I kept all my own essentials  (phone, keys, credit card and red lipstick) in my cross body bag so I was always hands free,” she notes, adding that prints are always an excellent way to disguise any stains. “I've been using my Louis Vuitton BB bag loads recently as the monogrammed print goes with everything and covers up any smooshed marks that my daughter Belle likes to decorate it with.” Gemma Rose Breger and Sam Silver  of This Is Mothership When it comes to footwear, all the experts recommend flats and trainers, but Davies says that a new pair of colourful boots may prove to be the only new hit that a fashion-forward autumn term wardrobe requires.  So far on the Royal Tour of Canada the Duchess of Cambridge has upped the ante with her wardrobe - think a killer £2,000 Dolce & Gabbana dress and being the first mum in history to wear cream to a children’s tea party. But today, for the final day of events, Kate proved she can make just as much of a sartorial statement wearing high street. For her visit to Cridge Centre, an agency that offers shelter, care and hope for children, women, families and the elderly, the ever-appropriate Duchess wore a jeans and jacket from Zara and a top from humble old H&M. Whilst the single-buttoned white blazer is a new purchase from Zara, the jeans-and-jacket combination is one the Duchess often turns to when she’s in need of something smart-casual, that trickiest of dress codes. Indeed, we last saw Kate wearing today’s H&M top on her tour of Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, when she paired it with jazzy £22 Gap trousers and a Smythe blazer. And this is the third time on her week-long tour of Canada that we’ve seen Kate pull on a pair of her beloved Zara jeans. (Cue the very serious question of how she keeps them so 'skinny' with no bagging at the knees given how often she wears them?). But if the Duchess might have been falling back on a well-perfected fashion formula (and why not? If it works, stick with it, we say), there were still subtle signs that she’s developing some new style tricks. Note the shoes; £278 Avery heels from J Crew - a new addition to her wardrobe, but perhaps bought well in advance of the tour, given they are already sold out online. With their block heel and tweed fabric - a nod to the current heritage trend - they make a pleasing change from Kate’s safe-but-staid patent nude court or Sebago boat shoe habit. And whilst props should be given to the Duchess for braving Zara’s sale rails like the rest of us (the Duke of York store off Sloane Street is her preferred branch, fyi - and with good reason given how well stocked it is), it’s worth pointing out that her royal status subtly shines through in other areas of her outfit; notably her jewellery. Aside from that engagement ring and the £1,090 Annoushka pearl earrings that are firmly becoming a favourite, Kate is wearing an Asprey charm necklace that would have cost in excess of £10,000. The necklace features charms from Asprey’s woodland collection that represent her family’s coat of arms - an acorn, an oak leaf and a mushroom - all set in 18ct yellow gold and featuring pave diamonds.  If Kate’s jeans-and-blazer combination struck the right note for a Royal at work on the final day of the Canadian tour, it also worked because it allowed her to easily switch up her look for the next engagement - sailing. In the back of the car (quite literally) en route to take a trip around the harbour, the Duchess slipped off her Zara blazer and J Crew heels  in favour of a more practical parka jacket and plimsolls. But true to Kate’s attention-to-detail with her clothes her Troy London parka wasn’t just a sturdy choice - but a show of support to her old friend Rosie Van Cutsem who recently set up the country casual clothing business with her sister Lucia Ruck Keene. Van Cutsem is married to one of Prince William’s oldest friends, also called William, who is godfather to Prince George. Van Cutsem set up contemporary British outerwear label Troy London with the ambition of creating timeless parkas that will work in both the city and country. “A fresh take on our bestseller, this new lightweight coat is made from 100% cotton milled in England with a dry wax finish,” is how the website describes the £350 parka that the Duchess of Cambridge is wearing. “A black sports-luxe lining provides 100% waterproof protection and brings an urban appeal to this casual but elegant coat with a cinched waist and drawstring hood.” The Duchess’s coat is currently still available to buy online - but for how much longer?  These days ad camapaigns have become just as much about creating a talking point as showing off nice bags and shoes. Versace's AW16 ad campaign released last week is no different. Donatella Versace enlisted photographer Bruce Weber for the first time in 17 years to create a family-centric set of images starring Gigi Hadid ,21, and Karlie Kloss, 23, alongside their imagined children and boyfriends.  A leather-clad Karlie Kloss is seen exiting a car with two children- who are definitely around school age- and a partner, while Hadid walks through Chicago holding her "son's" hand as her fictional boyfriend/ husband/ baby daddy pushes their "daughter" in a buggy. This glamorised spin on real-life is a  world away from the previous autumn/winter campaign which showed models lying in the snow in animal-print bikinis.  "With my collections, I’ve been thinking more and more about the real life of Versace, and the complexity of women’s lives," Donatella Versace explains to The Telegraph of her thinking behind this campaign. "They run their own business, look after their family, travel, share time with friends, all often in the same day. I wanted to show the fullness of the Versace life in our campaign, and Bruce was the only photographer who could capture that mood." The campaign has sparked plenty of reaction online, with many complaining that it's unrealistic to show twentysomethings Gigi Hadid and Karlie Kloss as mothers especially given that the age of children they're posing with means they'd have given birth aged 16 or younger. Meanwhile others have claimed it's racist to show Hadid front and centre with a black partner and children, one of whom is chained into its buggy- although many have also retorted that those people "really need to get a grip. You're looking for something that isn't there." "My name is Versace - I don’t know how to do things quietly," Donatella reasons, "that is just my blood and my family. We make a noise, shout loud, never hold back on our opinions. This is why our campaigns have always been so bold, because my family has always provoked. Life would be so boring if we all did the same thing." Given Versace's long-history of working with the biggest supermodels of the day- her brother Gianni was famous for forming close partnerships with the likes of Naomi Campbell, Claudia Schiffer and Kate Moss who would always walk in his shows- it's hardly surprising that Hadid and Kloss are the no-brainer choices for Versace now. But Donatella says it's more about the models' integrity and attitude than just their impressive follower count and fame. "Versace is about individuality. It is about believing in yourself and showing your true character to the world. I love Gigi and Karlie because of their amazing strength of character. They are their own women who will not compromise their individuality for anyone. I wanted to create imagery that was all about their brilliant individuality." When Weber and Versace worked together almost twenty years ago, their work was equally provocative. Think- a topless Helena Christensen being touched by a male model as she takes pictures of him, mixed race couples embracing and not wearing very much and a denim campaign which shows a line up of groins pressed up against each other. In short, just the sort of thing which would still elicit a reaction now.  "Shooting our first campaigns with Bruce are some of my most special memories of my Versace life. It was a different time then, no constrictions or constraints," the designer says of how much has changed since they last worked together. "We could shoot for days, dream big, make the impossible happen. We travelled to the most exciting places in the world, such as Buenos Aires. It was in the days before digital, and no-one had cameras on their phones. It was a magical time." Gigi Hadid starred in her first Versace campaign last year, and has opened and closed several shows for the house so is now a firm favourite. "As soon as I met Gigi, we clicked," Versace says of her relationship with the model. "I love that feeling when you meet someone new, and you know straight away you’re going to be friends. Gigi is a true supermodel because not only is she stunningly beautiful, she is also gracious and works incredibly hard. She is a natural supermodel, and a perfect Versace woman." Hadid's huge following online (she has over 18 million followers on Instagram) is often regarded as a key part of her supermodel status. 61 year-old Donatella joined Instagram herself a year ago, posting her first selfie on set of the AW15 campaign with Gigi. "It was a very happy coincidence that my first post was with someone who understands social media so well," Versace explains. "So many people are scared of Instagram or social media, but it’s amazing to watch young people today and see how much it is a part of their lives. The new way that they communicate is very inspiring to me. They are so curious about the world, following people of so many different nationalities and backgrounds. Getting to know Gigi has made me fall in love with social media, and the new way it lets me see the world."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Christian Louboutin will go to great lengths to outfit his prized garden; seven hectares of high-maintenance landscaping at his 13th-century French château in France’s Vendée region. “I do have the, how do you say? Green fingers,” he laughs. “I will always bring back plants from my travels. Perhaps I shouldn’t say this, but I’ve been smuggling them from everywhere. The only place I don’t think I’ve brought a plant from is in England, though, which is odd because I spend so much time here.” As such, the garden at Château de Champgillon, a property he has co-owned with his business partner Bruno Chambelland for more than 25 years, is established and thriving, filled with everything from Chinese and Japanese wisteria, to an orangerie growing kumquats and mandarins. The team at contemporary gardening magazine Rakesprogress were so taken with his lot, that they commissioned photographer Jane Hilton to capture a series ‘Digging His Heels In’ which is on display until the end of this week on Covent Garden’s Floral Street. Hilton’s images capture Louboutin in a blissed-out state, sniffing great peonies and pottering around lawns with friends. “I find gardening very relaxing now,” he says of how his work makes him feel. “From an early age I have been an Animist, even before I understood what that meant. I don’t believe in God, I believe in energies and life of different forms - trees, plants, animals. When I did discover what it meant I felt totally at ease with the idea.” Louboutin almost made landscape gardening his full-time career at the end of the 1980s. He had dropped out of school in Paris at the age of 16, gained, by pure luck and charisma, an internship at Christian Dior after meeting Countess Hélène de Mortemart and had worked briefly as a secretary to Roger Vivier. In 1988 he made a sideways career move and began working on topiaries and gardens while he contributed to Vogue, before realising that his true passion was in fact to design shoes, and founded his eponymous line in 1991. “When you’re a designer you look at the line structures, forms and colour combinations of everything you see,” he explains of how the two disciplines relate, for him. “Many designers think of paintings, but if I close my eyes I would see nature. The colours and the textures just add up for me. A magnolia is a thick leather, probably patent. A pansy is definitely suede or velvet. When I think of what colours look good together on a shoe, it’s usually ones that I have thought look good together in the garden. I don’t make moodboards, this is how I research.” His gardening uniform is a basic one - a panama hat and wellingtons. “I am never barefoot,” he says. “It’s mostly wellingtons and not of my own design, but perhaps soon I will make some. I always carry a secateur, even if I’m only going outside for five minutes. There is always something to clip and if there is truly nothing, I will clip my nails instead.” The Rakesprogress pop up at 13 Floral Street, Covent Garden, is open to the public until 7th December. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The 2016 awards season will kick off on Sunday night with the Golden Globes, but there’ll be one person noticeably absent from the post-event fashion dissection to which we have all become so accustomed; Catherine Kallon. You may not recognise her name, but if you’re a follower of red carpet fashion you’ll almost certainly know her website RedCarpetFashionAwards.com, the one-stop-shop for celebrity outfit identification and analysis. Kallon was working at a sports marketing company when she set the site up as a hobby in February 2007. It was born out of three things; an obsession with catwalk goldmine Style.com [now voguerunway.com], a frustration with magazines and TV programmes that incorrectly credited red carpet gowns, and a quest to escape the laddish topics of conversation that permeated her male-dominated workplace. It was the middle of awards season so she set about updating it a few times a day, meticulously identifying the designer outfits worn by celebrities at the previous evening’s event, placing them side-by-side with the corresponding catwalk image, adding her own measured opinion and commentary and showing readers, where possible, where they could buy the same outfit online. She noticed her first significant surge in traffic on the night of that year’s Oscars ceremony when the site garnered quadruple its usual amount of visitors. She quickly realised she was filling a niche in the web market. “I was amazed at how much people were responding to it and thought ‘Instead of me doing this just for awards season, how about I do it every time there’s an event?’ and soon after that I was like ‘Oh there’s an event every single day’,” she says. So she did. When the recession hit in 2009 she found herself without a ‘proper’ job but with a lot more time to spend on the website. Consequently, her traffic spiked and she came across a way to start earning an income from it - Linkshare, an affiliate program that allows you to earn money if a reader clicks on a product link from your website and then goes on to buy that product. A four-figure cheque soon followed and she realised her hobby was a viable career option. Brands wishing to advertise on her site soon came knocking and the site only continued to grow, boasting up to 120,000 hits a day. But now she’s giving it all up. On December 31, 2015, she made her final post, titled Thank You And Goodbye. “I took a while to think about it, and without getting into too much detail, I have decided that this will be my last post on the site,” she wrote amid a longer note. The post has so far received just shy of 400 comments, each one including thanks to Kallon for what she has given them over the years. But, why? Well, put simply, she is a victim of her own success. “I would definitely say that’s the best way that you could describe it,” she says. “It just became too unmanageable; there were too many people that I wanted to write about. I felt like I wasn’t working to the best of my abilities, and I felt like the site had grown bigger than me.” The number of events happening each day has increased dramatically since 2007, as has our collective appetite for red carpet analysis. “Sometimes there’d be 15 actresses at an event, and then there’d be three of these events in the night and it was just becoming too much,” she explains. “The site needed a team of people,” she adds. “I’ve been so obsessed with it. I look at my website several times a day and read people’s comments so I understood, from a reader’s point of view, that they were frustrated. They were sending me messages like, ‘Why haven’t you featured this person?’ or ‘Why haven’t you featured that person?’ I would get these messages every day.” Though she did have some contributors and more recently help in the form of writer Rachel Watkins, Kallon found readers wanted her voice, so it was something of a catch-22. They liked her opinionated but never nasty tone, and how it always encouraged the readers to get involved and join to conversation via the ‘comments’ section. She acknowledges that RedCarpetFashionAwards.com was a key player in creating and feeding the insatiable hunger we now seem to have for immediate information. It sounds a little like Frankenstein’s Monster – she made it, it defeated her - except Kallon’s not defeated. She’s graciously bowed out before it got to that point. She’s now taking a break while she evaluates what she wants to do next. In the meantime, she’s got nine years of success to look back over, and she learnt a lot. In that time, the spotlight on the red carpet has become blinding. “It has changed drastically,” she says. Everyone is now “playing the game”, even the older generation like Meryl Streep and Helen Mirren, who would previously blend in to the background in nameless outfits but now wear the same big-name designers as their younger counterparts. “I think it’s because of how important it is; nobody wants to be seen to be making a mistake.” The increased visibility of the red carpet thanks to sites like hers has also changed the way the fashion industry works, she notes. “When I started, it was very much the same key designers but now you can see that stylists are actively looking for the next big thing… take Prabal Gurung. Zoe Saldana was the first to wear him and then he just exploded. Before you knew it Michelle Obama was wearing him,” says Kallon. It has also allowed her valuable insight into the inner workings of celebrity image, which made the #AskHerMore campaign mounted by the likes of Reese Witherspoon and Cate Blanchett during the 2015 awards season a little grating. It urged red carpet reporters to ask about the work of the actresses they were interviewing, not what designer they were wearing. “I understood what they were saying to a certain degree, but there’s a designer that’s been sitting in a room for the last six months designing, sketching, and his atelier have been hand-sewing these things for sometimes 600+ hours,” says Kallon. “So I think a name-check wouldn’t hurt, and then [after that] they can go on with the rest of what they need to talk about. At the end of the day, if you didn’t want people to care what you were wearing, why did you come in that dress?” Her personal red carpet superstar is Elizabeth Banks, who she admits she’s “obsessed” with. But in terms of big-hitters on her website, Kate Middleton, Jennifer Lawrence, Emma Stone, Olivia Palermo, Rihanna and Kim Kardashian led the charge. She thinks the site’s popularity was down to our unstoppable obsession with celebrity and wish to replicate their style. “A lot of people have commented on my [final] post that they feel like their style has evolved as a result of the website, because they see how a certain dress can look with a certain shoe, they see how you can wear a plain ASOS dress with a pair of Sophia Webster heels,” says Kallon. “And I think that’s why people want to know - they want to know if they can afford it, or if they can recreate it from Zara, or even just buy it directly from the designers themselves.” This year, for the first time in nine years Kallon will watch the forthcoming awards ceremonies and their accompanying red carpets - and she'll actually get to see the gowns move. "I’ve always seen them static [in photographs] because as soon as it starts, I'm refreshing, refreshing, refreshing to get the pictures to come in so I can post.  So it will be nice to sit and watch it from a spectator point of view." But for millions, her point of view will be sorely missed. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Zsa Zsa Gabor, who has died aged 99, is a reminder that the fashion world's self-proclaimed It girls like the Hiltons and the Kardashians are no invention of the modern age. Nine-times married Gabor is their logical predecessor. She made it her business to drip with diamonds, dress as ostentatiously as possible and gallivant her way through the past almost century doling out lessons in living fabulously.  When she was interviewed by People magazine in 1975 about her relationship with sixth husband Jack Ryan- who had made his millions from creating the Barbie doll- Gabor emphasised her adoration for him by saying what a seismic sacrifice it had been for her to stay indoors for two whole months with him luxuriating in coupledom instead of being out partying and showing off her wardrobe. 'Not once did we really go out during those two months. And usually that is the biggest pastime for me,' she said. 'I love to put on diamonds and beautiful evening gowns and make my girl-friends upset. It’s a wonderful feeling.' Dress and diamonds were the magical elixir of Gabor's existence. She first shot to fame (notoriety?) in 1951 when she was drafted in to appear on a chat show called  Bachelor’s Haven. Married to George Sanders at the time, she wore a dress by Balenciaga, the must-have Parisian couturier of the day, which was accessorised with a diamond bracelet and 20-carat diamond ring. When the host remarked on the dazzling beauty of her bling, Gabor retorted  'Oh, dahling, these are just my working diamonds.' It's little wonder then that Sanders would compare Gabor to some of history's most legendary glamourpusses in his book Memoirs of a Professional Cad. "Every age has its Madame Pompadour, its Lady Hamilton, its Queen of Sheba, its Cleopatra. I wouldn’t be surprised if history singles out Zsa Zsa as the twentieth-century prototype of this exclusive coterie." Think of all the tropes of glamour and Gabor, who had been crowned Miss Hungary as a teen, embodied them all. While it was widely acknowledged that she was probably not the most gifted of actresses, she was nevertheless cast in dozens of films over the years. One of her most famous was Moulin Rouge in which she outdazzled the rest of the cast in the sumptuous costumes designed for her by Elsa Schiaparelli. "The most beautiful girl ever to be on a television screen," trumpeted the Hollywood Reporter in response to her performance. It is her off-screen wardrobe though which truly marked Gabor out from her contemporaries. Quiet sophistication and elegance were nowhere to be seen in her repertoire. Instead 'more is more' was the mantra. Naturally, she was one of leopard print's greatest ambassadors, with streams of images from throughout the decades showing her wrapped in exaggeratedly cut animal print coats.  A pair of leopard ankle boots she owned and often wore with a co-ordinating cover-up were so well-loved that she wore them for six whole years - a longer time span than she managed with seven of her husbands.  Over the course of her many weddings, Gabor charted the changing nuances of her style. For her second marriage in 1942 - to hotelier Conrad Hilton (yes, grandfather of those noughties institutions Nicky and Paris) - she wore a glittering gown with beaded bodice and matching shawl wrap. It was all out Barbie for her wedding to Ryan meanwhile, with an elaborate head dress; while the ninth ceremony of Gabor's life to Frédéric Prinz von Anhalt in 1986 was somewhat dominated by the  layers and layers of creamy whisps which formed a huge band around her shoulders and trimmed her baby-blue dress. More refined was the look for her wedding to investment banker Hubert Hutner for which she chose a sleek sheath dress, feathered hat and pearls.  Gabor's best fashion moments teetered on the brink of parody - it was rare that she was not dressed in designs that forced her to occupy more than three times the space her body took up; the rest accounted for acres of taffeta, tulle and ruffles. She would have been a gift to the age of Instagram. When she was interviewed by Dame Edna Everage she chose the most frou-frou dress imaginable, complete with with 'Zsa Zsa' embroidered on the front. She was almost certainly playing Barry Humphries' Dame at her own game - and winning. According to her fan site, Zsa Zsa Gabor's wardrobe usually contained around 5,000 items of clothing. It's a fact which might seem fair for a world famous woman who had spent years racking up red carpet and party appearances. But, the account claims that in fact her stocks were cleared every year or so and auctioned for charity, leaving only a small selection of her most treasured dresses. Which means she must have had quite the shopping habit. Indeed, she is said to have been irate when Hilton attempted to curb her spending to $250 a month - not a tiny sum in the 1940's.  Like the Beckhams, Kardashians and Hadids of today, Gabor used the airport as her catwalk. Furs, luxe silk scarves and lashing of Louis Vuitton luggage were her signatures as she traveled the world on the arm of one man or another.  Her refreshingly fearless and confident approach to style is evidenced in the pictures of her in later life, stepping out in  thigh grazing mini skirts when most women would be more likely to be seen in slacks from Country Casuals.  In 1989, Gabor was arrested for slapping policeman Paul Kramer after he pulled her and von Anhalt over in their $215,000 Rolls Royce. Appearing in court to hear the verdict on the offences, Gabor made the moment her own by wearing a characteristically flamboyant orange and black floral dress. In 2001, a similar dress which Gabor had been wearing at the time of the offence was auctioned to pay for her escalating medical bills. "Tight enough to accentuate womanly curves, loose enough to slap a cop in the face," quipped gossip site TMZ.  "That would be wonderful. I'd have time to write my book," Gabor told reporters when asked how she'd feel about going to jail. But the reality was more sobering. "At first I was petrified. They even took my make-up away," she later complained. Even at her lowest moments, glamour and glitz was always front of Gabor's mind - a rare breed of fabulous for which she will long be remembered.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  “It’s quite crowded out there,” says Jimin Lee, founder and creative director of J.Cricket, as she describes fashion’s current state of affairs. “It’s tired as well.” This statement comes from a long-time fashion buyer who has spent years anticipating what women want to wear. Which is why she is approaching her newly launched, own-brand collective with the freshest of eyes. Armed with knowledge of what's missing in women's wardrobes, Lee aims to create "a classic vocabulary, but reinterpreted"; made by a talented collective of freelance creatives, through discerning collaborations with designers and pattern-makers across the world. The first item to make it into the collection was the Slide – a mesmerising Transformer-type bag designed by Paul Graves, an artist and photographer, that comes in bubblegum pink, cobalt and silver, or khaki, navy, calamine and orange colourways. Next for Lee was a selection of sleeveless coats. “We often see a gilet in a traditional fashion collection, but it’s usually just like a jacket with its sleeves cut off. I wanted to have sleeveless coats with volume to the back that make them much more dramatic.” It’s an easy layering piece that most of us forget about, until we see one like this that can play with anything else in our wardrobe. And now J.Cricket offers a shirting collection; folded and billowing, patterned or plain. In pinstripe, polka dot, crisp white and leopard print, like a Pick'n'Mix stand – there’s something for everyone. “There’s a boyfriend shirt, a tuxedo tunic, a scarf blouse. We worked on the volume, the shape and the silhouettes more than anything, and then interpreted them in classic and printed fabrics,” says Lee. Like all judicious gallerists and curators, Lee, who is Korean-born but grew up in the Philippines before working with Saks Fifth Avenue and Chinese department store Joyce, also has a focused business plan. J.Cricket is currently only available to purchase through trunk shows, the idea is to add to the collection slowly and carefully. “I like the idea of exclusivity, limited-edition, and doing more push around the brand for a concentrated period of time rather than letting things get lost,” she says. “I’m trying to keep things very small instead of giving in to the urge to blow up and make things more impressive.” But whatever she says, as someone always looking for stealth, brilliantly-designed wardrobe staples, I’m already impressed. jcricket.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Meeting young air cadets at the RAF base in Peterborough today, the Duchess of Cambridge chose to nod to the occasion by wearing a double-breasted, military-inspired jacket by Philosophy di Lorenzo Serafini. Choosing clothes with details that reference uniforms has proven frequently to be a hit in the Duchess’s fashion playbook, as it makes her look both approachable and formal to an audience of servicemen and women. Kate wore Stuart Weitzman boots, Joseph poloneck top and Kiki McDonough earrings with the jacket, which is from Lorenzo Serafini’s resort 2017 collection for Philosophy, a brand that the Italian designer has headed up since 2014. It’s the second time that Kate has worn a Philosophy piece, the first being when she wore a jacket designed by Alberta Ferretti for the brand in an official portrait back in 2011. Priced at £760, today’s coat is now almost sold out on Net-A-Porter.com. The sartorial tactic of wearing military styles to military events is one that several women in the Royal Family have employed throughout history, including Princess Diana and The Queen. Diana famously wore a fully-frogged white jacket and skirt to a passing out parade at Sandhurst Military Academy in 1987. Indeed Kate has previously commissioned bespoke looks by Alexander McQueen (a brand that famously plays on, and is inspired by British heritage) as well as a wardrobe full of coats by British designers that nod to both nautical and army uniforms. In 2014, she wore the above double-breasted Alexander McQueen blouse and skirt on a visit to World War Two heritage site Bletchley Park, and in 2011 she presented medals to the Irish Guards at Victoria Barracks wearing a navy coat with epaulettes. The look is markedly different to the McQueen off-the-shoulder gown that the Duchess wore to the BAFTAs on Sunday night - offering a bit more of a ‘message’ to onlookers, as opposed to her red carpet ensemble which seemed to be simply about her having fun with fashion. Today’s look balanced heritage and authority - not to mention that she chose red, rather than navy, for Valentine’s Day.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Luxury shoe brand Aquazzura feted the launch of its second stand-alone store in London last night, and found itself among unusually glamorous male company. Mingling among the Mayfair boutique were suave gents wearing all-black outfits and, notably, glossy gold Aquazzura heels. That’s right, heels. How did the dandies stay upright against the flow of champagne and intrigued females? The Christy Pump, which retails for £455, is just one product of Colombian shoe designer Edgardo Osorio’s  mission to craft a “beautifully simple, sexy shoe that [people] can actually walk in.” The process of creating Aquazzura’s popular Sexy Thing heel, for example, takes up to 12 fit trials under Osorio's supervision, assisted by a technician in his seventies with more than 40 years of podiatric experience. Each heel, Osario told The Telegraph’s Ellie Pithers, is perfectly weighted to distribute pressure evenly across the shoe; there is memory foam in the soles; and the cashmere suede (and the newer nappa leather version) moulds to the foot by the third wearing to ensure maximum comfort. Back to the male revellers, who almost stole the spotlight from Poppy Delevingne, who the party was also in aid of. The fashion plate and full-time socialite has teamed up with the cobbler for a nine-piece collection inspired by her travels and Moroccan wedding (think moons and stars artfully littered on the brand’s signature lace-up flats and heels). Delevingne, whose Resort collection launches in December, has previously said it is the “sense of humour” behind Osorio’s shoes that attracts them. How fitting, then, that the model invited select guests, and the troupe of haute hommes, from the store's opening soirée to a private venue, transformed into a Moroccan Bedouin tent with gold life size palm trees and pineapple installations (Aquazzura’s logo), to carry on the celebrations. Here’s hoping those Christy Pumps passed the dance floor test.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Naomi Campbell might be renowned for her fiercely independent attitude and untouchable glamour but there's a tender back story from the beginnings of her career which offers a fresh view on the Streatham-born supermodel. When, aged 16, Campbell moved alone to work in Paris, Tunisian designer Azzedine Alaia took her under his wing. Their relationship became so close that she called him 'papa'- a sign of affection she still shows to this day.  In a 26-page feature in the new issue of biannual fashion and culture magazine AnOther, Campbell is photographed by Alasdair McLellan and styled by Katy England wearing Alaia's legendarily elegant yet powerfully sensual designs. She stars alongside Iris and Rafferty Law and Kate and Lila Moss in the epic tribute to the designer.  "I will never be part of anyone or anything that's disrespectful to my papa" Campbell tells AnOther magazine editor Susannah Frankel of her enduring loyalty to Alaia. In 2009, Campbell refused to attend the Met Gala because she felt his work did not receive the coverage it deserved in that year's 'The Model as Muse' exhibition.  Campbell- now 46- also recalls her exploits in Paris while living with Alaia. Her tales could be those from any loving, protective father and his daughter- with a few fabulously famous extra characters added in.  “I met him and that was it,” she says in the interview. “He called my mother and told her I had to live with him. He said I shouldn’t be in Paris aged 16 by myself. He said I needed protecting and he was going to take me in.” “I used to sneak out at night to go to Les Bains Douche with Grace Jones and Iman,” Campbell remembers. “I’d have to put my stuff downstairs by the door but the dogs would always start barking when I left so he would wake up and know I wasn’t at home. Then Papa would arrive. He’d get a call and they’d tell him, “Your daughter is here.” So he’d come down and look at me and if I’d put the outfit on wrong he’d fix it and then say, ‘Now you’re going home!’ I’d say, ‘No! Please Papa, can I stay?’ Even the chance to see a music icon perform didn't avert Alaia from his paternal insitincts. "I remember one time Prince was going to come and play live," Campbell tells AnOther, "but he was like, ‘No. Home.'" On another occasion, Campbell recalls, she fell down the stairs. “We had no ice in the house. We’d run out. But we had a frozen leg of lamb. I remember he put that on my head. Papa, if it was his last egg, his last piece of bread, he’d give it to you. To me he is family in every sense of the word.” Alaia was also on hand to offer reassurance and encouragement to Campbell in the early years of career when she was perhaps not equipped with the confidence she has today. "For years he told me, don't wear too much make-up, you don't need make up" she says. "Now finally I don't wear so much but back then it was a security blanket." Alaia's determination to instill confidence and independence in a young Campbell can be traced back to the designer's own singular way of doing things. He is almost unique in the fashion industry for not conforming to the standards show dates, instead preferring to show a new collection as and when he's ready- and any shop that orders his designs will have to wait until he's satisfied they're ready for customers to buy before he delivers them.  “I live with the climate. I am like fruit. When I’m ready, I’m ready, There are no rules, it’s a way of life” Alaia says to AnOther by way of explanation for setting his own timetable.   AnOther's latest issue will go on sale on Thursday 15th September   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge is not usually one to be relied on for experimenting with the latest trends, mostly sticking to her failsafe favourites of elegant coats, pretty dresses, nude heels and breton tops. For tonight's Sports Aid 40th anniversary dinner however, the Duchess experimented with one of spring/ summer's trickier themes- the 'cold shoulder'. Kate chose a sleek royal blue (how appropriate) column gown by Roland Mouret for the occassion which she hosted at Kensington Palace. With cut-out scoops at the top of the arms and thick shoulder straps, the dress offered the subtle flash of shoulder skin which is very 2016. It's a trend which was born on the catwalks, thanks to the likes of Givenchy, Erdem and Chloe but which has been widely taken up on the high street with shops from Zara to Marks and Spencer offering their take on the look. It wasn't just the cut-out shoulder detail which showed that Kate might have been reading her Vogue- she was on the cover of the most recent issue after all. She accessorised the dress with a pair of chunky gold hoop earrings which bore some resemblance to a pair recently worn by Rihanna- who'd have thought it? Another modern touch came via the chunky exposed silver zip which ran right down the back of the dress. The Duchess kept her accessories faithfully classic though with black strappy sandals and a simple matching clutch. As part of the evening, the Duchess also delivered a short speech giving her support to the Sports Aid athletes who are hoping to compete at the Rio Olympics in August. The Duchess on @TeamSportsAid : "I am immensely proud to be their Patron and I can't wait to cheer on our team competing in Rio." While the Duchess often opts for specially-commisioned outfits, this piece by British designer Mouret- who shows his collections at Paris fashion week- is still available to buy on luxury site MyTheresa with a price tag of £2095 and in the sale for £1,255 on Mouret's own website Harrods also have a blush version priced at £2099. Mouret shot to fame in 2005 when he created the 'Galaxy' dress, an ultra-flattering, figure-skimming midi length style which proved an instant with celebrities from Jennifer Aniston to Cameron Diaz and Dita von Teese- in fact, if there was a dress which summed up the late noughties, the 'Galaxy' would be it. Mouret quickly became a favorite of Victoria Beckham and her first collection of dresses was widely reported to have been inspired by him- she even employed his pattern cutter to ensure her designs had the same effect.  This isn't the first time that the Duchess of Cambridge has looked to Mouret for a glamorous evening gown either. She has twice worn a floor-skimming cream dress with a split to the thigh by the designer; first for a dinner at Claridges in 2012 and again for the premiere of 'Mandela' in December 2013.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Alaia Baldwin is the latest member of the Baldwin acting dynasty to make it as a model. She follows in younger sister Hailey and cousin Ireland’s footsteps as the latest signing at State Models, a newly-founded talent pool that was established during New York Fashion Week. The daughter of Stephen Baldwin - the youngest of the four Baldwin brothers - and Kennya Baldwin, a Brazilian graphic designer, 21-year-old Alaia is the third girl from the genetically-blessed family to be snapped up by an agency. The Kardashians had better watch their thrones as the Baldwins are hot on their heels. Younger sister Hailey, 18, has already been welcomed by the fashion industry, walking the runway for Tommy Hilfiger and Philipp Plein just a few weeks ago at New York and Milan fashion weeks. She has also been the face of Topshop for spring 2015 (a role she handed over to her model buddy Gigi Hadid for autumn). Meanwhile, her cousin Ireland, 19, has been making her own headlines. The daughter of Kim Basinger and Alec Baldwin (the oldest Baldwin brother) has been shot for W Magazine, Elle, and Vanity Fair and appeared at New York Fashion Week for Son Jung Wan SS16. Alaia, 21, is yet another celebrity daughter to strike it lucky as a model, the latest in a wave of celebrity family signings including her sister’s model squad Gigi and Bella Hadid and Kendall Jenner of Kardashian fame. The Baldwin girls’ good looks clearly run in the family as their uncle Billy was a Calvin Klein model back in 1986. With a fashionable name like Alaia after the great Azzedine - there’s no wonder that this latest Baldwin babe has been called up for model duty.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Coldplay's latest music video for 'Hymm for the Weekend,' starring Beyonce, was released on Friday afternoon and has already had 15 million views on YouTube. Numbers that are arguably more One Direction than Coldplay. The video was filmed in Mumbai, with scenes shot on location at the Holi Festival, and has sparked a debate about cultural appropriation, largely because Beyonce plays a Bollywood star and wears traditional Indian dress. Small independent New York-based designer Laurel DeWitt has found herself in the centre of it, as she created the elaborate floral crown that Beyonce wears in the video.  So how did a relatively unknown designer end up in one of the most talked about Beyonce videos to date? Laurel tells The Telegraph: “Her stylist Zerina Akers reached out to me and needed some crowns for Beyonce. I am a little designer in New York and in the independent fashion scene am known for my crowns and headdresses. It’s her job to know people like me.” via GIPHY This is a Beyonce project, so it was obviously a tell-no-one top secret operation. You don’t even know you’re working on a Beyonce video when you are working on a Beyonce video: "Her stylist worked with me and told me she was looking for Indian vibes, very regal and colourful. At the time I didn't know what it was for. "I didn't know it was for a video or for Coldplay. It came out maybe a few weeks after they filmed it back in November, so I've been waiting patiently!" Most designers working on a bespoke Beyonce piece would have an entire team dedicated to Beyonce's look, but Lauren worked on the piece for a month all by herself. Laurel tells The Telegraph: "This crown was custom for her [Beyonce], with a metal structure underneath and floral applications. All the flowers [25 or so] are hand cut with metal and there are multiple layers on each flower." So how does she make the flowers from metal? "They are raw sheets of metal which I cut and form with my hands. I then ink the metal, with this special ink, and hand-painted every single piece. I'm literally bleeding when I make it." The crown may be made of 100% metal, but it’s not as heavy as you might think, as she used lightweight aluminium, brass and steel: “It’s actually really light because Beyonce needed to move in it.” And hand-crafted metal flowers don’t come cheap, as Laurel reveals that her smaller crowns start at $5,000 and Beyonce’s would have cost approximately $15k. via GIPHY Laurel explains: “It's one of a kind. You can't find anything else like that in the world. There is only one of each crown and each layer of the flowers is inked and coloured by hand. It's a lot of work.” Laurel’s entire business model is based on creating custom pieces for celebrities, and judging by her last commission her plan to dress stars is working. She explains: “I did the chain top in the Nicki Minaj Anacondo video, Gaga has commissioned me and Amber Rose wore a dress for the VMAs and walked in my fashion show. That's who my market is. I'm a small independent company, with very limited resources. My theory behind it was to create spectacular one of a kind pieces that become so exclusive and can't be found anywhere else, so that the stylists come to me.” Speaking of how she plans to expand her label, she says: “My background in fashion is doing handbags for Kenneth Cole, Juicy Couture, Target. So eventually when I do have the resources to produce a line worldwide, I'll have a brand built up with A List people wearing it and can then take elements from that into a mass produced line.” Everything (and we mean everything) in Laurel’s collection is made of metal, including capes, gowns, bow ties and t shirts. “The crowns are not the most comfortable, but a lot of my other pieces are wearable. They are heavier than normal garments, but are still light as I’ll use aluminium or other lighter metals.” She comes from an arts background, and has had her crowns displayed in galleries and museums. She tells The Telegraph: “I was asked to do a presentation at the Smithsonian Institute of African Arts in the Egyptian wing, so I made an Egyptian headdress. "That was my first crown. I had no idea what I was doing, and then every season I tried to make bigger and better crowns and crowns became a signature of mine.  "I went to Pratt, a really good art school in Brooklyn, and I'm an artist before I'm a fashion designer so for me they are art pieces." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  President Donald Trump’s campaign manager Kellyanne Conway was clearly keen to stand out at today’s inauguration ceremony - however her outfit has possibly attracted the world’s attention for all the wrong reasons. Her military-style paneled coat (which certainly is red, white and blue, through and through) set social media alight, with critics quick to create memes after Conway called her attire “Trump revolutionary wear.” No doubt Conway had hoped that the coat's colourway would play into the top lines of Trump’s first speech as President - putting America and its businesses first.  But many have been quick to point out the fashion failings of her style statement, in that her £2,030 wool coat is by Italian label Gucci, and its designer, Alessandro Michele, was inspired by the city of London, when he debuted it in his resort 2017 catwalk show at Westminster Abbey. On the catwalk, the coat was teamed with a sapphire fedora and embroidered satchel. But worn with an outstanding scarlet hat, matching gloves and a red handbag, Twitter users compared Conway’s look to Paddington Bear’s and suggested that its Napoleonic-era vibes were reminiscent of historical costume. Today also happens to be Conway’s 50th birthday, causing tweeters to speculate that she may burst into song in her jubilant attire, or even lead a marching band. Named Donald Trump's campaign manager back in August 2016, Conway was the first woman to ever run a Republican presidential campaign. The mother-of-four has been a dedicated member of the Republican party for thirty years and has been a long-running adviser for candidates who want to appeal to female voters. Educated at Trinity College in Washington, as well as at Oxford, she co-authored a book in 2005 called What Women Really Want: How American Women Are Quietly Erasing Political, Racial, Class, and Religious Lines to Change the Way We Live. A former pageant-winner, Conway’s personal style seems to have always been fun and shouty; Republican red has long been her go-to colour, often layered with decadent metallics or shearling coats. At the events leading up to the inauguration, she’s opted for one-shoulder gowns as her signature silhouette; wearing a white knee-length dress at the Chairman's Global Dinner on 17th January, and a red fluted-hem number, accessorised with stylish earcuffs, at the Candlelight Dinner on the eve of Donald Trump's Inauguration.  What she will choose to wear at tonight’s main event remains to be seen, but one thing’s for sure; Kellyanne Conway is unlikely to be the one sneaking in through the back, in a demure little black dress.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When the doors open to Kensington Palace’s ‘Princess Diana: Her Fashion Story’ exhibition next February, those lining up to peruse the collection on display will no doubt range from Hackney hipsters too young to remember her when she was alive to Home Counties ladies who grew up with 'Lady Di' as their fashion barometer. Because while it might be almost twenty years since the Princess of Wales died, her inimitable style is as popular and obsessed-over as ever. As a public figure who embodied glamour, intrigue, duty and mystery, Diana's wardrobe was one of her most powerful tools of communication. Her outfits for foreign tours were always carefully diplomatic; in Japan in 1986 she carefully chose a red polka dot dress to represent the country’s rising sun motif; in Pakistan she wore green, a customary colour of respect. But it was in her choice of evening wear when she really let go and so enjoyed some of her most memorable fashion moments. After dark the designer dresses she wore were often laced with attitude and often not-so-subtle messaging. She could have invented the word statement dressing with her black off-shoulder cocktail dress by Christina Stambolian which she wore to the Serpentine on the night that Prince Charles admitted to his infidelity in 1994. Then there were her playful off-duty looks which included jazzy jumpers for polo matches and American football-style bomber jacket for days out with William and Harry. It’s little wonder Diana came to epitomise late 20th century fashion and was strategic in using it to her advantage. "She was always very thoughtful about how her clothes would be interpreted, it was something that really mattered to her," remembers Anna Harvey, Vogue’s former deputy editor who helped the Princess to craft her image after they bumped into one another in the corridors of Vogue. Diana was looking for help after a royal blue suit she chose for her engagement announcement had been given a lukewarm reception. "She was aware of her position and the fact she was representing Great Britain. She was always very clever when it came to flattering people’, says Harvey. "We all remember her as an elegant beautiful woman who loved fashion. It would be no different now I am sure. She would be an example to us all with what she wore and how she wore it." The new retrospective announced last week is not the first of its kind- in 2007, Kensington Palace hosted 'Diana: A Princess Remembered' and the current 'Fashion Rules' exhibit includes some of Diana's clothes-  but it will be one of the biggest ever. Among the 26 outfits on display will be iconic items, like the navy blue Victor Edelstein gown which Diana famously wore to dance with John Travolta at The White House in 1985, through to less well-known items such as an Emanuel Couture check dress which was worn on a trip to Venice, also in 1985. Purchased by Historic Royal Palaces at an auction earlier this year, that dress is a neat example of the complex job which faces anyone trying to piece together a true retrospective of the way Diana dressed. It was bought in a posh second shop having been taken there by Susan Barrantes, the mother of Sarah Ferguson who was dropping off a pile of unwanted clothes belonging to her daughter and Diana. There is no definitive archive of the Princess’s vast wardrobe, instead it is a kind of diaspora, spread across the world after being dispatched to friends and charity shops or sold at various auctions over the years. The new exhibition will include items already owned by the palace as well as pieces loaned from Chile's Museo de la Moda (which began its collection at the Christie's 1997 sale), collectors in the US and more. One place where you will find a definitive deep-dive into Diana’s style though is on Instagram, the social media platform where fashion-loving millennials love to share nostalgic shots of the Princess. The account ‘Princess Diana Forever’ has amassed 130,000 followers with its constant stream of images. Recent posts have included a coy-looking Diana in retro Seventies ski wear on the slopes during her time at Swiss finishing school, a starkly fresh portrait taken by fashion photographer Mario Testino in 1997 in which she wears a one-shouldered sparkling white dress by Japanese designer Hachi and a quintessentially Eighties snap of the Princess in a frou-frou silk taffeta gown by Catherine Walker. The account is followed by those who might be too young to distinctly remember Diana from when she was alive, but who are enamoured by the fashion legacy she left. "There's a certain generation that will never forget her and she will always be their ultimate Princess, while people in their 20s are aware of her but perhaps don't know quite so much about her,"  says Harvey. Unlike many other women who are held up as style icons, there is not a single item or look which sums up Diana, but a plethora of moments and details; the luxe continental combination of blazers and denim which she turned to post-divorce could not be more different to the flimsy floral dresses which defined her early years, yet she made both her own. Diana’s effect on fashion was instant. As early as 1983, just two years after her marriage to Prince Charles, she was credited with helping to create a ‘jobs boom’ in Ireland where workers were ‘flat out’ trying to meet demand for Clarks’ ‘Princess Di’ shoes. The term Sloane Ranger wouldn’t have become so memorable without Diana as its poster girl; she appeared on the cover of The Official Sloane Ranger Handbook in pearls and ruffled blouses which quickly became must-haves. Later, Diana made household names of Parisian couturiers like Ungaro and homegrown designers such as Catherine Walker, always balancing patriotism with the allure of glamour. It is this eclectic style and enduring appeal that recently prompted the collaboration between fashion retailer ASOS and Sharmadean Reid, the founder of the interminably trendy WAH nails, on a collection in tribute to Diana’s looks, reimagining everything from the little black dresses she favoured for less formal evening events to the cycling shorts and sweatshirts which she wore to her gym at  the Chelsea Harbour Club. "Princess Diana stood for a lot of the things that girls feel are important,” says Reid. “You often saw her out jogging or picking her kids up from school. Ultimately, I think Diana was the epitome of the modern woman, she could wear uptown and downtown style and always looked amazing." Those who followed Diana’s fashion evolution in ‘real-time’ remain as captivated by her as ever. “I’ve been fascinated with her style since she wore the ruffle-neck blouses in the 80s. She was daring, fun, smart and posh,” says Stacey Duguid, acting executive fashion editor at Porter magazine. “I kept scrapbooks of her as a child – I still have them. To this day I remember how I felt watching her on the TV as she walked down the aisle.” While most Diana fans suffice with old photos, Duguid had a real-life encounter with the Princess. “I served her when I worked in Harvey Nichols in 1995. She was a size 10 on top and a size 8 on the bottom, and was super tall. I remember handing her a mid-blue Cheap n’ Chic Moschino suit. She pulled on the jacket, cropped with a small peplum, and the skirt was pencil, fitted, ending just above the knee. It was my most memorable fashion moment, which is saying something considering I’ve worked in fashion for 20 years.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  On a dour morning in Central London to discuss serious matters – mental health and suicide in young men – the Duchess of Cambridge brightened up proceedings by donning one of the many bright coats which she has collected since becoming a member of the royal family in 2011. Today she sported a vivid green, knee-length style by London-based designer Erdem, a style she debuted in 2014 on a trip to New Zealand - and also wore to watch the Tour de France in Harrogate in that same year.   On it's latest appearance the zip-up coat ensured that the Duchess was easily noticeable against the sombre backdrop of the hospital - a winning method that she has employed for several public engagements, with the exception of a memorial or military service for which black best befits. Even when she was pregnant with Princess Charlotte, the Duchess didn't veer away from colour, wearing a bright pink Mulberry coat for one of her last appearances before giving birth.  But mother-of-two Kate, 34, can’t claim this trick as her own. It’s a tactic employed by HM the Queen, and a canny one at that. “She may subconsciously be following the Queen’s style,” explains Ingrid Seward, author of The Queen’s Speech. “The Queen has always worn bright colours so she is visible in a crowd. She knows block colours are more flattering in photographs so frequently wears a patterned silk dress underneath a bright block-coloured coat. Material from the dress is often used to trim the hat in some way or other.” Whilst Kate hasn't gone as far as matching her the fabric on her hat to her coat, the Duchess did indeed wear a swallow-print dress costing £60 by Jonathan Saunders for Debenhams (bought way back in 2012) under her bright designer coat. “Kate’s colour co-ordinated look is not cutting edge fashion, but looks smart and good in photographs," says Seward.  And whilst the Queen gets her clothes custom-made rather than popping out to Debenhams, the Duchess's latest outfit choice shows the pair share another trait: re-wearing their investment pieces. Kate has purchased flamboyantly-coloured coats from luxury British brands such as Alexander McQueen, Mulberry and Emilia Wickstead for public engagements, which she wears on rotation. Jane Eastoe, author of Elizabeth, Reigning in Style says of the Queen's rewearing: "The Queen supports the old-school approach of investing in clothing that lasts; disposable fashion is not for her. She returns clothes to her couturiers for alterations and will ask for a new dress to be made to go under a favourite coat to extend its lifespan. Only on foreign tours are new pieces of clothing guaranteed as it would be considered undiplomatic to recycle garments previously seen elsewhere." In 2012, Angela Kelly, the Queen’s dressmaker, revealed that she keeps a log of every single outfit worn by the Queen, capturing every detail from the jewellery right through to the event, so that ensembles can be rotated accordingly. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
