 After last year's #Neonat90 fashion moment- when The Queen singlehandedly caused sales of neon products to rise 137% by wearing a gloriously bright outfits which confirmed that age really should be no barrier when it comes to making bold style choices- Her Majesty opted for a rather different message with her choice for this year's Trooping the Colour parade. Proving her ability to judge the nation's mood perfectly, Her Majesty moved away from the unashamedly statement making look of last year's parade, choosing a pale blue jacquard silk duster coat with matching shift dress by Stewart Parvin, with the Guards brooch pinned to her left shoulder. As always, Her Majesty was not without a hat as her finishing touch, adding a bow embellished matching pale blue design by Phillip Somerville, one of her favoured and longest serving milliners who created hats for The Queen from the early 1980s until his death in 2014. Reflecting the message which she released ahead of her birthday parade acknowledging the nation's somber mood in light of the recent terror attacks and Grenfell Tower fire , The Queen's choice of outfit struck a calm, subdued note.  But there was another element of Her Majesty's choice of outfit which made it utterly suited to the more solemn approach to this year's celebration: she first wore it  in Malta in 2005, making it 12 years old. By recycling her outfit instead of wearing something new, The Queen demonstrated sensitivity to recent events.  With a vast wardrobe of bright dresses, coats and hats to cater for the hundreds of public engagements which she carries out each year, The Queen- like other members of the royal family- tends to switch between new items, usually created for her by Stewart Parvin or Angela Kelly, her personal dresser and pieces she has worn before.  According to an interview which Parvin gave to The Sunday Times in 2012, there is a spreadsheet where the date and event which each outfit has been worn is recorded. After debuting today's look in 2005, The Queen did not wear it again until Ladies' Day at Royal Ascot in 2008. Parvin also explained that The Queen's preference for block colour is because they ‘elongate her; she’s only very tiny’ and that she chooses dresses thanks to their streamlined, unfussy look.  ‘There is always someone there photographing her. So when she gets out of a car, she can’t pull her skirt up, tuck her shirt in, tighten her things; she gets out and she’s ready,’ Parvin explained.  At the height of his work for The Queen, Phillip Somerville was creating 40 to 50 hats each year for her. “People say, 'What does she do with all those hats?’ Wear them out, I say. They get damaged and they wear out. She’d possibly wear hats at least 10 times, and that’s a long time. Most people would only buy a hat and wear it once and then they put it away in a box,” he once said. A note written to Somerville by The Queen in 2007 emphasises not only the close bond which she shared with the milliner but also a touching recognition of the unique position which she holds.  "Thank you for your letter telling me the outcomes of your business. I am very glad to hear you will still be able to work for me," she wrote. "I know how difficult business can be nowadays – specially with matching fabrics for someone like me, who must be almost the only person who wears hats constantly!" Although twelve years might seem like a long time to keep an outfit, The Queen by no means holds the royal family's record. That accolade goes to Princess Anne who in 2015 wore a mustard yellow coat and patterned dress which she had first worn to Trooping the Colour in 1980, making the look 25 years old.          © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It's the height of August holiday season, and Instagram is full of bikini selfies- most of them showing 'perfect' tanned, toned bodies and taken in luxury Grecian hotels or on sparkling Mediterranean beaches. Winnie Harlow joined the trend last night, posting an image which shows her almost naked, save for a beige thong. But unlike many of the other swimwear portraits currently doing the rounds on social media, Harlow's came with a determinedly body positive message.  The model, who was diagnosed with the skin condition vitiligo aged four, wrote: "the real difference isn't my skin. It's the fact that I don't find my beauty in the opinions of others. I'm beautiful because I know it. Celebrate Your unique beauty today (& everyday)!" The image is the latest example of Harlow's campaign to inspire women to feel good about themselves, no matter what obstacles they may face. "You are not just beautiful on the outside. Your attitude towards yourself is so inspiring ," wrote one follower in response to the image. "Keep shining that beautiful positive light." Another added: "So incredible to see @winnieharlow! Your skin is so beautiful and so are you for sharing to the world with such positivity. Love it!" Harlow had her big break in modelling in 2014 when she appeared on America's Next Top Model. Since then, she has become one of the best-known names in the industry, walking in shows for Ashish, Coach and Marc Jacobs as well as becoming a front row and fashion party fixture and appearing in Beyonce's visual album, Lemonade.   "My modelling career is about hard work," Harlow told The Telegraph last year. "There are a lot of people that would say my skin is what made my career, but my skin condition is not something new. It’s not like I was the first person to have it, it’s not new, so to be able to break boundaries with something that for years people have said is ugly, or something that should hold you back, it’s mainly hard work that gets you to where you want to be regardless of the boundaries that you're faced with." Harlow is part of a wider movement to counteract 'perfect' bikini shots with more realistic representations of women. Model Iskra Lawrence- who champions non-sample size figures- also posted a video yesterday which shows her dancing in a bikini, one of several she has shared recently. Her caption included the message: "maybe if we stopped picking each other's bodies apart we wouldn't have so many body image issues." Meanwhile, former British Vogue editor Alexandra Shulman was praised by hundreds of her followers last week when she shared a mirror selfie in which she was wearing only a bikini. Having encouraged designers to move away from creating tiny samples and featuring 'real' women during her Vogue tenure, the image was interpreted as a powerful statement by Shulman of a renewed determination to normalise different body shapes now that she is a free agent, even if she did nonchalantly caption the image 'Time for the boat trip'. "Brave" and "inspirational" were some of the most common adjectives used in response.  Whether there will ever be a day when sharing a selfie of a less than 'perfect' body is seen as a matter of normality remains to be seen, but until then plenty of women and girls will take heart from the bold gestures of Harlow et al.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge are on a two-day tour of Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, but today had to reschedule their visit to the islands because of heavy fog. Instead, the couple visited the Eden Project, where the Duchess made a surprising departure from her usual casual style, and swapped her signature Breton top and skinny jeans for a pair of jazzy printed trousers in a skinny fit and cropped above the ankle. The blue and white printed trousers are from Gap, and are currently available in the sale for a purse-friendly £21.99. The mid-rise skinny cotton trousers are a tricky style to pull off, and are at first glance reminiscent of the patterned pedal pushers that were popular in the Nineties. The Duchess balanced her statement trousers with her old-favourite conservative pieces, wearing her nude L K Bennett wedges, a navy fitted blazer by Canadian brand Smythe and a simple cream top. Although the Duchess's visit was a last-minute change to the schedule, her habit for dressing in literal tribute to the topic of her visits still came into play with the vibrant print complementing the tropical indoor rainforest at the Eden Project. The Duchess of Cambridge might regularly lean on designers including Alexander McQueen, Erdem and Jenny Packham, but her wardrobe is filled with just as many affordable, high street labels.  The Gap website reveals that the trousers were made by women who are part of Gap's PACE educational programme. The project, running since 2007, provides courses and support for women working in Gap factories, to open more opportunities to them.  Considering that every detail of the Duchess of Cambridge's outfits is carefully planned, it is likely she will have been aware of the origins of her trousers.  They could be her way of supporting an initiative to make high street manufacturing more ethical and sustainable.  When it comes to high street sweeps, the Duchess of Cambridge usually turns to British store L K Bennett, but she does own a number of pieces by Gap, an American retailer. Ahead of her royal tour of Australia, she was seen shopping in Gap in Kensington where she is believed to have bought classic children's-wear pieces for Prince George.  It’s not often that Vancouver finds itself in the eye of a fashion-storm, but in recent years Lululemon, the active-wear leviathan based there, has been whipping up a storm. This is the brand that dresses half of North America in yoga-inspired clothing. So comfortable are Lululemon’s leggings, drapy tops and hooded sweatshirts and so desirable is a yoga‑rooted, clean-eating lifestyle, that people wear Lululemon all day long. Some find Lululemon’s encroachment into our daily life a breath of much-needed reality. Others – the kind who consider comfort a secondary or tertiary consideration in their style strategy – are horrified. They might need to get over that. Last year Lululemon arrived in the UK. World domination is assured. But before that happens, Vancouver has another offering – one that promises comfort (the engine driving most innovation in fashion today) that’s on a level with that offered by Lululemon’s trackie bottoms, with considerably more finesse. The shared aesthetic is no accident. Kit & Ace – which has opened three stores in London in as many months, including a flagship (albeit pop-up) on Regent’s Street – is the brainchild of Shannon Wilson (above), who designed at Lululemon and is married to its co‑founder, Chip Wilson. Kit & Ace’s unique proposition is its Technical Cashmere™, a blend of cotton, Modal or wool with 6-8 per cent cashmere and a few other ingredients that make its T‑shirts and ribbed knits soft and cosy, but, perhaps just as importantly, machine washable and, unless otherwise specified, tumble-dry-able.  Part fashion, part technical, it’s an offering that takes the way many people already dress and makes it a little sleeker and more luxurious. Stretchy knitted dresses, cashmere-mix vests and fleecy bombers are designed to be layered. Some can be reversed or flipped upside down to make shorter versions. Most won’t crease, none of it should bag, and the pure cashmere pieces are guaranteed not to pill. Some of it is even waterproof. “Honestly, the invention of Technical Cashmere is one of the most exciting things I’ve ever been part of,” she says. “It has this luxurious handle which means we could meld European styling with a West Coast, laid‑back vibe.”  While Lululemon is about being active, Kit & Ace “is about being on the move. Most people don’t have much time to keep getting changed through the day.” Since the Wilsons have five children between them, she knows of which she speaks.  The label’s growing at a rapid pace – and there appears to be no shortage of money to invest in its evolution. Wilson recently hired a fabric scientist – Kit & Ace has five “proprietary” (like patented) fabrics so far. “For me, design always begins with the fabric,” she says. This is the way fashion’s going. “When I began at Lululemon in 1999, we said wouldn’t it be great if we could design exercisewear that people could wear to the office. Everyone thought we were crazy.”  Now she wants Kit & Ace to take people from the office to evening, off a plane or the school run and into a meeting. She doesn’t see why comfort means surrendering style. “After all, if you’re not comfortable, it’s hard to feel elegant.”  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The generally agreed etiquette when interviewing celebrities with, some – how shall we say - history, is that you go in gently. Start perhaps with a little fluffy questioning about whatever new product, religion or diet they’re currently plugging, in the hope that if you show sufficient good will, they’ll relax and open up about themselves.   No one, however, seems to have sent this particular memo to Tara Palmer-Tomkinson, who veers so far off plug during our interview, that at various points I feel honour-bound to wrest the conversation round to Desiderata – the label of Oxford shirt-cum-bodies (or kubbis) which she recently launched. But she’s not ready to talk about cuffs and snap fastenings yet. Three minutes into our meeting, she is demonstrating etiquette of another nature. I think it’s how to get out of a Lamborghini without flashing your knickers (clamp knees together at every swivel), but since she is simultaneously telling me about the oral sex lessons she received from a celebrated Madame, it’s not unambiguously clear. Nor is it certain whether she learned these valuable life skills while at one of her finishing schools or later. The discreet staff in Blakes Hotel take all this in their stride. The restaurant is practically empty, although it is mid-lunch time. They won’t be making much from TPT either, who has one banana milk throughout, while a good natured make-up artist, who has worked with Tara “for ever”, and I have tea and water. I don’t get the chance to ask whether this is her normal sustenance. Suffice to know that, tightly held in by one of her kubbis and an old Alexander McQueen tweed skirt, she’s as strikingly slender and nut-brown as the “notorious” It Girl who dominated all those column inches in the 1990s. Back then it seemed that Tara was omnipresent. Daughter of Patti (an Anglo-Argentine–Brazillian beauty) and Charles Palmer -Tomkinson (former Olympic skier) and sister to the virtuous Santa, who under her married name of Sebag Montefiore went on to become a successful novelist. She starred in Walker’s Crisps ads, on Tatler covers, attended openings great and small and was a runner-up on I’m a Celebrity. Yah! the title of her weekly column in The Sunday Times (ghost written by Wendy Holden, who cited PT as a major inspiration for a subsequent string of best selling social satires) was a literary landmark of sorts, pre-empting an era clogged with celebrity endeavours. Her partying days are far behind her. Her appearance at the Royal Wedding in 2010 (the Palmer-Tomkinsons are close friends of Prince Charles’s) was the first most of us had seen of her for years.  “I designed that dress you know. It looks quite simple, but underneath it was like Piccadilly Circus.” The style police were generally approving of the theatrically lady-like royal blue structure, which pleased her. Not that she cares about the press, you understand, “but you want to make everyone proud”. She resides not far away from Blakes, hermit-like, as she puts in, in a penthouse flat that, until recently, she shared with a squirrel she called Simon. By strange co-incidence, I once, briefly shared a room with a squirrel that wandered in mistakenly from a nearby meadow, and can confirm they are not soothing companions. They are feral flying rats with mass murder on their minds.  PT seems to have been fond of Simon however, commissioning her friend David Linley to design a house for him. “I’m not absolutely confirming or denying that Simon is not still sometimes on the scene,” she says enigmatically.  Except that she’s not enigmatic is she? One of her most endearing, troublesome qualities is that she is, a compulsive sharer, which may be a symptom of her need to people please. It’s all out there, the drink, the drugs but also the vulnerability, the intelligence. She has, she says, been clean for the past twelve or fifteen years. Co-incidentally, twelve or fifteen years ago is when the reclusiveness set in, although the morning we meet, photos of her having lunch at The Ivy with her old friend Duncan James, the dimpled singer from former boy-band Blue, are all over the mailonline.com. She thinks someone from the Ivy tipped them off. “I know you’re thinking, 'well why go to The Ivy then?’ but it wouldn’t make any difference. They’d still be there if I went to MacDonalds. They camp outside my flat. One time when I went out to my car in a bikini”- Hang on, Tara. You knew there were paparazzi outside but you still went out in a bikini? “It was a bikini top and I’d left some flowers in there…” There is an upside to Ivy-gate. “At least I’m not wearing a track-suit. I look quite smart in those photos, don’t I?’’ She does. Although not as smart as today. “The skirt’s good isn’t it, I must have had it twelve years.”  And the Kubbi, Tara, the Kubbi? “I’m the biggest consumer there is. Alaia – I’ve got all of Alaia. But look at this, “she raises an arm to reveal a huge hole in her purple Alaia cardigan. “I only bought it yesterday,” she sighs. “I love clothes and to make an effort… so why does everyone say my nose is awful. Is it so awful?” It’s not awful, I say carefully. But it does erm, show signs of  a life recklessly lived. Given what she’s ingested, I add truthfully, she looks remarkable. Line free, taut.   "Hah that’s true”. So did she have £6000 worth of surgery to rebuild her septum as widely reported? “Nothing! If people said I looked nice every day, I might have been tempted. But my face is really crooked and that’s that. It’s not all from drugs… or maybe I’ve got facial dysmorphia. I’ve been destroyed by the things people have said”.    A part of her always wanted fame. After school, she was scouted by the choreographer Terry Gilbert. “The selection panel had paper bags over their heads and they asked me to be a piece of pasta.” She got in, but it was not a success. “Nearly everyone was Russian so I couldn’t talk to them and I spent most of my time sitting on my own, eating crisps. I was the worst dancer in that school, but I was too afraid to tell my parents I wasn’t good enough”.   The Palmer-Tomkinsons sound a jolly bunch, but they are rather high achieving. Having a daughter famous for being famous may not have sat easily. So fame? Yes and no. “If you really want to know, I was quite pleased, in a way, to be on the mailonline”. But she doesn’t like the long lenses, “not when there’s a man looking at you at the other end of a long, fat thing and you can’t see him.”   So like a millennial Lady of Shallot, she keeps herself more or less occupied within her penthouse. Rising around 10 for a conference call with her “team” and another at 12.  In between, she plays the piano, a bit, and composes music, a bit. She recently went on one of Prince Harry’s skiing trip with injured soldiers, although not to ski with them, which would have made sense, given her ability, but to play her music to them. “I love composing,” she says. She wrote a song when her friend Isabella Blow died. “I’ll sing it if you like… they wouldn’t let me go to her memorial.” she adds sadly, “because they said I’d deliberately stolen the limelight at her funeral. As if…”   Anyway, the Kubbis. Oh yes. At 2pm she meets with her team face to face. It doesn’t sound too onerous. “Oh My God. You have no idea. I’m working to a three-year plan. I really want this to be a success. I didn’t want to use my trust fund, so it’s all money I’ve earned.  I was absolutely determined to take The Tube, so to speak”. So to speak? “I can’t remember whether or not I’ve ever actually taken the Tube”.   By team, she means her PRs, “Results UK or whatever. We’ve been through quite a few”. She doesn’t like the snobbishness of the fashion industry. “When I was a so-called It Girl – and by the way, I didn’t know what that meant at the time – I would be told that this label or that one didn’t want me wearing their clothes, because I wasn’t the right image.  But who knows? Maybe my assistant wasn’t telling me the truth”.  She doesn’t want Desiderata to be one of those snooty labels. “It’s Latin you know. I had a great uncle who used to talk to me in Latin. Amo, amas, amammmm. You know that song, “I’m every woman?” That’s what I want the Kubbi to be – something for someone doing everything, fat, thin, sober, drunk”.   You can tell she’s put a lot into Desiderata. Not just the money and the putative Tube taking. She knew what she wanted from years of “borrowing” her father’s Jermyn Street shirts and, who knew, from a brief stint studying fashion on a City & Guilds course. The cuffs have to be long, to the knuckles, the arms have to be narrow, “you want 70 per cent stretch, and I wanted them all made in Britain… and with every shirt, you don’t just get spare buttons in a nasty little plastic packet but with a needle already threaded…”  She’s warming to her Kubbi theme now. She even tries to sell me one, several times, for a knock down sum. No one in an interview has ever attempted this quite so directly. You have to admire her honesty.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s not often that a fashion designer precedes an interview by sending over a forensically-detailled, 14-slide Power-point presentation crammed with statistics from corporate behemoths, quotes from eminent psychologists and references to behavioural economics. But, then, Nina McLemore is no ordinary fashion designer. A former executive at Liz Claiborne, a company which filled a work-wear niche in the 80s, and founder of a private investment firm, McLemore has made it her business to create clothes- specifically perfectly tailored blazers- which help women to navigate what she calls the 'C-suite’ (that’s high-powered boardroom positions) with style, ease and confidence.  When Hillary Clinton addresses the Democratic Party convention later today, the chances are that she will either be wearing one of McLemore’s go-to-jackets, or one inspired by her style. The self-declared 'pantsuit aficionado' (according to her Twitter biography) has depended on McLemore’s key pieces as she has navigated her way from First Lady to Presidential nominee. From the bold turquoise jacket she wore to meet the South Korean president Lee Myung-Bak whilst secretary of state to the fuschia blazer she’s chosen for frequent TV appearences, Nina McLemore has been lending her sartorial support throughout.  For many of her high achieving fans from Pepsi CEO Indra Nooyi to American senator Elizabeth Warrien, it’s her no-nonsense approach to 'power’ dressing that has won them over. Even when she’s not even wearing McLemore’s label, Clinton stays true to her rules; when she appeared via video link to address the Democrat National Convention on Tuesday, it was in a pink jacket with the signature stand-up collar which McLemore favours ('it projects more confidence’ says McLemore.) The tailored jackets and trouser suits for which she has become famous are all founded on meticulous market research. Every detail is backed up with hard-to-argue-with and very pragmatic reasoning. For example, she rarely makes anything black and encourages her clients to wear bright hues. “Colour can change your attractiveness entirely and how people see you” she explains, “what a woman wants is skin that has a pink touch to it, not grey or yellow which is what black does. I’ve given many talks to law firms accounting firms. I walk in and 70-80% of the people are in black so of course they don’t stand out.” We just put the biggest crack in that glass ceiling yet.” —Hillary https://t.co/mYkaLIv861 The sleeves on McLemore’s jackets are cut to be around an inch longer than a standard sized jacket, but they come with linings in contrasting hues which can be flicked up to the exact right length for the woman wearing it, without her having to faff around with getting it tailored. The trick also lets them emulate the roll-up of shirt cuffs trick which has become a sartorial signaling favourite of male politicians in recent years. McLemore will never create a blazer with a power shoulder (too unflattering) and keeps the silhouette neat but allows plenty of room around the back and arms for ease of movement and gesturing. Anything else? “A jacket that’s buttoned is more slimming than jackets that aren’t.”  “Essentially, it’s all about the image that you’re portraying both to yourself internally and externally, it’s not just about how other people see you but also how you see yourself,” she explains, adding “there’s also an impact on your cognitive ability - so the research is showing that how you dress has a definite effect.” McLemore says this kind of prescriptive styling is a response to the uniform way of dressing which men have adopted in the workplace for years. “There is no uniform for women and our bodies have more places with shape than men” she observes, noting that women also have more interesting tools in their arsenal to play with; “We can change things with hair, make-up and shoes. The first message that women need to learn at a young age is that if they’re serious about their careers they need to dress a certain way. The fashion industry has adopted this very sexually provocative image so if you look at clothes in retail it’s very hard to find clothes that are projecting a powerful confident image.” There is constant bemoaning of the fact that high-profile women are more closely-scrutinised than men, but that, says McLemore, should be seen as an opportunity. “One of the things that I have noticed about the women who are chief executive officers or in high positions is that they are strong people and able to deal with really difficult challenges. They can be tough when they need to be tough but when there’s tension in the room they can deflate it with a sense of humour. It means the clothes you wear also can send that message of 'I’m a positive person’ – which is much more challenging for men in grey suits to project, short of resorting to a novelty tie.   And what of her most famous client? “As far as Hilary is concerned, the general consensus is that fashion is not her strength” McLemore says. “One of the challenges she has is that she does not photograph well. In  person she’s much more slim and much more attractive than she is on camera, so I think that she probably needs to think about clothes that make her look slimmer. But also clothes that appeal to a younger audience, because she is not particularly winning over huge numbers of young women.” With such conflicting campaign trail pressures, it’s little wonder that the cheerful appeal of tailoring with scientific levels of fit has become Hillary’s signature. McLemore’s rules mean that she can at least count on her clothes to make her feel confident and powerful. And, as she prepares to face Trump – a powerful armour will be everything. “The colour that looks good on everybody is blue, particularly if it has a touch of red in it. It’s the number one for getting a positive response from both men and women. Turquoise is flattering for everyone then coral and red. I don’t recommend pink unless it’s a magenta because it’s not flattering for most people- but green is also great.” “There’s a song that’s become extremely popular in the US from a new musical Hamilton, called “The Room Where It Happens.” Women from a very early stage in their careers need to think about dressing to succeed. Dressing in a way that the people in power see you as someone who is serious about her career and wants to be sitting at that top table.”  “The jacket is critically important because if you’re sitting at the table or if you walked into a room full of people, it’s what people see. Find one that fits well and is made of good material- it can be the one thing that just pulls everything together.”  Like Hillary and her beloved pantsuits, McLemore advises that getting dressed is much easier if you have a formula which you know will work. “Having a style which is yours makes it easier to get dressed in the morning. Figure out what looks good on you, what’s flattering on you and be consistent.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  For the inside scoop on what happened at last night’s Golden Globes, look not to the red carpet, but to the social channels of Hollywood.  In recent years, the idea of the democratisation of fashion has been knocked around by the industry as a thrilling sort of buzz phrase. Now that we have Instagram and live streaming everyone has a ticket to fashion week. Now that every department store from Bristol to Bali stocks Gucci, Prada, Burberry and any other European luxury label you can think of, this world of supreme luxury is for everyone (with a credit card).  And yet, in spite of this voracious international expansion, the store openings, the vexation over the Chinese market, the globe-trotting fashion super-shows, at its core there is an inconvenient and unpleasant truth: fashion is as racially un-diverse as it ever was. In 2013, Naomi Campbell, Bethann Hardison and Iman set up Balance Diversity, an initiative to highlight the lack of models of colour on the international catwalks, which keeps a tally of the level of diversity in the casting of fashion shows. In her speech at 2014’s CFDA awards, where she presented Hardison (a veteran model and model agent) with the prestigious Founders award, Campbell described their initiative gracefully, “It’s not a fight, it’s a conversation. It’s about making people aware in a civil way” she explained. But two years later, the numbers of ethnically diverse models being cast in fashion shows remain pitifully low. Having just sat through a month of fashion shows, if I noted a designer featuring three models of ethnicities beyond white Caucasian in a single show it seemed progressive. The Fashion Spot has just released its figures on the season, finding that less than 25 per cent of models who walked at New York, London, Milan and Paris fashion weeks were models of colour. This is a marginal increase on last season’s figures. Although over-all, London as a fashion city was less diverse in terms of casting than last September. New York, where Kanye West presented an entirely non-white cast for his Yeezy show, and Zac Posen cast a non-white majority in his, was the most diverse (with an overall percentage of 31.9 per cent models of colour cast). Last year, the South Sudanese model Nykhor Paul lamented on her Instagram account the poor preparation and skills from backstage make-up artists, saying “Why do I have to bring my own makeup to a professional show when all the other white girls don't have to do anything but show up?” Something Jourdan Dunn has also previously flagged up. This season, when faced with a make-up station of pale shaded foundations, the British model Leomie Anderson raised the same issue, posting a picture of her ‘black model survival kit’ on her blog and writing that “Being a black model can be hard when it comes to makeup during fashion week as not all makeup artists really know how to enhance our features or sometimes pick the incorrect colour which leaves us with ashy runway pictures! I now bring with me my own concealer, foundation, powder and brush and correct my make-up in the toilets. I don’t want to offend the artist who does my make-up but at the end of the day I want to look my best down the runway.” At the two most talked about labels, Balenciaga and Vêtements, both designed by Demna Gvasalia and styled by Lotta Volkova (described by vogue.com as ‘basically the coolest stylist in the industry right now’), the entire cast of both shows were white. The casting itself a mixture of ‘actual’ and street cast models (as well as some of their friends and Volkova herself, who opened the Vêtements show in an appropriation of a monk’s habit into a mini dress) had a clear provocation behind it – exalted by some fashion people as revolutionary. Which makes the fact that there was not a single woman (or man) that wasn’t white all the more jarring. What provocation is this? What street were they casting from? Given that all eyes of the industry were on these shows, that they have international stockists and intentions, it would be perhaps more refreshing if that was reflected rather than merely their Eastern Bloc roots. I asked a model agent friend, who has spent her career working at big name agencies, off the record for her experiences of racism in the industry. She reeled off a depressing monologue of examples: “I have experienced occasions when the model agency will have two models of colour on the board and a 'walk in' will come to the agency, looking absolutely amazing, great personality etc only to be turned away because, and I quote, 'we have one that looks like him/her already.’ I have been privy to situations when a model of colour was given a significantly reduced fee for doing the same job as her Caucasian colleague on numerous occasions. I have sat next to a well respected, loved model agent who stated that a black female model was amazing because "you do not get black girls that look like this.” I have had male models of colour almost cry at the prospect of having to go to Milan because of how they are treated.” This white out extends beyond the catwalks. A quick scroll around luxury online stores such as matchesfashion.com, net-a-porter, avenue32.com, mytheresa.com, shopbop.com, harveynichols.com, and it is striking that the women they use as fit models – i.e. the human coat hangers on which the clothing is presented, are overwhelmingly white. The high street online stores fare little better. Exceptions are Finery.com, Asos.com Topshop.com and H&M.com who use a mix of ethnicities in their visual merchandising. But, to return to that dubious idea of the democratisation of fashion: those model voices who speak out at their treatment, those who support the #blackmodelsmatter, those who continue to count and report and note the embarrassing, offensive out of step visual representation of the industry – this is a valuable democracy, and these voices must be heard louder and louder. It is important to report this. It is important to call this out. If fashion wants to be for all, to sell to all, to ram-raid every international market into buying its wares, then frankly the very least it can do is reflect that at its core. Encouragingly, to look at the eight finalists for this year’s LVMH Prize for young design talent is to see a truly diverse future for fashion: the current establishment would do well to learn something from these truly provocative talents. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s all very well owning a drawer full of tangled thongs and scary suspender straps, but what’s the point if the thought of actually wearing any of it fills you with dread? That’s Stephanie Seymour’s school of thought this Valentine’s Day as she launches her new lingerie line, Raven and Sparrow, in the hope of offering women something they will actually enjoy. “I think so much of today's lingerie is made for men,” says the supermodel, 48, of the reason that she wanted to start her own brand. “I wanted this collection to be specifically geared to the female customer. As a consumer I saw a hole in the market; I was looking for garments that were beautiful and alluring, yet had enough coverage to be wearable and comfortable.”   Seymour, of course, has form in the lingerie world, having posed for Vogue as well as being the original Victoria’s Secret Angel, modelling for the all-pink empire in the pre-Kardashian days when it was just a mail order catalogue. After road-testing the good, the bad and the just-plain-scratchy of the underwear market, she says she’s now more than qualified to design her own collection for grown-ups. “My hope for Raven and Sparrow is that the line has the sex appeal, but makes a woman feel beautiful, comfortable and confident,” she tells us. “This has been a dream come true - we’re putting delicate couture techniques into production.”   Seymour’s interest in lingerie extended beyond her former career on the catwalk and the supermodel tells us that she keeps an archive of historical undergarments, many of which inspired the pieces in her range. “I have been collecting for years,” she says. “I have pieces that span 100 years ranging from cotton pintucked bloomers from the 1920s, to more glamorous silk pieces from the 1940s and 1950s. We draw inspiration from all of these pieces in the collection.” Produced in partnership with designer Casey Paul, the focal points of Seymour’s debut Raven and Sparrow collection, though, are not bloomers. Rather, the hero buys are its silk slips and kimonos - pieces that she says are sexy enough to seduce in, or soft enough to sleep in, as these two needs are no longer mutually exclusive. “This collection’s colour and fabric palette includes mint green charmeuse and georgette, saffron gold washed silk, champagne blush charmeuse, and our custom floral print.  We wanted to start the line with a very feminine feeling, these colours are extremely complimentary to the skin tone.”   Seymour describes putting on the clothes as part of her “divine ritual of dressing for bed”, a routine that she says is about no-one but herself. “I feel like when you go through the ritual of taking care of yourself - of washing your face, taking a quiet bath and slipping something on that makes you feel good - you go to bed feeling good. For me, this makes all the difference and it even sets you up for the next day.” Enjoying getting ready for bed is surely something we can all get on board with? It certainly makes a lot more sense than getting our scary strappy knickers in a twist in an attempt to be sexy.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Awards season is no stranger to below-the-belt jokes at the podium. It’s an art that has been honed by the likes of Ricky Gervais, who has embarrassed many a celebrity with his barbed humour during multiple Golden Globes ceremonies. Seth MacFarlane gave the 2013 Oscars audience an equally good run for its money. So we’ve come to expect a certain amount of off-colour ribbing amid all the mutual back-slapping - and some might say these events are all the better for it. But this week, up stepped Stephen Fry to do his turn (for the 11th time) as presenter of the Baftas. Caught in his crosshairs this time was not a Hollywood megastar or entire institution (see Rebel Wilson’s quip about the “racist” Oscars) but the not-so-household name of Jenny Beavan. Shrugging off the black tie dress code, the award-winning costume designer was (somewhat ironically) clad in black leather jacket, white t-shirt, black trousers and grey scarf. No sooner had she accepted her award for Mad Max: Fury Rd than Fry deadpanned into the microphone: “Only one of the great cinematic costume designers would come to the awards dressed like a bag lady.” Cue a substantial outpouring of rage on Twitter, much to the annoyance of Fry, who did what is rarely advisable in such situations and sought to explain himself by tweeting back: “So just a word to the tragic figures who think calling Jenny Bevan a bag lady was an insult. She’s a dear friend and she got it. Derrr.” And there it could have ended, had Fry not subsequently deleted his account, prompting a further slew of headlines. The “dear friend” herself seemed none too bothered meanwhile, betraying no sign of rancour when she posed for a post-ceremony picture with Fry. She told the Telegraph: “Yes we are friends, and I am absolutely not upset, but I don’t want to talk any further because if I talk about it it will just create more fuss”. So who is  the unfamiliar woman at the eye of this particular Twitter storm? If you’ve never seen her before, you’ve probably seen her work, which includes costumes for The King’s Speech, Sherlock Holmes, Gosford Park, Sense and Sensibility, A Room with a View and BBC Two mini-series Casanova. Among her silverware, the 66-year-old boasts an Oscar for A Room with a View, an Emmy for Emma and a Bafta for her work on Gosford Park. Born in London to a cellist mother and violinist father, she credits both with her stoic work ethic and is frequently up at 5am sourcing fabrics, compiling mood boards and researching every inch of a character or time period. After studying at Central School of Art and Design (now Central St Martin’s), she was, in her words, “catapulted” into the world of costuming through fortuitous meetings and a stint of unpaid work on early Merchant Ivory films. Her big break came when she dressed Dame Peggy Ashcroft for Hullabaloo Over Georgie and Bonnie’s Pictures in 1978.  Since then, she has created costumes for Dame Judi Dench, Colin Firth and Helena Bonham Carter, dressed on-screen monarchs and several Winston Churchills and has over 50 titles to her portfolio. She lists Piero Tosi, Anthony Powell and Alexander McQueen as sources of inspiration and cites people-watching in Trafalgar Square and the Royal Academy’s café for further inspiration. But despite a career built around clothes, Beavan has form when it comes to dressing down for awards ceremonies. In 2011, nominated for best costume design in The King’s Speech, she arrived at the Oscars in a plain black suit made by a friend which, she told a journalist, she hoped would look smart but be “completely non-eventful”. “I have no interest in my own clothes or in clothes in general,” she has explained previously. “My love is creating character through clothes.” As for her relationship with Fry, the pair are certainly acquaintances. In 2011 she dressed him as Inspector Thompson in Gosford Park, then again in 2011 as Mycroft Holmes, Sherlock’s older brother in Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows. She said of the latter that she made a call to clothe him “very straight” in stiff white shirts and top hats: “He is so recognisable that my feeling was to keep it simple and very much in period without quirkiness. Stephen could add that!” But are they actually friends? John Bright, a founder of renowned costumier Cosprop and a close friend of Beavan’s is doubtful. “What a silly man!” he says of Fry the morning after the night before. “I wouldn’t have said they were very good friends. I think she will probably laugh it off but it might come back to haunt her in a quiet moment. It was such a strange thing to say. He has done this many times, and after Ricky Gervais comments at the Golden Globes you would imagine he would have the nous and the forethought not to say anything like that.” And worse, perhaps, it was just not that funny.  Bright, who hadn’t spoken to Beavan since the row, would rather have her celebrated for her “intrepid” approach to film. “She has the most amazing enthusiasm,” he says.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Baz Lurhmann has been developing his first television show The Get Down, which lands on Netflix this Friday, for over a decade. The legendary director, who has worked with the likes of Leonardo DiCaprio and Nicole Kidman, could surely have had his pick of established Hollywood 'names,' but he wanted to introduce a new cast of unknowns to tell this story about teenagers discovering hip hop in the South Bronx in the late 70s. One of these 'unknowns' now on the brink of stardom is Herizen Guardiola who plays the female lead Mylene, an aspiring singer trying to break away from her evangelical father, who is a strict pastor frightened of the disco music his daughter idolises. In the first episode, Mylene sneaks out to a disco club where she lights up the screen in her silver vintage 70s Halston dress. Herizen Guardiola's own wardrobe might be a little less sparkly than Mylene's, but she is poised to become a style star in her own right. Guardiola, who is acting for the first time in The Get Down, made her red carpet debut at none other than the Met Gala in a green Monique Lhuillier gown picked out by the Vogue team. A clear indication that she isn't going to remain a red carpet unknown for long. Guardiola prioritises her music career, and her voice is an integral part of The Get Down so she is sure to have her own recording contract shortly. "Music has always been my first love,” she said to InStyle. “My dad is a reggae musician and I was raised around the Marleys. Growing up around that world influenced me in a lot of ways. As a kid, I would be on stage with my Dad, you know, his little backup singer. He had us record a couple things on his album when I was about six. So I’ve been doing this a long time. Music is really who I am, I would say. It’s the way I express how I feel, and how I’ve learned to tell my story.” Her own style channels low-key New York street style, with ripped denim, varsity jackets, statement trainers and vintage band t shirts making up the majority of her wardrobe. "I'm a fan of fashion, but I'm not a fashionista," she explained to Elle. "I'm kind of grungy, something I always have is a nice leather jacket and smart sneakers. I'll spend money on nice sneakers. If I see someone wearing a really nice pair in the street, I will run up and ask where they got them from. Of course, Yeezys are really nice, if only I could afford them!" Partnering with a large fashion brand now comes with the territory of being an actress in 2016, and Guardiola is excited for possible brand collaborations. "I would love to shoot a really big campaign in the future – Prada, Gucci, Chanel – but I really want to focus on my music," she said to Elle. "The way I grew up, in a way, resonates with my character," she told Vogue. "I’m half Cuban and half Jamaican; my Dad’s a reggae musician and he was raised Cuban Catholic, and my mom was raised Baptist, but she’s a Buddhist and a nutritionist and yoga instructor. When I was young, I would go from living with my hippie parents to my [extended] family’s house, and I would have to put on the pearls and put my hair in a bow and dress really nice. That helped me with my character."  The fashion world might be mourning the imminent departure of Michelle Obama from the White House, and with it the end of one of the most captivating and fabulous eras in First Lady style but the state visit to Britain by Colombian president Juan Manuel Santos and his super chic wife Maria Clemencia De Santos has offered a soothing distraction for the past few days.  In her elegant tailoring, refined eveningwear and luxurious accessories, 60 year-old De Santos has evidently mastered the conundrum of dressing interestingly yet appropriately on the world stage, all the while ticking that other crucial First Lady box- supporting the fashion industry of your home nation.  Over the past few years, Colombian fashion has seen many of its designers become international names as the industry broadens its horizons. Johanna Ortiz had been creating her ultra-feminine flounced pieces for years when they were spotted by M'oda 'Operandi founder  Lauren Santo Domingo and became a street style sensation last year. The president's daughter, Maria Antonia, wore an Ortiz gown to the state dinner on Tuesday night.  It was to husband and wife design team Leal and Karen Daccarett that her mother, known as Tutina, turned to for the banquet hosted by The Queen. The duo are long-time favourites of De Santos. "Our aesthetic is very proudly Colombian- it's about colour, arts and crafts, volume and mixing materials. Everything we do is very feminine," they explain over the phone from Colombia.  "We have made lots of special outfits for her," they continue excitedly. The navy and white silk gown embroidered with pearls they created for this week's visit took about one month to make. "We create designs for her and then we decide materials and things like that together" they say.  The pair, who met while working in Milan ten years ago, are big fans of the look which De Santos has developed since her husband took office in 2010. "Her style is very classic, she doesn't want to be a trend setter, but she always supports Colombian designers. Colombia is living through a very special moment and and she helps with that." During this week's state visit, there has been none of the affordable/ designer balance which often comes with world stage dressing. Instead, De Santos' look has been an expensive showcase of Colombian fashion- with a smattering of stealth wealth accessories for good measure. The grey jacket and skirt which she wore for the first day of the tour is by Pepa Pombo, a label founded in 1978 by Pombo and now designed by her daughter Monica. The sleek knitwear was also recently worn by Amal Clooney while De Santos chose a dress from the brand for another recent meeting with Michelle Obama. That look was paired with a box bag by Barcelona-based handbag brand M2Malletier whose architectural designs offer a modern take on that traditionally neat style which is favoured by politicians and royalty alike.  Last night's deep emerald gown is by an as yet unidentified designer, but its aesthetic continued the week's sophisticated yet gently forward-thinking theme. With its drop tie waist and balloon sleeves, the gown nods to the volume-play which has become a Colombian fashion signature while the jewel-hue and deep burgundy lipstick should be noted as an excellent party season combination.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s official: Chris Martin really does have a thing for blonde, talented and photogenic actresses. Since ‘consciously uncoupling’ from Oscar-winning star Gwyneth Paltrow, his wife of 10 years, in March 2014, he swiftly moved on to fellow Oscar-winner Jennifer Lawrence. Despite never being photographed in public together, the Coldplay singer is said to have enjoyed a string of dates with the 25-year-old starlet, who recently spoke out about the gender pay gap in Hollywood. With Lawrence now out of the picture, the 38-year-old father-of-two is romancing another actress – but this time a British one – in the form of 31-year-old Annabelle Wallis. Pictures of the pair taken in Paris this weekend, which show them laughing, kissing and even appearing to tango down a street in the romantic city, are proof that Martin is consciously coupled-up once more. Reports suggest that they have been an item since August. Avid watchers of TV series The Tudors and Peaky Blinders will be familiar with Wallis; she played Jane Seymour in the former and with an Irish lilt serenaded Cillian Murphy’s character in the latter as undercover policewoman Grace Burgess. Born in Oxford, Wallis grew up in Portugal and attended an International School, meaning that her CV boasts that she can speak Portuguese, French and Spanish. She is ‘ranked’ 147 in society glossy Tatler’s ‘The Tatler List’, who writes of her “Immaculately turned out and annoyingly beautiful” but humourously observes: “Claims to be fluent in four languages but, after a glass of wine, she'll admit that 'fluent' is a slight overstatement.” The niece of award-winning Irish actor Richard Harris, Wallis’ star is certainly on the ascent. She’s flirted with Hollywood by way of a lead role in 2014 horror Annabelle and enjoyed small roles in X-Men: First Class and hit series Pan Am, but 2016 will see her play larger parts in Sacha Baron Cohen’s Grimsby, star alongside Breaking Bad’s Aaron Paul in drama Come and Find Me and play Maid Maggie in Guy Ritchie’s Knights of the Roundtable: King Arthur. Like Martin’s previous loves, Wallis possesses something of a passion for fashion. She was a guest at Chanel’s recent Paris Fashion Week show and her Instagram account reveals a slight addiction to the luxury brand’s iconic, quilted handbags. Her red carpet appearances are also consistently fashion-forward and covetable; Dior, Prada and Valentino are just some of the big fashion houses to have dressed her. At the Met Gala in New York earlier this year, she was kitted out in Dolce & Gabbana couture along with actress friends Brie Larson and Courtney Eaton, forming a striking trio at what is considered to be the fashion event of the year. Hollywood glamour aside, friendships with London-based designers Christopher Kane and Georgia Hardinge mean she’s au fait with sitting on the front row and championing British fashion on the red carpet. She’s a regular at the annual British Fashion Awards and fashionable parties in the capital – which she calls home – thrown by Louis Vuitton and Prada. Whether her romance with Martin goes the distance or not, Wallis is certainly a name and a face to have on your radar.

 You can’t deny the WAGS knew how to work a look. With their microscopic hot pants and super-sized hair, handbags, shoes and sunglasses, Coleen Rooney and co created an image that was designed to emphasise their tiny waists and excessive wealth. And, with their daily style parade in Baden-Baden in 2006 making international news, it wasn’t long before their look was being both emulated - and derided. The boutiques and labels the WAGS frequented experienced a surge of customers wanting to dress like their new-found fashion idols. But luxury handbag brand Birkin reportedly suffered  a so-called WAG-lash from customers who no longer wanted to be seen with the  same bag hooked on their arm as Victoria Beckham. So, ten years on - as Euro 2016  begins - where do we stand on the trends the WAGs made famous?     Can you imagine a summer in which you didn’t even question your skin tone? Not since the WAGs had a tan-off on their hotel sun loungers. Biscuit-hued tans have become so the norm that the fake tanning industry is now worth $1.2billion - and is forecast to grow by another 13% in 2018. The only difference today? It’s all about a gradual tan, thanks to innovative technologies like St Tropez’s In Shower Gradual Tan. (£14.50, boots.com) The Liverpool-based boutique Cricket favoured by the WAGS became such a shopping mecca, even the shop’s leopard-printed carrier bags achieved cult status - going for £25 on eBay in 2006. Today, Cricket’s still selling Chloe handbags to Liverpool locals and its 70,000 followers on Instagram. Hard to fathom but a picture of Alex Curren in a yellow Juicy Couture tracksuit and UGGs was credited as creating a waiting list for the velour two-piece. Even harder to fathom is the fact the Juicy tracksuit is back. The company closed in 2014 but US department store Bloomingdales has just announced it’s re releasing the cult tracksuit this autumn - and charging £320 for it.    “Can you really have hair extensions without looking like a WAG?” The fact we’re still reading this headline today shows just how ubiquitous Victoria Beckham and co made hair extensions. The answer, by the way, is yes. Today, Hershesons offer a £250 service of extensions from hair donated by virgins to Indian temples (yes, really) that’s said to release biotin onto the hair to encourage cell growth. Victoria Beckham was said to have packed 60 bug-eyed pairs for Baden-Baden by the likes of Versace and Roberto Cavalli. And in doing so, she made functional sunglasses into a fashion statement. Today the luxury shades industry is worth $13billion.   The bag brand Beckham used to hold over her mouth to disguise her smile has recovered from any WAG-lash. Last month, a crocodile-skin Birkin bag became the world’s most expensive handbag when it sold at auction for $300,000.  Louboutin platform heels were the WAG shoe of choice thanks to the way they elongated the leg - and flashed a conspicuous red sole. These days you’re more likely to see Victoria Beckham in (Adidas Stan Smith) trainers while Christian Louboutin has expanded into the world of beauty, creating nail varnish and lip lacquer which perfectly matches those signature scarlett soles.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Despite being the second richest man in the world, Zara founder Amancio Ortega usually keeps a low profile. But this weekend, the paparazzi caught the Spanish billionaire in a rare ‘display’ of mega-wealth in St Tropez, as boat watchers salivated over his £41.2 million super-yacht. For the fashion crowd, though, there was something else on board to catch the eye - and, alas, it wasn’t 81 year-old Mr Ortega’s (inevitably Zara-bought) bathing suit. His 33 year-old daughter and the heiress to his empire, Marta Ortega, was also present, and flexing her impeccable taste for resortwear. The appearance has, consequently, given us a rare insight into the woman who is likely behind 20% of the contents in an average British woman’s wardrobe. Marta acts as a senior creative consultant on all Zara Woman collections, and evidently has first pick of the new clothes before they hit stores. Despite her wealth (her father was worth £65 billion at last count) Ortega actually practices what she preaches, mixing her fully-stocked high street wardrobe with a few choice designer buys. It’s thought that she’s the one, over her two siblings, who will take over the family business if her apparent-workaholic father ever retires, and she has been working her way up the ranks since beginning her career at the family firm as a shop girl in the Oxford Street store, during her Business Management studies in London. With a circle of friends that includes Athena Onassis and Spain’s Queen Letizia (who is regularly spotted in Zara), Marta also is an established show-jumper, meaning that she’s a key figure in the Spanish equestrian social set. The entire family is, however, notoriously private, and great efforts have been made to keep her personal relationships out of the papers. In 2012, Marta married fellow champion rider Sergio Alvarez Moya in a private ceremony on her father’s estate, with an altar designed by sculptor Anish Kapoor - forgoing a bargain Zara look for a Narciso Rodriguez couture gown, just this once. After splitting some months ago, she is now in a relationship with Carlos Torretta, a model agent who establishes deals for Kendall Jenner and Adriana Lima in Europe. Torretta is the son of Roberto Torretta, the Argentinian designer and vice president of ACME , the Association of Fashion Creators of Spain and Carmen Echevarría, a woman who counts Jane Birkin among the clients at her Madrid boutique, meaning that this new relationship would only serve to seal the credentials of the first family of Spanish fashion. As she continues to rise at the company, and is establishing herself among the new Madrid fashion set, Marta Ortega is definitely a name worth watching. In fact, considering the fact that Zara's sales hit £535.2 million in the UK alone last year, she may already be the most influential name in fashion that you’d never heard of.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  At the Met Gala on Monday, this year's 'tech white tie' dress code was mostly interpreted to mean "silver sequins." But some embraced the spirit of Anna Wintour's directive more wholeheartedly and used the most high-octane red carpet as an opportunity to flag recent advances in design. Latex eveningwear was one development to have a moment in the Met Gala spotlight, with Beyoncé, Solange Knowles and Bella Hadid all opting for rubbery creations. Unlike most trends which come together after various designers gravitate towards a certain inspiration, there is one woman behind this latex red carpet movement, London-based designer Atsuko Kudo. She collaborated with Riccardo Tisci at Givenchy to create the nude pearl-embellished gown which Beyoncé wore to the Met Gala.  "We worked on the dress over the past few weeks in different periods of a few days and then would come back to it to make changes and edits," Kudo tells The Telegraph of how she and her team created Beyoncé's figure-cinching creation. "Unfortunately we cannot tell you how we applied the pearls - it’s a secret! We do apply pearls and crystals to the Atsuko Kudo range, but Riccardo chose some special pearls that are very beautiful, but we had to find a new way to apply them. I think the dress used approximately 2,500 pearls." Beyoncé's stylist Ty Hunter said of the artistry of the gown: "[Riccardo] had an actual artist hand-paint the dress, so if you notice the details, it was all hand-painted flowers, also pearls were put on as well." Although a latex gown might sound about as comfortable as a bikini wax/ childbirth/ Lady Gaga's penchant for impossibly-high platforms, Hunter said to Extra: "Believe it or not, people think this was probably the quickest dress to get in, most comfortable and less stress." Kudo explains that there is a 'ritual' to applying latex products, such as Beyoncé's. "You moisture your body first so you can slip into it. It's a lubricant product, that is nice on the skin, and you have to do a ritual to get into latex. It's like wearing a corset or high heels, it's not like cotton or something that's easy to put on, but it makes you look and feel amazing." Kudo believes that anyone can look amazing in latex, but only if the cut is perfect so it resembles a second skin. "You'd think latex is easy to fit, but it's difficult because everyone is a different height and shape and we make it to precisely fit the shape," the Japanese designer explains. "If we get the measurements right, latex will make you look amazing and works like shapewear. I don't want people to think latex is not flattering - it just has to be the correct size, because some people just go to any shop and try on and it's not the correct size so you don't get the right result. A good fit of latex can empower women." In order to ensure Beyoncé's latex fitted perfectly, Kudo's team worked from an accurate dummy of her body. "We didn't speak with Beyoncé about this dress but we were already making some Atsuko Kudo designed pieces for her Formation tour so we knew she liked latex," explains Kudo. "We prefer to do the fitting in person but it's not always possible. Often we work from just measurements and pictures. In this case, because we just did the costume for Beyoncé’s Formation tour and we made a body block of her, due to her not being in London and not able to do fittings with us." Kudo initially created this 'dummy' of Beyoncé's body to work on a red latex bodysuit which she wears on her current Formation tour. Beyoncé requested that the body fit in with her antebellum ( the period before the American Civil War in the early 1800s) theme which runs throughout her visual album Lemonade. "She wanted it to have some frill and pop sleeves, but at the same time wanted it to be super modern and be able to dance in it," Kudo explains of the brief for this look. "So it was where the frills across the chest and scoop neck came from rather than being super sleek and modern." Kudo studied at fashion college in Japan and then learned how to work with latex at a fetish shop in London. "It is different to normal, ordinary clothes," she says of the difference working with latex. "We cut differently and use glue, so we glue the seams together rather than sewing. You can sew, but we prefer to glue because you get more of a smooth finish." There has been a rise in latex on the red carpet, with the likes of Kim Kardashian, Miley Cyrus and Rita Ora wearing a number of Kudo's designs. Lady Gaga even wore a red custom full latex look to meet the Queen in 2009. "Beyoncé's dress for the Met Ball was another significant step forward for latex as a fashion fabric," says Kudo. "When a couture brand like Givenchy chooses latex to create a main garment for an important client who happens to be a super-star like Beyoncé then it’s a big change. My mission is to empower women though latex, and make the world a shinier place."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Do those nude court shoes and that floral fascinator look familiar to you? For her first appearance on her state visit to the UK today, Queen Letizia of Spain appears to have taken her fashion cue directly from the Duchess of Cambridge. Letizia, who usually is spotted in Spanish designer labels like Felipe Varela, as well as their high street hitters Zara and Uterque, instead chose an all-yellow look more suited to a day out at Ascot for her visit, meeting The Queen, Prince Charles and the Duchess of Cornwall at Buckingham Palace. A former newsreader on TVE, her go-to for formal occasions is razor sharp dresses and pitch-perfect suiting, yet this morning’s ensemble (a canary sheath dress and a lace-trimmed dress coat, teamed with buttercup gloves) resembled nothing that we’d seen her in before. Perhaps she had hoped to appeal to her hosts, each duly clad in their own A-line coats by their signature dressmakers Stewart Parvin and Anna Valentine. Certainly she timed it well to wear yellow just as the sun reemerged. But this was a chance for Letizia to show herself as a glamorous fashion rival to Kate and co. (and to highlight the best of her nation’s design talents, just as the Duchess might when she heads to Poland and Germany next week) so it seems ill-judged that she’s simply mimicked one of the Duchess’s look from the races five years ago, for her first moment in our country’s spotlight. Is this what people in the outside world think British style is all about? The Duchess of Cambridge has undoubtedly figured out what works for her on an international stage, and has honed a look that thousands want to copy. But nodding to Britishness can surely be about more than repli-Kating our fashion figurehead’s favourites, right down to the nude heels? There’s a banquet to be held tonight (which the Duchess will also be attending) offering a dress code that Queen Letizia is undoubtedly more familiar with. On previous gala occasions she’s been seen in cool caped dresses by Stella McCartney, or embellished Carolina Herrera numbers. Perhaps later we will see her go back to doing what she does best - and feeling comfortable in her signature clothes.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s just over a year since Blake Lively launched Preserve.us, her attempt at a lifestyle and e-commerce site that celebrated all things artisanal, from clothes to crockery. But today, she has announced that she will shut down the business on October 9 as she feels it never quite met its full potential. “We have an incredible team of people who do beautiful work, but we launched the site before it was ready, and it never caught up to its original mission: It’s not making a difference in people’s lives, whether superficially or in a meaningful way,” she told US Vogue. “And that’s the whole reason I started this company, not just to fluff myself, like, ‘I’m a celebrity! People will care what I have to say!’ It was so never meant to be that, and that kind of became the crutch because it was already up and already running, and it’s hard to build a brand when you’re running full steam ahead—how do you catch up?” she added. Alas, this isn’t Lively, 28, just admitting defeat – the essence of Preserve will be back, but rebranded and rebuilt as what it was always intended to be. Nevertheless, she is prepared for the media backlash that will likely succeed today’s announcement. “I know what it’ll look like, what I’m facing publicly, that people are just going to have a heyday with this,” she says. “But it’s so much worse to continue to put something out there—to ask my team to put something out there—that isn’t the best we can do. I’m going to take this hit, and the only way I can prove all the negative reactions wrong is to come back with a plan that will rock people. And I have that plan. And I’m so excited about it, and that’s what gave me the courage to do this, to say, ‘You know what, I’m going to give myself one more shot at this, and I really have to do it as well as I can do it this time.’” She hasn't given a timescale for the new project though we expect this time, she's taking her time to get it just right. It’s been a busy 12 months for Lively, who is married to fellow actor Ryan Reynolds. The couple welcomed their first child, a daughter named James, in December 2014.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Beyoncé took some time out from her 'Formation' tour this weekend to spend a day at the beach in Hawaii with her husband Jay-Z and daughter Blue Ivy. But of course a "day off" for Beyoncé is not your standard lazy sunday by the sea, reading your Kindle and eating ice cream for lunch. In fact, the outing proved an ideal opportunity for Queen Bey to promote her latest album Lemonade with a look which comprised a carefully curated selection of lemon-themed accessories. Of course, there was therefore no keeping this citrus-fruit themed outing a private Carter family moment- Beyoncé later posted 19 snapshots of the outing to her website, as well as adding a few outtakes to Instagram for good measure. Unsurprisingly, this latest beach appearence has raised a few important summer beach-dressing issues... Beyoncé is really taking ownership of lemons, wearing a zesty yellow cover up and a crown of six lemons plus a matching necklace adorned with lemons made by under-the-radar Budapest-based designer Sugarbird Zagreb. She then changed into a 183euro lemon print off-the-shoulder maxi dress by the same designer. The singer is pushing the lemons thing so much in fact, that she even stuck a lemon sticker over the apple on the back of her iPhone. Now that is dedication to the lemon cause. There's a serious visual strategy behind Beyoncé's lemon obsession which is fast ensuring that lemons overtake avocados as the new popular culture fruit du jour. It's all a not-so-subtle reminder of her latest album Lemonade, which was released at the end of April. The coverage of the album has been dominated by speculation about cheating within Beyoncé and Jay Z's marriage due to the highly personal lyrics which allude to a broken relationship. But the pictures on Beyonce.com of the couple kissing on the beach, with Beyoncé wearing a halo of lemons, send a clear (if bittersweet?) message that despite the angry tracks, the couple are still very much an item. Lipstick is rarely a make-up detail you would think to attend to on the beach. At the most you might stretch to a bright coral hue if you're somewhere particularly fancy.  But Beyoncé is pushing boundaries by pairing her brightly multicoloured clothes and accessories with a deep burgundy lip colour.  Now that she's made the case for experimenting with a red wine shade of lipstick, expect to see the look emulated in Beyoncé-at-the-beach copycat selfies, surely coming soon to an Instagram/ Facebook feed near you.  This is the summer of the one piece, but Beyoncé is also making us consider a surf-style cut in her tropical printed Mara Hoffman swimming costume with rash guard sleeves and cut outs at the waist. Although this print isn't currently available, there are a number of other graphic surf suits in Hoffman's collection. As a bonus, these pieces offer extra sun protection but are also good for keeping the chill at bay if you're booked to go to St Ives rather than Hawaii.    Mara Hoffman Rash Guard suits, available on MaraHoffman.com   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
