 It’s slightly discombobulating hearing Stella McCartney talk about the challenges of engaging with young people. Can it really be that much of a stretch? Then I remember she’s 44. Like her dad, Macca, there’s an eternally youthful Tiggerish-ness to her. Is it the vulnerable cast to those cartoonishly large, occasionally hurt-looking eyes? The quick bounce back? The apple cheeks? The stylishly sporty silk track pants, worn with men’s brogues? ‘Flat-fronted, elasticated waist, ribbed hems,’ she enumerates helpfully. ‘I practically live in them at the moment.’ There’s a bit of shoulder robing going on as well, with a tangerine cashmere coat, a lightly tanned, smooth face (does she, doesn’t she? I don’t know, and it seems rude to ask). Whatever she’s doing, it’s all working. She looks elegantly modern. There’s also the girlish voice, somewhat at odds with some of her weightier, chewier utterances. When she tells me about the way she deals with some of her five- and nine-year-old daughters’ more controversial clothes choices (‘I say to them, “Explain to me what is it you like about that?”’), she sounds like a head girl trying – and frankly failing – not to be bossy. We’re in a white cube of an office at her HQ on the outskirts of Notting Hill. It’s not until 10 minutes in that I realise her PR is sitting in. He’s hidden by a large computer screen. Then again, I’d understand if she never gave another interview at all. There was a time when she seemed to have decided not to. The issues that wind her up – animal welfare, the environment, longevity, the way fashion engages, or doesn’t, with young women – are so hard to square with the business in which she’s been working, with no small success, for more than 20 years, that she’s always going to lay herself open to accusations of hypocrisy. That’s before we get to her understandable desire for complete privacy. But there’s a new fragrance to promote. Stella McCartney POP is a sweet, youth-orientated cocktail of sandalwood and tuberose – ‘a very unfashionable flower, but I like it for that. And it only releases its scent at night.’ As a matter of fact, Alexander McQueen’s creative director Sarah Burton, and one other major brand I can’t currently reveal, have also availed themselves of tuberose in the past few months, for precisely the same reasons. She’s always been good at identifying the zeitgeist, has Stella. Arguably because she was born into it. But there are plenty of people who miss what’s in front of their nose. Stella gravitated to it like a homing pigeon. She’s still there, doing things like fighting to cast the women she thinks represent something other than superficial beauty. Women like Grimes, aka Claire Boucher, the Canadian-born artist-cum-musician-cum-video director, who is one of the stars of her new perfume campaign. ‘I look at Bailey, my nine-year-old, and she’s already old beyond her years. She’s very aware of advertising. We all are. I feel responsible… I never want to promote an ad that makes women feel bad about themselves, because when I was young, I never felt rich enough or fashionable enough or good enough. I felt talked down to by luxury fashion labels. There was a disconnect. They made me feel we weren’t right for each other.’ In print, there’s a fair chance that such a statement could come across as the Unbearable Pain of Being Famous and Privileged. But eyeball-to-intensely-blue-eyeball, I can tell you it’s convincing and likeable. Stella’s heart is in the right place, even if it sometimes trips up on its moral high-wires. She knows, for instance, that producing a perfume instantly raises all kinds of eco-objections, from packaging to harvesting. ‘We’ve simplified the bottle to cut down wastage, but, quite honestly, the minute you make anything, you are creating a footprint.’   She tells me there’s a lot of technologically advanced biomimicry in this scent. Translation: it comes from a lab rather than fields – in which solution there lies a whole other set of complex pros and cons. But the point is, Stella has built a luxury fashion brand in her home town, at a time when everyone said it couldn’t be done in London; a brand that employs 500 people directly, 250 of those in the capital. ‘That’s one of the things I’m proudest of – that the people we employ could work anywhere in the world, for any brand, and they choose to be here.’ The fact that her company is co-owned by the Kering Group means she has to deliver year-on-year gains. That’s not that easy when you refuse to work with fur and leather. She estimates her accessories business could have been five times the size if she’d caved on her principles. But she didn’t. Let’s not forget her clothes, because Stella sells a lot of them, not least because she’s always had the knack of being just sufficiently ahead of her customers to be able to inspire rather than alienate them. In the early ’90s she gave smart, working women a cool way to dress by eliding Savile Row tailoring with vintage-y looking camisoles and dresses: a soft/hard, masculine/feminine matrix that still works today.  But traditional blazers, once a mainstay of her collections, have apparently taken something of a back seat lately. ‘That’s a good thing,’ she muses. ‘It’s a sign that women don’t feel they have to dress like men any more. They can wear a dress to the office without feeling they’ve suddenly become this sexual creature. They’re less dictated to by the likes of me, and that’s great.’ These days, she’s rarely motivated by trends, which would be ‘deadly’, than finding ways to make clothes more planet- and eco-friendly (quilted coats filled with synthetic wadding rather than down and feathers; committing her label to only using recycled cashmere) and increasingly versatile. ‘Pockets. I love a pocket. I’m about helping women look as good as possible on the least amount of effort,’ she says. ‘I want versatility and comfort. Clothes that can go from the office to anywhere. We’re always trying on samples at work. If none of us would wear it, chances are no one else will.’ Stella’s own schedule is full-on. ‘There are some days when the balancing act doesn’t feel balanced at all,’ she says. She’s good at empathy and sounding normal, even if the details sometimes give the game away. ‘Today I couldn’t do the school run because we were launching the Team GB kit. But I’ll try to do the pick-up this afternoon.’ Ah yes. Launching the GB kit. As you do. Typically, Stella was early to the game of designer gym-wear collaborations. She began working with Adidas 12 years ago – the dark ages of women’s sportswear, when you cobbled together a look from what Stella calls, ‘crap sneakers and a T-shirt that you’d got free on the front of a magazine. I remember going to the gym and avoiding all eye contact. You didn’t want to sweat and you definitely didn’t want to bump into anyone you knew on the way home. It bore no relationship to anything you might wear the rest of the time.’ Stella undoubtedly helped change the conversation around workout gear, which, in turn, probably encouraged more women to get active, which has ultimately fed into mainstream fashion. She herself runs – from the school gate to the office – and remains an active horsewoman (she rides Western style in an enormous armchair of a saddle) as well as a fair-weather gardener. ‘I’m not out in the mud every weekend, but we’re good at potatoes, garlic, onions.’ As often as they can, the Willis-McCartneys (her husband is Alasdhair Willis, creative director of Hunter) pile into their car and head from their double-fronted stuccoed house in Notting Hill towards their home in Warwickshire, an imposing Queen Anne manor with an avenue of trees (a wedding gift from Tom Ford) and its own wood (a joint present from their other guests). ‘It’s important for us as a family to go and sit in the woods sometimes.’ She insists she and Alasdhair don’t talk shop. ‘Too busy running the kids to gymnastics or football.’ I can’t help wondering why she’s so keen to take on so many projects – presumably something to do with proving she’s worthy of her parents. I think she’s also driven by a healthy quota of outrage. ‘There are a lot of designers who are very f­— you when it comes to using fur,’ she says. ‘If it’s wrong to do fur, then they’re going to do it. ‘But given that there are only about three of us who don’t do fur, they’re not being very punk. They’re just complying with every other fashion house. The fur industry gets to fashion students so young, paying them to use it. But even if you don’t care about the millions of animals killed for fashion, it’s not sustainable, and it’s not modern. Every other industry tries to move forward, apart from the fashion industry.’ Whatever your views on fur, it’s refreshing to hear someone in the fashion industry publicly saying what they really think. Granted, she has more freedom than other for-hire designers, but it would still be easier for her not to express a single controversial opinion. If she no longer seems in retreat from the press, that’s probably because, with age, she’s gained genuine confidence – not the entitled-but-needy cockiness you often see in the offspring of famous parents, but a sense of genuine achievement. She says she didn’t feel a moment’s wobble when she turned 40. ‘Obviously we live in a society where ageing is feared. But, to me, the alternative to getting old isn’t that great. I’ve got friends much older than me, and much younger, and I love that. It means you get to teach as well as learn. I feel attitudes to ageing are starting to change.’ She could be right. After all, the demographics are with her – and she does have that nose for the zeitgeist. Stella McCartney’s POP, £74 for 100ml, Debenhams By Emily Cronin No matter how printed or embellished the clothes designers send down the runway may be, black and navy still rule their personal wardrobes. There’s been a lot of coverage lately about the death of heels, but Stella shows why they still have mileage. Simply put, they look sharp and make most outfits look sharper. Pointed toes and higher-than-high heels are key to refining loose looks. If they awarded degrees for shoulder robing, Stella would be an obvious recipient. Balancing a coat or blazer on the shoulders allows her to display more of the coat and the outfit underneath.  Any overview of Stella’s style choices makes clear that her favourite clothing colours are black, navy, cream, white, grey and camel, with a pop of red for variety. Prints are deployed sparingly. The effect is crisp and cohesive, not to mention effortless. When she does bring in a print, it’s likely to be leopard. In shoes, clutches, coats and gilets, it is one of Stella’s signatures. By sticking to accessories, it looks sophisticated and fun. Consider these photos: on the left, Stella wears a black playsuit at the Hunter show in London last September; she chose the same garment for her autumn presentation in LA four months later. That a fashion designer with access to all the novelty her team devises would opt to wear the same outfit to two photographed events suggests she loves it. And we love that.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The men's fashion shows aren't usually a magnet for mobs of screaming teenage girls, but there is one model bringing Beatles mania to Milan Fashion Week – Lucky Blue Smith. The 17-year-old, who has been crowned the Justin Bieber of modelling, has walked for Emporio Armani, Ralph Lauren, Phillip Plein and Ermanno Scervino in Milan this season and is being chased from show to show.  Madonna has landed the cover of Harper’s Bazaar’s February issue, marking the 150th anniversary of the magazine’s US edition. Shot by fashion photography duo Luigi & Lango, the 58 year-old star models a vault’s-worth of vintage jewellery, plus capes by Gucci and Dior, with custom lingerie by La Perla, Stella McCartney and Agent Provocateur. “I like pushing the envelope,” the pop and fashion icon explains of her art and her ethos in the accompanying interview, which hits newsstands on 17th January. “But I don't like to do it just for the sake of doing it. I don't like to be provocative for the sake of being provocative. I like to be provocative. I like to make people think. I like to touch people's hearts. And if I can do all three of those things in one fell swoop, then I feel like I've really accomplished something.” Her 1930s showgirl look was created by Arianne Phillips- the costume designer and personal stylist who has helped Madonna to reimagine her look countless times over the years-  with set curls coiffed by Andy LeCompte. Madonna’s image came under fire on several occasions in 2016, most notably when she wore a bum-baring Givenchy lace dress to the MET Gala in May, and started a debate about ageless style on social media after commentator Piers Morgan told her to ‘put it away’. “My dress at the Met Ball was a political statement as well as a fashion statement," Madonna wrote on Instagram in response. "The fact that people actually believe a woman is not allowed to express her sexuality and be adventurous past a certain age is proof that we still live in an age-ist and sexist society.” Madonna also reflected on the criticism she's received over the years in her interview with Harper’s Bazaar. “I've always felt oppressed,” she said. “I know a lot of people would go, 'Oh, that's ridiculous for you to say that. You're a successful white, wealthy pop star,' but I've had the shit kicked out of me for my entire career, and a large part of that is because I'm female and also because I refuse to live a conventional life. I've created a very unconventional family. I have lovers who are three decades younger than me. This makes people very uncomfortable. I feel like everything I do makes people feel really uncomfortable.” The editors of Harper’s Bazaar’s 32 editions around the world also had their say on a list of the 150 most fashionable women in the world today, of which, naturally, Madonna was a top choice. The Duchess of Cambridge, Amal Clooney, Kendall Jenner, Beyonce, Naomi Campbell and Michelle Obama were all also chosen for the list that celebrated The Cool Girls, High Society, Modern Mega Stars and the New Guard. “Our lists were more or less the same,” the US edition’s editor-in-chief Glenda Bailey, said. “These women are renowned for style around the world. And they all have such very different styles. This is in praise of the individual.” And there's no better example of individuality than Madonna.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Michelle Obama says "it's time". After eight years in the White House, the First Lady will be leaving the West Wing in January as one of the most popular presidential spouses America has seen. Appearing on the cover of Vogue for the third time in seven years, Mrs Obama said she would miss waking up to the view of the South Lawn and the Washington Monument. "But on the flip side . . . it’s time," she told the magazine in a wide-ranging interview. "I think our democracy has it exactly right: two terms, eight years. It’s enough. Because it’s important to have one foot in reality when you have access to this kind of power. The nature of living in the White House is isolating.” .@FLOTUS Michelle Obama is the cover star of our December issue! Read the full story: https://t.co/ihGSr9Obhl pic.twitter.com/OONghTYMP8 The 52-year-old has earned widespread praise for her self-described role as "mom-in-chief", particularly from her husband. "Michelle never asked to be First Lady,” President Barack Obama told the magazine. “Like a lot of political spouses, the role was thrust upon her. But I always knew she’d be incredible at it, and put her own unique stamp on the job. That’s because who you see is who she is - the brilliant, funny, generous woman who, for whatever reason, agreed to marry me. "I think people gravitate to her because they see themselves in her - a dedicated mom, a good friend, and someone who’s not afraid to poke a little fun at herself from time to time.” As First Lady, Mrs Obama campaigned for healthy eating, launched two education initiatives, became a style icon, turned herself into the First Lady of Popular Culture with appearances on TV shows, such as singing karaoke with James Corden, and stole the show on the Hillary Clinton  campaign trail.  She did, the mother-of-two notes, whatever she wanted.  “Everything we do is by choice,” she said. “I could have spent eight years doing anything, and at some level, it would have been fine. I could have focused on flowers. I could have focused on decor. I could have focused on entertainment. Because any First Lady, rightfully, gets to define her role. There’s no legislative authority; you’re not elected. And that’s a wonderful gift of freedom.” Her barmstorming speech at the Democratic National Convention and an emotional attack on Donald Trump in support of Mrs Clinton has spurred calls for her to run for president, especially in the wake of the business tycoon's election victory on Tuesday.  Could she follow Mrs Clinton's footsteps in trying to return to the White House as president after being First Lady?  “Absolutely not,” Valerie Jarrett, senior adviser to the president and a friend of the Obamas, told the magazine. Ms Jarrett argued that her speeches connected because she was not a politician and never will be. “Nobody questions her motives," she said. "Everybody knows exactly why she’s doing what she’s doing. There are no hidden agendas. She’s pure in mission, honest, kind, empathetic."   So if her future is not in politics, what lies ahead for Mrs Obama outside the White House? “I will take the same approach leaving as I did coming in,” she said. “I won’t know until I’m there. I’ve never been the former First Lady of the United States of America before. "But I will always be engaged in some way in public service and public life. The minute I left my corporate-law firm to work for the city, I never looked back."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This. Is. Not. A. Drill. The Spice Girls are said to be back and planning a concert at London's Hyde Park next summer. Geri Horner, nee Halliwell, Melanie Brown and Emma Bunton are reportedly said to be planning a concert at Hyde Park next summer to mark the 21st anniversary of the Spice Girls. A source said to The Mirror: "It gives them a year to plan everything and make sure their comeback is spectacular. It would be the most-talked about gig of the year." Earlier this year the three members of the group spent the past 48 hours in London’s Play Deep Studios, working on previously unheard material, according to The Mirror. The trio will release new material later this year, after the 20th anniversary of the band’s first single, Wannabe, in July. A handful of worldwide tour dates are also slated to take place in 2017, but will not include former bandmates Victoria Beckham and Melanie Chisholm. Known in their heyday for their distinctive style personas, the question on everyone’s minds is surely, what will they wear?! Does Mel B (Scary Spice) still have a penchant for leopard print? Has Emma (Baby Spice) been practising dance routines in her vertigo-inducing buffalo boots? And what about that Union Jack dress, Geri (Ginger Spice)? As much as we’d wholeheartedly enjoy a return of Nineties Spice fashion, we feel it’s our duty, as fashion press, and not former super fans, to offer some predictions, nay guidance, for the trio. Keeping their past signature styles in mind, here’s how we hope the Spice Girls reinvent themselves in 2016. It was all about pink, fluffy fashion for Baby Spice in the Nineties. Her girly character was maximised thanks to hair constantly styled in pigtails, bubblegum lip gloss and lollipops in-hand. The mother-of-two might still love  a pop of pink, but we very much doubt those ultra-mini hemlines are at the top of her wishlist to wear in 2016. If one label chimes with her feminine sensibilities, it’s Gucci, the brand bringing fun back into fashion under the creative direction of Alessandro Michele. Back in the Nineties, its sexy LBDs were a favourite of Posh but Gucci's turnaround now makes it ideal for Bunton's super-sweet tendencies. The chintzy prints, chiffon dresses and colourful accessories would nod to her saccharine style of yore, while acknowledging Gucci as the current ‘It’ brand in fashion. Michele’s hemlines all tend to flutter far below hot pants length which would give the look a grown-up spin. Clockwise from left:  Faux pearl-embellished wool and silk-blend mini dress £1,330, Gucci at Net-a-Porter;  Flora ring in rose gold, enamel and rubies, £ 1,550, Gucci; Blooms GG Supreme bag, £600, Gucci at Net-a-Porter;  Floral-print pumps, £585, Gucci for Net-a-Porter Nothing was ever too loud or brash for Melanie Brown, who cavorted through her Spice days in leopard print jumpsuits, patterned bralets and, quite frankly, little else. These days the fun-loving pop star, now 40, still has a tendency towards form-fitting fashion, but takes a more conservative approach to dressing. Olivier Rousteing, the creative director of Balmain, is the perfect modern day designer to dress Scary Spice. The Frenchman caters to a feisty girl gang, including Kim Kardashian, Kendall Jenner and Gigi Hadid. His signature leather, suede and studded pieces hug his muses’ frames, with an added flash of sass that would be perfect for a Scary comeback. Clockwise from left: Lace-up geometric-knit mini dress, £1,230, Balmain at Matches Fashion; Studded clutch, £775, Balmain; Akutai suede pumps, £975, Balmain Always the wild one, Geri’s spontaneous fashion matched her outspoken character. The singer made headlines after the 2004 Brit Awards where she took to the stage in that infamous Union Jack dress which had been crafted from a tea towel.  Fast forward to 2012 and Geri attended the opening night of Spice Girls, The Musical, in a baby blue princess dress. Totally over-the-top in comparison to her fellow Spices, it proved that the star still loves the limelight and maximalist style. If anyone can dress Geri, it’s Jeremy Scott, who is currently at the helm of Moschino. His zany and unpredictable creations are often the biggest talking point of fashion week, and his work with Katy Perry means he is well-versed in dressing pop stars. Go on Geri, we dare you.  The Duchess of Cambridge has joined women up and down the country by adding a Self Portrait dress to her wardrobe. Tonight, The Duchess attended The Recovery Street Film Festival and the world premiere of A Street Cat Named Bob in support of the charity Action on Addiction, of which she is patron.  Despite being a chilly November evening in London, The Duchess looked fresh and summery in a full-length white dress by the cult contemporary label which has sky rocketed to success in recent years, with its dresses becoming a regular sight on the backs of guests at weddings and other special occasions.  Self Portrait's founder and designer Han Chong was delighted to see The Duchess wearing one of his dresses. "It's a proud moment for me as designer to find Kate in one of my designs! She's such an elegant women and it's a dream to see. She looks incredible!" he told The Telegraph.  🎬 Watch Bob's audience with The Duchess of Cambridge. pic.twitter.com/VYevIWD5Pt 🎬 Watch Bob's audience with The Duchess of Cambridge. pic.twitter.com/VYevIWD5Pt The design chosen by Kate, who met film makers who had created works inspired by their experience of addiction,  features a chunky guipure lace bodice- a signature Self Portrait detail- with a prim raised collar and long pleated white skirt with a thigh split. In fact, the look would work perfectly as a bridal dress in its own right. Although the exact style worn by The Duchess is from the Resort 2016 collection  and is not currently available to purchase, a more seasonal version with a scarlett skirt is currently retailling on Self Portrait's website for £320.  As the fashion bloggers Go Fug Yourself pointed out, The Duchess's Self Portrait outing comes just days after Paris Hilton wore exactly the same dress to the amFAR inspiration gala in LA- an unlikely style match is ever there was one.  Of course, The Duchess- who was introduced to Bob the cat and his owner Jim Bowen at the premiere- styled her take on the look very differently, with her brunette hair glossily blow dried and carrying a burgundy clutch bag and heels in contrast to Hilton's bling-tastic tiara and white stilettos.  Self Portrait is something of a fashion phenomenon, with most dresses hitting on the sweet spot price point around £300 which is within reach of many women but still feels like a special investment. “Our handwriting is glamorous, but it’s not totally full-on and over-the-top. It’s got an edge to it; a unique quirk. It’s not a conventional red carpet dress,” founder Han Chong told Business of Fashion last year when the label was at the height of its growth, selling over 100 pieces each week in Selfridges and acquiring more than 250 stockists globally, an astonishing number for such a recently-founded business.  Although actresses, musicians, It girls and royals like The Duchess have access to gowns worth ten times as much as Self Portrait, the brand has nevertheless proved a hit amongst many famous women. Kristen Stewart, Beyonce, Reese Witherspoon and Madonna are just a few of those who have chosen Chong's feminine pieces. Even Michelle Obama has cottoned on to the appeal of the label's flattering cuts. The First Lady recently commissioned a custom-made design which she wore to give a speech at the UN General Assembly in September. " Very emotional! First Lady of the United States @michelleobama in a custom made @mrselfportrait dress yesterday. An honour to dress a woman that we admire and respect so much," Chong wrote on Instagram at the time.   Now that The Duchess of Cambridge has stepped out in Self Portrait, the juggernaut shows no sign of slowing.      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Unless you’re a Star Wars fanatic, you probably won’t have heard of Daisy Ridley. The 23-year-old, London-born actress has had small roles in TV series such Mr Selfridge, Casualty and Silent Witness, but is set to stare back at you from the side of every bus in the country – scrap that, the world – thanks to bagging one of the biggest parts in Hollywood. In Star Wars: The Force Awakens and the two films that will follow it, she plays Rey, the film’s lead character. Very little is known about her part, but that hasn’t stopped Star Wars obsessives already getting tattoos of her face (seriously). Ridley’s Instagram account reveals that her life is taking a very different trajectory to that of the average twenty-something, and when the film opens on December 17, she may never be able to enjoy anonymity again. It’s time to get Ms Ridley on radar, and here is what you need to know… Ridley and her Star Wars co-star John Boyega (also a Londoner) recently appeared on the cover of ASOS magazine. When Ridley asked who she’d most like to dress like, she responded ‘Diane Kruger, all day every day.’ The German model-turned-actress certainly never puts a stylish foot wrong, stepping out in directional looks from the most covetable designer brands. Kruger doesn’t employ a stylist, so it will be interesting to see if Ridley might reference some of her looks in the future. …As in, when people’s comments get nasty, she puts her foot down. The actress only joined the social media network three months ago, and rather endearingly shares some of the incredulous moments coming her way, i.e. seeing her face in giant proportions on billboards and on magazine covers. She’ll also post clips of her workouts, but when the haters go a step too far, here’s what she has to say: Could Ridley be this year’s red carpet answer to Lupita Nyong’o? Judging by her affection for bold hues, she may well take the fellow actress’s title. Filming The Force Awakens in Abu Dhabi was no piece of cake. As Ridley recalled to US Elle magazine: “We were told about this scorpion in Abu Dhabi that, if it stabbed you, you needed treatment within half an hour. There was this bit where I was lying in the sand, and if a scorpion got me, the nearest hospital was an hour away. So I was like, I could die right now. I could be dead in half an hour.” Ridley’s Instagram account is also a vehicle for all the people helping her on her remarkable journey. She’s only too happy to shout-out to the fabulous make-up team helping her look camera ready, such as Mary Greenwell, who could best be described as British make-up aristocracy. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  America in the sixties seemed the most glamorous, modern place in the world and Jackie Kennedy epitomized its appeal. But is that why she’s such an enduring figure? It’s more than half a century since she vacated The White House, yet Jackie Kennedy’s style is still considered not just relevant, but central to our ideas of what’s elegant and tasteful, to an almost weird extent. No other figure, apart from Audrey Hepburn, who was essentially Jackie’s celluloid doppelganger, and with whom she shared the same overarchingly influential designer, Hubert de Givenchy, has cast such a powerful or long-lasting penumbra over the world’s ideas of how to dress, eat and even live.  Johnnie Boden spends most of our time together doubled over in his chair, his head in his hands, his face screwed up, like a man in police custody. The founder of the eponymous 24-year-old mail order clothing company arrives at the posh member’s club, High Road House in Chiswick, ruddy-faced and tousled after cycling from his Acton headquarters, during which time he’s been totting up the number of his rivals who are currently discounting. “Fat Face, White Stuff…What are J Crew running at now, 40 per cent off?” Dressed head-to-toe in his own label (“Of course. Silly question”) including dark jeans with hipster roll-ups for which he apologises - “My daughter Katie styled me. I can’t really carry this off” - he is perhaps the most affably anguished man I’ve ever met. You might think, given the grimacing and visible fretting, that Boden was on the verge of bankruptcy. Far from it. In 2014 pre-tax profits were up 31 per cent to £32 million. The company now has 1.6 million customers across the world, (‘seven Glastonburys’ says Boden, for those who like to measure out success in British music festivals), with strong markets in America and Germany. Not bad for a company that started at his kitchen table as a hand-drawn catalogue selling eight menswear designs. There have been huge changes in retail since then, not least the takeover of online shopping. But what Boden says has changed most for his customer in those years is “The scale of improvement in women’s fashion education.” Women, he says, are more confident now about fashion.”When I started there were four or five styles that you carried forward every season – 60 per cent of the range you ran and ran, you just re-coloured it. And then suddenly… I always credit Trinny and Susannah because they said to middle-aged women, ‘You don’t have to dress your age’ and I think, for all their faults, they were very influential.” As a result of bossy Trinny and Susannah, repeated styles no longer cut it. The Boden customer wanted – still wants - new. But new in a Boden way. “There are hundreds of companies selling good versions of catwalk products but the important thing for me is that you can follow these trends but they’ve got to look right for the customer. There are some quite contentious trends at the moment – culottes, jumpsuits. We’ve done a jumpsuit, that’s done well. The peplum top, that was an absolute disaster. ”Why? “Not flattering. They make your hips look big. So that’s the acid test. Does she look good in it? I’ll say, if a Martian were to land and see women wearing these things would the Martian say you look really nice in that or you look ridiculous?'' Of course, it’s not the Martian but Johnnie Boden himself who’s the judge. Other trends he is currently struggling with include flares and high-waisted denim. ‘Would you wear a high waist?” he asks me. Yes. “Hmm. It’s a tricky one and I have to be led by the girls [his buyers and designers]. They’ll say, ‘We’ve got to have it”’ and sometimes I just say fine and occasionally I’ll think, no way.’ Loose, Bohemian styles don’t do it for his customer. ‘And there was a trend for outsized coats, which I was really opposed to and I fell quite vindicated when it didn’t work,” he says. “Our customer is nervous about oversized. They want to feel – the Americans particularly – pulled together.” Still, Boden has put its foot in the fashion water this season with its new Icons collection – a well-received range that includes stylish contemporary, more expensive pieces such as a big (some would say oversized) parka, neat tailored shirts, denim culottes and a printed tea dress. Johnnie even attended London Fashion Week for the first time in September. “Yes, it was good. Everyone was very friendly, there was a lot of energy. I thought the models were too thin though.” Having started his catalogue casting ‘real women’ – his friends – as a point of difference, he knows how important what models look like is to his customers. “The problem is that internally the staff are hard wired to go for the skinny model. They’ve been conditioned,” he says. “Actually in the early years we used some great models who have now become quite famous, like Caroline de Maigret. We used her for three years and then the team said, ‘She’s too old’ and I was really sad because I thought she was great, sexy.” It’s a tricky balancing act. “You don’t want to make the Marks and Spencer mistake of choosing those oversized models. Because it’s interesting how, when we have focus groups, we’ll show them size 12 models and they’ll say, ‘She’s a bit fat’. And then we’ve had problems in America where there was a very good 25-year old model mucking about in a lovely family shoot and they said, ‘She looks like the au pair’. I thought she was hot as hell…” Which was possibly the problem. Today the company is committing to further involvement with the fashion industry with its announcement on Future British, a programme to support new British designers as they build up their businesses. The winners for the inaugural season are: Caitlin Charles-Jones, a 26-year-old knitwear designer Samantha McCoach, 28, the founder of Scottish tartan brand Le Kilt, and the shoe designer Camilla Elphick, 26. Boden, in conjunction with the British Fashion Council, will give these winners financial support as well as business mentoring and marketing advice. “I remember, it’s bloody hard and it’s really nice to be able to help them,” says Boden. “We give lots of money to charity but this is much more authentic. We showed these girls round [the headquarters] this morning and their eyes… They were so flabbergasted by what they saw, you could tell.” There probably isn’t any one better to guide them than Johnnie Boden. For an individual to create a brand that has become as known and identifiable as Boden (whether you like it or not), and for it to survive the tough retail conditions of these decades, is no mean feat. From the beginning the old Etonian, former banker put himself on the line – using his own distinct voice for marketing – that jollyish, familiar middle class lingo that is now so firmly part of British branding, taken up by brands such as Innocence. “I know a lot of people look to us for that language. But it was bloody exhausting,” he says. “And unfortunately we slightly lost our confidence as we got hammered quite hard by the press. The whole ‘smug Johnnie and the middle class’ thing. That was quite bruising. So we toned it down a bit but it’s still there.” Having weathered the digital revolution – 90 per cent of sales come from online – next year Boden will put its neck out again by investing in bricks and mortar with a first London store. “It’s interesting how many strong brands have pretty rubbish shops actually,” he muses. “I think in terms of theatre Anthropologie is good. It’s like someone’s home. J Crew, the shops aren’t great.” What kind of atmosphere does he want his to have? “Lively, unexpected, uplifting. Rather like the catalogue. I don’t want to tell you too much but I’m having lots of debate on the décor. We’re building a mock shop at the moment and of course everyone’s very unhappy with my ideas.” He runs his hand through his hair, stares at the floor, frets some more. boden.co.uk  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge was quick off the mark in her promise to promote Indian designers during this week’s royal tour. For her second engagement of the trip on Sunday - a cricket match and tour of Mumbai’s most deprived areas - Kate wore a delicately printed georgette dress by Mumbai-born designer Anita Dongre. Dongre, who started her label seven years ago, told The Telegraph that Kate’s PA-turned-stylist Natasha Archer got in touch a month ago to request some clothes for the Duchess. “Her stylist emailed us and and we sent her a look book, then she came in and got some pieces for fittings,” says Dongre whose Rajasthan-inspired designs are already popular in India, where she has eight shops. However Dongre had no idea whether her designs had made the cut. “It was a real surprise. I was at home when I saw the pictures and was so delighted,” she says of seeing pictures of The Duchess playing cricket in her collection. All the more surprising was the fact that The Duchess’s team had altered Dongre’s design. The “Gulrukh” dress - from the SS16 Love Notes collection - was originally full length and included a traditional stole in matching fabric. “In India a lot of woman would wear this with trousers and a stole,” she says, pointing to the catwalk look from Lakme Fashion Week where the dress was shown in its original form. “Her stylist has taken the stole and converted part of that into the belt and then chopped it off so it can be worn as a dress. She’s amazing - it looks easy, breezy and so contemporary,” Dongre says of the DIY update by Natasha Archer. Archer - fondly known as Tash - began working at Kensington Palace as the Duchess’s PA but has added the role of stylist to her role over the past couple of years. She was first identified as one of Kate’s team of image-makers when she was seen carrying a suitcase into the Lindo Wing following Prince George's birth alongside her hairdresser Amanda Cook Tucker. Since then Archer has been credited with helping Kate to become more glamorous, regal and bold in her style choices. But, according to Dongre, Archer’s styling contribution is even more significant than first thought: customising Kate’s clothing to make them appropriate- and original- for her royal appearances. “She looked beautiful,” Dongre told The Telegraph from Mumbai. “I’ve always admired her sense of style. My clothes stand for a certain feminine elegance - I think she does the same.” And it seems that the famous ‘Kate Effect’ - whereby any item worn by the Duchess rapidly sells out - is still in full force. “We’ve been inundated with orders - especially from the US and UK,” she says of the influx which promted her website to crash temporarily. So, in a savvy business move, Dongre is now also offering Kate’s customised version of the dress. “The dress is still available online because we’re taking forward orders. I had a very small run introduction but people are willing to wait for it.” The website currently says that there is a 2-week wait for a $236.60 version of the dress worn by the Duchess while the original is for sale with a 6-week wait for $591.50. “The Indian media has gone completely gaga,” laughs Dongre. “Of course, we are now waiting to see what she wears next but it makes us feel very happy she’s wearing local designers.” Dongre says that the Duchess does have more of her pieces so is “keeping her fingers crossed” that we might see Kate wearing another of her designs before the week is out.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Trumps have shaken up the rule book on how to behave in public office and it’s causing some confusion further down the political ladder. Case in point this week has been Louise Linton, the 36-year old Scottish actress, recently married to Steve Mnuchin, Trump’s Secretary of the Treasury and a woman who attracted the wrath of many Americans with a rather ill-judged Instagram post. Monday saw her stepping off an official government plane after a trip to Kentucky with her husband, who was discussing tax reform with the senator. Maybe the topic had been a little dry, maybe Linton was bored, maybe she was still high on the honeymoon vibes, but why waste a good photo opp? So she posed for the camera on the tarmac, plane in the background, white suit, golden hair, bag crooked over an arm, scarf flying gently in the breeze and posted the picture for her fans. Come on, we’ve all done it. Maybe not on government time but what is social media if not an attempt to constantly impress and outdo all the people you care for in your life? This might have just scraped by with a rolling-eyed impatience from the people of America had Linton, an actress who has appeared in the film Cabin Fever and an episode of CSI: NY, not insisted on also tagging the brands of her luxury fashion apparel and accessories, just to, you know, really hammer home the point that she is living the dream. Yes, she really was carrying a #Hermes Birkin bag. No, your eyes weren’t deceiving you, the shoes were #ValentinoRockstud. #TomFord and #RolandMouret had also come along for the ride. The phrase “status update” has never rung truer. This did not go down well. After a severe dressing down by the public, which necessitated an official apology for her “insensitive” post, Linton may want to refamiliarize herself with the concept of stealth wealth.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The wardrobe choices made for Monday’s international Star Wars: The Force Awakens premiere were always going to be a hard act to follow.  Surely one of the most positive trends to come out of the fashion industry recently is that models are becoming increasingly visible the older they get. Today's example of an industry that looks like it's finally beginning to overcome it's youth-obsession is Naomi Campbell's campaign shoot for Italian underwear brand Yamamay.  The 46-year-old, who was one of the most powerful supermodels in the world back in the late 80s, proves she's still one of the most sought after faces in the industry with these Mario Testino shots. In November 2015 Campbell collaborated with the lingerie brand to design her own capsule collection of silky robes and luxurious underwear, called 'I Am Naomi Campbell.' Although her collaboration with a low-profile (in the UK, at least) brand might seem like an unlikely move, designing lingerie was a natural step for the model given her experience modelling for Victoria's Secret, Agent Provocateur and La Perla. This latest campaign shows a different, softer, side to the model. Instead of the purple silk robes and black suspenders she wore last time around, she is keeping it simple and much more natural in a pale T-shirt bra and matching briefs.  The 'Space' bra is from the brand's basic collection, and is designed to be a practical fit for women of all sizes. The bra cup is created from two flat layers with a 'spacer layer' in between to make it breathable and the stretch in the fabric means it can provide support for bigger sizes. Admittedly with her rock-hard abs and seemingly ageless skin, Campbell isn't exactly your 'average' 46 year old, but she is part of a group of grown up supermodels who are starting to call the shots in fashion. Last season Cindy Crawford, Claudia Schiffer and Naomi Campbell posed for Balmain, and Eva Herzigova, Yasmin Le Bon, Stella Tennant and Nadja Auermann were scooped up by Giorgio Armani.  "Fashion is much more open than it was, in terms of age, shapes and sizes," Rosie Vogel-Eades, fashion bookings editor of Vogue, who also has her own casting agency, previously told The Telegraph. "The people who are creating advertising have realised that they need to appeal to more of a 360-degree customer. It’s not the 18- to 25-year-olds who have the buying power now." This diversity is incredibly important to Naomi Campbell, who has claimed that she won't retire until the industry becomes more representative. “I didn’t work 28 years for it to be a trend," Campbell said in an interview with Nick Knight. "That's one of the things that keeps me wanting to work. I can't duck out yet; I feel I still have to represent.” One thing that is clear from the Yamamay campaign, however, is that Naomi Campbell is in impeccable shape. Back in 2014, Naomi Campbell gave Harper's Bazaar an insight into her workout habits, by detailing what she eats and drinks in an average 24 hours. On her menu was eight health-boosting drinks, including aloe vera and hot water with lemon and probiotics. She also noted that she does yoga or pilates, and then a dinner-time workout (in 2014, this was Zumba but we suspect she might have mixed this up these days.) Other Campbell rules include never eating past 8pm and doing a juice cleanse two or three times a week. A model who's honest about the work it takes to get her body in shape? Just another reason we're in favour of Campbell....  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Victoria's Secret models are often held up as the embodiment of perfection; seen as otherworldly creatures who never skip the gym, wake up with perfect bouncy hair and are tirelessly confident in nothing but their underwear. But Erin Heatherton has opened up about how the 'pressures to fill the demands of perfectionism' left her struggling with her body image. Instagram is often credited with perpetuating our obsession with perfectionism, with success measured by the number of Instagram likes you get on heavily-filtered images. But it can also be a platform for women to speak honestly about their body image. Heatherton posted an emotional piece about her struggles with her body confidence, which was accompanied by a picture of her wearing an 'Empowered by Failure' t shirt. The 27-year-old model, who was a Victoria's Secret Angel between 2010 and 2012, wrote: "In my moment of “failure,” I stood in the face of adversity. I was struggling with my body image and the pressures to fulfill the demands of perfectionism upon me. I am not perfect." She continues: "This feeling I once perceived as “failure” was, in truth, a powerful awakening for me to stand behind my purpose in life. I stepped away from hiding behind a fabricated version of myself. I no longer put actions behind my fears and insecurities." She finished the post by writing: "In the end, if you aren’t being true to yourself, then what the f*** is the point." In the post she tags in Empowered By You, which is an underwear brand which donates '20% of profits to microfinance loans to empower women out of poverty.' Of course she isn't the first model to speak out about struggling with body confidence.  Gigi Hadid has scored her second British Vogue cover, her thirteenth for the prestigious fashion magazine internationally. It's the latest major coup for the 21-year-old, who has enjoyed a meteoric rise in the modelling world the past three years. Along the way, she's also earned a reputation for being outspoken about body-shaming  and she addressed the topic again in the issue's accompanying interview. It's a cause which is bound to have endeared her to outgoing Vogue editor Alexandra Shulman who has previously spoken out against the impossibly tiny sample sizes created by fashion houses which in turn force models to conform to unrealistically tiny sizing.  In September 2015, Hadid hit headlines due to the candid open letter she posted to Instagram hitting back at trolls on social media who had suggested she wasn't thin enough to be a top model. "Yes, I have boobs, I have abs, I have a butt, I have thighs," she wrote. "Your mean comments don't make me want to change my body." Now, in her interview with Derek Blasberg, Hadid revealed the overwhelming support she had to her letter from her peers and reflected further on the pressures put upon models. "The response was crazy. From Victoria’s Secret Angels to my friends who are considered plus size, everyone texted me and said they appreciated me saying something," Hadid says. "The world puts so much pressure on fashion, then judges models for succumbing to that pressure." Shot by Mario Testino, Hadid appears in a high-slit silk dress on the March issue with a stripped back beauty look. Inside she poses alongside her brother, 17-year-old Anwar Hadid, who has just landed a Spring/Summer 2017 campaign for Hugo Boss. Despite her success- the model will soon unveil the second part of her collaboration with Tommy Hilfiger- a thick skin is required to deal with the dual pressure that comes from within the modelling industry and from those looking in via social media. Whilst a high follower count on Instagram often assists models in securing high-profile contracts, it's also the place they're most vulnerable to attack from naysayers. In a podcast with US Vogue  in 2016 Hadid said, "everyone is affected by the pressures that come from being on social media. We're all human. I'll never say that it doesn't affect me. Sometimes it's harder than others." Hadid is resolute in not allowing mean comments to knock her confidence in her body. "I never didn't like my body [growing up]. I was very athletic. I was proud of why my body was the way it was ... You do everything you can to be healthy and do what makes you feel good and feel happy. That's just always how I've looked at it," she added in the Vogue podcast. Part of Hadid's ability to rise above the criticism and remain grounded is no doubt thanks to her strong relationship with boyfriend Zayn Malik, who she began dating in November 2015. She spoke fondly of the singer in the new issue of Vogue, revealing that they both enjoy the simple things in life. “When I’m in LA I mostly stay in because it’s my time off and I like being with my boyfriend and doing art and cooking," she tells Vogue. "We like late-night movies and we order from this amazing place that does lattes and gingerbread cookies. I need coffee to stay up. I’m always like, ‘Babe, let’s go to a movie.’ Then I fall asleep halfway through and he’s like, ‘You’ve seen the first half of every movie out there and you have no idea how any of them end.’” See the full shoot in the March issue of Vogue, on sale Friday.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The star model at this season's London fashion week was not a newly-discovered young teenager- as is so often the case- but Jan de Villeneuve, a 72 year-old veteran model with a fabulous chic silver bob and the finest cheekbones a woman could wish for. Last Saturday evening, images of de Villeneuve striding the catwalk at Simone Rocha wearing a luxuriously cosy faux-fur coat and chunky platform sandals lit up social media. She was joined by fellow grey-haired beauties Marie Sophie Wilson and Benedetta Barzini as well as 50 year-old Cecilia Chancellor in Rocha's celebration of woman of all ages.  "This is my customer," the designer said after the show. "What I do is for all types of women and that's what I wanted to reflect in my casting." De Villeneuve's fashion week didn't stop there though. On Monday, she was back on the catwalk at Osman, showcasing an embroidered cape and cropped, wide-legged trousers.  "Life doesn’t end when you start getting a pension," de Villeneuve, who started modelling in 1966 told The Telegraph after her catwalk appearences. "Older women love fashion too. I’ve always thought it would be nice if people of all ages, shapes and sizes were included because that’s more relevant to day-to-day life." "The Simone Rocha show was wonderful, her clothes are totally amazing  and there were some wonderful tartan coats at Osman. It’s so fun to see all these things and try them on. It’s one of the joys of modelling". Rocha had decided to include a wider age range of models in her show, always a highlight of London fashion week, so de Villeneuve's agency- Models 1- asked if she wanted to go for a casting- "I just thought, why not?"   She's been in the modelling world for over 50 years and de Villeneuve says a lot has changed during that time. When she first began her career, models either did shoots or catwalks, but not both, with most fashion houses having in-house models to show their collections. But that began to change in the Seventies, when de Villeneuve took to the catwalk for designers she was friendly with like Bill Gibb, Ossie Clark and Thea Porter. Her first show was for Japanese designer Kenzo in Paris. "In those days, we had to do our own make-up and hair, then they would give you a few dresses to march around in," she remembers, adding that she would be paid in dresses. "Now it’s much more organised with an army of people doing make-up, hair and nails. Showbusiness and social media has come into it much more," she observes of the set-up at her most recent shows.  One might think that de Villeneuve has a complex beauty and wellbeing regime but refreshingly she's at pains to point out that that's far from true. "I would never want to have plastic surgery," she exclaims. "This weekend some of those pictures which appeared of me show that I have wrinkles. Perhaps I don’t always like it so much that I look older now, but I wouldn’t change it." She describes the simple beauty routine which has relied on to keep her looking brilliant for her age. "I don’t do anything special. I splash my face with water in the mornings 25 times. For years I have rubbed moisturiser into my skin before bed for about a minute if I can be bothered. I go to the gym maybe two times a week and I like to walk but I don’t buy expensive products. I have lemon juice and water in the mornings and eat lots of fruit. I used to detox a couple of times a year but I’ve always like nutritious food. It’s nothing that other people couldn’t do no matter what their size, shape or profession." Walking for Simone Rocha and Osman is just the latest in a long line of modelling adventures for de Villeneuve. Her career highlights include shooting a dog food commercial with Mario Testino- "I had to tuck a piece of chicken under my chin!"- and appearing on the cover of an all-ages issue of Vogue Italia shot in New York by Steven Meisel.  But her most treasured modelling memory was a three-week long shoot with Norman Parkinson in the Seventies. "We travelled through the South and West of America for British Vogue, it was just myself, Norman and the fashion editor and her assistant." De Villeneuve took a break from modelling to bring up her daughters and laughs that she missed the days of drugs and "big supermodel money". She has been taking jobs again since 1988, with her work ranging from high fashion editorials to T.K Maxx campaigns.  As such, she has amassed an ecelectic collection of clothes. "I'm a terrible hoarder but style on a budget is my credo," she says. "When I saw Gucci, I thought they must have raided my wardrobe from the 70s," she jokes, referring to Alessandro Michele's maximalist, vintage-inspired designs. Her two daughters, Poppy and Daisy, grew up raiding her wardrobe and now she's planning to save everything for her seven month-old granddaughter.  Now she's off to Paris to do a shoot with the avant-garde label Aganovich but she's still buzzing from London fashion week. "I was quite conflicted as a young model about making money from how you look. I’d gone to university and had a good degree so thought, ‘Should I be doing this?’ I railed against it when I was younger but now I don’t think about it because I look like an older lady. It was lovely this weekend to see there was interest in women of my age."          © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s the middle of January. Your skin hasn’t seen sunshine since July last year, in other words, aeons ago. Pale pink is the last thing you need to draw attention to this pallid tone, right? Ethereal dresser Rooney Mara has persuaded us otherwise. The Carol press tour quickly saw the 30-year-old establish barely-there pink as one of her signature colours (the other, in radical contrast, is black). With a snow white complexion, the ghostly rose embellished dresses tap wonderfully into spring’s romantic maximalist trend, but somehow manage not to wash out her features. Here’s how you can practice pale pinks too... With a blood red lip Mara somehow manages to disarm the tumbling grace of this Alexander McQueen gown (above). Rather than the nude studs, ruffles and cascading strands of chiffon, our eye is drawn immediately to her lip, and not the way the dress melts into her skin tone. Nineties-style chokers are enjoying a resurge of popularity. Unlike the popular black bands, a pale pink ribbon gives a wonderfully balletic air to a look and does not cut off the neck area.  The sci-fi hair 'do Mara sported with her ruffled McQueen at the BFI Film Festival also laced the look with a hard-edged surprise. We're not necessarily encouraging you to replicate this obscure double hair roll, but a scraped-back ponytail would provide the same impact. There’s nothing prim and girlish about letting the outline of your leg peek through your dress. Err on the conservative side and stick to carefully constructed sheer panels below the knee. Remember you want to undercut block nude looks, but not compromise your modesty. A rich camel coat warms up pale pinks, as opposed to washing them out as dark colours might. Wear yours over the shoulders of your dress so the mannish cut doesn’t steal the whole spotlight. A chunky camel knit would also look chic with midi and maxi pink skirts. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When the shoots are wrapped and the filming has finished, what sort of home does model and actor  Poppy Delevingne return to? It’s no surprise that the west London home of model and actor Poppy Delevingne is filled with style, glamour and a sense of fun. Throughout the house, which she shares with her husband James Cook (who is CEO  of his family’s aviation company), rich textures are combined with jewel and pastel tones,  metallic accents and chic, modern touches. Velvet cushions, fringed lampshades and figurative art prints give a feminine vibe, while pieces of vintage  furniture add an eclectic edge.  It is, in some ways, a house of  contrasts: the bedroom is soft and cocooning in powder-pink, while the sitting room is  party-ready, with dark, glossy walls, lightning-bolt mirrors and brass palm-tree lamps.  Yet the overarching aesthetic throughout is sophisticated, artistic and undeniably cool. Poppy has worked in fashion for over a decade, modelling for brands including Burberry, Anya Hindmarch and Louis Vuitton, but this summer she has indulged her love of interior design by teaming up with H&M Home, styling pieces from the company’s new autumn collection, and showing how to incorporate high-street pieces into a high-end look. We asked her what she loves most about her home and what inspires her decor choices. We bought it back in 2015 and moved in two years later. It  was a labour of love, to say the least. We gutted the whole house and removed all the staircases, so at one point, when  you stood on the doorstep, you could see from top to bottom. It was a complete overhaul, from renovations all the way through to decoration.  It’s very important to me. This  is the first home that I have owned, and I had so many ideas and things that I was inspired by. I also wanted it to be a reflection of James and me.  I would say it’s eclectic. There are parts of the house that are  totally modern, with clean lines and a look of simplicity; then others that are cosy and sumptuous, where we have used a lot of velvet and coated the walls in dark-coloured lacquer.   I love mixing old with new. So I tend to scour the antique shops on Golborne Road in Notting Hill and Kempton Market (a twice- monthly antiques market at Kempton Park Racecourse in Surrey), as well as The Conran Shop for modern pieces. I also love wallpapers by de Gournay and Barneby Gates, and fabrics by House of Hackney. My  favourite piece in the house is a custom-made velvet sofa in dragon’s-blood red by the interior designer Joanna Plant. I couldn’t have done the house without her.  I think you can use the pieces from this range anywhere. I love the use of marble, green tones and brass, and the glassware with gold edges is so chic and timeless.  It would have to be my pink bedroom. The walls are lined with linen and I immediately feel calm when I walk in. I also had my bath painted pink to match.  Much to the dismay of the tabloids, the loveheart bag that Pippa Middleton carried as she arrived at Covent Garden’s Bunga Bunga club last night was likely not a declaration of post-honeymoon bliss. Instead, the newlywed sister of the Duchess of Cambridge was giving a nod to the cause of the day, sporting a symbol with direct relevance to the Miles Frost Fundraiser she was attending and doing what fashion pundits would call ‘going literal’ with her clothes. This is the second time that British Heart Foundation ambassador Pippa has ‘gone literal’ at one of their events, as she also carried a similar clutch by Radley to one of the charity’s galas last year. Perhaps it’s in her contract to stockpile them, or perhaps she herself saw the opportunity to practise the strategy that her sister, and many other public figures, have been turning to recently. The Duchess of Cambridge is perhaps the most prolific champion of the literal dressing approach, wearing, say, a nautical-style, navy Alexander McQueen dress with epaulettes and frogging to open a sailing education centre in Portsmouth, or a floral printed Rochas dress to launch the Chelsea Flower Show. Sometimes the reference is subtle, and sometimes it’s glaringly obvious, but whatever nod the Duchess chooses to give via her clothing tends to go down well with her hosts, as well as giving her adoring fans (and the waiting fashion press) something new to talk about. Politicians are the other key group subliminally relaying the day’s headlines via their clothing, and on the campaign trail last month, Prime Minister Theresa May was seen employing sartorial tactics aplenty. Wearing Welsh designer brands while canvassing in Wales, or tartan jackets in Scotland may sound like a basic and blatant attempt to appeal to audiences, it can, when done the right way, successfully show that you’re connected to the cause. Pippa Middleton’s light entry to the realms of literal dressing shows that she feels some responsibility to impress as a public figure - a job that she didn’t really ask for, but that she’s trying to maximise in her own way. And as the paparazzi will be jumping over each other to take a picture of what she’s wearing anyway, she may as well utilise the opportunity to add a message into the moment. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Looking back, it seems almost bizarre that Theresa May has been reluctant to play the 'Tory Blue' card in her wardrobe so far as Prime Minister. After all, Margaret Thatcher often wore her political affiliation unashamedly head-to-toe, opting for cobalt dresses and suits throughout her years as PM for everything from conferences to elections and evening dinners. And every Tory leader since has had an electric blue tie or two in his arsenal. But today is the first time in her high-profile public life that May has been so vibrantly party political in her wardrobe choices.  As she travelled to Buckingham Palace to meet The Queen and state her intention to form a minority government with the support of Northern Ireland's DUP, May had changed out of the bright red Amanda Wakeley suit which she wore to her constituency count overnight- a choice which surprised many with its Labour-leaning shade- and into a distinctively Tory Blue skirt suit. The look,  by British designer Daniel Blake,consisted of  a modern tailored jacket with architectural peplum detailling and a shawl collar with a just-above-the-knee pencil skirt. The jacket is identical to the £595 'Orchid' jacket advertised on Blake's website. It is part of a Spring/Summer 2017 collection 'which can be  developed to a client's requirements.' She let the Tory Blue hue speak for itself, swapping her usual statement shoes for snakeskin kitten heels.   Daniel Blake appears to May's new favourite designer. After sourcing a black coat from his discreet label which specialises in immaculately tailored bespoke commissions, May chose Blake's pinstriped navy dress to announce the snap poll back in April, meaning she has bookended the seven week long campaign with his designs.  From announcing her intention to stand for the Tory leadership last summer to her eventual victory and the handing-over of power, May avoided blatant Tory Blue style statements in favour of more muted hues with the occasional flash of an unusual colour. Moving into Downing Street, May wore an navy dress coat by Amanda Wakeley with a fluoro yellow panel at the bottom. Meanwhile, her leadership campaign saw the former Home Secretary wear a Black Watch tartan Vivienne Westwood suit and an aubergine Escada shift dress.  During the campaign, May has worn a cobalt jacket by Diane Von Furstenberg on several occassions, a first hint of a more traditionally Conservative shade finding its way into her wardrobe.  Given the tumultuous events of last night's election, which saw May's authority severely diminished instead of strengthened as she had hoped, today was an appropriately crucial moment for the her to sartorially signal her party loyalty.  And although May swerved calls for her resignation, it did seem somewhat poignant that the blue suit was a modern take on the boxy blue blazer and co-ordinating skirt which she wore the night she first became an MP in 1997.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The stakes were high for Hillary Clinton at the first televised presidential debate last night. After her recent bout of pneumonia and the consequential questions about her health, Clinton needed to show the world that she was raring to take on Trump for the fight for the White House. She did this with meticulous preparations; hours of debate practice (sparring with the likes of  Alec Baldwin, who reportedly played Trump in rehearsals), poring over pages and pages of policy documents - and commissioning US designer Ralph Lauren to create one of her signature pantsuits in the fieriest shade of red. Yes, her choice of outfit (accessorised with subtly chic jewellery by Julie Vos) carried major importance, because have no doubt about it, whatever any figure in public life wears comes with meaning and shapes our perception of them (whether they - or you - like it). Clinton gets that and plays to it. Clinton's choice of red brings full circle a message first laid out in her debut post on Instagram, more than a year ago now. It showed a rail of red, white and blue tailoring and was captioned with the title of her book Hard Choices. Wry and knowing, the post signaled that Clinton was a step ahead of everyone else in understanding that what she wore - and, yes, how her hair and make-up were done - would be pivotal in creating the public image to win this election.  Consequently, Clinton has chosen suits designed by Ralph Lauren, probably the most-established and best-known American designer, for three key moments in the presidential campaign thus far. At her campaign's opening rally in June 2015, Clinton wore a cerulean blue Ralph Lauren suit with tapered-trousers, a slim lapelled jacket which hit flatteringly below the hips and a matching plain round neck top. Then appearing at the Democrat Convention to accept the Presidential candidate nomination, Clinton opted to wear a white Ralph Lauren suit. Given white is the colour of protest associated with the Suffragettes and Clinton was celebrating the achievement of being the first woman ever to be nominated by a major political party for the American presidency, her choice of outfit was widely interpreted as a feminist statement. Monday night's red means that Clinton has now covered off every colour of the flag with her Ralph Lauren wardrobe. But regardless of the trio it completes, red - a colour that stands for power and visibility - was a potent statement in its own right. It's not a 'good girl' colour, it says that the wearer has attitude and determination. For the Chinese, it also denotes luck and good fortune. If the white suit was about revelling in a moment of victory and taking a deep breath, red said that Clinton was determinedly on fighting form.  Choosing a bright colour was also a way for Hillary to stand out against the much taller and bound-to-wear-black/navy Trump (there had been some wrangling before the debates about the size of the lecterns they would stand behind, given she is almost a foot shorter than him). “Colour can change your attractiveness entirely and how people see you,” Nina McLemore, a workwear designer whom Clinton has called upon numerous times in the past, has told The Telegraph of why the Presidential candidate isn't afraid to use embrace block, primary colours. “What a woman wants is skin that has a pink touch to it, not grey or yellow which is what black does. I’ve given many talks to law firms accounting firms. I walk in and 70-80 per cent of the people are in black so of course they don’t stand out.” The collaboration with Lauren is fitting for another reason. In 2014, Clinton awarded Lauren with the James Smithsonian Bicentennial medal for donating millions of dollars to help preserve the delicate 'Star Spangled banner', the American flag raised at Fort McHenry, Baltimore in 1814 to celebrate victory over British forces. The flag inspired Francis Scott Key to write a song that eventually became the United States national anthem. Lauren, who has long used the stars-and-stripes flag as a motif in his all-American work, said he wanted to protect a crucial part of American history - and no doubt he'll feel the same way about being involved in dressing one of the candidates in what's shaping up to be one of the most hotly-contested presidential elections.  Yet, some critics have observed that Lauren might not be the smartest choice of designer for Clinton to associate herself with. "There’s a possible weak spot in the relationship," wrote Vanessa Friedman in The New York Times when Clinton wore Lauren to launch her campaign. "Because for a candidate who has been pushing her connection to, and understanding of, the middle class — and whose speech while wearing the pantsuit was largely about closing the income gap — Ralph Lauren is a relatively inaccessible brand. An average Ralph Lauren Women’s Collection pantsuit, which this was — not, in other words, a style from the more accessible line, Lauren Ralph Lauren — is a few thousand dollars... That is out of reach for most voters." But whilst it's true relatability is always an issue for politicans who are schooled to remember the price of a pint of milk, out of all the big name designers Clinton could have chosen, Lauren is the most accessible of them all with his diffusion lines. The woman or man in the swing states Clinton is trying to appeal to will hear Ralph Lauren and think of their jeans and polo shirts. And besides, no-one is criticising Trump for wearing wildly expensive tailoring. (He is, by the way - and his wife Melania wore Dolce & Gabbana.)   As for matching red lipstick to her red Ralph Lauren suit? US make up legend Bobbi Brown approves. "Whatever works in make-up to give you confidence, for some women it's concealer, for others it's a red lipstick," she told The Telegraph of the look, which attracted comment online during the debate. "Personally, I wouldn't be confident in a red lipstick because it doesn't suit me, but I feel my best with concealer and eyeliner. I always say you're either a red lipstick person or not. I don't think women should wear red lipstick if it doesn't suit them to try and feel confident. I thought the red lipstick worked for Hillary, I thought she looked good." There is constant bemoaning of the fact that high-profile women are more closely-scrutinised than men, but that, says McLemore, should be seen as an opportunity. “One of the things that I have noticed about the women who are chief executive officers or in high positions is that they are strong people and able to deal with really difficult challenges. They can be tough when they need to be tough but when there’s tension in the room they can deflate it with a sense of humour. It means the clothes you wear also can send that message of 'I’m a positive person’ – which is much more challenging for men in grey suits to project, short of resorting to a novelty tie."  Decisions of political clothing are Hard Choices, as Clinton has observed, but she chose well last night.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Game of Thrones fans were beside themselves on Monday night, as the self-proclaimed Queen from the south, Daenerys Targaryen, made her debut on northern soil. Needless to say, the draped silk dresses and breezy capes that had become the Khaleesi’s style signatures when she lived in Meereen were in no way adequate to insulate from the cold beyond the wall (winter has come, after all) and so she required a new wardrobe for the unprecedented occasion. The show’s costume designer Michele Clapton made a stand-out ‘fur’ coat for Daenerys, a striped black and white pelt accessorised with the character’s favourite three-headed dragon chain from the series, designed by jewellers Yunus and Eliza (and available to buy if you are a super-fan with a spare £2,600). “It was just extraordinary,” Clapton tells Making Game of Thrones of the coat’s design, which was armour-like in its structure with a high, standing collar to signify the character’s leadership qualities. “We created the fabric in the work room. It’s such a strong look for riding the dragon through the snow.” “Great to get such a positive reaction to Daenerys coat,” she wrote on Instagram yesterday, posting pictures of her initial sketch and the fabric development process. “Even better is that it is mostly fake fur and hand made in our own workroom… talented crew make costumes possible.” The fake fur in this case was constructed by Linea, but earlier in the series Clapton’s costumes made headlines after she revealed that she had sourced fabric for other fur-wearing characters, like Jon Snow and the Night’s Watch from IKEA. "These capes are actually IKEA rugs," she told an audience during a talk at the Getty Museum in Los Angeles, to great applause. "We take anything we can. We cut, and then we shaved them, and then we added strong leather straps, and breakdown which is like a religion on Game of Thrones." Anti fur organisation PETA had previously been in touch with Clapton when the series first launched, objecting to her use of fur. “Certain actors won’t wear it and we’ll respect that and we’ll always try to make it in fake fur instead,” she told The Telegraph at the time. “But when you’re depicting the things that we are a lot of the time it doesn’t work.” As a result Clapton says she will never commission new fur and has actively sought to find faux furs or, if real must be used for an effect, she will source vintage pieces from French markets. In short, you could have been forgiven for thinking that the car-to-table sashay was the fashion show everyone had come for. Graphic optical prints came on fur jackets and natty blazers. The change in business model is part of the see-now, buy-now strategy which many of the biggest fashion brands are now switching to. Ford is the first to show in this way but over the coming weeks, Tommy Hilfiger and Burberry will be among the other big names showing clothes which you'll be able to buy straight away.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
