 Pippa Middleton arrived for her wedding this morning wearing a spectacular lace-bodiced, high-necked wedding gown created by Giles Deacon. Her face was covered with a delicate bespoke tulle veil dotted with pearls and made by milliner Stephen Jones.  The bride also wore a Maidenhair fern tiara by Robinson Pelham,the Middleton family's go-to jeweller, and ivory satin pumps by Manolo Blahnik with pearl detailing, a customised version of the label's £715 Seneca bridal heels. As for her 'something old'? The same Robinson Pelham pearl earrings which she wore for her big sister's wedding in 2011.   "I was thrilled to work with Pippa on her wedding dress," Giles Deacon said of his collaboration with Middleton. "The dress is constructed with a cap sleeve, high neckline and features a corseted bodice with draping to the front and a heart-shaped detail at the back." "The bespoke silk cotton lace was hand appliqued to create an illusion of the dress having 'no seams'." "The lace bodice is embroidered with pearl detailing over an organza and tulle underskirt, which has layer upon layer to enable a floor-sweeping movement." "It's a privilege to show the craftsmanship that my team produces in London and a real testament to Pippa's support of British fashion," Deacon added. His coup - which had been rumoured since he was spotted leaving Middleton’s home last November- became a triumph for bride, designer and British fashion alike. Giles Deacon is an inspired, but perhaps unexpected choice from Pippa. When her engagement was announced last summer, it was widely thought that she would opt  for a gown by a traditional bridal designer from a Belgravia-based couturier au fait with designing for an English society wedding.  Until 2016, Deacon-who was born in the Lake District- showed his collections at London Fashion Week, delivering enchanting collections inspired by historical figures, mysticism and fairytales. Last year, Deacon announced that he would be pausing his ready-to-wear line to concentrate on couture instead, an area of his business which had grown over previous years. Besides commissions for private clients, Deacon had created striking red carpet looks for actresses including Cate Blanchett and Sarah Jessica Parker.  "For the last four years we've been quietly developing that side of our business and working with private clients and couture off the back of our fantastic red carpet pieces we've done and had great gals wearing," Deacon told The Telegraph at the time of the announcement. "It seemed like a good growth direction for us and to show it at Paris in Couture is where you show the best of what you can do." "There will be all sorts of ethereal, slightly darker romanticism and some witty touches," he explained of the refocussed strategy. While designing Pippa Middleton's wedding dress is undoubtedly the commission of a lifetime, it seems that Deacon has had mixed feelings about taking forays into wedding dress design in the past. "With wedding dresses, it's different. The bride wants X and the bride's mother wants Y and it becomes a nightmare," he admitted in 2009. Despite his reservations about managing the inevitable mother-daughter politics, Deacon's feelings on bridal design seem to have softened as the couture arm of his business expanded. "It'd be a logical place for us to go to and also seeing how popular the Bridal collections in New York are and how much they have grown," he later mused. In 2011, Deacon designed the non-Royal wedding dress of the year, creating a strapless, tiered skirt gown for model Abbey Clancey's marriage to footballer Peter Crouch. That dress is said to have taken two months of intense handiwork to create. Prices for Giles Deacon couture designs- which are made in his London atelier by a team of 20 staff- range from £8,000 for a bespoke day dress; the mid-tier eveningwear looks come in at about £24,000, and prices can spiral to £120,000 for extravagant wedding gowns. Deacon's girlfriend, the Game of Thrones actress Gwendoline Christie summed up the appeal of Deacon's designs in an interview last year: "He has two of my favourite attributes in artists: wild imagination and technical rigour. [His designs] can be practical, otherworldly, sculptural and mind-bending, but you always feel celebrated as a woman when you wear them… Their confidence somehow increases yours. It’s quite a power for a designer to have. His clothes have personalities."  "I want the label to be a very advanced couture house for the 21st century," Deacon added in the same interview.  A wish which he has come a step closer to fulfilling today.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Just as Barack Obama employed the power of rhetorical callback in his farewell address in Chicago last night - ‘Yes we can, Yes we did’ he said, reminding the world of the slogan which encapsulated his 2008 Presidential campaign - so Michelle Obama created her own sense of symmetry by choosing a dress by Jason Wu for one of her last appearances as FLOTUS. It was Wu who created the white, one-shouldered chiffon gown which Michelle wore for the first Inauguration Ball back in 2009, and to whom she has turned on countless occasions since then for everything from state dinner formality to smart-but-stylish daywear - as well as a second Inauguration gown in 2013.  A little over a week before she leaves the White House for the final time, Obama was understatedly elegant in a navy lace design by Wu - a designer born in Taiwan, raised in Canada, now living in New York - as she joined Barack and daughter Malia on stage after the speech. The moment held similar poignancy and meaning to the First Lady’s own final speech last Friday, when she chose a dress by Narciso Rodriguez, an American designer of Cuban descent, who was also responsible for her look at one of her earliest moments in the spotlight, making the dress she wore on the night that her husband was first elected POTUS. It is precisely this thoughtful recognition of fashion’s symbolic power which has made Michelle Obama so effective in her messaging throughout her eight years on the world stage. In the early days, she portrayed a deftly democratic touch by wearing plenty of affordable (and American) brands like J.Crew. She made an early decision to support emerging domestic designers, wearing clothes by Wu and his New York contemporaries like Joseph Altuzarra, Thakoon and Proenza Schouler. Then came designers from other countries, often worn as nods of diplomacy during foreign visits; Indian designer Naaem Khan was commissioned to create a gown for a state dinner with the Indian PM in 2009 while Brits like Christopher Kane, Roksanda and Preen were chosen during state visits to the UK. There has been plenty of fashion bravery from Obama too. She caused controversy when she picked a fiery red Alexander McQueen dress for a Chinese state dinner in 2011, eschewing an American designer. And she has developed a love for Azzedine Alaia, the Tunisia-born, Paris-based designer whose collections are highly exclusive. Towards the end of 2016, Obama had seemed to be moving even further from her policy of promoting American fashion, or choosing something with a political undertone. She wore dresses by Gucci twice; unashamedly maximalist and seemingly without any other agenda than ‘I really love this’. Ditto, a Dries Van Noten silk dress worn for the Presidential Medal of Freedom Ceremony. She did, however, mix her experimental attitude with excellent diplomacy when she wore a gold chainmail gown by Versace for the final state dinner of the Obama presidency with Italy's Prime Minister Matteo Renzi in November.  Obama has been assisted in her wardrobe decisions by two women during her time at the White House. Chicago-based retailer and buyer Ikram Goldman was responsible for carefully honing her image in the early days and was instrumental in that first Jason Wu dress. But after a couple of years, Goldman’s protege Meredith Koop took on the role. Goldman later told Vogue about the rather unorthodox delivery method which she used to get the Wu gown to Obama. “No one was allowed to see it. I go to Washington [D.C.], and I had the inauguration dress wrapped up in a tiny little bag in my backpack with her jewelry and everything she was going to wear that night. I walked with that dress crumpled up in my backpack to watch the President get sworn in,” she admitted. "It was all so secretive," Jason Wu told The Telegraph last year. "I was watching on TV, just like everyone else, to see what she was going to wear. As a designer, you want to be in fashion magazines, you want to have great shows. But to be a part of history, and that particular moment, that was a once in a lifetime." “She gave women the confidence to dress and express themselves in a way that made them feel comfortable, because she is an extraordinary, happy, and wonderful person,” Goldman added. “That exudes, and fashion just adds to it. You can’t have great fashion without a great attitude.” In an interview with Harper’s Bazaar, Koop discussed how she and Obama had embarked on a project to bring a greater variety of designers into the ‘First Lady’ fold.  "We really had to break that mold, highlighting designers from diverse backgrounds with varying levels of success and exposure became an important part of my role." "When [the first lady] wears an up-and-coming designer, it creates this feeling that anything is possible,” she continued.  “This is something the first lady talks a lot about with young people, how important it is to follow their dreams and work hard no matter what obstacles come their way. I wanted to translate that very message into her clothing." So, what will Michelle Obama wear to leave the White House next week? Isabel Toledo would be the name which completes the trio of Narciso Rodriguez and Jason Wu. She was another of Obama’s favoured designers in the early days, creating the lime green suit which she wore to the President’s first swearing-in ceremony. Toledo also has a Cuban background, which could be a clever nod to the Obama administration’s success in repairing relations with the country. Or perhaps Michelle Obama will surprise us and make a star of another on-the-rise designer one final time.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  She’s the Swedish-born ballet dancer turned actress who has taken Hollywood by storm, appearing in a string of hits, and winning a Best Supporting Actress Oscar in 2016 for her role in 'The Danish Girl'. Now, Alicia Vikander has followed in Angelina Jolie’s footsteps to gain six kilograms of muscle and don combat shorts and double revolvers as Playstation’s favourite action heroine, Lara Croft. Outside action-wear, her fashion credentials are more aspirational; for starters, she's a Louise Vuitton spokesmodel and Vogue cover star. So what is it about her sartorial choices, both on and off the red carpet, that have cemented the actress as a style star to watch? Firstly, it doesn’t hurt that 27-year old Vikander has the willowy limbs and graceful poise that ensure almost anything looks good - a combination of genetics and rigorous dance training at the Swedish Royal Ballet School in her formative years. Working with stylist Victoria Sekrier (the ex-model is Vikander’s sartorial right hand woman), she skates through awards seasons, premieres and appearances, perfectly balancing fashion-forward with entirely effortless. Versatile, timeless, with a getting dressed ease we all wish we could master, Vikander’s style blends understated minimal (sleek tailoring, neutral colours, pared back accessories) with an edge of bohemian - there’s something of the ‘Chloe-girl’ (a regular label in her wardrobe) about her style spirit- delicate ruffles, sheer details and pretty prints nod to feminine without being overly girly. As muse and model for Nicholas Ghesquire’s Louis Vuitton, it’s unsurprising that Vikander is a natural at red carpet dressing. And that Louis Vuitton is, of course, a staple in her event repertoire. Custom designs by the French house make up a large proportion of her red carpet appearances. In terms of silhouette, she is apt to mix it up, appearing one day in a high-necked, all-over lace gown, and the next a strapless creation, slashed (ever-so-elegantly) at the navel. Vikander punctuates her loyalty to Vuitton with a host of other big names - Gucci, Rodarte, McQueen. But, she is also an avid supporter of more under-the-radar fashion brands. Barbara Casasola is one of her favourites - the Brazilian-born, London-based designer’s clean lines and modern use of colour chime perfectly with Vikander’s aesthetic. And she is partial to sleek, modern designs by Gabriela Hearst, Brock Collection and Rosetta Getty. Away from the high-octane glamour of the red carpet Vikander’s ‘off-duty’ style is equally covetable. In a recent interview with The Telegraph, she described her look as ‘Scandi simple’ and the description rings true. Her day-to-day wardrobe (read flying/shopping/city living) rotates a series of tailored trousers, crisp shirts, cashmere sweaters and classic coats - always finished with a Louis Vuitton bag. The palette tends towards neutrals - tan, camel, navy, black - shot through with hits of colour and print. Several of the labels which underpin the actress's wardrobe are stylish names with a Scandinavian connection. Rodebjer, based in New York and founded by a Swedish designer, delivers luxury staples which recur in Vikander’s arsenal - slouchy sweaters, cropped trousers. Stockholm-based label Toteme was founded by influencer and editor Elin Kling; Vikander is a fan of their outerwear. And the actress has worn several pieces - from dresses to sweaters - by LA-based Anine Bing. Founded by a Dane, the label’s sleek staples and pretty prints chime perfectly with Vikander’s downtime aesthetic. She fuses these with a sense of dressed-down, Californian cool - think Sweatshirts from Ragdoll LA and luxury basics from Vince. Add in a pinch of European chic - French labels Sandro and Maje deliver just the kind of interesting pieces with the nonchalant edge that runs through the actresses wardrobe. On holiday, the bohemian edge that runs through Vikander’s style becomes more pronounced, wearing broderie anglaise, paisley prints and ethereal silhouettes from the likes of Zimmermann and Isabel Marant’s whimsical diffusion brand, Etoile. One thing's for sure, whether hopping aboard a yacht in Ibiza, walking the red carpet in LA or wandering the streets of London, Vikander's fresh, elegant, and completely effortless looks are setting her on the path to style icon status. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Cannes Film Festival kicks off tomorrow night, with a host of stars set to descend on the red carpet, including Nicole Kidman, Uma Thurman and Kristen Stewart. The event is a fashion spotter’s Riviera paradise, as the stars tend to choose European designer names and go for all-out Old Hollywood glamour, in honour of the festival’s 70 year history, and the film icons like Grace Kelly and Audrey Hepburn who came before them. Here’s our guide to what should be the most exciting red carpet looks of the week... Uma Thurman and Jessica Chastain join the jury for this year’s competition, meaning that we can expect glamour from the off. The two Hollywood power-stylists Elizabeth Saltzman and Elizabeth Stewart work with the actresses respectively, meaning that they should make for a dramatically glamorous red carpet duo on opening night. Dates for your diary: Cannes opening ceremony (Wednesday 17th May)  Nicole Kidman is set to be this year’s queen of Cannes with four films to promote, which means her stylist Julia von Boehm will be working overtime. Von Boehm took a lot of risks with Kidman’s recent awards season looks (the actress was nominated at the Oscars and the Golden Globes for her role in Lion) and opted for quirkily embellished looks by Armani, Chanel and Gucci, the latter of which came complete with sequinned parrots on the shoulders. What to expect in Cannes? More megawatt sparkle and more big European names. Dates for your diary: Premieres for How To Talk To Girls At Parties (Sunday 21st) The Killing Of Sacred Deer (Monday 22nd) Top Of The Lake (Tuesday 23rd) and The Beguiled (Wednesday 24th)   Two major stars will take to the red carpet on Thursday evening, with Julianne Moore and Vanessa Redgrave appearing one after the other. Moore will promote her role in Wonderstruck on the Grand Theatre Lumiere red carpet, before Redgrave will make her directorial debut with Sea Sorrow. We predict a Chanel showstopper from Moore’s long-term stylist Leslie Fremar, but are calling Redgrave as fashion’s one to watch, after she was spotted on the front row at London Fashion Week designer Roksanda Ilincic’s show in February. Dates for your diary: Premieres for Wonderstruck and Sea Sorrow (Thursday 18th) Kristen Stewart will present her second directorial effort, Come Swim, on Saturday and, as at pretty much every Cannes Film Festival she’s been to to date, it’s likely she’ll shun a gown in favour of something a little more casual. Stewart often picks a shift-style mini-dress, or a pencil skirt and t-shirt combo, in a statement against traditional red carpet glamour, however, as said tee is usually made by Chanel, her look is still pretty fabulous. Dates for your diary: The premiere for Come Swim (Saturday 20th)  She had a phenomenal fashion run as she promoted Elle last year and, after taking a break from the limelight for a couple of months post-The Oscars, Huppert is set to return to the red carpet at Cannes next week to promote her new film Happy End. Expect more elegant Chloe dresses, more Armani Prive sparkles and more edgy jewellery from stylist Jonathan Huguet. Dates for your diary: The premiere for Happy End (Monday 22nd) The annual amfAR Gala always falls in the middle of Cannes and is always a supermodel-fest; Heidi Klum, Jourdan Dunn and Adriana Lima attended last year. It’s often seen as the chance for those who don’t actually work in the film industry to dip their toes into the Riviera’s red carpet scene - and the dress code is usually sparkle-y, spangly and barely-there.   Dates for your diary: The amfAR Gala (Thursday 25th) © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Upstairs at Café de Flore is Sofia Coppola’s safe place for interviews. Her Paris apartment is a stone’s throw away and her parents’ apartment, where she often stayed as a teenager, is around the corner. It’s a Friday, sunny, and the lunch crowd is lingering, some eating tuna niçoise, some – like the louche young man planted in the corner with his laptop – being conspicuously literary, clearly conscious of the connection the café has to Paris’s people of letters.  Sofia, 44, picks her way through the crowd, smiling anxiously. She’s slight and dressed in dark clothes, but her clear skin and white teeth stand out across the room. When she arrives, she speaks so softly it’s like a murmur. She makes small talk about travel then stops, distracted by the window boxes blooming green and pink. ‘Oh,’ she says. ‘The flowers. Sorry. I haven’t been here since the winter. I haven’t seen that.’ There’s a sense that she’s a beat apart from everyone else. She reacts to questions with a kind of vague surprise. It’s hard to imagine her voice booming across a film set, like her father’s – Francis Ford Coppola, the grand auteur of 20th-century American cinema – is said to. But it certainly hasn’t held her back. As a kid she acted in her father’s films, but later decided to get behind the camera. She is the writer and director of six features, including Lost in Translation – for which she was nominated for three Oscars and won for Best Writing – The Virgin Suicides and The Bling Ring. Only the third woman ever to be nominated for a directing Oscar, she seems bashful about her achievements. ‘I don’t really think about it,’ she says. ‘Although maybe more now. I was asked to do a book of my work and I thought, “Well, there are so many books about men directors, maybe I should, just so that there are  more female voices out there."  But her lofty achievements do not exclude an interest in fashion – or beauty. We’re meeting because she has been collaborating with Louis Vuitton, reworking the original bag she designed for the brand in 2009, which she carries today in her favourite navy blue. ‘It’s a good size, it fits a lot,’ she says – revealing the inside of the bag, bulging with boxed French creams and lotions that she just swept up from the pharmacy. Given her flawless skin that appears bare except for a flush of sheer colour on her cheeks, I should have demanded the names and prices.  The newer version of her bag comes in a perforated leather – ‘I thought that was cute for spring’ – and with coloured piping. It looks like a small, chic sportsbag from the 1980s. She hasn’t got one herself yet, but she wants one in white for the summer. She started working with Louis Vuitton after making Marie Antoinette (2006), when she was taking time off from films to look after her elder daughter Romy, now nine (she also has a younger daughter Cosima, six, both with the French musician Thomas Mars). She has been friends with Marc Jacobs, who was then Vuitton’s creative director, since the 1990s. ‘And because of Marc, I met the bag department and they have a tradition of doing custom-made bags, so I did one and we turned it into a line. I guess it was in that time where bags were all about charms and hardware and just big, and so I designed something simple that my friends and I would like.’ She doesn’t do fuss. ‘No, but I want to look put-together even if I’m running around. I like something that’s not specific to a season that you can have for years and years. The quality’s beautiful. And for me it’s fun going into the office. I never have a regular job where I do that. Working somewhere like Vuitton, where they have every material you can choose from and they can make samples of anything you can think of, it’s a dream way to be creative.’  I wonder how the word ‘muse’ sits with her. ‘I don’t think of myself like that, but I’ve always loved fashion since I was a kid,’ she says. ‘I was obsessed from a really young age and when I was a teenager my parents encouraged it. I think my dad enjoyed it, he’d always ask my opinion about style.’ With a lot of stellar connections, doors swung open for Sofia. As a teenager she interned at Chanel for two summers. ‘I loved it. I’m from a small country town [albeit the Coppola vineyard in California] and there weren’t any like-minded people that were very sophisticated and my friends were, you know, pre-internet, so we weren’t connected. I used to get The Face  in the mail and that was my connection to the outside world. So to come to Paris in the 1980s was so exciting.’  She wasn’t planning to be a fashion designer. ‘I thought I’d be a fashion editor – like Diana Vreeland or something. I didn’t expect to work on films.’ There are possibly as many devotees of Sofia’s personal style as there are of her movies. She has been a permanent member  of the Vanity Fair Fashion Hall of Fame – a distinction bestowed on the likes of Coco Chanel and Lauren Bacall – since 2007, after appearing on the US magazine’s best-dressed list year after year. Today she is working her signature pared-down style in a navy striped Sonia Rykiel jumper, black jeans and sweet black Valentino block-heeled Mary Janes. She may have been a country girl, but she was surrounded by glamorous people. One of her first memories, she has said, is of sitting on Andy Warhol’s knee. But what she loved about them was not the showbiz razzmatazz but ‘the detail. How people’s personalities came through in their style.’ One family friend who she always thought tremendously stylish was Aurore Clémente, a French actress who was cast in Apocalypse Now and married Francis Ford Coppola’s production designer, Dean Tavoularis. Clémente had been a model who broke the rules by not wearing make-up and had her own simple, classic style. ‘She was this really chic woman – she always wore a man’s shirt, but before everyone else did. I also loved people like Agnès B in the ’80s. The way Parisian women dress, it doesn’t look like a lot of effort has been put in, but they always look chic and interesting. That made an impression on me.’  She says she doesn’t think about her style, but admits ‘a kind of uniform helps’. When she’s working, she wears a Charvet man’s shirt, made in Paris. ‘There are a few things I wear all the time – Acne jeans, the staples that you just know you like and don’t have to think about too much. And then it’s fun to dress up for special occasions.’ But mostly you will find her wearing navy blue. ‘Oh, it’s so boring!’ she exclaims. ‘My friend who designs shoes at Louis Vuitton, he’s always laughing at me. “Do you want it in navy blue, Sofia?” and I’m like, “Um, yes, I do.” My memoir will be called: Does This Come in Navy?’ Her daughters may have different ideas. Romy is currently hankering after a pair  of ‘emoji’ leggings that apparently all the kids are wearing in New York. She has also started questioning Sofia’s taste. ‘I was wearing those Tod’s driving shoes with the fuzzy lining [shearling] to take her to school and she said, “Why are you wearing slippers?” I looked down and she had a point.’ This summer, after directing La Traviata in Rome – her first opera – she’ll start working on her next film, The Beguiled, a remake of a 1971 Clint Eastwood film about a girl’s boarding school, starring Elle Fanning, Kirsten Dunst and Nicole Kidman. ‘I’ve never worked with her before but I’ve always wanted to,’ says Sofia of Kidman. ‘And to have the three of them together…’ She enjoys creating stories about women. ‘It’s hard for me to watch a movie with only men in it, without female characters. I can’t relate to it. I grew up around all boys and men,’ she adds, ‘my dad’s sets were mostly [dominated by] men and there were my brothers and cousins. I was with boys all the time.’ Did she have to shout to get heard? ‘No, because I was like the baby girl I got a lot of attention in an all-male family.’ She smiles. ‘But I do feel like I’m very into my feminine side because of that.’ By the time Sofia has left, adding a navy Louis Vuitton donkey jacket to her chic ensemble, the conspicuous typist has somehow managed to pass on his scripts to Sofia’s publicist. A woman in her 70s, possibly an academic, who had been having an erudite conversation with her lunchmate about the Middle East, leans over and says, ‘Is that woman you were talking to who I think she was?’ On confirmation, she is pleased. ‘She looks so like she does in her photographs,’ she says approvingly.    The SC Bag PM, from £2,480, is available from the end of May. In 2015, the Duchess wore a classic black dress-coat by Catherine Walker for the annual Irish celebration with a khaki hat, and the year before she opted for a tonal ensemble by way of a green dress-coat and jade accessories, both years finishing her look with a shamrock brooch worn on her lapel for the parade at Aldershot Barracks. There has also been a considerable amount of deliberation ahead of the Duchess' state visit to Paris this weekend, concerning what she will step out in in the city of chic.  Fashion designers have so far been divided on whether or not they want to partake in dressing the new First Lady. But one label that has definitely set its sights on Melania Trump is anti-fur organisation PETA. Their own first lady of sorts, Pamela Anderson, tells us that she has taken a direct approach in her attempts to woo Melania. “[It all started] when I saw that Melania Trump wore Ralph Lauren, which is a fur-free brand, to the presidential inauguration,” explains Anderson. “I thought we should send her a beautiful coat in the hope that she will wear it and inspire more women not to wear real fur when the alternative is just as glamorous. Eco-fur is warm, soft, less expensive than real fur, made from recycled materials, and machine washable.” As such, Pamela and PETA worked with Only Me, a Russian company that makes eco-friendly furs, to produce a black Persian lamb-look coat with a vegan leather sash belt, aiming to tie in with the winter collections that are currently hitting the runways in fashion capitals around the world. Knowing that everything Melania wears will now make global front pages and be heavily scrutinised, PETA’s founder, Ingrid Newkirk, says that they couldn’t have picked a more prolific ambassador to target. “Melania is a fashion icon now whether people like it or not,” Newkirk says. “We decided that since the world is looking at Melania Trump, we would ask her to be a style icon with a heart. Michelle Obama has never worn fur, the Bush wives never wore fur. When Nixon was in office he made a statement about the Republican ‘cloth coat’ and his wife never wore fur. So Pam is saying to Melania, ‘please keep this going’.” Anderson reveals that she also sent a handwritten note with the coat to the First Lady, hoping to appeal to her on a personal level. “I believe in being proactive and positive,” she tells us. “I know it will be meaningful to her coming from me, as an authentic gesture amidst a lot of negativity in the world. I thanked her for not wearing fur at the inauguration and told her that by remaining compassionate in her fashion choices, she will warm the hearts of many.” Let us now stay tuned to see whether the First Lady will deliver.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  As a three year old who is estimated to be worth £2.4billion to the UK economy, Prince George no doubt has designer babywear sent to Buckingham Palace daily. But for today’s Trooping Of The Colour ceremony, the Duchess of Cambridge opted to put Prince George in old clothes - and not just any old clothes but the exact same outfit Prince William wore in 1984. The blue-trimmed peter pan collar shirt and shorts set Prince George was wearing on the Buckingham Palace balcony today is the outfit his dad Prince William first wore to Prince Harry’s Christening in the early 1980’s. It’s not the first time Prince George has been seen wearing his dad’s old clothes. For last year’s Trooping of the Colour the toddler wore a blue frilled romper set Prince William had also worn at the ceremony as a two-year-old, which had been carefully stored away afterwards. And whilst the pink collared dress Princess Charlotte wore for today’s Trooping of the Colour is new, it also fits with The Duchess of Cambridge’s tendency to put her kids in retro-inspired clothes for formal occasions. British childrenswear designer Rachel Riley - known for her ruffled socks, Edwardian smock dresses and romper sets - has become one of the Royal kids go-to designers. Prince George has worn Rachel Riley outfits for most of his official outings, including Princess Charlotte’s Christening and the portrait that was released to commemorate the Queen’s 90th birthday. “They have chosen a very traditional look and are a traditional family,” Riley has told The Telegraph of why she believes the Duchess of Cambridge has chosen to patronage her label. “We have been doing very similar things for 18 years in that our collection is classic. The reason why I design clothes that way is because if they wear very simple things, it’s about the child, and it’s timeless in that you can’t really date a specific photo or put them in something that seems out of date. I think they are going for clothing that is classic and timeless, rather than clothes that draw attention to them.” Although the London-based designer is inspired by traditional children's clothes, she modernises the styles. “I look at photos of that historical period and of course what the royal children wear, but it has to have look relevant for today," she explains. "For example, Prince William wore a shirt and bloomer set, I don’t think we’ve ever seen Prince George in bloomers and I don’t think he would today. But shorts with turn ups is a traditional look, but is still relevant for today. When they are little, children traditionally would always wear shorts.” And just as anything the Duchess of Cambridge wears becomes an instant sell-out, so her kids are buoying up the retro kidswear market. "There has been a revival in the UK of parents buying into a more traditional way of dressing their children, which is reminiscent of how they, or their parents, dressed as children. We've noticed this especially since the birth of Prince George,” says Simona Saraz, Head Buyer at Igloo Kids, which specialises in designer childrenswear. Which is perhaps all the more reason Kate is keen to bring out William’s old vintage items when she can - at least, no competitive Norfolk mothers can replicate them. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Two of the fashion industry’s biggest names, Marc Jacobs and Tom Ford have insisted that they won’t be dressing Melania Trump any time soon, despite fellow icon Tommy Hilfiger’s comments last week that ‘any designer should be proud to dress her.’ ‘I have no interest whatsoever in dressing Melania Trump,’ Jacobs told WWD. ‘Personally, I’d rather put my energy into helping out those who will be hurt by [Donald] Trump and his supporters.’ Sophie Thealletwas the first designer to state that she would be boycotting any opportunity to clothe the new First Lady, releasing an open letter on Twitter that damned the Trump presidency. While some designers say that their reasoning is purely political, though, others have taken a more direct aim at Melania’s personal appearance. Tom Ford insists that he’d made his decision ‘years ago.’ ‘I was asked to dress [Melania Trump] quite a few years ago and I declined,’ he told The View. ‘She’s not necessarily my image.’ Melania’s signature version of power-dressing (a formula of sheath dresses, nude Louboutin shoes and expensive-looking handbags) divides opinion amongst the fashion elite, as many suggest that her glamazon vibe isn’t in-keeping with their ‘natural beauty’ or 'effortless style' ideals.  But for Ford, the rationale of why First Ladies shouldn't be wearing his designs goes further. ‘Even had Hillary won, she shouldn’t be wearing my clothes. 'They’re too expensive,’ said Ford, whose average day dress costs £3,000. ‘And I don’t mean that in a bad way. They’re not artificially expensive. It’s how much it costs to make these things. But I think to relate to everybody, you shouldn’t necessarily [wear such expensive clothes].’ The View’s host did, however, point out that Ford has once dressed Michelle Obama when she was going to Buckingham Palace for dinner with the Queen. ‘That, I thought, was appropriate,’ he reasoned. ‘I live in London, and so that made sense.’ Slovenian Melania, a former model who posed nude in her early career, wore looks by designers including Gucci, Roksanda and Ralph Lauren while on the campaign trail, however several designers were keen to point out that she had bought them ‘off the rack’ (or on Net-A-Porter) rather than by collaborating with the designer on a bespoke piece. Which is why American designer Cynthia Rowley has perhaps given the most sensible response of all to the burning ‘would-you-dress-Melania’ question.  ‘In the midst of this heated debate, the question actually seems somewhat irrelevant,’ she told WWD. ‘She can simply purchase whatever she wants, so how can we control it?’   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  I grew up in New Zealand at a time when fashion wasn’t really on the radar anywhere in the world unless you were buying haute couture in Paris. The thing for me was always music. I found David Bowie around the time of Space Oddity – everything he said and did was meaningful to me. He gave me a licence to be free. At school I also adored words. I wrote and illustrated my own books and, when I moved to London in 1974, I lived in a squat in Kilburn and did lots of music writing. In those days you could call up a pop star, ask to interview them and they would probably say yes. In that respect, my career path was very different from that of the young writers I work with today. They all need a plan, whereas everything that happened to me was a happy accident. I ended up in Toronto and the only place I could get a staff job was at a fashion magazine called Toronto Life  Fashion. This eventually led to my own TV show, Fashion File. I later joined Style.com and today I’m the resident fashion critic at the Business of Fashion website. I’m enthralled by fashion. It’s the mirror of our world. It takes so long to make a film or write a book but collections are created in weeks. They’re a reaction to what’s happening. Writing about fashion is like a game because it’s so open to interpretation. It’s easier to write a funny, snappy review of something you hate – though I often love the things that others dislike. Either way, the more you bring to a review, the better the writing is. An aspiring fashion writer should be curious, enthusiastic, fearless – and true to themselves. Often shows I see will bring cultural references to mind. I used to be wary of putting those into my write-ups, but changed my mind when I saw other reviewers do so, and now I’m known for it. Overall, womenswear is crazed and uptight, but it can be richer to write about than menswear, which is more relaxed. Sometimes I have to critique people I care about, or write bad things about my friends. Luckily they understand it’s just my job.  We have a confession to make. We might have misjudged Rebecca Hall. The British actress’ early career was defined by proper characters - nerdy Rebecca in Starter For 10, prudish Vicky in Vicky Cristina Barcelona - that seemed to chime with her own Cambridge-educated, English Rose persona. Then along came 2012’s Lay the Favorite, which saw Hall play a young cocktail waitress, who also happened to pursue lucrative sidelines in lap dancing and gambling. Her roles since have been equally diverse, and light years away from the polite ones we often think of her playing. Coupled with a choppy bob cut (initially snipped in 2014 and creeping up her ears each year), and an expressed interest in minimal, modern red carpet wear, Hall is definitely not as clear-cut as her résumé might kid us. New to Instagram - her profile claims she is ‘taking it one day at a time, battling my confusion and ambivalence about social media…’ - and currently on The BFG press circuit, the 34-year-old has once again made her way onto our radar. Her avant-garde outfit flourishes have commanded our attention almost as much as her witty Insta captions, and so we set about finding the formula behind Hall’s new red carpet success. Here’s what we learnt... White-and-black are Hall’s go-to shades, but make no mistake, this doesn’t qualify her as ‘safe’. Look closely, and each piece she wears has an abstract flourish to it. The white Dior AW16 dress she wore to the London BFG showcase, for example, featured subtle drop waist pleats and a high, wrap neckline that one wouldn’t expect from a fresh summer midi. For the glitzy LA premiere of The BFG, in which Hall plays Mary, the actress chose a cut-out Dion Lee bustier top and trapeze skirt with asymmetrical hemline. Plucked from Lee’s Resort 2017 collections, Hall stamped herself ahead of the curve and not afraid to experiment with silhouette and proportion. Hall is in good company with her choppy bob, as both Cate Blanchett and Sienna Miller enjoy the mussed-up side-sweep. The hairstyle not only gives edge to her whole look, but is the perfect platform to show off unusual earrings (Hall favours Delfina Delettrez and Eddie Borgo). Hall might be a fan of Dior and Valentino, but she was also comfortable being photographed in Balenciaga and Tome in Tank magazine’s summer 2016 issue. Brooklyn-based cool girl brand Suzanne Rae and budding celebrity favourite Monse pepper her day looks, and illustrate that she has got her finger on the pulse.   All in all, we think you'll agree Hall is the ideal grown-up dressing muse for the summer of 2016.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Lottie Moss has already walked at Paris Fashion Week and appeared in the pages of US Vogue, but she was yet to land her first cover - until now. Kate Moss’ 18-year-old half-sister has just unveiled her first magazine cover, for L’Officiel Netherlands, and she's got off to a sterling start with not one but three suitably high-fashion covers.  In one image, shot by singer-turned-photographer Bryan Adams, she wears a ruffled pink Gucci dress with a sequin bow detailing at the chest (a look which has already been worn by Dakota Johnson). In the second image she wears a pink tweed Dior dress, and in another cover, clashing Prada prints and oversized green circular Prada earrings. Lottie has so far adopted her sister’s tactic when it comes to the press: whatever you do, say very little. She is yet to go into any real depths about her relationship with her big sister, but according to the Daily Mail, she told the magazine that she tries not to compare her career to her sister's.  She says: "I am who I am and I do what I want, whether that is modelling or anything else. The success of my sister does not affect me in my choices. I feel no pressure in that respect." She also told the magazine that despite her surname, she gets very nervous when she meets A Listers: "My mother must laugh: "Your sister is Kate Moss and you become nervous when you meet a celebrity?" Lottie made her modelling debut two years ago, appearing in the pages of Teen Vogue and making her runway debut at Sonia Rykiel in March of last year. But recently her career has cranked up a notch: she was in an editorial for US Vogue with Kylie Jenner and Bella Hadid and was recently named the face of Botkier handbags.  Something tells us this won't be the last time we see Lottie looking back at us from the newsstands.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When the great white future hope of the Royals (aka The Cambridges) landed in Canada for the start of their latest foreign tour, last week, it was as a perfectly colour-co-ordinated family in navy blue.  Despite a ten-hour flight with two children under four, the Duchess herself looked ready for business in a Jenny Packham fitted dress and elegant hat. The hair seemed glossier - maybe a little darker – and bigger and bouncier than ever (thanks to the £300-a-day skills of hairdresser Amanda Cook-Tucker, who could be seen descending the rear steps of the Royal plane), and her outfit was custom-tailored with a slightly higher waist to lengthen her legs. Kate had set her stall out from the off: free from the awkward fashion deliberations that must have dictated last foreign tour (wearing high-price luxury clothes to visit street children in India is never a good look), this time she was going full on glamour. Over the next eight days, there was a killer £2k customised Dolce & Gabbana dress in forest green (a great colour on her) and a winning £1,190 CH Carolina Herrera red coat - an ensemble which had more than a touch of the Jackie O about it. At one point it even looked like she’d broken out of her safe-but-staid favoured patent nude court habit, with some new chunky heeled Tod’s shoes. The £41,487 estimated total cost of this year’s entire wardrobe marks a big difference from the last time the Duchess visited Canada in 2011 - when it totted up to approximately £19,065. Then, the newlywed Kate veered from outfits akin to something a City secretary might wear for after-work drinks, to old-fashioned matching dresses and coats in square-cut shapes that could have been borrowed from her mother, or even the Duchess of Cornwall’s wardrobes.  Kate was still mastering the art of diplomatic frockery, too – throwing in a nod to the host country, while still actually looking stylish. Looking back, her Canada day outfit of white Reiss shift dress (which she’d recycled from her engagement shoot) with a red, maple leaf-shaped hat was rather dressing-by-numbers (or flag motifs).  By contrast, on this trip she took the red theme and ran with it: the asymmetric-bodiced, midi-length Preen by Thornton Bregazzi dress (designed by a London based husband and wife duo, and again a new label for the Duchess) was perhaps the best thing she’s ever worn. She looked young, fabulous, and modern – and there was no mistaking this for something Carole Middleton might sport for Ladies day at Ascot. (Extra points, too, for Prince William sporting a burgundy colour tie that complemented That Red Dress.) At 34, with two pregnancies behind her, it looks like the Duchess is finally coming into her own keen sense of style confidence. And why not. She’s slowly – with the help of PA-turned-stylist Natasha Archer - educating herself away from safe designer choices and dipping a toe into previously unchartered style territory. The first signs of a sea-change came at this summer’s Trooping of the Colour ceremony. Such was the superstar glamour of her white Alexander McQueen coat-dress, Philip Treacy hat – slanted with that delicious pink flower on the side - and fashion-savvy oversized Balenciaga pearl earrings, that she almost stole the show from the neon Queen. Then came a dare-we-say-it rather sexy, white off-the-shoulder number by Barbara Casasola (a Brazilian born, London based designer who shows at London Fashion Week) for an Art Fund event at the Natural History Museum. But this Canadian tour has cemented the fact that Kate has started exercising some serious style prowess. Such is her new conviction for glamour, the Duchess even wore a cream designer dress to a toddler-littered, petting zoo tea party. A high-risk sartorial choice if ever there was one. The absence of high street dressing may wind some people up, but arguably a Princess should have an air of slight untouchability. Wouldn’t you rather have prospective visitors think, “UK – how glamorous”, rather than, “Ooh, I’ve got that Zara jacket”. That’s no doubt why, whilst the Duchess has always seemed to be a Breton t-shirt and jeans woman at heart, her most triumphant style hits come from when she is glammed up to the nines. Interestingly, when she does do casual – see the strange Holland & Holland safari jacket in the Canadian rainforest last week – it jars.  She already has the power and prowess of a style leader – everything she wears, whether it’s Topshop or top notch, sells out – but the fact that these days she finally looks comfortable in her refined Princess get-up perhaps marks a new fashion era. Maybe she’s finally accepting her place on the world’s best dressed lists, and has decided to really give us something to really talk about. This Jenny Packham bespoke number is a classic Kate shape – fitted and neat, with a slightly higher waist to lengthen her legs. There are however a few subtle updates. The puff sleeves add a fashion-frisson, as do the higher than normal suede – not patent! – Gianvito Rossi courts. This flirty Alexander McQueen number – a label she has long patronaged – is cute, but perhaps not her best shape. Whilst she obviously has the legs for it, she’d look more grown-up in a longer length. Note the new (around £600) Miu Miu clutch bag though – another brand she’s not carried before. All one can think, when running an eye over the grubby-looking old boots, saggy-knee’d Zara jeans and outmoded Holland and Holland safari jacket (that could have been borrowed from Prince Charles) – is bring on an evening do. This Preen by Thornton Bregazzi number – a design duo who are well known and loved in fashion circles for their skill at creating dresses that gently purr “put-me-on-right-now” – is possibly the best thing she’s ever worn. She’s worn this Hobbs green coat before, but is wise to hold onto it. The structured trench details and waist-belt suit her immensely – and feel more modern than her V-necked single breasted coats. Another style hit – thanks to this £2k bespoke Dolce and Gabbana number. The gold buttons add an essential regal edge, the puff sleeves suit her perfectly and the colour is just divine. Worth every penny. Carolina Herrera is another new designer for the Duchess, but she’d be sharp to invest in her more. The elegant dresser of any self respecting Park Avenue Princess, the task of dressing a real one will come as second nature. The chunky heeled shoes here by Tod’s – a step on from her stiletto courts – add a keen fashion touch (and are surely much more comfortable). Wearing a wrap jacket by Canadian designer Sentaler, she’s showing off her skill at diplomatic-fashion. The combination of brown suede R.Soles cowboy boots, however, don’t make this her best look. Her new-found commitment to glamour know no bounds – here she is in a pretty See by Chloe cream dress for the children’s party at Government House in Victoria. Let’s hope Charlotte and George wiped their sticky hands. What to wear when canoeing in front of the worlds media is a tricky sartorial ask. The Duchess however goes classic country casual in coordinating khaki trousers and blazer. Hopefully no one splashed her cream blouse.  For her visit to Cridge Centre, an agency that offers shelter, care and hope for children, women, families and the elderly, the ever-appropriate Duchess wore a jeans and jacket from Zara and a top from humble old H&M. Whilst the single-buttoned white blazer is a new purchase from Zara, the jeans-and-jacket combination is one the Duchess often turns to when she’s in need of something smart-casual, that trickiest of dress codes. For the final wave goodbye, the Duchess looked to Catherine Walker, a Chelsea-based atelier, which came to fame in the 1980s as Princess Diana's favourite designer. Kate's classic cream coat evoked Telegraph fashion director Lisa Armstrong's description of Walker's aesthetic: “The label guarantees a statuesque perfection that looks as good in photographs as it does across a crowded cathedral or state ballroom."    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We were so busy pouring over traditional red carpet gowns at last night’s Baftas that one of the best looks almost slipped through the net. Sandy Powell, the British, Oscar-winning costume designer, turned heads in what she called “a little homage” to the late, great, David Bowie. Powell, who was nominated for the costumes in Carol, told The Telegraph that she had was inspired by Freddie Burretti, a designer and tailor who created the turquoise suit which Bowie wears in the video for the 1971 hit Life on Mars. Burretti was a close friend of Bowie’s at the time, and created many of the singer’s Ziggy Stardust costumes. He was just 19 when he made the Life on Mars suit. “I’ve always like that suit, and I’d love to have one, one day” Powell told us. She designed the suit herself and had it made by a friend at east London atelier Whitechapel Workhouse. The shirt and tie were also custom-made especially for the event; London shirt specialist Dometakis provided the shirt, while Angels The Costumiers, one of the film industry’s leading  costume suppliers, created Powell’s tie. Incidentally, Angels were honoured at the ceremony last night with a Bafta for Outstanding British Contribution to Cinema. She completed the look with Stella McCartney’s Britt derby shoes in silver. Powell’s sartorial statement wasn’t directly linked to the singer's recent passing. “David Bowie was a big influence on my life and my work,” she says. “It’s something I’ve been meaning to do for a long time because it’s my favourite Bowie outfit. I did decide a while ago, and the Baftas provided the right opportunity to go ahead.” The similarities between the two are striking, not least because Powell’s signature red hair is almost exactly like Bowie’s in the hit music video. “It wasn’t meant to be a replica” she explained. “It was meant to be my version – a little homage.” The look garnered lots of compliments at the British film event of the year, with guests who understood  the Bowie reference “depending on their age”. Powell told us that the look made a difference from wearing a gown, which she didn’t want to do. It certainly did.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Meryl Streep arrived fashionably late at tonight's Oscars, a nonchalant move in the wake of the furore which has erupted over the past few days after Karl Lagerfeld accused her of abandoning the Chanel dress which was being made for her in favour of a look by another designer willing to pay her for her support- a version of events which Streep vehemently denies and which Lagerfeld himself has now withdrawn.  In the first moments of the Oscars ceremony, host Jimmy Kimmel paid tribute to Streep, who was branded 'over-rated' by President Donald Trump earlier this year after she gave a speech criticising him at the Golden Globes. Kimmel prompted the audience to give Streep a standing ovation, for which she graciously took a bow. He finished his speech by quipping, "Nice dress! Is that an Ivanka?" referring to the First Daughter's controversial eponymous fashion brand.   Ultimately, Florence Foster Jenkins star Streep had opted for a custom-made outfit by Lebanese designer Elie Saab. The daintily embroidered, off-shoulder navy design offered a classically elegant look which was given a modern twist thanks to the slim, tailored trousers which were layered underneath. The look included a sleek waist belt and suitably grandiose train (which Streep tripped on as she walked up the red carpet). Streep accessorised with a boxy navy clutch in the same material as her outfit, super-high heels and delicate drop earrings.  The 67 year-old Best Actress nominee- a record 20th nomination-also continued her recent defiant, statement-making habit of donning glasses with a pair of subtle, frameless spectacles which she put on once she was inside the Dolby Theatre The elegant Elie Saab look is the culmination of a saga which has overshadowed the past couple of days with Streep and her stylist Micaela Erlanger engaging in a war of words with Chanel regarding a cancelled Academy Awards gown order, with Streep being forced to deny that she was seeking to receive payment from the label she wore to the Oscars.  It all began on Friday when respected fashion industry website Women's Wear Daily (WWD)  published an interview with Karl Lagerfeld in which he claimed  that his design had suddenly been cancelled after Chanel refused to offer payment for Streep wearing their dress. “A genius actress, but cheapness also, no?" he was quoted as saying. "As a stylist working with a nominee for any major event, it’s industry standard for designers to propose gown ideas and sketches — some custom, some not depending on the occasion," Erlanger told Business of Fashion in a statement refuting Lagerfeld's version of events. "In the case of Chanel’s submission, which was presented with full knowledge that Ms. Streep and I — her stylist — were having conversations with various brands, we were shown sketches of a dress from their most recent couture collection. Although [it was] an exquisite gown from the existing collection, we decided to go in a different direction, with another designer." Erlanger continued: "At no point were there any conversations regarding monetary compensation. Nor were any other brands considered based on their willingness to pay for placement. This is not how my company operates and is very much a practice in conflict with Ms. Streep's personal ethics. Any reports or quotes stating otherwise are a complete fabrication."  Lagerfeld soon clarified his comments with a statement reading: “Chanel engaged in conversations with Ms. Streep’s stylist, on her request, to design a dress for her to wear to the Academy Awards. After an informal conversation, I misunderstood that Ms. Streep may have chosen another designer due to remuneration, which Ms. Streep’s team has confirmed is not the case. I regret this controversy and wish Ms. Streep well with her 20th Academy Award nomination.” The tone of Lagerfeld's words seems to have provoked Streep herself into speaking out on the issue.  “In reference to Mr. Lagerfeld’s ‘statement,’ there is no ‘controversy’: Karl Lagerfeld, a prominent designer, defamed me, my stylist and the illustrious designer whose dress I chose to wear, in an important industry publication,” Streep’s statement said. “That publication printed this defamation, unchecked. Subsequently, the story was picked up globally, and continues, globally, to overwhelm my appearance at the Oscars, on the occasion of my record-breaking 20th nomination, and to eclipse this honour in the eyes of the media, my colleagues and the audience. “I do not take this lightly, and Mr. Lagerfeld’s generic ‘statement’ of regret for this ‘controversy’ was not an apology. He lied, they printed the lie, and I am still waiting." For the time being at least, Streep seemed to have put the furore elegantly to one side, enjoying proceedings in her dazzling Elie Saab.               © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  I see choppy waters ahead under our new Prime Minister – for fashion writers, I mean. Some folk are already snarling at us for having the temerity to suggest that what anyone wears, particularly a female PM might be of interest. Don’t we know it’s 2016? Others sneer because we’re not doing more to point out what they see as her fashion “failings”. Both are wide of the mark. It’s as delusional to imagine that humans don’t judge on snap impressions (however much we try to mitigate against this primal instinct), as it is silly to expect Theresa May to take a leaf from Samantha Cameron’s style manual. We may deduce from the way that Mrs May dresses and the fact that her luxury on Desert Island Discs was a subscription to Vogue, that she has a soft spot for a fashion statement. But Samantha Cameron was married to a prime minister. Mrs May is the Prime Minister. There is a sartorial world of difference and the former self-evidently had more latitude for dressing outside the Downing Street box. Sam Cam is even believed to have taken some kind of sewing or pattern cutting lessons, in anticipation, it’s thought, of ultimately launching her own fashion range.  On the clothes front, I hope that Theresa May reaches a point where she is allowed to enjoy her fashion idiosyncrasies while simultaneously finding outfits that don’t distract us, or her, from the demanding job in hand. I have faith. Anyone who finds time to slot a weekly manicure into such a gruelling schedule must be formidably organised. A neat, sleek, elegant uniform, ideally British as often as is diplomatic (she wore an Amanda Wakely coat and matching dress and her trusty LK Bennett’s on day one) will semaphore both subliminally and obviously, something important about this country’s talents, efficiencies and openness. But don’t imagine Mrs May’s fashion duties end there. The Downing Street fashion-industry reception that was instigated by Sarah Brown, turned, under Samantha Cameron, into a glamorous, annual event and became a prestigious draw for international press and buyers weighing up whether or not to come to London Fashion Week. Never underestimate the appeal – to Brits and foreigners, including the most worldly magazine editors-in-chief – of peeking behind that black door. That’s why I’m intervening early on to ask Theresa May, here, to continue the reception tradition. This wouldn’t merely be a gesture to keep those influential guests coming, but an important signifier that the government takes the industry seriously and views it a worthy recipient of time and investment. There is much more that Theresa May, as PM, can do to help British fashion. And boy could British fashion use it. As things stand, British designers and textilers currently export 70 per cent of their products to the EU. They are desperate to know what kind of trading tariffs they might expect post-Brexit. There are also many skills that are vitally important to the future of the fashion industry, from senior managerial roles (Marco Gobetti, Burberry’s new CEO and Emmanuel Gintzberger, recently appointed CEO of Alexander McQueen, both come from EU countries) to seamstresses, machinists and pattern cutters (did Sam Cam know something?) that cannot currently be filled by UK citizens. Oh, and 56 per cent of designers on London Fashion Week’s Schedule – that twice yearly event that spawns millions of images of British creativity across the planet – were born outside the UK. Vital then, that in the short term, the fashion industry continues to be able to attract, transfer and keep EU talent. But surely there is also a golden opportunity now to institute a raft of worthwhile apprenticeship schemes. While we’re on the topic of education, Britain’s world famous fashion colleges should be cherished, maintained and built in. There is, for instance, no post grad business fashion course equivalent to a MBA. There’s more. Currently British fashion companies can send samples to EU destinations knowing they’ll arrive the following day – unlike sending to the US, where packages can get caught up in customs for a week, or South America, where they can be delayed for months. That speed is incalculably useful when say, Italian Vogue or French Grazia is hovering between shooting an outfit from a New York designer or a British one. This may seem a trifling consideration, but it’s the kind on which reputations are made. It’s also imperative, in the production process, that samples can pass quickly backwards and forwards between the design studio in the UK and the factory in Italy or Portugal. Then there’s the complex fashion supply chain – zips from Germany, lace from France, work-forces in Rumania and Hungary – which could become a stagnant web if steps aren’t taken to untangle it. That’s why, although I’ve a hunch she’s quite busy, I think it’s important Mrs May gives this her attention. The British fashion industry currently contributes £28 billion a year to the UK economy, once supply, manufacturing and design consultancies are included. This isn’t some spurious figure, but the conclusion of Oxford Economics, a research firm that regularly works with the government. It’s also a sum that has grown, by a third, since 2010. British fashion isn’t only a “soft” force that demonstrates Britain’s creative excellence to the world. It’s a serious revenue source and generator of jobs – currently around 800,000 With the pound low, we should also do our utmost to entice high-spending tourists here, particularly Chinese who far prefer shopping for luxury goods outside their country than within. So British fashion isn’t only a “soft” force that demonstrates Britain’s creative excellence to the world. It’s a serious revenue source and generator of jobs – currently around 800,000. With the pound low, we should also do our utmost to entice high spending tourists here, particularly Chinese who far prefer shopping for luxury goods outside their country than within. There are hopeful signs that Theresa May will be a potent, positive fashion protagonist. In 2013, she attended London Fashion Week, although it clearly wasn’t then part of her remit. Not content with perching for half an hour on the front row, according to Caroline Rush, chief executive of the British Fashion Council, she visited the stands of less established designers at the static exhibition next to the shows. “She spent an encouraging amount of time listening to their stories,” says Rush. Listening is always a good start. Now we need action.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Last night Samantha Cameron accompanied sister Emily Sheffield to the People, Places & Things charity gala at Wyndham’s Theatre. While her younger sibling, who is deputy editor at Vogue, paired her leopard print blouse and tailored trousers with two-tone court shoes, Cameron chose to team her own satin top and trousers with - wait for it - trainers. Predictably in some corners of the internet, so-called style watchers accused Cameron of disregarding the formal dress code expected of gala events (especially one held in - gasp! - a theatre!) In her trusty £60 Converse Chuck Taylors, which are obviously much loved (read: scuffed), Cameron was the only one rubbing shoulders in trainers. To us, it looked more like Cameron was doing what most modern working mums do: turning to trusty flats on a busy day. (The Lulu Guinness shopper stuffed with paraphernalia that wouldn't fit in her handbag and a stray crocodile clip hanging from the handle are also tell-tale signs that sure, she may be the PM's wife but she also has a life).  Canvas and leather All Star vintage 70 trainers, £60, Converse But Cameron is just the latest public figure to be called out for wearing trainers in a formal environment. In May, Fiona Bruce presented the 10 ‘O Clock News in a pair of cream canvas plimsolls that set social media alight within minutes of the programme starting. “Respect!” and “Love it!” some viewers wrote, while one flabbergasted Twitter user simply wrote “Disgraced. I do not pay my licence fee for this!” Though Bruce was actually recovering from a broken foot and later said she was forced to wear the comfortable lace-ups, there has been a noticeable - and refreshing - shift towards professional women wearing trainers. At her most recent New York Fashion Week presentation, Victoria Beckham took her bow wearing boxfresh adidas Superstars instead of her usual point-toe stilettos. “I just can’t do heels any more. At least not when I’m working,” she told The Telegraph. Creative director of Céline, Phoebe Philo, meanwhile, has been wearing adidas Stan Smiths for years. “I think women of all ages are embracing being comfortable now,” fashion features editor of InStyle and founder of En Brogue, Hannah Rochell, tells us.  “There’s so much more choice which means that you can wear trainers and be on trend rather than scruffy.” Indeed, Cameron’s Chuck Taylors are just the tip of the iceberg. Brands such as Senso, Northern Cobbler and Eytys all make minimal, leather styles that would be perfect for smart environments. Naturally, most high street stores have also jumped on the trend, and most stock simple sneakers to accompany a modern woman’s wardrobe. Of course, as with all things fashion, there are many nuances to getting the trainer look just right. "Turning up the hem of trousers up to show the ankles is always the best way to style a flat shoe," Rochell explains, before adding that “leather sneaker styles will always look a little sleeker.” Cameron’s Chuck Taylor’s might benefit from a spin in the washing machine, but her simple, white model certainly chimes with the uniform of fashion editors and designers, alike. And bonus: are probably comfortable, too.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  British actress Kristin Scott Thomas has lived in France for over three decades and seemingly thinks little of the style of the UK’s female population. In an interview with French magazine Marie France, the 55-year-old star of The English Patient lambasted the fashion predilections of the country she left aged 19. When asked about the differences between French and English style, the actress wasn’t shy in her views. “The French woman can be seductive, attractive, without ever being too sexy. There’s nothing vulgar, everything lies in subtlety. The English, it’s terrible… and it’s completely the opposite!” she said, adding: “For example, they dare to wear mini-skirts when they don’t have the legs for them. In France, that would clearly be bad taste. And actually, it’s funny, this concept of ‘bad taste’ doesn’t exist in England. Neither in beauty or fashion.” Scott Thomas was born in Cornwall but moved to France to become an au pair when she was told that would never make a good actress. Her career took off after moving to the French capital; after graduating from a French theatre school she was cast opposite pop star Prince in Under The Cherry Moon.  In 1987 she married French gynaecologist François Olivennes, with whom she had three children (they split up in 2005). The actress was interviewed as part of promotional duties for Lierac, a pharmaceutical brand of which she is the new face. In terms of fashion, she said: "The English, they concern themselves much more with what is in fashion. They follow the latest trends and end up all looking the same.” She criticised the national obsession with wanting to look tanned, and the usage of fake tan as a means to do so. “In summer, everyone is orange! And as soon as there are a few rays of sunshine, every is outside – borderline naked!” She praised French women for their 'faux natural' approach to style and beauty matters. "They take good care of their faces, and I get the impression that they are more interested in beauty treatments - which have a deep impact - as opposed to make-up. For me, the French aren't scared of using recipes passed down from their grandmothers, even in beauty." She also cited French actress and James Bond star Lea Seydoux as the woman who embodies French chic as its best. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We’re only halfway through the Royal Tour of Canada but it already seems that we’re witnessing a change in The Duchess of Cambridge’s style - a subtle but distinct move towards more daring, stand-out designs from a host of fashion's biggest names.   Far from recycling old dresses from Reiss as she did the last time she visited Canada - her first royal tour abroad in 2011 - this tour Kate has worn customised Dolce & Gabbana and shown more skin than ever before in an experimental Preen dress. Today the new, more confident Kate was out again, wearing a bold red coat by American designer Carolina Herrera and (very on-trend) block-heeled shoes by Italian luxury brand Tod’s. The coat, made of double-faced wool and cashmere mix blend, is new to shops and still on sale for £1190. It’s the first time the Duchess of Cambridge has worn Carolina Herrera, but the brand is a natural fit for a Royal growing into her status as one of the world’s most watched fashion plates. The Venezuelan-born designer turned her patrician upbringing into a billion-dollar-a-year company thanks to her inimitable spin on glossy, Upper East Side socialite style. “A woman who wears, lives and breathes her brand, Herrera never looks old-fashioned even though she exemplifies that most old fashioned of  traits – elegance,” The Telegraph’s Lisa Armstrong says of the now 77-year-old grandmother.  That is no doubt why Herrera one of the very few designers who can lay claim to the fact they’ve dressed the triumvirate of US First Ladies that is Jackie Kennedy, Hillary Clinton and Michelle Obama - and now a Royal. "I am so thrilled the Duchess of Cambridge chose the red CH Carolina Herrera coat. It highlights her beauty and timeless style,” Herrera told The Telegraph  of her new fan. Some are speculating that the newfound glamour in The Duchess of Cambridge’s wardrobe is thanks to her stylist Natasha Archer. The 29-year-old started working as Kate’s PA in 2014 but was identified as her image-maker when she was spotted taking dust bags of clothes into the Lindo Wing after Prince George’s birth. Ever since, Archer has been charged with scouting out (and customising) suitable outfits for public events - a task made all the more challenging because the Duchess likes her clothes to have significance and nod to the host nation. With that in mind, however, it’s perhaps not hard to see where the pair got their inspiration for today’s Carolina Herrera look. The Duke and Duchess were in Whitehorse, the capital of northwest Canada’s Yukon territory, to visit a telegraph station that the Queen had also visited in 1959. For her trip, the Queen had worn a bold block-colour pink coat - a tactic she often employs to ensure she can be seen by the crowds from a distance. If the Duchess of Cambridge's 1950's-style red coat was a subtle nod to the past, the outfit she changed into after leaving Whitehorse was a more obvious tribute to her host nation. The Duchess nipped back to her hotel to change into jeans, boots and a coat by Canadian label Sentaler before heading off to watch First Nation dancers in Carcross.  The tie-waisted coat crafted from alpaca wool is one of the up-and-coming label's signature pieces - and currently on sale for £588 on Sentaler's website.  Toronto-raised Bojana Sentaler planned to go into business, but a chance encounter with Karl Lagerfeld during her world travels steered her towards fashion. Her ultra-feminine brand was loved by fashion insiders for its ribbed sleeve detailing and hooded wrap coats but it shot to fame when the Canadian Prime Minister's wife Sophie Gregoire-Trudeau was photographed wearing it at her husband's swearing in ceremony.   “She needed a few things to wear and was so busy. I was in Toronto so I sent her some options,” Gregoire-Trudeau's stylist Jessica Mulroney told The Telegraph of the moment. “She wore a coat by Canadian designer Sentaler and people went crazy for it. We had created this media frenzy, like you see with anything Kate wears. Then we realised we had a responsibility to create more moments like that to give homegrown designers an international platform.” Ever since Gregoire-Trudeau has been on a mission to promote Canadian designers - and it seems her latest tactic is persuading her famous guest Kate to buy into the best of the country's fashion talent, too. Something tells us Sentaler are set for another media frenzy.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
