 With its complex layers of narrative, $100 million budget and vast cast, Westworld is the definition of a modern television epic. Taking inspiration from the 1973 film of the same name by Michael Crichton, it’s a Western with a futuristic twist - one where a hyper-real theme park allows the rich to indulge in their fantasies, including shooting the 'hosts' with no fear of retaliation. The series has been piquing intrigue since it first aired in the UK in last month, not least because it is a sumptuous visual feast. But given Westworld spans multiple time periods and stars a nuanced array of characters, the job of creating costumes for the series was a monumental task for costume designer Ane Crabtree and her team. She says it’s been the “hardest but most wonderful job” of her career, which has included shows like Pan-Am (which set trends at the time with its impeccable recreation of 60's air hostess costumes) and The Sopranos. So how did she approach the task? Despite being available to watch in abundance, Western films were not Crabtree’s starting point. “Of course, I looked at westerns that are quite well known, especially ones from the 1960s to late 70s, for inspiration” she tells The Telegraph. “But I’m never really a designer who likes to go to other people’s versions of a time frame because while the films might be awesome, for me the great pull is towards real life.” That connection to reality came by trawling images of people who actually lived in the Wild West from the 1850s to 1890s. “A lot of the time those photographs are actually people’s personal photos that you find online through their ancestry,” Crabtree remembers. “I feel creepy saying that but it’s the truth. That’s something that Jonathan (Nolan) and Lisa (Joy), the show’s creators, vibed with also. It’s actually the most interesting and individual way to research and that’s where you find true character, when you look at people’s versions of that time. Western clothing was invented to be worn long term and in harsh climates and also for hard work, but there’s also this really cool thread of individualism that was super exciting to add to each character by looking at those photos. The task of creating wardrobes befitting of the series’ intricate storyline required a great deal more than simply sourcing a pile of old cowboy hats and costumes. “The world of Westworld is so big you think ‘Oh god, how much am I going to need?’” Crabtree laughs. “In the end we actually had to build nearly every single piece for anybody that speaks because there’s so much detail. You get into the habit of making everything so it can be your vision and very story specific.” There were also some practical reasons why buying in costumes was so tricky. “Some days we hoped we could just go down the street and buy something but we never could. Actually, where we were shooting above Los Angeles was this very cinematic and desert-y location but it doesn’t allow for a lot of shopping. There was like one fabric shop!” Instead Crabtree and her 35-strong costume crew worked with artisans and specialist factories to create most of the costumes absolutely from scratch. “We had to not only make the clothing but we even had weavers in upstate New York making the fabric so it seemed authentic. In the pilot we had used this vintage fabric but we needed loads for the series so we had people in LA printing. We printed, weaved and dyed our own fabric to lend the authenticity to the show - so it was a beautiful circus! It’s next level costume design.” Blue has a long history as a colour of innocence and purity - look at any depiction of the Virgin Mary, and she’ll be wearing blue, so it seems a significant hue for Dolores Abernathy, played by Evan Rachel Wood and the oldest inhabitant of the show’s Western-themed theme park. “There are so many secrets on Westworld so I don’t actually know Jonathan and Lisa’s ultimate reason for having her in blue - it’s quite a giant rabbit hole of reasoning and inspiration,” explains Crabtree. “We wanted Dolores to stand out in the frame though. It’s a beautiful rich blue which photographs incredibly in the locations which we have. In reality also it’s a colour that existed back in the 1800s.” Some of the series’ most elaborate and beautiful ensembles are worn by Maeve the Madam (played by Thandie Newton) and Clementine (played by Angela Sarafyan), one of her best girls. “Their look comes from a lot of reading I’ve done about the ‘soiled dove’ which is a great term for a prostitute,” says Crabtree. “There are great books about it which I read 17 years ago and re-read for this. There weren’t a lot of job offers or things for a woman to do in the Wild West and of course being a prostitute or if you were lucky, a madam, was one of the main jobs. They do refer to that career as ‘soiled doves’ and how they were beautiful jewels in the midst of quite desert-toned Western clothes worn by the men, so they always stood out.” “Maeve is a strong, powerful character so her colour is this vibrant fuschia which stands out in the bar they work at. Clementine is the perfect green colour to complement Thandie. There’s a beautiful genesis which happens to both - it’s quite empowering and you see various elevations via costume of both their characters.” “In any gentleman’s story, the hat is one of the most important parts of the gentleman’s wardrobe and that carries over in the West,” says Crabtree. The Stetson cowboy hat is a vital signifier of Western accuracy, so Crabtree emphasises that these were the most complex and time-consuming aspects of the costume process. “In the West, it became a thing that the white hats were the good guys and the black hats were the bad guys- it became a kind of unsaid western rule; the Sheriff wore the white hat. The John Wayne or the Gary Cooper had the white hat while the dangerous villain or the ones who were dark and sexy had black. It’s based in reality but we use it for character story in Westworld,” says Crabtree. “It’s the hardest decision I tell you. It takes as long to decide on what hat style because it’s the first thing people see in these wide, expansive shots so it means so much.” She uses the example of Logan, played by Ben Barnes and William, played by Jimmi Simpson to illustrate the detailed meanings which a hat can bring. “We had quite a lot of fun with them. We did black on Ben and white on Jimmi,” she recalls. “They are compadres. I was lucky enough to meet them on the same day and got to create their characters separately and together which is quite rare in TV scheduling. Ben’s character comes from money and he is dangerous, sexy and in-the-know so his hats had more of a moneyed, European flair and came from research books and photographs. Jimmi had a slightly more modern Western hat, not quite the hero but with this optimistic, upturned brim. And a bit naïve too so there’s a lot of layers in their choice of hat.” Anthony Hopkins plays Robert Ford, the “creative director” of Westworld. “He’s highly intelligent and highly creative, a bit of a father figure in the park. He’s mysterious,” analyses Crabtree. She relays the story of how she cleverly played with costume to help Hopkins and his co-stars - including the young boy who (*spoiler alert*) is indeed his younger version. “If you look at episode two, there’s a host or robot who’s a little boy and we tried to mirror the look of Robert Ford in the little boy host. It has its roots in Edwardian times and we tweaked it for Sir Anthony. I often try to help an actor by dressing the other actors in the scene to either support him or antagonise them. In that case, it was to support and excite Mr Hopkins a little bit. I try to surprise them a bit on the first day of shooting and I think he was surprised and happy. Sometimes I don’t mention it but I let the actor show up and see what unfolds. Our job is costume, sure, it’s a shirt or a pair of pants but what it actually means is quite large.” Like Game of Thrones before it, Westworld is immersive, escapist and fantastical which seems to make it a ripe candidate for fashion-show inspiration. Might we see Maeve’s dramatic dresses or the intricately detailed Stetsons replicated on the catwalks next season? “That would be awesome” Crabtree exclaims. “It would be a 360 for me because it actually happened once with the only other Western that I ever did. It was a film called Dust 17 years ago with Joseph Fiennes. I remember that some fashion designers got influenced by it then that season. It would be amazing if it happened again.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. An adorable picture captured by actress and lifestyle guru Gwyneth Paltrow and shared on Instagram provided an insight into family life behind the scenes at America’s biggest sporting event.   Captioned ‘#Superbowl50 jacket game’, you could be excused for thinking that the slim figure on the left is Martin’s ex-wife, but it is in fact the former couple’s daughter, 11-year-old Apple.  The Duchess of Cambridge isn't usually one for following trends, but by stepping out in a new Erdem grey coat, matching John Boyd hat and Rupert Sanderson heels she's the latest person to buy into fashion's current vogue for Groutfits - a head-to-toe grey look that's proved so popular it now has it's own tumblr, FiftyShadesOfGroutfits.  But if her Erdem lace-detail coat for the Commonwealth Service at Westminster Abbey was on trend, she accessoried her look with her most traditional hat yet; a wide-brimmed creation by Princess Diana's favourite milliner John Boyd.  "John has been making this shape since the 1940's - it's a classic, flattering brim," the people at Boyd's Knightsbridge shop told The Telegraph of the Duchess's hat. The 90-year-old opened his shop in 1946 and remains the oldest working milliner in London.   This is the first time that Kate, who normally opts for fascinators, has worn one of Boyd's creations. The custom wide-brimmed grey peach bloom felt hat with a silk dark grey trim would have taken up to a week to make, with everything hand-stitched by Boyd's three-person team. Similar styles retail for £500.  But whilst the Duchess is new to working with Boyd, the milliner has a long-standing relationship with the royal family. Princess Anne first wore his designs when she was 16 and then commissioned him to make a yellow and white net saucer shaped hat for Prince Charles and Princess Diana's wedding. And Boyd was credited with sparking a 'hat renaissance' when he designed pieces for Diana, the Princess of Wales, in the 1980s.  He first worked with Diana on the pink tricorn that she wore with her 'going away outfit' after her wedding in 1981. "My new range was just being completed when Diana arrived, and sitting on a chair surrounded by ribbons suddenly took a tricorn shape in sparterie that was hanging on the door and said, 'I like that style, I will have it for my wedding,'" Boyd has said of working with the late Princess.  He went on create some of Diana's most iconic hats and witnessed first-hand the impact they had on the public. “Mothers would drag in their daughters with long faces shouting ‘God, you’ll look a scream in that!’, then suddenly they all loved it…hats with feathers, ribbons and veils like the Princess of Wales," the milliner has said of the Diana effect. "Diana was our best ambassador for hats and the entire millinery industry owes her a debt.”   So will Kate's wide-brimmed hat have a similar impact? "There has been a return to classic wide-brim styles recently, especially at this time of year when racing and wedding seasons approach," Boyd's representatives told The Telegraph - before offering some crucial advice for anyone thinking about copying the look. "We always think it's nice to tip the brim down to the right so it frames the face. Most hats tip over the right eye, it's a traditional thing."         © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Did the red patent, bar-strapped shoes that Princess Charlotte wore as the Cambridge family touched down in Poland yesterday look familiar to you? Royal fashion spotters were quick to point out that they were not a new pair from M&H, Rachel Riley, Peppa & Co. or another of the childrenswear labels that the Duchess of Cambridge likes to dress her two year-old daughter in. They were in fact a hand-me-down pair from Charlotte’s uncle, Prince Harry. Many items of royal clothing are carefully preserved, stored away afterwards for potential exhibits, but also in case anyone from the Royal family may wish to reuse them.  As Edward Enninful is announced as the new editor of British Vogue, we revisit The Telegraph's January 2016 interview with the acclaimed stylist, who was appointed OBE last year, in which he discusses how his love for fashion developed and his passion for promoting diversity. Edward Enninful’s eureka moment came when he was working on an editorial for Italian Vogue in the mid-1990s. He was styling a fashion shoot with the renowned American photographer Steven Meisel, the pair having been introduced by the Italian designers Domenico Dolce and Stefano Gabbana. ‘For the first picture, I put the shirt on, put the slacks on; picture one done,’ he says, holding court from a plush velvet armchair in the drawing room of London’s Soho House, one chilly December afternoon. ‘For the next picture I put the shirt on, rolled up the sleeves; picture two done. For the next picture I went to put the shirt on and Steven said, “I’m bored. What else can you do?”’ The stylist responded quickly to the affront. ‘From that moment,’ he says, ‘my styling moved up a gear.’ Enninful is one of the British fashion’s great success stories, emerging in the golden age of London street-style titles. He was scouted as a model for  i-D magazine on the London Underground in 1990, when he was a 16-year-old schoolboy. By his late teens he was running the magazine’s fashion department. Enninful has been responsible for some of the most arresting editorial and advertising imagery of his era, tackling industry taboos including racism and plastic surgery head on, working with the giants of photography and enjoying productive tenure at the two blockbuster Vogues – Italia under editor Franca Sozzani, US under Anna Wintour. He is currently fashion director at W magazine, uniquely placed to cast his exacting eye over an industry reinventing itself for the digital age.  To commemorate 25 years in the fashion business, at the start of 2015 Enninful was approached by the tech giant Beats by Dre, the headphone multinational kickstarted by former NWA rapper Dr Dre and record producer Jimmy Iovine, to collaborate on a major new film initiative. Acquired by Apple in a $3 billion takeover last year, Beats now controls an estimated 70 per cent of the premium headphones market, so its promotional campaigns are a very big deal indeed. First, Enninful was taken to see the largest billboard in the world, a recent acquisition for Beats on New York’s Times Square, to do with as he chose. The result, a year later, is a filmic reimagining of the seven deadly sins, shot by British Fashion Awards winner and fellow i-D alumnus Nick Knight, starring eight of Enninful’s favourite supermodels. ‘I’ve known Kate [Moss] since I was 16 and she was 14,’ he says casually. ‘I’ve known Naomi [Campbell], my gosh, forever. She’s like a sister to me. All the others I’ve seen since they started.’  Campbell reciprocates his understanding of their relationship. She refers to him as ‘a brother’, and says, ‘When I first met him it was just like meeting family. We connect on so many different levels. The sky’s the limit for Edward. He’s patiently waited for his time, and this is his time. He’s so respected by the greats. He’s worked his arse off to be where he is and I’m just so proud of him.’ Enninful says each of his preferred girls was quick to sign up to the Beats campaign. ‘Straight away Kate said, “I’m lust.” She claimed it.’  The film is still in production when we meet and plans to roll it out from its New York launch are getting ever more elaborate.   Never one to knowingly underplay his hand, he cast Lara Stone and Anna Ewers as a double-header to play Gluttony. Jourdan Dunn, whose first cover he shot for i-D after wooing her at a west London retail park (‘She loved Nando’s! She was obsessed! When she started she was so west London and I loved watching Jourdan grow into this icon’), was a speedy signatory. Karlie Kloss and Karen Elson followed. As each sin was to be represented by a block colour, he cast Campbell as an emblem of Black Pride in a voluminous Yohji Yamamoto gown. Ethnicity is a subject both feel strongly about.  During his quarter of a century in the business Enninful has become one of the major power brokers of the global fashion world. It was not supposed to be this way. Born in Ghana, he was raised in Ladbroke Grove, where his first-generation immigrant parents decamped when he was an infant, and where they endeavoured to protect their children from the evils of the metropolis. ‘I was really sheltered growing up, with six brothers and sisters,’ he says. ‘We played together all the time and I was living in a fantasy world, like most creative people. He knew little to nothing of fashion when it first came knocking but had been schooled in key technical skills. ‘My mother was a seamstress so I always grew up with her making clothes. I knew how to construct outfits, I knew how to sketch, I knew how to customise. But I could never imagine it as a career.’ The first of several fashion fairy-godfathers to play a role in Enninful’s ascendancy was the influential menswear stylist Simon Foxton, who spotted him on a Hammersmith & City Line Tube carriage the first day Enninful traded his milk-bottle spectacles for contact lenses. ‘I saw this man who kept staring at me. I was trying not to freak out. Then we got to King’s Cross, he came over, gave me a card and said, “My name is Simon Foxton and I’m a stylist for i-D and Arena and I work with Nick Knight, and I’d love you to model for me.” I was like Arena? Nick Knight? Modelling? I couldn’t imagine any of it.’ His religious mother was particularly suspicious of the stranger’s enquiry. ‘I remember going home, saying to my mum, “I met this man,” telling her  the story and my mum said, “No. That industry? No.”’ But Enninful was in safe hands with Foxton  – another genial fashion giant who wears his authority lightly.  Making the Beats project perfectly cyclical, Enninful’s first job was as a model for Nick Knight. He was greeted at Richmond station by Charlotte, Nick’s wife, and a whole new world began to open up for the shy young boy who had previously lived mostly in his own imagination. ‘My mind was blown.’ He began assisting Foxton within a year and was appointed fashion editor at i-D by another key father figure, publisher Terry Jones. ‘Now when I look back I think, my God, I was so young,’ he says. ‘It was such a different time as well. I met Craig McDean, who was Nick’s assistant, Corinne Day, Melanie Ward, David Sims, Kate; it was all sorts of people, a whole group of friends who were working for The Face and i-D. It was very special.’ There is something about Enninful, now 42, that defies preconceptions about the backstabbing, Devil Wears Prada world he inhabits at the top tier. He is a cosy figure with a teddy-bear disposition quite at odds with his fashion fabulousness. Most of his rock-solid credentials and relationships have been nurtured with genuine affection. He was incubated in his industry through a series of casual connections that became another sort of family; he first met Kate Moss after Foxton recommended him for a Pepe Jeans model casting. ‘I remember sitting there and Kate coming in. It was 200 quid! I wanted that job so badly. It was 1990 and she’d just started working with Corinne. I remember it like it was yesterday. The energy, the beauty, it was like love at first sight, exactly the same thing that I had  with Naomi shortly after and Jourdan years later. She just lit up the whole room. I didn’t get the  job but she did. So she went off to LA and made  200 quid. A couple of weeks later she was doing Levi’s. And a couple of months later she was doing Calvin Klein.’ At the outset of his career he was a hands-on operator, diligently working the fashion desk at i-D. ‘I had to write, I had to commission and I was basically the whole fashion department.’ His styling, he says, took an upswing in the mid-’90s. ‘I’d been experimenting with a lot of different things but  I hit my stride when I really defined what I like.’ He is one of fashion’s great narrative storytellers and, though obsessive about the minutiae of the designers he loves, builds an image around a character first and foremost. ‘I can’t just go in and throw clothes at a picture. I still have to have some kind of an idea of a character, of who she is, where she’s from. It’s almost like playing a child’s game. You have your dolls and you create characters for them. Fashion indulged that in me.’   His primary skill as a stylist, Naomi Campbell says, is his ‘elegance. Edward’s taste is not predictable but it is always elegant, sexy and never vulgar. Always beautiful and yet simple. His best quality as a stylist is he never overdoes something. Our friendship is defined by honesty with each other.’ The younger supermodel Karlie Kloss confirms she was nervous initially about working with Enninful. ‘He was and is renowned for his success in fashion at a young age. I remember being in awe of his journey and excited to work with such an icon. I was a little intimidated because of his impressive work and reputation.’ Over the years she has developed a fondness for him. ‘I’m honoured to count him among my friends and mentors.’  Enninful says even now he is racked with nerves before a shoot starts. ‘Oh, massively. My stomach’s churning. Then you’re trying to find something, you’re searching for it. It may take a day or two days but once you hit that moment, once you’ve created that first image that sets the tone, then it’s like something from above. You are off.’ He believes it is fashion’s responsibility to go beyond the surface of clothes. ‘For me fashion succeeds when it says something about the times we live in.’ On the race issue, he is constantly flummoxed by the industry’s approach. ‘I acknowledge the fact that I’ve been luckier than most, being spotted at 16, a black kid from Ladbroke Grove, not wealthy, from that class. But we need more diversity, from schools to internships to mentorships. That’s what I try to do. It’s very easy to say, oh, there’s one black model in a show and one black or Asian model in an advertising photograph, so we’ve filled the quota. No, it should be a continuous conversation. It shouldn’t even be an issue as far as I’m concerned. Beauty’s beauty.’ He thinks the digital world offers real opportunities for democratisation. ‘The brilliant thing now  with social media is that the industry is so globalised. If I go on my Instagram I can find a black kid in Memphis who is making clothes. or a kid in Ukraine who is obsessed with skateboarding. I feel the playing field is steadily being levelled. This is  a great moment because that kid who had no  doors into the fashion industry now knows how to leave a comment on my timeline; they can tell me exactly what they like to see, and what they don’t like to see.’   He is also encouraged by the new breed of supermodels who are both seen and heard, engaging with the world around them and building their own portfolios online. ‘The girls of today, and it started with Cara Delevingne, are so savvy and they learnt that they could make themselves greater by having a fan base that they can take to a client,’ he says. ‘So when you’re booking Gigi [Hadid] or Kendall [Jenner], you’re bringing a whole new audience with you. They [the models] don’t want to be the silent ones who don’t speak. They want you to know exactly what they’re doing and feeling, and we love it. The dynamics have changed.’ Enninful is not quite sure which of the deadly sins is his favourite. ‘I like them all,’ he says, laughing. ‘I’m certainly guilty of them all.’ He says the 16-year-old him would not be able to quite take  in the project he is about to launch. ‘That boy was very shy back then. The first time I went to New York I was 17 and I really felt like it was the crossroads of the world. I didn’t fathom that something I had collaborated on would end up on the biggest screen in Times Square. I honestly think that little boy would have passed out if he had known what was to come.’    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When ITV signed up the man behind cult TV show The Bridge to create new detective drama Marcella, it should have been obvious that a. The series would be great and b. it would spawn a new fashion obsession. Enter the £535 Woolrich parka jacket that lead detective Anna Friel wears near constantly on screen - and is already firmly on your wish-list. As well it should be. A parka is a sort of fashion anomaly: it transcends seasonality. A great cut khaki green parka with a thick fur (faux, hopefully) hood will always be in, and always be cool. A parka is now acceptable worn over your party dress (thank the exiting Creative Director of Saint Laurent, Hedi Slimane for that – a common trope on his catwalk), it offers an instant kick of subversiveness yet also makes you look shrewd: your skirt might be made of sequins but you’re not stupid enough to go out without a warm coat with a hood. It’s the classic London girl look: Kate Moss wears hers over a black leather mini skirt to Claridges, at their recent London Fashion Week show Burberry offered mustard-fur trimmed versions, whilst Net A-Porter are currently selling a shearling quilted parka by the French label Chloé for just shy of £4000. The one Anna Friel is wearing in Marcella is made by the classic all American lumber-jack and fashion editor favoured brand Woolrich (she’s wearing their £535 parka). On Friel, wearing it over her shirt and jumper, it serves to makes her appear less office-worker, more harried in the field, working mother. The styling is smart: the coat makes her seem entirely relatable. They’ve employed the same technique as that of Sarah Lund in The Killing in her Faroe Island jumper that became a cult hit – it’s something identifiably hers, yet everyone has a parka, whether it’s a beaten up relic from the mod-aping 90s or a more recent purchase. It helps to make the abnormal, the most feared thing seem commonplace – and thus aids the suspense. Murder isn’t something that happens to other people, it can happen to anyone in a parka. How chilling. By Gillian Brett Have you ever seen a woman work a shift dresses with the same impact as stone-cold First Lady Claire Underwood? For the key female protagonist in Netflix’s corruption-heavy, presidential drama, House of Cards, office-friendly pencil dresses are the key component in her killer look. ‘With her character we really wanted to have this armored, tailored, tight, nothing out of place feel,’ said House of Cards costume designer Tom Broecker. The high neckline commands authority, but the second-skin silhouette makes Claire’s sexuality her weapon of choice in the White House. Seek out similar styles in LK Bennett, Jaeger and Banana Republic. Saga Norén — the socially awkward homicide detective played by Sofia Helin in the Swedish-noir crime series, The Bridge — is like a female Sherlock Holmes with her signature wool overcoat. The archetypal cool Scandi-girl with an edge, Norén’s trademark  khaki military coat endured all three series, and her style credentials soared. The fervour was due, in part, to the accessibility of the look: just add leather trousers, Acne boots, unbrushed bleached hair and go. Google Saga Norén and a get-the-look is hard to avoid. Never before has the humble silk blouse achieved such levels of wantonness, than it did in its recent capacity as Detective Superintendent Stella Gibson’s wardrobe staple in BBC crime drama, The Fall. The perfect personification of its enigmatic, assertive and unashamedly sexy wearer — played by Gillian Anderson — DSI Gibon’s super-soft and perfectly pressed blouse soon assumed a leading role in its own right. In one episode, it muscled in on the action when a critical button came (artfully) undone during an important press conference. ASOS and French Connection both reported a spike in sales of their silk shirts during the first season of the show. Carrie Bradshaw’s shoe game is a thing of sartorial legend. So hardcode is her stiletto devotion that Miranda once calculated that Carrie had dropped around $40,000 over the years on shoes. But of all the iconic moments the Sex & the City star brought us over the years, Big’s marriage proposal with a pair of cobalt blue Manolo Blahnik’s in the first movie (we don’t speak of the sequel) is a unanimous favourite. We wonder how long the script writers toyed with Carrie saying ‘I Choo’ instead of ‘I do’ had she made it down the aisle. The trademark chunky sweaters worn by actress Sofie Gråbøl in Danish drama, The Killing, became almost as famous as the cast, to the point that it spawned a tribute website and sparked a legal battle to stop the spate of copycat designs that swarmed the high street in its honour. The iconic (for those who were glued to the show) star print sweater was originally made by Danish brand Gudrun & Gudrun for Gråbøl to wear as she hunted a serial killer around Copenhagen. Shrouding her femininity beneath the chunky knit, Lund developed an androgynous persona as a ruthless and driven detective.  Today US Vogue released its September issue, which is largely considered the most important and prestigious magazine of the year, and their choice of cover star is utterly unsurprising. Kendall Jenner has landed her first ever Vogue cover for the publication, and only leaves us wondering, surely this has happened already? It turns out, it hasn't. Jenner has appeared in numerous editorials for the magazine and some of the most sought-after campaigns in the business, but this really is her first time on the cover. In the Mert and Marcus shoot, Kendall shows just how diverse a model she is in images where she is alternately wearing romantic Valentino, a sporty Vetements puffer jacket and hoodie and Cher-esque Alexander McQueen sequins.  To accompany the shoot, Vogue sent writer Jonathan Van Meter to drive around Los Angeles with Jenner in her 1957 Corvette Stingray, meet her sister Kim Kardashian and go for dinner at her mother, Kris Jenner's, Calabasas home. In the interview, the young model opens up about fame, family and how sometimes what you really need is a good old fashioned bath.... “I’ve always been super different from all my sisters, especially my Kardashian sisters. They’ve always been into the glam thing and dressing up every day and being in the thick of it," explains Kendall. "Part of me loves that, but at the same time, I love dressing down and having my private life. It’s almost, like, empowering to know that no one knows we’re sitting here right now—because it’s not usually like this." She says that she has to try and find time to relax by herself away from the Kardashian whirlwind: "The second that I feel it getting the better of me, I have to go chill myself out—go take a bath or something to, like, disconnect from it. It keeps you real and sane and humble.” In the interview Kendall Jenner discusses the first time she met Caitlyn Jenner (her father Bruce Jenner transitioned to become a woman last July). "My whole life we would, like, catch her, and we would be like, What is going on here? I think we know, but do we?," she recalls. "At one point Kylie and I thought he was cheating on my mom, because he had makeup and nail polish. One time we found those squishy boob things. We found wigs. And then one time I actually ran into her. In this house. She had no idea." Jenner continues: "She would wake up really early just so she could dress up and move around the house and get that little kick for the morning, and then go back to being Bruce—take us to school, totally normal. So one morning I woke up at 4:00 a.m. so thirsty, came downstairs into the kitchen, and grabbed a bottle of water. And as I was coming back out, my dad was coming down the stairs in, like, a wig and makeup and shoes—the full nine. And she didn’t see me. I literally froze. Please don’t turn left. Because she could either turn left or turn right. Thank God she turned right and—to this day!—has no idea that happened. That was the first time I had ever seen her.”  “People say a lot of what they think, and it’s not always positive," says Jenner of the criticism of her family, who found fame with the reality show Keeping Up With the Kardashians. "And we never say anything. We just take it. And then when people meet us, they’re pleasantly surprised. Because we aren’t what people think. One of the best lessons I ever learned from my sisters is not to take everything so seriously." The overriding message of the cover interview is that Kendall Jenner takes her modelling career very, very seriously, and she says she wants it to last as long as supermodel Cindy Crawford's. “This is a career—I want this to last for a long time,” she says. “Not that I won’t venture out and do other things, but I want this to be like a Cindy Crawford thing: I want it to last until I am her age.  Melania Trump opted to channel Jacqueline Kennedy for her daytime look as she accompanied her husband now-President Donald Trump to his inauguration which took place this afternoon. The couple attended St John’s church in Washington early this morning and then went on to meet with Barack and Michelle Obama at the White House before the Inauguration ceremony. Melania's pale blue suit was created for her by Ralph Lauren, America’s most famous and prolific living designer. “With the historic swearing-in of her husband, Donald J. Trump, as the 45th President of the United States, the First Lady-elect will become America’s new First Lady wearing an American designer who transformed American fashion, Ralph Lauren,” a spokesperson for Trump announced this morning. "It was important to us to uphold the tradition of creating iconic American style for this moment," Ralph Lauren said in a statement to the New York Times.  With its demure knee-length skirt and bracelet-length sleeves, the ensemble immediately recalled the ladylike yet simple look which was coined and made famous by former First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy. In fact, the suit seemed to have taken direct inspiration from the Oleg Cassini design which Kennedy wore for John F Kennedy’s daytime Inauguration ceremony 56 years ago in January 1961. Lauren and Trump had, however, added some more modern elements to give Trump’s look a more updated feel. The double-faced cashmere jacket came with a raised shawl collar and cropped, wrap effect, serving the double purpose of shielding Trump from the 5 degree temperatures and adding a distinctive edge to an otherwise pared-back silhouette. Melania accessorised today's suit with elbow length leather gloves and suede stilettos in a matching shade of icy blue while her hair was swept up into a chic up-do. The pastel tone of the suit provided a sophisticated contrast to Donald Trump's vividly red tie.  Ralph Lauren had been mooted earlier this week as the designer who was creating Melania Trump’s Inauguration wardrobe. While his designs are now considered to be American classics, the 77 year-old who was born in The Bronx, New York has spent his career pioneering a distinctive preppy, easy and elegant style. His $6 billion company has outposts across the world while the Polo horse emblem is globally recognisable.  During his Inauguration address this afternoon, Donald Trump announced that his adminstration would encourage everyone to "buy American and hire American", another hint that his wife will be supporting the American fashion industry during her time as First Lady.  During the Presidential campaign, Lauren became closely associated with Trump’s rival Hillary Clinton, creating a series of bespoke pantsuits for the Democrat candidate. Clinton also turned to Lauren for the beige pantsuit which she wore to today's Inauguration. Yet, Melania - who has historically favoured European designers like Chanel and Gucci - was already courting Lauren by choosing his ready-to-wear pieces which she purchased in store. For the third Presidential debate, Trump chose a black Ralph Lauren jumpsuit and for her husband’s victory speech, Melania turned to another jumpsuit, this time white, from his collection. Yesterday, Melania kicked off her Inauguration looks with a military-inspired black coat by New York designer Norisol Ferrari, this was followed by a glittering gold evening gown courtesy of another New York name- Reem Acra. The trio adds up to suggest that Trump will be adhering to the glamorous  but covered up look which she displayed throughout the campaign while tweaking her designer choices to present a patriotic roster.  Given Jacqueline Kennedy’s profound fashion legacy and the clever blueprint she created for modern First Lady dressing, Melania’s decision to echo her style in today’s look seems a fitting homage. And a sign that Melania Trump will be using her clothes to send subtle messages in the way so many of her predecessors have.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Guess what? Turns out clothes matter. We know this because on Wednesday, the morning after Hillary Clinton claimed victory as the Democratic nominee (and its first female one) Tina Brown turned 75 per cent of her interview on the Today programme with Mishal Husain over to Hillary Clinton’s infamous Sergeant Pepper pantsuit and its aftermath. To recap: Nehru collared, unstructured and in one of those bilious primary colours that only female politicians ever seem to dig up, it was not a great suit. Surely, demurred Husain, Clinton’s much-vaunted failure to connect with the broad sweep of America’s electorate despite a concerted three decades-long campaign to do just that, couldn’t be pinned on her predilection for dodgy jackets? Well yes. And no. Brown’s assertion, and she’s by no means an isolated voice, is that Clinton’s style nous, never her strongest talent, has gone to pot this campaign. And just look at the results. “She’s better when she’s being herself, ie when she’s being stern,” said Brown. “She should stop being likable – it’s just so uncool. It’s needy. She should be more authentic – own her inner bitch”. “Can all that be communicated via clothes?” asked Husain, with an audible blue-stocking scepticism one can imagine Clinton herself deploying back in the early Nineties when brainy women like her really thought that clothes didn’t matter. The problem is not only that clothes matter, but that no one has quite figured out to what degree or how. In the big bang of political warfare, clothes can be highly volatile atoms. So can authenticity. Take Michael Foot’s “donkey jacket”. Widely excoriated – and worse, lampooned – back in 1981 when he wore it to the Cenotaph, it prompted one Labour MP to confess, in somewhat off-message, class-conscious terms, that he was “disgusted to see that the leader of Her Majesty’s Opposition looked more like an Irish navvy than a party leader”. Subsequently said jacket was often interpreted as a sign of Foot’s authenticity (Clinton take note) and charisma, although as a biography of Foot revealed in 2010, it wasn’t a donkey or a navvy’s jacket, “so much as a short blue-green coat bought by his wife Jill, at some expense”. The kind of thing you could drop two grand on at Dover Street Market. Will Jeremy Corby’s baggy shorts come to be reviewed as a symbol of his integrity in the face of the evil-suited apparatchik? Or what about Obama, widely admired one minute for his skinny cool tailoring, regarded somewhat suspiciously the next. Should the leader of the western world actually look cool? I’ll tell you who did embrace their authenticity – Yulia Tymoshenko’s plaits. Ukraine’s first female prime minister, who before being sentenced to  seven years in prison for alleged embezzlement, was best known internationally for her idiosyncratically patriotic hair-do which, while it may initially have played well to nationalists at home, evidently didn’t play well enough. If political dressing is problematic for men, it’s torturous for women. Sure we think we know what women in power should look like – Julia Louis-Dreyfus in HBO’s Veep, or Robin Wright in House of Cards. Both women are terrific ambassadors for female power, what with their mastery of tailored jackets, sexy-but-not-cheap -looking pencil skirts and shirts that never get rumpled. They’re also fictional – and caricatures at that. Penn is Lady Macbeth with buttery highlights. Louis-Dreyfus is a lovable klutz who, don’t ask her how, wound up chief of the most powerful office on earth. Outside the slightly misleading prism of TV, sartorial role models in the corridors of political power are elusive, which is why Margaret Thatcher is still so frequently evoked. Mrs T was undeniably well turned out, but she operated in an era when prime ministers’ clothes weren’t expected to be either fashionable or “authentic”. Having been coached for her diction and her choice of clothes she would have failed both tests. Punishingly, Clinton, it seems, must be both. After she appeared in Good Pantsuit this week (and earlier in the year in US Vogue, a publication she previously shunned for fear it would make her seem trivial, or too “feminine”), Robin Givhan, the Washington Post’s fashion editor congratulated her on finally embracing fashion. True, after decades of incremental gains, she is hovering tantalisingly close to success with those coat‑suits – much more flattering on pear shapes than all those eye‑searing blazers that hit her thighs at precisely the wrong point. The trousers and shoes are all working to conceal the cankles – boy, was she hounded for those cankles.   But she’s not really embracing fashion – nor, under any circumstances should she, fashion being an even more fickle ally than mere clothes. Rather she’s cherry picking the trappings of fashion. She has hired Michelle Obama’s former aide Kristina Schake to shape her style and – in a sign that even real politicians would rather follow the template of TV politicians – signed up a make-up artist who worked on Veep. And she’s raised her game, recently delivering a speech on wage inequality in a tweed Armani jacket that  apparently cost over $12,000 – an authentic choice given her own earning capabilities perhaps, but maybe not the wisest one in the circumstances. It was Schake who encouraged her to lower her guard against fashion because, rather than being the social grenade of Clinton’s youthful perceptions, it can be a useful ice‑breaker, even among intelligent women.  Having for years tried to lock down debate about her clothes, Clinton wryly observed, when her memoirs were published in 2014, that they could have been called The Scrunchie Chronicles, 112 Countries And It’s Still All About The Hair, a nicely judged, self parodying quip that simultaneously gently skewered the commentariat.  Far from making her seem trivial, Clinton’s subsequent detours, albeit succinct, into fashion chit-chat have helped her seem more rounded, less touchy. But authentic? Owning her inner bitch ?(Are we really ready to reclaim that word by the way and what would it look like – Cruella de Vil?) Surely for most of us finding a workable mode of power-dressing (and we all need outfits that make us look as though we know what we’re doing) is about accepting that sleight of hand is involved. It’s a question of fixing on an image that looks right and accustomising ourselves to it until it feels right.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When it comes to finding 'the dress', mature brides are often encouraged to opt for more low-key options; elegant pastel separates, say, or a cocktail dress instead of frothy, princess-like bridalwear. But perhaps this 86-year-old newlywed whose wedding pictures have gone viral proves that you can wear your fairytale gown to walk down the aisle at any age.  New Jersey resident Millie Taylor-Morrison married Harold Morrison on the 16 October, the week after her 86th birthday. She wore a purple satin crystal-encrusted gown with a full skirt, worn underneath a regal jacquard robe-style coat. Taylor-Morrison designed the outfit herself as she couldn't find anything that suited her style.  "I had a vision of what I'd like this dress to be," the bride, who used to be a model in the 1950s, told People. "So I asked a young man in my church who is an artist to sketch it and I took it to the dressmaker. Purple and lavender are my favourite colours. It was exactly what I wanted. I felt so wonderful.” Taylor-Morrison's granddaughter posted the picture of Millie on Facebook with the story about the couple, and it quickly started getting shared on social media. "This is my beautiful grandmother, Millie Taylor-Morrison, who was married over the weekend at 86-years-old," she wrote on Facebook. "She just turned 86 one week ago and her new husband will be 86 in December. My grandmother was married to my grandfather for 41 years when he passed away. She found love again almost 25 years later and our family couldn't be happier for her. This is a true testament that age is just a number and everyone can find love again." The couple became friends 60 or so years ago and Harold attended her first wedding in 1952. After Millie's first husband died in 1992 she started driving Harold to church and then looked after him when he was unwell. After he recovered they decided to get married.   "I used to sing in the choir and Harold attended my church," Millie explained to People. "I would be standing with the other choir members, waiting to walk out and he would come over and kiss me on the cheek before sitting down for the service. I used to admire him in church. He dressed impeccably and I admire that in a man." Millie proves that the mature bride has an advantage when it comes to looking like themselves on their wedding day - that they are more likely to be comfortable in their own style. "Although older brides (let’s say post-40) are often treated by wedding experts as geriatric mercy cases, deserving of special pity on the grounds that: a. they hate their upper arms, and b. it is no longer seemly for them to rock up at the register office in a multi-festooned crinoline, it seems to me that the mature bride holds some of the best cards," says The Telegraph's Fashion Director Lisa Armstrong. "For one thing, she probably has a much clearer idea than the twentysomething about what suits her, both physically and temperamentally. For another, she’s less likely to be swayed by a mother wanting to relive her wedding fantasies vicariously – or by anybody else’s preconceptions for that matter, partly because there are fewer preconceptions around." After all, as Millie Taylor-Morrison proves, brides look at their best when they are wearing exactly what they want to.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We are officially on countdown for the Oscars, which is just three days away. Guessing who will wear what on the red carpet can actually be easier than predicting who will win thanks to designer contracts. We'd bet serious money that Jennifer Lawrence will wear bespoke Dior and Alicia Vikander will wear custom-made Louis Vuitton. But what about those without long-standing relationships with brands? Designers often won't reveal if they are working on a dress at all, let alone whose dress they are designing, so finding out any teasers before the red carpet is out of the question. But we can do some calculated guesswork.  Here are some of the recent runway looks that we would like to see having a moment on the Oscars red carpet come February. We'd like to suggest just one rule: no tired strapless gowns please. Let's hope this is the year of risks (as well as the year that Leo wins an Oscar).   At 21, Saoirse Ronan is the youngest actresses nominated for a Best Actress award at the Oscars this year. When it comes to the red carpet Saoirse is always playful and not afraid of an eccentric print. We'd love to see her in a Gucci party dress or whimsical floral Valentino gown. Saoirse has said of working with her stylist Elizabeth Saltzman: "When I started working with her, I said, 'I don’t want to wear any pink, I don’t like flowers and I don’t like glitter.' All she’s put me in has been pink dresses, flowery trousers, glittery jumpsuits. She’s the best.”    It's always difficult to predict Brie Larson's next red carpet move because she isn't afraid of shaking up her style and trying something totally new. She has a thing for metallics and following on from her triumphant gold Calvin Klein Collection gown at the Golden Globes, we think I'm-dressed-like-an-Oscar sequins could be on the cards once again for the Best Actress nominee.    In 2014 Cate Blanchett was the best dressed at the Oscars thanks to her £60,000 Armani Prive show-stopping nude embellished gown. She's up for the Best Actress award once again and we'd like to see her bring the drama to the red carpet in theatrical Armani, Givenchy or Giles.   Julianne Moore isn't nominated for an award this year, but we have a feeling the Academy Award winner will be presenting. We would like to see her wearing one of the caped sequin evening looks which were shown at the Chanel Haute Couture show this January, or a slinky sequin gown by Givenchy or Tom Ford.    Best supporting actress nominee Rachel McAdams always looks beautiful on the red carpet in feminine florals, so our money is on these looks by Lela Rose, Oscar de la Renta and Marchesa. Rachel's stylists Rob Zangardi and Mariel Haenn said to WWD of her red carpet style:  “Old Hollywood, young and sexy but not overtly so. High fashion but not over styled.”   Rooney Mara is nominated in the Best Supporting Actress category this year for her performance in Carol. On the promo tour for the film Rooney wore white, black and pale pink directional looks by her go-to designers Alexander McQueen, Balenciaga and Givenchy. She might wear black, she might wear white, she'll probably wear Givenchy, but one thing is for certain: she won't wear anything colourful.    Jennifer Lawrence is nominated in the Best Actress category for her performance in Joy. It's safe to assume that she will wear Dior, and most likely Haute Couture. But if she wears a look from the catwalk, here are some potential gowns Jennifer could have first dibs on. Jennifer previously said of how she selected the gown (which she later, artfully fell over in)  when she won her Oscar in 2013: "We were going through a lot of pictures online, I saw it picture of it on the runway. It was just the most beautiful dress I think I'd ever seen. Now I get the Haute Couture thing - it's a big deal."     See the best ever Oscar dresses in the gallery below... © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Hollywood actress Naomi Watts has been promoting two films this month, The Divergent Series: Allegiant and Demolition, standing out on the red carpet in elegant, but never-boring, gowns. Her stylist Jeannan Williams talked to The Telegraph about the advantage of dressing an actress over 40, her recent red carpet disaster and how sometimes it is Watts' partner who makes the final decisions... Watts wore a ruffled Valentino gown to the Demolition New York premiere this week, but it was a last minute substitute. "For Demolition, we wanted to work with Valentino on something.  We were lucky enough to have four amazing looks from the new F/W 16 collection sent to us for Naomi's fitting, but the pieces didn't make it in time. Fed Ex Fail! Insert panic!" Williams says, "But Valentino were amazing, they stepped in with quite a few new gems for us including the gorgeous ruffled confection that she had tried for the SAGs and ended up wearing. We had hoped to revisit it and eedless to say it all felt kismet." “The advantage is she’s a pro," Williams says of dressing an actress over 40 (Watts is 47 years old). "There’s no carpet she hasn't seen before, which kills all the nerves. She has presence, she knows her angles, how to walk with grace and elegance, truly honouring the gown. She is a true movie star. She doesn't sweat the small stuff, she's incredibly gracious and humble." As for being over 40 on the red carpet, she says: "Age yes, she definitely keeps this top of mind and there are trends she won't do, but that's also kind of great. It's a part of knowing who you are, what works for you and having your own sense of style. I see this as a positive.  I push her out of her comfort zone just enough I think. Have you seen that body? She looks amazing and works hard for it, so there are ways to dress age appropriate, but still bring that 'wow factor'. " Watts wore a heavily embellished short Derek Lam look to the Allegiant New York premiere last week, because she needed a break from red carpet floor sweepers. "For Allegiant she definitely wanted something short, she was sick of gowns after award season.  The silver and black beaded Derek Lam fit the bill perfectly, almost futuristic, it had an edge, yet still sophisticated with an almost '20s feel." Red carpet dresses are usually returned to the designers, but Williams reveals that Watts could make an exhibition of her own collection of Oscars dresses. "Well the house of Armani spoils us rotten, Naomi was gifted her Oscars gown," Williams tells The Telegraph. "This has been the case in the past, so she has all three Armani Oscar gowns we have done together.  They are very special moments and hers alone, they tell a story. Who knows maybe someday there will be an exhibition of all her gowns and dresses, that would be quite a sight."  Williams tells The Telegraph: "Women need options: you never know how you will feel on the day. I almost always have two looks completely prepped for a big night and let her, or in the case of Oscars, Liev [Naomi Watts' partner, Liev Schreiber ] call it on the morning of. Often it comes down to something as simple as if the sun shines." "The reviews can be tough and they put a lot of pressure on a big red carpet day like the Oscars," Williams says of the instant coverage of the red carpet. "It all starts off feeling very intimate with little decisions made just between her and I, and then all of a sudden within minutes of her hitting the carpet thousands of people around the world are critiquing my work down to every minute detail. It can make you cringe and anxious, so I try to just be present." Does she pay attention to this critique? "Yes, I look, how can you not. As long as she's happy, feels good and doesn't get killed we both say OK and get on with our night and have some fun." They will also text their own opinions on the other red carpet looks: "She loves fashion, so we'll discuss our favorites, sometimes shooting off a few texts during the ceremony." How many emails go into one red carpet gown? "Thousands honestly.  So much back and forth, stuff coming in, stuff going out. My phone goes through 2/3 charges a day that's for sure." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Although The Duchess of Cambridge is mostly renowned for her elegantly timeless style, occassionally she chooses a look which suggests that maybe she does have half an eye on trends, after all. Last summer, she nodded to the off-shoulder look which was sweeping the high street at the time in looks by Barbara Casasola and Roland Mouret. And during the tour to Canada in September, her choice of a pie-crust collar dress from See by Chloe was a hint that she was fully aware of the ruffles-and-frills mania occupying shops and Instagram. Today, the Duchess displayed her fashion nous once again by debuting a pair of kick flare, cropped trousers by J. Crew as she visited the 1851 Trust's roadshow at London's Docklands which uses sailing to encourage young people to get involved in STEM subjects. She paired her new trousers with a white Zara blazer, white t-shirt and tweed J.Crew block heels which she first wore last autumn as she met young people enjoying their away day. Although the J.Crew style is no longer available, they do play into one of the key trouser looks of the moment and mark quite a departure from the Duchess's usual penchant for skinny cut trousers. Cropped, flared trousers have been something of a slow burner trend, emerging as a key piece thanks to designers from Prada to Gucci, Chloe and Alexander McQueen featuring versions in their collections. Meanwhile, denim labels including Mih jeans, Frame Denim and Current/Elliott have created more casual jeans takes on the look which have become a modern alternative to the skinny jean.   .@1851Trust Roadshows deliver a unique multi-activity STEM, sustainability and sailing day for local students around the UK The cropped, kick flare has been widely adopted by the style set- yes, some people got in there before Kate- with Alexa Chung, Rosie Huntington-Whiteley and Reese Witherspoon among  the celebrities to have trialled it, mostly pairing it with silky shirts and blazers. But of course any trends with the words 'cropped' and 'flare' in it was never going to be the easiest to pull off.  The abbreviated length exposes the slim ankle bone so makes them more flattering than classic floor-sweeping flares, but the proportions can still be on the tricky side, especially with styles like those chosen by Kate with a sharp central crease. As ever, it's all about getting the cut right- high-waisted, thigh-skimming rather than clinging and not too short, not too long are your key pointers.  Arguably, Kate was likely first drawn to her new J.Crew  trousers because they work brilliantly into her penchant for literal dressing i.e dressing as closely as possible to suit the occasion. Given today's visit was all about sailing, her navy and white colour palette and those shiny gold buttons are the epitome of smart-casual sailor styling.  Previous literal dressing moments have seen the Duchess wear a tiered white dress to Wimbledon, a floral tea dress to the Chelsea Flower Show and red in Canada, beside numerous outings to sailing-themed engagements in navy and cream.  Her visit came as her husband Prince William accompanied The Queen to visit the residents' whose lives were devastated by the fire at Grenfell Tower in West London this week.  When Pippa Middleton selected couturier Giles Deacon to design her wedding dress, it's fair to say that the decision raised some eyebrows. Not because Deacon wasn't supremely qualified for the role- after all, he is known for his fantastically imaginative collections and precise couture-level craftsmanship- but because he seemed like such a 'fashion' choice for a woman who usually sticks to high street and contemporary stalwarts like L.K Bennett, Warehouse and Kate Spade or Sloaney occassionwear favourites like Tabitha Webb.  But the week before her May nuptials to financier James Matthews, suggestion came that the rumoured designer of her wedding gown might not be a one-off high fashion decision but part of a wider strategy by The Duchess of Cambridge's younger sister to step up her style reputation. As she left her then-fiancé's Chelsea home for the Para-Snow ball, Middleton debuted a new blue jacquard dress by Erdem, the London fashion week designer whose shows are always a feast of romantically intricate dresses destined for the most ladylike of dressers.  Today, the new Mrs Matthews arrived at Wimbledon wearing a pale pink lace midi dress with sharp shirt collar detailling which was a more fashion-forward choice than anything she has ever worn for her annual pilgrimage to SW19. What's more, the £360 design is by Self Portrait- the cult label which has shot to fame over the past couple of years with its guipure lace dresses which have become a new go-to for occasion dressing. While you could never call the look experimental exactly, it certainly conjures a more sophisticated and informed feel than Pippa's previous choices. Paired with minimal accessories, sunglasses and a relaxed ponytail, she looked more coolly confident than ever.  Another area in which Pippa has plenty of sartorial experience is wedding guest dressing- naturally, she seems to land an invite to every society do on the calendar- and has been to two since returning from her rather epic world-tour honeymoon. First up was another dreamy Erdem creation- the floorsweeping, high-necked £2720 Kenzie dress- for the marriage of Jons Bartholdson and Anna Ridderstad. At the marriage of her good friend Camilla Campion-Howard to Oliver Jenkinson in Ireland this weekend, Pippa eschewed the polite printed dresses she usually chooses for such occasions in favour of a beautifully bold emerald-green shift by Royal College of Art-trained young designer, Alice Archer (top). It's the sort of thing which only a truly in-the-know, luxury-minded shopper might snap up.  "I was inspired by the artist Nobuyoshi Araki's bold and sensual photographs of flowers," Archer tells The Telegraph of her opulent 'Freya' design which was made in Como, Italy and hand-finished in her London studio. "The technique I use to achieve an almost 3-dimensional look is through the use of digital embroidery," Archer adds of her uniquely modern yet ultra-pretty signature. "In some cases, we finish with hand embroidery details. I programme every single stitch, so that even though the embroidery is made digitally it has the quality and texture of traditional hand embroidery." When Deacon's wedding dress was finally revealed, a statement from the designer read: "It's a privilege to show the craftsmanship that my team produces in London and a real testament to Pippa's support of British fashion." An investment in one of Archer's equally painstaking creations- which can retail for more than £2000- suggests that it's a scheme she is keen to keep up. Has British fashion just found an unlikely new champion?   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Ordinarily, the Pirelli calendar is a byword for smutty sexiness, albeit beautifully shot. Flip the cover (if you’re lucky enough to be one of the elite few to receive one) and you’ll find 12 NSFW images of scantily-clad or entirely nude models, often set in a tropical locale. But for 2016, the world famous calendar has changed tack and opted for an altogether different approach that celebrates the featured women for their achievements, and not as objects of titillation – something which the calendar is annually accused of. Partial nudity is still part of the package though, thanks to comedian Amy Schumer and tennis player Serena Williams, who both pose in their underwear for the black-and-white shots - but they are in the minority in this edition of the famed calendar. It’s all down the Annie Leibovitz, the photographer chosen to capture the latest edition, which takes on a book-like appearance this year, detailing the accomplishments of each subject with a paragraph of text. It was Leibovitz got to cherry-pick the line-up of women, too. “I thought of women I admired. I still can’t believe the women who agreed to do it,” explains Leibovitz. You’ll find only one model in the 13-strong line-up of women; 33-year-old Russian Natalia Vodianova, who has already appeared in the calendar a number of times before. Alongside her is a cast of strong, successful women from fields including music, film, literature, sport and art, with an age range of 19 (writer Tavi Gevinson) to 82 (Yoko Ono) - and they don't get their kit off. “I started to think about the roles that women play, women who have achieved something. I wanted to make a classic set of portraits. I thought that the women should look strong but natural, and I decided to keep it a very simple exercise of shooting in the studio,” Leibovitz said. “This calendar is so completely different. It is a departure. The idea was not to have any pretence in these pictures and be very straightforward.” At the press conference, the photographer added: “We need more than twelve months… There isn’t a beginning and there isn’t an end.” Schumer, wearing just a pair of briefs, was the last subject to be photographed, and Leibovtz thought it funny to portray the comedian as the only one who didn’t get the memo about the calendar not being nude-centric for 2016. “I felt I was more beautiful than I’ve ever felt in my life,” commented the star, 34. Leibovitz stated that retouching was kept to a minimum for the final images, and summed the collection of portraits as: “No-one was supposed to look like they had tried in these pictures.”  Yoko Ono, 82: artist
The second wife and widow of John Lennon, Yoko Ono is an established artist and musician in her own right. She is now the oldest woman to appear in the famed calendar, a record that was previously held by Sophia Loren. Serena Williams, 33: professional tennis player
As the official world number one, Serena Williams is widely regarded as the greatest female tennis player of all time. She recently diverged into a career as a designer and earlier this year showed a collection at New York Fashion Week. Fran Lebowitz, 64: author
Lebowitz started her career as a columnist for the Andy Warhol-founded Interview magazine and is now known for her sneering social commentary on modern American life. Her style too has become something of a signature; she favours Anderson & Sheppard suits.  Amy Schumer, 34: comedian, writer, producer, director and actress
You'll likely recognise Amy Schumer for her red carpet pranks, which include prat-falling in front of a bemused Kim and Kanye. The comedian and writer starred in her first self-penned film, Trainwreck, earlier this year and has seen her star ascend dramatically thanks to her honest, humorous observations on life as a woman today. Tavi Gevinson, 19: writer and magazine editor
Gevinson was just 12 years old when she started winning plaudits for her fashion blog Style Rookie in 2008. Three years later she turned her focus to culture and feminist discussion and founded digital publication Rookie Magazine, which boasts contributors inclduing Lena Dunham and Judd Apatow. She is a staunch campaigner for the equal treatment of disabled people in Russia; her younger sister, Oksana, suffers from cerebral palsy and autism and has been the victim of abuse numerous times. Yao Chen, 35: actress
Chinese actress Chen is the most-followed person on China's version of Twitter, Sina Weibo, and regualrly listed as one of the most powerful women in the wold thanks to her vast following. Just a simple Weibo post by her can raise thousands for worthy causes from her adoring fans. Patti Smith, 68: musician
It would be hard to find a more iconic figure than Patti Smith and her inclusion in the calendar seems oddly fitting, given her influence. Famed for her songwriting and poetry, she is also an acclaimed writer thanks to her memoir Just Kids. Agnes Gund, 77: philanthropist, art patron and collector and advocate for arts education
Gund is one of the most prolific art collectors of her generation. Born to a prominent Ohio family, in 2011 she was nominated by President Barack Obama as a member of the Board of Trustees of the National Council on the Arts. Kathleen Kennedy, 62: film producer
Kennedy is the co-founder of Amblin Entertainment with Steven Spielberg and Frank Marshall, and also the president of Lucasfilm and brand manager of the Star Wars franchise. Her body of work, which includes films such as E.T. and the Jurassic Park, includes over 60 films and 120 Oscar nominations.  Mellody Hobson, 46: president of Ariel Investments and the current Chairman of the Board of Directors of Dreamworks Animation
Businesswoman Hobson, who is married to Star Wars creator George Lucas, is often cited as one ofthe most influential women in the world thanks to her involvement with numerous high-profile oragnisations including the Starbucks Corporation and The Estée Lauder Companies Inc.  When Chitose Abe was in kindergarten all the kids were wearing bell bottoms. 'Since everybody was wearing them, I couldn’t like them,’ she says, with a shrug clearly meant to be interpreted as 'obviously’. 'So I asked my mother to make my trousers very tight.’ A week later one of her friends also turned up at school with skinny trousers. 'I was so upset I ran out of school,’ says Abe. 'I couldn’t stay when my friend had copied me.’   The unique, the exclusive, the inimitable is where it starts and ends for 50-year-old Abe. Over 18 years she has built up her label Sacai, both women’s and menswear, with a look entirely its own. Now sold in the most prestigious stores across the globe (including Selfridges, Dover Street Market and Net-a-Porter), it is applauded by fashion editors and buyers alike. Karl Lagerfeld has said she is one of the most interesting designers working today. The former Comme des Garçons employee, who has been established in Japan since 1998 but only started showing her collection in Paris in 2012, has taken modern wardrobe classics – the shirt, the kilt, the blouse, the biker jacket –  and given them an avant-garde twist. Never has a navy pleated skirt worked so hard to be something more. There are surprises in all her clothes  – inserts of contrasting  fabrics, knife pleats that fan open as you move, splits in seams, backs that fall open, exaggerated ruched waistlines at the backs of dresses. This fusion of statement and elegance that lends Sacai pieces a kind of era-less longevity came two seasons into her label. 'I realised that I always wanted to wear the same kind of clothes – a shirt or a biker jacket or a pair of trousers – but I could make them different, really new,’ she says. 'I wanted to make garments that everybody wears but turn it into something that could be made only by me. That’s when I began to think of this fusion, mixing the garments so they would become special.’ It is two days after Sacai’s autumn/winter 2016 catwalk show and we are in her concrete-floored showroom off a bamboo-planted courtyard, a cavernous space with the new collection lining its sides. At a score of tables in the centre, buyers from legendary boutiques are placing orders. Abe talks through an interpreter but is utterly engaging. She’s a curious mix of tranquillity and mischievous glee (backstage after her shows she squeals and bounces about on her platform sandals), and is fairy-tale beautiful with it – glowing skin, luxuriant hair. She wears a single gold and pearl sculptural earring by Sophie Bille Brahe and, just visible beneath her bandanna, a gold necklace with 'Chitose’ written in a tiny curly script. When she’s thinking of a response to a question she closes her eyes tight, tips up her nose and says, 'Mmmmm,’ until she comes up with an answer. 'I’m just trying to make what I want to wear,’ she says, 'and I always want something new.’ The clothes look complicated and indeed the design and construction are, but Abe puts a lot of time into making sure that they are also comfortable. She tries on everything before the runway show and then again afterwards, before the pieces are produced for retail. 'I try to make the clothes as easy to wear as possible, all without changing the design,’ she says. Abe was born in Nagayo, Japan. Her father designed air-conditioning and her mother was a patissier who taught her daughter to sew. Abe started making clothes for dolls, designed her first dress at 12 and immediately knew she was on to something when an older girl from school asked her where it was from. 'She was upset when she heard I had made it because she knew I was wearing something very special and she wouldn’t be able to find it anywhere,’ she says, still relishing the memory. After fashion college and working for a big textile firm, Abe started as a pattern cutter for Rei Kawakubo’s groundbreaking label, Comme des Garçons. 'Of course I was influenced by [Kawakubo] in a way, but she is not the kind of person who actually teaches people,’ she says. 'But I learnt from her that originality is very important – the originality of design but also the importance of originality in business.’ As a result Abe has kept full, independent ownership of her label. There are rumours that she has been in the mix for high-profile jobs currently vacant at Paris fashion houses. She doesn’t deny it. 'It is not something that I’m not interested in,’ she says in a roundabout way. 'But it’s important who you work with. I would need someone who would truly understand the creativity of the label Sacai and what Sacai would make. But I have been thinking about it.’ Abe is married to another Japanese design sensation, Junichi Abe of the label Kolor, with whom she has an 18-year-old daughter. 'Big girl now. Very same face,’ Abe says in English, beaming. The couple met at Junya Watanabe, which Chitose helped to set up. They have not worked together since and never will, Abe says strictly. They made a rule years ago that they will not talk about their businesses to each other. 'We are both in the same situation so it’s better not to know everything. I really don’t know what he’s up to,’ she says. 'It’s only when I’m doing the laundry and I find his clothes that I have a look and think, “Ah, so this is what his brand is like.”’  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
