 With over 60 celebrities to dress, filming which took place by night on the River Thames and a surprisngly strict budget, you might think that masterminding the wardrobe for Absolutely Fabulous: The Movie would have been a stressful affair but nothing could be further from the truth confirms costume director Rebecca Hale- "Oh yes, it was a joy a minute!" she laughs, "I’ve never had so much fun on a film, likely not to ever again!" For the unintitaited, this week sees the release of the much-anticipated film version of the hit 90s and 00s TV series which follows the outrageous escapades of fashionistas Edina and Patsy. Hale joined the Ab Fab team in the early 2000s back when Instagram and Snapchat were but twinkles in their creator's eyes and Kim Kardashian was just your average rebellious LA teen.  In fact, Eddy and Patsy's world has changed quite a bit since we last saw them (in a short series of special episodes for the Olympics in 2012) and there is probably no more potent way to show their new reality than via their wardrobes. "Most of the issues on Ab Fab are related to social issues that we have, albeit quite frivolous a lot of the time, but there’s always a message" muses Hale. "Life has changed dramatically since early 2000s- the whole way we socialise, we communicate on social media, we shop on the internet and life is completely different. It’s become much broader and a lot more insular all at the same time, so I wanted to be very aware of that," she explains. That awareness plays out most emphatically in the way we dress; "I think it makes you less creative because you are more governed by what Kim Kardashian or Miley Cyrus is wearing. You think 'Oh I want to look like her'. If you have no point of referencing, you’re going to make your own style." In lots of ways, Patsy and Eddy were predictors of what fashion would become in 2016. "Fashion has got so outrageous that I thought, before Edina was always outrageous and people go 'Oh my God, she looks wild'" explains Hale, "I discussed it with Jennifer and said I thought she needed to be toned down, otherwise it’s not necessarily right for the character now and they’re a lot older- although being age-appropriate  would never worry Edina!" So how did Hale pull off the costume director job of the year? Here she tells us some of her Absolutely Fabulous: The movie wardrobe secrets...  "Edina has a flow of Net-a-Porter clothes coming through the door, more being delivered all the time," says Hale of Eddy swpping her Harvey Nichols shopping habit for the online luxury site. "Bubble picks them up from the Net-a-Porter driver. The house is just full of Net-a-Porter bags." Like many of the references in the original Ab Fab, this extravagance is rooted in reality. "Where I live in Queen’s Park, I see four or five Net-a-Porter and Matches vans everyday" Hale tells The Telegraph. Net-a-Porter themselves were happy to help scatter as many modern day designer must-haves as possible across our screens by providing samples for Hale and her team to use. "We were very fortunate, in the sense that, we didn’t have the money, we’d never be able to buy a lot of clothes for everybody that came in, " says Hale, "Net-a-Porter were really kind and said it was a project they wanted to be involved with so they loaned a huge rail of clothes."  "I really love doing Saffy" emphasises Hale, " because you find shoes that look like Cornish pasties and all sorts. Julia (Sawalha) would talk about people we know and what they'd wear- she gets very involved." Long-time Ab Fab fans will remember Saffy's hopelessly frumpy sense of style which provides such exquisite contrast to Eddy's OTT look. Now that normcore has happened, there's even something a little bit aspirational about Saffy's style, but finding pieces for her to wear is actually quite a nuanced process. "It’s not always about finding the most ghastly piece of clothing," says Hale, "you might find a nice shirt and put that with a horrible pair of cargo pants from Mountain Warehouse. She’s just needs to be oblivious. "There are many people in the world who don’t really care what they wear and don’t really care what they look like, and in a funny kind of way, that’s more important because they’re worrying about other issues which are more important. It’s a combination of finding horrible old jumpers in charity shops and mixing them up with something that’s like a nice piece from Brora for example. It's good fun."  "Kate is THE fashion icon of the noughties. Initially I went to see Kate and my overriding ambition was that Kate had to stay herself," explains Hale. "She wasn’t playing a part, she was playing herself. I went to her stylist and said that we'd need a dress which stands out but we’ve got to be able to make it or borrow it from a designer and it’s got to be simple because you’ve got to wear it over a wetsuit because you’re coming out of the Thames in the middle of November!" Of course Moss had just th thing squirrelled away in her wardrobe. "She said 'I’ve got this dress which I think would be perfect! I was given it on my 21st Birthday from Johnny Depp'” remembers Hale. "It’s a very simple dress so we could recreate it perfectly.  So, in the end my seamstress just copied the dress that Kate was given by Johnny Depp- it had originally been made by a Hollywood costume designer." When your cast includes some of the best-dressed people in the world with access to incredible designer archives, it would almost seem a waste not to ask them to bring along a few options of their own. "Jerry Hall was one who was very happy to wear her own clothes, " recalls Hale, "she has this amazing Chanel piece which she looked extraordinary in." Of course, there's logical reasoning behind sourcing celebs' costumes from their own collections; "We thought 'well, you’re perfect,'" says Hale, "they’re playing themselves, so it’s appropriate they look what they would look like. It’s what you’d expect them to wear on the red carpet." With both of the girls, I wanted to hark back to the nineties, when Ab Fab was created," says Hale. "There was a lot of nineties fashion and images which we were inspired by, or there were designs that were slightly reminiscent of the nineties. "Most of the clothes that Patsy wore came from Betty Jackson and there’s always tailoring with a slight twist so it’s classic but it’s got something that’s different. So I kept that in mind and I went to Mulberry because they do really beautiful tailoring and really lovely clothes.  "Joanna (Lumley) and I went and talked to the people at Mulberry so that's where all her classics come from. But then you have the pieces of anarchy in there to mix it up, so when she’s going to a fashion party, that’s when I put her in Alexander McQueen- a bit more rock ‘n roll with a leather jacket." "Stella took up the mantle after Lacroix so she is what Jennifer’s idea is of the person who is the leader in fashion now" Hale explains. "Jennifer (or Edina) desires to wear her pieces  and what Stella doesn’t want her to wear them because she’s a social embarrassment!" Hale believes that despite McCartney's playful role, a serious fashion point about British fashion is being made with her involvement; "She’s an iconic fashion designer and very important within the film. I wanted to champion all British fashion from Stella to Westwood and the younger people who are just leaving college. I wanted to incorporate everybody and it was the perfect opportunity to do that."     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Donald Trump dropped a fashion bombshell during a post-Golden Globes interview on Monday. Responding to Meryl Streep’s dignified, mournful remarks about his unrelenting assault on decency, the non-fictional president-elect said he was ‘not surprised’ by Streep's comments as she's ‘a Hillary lover’ - but that’s ok, because he’s so popular, and so many people want to attend his inauguration, that there are no more dresses left to buy in Washington DC. ‘We are going to have an unbelievable, perhaps record-setting turnout for the inauguration, and there will be plenty of movie and entertainment stars,’ Trump told The New York Times. ‘All the dress shops are sold out in Washington. It’s hard to find a great dress for this inauguration.’ Could it be? Were the denizens of DC so ecstatic to welcome the Trump regime that they sent the women (all tens, no doubt) out to buy new dresses in such overwhelming force? Has Ivanka failed to fill him in about the existence of online shopping? Like many Trump statements, this one merited some fact-checking. Which was difficult, because no one shops in DC. It’s a territory relatively untouched by fashion, at least anecdotally, until the arrival of Michelle Obama. Or rather, it’s not that no one living in DC cares about fashion, though that’s a stereotype too - it’s more that anyone who’s excited about fashion finds it worth her while to hop on the Acela for three hours and go shop in New York. Back to the fact-checking. Hello, special occasion department at Neiman Marcus Mazza Gallerie… Do you still have dresses? ‘Yes, we do. We have a great selection.’ Nordstrom The Fashion Centre at Pentagon City - do you still have dresses? ‘No comment - but yes.’ CH Carolina Herrera? ‘No more comments.’ (Previously a sales associate told the Associated Press that dresses were still in stock.) That’s settled, then. Ladies of DC, rest assured: there are still dresses! One person who should have been having a little less trouble finding something to wear is future FLOTUS Melania Trump. Whilst some American designers such as Tom Ford and Marc Jacobs have been vocal in their determination not to dress Trump, others have come forward to offer their services to a woman who can put their designs in the global spotlight. Carolina Herrera said it would be ‘an honour’ to dress the first lady. Diane von Furstenberg said it was the fashion industry’s responsibility ‘to promote beauty, inclusiveness, diversity.’  Tommy Hilfiger, not exactly a noted gown designer, but an American fashion behemoth nonetheless, said ‘any designer should be proud to dress her.’ Italian maestro Stefano Gabbana certainly was; he took to Instagram to thank Mrs Trump for wearing a Dolce & Gabbana LBD to a ticketed New Year’s Eve party at Trump retreat Mar-a-Lago. Some took that enthusiasm as a clue the Italian design duo might be working on her inauguration look - a fashion move that would be controversial, considering no other First Lady has used a foreign designer for such a key event.   So what about Ralph Lauren, living legend and the man who has defined American style for well over a decade…? Well, she’s been there, done that, worn the bridal jumpsuit. But she did buy it from the store's rail, rather than having a custom-fitting like her husband's counterpart in the election, Hillary Clinton. Deduce from that what you will. Perhaps Mrs Trump will enjoy the ministrations of a special, surprising ally. Anna Wintour, the Vogue editor-in-chief and Condé Nast artistic director, invited President-elect Trump to meet Condé Nast executives at the company's New York headquarters last Friday. The meeting was off-the-record, so there's no telling what was discussed - but with past Trump critics Wintour, Vanity Fair Editor Graydon Carter (who once described Trump as a 'short-fingered vulgarian') and New Yorker Editor David Remnick in attendance, it can't have been breezy. Unless, of course, Wintour used the occasion to offer to reinvigorate Vogue's relationship with the future first lady. After all, Mrs Trump made something of a global debut on the February 2005 cover of Vogue. With Editor-at-Large Andre Leon Talley as her 'couture mentor,' Melania enjoyed a romp through leading Paris couture houses in search of her wedding gown. She wears her choice - a $100,000 Christian Dior Couture gown - on the cover. Past choices for high-stake occasions show Melania hewing to a narrow vision of femininity, one reliant on nipped-in waists, high heels and solid colours. Like Betty Ford and Pat Nixon, she's a former model, and she wears clothes well (though she may want to refrain from altering already fitted designs to fit even tighter, as in the case of a certain white Roksanda dress). One thing is certain: Melania will want to use the inauguration to make a statement. Not least because a First Lady's inauguration gown is traditionally a symbolic outfit, that sets the tone for their presidency - and often sparks a wider trend. Mamie Eisenhower’s 1953 pink gown, designed by Nettie Rosenstein, is said to be the reason why the bubble-gum colour dominated the 1950's. Jackie Kennedy opted for a white caped gown; designed to stand-out in both black and white media and make her easy to spot in the sea of guests. Lady Bird Johnson, meanwhile, opted to wear yellow for the 1965 Inauguration - a cheery, optimistic colour, for a bitter-sweet unexpected ceremony after John F Kennedy's shocking assassination.  Most of Melania's predecessors though have opted for red, white or blue gowns for inaugural balls, for obvious reasons. She might throw a curveball and nod to 1993's White House chatelaine (that would be Hillary Clinton) by wearing purple. Or do what no other First Lady has and wear a classic black dress, a fail safe option she's fallen back on a number of times. At least one DC-area retailer has a view on the colour she expects to rule the day on 20th January. ‘We have a lot of red gowns for this inauguration,’ said Krista Johnson, owner of Georgetown boutique Ella-Rue. Place your bets now.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s a bitterly cold Friday afternoon in Paris so there is great concern for Natalia Vodianova, who has gamely been posing on the balcony of the InterContinental hotel in nothing but a silk dress and jacket. ‘Get her a blanket!’ an assistant pleads. Moments later an enormous beige curtain complete with giant goblet pleats is bustled into the room. Greater divas than Vodianova might throw a tantrum seeing old curtains in lieu of something more luxurious, but she simply squeals with amusement and wraps the fabric around her waist to create a fabulous ballgown skirt.  They don’t call her Supernova (a nickname of which she is so proud, she uses it as her Instagram profile) for nothing.  In classic good-British-girl fashion Lily James opted to wear a dress by London-based designer Erdem at the London premiere of Pride and Prejudice and Zombies. The 26-year-old actress graced the red carpet in Leicester Square wearing an off-the-shoulder cropped top and a full-length tiered skirt from the designer's SS16 collection, whose black and grey asymmetric stripes gave a romantic Victorian feel to a modern navel-baring silhouette. She paired her ensemble with Jessica McCormack jewellery, and Aquazzura shoes. The Surrey-born actress has made her name in period dramas. She's currently starring as the beautiful and impetuous Countess Natasha Rostova in the BBC's adaptation of Tolstoy's Russian epic War and Peace, and she played kindhearted Lady Rose Aldridge in Downton Abbey. Both are performances that have led her to the lead role in Pride and Prejudice and Zombies - that of Elizabeth Bennet who faces not just trouble with Mr Darcy but also zombies. Her wardrobe for the Pride and Prejudice and Zombies global tour has seen her go high fashion, and representing her British roots by wearing homegrown designers. In addition to Erdem, Lily wore a dainty floral Alexander McQueen dress to the LA premiere in January - something her stylist Rebecca Corbin-Murray said she had to talk the star into. “I told her: 'If you want to be the movie star you have to dress like a movie star, even if you feel a bit silly,’ - especially when you’re English and you always act embarrassed about everything all the time,” she told The Telegraph of dressing Lily for the red carpet.  It was good advice. Lily's Erdem two-piece is the latest in a long string of strong red carpet moments which have contributed to the starlet claiming her place as one of The Telegraph's best dressed women of 2015. Working with her stylist, Lily has worn jaw-dropping evening gowns from the likes of Marchesa and Elie Saab and more directional choices from Mary Katrantzou and Balenciaga.  Give us a twirl, Lily James! #PPZPremiere 🙌 pic.twitter.com/IHzJgO6cMH It's not just the killer outfit that makes Lily stand out on the red carpet - the actress also knows it's all about the pose. “I made her stand in the mirror practising different poses and while we take pictures," her stylist Corbin-Murray told us of Lily's pre-Golden Globes preparation. "And then go through them and make sure that the way she is standing is the best for her and the best for the dress.” Something tells us that's a lesson she's also taken to heart for today's London premiere.  Elsewhere on the Pride & Prejudice Zombies red carpet, actress Ellie Bamber set off her porcelain skin and auburn hair with a delicate nude-pink tiered gown with petal appliqué, proving she's one to watch for future red carpet engagements. She's set to star in  Tom Ford's new film Nocturnal Animals, due later this year, which makes it likely that she'll have big name dress leverage when it comes to her turn in the spotlight. Bella Heathcote wore a slinky sequin-embellished 90s-silhouette dress with a powerful side split that required some serious poise when posing, while fellow Bennett sister Millie Brady was radiant in a baby-blue floorsweeper with criss-cross sparkle detailing.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When you’re a Hollywood star with a film to promote, the concept of maternity leave goes out of the window. Unless you’re actually in the delivery room during your latest film’s premiere, there’s no reason why you shouldn’t be smiling for the cameras and talking about your work – all while looking resplendent in the process. Take 30-year-old Carey Mulligan, who glided onto the red carpet in London last week in a playful and purple Chanel Haute Couture frock alongside her Suffragette co-star Meryl Streep.   Mulligan, who is married to Mumford and Sons singer Marcus Mumford, isn’t the sort to be papped falling out of nightclubs or at the opening of an envelope, so during her recent hiatus from the promotional circuit, she’s managed to discreetly go about her pregnancy, welcoming her first child just three weeks ago. Yes, three weeks. New mother looks away now - for there was no hint of baby sick on that Chanel dress, or any sign of a struggle for Ms Mulligan to slip into it. Instead she looked radiant and at ease as she posed for photographs in a rather blustery Leicester Square, discussing women’s rights and praising the domestic violence activists who had chosen to protest at the premiere. Earlier on in the day, she’d been dressed in more Chanel samples to make an appearance alongside Streep at the BFI London Film Festival, and her schedule hasn’t let-up since. Travelling to New York – undoubtedly with baby daughter Evelyn in tow, Mulligan has been showcasing her remarkable bounce-back in waist-cinching gowns by Roland Mouret and Alexander McQueen for public appearances, accessorised with a punchy red slip or her hair in effortless waves – not sleep-deprived eyes or a sense of humour failure.  The Duchess of Cambridge has tweeted a series of charming pictures of her daughter Princess Charlotte to celebrate her first birthday, on May 2. The set of four portraits, which includes the first photograph of Charlotte walking, were all captured by the Duchess, herself, with the caption: "We hope that everyone enjoys these lovely photos as much as we do." The photos follow the recent release of Kate’s first ever Vogue cover and fashion shoot, taken by Josh Olins, in honour of Vogue’s 100 anniversary. Although Princess Charlotte has mainly been dressed in Spanish childrenswear labels, such as M&H and Amaia Kids, she is also wearing an emerging British childrenswear designer in her birthday portraits. She wears a cream vintage-inspired cashmere cardigan by Olivier Kids, which is £59. Emma Davison, who previously worked at Cath Kidston, created the label in 2011 after the birth of her second child. "The cardigan Princess Charlotte is wearing was actually our first design," Davison tells The Telegraph. "My own daughter is called Rose and my nanny mentioned a stitch called the Rose stitch so that's how it came about. It's very close to my heart." "I started knitting for my children and friends children then I actually began to receive orders," Davison continues. "So my nanny at the time pitched in to help too. It was an old bonnet of mine which my mum found which inspired the whole thing, I wanted to make something similar. Now we have piles of vintage pieces and patterns."  Olivier have already experienced an impact on sales by their royal wearers. "Prince George wore one of our cardigans to the polo last summer and we immediately noticed a surge in orders, not just from the UK but from as far afield as Japan and America," she explains. "Even this afternoon we've seen a huge increase in visits to our website. The effect is incredible." The photo of Charlotte pushing a wooden trolley in the garden of her Norfolk home, Anmer Hall, shows her wearing a pale pink Peter Pan collared dress, with matching M&H cardigan, woolen Amaia Kids tights and dark Early Days pumps. A pink Amaia Kids bow is fastened in her hair. In the image of her playing with her Wheels On The Bus, a sound and action book by David Ellwand, Charlotte appears to be wearing the same M&H knit, which retails for £23 from the Spanish retailer. This is not the first time Kate has dressed Charlotte in M&H, and founder Margarita Pato has previously told The Telegraph that the brand saw an immediate impact. “Princess Charlotte wearing two of our floral dresses has had a huge influence on our brand,” Pato told us ahead of Charlotte's first birthday. “It’s especially important for medium sized brands like us - we only have five stores in Spain.” Whilst the dresses Charlotte appeared in were already sold out when the pictures broke (“we only offer ten per store of each dress otherwise all the girls will be in the same outfit”), the halo effect has left the brand planning to launch an ecommerce site which will ship to the UK, Europe and the USA. The soft cotton ribbed tights, £11, and hair bows, £2.50, worn in the same portraits (above), are both from Chelsea boutique, Amaia Kids. The clips are available in a multitude of colours, and are described as "the final touch to a cute look!" Another photograph shows the princess wearing a pale blue M&H dress peppered with flowers, Olivier Kids cream cardigan, baby blue woolen Amaia Kids tights and the same Mary Jane-style pumps from Early Days. The British brand, founded in 1952, prides itself on quality craftsmanship and using the finest soft leather. Princess Charlotte's navy  leather 'Emma' pre-walker shoes, which boast a pretty scalloped edge, retail for just £29.  The blue dress is the same style (but a different fabric) as the one from M&H's autumn/ winter collection which Charlotte previously wore in the recent portrait of the Queen surrounded by her youngest grandchildren and great-children and in a portrait of the Cambridge family from October 2015.  The brands worn by the youngster will undoubtedly experience the 'Princess Charlotte effect' over the next few days.  For all kinds of reasons, both complex and simple, TV generally makes a hash of fashion. But Absolutely Fashion: Inside British Vogue, a two part documentary which starts on Thursday,  probes further than most, delicately skimming past the clichés.  Throughout, film-maker Richard Macer deploys a kind of idiot-savant star stuck naivety. “We did wonder whether it was for real or fiendishly clever,” one Voguette told me. It was clever. The closer Macer gets to power, the less stereotypical his film becomes. He’s helped by his leading protagonists. There’s Alexandra Shulman, Vogue’s long-standing (25 years) editor in chief:  smart, “normal”, never reacting quite how you expect her to. His other star is Lucinda Chambers (who has been there even longer than Shulman), the magazine’s Fashion Director, whom I first met when we both briefly worked at Elle, before moving, one after the other, to Vogue. While I left after seven years, Vogue is her spiritual home. She began working there “sometime in the 1970s”, threads and loose layers of tulle trailing from her home made-tutus, and grafted her way from the petty cash department to the heady heights of secretary to its then editor, Beatrix Miller.  She was, she admits, appalling in both posts, however it’s notable she only left once, of her own accord, to help set up British Elle. Our first AbFash view of Chambers is the back of her head. She’s always on her way somewhere. In an industry where narcissism has become a vaunted, self-marketing tool, she doesn’t “do” social media, or dawdle outside the shows posing for the street style bloggers.  They should stick a mic under her nose more often though:  she is wickedly funny, does not suffer fools, and has an Austen-esque eye for detail and affectations. “Kate Moss isn’t in the office every day. We’re not swinging from chandeliers." “My first concern was that it would be very boring’”, she says of the six months filming process of the documentary. “Kate Moss isn’t in the office every day. We’re not swinging from chandeliers. To be honest, I didn’t think I’d ever watch it, but I suppose I’ll have to. It would be disrespectful to Vogue not to”. I don’t think she’s being disingenuous - she’s sufficiently honest to confess to being eternally disappointed when she sees pictures of herself, despite having a beautiful face. “Do I really look like a batty old woman?” Fear of flying, the wrong underwear, a rogue documentary maker and John Kerry all play a role in the frenetic life of Alexandra Shulman, editor of British Vogue. As she celebrates the style bibles 100th anniversary, here is an extract from her private diary of a momentous year at the magazine.
 _By Alexandra Shulman, Friday 14 October 2016_
**September 1, 2015**
Three nights ago, in a restaurant by the sea, just off a coastal road in Puglia, some children at the long family tables next to ours were playing with their pencil cases, lining up the coloured felt tips in order. Today, back in London, it is like the first day of term, and I wish I had a new box of coloured pens that I could bring into work with me, shiny and neat and full of promise. Though of what, I couldnt say.
September 1 was my fathers birthday. If he were still alive, he would be 102 today. Instead his ashes were shot into the sky 11 years ago in a rocket my brother, Jason, made from Evening Standards, the newspaper where my father \([Milton Shulman](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1462636/Milton\-Shulman.html)\) worked for more than 40 years. He loved being a journalist, having a soapbox and a public voice, whether that be theatre criticism or politics or anything, really just so long as he was heard. I dont feel that way about editing Vogue. Its Vogues voice, not mine.
Although I do, of course, have a choice in what that voice says. After three weeks on holiday, I feel disengaged and not sure whether I have any\-thing to say on any subject relevant to the magazine. It will take a few days to reimmerse. I put on a striped shirt from Zara that I bought before the holiday. Its refreshing to wear something new ammunition for the day ahead. A shirt feels as if it has a clarity of purpose, which will be helpful.
 Even so, its strange: a costume rather than the holiday clothes of the past days. Before leaving for the office, I go to Gails bakery down the road and buy croissants and a Chelsea bun for my son, Sam, whose flight home from New York is scheduled to arrive this morning. Hes been away for nine weeks. Im so excited to see him. Tonight Ill roast a chicken for us. I wont relax until I get the text saying hes landed.
**September 7**
Ive returned to work with five big projects to achieve: a centenary issue, [a big party to celebrate our 100 years](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/events/vogue\-100\-best\-dressed\-kim\-kardashians\-opts\-for\-sheer\-dress\-for/), the 2016 Vogue Festival, the filming of a BBC Two documentary about the magazine, and the successful installation of an exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery. When I consider them all, I want to go back on holiday.
**September 14**
The garden at home never looks lovelier than when Im about to get on a plane. Yesterday morning the figs had finally ripened enough to eat, and the sun was shining on the [new autumn colours](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/style/shopping\-on\-mount\-street/autumn\-fashion\-trends\-you\-need\-to\-know/) that are peeping through all the dusty green.
  As I left for Heathrow I felt sick, and waiting for the flight to New York I was feeling so bad that I nearly cancelled the trip. Ive hated flying since I was 19, and the degree of my terror waxes and wanes. Once weve landed, Im excited to look out of the window at the tarmac. If you believe youre bound not to survive a flight, arriving intact is hugely pleasing. [Diane von Furstenberg](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/new\-york\-fashion\-week/diane\-von\-furstenberg\-gets\-modernised\-jonathan\-saunders\-on\-raisi/) was my first show \(at New York fashion week\) and I went there straight from the airport.
  At the end, in true showman style, she appeared, fiery\-maned and running down the catwalk with her still\-incredible legs on display, shaking hands and locking eyes with the audience, reminding me of Bill Clinton. New York collections are often a commercial version of what Europe provides for the previous season. Its what America does so well: the designers turn someone elses idea into something that makes money.
 > "Ive made a massive error here and this film is simply going to be incredibly trashy and simplistic"
 Even on the first day, I could see the huge [Cline](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/cline\-introduces\-us\-to\-faye\-wong\-chinese\-pop\-sensation\-\-and\-your/) influence in the longer lengths, the silhouette, the heavy, clumpy shoes that everyone loves. When Phoebe Philo arrived at Cline in 2008, she seemed to tap straight into a style vein that so many women relate to. Unsurprisingly, the American designers hate the notion of copycatting, even more than their stereotype as successful sportswear designers.
However, commercially theyve had the last word, and over the past 40 years, the American market has been the primary powerhouse of the industry. Its changing now, though: China and other Far Eastern countries are becoming the leading players.
Nowhere is it clearer that we are in the last days of the American empire than in the fashion industry. Fabrics and designs are being tailored to the requirements of the Eastern market. The big brands are spending fortunes expanding there, and although many Middle Eastern women are hidden behind burkas, their wardrobes contain some of the most ravishing Western fashion.
  
 
 **September 19**
Last night was the London Fashion Week party I hosted with the \[US\] ambassador and his wife, Matthew and Brooke Barzun. It was heavenly, and I went to bed happy. I arrived at the neo\-Palladian Winfield House in Regents Park 15 minutes before kick\-off, to be prevented from entering by the massive security detail outside the gates, heightened because of John Kerrys stay.
But eventually I was led past the childrens skateboard slope the Barzuns had erected outside the front door, and into the house. Victoria Beckham arrived to the usual accompaniment of flashbulbs, but in terms of celeb power she was upstaged a few minutes later by John Kerry.
I imagine that he could have slipped in through a back door and headed to bed, or at least for a private drink upstairs, but he gamely confronted a heaving room of partying guests. Victoria was introduced to him almost immediately, and stayed talking to him for so long that I thought he might never meet anyone else, but he hung out at the party for well over the half\-hour I had been told he might be there.
  Hes so tall that eye contact is almost impossible if youre my height, and in a noisy room, ear contact is not that easy either. The social temperature of the room soared when news of his being here spread; he was the real stardust that transformed the party.
Later, I found Victoria on the terrace with her shoes kicked off. I asked her what she had talked to Kerry about. He said hed seen me at the UN, she answered, referring to a speech she had delivered earlier in the year, and he said, We gotta talk about Syria. Her look showed she found that suggestion as surprising as I did.
**November 10**
At dinner last night David \(Jenkins, Shulmans partner\) asked whether I knew that he liked endives. Endives? Yes, endives. You had them in the salad the other night. Are there any in this one? He poked around fruitlessly at the endive\-free plate. It reminded me of the newly married butler, Carson, finding fault with his poor wifes cooking at their marital dining table in Downton Abbey.
 Breakfast yesterday with Nicholas Coleridge, who runs the UK company. We both ordered mashed avocado with chilli flakes and lime, and poached eggs no toast. What have we come to? Are we simply fashion\-lifestyle victims?
Nicholas had a scribbled list of issues to talk to me about, which included the idea of an African Vogue supplement, and who I was planning to invite to the centenary dinner. George Osborne? Ed Vaizey? I answered that I was planning to ask Jeremy Corbyn, and Id see if Emily Sheffield, m[y deputy editor](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/what\-do\-you\-wear\-to\-a\-job\-interview\-at\-vogue\-four\-editors\-share/), could exert some influence on her brother\-in\-law, David Cameron. Theres only room for 300 guests and, given the number of big beasts in fashion, its going to be tricky to get the right balance for the guest list.
**January 3, 2016**
After 10 days break, I woke up this morning and went to the farmers market in the pouring rain. I stewed some apples with cinnamon, put on a stock to simmer, and wondered whether it would be possible to have a life of just reading all the books Ive now got piled up on the big table in the bedroom, and do very little work. I could run every day, make vegetable soups, let my hair go grey and And then what? Would I be content? David, who had just woken up, said that thousands of years of philosophers have pondered this same question.
**January 30**
Im 37,000ft above the ground and travelling at 560 miles per hour, or so it says on the map in front of me on this flight to Milan. Im also feeling thoroughly queasy, which is partly my flying anxiety and partly my total stupidity in waking up with a hangover from dinner last night.
David and I went to my friend Flora Frasers, and I was so gripped by the conversation between fellow guests Charles Saatchi and former Lib Dem cabinet minister [Chris Huhne](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/crime/11386970/Disgraced\-former\-cabinet\-minister\-Chris\-Huhne\-returns\-to\-Parliament.html) that I drank way too much wine. Charles, whether genuinely or simply to be controversial, described both Putin and Trump as magnificent, in his flat London accent.
 > "Victoria Beckham arrived to the usual accompaniment of flashbulbs, but she was upstaged by John Kerry"
 Chris is a passionate Europhile, and is looking extremely well in the aftermath of his jail experience. He didnt appear remotely rattled and was keen to hammer home his pro\-Europe stance. We left at the same time as Charles and his new girlfriend, Trinny Woodall.
Just before he left, as we stood in the hallway, he grabbed me and pulled me under one of the overhead spotlights and peered behind my ears. You havent changed, he said, explaining that he was checking to see whether Id had work done. Weird, undoubtedly.
  **February 4**
I must buy some new clothes. I have weeks of events and fashion shows coming up and nothing to wear. Clearly nothing is a relative term as I have two cupboards full of clothes, but nothing I have is new, and Im meant to look like somebody who has new clothes.
**February 17**
Last week ended well, so this week Im certain that something difficult will happen as a reproach to me for feeling too relaxed. Organising all the different strands of [the Centenary](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/understated\-glamour\-the\-duchess\-of\-cambridges\-first\-vogue\-cover/) is emotionally exhausting. One thing goes well; another veers into difficulties. Mario Testinos Decades shoot arrives and is luscious. But we still have the final Tim Walker portraits to nail: Tracey Emin has twice cancelled even as he arrived at her house.
 > "I wondered whether it would be possible to have a life of just reading all the books Ive now got piled up on the big table in the bedroom, and do very little work"
 Tim is getting a bit fed up. David Beckhams people want a number of different concepts to propose to David, if he is to agree to be included. I know that Tim wants to shoot him on a football pitch, kicking a crown into the air, which would be wonderful. But I have a feeling David might not think so. My fashion director, Lucinda \([Chambers](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/style\-lessons\-to\-learn\-from\-vogues\-lucinda\-chambers\-whatever\-you/)\), walks into my office saying she had a great meeting with \([David](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/david\-bailey\-jack\-nicholson\-turned\-me\-on\-to\-viagra\-very\-young/)\) Bailey about the [Ab Fab](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/events/everything\-we\-know\-about\-absolutely\-fabulous\-the\-movie/) shoot.
They havent worked together for many years, and I was worried about how they would get on. He told her he liked the energy of the unexpected and asked her why she hadnt had Botox. We have our monthly circulation meeting and start making plans for what we hope will be a high\-June centenary\-issue sale. The circulation team are projecting about a 25 per cent rise in year\-on\-year news\-stand sales, which is a big ask. I always feel maddened when I see someone reading Vogue at the hairdressers. Why dont you buy your own copy? I want to say, as I glower at them from my hideously unflattering gown.
The film crew have practically disappeared from the office and my staff keep asking me what I think [the documentary](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/alexa\-chung\-vogue\-documentary\-the\-future\-of\-fashion/) will be like. They are suspicious of director Richard Macers hapless approach and feel theyre being tricked in some way. I trust him about 70 per cent, but in the end I have no idea what will emerge. What on earth made me think it was a good idea to do it all those months back?
  **April 15**
Last night I took part in a discussion in the NPG theatre, focusing on changes in the fashion world since I first started my editorship. The audience asked good questions. One young woman had spotted that the [cover line](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/style/look\-back\-at\-100\-years\-of\-vogue\-covers\-as\-the\-magazine\-celebrate/) on my first issue, April 1992, had read, Do we still need feminism? and asked me if I considered myself a feminist.
I know I should unhesitatingly say yes. But, if Im honest, feminism is something I have rarely considered in a personal sense as opposed to the theoretical. If youve been brought up in a household of journalists, where it was always expected that as a woman you would work and be as successful as a man, it doesnt have the kind of emotional resonance it might for women coming from a different background or working in a different world.
But then, my father often shouted at me that no man would marry me if I didnt lose weight, or if I continued to argue so much. It didnt matter, though, since his love for me was never in doubt.
Last night, for the first time in years, I woke in the night and really wanted to see him walk through the door of the flat where we lived, put his trilby hat down on the hall table and come into the study where we ate dinner, with all the bustle and purpose and, it has to be said, self\-absorption he carried with him.
Id be able to smell the sweet scent of his skin that had always been the same from when we were tiny and crawled into our parents bed in the morning, and he would make a tent of the sheets with his legs in the air, which we could huddle under.
  
 
 **May 17**
I have my final dress fitting for the centenary dinner, and run into Erdems shop in South Audley Street with a variety of bras and knickers to try with it. The dress is hanging in the dressing room, a little like a child waiting to be collected from school.
I try it on with a pair of fine\-gauge Lycra cycling\-style knickers and a new bra, and it fits perfectly, though the shorts make me feel horrible. The lace embroidery now snakes across the sequins, and the boat neck is wide enough. Erdem stands back to survey his work and says, Its great. Really nipped and wicked, as he looks at me with those sloe eyes, adjusting the neckline to lie flat across my collarbone.
 > "I feel maddened when I see someone reading Vogue at the hairdressers. Why dont you buy your own copy? I want to say"
 He leaves the dressing room for a moment and I remove the shorts, which are clinging to my hips. I cant bear to wear such hideous underwear, even if it does give me a better shape. Standing in front of him in the shop we look at me again together in the mirror and he photographs me from the back and the front.
I ask him if he can see any difference from moments before, and he says perhaps the waistband is sitting a little better now the neckline is adjusted. I tell him about the removal of the shorts and hes polite enough to say that it looks better without, though I immediately feel Ive loaded him with too much information on the underpinnings of a 58\-year\-old woman.
   **June 11**
Yesterday Richard filmed me for the last time. He had wanted me to think of something that had some personal relevance, so I suggested we visit a huge old horse\-chestnut tree in Hyde Park, which I remembered playing under when I was very young.
After the filming he travelled with me in a car to the office and we joked a bit about this being the last time he would be filming me in a car. Then he leant forwards to fiddle with his camera and said, Theres something I want to tell you about the documentary. Kind of what were doing? Aha. Whats that? Well, you know I said I didnt want to use a voiceover narrator, that it was a bit tacky and overdone? Yes. I remember.
Id thought what a relief it would be not to have that clichd narrator. Well, weve had to change it a bit. And now, well, there is one. Or a kind of one. You know how usually theyre narrated by an actor? Well, we arent doing that. At this point I was becoming concerned by what he was about to say.
Um... Its going to be me. You know, not a huge amount of it. But its kind of about how a man who knows nothing about any of it goes into Vogue. My mind went into split screen one half thinking, Keep calm, theres nothing you can do about this and maybe itll be OK, the other thinking, Ive made a massive error here and this film is simply going to be incredibly trashy and simplistic. I couldnt believe Id allowed it to happen. Our one shot after so many years of refusing to let cameras into Vogue and Id blown it. This was now going to be a mocking Ladybird guide to the fashion world. What do you think? he asked.
  
 **June 23**
As I took my seat in a small room in Soho to view the documentary, the nerves took hold. Watching yourself in something like this is the most curious activity. I kept wondering what I was going to say, rather as if it hadnt been me sitting there, in far too many endless car shots staring crossly out of a rainy window.
Richard sitting behind me was still and serious as we watched his vision of Vogue for two hours. Through telling the story of a number of our shoots and the plans for the centenary issue, he certainly succeeded in getting across how much we all cared about what we did and, also, showed the hard work that goes into each issue.
Was it the film that I would love to have made about Vogue? No. I dont think it conveys how wide Vogue is nowadays, the influence it bears, the number of areas we are involved with, the fantastic journalism we include. Am I happy with how Im portrayed? Not particularly I seem very depressed through much of it, and prefer to think of myself as a funnier, lighter person than I seem on screen.
   I also dislike how I look most of the time, and cant understand why Im wearing the same blue top throughout most of the first programme. People will say, There she is, editor of Vogue and all. Youd think she could change her shirt.
Are there moments I really hate? Yes. The whole saga of the swapping of the Rihanna cover with the previous issue because of American Vogue jumping ahead of us is given a ludicrous weight, and when Richard says to camera that I rang threatening to pull the whole film if he talked to Anna Wintour about it, I felt misrepresented.
It was the one really devious thing he did. Of course, in the documentary when Anna is filmed she is hugely complimentary, which makes me look even sillier. I dont know what the rest of the office will think.

    It’s a Friday: if you want to find Chambers on a Friday morning, it’s Portobello Market or bust. I pause to scan her outfit and peer inside the white carrier bag containing this morning’s market trophies. From the top, she’s in dangly earrings (Grey’s Antique Market, another good place to track her down), an old Marni black and white stripy top, black vintage Dsquared2 trousers , Celine sandals, zero make-up and scrunched back hair. It’s quintessential Chambers – idiosyncratic-bordering-on- eccentric but also chic. Today’s carrier, she says, constitutes her ideal market haul: “Look at this polka dot dress, if I turn it back to front and get rid of those sleeves…and cut it there…I think it could look a bit  J.W.Anderson, in an ironic way. I might put a shoulder pad in there. And see this white 80s jacket with lovely pockets? “ I do, but I can’t visualise how even irony might rescue it. “I won’t wear it, obviously, but I bought it for inspiration.” There’s a caftan she bought for Toby the eldest of her three sons, now a photographer in LA and at the bottom of the pile is the Stefan Zweig she’s reading. How does she find time for it all? As well as being the woman to call when you need to advice on the best acupuncturist, shrink, picture hanger,  dyslexia coach or colour for your walls (currently brown btw).  “When I’m on something, I concentrate solely on that. And I’m good at making my pleasures – like the Friday Portobello trips - about work”. Chambers’ stories about fashion can be epic with elaborate sets, exotic locations and disparate romantic– or studio bound and minimalist. She may not remember precisely her precise age (“late 50s”), or what year she joined Vogue or married. However - and make of this what you will - she does know that the shoot in the documentary was her 422nd for the magazine.  She is unusually versatile although she and Shulman are, she says, constantly having “discussions” about what Shulman calls her bells and whistles.“Alex will say, 'that was a nice shoot before you put the chin straps on’” She tries to rein in her props, she says. “I know as I’m adding them that Alex will hate it….but it’s a compulsion”. On the Duchess of Cambridge: 'That girl next door is just shtick. You can’t do that job and be ordinary.' The relationship between an editor and their fashion director is usually feisty – both wanting the best for the magazine, but coming from different approaches. This is well played out in The September Issue, the 2009 fly-on-the wall film about American Vogue .But Chambers and Shulman are very different characters from Anna Wintour and Grace Coddington, US Vogue’s legendary Creative Director  (although Chambers worked for Coddington when she was still at British Vogue). It’s a testament to Shulman’s and Chambers’ mutual respect that when the Duchess of Cambridge was confirmed for the Centenary issue – a secret entrusted to only four people, Chambers was put in charge of the shoot. “I wanted to keep it quite generic because I knew one picture would end up in the National Portrait Gallery and because the Duchess felt she’s been photographed in quite a lot of evening wear already. But she’s very open. She’s intelligent and engaged with everything. That girl next door is just shtick. You can’t do that job and be ordinary. What strikes me is that she really loves William.” Chambers prepares meticulously, commissioning one-off pieces, working repeatedly with an A-list cohort of photographers. But as luck would have it in the shoot featured in the documentary,  “the model, Linesy Montero, wouldn’t take her ear-phones off, the set was hideous  “and Patrick {Demarchalier] the photographer, was losing interest. Sod’s Law. My shoots never go wrong”. (Not true: there was the time with Mario Testino when none of the clothes turned up and Chambers had to talk an incandescent Emma Watson back onto the set). What she has realised, “is that I’ve turned a disorder into a career. I can buy a ton of stuff and either wear it, make it into a cushion, or file it under 'inspiration”. She recently had a purge at her home in Shepherd’s Bush, but  there’s a strong probability it will seep back. “I’m a tart, aesthetically. I love sparkly, I love vintage, I love ethnic.  So many people working in fashion just look like one thing..it’ a sign of insecurity”. A bad shrink might trace this love of “stuff”  back to her childhood: Raised in London, despite the Celia Johnson accent and posh schools (Queen’s Gate and a convent) and a small role in the 1968 film Isadora Duncan in which she played Duncan’s (Vanessa Redgrave) daughter  there was no money after her father left. She failed her O’levels, didn’t get into fashion college. Her mother, a talented artist, was endlessly making things out of cornflake packets and eventually suggested they both apply to art school, mainly for the grants. So they did. At Vogue, when the petty cash officer wasn’t throwing things at her, Chambers would share her luncheon vouchers with Mario Testino, an impecunious Peruvian who lived in a squat near hers. “It was lean pickings in winter. Mario only knew how to shoot in natural daylight …God, I was so bad at so many things back then. Even the clothes I made fell apart while I was wearing them. If there’s anything I could say to young people it’s keep trying different things and eventually something will stick.” Absolutely Fashion: Inside British Vogue begins on BBC Two on September 8 at 9pm   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  She's familiar to most of us as the ultra-glossy, pulled-together First Lady Claire Underwood in House of Cards. But on the Cannes red carpet this week, Robin Wright was offering a style masterclass of a very different- but equally empowering- kind. In a series of glamorously sophisticated looks, Wright ripped up the rule book when it comes to dressing for one of the world's  most famous film festivals.  In the process, she also offered up a genuinely useful approach to agelessly fabulous style.  "Even though this is a prestigious film festival, you have to keep in mind that Cannes is warm, it's by the water - it seems like there's always a soft breeze blowing," says Kemal Harris, the stylist who put together Wright's Cannes wardrobe, of her inspiration for Wright's Cannes looks.  Wright's first major fashion moment came at the festival's opening ceremony when she stood out amongst a sea of gowns in glittering Saint Laurent mini dress. "It's hard to tell unless you're looking at up close but all of those stones on the Saint Laurent dress are stitched on individually by hand," explains Harris. "It's just phenomenal work!" Of course, the design served to highlight Wright's killer toned legs but Harris had the festival's celebratory theme in mind too. "This is the 70th Anniversary of Cannes so I wanted to find something that felt like a party dress," she says. "I was thinking a lot about the golden era of Cannes fashion. I imagined Betty Catroux wearing this dress to a Cannes screening and then kicking off her heels and jumping on a yacht with a bottle of champagne."  Catroux- the party girl model and muse to Yves Saint Laurent- would surely have approved.  The following day, Wright switched things up again in a Stella McCartney, slim-fitting suit which might have come straight from Claire Underwood's wardrobe, if it weren't for a smattering of tweaks and additions which transformed it from purely professional to modern and chic.  "I was looking for a chic tailored suit to balance out the many dresses and this one fit the bill," says Harris. "It's a great lightweight fabric and we flipped the cuffs to show a bit of skin." Harris finished the ensemble with Saint Laurent sunglasses (for an ultra-cool outdoor photo call look) and a pair of leopard print heels which added an extra dash of attitude. "The Schutz leopard print pumps are just a fun accent. Plus, all my clients tell me that the Schutz pumps are very comfy!" explains Harris. It made for a perfectly pitched look for Wright's appearence at Kering's 'Women in Motion' event.  "Effortless and sexy" is how Harris sums up Wright's final outfit, a teal slip dress by L.A-based designer Michelle Mason.  "The color is what initially drew me to it and then when I saw how good the fit was, I was totally sold," she says. "The jewel tone inspired me to add the raspberry heels and royal blue clutch. " Once again, the breezy, relaxed look created serious impact thanks to the unique contrast it offered to some of the more high-octane ensembles.   Wright did, however, have some compatriots in her glamorous red carpet rebellion; last night saw Susan Sarandon don a skintight maxi-length leather skirt, Vanessa Redgrave ditch heels for Converse and Uma Thurman throw on a leather jacket. The common thread? These are all women with the perfect counterbalance of poise and confidence to rule the red carpet, in their own way.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Jenna Coleman's second reign in the hit ITV drama Victoria comes to an end tonight and, as the series has developed to show the changes in the young Queen’s life, her wardrobe has had to adapt, too. “Over the course of series two we cover six years, starting just after the birth of [her first child] Princess Victoria in 1840,” Rosalind Ebbutt, the series’ costume designer tells The Telegraph. “Victoria is now married, established as Queen and has had a baby, so she's a young woman not a teenager.” Victoria’s style has also moved with the trends of the times, adopting the prettier, more refined silhouettes synonymous with the 1840s and abandoning some of the the pomp associated with her coronation look from the previous decade. “The more exaggerated, romantic shapes of the 1830’s have been left well behind and we’re definitely doing clothes of the 1840s,” Ebbutt, who has also worked as a costume designer on other period dramas like Anna Karenina, Vanity Fair and Downton Abbey, explains. “They've got a waistline, bell-shaped skirts and tighter sleeves - what you would think of as a typical early Victorian woman.” Ebbutt takes care to interpret, rather than copy, the real Queen Victoria’s outfits for the small screen, emulating some of her most recognisable looks but allowing for a little creative license. Following last season’s epic coronation gown, this series has had plenty of opportunities for a wow moment - notably her christening look. “We decided not to do a direct copy because we had her cream wedding dress and I didn't want to do another cream one,” Ebbutt explains of the adaptations she made to Victoria’s original christening look. “We found the palest ice blue brocade that looked so great on film and then we more or less made it the same shape as we can see in the painting [of the actual Queen at the christening]. “I always go with colours that Jenna likes and that will suit her, as well as being ones that look like a version of what you would see Queen Victoria in,” she says. “We have an overall mood board and colour palette for this series - blues, soft peaches, cream and some lilac.” Ebbutt says that, while the Queen may not have had Instagram, or even magazines, to give her new ideas about style, she was still totally informed about which shades and silhouettes were in and out. “I wouldn't have said she was cutting edge or an initiator of fashion, but she was a very fashionable figure, there's a slight difference,” she considers. “She was inspired by fashion plates [illustrations] of the period, and various French and English firms specialised in publishing them. Queen Victoria would have looked at them just as people now look online or in fashion magazines. Outfitting Coleman in period dress for an eight-part series is quite a feat, and Ebbutt says that she uses a mix of sourced pieces from vintage and costume shops, as well as making some bespoke dresses. “She does have about 30 outfits over the eight episodes, which is a fair amount, but probably nothing compared to what Queen Victoria would have owned,” she laughs. “It's quite dull if people wear the same thing all the time on TV - it's the code for a viewer that a new dress means a new day, or that a new event is going to happen.” One of the key pieces that she stumbled upon in a costume shop ahead of this series was an embroidered jacket, worn by Coleman in several scenes, including for the ‘churching’ ceremony which she takes part in after the birth of her first daughter. “That was a happy charm,” Ebbutt says. “I found it and thought its embroidery was absolutely perfect. We tweaked it a little bit, just slightly took it in, and the shape works nicely with a skirt and a blouse. Styling is a key consideration, Ebbutt says, as she can’t suddenly be seen to drop a more modern accessory into a scene, shattering the period illusion. It’s more berthas and bonnets than It bags. “A bertha is a collar, a low-hanging lace neckline on a gown which a woman’s maid would take on and off for her,” Ebbutt explains, “I have a lot of original lace and we find and rent them too. They wouldn’t wear precious jewellery in the day - more spectacular pieces are kept for the evenings - and you shouldn’t mix diamonds and pearls. There are lots of old fashioned rules like that.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The first weekend of Coachella saw a new breed of festival-goer graze the dusty Californian fields. Wealthy LA natives, dropping $20,000 getting 'festival ready’, with $8,000 shopping sprees, as well as Botox, lip injections and personal trainers. They weren't the only ones ploughing thousands into their festival wardrobes. Mad Men star Kiernan Shipka, 16, spent close to £10,000 on just three Coachella looks, with a pastel Dior ensemble, £5350, and Valentino denim twin set, £3980, in the mix. Meanwhile, 27-year-old actress Vanessa Hudgens thought nothing of splurging $170 on a jewel-encrusted manicure. This quest for attendees to look “blog-ready” has led to Coachella creating its own ‘season’ in the retail sphere, with online retailers drip-feeding festival product onto websites to capitalise on demand. In the two weeks leading up to the Californian event, 337 items including the word 'festival' in the product description were uploaded onto online aggregator Lyst. They say that Coachella shifts four times as much product than any other festival - with searches for merchandise directly linked to what celebrities are spotted wearing on site. After Taylor Swift posted that ‘chokers are the new flower crowns’ on Instagram this year, searches for ‘chokers’ increased 70% in the following five days on Lyst. Kendall Jenner’s Aquazzura Tulum sandals saw a 110% increase in page views for the style. And after Suki Waterhouse wore Tommy Hilfiger’s denim overalls, Lyst saw a 207% increase in searches for the brand. If all this seems like Coachella has reached peak shopping saturation point, take comfort in the fact there has been some movement against it. After 10 years of frolicking in the festival fields Alexa Chung decided to skip Coachella in favour of her own ‘Nochella’ party in collaboration with her tech start-up Villoid. Stylish friends Poppy Delevingne, Leigh Lezark and Mark Ronson chose to sup Pimm's Cups with Chung over rubbing shoulders with the ‘blog-ready’ Coachella cougars. Asked by Fashionista whether she was ‘over Coachella’ and the idea of trends starting at festivals, Chung replied: “Oh my God, the choker is so dead. No, thank you… No, it's fine. Look, everyone can do whatever they want, but I do think there is a certain thing with trends when they reach a tipping point and that tipping point to me, with the choker, seems to have happened a few months ago." Alexa’s dismissal of ‘festival fashion’ - she has previously called it “naff” - is no throwaway comment. Whilst brands like H&M and Calvin Klein hosted parties at Coachella this year, others are overtly moving away from a direct association with festival fashion.  High street giants Topshop and ASOS have both stopped offering a dedicated ‘festival’ section on their websites this season. "At Topshop we try not to think of dressing for a festival as a uniform," brand design director, Jacqui Markam, told Vogue. "It's more about real girls interpreting and having fun with their own style - not blending in with the crowd, but standing out." Topshop has chosen ‘Holiday Shop’ as its umbrella for all summer fashion, while ASOS has plumped simply for ‘Summer Shop’. So while it is dismaying to learn that searches for ‘hippy’ and ‘boho’ fashion were up 30 per cent in comparison to last year’s Coachella festival, we're still holding out hope that Glastonbury won't inspire the same money-spending mentality. Having Botox to look "blog-ready" amongst the mud-soaked masses? Now that really would be a festival fashion cliche too far. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Grace Kelly's impact on fashion is enormous; not only was Gucci's Flora pattern designed specifically for her and one of the most timeless fashion items, the Hermes Kelly bag, bears her name, but she was also one of the first stars to really hone a consistent 'signature style'. She is regarded as having the ability to make anything look elegant, even a cast for a broken arm - she once used a printed silk Hermes scarf as a sling.  "She always understood that being a stylish was part of her job," explains fashion historian Bronwyn Cosgrave. "How Hollywood sold movies was through image, glamour and the red carpet." To mark what would have been the princess' 87th birthday this Saturday look back at why how she dressed was quite so captivating... Grace Kelly was one of the first actresses to cultivate her own consistent signature style, which was simple, but refined and elegant.  "She determined what suited her and stuck with that style," explains Kristina Haugland, author of Grace Kelly Style. "It was really this that set her apart as different and gave her this image of being very reserved, which was in contrast to the other stars at the time." Her wardrobe was centred around classic American 'college girl' understated pieces, but she always looked incredibly polished and groomed whether wearing capris and a white shirt or an Edith Head gown. Haughland notes that it was said at the time that she was 'giving good taste a sense of glamour.' In an article in The Telegraph on 12 January 1956 entitled 'It started with Grace Kelly', fashion writer Winefride Jackson notes how Grace Kelly popularised an 'uncluttered line.' She writes: "Of one thing we may be certain - the fashion and beauty barometer is pointing to a return to the style of classic elegance. The new trend has been largely determined by the woman whose name is hitting the headlines hard just now - Grace Kelly." To achieve Kelly's 'new fashion technique' Jackson advises readers to "dress slim, uncluttered and practically adorned with chunky jewellery - except for stud earrings and one good bracelet." But she notes: "With the accent on the classic, accessories will need to be impeccable - no shabby or worn hand-bags, no grubby or wrinkled globes, no heels even slightly turned over. It is in the bandbox look from now on." Her beauty tip to readers is "hairstyles, most important to the whole effect are smoother and glossier." Grace Kelly might now be held up as the epitome of elegance, but she was seen by some as 'stubborn' when it came to dressing. An article in The Telegraph on the 17 April 1956 notes: "Miss Kelly comes of ambitious, determined and independent stock. That she has inherited these qualities she has already proved by her film career, and her stubbornness in wearing an enormous face-hiding hat for her arrival, despite the advice of her father who thought it was quite wrong. The Monegasques are still hurt by her thoughtlessness."  There was a huge level of interest in Grace Kelly, but this became hysterical in the lead up to her wedding to Prince Rainier II of Monaco in 1956. She said during a press conference on her journey to Monaco: "This is frightening. I am flattered by all this attention but I wish you would be more considerate of one another.” The press coverage was relentless, as Kristina Haugland explains: “This was before 24 hour a day coverage, but when she departed on New York the press even mentioned that the stockings she wore were seamless. There were details about where she got all of her clothes from, who they were by and where she was shopping.” Aware of the huge interest in her outfits, she used this as an opportunity to boost the fashion industry in America. “There was always a feeling that European designers were the top, but that she wore American designers on an international stage was seen as giving an american fashion a boost,” explains Haugland. When she arrived in Monaco, for example, she wore a navy blue coat and sleeveless dress by American designer Ben Zuckerman. Grace Kelly was one of the earliest stars to have a designer item named after her, as Hermes renamed its Haut à Courroie bag the Kelly. Grace Kelly and costume designer Edith Head discovered the bag in 1954 while shopping for accessories for the film To Catch A Thief, and noticed it in the Hermes window. The bag, which was first created in the 1930s, was a regular feature in paparazzi pictures of Grace Kelly, and it was said that she used it to conceal her pregnancy. "It started to be associated with her because she was pictured with it when the engagement was announced and was photographed when went back to California so was seen with it," explains Haugland. "This whole story arose that she used it shield her pregnant stomach and was on a magazine cover doing that but I’ve never been able to find any evidence of that, but it refuses to die. I’ve never seen a photograph like that and I've never seen a magazine cover like that. It is a rumour that has a life of its own." Grace Kelly might have been a princess with access to the likes of Dior and Gucci, but she wasn't unnecessarily extravagant and wore her favourite pieces for decades. She rewore the navy Ben Zuckerman coat she first wore to arrive in Monaco in the 60s when pregnant with Stephanie. “Someone said isn’t that a nine year old coat she said ‘yes I like it!” recalls Haugland. “She wasn’t the clothes horse you might think she is. Now we would think of someone like that having an immense closet and never wearing same thing again. "She certainly had a different attitude; it didn’t have to be new every time and not the most extreme. She wore jeans and people teased her about this old camel hair coat she had and loved and wouldn’t give up. She wore her favourite clothes over and over again.” At the 1955 Oscars she re-wore an Edith Head satin gown which she wore the year before to the New York premiere of The Country Girl. "This dress was seen as very different at the time," explains  Haugland. "Most of the stars were in large full skirts with fur coats and she wore a simple satin dress with a matching satin coat and in the newspaper accounts she was seen to be dressed very differently from the other actresses."  “For a long time in Monaco women were not supposed to wear trousers and wear hats at the palace, but she was often photographed wearing trousers with her family so those rules were relaxed,” explains Haugland. “She was conscious of her image of the Princess of Monaco, but she was careful that her family weren’t held to formal standards. She liked hats herself, but as hats started to wane from fashion and were no longer a must-have accessory the rule was eventually relaxed, but that wasn’t quite as revolutionary when it happened as it was bowing to change.” Grace Kelly had two wedding outfits for her religious and civil ceremonies, both gifts from MGM studios and created by the head costume designer, Helen Rose, who had created her looks for High Society. The iconic gown she wore to the religious ceremony took 30 seamstresses at the studio six weeks to make and had a high collar, elegant lace sleeves and a full skirt made of 125-year-old Brussels lace.  Instead of a tiara, she wore a beaded floral Juliet cap with a 90-yard veil and carried a pearl-encrusted prayer book and a delicate bouquet of Lilies of the Valley. For the private civil ceremony, Kelly wore a pink embroidered skirt suit by Helen Rose with another delicate Juliet cap. A piece in The Telegraph from 1956 notes that the hype surrounding the dress was feverish and sketches of the dress were only released days before due to fear of "copying pirates." The ceremony was an elegant affair, and many guests dressed in a Grace Kelly style. Winefride Jackson wrote in The Telegraph from her seat in the cathedral of Saint Nicholas: "Most of the women guests respected the prince's wish to avoid wearing black and white. Blue, pink, silver-grey and orchid mauve dominated their choice of pastel shades for floating chiffons, organzas, satins and brocades. But the outstanding fashion contribution was the style of hats. "There were tulle-swathed picture hats, many similar to the one worn by the bride on her arrival in Monaco, toques and mille-feuilles concoctions of multiple layers of net, often with a single rosebud tucked in front between the layers."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  As widely speculated, Yves Saint Laurent has confirmed that Anthony Vaccarello has been appointed as its new creative director, following on from Hedi Slimane. In a joint statement, Kering and Yves Saint Laurent confirmed the rumours that the former creative director at Versus, Vaccarello, is taking the helm of the label, showing his first collection during Paris Fashion Week in October 2016. “Mr Saint Laurent is a legendary figure for his creativity, style and audacity," said Vaccarello in a statement. "I am extremely grateful for the opportunity to contribute to the history of this extraordinary house.” “I am extremely happy to have Anthony Vaccarello take the creative helm of Yves Saint Laurent," the president and chief executive officer of Yves Saint Laurent, Francesca Bellettini said. "His modern, pure aesthetic is the perfect fit for the maison. Anthony Vaccarello impeccably balances elements of provocative femininity and sharp masculinity in his silhouettes. He is the natural choice to express the essence of Yves Saint Laurent. I am enthusiastic about embarking on a new era with Anthony Vaccarello, and together bringing the maison further success.” Note the house is referred to as Yves Saint Laurent in this quote, rather than Slimane's rebranded 'Saint Laurent.' Vaccarello has been at the helm of Versace's Versus label - a youthful label which Donatella's late brother, Gianni, put her in charge of - for only a year. In a statement Donatella Versace said of Vaccarello's departure: “While I’m sad to see him leave the Versace family, I wish Anthony Vaccarello tremendous success with his next chapter." "In the past several years, I have worked with three great young talents on Versus Versace: Christopher Kane, JW Anderson and Anthony Vaccarello," she added. "In each instance, their time on Versus Versace led to them making a huge advancement in their design career. I appreciated the chance to work with each of these three designers, and I enjoyed seeing what they brought to a brand I truly love. I’m proud that Versus can be such a remarkable global platform for emerging design talent." The largely unknown Belgian-Italian designer (he doesn't even have his own Wikipedia page yet) studied at La Cambre in Brussels and worked for two years under Karl Lagerfeld at Fendi, creating furs. The designer then founded his own label in 2009, with sexy power dresses and dangerously high hemlines at the core of every collection.  While you may not know his name (yet), chances are you'll recognise his work. Seeing as his aesthetic is focused on opinion-dividing little black dresses, with strategically placed straps and leather detailing, it didn't take long for his designs to be a fixture on the red carpet at music awards shows.  Jennifer Lopez wore his leggy black asymmetrical dress to the Grammys in 2013, and Vaccarello also counts Miley Cyrus and Alessandra Ambrosio as fans. But he received the most coverage for the daring ab-flashing gown that Gwyneth Paltrow wore on the cover of Harper's Bazaar in 2012 and the slinky minidress Gisele Bundchen selected for the Met Gala in 2013. "We chose each other," Donatella has previously said to The Telegraph of appointing Vaccarello. "What Anthony does is very close to my work. My woman is cool and sexy, and to combine those two things is not always easy. I’ve worked with JW Anderson, who is a great designer but he’s cool and that’s it. Not many have this quality of combining very cool and sexy. But it’s what women and men want." Vaccarello's predecessor, Slimane, was at the helm of Saint Laurent for four years. Although many critics despaired at his literal interpretations of existing street style, the house became the most commercially successful label of the new decade.   "The catwalk shows were conceived to seem edgy (obscure rock music, darkness, a cohort of soi-disant rebels strategically seated near the cameras) but the collections themselves became repositories of modern classics," The Telegraph's Fashion Director Lisa Armstrong said of his impact at Saint Laurent. "Biker jackets, slim black trousers, trench coats, jeans skinny black jackets, pea-coats…Slimane didn’t exactly reinvent, so much as lightly tweak them. Perhaps that was the mark of his shrewdness. He cut them in a way that worked for a lot of women, and styled them so that they looked youthful. For the doubters, it was reductive, simplistic fashion for those who had never mastered anything more sophisticated than superannuated rock-chick separates. To believers it represented the only style template that made sense in a modern context."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We’ve long extolled the virtues of the shirt dress. The humble wardrobe staple might not be about to reinvent the trend rule book, but it makes getting dressed a whole lot easier. Both breezy yet elegant, a shirt dress is a faithful friend that never fails to pull you together. Serving up new shirting inspiration this weekend, were Sienna Miller and Sophie Hunter, who both chose beautiful riffs on the dress style to wear to Wimbledon. First up, Hunter took her place in the royal spectator’s box wearing a white mid-length Temperley shirt dress stitched with symmetrical pretty black embroidery. (Side note: could Hunter and husband Benedict Cumberbatch be vying for a place as 2016’s best-dressed couple?) The theatre director left the button-down dress style fastened tightly at the collar for a preppy twist on the feminine cut and print, then threw a nattily-cut blazer on for good measure. With black accessories acting as an extension of the black embroidery, the whole look was utterly delightful for a British summer afternoon. Etta dress, £795, Temperley If Hunter’s dress hit a high note between preppy and pretty, then Sienna Miller’s symbolised the fluid, pared-down potential of the shirt dress. The actress watched Andy Murray take the title of men’s champion in a white Ralph Lauren sablé dress, which fluttered just below-the-knee in beautifully flattering proportions. Unlike Hunter’s starched collar, Sienna’s was left open, relaxed and in keeping with the 1930s silhouette of her day dress. For Miller, the ruffled neck feature, with delicate mother-of-pearl buttons stitched onto the bodice, was enough to occupy the eye. The mother-of-one kept everything else on her outfit minimal, choosing brown woven T-bar heels, tan sunglasses and a white shoulder bag as simple accompaniments. Eva dress, WAS £2,045, NOW £1,022, Ralph Lauren Don’t let these well-dressed women kid you that the shirt dress should be the reserve of formal wear. It’s actually a multiple-use item. Sure, you can wear it as a dress, but how about layering looser styles over trousers? With a roomy jumper worn over the top and the shirt tails left swinging, you’ll have a fresh take on workwear that is brilliant for combatting office air con. Hunter and Miller’s shirt dresses might sing of ladylike fashion, but there are myriad of minimal styles out there that could be toughened up with trainers or chunky boots for the weekend. Oh and did we mention how forgiving they are on derrières? Go forth and stockpile your own wear-anywhere stash of simple shirt dresses. You won't regret it.
