 During her years in the White House, Michelle Obama cleverly carved out a distinctive First Lady look, working with emerging designers and major fashion houses alike to create a look which blended fun, glamour and diplomacy- whether it was casual J.Crew cardigans, vibrant day dresses or dazzlingly sophisticated ballgowns. Meanwhile, Barack Obama stuck mainly to navy suits, black tuxedos and relaxed 'Dad' shirts.  Now the former First Lady has spoken about the double standards which exist in men's and women's style, and how she and her husband navigated the differences- with characteristic humour- during their White House years.  "This is the thing," Michelle Obama said at Apple's Worldwide Developers Conference in California earlier this week. "You talk about Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers. No matter what we do, he puts on that same tux. People take pictures of the shoes, the bracelet I'm wearing but they didn't comment that for eight years he wore the same tux, same shoes." .@MichelleObama is fun 😂 #WWDC17 pic.twitter.com/uDH8d4Of4Z Obama, who used fashion more powerfully than any First Lady since Jackie Kennedy, added that her husband would tease her about how effortless his getting ready process, even for the most formal of state occasions, would be. "He was proud of it too, he was like 'I'm ready, ready in ten minutes, how long did it take you? 'And I'm like 'Get out of here.'" During the same talk, Michelle Obama discussed how she coped with the somewhat surreal moments of waiting for guests outside the White House in front of the world's press. She recounted one occasion when she and the President were awaiting the arrival of the Chinese president and his wife. "We're standing there waiting for the cars to roll in," she said, describing the click-click of cameras flashing before them. "I was bored, so I thought 'let me make sure my husband looks good.'" The images of that moment became one of many adorable couple moments between the Obamas which went viral.  While Michelle Obama might have bemoaned the unequal levels of attention between her and her husband's style choices- a sometimes depressing but nevertheless universal truth when men's style is so much more a uniform than the huge variety of women's options- she still embraced dressing for the First Lady role and seemed to enjoy it. Of course, she didn't have to tackle the monumental task of dressing for her packed calendar of engagements alone. Stylist Meredith Koop became a trusted adviser of the First Lady, helping her to put together a wardrobe which worked for her but which also came to  influence the way millions of women the world over dress and helped the brands which she wore to add a combined total of $2.7 billion to their stocks.   "In the beginning, designers used the phrase 'first ladyish' to describe a certain traditional look. We really had to break that mold," Koop told Harper's Bazaar last year. "Highlighting designers from diverse backgrounds with varying levels of success and exposure became an important part of my role." Koop also underlined the inspirational power of the FLOTUS's style choices. "When [the first lady] wears an up-and-coming designer, it creates this feeling that anything is possible," she said. The theme of this year's Met Gala is “Manus x Machina: Fashion in an Age of Technology,” and Emma Watson used this as an opportunity to highlight the incredible advancements in eco fashion. Everything from the lining to the unique yarn, which is created using plastic bottles, is made from sustainable materials.  This was a collaboration with Calvin Klein and Livia Firth's on going project, the Green Carpet Challenge, with Eco Age. Watson's stylist Sarah Slutsky wrote on Instagram of the look: "Tonight, the stunning Emma on the red carpet at the Met Ball in a look crafted by the incredible team at Calvin Klein. With the help of Eco Age this five piece look is created from three fabrics woven from yarns all made from recycled plastic bottles." She continues: "Plastic is one of the biggest pollutants – being able to turn this waste into a high quality material is a real success story. Also this beautiful look was designed with the intention to be re-purposed for future use; the pants can be worn on their own, the train can be used for another red carpet - the ultimate #30Wears!" "We loved working with the team at Calvin Klein to create a look that is truly a perfect marriage of ethics and aesthetics," Eco Age wrote on Instagram of the look. "The body of the look is crafted from three different fabrics all woven from yarns made from recycled plastic bottles, the zippers are made from recycled materials and the inner bustier has been created using organic cotton." Lupita Nyong'o meanwhile wore a jade sequin dress with velvet straps, opting for a colour that truly reflects the 'Green Carpet Challenge.'  This year is fast shaping up to be a landmark year in the body confidence battle. After many, many summers dominated by images of celebrities with 'perfect' bodies on the beach and thousands of punishing  'beach-ready' diet plans and exercise regimes which come with the subtext that if you don't achieve nigh-on impossible goals then donning swimwear might not be a great idea, the world is fighting back.  Just weeks after H&M revealed  the beautiful 60-year-old Gillian McLeod  as one of their swimwear models and the #MySwimBody initiative supported by Ashley Graham was launched, JD Williams has enlisted Nicola Griffin, 56, and Jilly Johnson, 62, to front a campaign encouraging women of all ages, shapes and sizes to feel proud to wear a bikini. A YouGov poll conducted by the retailer revealed that just 4 per cent of women over 50 would feel confident enough to share a picture of themselves in a bikini on social media. In a bid to tackle those shockingly low levels of pride in their bodies, Griffin - who shot to fame earlier this year when she became the oldest ever model to star in Sport's Illustrated swimwear issue - and Johnson, a former glamour model,  are encouraging their peers to banish their bikini fears and share their selfies using #mybikiniselfie. "Youth is everything these days," Johnson tells the Telegraph, "but I just thought hell's bells to boundaries and protocol, it's time to throw the wraps and kaftans aside and just get up and do it."  While Johnson and Griffin undoubtedly look fabulous in the shoot they have taken part in to launch the campaign, Johnson is keen to stress that their confidence has not been easily-won. "It's true that I have been genetically blessed and never used to think twice about wearing a bikini," she explains, "I just never understood that lack of confidence but suddenly when I hit 40 I became very sympathetic and I finally understood what everyone was going through."  "I spent the years between 40 and 50 wearing appropriately placed wraps - and I think I pulled it off quite glamorously!" she laughs, "but now I have a devil-may-care approach, even if I'm not quite as firm as I once was. We're only on the planet a short time so we should make the most of it." It's a sentiment which countless women will identify with.  Johnson says that bikinis have long had a reputation as something only very young girls could wear. "I was still modelling swimwear into my 30s" she remembers, "but I always found it extraordinary that I would be handed the one-piece while the teen models would get the bikinis." She puts her newfound confidence down to the difficult life experiences which many women her age have been through. "My attitude to wearing a bikini was very different 20 years ago but I've have had friends who have been ill or I've lost - the girls I used to model with - some to breast cancer," she says, "that makes everything fall into place and you're more willing to just embrace everything." Of course as a former model, Johnson has a head start on many normal women facing the thought of wearing a bikini this summer. "I used to worry and would keep my movements to an absolute minimum if I was wearing a bikini, but there is nothing worse than a lady with no confidence. I think you have to pretend," she encourages, "you need to fake it until you make it. I always think that bulls--- battles brains." Her final rallying cry? "Us older ladies should be grateful for what we've got - wobbly bits and all. I'm 62 and past worrying, life is for living."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Demna Gvasalia sent stripey market-stall shopping bags down the runway at Balenciaga in March, they quickly became the latest 'Oh fashion!' joke, with many comparing the £975+ totes to the laundry bags you can buy in Thai markets for £1. The shoppers from the AW16 collection dropped on Net-A-Porter, MATCHESFASHION.COM and more at the beginning of this month, and now Gvasalia is having the last laugh, because these 'market bags' are selling. And selling fast. "We saw the Bazar bag on the runway and loved it so bought into this style across several sizes as we knew our customers would love it too," says Natalie Kingham, Buying Director at MATCHESFASHION.COM. "We’ve had a really great reaction to all sizes, but particularly the medium which has sold very fast. Our MyStylist and private shopping teams had requests for the Bazar following the runway show." It's a similar success story over on Net-A-Porter, which is backing the Bazar as the bag of the season. “We’re huge fans of the Balenciaga Bazar; it’s the bag of the moment," adds senior buyer at Net A Porter, Billie Faricy Hyett. "We bought six styles in total of the Balenciaga Bazar bag in different sizes; three in multicolour and three in leather. We had one style launch on the site last week, with further styles available from September." So why are people paying £975 for a bag that has been compared to a heavy-duty laundrette carry-all? Well it seems all of this virtual eye-rolling, only makes fashion people want it even more. "It’s a really iconic bag which is very tongue in cheek, taking an everyday product and making it feel luxurious which is very of the moment with the success of brands like Vetements," explains Kingham. "It’s also a really useful, functional bag that holds a lot and which can be used for many different purposes." "The main draw for me is the juxtaposition of the Thai market bag inspiration that’s been executed and styled in such a luxe way," adds Net A Porter's Hyett. "Demna Gvasalia manages to give a normal everyday item an unexpected twist and turn it into something high fashion. For me, the Bazar is the modern version of the classic granny shopping bag. The colourful print also makes it perfect for Instagram, so I’m sure we’ll see more of them across our feeds once it’s available on site." The bag is instantly recognisable, and is already appearing on some of the most influential arms in the industry. Fashion blogger Pernille Teisback wore hers throughout Copenhagen Fashion Week this month, with everything from a slouchy Vetements hoodie to a tailored, Prince of Wales check suit, and it was also carried by Russian fashion journalist Natasha Goldenberg to the shows in Copenhagen. Signs that it's almost certainly going to be a front row hazard at fashion month this September. We can almost hear the sound of the photographers shouting 'move your Bazars', instead of 'uncross your legs!' MATCHESFASHION.COM believes that part of the reason why there is such a huge buzz around this bag for Autumn, is because of the rise in popularity of instantly clockable, must-have bags, much like the it bags that reigned supreme in the noughties. "The it-bag is making a comeback and the Bazar falls into this category, explains Kingham. "Bags are one of our strongest areas, our customers tend to buy a new it-bag each season to add to their wardrobes." If you just don't get this bag, that's Gvasalia's point, as his aim with all of his work is to turn the entire industry on its head. At Vetements, he has made tracksuit bottoms, ripped jeans and slogan sweatshirts cult items, with hefty 'it item' pricetags to match. Not only can he sell a yellow DHL t shirt for £185, he can make it sell out too. But he wouldn't even pay for these clothes himself. "I wear prototypes but I don’t think I’m crazy fashion enough to go and buy those things," the Vetements designer previously told The Telegraph. "I’d rather go on holiday. I feel like it brings more use. Holidays are important. Holidays and quality time on your sofa.” As for the £975 striped leather shoulder bag he carried to said interview, he rolled his eyes at the mention of it and said: “This bag. This is just a prototype but the number of people who have stopped me in the street to ask where it’s from. Even an old lady came up to tell me this morning that she had the same one at home. I thought, 'I don’t think it is …’”   Balenciaga, Bazar medium grained-leather tote, £975  Balenciaga, Bazar medium grained-leather tote, £975 Balenciaga, Bazar striped textured-leather pouch, £345   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We are always on the look out for new faces to shape up the red carpet, and bring a fresh, daring approach to the premiere dressing game. Star Trek Beyond's Sofia Boutella is one of a new wave of actresses, including Soko, Bel Powley, Daisy Ridley and Alicia Vikander, who are turning their backs on traditional codes, and bringing a cooler, more honest approach to their red carpet wardrobes. The Algeria-born, Paris-raised 34-year-old actress may still be a relatively unknown, but she is bound to be a break out star in Hollywood with forthcoming roles in The Mummy with Tom Cruise and The Coldest City with Charlize Theron and James McAvoy. She has prepared for the many large-scale press tours that lie ahead of her by working with Rosie Huntington-Whiteley's stylist Cher Coulter to carve out a look which is making the fashion crowd take notice. This is a girl who clearly loves fashion, so much so that she started making her own jewellery over 10 years ago when she was 22- although she hasn't turned it into a commercial venture. "I make body chains that come from the neck, cross in the middle of your chest, then go around your waist," Boutella has previously said of her designs. "I mix them with feathers for a gypsy, bohemian style." To promote Star Trek Beyond at the end of last month, Boutella made unusual - but spot-on - choices, wearing a gothic black sheer lace Alberta Ferretti gown with stacked Messika jewellery to the London premiere and a short white lace Elie Saab dress to Comic-Con. "She's adventurous and brave," says Coulter, her British stylist, of her approach to fashion. "I think she'll surprise us with her choices. She is also individual; she won't be one to be obvious. She's a little bit of a break from the norm." As a jewellery obsessive, Boutella has one clear request when it comes to her styling - that she had plenty of rings and bracelets to liven up her look. "She always wants to make it interesting with the jewellery," adds Coulter. "Sofia did say she likes lots of rings, and bracelets and stacking jewellery. She's fun because she wants to go there and she cares about what she's wearing." "I like working with the new girls," Coulter says of working with actresses at the beginning of their careers to develop their red carpet look from scratch. "It's not easier, because you have to create relationships with designers so it's from the bottom up. With the new girls you are more invested in them and you help develop their look. What was interesting and challenging at the same time with Sofia was I did the whole first fitting over Skype." "You want to be in the room with a new client, which is tough, but you are already seeing it on a screen so you have that distance from it," Coulter says about their six-hour Skype fitting. "Because sometimes you can be like 'it looked great in the flesh' but it's really important what it looks like on camera, so that was useful." On the red carpet she might favour dramatic, even rebellious gowns, a quick scroll through Instagram makes it apparent that when she's not on the red carpet she keeps it more casual. Boutella favours basic grey t shirts, distressed denim, chunky boots and stacked rings.  Whether you're likely to watch her upcoming action films or not, you will certainly be seeing a lot of Sofia Boutella in every fashion magazine come 2017.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Sometimes, when we get dressed in the morning, we throw something on and run out the door without a lot of thought. But some outfits we know will be more important, and for many of 2016's most public figures, a key fashion choice has been able to cause headlines, prompt Twitter hashtags and even rattle the political landscape around the world. These are the looks that got everybody talking in the last year, and the ones that will probably make it into the fashion history books... She hadn’t meant to cause a controversy. She apparently hadn’t even realised the significance of the style of blouse. Yet Melania Trump’s shocking pink Gucci outfit had an impact because of its, well, shocking timing. She chose to wear her pussy-bow just days after it was revealed that her husband had made vile comments about grabbing women ‘by the pussy’. So was she really so naive that she didn't know her look was loaded with meaning? Or was she intentionally mocking the situation? “There is not a woman alive who puts on a head to toe fuchsia outfit, blows out her mane and doesn’t want to be noticed,” Victoria Moss, our Senior Fashion News and Features Editor concluded.   The theme of this year’s MET Gala was man versus machine, a dress-code that Madonna interpreted to mean wearing a sheer lace skirt by Givenchy, and subsequently flashing her bottom. Twitter had plenty to say about the 57 year-old’s exposed derrière, with commentators like Piers Morgan chiming in to tell her to “put it away”. Her response? "When it comes to women's rights we are still in the dark ages,” she wrote on Instagram. “My dress at the Met Ball was a political statement as well as a fashion statement. If you have a problem with the way I dress it is simply a reflection of your prejudice.” Kate’s Vogue appearance made headlines around the world, but what probably surprised fans the most was her relaxed cover-girl look. With fresh, minimal makeup applied by Sally Branka, Kate wore a country-casual jacket and white shirt by Burberry, passing on the opportunity to dress in cliche couture confections. "She didn't want to be dressed as a fashion plate and was not keen to be shot in gala gowns and tiaras," revealed Vogue Editor-in-Chief Alexandra Shulman. You’ve just landed the biggest job in British politics - so what do you wear on your first day at work? It was a dilemma that Prime Minister Theresa May had probably less than twenty minutes to solve, but her choice would make or break one of the most important pictorial moments of the year. In the end she picked a neon and navy coat by British designer Amanda Wakeley, plus her signature L.K Bennett leopard print kitten heels to enter Downing Street. It was seen as a perfect balance of power dressing and fashion fun, that ensured she stood out. We don’t care if she’s fictional, we can’t think of the last time a little girl made such a big statement with her clothes. When Eleven shed her institution’s nightgown and started hanging out with the boys (who tried to clothe her in their sister’s frilly dress) her shaved head and bomber jacket made a feminist statement that was wise beyond her years. She wanted to be pretty, but found that being pretty tough is way more exciting - what a message to offer up to over 14 million people worldwide with a single outfit. Made entirely of Swarovski crystals and worth over $9,000, Kendall’s 21st birthday dress was designed to pay homage to Paris Hilton’s birthday frock from the Noughties. It was a classic case of what goes around comes around - the model of the moment reviving the style of the original reality TV It-girl, who arguably paved the way for the Kardashian-Jenner clan and their modern media empire. Kendall’s look was liked over 3.1 million times on Instagram - the Millennial sign of a job well done. Jerry Hall’s Westwood gown was the most talked-about wedding dress of the year, starting a long-overlooked conversation about ageless bridal style. The 60 year-old bride chose a designer whose work meant something to her (Jerry and her daughters have walked in several Westwood catwalk shows over the years) and opted for a softly draped chiffon gown in ice blue, not white. Kate and William’s September tour of Canada presented many opportunities for the Duchess to wow in the fashion stakes. But it was her Preen dress, worn at the Government House reception in Victoria, that was considered the most beautiful of them all. In Canada red, the dress by British design duo Justin Thornton and Thea Bregazzi evoked a classically glamorous, mid-century silhouette. It nodded to both British and Canadian parties (especially when accessorised with a diamond maple leaf brooch) and flattered the Duchess’ figure so well that she later went back to Fenwick to buy it in black, too.   Hillary’s entire fashion campaign was built around pantsuits, but one in particular will go down in history as being the most significant of them all. As she accepted the Democratic presidential nomination, making history in the process, she chose an all-white suit. It was a look loaded with feminist meaning as the British and American women in the Suffragette movement wore white, and it fuelled the hope that she might yet crack “the highest and hardest glass ceiling” yet. Michelle Obama had one last fashion hurrah at her final White House State Dinner, stunning in this Atelier Versace gown made of rose gold chainmail. The critics were beside themselves, with most citing this as her best look of the entire administration, noting that her chainmail might represent armour, the warm colour might represent hope, and  just that the Obamas have shined like rockstars for the last eight years. The Queen has worn a rainbow of vivid hues in her time, but for this year's Trooping The Colour (how fitting) Her Majesty was celebrating both her 90th birthday and the fact she’s now Britain’s longest serving sovereign, and so she really wanted to stand out. As soon as she stepped out of the door she caused a stir, with #NeonAt90 and #HighVisHighness trending immediately on Twitter and sales of neon clothing rising by 137% in the weeks that followed. Perhaps most importantly, though, she reminded us all that anyone, at any age, can have fun with fashion and should never be afraid to experiment with bold looks. All hail.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Amandla started out in the industry in photo shoots for Disney when she was four and played Rue in the first installment of the Hunger Games franchise. But recently she has been venturing into the world of fashion - she is signed with modelling agency One Management, is this month's Teen Vogue cover star and attended Stella McCartney's presentation earlier this month. We expect that she will make an appearance (or 10) at New York Fashion Week, perhaps with her stylish 'squad' which includes Tavi Gevinson, Willow Smith, Kiernan Shipka and Lorde.  Amandla is a powerful role model and will speak candidly about feminism, black culture and bisexuality - she came out as bisexual on Snapchat. She made headlines last year for her viral video about cultural appropriation, ‘Don’t cash crop on my cornrows,’ and has made her own black feminist comic book.  In her Teen Vogue cover interview with Solange Knowles she admitted that she’s bored of being asked about her afro hair. She explained how she started embracing her natural hair: “I know when I used to chemically straighten mine, I did it because I wasn’t comfortable with my natural hair. I thought it was too poofy, too kinky. So for me, personally, when I started wearing it natural, it felt like I was blossoming because I was letting go of all the dead hair and all the parts of me that had rejected my natural state. But, you know, it’s not like that for all black girls. Some have their hair straight because that’s just how they like it, and it doesn’t mean that they accept themselves any less.” As for her style, Amandla has revealed that she turns to Instagram for inspiration. She told WhoWhatWear: “I love social media because you are able to find role models who are not necessarily the most conservative or what we see in the mainstream media. You are able to find people with voices and really cool style, and I’ve been able to find through Instagram some really sick women who I can relate to and identify with, and they have become the celebrities to me." She also spoke about her style philosophy: “This sounds cliché, but you are going to look the best in anything you feel comfortable in. I feel like while clothes are important, the most important thing is if they are what you want to wear and if they are who you are. How you wear it is 95% of it.” See more of Amandla's style over on her Instagram, @amandastenberg.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This evening some of the biggest names in Hollywood will walk the red carpet at this year's annual Met Gala. The event, which was fittingly dubbed the "Super Bowl of Fashion" by Andre Leon Talley, is orchestrated by Anna Wintour and sees designers and their muses pair off. So how do the stars prepare for a night that is arguably even trickier to dress for than the Oscars? "The Met Gala is the biggest fashion event bar none, but it's the most controlled event in terms of dressing," explains stylist Manny Ezugwu, who has worked with Jourdan Dunn on her previous Met Gala looks. "There is no wild card option. I guess there's not even room for that because it's so heavily managed by Anna Wintour and the Vogue crew in terms of who gets invited and what designers attend. So clients know what designers they are wearing, probably by fashion week in February. They don't know the look, but they know who they are going with then or even earlier." It is also a given that a celebrity face of a design house will wear the label to the Met Gala.  This is the one red carpet where you really can't predict what celebrities will wear as most of the pieces will be one-off creations. "The Met Gala is one of the few events that the majority of items are custom," explains Manny from the Muse Talent Group. "So the designers always have a theme in mind, so dependant on the relationship you have with brand you can really direct how you want it to look or the style you're going with. With Jourdan Dunn's Burberry gownin 2015 it was a really collaborative process about what we thought would make best dressed, and with Topshop the year before they listened to us in terms of colour and material." Cristina Ehrlich, who  has styled Brie Larson, stresses that unlike other red carpets, the Met Gala is really a collaborative effort. "It is different in the sense that it is truly a collaboration, between myself and my client and also the designer who the actress is a guest of and Vogue. It is not more difficult - it’s just a more collaborative process," she explains. "It’s not more political, but it is based around the idea of costuming verses a traditional red carpet, which is meant to promote a project or a movie an actress is working on."stresses that unlike other red carpets, the Met Gala is really a collaborative effort. "It is different in the sense that it is truly a collaboration, between myself and my client and also the designer who the actress is a guest of and Vogue. It is not more difficult - it’s just a more collaborative process," she explains. "It’s not more political, but it is based around the idea of costuming verses a traditional red carpet, which is meant to promote a project or a movie an actress is working on." Each year designers create a look to tie in with the theme of the exhibition at the Costume Institute. Ehrlich sees it as her job, however, to ensure her clients look in keeping with their signature style, rather than dressing to fit the theme. "My role in the process is to keep my client’s own aesthetic there, while the designer who is creating the gown works to incorporate the theme for that year into the look," she explains. The Met Gala is one of the trickiest red carpets to dress for, because unlike the Oscars or the Golden Globes where the stars walk across a flat surface, here they have to hike up the seemingly endless steps. Manny learned the hard way on his first Met Gala that you need to think carefully about the fit of the skirt. "The first Met Gala I styled was the one in 2014, and a tribute to Charles James, and Jourdan went with Topshop with Kendall Jenner, Chanel Iman and Toni Garnn," he recalls. "And we all had a say in what we wanted the colour of dresses to be, and they came back with mermaid-y satin ball gowns, but we hadn't thought about how they would move and walk." "There was this funny scene where we trying to load Toni and Jourdan in the car to get to the Met Gala and we had to put the seats totally flat so they could get there without the dresses getting creased. And then when they were walking, it was impossible  because it was one foot in front of the other. After that, from 2014 onwards, I was like "there needs to always be a slit." And so the next year, Jourdan and Manny ensured that there was a slit in her custom Burberry gown. Securing the perfect diamond necklace, or booking the hairstylist you love, can be difficult. "When it comes to accessories, it's so busy," Manny says of the rush to get diamonds. "Last year I went to Lorraine Schwartz with Lily Donaldson to pick up diamonds and there's even a hierarchy with that. Lorraine personally went out with a whole tray of jewels for Beyonce, so it's already a rush with the jewellery brands. But Lorraine is the queen of jewellery!" As for hair and makeup, celebrities can have their full look finished seven or so hours ahead of the event because artists are in very high demand and you have to book appointments weeks, if not months, in advance. When stars finally make it onto the red carpet, they have to stay focused when it comes to making sure their dress gets seen. "That red carpet is daunting, it goes on and on," Manny explains. "It's the one event you when you really need to peacock and try and get as much camera time as possible. You are better off at the beginning because you get early exposure, whereas towards the end the Rihannas and Beyoncés can be the last, last person there. There's the shot you need to have by the stairs and by the entrance, but are about 20 handlers (you go from one person to the other to the other) who motions you through. You can't just come when you want - you have your slot when to arrive."  Red carpet photographer, Andrew Walker, who has captured the last five years of Met Galas says in reality it is tricky to photograph every single look. "You get zero time with each celebrity," he explains. "They have to keep going. There are people right behind them, and it's impossible to linger. I have shot the Oscars and the Met Gala - and the Met Gala makes the Oscars look like kids play. The sheer number of A Listers with great fashion there is nothing like it - people literally get heat exhaustion because they are working so hard trying to take pictures of them all." Beyoncé will always have her own handler (if not handlers) walk the red carpet with her, so that they can make sure her dress looks camera-ready at all times. But even having a handler carry your dress is something that needs approval beforehand. "Handlers are allowed to help navigate depending on how the dress is," explains Manny. "It's up to a certain point and then you're left on your own. It needs to have approval beforehand to have someone walk on the red carpet with you. " But often designers walk the red carpet arm-in-arm with their celebrity and so they will do this 'dress fluffing' themselves.   Although most dresses are organised months and months in advance, if you are on the reserve list to attend you can be left with just one day to pull a look together. "There is also a reserve list so if anyone pulls out you'll get confirmation on Sunday, and then you have to get ready on Monday and scramble to find something to wear," reveals Manny. Talk about stressful!  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It can’t be easy being the assistant to one of the world’s most famous, most photographed women, Beyoncé. And that’s a point that was proved correct last night. The singer was posing on the red carpet of the rather uncatchily named TIDAL X: 1020 Amplified by HTC event when her faithful PA, Sam Greenberg, dutifully stepped in to adjust her crotch-skimming, cleavage-revealing Philipp Plein gown to avoid any awkward slips. Ever the professional, Beyoncé maintained her plastered-on grin as Greenberg tweaked before sniping what looked to be: “stop it”. Greenberg promptly retreated to the background, tail between legs. Ouch. The clip was posted by Beyoncé-fan Instagram account @beylite and has so far prompted over 2,000 comments. Greenberg revealed to Vogue earlier this year a little about her life as Beyoncé’s right-hand woman. Though she didn’t speak directly about Queen B (we’re pretty sure there’s a clause in her contract that stops that), she did reveal how she feels about the job: “I think that in this job it is about looking clean and looking cool, and not trying to be much in the spotlight because that isn’t why you’re there,” she said. “It is also representing whom you work for. For me, the fun of it is walking in and seeing that B’s stylist has pulled something from what I have or vice versa. It is a cool experience to learn from her and curate my taste along with hers because she is quite the style icon,” she added. A style icon that really doesn't like it when you touch her, that is... So, what lessons can we learn from this debacle? When Beyoncé says stop, you stop. And next time someone annoys you, try out her fake-grin-and-'stop it' and see what happens.

 What exactly the Duchess of Cambridge would choose to wear to her sister Pippa Middleton’s wedding today has likely been discussed as much by fashion commentators as what the bride herself would opt for. As one of the most famous women in the world (and one whose every outfit choice makes the front pages whether she’s attending a gala or popping to the shops) the Duchess will have found herself contemplating her wedding guest look from a very unusual position; no matter what she chose to wear, she would be at risk of upstaging the bride, her sister, on her big day. The Duchess’ understanding of this sensitive situation meant that what she actually did choose to wear today was a very clever sartorial tactic indeed. Kate completely steered clear of anything outlandish or attention-grabbing, sticking with her signature occasionwear silhouette, a rose pink midi-length dress, by one of her favourite labels Alexander McQueen. The first glimpse of Kate came at around 10am as she left Kensington Palace with the Duke of Cambridge in a Range Rover, her sculpted rose-topped hat by milliner Jane Taylor, and morganite earrings by Kiki McDonough visible to the awaiting paparazzi through the car window.  The next shot we saw was of the Duchess arriving at the church, leading a gaggle of bridesmaids and page boys into the service, including her own children Prince George and Princess Charlotte. Here we got the first glimpse of Kate's custom-made, full-sleeve dress by designer Sarah Burton, as she helped make adjustments to Pippa's dress just before she went down the aisle. L.K. Bennett, Erdem and Emilia Wickstead were all frontrunners to dress the Duchess today - all being brands in Kate’s occasionwear repertoire which could offer her something classic and understated, but still a little bit special. But when it came down to it, she turned to Sarah Burton, the woman who designed her McQueen wedding dress in 2011, and who has become a trusted aide.  London-based fashion house Alexander McQueen has dressed the Duchess of Cambridge on dozens of occasions since the royal wedding, including to Prince George's christening in and on the red carpet at the BAFTAs earlier this year. Burton will gamely adapt pieces from her runway collections to suit the Duchess (like when she switched a risque corset bodice for a more suitable off-shoulder top for said BAFTA appearance) and will also whip up bespoke outfits at a moment's notice when needed. Pippa, of course, became the world’s most famous bridesmaid at the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge’s wedding in 2011 (thanks largely to her own figure-skimming Alexander McQueen crepe satin dress) so she will know all too well what it can mean to have a star in your bridal party. While she didn’t quite manage to steal the show from the Duchess, it was a moment that put her on the radar for designers around the world, turning her into an unexpected fashion plate and a regular on the front rows at London Fashion Week. In not asking her sister to be an official bridesmaid and get ready with her on the morning of the wedding, Pippa showed that she didn’t want to be outdone on her wedding day, and, frankly, it seems fair enough - this is perhaps the only day that she will not be playing second fiddle as ‘the sister of the Duchess of Cambridge’.  The overall fashion verdict on the Duchess’s look, then? Poised, diplomatic and as sisterly as could be.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Despite being nominated for a Best Actress award at the Golden Globes last night, despite arriving in a dazzling Armani Privé gown and despite posing for pictures with Leonardo DiCaprio and the ilk, perhaps only film buffs were aware of Isabelle Huppert's illustrious career before she stepped onto the red carpet last night. But now the 63 year-old French actress has won the gong and won the spotlight, pipping Amy Adams (for her role in Arrival), Jessica Chastain (for Miss Sloane), Ruth Negga (for Loving) and Natalie Portman (for Jackie) to the prize and causing the headlines to hail her a ‘surprise star’. True, she might not have been a mainstream name before her critically acclaimed performance in Elle, but the fashion industry had caught onto Huppert’s magic some time ago. A front row fixture at Dior, Chanel and Armani (she attended the latter's couture show in July and likely picked her Golden Globes gown from the presentation), her irreverent, nonchalant sense of style has allowed her to play both muse and model for many designers over the years. Photographer Helmut Newton took a series of now-iconic, provocative portraits of her in the 1970s, and Mert Alas and Marcus Piggott shot her for Givenchy’s 2014 ad campaign, alongside Kendall Jenner and a gaggle of millennial models. Despite starring in over 130 movies since her debut in 1971, Huppert’s choice to always work with edgy directors and complex characters is part of what has defined her as an ageless cool-girl for so long. Her character in psychological thriller Elle is a businesswoman who is attacked and raped in her home, and previous roles like 2001’s The Piano Teacher, have all called for her to adopt dark personalities.   The fact that Hubbert is extremely private and very little is known about her, is also likely part of her appeal to designers on the hunt for a steady, reliably chic muse. The mother of three joined Instagram just three days ago and has gained 1,500 followers so far. Her day-to-day style consists of all the now-cliche markers of French chic; jeans, tailored jackets, skinny neckties and even Breton tops. But with her authenticity (she was born in Paris in 1953) the look suddenly feels sophisticated and easy. On the red carpet, her go-tos are equally archetypal - think smoking suits in red, white or black, black leather blouses and pussy bow dresses by Dior - but in the mix of flashing sequins, bodycon tops and ‘naked dresses’ on swarming Instagram right now, Huppert's is an easy approach that feels positively refreshing. At the Golden Globes last night she took some risks with her is-that-a-bare-midriff dress and Repossi earcuffs to boot. But the risks paid off and only added to her enduring appeal as an underrated, understated French style icon.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Azzedine Alaïa, who has died between the ages of 77 and 82, was, with Giorgio Armani, the most influential fashion designer of the 1980s, and one of the industry’s few innovative talents; his use of fabric to make clothes that hugged the body earned him the epithet “The King of Cling”. Like Coco Chanel before him, Alaïa’s genius was to use a previously overlooked material to create an entirely new mainstream fashion. Where Chanel made her name with jersey (previously reserved for men’s undergarments), Alaïa used stretchy fibres hitherto employed only for swimwear.  Today, the Queen stepped out in an all-purple ensemble to attend a Thanksgiving service that also marked 60 years of the Duke of Edinburgh Award.  Her particular shade of purple (shall we call it Cadbury?) packed a punch when set against Westminster Abbey's grey stonework, but also stood next to the Dean of Westminster in his contrasting golden cloak. But, of course, she knew it would. The Queen has 63 years of experience in using colour to stand out. Indeed, when she marked the start of her 90th birthday celebrations earlier this year, the Queen kicked things off in top-to-toe fuchsia. Created by Angela Kelly, who has been the Queen's personal dresser since 1994, the outfit would have been painstakingly planned. Likewise, opinion dividing the neon green dress coat and matching hat which she wore for the Trooping of the Colour- an outfit which prompted a 134% uplift in sales of neon items.  In a book released four years ago Kelly revealed that she sketches at least four different designs for a particular piece of fabric and that a fan is used to test how material will move in the breeze before the final creation is decided upon.  She also talked of the significance attached to colour in the Queen's wardrobe - both to ensure Her Majesty stands out in a crowd and to pay a subtle tribute to the event. Think for example of the dazzling green outfit that Her Majesty wore to touch down in Dublin on her landmark visit to Ireland in 2011 - or the white outfit The Queen wore on the Thames River Pageant that was designed to contrast against the boat's red seats.   “I have to be seen to be believed,” the Queen has said. And a colourful wardrobe plays a key role in fulfilling this mantra. From zingy violet and hot pink to lime and sunshine yellow, there is no colour that clashes with Her Majesty – the only one she avoids is beige, which does not allow her to stand out in a crowd.  In 2012 British Vogue magazine published a graphic tracking the bold spectrum of colour the Queen wore across the course of a year. The results were illuminating: 29 per cent blue, 10 per cent pink, 13 per cent floral. For schools, the Queen turns to jolly, bright colours and embellishment like ribbons designed to appeal to children. Yellow is her happy colour; black the one she only wears when expressing condolence.   So what does today's purple outfit prove? That as Queen Elizabeth II rounds off her 90th birthday year she's doing what she has in more than 63 years of dressing for the public eye - not putting a patent-court-shod foot wrong.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It appears that Meghan Markle’s recent visits to London have had some effect on her wardrobe. Burberry, Mulberry, Barbour, Hunter and more have all found a new place in the Suits actress’ wardrobe, as she has spent more and more time in the capital visiting her boyfriend, Prince Harry. So what has Meghan been buying? Yesterday, she was spotted shopping for flowers on London’s Kensington High Street wearing a classic waxed cotton Barbour jacket with Hunter wellingtons, a Brit-approved ensemble that royals from the Duchess of Cambridge to The Queen have all road-tested over the years, and would surely approve of.  Sienna Miller is enjoying a long summer of standing ovations, starring as Maggie in Tennessee Williams' Cat on a Hot Tin Roof. For anyone who has seen her performance at the Apollo, you'll know that Miller spends the evening in pared-back slip dresses, teetering heels and a glittering sequinned black gown. She looks modern and spectacular. But this stage style story continues each night once bows are taken and the lights come up. If Victoria Beckham has made airport style her own, then Sienna Miller is fast becoming the high priestess of the stage door look.  Plenty of actresses have understood the power of the swift dash from theatre to car in the past. When Elizabeth Taylor starred alongside former husband Richard Burton in the 1983 play Private Lives, the pair exited New York's Lunt Fontaine theatre together, him looking pristine in a navy jacket and burgundy tie while she was ostensibly understated in a black tunic, but enlivened the look with a chunky statement necklace. Meanwhile, when Katie Holmes was at the height of her Tom Cruise marriage fame in 2008, she used her daily arrival and departure from Arthur Miller's All My Sons to showcase a studiously casual ripped jeans and knitwear look.  The savvy nonchalance of Sienna Miller's post-performance wardrobe sets a new bar though. She's dialled down the look since the first showings of the play in July, when she was pictured wearing a delicately printed tea dress by Erdem. Aside from the tiered Chanel dress she wore for the play's opening party, Miller's choices have mostly been comprised of laidback culottes, tracksuit bottoms or jeans which she has worn with a variety of slouchy tees.  Earlier this week, she paired Everlane's 100% Human t-shirt (a purchase which generates a donation to the American Civil Liberties Union) with grey marl joggers and Adidas slides before stepping things up on Wednesday night with a Chanel t-shirt and battered skinny jeans. Last week , the vibe was similarly relaxed but significantly more luxe with a pair of Rockins' silk pyjamas.  Miller has given her stage door wardrobe a real touch by carrying the same roomy Proenza Schouler tote bag and wearing her beloved Gucci Princetown loafers or Adidas Stan Smiths on and off throughout the run so far, while a Dior Addict logo bag was a notable new piece this week. It's this artful juggling of relatable realism with a smattering of designer key additions which define Miller's take on the stage door outfit.  The Hollywood super stylist Kate Young, with whom  Miller usually works for red carpet appearences, doesn't seem to have masterminded the actress's clocking-off outfits (although she will surely have offered some helpful pointers), but instead Miller has been going with her natural instinct for effortless cool.  She's well-versed in the practice; during the summer of 2005 when Miller made her stage debut in As You Like It, she made the papers day after day with a parade of boho blouses,  embroidered hippie jackets and Chloe 'Paddington' bags.  With Cat on a Hot Tin Roof set to continue into October, Miller will no doubt  soon be offering up her stage door take on autumn style.        © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge hasn’t had a major glamour moment in a few months, but attending the Royal Variety performance at the London Palladium last night, she offered a  reminder of her ability to dial up the regal glitz when the occasion calls for it. While many pregnant women might struggle with what to wear for a black tie do with a burgeoning bump, Kate turned to one of her most trusted designers, Jenny Packham, for a solution in the form of a bespoke, embellished design similar to a look in her AW17 collection. On the catwalk, the dress came in cream with only a mini-length slip beneath the tulle. The Duchess’s version was, naturally, more demure  with a full length icy blue silk slip dress with a lace trim underneath a sheer layer with long sleeves embellished with clusters of crystal and sequins. Kate amped up the twinkly effect further still by adding sparkly Oscar de la Renta heels and a pair of chandelier diamond earrings which she has on long term loan from The Queen and has worn several times before.  Amongst the Duchess's online fans, comparisons were made with the pale blue, glittering look of Frozen's Elsa, a style reference of which Prince George and Princess Charlotte would surely have approved. For two other evening engagements in recent weeks, Kate has worn a black lace Diane von Furstenberg dress which she first wore in 2014. The decision to wear a new dress last night- one of the highlights of the royal calendar- evidences the careful balance of frugality and opulence which royal women seek to strike through their style choices.  Last night's gown is the latest addition to the Duchess's collection of  timeless evening looks from Packham. In Paris earlier this year, Kate debuted a new silver column dress with botanical-themed embellishments for a reception to celebrate British-French relations. Other Packham-designed highlights include a lace-backed turquoise gown which Kate wore for an Olympics dinner in 2012 and a similar red style which offered a diplomatic nod to the guests of honour at the Chinese State Banquet held at Buckingham Palace in 2015. Another niche in the Duchess's wardrobe which Packham has come to 'own' is the coming-home-from-hospital look. She was responsible for both the spotted blue tea dress and the yellow and white floral shift which Kate wore to bring home George and Charlotte respectively. So it seems likely that she will win the commission again when the Cambridges' third child is born in April.   Jenny Packham also counts Angelina Jolie, Rosie Huntington Whiteley and Kim Murray amongst her well-known clients who turn to her for glamorous red carpet failsafes. The designer's other expertise is in romantic bridal dresses, a speciality which may pique the interest of Meghan Markle if rumours of an engagement to Prince Harry are confirmed.   For now though, it is Kate setting the royal standard for Christmas party dressing.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Kate Winslet was so convinced she wouldn’t win a Golden Globe on Sunday night that she’d booked a massage to ease her nagging neck pain immediately after the ceremony in LA. She had to cancel it. Because, instead, the 40-year-old Brit picked up a Best Actress award for her role in the film Steve Jobs – latest proof that while Hollywood has traditionally honoured youth, the tides are slowly turning towards experience.  “I have been doing this for 23 years now,” Winslet said backstage of her win – in a category that was dominated by old-time Hollywood actresses. “Cate Blanchett has been doing it for probably longer, actually – and look at Helen Mirren and Jane Fonda. These wonderful women that we are so fortunate to stand alongside and learn from still. It is incredibly exciting to have that array of skill for all of us to be inspired by and to be a part of that.” If Winslet was right to celebrate the fact, it seems there are finally a richness of roles available to older female actresses on screen, we should all celebrate the knock-on effect: a red carpet that’s all the more interesting thanks to women who are bringing the same sense of individuality they’ve brought to their careers, to their sense of style.  Carol co-stars Rooney Mara (30) and Cate Blanchett (46) are a case in point, both choosing blush pink gowns for Sunday’s ceremony. Mara, whose signature look is always ethereal and edgy, appeared in a ruffled bias-cut style from her go-to label Alexander McQueen. In a barely-there shade of nude, the beautiful, antique-looking gown was pared down almost to the point of invisibility.  By contrast, Blanchett wore an intricate pale rose creation from Givenchy Haute Couture – a 1920’s-inspired caped style with shimmering fringing alternating with semi-transparent panels. Exquisitely complex and esoteric, and a world away from the easy-to-read flesh-flashing gowns of younger starlets, the choice of dress tells us something about Blanchett herself. (Capes, the ultimate in scene-stealing fashion drama, were big with the 40+ set at this year’s Golden Globes.)  “Cate and her peers are proving that women in Hollywood today, in their forties, are smart, sexy, and principled – to be admired not only on a superficial level,” Morag Ross, Blanchett’s make-up artist, told The Telegraph. “The fact that Cate continues to look assuredly glamorous, elegant and stylish on the red carpet demonstrates that it is possible to have a full career, a family and carry on displaying both brains and beauty as a mature woman.” No one demonstrates this better than Dame Helen Mirren. The actress has stated in interviews recently that she doesn’t like the word “sexy”. But when the 70-year-old Brit appeared on the Golden Globes red carpet, it was a struggle to come up with another term. Wearing a figure-hugging mesh-panelled black dress with plunging sweetheart neckline by Badgley Mischka, which perfectly showcased her age-defying hourglass silhouette and impeccable sense of style, Mirren blew kisses to waiting fans as she walked the carpet. Accessorised with her platinum bob casually tucked behind one ear and a cool $1 million-worth of Harry Winston diamond jewellery, it showed that Mirren possessed perhaps the most important trait for any red carpet dress: confidence. Oh, and diamonds.  “People want to see a bit of glamour and excess [on the red carpet], and there’s no better way to express it than with fine jewellery,” Mirren’s stylist Rachel Faconi told us of the thought process behind her outfit. “It’s all ‘go big or go home’ for me.” Of course, the idea of going big or going home is easier when you’re a Hollywood actress who’s had time to develop a relationship with a fashion designer who knows how to make a woman of any age look red carpet-worthy. Witness Julianne Moore, who took the designer of her blue sequin gown, Tom Ford, as her date down the red carpet.  You can only “go big” when you’re not afraid to take a fashion risk. Jane Fonda, nominated in the Best Supporting Actress in a Motion Picture category for her role in Youth, wore a couture creation by white-hot label-of-the-moment Yves Saint Laurent. The dress, a chic, long-sleeved cream column, dominated by a waist-length capelet of gigantic ruffles, was soon hitting the “Worst Dressed” lists worldwide, and was even decried by Vanity Fair as “pastry-like”.  But her stylist Tanya Gill told The Telegraph that is not something that bothers her – or Fonda. “At the moment in Hollywood, significant roles are being given to older women; they are collecting accolades and gaining steam on screen as well as on the red carpet,” she said of dressing 78-year-old Fonda for the 73rd Golden Globes – a ceremony younger than the actress herself. “Designers around the world are very enthusiastic to dress and adorn these [older] women who define stardom,” insists Gill. “Age is never a consideration for me when dressing Jane Fonda, as she truly masters every look she wears. It’s about an attitude and having the confidence to wear whatever you want.” Of course, risk-taking is undoubtedly more appealing when you have already built up a back catalogue of award-ceremony looks. For the new starlet who possibly fears this may be her first and last appearance, a more timeless gown may, understandably, be the dress you want to be remembered by.  And this is not to say we should ignore the stylings of the newest generation of actresses. Jennifer Lawrence (25) in fire-engine red Dior couture, Brie Larson in gold-beaded Calvin Klein Collection, and Kate Hudson (36) in glittering pink-beaded Michael Kors Collection all brought the glamour in cutaway or cropped ab-flashing evening gowns; clearly, stomachs are the new sexy. Meanwhile, newcomers Lily James (26) and Saoirse Ronan (21) both wore quietly chic takes on the classic white Greek-goddess gown – by Marchesa and Saint Laurent respectively.  But for the older actress, age brings experience; as to what works on you, and on the red carpet. And confidence. Lots of confidence. Take Taraji P Henson, 45, accepting her first Golden Globe for best actress in a TV drama for her role as ball-busting Cookie Lyon in Empire, also wearing white – an ultra-tight Stella McCartney strapless gown with train. Henson looked fiercely modern (and sexy with it), but she also brought a sense of power and attitude with her to the podium.  Not only did Henson snarl a very Cookie-like “Get off my train” as her dress was stepped on for the second time at the podium (a gif went viral on Twitter within minutes), but she refused to rush her acceptance speech: “I’ve waited 20 years for this! You’re going to wait.” As Hollywood veteran Orson Welles once put it: “Style is knowing who you are, what you want to say, and not giving a damn.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Just as Barbara Casasola’s native Brazil is having a moment in the global spotlight as it hosts the Summer Olympics, so Barbara herself – who has been showing at London Fashion Week since 2013- has seen her own star rise considerably lately. In the past year, she’s found a firm fan in Alicia Vikander who has worn a series of Casasola looks out-and-about during her film promotion activities. And in July, the Duchess of Cambridge arrived at an awards ceremony at the Natural History Museum wearing a cream, off-shoulder dress designed by Casasola which was met with a rapturous reception, hailed as a prime example of the more daring approach to fashion which Kate has begun to embrace.  Barbara herself is impeccably chic in an unfussy, modern way which may be one of her label’s best advertisements. She can be spotted backstage at her shows- which are often held in pristine modern art galleries- dressed in sleek tailoring and cashmere in muted hues, always speaking softly of her ‘sensual’ vision. Casasola’s collections could be succinctly summed up as minimalist, but that would be to do a disservice to the careful detailing and design quirks which go into her work. Take that dress worn by the Duchess of Cambridge. Yes, it was subtly sexy and supremely summery but behind its initial impact is a deeper meaning. “I am interested in raising awareness about Brazilian aboriginal tribes in any way that I can” Casasola explains. “This piece was inspired by body painting designs of the Kayapo, a tribe in the Amazon basin. You can see an image of it that I posted on Instagram some time ago. It was developed and made in Italy with knitwear specialists. It took some time to get the right yarn mix and gauge to match the pattern and silhouette. In the end, we used a transparent yarn for the pinstripes in order to get the right result.” On the subject of the Duchess herself, Casasola is characteristically discreet, saying simply; “I am very honoured that the Duchess of Cambridge wore the dress.” Although Casasola grew up in Brazil, she has been living in Europe for many years. After a foundation course in Fashion Design at London’s Central Saint Martin’s and a degree at Milan’s Istituto Marangoni, she worked at Roberto Cavalli and consulted for labels such as Lanvin before beginning her own business. Despite her international outlook, Brazil remains a constant source of inspiration . “It’s difficult to unpick these things, but nature’s definitely a big part of growing up in Brazil” Casasola reflects, “you can’t really shut yourself away from it. Even if you live in a big city, it always has a strong presence. Nature’s also a great leveler. I see that reflected in Brazilian art and architecture, which has also influenced me. I’ve been increasingly drawn back to basics; toward simplicity, clean lines and craftsmanship.”  Say ‘Brazilian style’ and you might think miniscule bikinis, va-va voom dresses and carnival-esque colours but Casasola offers a more nuanced interpretation; “For me Brazilian style is less a sartorial statement and more about a certain attitude. It’s difficult for me to put words to it, but Brazilian music communicates it really well. It’s pared-back and thoughtful but also very much alive, confident and sensual.” Casasola has clocked up an impressively elegant roster of VIPs  wearing her designs, from Solange Knowles in a bronze pleated skirt to Gwyneth Paltrow in a refined black culotte jumpsuit. Alicia Vikander- whose stylist Victoria Sekrier has encouraged the actress to experiment with under-the-radar labels like Casasola’s as well as big designer names- has also become a fan.  Most recently she opted for a crisp white jumpsuit with black piping to appear on ‘Good Morning America’ but a magenta pink silk crop top with  matching wide cropped trousers and a maroon version of the dress worn by Kate have also made it into the Oscar-winning  actress's wardrobe. Casasola and Vikander  have bonded over the choosing looks. "Sometimes you meet people and get an immediate sense that they're special. Alicia's one of those people,” Casasola says, “she's very real, open and true to herself. I think that reflects in her style. It's a joy to dress her.” “I don’t want to sound like it’s not thought through, but I really just design from a gut feeling” Casasola says of the elegant approach  which has captivated so many of the world’s most discerningly stylish women. “On the surface, it’s difficult to box-in the women that get attracted to what I do because of their diversity in terms of age and background. But they do share a certain attitude about life and having meaningful experiences.” Pleated black dress, £979.14, Barbara Casasola    Grey blazer, £445, Barbara Casasola White pleated skirt, £595.47, Barbara Casasola © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Earlier this summer Malia Obama, the 18-year-old daughter of President Barack Obama, was seen smoking what some suspected was a cannabis joint at Lollapalooza music festival in Chicago. The First Family has remained silent about the images, until possibly now. Malia seems to have learnt a thing or two from celebrities who have handled media storms by wearing a wink-wink, nudge-nudge slogan tee in paparazzi pictures. Obama was at the Budweiser Made in America Festival this weekend where she wore denim cut-off shorts and a classic white and black ringer tee with 'Smoking Kills' written across the chest. Some have suspected that this reminder about the dangers of smoking was Malia's own penmanship, as it does have a do-it-yourself feel about it. It is certainly a loaded choice of t-shirt given that this is the first time she has attended a music festival since the smoking incident. In the pictures Obama is also wearing a Harvard University baseball cap, a nod to the fact that she is going to be joining the university in the autumn of 2017 after completing her gap year.  Wearing a slogan t-shirt during a crisis is the oldest trick in the celebrity handbook. It perhaps all started when Brad Pitt and Jennifer Aniston divorced in 2005 and the likes of Eva Longoria, Nicky Hilton and Paris Hilton wore 'Team Aniston,' 'Team Jolie' and 'Brad I'll have your baby' t-shirts. There are endless examples of celebrities from Britney Spears to Kim Murray dressing in not-so subliminal messages to give a personal response to a scandal they're involved in. The award for 'the most press coverage from one slogan tee' this year has to go to Tom Hiddleston in his 'I heart T.S.' vest top that he wore beach with Taylor Swift. Malia Obama might have worn a baseball cap and ripped denim like your average teen at a festival, but she also was spotted spending time with Beyoncé who was celebrating her birthday at Made in America. Michelle Obama spoke movingly at this year's Democratic National Convention about how she attempts to give Malia and Sasha Obama a normal life, despite living in the White House.  "[It was a] journey that started soon after we arrived in Washington when they set off for their first day at their new school," Michelle said. "I will never forget that winter morning as I watched our girls, just seven and 10 years old, pile into those black SUV's with all those big men with guns. And I saw their little faces pressed up against the window, and the only thing I could think was, ‘What have we done?’" "At that moment I realised that our time in the White House would form the foundation for who they would become, and how well we manage this experience could truly make or break them," she continued. "That is what Barack and I think about every day as we try to guide and protect our girls through the challenges of this unusual life in the spotlight." And judging by her ironic choice of t-shirt, it looks like Malia Obama is intent on handling all of the challenges that come with being in the spotlight in the savviest and coolest of ways.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Fashion muse Giovanna Battaglia Engelbert is a shop assistant’s dream. “I watched the Burberry show on Instagram, and the next day I arrived in London and thought I’d check it out in the store. That day, I ended up buying two skirts and a coat from the new collection - I thought, I need this skirt right now. The shop assistant was like, 'oh, shall I wrap this for you?' And I said, ‘you don’t understand, I’m walking out of the store with this skirt .” A fashion editor for titles including Japanese Vogue and W Magazine, Battaglia Engelbert got her start in the industry as a model for Dolce & Gabbana at 17, but turned her back on it because she wanted more control over styling and make-up. An early adopter of Instagram, she built her profile quickly by using it to network and establish herself as a fashion authority beyond the pages of magazines; so when she attends the bi-annual fashion shows, today she attends not just as an editor, but as one of the ‘peacocks’, changing outfits multiple times a day - one moment feathers, the next, sequins, and all designer- all with the aim of being photographed by the waiting paparazzi. They’re a breed often scorned by the ‘working’ showgoers filing copy to deadline, though with brand partnerships worth a lot of money, this work to many of this new cohort. With very long legs and the deep pockets to match, 38 year old Battaglia Engelbert could be an easy figure to dislike, especially for the majority of us for whom clothes shopping entails hunting down for things that fit our bodies and our budget. However, Battaglia has a trump card that so many in fashion lack - a sense of humour. That sense of humour, along with an ability (and the nerve) to wear anything, is the basis of her book, Gio_graphy: Fun in The Wild World of Fashion (Rizzoli, £29.95), out this week. It’s a style manual - at least, of sorts. “It’s more about mistakes, this book, than a how-to guide,” she laughs, ‘like when you have to go from work to cocktails super quickly, you’re going to end up brushing your teeth with mascara.” It spans from everyday - how to wear red, how to style out a broken zip - to the extreme, like how to go to the loo in a ball gown. Both ends of the spectrum are illustrated with pictures of Battaglia Engelbert leading by example - which in this instance, means a photo of her on said loo in said ball gown. It’s the fantasy fashion life though which is the real appeal of the book. It’s Battaglia Engelbert’s spirit that we could all use a little of, her willingness to try, her ability not to take herself too seriously. To have fun. “Why not? I’m just saying that in my world, I think that being cool is a bore and being fun is more glamorous! At the end of the day, fashion is us changing costumes, it’s the things we put on our bodies to have a good time. I think the worst is to be victimised by the clothes you wear. To watch a girl who cannot walk in high heels, and see her suffering. It’s meant to be fun. Being fun is not necessarily me being a clown all the time, but I can’t be the one who takes myself super seriously, and says, ‘today I’m going to wear this minimal look because I want to look intellectual’. No.” Being brought up in Milan by parents who were both artists could explain how both Battaglia Engelbert and her sister Sara, a handbag designer, ended up as such creative freedom fighters. Now, she divides her time between New York, Stockholm, and, just lately, the English countryside with her husband, Swedish real-estate mogul Oscar Engelbert. The pair married last year in a ceremony that spanned days, countries, and multiple dress changes. First a Valentino gown for a small ceremony in Sweden, then Alaia to welcome guests to Capri the night before the wedding. “On the day of the ceremony, I had three because I couldn’t… I think each one of them was built for that purpose. I love fashion so much, it was a natural decision to have many changes. If I could have kept the big McQueen dress through the dinner, I probably would have done it. It’s just that I would have had to have had 50 less guests to make room for the dress, so I went for the guests instead.” The bride changed into a Giambattista Valli gown for dancing; metallic Prada was custom made for a party the following day. “I’ve been like this since I was eight years old. I think my style will evolve as I evolve. My mother was a good example of elegance, but then I went crazy bananas like any teenager. And I don’t have kids now, so I don’t know what I’m going to do after, when I have kids. That’s another chapter. I look at my girlfriends who have kids, and they have comfortable moments, and when they’re back in shape or whatever, they go beyond fashion, even more than before.” Women around the world look to her for style inspiration- intentionally or not, she can set even the unlikeliest of trends. Is there anything she’d never wear, I ask her. “Never say never.” Except... she hesitates. “I have to say, I would never wear crocs. Never, even if Christopher Kane made them. That’s where I draw the line.” For the rest of us, that’s probably a good thing. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Natalie Massenet MBE, founder of luxury online shopping website Net-a-Porter, is to be made a Dame for her services to the fashion and retail industries. The 50-year-old’s damehood was revealed in the Queen’s New Year’s honours list, along with veteran actress Barbara Windsor.    "I am thrilled and completely overwhelmed to be awarded this honour," Massenet told us in response to the news. "I also feel humbled by it because during my career I have been privileged to have worked with so many brilliant and inspiring people, all of whom have contributed to the success of our fashion industry."  Despite being born in Los Angeles, Massenet has dual American-British nationality thanks to her British mother, meaning she can take the title of Dame - unlike American actress Angelina Jolie, who was made honorary dame by the Queen in 2014. The title tops off a climatic year for Massenet. In September she resigned from Net-a-Porter, 15 years after founding the phenomenally successful e-commerce platform from her Chelsea flat. Her departure was abrupt but not unexpected; Net-a-Porter.com was due to merge with Italian online discounter Yoox.com and although she intended to stay on as executive chairman, it was not clear how that role would impact her day-to-day responsibilities over the business.   Massenet changed the face of luxury fashion retailing, and paved the way for many competitors to gain a slice of the action. In her parting memo she stated how now was “the right time for me to move on to explore new ideas and opportunities.”   One role that Massenet has kept on is that of chairwoman of the British Fashion Council. Since her appointment in 2013, she has helped elevate the profile of London Fashion Week and menswear showcase, London Collections: Men, and made the annual British Fashion Awards a glamorous, global showcase to celebrate the best in British fashion.   Massenet hinted that another venture could be on the cards when her parting email to staff at Net-a-Porter was made public. “As for my own future, my entrepreneurial drive is as strong today as it always has been, and my passion for innovation will continue to be my greatest guide in business,” she wrote. And so, in November, she registered a company called Imaginary Ventures Ltd. No one knows what direction the company will take yet but given that Massenet is subject to a 12-month non-compete agreement with Net-a-Porter, it won't be clear until late 2016. In 2009 the mother-of-two enjoyed a trip to Buckingham Palace when she was awarded an MBE. As you might expect from one of the most powerful women in fashion, her outfit choice was impeccable: she wore a dress by Roland Mouret and a headpiece by Philip Treacy. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
