 The tale of Hollywood actress Grace Kelly marrying a real-life Prince Charming, Prince Rainier of Monaco, is the ultimate modern day fairytale. Six decades later, the Palace have released never-seen-before photographs from their wedding day, proving that it is still the most dreamily stylish wedding on record. "It was such an incredible affair, and it's left such a mark on people," their son Prince Albert, reveals in an interview with People. "What it has meant for people has been incredible. For us, it was – and you'll have to ask my sisters [Princess Caroline and Princess Stephanie] – for us it was our parents getting married. But what it's meant for Monaco, for people around the world, and, how their story continues to fascinate people, that's something unimaginable."  "There were always pictures around the palace and other properties to remind us of the day," Prince Albert continues. "I got different accounts of the wedding, mostly from Mom. Then from others: from my aunts from Philadelphia who came over for it, from cousins. Those who attended who are still with us still talk about it."  But the one thing that stands out in all of the photographs is Grace Kelly's wedding gown, which still looks just as magnificent today as it did 60 years ago. Grace Kelly had two wedding outfits for  her civil and religious ceremonies, which were both gifts from her film studios MGM and were created by the head costume designer, Helen Rose, in the studio's atelier. Rose had created Kelly's costumes for a number of her most-loved films, including High Society and The Swan.  The gown she wore to the religious ceremony took 30 seamstresses at the studio six weeks to make and had a high collar, elegant lace sleeves and a full skirt. The dress was made of delicate rose point  Brussels lace, which was 125 years old, and a silk faille skirt with three petticoats;  a smoothing petticoat, ruffled petticoat, and foundation petticoat. Instead of a tiara, she wore a beaded floral Juliet cap with a 90-yard veil and carried a pearl-encrusted prayer book and a delicate bouquet of Lilies of the Valley. Kelly's shoe designer David Evins hid a copper penny inside her right shoe for good luck. For the private civil ceremony, Kelly wore a pink embroidered skirt suit by Helen Rose with another delicate Juliet cap. The wedding gown is one of the most influential gowns in bridal history, and has been referenced in many designs since including the Alexander McQueen dress which Sarah Burton designed for Kate Middleton when she married Prince William. Oscar de la Renta said of its significance:  "On her wedding day, Grace Kelly gave new meaning to the word icon. Her whole look, from the regal veil to the feminine lace details and the conservative gown, made her an ageless bride."  Prince Albert reveals to People that ahead of the wedding on the 19th April 1956, Kelly sailed from New York to Monaco on the S.S. Constitution, travelling for eight days with 50 family members, her six bridesmaids and 80 suitcases. In Monaco she was welcomed by her Prince and a crowd of over 20,000 people. "The whole Constitution trip was something Mom referred to at times," says Albert. "She'd say it was fun for the wedding party. It really bonded the whole Philadelphia side, her family and friends who came over together on the crossing.  "And she would talk about her dog, Oliver, being onboard with her."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.   Helen Ruth Elam Van Winkle, a.k.a. Baddie Winkle, is confounding every preconception which you might have about a. an Instagram star or b. an 89 year-old great-grandmother. Four years ago, with a little help from her great-granddaughter Kennedy, Winkle became an Internet hit thanks to her ultra bold, fearless and eccentric personal style. There are few fashion frontiers Winkle will not cross- mini skirts? No problem. Leopard print? Bring it on. Dungarees? They’re one of Winkle’s favourite items. It’s an attitude which is not only age-defying but also determinedly unswayed by any of the usual dos and don’ts. On the day that we meet, for example, Winkle is wearing head-to-toe blue camouflage print with a crystal choker and perspex flower earrings. With over 3 million followers on Instagram, there’s no doubt that Winkle is living out her Eighties to the full- and seemingly enjoying every minute of it- but her message goes beyond the artifice. Having lost both her husband and her son, Winkle says that clothes have helped her to gain confidence and happiness in the face of her losses. And while not all of us would be brave enough to adopt Winkle’s unique approach, she does have some advice to impart... Winkle is all about wearing jewellery around her face (better for selfies, she declares) but there’s one item in particular which she counts as a secret weapon. “I love a choker because it covers up the neck wrinkles, I have so many of them. Now I’ve got all my friends involved, so I’ve started a trend- I have plain ones, leather ones, jewelled ones.” “I’ve always loved to shop, it’s one of my favourite things to do.” It might be an obvious statement considering her new career but Winkle likes to mix up the places she frequents with everywhere from online shops to her local mall and L.A vintage stores being top of her list. Last year, she even appeared in a campaign for Missguided, whose usual customers are girls in their 20s. “I never wanted to wear ‘old people’ clothes so I’ve always dressed young,” she says. “I haven’t had anything done to me!” Winkle protests when the subject of plastic surgery arises. “I think I look old and I don’t really like that.” Old, maybe, but for a nearly-nonagenarian, Winkle looks remarkable. She puts this down to the good old-fashioned advice of using moisturiser and staying out of the sun, although she only officially stopped sunbathing two years ago- “I’d come in and look in the mirror and think ‘oh my gosh!’ Now if I want a tan I get a spray tan.” She’s also adopted some millennial favourite make-up tips courtesy of Kennedy, with contouring and highlighting now part of her beauty routine.   When we meet, Winkle is on a ‘bucket list’ world tour courtesy of Hotels.com which has involved stops in Paris, Brazil and at Niagara Falls. So, how did she tackle packing for such an adventure? “It was very hard. I packed comfortable clothes mostly because I was going to be on the go but I didn’t pack a lot of the fancy clothes I usually wear. I bring a lot of accessories instead.” She has also been shopping as she goes, with a purple beret and a crochet jumper among her haul from Dublin's vintage shops.  So packing light is not a priority, and Winkle says there’s no point worrying about it: “you always have, you always will,” she shrugs. Whether Kennedy, who has been accompanying her great-grandmother and her three suitcases feels the same, is another matter. “I’ve been though a lot of tragedy in my life,” says Winkle, “but that’s helped me to be outgoing I always knew what I wanted to wear, whether anyone liked it or not. Now I do some wild things. Clothes give you confidence, if you look good in them then you want to wear them.” “The more confidence you have, the better off you are and my clothes give me that. I know it’s hard for some people but being on social media has helped me a lot. I always thought I was shy but I don’t think I really was. My family and friends think I am fabulous.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  ‘After examining myself, I felt like looking at you and the different decades of your life in fashion and what it [sic] means to me’ read the notes that accompanied the Andreas Kronthaler for Vivienne Westwood AW18 show at Paris Fashion Week yesterday. If the brand name is rather a mouthful, it’s because it reflects an equally complex setup behind-the-scenes. Kronthaler is the creative director of Westwood’s brand, but while most designers working under a known name seek to make it their own, Andreas, as Vivienne’s husband, is keen to continue her work, rather than subvert it. In Westwood’s world, that means fashion as political and social statement - mixed with an element of performance art. Young men dressed in platform boots, tights, hairpieces and deconstructed tops, faces painted with pink circles and black lines, danced freely and expressively on raised platforms as male and female models - some professional, others friends of the brand like young Brit designer Matty Bovan - walked between them. The clothes spanned decades of Westwood designs, everything from 1950s wallpaper from her King’s Road shop to 1970s teddy boy tailoring to 1980s mini-crinoline skirts. Thanks to full-throttle club-kid styling (see the dress belted with a phallous on a chain), the overall effect was greater than the sum of its parts. Strip that away, and there were wearable pieces here: asymmetric dresses, full skirts, a floral cape. There were two brides, one veiled and one trailing fairy lights, and even a bouquet-carrying bridesmaid in flower-pailette sequins and silver hotpants. Not the normal strapless gown, but then for many fashion-forward brides, Westwood’s subversive - but crucially beautiful and form flattering - draped gowns would appeal. Lest we forget, Sex and the City’s Carrie Bradshaw was jilted in just such a Westwood gown. ‘God, how long we have known each other,’ wrote Kronthaler to Westwood, “how wonderful. I want to pay homage to you as my collaborator, my friend and partner, my teacher and of course as my muse.” The words were scanned from the handwritten original, spelling mistakes et al, on a piece of Eurostar-issue blue paper (Standard premier class, since you ask). “I still think today that you are the best dressed woman in any room.” Many couples claim that, after a few decades together, they are able to (almost) read each other's thoughts, and certainly finish each other's sentences. That level of understanding seems to be true here, with a symbiosis of passion and design. The designer’s bow was taken as a pair, hand in hand - Kronthaler taking the lead as cheers rang out, before quietly stooping to rescue a yellow tulip from his congratulatory bouquet when it fell into Westwood’s path. When she handed over the reins to her eponymous brand, Dame Vivienne Westwood left the sentence unfinished - but Kronthaler seems to know exactly what she was going to say. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  No one would have predicted seven years ago that around 13 million people would stay in on a Wednesday evening to watch a TV show about baking biscuits, but the Great British Bake Off has been filled with a number of surprising turns. Not least of which is that over the past seven seasons 81-year-old Mary Berry has become a style icon for viewers of all ages, capable of causing Duchess of Cambridge-style shockwaves on the high street.  The tipping point came when Berry wore a colourful floral printed silk £29.99 bomber jacket from Zara in 2012 - arguably still the most memorable moment from the past seven years in the tent. It sold out almost immediately, and versions were going for up to £200 on eBay not long afterwards.  The Zara jacket worked so brilliantly because it's bold print jarred with the typical twee styling associated with Bake Off's Cath Kidston-esque gingham tablecloths and the white picket fences. It's no surprise then that jazzy jackets quickly became Berry's Wednesday night uniform.  Almost every week since Berry has worn an unexpected statement jacket with her jeans, paired with little more than her cheery pink lipstick and non-moving hair. Mary Berry's floral bombers, bikers and blazers have now become their own personality on the show, causing just as much hype on Twitter as the final showstoppers. My kingdom for Mary Berry's sold-out Marks & Spencer stork-print bomber jacket pic.twitter.com/5o2eQIn9RG Mary Berry, can I just jusy that your jacket is simply divine! I want me one! I believe its from Zara. #TrendyMary pic.twitter.com/UMSugK4a Even professional style icon Alexa Chung was impressed with Berry's fashion nous. She recently told The Telegraph that Berry is a canny fashionista and asked if her boots were by Penelope Chilvers.  But whilst Berry is partial to a designer item every so often - her Hermes vintage logo belt, is a good example - part of the fashion genius she brings to Bake Off is that she always opts for affordable pieces which make her look stylish but still approachable to the wide BBC audience. This series her jackets have fallen mostly under the £200 price point, with designer only ever meaning 'Designer at Debenhams'. Highlights have included a cream £69 Marks and Spencer's zip-up jacket, a £142 white French Connection biker jacket with fresh yellow and green poppies (which swiftly sold out) and a £99 pink blazer by Joules. She also received praise for a H! by Henry Holland red, pink and cream Aztek printed jacket which retails for £45.50 at Debenhams.  So what does Berry make of her new role as a style icon? "I think it’s very funny that people are nice about the things I wear," she told Healthy Magazine recently. "I’d never have thought of myself as a fashion icon before everybody started telling me I was one!" She adds: "People should just wear what they want to, as long as it suits them and doesn’t look too young. I only wear things that I think suit my shape and age. I wouldn’t wear anything too short or low-cut."  The singer Céline Dion is launching a fashion brand this autumn. She couldn’t call it Céline, alas, as that one’s already taken, but Dion is planning to make her first mark on the industry with handbags, which will launch with American retailer Nordstrom in August. The Céline Dion Collection’s first drop is said to be comprised of 50 affordable styles, covering handbags, luggage and other small accessories, with prices varying between $58 and $298. A single image has been released offering a preview of one design - a black, top-handle bag with contrasting top-stitching, and a sculpted gold lock. The move comes at the end of the year that Dion found her fashion footing, hiring a new stylist, Law Roach, who she says helped her enjoy a new sense of personal style. Last January her husband of 22 years, René Angélil, passed away after suffering from cancer and, just two days later she lost her brother to the same disease. In June, Dion began to enjoy experimenting with new designers and established names and, when Roach took her to Paris Couture Week in July for the first time, the pop icon was seen cheering on the front row at the Giambattista Valli show. “I’m a firm believer that things happen when they are supposed to and I think that us partnering up when we did and having that amazing time was meant to be,” Roach told The Telegraph. “She was dealing with, and I’m sure she is still dealing with, the death of her husband and her brother. She was going through a lot of tragedy and, these are her words, the dresses and the bags and these lighter moments have helped her with her recovery.” Of Dion’s taste and aesthetic, Roach says that she’s open to trying on anything to see what suits her. “I can literally bring Céline any silhouette, any colour and she will want to see it on,” he says. “Some things just don’t work, that’s the nature of fashion, but she’s never afraid to find out.” Having sold over 240 million records in a career spanning more than 30 years, Dion’s change of tac in fashion will leave critics keen to dismiss this as ‘just another celebrity clothing line’. But Roach has insisted that Dion’s interest in fashion is not a new-found one - she’s only just discovering how best to showcase it. “She’s always been this girl though, the world just hadn’t noticed yet,” Roach told us. “People knew her as the voice and this legendary pop icon, but she’s letting you see another side to her now.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  With Mick Jagger and Jerry Hall as parents, it's not surprising that model Georgia May Jagger has one of the coolest, rock n' roll wardrobes around, overflowing with Studio 54-ready platforms, velvet and leopard print. This week we talked all things style with the British model and face of Thomas Sabo live on our Facebook account, where she revealed the story behind her recent bridesmaid look and explained the "funny things" she has taken from her mother Jerry Hall's 80s wardrobe.  If you missed the action on Facebook, see below for the highlights from the livestream... Georgia May Jagger has been a bridesmaid twice this year, firstly wearing a powder blue Vivienne Westwood dress with silver flats to her mother Jerry Hall's wedding to Rupert Murdoch in March of this year. Then in April she wore a striking red suit with chunky red platforms to the wedding of her brother James and Anoushka Sharma. So what are Jagger's tips for dressing for a summer of weddings? "I try to be comfortable because you are going to be there all day and I always see women with a bag with their high heels in it and I always try and wear shoes that I don't need to bring another pair or do something like that. It's hard though, because I've been going to more and more, it's hard to find outfits the whole time."  When it comes to bridesmaids dresses she is an advocate for picking your own look. "I wore a red suit for my brother's," she explains. "We just went with a colour, red, and then everyone just wore different things in red, so it's nice sometimes to have your own style. If you pick one dress for bridesmaids then it doesn't really suit everyone, so I liked being able to pick it." Jagger has been modelling since 2009, but before that she used to go backstage at London Fashion Week with her sister, Lizzie. "I used to go on half term to fashion week to keep my sister company when I was like 12 and it was really funny," Jagger says. "I got a bit of experience then - I thought it was really weird. People would often ask if I was waiting for the fitting and I'm like 'No! I'm 12!' I remember Lily Cole studying backstage for her exams - for a while I was going to New York at weekends and stuff and doing my homework on the plane when I was finishing off my A Levels." Starting out as a model must be incredibly daunting, but luckily for Georgia May Jagger she could turn to her supermodel mother, Jerry Hall, for advice on how to get ahead in the industry. "She always says always be on time and be nice to everybody," Jagger explains. "Because people might not remember the jobs, but they will always remember how you were with them. On the way up it's easy to ignore people or whatever, but on the way down that's when you need them." Jerry Hall was a supermodel of Studio 54 era, known for her love of leopard print, glitter and stacked gold jewellery. "My sister has all my mum's stuff because she is seven years older than me, so I have to borrow them off her, it goes through her," Jagger says of raiding her wardrobe. "I've got some of my mum's stuff - some really funny 80s dresses that are easy for her to pull off, but not so much me! She does go on about how she doesn't have any good things any more because we took them all, but I think she's fine!" Given Georgia May Jagger is the face of Thomas Sabo, we had to ask her what her approach is to jewellery. "More is more but I like lots of small things," she explains. "So I'm really into the Thomas Sabo Love Bridge bracelets because they have lots of engravings and you can get them right here in the shop.  While Donald Trump's third wife Melania prepares to become America's first foreign born First Lady since 1825, the President-elect's first wife Ivana - who was once described as “the ultimate symbol of strength, glamour and worldliness” - has now spoken out about her own political ambitions. "I will suggest that I be Ambassador for the Czech Republic," she told the New York Post this weekend. "That is where I'm from, and my language, and everybody knows me." Whether Trump grants her suggestion or not, it’s not just in political spheres that Ivana (who was rumoured to have advised her ex during his campaign) has been wielding influence of late. At a presentation about Net-a-Porter's focuses for the autumn/winter fashion season, Vice President of Global Buying, Sarah Rutson, cited the first Mrs Trump as a key fashion inspiration for the coming months. Singling out Hedi Slimane’s farewell Saint Laurent show, Rutson pointed to Trump in her 80s excess heyday as the template for a new uber-glamorous mood in fashion. From Slimane’s super-short cocktail dresses with elaborate bows to Isabel Marant's one-shouldered ruched tops and fishnet tights and Balmain’s hard-edged, power shoulder jackets, the va-va-voom which Ivana - who told a New York Times journalist "You don't have to put down the second name…Ivana is what the people call me" - once brought to the upper echelons of American society is back on the radar. After meeting when one-time champion skier Ivana was working as a model - what else? - in New York, Donald and his Czechoslovakia-born first bride were married in 1977. A mutual quest for world-domination ensued and the couple became the poster man and woman for the boom-fueled opulence of the 1980s. With her bouffant of blonde hair, Ivana probably consumed 99% of the world’s supply of Elnett hair spray- a feat she continues to achieve to this day. The beehive sported by Joanna Lumley's Patsy character in Absolutely Fabulous is said to have been inspired by her. Her wardrobe, meanwhile, made Dynasty’s Alexis Carrington look like a nun. Think elaborate taffeta creations with the look of a life-sized Quality Street wrapper, unashamedly oversized fur coats and the most bling-tastic cocktail dresses imaginable. And her tastes don't seem to have adjusted since then, with all her most recent public appearences still chiming with the 80s look she made her own.  “When she had first come to New York, she wore elaborate helmet hairdos and bouffant satin dresses, very Hollywood; her image of rich American women probably came from the movies she had seen as a child," was how Vanity Fair described Ivana's style in an analysis of the Trumps' eventual divorce in 1990. "Ivana had now spent years passing through the fine rooms of New York, but she had never seemed to learn the real way of the truly rich, the art of understatement.” But it is this very failure to achieve a minimalist, whisperingly-rather than screamingly- expensive style which may have made Ivana a new fashion muse. After years of desiring only Celine cream tunics, The Row's perfect black trousers and anonymous crisp mannish shirts, the fashion world has been crying out for Drama! Excess! Fun! Ivana, if you'll pardon the pun, comes up trumps. "It may not be the decade we remember with the utmost fondness, but the hard edged glamour of the eighties certainly made an impact this season" confirms Lisa Aiken, Net-a-Porter's  retail fashion director. Luckily she has advice for how to wear it now. "To keep the look modern, be selective and don’t try to replicate the era top to toe. At Net-a-Porter, we’ve bought into wide belts to bring that 80s cinched-waist silhouette to mini dresses and blazers. Balmain, Maison Margiela and of course Saint Laurent showed strong ones for AW16. In terms of accessories look for sharp stilettos, oversized statement earrings and chain handle bags, but wear them one at a time." Since the divorce from Trump (in which she managed to receive a $20 million settlement despite his impending bankruptcy), Ivana has married twice again. Both were short-lived marriages. So renowned had she become for encapsulating 80s glamour, that she spent most of the 90s capitalizing on it with her own fashion line- Ivana Haute Couture- which offered copies of her own designer wardrobe and jewellery. It seems she had even come around to her ex-husband’s thrifty ways, declaring: "For me, the real jewels are not that important now. I wear my costume jewels from my collection." Ivana also famously made a cameo appearance in the 1996 film The First Wives Club in which she advised: “Don’t get mad, get everything”. It’s a phrase which could take on new meaning as Donald Trump begins his presidency and she vies for a role in his entourage.  Rumours swirled about the power struggles in the Trump marriage and Ivana has made allegations about her ex-husband's violence towards her. So perhaps all the gilted jewellery, piles of brassy blonde hair and opulent wardrobe weren’t just an expression of an 80s anything-goes culture, but the sartorial solution to dealing with “the Donald.” So pile on the tackiest, sorry, blingiest costume jewellery you can find, pull on a sequinned cocktail dress with sleeves the size of Donald's ego and face the Trump presidency in defiant Ivana-style.  There’s normcore – and there’s Italian normcore. For evidence of the latter, I direct you to Virginia Raggi, Rome’s new (and first female) mayor. Raggi has deftly navigated the twin currents of political culture in Italy – the desire for its female MPs to drip gravitas and the deeply engrained reflex to vote for someone who looks like la Cicciolina.  “Raggi has been really smart,” says Persivale, “She can well afford designer clothes and bags - she’s a lawyer at a good firm in Rome - but she can’t afford them politically.  In September 2014 niche title Paper Magazine created one of the biggest cultural events of the year, and perhaps the decade, when they set out to 'Break The Internet' with the help of a naked Kim Kardashian. The image of Kim Kardashian balancing a champagne glass on her perfectly-sculpted derriere alongside the hashtag #BreakTheInternet sent a sharing shockwave through the web. The site received over 50 million hits in one day, equating to 1 per cent of all internet traffic that day in the US. Drew Elliott, Chief Creative Officer at Paper Magazine, explained to The Telegraph ahead of his talk at the FashTech Summit the method behind the social media madness: "We basically came up with this idea that if Jean Paul Goude shot Kim Kardashian it would break the internet, because it's great art mixed with the most famous woman in the world, so those two things paired together create that excitement."  'We started thinking like an entertainment company, as opposed to driving impressions' "The hashtag #BreakTheInternet is a way to create fiction and tension inside of social," he continues. "Did she break the internet? Did she not break the internet? Obviously she didn't, because the internet is unable to be broken, but it's a fun play on a notion of what is virality." But what this cover line did do is establish a new bench mark for viral success; "It puts it into the lexicon of pop culture and makes it a bar for if something creates a thunderclap of excitement." The key to making content go viral, Elliot argues, is to focus completely on the concept, rather than the distribution strategy. "We started thinking like an entertainment company, as opposed to driving impressions and all that kind of stuff. Of course we want to hit traffic, but at the end of the day when we can unearth something that people are excited about, then we win." He continues: "It's magic plus math, that's what you have to conquer. So many people have the focus on the math side of the equation, but if you don't have the magic you have nothing to count. Our focus is on the art and then when we get that right, that will drive the numbers. Everything we do is designed not to be viral, but to be important and to have a weight to it that lends itself to being culturally important." But when it came to distributing the images, Kim Kardashian certainly played her part in making it go viral. "She was a participant in it and emailed us and was like 'wow we're really doing it - we're breaking the internet,' Elliott explains. But it's worth noting that the Kim Kardashian issue also profiled numerous powerful influencers on social media, who had a combined following of over 127 million (that's almost half the population of America.) This month the youngest member of the Kardashian dynasty, Kylie Jenner, is on the cover of Paper's Instagram-themed issue wearing a bubblegum pink wig in a highly saturated, heavily-filtered image. Love them or loathe them, the Kardashians are an unstoppable force, monopolizing every corner of the internet. Elliot believes that their enduring power lies in their approach to content which in many ways is in line with Paper's own growth strategy. "They know their audience and know they have the platform to ignite things," he explains. "They too are their own publishers, with apps and websites, and just as we do as publishers, they keep reinventing what that is and what's interesting. It has longevity in that they continue to keep creating product and content that is still interesting. You still want to go to each of them for those milestones in their lives that are so personal to them and we can all share it. As micro publishers, they are doing things like we are, they are creating concepts, just with themselves as the icon." Just one example of this power and mass appeal came when Kim launched her Kimoji app last year; it averaged 9000 downloads per millisecond and prompted the Apple store to crash.  'She said to me a few months after the shoot had come out, 'I made Paper relevant and you made me cool.' Elliot argues that magazines are, despite the hysteria over plummeting circulation figures, still a powerful player in popular culture. "I was recently watching Entertainment Tonight and it was so interesting, ten of the segments in that one short show were all about magazines, when people are hell bent on that 'magazines are going to die'. Magazines are actually the brands that are creating content with celebrities and talent that is fresh and new and that's not performative. We're discovering a new side of an artist. I don't see magazines dying, what I do see is that digital is the ultimate revenge of the publisher because it breaks down that one piece that is really hard for us; that distribution is really expensive. That said, we can put something on digital for free. Our content can be as popular as a huge publisher, and for us it's brand-building, whereas for others it's brand-diminishing." The key to Paper's viral thinking, is to not to prioritise one platform over another. "The magazine is there to create almost like an event inside of digital, so it has a release date. It's like television, whether it's an awards show or whatever, you want to watch it and participate in that conversation and it's the same with magazines at this moment. If people see it on Instagram, I'm happy with that. If they see it on our website - great. If they see it in our magazine - awesome." As for creating its magic content, they work with, rather than against, celebrities. "We are not interested in covering things, we are interesting in collaborating," Elliott explains. "If you say 'We are going to send a writer to write about you,' immediately they are guarded. With us, they are involved. Lena Dunham told us it was her dream to be a Hollywood star and a director and that's what we did. It's not 'this is what we think of you' it's what they want, so they want to participate.' Kim Kardashian's cover is the perfect example of this collaborative attitude, as Elliott explained in his presentation at the FashTech Summit: "She said to me a few months after the shoot had come out, 'I made Paper relevant and you made me cool."  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  So the long-running rumours are true: Christopher Bailey is leaving Burberry after 16 years. “I am excited to pursue new creative projects,” Bailey commented this morning, “but remain fully committed to the future success of this magnificent brand and to ensuring a smooth transition." Burberry now and Burberry then are two very different things.  Once upon a time in the 90s, Burberry was still grasping onto a sepia-tinged nostalgia for the trench coat and trading on discounted takes on its famous check. Now, it is arguably the jewel in Britain’s fashion crown and a world famous barometer of Brit cool. The transformation has been credited to Bailey’s visionary influence, aided along the way by Rose Marie Bravo, the American CEO who first hired him, and Angela Ahrendts, who was at the company from 2006 to 2014. With new CEO Marco Gobbetti now in place- after Bailey himself took up that mantle alongside his creative responsibilities for a few years- the next phase in Burberry’s evolution will see it pitted against an ever sharper set of competitors in the luxury market; the rise and resurrection of labels from Gucci to Saint Laurent and Vetements in recent times will undoubtedly have fuelled a desire for radical change. "We have a clear vision for the next chapter to accelerate the growth and success of the Burberry brand,” said Gobetti, who oversaw the overhaul at Celine where creative director Phoebe Philo is rumoured to be on her way out, perhaps to Burberry? “Under Christopher Bailey the idea of Burberry became alluring, it’s developed such a strong personality,” says Lisa Armstrong, The Telegraph’s fashion director. “Everyone said that you could never create a big brand from nothing, but he proved it could be done. Anything he’s ever been told he couldn’t do, he’s done.” As fashion’s musical chairs game kicks into action again, here’s how Christopher Bailey transformed Burberry… ‘Digital innovation’ has been a buzz phrase for years but Burberry were all over the advent of digital and social media, being amongst the first to get serious about live streaming its shows which were always precision timed to happen at lunchtime GMT to catch as many people as possible around the world. There were raised eyebrows too when Burberry began to reveal its catwalk looks on Twitter before they were seen on the catwalk. “I’m not sure how much digital did for the bottom line,” says Armstrong, “but it showed that Burberry was a very modern industry leader, it was a great PR exercise.” The fashion schedule has become lately dumbfoundingly confusing as some brands have switched to a See Now, Buy Now model whereby customers can immediately buy what they’ve just seen pop up on their phone screens from the catwalk. Ralph Lauren, Tommy Hilfiger and Burberry are three of the major names to adopt the strategy but whether it’s actually working is yet to be seen. Do enough people have an impulse to click buy the moment they see something on the catwalk? Nevertheless, it was Bailey who led Burberry to take on this bold experiment. Cara Delevingne, Emma Watson, James Bay, Jenna Coleman, Eddie Redmayne, Tom Odell, Edie Campbell… these are just a handful of the once up-and-coming young Brits who Bailey helped to propel to global stardom by casting them in glossy Mario Testino shoots and high octane fashion shows. Of course, in return Burberry earned a mega dollop of cool factor thanks to its associations with the new bright young things. “Rose Marie Bravo took Burberry out of the coffin and blew the dust off, but Bailey has always really understood the romance,” adds Armstrong. London fashion week was on the up long before Bailey came along but Burberry’s lunchtime slot on Mondays (until two seasons ago) offered a Wow moment with the great and the good congregating in a magnificent tent in Kensington Gardens. Then they moved to the evening with their See Now, Buy Now strategy and high culture art exhibitions. Just like that, it became the dress-up party moment of the week. Bailey’s latest masterstroke came when he finally took on the heritage Burberry check in this September’s collection. After years of sweeping its signature print under the carpet (in a bid to shake off  the Daniella Westbrook et al associations of the early 90s) there were checks loud and proud on the catwalk- think Cara Taylor in a cap and raincoat emblazoned in them, Grace Bol in a checked anorak over a baby pink dress and Laura Toth carry a check tote. Rihanna has already worn the look head-to-toe too. “It was such a brilliant collection,” says Armstrong, “it really put Burberry on a new track.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Meryl Streep appeared at the podium at the Democratic convention in Philadelphia yesterday in support of Hillary Clinton, she did so in the most patriotic dress she could find. Streep was, quite literally, wearing an American flag as a dress.  While you might assume that this dress was specifically created for Streep to talk about Clinton's 'grit and grace', this was a look she already had in her wardrobe. Streep first wore the stars and stripes knee-length chiffon dress by French designer Catherine Malandrino in 2009 to promote the film Doubt in 2009 in Paris.  And Streep's not the only one to turn to the patriotic dress over the past 15 years. Halle Berry first wore a sleeveless version of the dress with stiletto knee-high boots when promoting Swordfish in 2001, Katy Perry wore the flag-printed dress over 4th July weekend in 2013 with John Mayer and Miss USA 2014 Nia Sanchez wore hers (with her tiara, of course) shortly after she was crowned.  Catherine Malandrino started her career working in Couture Ateliers in Paris, including Emanuel Ungaro, and launched her own label in 1998, showing at New York Fasion Week. Malandrino's business is still based in New York and is stocked in a number of American department stores, including Lord and Taylor and Nordstrom.  It's not surprising that Streep's outfit for the DNC was just as considered and persuasive as her speech. There is a long history of celebrities using fashion to show their support for a presidential candidate, with no-one being as committed to a voting-ready outfit as Katy Perry who in 2012 wore 'ballot paper' dress to show her support for Obama. While there has been a lack of celebrities wearing customised Trump ensembles, Clinton certainly has the fashion industry in her corner. Clinton collaborated with Tory Burch, Marc Jacobs and Dao-Yi Chow and Maxwell Osborne, Diane Von Furstenberg, Rag & Bone, Marchesa and Tory Burch to design 'Vote for Hillary' t shirts available on her website. The likes of Kendall Jenner, Emma Roberts, Olivia Wilde and Christy Turlington have been wearing this Clinton merch, and Anna Wintour even wore one on the front row at New York Fashion Week in February. Lena Dunham has shown how these political cheerleader outfits can be a powerful tool in an election, and has worn a number of red, white and blue custom-made pieces. "The clothes are just a way to bring even more energy and joy to the message," Dunham explained her patriotic looks in a caption on Instagram. Dunham's stylist Shirley Kurata previously revealed to The Telegraph that Dunham's decision to dress like an American flag was inspired by the custom 'Vote Obama' pieces Katy Perry wore in the 2012 election. "It is a quick and powerful way of showing who you support and what your ideological and political beliefs are," Kurata says of how fashion can be a powerful political tool. "And with the popularity of Instagram and the power of the internet, you can send that message through in a way that can reach hundreds and thousands of people in a matter of minutes.  I hope that people can use this power to inspire tolerance, peace, goodwill, activism, and positivity." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The luxury strategy for cutting back on consumption is to blow most of your budget on one or two everlasting pieces thereby ensuring you can’t afford to buy anything else. That’s the argument trotted out by Azzedine Alaïa junkies, and visiting his first ever store in London – the one with the spectacular staircase, an absolute must for Instagram traffic – the day before it officially opened this week, I can see a certain logic to it. Many of the clothes on the rails look familiar. There’s the chiffon goddess dress Stephanie Seymour wore, the tailored coat Naomi Campbell has in every colour, the little cardigans and shirt dresses that everyone from Michelle Obama to Victoria Beckham collects. Like Coco Chanel, Alaïa created his own vernacular: minimalist, a little sporty, albeit of the refined variety, always indifferent to ephemeral trends. If it works for you (you need to be bold, confident and have mastered the art of excellent posture I find) then it will always work. Carla Sozzani, sister of the late Franca Sozzani, the legendary editor of Italian Vogue, and no style slouch herself (she founded the concept stores Corso Como, which now span the globe) first met Alaïa 40 years ago. “I was working for Italian Vogue. I had heard about this man doing made to measure for a small group of clients in Paris…” It was mutual adoration at first sight. He made her a black jersey dress. She still has it, but, no longer wears it. “It’s not so much that it has dated “ she says. “But I have. I don’t have the same shape.” She is minuscule but one doesn’t always want to wear body con Lycra in one’s 60s. Alaïa was dubbed the King of Cling in the Eighties. However the tight, stretchy pieces were only one aspect. His tailoring is extraordinary: bonded, barely perceptible seams and darts that subtly reshape a woman’s body. He was the opposite of those designers who chuck on embellishment and gimmicks to create an effect – a radical innovator by subtle degrees. Not everyone’s a fan. Karl Lagerfeld, in an interview this month with Numero magazine, took aim at just about every sacred cow on planet fashion and declared that “by the end of his career all he did was make ballet slippers for menopausal fashion victims”. Sozzani smiles sweetly, rather as a Montessori teacher might when one of her pet pupils wets their cushion during show and tell. “I think to understand the root of that you’d have to go back to the Seventies and the rivalry between Azzedine and Karl when they were starting out”. It seems rather menopausal-ist. It’s not as if Alaïa wasn’t continuously tweaking right up to his death in November. “There are 22,000 designs in the archives,” laughs Sozzani. “I don’t think we’ll have a problem finding ideas with which to fill this store”. As someone who worked with Azzedine for four decades (she was fired from Italian Elle in the Eighties for putting an Alaïa dress on the cover of a key issue that was considered consecrated territory for Italian designers), Sozzani has become de facto curator of his legacy, involved in overseeing future collections, which will all be drawn from Alaïa’s library. It’s ironic that his first UK boutique (and a forthcoming exhibition devoted to him at The Design Museum this May) come posthumously. The shop, like the clothes, is a work of art, with furniture and fittings designed by inter alia Marc Newson, Gio Ponti, Renzo Piano, and that staircase by Kris Ruhs. Even if you walk away empty-handed your imagination and taste levels will be fired up… © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Quick pub quiz question; who invented the bikini? It wasn’t one of fashion’s household names - one of Coco Chanel’s many visionary ideas, or one of Monsieur Dior’s genius new silhouettes. Instead it was Louis Réard, a French mechanical engineer, who anticipated what women (and men) would want to see in 1946, but whose name has largely been forgotten, until now. Réard Paris re-launches today as a luxury resort label, leading with its French design roots, but fronted by new creative director Céline Adler, a former swimwear design consultant for Chloé and Nina Ricci. “As a swimwear designer, I am very familiar with the [original] style and it has always guided me throughout my creative career,” Adler tells The Telegraph of the reason she took the job when Richard Emanuel, the Chairman of Réard, called her to say that he wanted to start telling the brand’s story again. “Every brand has at one moment in time taken inspiration from this era. It is a time period that I particularly like as well, with glamorous Hollywood coming to light, and the historical and political context fascinates me.” While the new Réard will draw on its past, Adler is quick to point out that a lot has changed since the original hit the big time in the Forties, when the mechanic who had taken over his mother's lingerie business was making his first attempts at designing clothing. “We are not recreating 1950’s swimwear,” Adler says. “Since 1947, technology has changed the most, and with this comes progress in terms of fabrics and finishing touches. The possibilities are endless nowadays, whereas Louis Réard simply had cotton to work with, as Lycra was still not available. Today’s technology allows us to think outside the box and push ourselves creatively for every design, until it has been perfected.” The launch offering comprises 28 suit styles and colourways (with many named after the original Riviera icons) with prices starting at £120 and reaching £600 for the embellished one-pieces. Adler says that swimwear will be the focus for the launch offering, but that the brand will expand to produce four questions per year, including resortwear. “The first capsule collection focuses on swimwear - we work with 12 types of shapes and find creative ways to re-work them,” she says. “The idea is that we want every woman to be able to find their ideal piece. We are truly obsessed with having a perfect fit, with a sharp eye for details and finishing touches.” Fit was something that was particularly important to the brand’s engineer founder, and Adler suggests that the one thing that hasn’t changed about what women want from a bikini is for it to give them confidence in their shape. “Women will forever want the same thing when it comes to their swimwear, to find a product which is visually pleasing and desirable, but most importantly a piece that will make them feel beautiful and confident."  Taking the shapes back to those that flattered the original, curvaceous bikini-wearing icons of the era, Adler says, was an important part of this process. Because who wouldn’t still want a body like Bardot’s today? “I believe our bandeau will be very popular as it has curved lines which beautify the female form, a reference to the 1950's, were carefully thought out as to create a piece that is light, pure, and minimalist,” she says. “Purchasing a bathing suit is not always the easiest task for any woman, any body shape. It is a vulnerable moment for many of us, so it is important to respect this fragility and offer a real solution.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Remember ‘going out’ tops? The specific breed of top worn with jeans when going ‘out out’? Or on a dinner date with girlfriends? Well, you might have thought the concept got tired along with kitten heels and pashminas but Rosie Huntington-Whiteley is making them modern again. For the uninitiated, let us take a step back. A ‘going out’ or ‘nice’  top is one that boasts pizzazz. It might be made from luxe material, an unusual pattern or simply have a flouncy sleeve. Back in the Nineties all you needed was a splash of diamante on a blouse for it to be classed as ‘going out’ worthy. In the midst of Gucci’s maximalist fashion boom, and the flip-side of this eclectic movement which has seen women flock towards Scandi minimalism, we have forgotten about the simple fashion equation of wearing a beautiful top with classic denim. Enter Rosie Huntington-Whiteley. The Devon-born, LA native was recently spotted leaving Nobu, Malibu, in a cold-shoulder floral Magda Butrym blouse, black slim-cut jeans and Giuseppe Zanotti sandals. The yesterday, Huntington-Whitely was spotted at the airport in blue jeans with a decorative bomber jacket. In both cases, the look is pulled-together, but casual and uncontrived. The thing about the ‘going out’ top, you see, is that it will go with any pair of jeans. The ‘going out’ top does the hard work, and lets the denim tone down the look in a harmonious high-low balance. Rosie, 29, has been pairing her ‘nice top and jeans’ combos with a pair of minimal sandals, but the outfit would work equally well with a pair of pointy black pumps (heeled or flat) or black heeled boots. Like jeans, shoes come secondary to the top and should not compete for attention. Just a couple of months ago, the model-cum-lingerie designer sported another ‘nice top and jeans’ combo. (Forgive us for giving it such a basic moniker, but it does what it says on the tin, right?) Running errands in LA again, Rosie wore a cream blouse and leather skinny jeans. A black blazer balanced neatly on her shoulders, while chain-embellished accessories added a point of interest. The result was an elegant look which you can make work whether you're going to Nobu with Jason Statham or to your local Slug and Lettuce for a catch-up with the girls.  The simple nice top + jeans formula is also brilliant adapatable to your personal style. Skinnies can be swapped for flared denim or this season’s cropped flare jeans. Floral fans will count a catalogue of posy-printed blouses as their go-to ‘nice tops’, while others will covet Equipment’s luxe silk shirts and leather jeans, à la Kate Moss. With new studies showing the average woman spends 17 minutes a day deciding what to wear each morning, we can’t help but praise such simple dressing maths. After all, sometimes you just need a nice top and jeans, right?  When Margaret Thatcher embarked on her historic tour of the Soviet Union, her signature style was very much on show - complete with pearls, handbags and pussy-bow blouses. And while the Prime Minister sought help when planning her travel wardrobe, newly released sketches reveal she wasn’t afraid to put her own spin on her stylist’s suggestions. The woman behind Thatcher’s ironclad outfits was another Margaret - Margaret King, the PM’s ‘dress adviser’ and a director of Aquascutum, the British fashion house. The pair first met in 1979, shortly after Thatcher became Prime Minister, when she came into Aquascutum to buy a new coat. Their decades-long collaboration really began in 1987, when Thatcher was preparing for her trip to Moscow. ‘She needed a coat, but I wanted to do more,’ King told The Telegraph in 2013. ‘As our leader, I felt she should look absolutely devastating.’ King designed four coats - one for each day of the trip - and commissioned a dramatic, Russian-style fox-fur hat from royal milliner Philip Somerville. Her meticulous planning is visible in a set of sketches released for the first time today by the Margaret Thatcher Foundation archive. ‘The Prime Minister knew how important it was going to be, and how important it was she should look good. She was the first British prime minister to visit the Soviet Union, so it was a historic occasion,’ King added. 'She wanted the British to be proud of her and wanted to wear everything British.’ The eight sketches include style names, stock numbers and King’s choice of accessories for each outfit, including items noted to be ‘P.M’s own’. Photographs from the trip show that Thatcher made subtle changes to King’s ensembles, wearing the Somerville hat with a different coat and eschewing a hat altogether with another coat, this one in her favourite ‘Conference blue’ hue. But it worked: King said that Thatcher rang her within two hours of returning to London to say the clothes had been ‘sensational’. The PM appeared on her first international best-dressed list in 1988. Her outfits from the Moscow trip proved so pivotal to her image that one key piece - the camel-coloured cashmere coat with stranded mink collar - sold for £30,000 at auction in 2015. King and Thatcher worked together for the remainder of Thatcher’s time in power. Over the years she would usher Thatcher away from her favourite pussy-bow blouses and introduce colours beyond sapphire blue. But the Aquascutum suits remained a pillar of the Prime Minister’s wardrobe. ‘If Margaret trusted you to do something, that was it – she trusted you,’ King said. ‘I felt very close to her, and working with her was an amazing chapter in my life.’   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Last week, a young designer based in LA told me that to grow her business to the next stage, it would be useful- well, essential actually- to have some of the right actresses wear her designs on the red carpet. But that’s an industry in itself, so if she cannot afford to pay influential, chic women to don her wares when they’re in the spotlight then that valuable exposure is going to be almost impossible to achieve. The same principle applies to musicians on world tours. Each night they pack out venues filled with thousands of adoring fans, with images of their stage looks beamed around the world on Instagram. For her Rebel Heart tour- which finished in Sydney last week- Madonna worked with major names like Gucci creative director Alessandro Michele  and Moschino designer Jeremy Scott. Meanwhile, Adele is wearing only bespoke  Burberry for her 105 date sell-out world tour.  It’s understandable because this is a high stakes business and it takes serious expertise to create costumes which are suitably impactful but also comfortable for belting out a ballad or two. All this makes the fact that Rihanna is championing new talent on her Anti tour all the more heartening. She's got form when it comes to highlighting up-and-coming or more unknown designers. You might remember that at last year’s Chinese themed Met Gala, she was one of the only high profile guests to opt for a dress by an actual Chinese designer (the couturier Guo Pei) or that it was Adam Selman rather than a major brand who she worked with on the ‘naked’ dress which she wore to collect her Fashion Icon award at the 2014 CFDAs. For Anti, Rihanna and her stylist Mel Ottenberg have worked with two designers whose avant-garde approach has attracted the beady eyes of fashion insiders of late. For the opening look of the show, London-based Craig Green created a custom-made calico hooded cream coat which comes with his signature tie details, including a top-knot like detail on the top of the hood. Rihanna has numerous versions of the coat so that there can be a pristinely clean new one available each night of the tour.   "The coat was a long time in discussion and we created countless prototypes" Green tells The Telegraph. "Mel had a vision of the tour look being quite plain and stripped-back, which I guess worked with my look" adds Green who has been known to bring attendees of his shows to tears thanks to the ethereal atmosphere which he creates. He’s predominantly a menswear designer, but his minimalist  shapes and pared-back aesthetic have unisex appeal. "I love seeing my work on a female celebrity. It's a sign of the times that it's ok to mix it up now. Stores often tell me that women cross over to the men's department to buy my clothes."  Meanwhile, there is a lot of buzz right now around Y/Project, the label designed by Belgian Glenn Martens. He’s just been shortlisted as a finalist in the LVMH prize, a prestigious award which counts Karl Lagerfeld and Marc Jacobs among its judges. Martens is part of a crew of Paris- based designers who are bringing a dash of youthful verve to a city which has long been associated with the major fashion houses. Since his appointment in 2013, Martens has added womenswear  to his offering and now 50% of the men’s and women’s lines are unisex. For Rihanna, Martens created a slouchy brown trouser suit which Ottenberg has styled with a leather body suit by L.A Roxx, though if the proportions were tweaked and the leather swapped for a tee, you would probably want to wear it to the office.  Peppered amongst these new talent choices have been boots from Rihanna's Manolo Blahnik  collaboration, Dior sunglasses and an Armani Privé coat. It all comes together to form an excitingly offbeat look which will help propel these designers to the next level. "It's so beneficial to have that kind of support" says Green, "it means that my work reaches a different audience- plus my Mum and my sister actually know who Rihanna is, so it really means something to them."  The corset is the most loaded fashion item there is, with an uncomfortable (quite literally) history of whalebone-induced fainting and rib removal surgery all in the name of sculpting a Scarlett O'Hara 'waist-trained' silhouette. But whilst the Victorian corset might be a universal symbol of female confinement, it is back for AW16 - and in a whole new form.  Victoria Beckham, Prada and Balmain are a few of the key labels championing corsets for AW16, and they have already been worn by the likes of Rihanna, Victoria Beckham and Gigi Hadid. Instead of uncomfortable hidden shapewear or overly sexualised Burlesque costumes, this new wave of corsetry is designed to be worn by women on their own terms. At Prada corsets were minimal, rather than sexy, and worn as an accessory, layered over coats and suits, with the laces left loose and half-tied. At Balmain they were powerful and body conscious, aimed to mimic the Kardashian's love of shapewear, while at Victoria Beckham they were sleek, classic and minimal. “I used to wear a lot and it felt very sexy and feminine,” Beckham said to The Telegraph of the corset revival backstage. “I wanted to find a way to bring that back and feel new and fresh.” Ever the perfect brand ambassador, Beckham wore a black corset with tuxedo trousers at the Cannes Film Festival, proving that it is in fact a surprisingly wearable look. Gigi Hadid and Amy Schumer have followed suit, and worn sculpted corsets with black suit trousers. Rihanna, always the first to leap to a new trend, has been wearing corsets in the style of Prada, however, layering a lavender corset belt over a loose shirt dress and then performing at Sziget Festival this month in an Adam Selman brown corset belt cinched over an oversized T shirt. It's a powerful styling move, which has been called by some a feminist reclaiming of a garment which traditionally was used to control - and restrict - female bodies.  This isn't the first time that corsets have been 're-appropriated' as an empowering garment, of course, as in 1990 Madonna's iconic Jean Paul Gaultier corset with a cone bra ignited a debate about women's image being controlled by men. "Madonna's corsets satiricized male fantasy - they sprouted fake nipples," writes Carol Chillington Rutter. Corset belts could easily be a trend that never leaves the catwalks, but it's an AW16 styling trick that already in August appears to be resonating with some customers. Lyst has seen a 25% increase in searches for corsets over the last six weeks but only a 0.6% increase in sales. An indication, perhaps, that the public aren't fully committed to the trend?  Not so, according to the people at Net-A-Porter. The Prada belt corsets sold out almost instantly when they hit the site earlier this month. "Prada’s denim corset belt sold out immediately upon upload in both colours," says Net-A-Porter's Retail Fashion Director, Lisa Aiken. "The fabric is a slightly thinner denim so it sits very neatly over dresses and even knitwear without the fabric spilling over the sides." And if you're wondering how to wear the corset in a modern way? "Over the past few seasons we’ve seen ready-to-wear borrow inspiration from the lingerie category in so many variations; from bodysuits to slip dresses and now corsets, it’s empowering to see designers use these styles as a layering piece as opposed to something that was once hidden and worn under clothes as shapewear."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Following the death of Karl Lagerfeld at the age of 85, friends, peers and celebrities have taken to social media to pay tribute to the late designer.  Former Chanel muse, the actress Diana Kruger shared that she was 'heartbroken,' whilst the designer Victoria Beckham described him as a genius.  Read more of the tributes to Lagerfeld from his colleagues, fellow designers and celebrity fans below...  Alain Wertheimer, CEO of Chanel, said: 'Thanks to his creative genius, generosity and exceptional intuition, Karl Lagerfeld was ahead of his time, which widely contributed to the House of Chanel's success throughout the world. Today, not only have I lost a friend, but we have all lost an extraordinary creative mind to whom I gave carte blanche in the early 1980s to reinvent the brand.' Bruno Pavlovsky, President of Fashion at Chanel, said: “Fashion show after fashion show, collection after collection, Karl Lagerfeld left his mark on the legend of Gabrielle Chanel and the history of the House of Chanel. He steadfastly promoted the talent and expertise of Chanel's ateliers and Métiers d’Art, allowing this exceptional know-how to shine throughout the world. The greatest tribute we can pay today is to continue to follow the path he traced by – to quote Karl – ‘continuing to embrace the present and invent the future’.” Serge Brunschwig, Fendi Chairman & CEO said: 'Working with Karl Lagerfeld at Fendi allowed me to catch a glimpse of the secret of the continuous renewal of the House. I profoundly admire Karl’s immense culture, his ability to rejuvenate at all times, to taste all the arts, to not overlook any style, along with a persistent refusal to turn to his past, to look at his work in a mirror. He was restless and his exigent nature would never leave him. The show was just ending  that Karl would  always say, "And now number next!" He leaves us an enormous heritage, an inexhaustible source of inspiration to continue. Karl will be immensely missed by myself and all the Fendi people.'  Silvia Venturini Fendi, Fendi Creative Director for Menswear, Accessories and Kidswear said: 'I am profoundly saddened as today we have lost a unique man and an unrivalled designer, who has given so much to Fendi and to myself.  The Duchess of Cambridge blended the best of British and Indian fashion this evening at a reception held at Buckingham Palace to celebrate the 2017 UK-India year of culture. As she mingled with other members of the Royal family, including The Queen, and chatted with guests from both nations, the Duchess offered up a new lesson in the diplomatic dressing game which she has made her specialist subject. Kate had turned to Erdem, the Canadian- Turkish designer who has established his design label in London and become a favourite amongst high-profile women, for a delicate lace dress. The midi-length ‘Rhonda’ design comes pleated and shot with silver, giving an opulently shimmering finish. Although it is no longer available to purchase, the dress originally retailed for around £900. The Duchess added a pair of sparkling Oscar de la Renta heels to match the dress.  The Indian fashion designer Anita Dongre was one of the guests at the event, which made the Duchess’s decision to finish her look with a pair of earrings from Dongre’s eponymous label all the more fitting. Although the pearl drop earrings are no longer available on Dongre’s website, they epitomise the luxurious take on Indian craftsmanship which Dongre has sought to create since launching her business over twenty years ago. Much of Dongre’s jewellery collection comes at affordable prices, with earrings similar to those worn tonight retailling for around $100 US (c. £80). It is not the first time that Kate has worn Anita Dongre as a way to pay tribute to Indian fashion. When she and Prince William visited India last year, the Duchess chose the printed georgette “Gulrukh” dress from Dongre’s SS16 collection for an engagement involving a cricket game and tour of Mumbai’s most deprived areas. “It was a real surprise. I was at home when I saw the pictures and was so delighted,” Dongre told The Telegraph in April last year, also revealing that Kate and her PA-turned-stylist Natasha Archer had customised the dress. “Her stylist has taken the stole and converted part of that into the belt and then chopped it off so it can be worn as a dress. She’s amazing - it looks easy, breezy and so contemporary.” “She looked beautiful,” Dongre said from her base in Mumbai. “I’ve always admired her sense of style. My clothes stand for a certain feminine elegance - I think she does the same.” It seems that the Duchess was a convert to Dongre’s elevated take on timeless Indian style. Both on that occasion, and this evening, the Duchess has employed Dongre’s designs to carry a soft- yet highly effective- diplomatic message of unity and respect. This evening’s Erdem dress is just the latest addition to a growing collection of pieces by the designer the Duchess had added to her wardrobe lately and which are a powerful tool for her promote and highlight the best of British fashion. The Duchess has long been a fan of Erdem’s ladylike signatures- first wearing a dress by him on a tour to Canada shortly after her wedding in 2011- but this is the third look in almost as many months; in October, Kate debuted an elegant  checked coat from the Resort 2016 collection on a visit to Manchester while in January she chose a £1,050 ‘Evita’ dress for the launch of a Heads Together initiative in London. Events such as this evening’s UK-India reception throw into sharp focus how the royal family’s role will become more integral than ever as the UK exits the EU, underscoring a need to strengthen ties around the world and highlight the best that Britain has to offer. As such, what the Duchess chooses to wear for these diplomatically vital occasions carries great power, and tonight she played it meticulously. At the glittering royal reception guests were greeted by the sight of the palace decorated with a peacock - the national bird of India - projected onto the facade of the famous London landmark, an artwork commissioned by the British Council and the Indian High Commission. The canapes served reflected the Anglo-Indian theme, with a choice of spice-rich delicacies or traditional western-style morsels, created by Uday Salunkhe, executive chef at Veeraswamy, said to be the UK's oldest Indian restaurant, and  Mark Flanagan, head chef at Buckingham Palace's kitchens. The Queen arrived in the White Drawing Room at 6pm accompanied by the Duke of Edinburgh, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, and Princess Eugenie. The Duke and Duchess of Gloucester, Princess Alexandra and Prince and Princess Michael of Kent were also in attendance. Guests included former India cricket captain Kapil Dev, musician Anoushka Shankar - daughter of legendary sitar player Ravi Shankar - and her husband film director Joe Wright, and former EastEnders actress Nina Wadia. The Queen wore a purple Stewart Parvin dress woven with gold threads, meeting a line up of dignitaries including Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson, the Indian Finance Minister and Sir Dominic Asquith, the British High Commissioner to India.  Princess Eugenie introduced her grandmother to Aloka Mitra of the Women's Interlink Foundation, an organisation dedicated to supporting trafficked and exploited girls and young women. The ceremony was accompanied by an exhibition of priceless artefacts from the Royal Collection including a shawl woven by Ghandi on his loom as a wedding present for Princess Elizabeth in 1947.  There were also several painting and manuscripts dating back to the 17th Century - some of which may not have been seen in public since - and a welcoming garland presented to the Queen when she visited India in 1961.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s the go-to workwear fabric for those who want to dress like a boss. But, as Amal Clooney demonstrated yesterday, the power pinstripe is more versatile than you might think. Taking to the stage at the Texas Conference for Women, Amal wore a navy, striped sheath dress, believed to be from the Victoria Victoria Beckham line, with Paul Andrew heels. As a human rights lawyer, her office dress code may rarely leave a lot of room for flair, yet Amal (once again) has found a way to make a subtle statement with her workwear. A pinstripe suit, traditionally, is a look that exudes power. There are many fashion folklores about its exact origins, but its evolution has been traced through the striped jackets worn by British boaters from the 19th century and the suits that distinguished bankers in the 1920s. Actors have cemented its status as the businessman’s uniform over the years - from Carey Grant in 1943’s Suspicion through to Leonardo DiCaprio in The Wolf Of Wall Street in 2013. In women’s wardrobes, however, the pinstripe became a symbol of empowerment. Yves Saint Laurent created rebellious pictures of his statuesque muse, Danielle Luquet de Saint Germain, wearing a three-piece pinstripe suit and smoking a cigarette in the early 1960s. A few years later in 1967, Helmut Newton photographed Twiggy in a suit, brogues and tie for Vogue, encouraging women everywhere to try the Dandy look. By the time that Jean Paul Gaultier made Madonna’s Blonde Ambition tour suit, slashed down the front to reveal her iconic conical bra, all of the rules were broken, and the pinstripe was corporate no more. For AW16, designers have again seized the chance to play with this symbol, with young designers like Jacquemus collaging pinstripes with party fabrics, and bigger brands like DKNY cutting it into dozens of new silhouettes that are so #NSFW (that’s ‘not suitable for work’ for the uninitiated). The pinstripe now goes with everything - so long as you’ve got the confidence to stand tall in it - and, best of all, it’s universally flattering. So whether you’re looking for a subtle yet powerful addition to your workwear wardrobe like Amal, or fancy turning the pinstripe into your new party staple, here are five pieces that could work for the office, but should definitely not be reserved only for the boardroom...   Dress, £425, from Paper London Jumpsuit, £49, from Topshop Top, £99, from Jaeger  Dress, £620, from Victoria Victoria Beckham at Net-A-Porter  Deconstructed jacket, £615, from Jacquemus at Browns  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  At a glance, you could be forgiven for thinking that the new Louis Vuitton ad campaign features four promising young female models – emerging talent showcasing futuristic garb from a storied fashion house best known for its monogrammed luggage. Yet while all those cast are certainly new names to have on your radar (Scottish beauty Lady Jean Campbell, for example), one is in fact Jaden Smith - the teenage son of Men in Black actor Will Smith. The 17-year-old holds his own in an asymmetric skirt and tassled top in the image, which was released on Instagram by the brand’s creative director, Nicolas Ghesquière. The campaign, titled Series 4, was taken by revered fashion photographer Bruce Weber, the man responsible for Abercrombie & Fitch’s legendary black and white campaigns. Lending some serious street cred to the French fashion house, Smith is proof that the fashion world’s gender-fluidity movement isn’t going anywhere in 2016. If 2015 was the year that comeback brand Gucci made it hard to determine the gender of its catwalk models, 2016 looks set to be the one where the boundaries in ad campaigns become all the blurrier. It's a movement Jaden will be perfectly comfortable with. Last year, he demonstrated his commitment to gender neutral dressing wearing a monochrome shift dress to a friend's prom.  Ghesquière addressed Smith's involvement in the campaign by stating: "He represents a generation that has assimilated the codes of true freedom, one that is free of manifestos and questions about gender. Wearing a skirt comes as naturally to him as it would to a woman who, long ago, granted herself permission to wear a man’s trench or a tuxedo. Jaden Smith conveys something very interesting about the integration of a global wardrobe. He’s found an instinctive balance that makes his extraordinary attitude a new norm. That really inspired me in the creative process for this collection.” Jaden Smith is perhaps best known for appearing alongside his father Will in 2006 movie The Pursuit of Happiness. A film career followed: the 17-year-old was the star of The Karate Kid and has just finished a follow up to the movie. He's also an accomplished rapper and keen fashion fan, as photographs on his instagram account Chrisitaingrey prove.  Jaden isn't the only Smith to star in a high fashion campaign. Last year his little sister Willow, aged just 14, posed for Marc Jacobs in a campaign that also counted Cher, 69, and Winona Ryder, 44, amongst its cast.  It’s not often that a ghost story serves as a backdrop for some seriously chic fashion, but Personal Shopper, the new thriller starring Kristen Stewart, has just raised the bar. Stewart plays a personal shopper responsible for organising designer clothes and jewellery for a celebrity client. Though her character, Maureen, lives in jumpers and jeans, her glamorous job involves dealing with treasures from Chanel and Cartier - which, one imagines, is not a huge leap from the actress’s real life. Costume designer Juergen Doering was responsible for the wardrobe, and worked with director Olivier Assayas and the cast to piece together his own impression of how it should look. “First I read the script and I asked Olivier to tell me in three adjectives what he thinks about each character,” explains Doering. “Then I looked at the cast - so I led with the character first and the person second. Then I went to the actors and, without telling them what the director had said, I asked ‘How did you get this part and how do you see it?’ Because Olivier likes for people to feel the character and feel the clothes.” There’s a noticeable difference between Maureen’s day-to-day clothing and the more elevated style of her boss. “We were thinking that Maureen’s American, she’s in Paris, she’s wearing jeans, she’s a little bit rugged - sneakers, vintage, sweaters,” says Doering. “I looked at some vintage Fruit of the Loom sweaters at a shop in Paris, and was looking for things that you could believe a girl like this had picked at the flea market. The flying jacket in brown leather, very manly, for when she’s always on the bike - a young person will try things.” As the film progresses - spoiler alert - Maureen sneakily borrows and wears some of her client’s designer pieces, including a Vionnet organza gown with a harness, something that was specifically requested by Assayas. “I was looking in all the couture collections for a harness dress,” says Doering. “The director said ‘Maybe it’s a harness over a dress, or maybe it’s part of the dress.’ In the end I saw it at Vionnet and Olivier liked it immediately. We chose black because there is something ambiguous about her personality: she says she hates the job she is doing and the girl she is picking the things for, but when she comes to desire men, she wants to be that woman she hates.” Maureen also borrows a silver sequinned Chanel dress. As Stewart has fronted several Chanel campaigns, it was no surprise to see the fashion house popping up in her movie - though Doering says there was no contractual obligation involved. “We know the team at Chanel well, but if we didn’t find what we wanted, we had no pressure,” he says. “I asked the girls there, ‘Do you have something with sequins?’ and they said ‘Oh we have this old dress that no one has worn before.’ And I saw it and I thought ‘Oh, this is it.’” It may be the only time you’ll see Stewart in a Chanel dress that doesn’t fit like a glove: “Of course we didn’t fit it onto Kristen, because it is not supposed to be her own dress. She feels uncomfortable in the dress, it’s not hers - but she likes it because it’s not correct for her to wear it.” Though the contrast between Maureen’s casual wardrobe and this highly polished eveningwear is visually dramatic, it somehow feels like a natural fit for Stewart. The actress is known for her grungy personal style of T-shirts and Converse, but she’s also a muse for Karl Lagerfeld and a fixture on the front row. Working with her was easy, explains Doering: “Kristen knows her stuff. She loved Chanel before she was famous. For her it was easy to jump from the jeans to the dress, no trouble.” He clearly felt that they had a meeting of minds. “Often actresses they have no taste!” he laughs. “So it’s good to actually have a conversation with someone who knows.” Personal Shopper is in cinemas now   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
