 Lady Gaga paid tribute to David Bowie at the 2016 Grammys as only she could; with a high fashion performance of his greatest hits that broke the internet.  The singer started her homage to Bowie on the red carpet, riffing off the trademark blue eyeshadow and flame hair he made famous and wearing a shoulder padded dress-coat by Marc Jacobs that was a nod to both Ziggy Stardust and Bowie's "Aladdin Sane" album cover, which she had tattooed on her body over the weekend. The Marc Jacobs design was custom-made for Gaga but took inspiration from the New York designer's Spring 2016 collection, which featured heavily embellished blue jackets.  Gaga posted an instagram video of her looking teary whilst getting Bowie-ready make-up done before the 2016 Grammy awards. But it was her musical tribute to the main man which left the audience emotional.  Gaga ran through 10 of the icon's hits from the 70s and early 80s, including Space Oddity, Changes, Fame, Let's Dance and Heroes. She managed to capture the hugely varied, era-defining sounds that Bowie kept producing right up to his death last month.  Gaga's performance was a hybrid of her own trademark stagecraft - thrashing 'Little Monster' paw dance-moves and wide-eyed facial expressions - and that which Bowie made his own. Although she allowed the true strength of her vocals to shine on closing song Heroes, she spent the rest of her show imitating the late star's arch British accent, which inflected his voice on Space Oddity, Suffragette City, Fashion and Rebel Rebel.  The stage was filled with dancers and musicians helping Gaga to segue seamlessly, if chaotically, through 10 hits in six minutes, Chic's Nile Rodgers joined Gaga to play the instantly recognisable high-pitched guitar riff on Let's Dance. Rodgers had directed the "multi-sensory" performance and stuck around as it reached its crescendo in Heroes, perhaps the Bowie song which greatest reflects the sentiment behind Gaga's artistry.  Gaga said paying tribute to Bowie was probably the most challenging thing she's done in career because he influenced her so greatly and helped shape her identity. "When I was 19 years old ... I started to live my life like him. I began to consume art and fashion and art history and a combination of those things, performance technique ... and I only hung out with people that were artists and that was the way that he was and I learned that from him," she said. "What I'm trying to say is there's people that love David Bowie, and then there's David Bowie fans, and there's Bowie kids, who live like him ...and I can't express to you, I don't know who I'd be if I didn't have (him as) a figure in my life. I don't know what my identity would be." And, this being Lady Gaga honoring one of the music world's biggest fashion innovators she'd lined up some epic costume changes courtesy of Marc Jacobs to go alongside the music. The New York designer created a white encrusted suit that wouldn't have looked out of place in a Bowie video and Gaga's make-up artist Sarah Nicole Tanno used Sephora products to recreate the lightening bolt flash Bowie has become synonymous with. The look was thought through. Gaga had flown her stylist Brendon Maxwell into LA just a day before his New York Fashion Week show and pictures on instagram show him tweaking her outfits as she practiced her Bowie tribute backstage before walking the red carpet. Gaga and Bowie - two professionals to the end.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Season five of Lena Dunham’s hit TV sitcom goes is in full flow on Sky Atlantic, with only one more series of what has become one of our shows ever scheduled to be made. We’ve become voyeurs of the world inhabited by Hannah, Shoshanna, Jessa and Marnie, living vicariously thought their questionable life decisions, often-terrible choices in men and rollercoaster friendships. The clothes powerfully tell the story of the characters and where thy are at, so we spoke to the costume designer on the series, Jenn Rogien, to tell us more about her work with Lena Dunham, the show’s creator and star and its executive producers, Judd Apatow and Jennifer Konner. Set in Brooklyn, the show very much has the feel of the hip New York neighbourhood – but it’s an ever-changing one. “I could probably write a dissertation on the Brooklyn feel at this point!” laughs Jenn. “Season one started very thrift and vintage heavy, very quirky, and then by season five when we got to dressing some of the coffee shops you’ll see that it’s a very different look, more pared-down and monochromatic and incorporating a vintage item along with designer items, so there’s been a big shift and we try to mirror that and maintain that and be ahead of it where we can for the girls, the guys and most importantly, our background atmosphere on the show.” For season one, Jenn fitted Hannah Horvath (played by Lena Dunham) with Spanx and belts to cinch her waist and put her in heels, but it just looked wrong. “Our producers grabbed me and said: ‘This isn’t working… Hannah looks to good and we don’t think our audience will believe that she is this emotionally all-over the place if she looks this put-together. So we did – we stripped the Spanx and took out the belts and we took out the heels and then from there on out, I was very mindful of altering things to potentially look not as good... so the hemlines were in the wrong place for Lena – but for Hannah they were great – they made her look dishevelled, they made her look ill-fitted.” In season two, episode three, Hannah goes out clubbing one night in a big way. Part-way through the evening, she swaps top with a fellow clubber, sporting nothing but a yellow, netted tank top. Once you’ve seen the episode, it’s an image that is impossible to erase from your mind. “That’s the stand-out moment for a lot of people!” says Jenn. “That look actually started with another character, and so the challenge was to compose a look that didn’t strike anyone as unusual on this sort of club kid guy in the background, but then became outrageous for Hannah.” Jenn can't recall where she acquired the offending item; “We had gotten our hands on every available fishnet, string, net open-knit tank top that we could find! And so we had a rack of choices - we went everywhere, from club stores to any fashion brand that was doing a string vest at that point, to H&M , we covered every almost every store looking for that item.” "The standout moments are always always tied to a big emotional step for my characters," explains Jenn. "There are some Jessa looks from season one – the feathered vest she wore to the Bushwick party, that was absolutely ridiculous but somehow worked." Then she notes the scene where Hannah wears her pyjamas out on the street when she gets a Q-tip stuck in her ear. Jenn made the plastic dress by hand, which Marnie wore to impress the art collector. "It wasn’t fabric, it was a whole different game… it was PVC / smoke-coloured plastic over  gold crocodile-embossed vinyl. More importantly, it was all motivated by Marnie’s desperate attempt to please/ get the attention of this artist guy and it was really playing the emotional state that she was in, which is why for me it’s so significant. Because yes, it’s an outrageous costume, but it was even more about drawing our attention to where Marnie was emotionally in that episode." The show sees the cast pull off some pretty questionable looks, but it’s all in the name of art. Only if a garment or accessory is proving prohibitive to actually acting out a scene will it be given the chop. “It’s such a collaborative effort of a show and we know each other so well and we know the characters so well at this point that it’s a general consensus of ‘Oh, this isn’t working, it’s not right’ – it’s not anyone refusing” reveals Jenn. “On a show like Girls it’s incredibly hard to choose because all of them are so unique in their looks – and not just the girls, the guys and Hannah’s mom Loreen - we actually have a great time shopping for because she has changed so much over the series. It’s one of the great pleasures of the show, to have characters whose looks are so strong.” Girls is available to watch on Sky Atlantic on Mondays at 9pm © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Given her precedent for literal dressing, one might have assumed that The Duchess of Cambridge would wear florals for her appearance at The Chelsea Flower Show today. Not so. Instead Kate turned to a grass-green coat-dress by Catherine Walker, for the outing - which saw her and Prince William smelling the Princess Charlotte Chrysanthemum, a flower named after their daughter.  It's not the first time we've seen The Duchess wearing this dress - she first debuted it in Canberra on her 2014 tour of Australia with Prince William. But that doesn't mean that her outfit is not thought-through. Indeed, in a way, The Duchess couldn't have chosen to wear a more appropriate designer to the Royal Family's favourite flower event, given Catherine Walker started her work in Chelsea and went on to work extensively with Princess Diana.  Walker started selling clothes in 1976, when she used to walk down the King's Road in London holding a basket of her designs. Soon after she set up her first shop on Sydney Street in Chelsea - and it fast became the go-to destination for event dressing for the 1980's Sloane, including most famously Princess Diana.  French-born Walker first started working with Diana shortly after she married Prince Charles and went on to design over 1,000 dresses for the Princess, including the black dress she was buried wearing. After Princess Diana's divorce, Walker is credited with helping create so-called 'defiant' frocks, such as the black backless dress she wore the night Prince Charles went on national TV to admit his affair.  It's not the first time that Kate has opted to wear Catherine Walker's designs, in an apparent homage to her late mother in law. On her royal tour of Canada in 2011 she wore a grey sheath dress by Catherine Walker, on the day after what would have been Diana's 50th birthday.  It's perhaps also appropriate that this week the team behind Catherine Walker (the eponymous designer died in 2010), are doing their own tribute to the Chelsea Flower Show. On Wednesday 25th May, nine models will parade down the Kings' Road wearing evening dresses from the house’s Spring/Summer 2016 collection, accessorised with floral headpieces inspired by the English country garden. Including, perhaps, a dress we may well see Kate wearing herself in the not too distant future.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It is invariably a surprise to hear that even people at the top of their game don’t always get it right first time. Never more so than when Kim Winser – a woman with one of the best track records in British fashion retail – tells me that Autograph, the upmarket line she launched so successfully at Marks & Spencer in 1999, actually started life a year earlier as Top Tier. Top Tier? ‘Er, yes. Autograph’s better, isn’t it?’ she says diplomatically, laughing. We are sitting in a booth at Brown’s Hotel in Mayfair, and Winser, now CEO of her own womenswear company, Winser London, and dressed in a sleek black silk blouse and perfectly cut black trousers by the brand, laughs a lot while polishing off a good-looking chopped salad. Lunch should have been well out of the way, but she came straight from a meeting at Downing Street and it overran – by an hour. She is unable to divulge the contents of her conversation with the prime minister, but it is clear that Cameron is a fan. Three years ago he made her a trustee of the Natural History Museum, and she is often called in to discuss British business. ‘It’s usually 10 of us around a table. I look at the top guy from BP, for example, and wonder why I’m there,’ she says. Is she, I ask, the token woman? ‘Oh no,’ she says coolly. ‘There’s usually one other. But let’s put it this way: I never have to queue for the loo.’ What about women in her own business? ‘I’m a big fan of a balance of women in the workplace, and not only do I consciously seek to nurture female talent, but I believe we should encourage a workplace ethos that takes its cue from women, too. The economic facts are clear: women are more likely to be balancing work in the office and work at home, so they can be very innovative with flexible new ways of working – perfect given our digital age,’ she says, though she refuses to go so far as to describe herself as a feminist. Her relationship with Number 10 goes back to 2006, when Tony Blair gave her an OBE for services to the fashion industry. ‘He was more… social than Cameron,’ she says. ‘Chattier. David Cameron is very straightforward; he likes to get on with things. It’s all about business and he’s very to the point.’ Winser has spent her adult life working out what women want to wear and how they want to buy it. She started at Marks & Spencer as a management trainee, and in her 20 years there became the divisional director of womenswear and the first woman on the board. She moved to Pringle in 2000 and set about its impressive turnaround. Then she gave Aquascutum its mojo back, advised at Net-a-Porter during its ascent and became chair of Agent Provocateur after its acquisition by the private-equity giant 3i. ‘3i asked me which brand I wanted of all the ones they’d acquired, and I chose Agent Provocateur,’ she says. ‘I love its honesty.’ Finally, in 2013, she launched Winser London – the result of a lunchtime discussion with friends about a lack of quality separates at decent prices. ‘I quite often do things people don’t expect,’ she says of the business that started life in her conservatory. ‘And now we’re three years old on March 1.’ High-quality cashmere sweaters and scarves, and cunningly cut trousers and dresses (sold primarily over the internet) have propelled turnover way past its forecast figures. ‘America has gone from nothing to 15 per cent of total sales,’ Winser says. ‘And Paris is really getting strong.’ A straight-A student at her Hampshire grammar school, Winser also showed a talent for tennis. Spotted by an American coach as she practised at a local court, aged 17, she was invited to go and train in the US but had already applied to the M&S training scheme, offered to the brightest school-leavers; she had fallen in love with retail while working in a shoe shop on Saturdays. Home is now in Berkshire, where she lives with her son, James, 17, and their springer spaniel, Snoopy. She has always been a single parent, having separated from James’s father before he was born. ‘We just weren’t meant to be together,’ she says. ‘I like to go home every night to be with them,’ she continues of her son and the dog. In 2000, when Winser finally left Marks & Spencer and became an investor in Pringle, the Scottish knitwear company was ailing. ‘It had become a golf brand, and a discounted golf brand at that,’ she says. In six years she increased sales from £10 million to £100 million, and put the label on the global fashion map. ‘Then I went to Aquascutum and learnt a lot about trench coats. I used to have regular meetings with the Burberry team. Rose Marie Bravo was there then, and she used to say, “I’ll tell you everything I know about America, if you’ll tell me everything you know about the UK.” Then Angela Ahrendts came along – another fantastic woman.’ Ahrendts is now a senior vice president at Apple. ‘That’s why we had to find a store to sell Winser London on the West Coast, to keep Angela happy,’ Winser says. So should you find yourself in Napa Valley and in need of a cashmere wrap, head to Flats in St Helena. Why does she think women have had such success at the helm of international fashion companies? ‘Women bring an intuitive approach to business that comes from experience and the emotions that drive us to make decisions in both our personal and professional lives. That “gut instinct” can be so powerful, so spot-on,’ Winser says. ‘Womenswear accounted for £439 billion globally in 2014, and those buying decisions are being made by women, so it makes sense to tap into women’s feelings and experience within the industry.’ Winser’s three-year tenure at Aquascutum was a success, too. She brought in celebrities such as Pierce Brosnan to glam up the brand’s image and increased sales by 60 per cent. But she wanted to carry out a management buyout, and the Japanese owner chose to break the company into three parts. ‘I understand why, but I don’t think it’s right. It’s a brand and should stay as one entity,’ she says. Still, timing is everything. Her sudden freedom led her to work on strategic development at Net-a-Porter – ‘Natalie Massenet’s decision to go purely online, that was brilliant’ – and at Agent Provocateur, where, from 2009 to 2011, she led a global roll-out and raised earnings from £1.2 million to £3.3 million. You can see the sum of all these parts in Winser London, from the close connection to suppliers that she learnt at M&S to the direct relationship with customers that an online operation offers, and the presence of the right celebrity – Yasmin Le Bon this time. ‘With digital, you can see exactly who’s buying what, when. Anything you put Yasmin in will sell, sell, sell. The customers love her,’ Winser says. Le Bon’s affection for the brand also seems genuine. ‘Amber [Le Bon’s daughter] and I both wore the Lauren trouser suit for New York and London fashion weeks last season,’ she tells me. ‘And I’ve got the Audrey jumper in every colour.’ She accepted Winser’s request to front the brand immediately. ‘It wasn’t a risk, because anything Kim does is good,’ she says. They have known each other since the M&S days, ‘and I just enjoy working with her – even when she’s making me lie on a concrete floor for a cashmere shoot’. Le Bon is not the only celebrity to love the brand. Gillian Anderson is another. And Emma Watson wore a Winser London raincoat on leaving LA after the Oscars in 2014. ‘She was a trench-coat model for Burberry, so we really weren’t expecting that,’ Winser says, eyebrows raised. ‘Then she ordered the Audrey, then the wraps.’ The internet is awash with pictures of Watson dashing through airports swaddled in Winser London cashmere. But the success of the brand relies on more than celebrity approval. Winser’s focus is the customers.  ‘They’re the only people we present to,’ she says. And while bricks-and-mortar stores have opened in Marlow and Gerrards Cross – selling online allows brands to see exactly where customers spend money – she is also interested in the global market. ‘Especially in Asia and America, British products are associated with quality that you can trust,’ she says. ‘We’re seen as being very good in fashion. We start trends here. London Fashion Week isn’t the most commercial, but it’s exciting. And we own the best in fashion education.’ Students at the Royal College of Art and Central Saint Martins are currently working on projects for her. She has also developed close relationships with British mills and factories. ‘This fabric is made for us by Linton Tweeds in the north of England,’ she says, pointing out the subtle metallic thread running through her tweed coat. ‘But we have to work abroad, too. The best place to do silk is in China – that’s where this blouse I’m wearing was made.’ On her ring finger, a spectacular aquamarine, her birthstone, flashes in a glitter of tiny diamonds – a present to herself. She will be in Hong Kong for her 57th birthday having taken a role as a non-executive director of the Hongkong & Shanghai Hotel & Property Group. ‘They wanted a European non-exec, and someone interested in digital,’ she says. ‘I love a good concierge, but it’s nice to have an iPad set up in your room so you don’t have to keep ringing down. And they can acquire information about you that way. The more data, the better the service.’ As Winser has proved again and again, knowing what your customers want is everything. ‘I’ve chatted to supermodels and customers alike, and they all have something they don’t like about their bodies,’ she says. ‘The sooner we ensure fashion gives real confidence to women and makes them feel good about themselves and how they look, the sooner we will make the business of fashion a real success.’ © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  There is something of a military commander about J J Martin as she inspects the wood-panelled room in Liberty that is currently home to La Double J’s first London pop-up shop. Scanning the rails of clothes, her eyes fall on the table at the room’s centre, laid with the brand’s newly launched crockery and linens. Bread plates have been stacked on top of dinner plates, pudding plates on the left: navy and red geometrics have been paired with lemon yellow peacocks. “I don’t think they quite got it,” Martin half laughs, half sighs, as she begins to lay the table as intended – clashing, but harmoniously so. When you are playing with this much print, everything needs to be in its place. A customer beelines towards a pink silk ankle-length T-shirt dress covered in a 1900s wallpaper print. There are shop assistants within hearing – two, in fact, perhaps drawn over by the sight of 5ft 10in J J casually rearranging their displays – but Martin can’t resist. “Have you seen it in yellow?” she asks, plucking the dress’s yellow velvet sister from another rail. And when the customer emerges from the changing room: “Can you lift your arms? It might be a little small in the shoulder, maybe.” There is no hard sell – but then, Martin, elegant in matching skirt and shirt under a black cardigan, is sales tactic enough. “I love your skirt,” the customer asks. “Do you have it here?” What began in 2015 as a website selling Martin’s collection of vintage clothes and jewellery has come a long way. Realising that she couldn’t make a living from one-offs, she paired up with one of Lake Como’s oldest silk manufacturers, Mantero. “Dior – Mr Christian Dior – was using them, Mr Yves Saint Laurent was using them. Recently, I was in there and I saw reams of Vuitton; but these brands never speak about them. And I found that so sad, especially in light of how much Italy is losing in terms of its artisanship, and all of what they excel in, now that so much of it is being outsourced to Portugal, Romania or China.” Skirt, £535, Minidress, £455, both La Double J. An emphasis on home-grown Milanese talent – from Mantero’s archive prints to the Italian women profiled on the site, women who stood in as models when the company was too poor to afford them – runs through all that Martin does. Which is why it’s surprising that she’s not home-grown herself, but an American: J J stands for Jessica Jane. “I grew up with a hunter fisherman father and an extremely athletic mother, and there was no one in my family that even had a speckle of culture, fashion, beauty, taste – nothing. My brothers… one of my brothers is a professional beach volleyball player. We come from a very different world,” she laughs. Moving from her native Los Angeles to New York, Martin was working in marketing at Calvin Klein when she met Italian Andrea Ciccoli at a party. A year later, she followed him to Milan. “When I first arrived, he [Ciccoli] was like, you can’t eat like that. He’s not very rule-based, but he had this one thing: he taught me how to hold my fork and knife properly. Americans are terrible, I’ve got to tell you. And now when I eat with my family, I have to say, ‘You can’t eat like that!’ I’m glad that he told me, because he’s right. And now, when I watch Lindsay Lohan with her fork and knife…” she laughs. After three months of Italian classes, a chance meeting with Godfrey Deeny, the then European editor at large of Fashion Wire Daily (an early fashion news site), gave Martin her entry into journalism. “Back then, in 2001, the Italians didn’t even have websites. Nobody invited me to anything. It was a very valuable exercise in ego management,” she quips. Martin went on to write for The International Herald Tribune, Harper’s Bazaar USA, and Wallpaper. “It wasn’t until I moved to Italy at age 28 that I really got a proper fashion education. These women would glide by on their bicycles wearing Prada skirts and these perfectly starched white shirts and these little kitten heels and sunglasses, and they looked like they were out of a Fellini movie. I come from Los Angeles, where everyone is walking around from morning to night in their yoga pants, and in Italy, no one is wearing exercise clothes. Ever. No one is exercising.” She laughs. “That’s a downside.” It was the Milanese women’s ability to balance work and home that really struck her, though. “In America I saw women that were total career girls, and their home lives were disasters. But here in Italy, they had these amazing jobs and yet they were obsessed with the house: the aperitivo had to be like this, the table needed to be set like that, the food – they were domestic goddesses as well as corporate warlords.” The last few years have been about finding that balance. Martin now meditates twice a day, she does yoga most mornings – not the aggressive kind she practised in LA, but a calmer, “yin” form. “I go into the office at 12pm, never before. So from the moment I wake up until 12pm, I’m doing my own thing. I had to carve out that time. I quit all the magazines, I’m no longer a journalist. I’m doing this full time, but I make that time for myself.” She shares not only an apartment but an office building with her husband who, five years ago, co-founded The Level Group, which handles the logistics of taking luxury fashion brands online. Martin couldn’t have asked for better help in building her own business, with his in-house creative agency and team of graphic designers within shouting distance. Have they managed to keep their personal and professional lives separate, I ask. “Are you kidding me? It’s totally bled together. We’re an Italian family: screaming at breakfast, kissing at lunch…” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  What does one wear after, arguably, the biggest night in the fashion calendar? The Met Gala. Or the ‘Super Bowl of Fashion,’ as dubbed by Andre Leon Talley. While mere mortals might hibernate in loungewear, the A-listers face paparazzi outside every upmarket New York hotel, and JKF airport. To get home they must pass the photographers, and, in turn, the fashion press, who will once again pass judgement on their outfits. Some, as you may predict, welcome the spotlight. British model Jourdan Dunn was spotted strutting New York’s sidewalks in a moss green Vetements tracksuit and heeled boots (above). Jogging bottoms might not sound like revolutionary hangover attire, but Dunn’s joggers retail for a cool £375. The hoodie from the designer-meets-street brand has already sold out due to its cult status. No wonder Dunn was smiling. Fellow Brit beauty Rosie Huntington-Whiteley was an example of how to elevate casual basics into a pulled-together ensemble. She touched down at LAX airport in a comforting, over-sized Aztec-printed cardigan and skinny black trousers, but added glamour via some suede tasselled booties. With a trophy tote, statement shades and hoop earrings thrown into the mix, the look was more haute than hungover. For others it was a strictly denim day. Brie Larson, Emma Roberts and Jessica Chastain all made their post-Met escape in cosy crew-necks, jeans and trusty flats. Roberts’ kept her halo braid, albeit a slept-on version, in, and Brie Larson scooped up her tired locks into a baker boy cap. This was seriously fuss free fashion, and beauty. It was business as usual for party girl Poppy Delevingne, who celebrated her birthday over lunch with her close contingent of socialites, Alexa Chung, Sienna Miller and Harley Viera Newton. Wearing a classic Bella Freud ‘Ginsberg is God’ crew-neck, and barely a scrap of make-up, Pop-dog, as her friends call her, was the perfect pin-up for dressed-down days when, quite frankly, all you want to do is eat cake and talk about the night before.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  US presidential candidate Hillary Clinton may be canvassing for votes until 2016, but she’s already a clear leader in the fashion stakes. While her style has been subject in the past to harsh criticism (“dowdy” and “matronly”: two of the coldest insults known to fashionkind), times have changed. Now, her style signatures are suddenly popping up on the backs of catwalk show-goers around the world's fashion capitals. There’s a clear case for electing Ms Clinton as a new season style inspiration. Her penchant for pantsuits and bias towards bold colour are all excellent guidelines for our wardrobes, both for this season and beyond. The ex-US Secretary of State has been in the public eye for over two decades, which has given us a wealth of photographic resources for reference points, not to mention helping Clinton to cement a trademark look. Her pantsuit predilection is so famous that it inspired its own Reddit rainbow meme, and at the SS16 shows, a bevy of street style stars suited up à la Clinton. Maybe they wanted to get in on her internet game and go viral themselves? Both Clinton and her street style counterparts have some high-end validation from the likes of Dior and Gucci, whose colourful trouser suits were standout looks for AW15. The suiting trend is in full swing for spring, Versace and Paul and Joe having including them in their next season collections. Yet it’s looking back on the politician’s past that reveals perhaps a more iconic moment, as Lena Dunham discovered when she interviewed Clinton for her latest project, the Lenny e-newsletter. Yes, it turns out Hillary Clinton is an original supporter of the cold-shoulder trend, having selected a Donna Karan cut-out dress for one of her first White House state occasions in 1993. Dunham quickly identified that she could “bust it back out … for a potential inauguration” and indeed, cut-out shoulders are all the rage for spring, appearing at Proenza Schouler, Preen and Louis Vuitton. Clinton hasn’t ruled out a repeat cold-shoulder appearance, noting that “Donna [Karan] always says that no matter your age, your size, your shoulders always look good.” Cate Blanchett has already proved the point, wearing Proenza Schouler straight from the SS16 runway to a screening of her latest film, Truth. Hillary Clinton’s clothing choices have remained consistent yet never boring, despite the clothes-related criticism that, sadly, is one of the perils of being a powerful woman in the public eye. The largely unvarying cut of her pantsuits - longline jacket and straight leg trousers - creates that signature look that all style icons possess in one form or another. And as a potential future President of the United States, Hillary Clinton can save her energy for the important decisions. All she has to do when getting dressed is simply pick what colour pantsuit she feels like today.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Victoria's Secret angels are often presented as other-worldly creatures who can magically shed baby weight in weeks and smile their way through the midnight training sessions that are part of the preparation for the annual underwear show. But this week two Victoria's Secret angels have diverted from the usual 'it's fun to #TrainLikeAnAngel' message, and spoken refreshingly honestly about the pressure of maintaining their perfectly sculpted bodies.  Alessandra Ambrosio famously walked in the Victoria's Secret show in 2008, just three months after giving birth to her daughter, and walked in the show in 2011 when she was two months pregnant. The 34-year-old model has now revealed that she couldn't go through with the rigorous training required to lose baby weight so quickly again. “Your body will never go back to exactly what it was before pregnancy, whatever people tell you," Ambrosio tells The Edit. "It can’t. But I think I have a better body now than before I had kids. It’s partly because I work out, whereas before I didn’t, but also to do with the shape – it just looks more formed now and I feel better about it than I did. Not that it was easy getting back into shape post-pregnancy: after having Anja I only had three months to lose all the weight [before doing the 2008 Victoria’s Secret show] and I was on this 1200-calorie-a-day meal-delivery service that I hated. I couldn’t do that again.”  While there is no implication that the people at Victoria's Secret impose body demands on their models, Ambrosio revealed that there's a certain pressure that comes with knowing that the televised catwalk show was watched by 6.6 million people in the USA alone last year.  “It’s so stressful before the Victoria’s Secret show," she continues. "There’s so much pressure on us all – not just in terms of shape – and the energy gets sucked out of you, so my favorite thing to do afterwards is dance all night long. Yes, we’ll have a pizza party and drink, but I don’t even care that much about the food. It’s about being young, normal and carefree again.” Although Ambrosio reveals she will now drink red wine and eat the occasional chocolate bar, she had to teach herself not to get into an emotional-cycle of eating as it could damage her career. “I’ve been through that stage," she tells The Edit. "It started when I first began making my own money at 15. I’d go to the supermarket and fill my bag with cookies, ice cream and yoghurt: everything sweet you can imagine. And there were times when I would eat a whole packet of cookies. But then I taught myself not to do that, basically by reminding myself how horrible it felt the last time. Oh, and of course I would lose my job, so that was another incentive.”  It's rare for any models to open up so publicly about the work it takes to get their bodies in shape, so Ambrosio's comments are all the more surprising because they come in a week that another former Victoria Secret's angel Erin Heatherton also broke rank. The model told Time magazine that she felt so much pressure to lose weight for the shows that she even considered not eating in the lead up one year. "My last two Victoria's Secret shows, I was told I had to lose weight," she revealed. "I look back like, 'Really?' I was really depressed because I was working so hard and I felt like my body was resisting me. And I got to a point where one night I got home from a workout and I remember staring at my food and thinking maybe I should just not eat." The 27-year-old model, who was a Victoria's Secret Angel between 2010 and 2012,  added: "I realised that I couldn't go out into the world - parading my body and myself in front of all these women who look up to me - and tell them that this is easy and simple and everyone can do this. I'm willing to sacrifice my pride, in a sense, and my privacy because I know that if I don't speak about it, I could be withholding information that would really help women. It hurts too much to keep it in, and that's why I'm not keeping it in now." There's been no official comment from Victoria's Secret on Heatheron's claims. Victoria's Secret angels Candice Swanepoel and Behati Prinsloo are currently both pregnant with due dates in Autumn. Although it's unconfirmed whether they will walk in the show in November, there is certainly a precedent of angels getting pregnant at the same time and giving birth in Autumn, which some have speculated is planned so that they don't have to take a year out from walking in the show. At the 2012 show Adriana Lima walked just eight weeks after having her second child and Lily Aldridge walked four months after giving birth. "We only had five weeks to do it," Lima's trainer previously told Shape. "So we were working out twice a day, seven days a week, for two to three hours per session. We’d start around 9 a.m. and finish the first session around 11 a.m. or 12 noon. Then she’d be back in the gym at 5:30 p.m. or 6 p.m. to put in another couple of hours." When pictures of perfectly-positioned green juices and heavily-filtered workout selfies flood Instagram daily, it's refreshing (if a bit depressing) to hear a few models begin to speak so candidly about the effort it takes to keep their model in shape. And might just make you feel a bit better about that emotional-biscuit-binge you had last night...  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge is visiting three community projects in Edinburgh today, visiting St Catherine's Primary School in Edinburgh with the charity Place2Be, the charity The Art Room, of which she is also a Royal Patron and is attending a tennis workshop with Andy Murray's mother, Judy Murray.  The 34-year-old nearly always taps into the heritage of the place she is visiting with her outfit, so it's not surprising that she wore a kilt to her first appointments of the day. But what is perhaps more surprising is the label she looked to for said kilt: she picked a classic grey houndstooth long skirt by emerging London Fashion Week label with a Scottish heritage, Le Kilt. The 100% British wool skirt, with leather side buckles and a Kilt pin, is currently available for £470 on Le Kilt's website. Le Kilt was only founded in 2014 by Samantha McCoach, whose grandmother was a traditional kilt maker in Scotland for over 40 years. The London fashion Week brand gives traditional kilts a modern update, bringing a punky attitude to heritage tartan. The name comes from the popular 1980s Soho nightclub, Le Kilt. Designer Samantha McCoach said to The Telegraph about Kate wearing one of her pieces: "It feels great, it's fantastic to see the Duchess is supporting young new brands." She added: "This is amazing! I work with a lot of 'made in UK' workshops and factories, as well as British manufacturing and this is a huge support." Samantha says she has had lots of texts and calls: "My grandmother is over the moon." She is a fan of how Kate styled her kilt with a Max Mara coat, adding: "I love Max Mara, I still have an amazing camel Max Mara coat I brought from a charity shop in London whilst studying at the RCA." For her tennis lesson with Judy Murray, Kate changed into aqua Asics Gel Trainer, a white long-sleeved top by Nike and black exercise pants with white trousers down the leg (available on Saks Fifth Avenue) by another new London-based sportswear designer, Monreal London.  Stefani Grosse, Tennis player and former designer at Donna Karan and Calvin Klein, launched Monreal London in 2013, and produces modern tennis outfits with colourful spins on the traditional all-white pleated tennis skirts and dresses.   When the Duchess visited Dundee in October last year she wore another very Scottish outfit: a blue bespoke coat by Scottish designer Christopher Kane. Back in 2010 Kane told WWD that he wished she supported more British designer labels. 'It’s a shame she doesn’t wear more designers. I don’t really like the high street getting so much of the credit. I understand that there would be an array because you need to relate to so many people in the market, but she is a princess. If I were a princess, I’d be like, "Oh yeah, bring it on."'  It looks like she's taken these comments on board by championing two new British-based labels for today's outing.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  A lot has changed since 2001, the year Zoolander was released. Nothing more so than the way in which social media and mobile phones impact our everyday lives. Facebook, Instagram and Twitter were mere twinkles in the eyes of their respective inventors and being able to play Snake on a Nokia 5210 was about as advanced as mobile phones got. Those were the days. Derek, Zoolander’s model protagonist, was leading the way with his really, really, ridiculously tiny flip phone (fictional, of course) and for all we knew, that really was the future. But 14 years on, we now know it wasn’t. Phones have actually got bigger, thinner and exponentially more intelligent and interactive. Oh, and the selfie has become a ‘thing’. A really big ‘thing’. So, it seems only right that such changes are acknowledged in Zoolander 2, the forthcoming sequel to the greatest fashion industry parody ever made. The poster for the new sequel shows Derek and Hansel, his former male model enemy now cohort, pouting into the screens of their palm-sized Samsung phones, surely perfecting a selfie to post to their Instagram accounts. Indeed Ben Stiller, who plays Zoolander, has already harnessed the power of social media to promote the movie during the filming process. In March, he and Owen Wilson, in their guises as Zoolander and Hansel, took to the Valentino catwalk at Paris Fashion Week to film a scene, whipping up a social media frenzy in the process. He’s also started up a Zoolander Instagram page that already boasts over 600,000 followers, so we can rest assured that even if Derek and Hansel are just as dim-witted as before, at least they’ll be great at scoring ‘likes’ - and that's all that really matters these days, isn't it?  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Following today's sad news that Vogue Italia editor Franca Sozzani has passed away aged 66, we revisit an interview which she gave to The Telegraph in 2013 in which she discussed her creative collaborations, her charity work and her fearless approach to life. Of course, the rational part of you knows that fashion magazine editors aren't all pointy elbows, high heels at dawn and preposterous adages. You suspect that in real life Anna Wintour probably isn't the ice queen of popular legend. And yet still it is thrilling to find that the office of Franca Sozzani, the esteemed and influential editor-in-chief of Italian Vogue , is kind of a mess. Neither does it fail to impress that her hair is damp from the shower because it slipped her mind that she would be having her photograph taken. And when she sits down to chat and slides a box of chocolates towards me before leisurely picking out one herself… Well! I mean, she already had me with the messy office. Clichés wiped off the slate immediately, there's something languorous and otherworldly about Sozzani. Or perhaps astute and medieval. I can't decide. Her face is mesmerising: still blue eyes, quiet smile, like a da Vinci. She is 63 and girlishly slim, an impression enhanced by her choice of outfit: a black wool full Chanel skirt to the knee, a cropped wool Dolce & Gabbana jacket, a black top by Comme des Garçons and leopard-print Manolo Blahnik slippers. Accessories are a gold Cartier watch and dangling antique earrings; her hair is loose, legs bare. As behoves her position, Sozzani has her own style down pat. Unlike other editors, she refuses to wear clothes in the season they're designed for. Designers, she says, 'don't even try to dress me like that. 'I'll buy and wear later,' she says,'I mix old and new.' She has YSL shirts from the 1970s that she still wears. Sometimes she'll borrow something from a fashion house for a big event, but the truth is, she says, in her beautifully accented English, 'I like going in the shop to buy. I go shopping. Everywhere. I was in China and I went shopping all the time because I found these young designers who were making something good.' Sozzani, who this month celebrates 25 years at the helm of the most avant-garde of the international Vogue titles, has been quoted as saying that fashion is ridiculous. She clarifies this, smiling. 'It's not that fashion itself is ridiculous. It's the people in fashion who make fashion ridiculous,' she says.' When you look at the front row… Only at the shows you see those people. When [other] women go out and enjoy their life they want to be beautiful, they don't want to be ridiculous. There is no man who wants to be with a ridiculous woman. It's only the fashion crowd. They dress to be portrayed by bloggers and street style [photographers]. It became a fashion to be outrageous. 'We are not celebrities,' she says of herself and her sister editors, who are increasingly found in - sometimes self-propelled into - the spotlight. 'We are people who work as a messenger, to fashion and readers. We should not become our stars. And anyway, if you become [a star] it is because of what you do, not because you dress this way or you wear these glasses or you have this bag. That's not the point.' During her career Sozzani has certainly done more than work a good look. A former philosophy and literature student, she speaks English, French and a smattering of Russian and German, is a recipient of the Légion d'Honneur and a goodwill ambassador for a UN-linked organisation. Her July anniversary issue, photographed by Steven Meisel, will be out this week and, although under wraps when we meet, is guaranteed, as with previous special issues, to warrant collector status. 'It has six different covers and everything you would expect to be on the inside is outside,' she reveals. With a circulation of 120,000, Italian Vogue may not be the powerhouse of the 1.3 million-strong American title but under Sozzani's leadership it has gone from conservative Italian trade-pleaser to a visually arresting, risk-taking title that out-fashions the fashionable. And influences the influencers. Vogue Italia's language is photography. Sozzani has championed photographers now considered the best in the world - Steven Meisel ('For me the fashion photographer, you cannot compare him with anyone else'), Bruce Weber, Peter Lindbergh, Ellen von Unwerth, Paolo Roversi. She discovered many of them when she was editor of Lei , the Italian version of Glamour , and they were unknowns. Meisel was teaching in an art school and had only two pictures. 'One was two guys, the other was a Vespa, but he had something,' she says. It took only a single image by the British photographer Tim Walker. 'It was just a hand on a butterfly net. I thought, "This is amazing." So we start immediately to work. He has made some wonderful stories for us and I think he has become one of the greatest photographers.' Spotting new talent and working with that talent to create boundary-pushing images is what got Sozzani's Vogue noticed. And still does. 'All the magazines can have the same clothes. We go to the same show, with the same models,' she says. 'So if you don't change the point of view, you are just another catalogue. We don't need another catalogue.' In the past 25 years she has created shoots and special issues that have made international headlines: the Black Issue, the Curvy Issue, the Makeover Madness Issue 0f 2006, in which Linda Evangelista's face was wrapped in bandages in a send-up of plastic surgery; various supermodels shot as if in rehab. In each issue you'll usually find something challenging or unsettling. Last month Gisele Bündchen was photographed in various postures that glossily deconstructed the business of a professional beauty. In one picture her face was sprayed with blood as if she'd just undergone a gruesome facial. For Sozzani this isn't about sensationalism but rather recording the times. 'Fashion is not only about a piece of fabric,' she says. 'If you think about all the [fashion] movements we have had in the years, they came from a situation that's social, economical and political. So why should we not reflect our time? The name of Vogue is good but it's not enough. Inside you have to fill it with something that is contemporary so that later on you say, "OK, this was really the 1980s, this was really the 1990s." If you don't, it's like you have the most beautiful house but you put trash inside.' There have been moments that have been unwise. In 2011 Vogue almost undermined all the work of the Black Issue with an online accessories shoot entitled Slave Earrings. And an issue in 2010 after the BP oil spill with the model Kristen McMenamy in oily black clothes was seen by many as crass and exploitative. Maybe sometimes she's gone 'too far', she admits. 'Sometimes, yes, I think I am crazy. Why did I do something like that? But at the same time I do not regret it. When you see that you have made wrong, you just have to go on, to try again.' Besides, she has shown that the quiet lady of fashion has a voice that can reverberate around the world, which no doubt attracted the attention of Fashion 4 Development, the UN-linked organisation for which she is a goodwill ambassador. Sozzani now spends a lot of time in Africa and other countries looking at ways the fashion industry can help. And actually helping. 'They said, "Go around, make awareness." I said, "No, no, no, I want to work. I don't need another honorific name." The point is what you do and what you leave behind.' For one fundraising project, with Lavazza coffee, African designers were commissioned to customise boxes, while another one funded an embroidery school for women in Bali. ('They are paid from the beginning so you don't go to school and then after have a problem of finding employment.') And she has brokered deals with fashion labels such as Pinko, which put in an order with an Ethiopian factory to print and make 30,000 bags. 'That's a big order,' she says. 'People can really work.' She also invites local designers to show in Italy to gain exposure and find new buyers. She finds the work both stimulating and rewarding but also sees it as an act of duty. 'When I started with Fashion 4 Development, the motto was "Giving back is the new luxury". It was exactly perfect for me,' she says. 'I have had so much and now it is time to give back.' Sozzani was raised in Mantua, northern Italy, in a family that prized culture and education above all else. Her mother may have worn Saint Laurent couture but books came first. 'We were all in this mood,' says Sozzani. Her father encouraged Franca and her sister, Carla (who founded the renowned Milan concept store and gallery 10 Corso Como), to go to university. Franca then surprised everyone by getting married immediately after graduating. The relationship lasted just a few months. She only found a job on magazines, she says, 'because I wanted to get divorced'. She worked her way up from Vogue Bambini to, at 29, the editorship of Lei, then, eight years later, the top job at Vogue . It took a long time for her father to approve. 'For him it was like a waste of time. He said it was… You know, when you take care of the wardrobe of somebody?' A valet? 'Yes, he thought that was what I did!' She has never remarried but she has a son, Francesco, who is a photographer in New York. She is now single and lives alone. She describes herself as 'fearless - even in my personal life' and a tough boss. 'Because I am tough with myself. When my son was a child I said, "I work and you study. I don't work, I don't eat. You don't study, you don't eat." You can't be soft with yourself and tough with everyone else. No, I do, you do. We are exactly the same.' Sozzani hates labels and refuses to call herself a feminist. 'I think women are sometimes much more clever than men because we are used to doing many things at the same time - mother, maker, boss, wife. But I don't think that by saying I'm a feminist you change the world. It's by behaving like a feminist. I want to protect other women who can't stand up for themselves. But at the same time it seems a lot of women behave stupidly because they only want to get married and have kids and have a rich man and beautiful clothes. These women do not deserve anything from me.' Never afraid to speak her mind, she was one of the few people publicly to support the disgraced Dior designer John Galliano. She doesn't defend his racist abuse and agrees that he should have been sacked, but now, she says, he should be pardoned. 'I think he paid a very high price. So, I'm a supporter, honestly. Because I think all of us have to have a second possibility in life, and of course he said something awful, something that is not forgivable, but at the same time we cannot kill him.' She does nothing lightly. Not even blogging. Two years ago she started a blog (the only Vogue editor with one) on the vogue.it website on topics from new design talent to the art at the Venice Biennale, which she updates daily. Recently she has written about dreams, a theme to which she often returns. 'I cannot live without dreams,' she says. 'If you have a big dream you can make it. So you have to dream on a big scale. Martin Luther King said that he dreamt one day his kids would be appreciated for their character, their knowledge, not the colour of their skin. Forty years later we have a black president. So you have to think and fight for the big things. The dreams should be huge. Of course you can dream to have a bag,' she says, 'but that's a small dream.'   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Last night, it was announced that Francisco Costa would be leaving his role as womenswear designer at Calvin Klein. It’s all part of a new creative strategy from the owners of the Calvin Klein brand to bring all its collections under the eye of one designer, but also opens the latest chapter in what’s shaping up to be fashion’s year of musical chairs. Since Raf Simons’ departure from Dior and Alber Elbaz's dismissal from Lanvin, the delicate business of matching designers with brands has been a big fashion talking point again.  For the past decade, Costa has designed quietly elegant women’s collections which follow the minimalist spirit famously pioneered by Calvin Klein during the 80s and 90s. After Klein retired in 2003, Costa joined the business from Tom Ford. It’s remarkable that for so long he has been at the helm of one of the best-known names in fashion while remaining relatively under-the-radar. Calvin Klein’s CEO Steve Shiffman also announced that men’s creative director Italo Zucchileli would  be leaving. He thanked  “Francisco and Italo for their unwavering commitment to the Calvin Klein brand and their accomplishments over the past decade. They have both contributed immensely to making Calvin Klein a global leader in the fashion industry, and they have done so with dedication, focus and creativity.” So what does this mean for your wardrobe? “Francisco created these beautiful, icily perfect clothes. I remember Naomi Watts and Saiorse Ronan wearing some sensational dresses recently, but whether we ever saw that vision translated into stores I’m not sure” says The Telegraph’s fashion director, Lisa Armstrong. Calvin Klein’s identity is still firmly rooted in its associations with the pared-back glamour of the 90s. Indeed, many of Costa’s designs have riffed on those silky slip dresses worn by Kate Moss, Gwyneth Paltrow and Carolyn Bessete Kennedy, which have seen such a resurgence lately. Blogger Pernille Teisbaeck was pictured wearing a Calvin Klein slip at Coachella last weekend .  “Calvin and [his wife] Kelly were of an era which was all about that glamorous minimalism and aspiration. It was a great American fashion moment. Women loved Calvin Klein because it was so wearable- and that’s something that’s just as valuable now” says Armstrong. Whoever comes in to replace Costa and Zucchelli has a major opportunity to give that message relevance again. It’s been widely rumoured that former Dior designer Raf Simons might take up the mantle at Calvin Klein (although Shiffman hinted that no announcement will be made any time soon). It’s six months now since he left Dior, for “personal reasons” but whether he would actually want another high-pressured job at a global fashion brand is uncertain. Simons recently lamented the speed of fashion today, telling The Telegraph:  “Everyone is paying attention to the wrong thing in my opinion. There’s this huge debate about ‘Oh my God, should we sell the garments the day after the show or three days after the show or should we tweet it in this way or Instagram it in that way?’… You know, all that kind of bullshit. Will all that stuff still be relevant 30 years from now? I don’t think so. What we should ask is will we have enough creative people who are strong enough and willing to do what is necessary right now to follow that madhouse. Lots of people are starting to question it.” Meanwhile, there is also speculation that 82 year-old Karl Lagerfeld may soon retire at Chanel, with the forthcoming Resort show in Cuba possibly being his last. Hedi Slimane- who left Saint Laurent in March after three years of often controversial revolutionising at the brand- has been linked with the role which, if and when it becomes available, would be one of the biggest jobs in fashion. “There have been rumours about Karl leaving Chanel for years” says Lisa Armstrong, urging caution "but it would be interesting to see what Hedi did with the tweed jacket."  How to sum-up fashion’s complex and fascinating game of musical chairs? A recent post on Vogue international editor Suzy Menkes’ Instagram might help. Quoting Yves Saint Laurent’s partner Pierre Berge, she wrote, "Designers have become like footballers, they go to the highest bidder.” We'll just have to wait and see if Raf is willing to come out of retirement for a new team.      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.   We’re deep into the summer-event season: weddings, garden parties, Wimbledon, post-Brexit make-up friendship dos (too soon?), so it’s worth taking stock of the runners and riders for sartorial inspiration. Whoever decided that “event dressing” should mean a prim dress, matching shoes and handbag and a mesh satellite atop one’s head ought to be exiled (too soon?). But for anyone lost in a sea of pastel occasion wear, it does allow for a paint-by-numbers sort of approach. However, that doesn’t mean that if the mood so takes, you can’t mess around a bit (or even a lot) with this safe, if predictable, formula. The hardest part of getting spruced up for an event is perhaps not even the act of getting dressed; it’s more the perception of pressure from invisible (or not, depending how vocal your friends and family are) fashion police, and that thorny, generation-dependent idea of what is “appropriate”.   Last week, a New Zealand radio station published a picture on its Facebook page of a young woman in a strapless, clinging, Kardashian mini-dress and diamante-fronted stilettos, explaining that on attending a friends’ wedding in said outfit, she’d been pilloried by other women. The question posed was: “Is this dress too short for a wedding?” I’d argue that the length of the stretchy orange, brown and white printed dress was the least of its problems. Yet she had the figure to pull off the unforgiving frock, and obviously felt great in it. Was it appropriate? Perhaps not. It was more of a Saturday-night clubbing outfit. But I’ve seen worse offenders. And I don’t mean skirt lengths. Women at some of the poshest weddings I’ve been to have often looked abysmal, with their feet squashed into mouldy old shoes, a moth-eaten cardigan slung over their back, hair on end and a dress hitched up somewhere around 1986.  The woman in New Zealand had made a serious effort; her fellow guests just didn’t like it. But making an effort is the crux of event-dressing, the aim being to look your shiny, glossy best. People have spent time and money putting on a show for you, the least you can do is brush your hair. This might not always come easily but it shouldn’t be beyond us to add a little polish. The key, is to find your polish. Don’t feel comfortable in a dress? Wear smart, tailored trousers or culottes. Don’t want to wear a hat? You’re not the Queen, no one minds. Can’t walk in heels? Who cares, there are lots of gorgeous, smart flats out there. Don’t want to buy an outfit you’ll wear only once? Don’t. Buy separates rather than a dress and you’ll get maximum use out of them. And if you’re worried about turning up in the same outfit as another guest, wear vintage (williamvintage.com has great posh frocks) or old season (look on theoutnet.com or resale sites such as Vestiairecollective.com or Rebelle.com). Buying something new from a popular high street (or even designer) shop is high risk, but adding your spin to it will ensure you’re at least staking out your own style claim on it. And just think of the “who wore it best” sport you’ll provide for your fellow guests. Altruism is often a great gift.   You know what suits you and you stick to it. You’ve never met a navy jumper you didn’t like. You do a regular replenishment of your Breton tops – which when new, even if they’re from Zara – you know will work for any event. The trick:Mismatched separates. If you only buy similar items in similar colours, you’ll be able to blend your entire wardrobe together, ensuring failsafe – and no brainer - style. Fashion hell: Bright coloured florals. Look out for: Tailoring. A well cut jacket or coat will always bring an outfit together. You’re adept at meshing your own style with that of a dreaded 'dress code.’ Yes you’ll wear a skirt, but with a buttoned-up blouse and flats. The trick:A bright slick of lipstick brings a brilliant contrast to mannish tropes and will always make you look dressed up. Fashion hell: Kitten heels. Look out for: Dark colours. O’Connor’s outfit works because of that gorgeous yellow skirt, if she’d been in navy, while chic, it wouldn’t have had nearly the impact. The cream blouse and shoe are strong balancing neutrals. Your formula is, I love it, therefore I wear it. Seems to work. The trick:Clashing prints. Weirdly, two bold prints almost cancel each other out. It’s a so-wrong-yet-somehow-right approach. Helps if you have an arsenal of classy patterned pieces. Fashion hell: Looking like other people.   Look out for: High street prints. Tricky to get right and dangerously ubiquitous.   Printed skirt, £39.99, H&M; Elysee momentum watch, £200, Watch Shop; Savanna sunglasses, £45, Le Specs; Printed silk cassock top, £192, Maxmara; Block heel, £75, Dune You have a coat to go with every frock, you’ve never met a lawn you couldn’t effectively traverse in a mid-height stiletto and can blow-dry your hair to salon standard. You make gym gear look glossy. The trick:Doing head to toe colour is a Duchess of Cambridge classic. It’s also remarkably easy to do, and will neatly pull you together. Don’t be afraid of:Standing out. The Traditionalist comes into her own at events, this is your moment, seize it. Graciously, obvs. Fashion hell: Mismatched accessories.   Look out for: Anything too fussy. A slim fit coat is far preferable to a pashmina.    Needle & Thread embellished tulle gown, £275, Net-a-Porter; Teardrop fascinator, £35, Accessorize; Clutch bag, £165, Russell & Bromley; Ted Baker suede court heels, £120, ASOS In another life, you’d be on red carpets and a local at the Martinez, as it is, you make do with the neighbours yearly catered BBQ, where you satisfy yourself with everyone’s whispering admiration and declarations of 'You look just like whats’ername off the telly.’ The trick: Bold block colours – that suit you. You know why fuschia works and teal doesn’t. Do a contrasting shoe to amp it up even more. Fashion hell: Grey marl. Look out for: Items with a defined waist and sharp shoulders. Secretly, you’re quite taken with Melania Trump’s wardrobe.   Raey pleated knot shoulder dress, £425, Matches Fashion; Suede t-bar heels, £58, Office; Ring set, £40, Uterque; Clutch, £19, Accessorize You have racks of flowing dresses which you’ll wear to the supermarket with your husband’s jumper pulled over the top, and at weddings with a pair of velvet heels. You don’t really differentiate what you wear between lo-fi and high-level occasions. The trick:Floral maxi dresses can eat you up. Look for ones with slightly lower necklines, or sheer details (wear a slip underneath). Lighter, more flighty fabrics will soften the look. Fashion hell:Power dresses. Look out for: Being mistaken for the psychic entertainment.  Former Elle France fashion director Sophie Fontanel started chronicling her outfits on Instagram by accident. Mid-fashion shoot and frustrated with the mood on set, Fontanel put the clothes on herself and showed the 16-year-old model how to pose - "Be yourself, act natural!" Needless to say, a 52-year-old style star was born.  Fast-forward two years and Fontanel’s selfies have garnered her 69,000 followers on Instagram - and a profile in Vogue. Now brands, she tells The Telegraph, give the Parisian, who is still a fashion journalist, clothes from the showrooms to take home and photograph herself in. “When you do it, we sell it!” labels keep telling her. And are you surprised? A quick scroll through her feed is sartorial inspiration for everyone - whatever your age.  Her style - an eclectic blend of menswear, over-sized vintage shirts, pastel tailoring and a healthy dose of Céline - hasn’t always riffed off the same confident formula. Ten years ago, she tells The Telegraph, she had a wardrobe epiphany, and decided to break away from the simple, largely all-black dress code of peers - “Everyone in the fashion industry in Paris dresses exactly the same!” She started dressing for herself, stopped dying her hair brown and followed her intuition.  Here, Fontanel shares the other style lessons she's learnt along the way... “One day you can wake up and think your body is marvellous. One hour later in front of the mirror you can feel horrible - our opinion fluctuates all the time,” she explains, of keeping a nonchalant approach to getting dressed. "Don’t worry about the details. The most beautiful girl in town will have a lot of troubles.” Think big! “I love big skirts or pants that sit below the waist, and mannish shirts with voluminous sleeves,” says Fontanel, who believes they allow her to belt things differently and experiment with shape and silhouette.  “When you avoid black, you enter a new era of colour,” says Fontanel. “I now love wearing white, baby blue and pastel pink - very soft colours that are the polar opposite of the all-black outfits I wore in my youth.”  “I imagine myself as a mixture of Jackie Kennedy and Clint Eastwood,” the the 54-year-old tells us. “My look can be very feminine but also masculine, with large garments in soft colours.” “The key to all my looks is comfort,” she explains. “But not ‘comfort’ as in I have forgotten my femininity or elegance. If you feel comfortable, it is as if you are naked, and it is sexy! And if you feel sexy then everyone will know you have a good relationship with your clothes and with your body.” “In the below picture I think I look like a nurse!” she laughs of the clinical white palette and starched separates. "Remember not to take fashion too seriously. If I feel too serious, I can start to feel pretentious," she explains.  The striped Ralph Lauren shirt above cost Sophie £2 from a flea market. And that's what makes Sophie love wearing it all the more.  Fontanel has a thing for white shoes, as they make a striking contrast to filthy pavements. Keep them pristine and they will draw the eye immediately down, elongating the legs (see her white Kicker boots above). A leather Valentino skirt over a £5 nightdress? That's the Fontanel way. And, as she puts, it helps her feel a bit better about the fact that the skirt was "extortionate" even in the sale.  "This Valentino skirt can look a little matronly - it’s not very modern, I can seem very old in it," Fontanel says of why she's paired the more formal skirt with a breezy nightdress. Fontanel puts her Gurkee sandals (below) in the washing machine every week to keep them pristine. And that simplicity and practicality is exactly why she recommends the style. “I look like a cow, or perhaps a cowgirl,” Fontanel says of why she wouldn't wear this all ACNE menswear look on a date. Instead, she saves it for experimental friends who appreciate daring dressing.  En route to the Louis Vuitton Cruise show in Rio, her friends told her she would not find a single thing to buy in the city. Fontanel proved them wrong by taking this selfie of her brand new Osklen swimsuit, the best swimwear she has ever found. “When you try on a swimsuit in a fitting room, you feel uncomfortable and you just want to die,” Fontanel says of why you must persevere and have patience when shopping for swimwear. “When I found this Osklen one, it was a breakthrough moment.”  "I wore the below sequinned Sonia Rykiel jacket and nightgown to Cannes, but I was almost not allowed past the red carpet controller into the party - he was hesitating over my nightie!” What swung it? Fontanel says it was the oldest style trick in the book - smiling.  This sequinned look was, in fact, inspired by a vintage photograph of Audrey Hepburn in a Givenchy dress.  The striped shorts in the below picture did not start off life as a pair of striped shorts. In fact they were a pair of Céline trousers. “I saw them in the Cruise lookbook and gasped, they were perfect for me!" she says. "But then I started wearing them, and I did not feel sublime. I felt like I was in costume, it was too much!” As much as it pained her to cut away 80 per cent of the fabric, Fontanel reasoned that it would actually mean she'd wear them. And she does.  “It is very hard to find a good tee,” Fontanel acknowledges. "So stock up! Look for soft fabrics in the right length for your torso, and buy in a myriad of colours." Her punchy yellow tee is from a stall in Argentina. “I like baby blue,” Fontanel tells us. “I found my lover because he was wearing baby blue!” This outfit, she likes, because the heavy-duty black boots undercut the rest of the pale palette.  “I can wear the below Céline dress on the red carpet with heels, or pared down with a jumper/jacket and sandals.” And that's why Fontanel says she was happy to spend money on it.  Deciding that her leather pants were too rock ‘n roll for over 50, Fontanel cut them into a pair of city shorts. The modern cut now shows off her legs, and she wears the flea market buy to dinner with low-block heels. “When you get older, you can still wear ‘young’ clothes, but you have to choose them carefully,” she muses. “I like fresh, playful pieces that are often a little unladylike, like this Mickey Mouse jacket (below), which was £10.” The cheeky Insta snap below is Fontanel’s personal thank you to a friend, who urged her to purchase the leather skirt. “I thought it was old, dirty leather and that the fit wasn’t quite right, but she forced me to buy it!”  As Fontanel puts it: “You can show your body, it is important to be proud of it whatever your age.”    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Though designers flock to dress Olivia Palermo during the international fashion weeks, the American socialite made it clear this weekend that she has a penchant for high street fashion too. Running errands in her native New York, the 30-year-old It girl was spotted wearing an open-neck white cotton poplin Zara shirt with leopard print pocket stitched onto the left hand side. Palermo teamed her loose shirting, which costs just £25.99, with a pair of distressed skinny jeans, yellow pumps and a ladylike, top handle bag. The result was understated, yet punchy, owing to those colour-pop accessories. We could pick out various points of Palermo’s weekend get-up to hone in on - is it OK to wear skinny jeans again? Or, more to the point, distressed skinny jeans? - but it was her leopard print pocket that piqued our interest. With cheetah spots set to be one of the key patterns for autumn, Palermo’s Zara shirt is a chic - and cheap - entry point into the trend. Because, let’s face it, unless Bet Lynch is your style icon, leopard can be a tricky trend to wear. Cotton poplin shirt, £25.99, Zara For Kate Moss and Alexa Chung it’s all about the leopard print coat. For most of us, spending our winter coat budget on a spotty showstopper we’re forced to wear until February is not a decision we can take lightly. Enter Palermo’s micro-leopard solution. The flash of cheetah on her pocket is a nod to the animal print du jour without being overly shouty about it. A pair of leopard print pumps or a handbag would have the same impact, and can be added to plain looks for a touch of pizzazz. Equally, Palermo could throw a navy crew-neck over the top of her tiered shirt and no one would be wiser about the leopard lurking below. Palermo’s high street bargain is also a reminder that you don’t need to dent your credit card balance to buy into the new season trends. Rosamund Pike has continued as she began and side-stepped the ‘tights or bare legs’ question throughout her promo tour, and stuck to trousers for both day and evening engagements. The floor-skimming trouser length is elongating, while the nipped in waist is equally flattering, making this a winning silhouette. The British actress wore a similar style in black two weeks earlier at a BAFTA Breakthrough Brits evening, paired with a pink silk top with navy blue cuffs, proving that the high-waisted, wide-leg trouser looks equally stylish for both day and night. Effortless, pulled-together, as good with a jumper as a silk shirt and, crucially, chic whether you've shaved your legs or not- Pike proves that the tailored, statement trouser is  worth investing in now.  A well-connected friend of the Delevingnes, Jaggers and Princess Beatrice, Nikolai will have known Kate for many years through his mother, Countess Debonnaire von Bismarck. 56-year-old Debbie - as she is known - owns a small fashion boutique in London and Kate is a regular at the parties she throws at her Belgravia mansion. I took a lot of photographs, I painted with them, drank ouzo with them, fired guns with them — I became one of them.”

 The Duchess of Cambridge left Poland this morning, flying to Germany for the second leg of her latest European tour. Throughout the trip so far Kate has been communicating subtle messages via her clothing, and this morning’s coatdress by Catherine Walker & Co. was no exception. The brand is a thoroughly British institution (and one that was adored by Diana, Princess of Wales in her lifetime) but today’s meaning was all in the colour. Berlin Blue, or Prussian Blue, is a pigment that was first developed in Berlin in the early 18th Century, and became the lead colour for the Prussian Army and for other German military uniforms up until the First World War when grey became the staple. The hue is also known as Cornflower Blue - the cornflower becoming a national flower in Germany thanks to tales of Queen Louise of Prussia, who fled Berlin as Napoleon pursued, and hid her children in a field of the flowers. Given that backstory, it seemed appropriate that Kate was surrounded by her children dressed in the same hue as they landed at Berlin's Tegel airport.  If you adjust your set slightly, you may also want to see it as a Royal Blue - a decidedly British hue coined by millers in Somerset, during a contest to make a dress for King George III’s wife, Queen Charlotte, in the late 1700s. The debate as to exactly who can claim the shade as their own rumbles on, but needless to say the Duchess has been diplomatic in ensuring that there is something in there for everyone.   Coordinating her colour palette with her daughter, Princess Charlotte, Kate cut a graphic, streamlined silhouette on the airport runway, something that Catherine Walker & Co. co-founder and head of design, Said Cyrus, has previously told The Telegraph is a key consideration when he designs. “We don’t usually suggest a jacket, as our coatdresses present a single, elongated look which we think is more elegant,” he says. “Our coatdresses are made by skilled tailors and in photographs their strong silhouettes work well at every angle. The most popular styles are our Melrose Coatdress worn with the Florence Dress or the Melrose Dress.” The Duchess has previously worn Cyrus’s Melrose style coatdress on several occasions - perhaps most notably when she commissioned a hybrid version of it, mixed with the also-popular Rosa Coatdress, to wear to a church service celebrating the Queen’s 90th birthday last year. As she lands in Germany there will be plenty more opportunities to make a statement by dressing in labels established in the host nation, or even by adopting colours from the German flag. Don't laugh too hard at that last point - Kate did it in Canada right down to the maple leaves, and the people duly loved it.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
