 Legendary fashion photographer Bill Cunningham died this weekend at the age of 87, after suffering from a stroke earlier this week. The flood of photographs of Bill Cunningham in his signature blue anorak on social media confirms that he is one of the most loved, unifying figures in fashion.  Cunningham worked at The New York Times for 40 years, chronicling what the people of New York wore each day in his style column- 'On The Street.' The original street style photographer became a celebrity himself, described by the The New York Times as a 'living landmark.'  Each season the New York Fashion Week was always flooded with pictures of the photographer smiling behind his Nikon camera, wearing his humble uniform- khakis and a blue anorak. Anna Wintour famously summed up the industry's love of Cunningham by saying, "I have said many times that we all get dressed for Bill." The likes of Rihanna and Anne Hathaway rushed to have a photograph taken with Cunningham, but he never intended on being in the limelight. He wanted to document high society from a distance as a quiet outsider, rather than become a part of that exclusive world. “I’m a zero. I’m a worker in the factory," Cunningham once said about his place in the industry. "I’m like you and everybody else. I’m still enjoying what I do.” Cunningham was intent on remaining elusive and private, and it took eight years for directors to convince him to appear in the 2010 documentary about his work, Bill Cunningham New York. The film (which is currently on Netflix) shows just how serious he was about remaining an austere observer of the extravagant fashion industry. He would never take a glass of water at an event, let alone accept the many invitations he received to sit at the table alongside those stars he photographed. For decades he slept on a camp bed in a small studio above Carnegie Hall, surrounded by filing cabinets storing his negatives. He ate the same $3 breakfast every day, repaired his plastic anorak with tape and continuously tore up the cheques magazines sent him as payment for his work. "You see, if you don't take money they can't tell you what to do, that's the key to the whole thing," he said in the documentary about his simple, and never changing, lifestyle. He photographed everyone from Greta Garbo to Gigi Hadid, but he didn't stop to click just because these people were famous. "I’m not interested in celebrities with their free dresses," he famously said. "Look at the clothes, the cut, the silhouette, the colour. It’s the clothes. Not the celebrity and not the spectacle." In the 40 years he spent snapping the happenings on New York streets from his bicycle, he was documenting shifts in culture and attitudes, as well as hunting for beautiful shoes.  “Fashion is as vital and as interesting today as ever," Cunningham said of the important role fashion plays in society.  "The wider world perceives fashion as frivolity that should be done away with. The point is that fashion is the armour to survive the reality of everyday life. I don’t think you can do away with it. It would be like doing away with civilization." “His company was sought after by the fashion world’s rich and powerful, yet he remained one of the kindest, most gentle and humble people I have ever met,” Arthur Ochs Sulzberger Jr., The New York Times’s publisher has said following the news of his passing. “We have lost a legend, and I am personally heartbroken to have lost a friend.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Victoria Beckham, Anna Wintour and Anya Hindmarch, have all been recognised in the Queen's new years honours list, released today, for their services to fashion. Beckham will receive an OBE, Hindmarch a CBE and Wintour will be receiving her second honor as she is named Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire. The renowned editor is receiving her damehood for her ongoing services to fashion and journalism. A spokesman for the Cabinet Office, told WWD “Anna Wintour has been a tireless advocate for established and emerging designers. In the U.K. alone, she has promoted the careers of such talents as Sarah Burton, John Galliano, Christopher Bailey, Erdem Moralioglu and Christopher Kane”. News of Beckham's accolade was released earlier this week by the Daily Mail, with the singer reportedly telling her family over Christmas. The designer and former Spice Girl is set to be honoured for her contributions to fashion and charity work and is said to be "delighted and humbled for the recognition." In recent years, 42 year-old Beckham has focused most of her time on her fashion labels. She shows her main collection- Victoria Beckham, launched in 2008 - twice a year at New York Fashion Week, always creating one of the pinnacle moments of the event with a front row often dotted with her children (Brooklyn, 17, Romeo, 14, Cruz, 11 and Harper, 5) and husband David. Her own choices for the finale always create talking points, be it her decision to eschew heels for trainers or skinny jeans for ultra wide-legged trousers. Although fashion editors were at first skeptical of a pop star vying to create a credible design label, she has won many over with woman-friendly, fashion-forward collections. "There’s nothing wrong with constructive criticism, and I learn from that and better myself. I’m not expecting anyone to be sycophantic in any way, I never expected that," Beckham told The Telegraph last year. She has seen turnover soar to £34 million, employing more than 150 people at her offices in London and New York. She opened her first store on London's chic yet avant-garde Dover Street in 2014, adding Hong Kong to the portfolio in March this year.   She has also shown a mastery of her different customers, as au fait with the wants of her main line clients as those purchasing from the (slightly)  more affordable Victoria, Victoria Beckham collection which was introduced in 2012. ‘The VVB customer likes to have fun,’ Beckham told The Telegraph in September. ‘Not too much fun – because she also wants to be quite sophisticated and chic and cool. She does like fun prints, but she likes them in sophisticated shapes.’ Beckham is set to add an even more affordable offering to her fashion empire in 2017 thanks to a collaboration with American retailer Target. Going on sale on April 9th, the collection will include 200 items priced between $6 and $70 and will comprise womenswear up to plus sizes as well as kidswear, her first foray into clothes for girls, no doubt inspired by Harper.  "The timing just felt right," Beckham said to Business of Fashion of her decision to launch an affordable collection now. "I’ve made no secret of the fact that I wanted to put a collection out there for people who either can’t afford designer prices or don’t want to pay designer prices.” Beckham also devotes much of her time to charity. In December - with a little help from daughter Harper - she created a T-shirt to raise funds for World AIDS day. She also makes regular trips to visit projects across the globe as part of her role as a UNAIDS ambassador. The source added that: "She is especially thrilled that her philanthropic work as a UNAIDS goodwill ambassador, creating a voice and awareness for women with HIV that suffer prejudice and discrimination has been recognised in this way." In December last year, Beckham visited Ethiopia where she met children living with HIV and Aids. "We have come such a long way in the fight against Aids. Huge global efforts have created proven results, and more and more people are accessing treatment and prevention services. But we are not there yet," she said at the time. 'There are still people being left behind due to gender inequalities, stigma and discrimination and lack of resources.' In October, Beckham took son Brooklyn on a mission to Kenya where they spent three days promoting the cause, visiting newborns and taking part in a football match to raise awareness for a campaign promoting testing.  Victoria is following in the footsteps of husband David who collected his OBE in November 2003.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Only a matter of weeks since her last political protest for junior doctors, Vivienne Westwood and her husband Andreas Kronthaler have stripped down to play Adam and Eve in a surrealist-inspired short film called Trouble in Paradise, in support of the End Ecocide on Earth campaign. An alarming festive message from the queen of punk fashion, the film retells the Biblical tale of Adam and Eve’s expulsion from the Garden of Eden. Only this time, Westwood’s eco-activist leanings come to the fore as they witness their paradise being destroyed by pollution, deforestation, oil spills, and open cast mining, overseen by sinister apple-faced businessmen, as in Belgian artist Rene Magritte’s famous 1946 painting The Son of Man. 74-year-old Westwood wears a white bodysuit with red elbow length gauntlets, and platform boots reminiscent of the ones in which Naomi Campbell infamously fell, while 49-year-old Kronthaler is nude except for a silver fig leaf. The couple were married in 1992 when he was 25 and she was 50, having first met when Austrian-born Kronthaler was Westwood’s student on a fashion course at Vienna School of Applied Arts. They now work and live together: Kronthaler is creative director of the Vivienne Westwood company, and often walks out with her to take a bow at the end of the brand’s catwalk shows. The End Ecocide on Earth campaign aims to get “ecocide” - the large scale destruction of the environment - recognised as an international crime against peace, by proposing an amendment to the Rome Statute which entered into force in 2002. The Rome Statute is the treaty that established the International Criminal Court, which sets out four fundamental international crimes: genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and the crime of aggression. End Ecocide on Earth wants to add ecocide to their list, in order that environmental destruction is taken as seriously and punished as severely as atrocities such as the use of child soldiers, slavery and invading another country. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. It was through a penchant for browsing the shops at the museums where she exhibits her photography work that McCartney first decided that it was time to branch out. “I thought that instead of just selling books (she has a collection of coffee table tomes to her name), we should start to have more merchandise. Like Tracey Emin, who has a great website,” she says. “I started doing tests with scarves but I had so many images that I needed someone to reign me in. A friend of mine introduced me to Ruth Chapman from Matchesfashion.com so she came into my studio and was very inspiring.That gave me a brief.” The McCartney name is, of course, already synonymous with fashion, but Mary’s collection combines style and art in the thoughtful, elevated way that discerning women will appreciate. “I thought about doing flowers or nature but I decided that I wanted to do confident, graphic females- a bit sassy or a bit sexy,” she explains of the series of images- called ‘Body of Work’- which have been taken from her back catalogue and printed onto four square silk scarves and two enormous woven wool options. “It’s only when you hold them flat you see the full picture. I love the idea of someone buying one living with it and wearing it in and then framing it and thinking about the adventures that it went on.” The Dancer in Blue scarf, £385 at Matchesfashion.com McCartney- who counts The Queen, Harry Styles and Rihanna as well as dancer, actors and musicians among the personalities she has shot- maintains that practicality is always her first priority when it comes to getting dressed, whether it’s the jeans and jumpers which she can wear for long days on location, a party outfit which she can wrap up in her bag or mostly wearing flats or wedges so she can walk everywhere. It’s an instinct which she has brought to her scarves, too. “This is the sort of thing I would take on a trip, you can snuggle into it” she notes, holding up a black and white scarf printed with a nude model wearing a flower-strewn straw hat- though your fellow passengers would never know that when it’s wrapped around you,  and therein lies the appeal. The Dress-Up scarf, £1,118 at Matchesfashion.com “I’m not sure what this is the start of,” McCartney admits when I ask if this could be the start of a bigger fashion presence. “I love collaborating and where this has taken me. It’s been really inspiring so as long as it’s like that then I’m totally up for it.” And how about working with her sister? “Yes definitely, we’re always looking for ways to work together.” The Red velvet nude scarf, £385 at Matchesfashion.com Naturally, her family are a rich source of style inspiration for McCartney. She looks back at her mother Linda’s impeccably laidback early 70s look which feels as right now as it did then. “I remember pictures of her in a classic beige raincoat or a camel coat. She was wearing Converse in 1971 but I still wear that look now. I love both my parents’ wardrobes. I have memories of sitting in their wardrobes as a baby, surrounded by platform shoes.” One of her most treasured items is “a lovely fitted black dress made by my sister. It’s just above the knee in a pencil-cut style. That has gone around the world with me. I like anything that holds a memory.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When news first broke that Sports Illustrated's had photographed their oldest model - 56 year old mum of two, Nicola Griffin - for their latest Swimsuit Issue, it seemed the magazine had diversified from their usual hot-young-model-in-next-to-no-clothes fare.  But today has seen the release of pictures of supermodel of the moment Gigi Hadid posing in the water on location in Tahiti in some seriously skimpy swimwear.  "It's my third year doing Sports Illustrated," Gigi has said of the shoot. "When I got the call this year that I was shooting with Yu Tsai, in Tahiti, it was just perfect, there was nothing else I could ask for." Gigi Hadid, Chanel Iman and Lily Aldridge skipped the end of New York Fashion Week, to  promote the latest issue of Sports Illustrated, hitting the red carpet and partaking in meet and greats with the magazine. So how does the Swimsuit Issue, which was first published in 1964, still have ties with the biggest supermodels of the moment? Carole White, co-founder of Premier Model Management, tells The Telegraph: "Rachel Hunter, Tyra Banks, Heidi Klum have all been in Sports Illustrated - it's always been a draw and a big deal for models to do. Cindy Crawford and Stephanie Seymour did it, so they have the ability to get these models because they see the value in it." She continues: "It's a powerful commercial tool for a model - it's the magazine that men and women read so it leads models into big commercial brands once they have done it. Car adverts and cosmetics deals and so on, so it's a big deal for a model." Is a Sports Illustrated cover as important commercially as a Vogue cover? "It is very, very powerful in the United States. If you look at big Vogue girls who have done it over the years, it takes them into a different type of modelling if you like. It's not fashion, but swimwear, so it shows them in a different light. For a model a Vogue cover is the be all and end all, but a Swimsuit Issue is perhaps more powerful because it reaches more people." Carole has seen first hand the impact that a Sports Illustrated cover can have on a model's career. "Our girl Hailey Clauson is one of three cover stars this year and it exposes her massively to the whole world. If you're a newish girl it makes you very well known quite instantly and changes the way people look at you. We will probably get a lot of enquiries about Hailey because of it." Amanda Bretherton, President of Next Models London, agrees the magazine spread drives visibility. "In a similar way to Victoria’s Secret, to be recognised as one of the most beautiful women in the world is always wonderful and obviously the readership opens up these models profiles to a whole new audience. Sports Illustrated celebrates the beauty of women and reaches a wide global audience, that level of exposure can never be ignored." The SI traditionally sells more than a million copies on the newsstands and have over a million followers on social media. And it's success is, in part, because the magazine's concept hasn't changed much since 1964. "It's a funny magazine in a way, because it's almost timeless. It hasn't got an era and hasn't really changed, some of these pictures could have been shot in the 60s. It has stuck to its formula," says Carole. A formula that works for the publishers - and the supermodels it features.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Every year ahead of the Victoria's Secret Show an army of models hashtag pictures of how they are getting in shape with the hashtag #TrainLikeAnAngel. Now former angel Erin Heatherton has opened up about the downside of 'training like an angel,' saying that she felt under so much pressure to lose weight she even considered not eating in the lead up to one of the shows.  "My last two Victoria's Secret shows, I was told I had to lose weight," she revealed in an interview with Time Magazine. "I look back like, 'Really?' I was really depressed because I was working so hard and I felt like my body was resisting me. And I got to a point where one night I got home from a workout and I remember staring at my food and thinking maybe I should just not eat." The 27-year-old model, who was a Victoria's Secret Angel between 2010 and 2012,  added: "I realised that I couldn't go out into the world - parading my body and myself in front of all these women who look up to me - and tell them that this is easy and simple and everyone can do this. I'm willing to sacrifice my pride, in a sense, and my privacy because I know that if I don't speak about it, I could be withholding information that would really help women. It hurts too much to keep it in, and that's why I'm not keeping it in now." There's been no official comment from Victoria's Secret on Heatheron's claims. But it's not the first time the model has talked about struggling with her body image. Earlier this year she wrote an emotional post on Instagram about the pressures to fill the demands of perfectionism. "In my moment of “failure,” I stood in the face of adversity. I was struggling with my body image and the pressures to fulfill the demands of perfectionism upon me. I am not perfect," she wrote. Depressingly demonstrating that even those women with so-called model bodies feel insecure sometimes. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This week it is Haute Couture Fashion Week in Paris, where the likes of Dior, Chanel and Valentino will show some of the most beautiful clothes in the world. It is day four, and so far Celine Dion, Kate Moss, Naomi Campbell and Bella Hadid have already been spotted at the shows. Haute Couture literally translates as 'high sewing', and is the art of dressmaking on a luxurious and grandiose scale. All pieces are made by hand in ateliers in Paris that employ no fewer than twenty staff. See our crib sheet for more on the exclusive, and dreamy, world of couture. 9am (UK time): Maison Margiela 11am (UK time): Elie Saab 1.30pm (UK time): Jean Paul Gaultier 3pm (UK time): Viktor & Rolf 4pm (UK time): Zuhair Murad 5.30pm (UK time): Valentino Follow below for all of the live updates from Couture... The Telegraph's Fashion Director Lisa Armstrong writes about the Valentino show: "This time,  Grazia Chiuri and Pierpaolo Piccioli, her designer partner of more than two decades, teleported their collection to  C15th Rome. The music was Prokofiev’s Romeo and Juliet. This is a place of cardinals and bishops (scarlet, white or black ball dresses partially resembled ecclesiastical surplices), page-boys (leather knee boots worn with a doublet-and-hose inspired gold lace two piece),  flattened bosoms and stomachers, midnight assignations (you never know when a billowing crimson cape  will come in handy) ermine capelets (white mink embellished with tiny black feathers) and gauzy Juliette negligee style dresses. At times it looked a little too literal, although unpicking the historical references is always interesting – those drop shoulders with puffed chiffon inserts were a chic reinterpretation of the Tudor penchant for wearing  pristine white linen shifts underneath heavier over-dresses that were rarely, if ever washed. It will be interesting too, if Chiuri is to depart for Paris, to watch how these two designers, who have worked so closely together for so long, develop apart. There hasn’t been a split like this since Stella McCartney and Phoebe. All eyes will be on both houses as one united force becomes two." Read Lisa's full report here... New details to note were the dramatic ruff collars and cool buckle-up riding boots.  During her time in 10 Downing Street, Samantha Cameron has shown unfailing support for British designers, showcasing up-and-coming names on the world stage and supporting initiatives which help them to build established businesses. And, as a former executive at British accessories and stationery house Smythson with a Vogue deputy editor for a sister, Cameron knows that her fashion choices can carry meaning. So it was something of a no-brainer that she turned to Preen by Thornton Bregazzi for a defining moment in her and husband's lives, the announcement of Cameron's resignation.  For Cameron's speech this morning, in which he announced his plans to resign following the vote for a Brexit, Samantha Cameron wore a sleek coral, duck egg blue and white shift dress with an abstract check print over a botanical background from Preen's Resort 2015 collection. The dress is in line with Preen's design signature, blending modern graphic references with Victorian-inspired details- an offbeat but always elegant combination. It's not the first time she's chosen Preen for a big political moment. After last year's Conservative general election victory, Cameron wore an electric blue A-line dress with a bold black and lime pattern to accompany David to Buckingham Palace. Crucially, both these dresses satisfy Cameron's experimental personal style but in an appropriately sleek way. Neither dress is available to buy now, but an array of similarly flattering yet creative designs are available on their website.  So who are the husband and wife duo behind Cameron's big moment looks? Justin Thornton and Thea Bregazzi hail from Isle of Man where they met as teens before coming to London, training as fashion designers and establishing their label. In the 1990s, their shop in Portobello was a hive of stylish activity which drew the likes of Kate Moss and Cher, drawn to their cool little dresses and drainpipe trousers. Since then they've matured into one of the must-see designer labels at London Fashion Week, selling around the world and creating a diffusion range for Debenhams - Preen/EDITION.  In an interview with The Telegraph earlier this year, Thornton explained Cameron's easygoing approach to choosing her looks. ‘She just rang us and said, “Can I come to the studio and try on a few frocks?”’he recalled. Meanwhile, Bregazzi explained how they create their collections: ‘We just think of our group of friends and what they want [to wear]. Obviously we have some things that are made for the woman with the perfect figure but there’s not many of them, so it’s part of our job to make things for  “real” women as well.’   Thornton also explained their families' attitude to their roles. ‘Sometimes I just think they have no idea what we do’ he said, ‘but when it’s on the cover of the newspaper or a trip like that, they’re really proud.’ No doubt Thornton and Bregazzi's family and friends will be seeing their designs on newspaper front pages the world over tomorrow.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Every line of work comes with its own, industry-specific lingo, and the world of modeling is no different. At Premier Model Management’s office near London’s Drury Lane, the phrases ‘she’s been optioned’, ‘she’s doing an exclusive’ and ‘speak to the mother agent’ are the ones that fly most frequently across the table, as their team of bookers makes the final preparations for the London Fashion Week shows. “You have a first or a second option, which is like the status of a model’s booking,” Annie-Lou Jennings, Premier’s new faces agent, explains of the complicated bartering process that goes on between agents and designers. Until a girl is ‘confirmed’ the deal is not done, and the graded optioning system allows all parties to wriggle out of it should a better offer come along. “A girl might be [tentatively] offered a job, but you could be holding back to see if another one that she went to a casting for comes in, and you can’t commit until you know. It takes a lot of calls and negotiations to make that final decision and everything can change at the last minute.” Why all the back and forth, you might ask? Why don’t the designers just say, ‘that girl looks pretty, let’s go with her’? Every role a model secures comes with high stakes - designers want the hottest line-ups they can afford and, for the models, getting in with the right brands can lead to financial gain and career longevity. “A lot of the job is about strategies,” says Fanny Zakrisson, the agency’s senior women’s agent. “Each girl will have an agent working for her in New York, Milan and Paris, as well as her mother agent, which is usually her home territory and the person who discovered her. All of these [stakeholders] will talk and try to make the best plan for the girl’s career.” For newcomers hoping to make a successful launch into the saturated market, there are two lines of attack. An agent might gun for ‘exclusives’ securing one, special booking with a super-brand to catapult a model into the editors’ consciousness or, the other option, a divide and conquer approach, where you simply aim to get your girl of the moment’s face into as many hot-ticket shows as possible. “The strategy depends on their availability as some girls have commitments with university or other work,” Jennings explains. “We want them to work with as many nice people as possible to build their relationships and experience. And to have a good time and get to do things that they would enjoy - that’s the most rewarding thing.” Premier’s new girl to watch this season is Hannah Motler, a 16 year-old Brit who was scouted by the agency when she was just 12. Motler has spent the last two weeks making her runway debuts in New York, walking for the likes of Victoria Beckham and Marc Jacobs, chaperoned by her mum. “She’s our new superstar,” says Jennings. “She started with Calvin Klein in New York, that was her very first show, and then she’s done Coach, Helmut Lang and more. So fingers crossed she’s going to kill it for the whole season ahead.” Being thrust into the spotlight could be dizzying for someone so young (auditioning for Victoria Beckham must be a surreal experience) and the Premier team is there to coach and develop their talents. “[Hannah] saw David at the show and was really excited,” Zakrisson laughs. “She saw Kendall Jenner arriving backstage at Calvin Klein too, and called me to tell me about it,” adds Jennings. “I just said you’ll be rubbing shoulders with them now, so it’ll be totally normal.” As well as negotiating, the other key skill needed to be a good model agent is an ability to mother someone. The press is constantly plagued with accusations of designers mistreating young models, and managing the health and wellbeing of their charges, as well as setting realistic, achievable work schedules, is of paramount importance to the Premier agents. “I spend a lot of time talking to girls about what to expect and speaking to the mums,” says Jennings. “We’re really proud to nurture and develop the careers of key British models here.” Arguably the agency’s most famous British export is Naomi Campbell. Success for all parties is career longevity and variety. Campbell is now 47 and a bonafide supermodel, but some new starters are just using the opportunity to earn some cash and gain some work experience while they get through university. “Success in the short term is repeat bookings, or after the show the client may be interested in booking her for the lookbook, or studio fittings, or for the advertising campaign,” Zakrisson notes of the endless cycle of work available and the constant stream of jobs to fill. During September’s rush of catwalk shows, agents are expected to be on call around the clock. But they will be well compensated come October. “I switch my phone off when it’s done,” says Jennings. “And we’re each given an official sleep day. I go for a massage and read a book, or stay in bed and watch movies. That’s the best bit of all.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Anna Wintour, the editor-in-chief of American Vogue, has had a busy week. After attending the Met Gala on Monday evening, she was at Buckingham Palace this morning to be made Dame Commander of the order of the British Empire by The Queen.  London- born Wintour was awarded the honour for her services to fashion. It's an award befitting her unrivalled reputation as the most powerful and influential person in the industry. The editrix chose a pale pink Chanel Haute Couture double-breasted coat with a wide belt layered over a sheath dress, in keeping with her precisely defined personal style. Dark glasses, which 67 year-old Wintour is said to have removed shortly before entering the palace's ballroom, and nude Manolo Blahnik sandals offered signature finishing touches to a quintessential Wintour look.  “She couldn’t find where to put the brooch." Wintour said after her meeting with Her Majesty. "I congratulated her on Prince Philip’s service because obviously that’s so remarkable and such an inspiration to us all." She was accompanied to the palace by her 29 year-old daughter Bee Shaffer who recently became engaged to Francesco Carrozzini, the son of Franca Sozzani, the editor of Vogue Italia and Wintour's close friend who died after a battle with cancer last December.  Chanel is one of the select few labels which features heavily in Wintour's carefully curated wardrobe. This is the third time this week that she has worn a design by Karl Lagerfeld, the house's creative director. At the Met Gala on Monday, she opted for a gold-flecked column dress with feathered detailling at the knee. She was in Paris yesterday for Chanel's Cruise show, for which she wore a simple cream tweed dress.  During her 29 years at American Vogue, Wintour has helped to redefine the fashion magazine, ushering in an era of celebrity-centric covers while balancing the demands of creativity and commerce to keep the magazine agenda-setting.  A recent Business of Fashion interview hailed her 'President Wintour'. Beyond the pages of the magazine, Wintour has spearheaded a drive to bring fashion to the wider consciousness, especially through her work on the Met Gala which she has grown to become one of the biggest events on the global social calendar. Each year the event raises millions for the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute  which was recently renamed the Anna Wintour Costume Center in recognition of her momentous contributions.  In 2012, the international rumour mill went into overdrive with speculation that Wintour was to be made America's ambassador to Britain as a reward for her extensive fundraising activities for the Democrats. She was the fourth top donor to Obama's 2012 re-election campaign and was a key proponent of Hillary Clinton's campaign, even taking the unprecedented step of offering her Vogue's official endorsement. Although the ambassador eventually went to Matthew Barzun, it was proof that her influence extends far beyond the world of fashion, where she is relied upon by countless designers and businesspeople as an advisor and sounding board.  No doubt many will be paying tribute to Dame Wintour's unparalleled  contributions as she celebrates over the coming days.      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Posing with her friend, The Clash musician Mick Jones' daughter Stella, they each model a new style of braid, now named in their honour on The Braid Bar’s menu. Kate’s friend Sarah Hiscox founded The Braid Bar with Willa Burton in 2014, and the duo have previously cast other young West London faces including Maddi Waterhouse (sister of Suki Waterhouse), Iris Law (16, daughter of Jude Law and Sadie Frost) and Anaïs Gallagher (17, daughter of Noel Gallagher and Meg Matthews) in their campaigns. Lila Grace is not yet signed to a modelling agency, and her parents had fought hard to keep her out of the public eye while growing up, with pictures of her only being released at Moss’s 2011 wedding to Jamie Hince and on the red carpet at the premiere of Paddington in 2014. She did, however, pose alongside her mother on the cover of Vogue Italia last year, perhaps signalling that she is ready to move into the spotlight. As her mother has now founded her own model agency, it’s possible that Kate could be about to start managing her daughter’s career. So far there are two signings on the Kate Moss Agency's books; Louis Baines and Elfie Reigate (daughter of supermodel-turned-nutritionist Rosemary Ferguson and artist Barry Reigate) both of whom have already appeared in British Vogue.  Like Lila Grace, Kate was also scouted at 14 by Storm models, the agency that she stayed with until she set up her own firm last year. “I felt like I wanted to do things that were more than modelling,” Moss told BoF at the time. “It didn’t matter how much we would try and do it together with them, I was always going to be the little Kate that they’ve known since I was 14. It was like leaving home.” “I don’t want a young girl to feel bad if she has to wait around,” she recently told Vogue of her new role as an agent, and the motherly approach she is taking when looking after her young charges. “I was that person with Steven Meisel, even though I was the face of CK [Calvin Klein] at the time.  It was almost a given that The Duchess of Cambridge would have to succumb to Chanel at some point during her trip to Paris. A Princess in the City of Light, the home of high fashion? How could she resist the capital’s most alluring label? She could not. It came into play not for a glitzy evening reception but for a sedate daytime visit to Les Invalides. The Duchess chose a Chanel striped cotton tweed waisted frock coat with a box pleated skirt and bracelet sleeves in blue and red, to meet WWII veteran soldiers at the military hospital and survivors of the terrorist attacks in Paris and Nice on the second day of the Duke and Duchess’s official short tour of the city. Afterwards they surprised Saturday morning tourists in the city with a visit to the Musee D’Orsay and then posed for a picture-postcard photograph with the Eiffel Tower in the distance. Her black belt bore the luxury brand’s signature interlocked double C, as did the small burgundy quilted leather top-handle bag she carried. She wore burgundy fringed block heeled pumps by Italian brand Tod’s, which Duchess-watchers - and there are many of them - are familiar with from previous outings. She underlined her French luxury statement with a necklace, earrings and watch by Cartier - a jewellery house associated with the Duchess of Windsor, Wallis Simpson. The coat looked like a modified version of a look from Chanel’s 2017 pre-Spring ready-to-wear collection, priced on the website at £8,350. The Duchess has not officially worn Chanel before, although a cream jacket worn in Canada from her personal collection was said to be made by the brand. Today’s choice was met with approval by local media. It was a subtle sartorial homage to the French capital and a diplomatic move on a Royal tour which some have described as a “charm offensive” ahead of the triggering of Article 50 and the beginnings of Brexit negotiations with the European Union. On Friday the Duchess started the tour in British fashion labels, arriving in a Catherine Walker green coat she’d worn earlier in the day to a St Patrick’s day event in England and changing into a black Alexander McQueen sleeveless tweed dress for a reception at the British Embassy, hosted by Her Majesty’s Ambassador to France Patrick Llewellyn and his wife, Lady Anne Llewellyn. The Duchess changed again into a sparkling silver-blue gown by designer Jenny Packham for the black-tie dinner given by the ambassador attended by, amongst others, actresses Kristen Scott-Thomas and Audrey Tatou. Chanel’s long-standing and often outspoken creative director Karl Lagerfeld has in the past described The Duchess with approval but a slight disappointment in the carefulness of her sartorial choices. In the early days of the Royal couple’s marriage he described it as regretfully “right” that the future Queen chose to wear high street and mid-market clothing brands. “People would say they spent too much money, you know?” he said in 2012. “We live in a strange world.” It will perhaps be feeling less so for Monsieur Lagerfield right about now.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Will we ever really know what is running through Ivanka Trump's mind? Yesterday, the First Daughter- who now has an official advisory role in her father's administration- was forced to defend The Donald against accusations that he is unsupportive of women's equality and rights. "He encouraged me and enabled me to thrive. I grew up in a house where there were no barriers to what I could accomplish," Ivanka said, over jeers from the audience.  Meanwhile, many who oppose the President have defended Ivanka, having known her during her years as a businesswoman in New York. “Ivanka has had a long history with the magazine," Vogue editor-in-chief tells The Business of Fashion in an interview, "and I have respect for Ivanka and everything that she has achieved.” With Ivanka maintaining perfect poise despite the seeming contrast of the beliefs in women's rights which she has long campaigned for, and her father's agenda and reputation (a Vanity Fair article this week claimed that he only agreed that Melania could have their son Barron if she snapped back into shape after the birth), her fashion choices become more meaningful. Here we examine seven times she made a style statement, and what it might have meant... At dinner in Berlin last night- hours after facing that jeering audience- Ivanka Trump veered from her usual polished but safely elegant look to experiment with the odd earrings trend which has gripped fashion of late. Her glittering mismatched style were by Marni, but might they have been a not-so-subtle ploy to veer the conversation away from awkward topics and into lighter-hearted areas? Somehow, we're not sure Merkel will have bought it.  When you know you'll be sat on a stage inbetween Angela Merkel and Christine Lagarde, both powerful women on the world stage renowned for their dedication to sharp tailoring, how to set yourself apart? In a look which is a complete antidote of course: when Ivanka appeared at  the W20 summit yesterday, she opted for a floral tea dress. With its Fifties look, it couldn't have been more persuasive of a soft power message. While Ivanka's stepmother Melania has been channelling Jackie Kennedy for many of her First Lady looks, for her first major appearence on the world stage, Ivanka almost curiously seemed to be referencing an era even further beyond that.  Arriving at your father- the President's- Florida mansion for a family weekend/ Republican power summit is hardly your average Friday night activity, but even since her family's extraordinary rise to power Ivanka has often been at pains to emphasise how 'normal' she is via adorable pictures and tales of her young family. Here little son Theodore is balanced sweetly on her hip as she negotiates stepping off the plane. She's having it all- and wearing a skirt from her own label collection, which has seen sales rise by 346% in the first two months of 2017, at the same time. Clever.  What couple with a young family doesn't dream of an evening out, dressed up to the nines and child-free? That's what made this Instagram post by Ivanka Trump on 29th January so strategic in its aspirational messaging. What had passed the couple by though, was the chaos which her father's ban on immigrants from select Muslim countries was at that moment wreaking across the world. The pair had been on communications blackout for the previous 24 hours because they were observing the Sabbath. So what began as a well-meaning vision of youthful glamour became a controversial Marie Antoinette moment. Many even made unfortunate comparisons between Ivanka's $5,000 Carolina Herrera silver dress and the foil blankets which refugees are often given to keep warm in emergency situations. The First Daughter was said to 'feel terrible'.  With its full tulle skirt, delicately beautiful embroidery and  nipped-waist silhouette, the Carolina Herrera ballgown which Ivanka Trump chose for the Inauguration Ball in Janaury conjured  fairytale visions. The message seemed to be that while America may not have a royal family to call its own, Ivanka Trump was more than happy to step into the role of Princess with her handsome Prince at her side and gleaming smile. A classical message of hope which offered a stark contrast to the determinedly modern look of Melania Trump's Herve Pierre column gown.  There were plenty of shots from the Trump family's pre-Inauguration activities but the perfectly composed image chosen by Ivanka for Instagram of her exiting the plane- a vision in green- carried particular meaning. The colour is said to denote peace, renewal, nature and safety, all qualities which the First Daughter- keenly aware of some of the public sentiment surrounding her father's Presidency- will have been keen to show. Leading the way in front of husband Jared and little sister Tiffany, the set-up also places Ivanka front and centre of the Trump family power set up.   Ah, those halcyon days! When Ivanka Trump attended the Forbes Women's Summit in New York in 2015 it was in her capacity as an accomplished businesswoman who happened to be the daughter of Donald Trump, business magnate with rumbling-but-surely-not-serious political ambitions. Her fluted hem pink dress, statement bag and pointy heels were at that time proof of her success in carving out a name for herself as a designer catering to busy working women who wanted to look good easily. Little did she know that just over a year later, her personal brand would bring controversy to her father's presidency and be scandalously endorsed on live television by Kellyanne Conway, counselor to the President. You simply can't predict these things.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Alexa Chung kicked off London AW16 Fashion Week with a party to celebrate her April collaboration with high street retailer M&S. The thrice-crowned style icon invited press eager to see a glimpse of 2016’s hottest tie-up to play air hockey, sip pink fizz and listen to her brother DJ, while models, including herself, sashayed around in the archive-inspired pieces.  Not one to bow out of a fashionable party, Chung, who was named a BFC young style ambassador in 2012,  has subsequently graced Charlotte Dellal’s debut catwalk show, sat front row at designer pal Henry Holland's presentation and stopped by Emilia Wickstead's salon for good measure. Here’s what we can learn from Chung’s LFW wardrobe.... This monochrome lace look - courtesy of Erdem - certainly chimes with the designer’s prairie aesthetic, but could look a little twee for the daytime. Add a roomy trench into the equation and suddenly this works as a transitional look that strikes a high-low balance. Like Alexa, we also call upon ankle boots as an antidote to ladylike dresses. At Marc Jacobs’s Harrods beauty launch, the presenter wore a plain black crew-neck t-shirt underneath her leather mini dress. The same Uniqlo, M&S and Gap tees are probably lurking in your wardrobe too. Such basics allow you to wear skimpier dresses when a) the weather is too chilly to bare your shoulders or b) the occasion does not require such shoulder baring. We estimate Chung’s barely-there nylons to be 15 deniers. This might seem like foreign territory after living in 60 opaques all winter, but hear us out. Semi-translucent tights give more coverage than they might seem, and add subtle shading to legs that have not seen sunlight in months. Plus, we all know it takes a courageous dresser to wear such delicate tights, and who wouldn't want that insouciant look? Yes, that is a velvet waistcoat and trouser pairing below. But don’t gasp in horror! Waistcoats don’t require other dandy foils to accompany - ruffled blouse, smoking pipe - they work as standalone garments. Chung’s own deep blue vest works as as part of an all-in-one look when paired with matching trousers, and gives off a chic Studio 54 vibe. Try for a standout evening look you can guarantee no one else will be wearing. Throw on a mere wisp of a scarf and enjoy a beatnik air to your look. Chung’s velvet, tasseled one amps up the glamour of her velvet base layer and stops her lithe frame from looking washed out in her furry cover-up. A simple black skinny scarf would add the same point of interest and break up outfits.  Open-neck blouses have been banished this winter in favour of preppy pussy-bow styles and shirts channeling a Victoriana aesthetic. Dress down high-neck blouses with denim jeans, as demonstrated by Chung below. Another dandy-esque flourish from the showgoer, who took in Emilia Wickstead's AW16 presentation in a sharp blazer with floral brooch adorning the lapel. A cost effective and crafty way to spruce up jackets already in our wardrobe?  Everything you need to know about the vast collection of priceless Crown Jewels... Most of the present collection dates from Charles II - earlier items were sold or dismantled during the dissolution of the monarchy in 1649. Only four pieces remain from before the English Civil War: three 17th-century swords and a 12th-century spoon. Some historians also believe that a proportion of early Crown Jewels were lost when King John’s baggage train was caught in incoming tides at the Wash in East Anglia in 1216. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Ever since it was announced that Hedi Slimane had left the helm at Saint Laurent, the industry has been guessing about where he will take his rock and roll aesthetic to next. There were whispers that Slimane was working on his own eponymous label, however yesterday he issued a lawyer's letter via Twitter regarding the speculation that he had met with investors. PRESS STATEMENT FROM HEDI SLIMANE'S LAWYER, MAITRE HERVE TEMIME pic.twitter.com/jQ4SySgDKO "For the record, Hedi Slimane has never had in the past, let alone now, the intention or desire to launch a brand under his name," the letter from his legal representative said, "and therefore denies recent rumours (including in WWD) of alleged encounters with investors, in Paris or Doha, where Hedi Slimane has in fact never been." He also thanked the team at Saint Laurent, the designers in the atelier and Yves Saint Laurent's partner Pierre Bergé for their support in his time at the house. The statement reads: "Hedi Slimane wishes to extend a public and vibrant tribute to his entire team, to whom he will be forever grateful and loyal. Hedi Slimane dedicates these four creative and inspiring years to Pierre Bergé." The latest rumour circulating is that Slimane is heading to Chanel to oversee a new menswear division. Karl Lagerfeld is famously a fan of Slimane's work, and this week wore a gold Hedi Slimane for Saint Laurent jacket to  Chanel's show in Cuba. While it is most likely that, like Lady Gaga and Justin Bieber, Lagerfeld is just a fan of Slimane's sequin work, some are reading a lot more into his suit jacket. "Slimane has been studying the Chanel archive and is hard at work on his first menswear collection," sources from within the house tell Fashion Unfiltered. The piece adds: "And with the rumors that Lagerfeld is set to retire, the belief is that Slimane is being groomed to eventually take over design for the women’s collection, too." Lagerfeld, who has been at Chanel since 1982, revealed in a 2004 interview with The Telegraph that he decided to lose six stone to fit into Slimane's tailoring.  He revealed that he "suddenly wanted to wear clothes designed by Hedi Slimane, who used to work for Saint Laurent and now creates the Dior Homme collections. But these fashions, modeled by very, very slim boys, required me to lose at least six of my 16 stone."  But until there is an official word from Chanel or Slimane, let's file this under 'fashion designer rumours to take with a pinch of salt.' © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  As soon as David Cameron announced before last year's general election that he wouldn't seek to serve a third term as  Prime Minister, fashion industry talk soon turned to what Samantha Cameron might do next. During her husband's six years in Downing Street, her own career had taken something of a back seat. Although she continued to consult for British accessories label Smythson, Cameron had stepped back from her role as creative director to focus on charity work and supporting her husband.  That didn't mean her style presence wasn't still keenly felt. She savvily used her high profile position to promote British fashion, wearing homegrown designers for public engagements, attending London Fashion Week, acting as a judge in the BFC/Vogue Fashion Fund contest and hosting receptions at Downing Street for designers and industry insiders.  But once the Camerons departed number 10 in June, rumours began to swirl that Samantha and her aide Isabel Spearman, who formerly worked as a PR for Anya Hindmarch and is a close friend of Samantha's half-sister Flora Astor, would be going into business together with their own fashion collection.  It seems that there is now some firm evidence that a label is on the cards. On 5th October, 'Samantha Cameron Studio Limited' was registered as a private company, with Cameron listed as the company's director. Although the former Prime Minister's wife used to work at Smythson's head office on Bond Street, her new start up is based in the market town of Brigg, North Lincolnshire with a pub and tyre centre for neighbours. It's also near to Normanby Hall, the estate where she grew up, and where her father Sir Reginald Sheffield, has a home. There is no mention on the company registration of Spearman, who set up her own  image consultancy business after leaving No.10 in 2015 and who bore the brunt of the criticism directed at Cameron's resignation honours list when he put her forward to recieve an OBE in the summer.  Cameron - whose sister is Emily Sheffield, the deputy editor of British Vogue - has kept a relatively low profile since her husband's resignation, but was seen on the front row at Burberry's London Fashion Week show alongside two of the most powerful women in British fashion, BFC chairwoman and Net-a-Porter founder Natalie Massenet and BFC chief executive, Caroline Rush. Spearman, meanwhile, had a front row seat at Emilia Wickstead's show. Incidentally, Cameron was wearing a striped dress by Wickstead at Burberry, could those shows of support be a sign that Wickstead - renowned for her ladylike designs - is in on the plan too? During her time in Downing Street, Cameron's style choices were much analysed. She cleverly mixed British design talent like Roksanda Ilincic, Erdem and Preen with high street pieces from Zara, Whistles and Marks and Spencer, honing a way of dressing which seemed to strike the perfect balance between experimental and appropriate, gaining her the admiration of women around the world.  She displayed subtle sartorial wit too when she attended the funeral of Margaret Thatcher wearing a pussy-bow blouse, a style the first female British prime minister had coined as her own. And in May, she sparked debate when she bared her shoulders in St Paul's cathedral in a striped L.K Bennett dress for The Queen's 90th birthday celebrations.  Whether Cameron goes it alone or forms a formidable partnership with Spearman, there's no doubt that women craving a way to tap into her modern, elegant look will be watching closely.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Chitose Abe was in kindergarten all the kids were wearing bell bottoms. 'Since everybody was wearing them, I couldn’t like them,’ she says, with a shrug clearly meant to be interpreted as 'obviously’. 'So I asked my mother to make my trousers very tight.’ A week later one of her friends also turned up at school with skinny trousers. 'I was so upset I ran out of school,’ says Abe. 'I couldn’t stay when my friend had copied me.’   The unique, the exclusive, the inimitable is where it starts and ends for 50-year-old Abe. Over 18 years she has built up her label Sacai, both women’s and menswear, with a look entirely its own. Now sold in the most prestigious stores across the globe (including Selfridges, Dover Street Market and Net-a-Porter), it is applauded by fashion editors and buyers alike. Karl Lagerfeld has said she is one of the most interesting designers working today. The former Comme des Garçons employee, who has been established in Japan since 1998 but only started showing her collection in Paris in 2012, has taken modern wardrobe classics – the shirt, the kilt, the blouse, the biker jacket –  and given them an avant-garde twist. Never has a navy pleated skirt worked so hard to be something more. There are surprises in all her clothes  – inserts of contrasting  fabrics, knife pleats that fan open as you move, splits in seams, backs that fall open, exaggerated ruched waistlines at the backs of dresses. This fusion of statement and elegance that lends Sacai pieces a kind of era-less longevity came two seasons into her label. 'I realised that I always wanted to wear the same kind of clothes – a shirt or a biker jacket or a pair of trousers – but I could make them different, really new,’ she says. 'I wanted to make garments that everybody wears but turn it into something that could be made only by me. That’s when I began to think of this fusion, mixing the garments so they would become special.’ It is two days after Sacai’s autumn/winter 2016 catwalk show and we are in her concrete-floored showroom off a bamboo-planted courtyard, a cavernous space with the new collection lining its sides. At a score of tables in the centre, buyers from legendary boutiques are placing orders. Abe talks through an interpreter but is utterly engaging. She’s a curious mix of tranquillity and mischievous glee (backstage after her shows she squeals and bounces about on her platform sandals), and is fairy-tale beautiful with it – glowing skin, luxuriant hair. She wears a single gold and pearl sculptural earring by Sophie Bille Brahe and, just visible beneath her bandanna, a gold necklace with 'Chitose’ written in a tiny curly script. When she’s thinking of a response to a question she closes her eyes tight, tips up her nose and says, 'Mmmmm,’ until she comes up with an answer. 'I’m just trying to make what I want to wear,’ she says, 'and I always want something new.’ The clothes look complicated and indeed the design and construction are, but Abe puts a lot of time into making sure that they are also comfortable. She tries on everything before the runway show and then again afterwards, before the pieces are produced for retail. 'I try to make the clothes as easy to wear as possible, all without changing the design,’ she says. Abe was born in Nagayo, Japan. Her father designed air-conditioning and her mother was a patissier who taught her daughter to sew. Abe started making clothes for dolls, designed her first dress at 12 and immediately knew she was on to something when an older girl from school asked her where it was from. 'She was upset when she heard I had made it because she knew I was wearing something very special and she wouldn’t be able to find it anywhere,’ she says, still relishing the memory. After fashion college and working for a big textile firm, Abe started as a pattern cutter for Rei Kawakubo’s groundbreaking label, Comme des Garçons. 'Of course I was influenced by [Kawakubo] in a way, but she is not the kind of person who actually teaches people,’ she says. 'But I learnt from her that originality is very important – the originality of design but also the importance of originality in business.’ As a result Abe has kept full, independent ownership of her label. There are rumours that she has been in the mix for high-profile jobs currently vacant at Paris fashion houses. She doesn’t deny it. 'It is not something that I’m not interested in,’ she says in a roundabout way. 'But it’s important who you work with. I would need someone who would truly understand the creativity of the label Sacai and what Sacai would make. But I have been thinking about it.’ Abe is married to another Japanese design sensation, Junichi Abe of the label Kolor, with whom she has an 18-year-old daughter. 'Big girl now. Very same face,’ Abe says in English, beaming. The couple met at Junya Watanabe, which Chitose helped to set up. They have not worked together since and never will, Abe says strictly. They made a rule years ago that they will not talk about their businesses to each other. 'We are both in the same situation so it’s better not to know everything. I really don’t know what he’s up to,’ she says. 'It’s only when I’m doing the laundry and I find his clothes that I have a look and think, “Ah, so this is what his brand is like.”’  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Alexa Chung's first collection with Marks and Spencer launched on April 13th this year, 20,000 pieces had shifted by 4.30pm, with the hero item - the ruffled Harry blouse - sold out by the end of the day. It is no surprise then that Archive by Alexa will be back for another season, with the hope that Alexa will bring her 'fashion' touch to the high street store which has been struggling to find its place on the modern British high street in recent years. Today M&S has confirmed that it has worked with Alexa Chung once again on a 27-piece collection for winter, with Alexa re-imagining looks from the company's archive in Leeds. In a touching addition, all pieces in the line - which will be available to buy from 1st November - will be named after streets in Leeds where M&S was founded in 1884. Alexa's first collection included quintessentially Chung style signatures; think ruffled blouses, printed tea dresses, slip dresses, sugary pastel knitwear, a navy double-breasted jacket and black leather ballet flats. While we will have to wait to see her offering for winter, in an image released today to announce the news Chung wears a halter-neck black polka dot party dress which is presumably vying to be the must-have dress for the Christmas party season . If we could make a fantasy wishlist based on Chung's own winter wardrobe, The Telegraph fashion desk would kindly request the perfect pea coat, patent Chelsea boots and a blanket scarf in the mix.  What we do know, however, is that party dressing is at the heart of this collection. "For this second collection I wanted to focus on a more luxe evening wear vibe to lead us into the winter party season and was thrilled to once again to discover an abundance of inspiration within the Marks & Spencer archive," Chung said in the announcement.   It is a smart move to find inspiration in M&S' 132-year-old archive, as it serves as a stylish reminder of the 'good old days' of the high street brand. "It was so fun to be given the keys to the M&S archive and such a treat to get to cherry pick the very best of their vast collection of pieces,"  Chung told Vogue of working through the M&S archive. "I pulled from stored garments, in-house magazines and TV adverts from various points in the history of Marks & Spencer to create the collection that I believe looks every bit as relevant today as it did then."  The model and TV presenter is the perfect fit for Marks and Spencer. Chung has long honed a reputation as the poster girl for a modern spin on British heritage style, complete with easy but impactful styling flourishes. As well as the popularity of her first collection, she has been responsible for some of the chain's best-selling designs of recent years, including the tan suede midi skirt with oversized pockets which she helped to prove was a wearable nod to the 70s trend . Thr skirt was even credited as one of the reasons behind M&S's first profit rise in four years.  Chung has collaborated with a long list of fashion and beauty brands all looking to tap into her ability to make women shop - this includes successful partnerships with AG Jeans, Madewell, Eyeko and Nails Inc. But this year it has been announced that she is launching her own contemporary label called Alexachung. Although we'll have to wait until May 2017 for the launch, Chung told Business of Fashion “I’m not making something that has got a crazy high price point. I want to make sure its something that is speaking to just everyone on the street.”    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Sitting front row at a Chanel show on a balmy 25 degree evening in Cuba is a tough diary date to dress for. Tilda Swinton, the unflappable Chanel muse and actress, made this gig look like just another ordinary day in the office. The 55-year-old star chose a simple collarless white shirt and satin midi skirt for the occasion. It might not seem like a ground-breaking wardrobe choice (Satin? In heat?!) but Swinton understands the impact of crisp white cotton poplin. Her shirt of choice boasted a simple metallic pin at the nape of the neck and two as the sleeve buttonholes. Apart from these punctuation marks, it was just another starched shirt that could have been from Cos. The beauty of Tilda’s white shirt wearing, however, is how the Bigger Splash star styled it. Or, rather un-styled it. Because sleek shirting should be left alone as the main event on an outfit. Keep it bright, white (we dry clean ours to avoid greying) and an ivory shirt can be a trophy item of a very pulled-together woman. Note how the actress has added a punchy bold rose lip colour into the equation? While accessories add unnecessary distraction, a bright lipstick can take a white shirt from desk-to-dinner. Combined with the shirt price, this makes a very purse-friendly power pairing indeed. Shirts have been in the spotlight of late, thanks to brands such as Palmer // Harding, Joseph and 1205, which have all deconstructed classic tailoring methods and added special flourishes. Relying on a shirt to do the hard work for you is nothing new, however. And we have an unseen archive picture of Audrey Hepburn to prove it. The actress, whose enduring style legacy lives on, was captured behind-the-scenes at the annual film festival wearing a belted white shirt dress. A floppy sun hat is her only accessory. It’s also no coincidence that both Audrey and Tilda have both opted for long-sleeved shirting, which elongates the arms and highlights the wrist area (the daintiest part of a woman). So, as this week’s heatwave takes hold, make sure you have a simple, long-sleeved white shirt in your arsenal. It’s not much to ask, is it?  ‘Gender-neutral’ and ‘gender-blurring’ are the latest buzzwords in fashion. Talking points revolve around designers’ championing of models and campaign stars that have transitioned sexes, while clothing neither aimed specifically at men or women have become a matter of intrigue. But one model hoping to become less of a tokenistic pawn and more of a signal of real change when it comes to attitudes to gender in fashion is Hari Nef. In June last year, Boston-born Nef became the first transgender model to be signed by top modelling agency IMG. Joining the same books as Gisle Bundchen, Gigi Hadid and Chrissy Teigen, interest in the 23-year-old soared and she was interviewed and captured for US Vogue, and starred in a shoot for Swedish retailer & Other Stories, which was entirely put together by transgender creatives. Catwalk appearances at New York Fashion Week followed (for small, forward-thinking brands Eckhaus Latta, Hood by Air and Adam Selman, the eponymous label of Rihanna’s former stylist) as did a role in series two of Amazon TV show Transparent. Nef is now a contributor to acclaimed scriptwriter Lena Dunham’s Lenny e-newsletter, where she recently penned an essay on ‘being a visible member of a marginalized community’, and has struck up a friendship with one of the most powerful men in fashion, Gucci creative director Alessandro Michele. Michele has dressed Nef in his Gucci creations to for various public outings, but yesterday he invited her to take over the brand’s Snapchat account and star in Gucci Milan Fashion Week show – to model menswear , that is. Confused? You shouldn’t be, because as Nef explained to Vogue: “Being a woman is an option, being trans is an option, and they’re options that appeal to me. We need to listen to people, not labels, not semantics.” Michele is somebody clearly not defined by labels; since he took the helm at Gucci a year ago, his catwalk shows have featured models of indeterminate gender and his menswear collections have whipped the fashion team here into a waiting-list frenzy. Nef met the diminutive Italian designer when she requested a dress to wear to the Los Angeles premiere of Transparent – which incidentally, centres on a retired college professor transitioning as a woman – and invited her to have dinner together at the Chateau Marmont, where they hit it off. Yesterday’s red cape coat-clad turn in the Gucci show was a big deal, as it marked Nef’s first major catwalk appearance in Europe. The significance that she was book by a behemoth such as Gucci will have mattered, but that it was a men’s show? Much less so. As she explained to Dazed after the show: “He’s [Michele] a great guy and he sees people, he sees characters...he doesn’t really see a lot of the labels. To work with the team has been a joy. I can genuinely say it’s been amazing.” Here’s hoping that Nef’s refreshing outlook on labelling proves to be more than a one-season wonder with the industry’s tastemakers.         © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The fashion world is paying tribute to Anna Harvey, the former Vogue editor, Telegraph columnist and the woman who helped to shape the style of Diana, Princess of Wales.... I started working with Anna when I returned to London in 1985 to edit British Vogue. It was a moment of tumultuous change there; Beatrix Miller, the long-standing and beloved editor, had retired, and I turned up from New York, with a very American get it done attitude, and a staff with a very English way of doing things. Anna, blessed with the most impeccable manners, was incredibly welcoming: kind and generous and once you got past her reserve, revealed that wonderfully dry and self deprecating sense of humor of hers. British Vogue then, like all magazines, had plenty of larger than life personalities. Yet Anna was Vogue’s ballast, calm and respectful with everyone she worked with, and in everything she did. (It might have been not longer after I arrived that she let an up-and-coming photographer called Steven Meisel sleep on her floor when he shot for the magazine). And with all people like that, she became Vogue’s centre of gravity, the person everyone - myself included - would turn to for advice and help. It’s that, just as much as her considerable talents as a sittings editor, that I will fondly remember her for. Read more: Anna Harvey's fashion life, from Vogue to Princess Diana I first worked with Anna as a model.  I tried to walk out when I realised it was a lingerie sitting. The photographer was Henry Clarke but I thought I was too grand, although I wasn’t. Anna was the last person in the world to try and sneak up on someone and force them to do something.  The pictures were gentle and beautiful as befits her style. Later, we worked together as fashion editors at Vogue. Her shoots were classic and timeless, she got on with her job without making a fuss about how fabulous she was- that’s very unusual in this business. Anna was not avant-garde but she recognized talent when she saw it.  I remember her bringing Steven Meisel into the office. I thought, “Oh my God what’s that?" of all that black eye make up he was wearing! She was always very self-deprecating almost not believing in how good she was but she really was tireless  For years, any time I did anything and she read about it she would be in touch and congratulate me, I always found that incredibly touching the way she thought of others. She was never really given credit for all the amazing things she did. Most people these days do little and want credit and fame but she did everything quietly and it never occurred to her to seek fame from it. She behaved with. absolute grace. She will be missed. Without Anna, I wouldn’t be where I am today – she contributed greatly to my career in so many ways. Modest and so generous with her constant advice.  However, also graceful, patient and bestowed with a natural elegance.  A very dear and loyal friend, I will miss her forever.  I remember being on a shoot with Patrick Demarchelier for Versace with Christy Turlington in Paris. She was wearing a pale blue figure hugging sequin dress. Turlington said, “this would look great on Diana because she looks so fit these days”.  I took a polaroid and showed it to Diana. She loved it but foreign courtiers were an unknown to her.  It was at the time Diana was changing into the power woman she was to become in the Nineties. I showed it to Anna who said in her typical low key fashion “leave it with me”. Anna set up a meeting with Donatella and that was the beginning of Diana’s relationship with the Versaces.  She was steadfast in her support of the British designers. Everything else at the time was more marvellous- America, Milan and Paris. We were cottage industries in comparison.  But Anna championed us over the years. In this this business, you have your highs and your lows, some turn their back and she never did. As a person, as a professional, she was magnificent.  Anna gave me my second ever shoot on British Vogue. It was around 1984. We were in Paris and it was a hat story. Anna was wearing a pink Chanel suit, I remember her sitting looking so chic and elegant on a sofa in the studio. Camilla Nickerson (now Senior fashion editor at US Vogue) was her assistant. It really struck me at the time that she was so encouraging of Camilla, letting her take the reins. I was a new young photographer and to see someone behave in such a generous way, to be a real mentor was very inspiring to me. I have never forgotten it. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Ivanka Trump’s fashion line has responded to its recent controversies with defiance; sharing that this February was in fact its most successful month on record. Being dropped by major US department stores Neiman Marcus, Nordstrom and Bergdorf Goodman, has clearly not affected sales in the way that many thought it would, and company president Abigail Klem has described the Ivanka Trump Collection as a “top performer” for the retailers that still stock the brand. “For several different retailers Ivanka Trump was a top performer online,” Klem tells Refinery29. “And in some of the categories it was the [brand’s] best performance ever.” Further analysis by multibrand e-tailer Lyst confirms Klem’s comments, explaining that this February saw a huge recovery for the brand. “During the month of February the Ivanka Trump brand sold the 11th most individual items on Lyst,” a representative tells us. “However, in January 2017 the brand was 550 in order count, showing an incredible sales increase of 346 per cent from January to February.” “If you compare February to Ivanka Trump's average orders in 2016, the brand sales increased 557 per cent.” So what has prompted the exponential February growth? In theory, Ivanka has actually distanced herself from the label. Ivanka’s line experienced some backlash when Donald Trump was first elected, as audiences boycotted her products in the #GrabYourWallet campaign, which encouraged people to avoid buying any merchandise associated with the Trumps, in protest of the President’s ‘pussy-grabbing’ comments. The First Daughter’s ethics were also questioned when she, having taken on a new political role, began to regularly wear and promote products from her collection in television interviews. Accused of cashing in on the Presidency, Ivanka felt the best action was to take a leave of absence from her company,  a brand that she had built into a $100 million lifestyle empire off the back of a 2007 fine jewellery franchise deal. The First Daughter's brand name was in the press even more frequently in February, as polarising Trump campaign manager Kellyanne Conway plugged the fashion line on national television, telling Fox & Friends viewers to “Go buy Ivanka’s stuff,” in a "free commercial" that violated government ethics. “We are proud that our business is growing rapidly and that our brand resonates strongly with women who are inspired by our messaging,” Abigail Klem told us back in November, just after the election. ‘Over the past year many more women have discovered and become loyal to the brand, leading us to experience a significant year over year revenue growth.’ Despite Ivanka's supposed separation from her namesake label, she has still frequently been seen wearing pieces from the collection. She’s worn everything from a $89 skirt, to $135 black heels, to $2,900 earrings from her fine jewellery label, at high profile events in the last few weeks. As First Daughter, her fashion choices are closely watched and gain huge worldwide exposure. As  fans see more and more of her polished style, they may want to buy into it again.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Now you see it, now you don’t! Kate Bosworth’s ‘hip’ handbag went incognito last night, blending into her torso and all-black ensemble. “All about the hip belt,” the actress Insta-reported of her outfit choice to the Target Who What Wear launch, and, dare we say, Bosworth is right. The bum bag has been making waves on the fashion scene for a while. No longer the favoured compartment of excitable tourists eager to go hands-free, the fanny pack has received a sleek makeover at the hands of British high street brand Whistles, and design houses Marni, Chloé and Gucci. And if Gucci is doing it, you can expect everyone else to follow. Top to bottom: Gucci Dionysius hip bag, £900, Net-a-Porter; Marni embellished leather belt bag, £800, Net-a-Porter How to wear the hip-hugger? Take a tip from Bosworth’s monotone look and let your bum bag sit against a top, dress or trouser of the same colour. Black, as Bosworth shows, is an easy entry point, and you will likely have numerous black garments to act as the backdrop already. Top to bottom: Baby rider bum bag, £207, Loeffler Randal; Bleecker leather bum bag, £95, Whistles Once you have worked out the proportions (how it fits under your coat, taking it off and on in the bathroom) branch out into camel hues, which will look understated and chic against light camel knits in spring.  Shoe entrepreneur Tamara Mellon has filed for bankruptcy. WWD reports that New York-based Mellon has filed for Chapter 11 of the bankruptcy code, which means that she is entering a re-organisation plan for her business. The 48-year-old launched her eponymous accessories label in 2013 after co-founding luxury shoe label Jimmy Choo. Her designs are stocked at Net-a-Porter.com and include ready-to-wear pieces as well as shoes and handbags. But this type of bankruptcy doesn’t signal the end for Mellon; Chapter 11 is a very specific code used when a business is unable to pay its creditors. It is used as a form of bankruptcy protection, and can be applied to individuals as well as business. Rapper 50 Cent, real name Curtis Jackson, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy earlier this summer, enabling him to create a plan to pay his debts and how much of them he is able to pay. London-born Mellon worked as accessories editor at British Vogue before setting up a business with bespoke shoe-maker Jimmy Choo in the mid-1990s. She helped grow the brand into a household name, giving it a presence in luxury boutiques around the world. Choo sold his share to a luxury holdings company in 2001 and the brand was subsequently acquired by several private equity firms. Mellon walked away with an £85m fortune in 2011. She documented her tumultuous life in business in her 2013 memoir, In My Shoes. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
