 Poised on high black stilettos, in navy trousers and luxurious ivory satin shirt, tamarillo-red coat (all own brand obviously) draped from her shoulders like a cloak, Stella McCartney is posing by a giant coat of arms, surrounded respectfully by a flock of young British Olympians. Presenting her new kit collection for Team GB, ahead of Rio 2016, which begins in 100 days' time, McCartney is so imperious - like a modern-day Calpurnia - that it seems utterly appropriate she is flanked by stars like Jessica Ennis-Hill, Olivia Breen, Alistair and Jonathan Brownlee, and Laura Trott, forming a sort of trainer-wearing Praetorian Guard. Indeed McCartney’s regal presence even draws the eye away from the nation’s favourite diver Tom Daley.  And this despite Daley being clad in trunks which are as teeny on the hanger as off, measuring about two inches at their shortest seam (causing him to remark yes ‘my trunks are quite small’) Yet if McCartney has segued easily from Queen of Fashion to Queen of the Olympics, she is quite down-to-earth in the flesh, touchingly concerned how her designs for Team GB will be received. ‘’It is so hard to really read people’s reactions,’’ she says, backstage, sipping water, and laughing. ‘’Hopefully, they will be polite to me. ‘’I worry about what the athletes think of course, but that goes hand to hand with what the nation thinks.’’  In 2012, initial reaction to her first Olympic kit was mixed, with some of the public taking exception to the lack of red in the union flag design and muttering about Too Much Grey. This time round, the designs already seem to be more popular, and - in case you’re worried - there is plenty of red, white and blue. The only grey in the range seems to be reserved for a vest top - which is so baby-bottom soft that no-one will care about the hue. Certainly not our Olympians who seem to be hugely enthusiastic about all their new gear. McCartney admits: ‘‘They love it; they tell me they feel time and love and consideration has gone into it, and they appreciate that the fit is even better.’’ One of the challenges of the new kit was that sponsors Adidas were aiming to make it 10 per cent lighter than before, so there were strange new fabrics to incorporate. But McCartney was also keen it would fulfil other requests, like allowing the women athletes to feel more feminine. Most teams, she explains, have a unisex uniform, but she wanted to design clothes that flattered and had a slim fit for women where appropriate. This ties in with McCartney's signature pared-back but wearable designs for her catwalk collections, which are driven she explains by a desire to serve and connect with the women who are her customers. ‘‘These are the things I bring to the occasion,’’ says the designer. ‘’I fight the athletes’ corner. I want the best quality fabrics, but also insist on little details like two way zips. You are tightly governed by what various sport governing bodies allow, but I try to navigate around that so make the athletes feel better. You have to find a balance.’’  Browsing the rails, this means a classy dark blue swimming costume for sprinting past Australians, bright patriotic tracksuits for rostrum duty, but also a cosy Onesie for trawling the athletes’ village when you are too happy to sleep. How did McCartney find new inspiration this time round? ‘’I felt it was really important to create a coat of arms to draw on our heritage, something we could gift to the British Olympic Association and British Paralympic Association.’’ The armourial design is deliberately focused on unifying the nation with its entwining national flowers from the different countries, and paired blue and red lions rampant, joining up the Olympic and Paralympic teams.  The gold, silver and bronze medals on top represent the past as well as future intentions. The coat of arms - sometimes in outline, sometimes blocked in - is present across the Kit, but the union flag is everywhere too, and the letters GB more graphic and bold than formerly. ‘’I wanted to make it sporty and bold, to dissect the various elements and spread them across some items, and then bring them back together for others.’’ She adds: ‘’There were so many points of inspiration - I really wanted to deliver on my role.  The Olympics is so special; it brings us together as a nation.’’  Working with 600 athletes, some have inevitably become friends, although she resolutely will not tell The Telegraph who she likes best. Sounding a little like Sir Bruce Forsyth, she says ‘‘They are all my favourites’’. Although she does let slip that she misses retired Olympians Victoria Pendleton and Chris Hoy.  Does she feel maternal towards the young competitors at their first Games? "Some are babies, with their futures still to be determined, cooking up something for the next time.  ‘’But I do feel an emotional connection to those doing it again.  You can’t help but feel proud of them, especially when you learn how hard they train and some of them with little funding in God knows what conditions.’’ So, utilising a magic wand, what would be her Olympic discipline? ‘’Ooh, equestrian, no, swimming - no equestrian, definitely - a bit of dressage. Actually I’d love to do most of them - rowing, even javelin. Though perhaps not discus. I’m not sure that would be my thing.’’ She laughs and mocks holding a heavy object under her chin. What sport does she actually enjoy?  ‘’I do a bit of everything. I ride, I swim, run, dance, do a bit of yoga, pilates, so I am active, But not like these guys, my mind doesn’t work the same way. ‘’So it is fascinating to get into their way of thinking. One of the female athletes - she blows me away by how she fine tunes her body. She has this connection between mind and body, so she can feel the slightest change in a muscle in her ankle. ‘’Now this is not how I work. But when I walk into a room, I might notice a tiny speck of blue tack in the highest corner of the room. My visual mind is different to most people’s.’’ I’m not sure she is as different to the Olympians as she protests. McCartney, 44, is notorious for being a hard worker and for pole-vault-high standards - probably as much as any gold medallist. Even the room in which we meet, a cordoned off section of a municipal sports centre, has been carefully dressed - with a pale blue sofa and chair, a white fluffy rug and a scented candle. In a profession noted for obsessives, McCartney has a name for being the perfectionist’s perfectionist. How then, given that apart from running her global eponymous fashion brand, she is also mother to two girls and two boys with husband Hunter creative director Alasdhair Willis, does McCartney keep her cool? ‘‘It’s about finding that balance between work, family, and self,’’ she says, before insisting, ‘’But I don’t always tick those boxes. I do meditate - but I’m not really at 20-minutes-a-day of TM [transcendental meditation], I’m not there yet.’’ Perhaps she is more lenient with herself than first appears - "My mum used to say - and this really resonates with me: ‘It’s allowed.’ "So I think: I don’t meditate for 20 mins twice a day? It’s allowed. It’s allowed to feel stressed. It’s allowed to feel sad. You are allowed to let yourself off the hook.’’ Although, not - if you are called Jessica, Olivia, Jonathan or Tom - until September. Please.  The Head of Lower School at Thomas's Battersea, Helen Haslem, was thrown into the spotlight this morning as she the greeted Prince George- third in line to the throne- for his first day at school. In the weeks leading up to the big event there has been much fashion chatter about what her new pupil’s mother, the Duchess of Cambridge, might choose to wear on her first run to the school gates and how exactly she might fit in with the SW11 set. What Haslem perhaps hadn’t anticipated though, was that Kate’s loyal fashion followers would be out to analyse the outfit that she had chosen for the big day too. And in the end, it was her look which gleaned the most style analysis after Kate was forced to stay at home, suffering from severe morning sickness. The teacher wore a soft pink, knee length dress for the occasion - granted not a look that may be suitable for a day of finger painting and glitter throwing, but one that looked smart and approachable all the same. Making an impression on both new parents and new students is undoubtedly vital on the first day back, especially when the former is paying upwards of £7,000 per term for their child to be there. Commentators were, however, quick to point out the similarities between Haslem’s choice of silhouette and hue, with those favoured by the Duchess of Cambridge. Blogs like What Kate Wore identified the dress as being a £250 'Amana’ style from one of Kate’s favourite British brands L.K. Bennett. Does it matter what the teacher wore? Probably not in the grand scheme of things and perhaps tomorrow she’ll be in suede elbow patches, tweeds and every other sartorial cliche that has ever plagued the education system.  You will never find Queen Elizabeth following a trend but, as our forensic analysis of the looks from the latest catwalks shows, she is certainly responsible for setting a few. As Her Majesty approaches her 90th birthday, it seems that her carefully considered, traditionally British and always jolly approach to dressing has proved highly influential on the AW16 collections which will shape what we wear next autumn.  Given that the Queen has been in the global spotlight for the majority of her adult life, it’s hardly surprising that her unwavering sense of style has become iconic. As an article in Time magazine put it last year: “The Queen doesn’t have to change to keep up with the times. If she just stays as she is, the times will circle back to her.” In her official duties, Her Majesty is known for choosing bright colours which she wears head-to-toe so that she can be seen from far away or picked out easily in a crowd. This way of dressing is often seen as tricky or overpowering for those of us without plaque-unveiling responsibilities. However at Chanel, where Karl Lagerfeld showed numerous all-pink looks, and Gucci, where a bold turquoise outfit stood out, the suggestion was that now might be the moment to adopt the one-colour approach the Queen’s been pioneering for years. When she’s not cutting ribbons or hosting state banquets, her Majesty is renowned for being very much your classic British gentlewoman. She apparently loves nothing more than a good horse show or bracing walk with the corgis. This outdoorsy life requires a sturdy rainproof trench coat, just the sort of thing, in fact, which Phoebe Philo showed in various guises from sleeveless to loosely relaxed at Celine. Meanwhile, Christopher Bailey, who is renowned for his devotion to all things British at Burberry, created cosy tartan coats reminiscent of those favoured by the Queen for church. There was a lot of talk this fashion month about “everyday” clothes thanks to the rise and rise of Vetements (the label named after the word for “clothes” in French) and its lead designer, Demna Gvasalia who also made his Balenciaga debut. The first series of looks he presented looked like awkwardised versions of what one imagines Her Majesty wears on a normal day of summering at Balmoral - think demure houndstooth blazers with matching midi skirts and dresses. Who knew the sensibilities of a Georgian sportswear and denim-obsessed provocateur (that’s designer Demna) could have so much in common with those of the British monarch? Elsewhere designers riffed off the Queen’s reputation for topping off her off-duty outfits with a silk scarf, carefully knotted under the chin. This exact styling trick also appeared at Mary Katrantzou while Christopher Kane showed plastic versions which he said were inspired by his mum. Even Her Majesty’s more unusual and grand style inclinations - the things which come with the job - popped up at numerous shows. Various spins on regimental coats, complete with frogging details, were seen at Sacai, Christopher Raeburn and Dolce & Gabbana; all might have originated from pictures of the Queen back when she used to participate in the Trooping of the Colour, decked out in the ceremonial uniform of whichever regiment was being trooped. Meanwhile, gloves - a favourite of the queen throughout her reign - were a key accessory at Oscar de la Renta, Simone Rocha, House of Holland and many more. There were also looks which seemed to hark back to moments early in the Queen’s life such as Molly Goddard’s frothy tulle creation which was like an exaggerated interpretation of the gowns she wore during in the 1950s while Miu Miu’s tweeds and frills - a pair of plus-fours in particular - reminded the audience of images of a young Princess Elizabeth. And why not? Influencing a whole fashion season does seem a rather fabulous way to kick off your 90th birthday celebrations. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  So far on the Canadian royal tour, the Duchess of Cambridge has championed homegrown fashion talent in a colour scheme that nods to her guest nation, but for today's occasion she shifted gear: in a bottle green dress by Italian designer Dolce & Gabbana.  On the fourth day of engagements the mother-of-two touched down at the British Columbian airport of Kelowna wearing the Dolce dress cut from smooth stretch-crepe. The form-skimming  midi featured a ladylike bow at the neck and gold-acetate buttons to draw the eye down to the elegant cinched-waist detail. Like many of Kate’s looks, such as the Alexander McQueen day dress worn in Vancouver earlier this week, her Dolce & Gabbana dress is bespoke. The original, which appeared in the Milan Fashion Week brand’s AW16 collection, features a pocket watch motif embroidered onto the right chest. It is currently on sale at Matches Fashion retailing at £2,150. Kate’s dress comes without the Alice in Wonderland reference, but keeps the ruched shoulders and other feminine accents.  The Royal couple were in Kelowna to visit the University of British Columbia, where Kate and Prince William witnessed a volley ball demonstration - which perhaps made her glamorous outfit a touch surprising to seasoned Kate fashion-watchers. After all, in October 2013 the Duchess made her first solo public appearance following the birth of Prince George at an Olympic Park volley ball match for SportsAid, a youth organisation of which she is a patron, wearing slim-cut J Brand jeans, a Ralph Lauren Breton T-shirt, Smythe blazer and Russell & Bromley wedges. But in Canada there was no sign of sporty Kate joining the athletes on the pitch to make some spirited shots over the net. Instead, she looked regal in one of her go-to designers for polished, classic occasion dressing.  The Duchess has worn Dolce & Gabbana's signature long-sleeved lace dresses on a handful of occasions, including the Chinese state visit to London in October 2015, and the Festival of Remembrance in November 2015. It is the white lace Dolce dress that the Duchess wore to this summer’s Royal Ascot racing event that is perhaps most memorable though. The long white romantic dress, paired with dramatic hat, conjured up the famous My Fair Lady scene in which Audrey Hepburn’s Eliza Doolittle attends the races for the first time. “We are big fans of the Duchess Kate," Domenico Dolce and Stefano Gabbana have told The Telegraph of seeing The Duchess in her designs. "To us it is a great honour to see her wearing our clothes.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  If any further proof was needed that Cressida Bonas’s transformation from Prince Harry-dating aristocrat to high-end fashion plate is complete, her latest shoot should do just the trick. Bonas, 26, became tabloid fodder when she began dating the heir to the throne 2012. But the photogenic blonde and the Prince split amicably in 2014 – despite rumours of an engagement, and since then she’s been free to spread her wings freely and further her acting and dance career, and develop a passion for fashion. A new addition on the London party circuit, Bonas has been the guest at Topshop and Dior fashion shows and on the guest list for a recent Chanel soiree in the capital, all while dripping in each label’s wares. She’s also showed off her dance talent in a video for Mulberry and appeared on the cover of Miss Vogue. Now our friends across the Channel are taking note of Miss Bonas’ style credentials, with French style magazine Jalouse giving her its seal of approval by styling her and featuring her as its cover star. The fashion bible’s cover line pronounces: ‘Cressida Bonas, the girl who said no to Buckingham Palace and yes to Hollywood’. Inside, she models key pieces for the new season by the likes of Miu Miu, Dior, Gucci and Carven with a decidedly Sixties twist, picked by the magazine’s fashion editor, Helena Tejedor. Photographer Piczo captured the professionally-trained dancer in a variety of playful poses; in one image she cradles an inflatable hand while in another she looks studios in spectacles as she sips from a straw. The publication was clearly taken with its new ingenue, writing on the cover: “She is 26 years old, with a dancer’s grace and a crazy magnetism with the camera, be it that of a photographer or a film director. But, what is striking with Bonas is her paradoxes: those of a young, shy aristocrat who braved the flashbulbs during her relationship with Prince Harry in the same way that today she braves the world by choosing an acting career on the demanding stage of the West End or in Hollywood.” Bonas has three films set for release in 2016, the first being Tulip Fever, which co-stars Cara model-turned-actress Delevingne.  It is 11am on a cracker of an October day in the Derbyshire Dales. The hills are rolling, the sky is blue, the leaves are at their blazing-scarlet best. The John Smedley factory, a stoic stone building on the crest of a hill, is taking the spectacle in its stride. Since it was founded in 1784, there has been many a day like this. Inside the factory, Ken Brierley is more than halfway through the morning shift. Brierley, who has worked for the knitwear company since 1969 and met the Queen when she visited last year, is based in the ‘fully fashioned room’, where the classic core collection of John Smedley’s famous fine-gauge knits is made. His ‘old lady’, a 12-head knitting machine, has been his since he started. He must know it well. ‘I know it too well,’ he says with a roll of his eyes and a chuckle. By the time he clocks off he will have completed the front, back and sleeves of ‘four or five dozen’ garments, ready for the next stage of production. In the trims department, yards of rib are spooling on to the floor, while in the finishing room staff are checking garments, joining backs and fronts together and cutting necklines freehand with scissors that Jane Garner, one of three John Smedley neckline specialists, is brandishing at a panel of cobalt knit as we pass. As Jackie Turner, design manager for special projects and an employee of some 30 years, says later, ‘When you see the processes going on here, you can see that people have got a real skill in what they’re doing. They’re aiming for absolute perfection every time.’ State-of-the-art Japanese and German knitting machines aside, with its raftered ceilings and gappy floorboards, you could set a Victorian drama in this factory and not have to worry too much about authenticity. The leather-doored boardroom, complete with brooding portraits of the original John Smedley and his descendants (the business is still family-run), has an air of Mr Selfridge about it. And yet for all its extraordinary heritage, the past is not why I am here. In September John Smedley knitted its way into the future with Spectrum, its womenswear debut at London Fashion Week. Designed by Pip Jenkins, who within six years has risen from student intern to head designer (‘I was only meant to be here for two weeks’), Spectrum was launched on a line of models standing quietly in a contemporary-art gallery off Regent Street, to a crowd that increased in number and volume as the afternoon wore on. The collection of simply cut sweaters, dresses, skirts and trousers in a palette of only three colours – white, blue glass and sloe (a dusky purple) – was extremely well received. Modern without being trendy, it has all the elegant minimalism and considered luxury of Calvin Klein or Lemaire, those brands providing a welcome whisper in an increasingly loud design world. ‘The original inspiration was the refraction of light,’ says Jessica Mcguire-Dudley, head of marketing and design, as she goes through the collection in the factory showroom. ‘When you walk around the factory you see all this light coming in, hitting different textures everywhere.’ The limited palette helps to convey that sense of texture. John Smedley is a brand known for its wide range of colours, but by using only three the designers and factory could, Jenkins says, ‘really concentrate on the texture and the fibre. We wanted to showcase more of the things we could do aside from colour.’ For an old company – particularly a successful one – it is a challenge to innovate without alienating your existing customers. Rather than playing fast and loose with the classic collection, the team wanted Spectrum to be an alternative. ‘We have the classic customer, who I guess is probably in her 50s and interested in buying that made-in-Britain quality crew-neck or the fine-gauge roll-neck synonymous with John Smedley,’ Mcguire-Dudley says. ‘But this was about opening up to a different audience, still older probably, but more interested in a contemporary style.’ ‘We’ve gone really deep into looking at how knitwear works on a female physique,’ Jenkins says. ‘How by adding a silk you can have an androgynous sort of shape, but the fibre itself gives you a very flattering drape.’ Split backs and wrap details on sweaters, and a tank top with a curved back slightly lower than its front, contribute to the sense of modern chic. Full knitted looks are currently in vogue, and the team was ideally placed to exploit that. As Mcguire-Dudley says, ‘Pip and Chloe [Cooper, designer] have created all the garments so that they can be layered together.’ Mcguire-Dudley, 30, is a woman so committed to the John Smedley cause that she commissioned the factory to make her wedding dress – the only John Smedley bridal dress in known existence. With Jenkins and Cooper both in their mid-20s, she heads up an interesting and startlingly youthful creative team. When Mcguire-Dudley attends board meetings, she is the only woman present ‘and about 15 years younger than anyone else’, she says, laughing. ‘But, joking aside, you can’t do this without a progressive managing director like Ian Maclean.’ Spectrum follows a successful entry into London Collections Men three years ago and a unisex collection that launched earlier this year and is sold at Selfridges and John Lewis, among others. ‘That was a good example of how reactive the factory can be,’ Mcguire-Dudley says. ‘I saw women talking about wearing our menswear pieces on social media, so I suggested to Ian that we try a unisex collection. Within two weeks we had the product out, and it’s now one of our bestselling lines for menswear and womenswear.’ Spectrum – now available online and at the John Smedley store in Mayfair – will return to London Fashion Week in February as a new collection for a/w 2016, in another three-colour palette. ‘What we want to showcase,’ Mcguire-Dudley says as she stands at her favourite viewpoint over the factory, where a higgledy-piggedly collection of roofing materials is a reminder of the decades this establishment has behind it, ‘is that John Smedley is an old heritage brand, yes, but the cogs are still turning.’  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Some of the biggest names in fashion raced to distance themselves from photographer Terry Richardson yesterday as one the industry’s most influential editors told how she refused to work with him because of his sexually “exploitative” behaviour with young models. Justine Picardie, the editor in chief of Harper’s Bazaar, said she did not want her models subjected to Richardson's “”troubling” working methods - which included screening hard-core pornography in his studio during shoots. Ms Picardie said those in positions of power within the industry had the duty to ensure young people were not placed in similar situations with men like Richardson. She said: “I would suggest that young models should not be put in positions where they feel exposed and vulnerable.” Ms Picardie spoke out after Conde Nast International, the publisher of Vogue, GQ and other glossy fashion magazines, issued instructions to its editors on Monday banning the use of Richardson and ordering them to “kill” any photo shoots featuring his work. The decision came as disturbing allegations resurfaced that he had engaged in sexually inappropriate behaviour with young models during photo shoots. Following Conde Nast International’s decision to ban his work, the Italian fashion house Valentino - for whom Richardson shot one of their current high-profile campaigns - said it will follow suit. It stated: “The last campaign with photographer Terry Richardson was shot in July 2017 - there are no plans for a future campaign and we of course take these allegations seriously.” At the same time the Italian luxury brand Bulgari and the US jeans maker Diesel both said they were cutting ties with Richardson. Bulgari, who used him to shoot their 2017 accessories campaign, said  "there are no plans to work with him again at this time". A spokeswoman for the firm added: "Bulgari has a long history of working with different photographers on various projects. The campaigns that have been done with Terry Richardson have been one off initiatives." A spokesperson for Diesel said: “I can confirm that we are not collaborating with Terry Richardson for the Diesel campaign, and also that we don’t have plans to work with him.” Porter magazine, which used Richardson to photograph the model Bella Hadid in May, said it has now “ceased working with him and publishing his images”. Ms Picardie said she had decided not to use Richardson as soon as she took over as editor in chief of Harper’s Bazaar in 2012. She said: “A colleague of mine, when she had been much younger and working on a different magazine, had gone to his studio and there was explicit pornography playing on a screen beside her and there were pornographic images on the walls and she had felt that there was something very troubling going on in that environment. “I had only once been in his studio and again I was much younger, a long time before I was editor of Harper’s Bazaar, but again I felt troubled by the explicit imagery that was on the walls.” Ms Picardie added: “That overly exploitative vision of women was something I didn’t feel happy with.” She who went on to say she had regular disagreements with other fashion editors over Richardson’s work. Ms Picardie pointed out that the 52-year-old US photographer’s working methods were well known throughout the industry and that other editors had still made a decision to use his work. But she suggested there had been a failure to protect more vulnerable, inexperienced models from Richardson and others like him. “Adults have to take some responsibility for what’s going on in their industry. It’s right to say to young girls this is probably not a good situation for you to be in, I would also say the same to boys. You need to be cautious and we need to protect them from exploitative situations,” she said. Richardson responded to Conde Nast’s decision by admitting that his controversial working practices involve “interacting” with models in a sexually explicit way. The photographer - who has been accused of persuading models as young as 19 to perform sexual acts on him while taking their photograph - says he only ever engaged in consensual behaviour. But on Tuesday he admitted he sometimes behaved in a sexually explicit manner with models during photo shoots.  As the world says goodbye to Nancy Reagan, Bronwyn Cosgrave remembers the woman who brought Hollywood glamour to the White House... Nancy Reagan spent eight years as First Lady of the United States of America, but it was perhaps her first appearance in the role that summed up her defiant attitude that style mattered - whatever the cost. For her husband’s January 1981 White House Inauguration she commissioned two of her favourite designers to create outfits that would make a statement.  For the daytime ceremony Adolfo Sardiña, a Cuban American, made her a matching dress and jacket in 'Republican red’ paired with a “toque” based on a hat he’d created for the Duchess of Windsor. For the evening’s ball, she wore an off-the-shouldered white column gown by James Galanos. The finishing touch were crystal and rhinestone embellished satin court shoes that were handmade for the First Lady by David Evins, the shoe designer who famously shod Marilyn Monroe. The outfits were hailed as patriotic and daringly elegant, but became even more of a talking point when, days later, it emerged that the total cost for her attire was $25,000. “More than twice my annual salary,” said one disgruntled reader in a letter published in the New York Times.  Not that it bothered Nancy. She paid no mind to Washington’s style conventions of the time that a 60-year-old woman entering the White House should see clothes as something that help you disappear. Rather, Mrs. Reagan took charge of her own look and projected an individual brand of luxury which her long-time friend and sartorial collaborator, Galanos, defined as "ultra glamour." It was Reagan’s background as an actress in Los Angeles that helped in her mission to bring Old Hollywood glamour to the White House. She had been contracted to Metro-Goldwyn Mayer, Hollywood’s “studio par excellence”, which featured a wardrobe department which rivalled a Paris couture atelier. At MGM Reagan - who was 5 foot 4 inches and a UK size 6 her entire life - realized that to project an image she needed more than just clothes. MGM’s leading ladies like Gardner and Elizabeth Taylor became glamor icons by forging close relationships with expert costume designers whom they completely trusted to make them look fabulous - no matter the camera angle - and from whom advice was sought on all appearance-related issues including makeup, hair and jewels.  Reagan’s Hollywood training also meant she could charm her way out of the criticism she faced for her extravagant style. Unlike Mrs. Kennedy, who notoriously ordered her New York dressmaker, Oleg Cassini, to copy couture originals which a personal shopper sourced for her on the sly in Paris, Reagan was unashamed about taking designer freebies. At a dinner for press reporters in 1982 she famously dressed herself as a bag-lady and sang a song, entitled “Second-Hand Clothes” as a nod to the criticism she was 'out of touch’ with the American people. It was met with riotous applause, and allowed her spendthrift ways to continue. Clairol, which manufactured her hair colour, eventually disclosed that they had allocated $100,000 to pay for the services of her hairstylist, Julius Bengtsson. Reagan’s fashion defiance was, in part, a reaction to her predecessor Rosalind Carter - whose husband Jimmy Carter’s “frugality bordered on the unrealistic.” Mrs Carter had sported “off the rack...versatile...clothes that work for someone who works,’’ her press secretary, Mary Finch Hoyt once explained. But, perhaps as a result, the significant political waves she made as the First Lady - successfully completing a solo policy making mission to Latin America in 1977, for example - received very little attention.  After the “dowdy Carter years,” the Reagan administration believed the White House needed a pizazz that matched the economic optimism of the 1980’s. Nancy realised that to project this she needed to use fashion as a kind of political costume.  “Like Jacqueline Kennedy she understood the connection between style and substance,” wrote Bob Colacello, a biographer of Ronald and Nancy Reagan. But while she was profligate, Reagan also made it her mission to dress patriotically. She wore red, originally, in 1966 when her husband announced his intention to run for Governor of California - and it became such her signature colour as First Lady that it became known as 'Reagan Red’.  “I always liked red. It’s a picker-upper,” she once told W Magazine of her red Chanel-style suit she wore to promote her anti-drug Just Say No program. But there was more to it than that. “Today 'power Republicans’ wear red,” American Vogue noted. Donald Trump’s wife Melania, for example, has a penchant for the colour. “But for Nancy - who started it - it wasn’t red as power or even sex,” Vogue went on. “It was to appear earnest but important. Looking earnest is a good strategy. No one can afford to look sinister in Washington.” Reagan also identified a host of up-and-coming American designers who could help her forge her approachable yet imperious signature style. On the Presidential campaign trail and during her White House years her patronage of Caroline Herrera, Bill Blass and Oscar de la Renta elevated the American designers to international heavyweight status. '’Fashion is a big business,’’ Mrs. Reagan reflected of their success.  But was Reagan simply ahead of the curve? At the 2008 Inaugural Ball election night in November 2012, Michelle Obama brandished 18K white gold “triple dangle”diamond earrings that were on loan from Loree Rodkin with her Jason Wu white column gown. Proof, perhaps, that Nancy Reagan’s mission to bring glamour to the White House is one which is very much still being pursued by its women today. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The exhibition of Princess Diana's wardrobe- Diana: Her Fashion Story- which opened at Kensington Palace last week charts how the late Princess cleverly strategised her wardrobe to be pitch perfect for the various roles which she was expected to fulfill. One of these categories was what Diana herself labelled a 'caring wardrobe' where pieces were chosen for their cheerful yet practical look. This meant bright colours or patterns which still looked smart and appropriate, often with jangling or interesting jewellery which children could play with- and a steadfast no hats rules because, as she once said,  "'you can't cuddle a child in a hat".  Unsurprisingly, suits in vivid colours became a cornerstone of Diana's 'caring' repertoire thanks to their purposeful but still eye-catching qualities. It seems those tailored looks were such a good idea that the Duchess of Cambridge has now coined a similar approach for her daytime charitable engagements.  Colouring and "what's your favourite cartoon" ... The Duchess meets other residents @RMHCUK pic.twitter.com/iMEluCCdSp This morning, for example, Kate visited new accommodation  created by the Ronald McDonald House Charities for the families of patients at Evelina Children's Hospital in London. With meet-and-greets with young children and their families as well as craft activities on the agenda, the Duchess turned to a versatile yet polished look by New Zealand-born designer Rebecca Taylor.  In the kitchen HRH meets families who benefit from services at @RMHCUK - here children are taking part in crafts and decorating pancakes. pic.twitter.com/AtS1r2ngtA She has worn the blue skirt suit a couple of times before, first in 2012 for a reception celebrating the Scott-Amundsen Centenary Race to the South Pole then again in 2014 in Wellington, New Zealand. The fact that this isn't a new outfit means that The Duchess is deflecting some of the attention which a new outfit would have attracted. Thanks to  its frayed edges, bright hue and tactile tweed fabric, the smart two-piece takes on an approachable, child-friendly air. A look back at the Duchess's previous looks for hospital, school and charity visits shows that she has developed a 'caring wardrobe' look of her own. In January, she visited East Anglia Children's Hospice (EACH) in Norfolk wearing an emerald green skirt suit by Hobbs with a lace-collared blouse underneath while in February she recycled a scarlett Luisa Spagnoli look for a school visit.   During that 2014 New Zealand tour, Kate opted for a similarly bold green coat by Erdem to drop into The Rainbow Place Children's Hospice in Hamilton. In 2012, she made her first speech as a member of the royal family at EACH wearing a cobalt blue tailored dress by Reiss. 'Bright, interesting but polished ' is the mantra which ties all these looks together.  Princess Diana excelled at these careful balances and would also often choose bright skirt suits for her 'caring' engagements. At the opening of the Liverpool Women's Hospital in 1995, she opted for an orange version of the look. Visiting St Mary's hospital in 1989, Diana nodded to her 'Dynasty Di' reputation in a power-shouldered, red blazer with gold buttons. And at the Royal Marsden in 1993, she co-ordinated her turquoise jacket and  pencil skirt with a matching bag and heels.  “Although she didn’t want to be known as a clothes horse, she learnt how to use fashion to help her do the job to hand,”  Eleri Lynn, curator of Diana: Her Fashion Story notes. “She crafted her public image carefully, and used it to engage and inspire.” Although, the Duchess of Cambridge has always sought to distance herself from comparisons with Diana, it seems that the late Princess's 'caring wardrobe' rules are as effective today as they were 30 years ago.      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  You can’t move these days for box-fresh adidas Stan Smith trainers or ‘power leggings’. Sportswear has crossed the fashion frontier to such an extent that it’s a way of life. Trainers and sporty silhouettes speak not only of physical strength and inner confidence but also that the woman wearing them has stuff to do and doesn’t want to be impeded by a cinched-in dress and heels she can only mince around in.  It’s no surprise, then, that celebrities are cashing in on the trend: Rihanna is the creative director of Puma’s womenswear line; Kate Hudson is the co-founder of sports/fashion brand Fabletics; Rita Ora has her own range with adidas; Rosie Huntington-Whiteley launched a sell-out activewear collection with Marks & Spencer. And now the queen bee has entered the arena – this week, Beyoncé launches Ivy Park. Named after her daughter, Blue Ivy, and co-founded with Sir Philip Green, the activewear label is the singer’s invitation to talk about the value that sport adds to women’s lives. ‘When I’m working and rehearsing I live in my workout clothes,’ she says. ‘But I didn’t feel there was an athletic brand that spoke to me. My goal with Ivy Park is to push the boundaries of athletic wear, and to support and inspire women who understand that beauty is more than physical appearance.’ It’s a compelling message, and one that the two-minute film she has made to accompany the launch – a rousing narrative over grainy black and white footage of sun-drenched trees in Parkwood, Houston, where Beyoncé went running as a child – is as evocative as it is stylised. The message is that every woman can do sport, and also go on to achieve great things. ‘Where is your park?’ Beyoncé asks, using the metaphor not only as a place to become strong but also as a woman’s ‘safe’ mental and emotional space. As a marketing  tool, its very inclusivity is canny. Clare Varga, of global trend forecasting agency WGSN, says: ‘Launching a fitness line is the go-to thing right now. It’s been described as the new celebrity perfume. It’s another reflection of how important fitness and wellbeing is, and how it’s vital for stars to be seen “working out”. Sports brands love it too because celebrities have a greater reach than today’s sports stars – they can touch a new audience.’ The ‘athleisure’ market (that’s luxurious gym/leisure wear, by the way) is now worth a staggering £4.5 billion in the UK, according to consumer market research group NPD. Globally that figure is around £173 billion, up 17 per cent on the previous year and expected to hit an estimated value of £229 billion by 2020. The latest figures also suggest the wider healthy-living industry is now worth £3.4 trillion globally – nearly three and a half times larger than the worldwide pharmaceuticals industry. Dressing as though you exercise (even when you don’t) has become one of the many aspirational fashion tropes: luxe sportswear offers elevated comfort dressing, whatever your aesthetic. Little wonder, perhaps, that this month Selfridges is opening a 37,000 sq ft space dedicated to bodywear, targeted at every shape. A survey by Macy’s department store, reported recently in the New York Times, revealed that last year Nike was the most-Instagrammed fashion brand, with nearly 48 million hashtag mentions – more than twice that of its closest competitor, Prada, and almost six times that of Michael Kors. Nike has clocked up tens of millions of downloads of its running and training club apps. These are not just passive followers on Twitter or mindless likes on Instagram, but millions of women actively engaging with Nike, using its technology to exercise. It’s a level of interaction that most brands can only dream of. Nike’s growing hold over upper-income teenagers (the world’s most attractive demographic, according to Scott Galloway, a professor at NYU Stern School of Business) also means it is poised to outsell the denim sector, which saw sales dip by eight per cent last year. It seems that if this trend continues, there may soon be 20-somethings out there who have never even owned a pair of jeans. Athleisure, as Net-a-Porter can verify, is a serious money-spinner. Since the retail site launched its sub-category Net-a-Sporter 18 months ago, it has doubled its spend on stock and there has been a 75 per cent increase in the number of brands it sells.  Heather Gramston, buying manager at Selfridges, says that Ivy Park is one of the most highly anticipated launches this year, maximising Beyoncé’s appeal as the ultimate active woman and creating a product that is both accessible and inspiring to a diverse mix of women. The marketing and PR honchos at Ivy Park are keen to stress that this is no flash-in-the-pan celebrity collaboration – the 228-piece collection has been rigorously tested by the singer. The label aims to promote a powerful message of self-assurance, confidence, inclusivity and diversity, the cornerstones for a generation reared on mindfulness – and it is democratic and accessible. A sports vest costs only £14, the lowest price of an affordable range that will be available to buy from retailers as diverse as JD sport, Topshop and Net-a-Porter. Even hi-tech performance leggings, in three waist heights and with in-built knickers to avoid unsightly VPLs, will only cost £40. The memo is clear: these clothes are not just for women who do pilates and yoga and have the premium sportswear labels to prove it. Apparently, Beyoncé found it depressing that up to 80 per cent of girls give up sport at the age of 13, and as such the collection has been designed to appeal to younger women too. Most of the range is slouchy with a tomboy feel that recalls Alexander Wang leisurewear. It will appeal to design-conscious women as much as it will win over an awkward teenager who balks at the thought of having to wear something that hugs every curve. As Natalie Kingham, buying director at matchesfashion.com, observes, this also feeds into a shift in buying habits that has style aficionados mixing activewear clothing with other pieces in their wardrobe.  Trend forecaster Clara Varga sounds a cautionary note, however. ‘Celebrities  will need to think through ranges like this carefully,’ she says. ‘Fitness needs to be real – it’s an industry that values authenticity – and if they’re seen as faking it or jumping  on a bandwagon, they’ll get brutally rejected, pronto.’ Somehow we’re guessing that this may not be something that Beyoncé, at least, needs to worry about.   Vest, £15, Ivy Park (topshop.com)  Seamless capri  pants, 332, Ivy Park (topshop.com) Shorts, £16, Rosie  for Autograph (marksandspencer.com)  Fenty x Puma by Rihanna  a/w 2016 Sports bra,  £35, Fabletics  (fabletics.co.uk) Leggings, £72, Fabletics (fabletics.co.uk) © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Celebrity wardrobes are notoriously bigger, fuller and flashier than most, but a new video inside Oscar-winning actress Catherine Zeta-Jones’ closet reveals an incredible approach to storing her clothes - and hints at a possible new clothing venture. The cavernous, department store-esque room is filled with floor-to-ceiling display cabinets, arranged in a way that makes us more likely to compare it to the inside of Liberty, or the warren-like Browns boutique, than the average woman’s Ikea PAX. The video whizzes around her impeccably stocked displays - pride of place are the Hermes bags, sat next to a wall of printed silk scarves. Chanel handbags in a rainbow of colours lined the shelves and an entire section is devoted to twenty-plus black, navy and marl jackets, with a section of boucle (likely Chanel) box jackets below. So what tips can we possibly take away from this, when tidying away our own style stashes? The categorisation of products here is interesting - this is a woman who knows exactly how many jackets she’s got to choose from, because quite simply, all of her options are in one place. Having everything on open display is also a helpful tactic as she can consider every visual option in front of her when trying to throw an outfit together in a hurry. It will also prove more economical (if that’s a consideration for Zeta-Jones) as seeing and remembering all of the things that you’ve got will encourage you to get more wear out of them. In recent weeks the 47 year-old has been posting more and more fashion-related snaps on her Instagram page (using the hashtag # StyleByZeta) leading many to consider whether she may be plotting a new fashion line or designer collaboration. A week ago she posted a picture of herself with white lace fabric, asking her half a million followers what their favourite materials are. Yesterday, too, she posted a shot of a sewing machine detailing how she ‘loves working with lace’. Perhaps the greatest indicator of what her label could look like though, is the moody fashion pictures that she posts on Mondays under the hashtag #MuseMonday. From vintage Emilio Pucci shoots, to crochet ensembles - there is a thread of feminine silhouettes and textural fabrics forming, that would certainly align with the hints of lace fabrics.  Maybe it's all a hobby, but we will certainly be staying tuned for more clues if and when she drops them.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Elle Fanning is just a tender 18 years old but is already onto something like her 25th film. The Neon Demon is out in cinemas today and is  like a dark, horror-spin on The Devil Wears Prada- same acerbic put-down of the fashion industry but with much more blood and a lot less Harry Potter and laughs. Directed by Nicolas Winding Refn (of Drive fame) the sinister, intense and gripping  tale tells the story of bright-eyed Jesse, played by Elle, who arrives innocently on the LA modelling scene and finds herself sucked into a world of extreme jealously and psychological torture. From a lot of what you hear about what it’s like to be a model, there might be only a few degrees of separation between the film and real life. For that reason, Elle was a savvy choice to play Jesse.   Besides her acting work, she has starred in ad campaigns for Marc Jacobs and Miu Miu in the past and has been going to fashion week shows since she was 13- Chanel couture was her first, which isn’t a bad place to start. “I’m a massive fashion geek!” Elle says when we meet a few hours before London premiere of The Neon Demon.   She agrees that Refn’s film bears some comparison to reality. “Some of it’s true but it’s an exaggerated truth. There’s dark in everything but especially in the modelling world where it is all about people judging you by your appearance” she says carefully, “there is definitely a  truth to it, when  people are saying no to you just because of the way you look, or your body type. That is very harsh.” For Elle, growing up in the spotlight added its own pressures. “I started out acting when I was young so I grew up physically in films. You watch films back and you think ‘Ah I was so awkward then!’ There’s a point, for a girl, where you start becoming aware of your body, you become self-aware but then it’s like the world becomes a magnifying glass too. You’re on screen also going through a change, so it can be uncomfortable. There are times where you’re totally insecure.” There are few signs that insecurity has had any lasting effect on smiley, perky Elle however. In fact, she seems to approach fashion in the same way any other style-loving teen would. She’s always had an experimental approach to getting dressed, and was encouraged by her parents from an early age to be confident. “If you start becoming insecure about your style, then you’re just going to be safe, but I never wanted to be safe and I still don’t” she says,” I’ll be like, today I want to look like a skate-boarder but then tomorrow I’ll want to put on my little lady outfit.” “I would go thrift shopping when I was 9 and get vintage bathing suits and then wear them out and about” she remembers. “Marilyn Monroe was my style icon when I was young so that was pretty hilarious.” Of course, most teens aren’t juggling what-to-wear-to-hang-out-in-at–the-weekend dilemmas with conumdrums about red carpet looks. But Elle developed a clever tactic  for her professional appearences early on. “I’d never want to look older than I was. If it was like 'Granny older' then that’s OK but not older in a ‘I’m trying to look sexy way’. People go through that phase when they’re 13 or something, but I don’t know if I ever went through that” she remembers. Her penchant for Granny dressing  might explain why she’s taken a shine to Alessandro Michele’s Gucci collections (he’s renowned for his vintage detailing)  which she’s been seen wearing everywhere from airports to awards ceremonies. The audition for The Neon Demon threw up another rather niche ‘what to wear’ moment. “I was a big fan of Nick’s.  You see one of Nick Refn’s  films and you know it has his stamp on it which I find very inspiring” she says, “I found out he was doing a movie based on the fashion world with models which doesn’t sound like Nick Refn. He’s like the king of gore, violence and masculinity. Then he asked me to come meet with him in LA. I hadn’t read the script or anything.  I just knew it was about models so I thought ‘What do I wear?!’  I was like, ‘Well I’m tall, I’ll just do the classic model look!’  I think I wore a little pink, crop top with high waist black slacks and black heel boots. Let’s make my legs look long! I remember that precisely because I was so nervous.” Off-duty, Elle says her ideal going-out look would go a little something like this: “It could be like a little baby doll dress, with a choker- I am really  into the choker trend.  I also have a very long neck, you can’t really tell but you can show it off! And maybe fish nets and then loafers of some sort.” Why loafers? “I go for flats if our guy friends are around because some of them are much shorter! So I wear them to not make them feel bad!” Her two worlds came together during May’s Cannes Film Festival where  The Neon Demon press duties meant she had to miss her prom back in LA. No matter.  The speed with which the internet reacts to the red carpet in 2016 can make actresses scared of taking fashion risks, and take refuge from online critics in safe, but bland, gowns. On the Baftas red carpet there was one star laughing at the 'no print, no colour' norm: 23-year-old red carpet newbie Bel Powley.  The young British actress was a rainbow in human form at the Baftas on Sunday evening, wearing a striped metallic Gucci gown with spindly spaghetti straps and a tightly-pleated skirts. She then added extra disco with stacked silver Gucci platforms. Her stylist Cher Coulter said to The Telegraph about her fearless approach to the red carpet: "She is young and cool and she's the perfect person to spice up the red carpet a bit. That's what we need. The reason I love working with her, is because she's willing to take risks and she's not scared." And her risk-taking doesn't just stop at the dress: "She likes accessories - when she tries on a Gucci outfit she likes putting on the flowers, and the badges, and the rings, and embraces what is brilliant about his [Gucci's creative director Alessandro Michele's] collection and his aesthetic, whereas other people might be terrified to really go there and she's not. She wore the really stacked shoes at the Baftas, and just went for it." Bel embarked on her first press tour in July 2015 for Diary of a Teenage Girl and has already found a friend in Gucci. Her stylist, who also works with Rosie Huntington Whiteley, tells The Telegraph about her relationship with Gucci: "I've only just started working with Bel. I think her and Gucci are the perfect match of brand and celebrity. Gucci is the it label right now anyway, but she is the perfect girl for them; their clothes fit like a glove as if they are made for her body." The Baftas was Bel's first awards show, and Cher explains how the approach is different with a red carpet 'fresher': "It's exciting because it's unpredictable, and if you work with someone from the beginning you can help nurture that. It's harder to start working with someone when they are three years into a red carpet routine and you have to try and change it. It's very difficult for someone to go from wearing simple tight dresses by one designer to try and work with new designers to change their look. It takes a minute." As for what we can expect from Bel's future on the red carpet, Cher says:  "You don't want to predict it but it's going to be fun and fashion, without looking ridiculous, because we all know on the red carpet you are seen from every angle and you still want to look flattering. You're not going to turn up in a sack, and if it's a sack, it's a short sack to show off your legs. I think she'll stick to liveliness, print, colour, texture." This certainly isn't the last time we'll see Bel rocking Gucci, but as for other labels Cher says they are drawn to "richer collections with depth" including Chanel, Sonia Rykiel, Rochas and Giambattista Valli.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The past few weeks have provided jolt after jolt of proof that racism is still rife in the world. From horrific scenes in Dallas and Baton Rouge, the anger sparked by the shootings of Alton Sterling and Philando Castile to the shocking abuse which drove Ghostbusters actress Leslie Jones to close her Twitter account, it's apparent that racial tensions and incomprehensible attitudes are still never far from the surface. And there is no denying that racism in fashion- a platform which has a huge visual impact and, therefore, responsibility- is just as systemic, deeply ingrained and pervasive.  And yet in the past few days there have been some encouraging signs that fashion might be gingerly beginning to realise the importance of using a diverse cast of women. Example number one comes from comments made by supermodel Chanel Iman in an interview with Teen Vogue. "I feel like fashion's opened up a lot" she observed, "with having rappers in campaigns, and more color on the runway, but of course there's room for more of it, and more diversity. It's nice to be part of a culture change." She added that her own perceptions of how she has been received have also shifted since she began modelling over a decade ago. "I think it was a struggle when I first started, just because it was always one black girl per show, or campaign, or whatever it was" she remembered, "I couldn't stand it, because I just felt like I was being judged a lot, rather than accepted for who I was." Iman's comments come in the wake of a powerful open letter written by model Ebonee Davis encouraging the fashion industry to take a leading role in changing how black models are perceived. She describes the day when one moment she is celebrating being featured "with my natural hair" in Calvin Klein's new adverting campaign, and later hears the news of Alton Sterling's killing. "I scrolled through a stream of tweets filled with grief, sorrow, anger and bewilderment until I regrettably found the footage of his murder" Davis wrote on HarpersBazaar.com. "Heartbreak instantly consumed me; a man's entire existence had once again been reduced to a hashtag." Davis's devastation contrasts painfully with the elation she had felt at being featured in the Calvin Klein ad campaign: "Last week, I received an email from my agent at MC2 Model Management. The contents: a photo of myself—nostrils wide, lips full, hair defying gravity in all its natural glory—in Calvin Klein's Fall 2016 campaign and a message that simply read, "Really proud of you." My heart swelled. I thought back to how hard I had tried to assimilate into the fashion industry—straightening my hair, wearing weaves and extensions. I was told that brands only booked black girls if they looked like they'd been "plucked from a remote village in Africa" or like a "white model dipped in chocolate," and from the start of my career in 2011, I lived by those words. Until last year when I made the decision to wear my natural hair." Davis underlines the vital role which fashion has to play in helping to change perceptions and open conversations. "As artists in the fashion industry, we are the embodiment of free speech" she writes, "we set the tone for society through the stories we tell—fashion, the gatekeeper of cool, decides and dictates what is beautiful and acceptable."  Like Iman, Davis acknowledges that there's plenty more to be done, but she has an outline for how to make the industry take responsibility. Firstly, she urges make-up artists and hairdressers to learn how to deal with black skin and hair- you may be surprised to hear that dark foundations are not a standard issue part of many technicians kits. Model Leomie Anderson has opened up about her backstage struggles on her blog. “Being a black model can be hard when it comes to makeup during fashion week as not all makeup artists really know how to enhance our features or sometimes pick the incorrect colour which leaves us with ashy runway pictures," she wrote. "I now bring with me my own concealer, foundation, powder and brush and correct my make-up in the toilets. I don’t want to offend the artist who does my make-up, but at the end of the day I want to look my best down the runway.” Davis goes on to asks "models, fashion designers and public relation agencies" to "use your personal platforms to speak out against injustice and show your support rather than standing by in silence." But her main message is this: "Most importantly, love black people as much as you love black music and black culture. Until you do, society will continue to buy into the false notion that people of color are less than—a concept already deeply embedded in America's collective psyche which is reinforced again and again through depictions in media. The time for change is now." Another joyous signal that fashion is leading the way when it comes to tackling racism comes with the news today that Tiffany & co., probably the most famous jewellery company in the world, has enlisted Lupita N'yongo as one of its first ever celebrity 'faces' for a campaign called 'Legendary Style' which has been created by Vogue creative director at large, Grace Coddington. Then there's Willow Smith, Chanel's latest young ambassador. “It’s not every day that a 15 year-old black girl with dreads gets elected to be the Chanel ambassador” she recently told The Telegraph,“I know a lot of girls that look like me feel that they’re not beautiful and feel like they don’t have a place in the media or a place in the world.”  Despite these encouraging messages, there is still a woeful lack of black models on the catwalks and in campaigns. Just this week Prada released an epic Autumn/Winter advertising campaign featuring 27 models, but only three were black. Last fashion month, less than 25% of models on the catwalk were black while 78.2% of models featured in the Spring/Summer adverts were white. At least there are signs that, with the help of a clutch of model activists, fashion might be on its way to a more positive place.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  "Fashion dies, but style remains," Yves Saint Laurent once observed, in a clear prediction his creations would stand the test of time. It is a claim hard to refute from the man credited with inventing the modern woman's wardrobe. But now the late king of Haute Couture's business and life partner, Pierre Bergé, is about to take Saint Laurent's canonisation to another level by opening two museums in autumn next year - one in Paris, the other in his beloved Marrakech - to honour the French designer's plethoric oeuvre spanning four decades. In terms of exhibits, the curators are spoiled for choice given the the 5,000 Haute Couture garments and 15,000 accessories painstakingly archived at the Fondation Pierre-Bergé-Yves Saint Laurent, from the seminal Smoking to the Mondrian dress. "We have kept everything," Bergé tells The Telegraph in the Avenue Marceau mansion that the designer worked in for 30 years, today home to the Fondation. On an upper floor, a space-age conservation room keeps Saint Laurent's myriad creations at carefully controlled temperatures and humidity. Dresses that leave its confines spend a month in quarantine upon return starved of oxygen to kill off the dreaded clothes moth. Visitors are required to don hospital-style protective white blouses and shoe covers to avoid contamination. It might sound extreme but such precautions are understandable given the phenomenal fashion firepower within. Hanging in one moveable wardrobe is the little black dress with contrasting white silk French cuffs and collar worn by Catherine Deneuve in Bunuel's Belle de Jour. In another drawer lies the Iris jacket worn by Naomi Campbell in 2002 from the Vincent van Gogh collection. "We are the only ones to have such a collection; neither Balenciaga, nor Dior nor Chanel can claim this, because they didn't keep the original outfits, only the customers' models," says Bergé. These were usually altered to suit clients' tastes, with dresses changing colour, seeing sleeves added to avoid baring arms, and necklines made less risqué, "not to mention sizes," he said. Saint Laurent was keenly aware of his legacy and knew that one day his creations would end up in a museum, says Bergé, whose business acumen coupled with the couturier’s talent made them both fabulously rich. "During each collection, he'd say, 'that will go in the museum',” Bergé recalls. "He was aware, and he was right, that he was the last of the great couturiers." For the new Paris museum, the building's current exhibition space will be doubled in size and completely refurbished in the style of Saint Laurent's original atelier. Meanwhile, in Marrakech, a 43,000 sq ft museum in local terracotta and granite, on - fittingly - the Rue Yves Saint Laurent, will be unveiled just 50 yards from the Jardin Majorelle, the flower-strewn garden where the designer's ashes were scattered. Around 60 original creations out of a rolling stock of 350 will be exhibited in a permanent space - many such as the Bougainvillea cape, inspired by local colours. However, four, including the Mondrian dress, will be copies because Bergé says he "couldn't bear" to see them leave Paris. With so many pieces to choose from, what are the most ground-breaking? "You can't separate them out, but his male suits that he dressed women in were revolutionary,” he says. With everyone from Jane Birkin to Susan Sarandon wearing an homage to Saint Laurent’s famous 1966 Le Smoking on the red carpet at this year's Cannes festival, was the designer aware at the time of how revolutionary his dinner jacket was and would continue to be? "It is the one piece of clothing that is 100 per cent masculine, so to get a woman to wear it was quite something,” he says. “At the same time, if a woman is to wear a masculine piece of clothing, she has to develop her femininity and her weapons of seduction.” All of Saint Laurent's work was a feminist statement, Bergé insists. "He accompanied the social revolution going on in the world at the time towards women's equality, for example, and it is wonderful that he did so. You only have to look in the street, women don't know it but they all have something from Saint Laurent.” By contrast, Bergé believes that the talking point fashion of today - such as Madonna's bondage-inspired Givenchy concoction at this year’s Met Gala - is far from revolution. "I have a lot of respect for Beyonce and Madonna, but that has nothing to do with fashion, and certainly nothing to do without Saint Laurent. It's marketing, that's not the same at all," he remarks. "As for Cannes, I'm in the habit of saying: It's hard to know what is more 'borrowed' (fake), the dress or the starlet. It's bluff and phoney marketing." Indeed, Bergé is unequivocal in pronouncing Haute Couture "dead", saying the "art de vivre" to which it catered from its 19th century founding father, English designer Charles Worth, to Dior and Saint Laurent is now a bygone age. "Today, the fashion houses supposedly continue to turn out haute couture but they don't have customers, because I don't call Russian prostitutes customers," he says. "They continue to offer it in the belief it will sell ties and perfume - that's their right but I don't believe it and think it is condemned to die out.” Bergé believes only three companies have understood today's fashion: Zara, H&M and Uniqlo. "I don't even know the bosses but they've got it right. There is no longer a need for fashion designers giving people orders on what they should wear, and tying them to dress codes,” he says. "Freedom is about allowing people to do what they want. Uniqlo and Zara brushes with ready to wear design, but crucially with a price to quality ratio that corresponds totally with the way people live their lives today. You buy something for not much, it doesn't last long, you throw away and buy another. It's the same for everything today." He sees the cult of the celebrity designer and all the tumult over changes in top designers as "dangerous". "Turning designers into stars, including Saint Laurent, has been totally idiotic. In Saint Laurent's time, the product was what counted most, we didn't turn a couturier into a footballer or rock singer. Marketing never entered this house," he says. Berge won’t be drawn on the recent departure of Saint Lauren's chief designer, Hedi Slimane except to say: "He is a very close friend, who I love and admire very much." But he appears less convinced than most by Slimane's ode to the 80s in his swan song at Paris Fashion Week. "I hate nostalgia. Fashion cannot be nostalgia, fashion is conjugated in the present tense. That's why all these couturiers who do revivals of various decades don't interest me," he says. As for Saint Laurent's new creative director, Vaccarello, Bergé says he was "touched" he had come to see him in person that morning - and respects Saint Laurent owner Kering's decision. So does the house continue to live up to Yves Saint Laurent's legacy? "They don't do haute couture whereas Yves Saint Laurent did, so there is no comparison possible,” is all Bergé will say. “That is the truth." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Poor Blake Lively. The actress stars in Café Society, Woody Allen’s latest film, and has spent the past several days fulfilling her contractual obligation to promote it at the Cannes Film Festival. That she’s done so while pregnant has made Lively the focus of internet-wide scrutiny. Correction: it’s not Lively getting the attention, per se. Rather her baby bump. Google ‘Blake Lively bump Cannes’, and you’ll find 1.2 million hits. ‘Blake Lively Puts Baby Bump on Full-Display’ [sic] from HuffPo Canada, something about ‘Blake Lively’s supernatural pregnancy hair’, and thousands of stories about Lively as she ‘shows off’ her baby bump are just some of the pickings. Vanity Fair effectively launched a Blake Lively pregnancy truther movement with their (tongue-in-cheek, but still somewhat misguided) story, ‘The curious case of Blake Lively’s disappearing and reappearing baby bump at Cannes’, in which a writer scored Lively’s ‘bump level’ in different outfits on a scale of one to five. There’s something so leery about the way we scrutinise celebrity ‘bumps’ - as if these bumps are entities separate from the women carrying them, rather than external indications of very internal, very private experiences. The second a woman in the public eye comes out as pregnant, her abdomen becomes an independent object of public discourse. Substitute ‘bump’ for ‘boobs’ anytime it’s mentioned, and you’ll see that this apparent mass interest in bump style is merely voyeurism concerning a different body part. And there’s no way to win. If women orchestrate art-directed Instagram reveals of their foetus’s gender or wear shape-conscious outfits when pregnant they’re accused of‘flaunting it’. But anyone who declines to draw attention is said to be ‘hiding’ the bump. When Carey Mulligan kept her pregnancy under wraps with loose-fitting clothing and declined to confirm her status, coverage centred on her unflattering red-carpet choices. Worse still is the suggestion by some this week that Lively is ‘using’ her baby bump. (How? To show that she’s pregnant and fabulous? Help her do her job of obtaining coverage in a gown-saturated environment? Demonstrate that she’s not slowing down just because as well as acting, she can own the red carpet and create new life?) Apparently that leaves just two ways to treat pregnancy in event dressing: either you’re brazen, or you might just find yourself being whispered about being fat.  “There’s an awful lot of pressure on women to look stylish when they’re pregnant - and yet it’s one time when women should not be critiqued, criticised, observed,” says Stacey Duguid, fashion writer and co-founder of Nico and Nate, a motherhood- and style-focussed blog. “They should be left alone to get along. There’s no such thing as pregnancy style - it’s called survival.’ See, all that most women want when they get dressed during a pregnancy is to feel as close as possible to ‘normal,’ which for most of us means reaching for the stability of our pre-pregnancy frames. “Trying to stay true to who you are is key,” says Ariane Goldman, founder of Hatch Collection, a range of fluid dresses and separates just as appealing before and after the bump. While celebs have the luxury of access to custom pieces, for everyone else, “it’s more about taking something simple and zheuzhing it up with accessories. Invest in pieces that are beautiful on the belly but that also make you feel special.”  So what did Lively hope to accomplish by dressing so spectacularly at Cannes? Just guessing, but she probably wanted to feel glamorous and confident. If it took custom pieces from Atelier Versace and Giambattista Valli to get her there, more power to her. Look a little higher on the photos of Lively making the rounds, and you’ll notice that one constant is a smile. In most photos she radiates happiness, despite the scrutiny and sky-high footwear. Now that is the right kind of flaunting it. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Few women can have a diary filled with such a number of diverse engagements as the Duchess of Cambridge. And when you’re called upon to watch a traditional Maori presentation in New Zealand one day, and then visit a prison in Woking the next – all in front of the world’s media – it can’t be easy finding the right outfit. It’s lucky, then, that one British couture house has something for, seemingly, every formal occasion you can wave a fascinator at: Catherine Walker. The Duchess attended today's Order of the Garter service at Windsor Castle wearing a red coat dress by the label, which came to fame in the 1980's as Princess Diana's favourite designer.  It's not the first time we've seen Kate in this outfit - she first debuted the punchy ketchup-coloured outfit on the royal tour of Canada back in 2011 - nor the first time The Duchess has relied on the Chelsea-based atelier. In May, she wore a bright green belted coat dress by Walker for the Chelsea Flower show, and just last Friday Kate was pictured at one of the Queen’s numerous 90th birthday celebrations in an icy blue embroidered number by the designer. Walker started selling clothes in 1976, when she used to walk down the King's Road in London holding a basket of her designs. Soon after she set up her first shop on Sydney Street in Chelsea - and it fast became the go-to destination for event dressing for the 1980's Sloane, including most famously Princess Diana.  French-born Walker first started working with Diana shortly after she married Prince Charles and went on to design over 1,000 dresses for the Princess, including the black dress she was buried wearing. After Princess Diana's divorce, Walker is credited with helping create so-called 'defiant' frocks, such as the black backless dress she wore the night Prince Charles went on national TV to admit his affair.  The eponymous designer died in 2010, but today the label continues under her husband Said Cyrus's direction.  “No one could ever accuse Catherine Walker of making her clients look youthful but impeccable dependability is the signature of this designer - and of the house that bears her name,” explains The Telegraph Fashion Director Lisa Armstrong of Walker’s enduring Royal appeal. “The label guarantees a statuesque perfection that looks as good in photographs as it does across a crowded cathedral or state ballroom."  Armstrong also remembers to this day the detail Walker and her team put into every design. "I visited Catherine, who died in 2010, several times in her shop and work-rooms and was fascinated to hear her navigate her way precisely around an outfit. No detail was left to chance. A Catherine Walker bodice or jacket always sat perfectly, its aim to elongate the torso as much as possible in order to create the most elegant, upright silhouette. The sleeves did not rumple or twist like almost every other sleeve you see. That, explained  Catherine to me one day, was because most sleeves are ready-to-wear. A proper couture sleeve is seamed differently - there is no visible join. It is inserted differently too. It sits high and is cut narrow, for maximum elegance, but it also allows for movement and royal arm waving.” As such, it's hardly surprising that both Kate and her mother Carole have turned to the label for high stakes occasions. Carole Middleton wore a blue coat dress by Catherine Walker for the Royal Wedding that was strikingly similar to Kate's outfit last week - something the design team say is true to the brand's DNA. "The signature of the house falls into two distinct areas – sumptuous hand embroidered evening wear, and beautifully cut bespoke tailoring," a Said Cyrus, who now heads up Catherine Walker told The Telegraph. "Common to both those categories is the focus on ageless design and craftsmanship. This is ageless in more than one meaning of the word.  Last season we sold the same design to a client in her 60’s and also to a girl to celebrate her 18th birthday. Same design both made to measure." The iconic status Catherine Walker's creations still hold became evident last month when news broke that one of the green sequinned dresses she created for Princess Diana was set to fetch £100,000 at auction.  “It's not true to say her clothes don't date," says Armstrong. "Some of her  1980s designs for Diana are clearly of their time - but they always retain an aura of imposing dignity and their photogenic flawlessness.” So how does it compare when The Duchess of Cambridge steps out wearing one of Catherine Walker's new designers? As you'd expect the label won't be drawn on comparisons - but they do admit the speed with which keen Kate watchers race to identify and then copy her outfits has impacted the business.  "Over the past 40 years the most striking change has been driven by the arrival of the internet," Cyrus says. "In 1980 if you wanted to know who wore what the answer was on TV or in print, often in expensive magazines. Nowadays clients in the USA, central Asia and China have looked at our website and ordered using a new service we have started called e-couture." No doubt after today they'll all be asking for red.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
