 In true Vivienne Westwood style, the British designer has waded into the latest political row – by designing T-shirts that support the on-going junior doctors’ fight against proposed changes to their contracts. Part of the #wearyourNHS campaign, the t-shirts show the slogan ‘Support Junior Doctors’ over a black heart shape on a white background. “Doctors are dealing with matters of life and death every day,” Westwood explained of the heart-shaped design. “I’m very pleased with this t-shirt as government policy will wreck the health service.” The government plans to impose a new contract on doctors up to consultant level next year, which would reclassify their normal working week to include Saturdays and up to 10pm every night of the week except Sunday. Medics argue that the new contract is unfair for doctors and unsafe for patients, imposing unfeasibly antisocial working hours on doctors and causing them to lose out financially, as hours that were previously considered overtime will be replaced by standard pay. It wouldn’t be a Vivienne Westwood design without also referencing climate change, and the Wear Your NHS t-shirts are no exception. The t-shirts have an Ecolabel rating of A, meaning they are organic, low carbon, and ethically produced, while the design includes the maxim ‘We have no choice between a green economy and mass extinction’. This isn’t the first time Westwood has used her design talent for political ends, recently producing a 'Save the Arctic' t-shirt for her own brand and having teamed up with civil rights group Liberty and designed a limited edition range of t-shirts and babywear that declaimed “I AM NOT A TERRORIST, please don’t arrest me” back in 2005. Dame Westwood is one of Britain’s most politically active designers, having been a vocal long-time supporter of the campaign for nuclear disarmament as well as supporting a wide range of causes, including Scottish independence and opposition to fracking. The #wearyourNHS t-shirts meanwhile, are designed to show support for junior doctors, with proceeds from each sale going to the Junior Doctors Campaign and medical charitable organisations. The t-shirts are on sale at the Wear Your NHS website, and supporters are encouraged to Instagram or Tweet photos of themselves wearing the shirts with the hashtag #wearyournhs and upload them to the campaign site. Campaigners fear that the new contract will lead to many junior doctors choosing to leave the country or medicine altogether. The protest has currently at boiling point, as 38,000 junior doctors have voted in favour of strike action in December - the first ever to take place in the history of the NHS.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Last night, the BFC/Vogue Fashion fund awarded its annual £200,000 prize to Sophia Webster, the designer whose pastel shoes with butterfly wings show every sign of becoming one of Britain’s most successful footwear labels.  It comes as no surprise that Sophia Webster used to be a competitive freestyle disco dancer. She has the lust for shimmery pastels, the poise and determination. There’s a reggae DJ father in the mix too. And a mother, who is a principal of a London secondary school and had different ideas for her daughter’s future. Maribel frill multi sandals, £395, Sophia Webster Instead of stage school, Webster attended Camberwell College of Arts where she found herself drawing repeatedly, sketching the model’s shoes in the life drawing classes. Her tutor told her about Cordwainers, the world-renowned footwear design course, at the London College of Fashion. Her current HQ in East London speaks to the showgirl and the serious shoe designer (she really can make shoes, having practiced when she worked for Georgina Goodman and the upscale Italian shoe label Casadei). It’s a quaint Victorian two and half story former printworks CK on a back street, that only a few years ago, was more shabby than chic. Webster’s interiors are part Dickensian, part Legally Blonde.  (Or maybe Hans Christian Anderson: from the waist up, she looks like The Little Mermaid and sounds like The Little Match Girl).   A wooden mezzanine, where she designs, juts out over 30 employees, beavering away on orders, designs and marketing. The walls and shelves are garlanded with racks of heels shapes, pom-poms, pictures of Hello Kitty styled as Frida Kahlo (two of  her idols). In case that’s not sufficiently girly there’s a sign hanging from the mezzanine spelling out her name in pink neon. Piper gem silver flats, £325, Sophia Webster  Next door they’re noisily constructing a Nobu Hotel, a development that seems appropriate to Webster’s own meteoric rise.  Arguably she’s doing well enough not to need the £200,000 that the BFC/Vogue fashion fund offers to its winning finalist. However the money isn’t awarded to the candidate most in need but the one who the panel (which comprised of ten industry experts, including Vogue’s editor in chief, Alexandra Shulman, Victoria Beckham, Joan Burstein, the founder of Browns boutique and one journalist, me) believes is at a stage where it will be most helpful to the expansion of their business. Flamingo frill flat sandals, £395, Sophia Webster  Her ascent seems seamless, but it’s the result of slog and talent. After Cordwainers, she was accepted onto the Royal College of Art’s prestigious MA. While still a student there she designed a collection for River Island, interned at Nicholas Kirkwood and at the age of 27, launched her own company. Kirkwood was so struck by her sales pitch, he let her use part of his studio to work from. He also, semi-formally, vetted her then boyfriend, Bobby Stockley, a former electrician (handy with that sign), whom she married in 2013 and who now helps run the business from the basement. “I tried it up on the mezzanine,” he says. “But there was too much chat.” It’s not hard to see why Kirkwood was impressed with the pair of them. Webster is one of the clearest-sighted nascent brand builders you could meet. Even when shoes took a turn for the clompily androgynous recently, she stuck to her first principles, introducing flatform-lace-ups that looked about as masculine as frosted fairy cakes. Having set herself the task of designing a fresh pair of shoes every day when she was at college she always knew exactly what she wanted her line to look like - and when to debut. “I started with a pre-collection rather than a 'main’ because that’s the one retailers have the biggest budgets for.”  Webster’s whimsical styles with their butterfly winged backs, flower encrusted straps, ruffled crests, sherbet-colour patchworks and neon trims were so distinctive they immediately carved out a niche in a market that until that point seemed saturated with whimsical, distinctive designs. Romy white drawstring bag, £550, Sophia Webster Webster was that still relatively rare spark: a young female shoe designer making high impact shoes with lots of detail for “girls like me, from ordinary backgrounds, who had been brought up on the glamour of Sex and The City shoes, but were never going to spend £600 on a pair.” Pricing was key. They weren’t going to be cheap but something between high end high street and luxury: aspirational, distinctive, something she could imagine her friends saving up for. Lilico Underwater sandals, £450, Sophia Webster She considered manufacturing in China, “where contrary to what people think, there are some incredibly factories” but fancied a tan so has spent the last four years flying back and forth to Brazil – on one occasion, when she was pregnant with her daughter Bibi, now almost two, for one day. “It was definitely challenging,” she muses. “There were lots of things I could have got made in Italy that Brazil wasn’t geared up to do.  But Italy would have made the shoes too expensive for her market. “The limitations were good for me because I had to work out other methods. They didn’t do 3-D printing for instance, so that meant a lot of the effects I had in my head had to go. But out of that came all the colour combinations”. Those sugar almonds and acid mixes became a signature – although not without some macho resistance from the factory. “There was a lot of 'Oh my God’ when they saw some of my colour palettes,” she says.  “But on the other hand, they were willing to take me and my very small orders on. At the start, they would happily make just 12 pairs of some styles, if that’s all I needed.” Flossy leather pouchette, £225, Sophia Webster Last year Webster sold 60,000 pairs of shoes - she sells in 200 shops around the world including Harvey Nichols and Selfridges - and turned over £9 million. This year she will sell 85,000 and has just launched a range of instantly identifiably handbags. Riko pastel low top sneakers, £250, Sophia Webster By 2018 she’s on target to do £20 million. Bobby is the pragmatic one who tells her, not unreasonably, they need some flats in the collection, based, on his sound observation that most women are currently wearing flats – including his wife, who is in a pair of Webster trainers when we meet.   As a token of her appreciation she’s named a shoe after him, and also in their daughter. You sense that in the Webster/ Stockley household, there is no higher honour. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  There was bemused uproar this morning as it emerged that the speech given by Donald Trump's wife Melania on the opening day of the Republican convention was in parts plagiarised from a speech given by current First Lady Michelle Obama in 2008.  Designed to give a more personal insight into 'The Donald' and his family, Melania's speech touched on classic Obama themes of ambition, determination and respect for others, all uttered in often near identical form to an address FLOTUS delivered to the Democrat convention where her husband was officially selected as Presidential candidate. That Melania delivered said speech at the equivalent event whilst wearing a cream 'Margot' dress by London-based designer Roksanda Ilincic only underlines the fact that she's been taking lessons from Michelle's playbook, because Ilincic also happens to be one of Obama's favourite designers.  Obama has worn Ilincic's designs- renowned for their elegant yet bold silhouettes- on numerous occasions during her time at the White House. A vivid purple dress with draped neckline has served for everything from a talk at Georgetown university to visiting Westminster Abbey during a stay in London. In March 2015,  the First Lady opted for a pattern-splashed, nipped waist design called the 'Lansdale' arriving on a visit to Cambodia. Fascinatingly, this is the second time this week that Michelle Obama has been credited for inspiring the fashion choices of another woman in the limelight. When Samantha Cameron departed Downing Street for the final time last Wednesday, it was in a near identical Roksanda dress to Obama's Lansdale dress. Roksanda is having quite a moment.  A spokesman for Melania confirmed to WWD that she purchased the $2,190 dress herself via Net-a-Porter and now it's already sold-out. The 'Margot' is one of Roksanda's most successful and long-running designs which has garnered an eclectic group of fans over the years. Coleen Rooney wore the fuchsia version to Aintree in 2012m while gamine actress Ginnifer Goodwin and businesswoman Helena Morrisey were also spotted in the design. Now that Melania has joined the Margot club, it can surely be declared the most democratic design of our time? From Liverpool to Trump's wardrobe, it's quite the trajectory.  The Michelle comparison is unavoidable in light of the speech's Obamaisms (see below), but there is a genuine personal reason why Melania might have chosen to wear something by Roksanda for her biggest moment yet on the campaign trail; Ilincic and Trump both hail from the former Yugoslavia. Melania was born in the town of Sevnica which is now part of Slovenia, while Ilincic was born in Belgrade, the capital of Serbia. Both women left their home countries, with Ilincic establishing her now decade-old and highly successful fashion business in London and Trump heading to the US for a career as a model and businesswoman. Whatever you think of Trump's politics and the prospect of him entering the White House come November, it seems his five-language speaking wife (who his camp is claiming will be a 21st century answer to Jackie O) has already honed an idiosyncratic take on diplomatic style, using a dress to tell her own story, if not a speech.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Last night he won the International Designer of the Year Award at the British Fashion Awards. The One Direction heartthrob, 21, turned up at Sunday night’s American Music Awards in an eye-catching custom-made floral Gucci suit, complete with flared trousers and a natty floral garland in place of a tie. His individuality was highlighted by the fact that his three bandmates had plumped for rather run-of-the-mill grey, navy and black suits, leaving Styles looking a little like he’d been duped into believing the dress code was fancy dress - a bit like when Bridget Jones turns up at a Tarts and Vicars party in a Playboy bunny outfit. We feel your pain, Harry.  How do you make sure that you don't turn up to a wedding, office Christmas party or  birthday soiree in the same get-up as someone else? Buy vintage of course. If you've been day-dreaming about turning up to an event in a beautiful, one-of-a-kind piece, which has people wondering where exactly you managed to find such a showstopper, then former interior designer and ''Vintage King'' (aptly dubbed so by British Vogue, Harper's Bazaar and The New York Times) William Banks-Blaney is here to help. ''I have always loved vintage and knew so many women who loved the idea of vintage but were terrified of shopping for it'' the vintage connoisseur tells The Telegraph. Banks-Blaney founded William Vintage in 2009 to sell the kinds of clothes he and his friends dreamed about finding; ''fantastic, wearable vintage clothing in perfect condition''. William Vintage offers an enormous array of vintage  gems; from the perfect work suit or weekend coat, to an exquisite formal gown. Personally responsible for scouring the globe and hand-picking pieces to sell in-store and online (his Eccommerce site launched earlier this year), who better to impart their vintage-buying-and-wearing-wisdom on us than HRH himself?  ''You should start with a piece that you know how to incorporate into your wardrobe and don't over think it'', Banks-Blaney tells The Telegraph. ''It may be vintage but you already know how to wear a dress, so the same rules apply'', he continues, suggesting a chic 1960s coat or a knockout LBD as a good starting point.  Banks-Blaney recommends always limiting yourself to one vintage piece at a time. ''I love vintage but I don't like dress-up, so always mix it in with contemporary,'' he tells The Telegraph. ''Celebrate all aspects of fashion and find your own language''. There's nothing you can't find vintage, so what you buy is down to personal choice. Banks-Blaney says that, while he loves vintage clothes, he prefers contemporary accessories, suggesting that pieces look far more relevant and clean as part of a combined look.  Great Unknown black trouser suit circa 1970, £345, William vintage ​ Banks-Blaney suggests that,  just as with contemporary clothing, you think about what you want and expect your vintage clothing to do for you and always bear the fabric in mind. ''If it's silk, chiffon of velvet it's going to be more delicate and less hard wearing than wool or cotton, so you will need to find a great dry cleaners, as chemicals kill your clothing no matter how old or new they are''. Banks-Blaney emphasises that if you ''shop well and invest sensibly, you should never need to part with beautiful vintage clothes''. Global gold dress circa 1962, £475, William Vintage​ What about when it comes to having vintage pieces tailored? At William Vintage they have a saying ''you never turn a maxi into a mini''. ''For premium vintage pieces like 20th century haute couture it's important they are not tailored as this will reduce their inherent value, while an inexpensive, fun dress is something you can tailor to improve its fit,'' Banks-Blaney tells The Telegraph, also urging that any tailoring work you do have done, is carried out well and with as little impact as possible on the item.  Thea Porter couture navy heart print dress, £1975, William Vintage To avoid falling prey to con artists and fakes, Banks-Blaney advises that you always purchase your vintage pieces from a reputable source and that you start slowly and enjoy the sense of discovery that comes with finding a piece of vintage that you love, so that your eye and understanding of vintage improves. ''If you're considering buying something and the sales executive can't tell you what you need to know - walk out!''  Yves Saint Laurent beige coat circa 1972, £825, William Vintage A new four part series on BBC Arts,  looking back at four hero looks in cinema history (including Audrey Hepburn’s infamous black dress in Breakfast at Tiffany’s and Alicia Silverstone’s yellow tartan skirt suit in Clueless) hosted by William Banks-Blaney, will be available on BBC iPlayer from 18th November 2016.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Yesterday, we saw Delevingne rock a checked Alexander Wang suit with played with proportion via an oversized blazer and drainpipe trousers; later, she wore a custom-made Burberry suit for the film’s London premiere. “As a nod to Cara's home town, it was only appropriate that she wear a British designer,” says Haenn. We’re accustomed to see Delevingne wearing the likes of Burberry and Chanel- both labels she has modelled for in the past- but Haenn is also mindful to include unexpected names in the mix (Dion Lee and Mugler are a couple she’s worn this week). “We don’t want to limit her so we look at everyone’s collection for the season and what their inspiration and theme was, so there are the usual suspects which we lean towards because of who she is, but we’re always looking to push outside that boundary too.” While the former supermodel might have been quoted today as saying she doesn’t care about how she looks, Haenn says she definitely plays a vital role in choosing the outfits she’ll be photographed in. “She’s great at trusting and trying things on, but she has an opinion too.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  In today's genius fashion marketing news Amanda Wakeley, one of London Fashion Week’s more established but less edgy names, has tapped a photogenic food entrepreneur for its latest campaign. Ella Woodward, the clean eating food blogger, author, Telegraph columnist and deli owner better known as Deliciously Ella, is the star of the brand’s adverts for SS16. The brunette models sleek evening dresses and smart separates from the brand’s new collection, and is pictured in a classic car parked in London’s Chelsea neighbourhood. It is her first modelling assignment but Woodward looks like a natural - no doubt her plant-based, dairy-, gluten- and sugar-free way of eating has given her the complexion that rivals most top models.  Casting 24-year-old Woodward is a savvy move for the brand. Founded by former model Amanda Wakeley in London in 1990, the label is older than its new spokesmodel. And it's part of a bigger campaign to profile entrepreneurial women on its website through ‘The Wakeley Women’ series,  which will feature interviews with successful women in business.  The association with Woodward will no doubt serve to help a younger generation to discover Wakeley’s brand; Angelina Jolie and Amanda Holden champion her designs on the red carpet, but it’s Woodward’s social reach (she has 650,000 followers on Instagram) that could prove to be priceless. Woodward, the daughter of former Tory MP Shaun Woodward supermarket heir Camilla Sainsbury, became the leader of the clean eating movement quite by accident. It was while studying at university that she became ill with postural tachycardia syndrome (PoTS), a rare disease which causes an abnormal increase in heart rate after sitting or standing. Woodward's case went undiagnosed for some time, so she suffered from extreme exhaustion,  severe bloating and dizziness without knowing the root of the issue. A Haribo fanatic who couldn’t cook and hated vegetables, Woodward turned her diet around after  researching alternative therapies and coming across a book by American cancer survivor Kris Carr, who had adopted a diet of plant-based foods.  She began by blogging her cooking endeavours and eventually came up with vegan-friendly alternatives to brownies (The Deliciously Ella version feature dates and sweet potatoes) and pancakes. Her health improved dramatically and while doctors can't explain how she cured herself, she has become a case study to help others suffering from PoTS. Woodward is due to marry late this year – her fiancé Matthew Mills also happens to be her business partner and the son of another former Labour MP, Tessa Jowell.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. "But in terms of equal pay I need to be paid the same as the guy who has equal billing with me. Otherwise I won't do it," she asserts,  "because if you accept less, you're just letting everyone else down and continuing the cycle." With 31.6m Instagram followers to her name, Cara has created a community of fans who she encourages to "Don't worry be happy, Embrace your weirdness, STOP LABELLING, START LIVING." She tells Vogue that her online following has led to worries that this could be the only reason that she is cast in films; "My greatest fear is always that I have just been hired because of my number of followers." Cara Delevingne with Annie Clark Delevingne has also been at the vanguard of an open approach to sexuality, confirming last year that she is in a relationship with Annie Clark. "I'm completely in love.....Before,I didn't know what love was - real love.  I didn't understand the depth of it.  I always used to think it was you against the world.  Now I know the meaning of life is love.  Whether that's for yourself or for the world or your partner," she says in the interview. "As a child I used gay as a bad world.  as in, 'that's so gay'.  All my friends did," Delevingne admits. "I'm obviously in love, so if people want to say I'm gay, that's great.  But we're all liquid - we change, we grow."  For most of the last decade, Daphne Guinness – muse, model, heiress, film producer, philanthropist – has, in one way or another, continued putting on an extraordinary and accomplished show of apparent exhibitionism: in Alexander McQueen feathered robes; rubber dresses; black and white hair striped like a badger, styled like a Duchess – while dealing with intense personal grief. First, owing to the suicide of the eccentric fashion editor Isabella Blow, who drank poison in 2007 (Guinness knew she was depressed but thought she was getting better), then the suicide of McQueen (‘I didn’t see that coming’) – both  victims of severe depression, both considered by Guinness as ‘my family’. ‘To be perfectly honest, I do feel slightly abandoned,’ she says. ‘Swallowing poison and hanging… It’s a terrible thing. I still go through it. Issy really was my best friend.’ On top of her confusion and sense of abandonment has been, or rather still is, the complicated and often melancholy nature of her on-off 10-year love affair with the married French philosopher and timber heir Bernard-Henri Lévy, who she confirms is the ‘love of her life’. The relationship has been punctuated by estrangements and the usual vows to walk away, and yet it is not over and Lévy has still not left his wife, Arielle Dombasle, the French actress and chanteuse: ‘You say it, you know it… You have taken a view of the circumstances, your life, whatever, and you still can’t see it,’ says Guinness, with a childlike honesty. ‘But I believe in love. I’m a terrible romantic. I can’t calculate anything. It’s so easy to tell everybody else what they should be doing with their lives, but when it comes to my own, I have no idea. I’m about as good as when I was two.’ I meet Guinness in London, at Claridge’s hotel, for lunch, although neither of us will eat or drink anything. She is upstairs in a suite, running late. When she finally arrives, she picks her way through the tables in her silver-sprayed Noritaka Tatehana boots (imagine platform boots with heels that are invisible), causing fellow diners of all ages to crane for a better view, like ugly ducklings turning their necks at the arrival of a beautiful swan, with feathers both white and black.  The heel-less boots give Guinness, 48, an unnatural height (she always wears them – she is 5ft 5in without – and walks on tiptoe when at home), and her hair, bar the stripes, is more black than white. She is wearing a frock coat of her own design, a black shirt with long ruffled cuffs and a pair of sequinned leggings, which, she says, are her uniform these days: ‘I tend to wear the same things all the time.’ She pulls at them in a gesture of ‘these old things’, and her tiny limbs are somewhere underneath. It’s a mannish, dandy-ish aesthetic. Aside from the beauty of her face, it is no wonder she has been such a successful muse. The spare lines of her physique are a fashion photographer’s dream and hint at the extreme self-control of a model (she once incurred intense criticism for saying ‘I’ll eat when I’m dead’ while on a shoot for The New Yorker). She wears heavy black-rimmed glasses, much like a pair I later see on Tony Visconti, David Bowie’s music producer, who has produced Guinness’s first album, Optimist in Black, released this month. She seems uninterested in her clothes, and I suspect that a comment made about her in the past – that her appearance is so interesting that it suggests it is the least interesting thing about her – is true. She certainly sees it that way. ‘I do feel that words are much more interesting than anything else,’ she says. ‘I never really understood what I am doing in the visual world, to be perfectly honest.’ She looks even more arresting for being in the art deco surroundings of the old-school hotel, a situation that will be repeated later in the afternoon in a room at Number 10, with Samantha Cameron, when she goes to receive an ICAP cheque for the Isabella Blow Foundation, the charity she founded in her friend’s memory from the proceeds of selling off a chunk of her own wardrobe at Christie’s in 2012.  The foundation is, for Guinness, a lasting legacy of Blow. Recently, it has been working with the Samaritans on a project to protect more people from the serious consequences of depression, while also providing scholarships to art students to attend Central Saint Martins. Guinness’s move into music – writing and singing – is not as random and dilettante as it sounds, despite the fact that in the past she has dabbled with so many areas of the arts. She has produced and starred in short films (one of which, Cashback, was nominated for an Oscar), has written, has painted and has designed clothes. All of this proves that she has been doggedly determined to put to use her rumoured multiple-million divorce settlement from the Greek shipping heir Spyros Niarchos, either by helping to fund others in their creative projects (McQueen was a beneficiary) or by exploring her own creative instincts.  Guinness has been making and self-funding the album for the past three and a half years. The music is rather different from her other projects because it has its roots in who or what she always wanted to be, which was an operatic soprano. Another analysis is that, because it means more to her, it has laid her bare emotionally for the first time. If she has spent her life dressing up, supporting others, then this now, she admits, is the real her. ‘I began in music,’ she says, ‘and I ended up there.’ But there has been an awful lot in-between. ‘You have to have that experience to be able to put it in a song. If I’d written the songs at 20, I wouldn’t have had that experience, with all its highs and lows.’ It has taken her 30 years to have the courage to return to it. Guinness, the daughter of Jonathan Guinness, the 3rd Baron Moyne, heir to the Guinness fortune, discovered she had a voice while at St Mary’s boarding school in Wantage, Oxfordshire. Her childhood was divided between a house on Kensington Square, Ireland and an estate in Cadaqués, which she has described as a ‘Spanish Wuthering Heights’. There were also spells in the north of England when her father tried unsuccessfully to become a Conservative MP. Despite the privilege, her life was not charmed. Guinness is wary of casting herself as a messed-up little rich girl. It’s not so much this portrayal of herself that she minds; it is more that she is at pains to emphasise that her troubles were no worse than those of most other people. What she does identify to me as a consistent theme of her life is the need to be ‘part of a family, and very much fashion people, and now it is music that is my family’. It’s a telling, transparent comment, which reveals that she has always looked beyond blood ties for emotional stability. ‘Funnily enough, I think I was pretty happy. Probably about five years ago, I thought, actually, my childhood wasn’t bad. I was left to my own devices. But people plant things in your brain.’ Guinness’s mother, Suzanne Lisney, was emotionally detached, and Guinness admits she was often left entirely on her own at the various Guinness properties. When she was five, Tony Baekeland, a family friend who was staying at the house, took her hostage with a knife. She could taste the blood in her mouth. He eventually released her but the next day murdered his mother and then, later still, when released from prison, attempted to murder his grandmother. (The story was told in the book Savage Grace, made into a film in 2007 starring Eddie Redmayne and Julianne Moore.)  When Guinness was 13, it was discovered that her father had a secret family with his mistress, Susan (Shoe) Taylor, and that Guinness and her brother Sebastian (five years her senior and involved in the art world, he now lives in Spain) had three more half-siblings, on top of the three her father already had with his first wife.  Added to this was the legacy of her grandmother Diana Mitford’s decision, in 1936, to marry Oswald Mosley, founder of the British Union of Fascists, at the Berlin house of Joseph Goebbels, with Hitler as their guest. (Mitford’s first husband was Bryan Guinness, Daphne’s paternal grandfather.) Guinness is an absolute spit for Diana Mosley, with the same beautiful, refined face and bone structure. It is a kind of bygone beauty, rarely seen these days. ‘Funnily enough, last night my father was saying how much I reminded him of her,’ she says. The fact that Diana – who Guinness was much closer to emotionally than her mother – was publicly reviled for her decision to leave her first husband for a fascist has been a source of ongoing sadness for Guinness: ‘She was extremely clever and the image of her is not what she was at all. She was very funny and warm, but you can’t say that about her because of who she is and who she married. Oh gosh, I wish she was still here and I could ask her all those questions.’ Guinness, while perplexed by her grandmother’s decisions, was with her in Paris when she died in 2003, perhaps recognising in Mitford a hopeless romanticism at the expense of all else.  Guinness’s own romanticism, expressed in the past 10 years through her liaison with Lévy, was present way back when she was only 17 and fell madly in love with Spyros Niarchos, a son of the Greek shipping billionaire Stavros Niarchos. Guinness had been destined for the Guildhall School of Music, but after meeting Niarchos during a skiing holiday at the age of 17, stubborn and determined, she abandoned all former plans to train as a singer. By the age of 19, in 1987, she was married. ‘It was love,’ she remembers. ‘What can you do?’ He was her first boyfriend. She quickly had her first child, Nicolas, now 26, then two years later had Lex, then, after a five-year gap, Ines, now 19.  For more than 10 years, she disappeared into the private, protected world of the international elite, jetting around from New York to St Moritz to Spetsopoula, the Niarchos family’s private island, barely seeing anybody, certainly nobody from her old life. Friends have said since that her life during this phase was a gilded cage, although she adored being with her children. She did go to the couture collections, particularly Valentino and Chanel, with the other international-elite wives, and occasionally she would have a clump of dyed pink hair, but she was not the visually exotic creature she is today. ‘I was frozen in time,’ she says now.  Guinness rarely talks about this part of her life. ‘I perhaps should be more paranoid than I am,’ she says when I ask her. ‘That’s why I get terribly nervous about saying anything at all. You have to be careful what you say and in which context.’ She is rumoured to have got a divorce settlement in 1999 of £20 million, although that has never been confirmed.  Given her early passion for music and its re-emergence now, it is poignant when she admits that Niarchos did not like her to sing or listen  to classical music during their marriage. ‘He thought when I listened to classical music it depressed me,’ she explains. ‘Funnily enough, funeral marches made me happy. I missed singing so much…’ She trails off. ‘I love my ex-husband,’ she says, almost immediately. ‘He’s adorable. What you are when you are 17… You go through transitions and you don’t know what baggage other people are bringing, or why they would think it would be depressing for you. Maybe I wasn’t articulate enough to explain. He wasn’t doing it in any bad way, but that’s where he was coming from.’ Guinness also admits she thinks she probably suffered from postnatal depression. ‘I was too young. I don’t think it was easily recognised then. In hindsight, it must have been difficult. What do you know about hormones when you are 17 and from an English public school? No one talks to you about things like that.’ But she also says, ‘I think I was made to feel like I was depressed in my 20s. People kept saying, “You had a difficult childhood. I don’t know how you got through it, all those crazy people.” And I was thinking, “I was pretty resilient.”’ Emerging from her marriage and finally returning to London in 2000, she says, was like ‘having done a spell inside’. I had been worried I would not like the album, that it could be a new creative toy for Guinness, less involved in the world of fashion without McQueen and Blow (saying that, the fashion photographers David LaChapelle and Steven Klein are still among her closest friends).  But she has a beautiful voice, reminiscent of the cool (in both senses of the word) detachment of Nico, and she brings a sadness and integrity to the lyrics.  It is ironic that a woman whose public persona is built entirely on artifice, who is the mistress of reinvention, is, in person, entirely free of emotional artifice. She is simultaneously childlike and old-fashioned, so at odds with the icy control of her appearance. ‘Childhood, relationships, life in general – it’s a distillation of all of that. It’s deeply, deeply personal,’ she says. ‘I’m trying to make a joke out of it, I’m trying to think, oh maybe it’s not that bad, everybody is going to find what they find in it, nobody is going to care that it is me singing it. But the awful thing is, every single world is true. I can’t sing a word if it’s not, can’t do it. Simply can’t do it.’ The themes of the album are not a surprise: Fatal Flaw, The Long Now and Joke deal explicitly with her destructive or at least imperfect relationship with Lévy: for example, how he once ended it in a letter. Ten years is a long time to be a mistress. In Joke there are lines based on a famous Lévy analysis of her: ‘Call me a concept/I think that’s rather suspect/Cancel my subscription to your self-crucifixion’; as well as, ‘You are an appalling liar and I’ve just left.’ In Fatal Flaw she says, ‘Love is a kind of madness’; and in The Long Now, ‘I know it’s my disease that I aim to please.’ In the notes accompanying the album she explains that this song is ‘about a relationship which has gone really bad’. For a brief while during our meeting we talk as if the relationship is over, but Guinness really can’t bear to lie. She admits that songs about Lévy – clearly written during an impasse in their relationship – make for awkward listening given their affair is ongoing; although he has laughed and said ‘fair cop!’.  In the title track she deals with feelings about Blow and McQueen’s suicides, and how she refuses to follow them that way, however low she has felt. Writing the song, she recalls, ‘was a very, very dark time’. ‘I’m really trying. I’m really trying,’ she says of her capacity to soldier on and look for inspiration, for new projects, for ways of finding meaning in life. Her return to music was triggered three and a half years ago while spreading the ashes of her elder stepbrother, Jasper, near the Guinness family monastery in Cadaqués (he died of cancer, aged 57, in 2011). Once again, she found herself dealing with death. As she wrote later in the song Optimist in Black, of losing her brother, Blow and McQueen: ‘They made for the exit/The shining light of the exit/Vaporised to who knows where/But I remain unchained/An optimist dressed in black.’  There at the monastery, out of the blue, she said to an old family friend, ‘Let’s go to Ireland and do a cover of a Dylan song!’ It was another act of reinvention, but I suspect, too, one of self-preservation. It is hard to pin down exactly how Guinness divides her time. Conversationally at least, she can be prone to vagueness, although her intelligence and intellectual curiosity – books, plays, poetry, philosophy – are evident. She has sold her Manhattan apartment (where she upset her neighbours by overflowing her bath multiple times) and explains she is currently staying at Claridge’s because of yet more plumbing problems, this time with her London flat. The reason she was late to our non-lunch was because she was upstairs working on a lyric. Her two boys are in America: Nicolas is head of the fact-checking department at The New Yorker (he graduated from Yale), while Lex is making music in New Orleans. Ines is reading philosophy at Trinity College Dublin. Guinness is palpably proud of them. ‘They are all so much more brilliant than I am,’ she says. ‘They are grounded and real people. Wow!’ Not one member of her family, she says, has heard the album. I get the impression she’d rather that nobody listened to it – she admits she didn’t want to release it – and that nobody watched the three accompanying music videos on YouTube. One of these, Evening in Space, inspired by Bowie and 1960s psychedelia and directed by LaChapelle, sees her writhing around naked simulating having sex with a spray-painted neon-pink ‘alien’. It’s quite a thing to behold, but then for Guinness, dressing up, or undressing, acting, are so much less exposing than writing the lyrics themselves. (To mark the McQueen exhibition Savage Beauty at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, in New York, she got dressed in the shop window of nearby Barneys.) Guinness has not made the album for the fame, and certainly not for the money, but says ‘the whole process is payment in itself’.  When she began her journey to make Optimist in Black, Guinness hired the Grouse Lodge studios down the drive from Coolatore House, in County Westmeath. She loved it there so much that she now rents Coolatore House.  When Guinness (working with Pat Donne, an Irish producer and co-writer on the album), realised she had mounting demos, she drew up a list of producers. Tony Visconti was at the top. He agreed to meet her, he says, because of who she was, but with no expectation. ‘She came dressed with all her glitter like the Queen of the Ball,’ he remembers in a small film they made to mark their collaboration at Avatar Studios in New York. ‘I was completely taken aback by her appearance. But what I wasn’t prepared for was the quality of the music. Daphne likes to say she is a non-professional, but she can sing, and she can sing with something that is rare among even a lot of professional singers. She sings with genuine passion. It’s in her heart, it’s in her soul and she becomes the song.’ ‘It’s coming from somewhere,’ says Guinness, ‘and I can’t stop. And I’m quite glad I’ve got all these things stacked up in my head and I’m writing them down and recording all the time, because, who knows, maybe it will dry up, but at the moment I feel like an aerial.’ Optimist in Black is out on May 27, with singles The Long Now and Marionettes available  to buy and stream now daphneguinness.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Cecile Reinaud launched her label Séraphine 15 years ago, there wasn’t much of a maternity fashion scene to break into. “To be honest it was nonexistent,” she laughs. “Brands assumed that women would need baggier clothes, but they were badly cut. No one had thought about the fact that a woman might want a sexy pair of jeans while she was pregnant.” Reinaud had started thinking about her business plan several years earlier, after witnessing the impact of Demi Moore’s now-iconic, bump-baring Vanity Fair cover and appreciating that stigmas around motherhood were changing. Where once women may have wanted to cover up their pregnant figures, the new generation wanted to maintain their personal sense of style, right up to their due date. “She really was the first person to bring some sex appeal to being pregnant,” Reinaud says of Moore. “Before that, women generally felt embarrassed, or that they should be hiding their figure. In the last 15 years though, so much has changed. There is now a whole generation of career-driven women who are having their children whilst working, returning to work and even nursing when at work, and so workwear is one of our big markets now.” Reinaud launched her label after inventing the UK’s first designer maternity jeans in 2002 - “great-fitting jeans in nice washes, but with a discreet band over the belly. It was the star product. It was before the internet so we started an old fashioned waiting list with people leaving their phone number.” After starting with the essentials, Reinaud has gradually built Séraphine into a business on track to turn over £20 million this financial year, and a recipient of The Queen's Award for Enterprise. “I started with the essentials like jeans, then expanded each time we saw a new demand,” she explains. “Now the range is really broad, from maternity underwear to swimwear to a corporate wardrobe to ballgowns. The average woman now attends three weddings during her pregnancy, so people need something great to wear at these events.” “The biggest part of our business now is selling dresses, because when it comes to denim we’re not the only brand doing maternity jeans anymore,” she continues. “From a dress, the customers want something stylish, flattering and versatile - you need to be able to style it up or down, because however many pieces you buy, your maternity wardrobe will never be as big as your normal one. The other successful things about our brand is the pricing. Even though we dress famous celebrities and royal families, an average dress is £55-£60.” A pivotal moment for Séraphine came in 2013, when the Duchess of Cambridge wore the brand’s £49 Jolene Knot Front Dress for her first official family portrait after giving birth to Prince George, an image that made front pages around the world.   “That picture gave us a huge springboard and we became an internationally recognised brand because of it,” Reinaud says of the interest she received, particularly from American audiences who were infatuated with getting Kate’s look. “For me as an entrepreneur it gave me such a boost to think of this dream endorsement. I had to run with it.” The timing, she reflects, was perfect, as the brand was approaching its 10 year anniversary,  the business was profitable and an established production system was in place. When the picture was released, the dress sold out in two hours, but the team was able to swiftly restock making the style a staple in every collection going forward. “We were prepared to an extent because we knew that she was our customer in the store,” Reinaud explains. “But you don’t know where and when something will be worn, or whether it will be in the public eye. We had read articles about what [the Kate effect] was doing for brands like L.K. Bennett and Reiss before us, so we were slightly aware that you need to be quick to react. We put an enormous amount of logistical work in to make the most of that opportunity.” Since that first picture, the Duchess has returned to shop at Séraphine several times. Now expecting her third child, she was pictured earlier this month in the brand’s Marina coat, a piece that she had originally bought when pregnant with Princess Charlotte back in 2015 and had worn on a visit to New York with the Duke of Cambridge. “To see her bring it back out was really nice because she’s just like any regular person - you have these pieces that you love and want to keep hold of,” Reinaud says. “On the third pregnancy, why shouldn’t you refer back to your clothes from the second? A lot of women have children two years apart or so, and they want to have these essential things that they can come back to again in their maternity wardrobe. It’s such an important factor for us when designing.” Reinaud says that the biggest achievement, for her, is considering the diverse range of women that make up her clientele. From Holly Willoughby to Anne Hathaway, she’s managed to provide solutions for all tastes and all body shapes - no mean feat when dealing with customers who are expanding, breastfeeding, and trying to carry on as per. “Your body changes and it is a challenging time where you don’t know what to expect,” she says. “You need more than ever to feel empowered by a good wardrobe.” “When I dress a rockstar like Gwen Stefani, who likes to wear leather pants, and someone like the Duchess of Cambridge who needs to be the epitome of elegance, I think I’ve covered a full spectrum of women. I feel proud that each person can recognise themselves in a part of the collection, but more importantly find something that suits them at a time when their body is changing and there is a lot going on.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Bennett's 'Addison' dress, which has delicate sheer sleeves and a jewel-coloured flecked-print, and is currently in stock for £325.  Whatever the uncertainty of our times, some things can always be relied upon. And one of those things is that: whenever a coming starlet finds herself with a career to launch, she will do so by means of a bikini. For, despite celebrating its 70th birthday  today, the bikini remains eternally young in the matter of strategic flaunting of assets, as it does in putting the fear of God into the rest of us.  From Brigitte Bardot’s decision to storm Cannes in one in 1957, via Carrie Fisher becoming every schoolboy’s fantasy in a metal number in 1983’s Return of the Jedi, to model Kate Upton’s progression from busty unknown to celebrity du jour after appearing on the cover of Sports Illustrated spilling out of a micro-bikini, for a miniscule garment, the two-piece has considerable  impact. Anyone who has had the pleasure of admiring the athletic “bikini girls” at Sicily’s Villa Romana del Casale will know that it is not entirely a new phenomenon. But Christianity ushered in a focus on hiding the shameful female form, swimming or otherwise. By the 18th Century, an all-encompassing chemise built of sturdy wool was required to take the waters, while the Victorians advocated bloomers and long-sleeved tunics. By the turn of the 20th Century, swimsuit shapes, however,  were beginning to replicate changes in underwear design. As suntans became popular, midriffs became increasingly exposed, while still considered fit only for private consumption. Accordingly, it was not until July 1946 that this was taken to its logical conclusion and the bikini - as we know it – took shape, its creator a Parisian named Louis Réard. Fellow designer Jacques Heim had released a similar design, called the “atome,” earlier that year, but it proved less winningly skimpy than his rival’s 30 square inches of material.  Fashion historian Amber Butchart, whose forthcoming book, The Fashion of Film, looks at cinema’s impact on style, tells me: “The modern bikini was invented the same year Churchill first referenced the ‘Iron curtain,’ and the year after the destruction of Hiroshima. It was named after Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands - site of American nuclear tests - as its creator claimed it would make an impact of atomic proportions.”  “Indeed, the bikini was so scandalous when it premiered that Réard had difficulties finding a model to wear it, so had to hire the nude dancer Micheline Bernardini. Still, as the post-war economy boomed and the jet age began, as the the bikini offered more tanning options that a one-piece it quickly caught on.”  The French perceived it as a symbol of youth, freedom, and a rebellion against a more moralising past, le Figaro opining: “People were craving the simple pleasures of the sea and the sun…It was a celebration of freedom and a return to the joys in life.” It no less spelled sex. In the early 1950s, beaches across Europe endeavoured to ban bikinis, the Vatican declared it sinful - even the Miss World competition turned up its nose; all of which made it the obvious weapon for self-publicists.  A 17 year-old Brigitte Bardot sported a two-piece on every beach in the south of France for her debut in 1957. Five years later, Ursula Andress emerged from the sea sporting a belted incarnation as Honey Ryder in Dr. No (a move replicated by Halle Berry in Die Another Day). While in 1966, Raquel Welch was unveiled in a fur bikini in One Million Years BC, propelling her to the status of Playboy’s “Most Desired Woman” of the 1970s. By this stage, the bikini had gone from scandalous to ubiquitous. The 1970s saw it championed by taut-bodied types such as Cheryl Tiegs, the Eighties by fitness fanatics. Despite Baywatch beauties being consigned to straining one-pieces in their capacity as health and safety professionals, by the end of the century, the bikini had become the world’s most popular beachwear: an $811 million annual earner, and the power behind subsidiary industries such as tanning and waxing.  Today, it flourishes in a thousand forms: tankinis, monokinis, camikinis, hipkinis, trikinis, skirtinis, pubikinis (don’t ask). As Amber Butchart notes: “The bikini has become synonymous with a certain kind of paparazzi-tinged lifestyle, heralded by Princess Diana in the 1990s. Its links to celebrity reached an apogee with the ‘schlong thong’ or ‘half-tan pants’ worn by male members of the The Only Way Is Essex cast - proof that diminishing swimwear is now also a male concern.”  It has also become politicised, as the row over last year’s Protein World bikini brandishing advertisements demanding: “Are you beach body ready?” proved. The Advertising Standards Authority banned the posters from the Underground, after protesters had the temerity to suggest that merely being in possession of a body might be sufficient to qualify. Still, if even a goddess of Helena Christensen’s proportions can lament: “It’s really intimidating to go on the beach in a bikini,” many of us feel – if not body shame – then a distinct reticence about the exposure said outfit affords.  For those who wish to give it a go, the advice of how to look good in a bikini is as lunatic as it is legion: from Margot Robbie’s three days’ surviving on carrot sticks, via the Victoria’s Secret models’ masochistic pre-show regimes, to my favourite women’s magazine tip to build a trench around one’s body in the sand to “cunningly conceal those extra curves”.  More sensible and less extreme advice comes from swimsuit entrepreneur and bathing belle Melissa Odabash who suggests avoiding overhead lighting and applying copious fake tan before going anywhere near a two-piece. She insists that to look your bikini best always  opt for a snug fit rather than a concealing yet unflattering larger size, and to pick out a colour to suit one’s skin tone - offering navy as a trusty stylish failsafe.  Busts should be supported (lifting the breasts also makes waists seem smaller), or can be simulated via halternecks and frills. If still in doubt, one can always solve the beach body issue as I choose to - by refusing to ever stray near one.  So, Samantha Cameron registered Samantha Cameron Studio Ltd with Companies House last week. That doesn’t automatically mean we’ll be seeing a Sam Cam fashion show any time soon. Registering a new company for a few hundred pounds is often as much about ring-fencing a name as world domination. However, what with her two decades at Smythson and her genes – her mother, Annabel Astor, co-founder of Oka, the successful furniture venture is a serial entrepreneur – the auguries are positive. When she first joined the luxury stationers, back when her husband was a relatively obscure PR, she did most of the designing and was behind its launch of bags. According to close sources, even while still in Downing Street she took dress-making lessons. Many designers can’t actually sew, but if you want to produce clothes that fit properly, the rudiments of pattern-cutting and basting are handy. Then there’s her personal style. There are those who believe this is not a feminist-friendly subject. It is when you’re launching a studio. Sam Cam’s is interesting, speaking as it did to many dilemmas among women who are interested both in fashion and in presenting a serious front. Often the two have been considered mutually exclusive, but along with Michelle Obama, La Cam wasn’t afraid to express her creative side or her unabashed enjoyment of clothes. Arguably both women helped free us from the drearier rules of corporate dressing. Power-fashion? If she can translate that into her own line, and given her enjoyment of fiscal prudence (“I love a bit of accounting,” she told me. “There’s something very satisfying about making the books balance”), she should go far.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Paris Jackson, the late Michael Jackson’s daughter, appears to have landed her first major fashion job. She was photographed modelling in Paris at a shoot which is reportedly for a future Chanel advertising campaign . Spotted on location at the Eiffel Tower today, she wore a white pussy-bow blouse and pencil skirt, waving French and American flags as she posed on top of an army truck surrounded by male model cadets - in fact, she looks like a mix between Madonna in the Eighties and Marilyn Monroe or Jayne Mansfield, both starlets who took their turns as forces sweethearts entertaining the troops. In other shots, she wears classic French Breton stripes and a silk scarf in her hair.  The 18 year-old has no prior fashion experience but appears to have landed what is probably the most coveted modelling job on the planet.  Thanks to the Chanel blessing, Miss Jackson is now virtually guaranteed to be a star on the rise. Chanel has a track record in spotting and nurturing new talents before they break. The fashion house's previous campaigns have launched the likes of Lily-Rose Depp, Kristen Stewart, Willow Smith and more bright young things to instant star status. But beyond the initial hype, whomever Karl Lagerfeld deems worthy of fronting a Chanel advert will likely achieve a long-term fashion career, as his blessing often results in extended partnerships with the brand, as well as encouraging interest from competitors. That relationship, for Paris Jackson, may well start officially at the house’s couture show on Tuesday as new campaign stars are regularly invited to sit on the front row, and enjoy even more exposure, as well as a nice outfit for the occasion. She may even make her catwalk debut in the show, as Lily-Rose Depp, Lottie Moss and others have done before her. With almost a million followers on Instagram, Paris’s profile has been on the rise in the last month or so, after she turned 18 and made the decision to pursue an acting career. She made her first big red carpet appearance last week, attending a Golden Globes after-party with her friend Sofia Richie, the daughter of the singer Lionel Richie. Aside from the odd Insta modelling moment, Jackson’s social media profile looks just like any other 18 year-old girl’s. It seems to serve as a moodboard of style references (Stevie Nicks and Baddie Winkle) and a place to document pictures from her travels (there are, of course, plenty of pictures of Paris in Paris). Via Twitter and Instagram, however, Paris has been quick to defend her privacy, as well as her father’s legacy, after she branded Joseph Fiennes’ recent casting as Michael in new Sky Arts dramatisation as a ‘blatant disrespect’. As the attention on her will no doubt build in the coming months, it will be interesting to see how Paris chooses to handle life in the public eye. Aligning herself with a fashion powerhouse like Chanel will undoubtedly be a good move, though.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The word 'luxury' at Glastonbury Festival for most means gluten-free burger baps or posh Wellies that don't split at the first sight of rain, but hidden among the sea of tents and muddy puddles is another world of facials and hot showers, where some festival goers will have two blowdries a day and can shop from on-site boutiques stocking designer labels. At Glastonbury's luxury campsites, a five-night stay will set you back around £10,000. Guests don't just have access to luxurious beds and warm 'glamping' tents, but Gwyneth Paltrow-approved, vitamin-infused loo roll (worth £100 a pop), a bar stocked with Aperol and Grey Goose instead of cans of Red Stripe and chauffeurs on stand-by, ready to escort you to the Pyramid Stage. These festival-goers don't have to worry about portaloo-appropriate footwear, so their style is in a league of its own.  There are subtle cues which make these VIPs stand out from the mud-splattered general festival population, as one of theupmarket campsite insiders tells The Telegraph: "You can nearly always tell which ones are staying with us- they'll be wearing insane jewellery and beautiful clothing." "Our guests come in two extremes; some arrive with a huge number of suitcases and are wearing a different outfit every second of every day," the insider tells The Telegraph. "Others have just hopped down to the festival from the city and barely bring anything with them, then expect to be able to buy everything they need here on site." At Camp Kerala, a luxury camp on an adjoining farm to Glastonbury, there is a boutique called Cocoon where guests can pick up everything from authentically bohemian tie-dye dungarees to seriously luxe items like Zadig and Voltaire leather jackets and Camp Kerala's own range of cashmere jumpers and denim shorts. Instead of lugging their outfit options in bin bags and backpacks like the general masses, glampers will airlift in their wellies. "Lots of our guests arrive by helicopter," says someone who works on one of the luxury campsites. "A couple of years ago, we were expecting a party to arrive by helicopter and we had a message over the radio to say they were landing, but then a second helicopter came into land. It turned out they had brought one just for their luggage." According to Lyst the average UK Glastonbury shopper spends £165 on festival items- almost as much as the festival ticket itself- but those with VIP wristbands wear outfits worth a thousand times that. "Some of the jewellery our clients wear would be worth more than most people's houses," says the campsite insider, "that's a popular thing to wear because it's easy to keep on you, unlike a designer handbag." Chloe Lonsdale, Founder and Chief Creative Officer of British denim label Mih Jeans, who is attending Glastonbury this year, is sure there will be a number of high fashion looks hitting the fields. "You look at Coachella and all the big, high level brands are there," she explains, "a lot of the brands showed summer collections that were all about that 70s style, so it's like the perfect place this season for a rainbow long Chloe festival dress, but to pull that off you definitely need a very high level of glamping." While they might be investing in doing Glastonbury the luxury way, the VIP crowd ultimately wants to look like they are there for the music rather than the posing- this isn't Coachella after all.  "I was in the VIP area last year, it was really low-key and anti-Coachella, and more 'fashion' than festival," says ThePool.com's Stacey Duguid. "People were wearing black leather jackets, those little Le Chameau ankle wellies, Rockins skinny scarves, black t-shirts and black jeans. Everyone backstage with the bands is in these key black pieces, shying away from an overly commercial look." It might be a quieter look, but it is still built around covetable 'fashion' items, such as Gucci cross-body bags and £2,000 Saint Laurent leather jackets. "We have definitely seen an increase in spending on customers' Glastonbury wardrobes, as they are now investing in a festival wardrobe the same way they might for a holiday," says Sepideh Shayan, Head of Style Concierge at Harvey Nichols. "However they are spending on high-quality items which will take a permanent place in their wardrobe and be worn far beyond the festival season." As for what the VIPs are buying, Shayan adds: "The key item to elevate a practical festival outfit is a statement jacket, such as this £720 silk crepe de chine jacket from RED Valentino which is perfect to layer over a mini dress or wear with jeans if the weather turns.  Dressed up denim has also been popular this festival season and Sandrine Rose’s eclectic embroidered denim collection has been a favourite for Glastonbury-goers, with jeans ranging from £275 to £375." Other key pieces proving hits with the VIP crowd are Rag and Bone £165 fedoras and Tabitha Simmons £625 ankle boots. A carefully planned beauty regime is just as essential to the VIP Glasto look as a Rockins scarf. Guests will plan their beauty approach months in advance; the festival makeup brand ItsInYourDreams, which is stationed at the luxury campsites, receives enquiries about festival beauty as early as September the previous year and then are sent specific look requests in March, four months before the festival actually kicks off.  Celebrity Goop-approved facialist Face Place also works with attendees months before the festival, helping clients to achieve the no make-up, makeup look with a series of pre-Glasto facials: "For our clients a festival is an event where beauty and fashion is as considered as a wedding for example" says Face Place's Eilidh Smith, "a few facials in the weeks before the festival ensures the skin is blemish free and radiant, and for best results our clients have a final treatment as close as possible to the festival as they would for any big event, to ensure the skin is hydrated to the optimum." There has also been a rise in the Glastonbury elite having 'hair fillers'. Shayan explains that this has been the most in-demand beauty request at Harvey Nichols in the Glastonbury lead-up.  "A popular pre-festival treatment has been Hershesons revolutionary ‘hair fillers’ which are ultra-tiny extensions," she says. "Added to limp hair they are designed to boost volume rather than length, and will help achieve a natural look that will last with minimal styling."  Even once they're on site, the VIP crowd has access to a host of beauty facilities from a fully equipped Clinique spa to a Kevin Murphy hair salon, where guests often visit at least twice a day, in the morning and then again before the evening sets begins. And we thought bringing an unopened can of dry shampoo was being prepared.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It's the lifestyle site that has divided readers over jade vagina eggs and "conscious uncoupling" but Gwyneth Paltrow's infamous Goop just got a whole lot more inclusive with its latest launch.  Teaming up with Universal Standard, a "size-inclusive" clothing company that counts Paltrow as one of its backers, the site has launched a capsule collection spanning from a US size 00 to 40 (UK size 2-44). Whilst Goop has sold a wide-range of clothing brands including Tibi, Ellery and Joseph since 2012 alongside its own apparel label that it launched in 2016, this capsule collection marks the first time that a size above a US 12, the equivalent of a UK 16, has been made available on the site.  Described as a "clean-lined, sophisticated capsule," it features five pieces including a dress, jumpsuit, peacoat, and tuxedo jacket with matching cropped trousers, a look that Gwyneth has been pictured wearing several times on the red carpet. The plus-size market, valued at £6.5 billion in the UK, is an area that more and more fashion brands are slowly beginning to explore. Earlier this year Marks and Spencer launched a Curve range offering 100 pieces ranging in size from a UK 18 to 32, whilst last year Ashley Graham became the first plus-sized woman to feature on Forbes' highest-paid models list.    Unlike most brands that fit a piece of clothing on a single model and then increase or decrease it proportionally for other sizes, Universal Standard adjusts every single item for each size. "Every notched lapel, every swingy wide leg was engineered to work with the proper proportions," explains the site. "Add in the true-black palette and move-with-you fabrics and you have a collection that is sharp, smart, efficient, and beautiful."  Launched in 2015 by former fashion journalist Alex Waldman and private equity specialist Polina Veksler, the brand aims to bridge the gap between straight and plus size clothing.  It has since expanded into loungewear, activewear, workwear and jewellery.  The Goop collaboration makes its second partnership; in July it teamed up with J.Crew on two special collections, taking the retailer's largest size offered from a US 24 to a 32. Speaking to The Business of Fashion about the Goop collaboration Waldman said:  “this is really about making [size inclusivity] the new normal through a variety of channels. The thing that should determine [your clothing] choices should be your taste and your budget. We don’t need any more barriers than that.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Melania Trump became America’s First Lady, she initially experienced a backlash from some of New York’s most revered designer names, as Marc Jacobs, Tom Ford and more refused outright to dress her. But three months into the role, Mrs Trump has started to set her own style agenda, and is building a trusted clique of talents to help her define her polished new signature look. As well as buying off-the-rack pieces by designers including Calvin Klein, Michael Kors and Alexander McQueen, Melania has introduced us to a roster of less familiar New York names - boutique brands and bespoke designers who perhaps haven’t experienced such exposure before. One such name is Alice Roi, the 45-year-old Manhattan-based womenswear designer who founded her label in 1999 and has produced a series of nipped-waist coat-dresses for the First Lady. In turn, Melania’s wearing of Roi’s designs on the biggest of public stages has helped to bring her business back into the spotlight, after the designer took a hiatus in 2012. Now Roi has spoken for the first time about her experiences of dressing the First Lady and helping her to hone her First Lady look.  “I think Melania has already begun to have an influence on fashion,” Roi tells The Hollywood Reporter. “There is nothing sarcastic about her style, nothing experimental. It is very true and solid. Her style is straightforward and traditional, but not dowdy or heavy. It remains light, elegant, clean and almost above-it-all." “Above-it-all” has become a key sartorial principle for a First Lady who doesn’t want to worry herself about bickering designers or fleeting trends. She’s turned to a tried-and-tested silhouette which borrows from the Jackie Kennedy school of thought in her first few months at The White House, and so far it’s been successful in projecting the polished and powerful glamour she now strives for, even if at times she’s been accused of going too archetypal, like a ‘soap opera’ First Lady. “Melania does favour a 1950s silhouette, in which the waist is emphasized,” says Roi of the pieces that she’s created for Trump to date. “It is not my usual go-to silhouette, but she nails it. It never looks literal or dated or forced. Rather, it looks like a refreshing, modern take on femininity and elegance." It helps that Trump has known Roi for 11 years, their first collaboration being on a maternity dress when she was expecting her son Barron, now 11,  after they met and “attended a few parties together”. Their work together has been natural and easy, according to Roi, who reveals that Mrs Trump has been heavily involved in the crafting of her own new image, right down to the pockets. “The coat had many different iterations,” explains Roi of the back-and-forth between the two when developing a coat that she wore to travel to Florida on Air Force One last month. “Big pockets, notch collars, and at one point it looked like a proper hunting coat. But in the end, Melania wanted it simpler and simpler. And she was absolutely right. I think we work well together because she tames my narrative.” “I guess the best word to describe [her new style] would be 'graceful’.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  With cinched-in waists and long, dream-like skirts languishing around the heels, the debut of Christian Dior’s New Look in 1947 Paris set haute couture in motion. As France struggled to extricate itself from the post-war abyss, where sickness and starvation were rife and industrial production stagnated, this opulence provided a way out from the misery that had reigned throughout the conflict. In the words of Carmel Snow, then editor-in-chief of Harper’s Bazaar, who attended Dior’s 90-piece runway show that bitterly cold February, “Dior saved Paris.” A much-anticipated new TV series, The Collection, captures the glamour of that era in exquisite detail - just as  Mad Men did for the following decade - and is already being compared to the phenomenally successful US drama, which was followed as much for its stunning fashion and set designs as for its writing.  While Mad Men captured the advertising industry in mid-century America,  The Collection explores the power of design in a Forties Parisian fashion house, run by the Sabine brothers, who are desperate to leave the troubles of the war behind. Driving the operation is Paul (played by Richard Coyle), business-minded and intent on success at any cost, while his younger sibling, Claude (Tom Riley) is the designer and “true genius” behind the label. Teaming up with a business partner who can bankroll the costly materials required, they seek to cement their city’s status as the leader of the global fashion revolution. “This is such a strong moment in fashion, but it’s rarely seen on film,” explains Chattoune, the Cesar Award-nominated costume designer who, with her partner Fab, created some 40 bespoke pieces for the series. “We see so much of wartime and Fifties fashion, but this was an amazing opportunity to show how important clothing was in 1947 France.” Taking inspiration from more than 2,000 images stored in Paris’s fashion libraries – though avoiding much of Dior’s work because “we didn’t want to be too close to him” – the pair curated a wardrobe of richly hued satin dresses (one of which required 70 metres of fabric) , wide-brimmed hats and emerald minks for the show.  “The show is all about post-war reconstruction; people were starving, but they were also starving for fashion.” After the liberation of Paris from Nazi rule in the summer of 1944, La Theatre de la Mode, a touring exhibition featuring exquisitely dressed mannequins one third of their normal size, was born. With the industry hit hard by shortages of thread and cloth, and numerous couturiers fleeing the country during the occupation, restoring its reputation was of consequence to both its high fashion credentials and the economy, too. “They wanted to establish in people’s minds that Parisian haute couture was the only one that counted,” says Anne Seba, author of Les Parisiennes; How the Women of Paris Lived, Loved and Died in the 1940s. “There were fears that the Italians might knock them off the top spot, and American designers were edging ahead with cool, elegant couture, so the French couture houses wanted to remind people that nobody could make bespoke clothes like theirs.” Paris’s predilection for specialist clothing was indubitable before the Second World War began, with more than 70 couture houses including Dior and Cristobal Balenciaga already registered in the city, but the Theatre de la Mode was a much-needed reminder of what they had to offer. As the Sabines’ investor Jules Trouvier (James Cosmo) surmises, the industry had to “remind women that Paris is where it begins and where it ends.” It worked: having been on tour in cities across Europe and the US for a year by the time Dior’s New Look arrived, the appetite for French fashion had been whetted. Yet while American journalists were loud to praise Paris’ return to glory, things were frostier in Britain: corsetry had been banned unless medically necessary and the fabric restrictions introduced during the war were still in place, making the notion of floor-skimming garments a near-unthinkable luxury. British Vogue omitted Dior from its pages and reactions to those who wore such finery were decidedly adverse. “People shout ordures at you from vans,” Nancy Mitford wrote of her experiences in haute couture; a Maison Dior photoshoot saw its models attacked by stallholders angry at their willful extravagance during hard times – an episode reimaged in The Collection. “I think this was a moment when fashion really was political, when fashion mattered,” says Kate Croft, the show’s executive producer. “Post-war Europe was a very difficult, ambiguous time, and yet in the midst of dreadful hardship and unrest, this industry rises phoenix-like out of the ashes. “The dresses are a metaphor for transformation.” The concept of sloping shoulders, full busts and wide skirts was a major departure from masculine wartime fashions and the loosely cut pieces that had preceded them. “The New Look, and the designs it inspired, were intensely feminine,” Sebba adds. Women had been given the vote in France a year earlier and the post-war focus was on family, rather than sustaining a professional career. “They were fighting to keep their jobs, but the impetus was on men getting back into work, and women going back to taking care of things at home. “To see people playing into traditional ideas of femininity by wearing such extravagant clothing made the garments even more controversial.” As Paul Sabine tells Trouvier, “Our next collection will allow men to be men again, by letting women be women – as feminine as they long to be.” For Fab, Chattoune’s design partner, recreating these “princess dresses” for the show was “intimidating, because it’s easy to make them cliché. But I put myself in that period and imagined how I would design clothes if I lived then”. The intricacies of the 1947 originals meant their recreations had to be just as exact: getting the structure of each gown right required numerous precise patterns to be cut; “enormous hems” and 1,200 individual pieces made for a “long, complicated process.” Chattoune and Fab’s focus was on the "eight", also known as the "Carolle" – Dior’s trademark silhouette of exaggerated shoulders belying a waif-like waist, and ramping up the volume of each skirt by joining eight circles together, where they would usually have one. With many of the dresses requiring 50 metres of fabric instead of the customary two, “it’s like wearing 25 outfits at once and so the dresses are unbelievably heavy. Couture is not for everybody!” Chattoune says. The fruits of their labour are every bit as lavish as one might hope: Chattoune particularly favours a red dress worn by Paul’s wife, Helen (Mamie Gummer) which is made of “the most beautiful double-laced satin ever”, and the glimmer of heavy set silks is rarely out of shot. With the addition of “short and clunky” heels, The Collection offers a glamorous snapshot in time.  “This is a Paris that most have seldom seen dramatised,” explains the show’s creator, Oliver Goldstick. “Not the Paris of Gene Kelly dancing along a sparkling Seine, but a haunted Paris, still trembling with distrust and anxiety,”  Now, through gowns just as devastating as the storyline’s unfolding dramas, they will.  Why do so many of us fantasise about emptying our wardrobes and starting again? How come there are more than 200,000 posts on Instagram about wardrobe and closet organisation? When did ‘closet styling’ (as opposed to styling oneself) become a thing? Sure, some of it’s guilt – we stare into overflowing cupboards each morning; we can’t find anything and if we do, it’s not quite right; then we increasingly feel pangs about indiscriminate consumption.
