 Long, white linen curtains fluttering gently in the hot breeze, tall French windows opening onto a 19th-century wrought-iron balcony, and beyond that, the Jardin de Luxembourg with its colony of beehives (this most formal of parks has got with the organic age)… could Julie de Libran’s apartment, where she lives with her Cognac-selling husband and 10-year-old son, be any more Parisian, or her lifestyle incorporate any more of the city’s idyllic tropes? As it happens, yes. Parquet floors, an eclectic mixture of art, books, old and new furniture (the former from the smart bit of Clignancourt’s famous flea market, the latter often commissioned to her specifications), and a brisk 15-minute walk every morning to her office above the famous Sonia Rykiel flagship store on the Boulevard Saint-Germain, where she took over as creative director in May 2014. If de Libran appears to have Paris, not always the easiest, most accommodating of capitals, laid out on a plate, perhaps that’s because it takes an exile of sorts to make one appreciate one’s home. For more than half her life, she lived outside France. Yet as we sit, then sprawl (it is a rare 2016 heat-wave) on her capacious blue velvet sofa (one of her commissioned pieces) alongside the flaked-out Gaston, one of her two Burmese cats (the other is Gastine), I’m struck by how Parisian – modern Parisian that is – she looks. It’s not the clothes themselves: her white, frayed-hem kick flares, the khaki silk blouse that’s just luxe enough not to need a jacket and brown platform sandals are the basic grammar of the international style conversationalist. It’s the way – and this sounds such a cliché – she wears them, with wavy, waist-length hair that on first impressions seems quite untamed, but isn’t, with a classic gold Cartier Tank watch, a chunky silver tiger-head medallion and a skinny diamond eternity ring. This is not the sports-chic option (those heels are easily 10cm high) that so many women have embraced as uniform for today’s smart-casual workplace, but something subtly different. Undone but done. Spontaneous and easy, but honed. Irreducible. It is a stylistic idiom that Coco Chanel, with her slouchy skinny cardigan-jackets and ropes of real-faux jewels would recognise and it’s certainly a continuum of the breezy, assertive swagger that Sonia Rykiel, who passed away last month at the age of 86, embodied when she first hit the fashion scene in 1962. “She was such an iconic woman,” muses de Libran in her perfectly modulated English. For once the word isn’t being traduced. “You can’t imagine how influential she was when she started. Women didn’t just want to wear the clothes, they wanted to be her, or to have some of that attitude. There was a time when you would see all these Sonia lookalikes, with bright red crimped hair. Her style, legacy and spirit will never be forgotten.” We discuss what that spirit was. Confident? Jaunty? Liberated? Politically, sexually, socially, Rykiel’s rise surfed the second wave of feminism, when the scaffolding of the haute bourgeoisie in France seemed as though it might be about to collapse. She was all of the above and fearless. The one piece of advice she gave to de Libran when she arrived at the helm? “She told me to know when to say no, and to stick with what I do.” So far, so good. In the two years that Libran has been in charge, she has quietly, without the fanfare of massive advertising campaigns, revolutionised the label’s collections, redefining the qualities that made Rykiel so loved in the first place. Revisiting all the Rykiel signatures – the skinny knits, the high-waisted flared trousers, the stripes, the strong-shouldered but comfortable jackets with their female swagger – she’s made them seem fresh again and at a price that, while hardly cheap, seems accessible compared with other big-name luxury fashion brands. As for the Rykiel bag: Le Copain (it means “buddy”, which sums up its friendly appeal perfectly), it is a nifty quilted gold chain number that comes in various colourways  and clocks in at around £350 but looks far more. “A big part of what made her great was the practical things,” muses de Libran of her striking predecessor. “So much of the knitwear had sleeves with vents, or sleeves that could be removed. Her dresses had opera pockets that were really slits – so you could move freely, and also it was quite naughty. Her tailoring was so strong, but comfortable. There was stretch before other people were doing it. Elegance and comfort. Her technique was amazing…” De Libran is no slouch herself, technically, although she denounces her pattern-cutting abilities (how many designers can pattern cut at all?). She studied not at those fashionable seats of fashion learning, London’s Central Saint Martins or Parsons School of Design in New York, but at Instituto Marangoni in Milan. “That was my father’s doing,” she laughs. “He thought the Italians were fantastic – their taste, their simplicity, their sense of colour. He thought they couldn’t be beaten.” This was the same father, an aristocratic wine cultivator, who transported his family, when Julie was eight years old, from Paris to the USA. They went first to the East Coast, which was too cold for her mother, then settled in San Diego, California, where de Libran père opened a restaurant. For de Libran, it was a form of paradise: a Provençal climate with American freedom, American beaches, and an American work ethic. “I was doing part-time jobs from the age of 12,” she says, “although looking back, I always kept a sense of Frenchness about me, mainly through the way I dressed.” There was a very brief Goth period, with shaved hair. “I wasn’t very good at being rebellious. I realised recently that I’m very, very shy – even more when I was younger. Clothes were how I expressed myself.” Her mother, who now works as an interior designer in North Carolina, was a huge influence. “Watching the way she put herself together, the way she styled everything, the way she wore a scarf…” We contemplate the role of the scarf in French style, and how there is always some kind of accessory that puts the right accent on an outfit. After 18 months on the “foreigners” course at Marangoni (she arrived in Milan speaking no Italian) she was offered a job working for Gianfranco Ferré. One of the giants of Italian fashion (metaphorically and literally, he was a bear of a man) he was also creative director of Dior, and  an exacting taskmaster. “He was super super strict with us,” recalls de Libran. “He was strict in everything. In his clothes too.” Famous for sculpted tailoring, “he would cut and reconstruct his toiles for hours. It was incredible training.” It’s an indication of de Libran’s strong sense of personal style that while she admired Ferré’s famous white organza shirts and precison flourishes, she never adopted that look for herself – perhaps because while strikingly beautiful and theatrical, its icy perfection was very much a man’s view of how a woman might dress. After two years, she was ready for Paris – the city she hadn’t lived in since she was a child. The rigorous training at Ferré had left her hungry for more. She enrolled on the Chambre Syndicale’s haute-couture course, source of her pattern-cutting doubts. “At least it taught me my strengths. I don’t have the patience for the meticulous technical demands of pattern-cutting, but I discovered I could be a designer without having to sew my own clothes. I’m better at cutting and draping and doing it by eye than making a pattern.” She does have patience though – you can tell from her quiet, thoughtful modulation. Then there’s her impressive CV. She has worked at the right hand of more major designers than almost anyone else I can think of. After the Chambre Syndicale she joined Jean Charles de Castelbajac, before moving back to Milan two years later to work for  Gianni Versace, and then his sister Donatella, then, from 1998, for Prada, where she stayed for a decade before returning once more to Paris to work for Marc Jacobs at Louis Vuitton, where she remained until shortly after he left, departing in January 2014. Adapting to the wildly different philosophies of the above must require some of the same skills as an actor, I suggest. “That’s quite true,” she laughs. “It’s certainly left me with a very eclectic wardrobe,” much of which she keeps in its own room in her apartment, which, it should be noted, is not huge. More than that: she was at Versace in the years when Princess Diana became one of his most loyal customers, at Prada when the brand was just beginning to dress celebrities. “That was interesting,” she says, with careful under-statement, “because at that time, in the late 1990s, Prada didn’t really do eveningwear. Actresses, or their stylists, would come with a very strong idea of The Dress – really fitted, very red-carpet classic.” De Libran knew that would never do for Miuccia Prada, so would spend months listening, sketching and acting as go-between in the holy triumvirate of stylist, actress and designer-in-chief. It must have felt like being a therapist at times. “Definitely,” she says. “But clothes are therapy in a way, and that’s what I love about them.” De Libran was so good at therapy that when Prada opened an office in Paris in 2003, it was she who headed up the celebrity dressing: Gywneth Paltrow, Clare Danes, Uma Thurman et al. De Libran would fly between Milan, Paris, New York and LA, attending the fittings and working up designs that would meet the approval of all parties. “It really helped me understand women more,” she reflects, “and to dig into that relationship we all have with our bodies and clothes. In that respect, French and American women are very different. It’s been an incredibly useful education.” At Vuitton she learned what it was like to start with a blank page for each new collection and to play with fireworks. Jacobs is mercurial where she is calm. They made a dream team. “Marc loved to change everything up, each time.” She worked with him on the show, across the women’s collection, accessories, jewellery, directing the studio… “It was exhilarating.” But, she says, Miuccia Prada’s is the aesthetic closest to her own. “That was part of the allure of coming to Sonia Rykiel. To me she was the French Miuccia Prada of her time.  She was always a reference for the design teams wherever I worked. When I was offered the job – and it was such a short distance from my apartment – it just felt absolutely right.” Ah yes, the apartment. It used to belong to her husband’s parents – somehow the fact that they casually handed it down seems evidence of more Frenchness, although she redecorated, stripping away the tapestries and rugs and replacing them with different talismen of arty, bohemian life. What’s striking about its eclectic elegance is how lived in it feels. There is nothing sterile or over-styled about it. How can it be with a 10-year-old and two opinionated Burmese cats who leave little tokens of their disgust around the place when the family periodically decamps to its country retreat? “Oh that,” shrugs de Libran, referring to Gaston and Gastine’s misdemeanours. “They like to make their feelings clear.” It’s an inordinately civilised existence. She rises at 7.15am, sees her son off to school, greets her trainer at 8am who directs her through her yoga, Pilates and TRX sessions, and arrives at the office at an acceptable 10.30am. Don’t be deceived by the seemingly leisurely pace. In short order, she has transformed Rykiel, root and branch, most recently designing and overseeing its new retail concept – a delightful meeting of clothes, accessories and shelf after shelf of books, highlighted with scarlet walls and woodwork. It seems a quintessentially Rykiel combination. She works until eight most nights on the brand’s eight collections a year (lunch is delivered from a nearby restaurant that caters for de Libran’s vegetarian needs), finds herself working at weekends and on holiday… As for that apartment, it may be eclectically boho – but everything in its place. “I cannot leave without tidying up every morning,” she notes. Undone, but done. Spoken like a true Frenchwoman. soniarykiel.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Fashion’s colour-blocking queen Roksanda Ilincic has long held an affinity with design and architecture. It was her original subject of study at the University of Arts in her home city of Belgrade, before she followed her first love, fashion, and headed to London’s Central Saint Martins. She is renowned for creating glamorous dresses characterised by fluid drapery and bold shapes in contrasting shades  – Ilincic’s designs are as striking as they are easy to wear. So it’s no surprise she’s a devotee of modernism. Today her appreciation of form and function is also channelled into a passion for chairs, which she collects, or simply admires from afar. Here she explains what she finds so captivating about the art of seating. "I love to collect chairs. I view them as sculpture. The right chair can completely change the feeling of a space, in the same way an artwork can. My mum collected furniture and ceramics. Her taste is more classic than mine though. I prefer modernist and midcentury designers, she was drawn towards art deco. My parents’ house was filled with furniture and objects, but the first chair that I bought was a very simple plastic Sixties one. I bought it for my bedroom when I was a teenager in Belgrade. I was excited by its bright orange colour, but sprayed it red after a while. I was into black with pops of colour at the time, so I had a painted wardrobe and this chair. It was a forerunner of what I’m doing now, but eventually colour took priority over black. Fashion was always my first choice but it seemed more realistic to study architecture. I thought it would lead to a job so I could support myself and live independently in Serbia. I felt that fashion wouldn’t provide me with as many possibilities after graduation. But while I was studying I read about Central Saint Martins – and Professor Louise Wilson in particular. I realised that most designers I admired had taken her course and that’s what made me come to London to try my luck. It changed my life. Soon after I arrived in London I went to a Sotheby’s auction where I came across a pair of very beautiful 1950s wooden rocking chairs. After I was lucky enough to buy them I discovered they were by a Slovenian designer called Niko Kralj – Slovenia was part of former Yugoslavia, where I was born. It was interesting that I made this journey to London and ended up buying something from home. They’re plywood with oval cut-outs, and they fold up like deck chairs. I still have them. I love them. Eileen Gray is one of my favourite designers. I love the incredible modernity and practical nature of her work. Take for example her Transat chair; it works like a deck chair and was inspired by the steamer chairs found on ocean liners of the time. She designed it for her villa in 1927, but it could have been designed now – this applies to all the designers that I love.  I feel there are similarities between Gray’s modernity, practicality and relevance, and my work. I love to experiment and push perceptions of femininity and beauty, but at the same time I keep my feet on the ground and appeal to women who need to live fast. Designers like Gray were doing this in their work – creating striking design that also functioned well. That’s why my dresses have that element of making you feel comfortable. I think about form and function; about the construction of the dress – how you move.  In the past when I was passionately buying vintage pieces I would discover a lovely dress but it might come with a corset, or you couldn’t sit down properly, or it was made out of  polyester, which doesn’t allow your skin to breathe. After wearing those pieces, once I started designing myself, I wanted to make a difference. I believe I’ve proven that wearability can co-exist with creativity. I seek out chairs online as a way to unwind. I am obsessed with browsing, regardless of whether I have space, or want to buy anything. At the end of a busy day I’m often in bed on my phone looking at websites like 1stdibs and Pamono. I really covet pieces by the Brazilian modernist architect Lina Bo Bardi. It’s that combination of beautiful metal with leather. She also loved circular shapes, there’s an incredible lightness to her designs. They look like they’re floating, just like her house. Actually there is something about Brazil and its aesthetic that I am really drawn to, because I also love Oscar Niemeyer. I was lucky enough to go to Brasilia and experience the whole town almost by myself one Christmas when it was virtually deserted. It was amazing to see Niemeyer’s architecture, but also his furniture in all its glory, how he imagined the chairs and the purpose for which he conceived them. They took my breath away, particularly those beautiful lounge chairs with stainless steel bases. Sometimes you find them in hotel lobbies, looking like time hadn’t moved on from when he first put them there. Pierre Paulin is another hero. I love his Ribbon chair, but also his early leather and steel designs. I have a couple of his pieces, including the beautiful Butterfly chair.  I don’t think that any particular chair has influenced my work directly, but there’s definitely a synergy with shape, colour and movement. Above all it’s about the feeling that my clothes and these chairs evoke by their very existence – a feeling of excitement, or happiness, from seeing these beautifully formed objects in colour." roksanda.com  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  What is it with the human scalp that makes us want to put a (semi circular) ring on it? From Tenniel’s illustrations of Alice Liddell to the Duchess of Cambridge’s adoption of an animal print one this week, the visual history of humans is littered with the Alice banded. I’ve been there. When Helmut Lang styled his models with bands as skinny as a length of dental floss, I pimped myself similarly. When I first discovered Martha Graham, the Mother of Modern Dance, I spent a year persevering with wide black stretchy bands worn brutally forward on my head with predictable results. I’ve done velvet, jewelled and leather bands, bands constructed like bra straps (very big in 2005). They all hurt and looked like hell. The AB has been lampooned as the Holy Sepulchre of the Church of Sloane, yet those of other beliefs can and do wear them – often with far more aplomb. I’m thinking Emma Watson, David Beckham, Tamara Rojo and Charlotte Casiraghi. But why needlessly burden one’s beauty with something so challenging and ill-suited to its putative job of keeping hair tidy? Perhaps because you are so macho and footballery you need an Alice band to stop all that testostrone leaking, or so beautiful and text-book ovoid of face, you experience frequent urges to wrap a ribbon around your perfection. Alternatively you are stuck in a moment in the 1980s, when Fergie, Duchess of York was, very briefly, a bit of a style darling. The top line here is that there is a stringent psychological test to be passed before contemplating this Black Run of style accessories. If the answer to all of the above is no, I strongly counsel abstinence. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  “No pain, no gain” used to be the mantra of the fashion industry, but it seems suffering to look good is a thing of the past. John Lewis announced this week that the popularity of “pyjama-style clothing” was soaring, with sales from its own brand “loungewear” up 29 per cent on last year in the week before Christmas. Meanwhile, plus-size retailer Simply Be has reported sales of pyjamas rocketing by 63 per cent.  If you’re assuming “loungewear” is fashion speak for “slob-out gear”, nothing could be further from the truth. Soozie Jenkinson, head of lingerie design at Marks and Spencer, defines the concept as “super soft fabrics layered in contemporary yet easy silhouettes”. In response to the “surge in popularity of the loungewear trend as a whole,” the store has had to significantly increase the cashmere offering in its premium Rosie for Autograph collection. John Lewis claims its sales reflect the trend for people to look for “relaxation time” at home, but if your loungewear looks this good, why hide it away? According to Jenkinson, “boundaries between formal and casual dressing are increasingly blurred. The importance of modern loungewear both for wearing in and out of the house has become an increasingly important and popular category, and has grown significantly over the past decade.” Sure enough, everywhere you look there are people out and about wearing what would formerly have been considered stay-at-home clothes. At one end of the spectrum, it’s no longer a surprise to see people in pyjamas at the supermarket, or in their cars on the school run. At the other end, Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg has taken loungewear into the boardroom with his trademark hoodie look. Nor does age seem to be a barrier to entry: at my local pool everyone from my toddler daughter to older teens leave, post-swim, in a cosy onesie (animal all-in-ones seem to be the look of the moment). Meanwhile, a colleague claims her sixty-something-year-old father-in-law lives in leisure wear around the house but gets dressed up to go and buy his daily paper - then changes back when he gets home again. In short, the lines of demarcation that once cut a neat divide between the different spheres of our life - the bedroom, the sitting room, the street, the shops, the office - are being eroded. Where once we would have worn pyjamas only in the bedroom, and unfailingly donned a tie or heels before our commute to work, such sartorial niceties seem to be on the way out, while in-between, crossover items like leggings, sweat pants and delux nightwear are on the up. “What we bought [in 2015] may say more than we realise about us and the year we’ve just had…and how we live today,” said shopping guru Mary Portas on Channel 4’s What Britain Bought in 2015 on Wednesday. By the same token, what we didn’t buy is also significant. Included in the latter category, she discovered, were thongs and fishnet stockings at John Lewis. Instead, Portas reported “one of the biggest selling categories [across UK retail in 2015] was 'athleisurewear,’” something she defines as “athletic but it’s also leisure - upmarket leggings and tops”.  The trend was kickstarted by Stella McCartney designing kit for the GB Olympic team in 2012, but by summer 2015 big name celebrities were fighting to collaborate with big name brands, and athleisurewear was put on the map.  The amount of time we’re spending at home is one explanation for the growing popularity of loungewear. In these straitened times, nights out have been replaced with nights in curled up with Netflix and adult colouring books. Online shopping has taken over visits to the supermarket, high street or giant shopping centre (on Black Friday 2015, Amazon sold 86 items a second).  So what exactly do we need to get dressed up for anymore? Certainly not our jobs. According to the Office for National Statistics, there were a record 4.2 million home workers in the period from January to March last year, up by 1.3 million on 1998 when comparable records began. Thanks partly to a more flexible (and round the clock) work life, enabled by the rise of the internet, at-home working is increasingly becoming the norm and with it, a more relaxed attitude to workwear.  Back in October, when the BBC’s then political editor Robert Peston caused a stir by claiming it was “bonkers” that people expected him to wear a tie, he may have offended Today presenter Justin Webb (who protested that “formality … does concentrate the mind”), but his views reflected attitudes in homes – and offices  - nationwide. What better poster girl for the trend than Robin Wright as ultra-modern First Lady Claire Underwood, working chicly on her laptop in La Perla silk pjs in House of Cards? (How fortuitous, too, that the actress has recently launched her own line of “luxury sleepwear”, Pour Les Femmes). Even David Cameron, the Prime Minister, has admitted to wearing pyjamas while working early in the morning.  While Mr Cameron is yet to share a selfie to prove this, the phenomenon of stylish celebrities displaying their lives to us 24/7 on social media has helped gift loungewear a huge boost in sales. As Laura Costin of Simply Be points out, “famous faces including Selena Gomez, Miley Cyrus, Rihanna and Cara Delevingne regularly share selfies of themselves wearing pyjama-style clothing.” The rest of us are hardly immune: sharing every aspect of our lives on Facebook, we invite the world to see us in all our dressed-down glory. With the public and the private spheres thus blurred, the pressure to up our downtime game is on.  All of which reflects the increasing informality of society at large, not just where fashion is concerned but in everything from our language to our eating habits. But it was Coco Chanel who popularised pyjamas as eveningwear for the more daring ladies of high society back in the 1920s with her “lounging pyjamas”, based on the silk pyjamas she stole from her lover, some nine decades before we became accustomed to seeing the pyjama on the high fashion catwalks, and street style blogs. Gucci, Dolce & Gabbana and Alexander Wang have presented silky pyjamas as a relaxed yet elegant take on eveningwear. Pjs even appeared on the Spring 2016 menswear catwalks at Versace, Dries van Noten and Louis Vuitton - and also in the audience, at least on some of the more fashion forward (male) style editors.  Where the catwalk leads, the high street follows. We may not yet have lost the art of the dressing up, but the age of casual is upon us and - early indications suggest - in 2016 it will not go away. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  In 2015, Kim Kardashian #broketheinternet with her Paper magazine front cover. You'll remember the one; shot by Jean-Paul Goude, Kim's famous derriere front and centre, Vaseline-d to the hilt and nude aside from a pearl choker and satin evening gloves. That 'Break the Internet' cover line became a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy, with the implied assumption sending the shots viral, if not literally doing what they said on the tin (leave that to hackers and cyber terrorists).  Now Kardashian has done it again but with a set of photographs which couldn't be more different. For the latest issue of Interview magazine, she has been styled as a retro-throwback, picture perfect tribute to Jackie Kennedy. She has the bouffant hair, immaculately tailored shift dresses and gleaming pearls. Her clothes are sourced from a patriotic selection of labels including Ralph Lauren and Michael Kors. Any political spin doctor would be delighted to see the common-touch H&M look in the mix while there is extra authenticity thanks to a smattering of vintage Chanel bags and jewellery. Daughter North West makes a meticulous accessory too in her sweet, traditional little girl look.  This is Kim Kardashian as we've never seen her before.  Admittedly, that's saying something given the constant stream of selfies, red carpet and street style images which she feeds us- it was pink hair and thigh high pink boots on Friday. But these pictures are also incredibly familiar. Jackie Kennedy remains a style icon who is continually credited as inspiration by designers, we obsess over her image as much we do living, breathing celebrities more than twenty years on from her death and more than fifty years after her spell in the White House.  There's a purpose to Interview magazine's ploy. They declare Kardashian to be 'America's New First Lady.' With Michelle Obama off the scene and Melania Trump undoubtedly glamorous but tainted by the controversies of her husband's administration, this is an acknowledgment of  a Head Woman vacancy in the national psyche. So why not dress her up as the most famous First Lady of them all, just to underline the point?  Kim might seem like a depressing choice-all that talk of make-up and men- but she does makes sense. In terms of power and influence, it is her family who fascinate America- and the world- like few others. She speaks carefully in the accompanying interview about how she considers issues like race and transgender rights, conflating national concerns with those experienced by her own family. "We want to raise our kids to be really aware," she tells interviewer Janet Mock. "I think that’s all you can do. The more you talk about things and keep them out in the open, the more they won’t be taboo." It's a perfectly poised performance and one you could barely relate to a woman who often favours belfies (that's bum selfies) as a means of publicity.   If, for now, Kim Kardashian is a substitute for the official First Lady then maybe it would have been more refreshing to offer a more visually modern spin on what she makes of that title, as Michelle Obama dressed for the version of the role which she created for herself.  But there's nothing quite like leaning on a very stylish historical stereotype. Just, in fact, as Melania Trump did when she channeled Jackie's Inauguration look in her own Ralph Lauren skirt suit in January. Genius, bizarre or a little bit of both, Kim as Jackie will probably aid the former in her mission to cement herself as a celebrity with the same long-term kudos as the latter.        © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Mary Kate and Ashley Olsen have been working since they were nine months old. But today the sisters turn 30 years old, which seems a fitting opportunity to analyse their style.  When it comes to dressing they are the anti-Kardashians, hiding behind bundles of cashmere and wearing quiet but luxe accessories by their label The Row. Their anti-paparazzi style has become so notorious that there are plans for an exhibition filled with images of them hiding behind Birkin bags and Venti Starbucks cups to run away from the paparazzi.  The Olsens have turned their low-key aesthetic into a fashion empire with their labels The Row and Elizabeth and James. But you don't need to be able to afford their £750 Mary Janes, £200 t shirts or £2,000 back packs to buy into the Olsens' scruffy but expensive aesthetic. Here are 10 styling tips to take from the super chic twins: 'No I don't want milk in my Americano, and no I won't wear colour just because it's August,' you can almost hear the Olsen sisters saying.  As the pair prove time and time again, black can still look chic in the summer. And bonus; doesn't show up sweat. The Olsens turned their back on heels way before Kristen Stewart dared to wear Converse on the red carpet, wearing sandals to awards shows in 2004. The Olsen shoe-drobe consists of Birkenstocks, leather flip flops, black loafers, Mary Janes by The Row and Chanel pumps.  A crisp white shirt with rolled up sleeves is a key part of Ashley Olsen's working wardrobe - a classic styling tip we can all learn from.  In 2006 Mary Kate Olsen was inseparable from her vintage beaded handbag, wearing it on the red carpet as well as to run errands. The Olsens are all about investing in pieces that will work for all occasions. Every item in the Olsens wardrobe must pass the coffee test (how will I go to Starbucks in this?). The Olsen twins are all about drowning in layers and piled up accessories, but sometimes they use stand-out pieces to distract from what is underneath. Mary Kate Olsen joked: "I love getting amazing jackets, because you can wear your pajamas underneath and everyone's like, 'Oh, fabulous jacket,' and I'm like, 'You should see what's underneath!'" This is once again part of their lifelong mission of snubbing the paparazzi. But can also be used by you in normal life to avoid anyone who tries to make contact first thing in the morning.  The Olsens have a bigger is better approach to accessories, and ten years after they were first seen lugging weighty Fendi Spy bags, they still favour epic totes. "I feel like when I carry a bigger bag, it looks like it's a huge bag because I'm really tiny," Mary Kate Olsen has joked about their thing with big bags. "But I do think it's important to have the space that you need, because we throw everything in our bags at all times. I think every woman does. "  In 2013 the Olsen twins went to the Met Gala in vintage Dior and Chanel clashing, shapeless outfits that many dismissed as "weird". The Olsens might favour basics, but they also aren't afraid of wearing something most people will hate. "I wear weird things sometimes," Mary Kate Olsen has said. "I like to drink coffee. Neither of those things have anything to do with who I am." Mary Kate and Ashley might like hiding in seemingly never-ending fabric, but they know how to play with proportions. Their Met Gala gowns are usually dark, moody and show very little skin, but they will be nipped in at the waist so they don't disappear. Mary Kate has said they learnt the importance of shape because of their height (they are 5'2): "When I was young, clothes were really just about what fit, because Ashley and I were so tiny.  J.W. Anderson beat Victoria Beckham to the Womenswear Designer of the Year at this year's British Fashion Awards, but there was only one man in the frame for the Fashion Creator prize. Photographer Nick Knight OBE was honoured with the Isabella Blow Awards for Fashion Creator, an award that has previously gone to stylist Edward Enninful, Professor Louise Wilson and Lady Amanda Harlech. Knight’s career began in 1982 with the release of his first book, Skinheads. He has since gone on to become one of the most prolific fashion photographers and filmmakers in the world, regularly collaborating with designers including Alexander McQueen and fashion influencers including Lady Gaga and Kanye West (he famously directed West’s Bound II music video). He regularly contributes to publications including Vogue, i-D and W magazine and his work has been exhibited around the world.  Here’s a question that might seem pretty straight-forward to answer: should twelve-year-old children be modelling grown-up clothes? On the cover of a magazine. A magazine aimed at grown-ups. That’s a simple ‘no’ right? Except of course when the twelve-year-old in question has (gasp!) 1.3m followers on Instagram, and is the star of cult Netflix super-hit, Stranger Things.   Here’s another question: does that make it OK? My answer: still no. However, fashion, that contrary little imp of opinion would clearly beg to differ. When child actress Millie Bobby Brown was unveiled as the star of a twenty page cover shoot with little known arts magazine So It Goes, which goes on sale today, style watchers reacted with breathless enthusiasm, fawning over the girl in a quite extraordinary manner. ‘Millie Bobby Brown lands first fashion cover!’ squealed the delighted headlines. At no point did anyone raise the issue of whether a twelve-year-old child should be modelling a £4000 Chloé dress. Let alone, whether that makes you actually want to buy one in the first place. That’s what she’s wearing on the front cover of So It Goes. But Chloé aren’t the only designer courting Bobby Brown. In a recent interview, the magazine’s creative director, James Wright confided that, “Every brand, bar none, reacted with an almost discerning level of excitement about the possibility of lending clothes to Millie.” I, like any self-respecting child of the Eighties who had a penchant for Eerie, Indiana and The Goonies, fell entirely for the misty-tinted spine chilling retro nostalgia of Stranger Things. I watched the whole series (admittedly, only eight episodes long) in three days. And yes, the character of Eleven, played by Millie Bobby Brown, was entirely beguiling. And yes, if I have a Halloween party to attend this year, sure I’ll crack out a baby doll smock dress, drip some fake blood from my nose and snack on frozen waffles. Provocative use of minors is, of course, nothing new in fashion. In 1980 a fifteen-year-old Brooke Shields declared in a Calvin Klein advert that ‘nothing gets between me and my Calvin's’. Two networks in New York banned the advert for its risqué implication that the teen Shields, photographed with her plaid shirt billowing open, wasn’t wearing underwear underneath her skin-tight jeans. A decade later sixteen-year-old Kate Moss was photographed topless by Corinne Day for The Face. At the age of 38,  Moss admitted in an interview with Vanity Fair that during the shoot with Day she’d “lock myself in the toilet and cry and then come out and do it. I never felt very comfortable about it.”   The trajectory of child stars, shuffled before their time into adult worlds and spaces has rarely ended without issue. Who can forget Britney Spears’s 2007 bald breakdown in front of the world’s media. Or indeed Drew Barrymore - who at aged seven became a cult sci-fi star thanks to her role in ET - later taken to Studio 54 by her mother, and then to rehab at aged thirteen. This current courting of youth is something that the social media obsessed fashion industry is fast turning its attention to. At the past round of fashion weeks, Brown herself sat front row at Coach’s New York show (alongside her co-star Winona Ryder and Emma Roberts). At Dolce & Gabbana, the designer duo unveiled their ‘Millennial’ front row - a cacophony of 18-24 year olds, beloved to their hundreds of thousands (in some cases, millions) of Instagram followers - and this week, 23-year-old ex-One Direction singer Zayn Malik has been announced as the new creative partner for Versace’s younger line, Versus. For anyone, however, who may not be seduced by teenagers flogging them luxury items, a more reassuring movement is concurrently taking shape. This month British Vogue unveiled their first ‘Real’ women issue, featuring artists, historians, Cross-Rail employees  and their own staff instead of professional models; Bottega Veneta booked 72 year old Lauren Hutton for its Milan fashion show, whilst Versace offered a cross-section of model ages in its show - including Naomi Campbell (46), Carmen Kass (38) and Mariacarla Boscono (36). Fashion has always been a contrary, opinion dividing beast, but where do we draw the line? Perhaps in separating it away from fiction. Do I want Millie Bobby Brown back as Eleven in series two? Hell yes. Do I want to see a twelve-year-old in a fashion shoot, or read an interview with one? Erm. Not really. Yes, she’s cute. But hyped up fawning over the ‘look’ of a minor is creepy at best. And where does it all lead? In another worrying youth-provocation, a tattoo artist called Kat Von D launched her new make-up range in London by furnishing Kings Cross station with a giant model of a lipstick. The name of the lipstick? Underage red. Still, it’s all just locker room banter right? No harm in any of it. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  You don't need to be a Prime Minister diminished by a disappointing election result to understand that on some days, clothes and make-up can take on an armour-like function, acting as a brave front for battle. For Theresa May, that battle today is thrashing out a plan to save her leadership and create a viable government for her country but the same rules would apply too for big work meetings or a tense family occasion. So it was perhaps unsurprising that when the Prime Minister arrived at the count in her Maidenhead constituency overnight, she looked more polished and put-together than at any other point during the campaign, a look which projected a poised readiness for power in spite of the emerging poll results to the contrary. Although May has never veered from her stylish-yet-professional signature look over the past weeks, she has been notably pared-back in her style choices. Not today though.  The Prime Minister seemed to have spent some of her down time on polling day having a blow dry and perhaps even a subtle trim as her cropped hair looked a notch neater and sleeker than it has during previous appearences lately. She also added some bolder elements to her beauty look, with more definition around her eyes and a swish of complexion-lifting red lipstick. Despite being the middle of the night, her look spoke of a woman ready for action, even if the slight crackle in her voice acknowledged that events were not unfolding quite as she had expected they would back on that walking holiday in Wales when she resolved to call a snap general election.  While May didn't pick a new outfit, as she did when she wore a pinstriped dress by Daniel Blake to call the election in April, she did turn to a tried and trusted option which has served her well at major moments of her Downing Street tenure so far. The tomato red Amanda Wakeley skirt suit with black belting detail was perhaps a surprising choice given its obviously Labour-ish hue (a conciliatory nod to Corbyn, who turned out to be a stronger opponent than she could ever have imagined?) but it's clearly a look which May feels comfortable in, having chosen it for her meeting with Donald Trump in January and for her appearence on the Sky/ Channel 4 leaders debate late in May. She even added the same final flourish- an Hermes scarf- on all those occasions.  While the hours and days ahead will see May fighting for her political future, her look last night confirmed that she not only enjoys fashion- as she has proudly said countless times before- but that it has a more profound ability to armour her for the most testing of challenges.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Meghan Markle’s glamorous new shoot for Vanity Fair has made front pages around the world today, as fans praise her bold declaration of love for our Prince Harry, and critics question the publicity-seeking motives of the up-and-coming American actress. Draped in Carolina Herrera silk tulle, she certainly looks princessy, and in the accompanying interview Markle secures her status as a potential fashion plate, giving a diplomatic nod to British-Canadian designer Erdem Moralıoğlu (‘a designer I’ve been wearing for years’) as well as ticking the relatability box with a story about a time she dashed into H&M to buy an emergency dress before a life-changing audition for the TV show Suits. The appeal of posing for Vanity Fair is obvious. Trying on couture gowns under the guidance of the magazine’s fashion director Jessica Diehl, having supremely flattering portraits taken by the legendary Peter Lindbergh (whose former subjects include everyone from Kate Moss to Penelope Cruz) - it all sounds like a dreamy scene from some sort of Sex and the City-style movie. And a lot of Markle’s life in the media to date reads like a rom-com in its perfectness. Her jobs as an actress, a women’s rights campaigner and a lifestyle blogger, plus her general sense of poise, are well documented in the press, as well as in the posts she offers about herself on her Instagram page. So aren’t we being hypocritical if we dismiss what is essentially a presentation of her 'best self’ as being fame-hungry? Fashion shoots are always supposed to offer a fantasy, extrapolated version of their subject, and aren’t words like ‘polished’, ‘perfect’ and ‘glossy’ symbolic of the very traits that we as a society seem to praise most about, say, the Duchess of Cambridge? Granted, when Kate starred on the front cover of British Vogue’s centenary issue in June 2016, she had specifically requested to ditch the diamonds. “It was very clear from the outset that these pictures were to be of the woman herself rather than of a figurehead, and that they would be as informal as possible,” editor Alexandra Shulman said at the time. “The Duchess liked the idea of being photographed in the countryside, and she wanted the pictures to reflect an element of her private existence. She didn’t want to be dressed as a fashion plate and was not keen to be shot in gala gowns and tiaras.” Vogue’s fashion director Lucinda Chambers instead dressed her in jeans, t-shirts and country casuals; “The same as the rest of us.” Glamorous and accessible? What's not to like? The late Diana, Princess of Wales, meanwhile, appeared on three Vogue covers and numerous Vanity Fairs in her lifetime, in various states of deb-worthy and cool-casual attire. In 1971, arguably her favourite fashion decade, Princess Anne modelled bohemian silhouettes for Vogue’s September issue. Princess Eugenie’s done Tatler, Prince William posed for GQ and Attitude in the last year alone, and Vogue has photographed Princess Margaret, the Queen Mother, and even the Queen herself over the past 100 years. Did they each give away details about their blossoming relationship at such a crucial stage as Markle’s in the accompanying interviews? Probably not. But they did use the opportunity to present some insight into their personal lives and style? Absolutely. Will you really deny the girl the chance to enjoy getting dressed up and relishing in her fantasy life for a moment - something that millions do on their own social media pages every hour? If so, I think you’re just being mean. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Van Custem is married to one of Prince William's oldest friends, William Van Cutsem, who is the godfather to Prince George and they live in the countryside in Norfolk, the same county of course as Anmer Hall.  "We started the brand in 2014 in reaction to what was available for women who wanted to move between the city and the countryside and have a versatile wardrobe that worked for both environments," Van Cutsem told The Telegraph last year. "It became a common thread that women would leave the city to the country and have to reinvent their wardrobe. We wanted to create something with durability, but add a luxury feel with high quality fabrics and leather detailing and fur and faux fur, adding a luxurious element so it's something a little more stylish but works from a practical point of view."  During her six years at Downing Street, Samantha Cameron inspired professional women across the country with her elegant, eclectic and modern approach to workwear. Now, she's taking the next step in influencing the wardrobes of the nation by launching her own fashion line.  Cefinn (the first and last letters are the same as the Cameron surname while the middle letters represent the initials of her four children- Elwen, Florence, Ivan and Nancy) goes on sale today on its own website, Cefinn.com, as well as via Net-a-porter.com and Selfridges. The 35 piece collection is designed to be "urban uniform for busy women who love fashion," according to Samantha Cameron, who first revealed news of the collection in British Vogue.  As you'd expect from a woman who had to dress for everything from the school run to a state dinner with the Obamas during her time in Number 10, Cefinn is a collection of easy-to-mix separates and dresses you can throw on and run out the door in.  There's also a hefty dose of versatile workwear, such as the sleeveless wool top and matching midi skirt Cameron was photographed in for the Vogue feature. With its red trim, tie-waist and kicked hem, the look was sleek enough for the office but also ripe for dressing up come the evening. Prices start at £150 and go up to £450 - a happy medium of Sam Cam's preferred stable of favourite labels, which range from LFW names like Christopher Kane, Roksanda and Preen, to the high street and mid-level brands which she calls on regularly, such as J Crew, Joseph, Zara and Marks & Spencer. “I felt that there were a lot of American and French brands out there that fit that bracket of designer contemporary with the right price point and the right styling but there aren’t many British brands which fill that space,” she explained to Vogue of part of the reason she chose to launch Cefinn.  Samantha apparently spend months perfecting the right shade of 'poppy-red' - and you can tell. The punchy colour of this funnel neck midi dress (£270) makes it a standout piece for desk-to-dinner dressing. The boxy black jacket (£290) would also be a brilliant wardrobe addition: the zip and sloped collar make it unusual enough for a smart work or weekend look.  Cameron has also cleverly ensured there are matching separates, which when worn together make a refreshing alternative to a suit. This zip collar crop top (£150) would look as good with jeans as it would the matching midi skirt (£190). As well as being a savvy shopper, Cameron has plenty of behind the scenes experience in fashion, having worked for Smythson for two decades. After her husband became Prime Minister she announced she was stepping down from her role as creative director of the stationery and leather goods brand to take on a part-time creative consultant position. When she first joined the company she was extremely hands-on, spearheading a large amount of the design work and playing an integral part in  launching its handbag collection - in fact, the Nancy bag is named after Cameron's daughter.   Adding to this, Cameron hasn't overlooked the practical skills involved in starting a clothing label. Samantha secretly took a dress-making course during her husband's time as PM and has long made her own clothes.  The 45-year-old has also cultivated close connections in the fashion industry in her role as an ambassador for the British Fashion Council. She hosted a number of receptions for designers at Downing Street, was a regular presence on the front row at London Fashion Week, and acted as a judge in the BFC/Vogue Fashion Fund contest.  During David Cameron's tenure Samantha earned a reputation as a taste-maker, allied with her peer, former First Lady Michelle Obama, as defining a new code of dress for women in politics. Adopting a less formal approach than their predecessors, they proved power-dressing is something you can have fun with. Silhouettes that accentuated her figure, while also possessing a directional quality became Cameron's signature - like the patterned fit and flare Roksanda dress she wore as her family departed Number 10 following  David Cameron's resignation. Cameron brought flair to her wardrobe with exuberant colour and print choices and never shied away from making statements in other ways. She caused controversy when she attended a thanksgiving service in celebration of The Queen's 90th birthday in a sleeveless L.K Bennett dress and nodded to Margaret Thatcher's sartorial legacy when she wore a pussy bow blouse to the former PM's funeral.  So despite the fact Cameron is the first among political spouses to launch a fashion label, The Telegraph's fashion director Lisa Armstrong believes she has the connections and clout to make it a viable venture. "With her two decades at Smythson and her genes – her mother, Annabel Astor, co-founder of Oka, the successful furniture venture is a serial entrepreneur – the auguries are positive," she comments. Citing the "ability to express her creative side" and the "unabashed enjoyment of clothes" which Cameron showed during her husband's time as Prime Minister, Armstrong asserts: "If she can translate that into her own line, and given her enjoyment of fiscal prudence (“I love a bit of accounting,” she told me. “There’s something very satisfying about making the books balance”), she should go far." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Before new cult label Monse had even presented its first collection at New York Fashion Week in September, Sarah Jessica Parker and Amal Clooney had already been spotted wearing pieces from the label. With a client list that even the most established design houses would be proud of, it's not surprising that despite only having a five-person team, Monse's debut collection ended up on Net-a-Porter. Most start-up labels spend years trying to be noticed by mainstream press and buyers, but Monse is a brand on fast-forward. The one-year-old label has designed costumes for Selena Gomez's tour, collaborated with Sarah Jessica Parker on her Met Gala look, dressed Best Actress winner Brie Larson for the Oscars after-parties and has quickly become Amal Clooney's new go-to label. While Monse might only be in its infancy, its founders Laura Kim and Fernando Garcia are certainly not new to the game and spent a combined 18 years working at American design giant Oscar de la Renta. "We met at Oscar de la Renta," Kim and Garcia tell The Telegraph of launching their label. "Because he liked a very small team, we got to know each other very well and work with each other's aesthetics. This became instinctual to check on one other's approval before showing an idea to Oscar. As soon as we found ourselves in a position of finding out who we were outside of a major fashion house, we decided to take the leap and explore that on our own which resulted in the creation of Monse." Their label is understandably informed by their training at de la Renta, mainly with their focus on wearability.  "Working at a revered house and with Oscar taught us many things, one of which was designing clothes that women can wear. Listen to those with experience and always have fun at work." Monse's A-list fan club has certainly been key to the success of the label. "The fact that the most stylish women in the world prefer to put our clothes on their backs – this gave us an immediate validation," the designers say of the impact of celebrity dressing. "The few that have worn Monse, we have complete admiration for their work ethic and talent and are honored to be considered worthy of dressing them." Monse made headlines around the world when Sarah Jessica Parker decided to defend the Met Gala outfit she created with Kim and Garcia. Parker responded to a fashion blogger who claimed her outfit- which was inspired by the musical Hamilton- didn't fit the tech white tie dress code, and wrote on Instagram: “Always welcome thoughts, but I’m a stickler for the theme and pay close attention to what it means. Every year with great consideration, research and conviction. The understanding of man and machine, how they intersect, when and why is what we considered. Perhaps you weren’t aware of the technology used in the details and embellishments of the design. Or perhaps you simple didn’t like that I wore which is completely fine but you can’t accuse me of not paying close attention and adhering to the theme. With respect and warmest regards, sj.” "There was a lot of research and thinking of how to interpret an 18th century men’s wardrobe applied with today’s technology," Laura Kim and Fernando Garcia said of Sarah Jessica Parker's Met Gala look. As for Parker's decision to defend her outfit on Instagram, they add: "We thought it served its purpose because she didn’t look another silver robot." The label is also finding fame with the Snapchat generation, as Laura Kim and Fernando Garcia worked with Selena Gomez on her recent tour wardrobe. Gomez opens her show in a Monse catsuit covered in 96,480 Swaorvski crystals with a deconstructed black gown over the top. "It was adapting our experience of ready-to-wear and applying it to something that is comfortable enough to move around in on stage," the design duo told us. "Christian Classen (Gomez's tour stylist) had a very clear idea of what the styling of the tour would look like and it made everything a lot more simplified in terms of process. We had a couple of fittings where we tweaked things here and there, but, overall, Selena was loyal to the “look” that Christian and I were going for that ultimately represented their (Christian and Selena’s) aesthetic done in the Monse way."  See our edit of the best Monse pieces to shop online below...  Monse + Mariela Montiel striped duchese-satin point-toe flats, £645 Monse one-shoulder stretch-cotton twill shirt, £730 Monse striped duchesse silk-satin wide-leg pants, £1,725 Monse button-detailed stretch wool-blend dress, £1,900   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  France’s First Lady Brigitte Macron met America’s Melania Trump in Paris this afternoon, prompting the political version of last night’s royal fashion ‘face-off’ between the Duchess of Cambridge and Queen Letizia of Spain. The new fashion strategy at play for global political figures now is a balance of diplomacy (showing subliminal allegiance to a particular nation, or your own, by wearing a native designer), personality (because a good First Lady has always had ‘good taste’) and figure-flattery - Obama’s collaboration with tailor Christie Rilling set the precedent that everyone must look incredible in their well-fitted clothes.  This morning Pippa Middleton confirmed her engagement to James Matthews, by flashing her engagement ring to the photographers waiting outside her London home, telling them she "couldn't be happier." Rumours emerged last night that Pippa Middleton's boyfriend of a year James Matthews proposed to her over the weekend during a walk in the Lake District, but she artfully hid her left hand behind her back when she was out and about last night to avoid giving anything away. But this morning when the Duchess of Cambridge's younger sister left her London home, she balanced her left hand over the strap of her brown leather shoulder bag to give photographers a clear shot of the impossible-to-miss engagement ring.  So what do we actually know so far about Pippa's ring? Matthews proposed with a large octagonal diamond ring, with a central stone thought to be at least 3 carats. The Telegraph Luxury's jewellery expert Annabel Davidson reveals: "It looks like an Asscher cut diamond with a halo of channel-set diamonds, either in platinum or white gold. It looks quite Art Deco in style especially, with all that metal around the halo instead of the little diamonds being claw-set. That central stone looks upwards of three carats." Diamond expert David Christopher Allen, Creative Director of 77 Diamonds agrees on the cut, commenting: "It is Art Deco in style with an octagonal halo of round diamonds surrounding what looks to be a 4 carat Asscher cut diamond. Asscher cut diamonds are step cut inside, which means there are fewer facets than standard shapes such as round or princess square cuts. This means that their clarity has to be of the highest quality and close to flawless to show off the beautiful structure of the diamond." Sarah Sheard, manager and diamond expert at Hatton Jewels which values jewellery, suggests: "The main stone appears to be around 3.5 carats with a total of 5 carats on the whole ring. The ring itself is platinum. The diamonds have an excellent clarity and white colour, as you'd expect given who it has been made for." As for price, Allen adds: "A diamond and ring of top quality could fetch upwards of £200,00." Meanwhile Sheard adds: "I would value the ring at between £150,000 and £180,000." How do you style out a ring worth the same as many people's homes? Middleton offset the diamonds with a modest outfit, selecting a summery white embroidered £110 Whistles dress with three-quarter length sleeves, which is now no longer available. She paired this with a classic tan leather over the shoulder bag and flat brown leather sandals.  As for which jeweller designed the ring, Davidson reveals: "There aren't any design signatures viewable to make it clear who designed it." The Middleton family have made a number of jewellery purchases from the London jewellers Robinson Pelham, including the diamond earrings which the Duchess of Cambridge wore on her wedding day- a gift from her parents Michael and Carole Middleton. Pippa and Carole also both wore pieces designed by Robinson Pelham to the royal wedding. As to whether they have designed Pippa Middleton's engagement ring, Robinson Pelham says it can not comment on clients or commissions. Although it has been suggested this is a vintage design, Joanna Hardy, a fine jewellery expert, explains that the design is a modern interpretation of a classic Art Deco style. "With an Art Deco ring you would have baguette diamonds around the outside, so to have changed for modern round cut diamonds. that definitely is a contemporary twist," she explains. "It seems that there is a bit of space around the setting of the Asscher cut diamond, which is a twist as with an Art Deco ring you would have diamonds or metal next to the main stone. The fact that you can see the gap gives a sense of lightness, which you wouldn't see in a traditional Deco piece, and it makes it look elegant." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Hunger Games star Jennifer Lawrence is revealing all manner of cleavage as she promotes the final instalment of the popular film franchise: Mockingjay Part 2.  After revealing a lot of front in Berlin by way of a plunge-neck gown, last night she balanced a more demure neckline with a flash of what is known as 'side boob'. Her Dior Haute Couture gown, split entirely at the side and held together with a couple of delicate chains, meant the actress had to forgo a bra and reveal much of her torso in the process. The 25-year-old, who won an Oscar for her performance in 2012 film Silver Linings Playbook, was joined by co-stars Julianne Moore, Elizabeth Banks and Jenna Malone on the red carpet in Leicester Square. Kentucky-born Lawrence was signed up as a Dior ambassador in 2012 and stars in advertising campaigns for is Miss Dior line of handbags and Dior Addict lipsticks. She has avidly worn designs conceived by Raf Simons, the brand's ex-creative director, who announced his departure last month.

 You know Ross, Monica, Rachel, Chandler, Joey and Phoebe maybe better than your own friends - I couldn't tell you my actual mates' middle names but I know Chandler’s is Muriel - but you might not be familiar with the woman behind their TV-defining style: Debra McGuire. McGuire pulled off the greatest coup in TV fashion history, taking ordinary clothes like tank tops, argyle sweaters and plaid shirts and making them suddenly aspirational - and in doing so, firmly cementing Rachel, Monica et al in our hearts. Over ten years, Friends defined 90's style. Jennifer Aniston's "Rachel" haircut sparked salon frenzy as thousands of women flocked to their hair stylist to copy the 'do, and just re-watching Series One is like a visual checklist of all our favourite pre-Millennium styles including crop tops, slip dresses and oversized shirts. So how did Debra McGuire make all our favourite Friends fashion moments happen? We found out some on-set secrets:  "The greatest compliment I ever got was a few years ago from Tom Ford," Debra tells us. "I got a note from Richard Buckley, his partner, saying they watched the show every night when they have dinner, and that Tom wanted me to know that the clothes looked better than ever. I like to think he felt that the clothes had stood up to the test of time." "I come from the fine art world, and I wasn’t really interested in television - I couldn’t stand the way the people looked. And since I’m a painter, I thought the best way to begin is to think about the costumes as if they were in a two-dimensional painting. Because there were six characters and they were together a lot of the time, the idea was to create a tableau, and to work with the production designer and set decorator to co-ordinate an ensemble look that was unique and visually enticing on a two-dimensional surface, considering color, line, and texture." "To this day, in 2016, I get at least one email a week saying, 'My wife and I are watching Friends and I loved that dress - where can I find it?'," McGuire laughs. "I always write back and say 'That was 20 years ago!'"  "At the beginning Marta Kauffman (the Friends co-creator), wanted the cast to wear jeans a lot, and I was like, 'Absolutely not!' I lived in New York for a long time, and I don’t think I ever wore a pair of jeans. People looked fabulous all the time in New York then."  ​ "So I wanted to find a great leather jacket for Joey, something that could be his best friend, and the one I found was Armani, which was a riot because he never could have afforded Armani," Debra reveals. "We made it look like a poor man’s choice, but really it wasn’t. And that was the case for a lot of things actually, which is very funny." "When I was in London doing Friends, for the episode when Ross gets married, I went to this boutique called Idol (now sadly not there anymore) and bought so much stuff for Phoebe and for Rachel. And some of those pieces are the most loved pieces by the fans. There was a strapless yellow dress that Rachel wore that I think I got thousands of emails over the years just about that dress." "It's a very common thing for actors to borrow their costumes but you know what? I think they didn't want to," Debra insists. "I don’t think they wanted to be seen as their characters." "For a 30 minute episode, the scripts sometimes spanned six to ten days, which means at least six outfit changes for the six stars, then three guest stars with three changes, so we had between 50 and 75 changes per episode," says Debra. Including that Rachel wedding dress , Ross's leather pants and... too many others to mention.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  British model Liberty said ‘I do’ this weekend as she tied the knot with billionaire music mogul Jimmy Iovine. 37-year-old Ross and 62-year-old Iovine held the ceremony at their Malibu home in Los Angeles on the evening of Saturday, February 13. The newlyweds were pictured barefoot at the beach, where Ross threw a garland into the Pacific Ocean and a skywriting plane endeavoured to pen their initials in the sky, except the result was ‘J heart M’ instead of ‘J heart L’. The couple then hosted a reception for around 300 guests the following day – Valentine’s Day. Attendees were asked to wear red in honour of the romantic date, and big-name guests such as Oprah Winfrey and Helen Lasichanh, singer Pharrell Williams' wife, were only too happy to oblige. This is not Ross’ first marriage. The London-born model, who has modelled for Dior and Vogue, wed fellow Londoner and film director Rupert Sanders in 2003, and moved to Los Angeles to help further his directorial career. The former couple have two young children, a boy and a girl. But it was Sanders’ admitted infidelity with his Snow White and the Huntsman cast member Kristen Stewart which catapulted Ross’ private life into the tabloids in 2012. The two were pictured kissing, and Sanders publicly admitted the affair. Ross later declared that the marriage was over, and the pair’s divorce was finalised in 2014. Iovine, who is 25 years Ross’ senior, has four children. He is the co-founder of Interscope Records and founded Beats Electronics with rapper Dr. Dre in 2006, which was subsequently sold to Apple for $3bn in 2014.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Kate Moss has created countless fashion moments in her long and illustrious career. Tonight, there's a new one to add to the roster. For the first time in 15 years, the British supermodel took to the red carpet at the Loving premiere at Cannes film festival. That  would probably constitute a 'moment' in itself. But Moss does not do things by halves; her appearence came with an added soupçon of glamour and intrigue in the form of little sister Lottie. Just to fully cement the momentousness of it all, the half-siblings even wore gowns in matching red hues which were as bright as the red carpet (though there was no danger they would be blending into the background.) Kate wore a slashed-to-the-hip, one shouldered gown from the archive of American fashion house, Halston.  She was styled for this rare red carpet appearence by Alexis Roche. He's the stylist boyfriend of her good friend John Galliano- the former Dior designer who is now creative director at Maison Margiela and who Moss commissioned to create The Great Gatsby-inspired dress for her 2011 wedding to Jamie Hince. Roche has also worked with Amal Clooney in the past and styled Kendall Jenner in Roberto Cavalli couture for her Cannes red carpet appearence last night.  The supermodel is in the South of France for Thursday evening's AmFar gala which is set to be a high-octane, star-studded affair. Carine Roitfeld, the former editor-in-chief of French Vogue, is masterminding an opulent show which will pay tribute to the  glamour of legendary 70s New York night club Studio 54. This was the height of Halston's heyday, when the designer made millions and dressed the likes of Bianca Jagger, Liza Minelli and Elizabeth Taylor for their hedonistic nights out. His flowing, Grecian inspired gowns and halterneck jumpsuits are still synonymous with the era today. So Moss's outing tonight is a very clever precursor to Thursday evening- and a reminder of how fabulous Halston's designs still look today.  Roche and Moss accesorised the striking red dress with a pair of earrings 18.95ct diamond earrings, a 9.12 ct diamond bracelet and another 103.89ct bangle, all from Chopard's High Jewellery Collection.  Her peep toe black stilettos are by Parisian shoemakers, Maison Ernest. Of course, all that adds up to a megawatt Kate Moss moment but the presence of her 18 year-old half-sister, Lottie, only added to the occassion. The younger Moss was dressed for her first major red carpet appearence in a floor-length, backless dress by Dior Couture and a Chopard necklace, earrings and rings. Her look was edgier and more grown-up than usual this evening, with graphic eye make-up and her hair pulled back rather than  worn softly around her face.  Kate and her little sister have only been seen together in public a handful of times before, most notably at Topshop's February 2014 London Fashion Week show and when Lottie acted as one of her sister's bridesmaids in 2011. With both of them expected to be in Cannes for a couple more days, expect more Moss moments to come.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Once a Disney teen icon Selena Gomez is now well on her way to power fashion It girl status. The stylish rise and rise of Gomez was confirmed this week by her first campaign for Louis Vuitton. The pop singer is the face of Louis Vuitton's latest campaign, LV Series Five, photographed by Bruce Weber alongside models Jean Campbell, Erika Linder, Natalie Westling, and Rianne Van Rompaey. Gomez has admirably avoided taking the route of her former tween collegaues, eschewing the temptation to rebel with a radical haircut or by posing naked. Instead she's executed an elegant transition from cute to cool via  lunches with Anna Wintour, enlisting the services of the most sought after stylist in Hollywood and forming an alliance with Ghesquière at Louis Vuitton.  It's an unsurprising casting given Gomez' close relationship with the house, which was confirmed by her joint cover with creative director Nicholas Ghesquiere on the June issue of Vogue Brazil. The cover line described Selena as his 'muse'- a fitting label given she has become a fixture on the Vuitton front row and has worn custom Louis Vuitton for a number of key red carpet events, including the Met Gala and the Oscars. With her 80.5 million followers on Instagram- the highest follower count on the platform- Gomez is a smart choice of brand ambassador.  Selena Gomez found fame on the Disney Channel's series The Wizards of Waverly Place when she was 14, and became one of the most written about young stars on the internet thanks to her on/off relationship with Justin Bieber. For five years the teens were at the centre of an endless stream of 'Are they dating? Are they not?' stories, but Gomez has now said that she is "beyond done" talking about her ex-boyfriend.  It's not just Louis Vuitton which you'll find in the 23-year-old singer's wardrobe. She has also exhibited an experimental attitude to her look, recently choosing to wear buzzed-about, fashion-insider labels like Vetements and Monse. The singer is currently on her worldwide 'Revival' tour, where she has turned to an eclectic variety of designers from Karl Lagerfeld to Sonia Rykiel and Vionnet for her on-stage wardrobe.  New York based label Monse is only two-seasons old, but is already considered an up-and-coming name to know and has been worn by Amal Clooney and Sarah Jessica Parker as well as Gomez. The brand's founders, Oscar de la Renta alumni Laura Kim and Fernando Garcia, worked with Gomez to create a catsuit covered in 96,480 Swarovski crystals and a black gown. "It was adapting our experience of ready-to-wear and applying it to something that is comfortable enough to move around in on stage," the design duo explains to The Telegraph. "Christian Classen (Gomez's tour stylist) had a very clear idea of what the styling of the tour would look like and it made everything a lot more simplified in terms of process. We had a couple of fittings where we tweaked things here and there, but overall, Selena was loyal to the “look” that Christian and I were going for that ultimately represented their (Christian and Selena’s) aesthetic done in the Monse way."  Creating a very clear 'look' has also been Selena Gomez's strategy when it comes to red carpet dressing. The other personality behind Gomez' notable fashion climb is her stylist Kate Young, who was crowned the most powerful stylist in Hollywood this year, thanks to her work with Dakota Johnson, Natalie Portman and Sienna Miller. Young monopolises best dressed lists by creating a signature look for each of her clients, so that their red carpet history is cohesive and instantly-recognisable. "What I try to do is really think about each individual client and curate a look for them that has a clear vision behind it," Young explains to The Telegraph. "A sense of who they are and how they look best - physically look best in terms of silhouette and colour and that kind of thing - and then style wise - find their personal style and hone it and work on it so that every time they go out in public and premieres they present this image that's like a really stylised version of themselves." As for Selena's signature look, Young explained to Vogue: “There’s an overall mood that we’re going for which is young, modern, clean, and sexy without ever being fussy. The clothes are effortless, and there’s a lot of American sportswear influence." Young doesn't just advise what her clients should wear on the red carpet, but instructs them on how they should behave while they are being photographed.  "I think everyone is so wrapped up in red carpet and images and stuff that they forget obvious basic things in a way - if you're comfortable, you look more beautiful," she tells The Telegraph. "When you go to a party you should look grateful to be there and smile and look happy. There are things that I try to say to remind people - that these are parties. I try to encourage that in my clients, because when you remember that you see that in them and you see them looking more beautiful. I don't want them to wear shoes they can't walk in or they'll trip in or a dress they're tugging on, because that's not beautiful even i it looks good in a picture."  It's safe to say that the Duchess of Cambridge is not renowned for her unmitigated willingness to embrace the latest catwalk trends. But today, fashionistas the world over are welcoming a new member of the Gucci fan club after Kate chose a tweed mini dress by the Italian label for a visit to open the V&A museum's new Exhibition Road quarter. Gucci has enjoyed a remarkable resurgence in its must-have status in recent years following the appointment of Alessandro Michele as creative director in 2015. His luxe, vintage bohemian aesthetic proved catnip to fashion lovers who have clamoured to wear his reinvented Horsebit loafers, decadently chic handbags and smart-meets-madcap ready-to wear pieces. The Duchess's choice of look is on the more classic skew of the Gucci spectrum- which also includes a cornucopia of glittery rainbow knitwear, jazzily printed silk bomber jackets, slick tailoring and bow-embellished blouses. The dress is part of the Pre-fall 2017 collection in which a red version of thedress was styled in Michele's signature maximalist spirit with sporty striped leggings, silver bow heels and Gucci-logo beige socks.  For today's visit Kate kept things more pared-back and suitably regal, wearing the above-the-knee dress with L.K Bennett navy heels, a bright red clutch bag and her favourite Annoushka pearl earrings which co-ordinated perfectly with the dress's GG pearl buttons. The £1,790 dress is still available to buy on Net-a-Porter in Kate's tweed material but also in bright red.  "Vintage is my vocabulary... like the notes of a musician,"is how Michele summed up his design approach at the Vogue festival in 2016, where he took to the stage alongside the magazine's then-editor Alexandra Shulman. "I never want to go out wearing something sad," he added of his enthusiasm for creating joy-giving pieces.   With its abbreviated length, tweed fabric and neat button and pocket detailling, the shift dress recalls the elegant look which Jackie Kennedy made her own in the early 1960s when she often wore pieces inspired by Coco Chanel's designs. That connection makes sense for Kate who has often nodded to Kennedy's style codes in her wardrobe choices, from her houndstooth skirt suit by Eponine London to her penchant for chic pillbox hats.  Kate's outfits are often laden with meaning and diplomatic nods, whether it's a decision to support a British fashion label or dressing 'literally' such as sporting floral prints for the Chelsea Flower Show. Today's look is more nuanced, but is sure to go down well with the cognoscenti art and culture crowd at the V&A who will likely know of Michele's era-defining designs.  The Duchess and her stylist Natasha Archer may also have decided that today was the perfect time to add an unexpected curveball into their repertoire. It's a strategy which Anna Harvey, Princess Diana's stylist, discussed in an interview with The Telegraph this weekend. Referring to one of Diana's best known looks- a checked black, red and white skirt suit by the Italian label Moschino- Harvey explained that "every now and then I would slip something into the mix, to liven things up a bit, to change the pace a little, and she couldn’t resist it." Instead of opting for a British or Canadian designer for this look which was worn in Toronto, Harvey and the Princess fell in love with the 'wit' of the Italian suit.  It's a thought process which seems to have repeated itself today, to brilliant effect.      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
