 The elegant Place Vendôme in Paris’s exclusive 1st arrondissement is the epicentre of the fine jewellery world. When the rich and famous need diamonds, this is where they flock. Around the edges of the square lie boutiques belonging to the biggest and most storied names in the business; there’s Boucheron at number 26, Van Cleef & Arpels at number 22 and Chopard at number 1. It has been a hub of glitz and glamour since Mellerio dits Meller – said to be the oldest family company in Europe – established its Paris jewellery salon nearby on Rue de la Paix in 1815. At number 6, a small revolution is in the works. Next month, the relatively new maison of Repossi will open the doors to its renovated store, designed by the avant-garde Dutch architect Rem Koolhaas and his OMA practice. It promises to be a cool, clean-lined antidote to the traditional grandeur of its neighbours. For Gaia Repossi, whose great-grandfather began the company in Italy in 1920, the store is the latest innovation in her quest to bring a modern outlook to a world steeped in tradition. It’s no exaggeration to say that since she took over from her father, Alberto, as artistic and creative director in 2007, Gaia has brought a radical breath of fresh air to fine jewellery. She has not only made customers rethink what luxury means, but her designs have sparked trends – if you’ve taken to stacking your rings or wearing an ear cuff, then Repossi is the woman you have to thank.  Clockwise from top left: White Noise ring, £8,985, Dover Street Market (shop.doverstreetmarket.com); Serti sur Vide earrings, £19,230, Dover Street Market (shop.doverstreetmarket.com); Antifer Pink 4-3 ring, £1,830, Net-a-Porter (net-a-porter.com); Berbère monotype pink-gold ring, £2,750, Harrods (020 7730 1234); Berbère earrings, £3,480, Dover Street Market (shop.doverstreetmarket.com) Sitting in her minimalist office just around the corner from Place Vendôme on the Rue Saint-Honoré, 29-year-old Gaia is most noticeably not dripping in jewels. A single, pared-back band glints on one finger. She’s barefaced, her fawn-coloured hair is pulled back in a low bun and she’s wearing a quietly chic grey knit and black jeans. It’s an enviably refined yet low-maintenance look, which has made her a popular subject for street-style photographers. In fact, she has become her company’s best advertisement, embodying the modern yet timeless look that Repossi jewellery has come to encompass. She had never planned to get involved in the family business, which has counted the Monaco and Saudi royal families among its clients. ‘Jewellery was my father’s universe when I was growing up. I would go into the safe and look at all his drawings,’ she remembers, speaking in the soft international accent she has picked up living between Paris, Italy and New York.  ‘I grew up seeing my mother wearing it; she was the female figure that my dad would create for, so a lot of his designs were according to her taste.’ Despite her early immersion in all things jewellery, Gaia was resolute that she would rather study fine art. ‘I felt the jewellery world was very conservative,’ she explains. ‘It didn’t click for me as a passion at all, I think it had just become so normal.’ During her degree – and a master’s in archaeology and anthropology – Gaia found herself dabbling in her father’s work, offering up opinions and ideas for designs and campaigns. For her first collection – a collaboration with her friend Eugenie Niarchos called Czarina – she insisted on styling a necklace with a T-shirt, a high-low mix never seen before in haute joaillerie.  Back then, her father told a newspaper, ‘Times have changed. Mothers are now copying daughters in fashion, not daughters their mothers.’ Gaia is sanguine about her vision. ‘I didn’t have a choice but to change this industry.’ She hasn’t wiped the slate completely clean: many of the artisans from the Italian workshops in Valenza have been with the company for years, including the chief of the atelier, who began working with Gaia’s grandfather 40 years ago. It’s a combination that last November attracted investment from luxury group LVMH, which means Gaia can now work on careful expansion and keeping up with ever-increasing demand.  ‘Modern’ and ‘minimal’ are the first words that spring to mind when you see a Repossi creation, but inspiration comes from Gaia’s vast knowledge of ancient civilisations, art and architecture. The White Noise collection’s artfully curved, scribble-like pieces draw on references to sculptors Alexander Calder and Richard Serra. Meanwhile, the signature Berbère rings and earrings are comprised of between two and nine bands of metal that take their cues from the tribal tattoos of the North African Tuareg Berbers but are ‘made refined and sophisticated for now’. ‘When I look at those tribal references, it’s not about copying it,’ explains Gaia, ‘but they always make me think, “How come that woman looks so elegant?” There are no diamonds but it’s beautiful and it works.’ She filters these observations through her obsessively mathematical design systems but is always pragmatic about how women need their jewellery to work for them. It’s probably this philosophy that has won her such success. ‘If you’re a working woman you can’t wear frou-frou skirts and over-the-top jewellery to the office. So I think about a smart woman: what does she want to wear? She has to work and travel but wants to look clever too.’ Gaia has also been trailblazing in the way that she considers how jewellery will flatter the wearer. ‘I don’t think our jewellery looks so nice on its own but once a woman puts it on, then it’s transformed – it should never be an object to look at,’ she muses. Her earrings are placed so that they fall in line with the jaw and her rings are engineered to gracefully elongate the hand. ‘I think intrusive jewellery [big rocks] can really age a woman,’ she advises. ‘Everything should always be enlightening.’ Unlike many fine jewellers who begin with a particular stone, Gaia’s starting point is always the design and she mostly limits herself to working with pavé diamonds.  She has continued her father’s experiments and has also introduced gold plating with lilac rhodium, resulting in jewellery that is strikingly different to anything else you would see on Place Vendôme. ‘For our older clients with a more classic style, it took a while for them to get used to our new aesthetic,’ admits Gaia. ‘Now our pieces have become classics for them, just as much as for our younger clients.’ ‘I bought a Berbère ring when they first came out,’ recalls Sophie Quy, Net-a-Porter’s fine jewellery buyer. ‘I still wear it all the time and it feels so fresh.’ Gaia has been, she says, ‘Truly instrumental in modernising fine jewellery, opening up the idea that a woman can buy a piece for herself and wear it day-to-night.’  The most expensive Repossi sale to date on Net-a-Porter was a one-off design that cost £35,000, but the beauty of the house is that the entry level is the same as for a mid-priced designer handbag: a gold ring from the Antifer collection (named after a Normandy cliff) retails at £450. Repossi has also become an unexpected hit on the red carpet. Mature actresses such as Tilda Swinton and Cate Blanchett, as well as their younger counterparts, including Alicia Vikander, Emma Stone, Carey Mulligan and Dakota Johnson, have seen the appeal of Gaia’s innovative designs, whether they opt for a scattering of subtly twinkling rings or a statement-making ear cuff or choker. Gaia puts the success down to Repossi offering a cool alternative to the stuffier options of other jewellery houses. ‘When you’re young and on the red carpet, you want something that reflects your style,’ she shrugs. ‘It wasn’t something we planned on doing but it’s kind of come to us.  With the first weekend of Coachella behind us, we can start to deduce the trends emerging from the festival. Each year the event, which takes place in Palm Springs, sees a stream of celebrities in attendance draped in sequins and tassel-laden kimonos, and wearing teeny tiny denim shorts and barely-there crop tops.  (According to Lyst, Kylie Jenner's appearance in a nude mini dress sparked over 23,000 searches for similar pieces, and Sofia Richie's choice of a white bra top and Reebok windsuit also  prompted a 74% surge in searches).  But besides the bedazzled body suits (Rihanna chose one by Gucci), the completely sheer dresses and the skin-tight lace-up trousers, there were some wearable trends too- honestly. Here's what we've seen so far.... While, generally speaking, English festivals make wearing below-the-knee dresses a bit of a challenge (unless you don't mind the hem being splattered with mud), a three-day party in the Californian sun makes this infinitely easier - particularly if you're swanning around the VIP area. Pretty printed dresses were everywhere over the weekend, from Emily Ratajkowski's dark variation by emerging New York label Markarian, to Selena Gomez' bright tea dress by Harley Viera Newton. Paired with trainers or boots, a patterned dress provides the bases for a flattering, effortless festival outfit.  Never one for the adoption of generic dress codes, Kate Bosworth covered up in an all-white ensemble, punctuated with black accessories, proving that monochrome makes for a chic festival look.  The simplicity of black and white offered up by both Bosworth and model Sadie Newman, among others, provided a welcome diversion from the multicoloured, embellished pieces chosen by the majority of festival-goers. Vintage-style jeans were the option-du-jour for many festival attendees, undoubtedly spurred by Levi's star-studded brunch that took place on Saturday.   Guests paired their denim with everything from sweet folk blouses to sporty tank tops and asymmetric ribbed tops, making a case for the versatility of a good pair of jeans and their value at a festival.  According to Lyst, the weekend's festivities saw a 333% increase in searches and a 126% increase in purchases of round sunglasses, fuelled no doubt, by all the celebrities opting for the popular style.  For those heading to a festival this summer, if flower-garland headbands and cutout swimsuits aren't for you, then vintage-inspired eyewear might grant your outfit the festival spin you're looking for in an acceptably low-key way. The circular style endows even the simplest of outfits a cool edge, as proven by Nicole Richie's black maxi dress, basket bag and oversize sunglasses combination.  Despite the fact that temperatures were upwards of 30 degrees, many festival-goers opted for chunky boots, rather than trainers or sandals - understandable given that Coachella is set in the dusty Sonoran desert. Ergo, the ideal terrain for track sole boots.  Practicality aside, lace-up boots are an excellent way to toughen up the ditsy floral dresses, folk blouses and floaty kimono-style cover-ups which make up the go-to festival uniform.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It has been 55 years since Marilyn Monroe sang “Happy Birthday Mr President” to John F. Kennedy wearing a sheer Jean Louis dress, hand-embellished with 2,500 crystals, but her look is as relevant and influential as ever. Earlier this week, reality star Kim Kardashian-West became the latest celebrity to wear Gucci’s new season mesh bodysuit posing in a photoshoot and Snapchat posts as she promoted her new makeup line to her millions of followers. Back in April, Rihanna wore a slightly more demure incarnation of the same look, layered under denim shorts and a vest top at the Coachella festival. Wearing nothing but sparkle is nothing new, but for stars hoping to shine on the now overly-saturated red carpet or on crowded social media feeds, returning to a ‘dazzle ‘em’ approach is considered a fail-safe - especially for anyone with hopes of dominating on the internet the following morning. Arguably, one's filter adjusts to the quantity of flesh and sequins now floating around in the ether, and it takes a lot more to shock us in the fashion stakes now than it did even a year ago. That said, when Gucci debuted said bodysuit on the catwalk in February, the interests of celebrity stylists were evidently piqued. Complete with what looked like a knight's chainmail coif redesigned for a rave, the brand's showman designer, Alessandro Michele's, interpretation was Instagram bait too tasty to ignore.  Kardashian-West and Rihanna have both been savvy in adopting the most-talked-about piece from Gucci's Milan Fashion Week show, and styling it their own way. For Rihanna, that was about making it festival-ready. Kardashian-West, meanwhile, has previously cited Cher as a muse and, right down to the poker straight, long black hair that she now sports, her interpretation mirrors designer Bob Mackie’s work in the Seventies and Eighties. “When Cher came along she wasn’t used to wearing anything glitzy but the minute I put anything like that on her, she perked up and became this amazing star,” Mackie told The Telegraph earlier this year. “People would tune in to see what she would wear. She was a beautiful young girl, she was one of the first girls to look that way; with her bellbottom flares, long, straight hair parted in the middle.” Mackie, arguably, is the one responsible for the entire category of ‘naked dresses’- and bodysuits that has emerged- he also had a hand, as Jean Louis’s sketch designer, in creating that original dress for Monroe. From Jennifer Lopez in Versace, to Beyoncé in Givenchy, extrapolations and reinterpretations of his work have been coming thick (well, thin) and fast in the last few years. His view? Quite simply, “everything comes back.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  There are few individuals in the modern age who have come up with a sartorial signature that is world renowned and instantly recognisable. Jacqueline Kennedy and Margaret Thatcher managed it to some degree. But no one has done it with more success than HM Queen Elizabeth II, a woman whom has forged her own indelible identity and created the defining style of modern monarchy. On the eve of her 90th birthday, the longest reigning British sovereign continues to be the blueprint, the gold standard, the measure of what it is to be and look like a queen. She may have made this appear easy, but it can’t have been. Dress has changed somewhat since her coronation in 1953. Imagine if she’d received a full, future-proof style briefing back then. “Your Majesty, we need to create a look for you that will not simply define you as the figurehead of this nation for the next century, but remain magisterial, relevant and age appropriate through twelve Prime Ministers, the TV Age, the Swinging Sixties, glam rock, punk rock, Sloane Rangers, Charles and Diana, boom and bust, the digital age and a televised stunt involving Daniel Craig. Initial thoughts?” “Well, it sounds like one shall be requiring a stout pair of shoes,” might have been her stoic response. Queen Elizabeth II began her monarchy with a strong sense of duty and the influence of her father. Following the abdication of Edward VIII, King George VI wished to distance his monarchy and his family from the haute couture flamboyance of Wallis Simpson. The Queen has never attempted to be a fashion-plate. As the designer Karl Lagerfeld, a confirmed royalist, has observed: “She is never ridiculous; she is flawless. For this job, in our day, she is perfect.” A teenager during the Second World War, she grew up with the same clothing rations as the rest of the country. For her wedding to Philip Mountbatten in 1947, the Queen famously saved her ration cards to pay for her dress. To this day she remains thrifty, with an enthusiasm to make-do-and-mend - her shoes and bags are sent back for repair time and again. Service to the people is everything. She has always been a working queen and her clothes reflect that. “Her whole wardrobe is based on complete practicality,” Stewart Parvin, the British designer who has created many of her outfits over the past decade, has said. As a trained mechanic in the Women’s Auxiliary Territory Service she would have learnt the value of a uniform and as monarch has created and adapted her own. The combination of a block-coloured coat and dress, the black patent shoes (each new pair is 'walked in' by a member of the Palace staff with the same size 4 feet to ensure her utmost comfort), the matching bag, hat and gloves are so synonymous with her that even if the Queen was not wearing the outfit it would be recognisably hers. She is not afraid to stand out from the crowd. Indeed, she views it as essential - “I have to be seen to be believed,” she has said. And to maximise her visibility she has more official appointments during the day than the evening and a day can encompass up to five outfit changes.  Since 2012, when British Vogue magazine published a graphic tracking the bold spectrum of colour the Queen wore across the course of a year (29 per cent blue, 10 per cent pink, 13 per cent floral), there has been a surge of interest in this aspect of her wardrobe. If anything the clothes have become brighter as she has got older, setting a stylish example of how to age with both elegance and brio. She has worked with only a handful of different couturiers including Norman Hartnell, her mother’s favourite, and from the 1950s, the Savile Row tailor Hardy Amies. "I do not dress the queen,” Amies once said. “The queen dresses herself. We supply her with her clothes – there is a difference.” Her style has changed only slightly in reaction to the different decades, becoming softer in the 1970s with the help of the designer Ian Thomas and in the 1980s - when her children and their spouses dominated the front pages - perhaps more conservative. Most recently the dressmaker and milliner Angela Kelly has served as her Personal Assistant and Senior Dresser, and with additional designs from Parvin has created some bold signature pieces, particularly during the Diamond Jubilee. With her recurring sartorial motifs – the headscarf, the brogues, the pleated skirts, the frame handbags and the dress coats – being frequently referred to in high fashion collections, the Queen has created an image that will endure. That she did so in one of the most fast-moving centuries ever is a remarkable achievement. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  What Michelle Obama wears often gets as much attention as what Michelle Obama says. More, even.  Roger Saul’s fate changed the year he sold his stake in Mulberry. Shortly after he parted ways with his multimillion-pound fashion label in 2002, the farmland that was historically part of his house in Sharpham Park, near Glastonbury, came up for sale.  Saul and his wife, Monty, a former Dior model, didn’t hesitate. They bought it, thereby bringing together the house, a former hunting lodge and its grounds for the first time in 100 years. ‘We suddenly had 300 acres. I thought, whoah – what are we going to do with that?’ says Saul.  The answer came with a visit from his sister, Rosemary, who had bowel cancer and was looking for an alternative diet. She suggested her brother grow spelt instead of the wheat he was thinking about farming. ‘I’d never heard of spelt and hadn’t a clue what she was talking about,’ says Saul. But he was sold on the idea when, after some research, he found that spelt, a high-fibre wholegrain, had many health benefits  – and tasted good, too. Nobody was growing large amounts of spelt in the UK at the time – and he soon discovered there was good reason for this: spelt is 40 per cent chaff. Unlike wheat, spelt has to be stored in its husk, meaning higher storage and transport costs. Removing the husks is also expensive work, requiring additional machinery.  Saul decided to make his spelt organic, further adding to the costs and difficulty; the crops have to be rotated to replenish the soil's nitrogen, so his fields can produce a harvest only every two and a half years. The result is that he gets only one tonne of spelt for every 12 tonnes of wheat he could have cultivated. But he was determined to push ahead, and today Sharpham Park produces 500 tonnes of spelt a year and has a score of loyal customers, including Waitrose, Ocado and Whole Foods.  Saul has also reintroduced deer to Sharpham Park, which had historically been home to deer as far back as the year 1100. It is, he says, a little ‘window dressing’ of a very decorative kind. Despite the risks, the progression from fashion to farming was a natural one for Saul, who says both are creative processes, offering the chance to build an idea into reality. ‘You go through life and think, OK, right, better go that way now.’ For Saul, that direction is spelt farming.  Celebrating 25 years in your job would usually either go unmarked, forgotten amongst the daily targets and to-do lists or be celebrated with a swift round of drinks at the pub after work. But that was never going to be the case for trailblazing fashion stylist Edward Enninful who is celebrating his 25 years of working in the industry with a high-octane 13-minute film starring eight of his supermodel friends - Kate Moss, Naomi Campbell, Karlie Kloss, Jourdan Dunn, Lara Stone Anna Ewers, Mariacarla Boscono and Karen Elson.  At the start of 2015 Enninful was approached by the tech giant Beats by Dre, the headphone multinational kickstarted by former NWA rapper Dr Dre and record producer Jimmy Iovine, to collaborate on a major new film initiative. Acquired by Apple in a $3 billion takeover last year, Beats now controls an estimated 70 per cent of the premium headphones market, so its promotional campaigns are a very big deal indeed. Enninful's vision for this modern model spectacle was a retelling of the seven deadly sins. The Fashion Director at American style bible W magazine enlisted his friend, the renowned fashion photographer and founder of pioneering fashion film site SHOWstudio Nick Knight to create the masterpiece which has been made in association with Beats by Dr Dre and features custom-made designs from Alexander McQueen, Prada and Marc Jacobs.  BeatsxEE25 from SHOWstudio on Vimeo. The two have known each other ever since Knight's friend, the stylist Simon Foxton, spotted Edward sitting on his bike as a teenager and asked him to model for i-D magazine. Enninful quickly became entrenched in fashion and got a job as Foxton's assistant, although not before he'd finished a qualification in accountancy to keep his parents happy. When it came to interpreting the seven deadly sins therefore, it's perhaps understandable that this duo of fashion image makers were never going to settle for age-old interpretations of lust, gluttony, greed, pride, envy, wrath and sloth. "It’s not a moralizing approach or telling people how they should live their lives," Knight explains to The Telegraph. "When you think of the seven deadly sins it always feel very old and biblical - like it's from a long time ago - so trying to modernise them was interesting. It's about setting your own moral compass." Each supermodel adopts the 'role' of one of the sins (each of which was explored in academic detail by Knight and his researcher Rei Nadal), with the film moving through dramatically changing moods from the pulsating drama of  Naomi Campbell's 'Pride' segment through to the soft, saccharine feel of Anna Ewers and Lara Stone as gluttony. "Lara said she wanted to be gluttony as soon as we asked her to take part," remembers Knight. "Kate wanted to be lust; I mean she IS lust." There was no model drama either. "These girls are Edward’s favorites. He gave me a list of who he wanted to be in the film and nobody said they were too busy - all those girls did it for Edward as something special, something nice for a friend." Knight was one of the first fashion insiders to realise the potential which the internet and fashion film offered; he orchestrated the first ever live broadcast of a fashion show with Alexander McQueen's spring/summer 2010 Plato's Atlantis collection. So true to form, there's a lot of reference to digital with 'Like' buttons, social media posts and trolling popping up throughout the film. Depressingly, they didn't have to look far for the nasty comments.  "We did a teaser for this video in Times Square a few months ago and the comments which are in the Jourdan Dunn segment are literally the ones which were written about her from that," Knight explains. "They’re very vitriolic - people hide behind the facelessness of the internet to say things which you wouldn’t say in real life and are actually quite harsh." Knight calls it "a modern form of envy" but says that internet hate is not something which bothers him. "I don’t choose to read many YouTube comments under my work. Sometimes you do, and obviously you’re really happy then if someone is saying it’s the most wonderful thing they’ve ever seen but the comment underneath will say it’s trash and I should be shot. I don’t think artists should spend much time acknowledging their audiences anyway." The film references other forms of modern 'sin' from the "greed of Wall Street, bankers and the finance market" to sexting and online porn. "All industries have a fair amount of sin," says Knight. "Lawyers, big business, the medical profession, the record industry, film... it's because people are inherently good and bad at the same time." But Knight thinks that fashion has been "unfairly labelled" in a more negative way than it should. "Fashion is maligned in the press and I think that's from our protestant culture where vanity is considered a sin. It's unfair because it’s really just about self-expression - what you choose to wear says something about yourself. It’s one of the most democratic art forms in a way. Fashion isn’t just the runways of Paris and New York, it's at its most interesting when people decide how they they are going to express themselves." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Often, it’s the quiet voices that ultimately make the greatest impression. At 71, Carla Sozzani has, in her own delicate way, shaped the fashion world for half a century. As a magazine editor in the ’70s and ’80s she worked with Norman Parkinson, David Bailey, Arthur Elgort, Robert Mapplethorpe and Helmut Newton. Together with her younger sister, Franca, the two Mantua-raised women would come to be linchpins, not just of Italian style but of the industry as a whole. Franca, who died from lung cancer in 2016, was the visionary, controversial editor of Vogue Italia. Carla created the first ‘concept store’, a place for people to come, relax, learn, see, eat, read, drink, and, perhaps, even buy something. From earnest beginnings in a disused garage on a street in central Milan, she is now the matriarch of an international empire, with 10 Corso Como stores in Seoul, Shanghai, Beijing and opening this month, New York. ‘My dream was to make a magazine come to life, but instead of having pages, I’d have book tables and clothes racks,’ Sozzani enthuses. ‘At the beginning it was very tough. Nobody could understand why the books would go with jewels and clothes, and why there was a chair at the cash till. 'I wanted to create a community where people could meet and do different things. I said, “This is slow shopping. Come here to buy a Yamamoto jacket that you don’t need, literally – right? So take your time, take time to give yourself a present…” It took a while, but now it’s everywhere.’  We meet in the unassuming looking complex in Le Marais in Paris that was the home/studio/store/museum of the late designer Azzedine Alaïa, who died at the end of last year. Sozzani and he were close friends; she’d worked with him as a consultant for years. She is a slight figure, delicately boned, her long blonde hair pulled back off her face and secured with a printed scarf. She’s in a simple outfit of an oversized white shirt and slim black trousers, but with the kind of detail and flair – the wide cuffs, crisp just-so cotton, sharp collar, studded Alaïa sandals – that betray a life spent in stylish company.  I’m led into the bustling back kitchen, where the remnants of lunch are being cleared from a huge table. Alaïa’s two dogs are settling into their beds in the corner. Since his death, life here has gone on as before, but without its diminutive inspiration. ‘Not a single person has left,’ Sozzani tells me, of the studio where the exacting designer ruled (he released collections when they were ready, rather than adhering to fashion seasons). ‘They’re all loyal to Azzedine and to carrying on what they created. That is his legacy, and it’s amazing, because,’ she adds with an eyebrow raised, ‘he was not always so tender. He could be very difficult, but they learnt so much from him, and they want to keep going for him. It is like a family.’  Since Alaïa’s death, Sozzani has been immersed in preserving his work. Earlier this year, she helped mount a long-planned exhibition at the Design Museum in London, as well as curating a rolling exhibition of his work, which is available to view here in Paris. She gestures to the gallery next to where we sit, filled with his dresses, ‘This is just one collection. There are 200,000 pieces in the archive.’ It’s a task that is keeping her busy, as is the launching of the store in New York. ‘The past two years have been very tough,’ she says softly, her eyes gently reddening, ‘I’ve lost the two people closest to me. Azzedine died only eight months ago. It’s been very important to have these distractions, to keep me going, to avoid falling in shadows and depression.’  For many years, the Sozzani sisters worked together in the same building in Milan, editing their respective projects –Franca helmed Lei and Per Lui magazines, before being given the editorship of Italian Vogue in 1988, where she fuelled frenzied headlines (covering everything from addiction to domestic violence and environmental catastrophe in the guise of fashion shoots) until her death. Carla worked on special issues of Italian Vogue, before being appointed launch editor of Italian Elle, creating its first three issues in 1987, after which she was fired.  Those issues have become highly sought-after collectors’ items. She’d commissioned Steven Meisel, Paolo Roversi, Nick Knight, Juergen Teller and Sarah Moon to shoot, ‘Everybody,’ she purrs in her gently accented voice. She included avant garde and progressive designers such as Rei Kawakubo’s Comme des Garçons, Jean Paul Gaultier and Alaïa. Notably, she didn’t feature much domestic talent. The Italian fashion contingent complained to her publishers Rizzoli and threatened to pull advertising unless she changed tack. Sozzani declined. ‘It was absolutely great in a sense,’ she tells me, reflecting on what has happened to her since. ‘I was very happy, I’d made the issues I felt I should make.’  After 19 years in magazines, she was itching to do something else. And so, at 43, she opened what started life as an art gallery and base for her small book-publishing house in a disused garage at number 10 Corso Como in central Milan. Corso Como is a designer shopping experience for those who have no interest in entering an austere, pretentious luxury store. It has a slightly homey feel, which is largely due to Sozzani’s taste, as well as the aesthetic handwriting of her American artist partner, Kris Ruhs (‘he’s always laughing at me,’ she says affectionately), who has co-designed all of the stores. The black-and-white theme would be harsh but for its naive rendering. It feels exciting to walk into the space – unexpected and joyful. It is both retro and modern at the same time, a wonderland that could have been imagined by Roald Dahl had he been more keen on Comme des Garçons than chocolate.  Equally the Perspex cabinets and circular tables are covered in the most enticing treasures born of Sozzani’s intense curiosity and excitement for something different, whether that’s a photograph or a candle or a necklace. She wants to ‘show things that are interesting and new, and to share this with other people. The reaction is always mixed, but you can’t please everybody. It’s impossible. Otherwise you’re a department store. 10 Corso Como isn’t a department store, it’s a point of view, to share with people who have the same point of view.’  Sozzani still tries to spend as much time in each store as she can, ‘To listen to the complaints. Otherwise you can never learn.’ From the beginning she hosted a heady mix of designers. She reels them off: ‘Jean Paul Gaultier, Alaïa – of course – Comme des Garçons, Yohji Yamamoto, Prada, Margiela…’ This summer, the Milan store featured an exhibition of Salvador Dalí with a recording of his voice, ‘It’s much more interesting than music. Time has to have passed so there’s no nostalgia, there’s just humour and the beauty of it.’ Her own collection of images – of which she has thousands from the talents she had worked with during her magazine career – is currently on display at the Helmut Newton Foundation gallery in Berlin.  The Sozzani sisters, both fiercely independent, led interwoven lives, often mirroring each other. They both had one child, out of wedlock, and were single parents. A son, Francesco, for Franca. For Carla, a daughter, Sara. They were equally devoted to their art and work. When Sozzani met Ruhs, her partner of nearly 30 years, he told her, ‘You must understand, my work will always come first.’ Sozzani clasps her hands with glee, ‘Wonderful!’ I said, ‘That’s perfect! Everyone says I work too hard, but for me it is not work. I do it seven days a week. I don’t need to go and sit by the pool for two weeks,’ she gestures to the room around us, full of her late friend’s work. ‘This is my pool.’ Neatly, both their children have ended up in the industry. When Corso Como was in its infancy, Sara worked for her briefly, but claimed her mother was ‘too soft’. Sozzani dispatched her to her aunt, ‘She was tougher than me, I knew Franca would be able to do with her what I could not.’ She is still working at Italian Vogue, currently as its deputy editor.  Francesco, a film-maker who made a touching documentary about his mother in the year before she died, united two grand houses of Vogue this summer by marrying Bee Shaffer, daughter of Anna Wintour, editor-in-chief of US Vogue. The wedding was held at Wintour’s Long Island estate under a complete media blackout. A couple of blurry pictures of the couple have emerged (alongside snippets of the guest list, said to include Fiat heir Lapo Elkann and Donatella Versace, and in a move that only Richard Curtis could have foreseen, Colin Firth reportedly officiated at ceremony). Carla describes the day as ‘very special, and beautiful, they are both so beautiful! The plan is to to have beautiful babies I think.’ She is understandably very close to her nephew; the New York store will provide even more opportunity for her to visit the city where he lives.  Sozzani credits her parents with instilling in her and her sister an intense work ethic and thirst for knowledge. ‘My father was an architect and an engineer, my mother was very intelligent and cultivated. They took us to museums all the time. We’d go to church on Sundays, not for religion, but because of the paintings,’ she pauses, and says, raising her eyes to the heavens, ‘You know, Italy…’ The two girls were also taken abroad early on, on trips to India and Africa. In the 1950s they were often sent to France ‘to the nuns’ or England where they would stay with friends in the summer holidays.  ‘I loved fashion,’ she tells me excitedly, her eyes glittering, ‘I used to make clothes for my sister’s dolls.’ Her father was ‘very strict’ but his daughters found ways to exploit his rules. ‘He put a system in place where we could get money to buy clothes if we were good at school. So we were incredibly good in school. We’d spend all our money in Pucci. Those beautiful colours.’ She laughs, delighted by the memory. ‘They used to do pyjamas, in solid colours, ah! The palette of colours.’  The American Corso Como venture is a novel proposition. The appeal of the pitch was the proposed space in the Seaport District (at the bottom of Manhattan island, facing Brooklyn on the East River), which is bidding to become the new shopping and entertainment destination in the city (move over Meat Packing).  When she visited the site, it resonated because it felt European, ‘All little red-brick, low-level buildings,’ she says enthusiastically of the historic, original commercial centre, with its warehouse still standing. Her thirst is always to do something new and different, ‘otherwise what is the point?’ The 28,000 sq ft space will house the Corso Como mix – a café, garden, restaurant, as well as her sharply edited curation of fashion – with exclusives from Prada and Alaïa, books – featuring the illustrator Lorenzo Petrantoni, as well as irreverent furniture from Seletti x Studio Job – and various other sharp design ephemera. The gallery will open with a Helmut Newton exhibition. If successful, it will put her at the centre of the city’s buzziest new district.  Sozzani rises at 8am and does Pilates every morning, retiring to bed at 11pm. In the in-between time she is buzzing with energy, frequently travelling between Milan and Paris, as well as touring her stores in Asia. Her curiosity and desire for the new have never waned. This she says, ‘is nature. You either have it or you don’t.’ Although while she is as turned on by fashion as she ever was, she has yet to see another Margiela – ‘he was the last true original,’ or Rei Kawakubo, ‘amazing’.  Having gone through her photography collection for the Berlin exhibition, her wardrobe is next. ‘I have a lot of clothes,’ she laughs, telling me that when her daughter moved out of their Milan apartment, she knocked her room through turning it into a wardrobe. Her archive, she says, will end up being donated to the Alaïa Foundation, which supports young talent, ‘not someone of privilege’, she says emphatically. ‘Azzedine came to Paris with nothing. He didn’t even have a bed. We need to give it to people like he was.’  10 Corso Como, 1 Fulton Street, New York, NY 10038; 10corsocomo.nyc  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  I’d been staring at Karl Lagerfeld’s portrait of Julianne Moore for quite some time before I clocked the flesh‑and‑blood Moore sitting next to it. Even in the crepuscular lighting of London’s Saatchi Gallery, which has been temporarily transformed into the world of Coco Chanel for its current exhibition, Mademoiselle Privé, she is dramatically, luminously pale. Mark Ruffalo, her co-star in The Kids Are All Right, said “she is filled with exquisite poise”. Allowing for Hollywood inflation, that still seems about right. The hair – currently mid‑red – is swept back into an artfully tousled ponytail. The clothes – tailored Chanel jacket with epaulettes and trousers – are black. The make-up is school of “professionally natural”. She is, obviously, a beautiful woman, but believably so. The few lines around her eyes and mouth look as artfully arranged as her hair but, since no surgeon is that good, they must be all her own work. She looks, in short, just the way she does in the many indie films that stud her stellar career – albeit with more expensive clothes. Even jetlagged, she is assiduously accessible. I should have guessed as much from her Twitter feed, which is a spontaneous stream that reads as if it comes direct from Moore, flitting as it does from gun control issues to pictures of the latest lipsticks L’Oréal has sent her. But that portrait is a blockbuster. In it, there are no facial lines, but several millions worth of Chanel diamonds, offset by a slanting neckline in bottle-green haute couture velvet – the dynamo combo she wore on the Chanel couture catwalk in Paris last July – and what I later discover the director David Cronenberg refers to as “hard” Julianne. When I realise that I’ve been hijacked by the virtual Moore over the real thing, I laugh, and so does she. She’s too smart to start arguing with the power of The Image. If she’d been born just a couple of years earlier than she was – she’s 54 – she might chafe at the current tyranny of the red carpet. Meryl Streep – an actress in whose league Moore undoubtedly now is – never looks quite as relaxed discussing frocks on E! as Moore does. Had success come sooner to Moore (she didn’t really resonate with the public until her turn as a porn star in the 1997 cult hit Boogie Nights; she was nominated for an Oscar for best supporting actress, lost out to Kim Basinger, but got to wear Chanel to the ceremony), she too might have been part of that generation of actresses that never quite saw the point of fashion. She would almost certainly have declined to be photographed by Lagerfeld, dressed, or semi-dressed, as a generic Greek goddess for the Pirelli calendar, which Moore did in 2011. As it is, she embraces it – and the L’Oréal contract she signed three years ago. “It’s not such a terrible thing to do, to have someone put you in a beautiful dress,” she says, of the red carpet hoopla. “You get to work with the designer, the atélier, the people who actually sew these dresses. The red carpet has become part of our cultural entertainment.” She did demur when a reporter asked her to lift her hem so the camera could film her shoes – “I said, I don’t need to do that. Let’s keep some dignity” – but with grace and humour. Friction is not her forte. Pragmatism, however, is – the by-product of a peripatetic childhood, perhaps. Her father was in the air force. The family moved from Alaska to Alabama to Germany. Part of the reason she is sanguine about the red carpet folderol is that she knows the L’Oréals, Pirellis and Chanels of this world enable her to take on the kind of juicy roles most commonly found in tiny, independent projects that cost around the same as those diamonds. Still Alice, a film about a professor diagnosed with early onset Alzheimer’s, for which she finally won her Oscar this year (in Chanel couture), “was a $4 million movie, so there were pieces in my on-screen wardrobe that were from my home wardrobe”. Like Moore herself, that wardrobe runs the gamut from memorable (Chanel, Tom Ford, her friend and some-time director) to accessibly forgettable. “I know you’re meant to look good even on the school run these days,” says Moore (she has a son, Caleb, 19, and daughter Liv, 12), “but I always looked terrible when I dropped them off. And I continue to.” I don’t think she’s kidding. She told US Harper’s Bazaar that when her children were small, the roll of paparazzi shots of Moore in cargo shorts, T-shirts and bandana was so bad, “my publicist was like, 'Get it together’ ”. On screen or in character, getting it together is clearly no problem for Moore, whose acting, while often understated, is physically technical. Without recourse to obvious wigs and pyrotechnic accents (although she plays a pitch perfect Dane in the forthcoming Maggie’s Plan), she has thoroughly inhabited tragic heroines, fruit loops (in Savage Grace she portrayed Barbara Daly Baekeland who has an incestuous relationship with her son, played by Eddie Redmayne) and Sarah Palin (in 2012’s HBO series Game Change). She can plumb the tragic as well as slyly seek out the ridiculous – sometimes in the same character. She is exacting about her characters’ clothes, which is why she adored working with Tom Ford. “He has such an incredible eye. If you’re trying to figure out who somebody is, you have to try to understand why they’re wearing what they’re wearing and what they’re saying by wearing it.” For a woman who is so serenely beautiful in repose, she has remarkably malleable features. As Cronenberg pointed out in a feature on Moore in The New Yorker, “she’s more angular from the profile and softer from the full on. Just by turning her head, she can go from hard to soft. She knows how to use that, too.” A shape-shifter who can look mesmerising, she can also blend seamlessly into a crowd. It’s the same with her house in New York’s West Village, on an unexceptional block – except that it’s the only one with plants outside. “I think that’s a New York thing, and maybe a London thing too… everyone tries to make themselves smaller. You live in a big city and everybody is in such close contact, so for all of us to live together in a civilised manner you have to go, 'Well, how much space do I actually need?’ ’’ Although on set she likes to study the monitor after every take, she admits “you can look at yourself on film until you’re blue in the face, but I don’t know what you’re going to learn”. She adds: “What’s important – the way you learn to act – is to watch, listen, try to understand what communication is. I can’t do it by myself. If you just told me to act something, I can’t do it. It’s a very collaborative process.” She has always been more drawn to film, where she can pursue intensive interior studies, than to theatre. “What’s so fun about making films is how many people and voices you need to make something come to life.” She is fortunate in being able to tell whether a script has legs. Some actors would balk if an old friend, especially one best known for designing clothes, asked them to read a script they’d written. But when Tom Ford sent her his treatment of A Single Man, “I read it and responded right away”. Ford was as astonished as the rest of the world when she said yes to starring in it almost immediately. “He said, 'Is that it? Don’t you want to know anything else?’ But it was very, very clear to me. When I waver, it’s usually a sign it’s not right for me.” From outside, her career, with its mix of the lucrative (The Hunger Games) and the quirky, looks more satisfying than ever. She has made some 50 films and shows no sign of slacking. “I’ve really noticed a change recently in the kind of work older actresses are being offered,” she says. “I think audiences are changing and I think the industry is realising there’s an audience for interesting stories and that the opportunities for women’s stories are huge.” In line with her peers, she acknowledges the current hot topic of sexism in Hollywood, while pointing out that it’s no worse than the sexism and inequality endemic in all walks of life. She won’t even indulge in a little whining when I ask for her views on the pressures placed on actresses to look perfect – and youthful. “Sure, I work out – I do Ashtanga yoga every day, though not at the moment [she injured her shoulder doing… yoga], and I’m careful about what I eat. But I know that male actors have an awful lot of physical scrutiny to deal with, too. That’s the nature of our business… it doesn’t mean that content doesn’t count. But why would anyone think that, when for centuries people have been objectified, that would all suddenly stop?” There speaks a pragmatist.  The one to watch on the red carpet this awards season? It’s not some fabulous ingénue or a young hot actress that nobody’s actually heard of. It’s Glenn Close, the legend, the icon, age 71. Close has always been stylish, sure. We’ve seen her fashion trajectory progressing since 1984, when at the age of 37 she made her first big red carpet appearance at the Tony Awards, wearing a white drop-waist dress and a coordinating choker. But in her latest round of promotional appearances for a career-defining role in The Wife (Close brilliantly plays a woman beginning to regret devoting her life to her husband) she is dressing better than ever - and by that I mean she looks more confident, more refined, and tailored to perfection. She’s making an exemplary case for a trailblazing trouser suit as red carpet attire, the antidote to all of the sugary princess gowns that are currently trending. If once the trouser suit felt stuffy and boring on a glamorous occasion, Close has made it her own; just on Monday we saw her tackle a lilac Alexander McQueen suit for a luncheon for Oscar nominees, before changing into a Dior toile de Jouy print one for another engagement later in the day. “She is a sucker for a good suit and strong shoulder,” explains Chloe Hartstein, the personal stylist Close turned to when she realised that she was going to need a strong wardrobe for a string of promotional tour appearances. “She likes anything that has a little or a lot of drama, something that she can play off of while walking the red carpet.” Hiring Hartstein back in the summer was a winning move, as it has undoubtedly helped her to take a fresh look at her failsafe fashion formulas. Hartstein listened and learned what Close loves to wear, and has helped her to find modern, interesting versions of her favourite silhouettes. Hartstein describes Close’s overall look as “regal”, something that has reflected in the duo’s choices; a cape-like Armani Prive gown for the Golden Globes, and a scalloped scarlet coat at the Santa Barbara International Film Festival. Everyone wants to dress Close at an age when, frankly, designers would once have turned their noses up. Her long-standing ethos; wear things that suit you (in her case tailoring), buy quality, buy classics, and don’t buy into trends, has served her well, to the point where it is now the most relevant conversation to be having in fashion. Now nominated for her seventh Oscar, she might finally get to take home the accolade this time. But regardless of the result on 24th February, she looks sure of herself and appears to be having the most fashion fun of her life. That in itself, I’d say, is a bit of a win. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Liv Tyler is despairing about the English weather – but not in the way you might expect. ‘It’s been so hot since I’ve been here!’ the actress told The Telegraph at the presentation of her second collection for British heritage brand Belstaff. ‘I hate summer dressing. My favourite thing is basing my whole look around a beautiful cashmere coat, a cape or a leather jacket. The winter months are my favourite because I can do lots of coats.’ Tyler, 39, has just made it through a whirlwind summer. In the past three months alone, she’s welcomed a baby daughter (Lula, her second child with fiancé Dave Gardner, is nine weeks old), travelled to Australia to film scenes for TV series The Leftovers and moved her young family to London, just in time to roast in a brief late-summer heat wave. But on the third day of London Fashion Week, Tyler seems the picture of serenity as she talked us through yet another project: her second capsule collection for Belstaff. ‘I really designed everything for myself and for all my friends,’ she says of the line. ‘I’ve tried not to overthink it too much and just created the things I love while honouring the history of the brand.’ While Tyler conceived of her autumn-winter collection, with its aviatrix-inspired cape, shearling-lined flying jacket and lace-up biker boots, as ‘a celebration of the feminine and masculine rolled into one,’ her spring-summer range is lighter, more bucolic. ‘This was more “summer garden party”-kind of thinking,’ she says. Drawing inspiration from the English countryside circa 1970 and Stealing Beauty, the 1996 film in which she starred, Tyler devised a line of light, feminine separates and tough-girl leather jackets. Standout designs include a four-pocket denim dress, a sage-green suede suit and the Alconbury biker jacket, a cropped, fitted design with covered poppers and epaulets based on a piece from Belstaff’s archives. A delicate yellow-on-black floral print appears in a blouse and a jumpsuit – chosen rather than a dress, ‘because it has a little more freedom,’ Tyler says. ‘Everything is very pretty, with a bit of an edge, but also something you can be quite strong and function in. It looks gorgeous but makes you feel like you can go on any adventure.’ Her current adventures seem more than enough to keep Tyler occupied. ‘I’m just so happy… There isn’t one thing in my life that I don’t feel grateful or lucky to be doing,’ she says. ‘All the jobs, and my family, and even moving – it’s definitely been intense, but it’s a complete joy.’ The Liv Tyler x Belstaff capsule collection is available now   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Herchcovitch's design was chainmail-like, glittering under the stadium lights. A message written in Portugese translates as: "Thank you for the opportunity to work with you. Best of all was exchanging experiences and stories of our children! And also get closer to known her sisters Patricia and Rafaela . Congratulations on everything!"  The Brazilian designer- until recently a regular at Sao Paolo fashion week and now concentrating on a new label called À La Garçonne'- explained to Vogue.com that Gisele's dress was four months in the making and that he was first approached by Claudia Kopke, the opening ceremony's costume designer. "Gisele knows exactly what looks good on her and what doesn’t, which makes the job much more objective and accurate" he said of the supermodel's involvement. "She was always present in the process. Bundchen made her final catwalk appearence at Sao Paolo fashion week last year, when she walked for Brazilian brand Colcci. At the time she said, "I am grateful that at 14 I was given the opportunity to start this journey. Today after 20 years in the industry it is a privilege to  be doing my last fashion show by choice."  A foreign fashion authority recently told me that the best thing about the way British women shop is their loyalty. Apparently in other parts of the world, shoppers are flippant when it comes to brands, and will actively seek the next, newest name rather than returning to something they love, and know will fit them well. How foolish, right? The Duchess of Cambridge, out in Manchester today to attend the Children’s Global Media Summit, was wearing two new pieces from two old favourite British brands. Her coat (L.K. Bennett’s £495 Delli in a heritage check) and dress (Goat’s £450 festive red Elodie tunic) offered silhouettes that she’s tried and tested before, but with updated fabrics and small design twists for now. Boring, you might think at first. But isn’t that the smartest way to shop? Goat’s founder, Jane Lewis, seems to think so. “Style should be effortless,” Lewis previously told The Telegraph. ''When I put something on I think, 'Does it look good?' and, 'Is it going to work for me today?'” What could be more effortless than knowing inherently that this shape of dress worked for you - and with those tights, these heels and that same jacket cut - on a previous occasion? Finding personal style formulas that are unique to you and suit your shape will eliminate all fuss when getting dressed in the morning, meaning that even on days when you have no idea what to wear, you’ve got something on standby. You must update the look in some way, though - this isn’t a case for literal uniforms. “I had an all-in-one in my first collection when I started Goat 14 years ago and I include at least one virtually every season because I like to wear them so much myself,” Lewis said of her own formula piece, which she owns in dozens of incarnations. “I turn to them time after time, for practically every situation.” Being brand loyal only serves this idea of easy shopping - Kate first discovered L.K. Bennett’s well-proportioned Ami midi coat back in 2011, and it worked, so why not return to pick from their 15 new season designs when she needed an update for formal occasions? Likewise, Goat has 70 variations of flattering figure-skimming mini dresses online and ready to buy right now.  So where do you go when you're looking for that one critical item that makes up your personal style formula? The place you bought it last time, of course. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Before Emma Watson delivered a speech at the UN General Assembly earlier this week about sexual assault policies in universities, she posted a picture on Instagram of what she was wearing. This wasn't your usual outfit-of-the-day post though. In fact, it was the subtle announcement of her collaboration with New York-based ethical brand ZADY. While most celebrity collaborations come about thanks to lengthy negotiations, it was Watson herself- a long time advocate of ethical fashion- who approached ZADY to create bespoke items for her to wear inspired by her style. As well as refreshing her own wardrobe, it was important to Watson that her fans would also be able to purchase the pieces, getting the look in a way which is reassuringly sustainable. Therefore, the entire capsule collection will be available to purchase on the 31st October. Watson will be posting pictures of the collection on her Instagram throughout October, and they will be available to pre-order online as soon she wears them. The elegant camel pencil skirt , which has a slit which can be worn at the back or the front, and the black rollneck wool jumper she wore to deliver her speech at the United Nations are already available to pre-order on ZADY.com for £151 and £134.  The idea behind the capsule collection is to have classic, timeless pieces that can be worn again and again. "It's good for work, it's good for evenings out- it's really a modern woman's capsule wardrobe," ZADY founder Maxine Bedat tells The Telegraph. "It was a bespoke collection. She said 'Can you create a collection for me for the events that I go to and around as a regular person as well?'" Bedat continues; "It was incredibly fun as a team to think what would look great on her, and it's about this timeless beauty and style so that was the inspiration that we were really thinking about - what will look great on her now and as we go into the future." "The pieces are designed for anything that a modern woman might do in a day, from going to a meeting to giving a presentation like she did yesterday, to hanging out with friends," explains Bedat. "It's a wardrobe that can bridge all of those things. Everything in the collection can be dressed up or dressed down, and be appropriate in all situations." The ethical standards of the collection were just as important as its style credentials. "It was about working with farmers and washers and spinners and dyers to make each piece sustainable," says Bedat.  "These pieces aren't synthetic materials and are natural fibres, so you can bury that piece of clothing at the final stage of its life and it would grow back into the earth, which is really important with sustainability because polyester is the number one fibre source in our clothing and is a form of plastic. "The farms that we use have very quality treatment of animals which is a major issue in the apparel industry, and there are no toxic dyes." Another factor that is important to Watson, a UN Women Goodwill Ambassador, and Bedat, is that the women producing these clothes are all treated fairly. "These pieces were all cut and sewn in New York with labour that is treated fairly for its work," Bedat tells The Telegraph. "What is important to Emma obviously is women's issues and the apparel industry is the largest employer of women globally, but 98% of those women aren't receiving a living wage. So it's really important to make sure they are being treated fairly for the beautiful work they are doing." Emma Watson might be best known for her work regarding gender equality with HeForShe, but she also takes sustainability in fashion very seriously. In 2015 she began taking part in The Green Carpet Challenge, working with her stylist Sarah Slutsky to ensure that all of the outfits she wears on the red carpet are created ethically. At the Met Gala for example she wore a Calvin Klein outfit which was created using recycled plastic bottles. "With the help of Eco Age this five piece look is created from three fabrics woven from yarns all made from recycled plastic bottles" Slutsky wrote on Instagram, shedding light on Watson's Met Gala outfit. "Plastic is one of the biggest pollutants – being able to turn this waste into a high quality material is a real success story. Also this beautiful look was designed with the intention to be re-purposed for future use; the pants can be worn on their own, the train can be used for another red carpet." We'll have to stay tuned to Watson's Instagram account to see the full capsule collection with ZADY, but judging by that pencil skirt we have a feeling she's going to make us want to shop... © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s The Met Gala on May 2 – the legendary annual party for 650 guests which last year raised $12.5m for The Costume Institute. This is because tickets are $30,000 dollars each (not a typo). For the first and last time in my life, I’ve been given a ticket, so my mission this week has been to get into official party-shape, and for a scruffy, short, broken-nosed girl like me, it’s been an alarming education.   Hair I went to a hairdresser in, appropriately, the Flatiron District. “I’d like glamorous American hair, please,” I said. “You don’t have enough of it,” he said. “Rude,” I said. “However,” he said, “you can buy these 11 big locks of swishy, long hair that I will tape permanently onto your head, therefore doubling the amount of hair you have. Then you can have a two-hour straightening treatment to make your hair silky. I will dye it, I will chemically gloss it, I will cut it and I will blow it, and at that point you will have glamorous American hair.” I was in the salon for three full days.   Eyes In Bling Lash in Greenwich Village, technicians with masks were applying individual permanent false eyelashes to dozing women lying side by side in pods. I lay down like a clone, two hours later was awoken by the terrible sound of my own snoring, and found I had acquired eyelashes that could hold down a part-time job fanning princesses. My eyebrows were then dyed, waxed, threaded, plucked and manually filled in. I had no idea you could inflict so many different processes on such a tiny amount of face.   Teeth Next stop, a dentist on Broadway for tooth whitening. “We can cast your teeth for a mould,” she said. “You inject a bleaching liquid into the mould every night and it will cost $300.” “Oh,” I said, “I was not expecting that.” “Or go to the pharmacy, buy adhesive White Stripes for $20 which you stick on for 30 minutes and your teeth will look like Tom Cruise’s.” So I did that, and they do. Body A hideous daily boot camp has involved treadmills, kettlebells, weights, medicine balls, fitness bands, rowing machines, exercise bikes and boxing gloves. It has been so exhausting that all I can do after each session is sit quietly and eat a pile of cakes. A Manhattan friend suggested I have a colonic irrigation as she said it makes your skin glow and you lose half a stone of 'body mass’ simply by slooshing 15 gallons of water where the sun never had any intention of shining. At the weekend however, I took my sons to a water slide resort in Pennsylvania and the big slides were so forceful that they basically did the same thing, rendering the appointment with a hose unnecessary. *pause to regain composure*   Dress It turns out wearing Zara to the Met Ball is a criminal offence, so a stylist offered to help me out by gathering a rack of appropriate clothes for a short woman in her 50s, and a tailor to inevitably take up the hem.  Predictably, the eight-year-old in me emerged and chose a silver sequinned swirly-twirly creation which doesn’t need me to hold my tummy in all night and only needed altering in four places; also a tiara and pale pink fake fur scarf. If it works, I’ll look like a party guest. If it doesn’t, I’ll be gracing the “worst-dressed” list (I’ve achieved that hard-earned honour before), filed under “Guests who came as Dame Edna crossed with My Little Pony”. The glamorous stylist has lent me silver platform shoes, real jewel ear-rings, some miracle underwear and the correct glitter colour to put on my nails. They even sorted another dress for the pre-party and a third one for the after party. Just to be clear, I haven’t been asked to the pre-party or after-party. If I am, I’ll be there wearing someone else’s hair, someone else’s dress, someone else’s eyelashes and even more make up than Donald Trump, but it will probably  still be me underneath. emmafreud.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  On the third day of her royal tour of India the Duchess of Cambridge wore three dresses, by Temperley London, fast-fashion label Glamorous and Anna Sui. For her final engagement of the day, at Bihu Festival celebrations in Kaziranga, the Duchess changed into a printed silk-chiffon and twill maxi dress by American fashion designer Anna Sui. The dress, which was shown at New York Fashion Week as part of the AW15 collection, has contrasting folk-inspired floral and animal prints and an embroidered trim. It is currently still available for £805 on Net A Porter. Earlier in the day the Duchess struck a balance between looking modern yet stately, wearing a Temperley London dress for a meeting with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi. The lace 'Desdemona' dress with panel detailing, a high neck collar and a fluted midi skirt is from the pre-fall 2016 collection and was previously available on Moda Operandi for £954. She paired the vibrant dress with her trusty nude court shoes and Natalie clutch, both from L.K Bennett. Designer Alice Temperley, who shows at London Fashion Week and is a long-time favourite of the Duchess, has previously told The Telegraph: “The Duchess is an inspiration. She’s very graceful, gracious and she’s a brilliant ambassador for British fashion. She mixes up designer and high street; the perfect modern-day woman.” Temperley designed the dress that Pippa Middleton wore to the royal wedding reception and has created a number of pieces for the Duchess, but she is very careful to be mindful of their privacy. “I’m not about banging drums or chasing after people and I will never ruin a relationship," she said in an interview with The Telegraph. "They know I will be discreet.” Prior to the lunch, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge visited street children at New Delhi's main railway station, where they heard first-hand accounts of the children's constant battle for survival. At the centre run by the charity Salaam Baalak, the Duchess wore a £50 patterned maxi dress by Manchester-based fast fashion label Glamorous with respectful long sleeves and a lace-up front. She paired the dress with £175 Russell and Bromley flats and the £8 Accessorize gold earrings that she wore on the first day of the royal tour in Mumbai.  During the tour the Duchess of Cambridge has championed both British and Indian fashion talent, wearing pieces by her go-to labels Alexander McQueen, Jenny Packham and Temperley, alongside Indian pieces. On her first day in Mumbai she wore a dress by Indian designer Anita Dongre, who revealed to The Telegraph that her PA-turned-stylist Natasha Archer got in touch a month ago to request some clothes for the Duchess. “Her stylist emailed us and and we sent her a look book, then she came in and got some pieces for fittings,” says Dongre whose Rajasthan-inspired designs are already popular in India, where she has eight shops.  Laura Carmichael once said that playing the dowdy Lady Edith in Downton Abbey was something of a gift. “I think it must be so hard to start your career with everyone going on about how gorgeous you are,” she said in an interview with Love magazine back in 2013. “I probably end up with more confidence than anyone because when people meet me they say, 'Oh, you’re nowhere near as dowdy as we thought you were.’” Nowhere is that statement more apparent than on the red carpet, where Carmichael shines. There’s just something about her. She’s polished, but not unrealistically so. She’s put-together, but also a little undone. She wears Christopher Kane with the ease that we wear Zara and never, ever looks uncomfortable. That’s no mean feat. Where co-star Michelle Dockery (who plays Lady Mary in the ITV period drama) is the archetypal 'English Rose' with her pale skin and raven locks, and Lily James (Lady Rose) the so-pretty-you-can-do-anything-with-her fashion plate, Carmichael is altogether more approachable, a bit more girl-next-door (if that can ever be meant in a non-twee way). She's a firm fan of London labels Christopher Kane and Erdem, and counts their eponymous founders as close friends. She's regularly spotted on the front row of both shows at London Fashion Week. As breathtakingly beautiful as these two designers' creations are, they are not bog-standard red carpet fodder. They don't cinch you in and oomph you up, Versace-style. They require the wearer to bring their own personality to the party, and then not to be overwhelmed - and that's exactly what she does. So, although she always appears sleek and polished (often with a nod to her days as a TVE newsreader in immaculately cut tailoring) many wondered whether tonight's ensemble would reflect her experimental approach to style, or play it safe?  Supermodel Christy Turlington Burns has today described a culture of ‘tolerance’ that exists in the fashion industry, towards the male photographers, designers and casting directors who mistreat and harass young models. Turlington Burns was responding to a week full of sexual abuse allegations in the film industry, made primarily against the producer Harvey Weinstein, as well as to a series of stories shared on Instagram by model Cameron Russell, in which other models detailed the ways that they had suffered in the hands of men in positions of power within the fashion industry. “I have been thinking about this a lot since the news came out [about Weinstein], and I can say that harassment and mistreatment have always been widely known and tolerated in the industry,” she told WWD. “The industry is surrounded by predators who thrive on the constant rejection and loneliness so many of us have experienced at some point in our careers.” Turlington Burns was scouted by the photographer Dennie Cody when she was just 14, but counts herself ‘lucky’, in that a chaperoning arrangement was set up by her mother and agents to keep her safe, and to ensure that she still went to school. She didn’t begin to pursue full-time modelling opportunities until she was 18, and says that she was never personally subjected to any abuse. “I feel fortunate that I did not personally experience anything traumatic, but also know that is not the norm,” she said. “I was lucky because my mom was with me a lot early on and then once I had some success, I was handled with extra care. We trusted the people who were supposed to be keeping an eye out for me. There were many times I could not believe who I was left under the care of on early trips to Milan, Paris or London. I would get off of a flight and find some creepy playboy type there to meet me.” Last week Russell shared accounts from numerous sources on her Instagram, prompted after a friend had told her about a male photographer who had assaulted her on a test shoot at the age of 15. “She has asked to remain anonymous but asked that I share her words here because the photographer still works in the industry,” Russell said. “She wants to encourage other women to speak up. We need a way to begin breaking the silence while remaining protected. We are not talking about one, five, or even twenty men. We are talking about a culture of exploitation and it must stop.” The British model Edie Campbell was one of the first to back her campaign to highlight those who abuse their power. "The question of consent is a particularly tricky one when it comes to fashion,” she said. “When we go on set, we enter into an unspoken contract: for that day we give our bodies and our faces over to the photographer, stylist, hairdresser, makeup artist. We give up ownership for that day. The power imbalance is huge, and the duty of care to that model is even greater as a result." Turlington Burns also describes a sense of feeling like ‘an accomplice’ and says that she might have acted differently if she had truly known how some of her collaborators had treated others. “In hindsight, I fear I may have played the “honeypot” that has been described in the stories about these predators who make other women feel protected,” she says. “Unknowingly, but still an accomplice of sorts. I might have been the assurance that made other young women feel safer. If I’d known how these men thought and behaved, I might have done more to stay clear of them.” The solution, she says, is to continue to strengthen and enforce the regulations in place to stop the use of underage models, as well as to monitor the appropriateness of themes of shoots, with penalties if standards are not adhered to. “The best way to protect young models is to keep them in school and off sets until they are adults,” she added. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Alexandra Shulman’s 306th edition of British Vogue has hit subscribers’ letterboxes today, allowing loyal fans of the title to get their first look at her final production as editor-in-chief. The September 2017 issue stars five of Shulman’s favourite models on the cover, shot by Mario Testino and aiming to represent the ‘past, present and future of modelling’. Veteran Vogue girl Kate Moss makes her 32nd cover appearance in Shulman’s tenure, and Stella Tennant returns for her fifth. Edie Campbell joins them to make her third, Jean Campbell her second, and Nora Attal making her debut. In an editor’s letter titled 'Wonder Years', Shulman talks through the changes she has seen in the industry during her successful 25 years at the helm, as well as highlighting exciting features in her final issue, including a profile of Cressida Dick, Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police. She begins by reminiscing about her debut, the April 1992 edition, which featured interview with an ‘up-and-coming’ actor Brad Pitt, as well as features on Hervé Pierre, the then-new designer at Balmain, and a review of upcoming Steven Spielberg film, Hook. “Some 306 issues, 1,600 fashion shoots and, at a calculated guess, 38,970 pages later, the world and Vogue have both changed enormously,” she writes. “News, whether current affairs or fashion, is no longer broken in print but arrives via a ping on a screen, day or night.” Indeed Vogue is about to undergo its biggest shakeup in a long time as her successor, Edward Enninful, officially started his new job yesterday, promising to push the magazine in new directions across both print and digital platforms. Enninful’s appointment was announced on 10th April, after Shulman confirmed her ‘Vrexit’ back in January. “Editing British Vogue has been the greatest of privileges and has meant that I’ve spent most of my days working alongside some of the finest creative talent around,” Shulman continued in her letter. “It is impossible to acknowledge everyone who made my years at Vogue so rewarding, but Lucinda Chambers, my fashion director for 24 years, and Frances Bentley, my managing editor, who kept the whole office on the road for an equal amount of time, have won my eternal thanks.” Indeed, many of the staffers who were so loyal to Shulman have since used her departure as a cue to leave Vogue too, prompting a natural ‘changing of the guard’ at Britain’s fashion bible. “Now it’s time for myself and Vogue to start on new journeys,” Shulman’s letter concludes. “I’m very excited to see where we both go.” See the full shoot in the September issue of Vogue, on general sale on Friday   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
