 This evening, the Cameron family departed the house they've called home for the past six years for the last time. And Samantha Cameron ended her Downing Street tenure in the same dignified style which has defined her time as Prime Minister's wife. Wearing a fit and flare dress by Roksanda, the London-based label designed by Serbian-born Roksanda Ilincic, Cameron cemented her reputation as being able to find a deft balance between experimental and appropriate clothes which woman the country, nay, world over have admired.   There isn’t a working mother in the land who doesn’t, at times, feel torn in several directions by the conflicting demands of modern life. As wife to the PM, Samantha Cameron had more balls in the air than most. Certainly, the ramifications were greater if she dropped them. During her husband’s six year term as Prime Minister, not only was she a career woman who juggled a family: in matters of conduct and in all things sartorial, she was an ambassador for Britain. Down days, off days and can’t-find-anything-to-wear days were not permitted. Whether she liked it or not, Sam Cam was forever in the public eye. It may not have been her intention to encourage women to embrace bright colours, mix high street with designer and furnish their working wardrobe with bold prints, but this she did, in a manner that made such risk-taking feel effortless. Unlike, for example, Amal Clooney, her style didn’t feel unattainable. With some judicious online shopping at the likes of COS, Whistles and L.K Bennett, women felt that they, too, could dress like Sam. It speaks volumes about her likeability that most women, regardless of their political persuasion, would be hard-pushed to find much about Mrs Cameron that is disagreeable. It is precisely this likeability which insiders believe she should put to good use in the next chapter of her life. As an ambassador for the British Fashion Council since 2011, her appeal has already been harnessed to the benefit of London Fashion Week. While previous governments have had an attitude to British fashion that can best be described as “ambivalent” (though Sarah Brown did much to change this during her husband Gordon’s time as PM), the fact that David Cameron’s wife already worked in the fashion industry - she was creative director at Smythson until 2010, and currently functions as a consultant - made her a natural and empathetic fit for the valuable work the British Fashion Council undertakes in promoting British fashion on a global scale. It is a role she takes seriously. Fashion designers are often anti-establishment by nature, yet it wasn’t long before Mrs Cameron had them eating out of her hand. She has the gift of making people feel included. The stiff white invitations to the receptions she hosted to mark London Fashion Week were more coveted than fashion’s cooler-than-thou denizens would admit. How could it not be a thrill to rubberneck the formal drawing rooms of Number 10? And, in the case of one designer, nick some toilet roll? British designers both established and fledgling were invited, as were visiting international press. The rooms thronged with guests including Anna Wintour, Salma Hayek, Naomi Campbell and Victoria Beckham.   Given that fashion directly contributes £26 billion to the economy, British designers don’t always feel as valued as they should, which is why Mrs Cameron’s patronage felt so important. More important still was that she went to their fashion shows, her very presence boosting the chances of international press coverage. She also wore their clothes, affording vital exposure to a host of designers including Christopher Kane, Jonathan Saunders and - her favourite - Erdem. Today was also not the first time that Cameron has worn Roksanda Ilincic's designs; she chose a fuschia and jade green top and skirt for a fashion reception in 2012 and a turquoise and navy shift dress to visit the Obamas at the White House.  Even when critics carped about the cost of these clothes, she remained defiant, rather than apologetically donning Zara. Wearing a £39 Zara skirt would not have boosted the British economy (although there were plenty of times that she concluded her grey suede Zara heels were a perfectly good accompaniment to a designer look.)  As a next move, some have conjectured that she could make millions from a “Goop-style website” a la Gwyneth Paltrow. This isn’t really her style. Mrs Cameron will be all too aware of the spectre of self-parody, and is too savvy to fall into the trap of, for example, Pippa Middleton, whose book of party tips invited ridicule. Others have claimed she is to launch a fashion label with Isabel Spearman, her former “Girl Friday” who now owns a brand consultancy. This has been denied by Spearman’s camp, though given both women’s friendship and industry experience, no-one would bet against them working together in some capacity in the future. Certainly, Mrs Cameron’s love of fashion runs far deeper than her role as clothes horse might suggest. Complimented on her grey flannel trousers at a Smythson press day several years ago, she cheerfully admitted she had designed them herself, then had them made up by a local tailor in west London. With a genuine love of clothes and a Rolodex dripping with stellar contacts, the truth is that Sam Cam can do anything she wants to do. In terms of her next fashion move, the question is surely not “if” but “when”.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  If we could all go back in time and advise our younger selves against that dodgy bandage dress or cropped 'pixie'-do we would.  But we can't. In truth this is probably a good thing because it would make looking at old pictures infinitely less enjoyable. But we can at least learn from our mistakes. From embracing their natural hair colour to managing a succinct wardrobe edit, or seeking advice from stylish acquaintances to knowing what things are better avoided: these are the sartorial lessons that women of every age wish they'd known all along.  ''Don't follow trends slavishly - figure out what shapes and colours suit you instead and stick to that,'' advises 33-year-old Roberta Benteler, founder of Avenue 32, who also recommends ''investing in classics, like a great coat or cashmere jumper, that will last a lifetime and never go out of fashion''. Another tip Benteler wishes she'd picked up earlier is to ''choose your colour palette according to your complexion and hair.'' ''A warm complexion and blonde hair welcomes colder colours like navy and grey, whereas a fairer complexion suits oranges and browns.''   ''Off-the-shoulder tops and dresses are the most elegant style for me to wear, but for too many years I was too insecure to show off my shoulders,'' says blogger Charlotte Groenveld of the style lessons she's only recently learnt.  ''I've also realised sunglasses without frames and skinny jeans are just not made for me,'' she continues. ''I have so many frameless sunglasses, but I never felt they actually looked good on me -  I've realised chunky frames are much better.'' ''If you haven't worn something in your cupboard for two years, the likelihood is you'll never wear it again - make some room in your wardrobe and donate it to someone who will,'' recommends 39-year-old fashion director and consultant, Caroline Issa. Issa also suggests investing in an evening suit: ''whether a formal tux, or looser tuxedo style or beautiful velvet jacket and trousers, when faced with a black tie dress code, you'll be sorted without having to run around looking for the perfect dress last minute.'' ''Ask stylish people you trust for advice,'' says 68-year-old model Maye Musk. ''As a dietitian and nutrition scientist I don't always understand the finer points of fashion - that changed 26-years ago when I started working with my stylist Julia Perry.'' ''I also wish I'd adopted the European way of dressing earlier - a smaller wardrobe with better quality clothes,'' Musk continues, ''and I should have let my hair go natural earlier and not waited until I was 60.''  What do you buy the woman who has everything? It’s a question you might be asking yourself in the run-up to Christmas if you’re a friend or family member of Carla Bruni, the Italian-born supermodel, singer-songwriter and wife of former French President Nicholas Sarkozy. “Something in cashmere,” she says, is on her gift wish list. “Warm, very soft and cosy. Or any of the large, gorgeous Burberry bags - I always carry a bunch of stuff around.” Bruni has been immersed in the world of Riccardo Tisci’s Burberry lately: she’s one of a number of brand ambassadors to have been cast in its festive campaign, including fellow Nineties supermodel Cecilia Chancellor, today’s models-of-the-moment Fran Summers and Ikram Abdi Omar, singer Mahmood and footballer Ruben Loftus-Cheek. If you’re not familiar with some of those names, don’t worry - neither was Bruni, who hadn’t heard of Loftus-Cheek before she met him on set. “I didn’t know about him,” she admits. “I actually don’t know much about football at all, which is an absolute disgrace for an Italian!” The pair poses together in one of the campaign images, Bruni seated on Loftus-Cheek’s lap, her arms draped across his shoulders. She describes the England midfielder as “lovely” and the photoshoot as “super easy.” In another image, she wears a white evening gown, her favourite look from the shoot. “It's cut like magic,” she says. “It’s everything I like in one outfit. Riccardo has a perfect technique and a great sense of modernity, he really knows how to use the past to reinvent the future.” It helps, of course, that at 51, she is still striking, with the same willowy frame that made her a catwalk favourite in the Nineties. It’s a period she remembers fondly. “It was all so much fun... I really enjoyed working with the photographers, the designers, chatting with the girls backstage, we all knew each other and lived together like a crazy travelling circus between Paris, Milan and New York.” Bruni was thrust into the spotlight once again in 2008, when she married Nicolas Sarkozy, France’s then-President. Over the next four years, she lived at the Élysée Palace and accompanied her husband on his official duties, usually clad in custom-made suits and dresses from Christian Dior and Hermès. She insists her style hasn’t changed much: she’s long been inspired by the likes of Patti Smith and Françoise Hardy, though it has evolved over the years. “I’ve always dressed quite simply, but there are some things I wouldn’t feel comfortable wearing at my age, like miniskirts for example.” Not that she has much call for miniskirts these days - her life couldn’t be further removed from fashion. “Writing music is the opposite of living in the fashion world, it’s all about living inside of yourself. Fashion is all about exchanging [ideas] with other people,” she says. “I hardly ever wear a dress in my regular life. A nice pair of jeans with a fitted jacket and a good pair of flat boots is my daily uniform.” These days, Bruni is also quite publicity-shy, rarely giving interviews, but it didn’t take much persuading to get her to take part in Burberry's campaign. “I've admired Riccardo’s work for a very long time and I love Mert and Marcus [the photography duo who shot the campaign] so I was thrilled, said yes and didn’t ask any questions,” she says. “The next thing I knew, I was on a train to London.” The festive season for the Bruni-Sarkozy clan is usually spent outside of Paris - though where that may be this year remains undecided. “I could end up in snow boots as well as in a summer dress,” she says. “If we go to our house in the south of France, it’s all about wood fires.” Bruni, who is mother to son Aurélien, 18, and daughter Giulia, eight, as well as stepmother to Sarkozy’s three adult sons, says whatever they end up doing, the children will be at the heart of it. “As with many large families, we always start celebrating beforehand,” she says. “Everybody gets to see each other and the kids can get spoiled.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge's off-duty wardrobe is always pinned around one thing: a classic Breton top, usually from a high-street favourite such as J.Crew or Me and Em. And it seems that she has applied the same 'Kings Road on a Saturday' approach to casualwear when dressing Prince George. To mark the Prince's third birthday today, Kensington Palace has released a series of images of George playing in the garden of his house at Anmer Hall in Norfolk and he is dressed in the Duchess of Cambridge's off-duty signature - stripes, stripes and more stripes.  Most importantly, nothing in his wardrobe would raise eyebrows at the tills. George wears an oatmeal jumper with navy stripes with a blue whale knitted on the front, which is by Spanish childrenswear brand Pepa & Co and is currently reduced from £42 to £29.40. The jumper is paired with cream shorts and his trusty navy and white preppy £15 boat shoes by Trotters - these canvas pumps are fast becoming George's version of Kate's nude L.K. Bennett heels.  The third in line to the throne wears navy shorts with a blue Breton T-shirt with a contrasting navy striped patch giving a pocket effect in the images which show him standing on a 'Catherine and William' personalised rope swing attached to a tree. This striped T-shirt is from London-based children's swimwear brand Sunuva and is also currently on sale from £28 to £9. Did the Duchess of Cambridge have a June sales sweep, perhaps? Sunuva told The Telegraph today that they will soon be restocking the T-shirt to meet the inevitable uplift in demand caused by the 'George' effect.  The photographs, taken by Matt Porteous, show Prince George in a much more modern context than we have previously seen. Instead of wearing stiff shorts, frilly old-fashioned rompers and traditional socks, he is dressed in a modern, low-key style wearing a number of striped pieces paired with shorts designed for playing. Estelle Lee, editor of Smallish magazine- the arbiter of taste among stylish Mums- says that Prince George's clothes in these third birthday pictures reflect his transition from baby to boy. "When they're babies it’s tempting to go to town with beautiful outfits," she explains, "but by 3 it's all about making life easier for yourself. They're wearable, washable and classic in style – perfect for romping about the gardens of Amner Hall with Lupo in tow." Prince George's Sunuva t-shirt, £9, available here (more stock coming soon) These new images also underline the very normal upbringing which the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge are determined to give their children. "Like her own wardrobe, The Duchess is choosing stylish but inobtrusive clothes for Prince George," says Lee, "she's not looking to start trends or make statements. It's all about conformity and not wanting to raise eyebrows at the nursery gates." It's not just the styles but also the sources of George's clothes which reflect this. "Trotter's is the absolute go-to for busy mums who don't want to spend ages getting the ‘right’ essentials for their kids," says Lee, "from haircuts to ballet tutus –they have a great edit of seasonal shoes, clothes and toys. It's a middle-class one-stop shop." Meanwhile, "Sunuva is the brand for best quality swimwear. It was the first to provide swimwear with in-built sun protection. Beautiful designs married with first class quality." And what about those stripes? "They're a middle class fail safe which will go with anything." George has caused the jumper from the Fulham-based Pepa & co to sell out in hours, as Pepa Gonzalez, founder of Pepa & Co tells The Telegraph: "I receive orders daily from around the globe and have been astounded at the number of orders today.  Our website has had a big lift in traffic this morning and we have had a number of orders today for the whale print jumper from around the world. We are now completely sold out of the whale print sweater but do have a few sizes of shorts left in stock." Emily Cohen, who co-founded Sunuva along with fellow Mum Sabrina Naggar, underlines the importance of The Duchess's support for British brands. "We know Kate is passionate supporter and promoter of young British brands and we are thrilled and hugely flattered that the Sunuva stripe T-shirt has been included in the official pictures of Prince George on his 3rd Birthday. Kate has impeccable taste and as always Prince George looks absolutely adorable" Cohen tells The Telegraph. As for the Duchess of Cambridge's own expansive breton collection, she has worn blue and white striped sleeved tops by the likes of Ralph Lauren, J Crew, Me + Em and Petit Bateau. This has become her established off-duty uniform, which she has worn everywhere from family trips to the polo to relaxed official engagements on royal tours to watching sport, such as at the London 2012 Olympics. She even wore a striped Petit Bateau long sleeved t shirt in her cover photo shoot for British Vogue.  In the images that the royal couple have released of Prince George and Princess Charlotte to date, they have worn very traditional childrenswear with an almost Edwardian feel. In the Queen's 90th birthday portrait, her great-grandchildren are arguably dressed even more traditionally than the 90-year-old monarch herself in  smock dresses from a bygone era and frilly socks.  It has been argued that they are dressed in this style so that the portraits will look timeless and classic, but the formality of these official photographs is also a significant factor. Childrenswear designer Rachel Riley - a label worn by George on several occasions - explained: “In the [90th] stamp portrait the Queen is wearing a formal dress and Charles and William are wearing suits, so it’s appropriate for Prince George, even though he’s two, to wear a formal outfit. Shorts and a shirt is appropriate for his age - he wouldn’t wear a mini suit and he wouldn’t wear anything too casual because everyone else is looking formal.” It is appropriate that George is wearing a playtime outfit that you would see in playgrounds across the country for these pictures of him playing in the garden. As Kate knows, wearing an every-day outfit is a way of giving the impression that despite the titles, vast wealth and worldwide fame, they are a 'normal' Norfolk family. "We are extremely honoured to have Prince George wearing our whale print sweater and taupe shorts in his official birthday portraits.  We are now six months into Theresa May’s Prime Ministership. But while political commentators still seem to be scratching their heads about what exactly ‘Mayism’ means, from a style perspective we can be reassured that the her doctrine is clearly defined: using her position to support British fashion, without sacrificing any of her trademark playful touches.  If anything summed that up it was the outfit May wore to host a reception to launch London Fashion Week, highlighting an industry that contributes £28billion a year to the UK economy. Precedent had been set by Samantha Cameron, who always used the opportunity to wear a dress by one of London’s homegrown talents like Christopher Kane or Roksanda, but somehow that didn’t seem quite May’s style. She solved the problem with an beautifully cut £150 white shirt from John Lewis’s Modern Rarity collection, designed by emerging British design duo Palmer//Harding. It was a look which nodded to the breadth of British fashion and the importance of supporting young talent without erring from May’s own tastes.   “Later we found out that she had gone to John Lewis herself to get the shirt and bought a few. It's a real honour to have such a stylish woman take the time to purchase our pieces on her own accord,” says Levi Palmer, giving fresh insight into the PM’s hands-on approach to her wardrobe.  Indeed, news last week that a package for May from that other great British high street stalwart Next had gone missing in her hometown shows the PM is an avid online shopper. And far from having a stylist, May is said to have been making regular visits to Fluidity - an independent boutique on the high street of Henley, less than 20 miles from her Maidenhead constituency, to flesh out her Downing Street wardrobe.  When looking for clothes, May tends to seek out British brands. Analysis by the Politics and Style blog, which has been charting May’s looks since moving to no. 10, shows that since becoming PM she's worn a piece from Amanda Wakeley almost 75% of the time. (And no, apparently she doesn't have a discount at the brand.)  Perhaps it's not a surprise that becoming Britain's most powerful politician has done nothing to deter May's attitude towards style. This is, of course, the woman who once told Desert Island Discs, “I enjoy clothes” and that her luxury would be a subscription to Vogue. Far from abandoning the leopard print kitten heels, colourful coats and bold jewellery she'd fostered such a fondness for during her years rising up through the cabinet ranks - and which had helped her to stand out in parliament - she's stayed true to her defiantly daring style. Since she became PM on July 13th 2016 we've seen her in steel-capped loafers, those £995 controversial leather trousers and, a month after her 60th birthday, a navy cocktail dress which both bared her arms and exposed her knees. “She sent a mighty signal to women who think that once they hit 60 they must cover up and resign themselves to invisibility as far as fashion is concerned,” wrote The Telegraph’s Linda Kellesy. The only thing May seems to have significantly altered is her adoration of kitten heels. The Politics and Style blog reports that since entering Downing Street flats have overtaken kitten heels as the PM's shoe of choice. (Ironic perhaps, considering the iconic 1990's shape is very much back in fashion after making a comeback on the catwalk).  "Theresa May is not your typical politician and throughout her career, she has used fashion to show her personality. She is paving the way for women in all professions to redefine what is ‘acceptable’ to wear in the workplace, demonstrating that you can be clever and like clothes. No longer should women be afraid to wear leopard print in the House of Commons or in the office!" says Laura-Emily Dunn, the blogger behind Politics and Style - who says she regularly has visitors to her site from Americans eager to see what May is wearing. "As the UK begins to rewrite its future post Brexit, it will become even more important for the Prime Minister to show her love of fashion, and by championing British designers and brands like Amanda Wakeley, Halcyon Days and Russell & Bromley, Theresa May will not only help to boost British business but also her presentation as a modern, forward thinking politician."  It may not have been May's intention, but it certainly seems that her unapologetic love of fashion is proving a refreshing antidote to the style rules so many women face, especially those who work in professional environments.  “I have grown used to the focus on my clothes and my shoes,” May told the The Telegraph shortly after becoming Prime Minister. “As a woman I know you can be very serious about something and very soberly dressed and add a little bit of interest with footwear.” That’s Mayism for you.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Coddington, the creative Welsh visionary who has helped shape the artistic direction of US Vogue magazine for 28 years, is stepping down from her position at the magazine. The Business of Fashion broke the news today that the 74-year-old’s decision will be effective immediately. But she isn’t cutting all ties with the style bible. “After more than 25 years at American Vogue, Grace Coddington will assume the role of creative director at large and take on additional projects outside the magazine,” said a spokesperson. “She will work on several Vogue fashion shoots throughout the year.” The decision certainly doesn’t mean that Coddington plans to reduce her workload; instead, she will collaborate on a variety of projects, starting with a fragrance in collaboration with Japanese fashion label Comme des Garç​ons. “I’m not running away from Vogue, because it has opened so many doors” she commented. “But it will be nice to collaborate, and nice to go out [and] give talks to people. It’s just another approach. I’m certainly not going into retirement. I don’t want to sit around.” The Anglesey-born former model has been responsible for creating many of the magazine’s iconic shoots since working under fellow Brit and editor-in-chief Anna Wintour from 1988. Over her career she has collaborated with the most revered photographers and in-demand models, creating some of the most enduring fashion imagery in the process. Last year, a book chronicling her most memorable fashion editorials, Grace: Thirty Years Of Fashion At Vogue, was reissued after first being published in 2002. Coddington entered public consciousness in 2009, when she emerged as the unexpected ‘star’ of The September Issue, a documentary-film revealing life behind the scenes at Vogue. At first she was reluctant to be filmed, but after director R. J. Cutler gained her trust, her relationship and creative wrangles with Wintour became the highlight of the film. In 2012, the cat-lover released Grace: A Memoir, a must-read that chronicles her childhood in Anglesey and her early career as a model during London’s Swinging Sixties, all peppered with doodles of cats and fashion personalities. Coddington was the model who sat for Vidal Sassoon’s groundbreaking ‘five point haircut' in 1963. She worked as a photo editor at British Vogue after modelling and a stint at Calvin Klein, started work at US Vogue on the same day as Wintour. She remarked today: “I really love Vogue, it’s been in my life always, they discovered me as a model at 19.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Emilia Wickstead married in Tuscany in 2011, she inadvertently created a starting point for a new tangent of her then-recently established label, which was fast gaining a reputation for its modern, polished pieces imbued with a timeless kind of simplicity.  The New Zealand-born designer created her own wedding gown- a column dress with sweeping full over-skirt and a fitted bodice, over which she layered a sheer, jewelled jacket for the daytime portion of proceedings. “The first wedding dress I ever made was for myself. It was at a time when I had my business up-and-running but it was still very early days and I thought this is my moment to do whatever I like,” Wickstead remembers. “My wedding dress was featured by Vogue and American Town and Country and from there people started to come to us because they had seen that dress.” Six years on, Wickstead’s bespoke bridal business has grown organically. Last year, she created Lady Charlotte Wellesley’s dress for her marriage to Alejandro Santo Domingo. The images of Wellesley arriving at the church in Grenada, Spain for the society wedding of the year were beamed around the world, with Wickstead’s grand yet streamlined and architectural design drawing much admiration. “That really pushed the level of bespoke bridal to another level altogether,” she confirms.  Now, Wickstead is finally launching a ready-to-wear bridal collection. The ten-piece offering spans a very modern jumpsuit to a regal gown, and plenty of options in between with prices ranging from £2,665 to £10,000. The Margo dress, with its thick shoulder straps and skirt which sweeps out from a nipped-in waist, is reminiscent of Wickstead’s own wedding dress. The Peggy offers a column, high-necked silhouette with an exposed back while the Tilda and the Claris seem to have been made for country nuptials in the breezy, gauzy fabrics which are a Wickstead signature.  “Anything I’ve designed for this collection would be what I’d wear if I could get married ten times,” says the designer who counts Gwyneth Paltrow, Emma Watson and The Duchess of Cambridge amongst her sophisticated devotees. “They are made to be worn and then looked at 35 years down the line and still make you think ‘That was beautiful.’" She cites Grace Kelly and Audrey Hepburn’s wedding looks, by Edith Head and Pierre Balmain respectively, as a source of timeless inspiration. "I think sometimes that’s been a little bit lost in today’s world of bridal so it was important to me to bring this old world back with this collection and to keep ticking that box.” So will Pippa Middleton arrive at St Mark’s church, Englefield on May 20th wearing Emilia Wickstead? The designer is, naturally, tight-lipped on the subject but she is an obvious contender for the commission as a London-based designer with an elegant track record and as a favourite of the bride’s big sister. One thing is for sure: it would be Middleton’s savviest sartorial decision yet if she has opted for Wickstead.      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge visited Roe Green Junior School in Brent, London on Tuesday where she launched a mental health programme for schools - the latest initiative from the Heads Together campaign. The duchess opted for a blue coat by the Italian, Max Mara-owned label Sportmax and a purple dress by Seraphine, the maternity label which she has favoured throughout her pregnancies, with Jimmy Choo navy suede pumps. So far, so textbook Duchess-style.  But Kate also added a pop of print to her outfit in the form of a Matiss-inspired printed scarf, designed by Beulah London, currently available for pre-order for £95. The label's raison d'etre is that "each and every product will support and empower vulnerable women." The Duchess has looked to this reasonably under-the-radar brand, which is the brain child of Lady Natasha Rufus Isaacs, an old friend of the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge who also happens to be married to a former boyfriend of the Duchess, and co-founder Lavinia Brennan, for public engagements on numerous occasions, most notably during the royal tour of India in 2016.  ''It's wonderful that she's worn our dresses before. She's a brilliant ambassador and it's great exposure for us on a global scale,'' said Lady Natasha, after the Duchess was pictured in a Beulah London poppy print dress.''A lot of people go on our site straight after she wears a dress," she conceded.  As well as producing flattering and feminine pieces, Beulah London was born out of a 2010 volunteer mission in Delhi during which Lady Natasha and Brennan were working to help transform the lives of women who had been trafficked into the sex trade. As a result, 10% of the profits of all sales go to the The Beulah Trust, an organisation set up by the founders in 2013, that supports projects creating sustainable livelihoods for victims of trafficking.   While Beulah is not a new label for the Duchess of Cambridge, this latest show of support comes days after Duchess-to-be Meghan Markle's appearance in Cardiff, during which she also showed her own commitment to ethical fashion; she chose a coat by cruelty-free designer Stella McCartney, a bag by DeMellier London which donates a percentage of its profits to children in developing countries and jeans by Huit Denim, which limits production in its Cardigan-based factory to 100 pairs a week, offers a free mending service and encourages customers to join its 'No Wash Club' to save on energy waste.  Could it be that the Duchess of Cambridge was spurred on by Markle's conscientious wardrobe choices? Both women are certainly aware of the attention which their clothes attract and are passionate advocates for good causes. So a strategy which combines the two can only be considered a smart move.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Voguefashion director Lucinda Chambers has been in the spotlight since she emerged as the star of the BBC documentary Absolutely Fashion: Inside British Vogue. Chambers joined Vogue in the Seventies and has worked her way up from petty cash handler to secretary, fashion assistant and finally director during her tenure. “She doesn’t 'do' social media, is wickedly funny, does not suffer fools, and has an Austen-esque eye for detail and affectations,” says Telegraph fashion director Lisa Armstrong. Her style, meanwhile, encapsulates her eccentricity. “I’m a tart, aesthetically,” she has said of her look. “I love sparkly, I love vintage, I love ethnic.  So many people working in fashion just look like one thing… it’s a sign of insecurity." This 'Fashion Month' there's been plenty of photographs of Chambers navigating the shows and parties, and thus a number of new season styling tips we can take from the original Voguette. She might eternally ask, “do I really look like a batty old woman?”, when she sees portraits of herself, but we'd have to disagree... Fear of flying, the wrong underwear, a rogue documentary maker and John Kerry all play a role in the frenetic life of Alexandra Shulman, editor of British Vogue. As she celebrates the style bibles 100th anniversary, here is an extract from her private diary of a momentous year at the magazine.
 _By Alexandra Shulman, Friday 14 October 2016_
**September 1, 2015**
Three nights ago, in a restaurant by the sea, just off a coastal road in Puglia, some children at the long family tables next to ours were playing with their pencil cases, lining up the coloured felt tips in order. Today, back in London, it is like the first day of term, and I wish I had a new box of coloured pens that I could bring into work with me, shiny and neat and full of promise. Though of what, I couldnt say.
September 1 was my fathers birthday. If he were still alive, he would be 102 today. Instead his ashes were shot into the sky 11 years ago in a rocket my brother, Jason, made from Evening Standards, the newspaper where my father \([Milton Shulman](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1462636/Milton\-Shulman.html)\) worked for more than 40 years. He loved being a journalist, having a soapbox and a public voice, whether that be theatre criticism or politics or anything, really just so long as he was heard. I dont feel that way about editing Vogue. Its Vogues voice, not mine.
Although I do, of course, have a choice in what that voice says. After three weeks on holiday, I feel disengaged and not sure whether I have any\-thing to say on any subject relevant to the magazine. It will take a few days to reimmerse. I put on a striped shirt from Zara that I bought before the holiday. Its refreshing to wear something new ammunition for the day ahead. A shirt feels as if it has a clarity of purpose, which will be helpful.
 Even so, its strange: a costume rather than the holiday clothes of the past days. Before leaving for the office, I go to Gails bakery down the road and buy croissants and a Chelsea bun for my son, Sam, whose flight home from New York is scheduled to arrive this morning. Hes been away for nine weeks. Im so excited to see him. Tonight Ill roast a chicken for us. I wont relax until I get the text saying hes landed.
**September 7**
Ive returned to work with five big projects to achieve: a centenary issue, [a big party to celebrate our 100 years](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/events/vogue\-100\-best\-dressed\-kim\-kardashians\-opts\-for\-sheer\-dress\-for/), the 2016 Vogue Festival, the filming of a BBC Two documentary about the magazine, and the successful installation of an exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery. When I consider them all, I want to go back on holiday.
**September 14**
The garden at home never looks lovelier than when Im about to get on a plane. Yesterday morning the figs had finally ripened enough to eat, and the sun was shining on the [new autumn colours](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/style/shopping\-on\-mount\-street/autumn\-fashion\-trends\-you\-need\-to\-know/) that are peeping through all the dusty green.
  As I left for Heathrow I felt sick, and waiting for the flight to New York I was feeling so bad that I nearly cancelled the trip. Ive hated flying since I was 19, and the degree of my terror waxes and wanes. Once weve landed, Im excited to look out of the window at the tarmac. If you believe youre bound not to survive a flight, arriving intact is hugely pleasing. [Diane von Furstenberg](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/new\-york\-fashion\-week/diane\-von\-furstenberg\-gets\-modernised\-jonathan\-saunders\-on\-raisi/) was my first show \(at New York fashion week\) and I went there straight from the airport.
  At the end, in true showman style, she appeared, fiery\-maned and running down the catwalk with her still\-incredible legs on display, shaking hands and locking eyes with the audience, reminding me of Bill Clinton. New York collections are often a commercial version of what Europe provides for the previous season. Its what America does so well: the designers turn someone elses idea into something that makes money.
 > "Ive made a massive error here and this film is simply going to be incredibly trashy and simplistic"
 Even on the first day, I could see the huge [Cline](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/cline\-introduces\-us\-to\-faye\-wong\-chinese\-pop\-sensation\-\-and\-your/) influence in the longer lengths, the silhouette, the heavy, clumpy shoes that everyone loves. When Phoebe Philo arrived at Cline in 2008, she seemed to tap straight into a style vein that so many women relate to. Unsurprisingly, the American designers hate the notion of copycatting, even more than their stereotype as successful sportswear designers.
However, commercially theyve had the last word, and over the past 40 years, the American market has been the primary powerhouse of the industry. Its changing now, though: China and other Far Eastern countries are becoming the leading players.
Nowhere is it clearer that we are in the last days of the American empire than in the fashion industry. Fabrics and designs are being tailored to the requirements of the Eastern market. The big brands are spending fortunes expanding there, and although many Middle Eastern women are hidden behind burkas, their wardrobes contain some of the most ravishing Western fashion.
  
 
 **September 19**
Last night was the London Fashion Week party I hosted with the \[US\] ambassador and his wife, Matthew and Brooke Barzun. It was heavenly, and I went to bed happy. I arrived at the neo\-Palladian Winfield House in Regents Park 15 minutes before kick\-off, to be prevented from entering by the massive security detail outside the gates, heightened because of John Kerrys stay.
But eventually I was led past the childrens skateboard slope the Barzuns had erected outside the front door, and into the house. Victoria Beckham arrived to the usual accompaniment of flashbulbs, but in terms of celeb power she was upstaged a few minutes later by John Kerry.
I imagine that he could have slipped in through a back door and headed to bed, or at least for a private drink upstairs, but he gamely confronted a heaving room of partying guests. Victoria was introduced to him almost immediately, and stayed talking to him for so long that I thought he might never meet anyone else, but he hung out at the party for well over the half\-hour I had been told he might be there.
  Hes so tall that eye contact is almost impossible if youre my height, and in a noisy room, ear contact is not that easy either. The social temperature of the room soared when news of his being here spread; he was the real stardust that transformed the party.
Later, I found Victoria on the terrace with her shoes kicked off. I asked her what she had talked to Kerry about. He said hed seen me at the UN, she answered, referring to a speech she had delivered earlier in the year, and he said, We gotta talk about Syria. Her look showed she found that suggestion as surprising as I did.
**November 10**
At dinner last night David \(Jenkins, Shulmans partner\) asked whether I knew that he liked endives. Endives? Yes, endives. You had them in the salad the other night. Are there any in this one? He poked around fruitlessly at the endive\-free plate. It reminded me of the newly married butler, Carson, finding fault with his poor wifes cooking at their marital dining table in Downton Abbey.
 Breakfast yesterday with Nicholas Coleridge, who runs the UK company. We both ordered mashed avocado with chilli flakes and lime, and poached eggs no toast. What have we come to? Are we simply fashion\-lifestyle victims?
Nicholas had a scribbled list of issues to talk to me about, which included the idea of an African Vogue supplement, and who I was planning to invite to the centenary dinner. George Osborne? Ed Vaizey? I answered that I was planning to ask Jeremy Corbyn, and Id see if Emily Sheffield, m[y deputy editor](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/what\-do\-you\-wear\-to\-a\-job\-interview\-at\-vogue\-four\-editors\-share/), could exert some influence on her brother\-in\-law, David Cameron. Theres only room for 300 guests and, given the number of big beasts in fashion, its going to be tricky to get the right balance for the guest list.
**January 3, 2016**
After 10 days break, I woke up this morning and went to the farmers market in the pouring rain. I stewed some apples with cinnamon, put on a stock to simmer, and wondered whether it would be possible to have a life of just reading all the books Ive now got piled up on the big table in the bedroom, and do very little work. I could run every day, make vegetable soups, let my hair go grey and And then what? Would I be content? David, who had just woken up, said that thousands of years of philosophers have pondered this same question.
**January 30**
Im 37,000ft above the ground and travelling at 560 miles per hour, or so it says on the map in front of me on this flight to Milan. Im also feeling thoroughly queasy, which is partly my flying anxiety and partly my total stupidity in waking up with a hangover from dinner last night.
David and I went to my friend Flora Frasers, and I was so gripped by the conversation between fellow guests Charles Saatchi and former Lib Dem cabinet minister [Chris Huhne](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/crime/11386970/Disgraced\-former\-cabinet\-minister\-Chris\-Huhne\-returns\-to\-Parliament.html) that I drank way too much wine. Charles, whether genuinely or simply to be controversial, described both Putin and Trump as magnificent, in his flat London accent.
 > "Victoria Beckham arrived to the usual accompaniment of flashbulbs, but she was upstaged by John Kerry"
 Chris is a passionate Europhile, and is looking extremely well in the aftermath of his jail experience. He didnt appear remotely rattled and was keen to hammer home his pro\-Europe stance. We left at the same time as Charles and his new girlfriend, Trinny Woodall.
Just before he left, as we stood in the hallway, he grabbed me and pulled me under one of the overhead spotlights and peered behind my ears. You havent changed, he said, explaining that he was checking to see whether Id had work done. Weird, undoubtedly.
  **February 4**
I must buy some new clothes. I have weeks of events and fashion shows coming up and nothing to wear. Clearly nothing is a relative term as I have two cupboards full of clothes, but nothing I have is new, and Im meant to look like somebody who has new clothes.
**February 17**
Last week ended well, so this week Im certain that something difficult will happen as a reproach to me for feeling too relaxed. Organising all the different strands of [the Centenary](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/understated\-glamour\-the\-duchess\-of\-cambridges\-first\-vogue\-cover/) is emotionally exhausting. One thing goes well; another veers into difficulties. Mario Testinos Decades shoot arrives and is luscious. But we still have the final Tim Walker portraits to nail: Tracey Emin has twice cancelled even as he arrived at her house.
 > "I wondered whether it would be possible to have a life of just reading all the books Ive now got piled up on the big table in the bedroom, and do very little work"
 Tim is getting a bit fed up. David Beckhams people want a number of different concepts to propose to David, if he is to agree to be included. I know that Tim wants to shoot him on a football pitch, kicking a crown into the air, which would be wonderful. But I have a feeling David might not think so. My fashion director, Lucinda \([Chambers](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/style\-lessons\-to\-learn\-from\-vogues\-lucinda\-chambers\-whatever\-you/)\), walks into my office saying she had a great meeting with \([David](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/david\-bailey\-jack\-nicholson\-turned\-me\-on\-to\-viagra\-very\-young/)\) Bailey about the [Ab Fab](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/events/everything\-we\-know\-about\-absolutely\-fabulous\-the\-movie/) shoot.
They havent worked together for many years, and I was worried about how they would get on. He told her he liked the energy of the unexpected and asked her why she hadnt had Botox. We have our monthly circulation meeting and start making plans for what we hope will be a high\-June centenary\-issue sale. The circulation team are projecting about a 25 per cent rise in year\-on\-year news\-stand sales, which is a big ask. I always feel maddened when I see someone reading Vogue at the hairdressers. Why dont you buy your own copy? I want to say, as I glower at them from my hideously unflattering gown.
The film crew have practically disappeared from the office and my staff keep asking me what I think [the documentary](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/alexa\-chung\-vogue\-documentary\-the\-future\-of\-fashion/) will be like. They are suspicious of director Richard Macers hapless approach and feel theyre being tricked in some way. I trust him about 70 per cent, but in the end I have no idea what will emerge. What on earth made me think it was a good idea to do it all those months back?
  **April 15**
Last night I took part in a discussion in the NPG theatre, focusing on changes in the fashion world since I first started my editorship. The audience asked good questions. One young woman had spotted that the [cover line](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/style/look\-back\-at\-100\-years\-of\-vogue\-covers\-as\-the\-magazine\-celebrate/) on my first issue, April 1992, had read, Do we still need feminism? and asked me if I considered myself a feminist.
I know I should unhesitatingly say yes. But, if Im honest, feminism is something I have rarely considered in a personal sense as opposed to the theoretical. If youve been brought up in a household of journalists, where it was always expected that as a woman you would work and be as successful as a man, it doesnt have the kind of emotional resonance it might for women coming from a different background or working in a different world.
But then, my father often shouted at me that no man would marry me if I didnt lose weight, or if I continued to argue so much. It didnt matter, though, since his love for me was never in doubt.
Last night, for the first time in years, I woke in the night and really wanted to see him walk through the door of the flat where we lived, put his trilby hat down on the hall table and come into the study where we ate dinner, with all the bustle and purpose and, it has to be said, self\-absorption he carried with him.
Id be able to smell the sweet scent of his skin that had always been the same from when we were tiny and crawled into our parents bed in the morning, and he would make a tent of the sheets with his legs in the air, which we could huddle under.
  
 
 **May 17**
I have my final dress fitting for the centenary dinner, and run into Erdems shop in South Audley Street with a variety of bras and knickers to try with it. The dress is hanging in the dressing room, a little like a child waiting to be collected from school.
I try it on with a pair of fine\-gauge Lycra cycling\-style knickers and a new bra, and it fits perfectly, though the shorts make me feel horrible. The lace embroidery now snakes across the sequins, and the boat neck is wide enough. Erdem stands back to survey his work and says, Its great. Really nipped and wicked, as he looks at me with those sloe eyes, adjusting the neckline to lie flat across my collarbone.
 > "I feel maddened when I see someone reading Vogue at the hairdressers. Why dont you buy your own copy? I want to say"
 He leaves the dressing room for a moment and I remove the shorts, which are clinging to my hips. I cant bear to wear such hideous underwear, even if it does give me a better shape. Standing in front of him in the shop we look at me again together in the mirror and he photographs me from the back and the front.
I ask him if he can see any difference from moments before, and he says perhaps the waistband is sitting a little better now the neckline is adjusted. I tell him about the removal of the shorts and hes polite enough to say that it looks better without, though I immediately feel Ive loaded him with too much information on the underpinnings of a 58\-year\-old woman.
   **June 11**
Yesterday Richard filmed me for the last time. He had wanted me to think of something that had some personal relevance, so I suggested we visit a huge old horse\-chestnut tree in Hyde Park, which I remembered playing under when I was very young.
After the filming he travelled with me in a car to the office and we joked a bit about this being the last time he would be filming me in a car. Then he leant forwards to fiddle with his camera and said, Theres something I want to tell you about the documentary. Kind of what were doing? Aha. Whats that? Well, you know I said I didnt want to use a voiceover narrator, that it was a bit tacky and overdone? Yes. I remember.
Id thought what a relief it would be not to have that clichd narrator. Well, weve had to change it a bit. And now, well, there is one. Or a kind of one. You know how usually theyre narrated by an actor? Well, we arent doing that. At this point I was becoming concerned by what he was about to say.
Um... Its going to be me. You know, not a huge amount of it. But its kind of about how a man who knows nothing about any of it goes into Vogue. My mind went into split screen one half thinking, Keep calm, theres nothing you can do about this and maybe itll be OK, the other thinking, Ive made a massive error here and this film is simply going to be incredibly trashy and simplistic. I couldnt believe Id allowed it to happen. Our one shot after so many years of refusing to let cameras into Vogue and Id blown it. This was now going to be a mocking Ladybird guide to the fashion world. What do you think? he asked.
  
 **June 23**
As I took my seat in a small room in Soho to view the documentary, the nerves took hold. Watching yourself in something like this is the most curious activity. I kept wondering what I was going to say, rather as if it hadnt been me sitting there, in far too many endless car shots staring crossly out of a rainy window.
Richard sitting behind me was still and serious as we watched his vision of Vogue for two hours. Through telling the story of a number of our shoots and the plans for the centenary issue, he certainly succeeded in getting across how much we all cared about what we did and, also, showed the hard work that goes into each issue.
Was it the film that I would love to have made about Vogue? No. I dont think it conveys how wide Vogue is nowadays, the influence it bears, the number of areas we are involved with, the fantastic journalism we include. Am I happy with how Im portrayed? Not particularly I seem very depressed through much of it, and prefer to think of myself as a funnier, lighter person than I seem on screen.
   I also dislike how I look most of the time, and cant understand why Im wearing the same blue top throughout most of the first programme. People will say, There she is, editor of Vogue and all. Youd think she could change her shirt.
Are there moments I really hate? Yes. The whole saga of the swapping of the Rihanna cover with the previous issue because of American Vogue jumping ahead of us is given a ludicrous weight, and when Richard says to camera that I rang threatening to pull the whole film if he talked to Anna Wintour about it, I felt misrepresented.
It was the one really devious thing he did. Of course, in the documentary when Anna is filmed she is hugely complimentary, which makes me look even sillier. I dont know what the rest of the office will think.
**[Inside Vogue: A Diary of My 100th Year](http://books.telegraph.co.uk/Product/Alexandra\-Shulman/Inside\-Vogue\-\-A\-Diary\-of\-My\-100th\-Year/19349052) \(Fig Tree, 16.99\), by Alexandra Shulman, out on October 26, will be available for 14.99 from the Telegraph Bookshop \(0844\-871 1514; [books.telegraph.co.uk](http://books.telegraph.co.uk/)\)**
    The jewellery trends seem to currently teeter between Scandi minimalism and more-is-more eclecticism. Rather than slavishly follow the latest ‘It’ looks, use trinkets to say something about yourself. Chambers has mismatching bracelets creeping up her left wrist and we imagine she’d tell a great yarn about each one were we to ask. Her crew-neck tops, knits and dresses are always punctuated with a round chunky chain or necklace. Not only do they spruce up plain garments, but they also frame the feminine part of the body. This is a simple, but an effective way to give shirts or t-shirts a dash of character. A small sleeve roll (don’t over do it) will add a casual element to whatever you’re wearing and highlight the slim lower arm area. Belts fastened around dresses can sometimes look a bit too done. A jacket or jumper, however, is a clever way of drawing in the waist while looking uncontrived. It adds a nonchalant, 'I’ve-just-thrown-it-on’ air, providing you don’t tie it too tightly. And - bonus! - you can wear it too. A bright cross-body strap breaks up plain ensembles and draws loose items of clothing in to flatter the figure. Don’t forget there are plenty of detachable straps around too if you want to jazz up your bag. It’s fine to wear all-black but why not throw the whole look off-kilter with a diverting white shoe? Chambers' bleached white-and-silver loafers make just enough of a statement.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  She has developed a reputation for mixing her favourite designer labels, including Carolina Herrera, Felipe Varela and Hugo Boss, with more affordable pieces from Zara, Mango and Uterque for engagements at home in Spain. But in London today, Spain's Queen Letizia blended her penchant for high street buys with a very diplomatic fashion statement.  For the last day of her state visit to the UK,  which included an official farewell to The Queen and Prince Phillip at Buckingham Palace followed by a tour of the Francis Crick  Institute, Letizia wore an ivory prom-style skirt by one of the UK's best-loved high street labels, Topshop. She teamed the pleated-waist design, which is now sold out but which was originally available for £80 (and then reduced to £30 in the summer sale), with a white wrap top with an asymetric neckline, a raffia clutch bag, a pair of pearl earrings loaned from her mother-in-law, Queen Sofia and burgundy suede heels by Spanish shoewear label Lodi.  Today's ensemble is exemplary of the elegantly grown-up style, with an occasional pep-up twist, which Letizia has made her signature. Since she began working with former Spanish Cosmopolitan fashion stylist Eva Fernandez in 2015, Letizia's already polished regal look has been elevated a notch or two; the addition of the decorative raffia clutch today was a case in point.  By turning to Topshop, Letizia did what many savvy stylish British women have known for years, looking beyond the denim hot pants and frilly crop tops to the store's impressive offering of sleek staples which would work just as well for a teen as their older sister, mum or even grandma. The midi skirt which Letizia chose today, for example, is shown online styled with trainers- perfect for the park maybe, but less so a palace. But simply add in her  heels and it becomes as sophisticated as the floral Carolina Herrera skirt which Letizia wore yesterday.  Queen Letizia isn't the first royal to recognise Topshop's arsenal of fashionable yet appropriate pieces. The Duchess of Cambridge injected a dash of  bohemian maximalism to her look during a tour to India last year when she wore a pale pink floral Topshop dress with black embroidery during a visit to the Indian village Pan Bari, where the royal couple fed baby elephants and rhinos. One of Kate's go-to maternity dresses-an empire-line, polka dot style- was also a Topshop buy.  Diplomatic dressing is a favoured sartorial tactic of many of the world's most high-profile women, who use their style choices to pay tribute to the places and countries they visit. Just yesterday, America's First Lady Melania Trump arrived in Paris wearing a red skirt suit by Christian Dior. Its silhouette echoed the Bar suit made famous by Mr Dior himself and celebrated the 70th anniversary of one of France's most prestigious luxury fashion houses.  On the first day of her visit to the UK, Queen Letizia offered up another tribute to the British fashion industry by wearing a claret trench coat by Burberry for a meeting with Prince Charles and the Duchess of Cornwall. Last night and on Wednesday evening though, it was all about displaying some of the Spanish royal family's most dazzling jewels as the Queen donned tiaras, necklaces, earrings and bracelets from her collection of precious treasures for banquets at Buckingham Palace and Guildhall.              © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Mark Twain’s maxim that there are no new ideas is particularly true of fashion. Designers can reinvent – and consumers rediscover – through a modern lens, but everything and everyone references something, even the future Queen of England. For the Duchess of Cambridge, finding a personal uniform that spans the Venn diagram of all her different personas is a tricky one. This week alone, she spent an afternoon as Mum-turned-Santa’s little helper in tartan at a Christmas party, an evening as poised and perfect Duchess in full regalia at a diplomatic reception, and a day as wife of the future King, showing her respect for the British armed forces.  For fashion designers, a catwalk show is the final climax following months of work and planning. Accordingly, they have become spectaculars costing millions of pounds (though the actual show usually lasts just 12 minutes) with designers competing for the most fantastic, the most elaborate, the most headline-worthy.   Richard Quinn, though, didn’t have an elaborate set built for his show during London Fashion Week in February, as Karl Lagerfeld so famously does at Chanel. He didn’t fly guests to a glamorous location (see Vuitton’s cruise show in Cannes this week), or begin his show with a breathtaking display of formation horsemanship (Dior, also in the South of France this week). But what Quinn did have was a V.V.V.I.P guest - Queen Elizabeth II. In an industry where celebrity sightings are the norm, Quinn’s royal spectator - who sat beside fashion royalty Anna Wintour - blew the rest out of the water. I meet Quinn, who was afforded his regal audience after winning the inaugural Queen Elizabeth II Design Award, in a slightly less regal setting - a railway arch in Peckham, ten down from the one that houses his dad’s scaffolding business. He’s transformed the space into a print works and design studio: the bold floral prints and metallic foil fabrics that graced his catwalk lose none of their impact set against the cement walls and with the sound of trains hurtling along overhead. Quinn’s next project builds on that dichotomy - from royalty to the high street, via a collaboration with Debenhams. The store is known for its designer partnerships, many of which continue for years - but for a fledgling designer who’s dressed Lady Gaga and Adwoa Aboah, it’s perhaps a surprising one. Instead of courting fashion’s ‘cool’ crowd, Quinn has his sights set on the mass market instead. Richard Quinn x Debenhams red coat, £130, blue dress, £125, yellow dress, £115  “Commercial isn’t a dirty word,” argues Quinn, “we’re not a vanity project. It’s a business as well.” Having studied fashion at the famous Central St Martins, he’s not oblivious to the many talented designers who prioritise ‘cool’ over ‘commercial’ - only to shutter their doors when they run out of money. As for those who might turn their nose up at a high street pairing? “That’s their hangup, it’s really not mine.”   This collaboration with Debenhams follows pairings with H&M and Liberty - despite the different markets, Quinn hasn’t struggled to maintain a brand identity - instead, he sees the benefits of association with these household names. “It’s an amazing opportunity to have something you’ve made in a vast range of sizes in so many stores, and online, and to reach a huge range of customers.” In the past month, Quinn’s bespoke designs have been worn by Amal Clooney at the Met Gala and Thandie Newton at the BAFTAs - and now, “a 15 year old who wants to go to prom” can wear his creations, too. Not that you should rule them out at any age - the floral party coat would work well for weddings or summer garden parties, and the lovely long-sleeved dress with A-line skirt looks sure to flatter. Quinn’s mother has been “dropping hints”, and Clooney’s mother, who accompanied her on a fitting, was equally enamoured. Making his brand - which prices dresses at around £2k - accessible to Debenhams’ customers is something that strikes a chord with Quinn. “There was a Debenhams on our high street growing up. I have memories going down Eltham high street with my mum and into Debenhams - there was a tea room where we had lunch.” Richard Quinn x Debenhams pink dress, £79, black dress, £85, navy dress, £125 That store shut its doors a few months ago, one of multiple closures across the high-street as a whole - just last week, Debenhams’ competitor Marks & Spencer announced plans to close 100 stores. Heritage names are struggling to compete with fast-fashion giants like Zara and Mango, and the booming online fashion market and the e-tail-only brands dominating it. As they strive to win shoppers back, any point of difference that could help to swing the balance - even a little - is worth championing. Quinn’s signature 1950s silhouettes and bold prints have been widely copied on the high street, but Debenhams - and Quinn - are ahead of the curve.  Many a designer's dream is to get their clothes on the back of a woman whose image will be beamed around the world. It's publicity which money can't buy. Well, you can buy it up to a certain level of the ladder, but there's a rung above that which forces a reliance upon careful relationship building and hefty doses of luck.  So it's been a brilliant week for Dior and Roland Mouret. On Tuesday, the Duchess of Sussex rocked up to Westminster Abbey in a chic nipped-waist navy dress by Dior.  Woody Allen has a habit of creating magical on-screen fashion moments, from Annie Hall in her Ralph Lauren tie to Cate Blanchett in her white tweed Chanel jacket in Blue Jasmine. His latest release, Cafe Society, might have had a mixed reaction from critics, but one thing is for sure: the costumes are as stylish and spot-on as in any vintage Woody film.  Set in the 1930s, Café Society follows 20-something Bobby Dorfman who moves from New York to Los Angeles and then back to New York to become the manager of a nightclub frequented by the fashionable and well-connected 'café society.' On screen, this translates into club scenes where women wear millions of pounds worth of diamonds, priceless Chanel originals and dresses made with flecks of real silver. This is a world where even the extras look like they have stepped out of a vintage Vogue editorial in spectacular couture.  Clothes function almost as their own character in Woody Allen films, and no-one understands this more than his long-time costume designer Suzy Benzinger who has now worked on six of his films, including Blue Jasmine. On the eve of Cafe Society's release, Benzinger tells The Telegraph about Woody's understanding of fashion, being given the sacred keys to the Chanel archive and how Hollywood studios dictated taste at the time... The silver gown that Blake Lively wears in a New York party scene were she meets Bobby for the first time was actually made from an original fabric made with real silver. "Over the years I collect fabric and keep it in case we need something for a film," explains Benzinger. "That silver metallic gown is made from Lamé. Lamé  now is a little flimsy, but I had the real thing, the silver fabric that tarnishes so you have to paint it because it has real silver in it. I had thought ‘who can wear a dress like this and carry it off?’, but when we put it on her body it was like ‘forget it, like I’ve saved it for her alone.’" Benzinger didn't just create her own costumes, but worked with Parisian Couture houses including Vionnet, Schiaparelli and, most significantly, Chanel. Working with these designers was essential, as she notes that this period was "the beginning of putting names in fashion."  "Chanel was so helpful to me, because we don’t have the money to afford real jewellery in the film. So Chanel sent millions of dollars worth of jewellery and 15 bodyguards  for the club scene for  Blake and Kristen," explains Benzinger.  "I went to Paris and went through their archive to pull looks for Kristen.  It is the most wonderful history lesson on the face of the earth. It  wasn’t that Kristen worked for Chanel, but in my research Chanel popped up all the time in  Vogue  even though they didn't have a shop in New York yet." "I didn’t use the original pieces but copied them," says Benzinger. "The archival pieces are laid out in climate controlled drawers so I picked things that would be good for Kristen and then Chanel copied them in the Atelier. They close in August and I was there in July and so they only had one week to make all these gowns and - they do know Kristen's size - but they were perfect." "They made two evening dresses and the little pants with buttons she wears to the beach are copied from a 1930s Chanel design." At the beginning of the film Stewart's character has no money, but she is still outfitted by Chanel: "The little white shorts she wears in the film are also Chanel. I said to them ‘guys she is really poor here’ and she wouldn't have Chanel, so they made a few adjustments to make them look a little less chic which is hard for them I tell you. But they were totally based on one of their original designs." "Chanel never say no to Woody," adds Benzinger. "They are so generous and kind. The funny thing with Woody and the fashion industry is they get him, these designers are designing four times a year and when you are working with Woody you work all the time and never leave the building - and that’s how Karl works too. Karl is the real deal and there till 12pm with sketches and swatches, and Woody is like that. He is a workaholic - he writes, edits, directs, scores and does everything. People in fashion understand that - everything is wonderful and beautiful but it takes a lot of time to get there." "It is on Karl’s say so we get all this stuff done," she adds. "Of course I’ve met him, talked to him, thanked him, and he’s been so generous, he’s a wonderful wonderful man, but he’s busy I don’t think he has time to chat about Woody Allen films with me!" Blake Lively's character Veronica's glamorous New York wardrobe is based on the designs of Carolina Herrera. "When we try to incorporate contemporary design into these films I try to find the equivalent for the people for now who it would have been then and for Blake it was Carolina Herrera," explains Benzinger. "For us New Yorkers she has that elegant, beautiful, timeless quality and with Blake I wanted to use Carolina as much as I could as I wanted that feeling. I shouldn’t say I copied Carolina, but I was very heavily influenced by her - I tried to put Carolina Herrera’s head in my head for Blake." The script is divided between the high societies in Hollywood and New York, showing a clear divide between how women dressed in these American cities. "The women in Hollywood dressed for fantasy and dressed like no women dressed anyplace else," explains Benzinger. "It was all about image and they did things that were not real for California. The starlets would dress up at the studios before going to premieres and things, and the studios would give them furs to wear in California in the summer time. All the stars wore furs, with orchids in the furs and all this other nonsense and they did it for image to show the rest of the world what Hollywood was, and if you weren’t in Hollywood you didn’t know that it was actually 95 degrees. The images were so controlled; the women didn't look uncomfortable and the satin gowns weren't wrinkled."  This is in stark contrast to how women dressed in New York, where they were guided by the fashion houses in Paris rather than studio heads. "When we get to New York, we show more of a reality," explains Benzinger. "The women in the New York clubs at the time were influenced by European design. I laughed at all these pictures from Hollywood of Marlene Dietrich in her huge furs - it was the Hollywood fantasy that still continues today of course." Considering the costumes are central to all Woody Allen productions you might expect that actresses would be heavily involved in the process, but Benzinger reveals they follow Wood's lead. "This is a tribute to all the girls on these Woody Allen films, pretty much without exception when they come to Woody films because they want to tell the story," she explains. "They want to do whatever Woody wants, with their head open and ready to go. It’s hard because Woody works extremely fast and you do a lot of gripping scenes in one day, so they are much much more concerned with the scripts and can they deliver the acting part. Blake was like ‘whatever you want to put on me, put on me.’ The Woody hours are insane - you’re on set at 5 o'clock in the morning and it’s tough" As for Allen's own involvement in the clothes, she says: "He is very attuned to fashion and knows what looks good and doesn’t. I have gotten over the years letters from agents saying 'she would prefer to wear this, she is a spokesperson for that, and she loves wearing Dolce & Gabbana and I think ‘Ok but a school teacher wouldn’t be wearing Dolce & Gabbana,’ But Woody Allen casts actresses who want to tell the story."  Politics aficionados will be well aware that Theresa May is facing the biggest challenge of her Prime Ministership so far this week as she attends the G20 summit in Huangzhou, China. As the first big meeting of world leaders since the Brexit vote, May's task is to execute a faultless diplomatic mission to show that the United Kingdom has a clear direction, steady leadership and is ready to play its role on the world stage as it leaves the EU. While we would never suggest that such a monumental task could be achieved through one simple wardrobe choice, May's decision to don a red suit to arrive at the meeting on Sunday is nevertheless laden with meaning.  The vivid, almost-orange hue of May's jacket and dress chimes with the colour which is traditionally used in Chinese culture to symbolise luck, vitality and happiness. During Chinese New Year celebrations, red lanterns line the streets, gifts of money are given in red envelopes and brands create special edition red versions of their most important designs to appeal to those buying gifts.  China's communist party also use red as their most prevalent identifying shade, meaning May's suit was politically, as well as culturally, flattering. By arriving in red, May was able to offer a not-so-subtle sign of respect to the hosts before she had exchanged even a single word with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Clever. Amongst a sea of politicians in grey and navy suits, May also ensured that she stood out. However she was not the only world leader present to exercise a little sartorial diplomacy; South Korea's President Park Geun-Hye also met her Chinese counterpart wearing a deep red jacket with mandarin collar.  There are also plenty of examples of politicians and royalty paying tribute to the sacred symbolism of red in Chinese tradition as a way to signify their consideration and respect for the Chinese officials they are meeting.  When Hillary Clinton met Chinese Foreign Minister Yang Jiech in January 2011 at the White House, she opted for a bold red jacket to welcome her visitor as they signed a memorandum of agreement between their two governments during President Hu Jintao's state visit to the US. In the same week, Michelle Obama nodded to China's national colour with the red Alexander McQueen gown she chose for the state dinner. Three years later, Obama visited Beijing as a guest of the new President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan ​and was pictured in an elegant Naeem Khan red design- daughter Sasha even joined in with the respectful dress code in a red dress of her own.  Meanwhile, The Duchess of Cambridge- who has shown an excellent command of the intricacies of diplomatic dressing- pulled off a particularly glamorous tribute to Chinese culture when she wore a bright red Jenny Packham gown for a state banquet in honour of President Xi Jinping at Buckingham Palace last year.  Given the G20 is Theresa May's first international summit as Prime Minister, could her careful style choice be a sign that she will be employing her well-documented love of fashion for political purposes?                 © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Since her husband's Inauguration in January, Melania Trump has maintained a relatively low public profile, appearing on just a clutch of key occasions. But this week has been a busy one for the First Lady. Kicking off with the release of her official White House portrait - which sparked controversy thanks to her decision to wear Dolce and Gabbana, rather than an American designer - and continuing with her taking part in the politically and sartorially high level visits of the King and Queen of Jordan, and now the Chinese President and his wife.  All these public appearances mean that the First Lady's fashion strategy is becoming ever clearer, and no look has epitomised her approach better than the £3000 Valentino red dress which she chose for last night's dinner with  President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan, who is known for her elegantly ladylike look.  Mrs Trump has been wearing a lot of Republican red, so as to perfectly co-ordinate with her husband's regular choice of tie. But the bold hue was yesterday reframed with a flatteringly diplomatic meaning; red is China's favourite colour, featuring on the flag and used to exemplify luck and happiness.  But while Melania's dress offered an outwardly on-message look, it also exemplified her defiance in continuing to wear the international designers which are her natural territory. The midi-length, daisy-embellished dress is a ready-to-wear look which Trump likely purchased in store or online rather than working directly with the Italian label.  The anatomy of the First Lady's Chinese visit look recalls the gown which Michelle Obama opted to wear for the state banquet during the visit of then-President Hu Jintao in 2011. Obama's decision to wear a dress by Alexander McQueen, rather than a US or Chinese designer, caused outcry among veteran American designers.  'My understanding is that the visit was to promote American-Chinese trade. American products in China and Chinese products in America. Why do you wear European clothes?' said Oscar de la Renta. Meanwhile, Diane Von Furstenberg said: 'Our First Lady Michelle Obama has been wonderful at promoting our designers, so we were surprised and a little disappointed not to be represented for this major state dinner.' So far, Melania Trump has received little criticism for choosing Alexander McQueen, Karl Lagerfeld and Givenchy over American labels for some key moments (although Michael Kors, Ralph Lauren and Calvin Klein have been worn). Perhaps that's because many in the industry are anti-Trump and have expressed their reluctance to work with the President's wife.  ‘I have no interest whatsoever in dressing Melania Trump,’ Marc Jacobs told WWD after the election. ‘Personally, I’d rather put my energy into helping out those who will be hurt by [Donald] Trump and his supporters.’ ‘I was asked to dress [Melania Trump] quite a few years ago and I declined,’ added Tom Ford. ‘She’s not necessarily my image.’ Meanwhile, Peng Liyuan represented a modern, sophisticated spin on the Chinese cheongsam in a midi version of the classic style decorated with a delicate floral print. In contrast to Mrs Trump's glossy international tastes, the 54 year-old First Lady tends to patronise under-the-radar Chinese designers such  as Ma Ke or Jihong Mae who are renowned for their exquisite craftsmanship.  'Ms Peng’s style restores the allure of femininity and she is utilizing it as a powerful tool to improve China’s image to the outside world,' Shaway Yeh, editorial director of China's Modern Media publishing group told The Telegraph in 2015. 'Inside China, her confidence and ability to hold herself in international society is a boost to national confidence. Her style is more about elegance than beauty or glamour. Elegance is the ideal for Chinese women from the cultural class. On top of that, she is a star in her own right - that has never been seen before in a politician’s spouse.'                   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
