 Gigi Hadid is one of the most in-demand supermodels in the world at the moment, so it's perhaps little surprise that she was chosen as the cover star of the launch issue of a new edition of Vogue.  However, since the image of  the elder Hadid sister gracing the cover of the inaugural Vogue Arabia was released yesterday, controversy has ensued.  On the cover- which was shot by iconic photography duo Inez and Vinoodh- Hadid wears a custom-made jewelled veil and is styled by Lady Gaga's friend and stylist, Brandon Maxwell.  It's a powerful image which is at once glamorously high-fashion, whilst also nodding to the modest dress codes which many of the magazine's readers will abide by.  While Hadid might seem like an obvious choice from a pure fame point of view, there's a subtler reason why Vogue Arabia's editor, Deena Aljuhani Abdulaziz, might have chosen her to set the tone for the newly introduced publication which is using 'reorienting perceptions' as its cover line; Hadid's father is Mohamed Hadid, a Jordanian-American businessman, born in Nazareth with Palestinian origins. As such Hadid has very personal ties to the region. "I think the beautiful thing about there being international Vogue's is that, as a fashion community, we are able to celebrate, and share with the world, different cultures," Gigi wrote on her Instagram page. "Being half-Palestinian, it means the world to me to be on the first-ever cover(s) of @voguearabia, and I hope that this magazine will show another layer of the fashion industry's desire to continue to accept, celebrate, and incorporate all people & customs and make everyone feel like they have fashion images and moments they can relate to... & learn and grow in doing so." Her reasonings are heartfelt and chime with Abdulaziz's argument that Vogue Arabia is an opportunity for the world to see the Middle East in a different way. “Vogue Arabia is a magazine with the authority and insight needed to capture the creativity of a distinctive, evolving, and often misrepresented part of the world,” Abdulaziz says. “The collage of countries across the Arab world are long-deserving of a place in fashion history and there’s no better first ‘face’ to lead the charge for Vogue Arabia than Gigi — a model who defines tomorrow’s entrepreneurial and dynamic generation.” Many have been supportive of Hadid's cover. "People she is one of us she has every right to embrace our culture.... she is just as much of a Arab as the other Arab models... at least she ain't ashamed of it," wrote one Instagram user. "I am so proud of you! I know this means a lot to you and your Arab fans!" added another fan on Twitter.  But many were upset by what they  interpreted as  a western, non-Muslim model appropriating the cultural practices of the Middle East. "She can't just randomly wear it like its a piece of clothing every one can wear. It's not fashion," said one Instagram commenter, referring to the hijab shown both on the magazine's cover and in the shoot inside.  "If you were really a muslim you wouldn't be able to do half the things u do now, so please don't appropriate the hijab again," another wrote. Others expressed anger that Hadid rarely refers to her heritage or speaks out on Palestinian issues. "You're only Palestinian when it suits you and when it means you get a vogue cover," was one such observation. Meanwhile, some of the criticisms weren't targetted directly at Hadid, but did question whether this was a missed opportunity for Abdulaziz to anoint a new star in her first issue: "How come no Arabic star or model was used for the cover?" With Islam's modest dress codes a topic of near constant debate, Hadid's cover is likely to be the first of many  conversations which Vogue Arabia's fashion editorials will prompt.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Alexa Chung has a habit of making people shop, whether she's persuading us to invest in her eponymous Mulberry bag or even a plain navy jumper. Now she is bringing her stock-shifting  power to M&S, curating her own collection called Archive by Alexa which will be released in April.  The collection includes 31 pieces of  ready-to-wear, all of which are Alexa reimagining looks from the M&S archive. "It was so fun to be given the keys to the M&S archive and such a treat to get to cherry pick the very best of their vast collection of pieces,"  she told Vogue of the collaboration. "I pulled from stored garments, in-house magazines and TV adverts from various points in the history of Marks & Spencer to create the collection that I believe looks every bit as relevant today as it did then." Pictures show her rifling through slip dresses and studying that Chung classic, the loafer. The high street giant has been struggling sales-wise for a number of years. M&S reported miserable Christmas results for general merchandise sales, including its clothing, which was down by over five per cent for the 13 weeks over the 2015 festive period, prompting the current M&S chief Marc Bolland to resign. The new chief executive Steve Rowe promised to deliver more of the much-talked-about one-off fashion hits, such as a  pink wool coat in the winter of 2014 that won so much press attention it became known as ‘That Pink Coat’. At 32, Chung is seemingly a great fit for the brand, her style combines a grown up elegance with fashion kudos and authority which should appeal to lost customers in need of style classics.  “Alexa Chung has always been a champion of the British high street," Earl explains. "And her style is internationally recognised so it has been hugely insightful collaborating with her on this unique and exciting project.” Chung was instrumental at popularising the 1970s-inspired tan suede skirt when she was pictured wearing it. The skirt went on to be credited as one of the reasons behind M&S's first profit rise in four years. And the Alexa effect hasn't just hit M&S. In 2010 Mulberry's profits soared by 79 per cent thanks to the 'Alexa' bag, and six years later the denim skirt she designed for AG Jeans sold out almost instantly. Other celebrity collections at Marks and Spencer have also worked; Rosie Huntington Whiteley's lingerie collection sold three times over its expectations when it launched in 2012.  All of which means Alexa Chung's Archive collection is being greeted as welcome news by fashion insiders who have a long-held affection for M&S - despite its recent troubles. "I think it's a brilliant idea," says Lisa Armstrong, fashion director at The Daily Telegraph. "Getting Chung to pick 31 pieces from the archives gives it credibility. Whether it's true or not, people believe M&S was so much better in the past."  This week marks the 21st anniversary of Clueless and, to use Cher Horowitz' catch phrase, 'As If!' we were going to let that date pass us by unnoticed.  From Cher's Alaia to Dionne's black and white hat, the costumes are like an extra character in the film; Cher Horowitz had a staggering 60 costume changes during filming. "Amy [Heckerling, the director] wanted Clueless to be different," costume designer Mona May explained to The Telegraph last year. "When the movie was made, there wasn’t a lot of high fashion. Grunge was in. We went to high schools all over LA to do scouting, and everyone wearing ripped jeans and baggy clothes." via GIPHY "There were just racks and racks of clothes," Stacey Dash who played Dionne remembers. "We did fittings for a whole week, that is so rare for a film. Usually you do two days, and we did seven, 10 hours a day of fitting. That’s how many clothes we went through, racks and racks and racks. Then Amy just designed things specifically for us, too." "I think the groundbreaking thing was how Clueless changed the way girls dressed. The movie came out and flipped the nation in a sense, every girl had to wear the over-the-knee stockings," May recalled. It might be 21 years since we first met Cher Horowitz and her pink fluffy pen, but if you look closely at this summer's trends, it seems the Beverly Hills teenager and her circle are still just as influential now. These are the trends from Clueless that are still making an impact in 2016... The most iconic look in the film is Cher and Dionne's matching plaid - the origins of the 'twinning' street style phenomenon, perhaps? Mona May said of the look: "When Alicia put on that yellow suit, it was like, “Oh my god. Here it is: this little girl who rules the high school, who dresses perfectly, and has this little ensemble that nobody had ever seen before. Wow, here she is.” The plaid suit paired with over-the-knee socks and a buttoned up cardigan is a look to be saved for fancy dress, but there are a couple of styling tricks to employ from Cher's look. First lesson, if you are planning on running a high school, it helps to have a uniform. But more seriously, Cher's buttercup yellow is the colour of the season. This sunny shade isn't just a difficult-to-copy runway trend, as Net-A-Porter has noted a 100 % increase in sales of yellow products from May to June. And checks were also all over the catwalks for AW16, with plaids, ginghams, tartans and Prince of Wales checks spotted at the shows.  Miu Miu, check mini skirt, £505; Gucci, pleated mini skirt, £645;  Gucci, ruffled shirt, £725; Topshop, Karter loafer, £62 Whistles is also championing Cher-esque plaids next season, with yellow check shift dresses and flares in their September AW16 drop.  Slip dresses were the key to Cher Horowitz' after-school wardrobe, including both white and red spaghetti-strap 90s slips. Her Calvin Klein white slip dress is perhaps the most iconic look of the film, as it led to this dialogue with her Dad: "Cher, what are you wearing?" "A dress!" "Says who?" "Calvin Klein!" Slip dresses are big news this season, and its still Calvin Klein making the best version of Cher's favourite dress. To make this a little more 2016, layer over a white basic t shirt - a trick which has been deployed by the street style set. Cher layered a spaghetti strap cami over a white t shirt for gym class, so this is a twist on her signature look she would certainly approve of.  Calvin Klein Collection, slip dress, £815; Topshop, black slip dress, £29;  Topshop, soft-washed white tee, £12 Dionne was all about accessories, wearing statement hats, flower pins and socks, meaning that if Clueless was made in 2016 she would most definitely be first in line for Alessandro Michele for Gucci's eccentric brooches and colourful berets.  & Other Stories, shiny ribbed socks, £7; Gucci, striped beret, £170; Gucci, floral brooch, £190 While you might not think of Ms Geist as a "total Betty", after her style-over by Cher she is actually rather 2016. Her Mansur Gavriel-esque block heels, silk neck scarf and V-neck jumper are all items you'll see in the shops now and over the next few months. At @TheGAcademy The Duke and Duchess and Prince Harry find out how students are developing their skillset for careers in broadcasting pic.twitter.com/MC10WiFHv8 Renowned for minimalist yet precise tailoring and elegant silhouettes, Armani is a label which it makes sense for Kate to add to her ever-increasing wardrobe for public duties. The house was founded by Giorgio Armani in 1975 and is now a multi-billion pound empire comprising several different sub-collections. Armani Collezioni is a diffusion of the main catwalk collection, offering similarly sleek pieces at lower prices.  The Duchess owns one other item from the Italian design house- a red coat which she first wore to Prince William's Sandhurst passing out parade in 2006 and which she wore once again during a visit to Scotland in 2013.  "I wanted my outfits to spark their awareness of the fact that they are the protagonists of a fast-moving society. Creating fashion does not just mean creating clothes – fashion is also a workshop in which attitudes are experimented with and new perspectives adapted," Mr Armani wrote in an autobiography published in 2015.  Over the past four months, Kate has chosen skirt suit six times for various engagements. She debuted a purple jacket and prom-style skirt by Oscar de la Renta for the Guild of Health Writers conference in February and an emerald green tweed look by Hobbs for a hospice visit in January.  Those who covet the wardrobes of Alexa Chung, Kate Moss and Gisele (and let's face it, who doesn't?) will be buzzing with excitement to hear that today marks the launch of supermodel and philanthropist Toni Garrn's charity supermodel sale. ''I’m super excited to take the physical sales to new cities this year.'' What gems can we expect to find being auctioned off in the supermodel sale? Highlights include a fabulous Gucci suit donated by Issa, a vintage denim jacket courtesy of Moss and Stella McCartney's signature star print platforms pilfered from Bailey.  And as well as the donated items, which have been divvied up between the online auction and the three cities, Garrn has also teamed up with designer Bella Freud, known for her quirky slogan knits, on three different grey and white t-shirts featuring the words 'Girl Empowerment,' 100% of the profits of which will also go straight to the Toni Garrn foundation.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  As The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge embark on their week-long tour of Canada, they continue a long tradition of royal tours to the Commonwealth nation. Over the years, The Queen, Princess Diana and even Kate herself have visited Canada multiple times - the country was the first one The Duchess visited with William following their marriage in 2011 - meaning there have been plenty of royal fashion moments. Here, we look back at some of the most memorable. When one is visiting the cold climes of Tuktoyaktuk in the Northwest Territories, it is only sensible to take tips from the locals when it comes to keeping warm. When The Queen, The Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Charles and Princess Anne made a stop in the village during their Canadian tour of 1970, they donned traditional Eskimo parka coats with patch pockets and fur trims. The royals added their own distinctly British style details to their look though; note Anne’s houndstooth trousers and The Queen’s beloved headscarf. It’s not often that you see the royals in fancy dress but Prince Charles and Princess Diana were excellent sports in 1983, donning full period costume for a historical reenactment barbeque in Edmonton. Diana's dress took some careful planning. Months before the trip, she enlisted the services of costume designer John Bright, who went on win Oscars for his work on A Room with A View and Sense and sSnsibility. He sent a selection of options to Kensington Palace and Diana handpicked this pale pink, ruched design.  The dress came with a back story; it had first been worn by the actress Francesca Annis when she played the role of Lillie Langtry in the Lillie TV series in 1978. Langtry had been the mistress of Prince Charles's great-great-grandfather, Edward VII.  Literal dressing - whites for Wimbledon, nautical for anything seaside related - has become a cornerstone of the Duchess of Cambridge’s fashion modus operandi.  One of the first (and most brilliant) examples of this came when she opted for a bespoke red maple leaf hat by Sylvia Fletcher of Lock & co. during the Canada Day celebrations which she and William took part in during their first ever tour tour together in July 2011, shortly after their wedding.  During the same tour, the Duchess also often pinned the 11-point maple leaf brooch to her outfits. The brooch was first worn by The Queen’s mother during her tour of Canada in 1939 and has been a regular feature of royal Canada tour wardrobes ever since. During a visit to Vancouver in 1986, Princess Diana attended a gala entertainment evening where Canadian Bryan Adams - who had written a song about the Princess - was among the guests she met. In keeping with the night’s relaxed feel, Diana swapped her usual taffeta gowns in favour of a black tuxedo jacket with button embellished jodhpurs by Jasper Conran which she wore with a frilled shirt and a Butler and Wilson snake brooch. It was a proper “I’m with the band” look.  When Norman Hartnell created the gown to be worn by The Queen at her coronation, he was conscious that it not only had to be beautiful, but layered with meaning. “Hartnell realised that the dress would be under international scrutiny so I think that weighed very heavily on his mind,” Caroline de Guitaut, curator of the Fashioning a Reign exhibitions which celebrate 90 years of The Queen’s wardrobe, told The Telegraph earlier this year.  And so it was that alongside wheat sheaves for Pakistan and lotus flowers for South Africa, the gown was embroidered with maple leaves as a nod to Canada’s vital role in the Commonwealth. Unlike a wedding dress, which tends to be worn only once for the Big Day, Queen Elizabeth’s coronation gown traveled the world with her in the years following the ceremony. In 1957, she finally wore it on Canadian soil for the opening of parliament in Ottawa. Another standout moment from the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge’s 2011 tour to Canada was their trip to the Calgary rodeo. The Duchess entered into the spirit of the occasion in her stetson, Alice Temperley frilled blouse, jeans and authentic cowboy boots. With William’s co-ordinating get-up, including a checked shirt, the couple made a very convincing cowboy and cowgirl.  Princess Diana mastered the art of diplomatic flattery via her fashion choices, and there are plenty of examples of her choosing red and white whilst in Canada in a nod to the colours of the country's flag. But the best is surely the red dress Diana wore in 1983 - complete with a maple-leaf collar...   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Actress Jessica Alba has created a billion-dollar beauty empire with the Honest Company, but now she is tackling one of the trickiest areas of women's wardrobes: jeans. This month sees the launch of Alba's first ever designer capsule collection with New York denim brand DL1961, which claims to give a 'contoured' denim look.  If you see any paparazzi pictures of Alba from the last decade, chances are she is wearing a pair of jeans as they are the core of her wardrobe, with her owning more than 20 pairs. "Jessica has the ultimate feminine shape, and she works day and night on it. But when we met her she was like there's so much denim out there and I'm such a girly girl and yet we're always complaining about jeans," says Sarah Ahmed, the Creative Director of DL1961, of why the pair decided to work together. "The way our fabric is engineered it sucks you in, and contours you and gives you that power sculpted look and she's a business woman so, lights went off."  As for how they claim to 'contour' the body, Ahmed explains: "The fabric is revolutionary as we weave it ourselves and is a tight weave. In addition, everything from the pocket placement to how we tighten and lift it at different points in the butt or the waist, is designed to sculpt your body. But you don't need to be a certain size or shape to have the benefits of it." Instead of just creating a fit that'll work for the Jessica Albas of this world, the 18 different styles in the collection all aim to flatter a number of body types. During the design process she did the fittings on four different women to try and create one pair that flatters all. "We have 65 women in this office and we made sure we tried the jeans on women with different body types. We saw across the board there was consistency in our aim," says Ahmed.  There are a number of different styles, including classic straight cut jeans, flares, rolled up boyfriends, ripped-up black jeans and leather-effect rocker trousers.   Here Sarah Ahmed explains her four hero styles from the collection: No.2 Ankle high rise -£180: "It is these dark muted washes and colours, and this olive green colour and dark grey." No.6: The boyfriend - £196: "It is a very tapered, slight drop crotch, fitted at the ankle, so is a very versatile cut." No.7: The jumpsuit - £294: "I was travelling for three weeks and every plane ride I wore that jumpsuit and it was the most comfortable thing, but is still very stylish." No.5: Flare - £196: "Jessica called this the power flare for her power meetings - she said 'I need to wear it when I know I have an event afterwards, and wear a nice top with it or a blazer, and it gives you a very sleek, contoured look'."  It’s no secret that human rights lawyer Amal Clooney has become something of a workwear style icon in recent years. What is only just becoming apparent is her love of vintage fashion, however. Case in point #1: Clooney arrived at the Cannes Film Festival, to promote husband George Clooney’s latest film Money Monster, wearing a bubble hem skirt. Yes, the 38-year-old dared to wear the voluminous round hem, a divisive  silhouette beloved of Princess Diana and Madonna in the Eighties. Thankfully this ode to the naff prom fashion ended there and Amal looked back to the Sixties for her next vintage foray. Case in point #2: Holidaying in Rome with George this weekend, Amal modelled two outfits that would not have looked out of place on Sixties style icons Audrey Hepburn, Jean Shrimpton and Jane Birkin. For the couple’s meeting with the Pope, whereby her actor husband was presented with the humanitarian award, Amal wore a black lace Versace dress with turban style wrap hat. Had the dress been made from colourful, swirling satin, Amal’s look could have been an ode to Biba, the British label that epitomised Sixties fashion, and often included turbans to offset its zany prints. Stepping out of their Rome hotel on Monday, Amal swapped her turban for another swinging Sixties staple: a thigh-skimming dress coat. The gold brocade confection featured a neat round-neck collar, elegant gold buttons and a three-quarter sleeve. And this is where confirmation came of Clooney's faithful ode to the 60s; the coat was not a modern reinterpretation of a classic style but an early 1960s original design by legendary couturier Cristobal Balenciaga which Clooney sourced from London vintage store, William Vintage. It's not the first time she has turned to vintage expert William Banks-Blaney. Back in February, Clooney chose a 1981 Yves Saint Laurent gown for an appearence on the red carpet at  the Berlinale International film festival.  She offset her cover-up with a block-heel suede court shoe, with a heel height also reminiscent of the elegant style of the decade. Dangling from her hand, meanwhile, was a hat box, presumably housing the aforementioned turban.  “Undeniably, one of the biggest advantages to working on Cleopatra in Rome was Bulgari’s nice little shop" Elizabeth wrote in her memoir My Love Affair With Jewellery. "I used to visit Gianni Bulgari in the afternoons and we’d sit in what he called the ‘money room’ and swap stories” she continued. Elizabeth Taylor is famed not jut for her acting prowess, but also for her diamond addiction. The actress owned one of the most beautiful - and expensive - jewellery collections in the world. Following her death in 2011, Taylor's jewellery, wardrobe and other personal items were auctioned at Christie's in New York. The sale smashed records, drawing bidders from around the world and fetching over $100 million. It was the most expensive jewellery auction in the house's history, with 26 of the lots selling for over $1 million. This week, some of Taylor's most treasured pieces have been gathered together once again by Bulgari. The rare and highly personal jewels are worth a cool $30 million between them. The spectacular- and highly meaningful- items are on display at Bulgari's New Bond Street London flagship until this weekend. It was down to Lucia Boscaini, Bulgari's Brand and Heritage curator, to bring the collection together and here she shares the stories behind a number of the pieces in the collection... On display in the exhibition is an emerald engagement ring with a 7.4 carat square emerald surrounded by 12 diamonds, totalling 5.3 carats. Richard Burton gave this to Elizabeth Taylor during the filming of Cleopatra in 1962. "This ring was already in the store," Boscaini says. "At that time the couple used to come to the store often, as they preferred to go places where they could be in privacy for a while. Being friends of the Bulgari brothers, they used to come often as they were able to be in a sort of private room only for them." There are a number of gifts from Richard Burton in the exhibition, including an emerald and diamond Bulgari necklace which was given to Taylor as a wedding gift in 1964. The pendant on the necklace was a brooch that Burton had given the actress as an engagement present two years earlier. Taylor wore this necklace to accept her Academy Award in 1966. "Richard was so romantic that he'd use any excuse to give me a piece of jewelry," Elizabeth Taylor wrote of his presents. "He'd give me 'It's a beautiful day' presents or 'Let's go for a walk' presents. Over the years I've come to think of these as my 'It's Tuesday, I love you' jewellery."  "Burton gave Taylor the sugar loaf sapphire for her 40th birthday," Boscaini explains. "He wanted to have this special stone - it's an intense blue with a touch of violet which looks like Elizabeth Taylor's eyes. The sugar-loaf cut is like a pyramid so it's not easy to mount this stone as it's 65 carats, and it needed to have a special jewel around it to maintain a good balance and anchor such an exceptional stone." "This is the most expensive jewel we have owned by Elizabeth Taylor worth $6 million, and the second is the emerald brooch ($5 million) and third is the necklace ($4.5 million)" Bosciani tells The Telegraph. The total value of collection by Bulgari is 30 million dollars. In the exhibition there is also a platinum, emerald and diamond brooch given to her in 1960 by her third husband, Eddie Fisher. "That was a 'recovery gift' - Eddie Fisher wanted to offer her something special to maintain the relationship as he knew she was having an affair with Richard Burton," explains Bosciani, "the legend goes that when she wanted to go on with the relationship with Richard, Eddie Fisher asked for the brooch back and apparently she answered 'No, I'm paying for it myself, because I can stay without you but I can't stay without it.' Of course that's a legend, but she was a woman in control and was very rich and was used to buying jewellery for herself." Proving that Taylor by no means relied on the men in her life to buy her jewellery, the "Trombino" 1930s sapphire ring in the collection was a present from Elizabeth Taylor to herself. She bought it to match the sapphire necklace given to her by Richard Burton - although they weren't created as a set.  The Elizabeth Taylor collection of Bulgari jewels is at the Bulgari New Bond Street boutique until July 16th © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  In fashion circles, ‘authenticity’ is the word of the moment – but it tends to function more as a marketing tool than as a concept of any great depth. Mega-brands know that pleading authenticity is a smart way of connecting with their customer. ‘Look! We hand-stitch things! We use artisans! We’re not a multimillion-pound luxury goods house churning out hundreds of thousands of products at all!’ Uh-huh. US accessories brand Shinola has more claim to authenticity than most. Based in Detroit, it manufactures in the Midwest city and is staffed by Detroit locals. A relatively recent arrival to the label is Carolyn Murphy, the all-American supermodel with the glacial Grace Kelly looks, who has been women’s design director since 2013. Her relationship with the brand began after she was cast by photographer Bruce Weber in Shinola’s first advertising campaign; now she designs their bags, too. You’d think Carolyn would already have been quite busy enough as Estée Lauder’s longest-serving face (14 years and counting), lingerie designer (CheekFrills), spokesperson (for Ugg’s Classic Luxe line) and mother to 15-year-old daughter Dylan Blue. But so impressed was she by Shinola, she longed to work for them. ‘I’d been in fashion for 22 years. I’d done a few collaborations before, but theirs was one of the first relationships that seemed authentic, in terms of what we believed in.’ It takes grit to be in fashion for 22 years – a mix of stamina and beauty, two qualities Carolyn has in spades. Like Shinola, she feels authentic – far warmer and unguarded than her pristine blonde persona might suggest, the opposite of a token model spokesperson. ‘Shinola has had to climb mountains – there have been naysayers, because they’re challenging a lot of American companies to rethink their business model. You have other American companies who don’t give a s—. It’s no surprise our economy took a crash in 2008. Importing so many things from overseas... why aren’t we creating jobs in America? Why aren’t we building things? 'This is important to me because I consider myself an American. Granted, my family came over from Europe – from Wales, in the 1800s – but since then, they’ve had a farm in Virginia. I come from a good old American family. Why did they come here? They came for a better life; to have their own life. That’s something that was ingrained in my DNA.’ While many of Shinola’s pieces are produced in the US, Carolyn admits that ‘we have to be careful, because realistically there are going to be times when not all the parts are made there. But the intention is that you’re providing jobs for people in our backyard. It’s assembled in Detroit, it’s handmade and there’s some meaning here.’ It can be hard to feel as though you are living a meaningful life when the tenets of your profession are so wildly superficial. And while she might not be the first 40-something model to have embraced clean eating and meditation, she is possibly the least annoying. Ask her to confirm that her own approach to ageing is well-balanced, and she exclaims: ‘No, it’s not! I find it so peeving when you see these models who are like, “Oh, my green juices and my workouts” and everything is so perfect. 'It’s not reality. If I were really to post pics or have a dialogue about the struggles with ageing, it would be, “Oh FFS, am I supposed to stop laughing all the time because the lines keep growing?” I like the road maps of my life; I like being able to move my face around. I’m not against [having] any help – there are ways to go about it, and it’s a personal choice. But I have the most minimalist approach to it. I don’t like killing myself at the gym or having a cabinet full of products.’ She agrees that acceptance of the ageing process is as tricky as it is important. ‘That’s the hardest part for most of us. It’s really difficult from my perspective. Say I’m in a fashion show and walking behind a 15-year-old from Denmark who has porcelain skin… it’s very humbling, but at same time, what are the assets of being older? 'I like the fact that I’m wiser, and have earned the lines I have. I spend time with Christy Turlington: she is unbelievable! She’s got great skin, she exercises, but she loves her coffee and she loves a glass of wine. It’s all about balance, and enjoying your life.’ It’s clear why Estée Lauder has held on to Carolyn. As well as being eloquent, she’s relatable – the most valuable commodity of all. ‘I still have “pinch-me” moments where I can’t believe I represent the brand. I grew up with it,’ she says. ‘I don’t think some of the newcomers within the brand have that connection, so maybe that’s why I’m still there. We are all ageing together, and ageing is a wonderful thing, in some ways, and not so wonderful in others. I’ve had moments where I think to myself, “I’m almost 42 and still working.” I don’t know what the formula is, other than to give 110 per cent to whatever I do.’ She says she was ‘really reticent’ about modelling. ‘I started later than most – at about 19 or 20 – and even then it was to earn money to go to college and be a writer. I loved creative writing. I hadn’t grown up thinking, “Oh, I want to be a supermodel, I want to be famous.” That wasn’t my intention at all.’ Her laid-back attitude was typical of the decade in which she was discovered – a time before models were the ultimate ‘Brand Me’s. ‘That was the beauty of the early ’90s, and of grunge: the attraction of seeing these pics of Kate Moss and [Australian model] Emma Balfour that David Sims had shot. They were riveting but relatable. I could relate to thatgirl, that music, that art. It was a wonderful time. You’d be hanging out with Marc Jacobs until 2am, listening to the soundtrack he might play in the show the next day. ‘It was almost like we were all artists – the joy of being in a studio and listening to Massive Attack and Portishead, and buying slip dresses from Portobello Market. I’d pluck most of my eyebrows off, or experiment with hair colour, but that’s what we did – there wasn’t this uniform, bombshell Victoria’s Secret hair where we all looked the same. We were celebrated for our differences. We were unique individuals, whether it was the way we dressed, wore our hair, what we listened to, how we behaved – which was super-unpredictable – and we weren’t plugged in all the time. It wasn’t corporate. Now everything is very corporate, very well-planned and thought-out.’ This seems a good time to mention social media, which most models agree is A Good Thing because it gives them a voice. ‘I think it’s a disaster waiting to happen,’ she says flatly. ‘There is such an inauthentic element to it. Anybody, myself included, can curate what the world should be seeing. 'It saddens me, not only that we believe in it but that we also think that it’s important. To place importance on gathering numbers is ridiculous. I don’t want to post pictures of myself and there are two reasons for that: one, I consider myself a private person, and two, I think it’s silly. It comes across as supercilious, just constantly self-promoting. I’d rather share things that are of some importance to me, but even then there’s a voyeurism I find super-uncomfortable. ‘I also find it takes away from connecting to people. A lot of the time, I’ll sit in a chair with a hair and make-up artist and they’ll say, “God, we’re so glad we have you,” because they’re so used to having a model whose nose is stuck in her phone that she doesn’t know how to communicate.’ Does she think people have lost the art of conversation? ‘They have. It’s sad. Not me. Not Motormouth Murphy. I can talk forever!’ Ironically, our interview is taking place via the medium we’re flaming: the screen. Clearly, it’s useful when you’ve had to cancel your trip to London, allowing you to conduct an interview via Skype and then, when Skype doesn’t work, via FaceTime. Why the change of plan? ‘I ended up having to work here [in New York] but also
I was battling a parasite.’ It’s no mean feat to appear relatable even when you live the sort of life that lets you cancel work plans because you are battling a parasite, but that’s her – as authentic as any multi-millionairess model can be, with the parasite to prove it.  When J.K. Rowling walked the red carpet at the premiere of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child last week, photographers in the pens all zoomed in on her metallic Sophia Webster shoes with Golden Snitch-esque wings fluttering off the ankles. It's not surprising given that Sophia Webster's objective is to design things that will look good in photographs, a clever strategy in a world dominated by imagery. "My shoes lend themselves to Instagram: They are colourful and visual. I do design them to be photographed. And a lot of people do buy them because they will look so good in pictures," explains the London-based accessories designer. "My speech bubble bags I did design with Instagram in mind, because I think ‘Oh people will like that on a night out.’ And we all know that these days a night out only happened if it was documented on social media.  Here's Sophia Webster's guide to maximising the power of Instagram... Webster only founded her label in 2012, but the growth in just four years has been astronomical - and she attributes much of this success to how she uses Instagram. The social network is at the heart of Webster's strategy, from dictating design to production runs and helping her to really understand her customer. "It’s definitely been really instrumental in being able to communicate directly with the customer globally," adds Webster. "It gives you an access to them so you can have a real conversation and feedback- I always read the comments and people’s requests." She also uses Instagram to gauge interest for production runs. "As a brand we are agile and flexible," explains Webster. "It was National Watermelon Day recently , and we have watermelon shoes that always get loads of likes on Instagram and always sell out completely so we did a special run of them as a treat for our followers because we know they love those shoes." As for using Instagram as a branding tool, she says the secret is creating a distinct recognisable aesthetic. "You have to be consistent, and also consistent in the quality of images you provide and use," advises Webster to anyone looking to create an Instagram brand. "We are really lucky we get a lot of pictures and some are amazing so we regram them. We are very selective, but are lucky to be in a position that we can be. Our offices are in Shoreditch so we also do street style recces and then have a hashtag #SophiasStompingGround and take pictures of the shoes in the area. It gives the right personality to the picture and it is our brand - luxury with a bit of attitude." Webster has also had huge success creating shoes for the most photographed day of many women's lives, with her collection of statement wedding shoes. This is an area she is looking to expand: "The ice blue pumps sell out every single time. I am adding some new styles into the bridal collection next time we do another production run, and we have made the store a real bridal destination for trying on. We have a dedicated bridal area and then some exclusives. It just widens the customer - everyone wants to get something special for their wedding day." And with 'Wifey for lifey' stitched in every sole, she ensures these are shoes that are photographed just as much as J.K Rowling's gold pumps. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  "I love coming to London Fashion Week," says Glenda Bailey. "I wave over at the front row and everyone waves back! It’s so nice because of course nearly all the editors were part of the team when I was editing Marie Claire." This is textbook Glenda Bailey, editor-in-chief of US Harper’s Bazaar, the opposite of the icy cool aloof magazine editor and an astute self publicist keen to remind us that her skill for spotting talent goes way back to her first big job as a magazine editor in the early Nineties. If you’re old enough you may remember the 1995 fly-on-the-wall Channel 4 documentary Absolutely Marie Claire ("I was the first to ask the cameras in" Glenda reminds me) or the American Express ad featuring Bailey lampooning herself. It was the era of Ab Fab, the heyday of Harvey Nics, and Bailey was the most successful magazine editor in Britain, creating a magazine whose unique mix of gritty reportage, witty sex features and designer shopping was as revolutionary for its time as Cosmopolitan was in the Seventies.  Then, like Tina Brown and Anna Wintour before her, Bailey made the giant leap to America and made up the trio British female editors at the top of American publishing. She turned around US Marie Claire in five years – increasing sales by 80 per cent – and then moved to US Harper’s Bazaar where she has been for the past fourteen years – now, officially, part of the American establishment. But Bailey’s extraordinary success as an editor does not begin to explain her iconic status or the curiosity she still inspires. She is famous because she broke the mould – a working class girl from Derbyshire who neither looked or acted the part, she proved that you don’t have to be connected, beautiful or reed thin to be a serious contender in the most elitist environment in the world.

Apart from her tendency to use "super" for emphasis – as in, "I am super lucky" - there is nothing about the 57-year-old Bailey to suggest that she has lived in New York for almost twenty years, editing one of the most powerful fashion magazines in America. Yes, she is wearing Louboutin heels, and a black and white Valentino dress, and okay, her earrings are diamond and her specs are Prada. But she’s still the Glenda Bailey of old with the unruly, frizzy red hair, the gash of dark red lipstick, and a pronounced East Midlands accent. "I think it would take more than editing a magazine in America to change me," she says, with a surprisingly girlish laugh. "I’ve still got my accent. I come back to Derbyshire at least twice a year to see my sister and nephews and my friends of course." On the airs and graces scale Glenda is firmly at zero. Her self-belief, on the other hand, remains off the scale.

My favourite Glenda story (and there are many) is the one about her pursuing the MD of a publishing company onto the dance floor to pitch herself as a future editor while they both gyrated to Satisfaction. She was 26 at the time, suffering from pneumonia, and she got the job. Apparently she has always been supremely sure of herself. "I think fear is a great motivator," she says, fixing me with a look. "I lost everything. I was at fashion college and my mother died. Then I was only out of college for 18 months, when my father became ill. So I went home and nursed him until he died. And it was coming back to London on the coach, with my best friend and my boyfriend’s sister, when I said: 'I am going to edit a fashion magazine now, because I have nothing to lose, and you can come and work on it!'"  And that’s exactly what happened. "It is a fairytale," says Bailey matter-of-factly. She and Stephen Sumner, an artist, have been a couple since 1977, "That’s my belove," she says, pointing out a bald man at the opposite side of the room dressed in a suit and designer specs. "It was a holiday romance that never ended."

Still, there is, even according to Bailey, a downside to being editor of Bazaar - which she acknowledges in the introduction to Bazaar Models, the coffee table book of fashion images she is here to promote. "I can tell you that it’s not always easy being a mere mortal in a room full of goddesses," she writes. So, how exactly does she cope? "Well, once I went on holiday with Demi Moore and as we arrived – I said to Steve 'Oh God'. You could see her coming out of the water, and then she greeted us at the door wearing this fabulous white bikini…the holiday could have been ruined at that point! But she is just a great girl and such fun." And yes, this is really the world she inhabits. Batting away thoughts that any of it is really threatening - "I think the whole point of fashion and beauty is making the most of your looks" – she prefers to focus instead on the many perks. Among the high points, she says, have been Sting singing at her launch party, Debbie Harry performing at a Hallowe'en do and a Patti Smith set at a recent Christmas event. She has the likes of Gwyneth Paltrow on speed dial, all the top models, "the designers and presidents have all become friends over time". Presumably she also has the country retreat on Long Island? "No. I don’t have time." Oh, but Anna Wintour does.

The two British editors are in direct competition (American Vogue being the top dog) and could not be more different if you’d made them up. Wintour is said to have been the inspiration for the chilly editor in The Devil Wears Prada, whereas Bailey’s defining characteristic is unbridled enthusiasm. Does she find the constant comparisons a bit tedious? "No," she leans forward, politely poised for the next question. Famously Anna Wintour rises at five to play tennis. Is she an early riser? "No." Tennis player? "No." What does she do for exercise? "Well," she peers down at her right wrist, "I’m sure this hand is more developed because of all the credit card swiping. Ha ha." One of the oldest urban legends associated with Wintour is that she only eats rare steak and Bailey is happy to play the other side of the coin: "drink, food, yes all of the above. Lovely, yes. I believe in over-indulgence in everything you enjoy!"

One thing Wintour and Bailey do have in common is an incredible work ethic. "I don’t quite know what the definition of a workaholic is?" she says, smiling like a politician. Someone who is focused on their work to the exclusion of all else? "Well, I am very focused, that is true, but equally I really believe that it’s important to have that work-life balance. And come 6 o’clock on a Friday, unless there is an absolute catastrophe, my team are not going to hear from me until Monday morning. Because one thing I know is if I email them, they have to respond, so, weekend ruined!" The same goes for maternity leave: "I have never once called: it is their personal time and I want to respect that." Is it possible that the real reason Bailey has a reputation for living and breathing her job is because she doesn’t have children herself? "No," she says firmly. "I think it is to do with the workplace, because I am very decisive, and I take work seriously and have great expectations of people who come to work for me." Which brings us to the big question: what happens next? Does she have her sights set on Vogue, the biggest job in town? "I think I have the biggest job and I think I am very lucky," she says unblinking. But you’ll notice she didn’t say no.

 Alexa Chung may be about to invade the high street thanks to a new collaboration with Marks & Spencer,  but the model-slash-presenter isn’t too much of a big thing to lend her cool credentials to an underground label, especially one founded by one of her closest friends. Followers of Chung on Instagram will no doubt be familiar with her partner in crime, Tennessee Thomas, a woman who has almost as many strings to her professional and creative bow as her famous friend. She describes herself as a DJ and a drummer - her father is revered drummer Pete Thomas, a Sheffield-born musician who has provided beats for Elvis Costello, The Attractions and Arctic Monkeys. But the 31-year-old is also the founder of a shop/clothing line/community clubhouse called The Deep End Club products, which is located in Manhattan’s hip East Village. The Deep End Club acts as a hub to unite eco-conscious artists and activists and sells creations, book and music by local creatives. Now, Thomas has decided to create her own line of ‘Deep End’ clothing, which launches this week. And who better to model her debut than Alexa? The slender Brit showcases The Deep End Club’s ‘Give a Damn’ slogan t-shirts ($45) in a Seventies-themed shoot: pinstripe trousers, metallic platform boots and wood-panelled fixtures all feature. The 32-year-old looks at ease in Thomas’ collared minidresses that look as though they were designed with her in mind: one comes in silver ($325) and the other in black silk velvet topped with a white Peter Pan collar ($280). The shoot was captured in locations around New York City – the adopted home of both of the friends – including an empty theatre and a subway station. Chung has previously spoken about her desire to start her own label, but has so far collaborated with US retailer Madewell and most recently on a capsule denim collection with AG Jeans.  When Sophie Gregoire-Trudeau, the wife of Canada's Prime Minister, was photographed alongside The Duchess of Cambridge this weekend, her outfit helped to accomplish the next stage in her carefully orchestrated ‘project’ to promote under-the-radar Canadian designers. Her elegant purple dress with bow detailling at the shoulders is by Editions de Robes, a Montreal-based label founded by Julie Pesant which specialises in beautifully-made dresses. Meanwhile her jaunty trilby, which cleverly mirrored the angle of The Duchess of Cambridge's Lock and co saucer, is by The Saucy Milliner, another Canadian brand, this time based in Toronto.  This strategy of wearing exclusively Canadian brands is one that Gregoire-Trudeau and her old-friend-turned-style-advisor Jessica Mulroney have been working on ever since they inadvertently created a fashion moment with the cream wrap coat Trudeau wore to see her husband Justin sworn in as Prime Minister last year. “She needed a few things to wear and was so busy. I was in Toronto so I sent her some options,” Mulroney remembers. “She wore a coat by Canadian designer Sentaler and people went crazy for it. We had created this media frenzy, like you see with anything Kate wears. Then we realised we had a responsibility to create more moments like that to give homegrown designers an international platform.” Since then, Gregoire-Trudeau and Mulroney, who is married to Ben, the son of former Canadian Prime Minister Brian Mulroney, strategise public outfits. “It’s a fun process, like girlfriends when they get dressed to go out. I do the research and speak to a lot of the designers,” she explains, tipping Greta Constantine as another label to watch out for Sophie wearing during Kate and William's visit. Mulroney says Gregoire-Trudeau's yoga-honed figure makes her a dream to dress - and makes niche designer’s dreams come true. “We’ve heard stories of designer’s careers completely changing,” she says. Gregoire-Trudeau chose pieces by Toronto-based jeweller Dean Davidson when she visited The White House in March, and promptly sent his business into "another stratosphere."  "He said because of that moment he’s getting appointments with retailers that never picked up the phone before, he's getting orders from Europe and Asia" Mulroney tells The Telegraph. Still, the duo’s project landed them in hot water earlier this year when it was revealed that some items had been gifted or loaned from designers. “It’s a practice which is normal in the fashion industry, but the pair learnt that you can’t do that in a very public role,” explains Odessa Paloma Parker, fashion editor at the Toronto-based newspaper The Globe and Mail. And this week there have been further political considerations for Mulroney to take into account when planning Gregoire-Trudeau’s outfits. “We were contacted by Kensington Palace a few days ago and informed about what colours the Duchess is wearing,” she explained the day before the tour began of the fashion diplomacy at stake on this tour. Not that Mulroney is bothered. “They’re both so young and beautiful that even if they both wore the same colour, I don’t think it would be a bad thing.” As it turns out, The Duchess (in Jenny Packham) and Gregoire-Trudeau made a perfectly complementary duo in autumnal hues of teal and purple.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  With his eclectic and flamboyant aesthetic, Alessandro Michele has not just made Gucci the most in-demand brand in fashion; he has altered the entire fashion landscape. After years of pared-back, Céline-style minimalism, Michele’s new Gucci champions a maximalist approach: ruffles, frills, prints, layers, a cacophony of colour – all of which both critics and consumers have welcomed with open arms. Discretion was the minimalist’s buzzword; anonymous, logo-less handbags replaced the heavily branded “it-bags” of the Nineties and Noughties. Logos became fashion’s anathema. In swinging the fashion pendulum towards flamboyance, Michele has also re-embraced the logo, resurrecting the neglected double G motif of Gucci’s 1980s heyday and reinterpreting it for a modern audience. “Logos still touch and talk to customers, but fashion is an industry of the new, and if you rely on a logo because of your heritage, you’ll get left behind,” said Marco Bizzarri, Gucci president and CEO, speaking at the New York Times International Luxury Conference last month. Bizzarri explained how Michele has breathed new life into the retro monogram, making it “an ode to joy, not something worn by the devil”. In a way it was surprising that Gucci’s new direction is led by an emblem from the past. One of Bizzarri’s first moves when he was appointed as CEO in January 2015 was to remove all the historical images from the walls of the company’s Italian design offices. “If you are constantly inspired by the past, how can you do something modern?” It was a move questioned by many of his 11,000 employees, he says. “Everyone thought I was crazy. But I wasn’t trying to erase the past, but relate to it in a different way.” Bizzarri needed to find a creative director who shared his vision to “make Gucci an iconic fashion house again”. Instead of choosing a high-profile name to follow in the footsteps of Tom Ford and Frida Giannini at the helm, Bizzarri appointed the relatively unknown Michele, who’d worked as an in-house designer at Gucci since 2002. An initial coffee meeting turned into a four-hour lunch, and as Michele discussed his vision for the future of Gucci, Bizzarri began to realise “maybe we have the right guy here at Gucci already”. After being appointed creative director in January 2015, Michele famously had just five days to create the autumn/winter men’s collection, with the women’s show a month later. “We threw away the collection prepared by Frida Giannini and created a show in five days,” says Bizzarri. “The only way to communicate our future strategy was via the catwalk show.” The double G monogram made an appearance in belt buckles in those first shows, and since then Michele has run with the theme, featuring it on accessories and clothing alongside other Gucci house codes such as the equestrian bit and red and green stripes. Statement made: the logo is back. “I saw it as a rebirth of the double G logo,” said Michele in a video interview shown at the conference. “In the past, Gucci has been a bit ashamed of its logo, but it should be proud of it as an emblem of 95 years of history. The logo is an incredible powerful asset for Gucci and it should become as desirable as a leather bag.” Importantly, Michele takes a playful, almost irreverent approach to the Gucci logo, daubing it with flowers or pairing it with cartoonish motifs in accessories that appeal to a younger demographic. “I couldn’t wait to get my hands on the logo,” said Michele. “It’s like drawing on the Mona Lisa. The double G is like a hieroglyph that everyone knows and I use it as the cherry on top of my designs.” It was a risk – and opinions were divided at first – but one that paid off. “Alessandro had complete creative freedom, within the framework of the brand,” says Bizzarri. “The way he played with the logo was a big success. We sold 600,000 products from the new collection and attracted half a million new customers.” In line with this spirited new approach was Gucci’s decision to partner with New York graffiti artist Trouble Andrew for autumn/winter 2016, inviting him to tag coats, bags and skirts with his counterfeit ‘Gucci Ghost’ GG. “Social media offers a huge opportunity to interact,” says Bizzarri. “The Gucci Ghost partnership played out over Instagram and Snapchat. It allows us to evolve the logo and give it modernity.” The logo then is alive and kicking at the house of Gucci, and given the brand’s current status as the hottest label in fashion, it might be time to wave goodbye to anonymity. “The logo is not over, but it needs to find ways to evolve,” concluded Bizzarri. “It requires a playful, spontaneous approach – you need to treat it in a lively way.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Jenna Coleman is about to star in one of the most anticipated TV shows of 2016, Victoria on ITV. The Doctor Who actress might still be relatively new to the red carpet game, but she has an almost impeccable track record when it comes to event dressing, sticking to elegant, but never-boring, vintage-inspired looks. Her high success rate on the red carpet is partly down to her stylist Rebecca Corbin Murray, who was the one behind Lily James' near-perfect Cinderella princess style. Here the British stylist breaks down Coleman's winning approach to red carpet style, which something tells us is only going to become more prolific in the wake of Victoria... While promoting Victoria so far, Jenna Coleman has worn feminine, but contemporary, dresses by Peter Pilotto, Victoria Beckham and Erdem. "It’s not like a movie tour unfortunately so isn't as big, but I think moving forward we’re going to stick with this vintage look, worn in a very modern way," adds Corbin-Murray. "Jenna likes dressing quite elegantly, with feminine and romantic pieces. I don’t think you will catch her in anything super skin tight. Especially with the AW16 trends rich, luxe, decadent pieces, which can be done in a really cool way." Rebecca Corbin-Murray says she doesn't work by following the current trends, but prioritises her clients' body types. "Designers have created this idea of trends, but it’s not something we really follow because my girls have realistic body shapes," she explains. "They’re just normal girls with normal bodies to be quite honest. Our main concern is working with silhouettes and finding the right shapes to work with and hide what they think are their flaws or wobbly bits or things they don’t like, and to emphasise the good bits. It’s always nice to be on trend a little bit, but I think it is more important for the girl to emphasise her assets." "In the beginning she was quite unknown," says Corbin-Murray of how they started working together. "It’s always quite hard with a new actress to enamour them with the brands. Jenna also has got a very strong sense of style herself and a really good understanding of her body shape, and what suits her and doesn’t suit her. That’s always made her quite insightful to work with. She likes a vintage sort of feel to things, so I think that comes out in a lot of the outfits we choose. She’s maybe quite English as well, so that maybe makes her veer to the vintage side of things." "I like to support our home grown designers," Corbin-Murray says of the labels she chooses for Jenna. "Great brands have started and just disappeared, and you have to take off your hat to the designers that have managed to get the funding. It’s so tough to be a new brand in this economy today, so I think it is really nice to support the home grown ones, just because they are incredibly creative and throwing out the most amazing clothes." Corbin-Murray says that her favourite of Jenna's looks to date is the white Emilia Wickstead dress with cut-out detailing at the waist she wore to this year's Serpentine Gallery party. "We went into meet Emilia and she had never met Emilia before and it’s nice to go as much as you can into fittings with the designers," she explains. "Designers are inspired by the people - well they’re inspired by everything - but they’re often inspired by the people and so once the designer meets that person they have a much better sense of scale, of body type and of their personality. So you know they are much more interested in dressing them next time, or maybe they have designed something this season and they’re like 'I had that person in mind when I was drawing this or creating this piece'. It’s a collaboration all round."   "I do have quite a few English roses," remarks the British stylist about her client list, which includes Lily James, Sophie Turner and Jenna Coleman. "They can do that whole big gowny, romantic, English rose thing. I think they really have that English quirkiness so they can really add this twist or an edge where you wouldn’t expect one necessarily. All of them are quite playful, they like taking risks, they all love fashion. And this idea of the classic English rose- I wouldn’t say we're f****** it up, but giving it an edge- just giving it a little wit!"  Even before he discovered his vivid alter egos, David Jones was a snappy dresser – a dedicated follower of fashion with a taste for flamboyant lapels and statement hair. His manner, in the early days, may have been confined to the not-so-wild borders of Bromley, but he was never one to dress down or dilute his message. Clothes, as he quickly established, were a strategic means of self-expression. Once he began studying mime and dance, fashion, together with an on-point haircut and psychedelic make-up, would play a huge part in his transformation into an artist. Really, it was through his clothes that in, 1973, I along with thousands of other teenagers, came to know David Bowie. His music was all pervasive by then – catchy and memorable, but to an eleven year old, not strikingly avant-garde. (Not that most eleven year olds, in 1973, knew avant-garde from Carry on Up the Khyber.) However when the songs came together with that blazing red mullet (courtesy of Schwarzkopf) and the Aladdin Sane lightning flash, you knew you were in the presence of something thrillingly odd. More thrillingly, the oddness was going mainstream. Aladdin Sane was everywhere in 1973, so ubiquitous, he had even infiltrated my school  -  Dorchester Grammar, a rural  establishment hitherto impervious to fashion and, so it seemed to me, anything colourful.  Like a West Country kabuki tribe, the girls in the fifth and sixth form marched arm-in-arm (forbidden) down the corridors with their spiky orange hair-cuts (not forbidden, but only because the rules had yet to catch up), alabaster faces and tweezered-to-the-brink-of-extinction eyebrows in tribute to their hero, terrifying my fellow first years and me. Fresh from worshipping David Cassidy, we had never seen anything like this red army with their Marlene Dietrich meets Martian style tics - not the cavalier shearing of the hair, the jolie-laide pallor or the remnants of glittery make-up (wearing make-up to school was also forbidden). The fan-girls were unsettling and mesmerizing in equal parts - much like their hero. It was one of those rare moments when the zeitgeist, politics and exploding social mores manifest themselves in a singular, decorative image. It’s that cultural white heat that allows Aladdin Sane to resonate even now, inspiring two Kate Moss-as-David-Bowie Vogue covers alone, long after the shock factor has subsided. Sane and Ziggy were fertile grounds for fantasy dressing up. For Aladdin Sane’s 1973 tour, Bowie collaborated with designer Kansai Yamamoto on a jumpsuit with vast, semi orbular legs - another is-it-a-bird, is-it-a-human moment that pre-empted the following decade’s obsession with post-apocalyptic Japanese design. The one sleeve patterned stretch knit unitard he wore as Ziggy Stardust was another eye-popping Top of the Pops moment. Watching Bowie smash elegantly through another social taboo often seemed like watching history in the making – not an experience often associated with TOTP, but a compelling reason for switching on when he was scheduled to appear. The unitard, which surely inspired Body Map’s collections a decade later, ignited one of London’s many fashion revivals, even though Bowie himself soon moved on to Berlin and then the USA. Not that leaving London stymied his style. Bowie fashion influences include arresting nail colours (still a huge trend in 2016), swooping blue eye-shadow (ditto), wedge-blonde hair dos and razor sharp tailoring, on both men and women. The ice-blue trouser suit Freddie Burretti designed for the 1972 Life on Mars? video was the catalyst for a recent Jonathan Saunders’ collection. And the list of beneficiaries of Bowie inspiration goes on. The New Romantics, New Order, Madonna, Kate Bush, Kate Moss, Gaga, Florence, Jean Paul Gaultier, Balmain and many more, have openly paid homage to his influence on their style and careers Did I say the legs on that Yamamoto jumpsuit were vast? One of the most striking if unregistered aspects of the 2013 blockbuster V&A Bowie retrospective was how teeny his clothes were.  When Moss collected the Best Male Solo Artist award at the Brits the following year on his behalf, she wore one of his romper-suits: the man who confessed that at one point in his life, he had survived on "red peppers, cocaine, and milk" often resembled nothing so much as an  etiolated electrified streak. If Bowie unwittingly helped ignite a mania in fashion for extreme skinniness, he also tilted it in positive directions. His own cultural vampirism – he cherrypicked from pop art, with Dada-ism, Brechtian and Japanese theatre, Lindsay Kemp mime, language and sci-fi and breathed fresh life into them - helped join the dots between fashion and art, placing the former at the centre of popular culture.   Without doubt however, it’s Bowie’s androgyny that has had the most lasting footprint. Unlike other agents of glam rock, Bowie’s gender fluidity managed to shock because it wasn’t mere posturing. While the members of Slade and Sweet went out of their way to demonstrate their machismo, Bowie, with breath-taking insouciance, flouted his bisexuality. Somehow he escaped getting beaten to a pulp, possibly because, as an early school report noted, along with being “vividly artistic” he was a gifted brawler. Besides, for all the chauvinistic swagger of the 1970s, there was also a blossoming of sexual and artistic experimentation, much of which Bowie communicated through his costumes. As the shock impact of Ziggy and Aladdin waned, Bowie skillfully manipulated the ostensibly conventional. Two decades after Ziggy, he sang at the Brits, a picture of establishment elegance in one of those impeccable dark, slim suits that had become a signature of his, until your eye snagged on those kitten heels - a cheekily subversive gender bending flourish that suggested he hadn’t lost his taste for mischief. He began wearing those sharp-edged suits  in the late 1970s. With their 1940s gangster angles they were simultaneously polite and menacing - and they set the sartorial course for millions of yuppies in the loadsamoney decade that followed. That may not have been Bowie’s intention. His aim, in the early days at least, was to depict a solitary, alienated figure in a dystopian world. His genius meant he reached out to millions. • Learn more about David Bowie's creative work and collaborations with the book David Bowie Is, available from the Telegraph Bookshop  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Top models and best friends Cara Delevingne and Kendall Jenner have been immortalised in wax form at Madame Tussauds in London as part of a special London Fashion Week experience. Visitors can go backstage with the duo, capture selfies and walk the runway with the catwalk pros. But we wanted to know more: how long does it take to make Delevingne out of wax? And how did they replicate her infamous, bushy eyebrows? We spoke to her sculptor Jim Kempton to find out exactly what goes into making a wax model... Delevingne's fitting took three hours in her hotel room in Canada, where she was filming, but sometimes the makers can only get five minutes with a celebrity. Kempton tell us, "anything is better than nothing. We are aware that we don’t want to put the sitter through it and it won’t work so well if Cara says to Kendall it’s an arduous process." They will travel all over the world to take measurements of celebrities: "Even if we only have time to take a photograph from the optimum distance and a width of tragus or something that will give us a lot more than guessing from picture agency pictures. We once did a fitting at Heathrow just before someone got on a plane." They don't use a 3D scan like you might think, instead everything is done through traditional measurements. Jim explained how they ensure the face looks realistic: “We use a pair of calipers and use the tragus on the ear as a reference point to measure to all the points on the profile and take 100 or so measurements on the head. Then we take a similar amount of photographs, making sure we photograph up and down and 360 degrees around the head and use different lenses so we get a full range of looks." They then take around 50 measurements on the body of the bone lengths, widths and depths.  There is a team of 20 people creating each model, including sculptors, colourists, hair and makeup artists and stylists. The whole process takes a total of four months. "The main mass of the hair and the direction are absolutely critical, so in recreating them we faithfully copied them hair by hair," Kempton explains. "Our hair and makeup department painstakingly inserted every hair one by one. We have to make sure the hair we are inserting is real and the root is inserted, rather than the tip. Even if you have it in the wrong way then the lie of the hair wouldn’t sit right, so it’s such a detailed process. If one eyebrow hair is out of place it’s not going to look exactly like her." "Cara was quite adamant that she wanted us to have her recreate a Saint Laurent dress [that she wore to the Paper Towns LA premiere]. Saint Laurent have made a replica version for us." Kendall however, is wearing a plain white dressing gown, as she is recreating a moment where she was backstage at fashion week having her makeup done.   Stars will always reveal the products in their makeup bag so that the colour of their make-up is accurate, or sometimes they will even handover make-up from their handbag in the fitting. Kempton says, "with the Saint Laurent dress, Cara’s wearing quite a deep red lip which slightly goes over the lip line and so makes it look slightly different to the natural smile we photographed in the fitting. The makeup artist who did the colouring ensured that we are really faithful to that one moment, so we make sure the amount of eyelashes she has is the same and they are flicked up in exactly the same way. Otherwise you lose the essence of Cara underneath that make-up."  Cara has (at last count) 18 tattoos, with many intricate designs such as the lion on her left index finger. The head is made of wax and the body is made with fiberglass, so they have two different techniques for tattooing the models: "For the head we etch into the wax and then work a darker coloured ink wax into the fine grooves that have been etched. Then we use paint for the body." Kempton says: "It would be possible to create one of her faces, but they are such a quick snapshot so that wouldn’t portray the spectrum of expressions and her elegance. By doing something slightly more passive, it means that you can get a glimmer of what’s going on behind - she might be about to burst into one of her kooky impressions. If we stuck with one, it might be a bit like when the wind freezes and not a real portrait of her." Cara is walking on the catwalk and Kempton explains that celebrities always have a lot of input into how they are standing: "We might go along with an idea, but the most important thing is that the sitter is relaxed and is completely natural. You can recognise someone from the back and from a distance because of everyone’s own characteristics in the way they walk and hold themselves, so it’s important that we don’t contrive it too much and they are relaxed in themselves so the public that then come and see the wax figure get an idea how it would feel if they were in a close proximity to them." Before wax is poured onto the model, the celebrity gets to look at the scultpure and confirm whether they think it looks like them. He says: "When I was happy with Cara's head I sent a photograph and she approved it straight away. We always make sure the talent has input into what we’re sculpting and creating – it’s essential that they are aware of the stage their figure is at. We have even previously done video calls!" Cara Delevingne and Kendall Jenner's waxworks will be revealed at Madame Tussauds in London on Monday, February 8 as part of the attraction's London Fashion Week experience. Tickets start from £23.80 when you book online.  This interview has been condensed.  Anti-fur protesters may have placarded fashion week’s show venues, but political point-making has become almost as common on the catwalk and red carpet of late. Sunday night’s BAFTAs saw actresses dress in black in support of Time’s Up, and Dior’s We Should All Be Feminists t-shirt, which spawned a thousand high-street copies, was named 2017’s ‘dress of the year’ by The Fashion Museum, Bath. “A 450 quid t-shirt, that would keep two cotton farming families going for a year,” says Katharine Hamnett over lunch. “And what do you achieve? It’s a reference of [Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie’s] book. But how watered down could you be? There’s a way out - you should be, but maybe you don’t want to be, and that’s fine.” As for the all-black red carpets: “Black is one of the sexiest colours in the world,” she says, “you think you’re making a protest? Wake up, look in the mirror.” Katharine Hamnett has made a career from pulling no punches. She designed her first politicised slogan tee in 1983. It read ‘Choose Life’ and was made famous when George Michael wore it in Wham’s Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go music video. “I was having an argument with Lynne Franks” - the PR widely accepted to be the inspiration behind Ab Fab’s Edina Monsoon - “she’s very interested in buddhism, and she put on this exhibition at the Commonwealth Institute. I said, ‘this is going to have absolutely no effect, you’d be better off printing the central Buddhist tenet, which is ‘Choose Life’, in giant letters on a white t-shirt’. So I went and did it - I just thought, why not?” That ‘why not’ mentality has carved Hamnett’s place in fashion history. It was cemented the moment she shook hands with then Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher in t-shirt branded ‘58% don’t want pershing’ - she whipped off her coat just in time for a photo, catching Thatcher unawares. It was “almost a practical joke,” says Hamnett, but the message reached further than she could have anticipated - she’s had offers from the metropolitan museum and the museum of modern art for the original t-shirt from 1984, though she’s yet to part with it. Her designs are some of the most copied in history and while for most brands, that would spell disaster, Hamnett realised early on that to be copied was to have her voice amplified. “I thought, that would make me happy, if they copied it. Make this worldwide: nuclear ban now, stop acid rain, save the sea, no war. They were regarded as quite radical at the time. American Vogue deigned to come and see me in my office: they took one long at the t-shirts and, without saying a word, they swung on their heels and walked out.”   Having launched her fashion brand in 1979, Hamnett shuttered her doors in 2004, frustrated with an industry-wide lack of interest in sustainability. But now the original t-shirt activist is back with a new collection (using organic cotton and producing sustainably), and a new plan. “The thing about t-shirts is, they don’t actually achieve anything unless you follow them up with pressure on your elected representative,” says Hamnett, whose latest designs are printed on the back with the guidelines of doing just that, plus a sample letter. ”I think it’s a feminist issue, isn’t it: we’ve only had the vote 100 years - start using it now.” Hamnett is marking that anniversary with Liberty, the exclusive stockists of the relaunched label. A century ago, suffragettes met in the department store - one of the few places women were allowed to gather unchaperoned - to make plans. In 1912, they smashed the store’s windows - ‘glass smashing for votes!’. After a hundred years of those votes, Liberty is marking International Women’s Day on 8th March by putting 8 women in those same windows, photographed by Mary McCartney: businesswomen, authors and fashion pioneers, hence Hamnett’s own spot behind the glass. Elsewhere in London, the Fashion and Textile Museum’s newly-opened exhibition - T-shirt: Cult Culture Subversion - also pays homage to the designer's legacy. At 70, she's throwing her hat back into the ring. 40 years ago, fashion wasn’t ready to hear what she had to say, but things can change - Hamnett's betting her business on it. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Tyra Banks, the 43 year-old model and head judge on reality TV show America’s Next Top Model, has made a move to banish ageism within the fashion industry by removing the upper age limit for hopefuls wanting to compete on her programme. The entrepreneur and executive producer, who has led the judging panel for 22 of the show’s 23 series, explained on Instagram that she constantly receives messages from fans who want to compete for the chance to win a prized modelling contract, but are older than the show’s previous age limit of 27. "You know I've stood for diverse beauty and erasing cookie-cutters when it comes to what is deemed beautiful,” Banks told her 4.9 million followers in a video post. “There have been 23 cycles of America's Next Top Model and every single cycle, we say, ‘You have to be 27 years old or younger.’ You know what I hear all the time? 'Tyra, come on! Why have an age limit?' So you know what? I'm taking that age limit off. You want to audition for America's Next Top Model? I don't care how old you are, honey, you just need to know how to smize [smiling with your eyes] and be open to learning how to work the runway like a supermodel." Signing off with the hashtag #ageaintnothingbutanumber, Banks’ post has been viewed over 300,000 times since it was uploaded last night, with fans praising the decision via the comments box.   Tyra's modelling career began in the early 1990s, when she was signed to Elite at the age of 16 and made appearances for American Vogue, as well as Chanel, Christian Dior and Marc Jacobs on the runway. She was the first African American model to grace the covers of GQ and Sports Illustrated, and made her first move into television with a part on The Fresh Prince Of Bel Air. Now  a multimillionaire, Tyra's business empire spans a production company (which produces America's Next Top Model and her chat show, The Tyra Banks Show) as well as several books and her own cosmetics company. She is a judge on America's Got Talent, starring alongside fellow supermodel Heidi Klum. Banks’ move comes after the fashion industry experienced its most age-diverse season of runway castings for years, as designers from Dolce and Gabbana to Simone Rocha included models in their fifties, sixties and seventies in their shows. That said, the total number of models over the age of 50 who were included in the autumn 2017 shows was still only 21, accounting to 0.29% of all bookings according to The Fashion Spot’s annual diversity report. Perhaps Banks and her team are hoping that by next year, there will be a new star name for designers to book - and someone who reflects the women actually buying their clothes.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
