 Alexander McQueen is one of Central Saint Martins' star alumni. The designer, who tragically died in 2010, is held up by students at the legendary fashion establishment as a design hero. One student hasn't just been inspired by the late designers’ genius however; she has embarked on a project to see if she could use DNA as a fabric.  Tina Gorjanc, a recent graduate from Slovenia, developed the idea of creating a collection made from ‘human leather,’ which is made in a laboratory using McQueen’s DNA. McQueen used his own hair in the labels of his first collection, and the owner of these pieces has agreed to give Gorjanc one hair in order to extract his genetic information for her research. The student submitted this concept as part of her final project for her Central Saint Martins degree in June, creating prototype backpacks and jackets using pig skins. She then worked in the lab to create test samples of  'leather' made from McQueen's DNA, to see if the technology would even enable this to even happen.  "You use a process which is called de-extinction, in which a biological agent is applied to the hair in the form of liquid  and you extract certain genetic information from it," Gorjanc explains to The Telegraph, "and then you use that information to reprogram already existing skin so it is the exact texture and colour and everything of the original source, so in this case McQueen's skin. It also depends on how much the hair sample is preserved as to how much information you can extract - fortunately McQueen's hair was preserved in a good state." "You can grow the skin using different techniques," Gorjanc elaborates. "We did it in a Petri dish in the laboratory, and you put liquid treatments and nutrients on the skin so it expands. After that when you want to create leather out of it, you actually need to kill the cells and the first layer and so apply a lot of heat onto it to preserve it. When the material is done and you have leather." She adds: "This process protects the biological information so you are not able to extract any more biological information from the leather, because the cells are dead. It is a typical technique that they use for any other leather." You could also use bio-printing to create this material, but that is more expensive.  The finished product looks like the leather you buy in the shops now, she claims. "While the skin is growing in the laboratory, it doesn’t really look like skin, because we are are just growing the first two layers of the skin. Visually, when you tan it and apply colouration to it, it can look just like leather," Gorjanc says. Of course this process throws up a number of serious ethical questions, but that is Gorjanc's intention. "The project is about how our biological information isn't protected, there are huge gaps in legislation because the technologies are evolving so quickly," the fashion student tells The Telegraph, "because of those loop holes we are able to extract genetic information from a human source- and it can be someone else's - and then produce something out of it like a product and then patent it. When you do that you patent material, that is including someone else's genetic information, which is an interesting concept." Gorjanc has applied for a patent application for this project, because she says the fact that you can patent someone else's genetic information is central to her point. She has no plans to make the collection for commercial purposes, but aims to demonstrate how genetic information could potentially be exploited. As for why she selected  McQueen to illustrate her idea, Gorjanc says his fame and fascination with pushing fashion to extremes make him the ideal subject. "One of the reasons I decided to use Alexander McQueen was to show that it doesn't have to be your parent or relative, it can be someone really big and they can't do anything about it because there is nothing to protect them. McQueen isn’t alive any more and he is a huge fashion genius, so you would think he would be more protected."  There is also the issue of obtaining a public figure's DNA. "A more practical reason," says Gorjanc, "is because of his hair labels, which are a rare source of authentic DNA material. If I got Marilyn Monroe hair from eBay there is no guarantee it is Marilyn Monroe's." It's almost as if McQueen himself foresaw the scientific possibilities which could arise from leaving traces of his DNA in his work.  Gorjanc argues that 'human leather' could actually be an ethical alternative to animal skins. "A lot of people are really grossed out by the whole procedure," she admits, "but in my opinion it's way less gross than other procedures at a leather farm because it doesn't include animal slaughter and is completely lab born and doesn't hurt any human beings. We are so grossed out by human leather, but then use animal leather in our every day life." There is one major difference with human leather however; it can get burnt. "If it isn't fully tanned (with a chemical of vegetable treatment) when you expose it to the sun it can get sun burnt because the human skin is more fragile than animal skin because it has less protected layers," the student, who is currently applying for funding, explains. "You can treat it as normal skin and apply UV protection or moisturiser, and we will try to develop a specific protection. It is really interesting how you can manipulate it in the laboratory, you can add freckles and moles because it is just a matter of condensing the melanin to one point. You can also apply other manipulation, such as tattoos." Thought-provoking, boundary-breaking and, well, just a little bit gross, Gorjanc's project has all the hallmarks of an experimental McQueen collection. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  In this age of global uncertainty, clothes have become a kind of panacea for a growing number of consumers. Designers are responding  to the political upheavals of the past year by injecting some much-needed humour into women’s wardrobes. Browns CEO Holli Rogers is already predicting that spring’s sartorial hit will be Rosie Assoulin’s smiley-face T-shirt. This cheery number, which reads "Thank you! Have a Nice Day!’" neatly sums up the jubilant mood of the coming season.  The logic goes that turning up the dial on the fun, the colourful and the crazy is the sartorial equivalent of Michelle Obama’s "when they go low, we go high" mantra. We may not be able to control the chaos of world events, but we still rule our own style. It’s no coincidence that a cartoonish aesthetic, of the sort you’d find if you rifled through an eccentric child’s dressing-up box, was in plentiful supply on the spring/summer 2017 runways. Alessandro Michele’s army of Gucci geeks displayed growing swagger in garish get-ups that ran from fuzzy crayon-coloured furs featuring zebras to tiered, tinsel-y coats that rivalled Grandma’s Christmas tree.  It was a similar story at Dolce & Gabbana, where sumptuous eveningwear was loaded with pasta and pizza motifs, and drums became bags, while Marc Jacobs tore a page from a psychedelic colouring book, covering clothes with the childlike scrawl of the London illustrator Julie Verhoeven. Even ardent minimalists would have to admit that these playful looks have potent pick-me-up power.  For Anya Hindmarch – whose empire is built on feel-good fashion – all this frivolity is nothing new. "An ironic, lighter and more irreverent approach has always been my thing. People love beautiful objects and increasingly, they want to show their character – that’s the point of fashion," she says. "Customers today are more confident with their style. There aren’t so many rules. It’s about putting a sticker on a beautiful handbag and not being too precious about it."   What’s surprising is who is consuming this cartoonish style. Though there’s no real rhyme or reason, says Hindmarch, often it’s older clients who are investing in the maddest pieces – like her cuddly, googly-eyed Ghost backpack that has also been spotted on Gigi Hadid and Kendall Jenner.  The same is true of the customer for the Lebanese designer Mira Mikati’s emoji-embellished styles. Though her fans run from twenty to fiftysomethings, at a recent London pop-up one of Mikati’s most ardent buyers was an 87-year-old. "She tells me that whenever she wears my clothes people stop her on the street. They smile. They start conversations. She literally makes friends through what she wears." Mikati began her career as a buyer, co-founding the upscale Beirut boutique Plum, before launching her own line some four seasons ago – largely out of frustration at the sameness of the mainstream collections. "I wanted to create something fun and colourful but easy to wear – that you can add to jeans and a white T-shirt, but that’s also a conversation point." Her clothes, worn by Beyoncé and Rihanna, are certainly that: pink parrot-appliquéd trench coats, scribble-print hooded tops and dresses clad with a family of monsters who spell out her Peter Pan ethos in scrawled speech bubbles that read "Never Grow Up’" The antithesis of normcore, these designs take their cue from her children’s toy trunk and the Japanese pop art of Takashi Murakami – who returned the compliment by donning one of her patched bombers. Mikati is clearly onto something. According to Roberta Benteler, who founded online fashion emporium Avenue 32 in 2011, it’s the cartoon aesthetic that’s really piquing women’s desire right now. "Anything that looks like a child’s drawing or a toy sells incredibly well," she says. "Brands like Mira Mikati, Vivetta and Les Petits Joueurs inspire the impulse to buy because they’re so eye-catching. You have to have it now because there’s a sense you won’t find it anywhere else."  The exponential rise of street-style stars and the social-media machine that now propels the fashion industry also plays a part in the popularity of these playful looks. "Designers are creating for the online world and customer," continues Benteler, who cites the Middle Eastern consumer as a big investor in these niche eccentric designs. "People find escapism in fashion and more than ever they need something to cheer them up. These are clothes that stand out on Instagram, and for designers that translates into sales."  In practical terms, in an effort to beat the warp speed of high-street copying, designers are differentiating themselves with increasingly intricate and artisanal styles that are harder to mimic. Just because these pieces have a childlike sensibility doesn’t mean they’re not beautifully crafted. "My aim is create a handbag that you can keep as a design piece," explains the accessories designer Paula Cademartori. One of her most successful designs – the Petite Faye bag, which comes in a whole rainbow of configurations – takes more than 32 hours to create at her Italian studio. "Even if the styles are colourful and speak loudly, they’re still sophisticated," says Cademartori, whose brand was recently snapped up by the luxury goods group OTB. It can pay to be playful.  One man with a unique insight into the feel-good phenomenon is Marco de Vincenzo, who combines his longstanding role as leather goods head designer at Fendi with creating his own collection. "When we first created the Fendi monster accessories for bags we were simply playing around," he says of the charms that still loom large some three years on. "The most successful designs are created without pressure, through play."  His own-line debut bag features an animalistic paw. ‘It’s about creating something new and different for women to discover,’ he explains. "You buy something because you love it, not because you need it. Fashion is like a game – it has to excite."  When it comes to distilling this childlike abandon into your wardrobe, take cues from super style blogger Leandra Medine, who balances madcap pieces, such as her first collection of colourful footwear under her MR By Man Repeller label, with plainer, simpler ones. "It’s all about wearing your clothes with joy, and having fun, but not looking ridiculous," says Cademartori. "You don’t want to look like an actual cartoon."  It’s advice that chimes with  that of Anya Hindmarch. "I love the idea of wearing a super-simple Comme des Garçons jacket and a white shirt with a really fun bag to mess it all up a bit." It’s a failsafe formula for dressing your way to happiness.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  In an era when fashion exhibitions highlighting the couturier’s exquisite technical skills and vision almost guarantee a blockbuster (the recent Dior in Paris and the forthcoming Alaia at London’s Design Museum, for instance), Monday morning’s news that Virgil Abloh has been appointed head of menswear at Louis Vuitton, replacing Kim Jones, who has departed for Dior’s menswear, seems a neat marker of fashion’s constant flux. It’s not that the 37-year-old Abloh isn’t a technician. It’s just that the native Illinoisian didn’t begin his career poised over a cutting table. But then Romeo Gigli, Rifat Ozbek and Gianfranco Ferre trained as architects. Giorgio Armani had plans to become a medic before switching to window displays. After completing a degree in civil engineering at the University of Wisconsin Madison, and a Masters in architecture at the Illinois Institute of Technology, on a course designed by Mies Van der Rohe (which he credits with teaching him the value of a multi disciplinary approach), Abloh worked variously as an intern at Fendi, a DJ- an occupation he still frequently practices- and a design consultant to Kanye West, for whom he’s produced everything from stage sets to merchandise. Like Olivier Rousteing, another erstwhile outsider, now head of Balmain, Abloh’s a formidable communicator with 1.7 million followers on Instagram. In 2013, Abloh launched Off-White, a street-wear label inspired by 90s hip hop styles and focused on high priced trackies and hoodies. It has been such a commercial success, and so championed by Rihanna, Beyonce, the Hadids, the Kardashians - social media mega-stars –that that no brand, it seems, is too mainstream not to want a share of its cool. Collaborations with amongst others, Nike, Vans, Moncler, Levi’s, Umbro and even Jimmy Choo followed. A joint-venture with Ikea is in the pipeline (announced, naturally, on Abloh’s Instagram feed). To his detractors (it’s fair to say he’s Marmite) he is a hype meister, extracting maximum dollar for minimum originality. To his many fans, he’s the ultimate democratiser who can, when necessary speak more conventionally luxurious language. Last September, he sent a Princess Diana-themed collection down his Off-White catwalk, paying tribute to her various phases, from Shy Di to Dynasty Di, with polka dot dresses, gauzy evening wear and some rather impressive, tailored leather blazers. Pastiche or prelude to greater things? The debate continues. The Louis Vuitton move had been rumoured for months, but has nonetheless provoked some consternation within the industry. Despite turning over more than £7 billion last year, Louis Vuitton positions itself assiduously at the apex of the luxury market. Or at least it does with its womenswear, where creative director Nicolas Ghesquiere makes much of his emphasis on craft and expensive materials. Last summer’s Louis Vuitton sell-out, limited collaboration with Supreme, another street-wear label highly sought after by (mainly male) affluent teens, rappers and, word has it, middle aged Chinese businessmen, took a different approach, and appealed to a new customer, an outcome not lost on the French behemoth’s CEO, Michael Burke. The under 30 male’s relationship with luxury is not the same as older customers who have certain preconceptions of service, product category and delivery methods. Far from seeing the queues for the Supreme collaboration as a betrayal of Vuitton’s luxury heritage, customers, Burke suggested, actually enjoyed being part of an Instagrammable moment. “It’s about placing yourself in a sub-culture. It’s not just waiting in line for six hours. It’s interacting with like minds. It’s the antithesis of buying online where everything is available to everyone, 24/7. It’s a moment. Miss it and it’s gone.” Burke, who previously worked with Abloh when they were both at Fendi, knows the latter is a skilled alchemist of “the moment”, as at home on video as he is behind the decks- articulate, affable and constantly multi-tasking. As an American of Ghanaian descent, he also brings some diversity to the ranks of European fashion’s somewhat homogenous top tier. Whether he has the gravitas to flesh out a Vuitton look that will stand the test of time remains to be seen. For the moment at least, what sells is sneakers, t-shirts, logos, backpacks and interesting looking, quasi-technical outerwear. Get these items right - and that means masterminding a compelling back story, advertising campaign and being in command of all your communication channels – and you can make millions. How long before the streetwear trend runs out of steam is anyone’s guess. There are signs it’s already panting, in which case there is that Princess Di collection as evidence that Abloh is more than a one trick pony. “Often,” says Burke, “you don’t know whether it’s a success until sometime later. What I will say is that in ten years, I will have to change half of this business. The issue is, which half? Keeping one foot in tradition and the other in the future is a nerve wracking dance”. Burke is a famously shrewd operator. So is Abloh.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Tuesday marked the first day of spring, and Catherine, the Duchess of Cambridge, chose a suitably seasonal look for her latest official engagement, wearing a bespoke mint-green coatdress and coordinating shift by Jenny Packham to host a symposium about early intervention for children. Her Royal Highness brought together academics, researchers, educators, practitioners and non-profit workers at the Royal Society of Medicine to discuss perinatal, maternal and infant mental health and the importance of supporting parents. It's no surprise that the Duchess turned to Packham to outfit her for such a high-profile event. She has worn pieces by Packham on more than a dozen occasions since 2011, and the London-based designer is often mentioned as one of the possible fashion names behind Meghan Markle’s wedding gown. Coatdresses have become one of the Duchess's wardrobe staples before and during her third pregnancy, but wearing an open coat over a matching dress struck a sartorial note that for many royal-watchers brought to mind another member of the family: the Queen. In fact the Duchess's green coat closely emulated one of Her Majesty's looks from 45 years ago: a mint-green silk coat and matching dress that she wore to the polo in June 1973.  During her decades in the spotlight, Her Majesty has identified brightly coloured coats and coordinating dresses as her failsafe event-dressing formula. Her priorities are to remain at all times dignified, appropriate and visible - "I have to be seen to be believed," she has said. Catherine could do far worse than to draw lessons from HM's approach (including the importance of weighting the hemlines of silk dresses with chains to avoid the perils of strong gusts), though she has updated the Queen's tactics in a manner befitting the millennial generation of royals. Her dresses tend to be shorter than the Queen's, she eschews hats on all but the most formal occasions, and her heels - whilst still sensible - are higher than Her Majesty's low block heels.  Even though the TV series Sex and the City wrapped 12 years ago, the hysteria surrounding the franchise shows no sign of dying down. So when it was announced that Sarah Jessica Parker was fronting Divorce - another HBO TV series set in New York - comparisons to the seminal noughties TV show came thick and fast. Aware of this, SJP and costume director Arjun Bhasin were careful to make sure that the clothes in Sky Atlantic's Divorce looked nothing like Carrie Bradshaw's - or Sarah Jessica's for that matter. "Sarah Jessica was a part of hiring me for the TV show and I think what she liked was I reacted to the character and the script, rather than her," Bhasin tells The Telegraph. "What we wanted to do with the character was something completely new. It becomes tricky for an actor when they become synonymous with a character because they can’t break out and do something else, so it was nice to restart the whole process from scratch and not keep that in the back of your mind." It helps of course that in Divorce Frances Parker is a mother of two going through a difficult break-up, battling through New York's brutal winter to get to work on the commuter train and home again with enough takeaway to pacify her unhappy children. Hardly a place fro Carrie Bradshaw's stilettos and attention-seeking outfits.  "It is a completely different show with a different mood," explains Bhasin. "The character is much older and has a different set of problems, a very different economic bracket and is in a different mental space, so it had to be different. If it's a parade of fashion there needs to be a reason why; why would a woman going through a divorce in upstate New York want to be a fashion show? It goes against the grain of what the story is about. But you do try consciously to stay away from things that seem like obvious choices and make new choices that are bold and interesting." So whilst Carrie Bradshaw's aesthetic was all about cult, must-have labels, in Divorce Parker wears almost exclusively vintage. "There was something about this show that felt nostalgic of a time, so we used a lot of vintage clothing and went back and used a lot of pieces from the 40s and 50s as bases to construct this character," explains Bhasin. "Almost her entire wardrobe is vintage, because there was a conscious effort not to do fashion brands, but we made it look very contemporary and modern. She isn’t brand conscious - she’s a classic woman, with two kids, she works, she has to commute in New York in the elements - it has to tick all those boxes so we did things that felt real to that." Whilst there are a few designer labels in the mix - Parker's handbags are vintage Coach, she wears some Ungaro dresses, an Armani trench and Hermes trousers - all of the vintage had to be customised to make it work on screen.  "We tweaked them to make them look more modern so it doesn’t look like she’s in a period film," explains the costume designer. "You have to restore them, alter them and fix them - we would change sleeves and collars, cut them down and add fabrics and line them. There was a lot of work that went into making them durable and workable for a contemporary situation." "She’s going through a divorce, she has kids, she’s not shopping every day and so we played with putting different pieces together and making a story," he explains. "You'll see her all dressed up, but she is still wearing the same old coat she wore the day before to go to work, but she’s paired it with a nicer dress. There is a certain seriousness to New York in the winter and the repeating of the coat becomes a symbol of that every day and mundane." There's other symbolism to Sarah Jessica's outfits, too. Arjun Bhasin also used costumes to show just how much Frances and Robert have grown apart. "Different people react to crisis situations in different ways and with Frances it was very much that she wanted to wake up every morning and keep it together. There was a sense she wanted to be neat and put together." Her husband meanwhile is scruffy, which shows how much they have distanced. "I wanted there to be a sense that he has had a past also, but it has collapsed," explains Bhasin. "He was possibly a suit wearing person at one point and has now given all that up and is a plaid shirt guy. He can't really get it together so starts throwing a tie on over flannel shirts, his suits are never quite right and he wears his construction boots with everything. He has let go of himself, and so visually they don’t go together. But you can imagine a time when they did, so you feel like this is something that was a thing and has collapsed."​ "We were very excited about the films of the late 70s and talked about the style of women in the late 70s and some other actors came into the forefront," explains Bhasin. "I always love films like Kramer vs Kramer,  American Gigolo and and some of the Woody Allen films in 70s set in New York. Those became the foundations of research, but there were also other iconic style moments I looked at, such as Katherine Hepburn and Charlotte Rampling and so we tried to build the character of Frances around those people. It’s classic, elegant and chic, but it’s not ‘fashion.’ It feels old worldy."  Since Alessandro Michele took the reins at Gucci in 2015, his designs have ushered in a new era of unashamedly beautiful, decorative fashion. Florals, sequins and jacquard are suddenly everywhere in abundance and the Kering-owned company has seen wholesale sales rise by 10% and own-store sales increase by 3%. If further proof were needed that fashion is in thrall to Michele right now, it came in the form of the whoops and cheers which the magnificently bearded Italian designer received from an audience of fans as he took to the stage at the Vogue festival in London last night - many of them also wearing Gucci loafers, carrying Dionysius bags or wearing his now trademark floral jackets and shimmering pleated skirts.  Dressed in an emerald green, elaborately embroidered bomber jacket with his initial on the front, stonewashed jeans, ribbed sports socks and black Mary-Janes with jangling silver embellishment, Michele spoke in vivid detail about his unique aesthetic and how it has come to dominate fashion. "Vintage is my vocabulary... like the notes of a musician," he told British Vogue's editor-in-chief Alexandra Shulman.  The designer discussed how he had spent 14 years working at Gucci, first under Tom Ford - whose style he described as "American and hedonistic" and then with Frida Giannini.  But it was after a four-hour impromptu meeting at his home in Rome with Gucci's CEO Marco Bizzari - which was originally meant just to be a chat before Michele departed Gucci himself - that the designer had the chance to pose his "one idea" for the house. This was the cue for Michele to tell the audience about his rather fabulous abode and - most importantly - his walk-in wardrobe. "It's a little room, it's like Alice in Wonderland," he explained. "It's like a toy store... I have shoes which aren't my size but I just buy them to keep, there are jewels, miniatures and paintings," he went on. Michele has used his approach to his own home in the re-design of Gucci boutiques - which Shulman described as "candy stores". As Michele put it: "With the stores, I just want to envision my perfect wardrobe." Beauty is clearly Michele's obsession. "I never want to go out wearing something sad," he proclaimed. But his idea of beauty is not a simple one. "I want to be confused by what I'm looking at," he said. "If you fall in love with a beautiful man, it's not easy. It's easier to be with an ugly man. There is a danger to beauty." Of his most recent show, Michele told the audience that he was imagining the end of the world. "It's a creepy aesthetic. It's sweet but also deep. I think the end of the world is when you  are in touch with something beautiful." Discussing how he creates his collections, he said, "I become mad, like a fever creating this story which goes from Elizabeth I to New York to the sea." Michele has passed on this free-spirited approach to design to his team, explaining that "in the beginning my way of working didn't make sense for them but now they are in this nonsense world too."  Michele has helped to drive a new gender-fluid approach to fashion with his work, recently announcing that the men's and women's shows would be combined but also adding feminine flourishes to menwear and traditionally masculine references to womenswear. His reasoning, once again, it comes back to beauty. "I wanted to talk about ambiguity because ambiguous things are the most beautiful," he said. "It is more about beauty than gender. I am in-between. Gender and sex are about rules which we have invented but we are animals, we belong to nature." The pressure faced by creative directors has been one of fashion's most contentious topics in recent years, but it seems that Michele's ability to live in a "dream" has helped him to remain creative, imaginative and - most importantly - happy.  "It's better if you don't know what you're doing tomorrow," he laughed. "Honestly, the only pressure is not having the time to do everything. It's a beautiful pressure. I don't feel the pressure of the market - otherwise I wouldn't be able to work." Instead of embroiling himself in the commercial aspect of the role, Michele declared: "I prefer to play like a kid." Anyway it's all part of the strategy which is making Gucci so desirable again. "For the last ten years, fashion has been full of product," he said. "But fashion should be about this amazing idea which you are trying to understand and then you are buying the idea, not the object." With his wide-ranging obsessions - at one point, he discussed being inspired by the women of the Tudor period "when you would have to scare with your clothes, one day you would be alive and the next you're dead" - Michele doesn't look set to run out of these fantastical ideas any time soon.  Just when we thought that Michele's appearance at the Vogue Festival had passed by in a celebration of all things beautiful and otherworldly, Shulman opened questions to the audience and a brave 12 year-old girl stood up and asked; "Is your fur ethically sourced? Because I was worried because I heard that you used kangaroo fur." She was referring to the fur-lined slip-on loafers which have become one of Michele's most recognisable creations. "I have to be honest, I love plants and animals. I'm fascinated by animals. We (Gucci) represent things which belong to the earth, it's impossible to ignore," Michele began. "If you have respect for the kangaroo and care about the way it died, it's completely different. I know it's hard. From my point of view, I'm not the kind of person who will say tomorrow, 'OK, I'll stop it.' I feel the power of the earth. It doesn't mean you should stop using it but you should care how about it has died." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The slinky dress that Marilyn Monroe wore for her iconic sultry performance of 'Happy Birthday Mr President' to John F. Kennedy is to be auctioned, and it is expected it will reach up to £2.2 million.  At the time this dress was just as provocative as Monroe's breathy bedroom voice. On stage at Madison Square Garden she stripped off her white fur to reveal one of the world's first 'naked dresses.' A predecessor to the totally sheer gowns that now are a common feature at music awards shows, this then-scandalous gown created by Hollywood costume designer Jean Louis was skin-tight and matched her skin tone, giving the illusion that she was wearing nothing but sequins on her bare skin.  The backless evening gown was covered in thousands of hand-stitched rhinestones and was designed to accentuate the famous Monroe curves, in the same way that illusion dresses favoured by Kim Kardashian and Jennifer Lopez are structured today. Legend has it the dress was so tight she had to be sewn into it.  Jean Louis was head designer at Columbia Pictures between 1944 and 1960. Louis created illusion dresses for actress and singer Marlene Dietrich for her tour, and it is thought that Monroe asked Dietrich who had designed her 'naked' dresses. The dress - which Marilyn called "skin and beads" -will be auctioned in November at Julien's Auctions in Los Angeles and the house estimates that it could sell for up to £2.2 million. According to reports, she bought the dress originally for £9,000 but as a piece of American history, its value has soared. In 1999 the dress was auctioned at Christie's and sold for $1.27 million, becoming the most expensive item of clothing sold at auction in history.  This is one of 500 of Monroe's personal items which are expected to smash records when they are auctioned off in Los Angeles this November. Among the collection is her used 1947 Revlon lipstick in pink 'Bachelor's Carnation', complete with smudges around the rim, is expected to fetch up to £13,500 when it goes up for auction 54 years after the singer's untimely death. “Such is the Marilyn factor that we estimate the lipstick will sell for $15,000-20,000 dollars, or probably much more. It’s so personal,” explains Martin Nolan, executive director at LA auction house Julien’s, to The Telegraph. “She’s this blonde bombshell who has been frozen in time,” Nolan who has been working on the auction for years says of the enduring fascination with Monroe. “We still think of her as that elegant 36-year-old who everyone feels they know and love, even if she was before their time. Ask an eight-year-old who Marilyn is, and they’ll probably know.” “No other celebrity has achieved the collectability of Marilyn Monroe. She transcends continents as she has fans all over the world and she transcends age groups as she has fans from five years old to 95 years old,” says Nolan, of why this auction is so important.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Missing, last seen June 2015: Lady Gaga’s crazy style. Reward for finder. Lady Gaga has been through many a wacky phase. Remember the tea cup phase? The Princess Diana phase? The Donatella Versace phase? The face-horn phase? See, more phases than the moon. Indeed the 29-year-old has made herself the queen of reinvention since hitting the spotlight in 2007 (much to the annoyance of her predecessor Madonna). But it seems she’s grown a little tired of her sartorial escapades. After all, a see-through plastic dress and 19-inch heels just aren’t practical sometimes. Or ever. Nowhere has this new direction been clearer than at last night’s Golden Globes. The singer and actress, who picked up her first award for acting for her role in American Horror Story, was resplendent in a fitted black velvet gown with exaggerated hips, sweetheart neckline and off-the-shoulder sleeves, custom-made by Atelier Versace. Her platinum blonde hair was cropped above the shoulder and styled in Marilyn Monroe-esque curls, her make-up was classic and she accessorised with Neil Lane diamonds. No flame-throwing bra, no bits on show, not even a whiff of a meat product. You see, Gaga is no longer gaga about hitting the headlines. Well, at least not for her dress sense. It’s all thanks to her stylist Brandon Maxwell. The pair have worked together for six years; Maxwell used to assist Gaga’s former stylist Nicola Formichetti (the man responsible for the meat dress and other such wonders), but when he went out on his own a few years ago, Formichetti told him to take the singer with him as his first client. Maxwell’s influence has been hugely apparent – the gimmicks are mostly gone, replaced with sweeping custom-made gowns by the likes of Azzedine Alaia, Valentino and Roberto Cavalli. Of course, Gaga often adds her own sprinkle of unconventionality in the form of bleached eyebrows or a jaunty wig - and her previous eccentricity does still made an appearance occasionally - but on the whole she errs more towards sophisticated than silly. His aesthetic has clearly rubbed off on the singer. When he was named one of Hollywood’s most powerful stylists by The Hollywood Reporter last (despite only having one celeb client), Gaga made a comment that seemed to confirm she was over going over-the-top: “So many people want to be more edgy and darker and avant-garde. But for me, it’s more interesting to celebrate being classic.” Of his new look for the star, Maxwell has said: “I guess it looks more timeless and elegant because in my mind that’s how I see her. Obviously I have my own style that I’ve grown up with and that I veer towards.” Last year he unveiled his eponymous label, which has proved startlingly popular. Gwyneth Paltrow, Reese Witherspoon and Kate Hudson are just a few of the big names to wear his beautifully-cut, simplistic but powerful designs, and of course Gaga herself. He documents every famous wearer with an Instagram post on his personal account.  “I want to make clothes that are almost a uniform for women and that last for years, that are timeless and classic and that are worth their money,” he told the New York Times shortly before his debut. His former boss Nicole Formichetti is also a fan of Gaga's new look. “Gaga became so iconic with these incredible outfits, I’m sure it was hard for Brandon to take over,” Formichetti told the New York Times. “But amazingly, he injected his sensibility. She became very sophisticated and beautiful, and it was more about her personality.” All hail the new Lady Gaga. Having first bared nearly all for its Burberry Body fragrance campaign in 2011 ­– save a strategically placed trench coat – this Christmas Rosie is back in the buff for Burberry, with only a monogrammed cashmere scarf to shield her modesty. Rosie’s nude is the latest shot to be revealed from Burberry’s festive, Billy Elliot tribute-themed campaign which has seen a multitude of famous faces from Elton John and Julie Walters to Romeo Beckham and James Corden strike a mid-flight pose while bouncing on a trampoline. It’s her fourth campaign for the British heritage brand which has a fondness for English Roses. Rosie, 28, also has a fully-clothed role alongside fellow model Naomi Campbell in the recently released three-minute campaign film that imitates Billy Elliot’s iconic opening credits, in which Billy bounces on his bed to the sound of T-Rex’s Cosmic Dance.  However, she decided on something a little more provocative for the accompanying stills, shot by Mario Testino. Well, there was also the small matter of trying to keep that scarf perfectly in place.  Thousands tuned in to watch Ariana Grande perform at the One Love Manchester benefit concert last night, with tickets raising more than £2 million for the victims of the terrorist attack in the city on Monday 22nd May. Anyone who wasn’t at the concert can still donate, though, as the One Love Manchester merchandise, as worn by Grande on the night, has gone on sale, with all profits going straight to the British Red Cross Society and its We Love Manchester Emergency Fund. Grande’s jumper retails at £40 on the specially set-up website uk.onelovemanchestershop.com, and is available in four different colours and sizes from small to xx-large. T-shirts bearing the same graffiti design are being sold for £20, as well as designs emblazoned with ‘I heart MCR’ logo and the specially-designed bunny ears logo - which merges the singer’s Dangerous Woman tour emblem with a peace ribbon. The black and pink T-shirt worn by Miley Cyrus during the concert is also on sale for £20. Prices start at just £5 for badges, meaning that people are able to donate no matter what their budget.  The wave of sexual misconduct scandals rolling through Hollywood, politics and the fashion world has engulfed another high-profile fashion personality, with photographer Bruce Weber facing accusations of harassment from not one, but two male models. Last week, the New York Post reported that model Jason Boyce was suing Weber for inappropriate touching during a December 2014 casting session at Weber’s flat. Yesterday, a second accuser, model Mark Ricketson, held a press conference with Boyce to say that Weber had also harassed him in a similar context. Both men described separate experiences of meeting Weber for casting sessions during which the photographer, known for his sexually charged work, instructed them to remove their clothes, fondle themselves and then engage in sexual activity. Boyce called the experience “terrifying and humiliating” during the press conference. “I have suffered from depression and anxiety as a result of my photo shoot with Bruce Weber, and want this behaviour to end now. I filed this lawsuit to show that this kind of abuse is wrong, and to hopefully stop it from happening to more of us.” For Ricketson, the encounter took a similar form, with Weber guiding Ricketson’s hand to touch his genitals during an initial meeting about a shoot. Although his experience took place 13 years ago, placing it outside the statute of limitations, he said he decided to come forward to corroborate Boyce’s account and support other victims. "I’ve ... talked to other young men who, like me, knew that if we protested or refused then we would be blacklisted, not just from the photo shoot, but likely from our agency," Ricketson said at the press conference, as reported by USA Today. "There is no safe place to go. If you wanted to work, you did what you were told." Models have long been among the most visible but least empowered participants in the fashion industry. Young models in particular describe a heightened awareness of their own replaceability, and a sense that anyone who complained -- for instance, about a lack of adequate changing facilities, food on set, or even inappropriate touching -- could be branded “difficult” by agents, bookers or photographers, and overlooked for future work opportunities. But the growing ranks of victims who have come forward with their experiences is leading a pushback, largely via social media. Model Cameron Russell has led the charge in the fashion industry by re-posting on Instagram anonymised messages from models, male and female, who recount abusive episodes, along with the hashtag #MyJobShouldNotIncludeAbuse. Lisa Bloom, the lawyer representing Ricketson and Boyce (she's also a former legal adviser to film producer Harvey Weinstein), said the modelling industry is “overdue for accountability for its exploitation of models.” "Others have told me that they left the business because they could no longer put up with the exploitation," she said at the press conference. "Some have said they thought being harassed and groped was just part of the business. But it’s not. Every worker, regardless of industry, is entitled to a workplace free of sexual harassment." Weber has built his career on sexually suggestive images of sweat-slicked, muscular models, most prominently for Calvin Klein and Abercrombie & Fitch, and glossy portraits of Hollywood stars. His nickname in the late 1980s was ‘starmaker’ for his power to catapult models to fame. Weber has yet to respond to the allegations. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Even if you have not heard of The Get Down yet, soon it will be all you're talking about. Baz Luhrmann’s highly-anticipated first television series, which lands on Netflix next Friday, charts the beginnings of hip hop in the late 70s, following the teenagers who discover Grandmaster Flash’s underground club in the torched, graffiti-splattered, gang battlefield, otherwise known as the South Bronx. The director's aim was to explore how high school students who had nothing ignited one of the most culturally significant, explosive movements in popular culture. "I thought, 'How did that creativity, that would go on to change the world, come from a place that was on its knees?'" Luhrmann told The Telegraph last weekend. These teenagers might have had very little, but the style in the hip hop club The Get Down is just as considered and influential as the highly-documented disco looks over in Manhattan at the infamous Studio 54 nightclub, which also opened in 1977. Even in the very early days of hip hop culture, a pair of trainers could elevate someone to legendary status, and so the red Pumas and customised jackets flashing across the screen in every episode are just as integral to Luhrmann's story as the epic soundtrack and central love story.  Luhrmann worked on the project for a decade with his wife Catherine Martin who served as executive producer and also oversaw the fashion alongside costume director Jeriana San Juan. Martin’s unparalleled knack for knowing how clothes can tell a story - an understanding that has earned her four academy awards for her work on other Luhrmann directed films including The Great Gatsby and Moulin Rouge - means that The Get Down is set to be one of the most exciting small screen fashion moments of the year.  Here Catherine Martin decodes the style in the Netflix series: The boys in the series idolize Shaolin Fantastic, the graffiti artist and dealer for the gangster Fat Annie, who parkour leaps between Bronx high rises in pristine, red suede Pumas. 'We hear, he has over 100 pairs,' the lead boys repeat wide-eyed. Just like in 2016, trainers signified status, and Martin worked with brands to reproduce the exact styles the kids were wearing in 1977.  "There are three sneakers that appear in the show that are considered acceptable," explains Martin. "Everything else was looked down upon because your mother had bought you a no-brand shoe and you were going to be a 'loser'. There were three shoes - Converse, the classic American sports shoe. There were Pro Keds, which are just about to be relaunched in the States, and the Puma. The suede Puma was the top of the top and certain colours were more difficult to get." Puma, Converse and Pro-Keds all re-made shoes in the correct colours and styles of the period for the series. "I explained that we were doing very pre-history of hip hop so we needed to have a multi-voice front of trainers, because it just wouldn’t be realistic to have everyone wearing Pro-Keds or Pumas and so they made us loads of sneakers all in the correct colours, because they subtly evolve over the period and there are so many sneaker freaks that we know we needed to be really accurate." As for why Shaolin Fantastic wears red trainers, Martin explains : "We gave a list to Baz of the colours that you could get at the time and he picked the red because it’s so iconic and looks so good on screen, but you would always try and get the most unusual colours. It was all about keeping your shoes immaculate and clean which is why they talk about him having 100 pairs. People carried around toothbrushes to clean their shoes - sometimes even today in the Bronx you still see people putting plastic bags over their shoes so they don’t get dirty." "If you don’t have many resources, what do you do?" Martin says. "You have to make style out of what you have at your disposal. You have pants, a t-shirt, you have sneakers which are the quintessential shoe of a teenager. The style was developed out of this very limited palette, so you’d match everything. You’d have red socks, red Pumas, a red t- shirt, a red jacket, because it doesn’t cost money to make things match." You would also show off everything you have which is new, hence the toothpaste-smeared sneakers. "You know how people still leave the sticker on the hat? That’s a relic of wanting things to appear new and perfect and clean," Martin explains. "It all comes out of developing style out of a very limited number of choices. When you don't have many resources, one of the most important priorities is that you have the money to buy something new, so there's an obsession on things looking crisp which is anathema to those of us who come from a different cultural background with vintage things looking old and distressed." The fashion in The Get Down is tribal, from the war lords in their customised jackets to the disco kings in their flared jeans. "That is very true to the reality because people wanted to associate and recognise those who were in the same sub culture as they were," Martin explains. "For gangs it was really important to fly your colours and then other gang members knew who you were and belonged with them. Similarly, people who were into hip hop wore garments that identified them with their peers. It’s all about as teenagers, really identifying with that subculture, like being a punk or a new romantic. Youth needs to separate itself from the adult world on one hand, but it needs to identify with a group and often that group is linked to a musical choice." A show about the birth of hip hop could easily be male-dominated, but The Get Down also shows strong, ambitious women, from formidable gangsters to girls defying their evangelical parents. "Our real baddy is a woman, which is great because you never see that, and she is - to quote the hip hop phrase - a bad a**," Martin says. "Within black culture in the United States certainly looking good has always been important within that community, whether it came out of the idea of Sunday best and women getting ready to go to church in incredibly well thought out outfits. It's very much about that pride in your appearance and displaying the pride in yourself by dressing well and not being afraid of your own sexuality. You see all of the girls really embracing who they are - they have a big journey in the show and we wanted to embrace that strength, that sexuality." The gangster owner of the club 'Los Infernos', Fat Annie, was based on an unlikely style icon from the time. "We used a lot of references strangely from Elizabeth Taylor and her kaftan moments in the late 60s and 70s. Despite being a larger than life baddy, she still took great pride in her appearance." The white Australian director recognises that it ‘is not my story to tell’, but to ensure it is believable and handled correctly he worked with a group of the founders of the hip-hop community. "It's the first show I've ever done set in a period that I actually lived through," says Martin. "One of the interesting things about this pre-history of hip hop is that people who were part of this movement are still alive. We had access to Nelson George who was there at the time, or Grandmaster Flash or Kool Herc." Mamoudou Athie who plays Grandmaster Flash in the series doesn't just wear a tracksuit like his, but wears some of the artists' own pieces which he has kept from the late 70s.  "We looked to a lot of photographic references, but also it’s about imagining yourself with the palette of clothes that would have been available to you in the 70s and then imagining the character. A combination of really researching what was available and making a closet for each of the characters as a whole and then pulling out things from the closet." As for whether Martin is worried about getting the look totally accurate, she says: "People spend their entire time writing articles about how inauthentic any period costumes I do are. I strive to understand the social milieu, the place these people are coming from and to work with the actor and the director to tell the story they want to tell. And ultimately sometimes, being strictly period doesn’t work to tell the story, but really with this show it is very accurate, but equally we’re not making a documentary." While you might assume that the wardrobe for a show set in the 1970s would be mostly vintage, Martin and Jeriana San Juan struggled to find the right original pieces from the period. "We used some vintage pieces [including archive pieces by Halston and Diane Von Furstenberg], but for the main cast most of it was made mainly because we were doing very specific things - it surprised me how much we actually made for the show. It was a huge amount."  In much the same way that The Great Gatsby ignited a trend for all things 1920s, The Get Down is sure to impact how we dress; from making you want a denim A-Line skirt within the first 15 minutes of the pilot to crowning Pro-Keds this summer's must-have new trainers. The Get Down will be available on Netflix on 12th August. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  On a hot Sunday in Paris last week, Paul Smith was backstage juggling a rubber fish. The fish was the invitation to his SS18 fashion show starting within the hour and he was anticipating the front row looking daft as they used them to fan themselves under the glass-roofed gym of the Lycée Carnot. “It’ll either be brilliant or I’ll be hiding,” he said. Sir Paul, 70, is not like other designers. He wears his eccentricity well. Like his famous suits, he comes tailored with a twist and over 47 years he’s made a serious and successful business out of it. He sells his clothes in over 70 countries, with 39 stores worldwide and hundreds of global franchises.  It’s the kind of publicity that many global fashion brands would have paid for if they could; dressing Prince Harry’s bride-to-be Meghan Markle for their first television interview as a couple, just hours after they announced their engagement to the world. But rather than a household name, the American actress chose a bottle green dress by under-the-radar Italian label P.A.R.O.S.H for her first big appearance, inadvertently giving the vintage-inspired line what was likely the greatest PR boost in its 25 year history. “It was totally insane, an amazing surprise,” founder Paolo Rossello tells The Telegraph, explaining that he had absolutely no idea that Markle had bought a dress from his company. “We were astonished to see Meghan with our bow detail dress. It was a dream.” The frenzy that Rossello and his team have subsequently experienced in the last 24 hours has, unsurprisingly, been unprecedented and is entirely comparable to that which the British brand Issa were overwhelmed by when the Duchess of Cambridge wore their blue silk ‘Sapphire London’ dress for her own engagement interview back in 2010. For Issa, overall sales doubled following Middleton’s initial appearance, after an immediate sell-out of the style in question. For Rossello? “The dress was sold out in less than one hour in all shops and online,” he confirms. The ‘Meghan effect’ was already a verified phenomenon before this, as several styles that Markle has been wearing since she confirmed her relationship with the prince last year have gone on to sell out, causing a rush of media and social media coverage. A plain white shirt by the New York designer (and Markle’s friend) Misha Nonoo was perhaps one of the greatest recent examples; despite its $185 price tag, the shirt became a global hit once fans cottoned on to the style’s name ‘The Husband Shirt’ - and the message it implied was that an engagement was imminent. Similarly, despite being priced at £489, Markle’s engagement dress likely appealed so strongly to fans because of its simplicity. “It’s a Parosh iconic dress enriched with bow for this season, but suitable for any occasion,” Rossello says. “I thought Meghan looked very sophisticated matching it with high heeled shoes and white coat -it was very feminine.” Rossello says that this ethos, and the constant evolution of seemingly simple designs, has always been key to his business. “The concept is to create simple clothing pieces enriched with special details that give a pinch of femininity to every look,” he explains. “I’m inspired by vintage prints, silhouettes and shapes, but mixing them with the new.” Earlier this year, Issa founder Daniella Helayel detailed how the Duchess’ wearing of her Sapphire London dress at her engagement ultimately contributed to the downfall of her relatively-young business. She struggled to fulfil the sky-high demand for that particular design and the rest of her label suffered as a result. Rossello, however, has a different outlook and many more years of production experience to help cope with the new interest. Fans still wanting to get their hands on Markle’s dress can rejoice; “Yes we are reissuing it, hopefully within a week” Rossello confirms. The only difference? “It will now have the name of ‘The Meghan’.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Unless you've been living under a rock for the past year or two, you'll know that Gucci is the most in-demand brand of the moment. To own a pair of designer Alessandro Michele's fur-lined loafers, a glitzy bomber jacket or Soho handbag is a knowing nod to the ardent adoration which his maximalist reinvention of the Italian house has inspired. And just when you thought Gucci couldn't get any hotter, Michelle Obama has only gone and worn one of Michele's dresses to appear on one of the biggest TV programmes in the US, The Ellen Show.  The design is from Gucci's spring/summer 2016 collection and is based on the La Carte de Tendre, a map created in 1654 by novelist and philosopher Madeleine de Scudery as a guide to romance. With spots marked with milestones like 'Generosity', 'Sincerity' and 'The Lake of Indifference', the artefact inspired what The Telegraph's fashion director Lisa Armstrong labelled 'madly pretty clothes'. Obama's dress comes with delicate sequin detailling around the neckline and waist and is still available to buy for £2,270. With its midi length, nipped waist silhouette, the dress conforms precisely with the flattering shape which has become a style signature during Obama's eight years as First Lady. But the comparisions with her wardrobe to date mostly stop there.  While Obama has undoubtedly ushered in a more playful, relaxed and feminine take on First Lady style- no more staid skirt suits and pearls to see here- her clothes have always come with a very considered message. Take the fact that she chose Jason Wu, then an up-and coming young 26 year-old designer working in New York, to create the gown she would wear for the Inauguration Ball in 2009- a decision with a clear agenda to promote young American design talent.  There have been countless occassions when Obama has exercised diplomacy with her fashion choices too. In the UK, she has worn outfits by homegrown names such as Christopher Kane, Roksanda Ilincic and Preen by Thornton Bregazzi. In South Africa, she wore an ASOS Africa top (the range raised funds for African charities) while Indian designer Naeem Khan was chosen to design the gown which Obama wore to welcome India's prime minister to the White House in 2009.  Wherever she goes in the world, Obama rarely misses an opportunity to promote young American designers, regularly calling upon Thakoon, Altuzarra and Proenza Schouler for her high-profile visits; and of course there's often a J.Crew cardigan thrown in for good affordability measure. So if 'Outfits with Purpose' have been Obama's thing until now, yesterday's Gucci look suggests that FLOTUS is finally ready to quite simply have fun with her wardrobe. There is no agenda to this divine Gucci look- it is just beautiful and exactly the sort of thing that you might purchase if you were a woman with a penchant for joyful prints and with sufficient funds to purchase.  And maybe this is reading too much into it, but after dedicating eight years of her life to helping her husband fulfil the biggest job in the world, by wearing a dress emblazoned with a map originally created to show the path to a happy relationship- perhaps it's Barack and not the rest of the world that Michelle is speaking to with her fashion this time?   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  British supermodel Jourdan Dunn is beautiful,of course, but her individual, outspoken and determined attitude has elevated her to become a true powerhouse in recent years. Not only does she walk in the biggest catwalk shows -she became the first black model to walk for Prada in a decade in 2008 but her latest was Balmain at Paris fashion week- but she’s now a front row fixture too (this season she was a VIP guest at Burberry and Michael Kors) and behind-the-scenes, there’s a major empire-building project on the cards. Dunn has already collaborated with high-street stalwart Marks and Spencer on a childrenswear collection called Lil Lon-Dunn inspired by her seven year-old son Riley and starred in her own cooking show- ‘Well Dunn’- on Jay-Z’s Youtube channel. The next string she’s adding to her bow is a savvy partnership with Missguided, the Manchester-based affordable retailler which is giving more traditional fashion brands a run for their money with its on-trend, fast-turnaround collections and friendly, community-centric messaging: customers are encouraged to post pictures of themselves on social media wearing their purchases with the hashtag #babesofmissguided. Most Missguided fans probably agree that Dunn is a babe. “I had a late one last night after the Burberry show and I had a really early call time today so I’m hanging right now,” she laughs when we speak to discuss the collection during London fashion week. Despite her high-level relationships with luxury labels, Dunn says that she and Missguided have been courting one another for well over a year. “They did a t-shirt with my name, and Cara (Delevingne), Naomi (Campbell) and Kate (Moss) on it,” she recalls. “I asked them to send me one and then Cara and Naomi Instagrammed it. They’ve always had love for me and I’ve had love them.” The enormous 96-piece collection launches tomorrow and is comprised of sportswear inspired designs which combine ease with youthful glamour- plus a few seriously sparkly evening pieces thrown in for good measure. “This is my street-chic style,” says Dunn. “I feel like Missguided consumers are girls like me or the girls who follow me. I wanted to create something practical, stylish and cool.” In fact, she’s designed everything with her multi-faceted life in mind, where one day she’s jetting off on a shoot while the next she’s at home hanging out with Riley. “For me, I’m not a Mum who takes my son to school in heels - that’s the last thing I want to do at 7 in the morning,” she says. “I just want to pull on a nice sweatpant- then I might put the heels on later. It’s about being effortlessly cool.” Dunn emphasises that it was important for her to create a collection which all girls could embrace. “I think the great thing about Missguided is that it’s affordable, cool stuff. I could easily have done something in a higher price range but I wanted girls to be part of my world and have Lon-Dunn in their wardrobe, whether they’re on a student loan or a tight budget or just have pocket money, they can get affordable pieces which still look great. But even people who have a higher salary can mix and match, I love to wear my designer pieces with sportswear and high street- it makes everything more interesting.” Dunn’s personal brand- which will see her expand her Lon-Dunn lines and bring out a recipe book in the not too distant future- has become just as much about her relatability and touch of the ‘real’ in a fashion world where it is so often only the veneer which is seen. Her message of solidarity is incorporated into the collection via the five girls she picked to help model it. Her ‘female collective’ includes Leomie Anderson, a fellow model who has become a campaigner for body confidence, Rina Sawayama, a singer who has used her insecurities to inspire her, Braina Laviena, a model and photographer who supports the Free the Nipple movement, Rainy Milo, an up-and-coming musician from London and Georgie Palmer, a young emerging model. “We’re in a time now more than ever when it’s important for women to empower one another and stand up for each other,” reflects Dunn. “I really wanted to have a cast of girls who are beautiful but also have a story and are inspiring and have something going on for themselves.” Lon-Dunn x Missguided is available from tomorrow        © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This weekend sees the return of Strictly Come Dancing, at 9pm tonight on BBC One Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman will introduce the series which will run up until Christmas. The wardrobe department is tasked with creating hundreds of sparkling costumes for the dancers and celebrities, but just because Tess and Claudia aren't wearing Tango-ready costumes, doesn't mean planning their outfits isn't an equally strategic operation.  Here Tess Daly's stylist James Yardley explains the months of preparation that goes into getting dressed for Strictly Come Dancing... This is the first series of Strictly which Yardley has worked on, and he wanted to take Tess Daly in a different direction, avoiding looks that sparkle as much as the glitter ball trophy. "I noticed in the years before she’s worn a lot of sequins, feathers, draping, that don’t tend to age a woman, but can age a woman in different parts of their life," says Yardley. "Tess is 47 but she doesn’t look 47, she is so young looking and I wanted to make sure her styling matched her youth. I wanted to have that Tom Ford at Gucci look, with strong shapes, no more draping and not too much embellishment. I have left a lot of the sequins to the dancers." "I started putting things together after the BAFTAs in May so it began very early," says Yardley of finding Tess's 30 looks. "Some are custom made and bespoke and some I buy off-the-rack and tailor, so I started thinking about how I wanted her to look very early. I then started officially just after the promo shoot in August with a fitting when I got 22 outfits out of the 30 done." Although all this planning means most outfits are decided far in advance, Yardley leaves a little room for last-minute changes and swaps. "There are new things dropping all the time, so it’s good to leave a few nights' outfits slots empty, so I can buy things leading up to the final." "I have a very thorough idea of what I want her to look like from the start to the finish of the series," explains Yardley. "There’s references of people who are a similar age to her, mainly Jennifer Lopez. In particular J-LO whole aesthetic from hair to styling to make-up is something that translates well onto Tess. People probably wouldn’t think  it would but she’s a really strong reference to put on her and a strong way of channeling her style." Claudia and Tess' stylists meet up weeks before filming to plot out what they will both wear for the entire series. "Myself and Claudia’s stylist sat down when we both had done our fittings and went through as far as we could, as far as to 14 shows, and tried to match them together," explains Yardley. "We have an idea of what Tess and Claudia will both wear on the same show. They both can’t wear the same designer, they can’t wear the same colour - they favour colour on Strictly so I took that one on because I know Tess likes colour." He adds: "We look at different weeks, and put them together one by one. When you sit down and look at it all it’s 30 gowns in total. Some that you see on the first meeting might not make it to week 7, but it’s good to have an idea of where you are going with the styling to show the producers. They spend the most time on screen so it’s important they look true to the brand." "I do love mixing my designers with mid to high end brands, when it comes to Strictly there is an expectation on her as a presenter and how she should look and what she should wear," explains Yardley. "Some of the brands we're working with include Halston, for the cuts because of her height, and Roland Mouret and Antonio Berardi." The Strictly Come Dancingfinal might be over Christmas, but Tess has already started planning her gown for the series climax, as this is arguably the trickiest night to dress for. "You want to go all out and do an amazingly insane gorgeous dress that’s going to knock everyone’s socks off, but it has to be cohesive and work with Claudia," explains Yardley. "In Tess’ case you have to be able to run around in it because it’s live TV and Tess does so much running around, so the heels can’t be too high, it can’t be too narrow on the ankles, it needs to have a split and movability."  London Fashion Week was just a whistle-stop visit for Olivia Palermo this season. In just 48 hours, the style influencer was papped sitting front row at six ‘big-name’ shows, and took it upon herself to wear a different outfit for each one. Note the gap between boot and jean? This requires some serious fashion maths. Palermo’s centimetre gap errs on the conservative side of the ‘trend’, but showing up to two inches is fine. Any more and you will run the risk of looking ill-proportioned. The fashion plate took in London’s sights in cropped Tibi trousers, a Topshop bomber, Louboutin pumps and Dior shades. Her high-low balance proves that bomber jackets (this season’s trophy cover-up) don’t have to evoke a sporty look. Invest in classics that will never date, like Palermo’s Dior sunglasses. With a Tibi polo neck underneath and a sleeveless jacket on top, the 29-year-old was a prime example of layering executed well. If you don’t already have a smart sleeveless jacket in your arsenal, now is the time to invest. Use as your layering essential during the transitional months when a winter coat is too bulky. Let patterned layers peep out at subtle points - check out the discreet polo neck blouse that’s barely visible underneath all other textures.  I wasn’t around to witness the fairytale moment of Diana Spencer’s marriage to the Prince of Wales in 1981, nor to be dazzled by how she carried herself as a thoroughly modern member of the Royal Family. I was probably too busy playing with dolls to pay attention to her Panorama interview. But, growing up, she was my go-to style icon – and remains so, 20 years after her death. I was nine-years-old in the summer of 1997, and living in Rome with my family. Hello! magazine was a lifeline for my homesick mother and there was rarely a week that Diana was not on the cover. I remember being excited by every new issue that landed on the doormat and became fascinated by this beautiful woman who featured in its pages: a Princess, yes, but not like the ones I’d seen in Disney films or read about in stories. Instead of having long hair, dreamy gowns and a handsome prince to save her, this one wore chinos and walked across landmine-scarred fields. She hung out on yachts in leopard-print swimming costumes and put her arm around people in hospitals, or tearful pop stars at funerals. I was mesmerised.   And then, she was gone. Diana’s death was the first “where were you when...?” moment that I can remember. We were back in the UK visiting my grandparents at the time, and it was my Grandad who broke the news to us all, booming “Diana’s dead!” from his bedroom door at 7am. All I remember about that morning is sitting around listening to the radio and watching TV, the tributes and reports about the circumstances of her death pouring in on a loop that felt like it would never end. “I thought I’d wake up and it would all have been a nightmare,” Mum remembers. The following week, back in Italy, we did all the same things as everyone else to try to make sense of what had happened. I might not have fully understood what was going on, but I queued to write something in the book of condolence at the British Embassy. We laid roses and went to a memorial service at an Anglican church. The following, sweltering Saturday, we watched the funeral on television. I was still wearing my pyjamas and it was the first time I had seen my father cry. I was swept up in the surrealness of it all. Maybe it is because Diana’s death became a seminal moment in my childhood, but ever since that week in 1997, I have come to admire her – idolise her, even. My fascination with Diana, in what turned out to be the final months of her life, helped shape my choice of career. As a fashion journalist, I have always been interested in so much more that the latest must-have item; for me, clothes are the most powerful tool by which we can say something about ourselves before we open our mouths, and there are few who played on that truth more expertly than Diana. She taught me that fashion, which I once thought of as a personal pleasure, could shape a public persona - whether you were a Princess or not.   Take that red jumper, covered in white sheep and one black sheep, by London knitwear designers Warm and Wonderful, which Diana used to wear to polo matches in the early Eighties. I can’t help but marvel at the mischievous undertones which it may - or may not - have had. I like to think it was her tongue-in-cheek way of recognising that she was different, perhaps not feeling entirely that she belonged either in the royal family or among the public who adored her. In the context of what came to pass in the following decade or so, that black sheep motif has become imbued with so much more potential meaning. This year especially, I have explored my enthusiasm for Princess Diana, interviewing her personal stylist Anna Harvey, the designers who dressed her and covering Diana: Her Fashion Story, the exhibition currently at Kensington Palace and which uses the Princess’s wardrobe to chart her remarkable evolution from shy teenager to global celebrity. In the process, I have learnt so much more about how she used clothes to her advantage and to amplify her message. Although she hardly invented the idea of dressing diplomatically, nobody had dared to do it with such panache. In 1986, she paid tribute to her hosts on a royal tour of Japan by wearing a white outfit covered in red sports to reflect the country’s rising sun motif. It struck the perfect note between deferential and jolly.   Diana gave us so many royal firsts - most notably, perhaps, shaking hands with Aids patients - but in her style choices too, she broke boundaries. No female royal before her had worn a trouser suit in public, but Diana took things up a notch by sporting bow ties with her Jasper Conran tuxedos, making an androgynous outfit instantly playful. Mostly she eschewed gloves, but when she did wear them, she would mix and match the colours or choose a dark pair, which was seen - would you believe - as rather daring. Often when she visited hospitals, she would wear bright, floral dresses - one of her most famous was a violet design with yellow blooms by Bellville Sassoon - to give the patients something cheerful to look at. If she knew she would be meeting small children, on would go a chunky necklace to give them something to grab and play with. She called it her ‘caring wardrobe’.​ If ‘People’s Princess’ is the epithet that best encapsulates Diana, then her clothes were one of her most important allies in creating that image. Even when she was off-duty (but still knew she would be photographed) her choices were brilliantly judged, like the Philadelphia Eagles varsity jacket she wore to visit Alton Towers with her sons in 1994 - casual, witty and utterly unregal. I am not alone in being fascinated by the minutiae of Diana’s style. She has become a muse for many millennials, who are too young to remember much about her life. On Instagram, we follow accounts which post streams of images of the Princess, and underscore the sheer variety of styles she experimented with. We are inspired to incorporate her signature looks into our own wardrobes. Indeed, recently, some of her most famous outfits - from tartan suits to blazers and jeans - were reimagined by the fashion website Man Repeller. While Virgil Abloh, creative director of streetwear label Off White, posted an image of his moodboard, covered in pictures of Diana as a teaser for his September fashion show.  In our digital age, where individual tastes can be cannibalised moments after they are posted online, and ‘street style’ photographs can make us all temporary fashion icons, I struggle to imagine anyone ever coming close to the impact Diana had. Which is why that week in 1997 makes so much more sense now, twenty years on, that it did back then. ​ © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
