 The usual style modus operandi of a Hollywood grande dame usually involves plenty of experimentation, eye-catching colours and striking silhouettes. After all, fashion has become a high stakes game in the film world over the past decade with sponsorship deals swirling and an actress’s ability to win best dressed awards becoming almost as much a consideration as her CV. Now that Angelina Jolie is more often found taking a behind-the-camera role as producer/ director, she is staking out the difference and largely eschewing the red carpet game in favour of a luxuriously purist wardrobe. It’s an approach which is at once practical (well, kind of), quietly confident (especially given her post Brad Pitt status) and more realistically grown-up than many of the style cues offered up elsewhere in Hollywood. Take her appearance on the red carpet this weekend for the premiere of The Breadwinner, her latest film about a young Afghan girl who dresses as a boy to help provide for her family. In lieu of a glitzy gown, Jolie was almost businesslike in a timeless white custom-made midi dress by Russian designer Ulyanna Sergeenko which she wore with nothing but beige heels and a diamond brooch. By day, Jolie’s pared-back preferences tend to play out in streamlined tailoring and a muted palette of neutral hues. Last week, she visited L.A’s Girls Leadership Academy in a black pencil skirt and cream silk shirt ensemble which The Fall’s Stella Gibson would have been proud of. In fact, much like Gillian Anderson’s character (probably one of the best dressed TV characters of the decade), Jolie’s style depends on a select few sophisticated staples which she can wear on rotation; no-brainer elegance. Of course, her glossy bouffant blow-dry and oversized sunglasses add the required soupcon of film star glamour.  Last month, Jolie expressed her dedication to minimalism in a camel-hued bodysuit, skirt and cardigan by Ryan Roche, a designer who works with a women’s co-operative in Nepal to produce many of her whisperingly chic designs. It was down to a red Valentino handbag to add a dash of colour- notably, it was Max Mara founder Achille Maramotti who struck on the combination of camel and red as supremely flattering when he founded the label in the 1950s. Naturally, most of Jolie’s pieces come in at luxury price points but that doesn’t mean something resembling her ultra-simple wardrobe couldn’t be put together with an astute visit to COS, Uniqlo and Me + Em. Luxe purism is a way of dressing which counted Katharine Hepburn and Carolyn Bessette Kennedy amongst its acolytes long before Jolie came along (although she's dabbled throughout her career) so why does it feel so right again now? For one, it’s a calm antidote to the plethora of choice out there and, whether you’re a mother of six film producer and UN Goodwill Ambassador or not, it will definitely make getting dressed in the morning easier.  I meet Abbey Clancy outside an advertising agency in Soho where she has just spent the morning discussing a campaign she is doing with Reebok – her second in as many years, squeezed in after the birth of baby number two 10 months ago, as you do. She’s wearing a T-shirt and jeans from H&M, a Burberry leather jacket, an unnecessarily towering pair of Saint Laurent boots (without them she is 5ft 9in), and a slightly stressed look on her beautiful face. She is busy, busy, busy – there’s a range of clothes she has designed for Matalan, her chief judging role on Britain’s Next Top Model, a couple of children at home and now, it turns out, a book. And not just any book: a novel. A Mills & Boon one to be precise, about a young girl from Liverpool with big dreams. Remind you of anyone? We jump in Abbey’s car where – reassuringly for one so glamorous – there is a child’s seat covered in baby detritus, and head to a smart hotel in west London where – reassuringly for one so svelte – she orders steak and chips followed by a chocolate fondant and vanilla ice cream. Abbey is often described as a WAG, but arguably she has been more famous than her husband, Peter Crouch, ever since she won the Strictly Come Dancing glitter ball in 2014; certainly she seems far busier than him, given that he has spent most of this season for Stoke sitting on the bench. Anyway, work has always been important to Abbey, even as a young girl from Liverpool with big dreams. At 14 she worked in a florist’s, at 16 she joined a girl band and by 20 she was gracing the pages of magazines, having come second in Britain’s Next Top Model, the show she now presents. She’s appeared in the swimsuit edition of Sports Illustrated and in fashion magazine Love alongside Cara Delevingne; unusually she manages to straddle both the worlds of high fashion and football. Her marriage to ‘Pete’ in 2011, three months after the birth of her first child, Sophia (now five), did not give her reason to hang up her high heels; superstylist Katie Grand had her posing naked on the back of a motorbike just weeks after the birth. (Their second daughter, Liberty, is nearly one.) ‘It is important for me to be self-sufficient,’ she says, gobbling down her steak, ‘not because I’ve got something to prove, but because I enjoy working and my whole family has always worked and it’s normal for me to earn a living. Especially now I’ve got two kids. It’s a breeze going to work. I’m like, “Ahhh, chill time!” At home I’m normally having a wee with Liberty strapped to me.’ Does she ever take a break? ‘No,’ she smiles. ‘I don’t.’  We are here to talk about Remember My Name, the Mills & Boon novel Abbey has sort of written. ‘I can’t dress it up really,’ she says, when I ask about the book. ‘I’m not coming out and saying I’m this brand-new author, I wrote it all myself. It was ghost written with an amazing girl from Liverpool. We brainstormed and tried to use events that have happened to me and my friends as inspiration for characters. ‘Then she obviously went away and wrote it with all our ideas and came back with it and then I went through it all.’ Did Abbey change much? ‘Yeah, quite a lot. Some of the characters didn’t come out how I wanted.’ It’s about a young singer who hits the big time, only to temporarily forget what’s important to her. In one bit, the protagonist admits to having been conned by seedy men promising her a big break. How much of it was based on actual events? ‘I don’t want to tell,’ she says wickedly. ‘It’s not about me. There’s one part of the book where she falls for this guy who’s tall, dark and handsome, and Pete’s like, “Babe, I thought you liked blonds”, getting all jealous, and it’s like, it’s not me!’ There’s a bit of sex in there, as there must be in all Mills & Boon books (Abbey reads a lot of Martina Cole). ‘I just sort of flicked past them [the sex scenes]. I had to read a piece out for Stella [watch it on our website] and I was like “blah blah blah hard on”, and I was like, “Oh my God, I said that out loud.” ‘So yeah. I don’t really talk about sex stuff outwardly with my family, and my mum, when she was reading it, was like “Oooooh.” I don’t think my mum thinks I have sex even though I’ve got two kids.’ Clearly, the business brains at Mills & Boon know that they are on to something – Abbey is the first celebrity ‘name’ to front a book. But Abbey says she didn’t do it for the money or the brand. ‘I just thought it would be fun, and I really enjoyed the process.’ She says she feels like a bit of a phoney because she didn’t write it herself. ‘But I just thought [it could be] a light-hearted book that girls can read on holiday with a bit of sexiness in it, a bit of drama.’ The book is dedicated to her friend Neale Pirie, who collapsed and died suddenly last year (a character in the book is even named after him). Abbey met him on the set of Strictly, where he worked as a stylist and hairdresser. ‘I saw him every week for the next three years, so he became really close to me. He was trustworthy, lovely, kind.  ‘He was the first person I’ve ever lost in my life apart from my nan, the first person who wasn’t family. It really, really affected me. And then I just thought it would be nice to have a little bit of him that will…’ She pauses. Live on? ‘Yeah.’ In a Mills & Boon book, I add. ‘In a Mills & Boon!’ She thinks that would have made him laugh.  When Abbey Clancy isn’t modelling or presenting or sort of writing books, she can be found in antique shops. ‘We love Lots Road,’ she says. ‘I love going there and finding like a 10 grand couch for £500 and having it recovered. It gives me real satisfaction to get a bargain. ‘I cannot spend these ridiculous types of money. Pete’s very, very down to earth and not flashy or anything. He’s not into clothes or cars or watches. The other day, he showed me a desk on eBay that he wants.’ I tell her about an antiques shop in west London I went to the other day. ‘Oh yeah, I’ve been there. I think it’s overpriced in there.’  The family has just moved (we have a long conversation about mortgages), and she is enjoying getting stuck into doing the house up. ‘Yesterday I went to B&Q to the knob shop to get some knobs for my wardrobe,’ she says proudly. ‘Pete’s like, “You’re going where? The knob shop?”’ She starts to laugh. She does the washing, makes dinner, does not go to football matches. ‘My brother was a footballer, still is. So my whole childhood I was dragged to football with my dad and my mum. I just remember being cold, bored to death, shivering, wanting to do some girly stuff but being stuck in a field. ‘So when I started going out with Pete, my feeling of football was not that it was about glamour and cars and houses.’ As she says astutely, ‘Pete’s career is amazing and I’m really proud to watch him play but I’m not a football fan just as he’s not a fan of dressing up in bikinis and [wearing] make-up.’ Her five-year-old is similarly uninterested in the beautiful game. ‘Sophia went to a sports camp for half term and they did football. She didn’t want to play and the coach was like, “Why don’t you? Your dad’s a footballer.” She said, “Yes, and that means he has to go away.”’  I wonder, in her private life, is she Ms Clancy or Mrs Crouch? The latter, she says. ‘But I do prefer my surname to Crouch,’ she adds, shortly before bemoaning the paltry number of chips on her plate (‘there’s only four like!’). ‘Clancy is a prettier name. Crouch is a bit blunt. But I’ve asked him. He won’t take my name. He’s drawn a line at that.’ She thinks he’ll probably go into management (they don’t talk about their careers at home, given how all-encompassing it is to have two children). Despite their hectic lives, the couple would have another baby. ‘I’d like another one, yeah. I have such horrific pregnancies. I’m so ill for nine months, throw up every day, so sick. But my births are amazing. Liberty was four minutes, Sophia 45.’  Professionally, she’d like to walk in the Victoria’s Secret show. ‘That’s my dream, but I think I’m a bit old now.’ She tells me about going to the show when it was in London almost two years ago. ‘I was pregnant and got a pizza on the way home and ate the whole thing in the car. I cried because I’d forgotten to get the cookie dough dessert. I mean, I was emotional and hungry.’ She gives a nonchalant shrug and tucks into her chocolate fondant. The woman is not a WAG.  Today, on day two of Haute Couture Week, Giles Deacon announced that he is temporarily closing his ready-to-wear line to enter into the fabulous world of Haute Couture. This means even more spectacular red-carpet worthy gowns like the printed masterpiece Cate Blanchett wore at the Cannes Film Festival last year. Giles spoke to The Telegraph about his decision to leave London Fashion Week and show in Paris from July: "For the last four years we've been quietly developing that side of our business and working with private clients and couture off the back of our fantastic red carpet pieces we've done and had great gals wearing. It seemed like a good growth direction for us and to show it at Paris in Couture is where you show the best of what you can do." Red carpet will be a focus for the team, which is certainly a good thing for awards shows everywhere given that he creates the opposite of seen-it-before gowns that we see so often on the red carpet. You won't see a Giles nude column gown. "I want to be very special eveningwear and the label to be a go-to place. There will be all sorts of ethereal, slightly darker romanticism and some witty touches.” Giles has an incredibly thorough and personal approach to red carpet dressing and he starts working on a dress six months (yes, you read that correctly) before an awards show. He explains why he starts so early: "Whenever we work with anybody we try to plan two or three events - one could be a big red carpet or something like going on James Corden's show, and then we'll work with them over a six month period. I find that much more interesting and we get better results - everything is designed and considered especially for the event.”  He doesn’t wait to hear if an actress is nominated to start working on their awards dress: "They usually have an idea and we can take a punt! We’ll start in the autumn for sure going through ideas with the actress and what else they have lined up and are attending. It takes time to get people fitted and it's got to be right."  So how long does it take to create his custom gowns? “The Gwendoline Christie Star Wars dress took about 10 days to create and the gown Cate Blanchett wore at Cannes took about a month. There was one dress from the swan collection that took three months to make which was a labour of love. There will be a number of dresses in the July collection which will have a similar workload." His red carpet career highlight so far was dressing Cate Blanchett for the Cannes Film Festival: “It wasn't just her wearing it, but to go down as one of the best of all time at Cannes when there have been so many corkers was incredibly flattering." Is there anyone else left on his red carpet bucket list? “I've not dressed Rooney Mara yet, I'd love to dress her she's phenomenal and Saoirse Ronan.” Bridal is also likely to be a focus for his label: "It'd be a logical place for us to go to and also seeing how popular the Bridal collections in New York are and how much they have grown.” He has designed wedding dresses before, including Abbey Clancy’s gown that he worked on for two months. Will there be wedding dresses in his July collection? “Who knows!” he laughs. Any bets on who will wear Giles Couture at the Oscars? We're keeping our fingers crossed for Cate. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  In the hotly contested world of celebrity style, there are countless categories- red carpet, fancy lunch, gym, to name just three- to be mastered. But few are quite so legendarily tricky as the airport look. After all, veer too close to genuine civilian territory and you risk looking simply sloppy in the inevitable snaps which will be captured of  your departure/ arrival. But getting implausibly dolled up could come across as just a tad try-hard- unless you're Victoria Beckham, in which case you are absolutely allowed to wear six-inch stilettos, cocktail dresses or louche mannish tailoring because you have made passport control your own personal catwalk, thereby absolving the need for any semblance of normality.  Meghan Markle not to be Beckham-airport-style-hall-of-fame level just yet, but as with most of the sartorial challenges which have been thrown at the Suits actress since she was catapulted into an even shiner spotlight than she already enjoyed when her romance with Prince Harry was revealed last year, she took her airport look in her stride this weekend as she jetted from Toronto to Texas for the ATX TV festival where she  participated in a read through of the pilot episode of Suits.  Although Markle has made very few public appearences since her relationship with Harry was confirmed, we do know that she is as at ease getting dressed up (see her Antonio Berardi and Erdem looks for a recent polo match and wedding as proof) as she is going casual, as she does when she dons sleek leggings and hoodies for her frequent yoga classes.  So how did her airport looks this weekend measure up? Finishing touches are also a crucial part of offsetting the more practical elements of a travelling look and Markle has these down to a T.  It just wouldn't be London Fashion Week without the models, who bring the new season collections to life in the jam-packed schedule of catwalk shows and intimate presentations. It might look glamorous, but it's also the busiest time of year on the model calendar. If a model's fashion week involves rushing from casting to casting in order to book the best jobs possible, criss-crossing across town for fittings and shows, and having your hair and make-up done and then taken off up to six times a day, we have to wonder, just how do models prepare - both mentally and physically? So we spoke to a couple of our favourite British models, Charlotte Wiggins and Matilda Lowther, and Select Models booker James Wood to find out just what it takes to get a model fashion week ready. Walking the runway under the watchful eyes of the global press means models need to keep in good shape. However fashion week doesn't require models to go into Superman-mode when it comes to their fitness routines. "I'm not really doing anything different, I'm just going more often. I'm on the way back from the gym now!" Charlotte laughs. "I've got a personal trainer - she's really good! She trains lots of models so she knows what the gist [of model fitness goals] is: to be lean and toned." Matilda's also ran the London Marathon this year and in between training runs, she also made time to head to the pool for a swim, and of course, a session in the sauna afterwards, saying "It helps to clear your skin!" "[I don't think our lifestyles change] that much, to be honest. Just trying to get lots of early nights, and drink lots of water!" Matilda shrugs, while Charlotte seconds her advice: "You need to sleep as much as possible, because it’s fashion week and you have no sleep!" No crazy crash diets here, folks - both Charlotte and Matilda are adamant about that. "It's just lots of fruit and veg, and keeping on top of [a balanced lifestyle], really." If anything, they just carry on their (admittedly, quite virtuous) eating routines as normal. "We eat pretty healthily anyway, there's no point in just eating badly and then cutting it out before fashion week," Charlotte advises. The long hours and hectic schedules require models to be fighting fit, so dramatically changing your diet just before the shows just isn't worth it. "It’s important to maintain a healthy body," Matilda says, "I’m quite against abnormally losing weight for shows."  Both Charlotte and Matilda are aware of their potential role model status when it comes to body size and shape: "Making sure you look healthy is important, especially when young girls are looking at you. You don’t want to promote something that’s unhealthy," Matilda says. Booker James also underlines the importance of food, recommending models to bring snacks along with them when they're on the go. "Here at Select, we always have so much fruit and bottles of water for girls to enjoy, but we always encourage the girls to take snacks with them, because as a model, you don’t know when your day’s going to end. You might get a last minute call to a fitting and you might not have time to stop to get something to eat. So if you have something nutritious and energy-rich, like a Bounce Energy Ball, to take along with you, it'll keep you going."  All the early starts do take their toll on model complexions, though. Matilda recommends the Elemis Pro Collagen Hydra Gel Under Eye masks (£46, Elemis) because "they help with puffy eyes when you get up early. Also there's a lot of eye make-up and it makes your eyes go horrible." Charlotte agrees "Your eyes get really sore, so I swear by eyedrops. You can get these Japanese ones (Rohto Eye Drops) that they use on shoots sometimes. They burn like nothing else, but they're amazing." Regarding hair, Matilda suggests that there's not much point getting your hair cut beforehand, adding "they just hack through your hair so much [at the shows]." Instead, James recommends that the New Face models that he looks after treat their locks in the run-up to show day to keep them in good condition. "If you’re doing a lot of shows, you’re having your hair re-done two or three times a day, so it’s quite damaging. We encourage models to treat it with natural oils like argan oil, which they can put on their hair overnight and sleep in. Then at the shows girls get their hair cut, and the dead ends cut off anyway." The perils of stripping off backstage also factor into the pre-fashion week prep: "I’ll definitely go and get a wax, you know?" laughs Charlotte, adding that the downtime before the shows start is a perfect time to get a facial "because [fashion month is] a long time where you can't sit back and relax with a face mask on." One of James's top tips to his rookie model charges is to make sure they're stocked up on music and books for the week.  "Unfortunately there is a lot of waiting time with castings, so anything to keep yourself entertained [is ideal]." "Standing in a room by yourself, waiting to go for a casting, is one of the most boring things ever," agrees Charlotte, adding "I've got Game of Thrones on my iPad."  But waiting for a casting doesn't mean staying in a screen-and-headphones bubble - it's also a time for socialising. Charlotte says "It’s also nice to talk to the other girls though, because some of them you only see at fashion week. It’s a good chance to catch up with the people you haven’t seen for a while." Clothing-wise, there's one thing that James says no model should be without: a pair of comfy shoes. "I cannot stress [the importance of wearing comfy shoes] enough. When you’re walking around town, wear comfy shoes, and carry your heels in your bag. Just change before you go into the casting - you can wear the comfiest shoes you want the rest of the time, but when you go into the casting you want to be presentable."  "Once in the casting, a model will always get away a bit better wearing a black court shoe. To a certain extent, the clients do need a blank canvas to see the girl walking, and a model needs to show that she can walk in heels, so wedges aren't the best option."  James says it's up to the girl to choose the exact style, his only guidance being to buy an affordable pair - "we recommend the high street" - that the girl feels comfortable in. "At the end of the day, if you’re going to 50 castings, you don’t want your feet to fall off because you’ve chosen the wrong shoe!" he laughs. When asked whether they secretly practice their walk or their end-of-runway pose, both Charlotte and Matilda burst out laughing. "When you first start, you do [practice] a lot - we had catwalk training! I think now I just wing it. Whatever comes!" Charlotte says, Matilda adding "Whatever happens, you know? Just walk the walk!" If anything it's not the walk that needs practice, it's trying to keep a straight face while doing it that's the key. "It’s funny if we’re in the same show together and we cross each other in the finale. Trying not to make eye contact and laugh is so hard! I'll be looking so serious, and then I see Tilly strutting her stuff going past, and I just can’t hold it in," admits Charlotte.  While giggling on the catwalk might not be the done thing, a sense of humour and a sunny smile is James's final tip for the roster of models he works with. "We appreciate it can be tough for girls when they're new to it all, and we’re here for anyone if they have any problems. Just remember that everyone’s in the same boat, so stay positive and be yourself - clients really do pick up on good energy!" "Having a smartphone is the way to keep in contact," says James. "When girls come in from other countries, it’s easy to just put in a new SIM card from England that works." James's next top tip is a fast-track to helping a model become a geographical whizz. "The first thing I would say is to download Citymapper. It's an app for getting around London and it shows you all of the tube and bus links. If you’re trying to get from one show to another, it makes it all so easy. When I’m in Paris or New York, I go straight on Citymapper to arrive at my destination without getting lost or being super late." All this city-hopping might drain your phone's juice, so James also suggests investing in a portable phone charger. "We bookers need constant communication with our models, because timetables and schedules can change throughout the day. We might have a fitting, or a fit confirm, or a go-see, and need to text a model saying 'Can you go now?' We’re fortunate now that we live in an age with Whatsapp and everything so it’s so easy to get in touch with them - as long as their phones have battery. I learned this the hard way when I was in Paris last season and my phone died after about an hour of constant emailing. A portable charger means you can be messaging all day and you'll still have that battery." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The London-based, New Zealand-born fashion designer shares a few of her favourite things Fashion indulgences?  Vintage jewellery. I collect from stores when I travel. Most recently in America I found a vintage golden ball Céline bracelet on a chain. I also love a colourful Missoni crochet swimsuit with matching headband. On your feet? Rochas. In particular, flat styles. I feel far more empowered, sophisticated and forward-thinking in flats than in high heels. Especially when I am working and hosting meetings. Favourite piece of jewellery? My ‘lucky’ bangles, passed down to me from my grandmother. I guess I call them lucky for totally sentimental reasons. They are gold, in a set of five, and are simply set. Favourite fragrance? Prada Infusion d’Iris perfume – my mother wears it so it feels like home away from home. It’s lovely to smell her scent at all times. Dream home? A Richard Neutra house. His design feels nostalgic, with such attention to detail and character in the furnishings. It gives an impression of a lifestyle from another era: one I wish I could have been a part of. Sight for sore eyes? A view of the beach anywhere in New Zealand. I love Pakiri Beach. Most cherished artwork? A picture my father painted in grey and cream – he was an incredible artist and passed away when I was four. It is the only work I have of his, so it’s very special to me. Favourite piece you own?  A pair of vintage royal blue vases that I found at a market. They are the stand-out pieces in my living room at home. Ultimate dish? I enjoy going for brunch at Granger & Co in Notting Hill, and having my all-time favourite: poached eggs and avocado on toast. I love the aesthetic of the space and the fresh, modern approach in the dishes. Design classic? I love the cleanness of Kaare Klint and Rud Rasmussen furniture, especially the wooden criss-cross under-bars of their sofas. One of my favourite pieces had a stripe design from the 1970s, which I dream of one day owning. Ultimate escape? I love to go back to New Zealand and visit my family, I’m such a home bird. Ideal watch?  A vintage Cartier yellow-gold Tank watch with an emerald-green strap. Dream drive? A 1970s Mercedes-Benz convertible. I imagine zipping around town in it, I love anything that’s already lived in another era. What do you collect?  Audrey Hepburn is part of a highly exclusive club of 20th century names who are as renowned for their extraordinary lives and talents as for their signature style. While Hitchcockian blonde Grace Kelly was all regal elegance and First Lady Jackie Kennedy blended European chic with American ease, Audrey Hepburn remains the high priestess of gamine simplicity. Although her appeal never diminishes, Hepburn's style will be firmly back on the agenda this autumn as Christie's host a major sale of her possessions, which is being offered by her two sons.  ‘We are thrilled to have been entrusted with the sale of items from Audrey Hepburn's personal collection,’  says Adrian Hume-Sayer, Director, Private Collections at Christie's. ‘Her name is one that instantly resonates, and her appeal and relevance remain as strong today as they ever were. The sales will offer fans and collectors alike the opportunity to acquire unique personal objects which have never before been seen on the market, and which will undoubtedly offer new insights into the remarkable life of a remarkable woman.’  Amongst the pieces for sale at the  27th September auction will be items from Hepburn's wardrobe which only serve to underline further the look for which she is so well known. A pristine  belted trench coat by Burberry is expected to fetch between £6000 and £8000. Hepburn's dedication to particular timeless staples is encompassed in a collection of ballet slippers in a rainbow of shades from classic black to cheery yellow and turquoise, which has an estimate of £1500. Hepburn's look is synonymous with Hubert de Givenchy, who first met the star when he dressed her for her second film Sabrina. He went on to create many couture dresses for the actress which she wore both on and off-screen. Included in the Christie's sale is a blue satin Givenchy cocktail dress worn by Hepburn in a photo shoot with William Klein for a fashion editorial promoting Two for the Road  in 1966.  “People have always talked about her grace, [and wondered], What was the secret of her elegance? What was her system? What was her style?,” Hepburn's son Sean Ferrer told US Vogue. He plans to write a book about his mother's style for release next year.  Ferrer also acknowledged his mother's enduring style appeal, even amongst those who have never known her alive (Hepburn died in 1993). “I think it’s safe to say that probably close to 50 percent of her base today is tweens and teens, which is quite extraordinary.” Besides pieces from her fashion collection, the auction- which also comprises a second online element set to run from 19th September to 3rd October- will include scripts from some of Hepburn's most loved films such as Breakfast at Tiffany's and photographs offering a behind-the-scenes glimpse into both her personal life and on-set goings-on.  For more information about Christie's auction, visit their website   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Today marks the birthday of one of the most influential designers to emerge from the 20th century, Gabrielle 'Coco' Chanel. 46 years after the designer's death, her legacy is as potent as ever; her signature boxy tweed suits, little black dresses and ballerina pumps are still associated with her gamine, revolutionary approach to style. But it is Chanel's chic handbags which are often seen as the pinnacle of investment pieces, but which one to buy? To coincide with the designer's birthday, the Parisian showroom and website specialising in the sale of pre-owned luxury items, Collector Square, has investigated the Chanel handbags which constitute the most worthy of investments. Of course, we would always advocate buying with heart as well as head, but just so you know, here are the 5 most collectible styles to keep your eyes peeled for... Undoubtedly the most well know of all of Coco Chanel's bag designs, the 2.55 (which refers February 1955; the month and year in which the style was introduced) was the result of the designer's desire to create a classic bag that was easy to carry around hands-free - a purpose is still serves for its owners today.  The rectangular lock was a detail designed by Chanel herself, and was the standard for all of  Chanel bags until the label's current creative director Karl Lagerfeld took to the helm in the 1980s. ''This model has increased in value by 70% over the last 5 years,'' says Jérôme Lalande, Collector Square's leather goods expert. ''It's extremely difficult to find on the second hand market, and can exchange hands today for between £2,500 - £3,500.’’ Chanel 2.55 bag, sold recently for £3,540, Collector Square An enduring classic, the Classic Flap bag was introduced by Lagerfeld the same year thathe took up the role of creative director at the French fashion house in 1983, using the same silhouette as Coco Chanel's 2.55 bag. ''This bag has increased its average value by an impressive 140% over the last 5 years,'' says Lalande. ''For the ultimate timeless Chanel bag, try to find an all black limited edition bag, with black accessories and hardware - these are the most rare, and therefore an excellent investment.'' Timeless Handbag in black quilted leather, Sold recently for £ 2,320, Collector Square The Boy bag was named after Arthur Capel - an English polo player and Chanel's lover, who she affectionately referred to as 'Boy'. Lagerfeld found a picture of Chanel sporting a hunting cross-over bag in the archives, which inspired him to create this model.  ''Designed in 2010, the Boy bag is still a relatively recent model and is only just surfacing on the second hand market,'' explains Lalande. ''As ever, savvy collectors should look for limited edition varieties of the Boy bag because these are likely to be worth more on the second market in the next few years.’’ Chanel Boy shoulder bag, £3,540, Collector Square The Chanel shopping bag dates back to the 1980s and comes in a wide variety of shapes, materials and colours. A particularly roomy style, the Shopping bag is the perfect travel companion. ''Convenient, urban and [slightly more] affordable, the Chanel Shopping bag can be used either as a handbag or a working bag,'' says Lalande. ''This model is a very popular collectable item, representing 1 in every 10 bags bought on Collector Square.'' Chanel shopping bag, £2130, Collector Square This boxy bag is defined by its vintage aesthetic. It's a go-with-everything accessory that is equally suited to being paired with jeans and a T-shirt as it is an evening dress.  ''Its silhouette is reminiscent of a vintage camera shape,'' describes Lalande. ''This handbag also has the advantage of being able to be worn underneath a coat, as it's smaller than most other Chanel bags,'' he adds. ''This style is quite hard to find on the second hand market and is coveted by Chanel Connoisseurs.''  The Rio Olympics 2016 are now just days away, so the eyes of the world will soon be firmly fixed on Brazil. So what better excuse to shine a spotlight on the gold medal-worthy fashion to hail from the South American nation? Here some of the country's most stylish editors and street style stars reveal how women approach style in a place where the average temperature is 27°C and all-black outfits are an alien concept... Marina Larroude started her fashion career at Vogue Brasil, and then went on to be Style Director at Style.com and Fashion Director at TeenVogue.com. While she now lives in New York, a world away from her home town Araçatuba, her Brazilian upbringing still has a huge influence on how she dresses every single day. Why she will never wear black "I lived in the countryside where it's summer all year around - about 80/90 degrees throughout the year," Larroude says. "You can barely wear jeans, so I love dresses. If it's 60 degrees in New York, I'll wear skirts and dresses and I just can't wear pants. I didn't own any clothes that were black growing up, so still wear lots and lots of colour, and lean towards cotton and dresses. I don't own a lot of black and will very rarely wear a black outfit - maybe once a year. I'm not afraid of wearing colour and gravitate towards pieces that have that Brazilian aesthetic, so always buy more resort and summer pieces." Why Brazilian women don't wear cut-off shorts and t-shirts- and they focus on grooming "Brazilian women dress quite glamorously, with off-the-shoulder tops, and sexy looks which are about the body," Larroude adds. "They don't dress down in cut-offs and t-shirts, so in the heat they'll wear a beautiful, vibrant cotton dress and never look too casual. Women  really embrace how feminine they are and that's a beautiful thing - they don't want to be cool, but want to look pretty all of the time." "The thing about Brazilian women is you can't put on a lot of clothes, so they dress up with their beauty, body and hair - they go to the hair salon all the time and have perfect skin. That's the only way can look dressed up. If you go to Rio or Sao Paolo, women are always very, very polished," Larroude explains.  Marina Larroude's Brazilian labels to invest in: "My favourite label for swimwear is Jo de Mer, it's fashionable and cool and not just a basic bikini set. Martha Medeiros does very unique lace dresses, which take over 300 hours to make each piece and are created in a community where women hand make the lace. Lane Marinho also create made to order shoes which are very special." While in Rio, Larroude advises visiting Via Flores which stocks a number of Brazilian designers and NK Store for stylish buys. Brazilian fashion blogger and street style star Helena Bordon practically grew up at fashion week, attending alongside her mother is Donata Meirelles, the Style Director at Vogue Brasil.  In Sao Paulo, it's all about being practical but stylish "I'm a proper Paulista - this is what they call people who are from Sao Paulo. I am always going around from one meeting or shoot to another so I always try to keep my style casual but with a twist," Bordon says. "Brazil is a tropical country so we tend to wear lighter things, but I love a good pair of jeans, a white t-shirt and amazing shoes - for the day I am obsessed with cool flats and sneakers. Living in Sao Paulo, I have learned to be practical but always make sure accessories are on point." Brazilian women have fun with fashion "Brazilians love prints, flowy dresses and fabrics and a cool pair of sunglasses and flats. It is super hot here all year round so we want to keep it fresh but always with a fun twist. I think we like to have fun with fashion," Bordon explains. "Brazil is all about colours and cool prints, and a 'sexy' effortless style and the bodies are also on point!" The Brazilian brands to name check Bordon recommends Adriana Degreas and Lenny for swimwear, Patricia Bonaldi for evening dresses and Bob Store, because she says "it's a great balance between Brazilian style and New Yorker style." Thássia Naves is one of the most influential fashion bloggers in Brazil, with over 2 million followers on Instagram.  On always having a Brazilian spin on her looks "I really like the Brazilian reference and always adapt it to my day to day looks, with exuberant colours, prints and tropical mood adding my personal edge to it," Naves explains.  Brazilian designers to know "Pat Bo, Adriana Degreas, Gig, Coven, Martha Medeiros, Vitorino Campos, Lucas Magalhaes, Skazi, and Isabela Capet, to name a few." Naves' three tips for getting the Rio look: 1. Always add a dash of colour to highlight your look. 2. Keep a little skin on display to complement your overall look, for example with bare shoulders. 3. Accessories always mix up the look, and are full of personality.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Canadian model Winnie Harlow was diagnosed with vitiligo at the age of four - a skin condition that causes white patches to develop on the skin due to a lack of melanin. She was called a "cow" and a "zebra" at school and dropped out at the age of 16 due to extreme bullying. Despite the difficulties of her early years, Harlow became a model, challenging the narrow portrayals of beauty in the fashion industry by appearing on America's Next Top Model and working for the likes of Diesel and Ashish. In December 2015, Winnie received a call from Beyoncé's assistant asking if she would appear in her visual album Lemonade, and a day later she flew out to New Orleans to start filming.  Lemonade features a number of black women who have at some point been targeted because of their race. Winnie appears alongside actress Quvenzhané Wallis who was referred to as 'little q' and a c-word on Twitter during awards season when she was 9 years old, Zendaya who was the target of offensive comments about wearing her hair in dreadlocks to the Oscars, and Amandla Stenberg who experienced racist remarks when she starred in The Hunger Games at the age of 12. “It was an honour for everyone who was cast for this video, just knowing that Beyoncé views us as a strong woman in our field, it’s an honour," Winnie said to The Telegraph about being included in Lemonade. "For me personally, I have vitiligo, so my whole career it’s always been this very odd debate ‘Does she want to be white? Is she white and black? Is her mum white?’ It’s always been this question of my background, my race and what I stand for," Winnie explains. "I feel like Beyoncé has got this backlash too that she doesn’t stand up for her background and so on and so forth, because her music was reflective of a certain time," she adds, "I feel like she’s really coming into her own in her art. In her music she’s able to open up and express what’s important to her, and I’m grateful to express what’s in my career because of trailblazers like her who have worked hard for what they want to be heard for." ' My skin condition is not something new. It’s not like I was the first person to have it' As for breaking barriers with her modelling, she doesn't want her skin to define her. "My modelling career is about hard work," says Harlow. "There are a lot of people that would say my skin is what made my career, but my skin condition is not something new. It’s not like I was the first person to have it, it’s not new, so to be able to break boundaries with something that for years people have said is ugly, or something that should hold you back, it’s mainly hard work that gets you to where you want to be regardless of the boundaries that you're faced with." In the video 'Freedom' black women hold up pictures of men they have lost in their lives. Among them are the mothers of Eric Garner, Trayvon Martin and Michael Brown, young black men who were killed by police in the United States. Harlow chose a picture of her great, great grandfather. " Beyoncé's personal assistant text me and said ‘the concept is loved ones that have passed, but a strong figure in your life, it’s more like the loss of a father figure.’ My grandfather is still alive but he’s such a strong father figure in my life and I am very close to him. I haven’t lost him, so I wanted to use someone super close to him, which was his father. He looks so much like my grandfather, and people always tell me that they are a replica of each other so I feel like I have got to meet him through my grandfather." Beyoncé may be one of the most celebrated artists on the planet, but Harlow says that she was very humble on set. "I arrived from the airport and went straight to hair and makeup. Beyoncé was walking off set to do a wardrobe change, so I thought she would come back, but she ran directly to me. She gave me a hug and thanked me for coming so last minute. It was a shock to see someone so big being so humble and grateful for us to take time out of our lives to create something dear to her heart." Beyonce's husband Jay Z was also very welcoming, "he came over and gave me a hug and said thanks for coming out, I was like 'this is epic.' The whole family was there." Winnie says that Beyoncé was involved in all aspects of the production."She would look back at the roll back and see if something was out of place; that's something that is mainly the director's job, but she had a hand in. Even runners - someone who should ask 'are you ok? Are you warm did you eat?' - she asked those questions as well. Things she shouldn’t worry about, she was so interested in knowing if we were ok. I was filming a scene with her and she was like ‘did you get to eat?’ and I was like ‘err yeah did you get to eat?!’" "Working with her is amazing because she’s able to talk to everyone" adds Harlow. "I’ve seen her talk to a five year old with the same interest as a sixty year old. I feel like I learned from her, from talking to her, of course, but also from just watching her and how passionate she was about getting the job done." via GIPHY One of the most beautiful visuals in Lemonade is when Beyoncé leads a line of women through the water in matching ethereal sheer dresses. The shot  was filmed in December, so wasn't quite so serene as it looks in the film. "Her dancers were telling me it was freezing cold," Winnie says of this scene, "but they couldn’t even complain because she’s doing the hard work with us. It’s not like she expects us to just do it, she does it with us." Winnie also saw Beyoncé's determination first hand. "We filmed 'Freedom' where she was singing a cappella to us, and she had a thin sheet of a dress - it was almost nothing. We were all pretty layered up and if we asked for a coat or a blanket, they would find it for us in five minutes, but she couldn’t wear certain things because she’s trying to get the shot. We are all shivering, but she’s standing there so strong for the film." The day before Lemonade was released, Beyoncé sent personal thank you emails to those involved. Harlow says, "she thanked me for being a part of her creation, and how dear to her heart this work is and it’s the biggest thing she’s done in her career and how grateful she was for me being a part of it. I don’t expect Beyoncé to ask me how I’m doing, if I’m cold, if I’ve eaten, or the day before the release of the biggest project of her life to email me to thank me for being there and coming so last minute."  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It may not be a mystery on the scale of an Agatha Christie novel, but the curious case of The Duchess of Cambridge's Royal Ascot outfit yesterday has had us stroking our chins. Kate made her second-ever appearence at Royal Ascot just a year after her first wearing a dress which was different- but the same. 2016's look was by Dolce and Gabbana while yesterday's was a bespoke creation by Alexander McQueen, the Duchess's go-to label for bespoke pieces. Yet, both were made of white lace, they were of modest length and came with fitted, long sleeves. Barely discernible differences were the latter's high neck and fuller, stiffer skirt.  Clearly when you are one of Britain's most senior royals, you have full prerogative to have several versions of a very similar outfit in your vast wardrobe and Kate may have any number of reasons for debuting a recycled-but-not-recycled look yesterday (perhaps she spilled red wine on the last one? Or George and Charlottte got paint covered paws all over it?) but the conundrum has thrown new light on  the Duchess's style recycling habits.  Here, we analyse her 5 style recycling rules... A duchess's duties include countless foreign visits which in turn call for the occasional diplomatic fashion gesture. Naturally, certain colours will be useful for more countries than one, and red is probably chief among those. So it was only right that when Kate attended a Wales v France rugby match in Paris in March, she revived a red Carolina Herrera coat which she had first debuted in Canada the previous autumn. Handily, red is the national colour of both Wales and Canada.  While Kate is perhaps not renowned as the most experimental of dressers, she has- to her credit- tried countless silhouettes from neat pencil-skirted suits to sheath dresses, prom skirts and cropped trousers in her time. But there are a handful of looks which have clearly gone down so well in the Kensington Palace dressing room that Kate has re-ordered them in different colours or slightly tweaked designs.  Most recently, that was the red Preen 'Fenella' dress which Kate first wore in Canada and then wore in black to an awards ceremony a couple of months later. Rewinding the clock further back, at a garden party in 2012 Kate wore a pale pink, pleated skirt dress by Emilia Wickstead which she now also owns in turquoise whiles her archive also includes a similar Alexander McQueen style in pillar box red.  Of course,  wherever the Duchess goes the attention will be on her but one way to shift a little of the focus is to wear a look which we are already familiar (this was a tactic employed by Princess Diana who knew that paps would get less for their photos if she was wearing a familiar outfit). Earlier this month, she wore an old favourite Rebecca Taylor tweed suit as she visited victims of the London terror attack. Now that Kate has been through two pregnancies, some of her maternity pieces have been seen on a couple of occasions such as the baby pink , pearl-buttoned coat she wore for the Commonwealth service when expecting Princess Charlotte and Trooping the Colour whilst pregnant with George.  Plenty of the Duchess's casual wardrobe falls into this category of repeating too: Zara skinny jeans, Penelope Chilvers boots and a Troy London parka are all pieces which have been seen more than once.  Perhaps one of the Duchess's most famous repeat looks is her Alexander McQueen navy and cream nautical blouse and pencil skirt which she has worn several times since debuting the look in 2011, often for sailing themed visits.  Although it might be subtler to be less literal, it's clearly a way of dressing which Kate enjoys and so might explain her insistence on always (well, twice) wearing white lace to Ascot- especially if she is a big fan of My Fair Lady.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Rachel Trevor-Morgan’s atelier is at the end of a little winding passage in London’s St James’s area and up the creaky staircase of a higgledy-piggledy hatmakers’ building, which has been at the site since 1765. It feels like stepping into a Dickens novel.  Trevor-Morgan opened her millinery workshop in 1990, after training with royal hatmakers including Graham Smith and Philip Somerville, and is now in Her Majesty’s small circle of go-to milliners. She has held the royal warrant since 2014 but began making hats for the Queen in 2006; she has worn them to Royal Ascot, her 80th-birthday celebrations at St Paul’s, her diamond wedding celebration at Westminster Abbey – and there is every chance that at today’s royal wedding, the Queen will be wearing a Rachel Trevor-Morgan.  Sitting in an elegant little fitting room, filled with her latest confections – colourful clusters of handmade silk flowers, artful combinations of feathers and straw twists, and jaunty saucers with intricate bows – Trevor-Morgan explains that her love of hats originated from watching her mother dress up in them when she was a child. ‘I always love looking back to the ’40s and ’50s when everybody wore hats all the time and they where just part of your outfit,’ she says. Now her signature look has ‘quite a soft feel’. ‘It’s very feminine,’ she says. She makes her hats using traditional techniques with the help of three assistants. ‘I’m extraordinarily lucky because one of my assistants has worked for me for 25 years and another for 10 years, and they are utterly brilliant,’ she explains. ‘We hand block our hats and make our own flowers. I’m very hot on the hand-crafting and the finish. By making our own trimmings we can do something that other people don’t. 'If a client comes in with a beautiful print dress, we can make the flowers to match, which might involve dying three or four colours and putting them together to make a spray of flowers.’ She loves to wear them herself. ‘I will always wear one if I’m going to weddings or banquets, not that I go to many.’ She adds, ‘I love being in my workroom out of hours and just working on my own; for me, there’s nothing nicer.’ © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Amal Clooney went for one of her first evenings out after giving birth to twins Ella and Alexander earlier this month, she was understandably keen to add a dose of glamour to the striped jumpsuit which she wore for the outing. That extra zhuzh came in the form of a pair of shoulder-grazing, tasselled earrings in metallic pink.  It turns out that rather than sourcing her statement-making accessories from one of the big name designers which she usually favours, Clooney's new earrings are a sample from the burgeoning collection of her little sister, Tala Alamuddin.  Called 'Totally Tala', the former events planner has been sharing tasters of her debut collection on her Instagram for the past few months. Fringing seems to be the signature detail which runs through the line with opulent fringed handbags in a bright palette of turquoise, yellow, purple and cobalt among the standout pieces. 80s-inspired biker jackets and cut-out leather chokers also make an appearence.  It seems that Amal has been a willing guinea pig for her sister's new venture.  The mud at this year's Glastonbury Festival has been one of the sludgiest on record, with the fields being churned into a gloopy glue, with scenes comparable to a Game of Thrones battle scene. Some festival goers have well and truly embraced their inner Kit Harrington and rolled around in the brown stuff.  Joining the likes of Alexa Chung, Lottie Moss and Cara Delevingne in this year's Glastonbury mud bath is Game of Thrones star Natalie Dormer, who has the definitive answer on how the festival compares to the Game of Thrones set. "You'd have to ask Kit Harrington, I can call him if you'd like?" she tells the Telegraph. "I tried to pack as lightly as possible, as you have to traipse it all over the mud," Dormer tells The Telegraph of her low-key approach to festival style.  As for what she packed for Glastonbury, she says: "You need some baby wipes and an anorak and some shades, as the weather seems to change every five minutes." As for her beauty essentials she reveals her one Glastonbury saviour is Dermalogica SPF50- "You've got to look after your face when you're standing in the middle of the crowd, rain or shine." Festival fashion has got a bad reputation of late, thanks to an over-saturation of clichéd flower crowns, carefully applied glitter and tiered maxi dresses. "I think any goes," Dormer says of where she stands on the divisive term 'festival fashion.' "I've seen men wearing capes and tight bodysuits with glitter.  Hedi Slimane’s latest catwalk collection for Saint Laurent might have been an homage to the 1980’s that was brilliantly constructed but difficult to wear in reality by anyone other than Lady Gaga, but his latest campaign seems designed to do the very opposite: appeal to grown-up women. Slimane has signed 69-year-old Jane Birkin for his latest campaign. The French actress, whose style inspired the world’s most famous handbag The Hermes Birkin bag, is pictured grinning casually whilst wearing one of Saint Laurent’s most iconic items - Le Smoking tuxedo. Slimane broke the pictures of Birkin on his twitter feed, which had been taken in Saint Laurent's newly revived couture house earlier this month. It's a rare fashion appearance from Birkin, whose nonchalance style has been much copied and commented on since she the 1960's despite the fact that she keeps a low profile. Of course, it shouldn’t be controversial that a grown up woman is modelling the epitome of a grown up jacket - and one that starts at £1,690. But until very recently, the average age of a model in super-expensive clothes was around 18. Still, it seems that change might be afoot. Sophia Loren, 81, has featured in Dolce & Gabbana’s new campaigns and Bette Midler, 70, was cast by Marc Jacobs as one of his Spring campaign women. But, whilst some might critique that the casting of these mature women is as tokenistic as fashion’s long-held obsession with youth, it would be churlish to deny there’s been a refreshing movement to reflect and cater to a wider demographic in fashion campaigns this season. For Balmain’s campaigns, designer Olivier Rousteing reunited three of the original “supers” – Cindy Crawford (49), Naomi Campbell (45) and Claudia Schiffer (45). Calvin Klein’s joyful pictures showed mother and daughter Lisa Bonet (48) and Zoe Kravitz (27), all full of beachy abandon. And earlier this year Giorgio Armani launched a range of everyday luxury classics called the New Normal with Yasmin Le Bon (51), Nadja Auermann (44), Stella Tennant (45) and Eva Herzigová (42). Armani says the collection reflects a “desire to dress women in their daily lives. It offers garments that maintain the values of elegance and dignity, and at the same time a reflection of modernity.” This from a designer who also triumphed at the Oscars by dressing three older red carpet icons Cate Blanchett, Naomi Watts and Charlotte Rampling in stellar dresses. If fashion designers have finally started realising that grown-ups want to see their clothes on women they can relate to, it’s about time. “For too long fashion has targeted very young girls, ignoring the swathe of older, confident consumers who have a high disposable income and are unsaddled by debt. They are a powerful and stylish army and don’t particularly want to dress in a uniform of wrap dress and nude court shoes,” Stella Editor Marianne Jones, 50, once said of this stylish demographic of women. But whilst the signs are encouraging, there’s still a long way to go. Recent research showed that 58% of the approximately 12 million females over 50 in the UK (four million of whom are between 50 and 64) said they felt woefully under-represented on the high street. So let’s hope Birkin’s beautiful imagery for Saint Laurent isn’t just another designer fashion campaign designed to make headlines around the web - which loves nothing more than a controversial fashion image - but another sign that the industry is beginning to acknowledge that grown-up women can sell clothes. Because grown-up women are buying clothes.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. The New York based designer is used to high profile clientele; he created a bespoke gown for Michelle Obama’s first State dinner at the White House in 2009, and has dressed Beyoncé, Taylor Swift and Emily Blunt for the red carpet, as well as Queen Noor of Jordan (30% of his clientele is based in the Middle East). The Mumbai-born 57-year-old, who moved to New York aged 20 becoming an assistant to the famed fashion designer Halston, has a textile heritage, and still uses his father’s India based embroidery workshops. His collections pick influences from global artisanal aesthetics, cleverly melding them together into modern designs which offer an exotic outlook but without being too pastiche; the Duchess’s dress, nods to traditional Mexican embroidery patterns.   The impact of the Duchess choosing his design has not been lost on Khan, telling the Telegraph, “This is my happiest morning.  Last night, Rihanna was photographed in New York wearing a t-shirt printed with  an image of Hillary Clinton wearing a Yankees cap in 1999. Meanwhile, earlier this week, American Vogue officially endorsed Hillary Clinton for President. “Vogue has no history of political endorsements. Editors in chief have made their opinions known from time to time, but the magazine has never spoken in an election with a single voice” read the endorsement’s introduction. Given the profound stakes of this one, and the history that stands to be made, we feel that should change.” The article goes on to list how her stance on everything on guns, tax, immigration and LGBTQ rights had encouraged Vogue’s decision. Anna Wintour, the powerful editor-in-chief of American Vogue, has been a long time supporter of the Democrats, raising huge sums of money for campaigns and hosting lavish fundraisers. At one point it was even rumoured that she might be in for an ambassadorial role as a reward for her efforts.  But fashion’s support for Hillary is different to the industry’s often natural backing for centre and left candidates.  As Rihanna's t-shirt succinctly proves, it has also co-opted her as a kind of style heroine, enamouring her to readers via the vast amount of ‘throwback’ imagery which exists of this politician who has spent much of the past thirty years in the public eye and who hasn’t shunned style in the process.   Vogue’s endorsement message, for example, wasn’t headlined with a recent image of Clinton on the campaign trail, but a softly glamorous portrait by Annie Leibowitz from the magazine’s December 1993 issue, showing Clinton with her head resting on her arms and her hair gently blown away from her face. Meanwhile, US Harper’s Bazaar has also just published an article penned by Hillary about the admiration she has for her late mother, Dorothy Howell Rodham. Images of Clinton in a gold gown when she won a Grammy for Best Spoken Word Album (for her book 'It Takes a Village and Other Lessons Children Teach Us') and beaming in her oversized red glasses and big gold bauble earrings are used as stylish introductions to the piece.  The Instagram account @HillaryStreetStyle has also amassed over 18,000 followers since it began earlier this year. “As Hillary started running, I saw a lot of coverage of her evolving style, but I felt there was room in that conversation” says the account’s founder, who wishes to remain anonymous. “I wanted to view her style through the lens of other celebrities style rather than as ‘political fashion.’” To that end, @HillaryStreetStyle posts brilliantly observed collages showing Clinton next to celebrities wearing strikingly similar looks; there’s the post where she’s stepping off a plane in a pistachio pantsuit next to Mick Jagger in an identical look, or a line-up with her sandwiched between Kim Kardashian and Taylor Swift, each of them sporting sleek black tailoring.  “There are other mashups that I wasn’t too thrilled about, but once I see the response on the account I become pretty fond of them,” comments @HillaryStreetStyle, "For example, the Tim Kaine mashup—I never expected people to be so enthusiastic about the Clinton Kaine ticket in turtlenecks.” “I feel like people are really rallying around pantsuits this election!” adds @HillaryStreetStyle. Clinton herself has encouraged the pantsuit mythology with her Twitter biography reading; “Wife, mom, grandma, women+kids advocate, FLOTUS, Senator, SecState, hair icon, pantsuit aficionado, 2016 presidential candidate.”  Meanwhile, Clinton’s Instagram strategy has also tapped into the trend for throwback imagery. Before each of the debates so far, a glamorous non-recent image of Hillary has been posted. She celebrated husband Bill’s birthday with an intimate shot from their wedding day for which she wore a fabulously bohemian white dress, a strikingly different look to the tailoring and bright colours we see her inhabit today. “I think interacting with the world as a woman requires reconciling politics, stereotypes and fashion on a daily basis,” analyses @HillaryStreetStyle, “I do think it is interesting how Hillary has used fashion in this campaign, particularly because it is different, in my opinion, from how she has used it in the past. Sometimes, we forget that Hillary has been running for office since 2000, and way before that in support of Bill. The campaign’s fashion discussion for her senate and first presidential bid was very different. It is hard to say whether the change is the result of a shift in culture, feminism, fashion or her as a candidate or perhaps all of the above, but I’m enjoying it.” So has fashion and Clinton’s embracing of stylish throwback imagery actually helped the campaign? Perhaps not, but there may have been a subliminal advantage.  “From a personal perspective, I think it always humanizes people in the public eye to see where they came from and what they were like when they were younger, whether it is a celebrity or a politician,” says @HillaryStreetStyle. Arguably, when fashion publications or Clinton herself highlights her style, it creates an element of positivity, relatability and glamour which, as all successful politicians know, has become a crucial element in winning over voters.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Kelly Klein has been involved in the fashion industry from all aspects; firstly as a fashion student at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York; formatively as a design assistant at Calvin Klein and Ralph Lauren – eventually marrying Klein himself - and subsequently, as a photographer. Born Kelly Rector, Klein dabbled in modelling and showjumping before pursuing design, and became engaged to minimalist designer-of-the-moment, Calvin Klein, in 1986. They wed in Rome while they were on a buying trip in Italy, but separated 10 years later and divorced in 2006.
 Klein has primarily worked as an art book producer over the years, but in the mid 1990s carved a niche as a fashion photographer, taking her camera with her on far-flung travels and enjoying commissions for international editions of Vogue and Harper’s Bazaar. And for the first time, she has produced a book all of her own by releasing a retrospective of photographs that document her endeavours behind the camera.
 Starting out in the mid 90s meant that she was one of the first to shoot a young Kate Moss and a fresh-faced Gisele Bündchen.
 “Hopefully my work shows how blessed I feel to have spent time with these remarkable people” Klein writes in the opening of her new tome, which is published by Rizzoli. “When I shoot them I try to apprehend their natural beauty, especially when it comes to supermodels—there’s something free, instinctive, and effortlessly charming in the way the girls look when they arrive on set, without makeup, just their everyday selves. That’s what I try to preserve. Even after hair and makeup, my job is to see their unrehearsed, natural uniqueness and translate the beauty of it, carry it over, into the final image.” Klein never trained formally as a photographer, but cites watching how watching the “great practitioners” - Irving Penn, Bruce Weber, Richard Avedon, Patrick Demarchelier – at work helped educate her.
 The foreword of Photographs by Kelly Klein is written by her friend, fellow New Yorker Aerin Lauder - the beauty businesswoman heiress of the Estee Lauder cosmetics company. The 45-year-old recalls seeing Klein, 58, for the first time in a restaurant in the Hamptons and their impression she made on her. In Lauder’s words, “she just glowed”. She writes how: “This book is a portrait of her life in pictures. What makes it even more special is that she is a very private person, so it feels very open and generous of her to share it with us. Kelly has an amazing eye, and when something intrigues or inspires her, she reaches for her camera. It makes perfect sense that she would be a photographer, because the impulse behind taking a picture is to cherish, to save, to preserve. Kelly portrays beauty in every aspect of her life.”  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Autumn/ Winter 2017 collections herald the opportunity for the show-goers to interpret the trends seen in the Spring/Summer collections which are just hitting shops now. As fashion month draws to a close- and we all begin to consider switching up our style for Spring-  we're taking a look at how the street style set took on and mastered the trickiest trends of the moment, while pounding the  New York, London, Milan and Paris pavements.   From crop tops to frills, and from 80s to oversize: take notes from these fashion plates on how to master these new looks... Balloon sleeves - the tricky trend championed by Isabel Marant, Jil Sander and Simone Rocha, to name but a few - have fast become a street style staple. Why so? They're a sure-fire way to add a little day-time-appropriate drama to you look.  How do you make the 80s-inspired aesthetic seen all over the Saint Laurent, Gucci and Balenciaga catwalks work in 2017? Keep the ruched sleeves and kitten heels, but opt for gingham over Lurex  and swap black trousers for denim to tone things down a notch.  If, after seeing them marched down the catwalk at Victoria Beckham, Alexander Wang and Altuzarra, you vowed never ever to wear a crop top, this might force you to re-consider. Avoid having to bare your midriff and follow Red magazine's Merchandising Director Sophie Hooper's lead by pairing yours with an oversize white shirt- genius.  As glamorous and girly as frills are, they do have the potential to be unflattering. Too big, and they can add unwanted bulk, too small and they can look a bit twee. If you're after an easy way to introduce ruffles into your wardrobe, opt for dark, subtle frills, like those on Net-a-Porter's Fashion Director Lisa Aiken's fabulous maxi dress.  Yellow was strewn all over the Spring/Summer 2017 catwalks, with Tibi (where a saffron hue dominated), Céline (where a paler palette was adhered to) and Chloé (where pieces were a shade of mustard) among the myriad designers to lift our mood with the happy colour. The good news is, whatever your preferred nuance, yellow looks fabulous with neutral colours, punchy prints and primary colours. Ergo: far easier to wear that you might think.    Christophe Lemaire, Stella McCartney and Marques'Almeida were among the multitude of designers who showcased capacious clothes for spring, proving oversize doesn't have to mean unflattering. A good place to start is knitwear and outerwear (because let's face it, both are always better on the roomy side).  It's all well and good oogling Prada and Gucci's Oriental-inspired creations from afar, but how should you work embroidered, feather-laden pieces into your wardrobe in real life? Mix them in with every-day pieces for an eclectic get-up that doesn't look like it's been plucked straight from the catwalk. This show-goer, who's wearing a kimono-style-dress over jeans, has got it spot on.  Not the most practical of trends but oh-so-chic, all-white everything, which was seen at Alexander McQueen, Céline and Valentino, was taken on by some brave show-goers this season. Among these was Caroline Daur, who threw an angle-grazing trench coat over her white jumpsuit to excellent effect. The tip to take? White lends itself well to being paired with other neutral pieces.  Balenciaga, Chanel and Dolce & Gabbana all made a strong case for lace in their Spring/Summer 2017 shows. Yasmin Sewell tackled this  difficult trend, by pairing a lace skirt with colourful boots and leather coat, which removed all bridal connotations and resulted in an uber-cool outfit.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  I set my alarm clock for 6am but I always wake before then. I like to be the first person in the office so I can clear my head before my meetings begin. First I pick out what to wear – I’ve an armoire in my dressing room that I picked up at Chelsea Market, which looks deceptively small but it could give Narnia a run for its money. I then put on eyeliner and red lipstick (I never leave home without these), and take a cab to work, stopping by Hu Kitchen to pick up a delicious organic coffee.  My office is 15 minutes from home, in a former factory in the Garment District of New York. When I started my fashion house in 1981 there were just a handful of us working from my loft apartment, but now there are 40 staff. We do everything there: drape garments, make patterns, sew the first samples and host clients.  My schedule can be a little stressful, so when I’m not working I like to lose myself in an art exhibition or go out for dinner with friends. I’m on a diet at the moment, though,  so I tend to have spinach and tuna for lunch, and chicken soup for dinner. I’m not a great cook but I follow my mother’s recipe. If I haven’t made plans  I snuggle up at home and watch Peaky Blinders, my current guilty pleasure.  My weekends are spent visiting my parents’ place near Detroit or scouting New York antique shops in search of furniture, especially art-deco pieces. I recently bought an apartment across the hall from mine with a view to expand there – so far I’ve bought a verre églomisé desk.  Some weekends I’ll just stay at home. There’s nothing I love more than devoting a day to tidying my many wardrobes.  Audrey Hepburn might have been 97 years-old today, May 4th, but her classic sense of style is still as relevant now as it was in her Hollywood heyday. Among her most memorable on-screen moments, there are some killer costumes, or rather sartorial gems, to replicate in real-life. Here are our favourites… Hubert de Givenchy’s breath-taking gowns might foremost be at the centre of Funny Face, however it's Hepburn’s minimal style as book clerk Jo Stockton that captured an intriguing community of bohemians and pseudo-philosophers. The formula for beatnik style success? A dark cocktail of black polo necks, smart black trousers, utilitarian loafers and white socks. Boat necklines and dresses boasting raised necks are synonymous with Hepburn’s style on-and-off screen. The actress favoured dress cuts that masked her collarbone, but often cinched her petite frame with a large belt. Today this form-fitting dress style still holds its own in the boardroom, or as part of a working woman’s 9-9 schedule. Zipping around Rome as tearaway Princess Ann on the back of Joe Bradley’s motorbike, Hepburn’s performance earned her the 1954 Best Actress Oscar and ingrained that iconic Fifties silhouette into mindsets worldwide. For the spree around Rome, Hepburn reportedly sent back costume designer Edith Head’s sketches and recommended a simpler neckline, wider belt and flatter shoe. Her lace-up ballet flats chime with Aquazzura’s current Christy pumps, which make the perfect accompaniment to the flared midi skirts of Princess Ann, but also the slim cropped trousers worn often by Hepburn herself. Crew-neck, tailored cropped trousers and ballet flats; it's the fuss-free uniform of Sabrina Fairchild and one that still rings true with any woman with an ounce of fashion nous. Stock up on classic black and navy styles, and use them as the perfect ‘don’t have to think about it’ spring shoe staple that will outlast any seasonal trends. Responsible for shrouding Hepburn as Holly Golightly during her traumatic, rain-soaked search for pet ‘Cat’, it is Hepburn we have to thank for bending-the-belt rules of trench coats. Ignore the buckle and knot tightly around the waist before offsetting with bumper cat-eye shades and a head scarf. Givenchy’s black column gown, complete with draped pearls, wide-brimmed hat and cigarette holder, is unabashedly the pièce de résistance of Breakfast at Tiffany’s, but her other dresses reek of elegant cocktail hours and elegant soirées. Pale gloves and kitten heels might look a little contrived nowadays, but don’t forget to add a pair of bobby dazzlers to your ear lobes. Avoid looking too put-together by letting the straps of cinched-waist dresses perch lightly on the shoulders. It’s these subtleties that single Hepburn out as a savvy dresser worth her salt still in the industry. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This Sunday marks the third anniversary of the collapse of the Rana Plaza factory in Bangladesh which killed 1,133, injuring 2,500 garment workers, most of whom were women.  In the wake of the disaster, Orsola de Castro and Carry Somers (who have both run their own ethical fashion labels) founded Fashion Revolution. The organisation seeks to challenge the fashion industry to provide greater transparency, safer work places, fair pay and to address the rising environmental repercussions of the extreme levels of garment production. The underlying question must surely be: does anyone care about this? The economic titans of retail, attached to their buoyant profit margins at any cost are one thing. But add to them a Verruca Salt demographic existing in a constant state of want, purchasing items because of their low cost rather than whether they’re required. Clothes have become a dangerously disposable commodity. On Monday in Westminster, the Fashion Revolution collective staged "Fashion Question Time" to debate this crisis of ethics. Led by Labour MP Mary Creagh, with a panel including Livia Firth, founder of sustainability brand consultancy Eco-Age, and Jenny Holdcroft, policy director of IndustriALL, whose work involves implementing the Accord on Fire and Safety Building Safety in Bangladesh, the voluntary agreement signed by 90 global garment brands in the wake of the disaster. When asked how much has changed in the last three years, the findings were not particularly encouraging. Livia Firth said, “brands are still acting with impunity, they’re doing a lot of cosmetic work but none of the groundwork. When I spoke to garment workers at the Rana Plaza memorial last year, they said there was no difference to their working conditions.” Jenny Holdcroft explained that while the accord had raised awareness, “we have to change the entire industry. It’s not within the capacity of a single company to change it”.  The driving force of the problem is the systemic issues in the supply chain.  “It’s so complicated, so it’s always someone else’s responsibility," an exasperated Firth said. "They don’t want to change the industry, because if we all stopped buying clothes they would lose profits.”   To try to establish a better dialogue within the industry, they have launched the Fashion Transparency Index, which (available to view online) features 40 surveyed brands from Prada to Primark and its findings on their supply chains. Disclosure did not come easily: out of the 40 brands surveyed only 10 answered their questionnaire, with some claiming competition as an issue for their reluctance to reveal how and where they manufacture. The highest scoring include H&M which recently launched it's "Consious Collection." While such so-called halo-effect offshoots of a fast fashion brand provoke some cynicism, it’s worth noting that the company is doing more in this area than other low cost retailers. Other high scorers were Levi Strauss & Co and Inditex (Zara, Massimo Dutti, Uterqüe).   Stripe bateau neck box top, £140, u-neck long tank, £85, wide leg pant, £175, backpack, £230, double sandal, £135, Eileen Fisher Beyond this, there is the issue of women. The garment industry offers crucial work, yet it is too often dangerous, debilitating, in some cases enslaving work. Firth quoted the founder of ethical fashion label Edun, Ali Hewson, '“We wear the stories of the women whose clothes we wear.”’    Fashion Revolution ask that you buy nothing unless you will wear it at least 30 times. That might seem paltry, but look at every single piece in your wardrobe and see if you can meet their challenge. Then question, who made my clothes? The answer is something we must all demand.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
