 Today Woody Allen's latest film, Café Society. starring Kristen Stewart and Blake Lively hits cinemas and the costumes are just as on-point as any vintage Woody film. Woody Allen's costumes have become renowned for functioning almost as an extension to the characters, with the director creating leading ladies whose complicated personas are expressed through their style . Before we fall for the 1930s satin gowns, preppy shirts and pinned curls of Cafe Society, here's how Allen's previous films have proven to exert a lasting influence on fashion... Diane Keaton's thrown together menswear look in Annie Hall is one of the most influential looks in the history of cinema. Although Ruth Morley was the costume designer, the quirky layering tailored separates, ties and hats was inspired by Keaton's own personal style. Woody Allen explained in an interview back in 1995 that he gave Keaton the freedom to decide how Annie Hall would dress: "She [Keaton] came in and the costume lady on Annie Hall said, 'Tell her not to wear that. She can't wear that. It's so crazy.' And I said, 'Leave her. She's a genius. Let's just leave her alone, let her wear what she wants.'" Keaton has explained how she developed the slouchy menswear look: "Woody’s direction was the same. Loosen up the dialogue. Forget the marks. Move around like a real person. Don’t make too much of the words, and wear what you want to wear. Wear what you want to wear? That was a first. So I did what Woody said: I wore what I wanted to wear, or, rather, I stole what I wanted to wear from cool-looking women on the streets of New York. Annie’s khaki pants, vests, and tie came from them. I stole the hat from Aurore Clément, Dean Tavoularis’s future wife, who showed up on the set of The Godfather: Part II one day wearing a man’s slouchy bolero pulled down low over her forehead. Aurore’s hat put the finishing touch on the so-called Annie Hall look. Aurore had style, but so did all the street-chic women livening up SoHo in the mid-seventies. They were the real costume designers of Annie Hall." American label Ralph Lauren are named in the film's credits as providing a number of the costumes, including the tie and jacket. Ralph Lauren are still benefiting from the Annie Hall connection; at the AW16 show at New York Fashion Week models wore classic taupe tailoring, shirts and ties. Mariel Hemingway, as Tracy, the 17-year-old girlfriend of twice-divorced 42-year-old comedy writer, Woody Allen (Isaac), is the stylish focal point of Manhattan. Wandering around New York, Tracy plays the sartorial Sloane Ranger in an oversized Oxford shirt with crew-neck jumper thrown over her shoulders. Cut  to a scene in the diner and she sips a milkshake in plain cotton basics that suit her student budget but also enhance her  relaxed demeanour. Isaac’s ex-wife Jil, played by Meryl Streep, is now a lesbian and writing a confessional book about their marriage. Streep’s fashion is an exemplary exercise in masculine meets feminine. Her uniform is a crumpled, over-sized shirt tucked in a flared midi skirt. A plain look that lets her sweeping hair do the talking. Nearly 40 years later, Streep and Hemingway's looks are still setting the benchmark for how to do relaxed elegance whether your shirts and knits are from Uniqlo, J Crew or Armani.  It girl Chloë Sevigny stars in the tragedy half of Melinda’s story (the 2004 film is split into two halves), as prim friend Laurel. She rarely strays from pretty ice cream shades of conservative tailoring that is pulled together by pearls, a tortoiseshell headband and ladylike handbags. Collegiate chic, eat your heart out. In Woody Allen's 2013 film Blue Jasmine Cate Blanchett plays a rich Upper East Side socialite who looses her fortune when her wealthy husband is found guilty of fraud, and is left with no option but to move in with her sister Ginger in San Francisco. Costume designer Suzy Benzinger uses Jasmine's wardrobe to show her clinging onto her extravagant lifestyle, as she arrives with monogrammed Louis Vuitton luggage and wears 'I summer in the Hamptons' ensembles by the likes of Chanel, Oscar de la Renta and Fendi while working as a receptionist. The cream boucle Chanel jacket is perhaps the most memorable item in the film, and it was created by Karl Lagerfeld especially for Blanchett. "I called up Lagerfeld and I have to tell you, I was astounded," said costume designer Suzy Benzinger. "I sent a note and in two days he shipped out two custom made jackets for Cate Blanchett and with the most beautiful note. And I just thought, 'oh my god,' and he just said 'For Cate, I'd do anything. When the jackets arrived, I said, 'How could he do this?' It was right during the fashion shows and everything and he turned them around and sent them to me. Cate put it on and it was perfect." Benzinger sent one Chanel jacket to the dry cleaners and had it washed multiple times so it would look worn, and so would contrast how pristine the jacket looked in earlier scenes.  Although the script does require Blanchett to wear luxury brands, Forbes notes that there was a tight costume budget which has been reported to be $35,000. Berzinger found many of the pieces at discount stores, such as the Marc Jacobs trench coat she found on sale for $39.97 and the Valentino cocktail dress was bought for only $350.  Not only will the Blue Jasmine wardrobe offer a reminder in years to come of the designer investments which were worth treasuring in the 2010s, but the chic styling helped to define the modern way to do grown-up dressing. Penelope Cruz is utterly magnetic as Javier Bardem’s emotionally unstable ex-wife María Elena. Her eclectic, beatnik style matches her mood swings, causing uproar in breezy sundresses, platform heels and boater hats. None of her looks would be complete without mussed up hair and a cigarette hanging out of her mouth. But the key pieces which define her look are the satin, lace-embellished slips which offer a rebellious update on the glamorous-grunge mood coined by Courtney Love in the 90s. With Cruz's latin spirit, the slip became sexy again. Hannah (Mia Farrow) and her family are a prime example of Eighties normcore fashion. The sisters favour patterned, button-up shirts, sweater vests, over-sized mannish coats and blazers, and brandless accessories. Nothing is ever too bright, brash or glamorous, exactly how the unpretentious style should be. The fact that this was just how all style-unaware families dressed at the time is no matter; Hannah and her Sisters was the definitive template for the anti-fashion fashion craze which hit in 2014 and is still influencing those who love a novelty knit and geek-chic trainers now.  Woody Allen's 2014 film Magic in the Moonlight might have been slammed by the critics, but putting the problems with the script aside, the costumes were as fabulous as ever. The film is set on the Riviera in the 1920s and sees Emma Stone play a medium called Sophie who works with the (gullible) wealthy people who summer on the Cote D'Azur. She wears drop-waisted shift dresses, elegant 1920s swimsuits, berets and flower-adorned hats resting on her short bob. Hats and headpieces are central to Sophie's look, and costume designer Sonia Grande explains that this was inspired by the painter Leo Gestel. “[He] had a way of painting women in hats with many flowers that I used a lot, particularly in the character of Sophie," she explained to The Post. "Because of the way the hats transform the faces of the women he was painting. For the millinery of the film I looked to him.” Magic in the Moonlight's main style legacy? Bring F. Scott Fitzgerald-era chic into the 21st century.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Lucy Yeomans has just got back from the Paris Couture. I know this because, where else would the editor in chief of Porter – the flagship magazine of Net-a-Porter, the biggest luxury on line fashion website in the world – be at this time of year? Also I have been peeking at her Instagram account which features – among other envy inducing snaps - a photograph of the brilliant blue swimming pool at the Hotel Bristol. This is the life of the glossy magazine editor: fabulous five star hotels; made to measure clothes; bunches of flowers courtesy of Dior (or blooms as they are known in the upper echelons of fashion). So meeting her on a immaculate offices of Net-a-Porter in West London, I am expecting the editor of the frontispiece of this operation to be as immaculate as her environment. A bit scary. Very thin. Wearing black and a tight smile.   Forget all of the above. Yeomans, whose office is surprisingly small, is soft spoken, smokey eyed, wearing a slouchy navy polo neck a soft skirt (the new mid length, naturally) and boots, with swooshy Duchess of Cambridge styled hair. At 44 years old, she reminds me a bit of the bad CIA station chief Allison in Homeland, which is probably the hair but also something about her composure. She doesn’t, as you might assume, pull her wardrobe from a rail of edited clothes once every season. ‘Oh No’, she says, ‘I’m not sample size so that can’t happen’. Yes she has a personal trainer, but that’s a new development. That snap of the Hotel Bristol pool, she didn’t actually swim in it; she was too busy rushing between meetings (admittedly including lunch with her friend the model and philanthropist Natalia Vodianova). Still, however much she might protest otherwise, Yeoman’s lives at the white hot point where glamour and big business meet. Her job is not to strike awe, but to tempt her readers into buying and then deliver the goods literally (Net-a-Porter’s promise is order it at 10am be wearing it by 5pm).   In these offices they know how many of which item they have sold by the end of every day  - whether a banker has ordered a leather coat in New York or a lawyer a Gucci dress in London – and all this information is at Yeoman’s fingertips.   So determined is she to make Porter ‘useful’ and ‘all about what works for Her (the reader) rather than the fashion industry’ she has banned the word “trend”.  ‘Ha! Yes I have’, she chuckles. Why ? ‘Because How to Dress Now…that’s what women want from us. I think magazines have to work harder now. For so long we have been this delicious inspiration but so often the reader experience is really poor’ she says. ‘And it can feel cliquey’. What and who is fashionable seems certainly be shifting away from groovy young girls to fashion for grown-ups and grown up fashion.  We are talking on the same day that Georgio Armani has launched their New Normal campaign fronted by Nineties top models including Yasmin le Bon who is 51. Balmain’s spring/summer campaign this year reunites three of the original supermodels, Cindy Crawford (49), Naomi Campbell (45) and Claudia Schiffer (45). It’s this move away from obsessing about youth to a recognition that with age comes style and experience - that Yeoman understands and is ready for.    The current issue of Porter (on sale Feb 5) features all female photographers including Sam Taylor Wood photographing her daughter, and Catherine Deneuve pictured by Nan Goldin. On the cover is Amber Valletta, aged 42, another one of a tranche of models who were big in the Nineties. Forty and fifty-somethings, women with busy professional lives, families, the beginnings of wrinkles and bodies that require assistance to look good are suddenly in the forefront of fashion, including the designers.   ‘It’s true there is Phoebe Philo’ (the influential Celine designer who is in her forties and a mother of three) ‘and there is Stella (McCartney) and Anya Hindmarch and Sarah Burton (of Alexander McQueen). Stella’s bag collection is all about women on the go and I think all this has crept up and influenced fashion in a really interesting way’. If anyone epitomises a woman ‘on the go’ it’s Yeomans. Now settled in a loft style apartment in West London with her partner Jason Brooks an artist, ‘with the Marlborough Gallery’, she took on the editorship at Porter just four and a half months after giving birth to her daughter, Red – who she gave birth to as she hit her forties.  However, taking on such a high-profile position with a small baby was plain sailing compared to the pregnancy.    ‘I had Hyperemisis gravidaram (the same condition the Duchess of Cambridge has)’, she says. ‘I was really sick. I was half a stone lighter when I was six months pregnant than I am now…and I was really worried about having a baby.  I went into it saying ‘Ok Darling: just so you know in France they only breastfeed for three days. Just letting you know I'm not going to be very good at this…then she came out’ - she smiles - ‘ and she was the easiest.’ At 44 she hasn’t ruled out having another child: ‘I would love to if it happened’, but she has no regrets about having come to motherhood late. ‘For me it was about meeting the right person. I don’t actually think it had anything to do with my work.’ Age, as far as she is concerned, is not a topic to get hung up on. What about when it comes to looks, I wonder? It’s one thing being fortysomething, another if you are having to socialise in the fashion world with the world’s best preserved forty-somethings? ‘Ok I have had a tiny sprinkling of Botox around my eyes’, she says. ‘I don’t mind admitting that. I don’t know if I’d do more. But my ageing mentor is Diane von Furstenberg and she hasn’t had plastic surgery. It’s whatever works for you.’   In any case she looks much the same as she did fifteen years ago. I interviewed Lucy Yeomans once before, in 2001 when she was 29, soon after she had been appointed editor of Harper’s Bazaar (then still Harper’s & Queen) and she is just as driven now as she was in her twenties. It was while working at Tatler that she decided ‘I wasn’t as in control as I would like to have been’ and wrote to the publisher of Harper’s telling him why she was the right person for the top job.   Half a day into her next job, at Vogue, they called and offered it to her, and she was there for the next 12 years, bringing Harper’s out of the dusty dark ages into the celebrity driven light. Right from the start she was in at the deep end of the London social scene. Ronnie Wood threw a party for her at his private members club the Harrington Club, she hung out with J Kay of Jamiroquai and Alex James and was photographed at parties with George Clooney. It seemed she was in the right place every night, though she came across as more sophisticated and self contained than most of her peers. Lucy Yeomans never did do grunge. It seems she has always been in control of her own image as well as her destiny. However, she does have one big regret.  Her mother died 15 years ago of a brain tumour, ‘And that she didn’t meet my little one is a massive sadness to me’. Her eyes briefly mist over. You also get the sense it’s sometimes lonely at the top, especially since Natalie Massanet her friend and mentor, walked away from Net-a-Porter last September, with reportedly upwards of £100 million. She doesn’t deny her job is very hard work and stressful: ‘I am an insomniac beyond belief’ she says. ‘I wake up at three and just worry until it’s time to get up.’ Which, just briefly, gives a glimpse of the paddling that may be going on under the surface, as the swan floats elegantly by. ‘Fashion is armour for all of us’, she says smiling. ‘Your armour to do battle in.’   To see the full feature on ‘The Female Gaze’ buy the latest issue of PORTER, on sale globally on Friday February 5.  Devoid of a Twitter or Instagram account to convey her emotion at the passing of legendary singer David Bowie, Kate Moss did what she does best, and expressed herself through her choice of clothing yesterday afternoon. Pictured out and about near her north London home, the 41-year-old donned a black and white T-shirt emblazoned with the late performer’s face. Her companion for the afternoon, an unidentified male, also sported a T-shirt bearing the poster for Bowie’s Sound+Vision Tour from 1990. And Moss’s sartorial tribute didn’t end there; her metallic purple platforms looked like they could have been borrowed from Bowie’s own archive, and we bet the Starman singer would have approved of her shaggy coat and top hat – just the sort of attire to disrupt the genteel neighbourhood of Highgate. Moss was one of many within the industry to pay her respects to Bowie, who passed away aged 69 after an 18-month battle with cancer, in a maverick manner. Burberry model Hayett McCarthy painted the words Bowie across the palm of her hands and opened them up to photographers while walking in the menswear show yesterday afternoon. Male models in the show meanwhile, all sported glitter make-up around their eyes as a nod to the sad news. “I was just going to put it on one male model and then suddenly they all wanted it,” Christopher Bailey, the brand’s chief executive, told Telegraph Luxury. Guests took their seats to a Bowie soundtrack and the show itself featured performances by Benjamin Clementine with two of the tracks entitled Condolence and Adios. “It didn’t feel right to do a show that was celebratory today, when the news is so profoundly sad,” Bailey explained. On Instagram, thousands of images of the 69-year-old performer throughout his career were posted in homage of Bowie’s legacy, but model Alexa Chung, a keen drawer, doodled a line drawing portrait with the words ‘I love you’. American designer Jeremy Scott, who showed his latest collection for Moschino in London on Monday afternoon, revealed that the range was in part inspired by Bowie. He wrote: “My recent Moschino men’s show opened with Bowie inspired silhouettes.  Whether you're off on a beginner's budget ski trip with friends or prefer just to kick back in a luxe chalet until it's time for apres ski, packing for the slopes is never straightforward. Whilst for a sun holiday you can quickly fling several swmsuits and a couple of printed dresses into a bag then pick up the sun cream in duty free, this type of laissez-faire attitude sadly does not apply to a ski trip. Instead, it requires military planning alongside a zero-tolerance policy to thinking you can just buy the essentials once you're there, that is unless you enjoy spending hundreds of pounds on  socks you're pretty sure you could get for a quarter of the price back home. Then there's the actual outfit planning.  Once, ski wear was limited to performance and outdoor clothing shops - nowadays there's myriad luxury fashion brands creating salopettes and ski-suits.  Here, three fashion insiders with a penchant for skiing share their tips on how they look stylish whilst still mastering the slopes...  Go-to ski destination?  I learned how to ski at such a young age – by the time I could walk I was already on the slopes! This was always in Italy, but into my teenage years we had our own place in Jackson Hole which is my all-time favourite ski spot. I love the terrain, the fresh mountain air and the rugged Wild West cowboy town nature. It’s the perfect winter getaway. Since I’ve lived in London I’ve visited Kitzbühel, which has such amazing food and après ski. Who do you ski with? I mainly ski with family but occasionally friends too. Talk us through an average ski day?  When I was younger I was always the first in the lift up the slopes and the last in the lift down. Now, I’m much more relaxed and I’m out of the chalet at around 11am. I enjoy the socialising aspect, as well as the dining, so I prefer to have a super long lunch around 2pm and then head down, often in the pitch black. What's your go-to look for a day on the slopes? A great jacket, along with overalls over pants, a sweater, and lots of base layers. I do love all the new onesies this season which are super 70s but also chic and fun, particularly those by Cordova. What should we look for when choosing a ski jacket? I usually go for something more fitted with colour blocking. Moncler Grenoble is my go-to brand for jackets, I love their Lamar quilted styles. And for pants, overalls and knits I often choose Perfect Moment. Their Allos colour-block ski suit with retro bootcut flairs is a current favourite of mine. Do you like bright colours or do you stick to a more muted palette? Usually I go for olive, navy, black and white pieces – I think they’re more glam.  Elizabeth's must-haves  Cold-shoulder Fair Isle wool sweater, £1095, Monse, Aspen striped stretch ski suit, £950, Cordova, Two-tone textured-leather and suede ankle boots, £510 Proenza Schouler   What are your tips when it comes to layering? Definitely lots of base layers as it can get so hot but equally just as freezing. Falke and P.E Nation are both great for this. What are your go-to ski socks for preventing blisters? I would say invest in a great pair of boots that fit you well - you will never have pain or blisters if they’re the right size. Equally, make sure you have enough room to move your toes as this is how heat is circulated. For ultimate comfort I highly recommend Stella McCartney’s Eclypse leather snow boots worn with Falke’s ski socks, which are so soft and practical. What beauty products do you bring in your ski pocket? Your skin is prone to dehydration when you’re on the slopes so ensure to lock in moisture with a great lip balm, hand cream and sunblock, applying these generously throughout the day. My favourites are Make Beauty’s Marine Salve, Grown Alchemist’s intensive hand cream and Elizabeth Arden’s City Smart SP50 Hydrating Shield.  In the evenings after skiing I like to use Dr Barbara Sturm’s calming serum to soothe the skin, as well as lots of hydrating face masks, such as those by Joanna Vargas’. How can we avoid helmet hair? You can’t! But usually wearing your hair up in a ponytail along with the right products is a start! I use Sam McKnight’s Modern Hairspray for a strong hold. What's your après ski style? Super relaxed - oversized cosy fun knits, with comfy leggings and big snow boots. Do you ever pack a pair of heels? No!  But lots of boots.   Go-to ski destination?  I have been going to Madulain, a small village near St. Moritz for thirteen years. It's where my husband’s family has been visiting for over thirty years.  Who do you ski with?  I cross-country ski with an instructor. I find it thrilling being in the middle of the trees, skating along, with the wind blowing in my face. You use such much power, it reminds me of running which I love also. Talk us through an average ski day?  We leave the house just after 8am to drop my son off at ski-school. Then on an ideal day, I wait until after 11am to hit the trails because as the sun rises, a corresponding  pressure falls on our part of the valley that creates incredibly cold conditions. The type that will freeze your eyebrows!  What's your go-to look for a day on the slopes? Cross-country skiing calls for a technical windbreaker, a thin fleece, thermal top, technical leggings or ski stirrups. I wear an old Prada Sport ski jacket, Odlo or Moncler pants and an old Marni balaclava. I also have down-hill ski suits from Perfect Moment and Moncler. Tamu's must-haves Victoire zip-through sweater, £290, Fusalp at Matches Fashion, Jumpsuit, £1476, Cordova,  Crew neck top, £65, Odlo  Do you like bright colours or do you stick to a more muted palette?  I love wearing black and navy for cross country. But I have nice colorful après ski outfits as well. What are your tips when it comes to layering?  I am a big fan of layering because I suffer from the cold. Thin layers are the best and Odlo makes reliable technical thermals. I also love a Uniqlo thermal turtleneck. If you are cross-country skiing, layer a ski sock designed for a thinner style boot over a thermal sock that are paper thin. What beauty products do you carry? Dr. Paw Paw’s lip balm and Coola SPF sunscreen stick. How can we avoid helmet hair? I have very short natural hair that does not agree with wool caps, so I always wear a silk scarf underneath. What's your après ski style? I love a great parka, stirrups and great knits. Do you ever pack a pair of heels? Always. We wear them at home for dinner and sometimes out. My mother-in-law used to wear sandals sans tights out at night. I can’t wait to see what she does this season! Go-to ski destination? Gstaad with the family or Chamonix with friends for more extreme skiing Why do you love it there? Gstaad is a perfect ‘chocolate box’ Swiss mountain village with a wonderful family environment and skiing. Chamonix is much more hardcore skiing and après ski! Who do you ski with? We ski in Gstaad with our five kids, grandparents and friends who come to stay with us with their kids. Skiing is a great group sport for any age and of most levels. In Chamonix we ski with Thierry Donard, who is the original founder of Perfect Moment, and now an extreme sports filmmaker. He skied for France in the World Cup and my husband, Max, skied for the Swiss National junior team so skiing with the two of them and a group of other extreme skiers is always an adventure and a lot of fun if challenging at times!  Talk us through an average ski day?  We used to love being the first ones on the freshly groomed pistes in the mornings but having five kids changed that plan. It now takes us two hours and a near divorce to get everyone ready and in the car! There are never seven sets of matching ski gloves to be found and don't get me started on socks.  What's your go-to look for a day on the slopes? I always wear one of our ski suits, such as the Allos all-in-one. They are super flattering and more sophisticated than the jacket and cargo pants combo that I used to live in. I have tried to create different ski pants for different shapes - from high-waisted flares to loose fitting cargos. What should we look for when choosing a ski jacket? Technical fabric is key. If you are cold and wet on the slopes, it is a miserable experience. Read the label and don’t be fooled by a cool designer or cheap brand. Pockets are also key, lots of them, plus an inside snow skirt for added protection, when you nose dive into a pile of snow. Do you like bright colours or do you stick to a more muted palette? I love bright colours on the slopes and always dress the kids in our chevron jackets so I can spot them, usually far ahead of me. Having said that, I also think plain white is super chic. If I was going to choose something more subtle, I’d go for an all-in-one in black & white or navy & red. What are your tips when it comes to layering? We use the best technical fabrics on the market from Switzerland and Japan so our pieces are very warm, meaning I don’t need to layer too much. I usually wear a Perfect Moment base layer and a Polo neck jumper, or a Perfect Moment Merino wool Starsuit, which is always fun to strip down to for lunch or après ski. Jane's must-haves Caribou waterproof nubuck and rubber boots,  £150, Sorel, Deep-V fine-rib cashmere dress, £395, Raey at Matches Fashion, Merino wool Tignes sweater, £200, Perfect Moment  What about footwear?  Sorrel boots are some of my favourite and you can’t beat the good old Moon Boot for kids.  Falke make the best ski socks on the market for adults and children, they’re worth the investment, as you will have them for years. What beauty products do you bring in your ski pocket? I always use Sarah Chapman Skinesis Morning Facial in the morning before skiing or the Charlotte Tilbury Miracle Glow cleanser mask & balm is amazing too. On the slopes, I carry Sisley sun cream with a SPF 30 or Fotoprotector by ISDIN with a SPF 50 for delicate spots plus a Piz Buin lip balm. The Guinot face mask is the best remedy for dry skin, after a day on the slopes. And coconut oil is also great, you can use it for hair, face & body, everything.  Do you ever pack a pair of heels? Yes usually a pair from Jimmy Choo in case we go somewhere smarter, like Leonard’s at the Le Grand Bellevue or to a friend’s chalet for dinner. Of course, I wear boots to get there, and then change on arrival! © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Miuccia Prada will be honoured with the outstanding achievement award at The Fashion Awards 2018 in partnership with Swarovski, it was announced on Monday.  The prestigious award, which will be presented by the British Fashion Council at the annual ceremony at London's Royal Albert Hall on December 10th, acknowledges the contributions made by noteworthy individuals to the global fashion industry. Previous winners include Donatella Versace, Ralph Lauren KBE, Karl Lagerfeld and Dame Anna Wintour, to name but a few. “Mrs. Prada’s intuition for the zeitgeist and her blending of multiple creative disciplines including fashion design, art and architecture since the beginning have made her a pioneering force in our industry," says Stephanie Phair, Chairman of the British Fashion Council.  Miuccia joined the Prada family business (first founded in 1913) in 1978, when it was a relatively small operation with a focus on leather goods and accessories. Her first big success within the company was a line of black nylon backpacks launched in 1984, which have come to be a Prada staple.  She then went on to create Prada's first womenswear collection in 1988, and menswear in 1995; both received critical acclaim and marked her as a designer to watch. Over the last four decades, Miuccia has shown over 100 runway collections that serve as presentations of her nonconformist fashion ideas. In 1993, she expanded the Prada group to include Miu Miu - a younger brand with a playful feel, that Miuccia refers to as her "other soul". Other additions to the Prada group include footwear brands Church's and Car Shoe, as well as historic Milanese pastry shop Marchesi 1824. Also in Milan, the Fondazione Prada - a vast exhibition space - was opened in 2015. Miuccia has transformed Prada into one of the most globally respected brands in fashion, and as she continues to reflect her creative, informed self through her collections,  Miuccia plays a key role in defining the future of the the industry. The Fashion Awards 2018 will take place on Monday 10th December at the Royal Albert Hall, London.  By the age of 70, most women have their style locked down, sporting silhouettes that they have worn for the past few decades and not veering away from what they know works for them. On Wednesday night, the 70-year-old Dame debuted a new winning red carpet look at the New York premiere of her upcoming film The Eye in the Sky.  This year, Princes William and Harry have been marking 20 years since their mother's death with a series of documentaries and interviews paying tribute to her achievements. Poppies are a familiar motif, most famously used to remember fallen soldiers but they have a wider significance of healing and memory for loved ones who have died. Although they came with a somber meaning, the pattern on the Duchess's dress was cheerfully bright, reflecting the eye-catching prints which Diana herself used to love to wear, especially when visiting hospitals, children and charities.  Along with pie crust collars and ruffles, pussy bows were a romantic flounce which Princess Diana made her own early in her marriage. On the day that her engagement to Prince Charles was announced, she wore a blue and white speckled pussy bow blouse which she had bought in Harrods and was photographed wearing pale pink chiffon blouse by the Emanuels in Vogue soon afterwarsds; in fact, she loved that blouse so much that it led to her asking the couple to design her wedding dress. Later, Diana would often layer a white shirt with the pretty tie detail underneath tailored jackets and coats for public walkabouts and visits. Last year, she wore a pie crust collar dress to a children's tea party in Canada while the polka dot blue dress by Jenny Packham which she chose to leave the Lindo Wing after giving birth to Prince George drew immediate comparisons to a similar style by Catherine Walker which Diana wore after having William.  Perhaps the most famous Diana-related item in the Duchess's repertoire is her sapphire and diamond engagement ring which William gave to Kate so that she would be part of his marriage and adult life.  This London Fashion Week we'll all have the chance to hang out (and take a selfie) with catwalk queens Cara Delevingne and Kendall Jenner. CaKe (that's the name they like to go by) have just landed a major LFW modelling gig - nope, they've not got their own catwalk show, they've been turned into wax models.  Cara and Kendall are the latest stars to get the Madame Tussauds treatment for a special LFW attraction at the waxwork museum which will show what fashion week is really like behind-the-scenes. So if you've always dreamed of going to London Fashion Week but haven't made it onto the front row yet, this is your chance to see what it's all about with CaKe as your tour guides.  You'll also be able to take a selfie or 10 with Delevingne and then if you want to follow in her fashionable footsteps, there will be a catwalk where your model strut will be judged by fashion's gatekeeper, US Vogue editor-in-chief, Anna Wintour. 23-year-old Delevingne is clearly pleased with her turn as a wax model, as she posted a picture of her double on Instagram with the hashtag '#WaxCake'. We'll have to wait to see just how realistic their wax counterparts are, but Madame Taussauds has revealed that both models worked closely with the sculptors to ensure that their waxworks look just like them. The museum even has a picture of Kendall in a fitting to prove it. This is London Fashion Week we're talking about, so obviously we will see some very well dressed waxworks; 'Wax CaKe' have lucked out in the wardrobe department - Delevingne will wear a Saint Laurent dress. This is the model friends latest joint venture: earlier this month we brought you the news that a CaKe clothing line might be coming our way soon. The Sun reports that Kendall and Cara have trademarked CaKe after they were spotted wearing t-shirts with their logo on it over the summer. The 'source' reports that they already have designs for tops and hats and haven't ruled out a complete collection.  Tempted? The London Fashion Week experience will be open from Monday, February 8 to Sunday, February 21. This sweeping history of the past century viewed through a prism of exquisite fashion was mounted with unprecedented imagination thanks to set designer Nathalie Crinière.  The selfie queen announced at the Vogue Festival earlier today that she 'hates most of her old makeup looks' when she watches past episodes of her and her family's reality show, Keeping up with the Kardashians, saying the 'crazy hair and bad make-up makes me cringe.'  Wearing a sparkling gold dress, she took to the stage at her panel discussion titled Fashion, Friendship and Fabulous Lashes. Old friends, global makeup artist, Charlotte Tilbury and reality megastar, Kim Kardashian West were lead by Vogue's Fiona Golfar to discuss all things beauty. 'I just wore too much, I loved false eyelashes and used to pile them on, but now I'm really into nontouring... I'm trying to wear less makeup and my husband loves it,' she said of her plans to step away from her previous heavily-contoured look.  Said husband, rapper Kanye West was sat front row and regularly took snaps of his wife on his phone as she occasionally smiled at him during her discussion. 'Now I strobe with highlighter rather than using a bronzer to contour as it just looks too heavy, I'm going for a lighter makeup look now.' Gesturing towards her eyes, she told the audience she wasn't wearing any fake eyelashes or hair extensions, a clear move towards her new natural look.  When asked by Golfar if she'd ever stop contouring altogether, Kardashian West replied 'no, I'll always contour my nose - I know people think I've had a nose job but it really is just make-up!' The two friends went on to discuss going bare-faced in front of their husbands, and to the packed auditorium's surprise, Tilbury revealed her husband had never seen her without full makeup. She even wore it while giving birth, and reapplies it before bed each night. 'For my first baby I wore full makeup giving birth, but none for my second,' Kardashian West stated, referring to the birth of the couple's son, Saint, five months ago. Although she plans to tone down her makeup look, she says their three-year-old daughter, North 'loves playing with make-up just like I did. I went to make-up school when I was 14, and I'd do the same for her.'   Wondering what the toned down Kim Kardashian West's go-to makeup products are? 'An eyelash curler, a lipstick in the perfect nude that Charlotte created for me, a Joe Blasco foundation, a blush, a Smashbox bronzer, a mascara - Charlotte's Legendary Lashes, a little MAC Kabuki brush and a gold eye pencil from Kardashian Beauty,' the star told the audience, who were frantically recording and taking notes, and are probably off to buy a highlighter.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Thanks to an as yet under-the-radar scoop in the latest Porter magazine which presciently interviewed Divorce Lawyer Of The Moment, Laura Wasser, about her style, we now have unprecedented insight into how the Brangelina proceedings will unfold. So let’s dissect what she says about her working wardrobe – and what that means. Because you should never underestimate the psychological clues provided by a person’s choice of handbags and shoes. Power Piece: “A sheath dress in black, navy or gray [sic]. I have a Dolce & Gabbana one with leopard print lining.” (Translation: If you’re sitting opposite me, I am going to scare the crap out of you) Fashion Icon: “Isabel Marant.” (Translation: I’m also an earth mother. Errant Husbands with anger and child-care issues, beware) Heels or Flats: “That’s a no-brainer. I always wear five inch heels and did so through two pregnancies.” (Translation: Earth Mother who’s taller than you) Most Treasured Item: “I have two rings made by Gabriella Kiss that I always wear. They were given to me by the father of my elder son.” (Translation: I stay friends even with ex husbands and former clients. Especially former-clients. ) Handbag:“I don’t like to carry a briefcase so I use a Lanvin or Balenciaga tote for my work folders and put in a fold-over clutch inside by my friend Clare V for my lipstick and phone.” (Translation: I have an eye for the quirky detail and contacts everywhere) Beauty Essential: “I don’t wear mascara but I always curl my lashes….and lipstick, lipstick, lipstick. Nars and Tom Ford.” (Translation: Expect the unexpected). Pants or Skirts: “Definitely skirts….I live in California so my legs are always brown.” (Translation: whatever happens in court, we’re going to look great). © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Even after the surprising ruptures of late 2015, this morning’s rumours about Hedi Slimane’s imminent departure from Saint Laurent seem initially far-fetched. Yet the normally reliable Women’s Wear Daily is running with the story, even suggesting that Anthony Vaccarello, the Belgian designer currently working wonders at Versus, is in Kering’s (the company that owns Saint Laurent) viewfinder as a successor. Does any of it begin to make sense? Slimane may have had a bumpy ride with most critics. (Heads up, I’m one of those underwhelmed by his creative contribution to the Saint Laurent legacy). Yet no one can argue with his runaway commercial success there. Since Slimane’s first womenswear collection for Saint Laurent landed in October 2012, the hitherto sluggish brand has been a top performer globally. The secret of its success? The self-same factors that irked the cognoscenti – the conventional, expensive classics masquerading as edgy streetwear. Saint Laurent became the aspirational source for well cut black trousers, tuxes, pea-coats, trench-coats, suede boots, kitten heels , sensible roomy handbags… it may have been drenched in a petulant teenage sensibility in Slimane’s rock ‘n’ roll catwalk shows, but in reality, it all slipped seamlessly into a boardroom meeting. That’s some kind of clever. To dress classics up as a two fingered gesture to the establishment is a peculiarly modern display of genius. Slimane has been undeniably astute in recognising that sharply engineered, simple, timeless, any-age items weren’t available elsewhere – and spinning them into something that appealed to high spenders. So why would he want to quit now? Speculation that he and Kering have failed to agree on a mutually pleasing new deal may seem predictably reductive – but it’s predictable for a reason. There is an emerging pattern of designers comparing their gilded terms with those of their peers, and finding them wanting.  Raf Simons allegedly left Dior last Autumn partially because he was unhappy with the salary and resources LVMH was offering him, compared with Nicolas Ghesquière’s package at Louis Vuitton. But it’s surely more complex than that. No designer at this level is motivated entirely by money. Slimane may feel that he’s achieved all he can at Saint Laurent. Having put it back on its feet commercially, and with Gucci hot on its heels (at least one major retailer told me last autumn that Gucci is poised to overtake Saint Laurent’s sales), he may want to leave while he’s ahead. For once, Twitter has no pat answers: so far tweeters have merely repeated the question. Vaccarello, while better known than Alessandro Michele was this time last year, is a relatively unknown proposition.  Nonetheless, so far 33-year-old  has steadily risen through fashion’s ranks,  coming first in the Hyères International Festival of Fashion and Photography, for his collection inspired by porn star La Cicciolina, thereby displaying promising PR skills and nabbing Karl Lagerfeld’s attention at Fendi. Since then, he has authored a well received mini-line of mini leather and organza skirts for Maria Luisa in Paris  - and more fully fleshed collections for Versus Versace, where he has been creative director since early 2015. Perhaps not insignificantly, in 2011, Vaccarello won the prestigious the Association Nationale pour le Développement des Arts de la Mode, or ANDAM fashion award – whose sponsors include both Kering – and LVMH. But it’s Vaccarello’s Versus Versace collections that are  most instructive vis-à-vis this story: electrifying, etiolated tailoring combined with rock chick sexiness. And as he proved with the safety-pinned tributes to that infamous Liz Hurley dress in his SS15 Versus Versace outing, he knows as well as Slimane, how to re-point a label’s codes for a new generation. He is also very at home with black. So if – and it’s still an if – the rumours are true, what are the lessons? That no designer, however successful, is indispensible. That egos will only be appeased up to a point. That the industry increasingly treats the archives of some of its most venerated houses like oil reserves – assets to be constantly mined but not necessarily added to. 2016 is off to an interesting start.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This weekend, Texan model Jerry Hall will tie the knot for the first time – officially. The 59-year-old will wed 84-year-old media mogul Rupert Murdoch on Saturday at St Bride’s Church on Fleet Street, an appropriate choice considering that the historic building is considered to be ‘the spiritual home of the media’ due to its setting on a street which was once lined with newspaper publishers. Contrary to popular belief, this will be Hall’s first official marriage. She wed Rolling Stones rocker Mick Jagger, the father of her four children in the late Seventies, but their Hindu ceremony, which took place in Bali, was declared invalid only after Hall had left Jagger in the late Nineties over his continued infidelities. Having walked for all the top designers during her catwalk career, Hall won’t have been short of options when it comes to who's making her dress for The Big Day. But the back catalogue of Hall's best looks through the years gives us some clues as to what style she'll pick on her wedding day.  There'll be some shoulder on show As our fashion director Lisa Armstrong recently pointed out, shoulders are the last part of a woman’s body to age, so Jerry, with her supermodel disposition, could more than get away with sporting an off-the-shoulder, sweetheart neckline for her big day. …and a fishtail silhouette Hall is fond of creating that Jessica Rabbit style silhouette with a fishtail dress - one of the bridal world's most popular styles. …or she could go down the twin set route Having modelled all manner of shoulder-puffed power suits through the Eighties, Hall recognises the function of an immaculately tailored two-piece. A crisp white or ivory jacket with a co-ordinating pencil skirt is a sophisticated choice for a bride who is perhaps past a floaty, princess moment. Her hair will definitely be side-swept and tousled within an inch of its life No-one gives a better side-parting than Ms Hall. Her hairstyle hasn’t chance in the four decades that she’s been in the spotlight, so why should it now? …and could well contain flowers We’re not talking a Woodstock-style headdress, but just a small rose or something discreet to nod to the romance of the union that is taking place. Her red lip game will be strong Jerry Hall and red lips go together like bread and butter, so we’d put money on the statuesque beauty sticking to her signature look. Her shoes will almost certainly be flat At a towering 6ft, Hall is a fan of flats and kitten heels, and who can blame her? Comfort is key and when it comes to her big day, she won’t want to tower over Mr Murdoch. We wonder if Manolo Blahnik or the likes has created a one-off pair just for March 5. We haven’t ruled out a pashmina Hall loves to drape elegant shawls over her frame, and the air in the City of London could well be nippy. We predict that dutiful daughters Georgia May and Elizabeth will be armed with one and standing by. …or a fabulous (faux) fur With temperatures for the weekend set to peak at just eight degrees, maybe Hall should raid her coat cupboard and pack something more substantial than the aforementioned pashmina. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  What we love most about global singing sensation Adele – aside from those weepy power ballads and her potty mouth – is that despite colossal success and wealth, she hasn’t forgotten her roots. This month sees the Hello crooner’s second ever US Vogue cover (her last appearance was in 2009), and the accompanying interview is a delight to read.  The Londoner opened up to Hamish Bowles, the publication’s European editor-at-large, a fellow Brit whose colourful, dandy style evokes a sort of bygone charm. The two go to upmarket food emporium Fortnum & Mason during the course of the interview – which is perfectly imaginable. But what’s really brilliant are the anecdotes of them visiting catalogue shop Argos. Bowles describes the retailer as "far from a celebrity hangout”, (no kidding) but 27-year-old Adele is quite at home there. “I used to buy my jewelry from here,” she admits, as they look at a cabinet of trinkets, and makes the most surprising admission of all: “I couldn’t wait to have a mum necklace.” Adele and half of Tottenham, Brixton (London neighbourhoods where she grew up), Manchester, Newcastle... aspired to own tacky Elizabeth Duke pieces in the late 90s, and its refreshing that despite now being able to afford a case-full of Harry Winston diamonds, she doesn’t consider herself too fabulous for the wares of Argos. (As an aside however, she does admit that she is an “absolute germaphobe,” and winces at the touch screens used in store as opposed to the traditional catalogues, but puts it down to her throat surgery). The interview also sees Adele reveal that her recent weight loss – in an attempt to improve stamina for her upcoming tour, she gave up alcohol – means she can buy off-the-peg clothes much more easily than before. “Now I fit into normal, off-the-shelf clothes” which means that she has acquired a new-found shopping habit. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Born in Paris, Christian Louboutin began work aged 17 at the Folies Bergère music hall, before his obsession with shoes led him to work for French designer Charles Jourdan and later Roger Vivier. Louboutin set up his own company in 1991, opening a store in Paris. He became known for vertiginous heels with glossy red soles – a feature he trademarked in 2007 – and now sells over one million pairs of shoes a year. In 2014 he branched out into beauty, with a range of nail polish, followed by lipstick and fragrance. He has houses in Paris, Lisbon, Aleppo and Luxor, along with a houseboat named Dahabibi (My Love Boat) on the Nile. I started working at the Folies Bergère because I’d done drawings of shoes for the dancers, but I never made a pair of shoes there – I made coffee, helped the technicians, resewed costumes. When I joined I was everyone’s little darling but after six months I became part of the furniture and the girls started to get annoyed with me being around  all the time, so it was probably time to leave. Roger Vivier was the first person who made me think that designing shoes could be a real job, a beautiful job. I was his assistant when he was working on his retrospective in Paris, and he became a mentor to me. The funny part is that he was quite competitive. One day he described someone as being ‘our age’. I was 24, he was 80! I couldn’t believe it, 60 years made no difference to him. But that’s why he was always so alive, so vivid and enthusiastic. Sometimes the shoe is not the master of the ceremony.Christian Dior once told Mr Vivier that a good shoe is able to appear but also able to disappear. It doesn’t apply to all of my shoes but it’s very good advice. You have to look at the woman first. As a designer you should always remain true to yourself. You have to believe in your own creativity. Every time I have gone with someone else’s choice, I was wrong. For instance, one time the buyers said they wanted a thicker heel and for some reason I said yes. But the balance of a shoe comes from every line. That shoe was not successful at all. And actually I was pretty happy because it means that when I’m true to myself my customers can see it. When I looked at my first prototype, it wasn’t as good as the drawings. From the back, it was monochromatic – very, very black. So I grabbed a bottle of red nail polish from a girl in my studio and painted the entire sole. The red sole quickly became a silent recognition of my brand, and later a trademark. But the court case over that trademark was very painful. I’m not an aggressive person, I just thought the company that copied me could have done other things.  I wouldn’t sell myself for celebrities, I don’t see the point. I was most flattered when I saw the French singer Sylvie Vartan wear my shoes. She was very big in the 1970s, and I couldn’t believe that someone from my childhood was actually wearing a shoe I had designed. It has required a lot of strength to stay independent. It’s difficult to resist when people offer you something amazing. In 25 years I’ve met thousands of people who’ve given me advice, and someone else will always give the exact opposite advice. Everyone has an agenda. That’s why you have to stay focused and decide for yourself. The only regret I have is that my mother died before I started my company. I owe my stability to the education she gave me and how loving she was, so I regret that she didn’t get to see that she did a great job. There were a lot of signals that I should go into beauty.There was fake Louboutin nail polish so it clearly made sense, and of course it’s part of my story. It took me two years to be happy with the polish and lipstick, then I moved on to fragrance. It needs to be organic and well digested; I don’t want to do things just for the sake of doing them.  Don’t limit yourself; the sky is the limit! As a young designer, you should not look too far into the future because you may be surprised  by your trajectory. When I started, I never imagined that 20 years on I’d still be in business, selling a million pairs of shoes a year. If I’d projected this far I wouldn’t have predicted the way it has happened. Don’t necessarily focus  in a straight line because there are a lot of opportunities that you’re not expecting, maybe that don’t even exist right now.   christianlouboutin.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We all know Celine Dion as one of the best-selling musicians of all time, queen of the love ballad and the woman who was responsible for at least three of the cassettes in every 90s family car. But for all her astonishing achievements, Dion has never been particularly well-known for her style (which is fair enough when you're busy smashing out hit after hit).  So when the Canadian singer arrived at Dior's show at the recent Paris Haute Couture Fashion Week in the established fashion editor uniform- black on black on black- it was the first sign that she might be entering a new phase of her life, on a mission to reposition herself as a part of the fashion crowd. A month on, she is still taking her fashion rebirth very seriously indeed. This weekend, she wore seven different outfits in 24 hours, all sourced from big name fashion houses such as Gucci and Versace. Another sign of Dion's commitment to establishing a reputation for style as well as songs comes in the form of Hollywood stylist Law Roach, who she hired just weeks before Paris fashion week to mastermind her style overhaul.  Roach, who styles tween stars Ariana Grande and Zendaya, has been dressing the 48 year old in key pieces by Gucci, Balmain, Balenciaga, Celine, Chloe and Saint Laurent. The loud prints, sweeping coats, bold colours and stilettos are all in keeping with Celine Dion's diva persona, but he has also balanced this with some unlikely twists that you wouldn't expect from Las Vegas-era Dion. There is also evidence that Dion has thrown herself wholeheartedly into these fashion experiments. Earlier this month, the 'My Heart Will Go On' singer was seen out and about in the cult Titanic hoodie by Parisian label Vetements, creating the most meta of fashion moments. Meanwhile, Roach has also tempted her to try head-to-toe Gucci catwalk looks and styled her hair in a 'Hackney hun', that's the half-up, half down style you'll have spotted on the tween crowd. There is a very personal significance to Dion's renaissance. Six months ago, her husband off 22 years René Angélil died of cancer. Over the weekend, Dion opened up to the Today Show about her difficult year. "It's been a journey. It's been hard seeing the love of your life suffering for the last three years. It's been really hard, but millions of people are going through this. And I feel very strong because not only that he loved me so much for many, many lives to come – he gave me three magnificent kids, so much knowledge, stability and confidence."  Dion seems to be dressing for a new chapter, using fashion to find extra confidence, strength and project a positive outlook. "I have to say that, coming here after the passing of my husband after not even six months (later), it could have been way easy for me to say, 'You know what, I'm not in the mood of dressing up and having the purse and seeing the fans and having a good time and singing, giving a part of your soul (sic)," Dion said to Entertainment Tonight. "But knowing that he (Angelil) loved the industry so much - he made me who I am today since (I was) 12 years old - I went back on stage before he passed, he wanted me to really be the artist I always wanted to be, and I knew that for a long time." "She’s really enjoying herself,” Roach told People “I know she’s enjoying herself and we’re enjoying each other because we tell each other every day. I’m here almost every day and it makes me so happy to see her so happy. If I had a small piece of [creating] that with the clothes and the fittings and the shoes and the bags, then I am overjoyed.” “I think she’s really enjoying fashion and being out and being seen and getting photographed,” he added. “Fashion is the most interactive art form. It’s nostalgic and it can take you to another place. If you feel beautiful and pretty, you can’t be sad and miserable. It’s just impossible.” As for what the styling process is like between the two, Dion said to Entertainment Tonight: "Working with Law Roach is quite an experience to be honest with you. He brought me out of my closet and now flowers are growing. Even my kids are like, 'We want a bow like this, we want a dress like this' - even if they're boys. They're into fashion, they're into characters, everything they say they like, whether it's for a girl or a boy, they want it." Something tells us that there's plenty more to come from Dion's big fashion misson. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The supermodel Kate Upton has accused Paul Marciano, one of the founders and creative directors of American denim label Guess, of emotional harassment and sexual misconduct. “It’s disappointing that such an iconic women’s brand @GUESS is still empowering Paul Marciano as their creative director [sic],’ she wrote on Twitter, using the hashtag #metoo, which was established after the Harvey Weinstein scandal broke across the film industry and victims of sexual misconduct in all walks of life began to share their stories on social media. Upton did not say whether she was referring to a personal case or speaking on behalf of someone else. “He shouldn’t be allowed to use his power in the industry to sexually and emotionally harass women,” she added. As a well-known voice within the fashion industry making a direct accusation, Upton’s words could potentially serve to start a ripple effect, much like that which women in film were able to propel after Ashley Judd and several others spoke to the New York Times, confirming the paper’s initial inquiries about Weinstein. The model, 25, has posed in at least four Guess advertising campaigns for lingerie and accessories, mostly in 2010 and 2011 when she was 18. The brand was credited with propelling her career into the commercial big league.     To date, a number of established fashion photographers and designers have been the subject of rumours, but with many victims wishing to remain anonymous, and with many models said to be scared of the consequences that speaking out could have on their careers, it has been difficult for the press to report on concrete circumstances, or even give names of offenders, in the same way that was possible in the film industry’s cases. At the end of last year Cameron Russell, an American model who has walked for Louis Vuitton, Prada and Victoria's Secret, had begun to allude to the fact that sexual misconduct was rife within the fashion industry, and spent weeks reading and re-posting stories on her Instagram account from fellow fashion models who claimed to have suffered at the hands of casting directors, designers, photographers and other men in positions of power. She rightly, however, respected the wishes of those who shared their stories with her, and blocked out names of all involved. The campaign started a much-needed conversation, and several agencies and media publishing houses took action as a result to protect their charges, but a witch hunt was inadvertently prompted, as readers began to try to fill in the blanks for themselves. Since then, more direct allegations have been made by male models, as 15 current and former male models and 13 male assistants spoke out against esteemed photographers Mario Testino and Bruce Weber. Many brands and publishers, including Condé Nast, have suspended ties with both Weber and Testino in light of the accusations and this week Condé Nast published a strict new code of conduct to be upheld on all fashion shoots, including a note that ‘subjects should not be left alone with a photographer, makeup artist or any other participant any time during a shoot.’ In accusing Marciano, who has yet to respond to the allegations, Upton has given us another potentially pivotal moment. Guess is a powerful fashion brand, founded by brothers Georges Marciano, Victor Herrero (currently serving as CEO), Maurice Marciano (Director and Chairman Emeritus) and Paul Marciano (who also serves as Executive Chairman of the Board) 37 years ago. Its revenue was more than $2.2 billion in 2016. This case is different to those of the independent photographers, who, if guilty, will see their reputations suffer and incomes dry up when they are no longer hired by brands that don’t want to associate with them. It will be up to Marciano's brothers and their board (as well as the police, of course) to decide if the claims made against him should be investigated and determine an appropriate course of action. And, of course, their primarily female customer base may speak by taking their wallets elsewhere. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. There is a wealth of luxurious loungewear out there as a feel-good alternative to old t-shirts and grey tracksuit bottoms and Trott has tracked down some of the best of it with her painterly floral pyjamas by Cyberjammies. We're particular fans of the times she matches her leggings to her trainers.   Stella McCartney has famously created Team GB's Olympics kits (lucky athletes) but of course the British designer is just as well known for her flatteringly modern dresses, beloved of the likes of Gwyneth Paltrow, Nicole Kidman and Kate Moss. So of course Trott wasn't going to miss out on the chance to wear a McCartney design not created in performance fabrics. For a recent photo shoot, it was all about  an elegant asymetric red dress.  Tony Porter, 80, has enjoyed several careers over the course of his life. From selling paint in Kenya to selling clothes at Biba, he ended up buying Burgh Island off the coast of Devon and restoring its historic Art Deco hotel. But somewhere in-between the above, he founded his own fashion PR business in London in the Sixties and laid the down the foundations for London Fashion Week as we know it today. Here, as he releases an autobiography chronicling his colourful life, he exclusively reveals exactly how the British Fashion showcase came about… Porter thought it was “ridiculous” that Paris and Milan hosted journalists and buyers twice a year, but that London, with its thriving fashion scene, was out of the loop. “There was nowhere for them [press] to go and find everybody in one place and one time in Britain. So I went to an organisation that existed then, which was called the Clothing Export Council of Great Britain, and I went to them, “Don’t you think it’s about time that somebody got this together?” That was in 1971. In the beginning, it had to be called British Fashion Week because it was supported by the Export Council and the British Knitting Council. The Clothing Export Council of Great Britain didn’t have any budget to get the event going, but its director agreed to match whatever Porter could raise from the designers that wanted to show.  Says Porter, “So I went round the top designers at the time, and introduced myself, and they were a great support, especially Jean Muir, Zandra Rhodes, and Bruce Oldfield." He raised £500, which the CECGB matched, then "I printed a little brochure and used the money to send it out to overseas press!" …but it quickly snowballed. “It was just wonderful the way everyone seized onto the idea” says Porter. “Not only did individual designers join, like Caroline Charles, Betty Jackson, but groups started to form, like the New Wave, there was one called Fashion Promotions too.” In the five years that Porter worked on promoting the event, that number became 25. Porter persuaded editors from the New York Times, International Herald Tribune and the Los Angeles Times to cover the event. “I was able to meet really important overseas press at the airport and take them to the hotels and prime them on the way about which designers were showing when, and where possible, to give them an idea of what they’re going to see,” recalls Tony. “I did this for five years, always making them welcome, and they came to my house, and we really got on well.” On nights were parties were scarce, he would host his own in West London. “Of course they had absolutely no IT in those days,” he says. “They [the editors] used to go back to their hotels in the evening and phone the stories through. They wrote really lovely pieces.” Does Porter think people got paid to attend fashion shows in the Seventies? " Oh, I don’t think so... I think I would have heard, if that happened" he says, clearly shocked. "I didn’t even know if happened now either. [Back then] designers made quite sure that not only the important press were in the front row, but also famous people that wore their designs. That was always picked up by the media, a photograph of one of those." When he logged on recently to see what London Fashion Week was all about now, Porter says he was absolutely "gobsmacked" to see the sheer amount of names showing. "In a way, it’s a dream come true because we tried so hard to get the idea across. I just had this idea that something should be done." Tony Porter’s autobiography, 'Whatever Next', is published by Matador and is priced £9.99 © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Raf Simons departure was announced yesterday – to the shock of the fashion world – and takes place with immediate effect.  His three-and-a-half year tenure at the brand has brought the storied fashion house, founded in 1946 by the late Christian Dior, back to the forefront of fashion. His directional but wearable collections, must-have accessories and utterly Instagrammable shows made him the dream appointment and the balance sheets at Dior reflect this.
 The 47-year-old Belgian is leaving to concentrate on his eponymous menswear brand and spend more time enjoying life’s pleasures outside of the fashion sphere.
 He said in a statement that his time at the helm of the brand was an “immense privilege”. Here’s what we’ll miss about his reign the most:  Those double-pearl earrings you see in every high street store these days? Those were conceived under Raf’s reign.  As were the opinion-dividing bejewelled 'fusion trainers' that no street style star worth her salt wouldn’t have been seen dead without. Then there’s the beautiful pastel bags, inverted-heel shoes and the latest smash hit: Perspex-heel boots. OK, so Jennifer Lawrence may have fallen over in the Dior gown she wore to collect her ‘Best Actress’ Oscar in 2013, but we won’t be quick to forget how resplendent she looked in it. Simons’ edgy designs helped the likes of Emma Watson come out of her goody-two-shoes Harry Potter persona and embrace a directional dress-over-trousers look at the 2014 Golden Globes. 2013 was Carey Mulligan’s Great Gatsby year, and who did she choose to step out on the red carpet at Cannes…? Under Simons, Dior appointed its first campaign star of colour: Bajan popstar Rihanna. He has also been instrumental selecting iconic women in the spotlight who shine on the red carpet in the brand’s designs. See Jennifer Lawrence for more proof of that… Simons’ catwalk sets were more than horticultural installations and mere passageways for models to showcase clothes.  After convincing his bosses to adorn every single piece of wall with flowers for his Haute Couture debut in 2013, he continued with the flower-filled theme in some way, be they dangling from the ceiling or, for his last show, erecting a mound of delphiniums in a square in the Louvre. In 2014, he took a break from flowers and flew the fashion pack to the French Riviera for a Cruise show staged inside the futuristic ‘bubble palace’ commissioned by fellow fashion designer Pierre Cardin. Simons - who had no experience of Haute Couture and had only started designing womenswear at Jil Sander in 2005 – was credited with steering Dior away from the flamboyant and theatrical tendencies of his predecessor, John Galliano, and embracing a fresher, more modern silhouette. His subtle nod to the maison’s archives saw him breathe new life into the late Christian Dior’s iconic Bar jacket and create modern classics. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Just when we had begun to accept the fact that retailers are replacing bikinis with boots and coats, Kate Bosworth knocked us straight back into our summer haze. The actress, 33, stepped out in New York wearing a floral Giambattista Valli suit with boxy jacket and high-waisted slim-cut trousers. Needless to say it was a #swoon moment on The Telegraph fashion desk. Peppered with enough posies to put any avid gardener to the test, the climbing ramage and anemones were an unabashedly pretty alternative to the abstract florals that have been at play this season. The saccharine suiting hails from the Paris Fashion Week designer’s Resort 2017 collection, which also boasts daisy strewn lace dresses, 3D petal embellished trousers and blooming bomber jackets. Bosworth’s suiting is the pick of the bunch, and is the perfect reminder that a) florals can still look original, and b) suits are a brilliant option for occasionwear. Though the Blue Crush star was stepping out to an evening engagement with Kim Crawford Wines, her co-ords would not have looked out of place at a wedding. In fact, the conservative cut, which covers her arms, legs and décolletage, is the perfect solution to those late summer nuptials in the diary, when the evenings will undoubtedly get chilly. The trick with busy printed suits is to nail the cut. Take your separates to a local tailor (most dry cleaners do alterations) to make sure the shoulder seams sit directly on your shoulders, and the trouser hem falls just above the ankle bone when worn with  heels. Speaking of heels, simple, high sandals are a must to elongate your silhouette. Keep all other accessories to a minimum to let your suit speak for itself. The beauty of buying co-ords is that you can wear them as separates with plain accompaniments, as demonstrated by Victoria Beckham last week. Bosworth’s Valli trousers would look equally chic with a simple black camisole tucked in, while the jacket would make an eclectic addition to A-line skirts and pussy-bow blouses. Three for one?  The French fashion designer Sonia Rykiel died this morning, aged 86, after a twenty year battle with Parkinson’s disease. Born Sonia Flis in Neuilly, Parisian suburb in 1930, to a Russian mother and Romanian father, Rykiel was the eldest of her four sisters. Writing in The Guardian in 2012, she discussed the disease – which had also claimed her mother - referring to it as the “putain de Parkinson's” (the bitch Parkinson’s). Of her early life she mused that, “I wasn't remotely interested in clothes. I came from an intellectual Parisian family. My father was a watchmaker; my mother was a housewife. We discussed politics, art, sculpture – never fashion.” Yet, having married women’s dress shop owner Sam Rykiel in 1953, fashion found its way to her. It was natural instinct that led her to develop clothing, instigated during pregnancy (her daughter Nathalie was born in 1955, followed by a son, Jean-Phillippe in 1961) when she found nothing she wanted to wear. She asked an Italian knitwear supplier to create her a dress and subsequent sweaters followed – designed to her precise specifications: the arm holes were cut high, the fit shrunken, and they clung to the body. At the time, knitwear was unforgivingly thick and unflattering. Rykiel injected a practical, yet stylish modernity. Friends soon ordered her little sweaters which were produced in vibrant colours, and stripes – a design signature which has endured to this day - and earned the nickname the “poor boy” sweater. Spotted in the window of her husband’s store, the sweater was featured on the front of French Elle – notable at a time when Haute Couture was the usual cover star attire. Rykiel was following on the path of liberation-by-fashion set by Coco Chanel, and is perhaps her most natural successor in terms of legacy. Her clothing (she opened her first eponymous store in 1968, aided by her then ex-husband Rykiel) struck a chord with women who sought freedom away from old fashioned, restrictive styles and a sense of individuality. She democratised fashion away from the rarefied world of couture, proposing that women of all ages could wear her clothes, as well as pioneering stylistic techniques such as exposed seams, raw, unfinished hems and even slogan sweaters (the first in 1971 read “Sensuous”). From those initial knitted sweaters, success followed quickly, Women’s Wear Daily crowned her the “Queen of Knits” in 1972. Audrey Hepburn, Brigitte Bardot and Catherine Deneuve were early fans. She was the true mother of the so-called ‘Left Bank chic’, where she lived and had her store, the first of which opened on the Rue de Grenelle; frequenting Café de Flore, the famed café of intellectuals, which has in her honour a table and sandwich named after her. Andy Warhols’s painting of her hung in her apartment, “I think he liked my hair” she said of the work. That signature blaze of striking red hair worn in a shoulder grazing bob with heavy fringe provided the fashion world with an instantly recognisable and distinctive figure. Rykiel’s London debut in the Seventies came via taste-maker boutique Browns, run by Sidney and Joan Burstein. The families became further intertwined when their son, Simon Burstein, married Rykiel’s daughter Nathalie. Now divorced, the couple had three daughters, one of whom, Lola works for the Sonia Rykiel office in New York. Speaking to the Telegraph, Joan Burstein commented that “ She was truly a unique and wonderful woman in every way. I still have clothes from her first collection that we ever stocked at Browns. She played a very important role in my life.”  In 2009 Rykiel was awarded the Order of the Légion d’Honneur in recognition of her 40 years service to the French fashion industry. These days, although the business was sold in part to Hong Kong based investment firm Fung Brands (the Rykiel’s retain a 20% share) in 2012, the family are still involved. Nathalie Rykiel who took over from her mother in 1995, remains as Managing Director. The brand has been invigorated of late by its artistic director Julie de Libran, who since joining the company in 2014, has brought the label back to form. Such is the force of its founder that in the latest collection, de Libran included a whimsical print featuring the faces of Sonia, her daughter Nathalie and granddaughter Lola. As it drops into stores in the coming weeks, perhaps there is no better timed homage. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
