 Even in a posh Parisian hotel at 10am on a Tuesday morning, Carine Roitfeld rocks a fierce look. Black pencil skirt, fishnet tights, a white shrunken T‑shirt printed with her own image, a leopard-print coat thrown over her shoulders – it’s vintage haute-punk Roitfeld, down to the smudgy black eyeliner and mussy brown hair. Roitfeld’s sexy uniform is usually a smattering of luxe, hot labels – Givenchy, Tom Ford or Christopher Kane – but today it’s head-to-toe high street. Everything she’s wearing she has designed as part of her new collaboration with the Japanese chain Uniqlo. “Honestly, it feels like me. I don’t feel different,” she says, with a Gallic shrug. “I’m wearing Uniqlo [but] I feel exactly the same.” Roitfeld, 61, who is much softer and warmer in person than her rock’n’roll image might suggest, is the former editor-in-chief of French Vogue who, by the end of her decade-long tenure at the magazine, had become as much renowned for her edgy, sexy personal style as her risqué editorials. In the Nineties she had established her name as Tom Ford’s stylist during the designer’s Gucci years, when the campaign imagery they shot with Mario Testino created the definitive glossy look of that decade and propelled the label to superbrand status. Now the mother of two, and recent grandmother, is editor of her own fashion magazine CR Fashion Book, and global fashion director for Harper’s Bazaar. Uniqlo in its turn has been enjoying great success with collaborations that have a particularly French flavour. Two years ago it launched a collection designed by the former model Inès de La Fressange, now in its fifth season. And earlier this month a new range designed by Christophe Lemaire, the French former creative director of Hermès, practically sold out within the day. Like the de La Fressange collaboration, the Carine Roitfeld collection, which goes on sale on October 29, is based on her individual style. “Most people think I’m very 'night’ in the way I dress, but for me it’s my uniform for working, and it’s also what I wear for going on a plane, for going to dinner – I will not change so much,” she says. “I think for Uniqlo it’s more feminine, more sexy, than they are used to, so it was challenging for them, but they got it. They understood the little details that were important to me. Because if I come to visit Tom Ford and I’m in my Uniqlo I don’t want him to look at me and think, 'Eurgh, what’s that? It looks cheap.’ No, not at all.” She’s keen to point out that she’s not a designer – she came up with the ideas and Uniqlo delivered them. “I’m not in competition with all my friends – not with Riccardo Tisci, Karl Lagerfeld or Tom Ford. I’m not planning to jump on the new look of what Miu Miu did yesterday or Givenchy did last winter, you know. I want to stay friends with them! I’m just a woman with a certain style. To me it’s quite a boring style, I’m always the same.” But at a time when creating a “personal brand” appears to be the apex of career success (whether you’re six, 16 or 60), and what you look like is so much a part of it, the secret of Roitfeld’s “boring style” – so nonchalant, so Parisian – is something we want to be privy to. So here are some of her pointers: “It’s about the French attitude and the French way of wearing. We are very picky. I always have my hand in a pocket. Usually there is no pocket on a pencil skirt, but in this collection there is. It’s all little details, nothing revolutionary, you know? It’s not a new jacket with four sleeves.” “I’m always wearing the same. Even if elements are different, it’s always the same silhouette. So the trousers in the collection are a continuation of the pencil skirt, with the pockets and the same silhouette, slim and fitted at the waist, not too long. It’s all about length and proportion.” “I usually spend a lot of time at the tailor’s. I get everything altered so the fit is right. It makes all the difference. I always have the coat a little shorter than the skirt [about half an inch]. Although now Uniqlo has made it all perfect for me, so I’ll never have to go to the tailor again.” “I’m very ambiguous about women and men. I mean in a fashion sense, of course. So most of the tailoring I like is very 'man’: the material, the finishing, the shoulders. The tail of the coats is very man. So it does not look cheap. A man never looks cheap.” “You will see a lot of slip dresses in this collection because this is a very French tradition – although it was quite revolutionary for the Japanese. I love fashion and to mix pieces, but you need to have a base. I will wear this under my ‘ladder’ sweater or put on a jacket for the evening. Or under a skirt so you see a little bit of the lace at the bottom.” “I love leopard print so I made a coat but you know my leopard is very dark, it’s not yellow, not aggressive. So even if you’re a grandma like me you can wear leopard. My granddaughter always says, 'Oh, Grandma, I love your fur!’ ” “I like to show some skin, it’s nice. So the slip dress is good and a camisole top. Also I don’t make the neckline of the sweaters too high because I like the collarbone to show. And you can push the sleeves up on your jumper, of course.” “I always like tights so for the first time Uniqlo has done fishnets, just for me.” “I travel a lot, so if I have the same base I make it easy for myself. I wear black because I like it, but also because it’s easier – you don’t have to match the pink shoes with the pink dress. So black, leopard, camo, a slip dress, tailoring, I can mix it all up. Is there ever a time when black doesn’t work? For a wedding. That’s a big problem for me. I like white, too, but you cannot wear it to a wedding, so it’s a big problem. Although the last time I had to go to a wedding, believe it or not, I was in bright pink.” “Because I travel so much, I’ve decided not to check in my case now. So we’re always trying to find the best and cheapest trolley – I think mine is from Muji. But it makes it quite fun to pack. So you just put this slip dress in and a jacket for night and you mix up leopard, lace, black, camouflage – all my key things. You don’t have to buy too many things, but the right things. Also, the trousers and the skirt we have made for Uniqlo are polyester, which does not wrinkle, so it’s good for travelling. See, we really think about this sort of problem. It’s very easy, very washable, but with attitude.”  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  There are many ways of measuring a star’s staying power. But one of the best barometers must belong to Marilyn Monroe – whose used lipstick is expected to fetch up to £13,500 when it goes up for auction 54 years after her death. The 1947 Revlon lipstick in pink 'Bachelor’s Carnation', complete with smudges around the rim, was discovered in a secret compartment of one of the actress’s evening bags by auctioneers who had spent years hunting down Monroe’s possessions for a “once-in-a-lifetime” auction. “Such is the Marilyn factor that we estimate the lipstick will sell for $15,000-20,000 dollars, or probably much more. It’s so personal,” explains Martin Nolan, executive director at LA auction house Julien’s. It’s one of 500 of Monroe’s personal effects that are set to smash records when they are auctioned off in Los Angeles this November. But, before then – and in honour of what would have been the actress’s 90th birthday today – everything that is up for sale is being exhibited at London’s Chelsea Harbour Design Centre. It includes everything from her Gucci address book (containing a who’s who list of telephone numbers) to beloved clothes and her personal correspondence and art works. So why is Monroe still so fascinating 54 years after her untimely death? “She’s this blonde bombshell who has been frozen in time,” Nolan says of the actress, who was one of Hollywood’s most bankable actresses but struggled with depression and addiction, before overdosing in her LA home in 1962. “We still think of her as that elegant 36-year-old who everyone feels they know and love, even if she was before their time. Ask an eight-year-old who Marilyn is, and they’ll probably know.” Nolan has been orchestrating the auction for a few years now. It brings together two separate private collections. The first from the estate of Hollywood actor and Marilyn’s acting teacher Lee Strasberg, who along with his wife Paula, was Monroe’s closest confidante and was left all of her personal effects in her will. The second collection comes from David Gainsborough-Roberts, a British man who became enthralled by Marilyn in 1988 and began investing in items owned and worn by the star. Now he’s decided, according to Nolan, “that Marilyn is bigger than him and that his collection should go to good homes.” Nolan believes part of the reason the auction will be record-breaking is because it includes some of Monroe’s most personal items. “My favourite piece is a miniaudière evening bag which is gold and bejewelled in amber with a black velvet lining,” says Nolan. He describes how the bag is still filled with all the accoutrements of “a night out on the town”: there’s a gold tray containing loose powder, eight Phillip Morris cigarettes “in perfect condition” and even 2 dimes “which is what you’d need to call a taxi home – it’s a true picture.” Another handbag contains a matching set of comb, compact and cigarette lighter – all exactly as you imagine Marilyn left them when she flung them aside on getting home from an evening out. Despite the fact that Monroe’s films grossed $200 million by the time of her death and she made 'Diamonds are a Girl’s Best Friend' one of the most iconic lyrics of all time, Nolan says she owned surprisingly few lavish items. “She actually had very few fine jewellery pieces of her own. For her it was all about the costume jewellery, but obviously when she wore it, it had that wow factor.” Among the paste necklaces and bracelets by costume jewellery specialist Albert Weiss is only one piece which does include real diamonds; an elegantly dainty cocktail watch from Swiss watchmakers Blancpain. Its face value is $80,000 to $100,000 but, once again, Nolan says that the sky’s the limit when you know that it graced the wrist of Monroe. “No other celebrity has achieved the collectability of Marilyn Monroe. She transcends continents as she has fans all over the world and she transcends age groups as she has fans from five years old to 95 years old,” says Nolan, of why this auction is so important. “It’s very rare to find items from her life or career and this is the last ever auction of its kind.” Among the other fashion highlights are a well-worn pair of tan leather wedge sandals which Monroe wore as a 21-year-old model when she was still known by her birth name, Norma Jean. Then there’s a black cocktail dress from her personal wardrobe, by one of her favourite designers Ceil Chapman, and the iconic beaded dress from 'Some Like it Hot', which was so tightly-fitted that she had to be lifted on and off the piano which she sat on to perform in it. But whilst Monroe used clothes and make-up as a tool to perpetuate her glamorous image, some of the most touching items in the auctions are the ones that emphasise the mundane. Alongside the diamond watch, are receipts for bacon and lard, an insurance document scrawled over with a recipe for stuffing – and a journal, in which she’d written that she was “Alone!!!!! All alone.” “Marilyn created this public image, brand even, around herself as the humorous blonde bombshell. It made her famous but she couldn’t escape it,” says Nolan, of the woman who spent most of her childhood in foster homes after her mother was hospitalized for schizophrenia.  “She had a hard life, getting married three weeks after her 16th birthday. There was no one who loved her unconditionally but she was always searching for that. It was very sad.”  Marilyn: The Legacy of a Legend is on show at the Design Centre, Chelsea Harbour until June 20th.  In her role as First Lady, Melania Trump will be meeting power players from across the globe: from Queens and Presidents to Prime Ministers and Princesses, part of her unofficial job description is to welcome them all to the White House. Yesterday, the FLOTUS greeted King Abdullah and Queen Rania of Jordan to Washington, where the King and President held talks while the Queen and Mrs Trump visited a girls-only school.  Queen Rania is renowned as one of the world's most stylish royals, with a penchant for polished international designers including Dior, Alexander McQueen and Elie Saab. So how did Melania Trump approach dressing for her meeting with the Queen? Firstly, she turned to Hervé Pierre, the former Carolina Herrera creative director with whom she collaborated on the white column gown she wore for the Inauguration Ball. He created an emerald green, figure-hugging dress in the style which has come to define Trump's political wife look, with scarf detailing adding a thoughtful finishing touch. Cinched at the waist but with a covered up neckline, the look encapsulated the more covered up look which Trump has lately made her own but with a nod to the glamour of the Trump woman aesthetic (see also, Ivanka and Tiffany, plus Lara, wife of Eric, and Vanessa, wife of Donald Jr.). Mrs Trump's decision to work with Pierre again suggests that their collaboration may become akin to that of Oleg Cassini and Jackie Kennedy. Cassini became a personal couturier to Kennedy, creating the majority of her First Lady looks and helping to hone her distinctively elegant style. 'He knew that she had very demanding tastes,’ explains Lauren Marino, the author of Jackie and Cassini: A Fashion Love Affair. ‘He talks about looking at her as a geometric figure and as an Egyptian princess. He was on her level – she didn’t have to explain to him what Tintoretto yellow was. He got it... He brought in the one-shoulder gown and the empire dress, which were quite daring at the time – particularly for a First Lady.'  Although Pierre has so far only created two looks for Mrs Trump, a sleek yet glamorous theme is already emerging.  The choice of colour for the dress may also be a respectfully diplomatic nod from the First Lady. Green is one of the colours of the Jordanian flag and is particularly important in the Islamic faith as it is said to have been a favourite of Prophet Muhammad. It is also considered to represent paradise in the faith.  Mrs Trump was criticised earlier this week for choosing to wear Dolce and Gabbana in her official White House portrait, rather than an American designer. Designer Stefano Gabbana expressed his delight at the First Lady's choice, writing 'BEAUTIFUL... Thank you' beside a picture of the portrait on his Instagram account. Although the First Lady may not be taking the most traditional of sartorial decisions, her look for yesterday's meeting underscores a determinedly personal strategy which also shows some awareness of the political potential of her choices. After all, she has made #PowerOfTheFirstLady her signature hashtag.  Meanwhile, Queen Rania stayed true to her ultra-chic reputation, opting for an elegant black coat dress with a minimalist white foulard which echoed Melania's dress. Both women wore Christian Louboutin heels.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  So, Kim Kardashian and daughter North West stepped out in matching floor length sequin £7000 dresses by label of-the-moment Vetements to attend a Kanye West concert in New York last night. The paps went mad for the show-stopping twinning look - and we were left to wonder if this matching show was a well orchestrated photo opportunity from the Kardashians (probably), or simply a cute mother-daughter dressing up moment (that too). Ditto, matchy-matchy looks regularly pop up on Beyonce Knowles' Instagram account; with her and gorgeous mini me daughter Blue Ivy, wearing matching floral dresses and show stopping gowns, often sourced from that other designer du jour, Gucci. While some might wonder if kids have replaced handbags as style accessories, I personally think that to question these mother-daughter matchy-moments is churlish. Because matching with your offspring is good old-fashioned fun. Just for fun’s sake. Yes, these celebrities might do it in a more OTT fashion than we do, and yes, wearing the same outfits improves chances of a good photo op, but as someone who has photographed mother-child matching moments for my own Instagram account, I don’t think it is rooted in anything bad, and therefore - why the fuss? When I see the picture of Kim and North, I don’t think, 'how hideous!' Instead I think, 'wow they must have had a good time getting ready for this.' It makes me smile. Also as a side note, I feel it’s cool that North West is wearing trainers with her dress, it’s not as if the 3-year-old is dressed in heels. As a mother of two young boys, Rafferty 5 and Fox, 3, I know the joys to be had of dressing together in corresponding outfits. We haven’t done floor length sequin gowns, yet (although, to be honest, my kids would probably revel in that level of dressing up) - but we have matched in distinctive Ralph Lauren striped jumpers; my own Selfish Mother MOTHER and BOY #Goodtees; and matching ‘Since 2011’ tops. Matching clothes with your child is a bit cheeky, it’s a little bit silly, but beyond that - it’s a lovely bonding moment between you and them. Really, it is. You feel like a team when you’re wearing something the same. And, for 3-year-old North West, facing a legion of (probably) mildly scary paparazzi, I think that dressing the same as her mother is likely to make her feel safer.  Matching outfits makes it feel like it’s you and them against the world; a knowing nod-and-a-wink at your parent-child relationship. It also puts emphasis on how important they are to you - which is especially relevant when the parent is a superstar attending a busy event where the star attraction just happens to be your Dad.  Matching your kids may have been a bit naff back in the day, when in the early 80s there was a trend for matching Christmas jumpers or in early 2000s, when Daniella Westbrook and child stepped out in matching Burberry check. But recently the trend has been gaining momentum in a cool way - with brands such as Nor-Folk, Tease and Totes and Stella McCartney all making super matching looks, that self-respecting parents want to buy into. Matchy-matchy is well and truly hitting the mainstream now with Beyonce and Kim’s seals of approval. Only time will tell if it gains momentum or if they kill it off completely. I do wonder if there’d be such a fuss if say, David Beckham and his sons stepped out in matching suits? They probably have, but we may missed it for lack of furore. Molly Gunn is the Editor-in-Chief of SelfishMother.com.  Rihanna proved that what they say about her is true - she really is the most influential celebrity. Yesterday she tweeted a picture of herself wearing a set of $9,000 Dolce and Gabbana jewel-encrusted headphones, captioned "listening to ANTI" (her long-awaited ninth album), and despite the steep price tag, they sold out within 24 hours, as reported by Digiday. If you were any doubt as to the power of celebrity influencers to spark a trend, you simply can't deny it any longer. listening to ANTI 🎈 pic.twitter.com/AgqlhU0GEz Embellished with Swarovski crystals and pearls, the headphones are well outside the average Joe's price range, but whatever Rihanna's fans want, Rihanna's fans get, presumably selling a kidney just to accrue a bit of the star's aura for themselves through the gold-heavy audio equipment. Similar sparkle-spattered headphones debuted on Dolce & Gabbana's AW15 ready-to-wear catwalk as part of a collaboration with premium headphone line Frends, although Chanel was the first to combine extravagance with earbuds in AW14 in the house's legendary supermarket-themed show. Rihanna is well-known for igniting trends, propelling bandanas and brothel creepers back into the mainstream, and memorably bringing old-skool Notting Hill streetwear brand Boy London back into circulation a few years ago. It's not just clothing that she's influential in, but beauty too: the prevalence of wickedly pointed stiletto false nails on girls across the world can be attributed to her.  But no-one could have predicted she'd spark a run on Dolce & Gabbana accessories with four-figure prices, except perhaps the NPD Group. In its research, it indexed the number of brand preferences of a celebrity's fans, and Rihanna came out on top with almost 3.7 times as many strong brand endorsement opportunities as the average big-name celebrity. Even more interestingly, four wheel drive manufacturers Jeep came through as the brand for which she'd be most influential.  'Totally outclassed' is the conclusion of many pundits following Floyd Mayweather's victory over Conor McGregor in their record-breaking fight which took place in Las Vegas last night.  One detail of the evening is certainly in no doubt; when it came to fight night style, Mayweather's bespoke Philipp Plein robe and shorts were some of the most opulent and flamboyant the boxing world has ever seen.  The designer, who has become renowned for the ultra-glamorous Jetset look which he has coined, first met Mayweather- a long time client- in the South of France earlier this year at the Resort show he hosted at his villa in Cannes. Mayweather modelled in the show and, set to emerge from a two-year hiatus for his McGregor showdown, it seemed only natural that the pair would decide to work together.    "Floyd’s gear needs to be both functional and fashionable," says Plein. "So within the guidelines of the sport I created pieces for the fight that represent my view, my lifestyle and my taste. " This was to be no normal boxing ring look. "Luxurious and unexpected materials like python and crocodile are used instead of the classic sport and technical fabrics," Plein explains of structured zip and split sleeve detailed jacket which Mayweather walked out in which was finished off with a gold-lined hood, black face mask and cap.  "Floyd’s classic black and gold colors are reinvented using embellishments in Swarovksi crystals," he adds- spectators last night cannot have failed to be dazzled by Mayweather's glittering TBE (The Best Ever) slogan stamped across the back band of his shorts.   Plein and Mayweather's partnership will stretch far beyond the custom designs for last night's fight, however, with plans for an ongoing two year collaboration which will see Mayweather work with the label on special collections.  "I think it is important nowadays to develop a real relationship with the personalities who are associated with the brand, there is a real investment," says Plein. "I also think that in this historic period of transparency through social media, the consumer can tell the difference between actions that are authentic and those that are just paid sponsorships."  "Sport stars are the heroes of our times," he adds. "They are icons, and represent what a man can look up to and emulate in many ways, including style and fashion. This can only make men more and more conscious of their own style." The boxing ring may be a rather unexpected fashion show case,  but it may yet prove to be a highly influential one.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Would you believe that today marks the 15th anniversary of Legally Blonde?  The cult film saw Reese Witherspoon wear more pink than Paris Hilton and graduate at the top of her Harvard law class, while also teaching us how to 'bend and snap.' Reese Witherspoon is marking the occasion with a 'bend and snap' Boomerang and a 'pink' takeover on Instagram, asking fans to share pictures of them wearing pink or posing with pink accessories with the hashtag #ThinkPink. Of course pink is Elle Woods' signature colour and the costume designer  Sophie de Rackoff explained that this was decided after they visited a university campus. "It was all organic and intuitive, I designed costumes for Elle Woods that moved the story forward and fitted the moment," de Rackoff told Elle US in 2012. "Reese and I actually went to visit a sorority house in the early prep, and it was just obvious that pink should be her signature color." The costumes in the Legally Blonde franchise became so iconic that the pink Jackie O inspired suit Witherspoon wears in the sequel was included in the V&A's  'Hollywood Costume' exhibition in 2013. But it wasn't just about the costumes. Fans will remember that fashion has never played such an integral role in a murder trial before with Woods using her knowledge of hair maintenance and shoes to help solve the crime and acquit her innocent client. In celebration of Legally Blonde's milestone birthday, we've picked out Elle's most genius fashion and beauty quotes... via GIPHY Elle Woods manages to solve a murder case by using her beauty expertise to realise that the victims' daughter, Chutney Windams', alibi is false.  Elle: "Chutney, why is it Tracy Marcinco's curls were ruined when she got hosed down? Chutney Windham: Because they got wet. Elle: Exactly.  Pippa Middleton arrived for her wedding this morning wearing a spectacular lace-bodiced, high-necked wedding gown created by Giles Deacon. Her face was covered with a delicate bespoke tulle veil dotted with pearls and made by milliner Stephen Jones.  The bride also wore a Maidenhair fern tiara by Robinson Pelham,the Middleton family's go-to jeweller, and ivory satin pumps by Manolo Blahnik with pearl detailing, a customised version of the label's £715 Seneca bridal heels. As for her 'something old'? The same Robinson Pelham pearl earrings which she wore for her big sister's wedding in 2011.   "I was thrilled to work with Pippa on her wedding dress," Giles Deacon said of his collaboration with Middleton. "The dress is constructed with a cap sleeve, high neckline and features a corseted bodice with draping to the front and a heart-shaped detail at the back." "The bespoke silk cotton lace was hand appliqued to create an illusion of the dress having 'no seams'." "The lace bodice is embroidered with pearl detailing over an organza and tulle underskirt, which has layer upon layer to enable a floor-sweeping movement." "It's a privilege to show the craftsmanship that my team produces in London and a real testament to Pippa's support of British fashion," Deacon added. His coup - which had been rumoured since he was spotted leaving Middleton’s home last November- became a triumph for bride, designer and British fashion alike. Giles Deacon is an inspired, but perhaps unexpected choice from Pippa. When her engagement was announced last summer, it was widely thought that she would opt  for a gown by a traditional bridal designer from a Belgravia-based couturier au fait with designing for an English society wedding.  Until 2016, Deacon-who was born in the Lake District- showed his collections at London Fashion Week, delivering enchanting collections inspired by historical figures, mysticism and fairytales. Last year, Deacon announced that he would be pausing his ready-to-wear line to concentrate on couture instead, an area of his business which had grown over previous years. Besides commissions for private clients, Deacon had created striking red carpet looks for actresses including Cate Blanchett and Sarah Jessica Parker.  "For the last four years we've been quietly developing that side of our business and working with private clients and couture off the back of our fantastic red carpet pieces we've done and had great gals wearing," Deacon told The Telegraph at the time of the announcement. "It seemed like a good growth direction for us and to show it at Paris in Couture is where you show the best of what you can do." "There will be all sorts of ethereal, slightly darker romanticism and some witty touches," he explained of the refocussed strategy. While designing Pippa Middleton's wedding dress is undoubtedly the commission of a lifetime, it seems that Deacon has had mixed feelings about taking forays into wedding dress design in the past. "With wedding dresses, it's different. The bride wants X and the bride's mother wants Y and it becomes a nightmare," he admitted in 2009. Despite his reservations about managing the inevitable mother-daughter politics, Deacon's feelings on bridal design seem to have softened as the couture arm of his business expanded. "It'd be a logical place for us to go to and also seeing how popular the Bridal collections in New York are and how much they have grown," he later mused. In 2011, Deacon designed the non-Royal wedding dress of the year, creating a strapless, tiered skirt gown for model Abbey Clancey's marriage to footballer Peter Crouch. That dress is said to have taken two months of intense handiwork to create. Prices for Giles Deacon couture designs- which are made in his London atelier by a team of 20 staff- range from £8,000 for a bespoke day dress; the mid-tier eveningwear looks come in at about £24,000, and prices can spiral to £120,000 for extravagant wedding gowns. Deacon's girlfriend, the Game of Thrones actress Gwendoline Christie summed up the appeal of Deacon's designs in an interview last year: "He has two of my favourite attributes in artists: wild imagination and technical rigour. [His designs] can be practical, otherworldly, sculptural and mind-bending, but you always feel celebrated as a woman when you wear them… Their confidence somehow increases yours. It’s quite a power for a designer to have. His clothes have personalities."  "I want the label to be a very advanced couture house for the 21st century," Deacon added in the same interview.  A wish which he has come a step closer to fulfilling today.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Melania Trump took to the dance floor at the Liberty Inauguration Ball last Friday evening, her choice of dress was, naturally, much anticipated. But few expected that Mrs Trump, renowned for her love of big designer labels and couture, would chose the moment to give an unknown industry name their own major moment in the spotlight- Karl Lagerfeld, Ralph Lauren and Carolina Herrera were just a few of the household fashion names which had been linked to the commission.  Yet, that is exactly what she did in asking Hervé Pierre, former creative director at Carolina Herrera, to help her to mastermind the gown. Now French-born Pierre has revealed the story behind Melania Trump's strikingly simple Inauguration look, discussing his fashion career and the machinations which led him to get the job of designing the closest thing America has to a royal wedding dress.  The New York Times interview reveals him to be witty- “I was Prince Philip walking always two steps behind her,” he recalls of his 14 years working for Carolina Herrera- but unassuming, with a discreet attitude which would have stood him in excellent stead when he designed for previous first ladies and other high-profile clients in his former roles. “If I work in shadows, it’s because I know how to park my ego. You can’t have an ego designing for the first lady,” he explains, adding that despite the fame which designing Trump's gown has brought him, he has no plans to open his own label, preferring to continue taking private commissions.  French-born, US citizen Pierre also offers a frank insight into Mrs Trump's style and way of working. Here's what we learn... "I almost dropped the phone," Pierre remembers of the moment he received a text from Mrs Trump on the morning of January 3rd. “I have a favor to ask. Would it be possible in this kind of time frame for you to design my gown?” read the First Lady-elect's rather casual request.  This remarkably laidback way of working continued throughout the process Pierre explains, with little mention of the pomp and circumstance one might expect from a visit to the family's glitzy Trump Tower abode. He sat down with Melania later on the day he got that initial text (he had been recommended to her by friends, possibly Stephanie Winston Wolkoff). “Each time I met with her, we were alone,” he says. “I never saw a maid. And never once did she look at her phone.” While Melania Trump might have seemed inextricably linked to bling and overt glamour in the past, she's worked hard to update her look for the role of political consort. Pierre reveals that her brief to him was that she wanted something “sleek,” “modern” and “form-fitting.” Pierre took that idea a stage further: “a modern look with laser-sharp tailoring, something hard, almost mean.” Mean? Can't think where he got that vibe from.  There was controversy earlier this week when Melania's offficial White House biography briefly mentioned the jewellery collection which she once designed. While the line is now defunct,  Pierre's account shows that her design instincts are as strong as ever. The New York Times explains how: "She wanted the small band sleeves of her décolleté-baring dress to form a straight line from shoulder to shoulder. He pressed for a curvier outline but ultimately changed his mind. She also envisioned a slender white ribbon encircling her waist. He argued for claret, and prevailed." “Fashion is a little bit like cooking,” Pierre said of the design process. "The red had a purpose, like when you put something very spicy in a dish, and it takes over a little bit of the flavor.” Despite her husband's controversial Presidency, it seems plenty of women still want to emulate Mrs Trump's undeniably chic look. “My phone has not stopped ringing," says Pierre.  Like numerous high-profile women before her, it seems that Melania is keen to please with her outfits and will be studying feedback on her every outing. Pierre confides that during the journey back to New York last Sunday, both he and the First Lady were engrossed in their Twitter feeds.  Steve Rowe, the new chief executive Marks and Spencer appointed today, has his work cut out for him – all £810,000-per-annum-salary of it. The announcement that the current chief, Marc Bolland, is stepping down in April after six years in the job, came as the firm reported miserable Christmas results for general merchandise sales, including its clothing, which was down by over five per cent for the 13 weeks over the festive period. Rowe is an inside man. Currently executive director of general merchandise, the store has featured large in his life and career. His father worked for M&S and he’s been employed by the British store for 25 years – his first job was on the shop floor in Croydon when he was 15. He’s scaled the company ever since, taking on roles including director of retail and e-commerce. He will need all that experience to tackle the problem of what to do with what is currently the most flailing British brand on the high street. While Next also announced disappointing sales, blaming the drop on unseasonably warm weather in December, M&S has had recurring problems in general merchandise for a number of years. Its fashion offering appears to be particularly hard to get right, despite the efforts of Belinda Earl as style director. There have been successes. There is no doubt that the lingerie range Rosie for Autograph, designed by the British model Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, has been one from the off. It sold three times over expectations when it launched in 2012 and  the collection has now expanded to include fragrance and active wear. The store has also attracted customers with much-talked-about one-off fashion hits, such as a  pink wool coat in the winter of 2014 that won so much press attention it became known as ‘That Pink Coat’ and, similarly, last spring, a 1970s-inspired tan suede skirt worn by Alexa Chung. But the womenswear offering failed to produce the same level of excitement over a single garment this winter. One of the problems - which Next has also admitted to - is stock levels. Neither store has enough of it. When there is  unexpected demand for something that works, they can’t meet it. And impatient consumers who now demand fast service have other retailers with different production models – Zara, H&M, Primark - more than ready to service them instead. “There's definitely been an availability issue at M&S,” says Lorna Hall, senior retail editor at trends forecaster WGSN. “Earlier in the season, soft, unlined coats which are great for layering and belting did really well for them. It's a trend which has been around for a little while so the customer was beginning to understand it and want to buy into it. But as the months went on they simply didn't have the stock in place to carry on meeting demand.” Other British high street stalwarts have succeeded where M&S has struggled. Jigsaw’s Christmas results, announced last week, bucked the decline in winter retail sales in December. So it is possible for quality British fashion stores to get it right. Jigsaw’s autumn advertising campaign, which highlighted the longevity of its garments with the tagline ‘For Life, not landfill’, appears to have been on the money. It attracted customers into store and is proof that quality counts. Jigsaw’s designer, Shalina Partim, has turned around the retailer’s offering in a couple of seasons, creating womenswear that feels contemporary without chasing obvious trends or copying designers. It is proof that great fabrics and interesting colourways matter to shoppers. It has not been all bad news at M&S though. It had an “excellent quarter” for food, with record sales cashed up during Christmas week - perhaps no surprise when you can sweep up your M&S groceries at the train station, the petrol station and the service station. But is it possible that the omni-presence of its food is doing no favours to its fashion offering? While the M&S Simply Food brand adds a bit of cachet to the local garage, do we still want to buy our fashion from somewhere that also sells Percy Pigs and Indian take-away for two on the M1? You might, as I did recently late night at the M&S in Waterloo, bung a pair of opaque tights into the basket alongside a pint of milk, but a coat or a dress? That’s less likely. And another issue for Steve Rowe to chew over before April. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Launching a handbag line at the age of 21 is a feat in itself, but when you can't draw or sew and have been paralysed for over year, it would seem to be an impossible task. Yet that is what Charlotte Elizabeth Jones has done, building her accessories business from her bed. The 21-year-old from Hertfordshire first had the idea to create her own handbag label at the age of 16. "I had a heart operation in 2012 and I had to leave school at 16 because of it. I couldn't get A Levels or go to uni, and it was hard to find employment because of my physical health conditions," she explains to The Telegraph. "I'm one of three sisters and noticed we were never happy with an every day handbag. I had such a clear a vision of what I wanted it to be - very clean cut, minimal and inspired by classic 50s handbags, when it was an experience to have a handbag." Despite her strong ideas about what she would create, Charlotte had no design training or experience within the industry. In 2014, when she was 19, Charlotte attended a four-day Prince's Trust course to learn more about setting up a business, but two weeks later she suddenly became paralysed, meaning she couldn't even speak, let alone hold up a pencil.  'I couldn't produce tears for six months, but I was crying' "I suddenly just collapsed," she recalls. "I had had flu-like symptoms for nine months before, but had been told everything was fine. I had a heart arrhythmia that was never supposed to come back after my heart operation, so it was a freak episode. I collapsed and basically lost all muscle ability within seconds. I remember gripping onto my sister's hands and I genuinely thought I was dying. I lost all ability to talk, I was shaking constantly and had gone so pale. When I went to hospital they thought I had had a heart attack or a stroke, which was obviously terrifying to hear at the age of 19. Then I was discharged and told I had anxiety, and finally after a tough battle I was diagnosed a year later with  postural tachycardia syndrome (PoTs) and following on from that I was diagnosed with ME." "The day it happened and I came home my parents had to hold me up as my feet couldn't work," she continues. "It was as if my heart had given up; I was at 200 beats per minute which is three times the resting heart rate. I remember looking at the stairs and seeing Mount Everest - it was honestly completely unattainable. I was carried up to bed and then remained there for a year." "We have this place in our body called the autonomic nervous system," Charlotte says of the condition PoTs, which Ella Woodward of the food blog Deliciously Ella also suffers from. "If you imagine a car, that's the engine; the control centre that makes your body work. It affects everything from your heart rate to your digestion to even producing tears - I couldn't produce tears for six months, but I was crying. I couldn't go to the loo, I couldn't lift my hand off the bedside, I couldn't smell, I was just laying. I couldn't even have the curtain open a centimetre because the light would trigger me to faint. At one point I couldn't speak." Unsurprisingly the situation left Jones feeling desperate, and led to depression and anxiety, which was exacerbated by her fight to receive a diagnosis. "At one point I gave up. I had lost most of my memories and couldn't think properly and thought 'what do I have to live for? If no one is believing me how will I ever be able to stand up again?' It's more terrifying than you could ever believe, especially when doctors disbelieve you and think it's all in the mind." Jones explains that the idea of creating her own label was something that stayed with her throughout her paralysis and spurred her on to start pushing herself to try to get it started. "I thought if I can create something through all of this I can do anything," she explains. "That's why my business is so special to me as it started at the absolute rock bottom. It has been with me through my worst moments." She became paralysed in June 2014, and in the Autumn of that year began thinking about her first designs. "Because I lost the ability to use my hands and muscles, I couldn't draw, so I was trying but it was very childlike," she says of those first designs. "My sister's boyfriend is a designer so he drew more specialised sketches so people would know how to make them."  She then spent a year finding her manufacturer and leather and brass suppliers, which are all based in Britain. "In January of this year I had my prototype come through and the final design. It seems quite a long time, but it was short for me because I was so unwell, everything was on a different time scale," she explains.  A year on from her diagnosis, Jones has taken her first steps outside and has set up her own online shop, selling her  minimalist chic- and affordable- Bloomsbury bags for £129.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The character of Donatella Versace makes her entrance - and it is an entrance - near the end of the first episode of The Assassination of Gianni Versace. Clad in her signature spray-on jeans, black roll-neck and double-breasted suit jacket, she is impossibly glamorous, even while grieving. With Penelope Cruz playing Donatella in Ryan Murphy's take on the Versace assassination, a follow-up to 2016's The People v OJ Simpson, the show offers a potted retrospective of the iconic style of the Italian house, and the personal style of the woman at its helm. Cruz’s transformation into Donatella is uncanny - he has the original's platinum-blonde hair, permanent tan, full lips and dark, smokey eyes - and a wardrobe of classic, covetable vintage Versace (or replica-Versace) pieces. For a woman who once said, 'You can be too boring, but you can never be too seductive’, seduction and glamour are in her DNA. Day-to-day looks remain true to the tried-and-tested formula reflected in Cruz’s opening appearance: tight black trousers - which Donatella declares to be ‘essential’ for every woman in her US Vogue 73 questions interview - black boots, a tailored jacket, or shirt, accessorised with an endlessly rotating collection of gold jewellery. In September last year, two decades after Gianni Versace was murdered on the steps of his Miami Beach mansion,  Donatella, creative director of the Versace label since the designer’s death, turned her spring-summer 2018 show into a tribute to her late brother. With five of the original supermodels returning to walk the runway in honour of the late designer, the show has already gone down in fashion history. At the centre of the five was the instantly recognisable figure of Ms Versace, dressed in her go-to daytime black with gold accents. Her own style has become as iconic as the gold chainmail sheaths worn by Cindy, Naomi, Carla, Claudia and Helena. Though the Versace aesthetic has evolved, perhaps matured, during Donatella’s tenure, a flick back through 30+ years of her own looks demonstrate that, save a gradual exaggeration of her physical appearance - slimmer, more platinum, smokier eyes - her personal style has remained virtually unchanged. And, as Donatella, Cruz’s on-screen wardrobe is expertly judged. Daytime wear varies between minimal, streamlined silhouettes and sharply cut tailoring. For evening, she showcases a rotation of sheath dresses. The palette is minimal - mainly black, with a flash of red, metallic, and the occasional Versace print, always accessorised with her signature gold jewellery. The first three episodes have shown a grieving, business-like Donatella, though future episodes will reveal flashbacks to high-glamour appearances - a particular highlight promises to be the Belt dress worn for Vogue’s 100th anniversary party. For the red carpet, she ups the ante in ultra-slim fit (she is a fan of Alaia’s bodycon designs alongside her own label), corset-cinched waist, sculpted bust, floor-length silhouettes. Sequins/beads/feathers/rhinestones deliver maximum glamour. The Donatella version of her brother’s all-out glamour that plays out on the runway and in the Versace collections, is somehow more feminine - a modern evolution on the 1980s campaigns where supermodels draped themselves over mahogany muscle men. The same can be said of her own style. In December, Donatella was awarded the Fashion Icon award at the Fashion Awards. She accepted her prize in a gown that seemed to fuse her own style with the aesthetic of the label she has led for the last 20 years. Nipped at the waist, sculpting and cinching of the torso and bust, sleeveless, floor-length, slashed to the thigh, the silhouette was pure Donatella. The all-over print - an instantly-recognisable motif from the Versace archive - perhaps, a tribute to her late brother? © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  With fashion month in full swing, the issue of model diversity is once again back on the agenda. At the opening of London Fashion Week this morning, a group of models aged 47 and beyond took to the pavements to protest against their lack of representation on the catwalks. “Too old to walk for LFW?” and “Grow up London Fashion Week” were among the slogans which the models' signs read.    "It's meant to be a gentle reminder that we're still out there and fit for work - don't put us out to pasture now," says 63 year-old Jilly Johnson who was one of the protest's ringleaders. It has long been rare to find any models over the age of 25 as part of the line-up in a major catwalk show, but the women who were out in force today- all working models themselves- say that those labels are missing out on a huge business opportunity by not including a diverse age range in their shows. "People seem to think that once you reach 40, you're not interested in clothes and you don't buy anything but that's simply not true," Johnson explains, "a huge percentage of  clothes are bought by older women so fashion is making a huge mistake by ignoring that grey pound." With some surveys suggesting that as much as 50% of consumer spending comes from that powerful "grey pound" demographic, the models- who were brought together by the retailer JD Williams for their #GrowUpLFW initiative- say that by using older models, designers could better tap into this hugely profitable market. "I think if brands recruited more mature ladies, they would gain more followers," Johnson states.     Johnson emphasises that there's not necessarily anything wrong with having younger models- "I love those girls"- but she does point out that it's not exactly helpful to women who might be interested in buying the clothes. "Often they are a size 4 or 6, but we want to know what the designs will look like on a real woman." Although the elegantly blonde Johnson and her fellow models are all slender and look brilliant for their ages, she says: "We're not perfect, but I'd argue that that's what makes us more appealing. We may have a bit of a turkey neck or jelly belly but at least we're not too good to be true." Joining Johnson at the protest was Liz Horne, a 50 year-old brunette with fabulous flashes of silver-grey, who explained that although she still had work coming in, bookings start to drop off once a model reaches 30. She was also passionate in her message that clothes should be shown on women nearer the age of the typical designer fashion customer.  “I don’t want to see girls my daughter's age wearing clothes that are meant for women of my age to buy,” she says. “It’s not appealing. I don’t see any representation of women like me.”   Her friend  Gina Michel, who still models swimwear at 47, agrees. “It’s more representational and aspirational to see an older model. Liz is an aspirational 50 year-old. Why wouldn’t you want to see her in clothes?” So, how successful can the protesters expect their campaign to be? There's a plethora of positive signs that the industry is waking up to the power of the older woman. Perhaps the watershed moment was when Phoebe Philo, creative director at Celine, chose then 82 year-old author Joan Didion to star a campaign in January 2015. Since then, Armani has turned to 52 year-old Yasmin Le Bon and 46 year-old Stella Tennant while Saint Laurent featured 71 year-old Joni Mitchell and 43 year-old Amber Valletta walked at the Michael Kors show in New York earlier this week. “Who would believe at 68 you’d be getting better jobs?” Maye Musk said in an interview with The Telegraph last year of her 'greynaissance'. “I wouldn’t have believed you if you told me that when I started 53 years ago. But it’s just so much fun.” This Sunday, The Sunday Telegraph's Stella magazine stars British supermodel Cecilia Chancellor on its cover. At 50, Chancellor has been modelling for nearly three decades but is making a comeback with recent work including shoots with Peter Lindbergh and a Miu Miu campaign.  Last fashion season however, just 13 over 50 year-old models appeared on catwalks throughout the month, a statistic which shows just how tokenistic their inclusion can still be.  "Recently we've seen the likes of Lauren Hutton covering campaigns which is lovely to see," adds Johnson, referring to Hutton's recent starring role in Bottega Veneta's Srping/Summer 2017 show and subsequent adverts. "I think someone should ask Twiggy back on the catwalk, I know she'd be up for it."  Maybe next London Fashion Week, that wish could become a reality.                        © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Brazilian supermodel Gisele Bündchen is set to take a starring role in the opening ceremony of the Rio Olympics tonight. Gisele- she's a member of the breed so famous that they can be easily identified by their first name- landed in her home country this week with her children Benjamin, 6,  and Vivian Lake,3, leaving her husband- the American football star Tom Brady to celebrate his birthday alone. Now that's true dedication to the Olympic cause.  So as she gears up to represent Brazil in front of an expected 900 million viewers globally, here are some clever facts to drop while you're watching... Gisele outperformed her closest rival in the earning stakes by an enormous $35 million earning $44 million to Cara Delevingne's $9 million in 2015 alone. It was her ninth year at the top earning spot, so little wonder her fortune is estimated to total $336 million. The 36 year-old supermodel is keen to play down her wealth though, and told The Wall Street Journal "who are they speaking to when they come up with these numbers? Not my accountant that's for sure." Nevertheless, thanks to lucrative contracts with the likes of Chanel, Givenchy and Brazilian behemoth Colcci, Gisele's face is still one of the most recognised in the world.  Gisele arrived on the modelling scene in the late 90s when the look-du-jour was all pale and waif-like, an aesthetic which had been branded 'heroin chic'. With her more curvaceous proportions and athletic look, Gisele offered an entirely new look which proved to be a turning point in fashion and was celebrated with countless photo shoots which emphasised her curves.  In July 1999, Gisele graced the cover of American Vogue with her glossy hair blowing in the wind, bronzed skin and a girl-next-door grin. The cover line read: "The Return of the Sexy Model." Her look referenced the supermodels of the 80s and early 90s- think Claudia Schiffer and Cindy Crawford with their bouncy blowdries and toned figures- but has also influenced the rise of her fellow Brazilians like Alessandra Ambrosio and Adriana Lima today. A true trailblazer. Like all the best models, Gisele has an excellent story of discovery. During a school trip from her home town of Horizontina to Sao Paolo, she was innocently eating a Big Mac when a model agent approached her. It wasn't her first brush with modelling ambitions though. Her mother had sent Gisele and her five sisters (yes, five) on a course to master the basics of the trade a few years before- perhaps that's where she picked up her distinctive catwalk strut.  In 2015, Taschen announced the publication of a tome which would chart Gisele's modelling career via a 536-page, carefully-curated selection of images which had been taken of her over the years, to be co-edited by Gisele herself. The book's cover showed Irving Penn's landmark 'Return of the Curve' portrait which had been featured in US Vogue in the early days of her career. 1000 of these special edition books were printed and sold out on pre-orders before the book's official release date.  When it comes to yoga poses on Instagram Gisele Bündchen is the ultimate inspiration, posting endless pictures of her doing headstands on the beach and practicing her daily meditation. Bündchen has previously said about her get up and go attitude: "I'm not a potato sack; I've never sat on my couch. If I'm home, I'm cleaning, feeding my dogs, doing stuff. Life is too precious to waste time." Gisele Bündchen and Tom Brady's chef Allen Campbell opened up to Boston.com about just how restrictive their diets are. "Eighty percent of what they eat is vegetables," he explained. "[I buy] the freshest vegetables. If it's not organic, I don't use it. And whole grains: brown rice, quinoa, millet, beans. The other 20 percent is lean meats: grass-fed organic steak, duck every now and then, and chicken. As for fish, I mostly cook wild salmon." He continues: "No white sugar. No white flour. No MSG. I'll use raw olive oil, but I never cook with olive oil. I only cook with coconut oil. Fats like canola oil turn into trans fats. ... I use Himalayan pink salt as the sodium. I never use iodized salt. "No coffee. No caffeine. No fungus. No dairy. The kids eat fruit. Tom, not so much. He will eat bananas in a smoothie. But otherwise, he prefers not to eat fruits." Gisele has previously said of her diet: “I haven't drank soda in 10 years. My kids eat what I eat. The first (solid) food my son had was papaya and then avocado.” Gisele has five sisters, including a fraternal twin sister named Patricia, who is her manager. In 2010 the model was criticised for her comments to Harper's Bazaar about breastfeeding. She said: “Some people here think they don’t have to breastfeed, and I think, ‘Are you going to give chemical food to your child, when they are so little?’ There should be a worldwide law, in my opinion, that mothers should breastfeed their babies for six months.” She also raised eyebrows with her quotes to Vogue about pregnancy: “I did kung fu up until two weeks before Benjamin was born, and yoga three days a week. I think a lot of people get pregnant and decide they can turn into garbage disposals. I was mindful about what I ate, and I gained only 30 pounds.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  As longtime partners in design Katie Hillier and Luella Bartley launch their own label’s second collection, the duo reveal their vision for the Hillier Bartley woman A couple of years ago, I found myself queuing at the till of an American retailer, carrying a huge pile of Marc by Marc Jacobs clothes. Let me be clear, these were not clothes I would usually buy. But in a sort of fashion #squadgoals moment, I had succumbed in the hope of acquiring, by osmosis, even a little of the attitude and spirit that they represented. The design duo behind the label, Katie Hillier and Luella Bartley, had debuted their vision for Marc Jacobs’ second line at their first electrifying catwalk show for the brand some months earlier, and the industry was abuzz. I realised right there that I was under a Hillier Bartley enchantment, powerless in the spell of their peculiar magnetism. An established name in the ready-to-wear business and the 2008 Designer of the Year winner at the British Fashion Awards, Bartley’s eponymous label was one of London Fashion Week’s hottest tickets right up until its shock closure in 2009 when its Italian production arm went out of business. Bartley stepped out of the fashion limelight for a while, releasing a book, Luella’s Guide to English Style, the following year, and bringing up three children in Cornwall with her fashion-photographer husband, David Sims. An idiosyncratic designer with a quirkily feminine British aesthetic, you can recognise a Luella outfit a mile away. I have a sweater from her little shop on Brook Street that feels as relevant today as it did when I bought it eight years ago. I like to think it was modelled on something Queen Elizabeth II once wore. Hillier, meanwhile, has quietly built an impressive accessories empire – including a fine jewellery line, Hillier London – away from the public gaze, but is a name to conjure with for fashion industry insiders. Mulberry, Asprey, Loewe, Salvatore Ferragamo, Marc Jacobs, Stella McCartney, Victoria Beckham, Joseph… the list of brands – all very different from one another – that have called upon her design skills is endless. As is her tally of hit handbags. While the duo first teamed up in the late 1990s – Hillier hand-making the beaded belts to accessorise Bartley’s early catwalk collections – the Marc by Marc Jacobs gig they undertook in 2013  was the first time they had collaborated on equal terms, with Bartley as women’s ready-to-wear design director and Hillier as creative director. "We thought, why not?" says Bartley. "It’s an amazing opportunity and we’re going to have fun doing it. And we did." The four exuberant collections that followed, before Marc by Marc Jacobs was absorbed into the main Marc Jacobs line in early 2015, showcased the duo’s collaborative aesthetic, cementing their partnership and allowing the idea of what would come next to form.  "I was working on my handbags, getting quite far along in the development stages, but there was something I didn’t feel confident about," Hillier explains. Hillier asked Bartley for guidance, and it occurred to them that they should do the whole thing: shoes, accessories and ready-to-wear. Hillier had always worked in ready-to-wear but, she says, "Designing clothes was the missing piece," and with Bartley’s involvement the idea was born. According to Hillier, working in partnership was "the most fulfilling and exciting bit. Truthfully I didn’t really care what we were going to do." Again with little fanfare, the pair revealed their latest enterprise: luxury label Hillier Bartley, last March, making it clear from the off that this project was to be about exclusiveness through elusiveness. It was a very simple premise, given the designers’ shared aesthetics – they both play with masculinity and femininity as well as a spirit of Englishness, which is simultaneously aristocratic and inspired by street-culture. The first collection, for autumn/winter 2015, wove together inspirations as diverse as British subcultural music icon Ian McCulloch and the teddy bear carrying Lord Sebastian Flyte from Evelyn Waugh’s Brideshead Revisited. Another shared idea was to create ‘hero’ pieces: standout styles using luxurious fabrics. "It was as simple as that – for the first season, anyhow," says Bartley, mock-ominously. "At the start, we didn’t want to do anything but tailoring and coats, because I don’t like dresses. Which is odd because Luella [the label] was all about dresses. I don’t think I wore a dress for years after that." "But I wear lot of dresses," Hillier interjects. "Well both of us have done the scruffy, indie-kid thing," says Bartley, "and although it can work in your forties, I certainly wanted to explore a more feminine side of my personality, which you can’t really do without dresses. Our fitted dress with the tuxedo scarf felt like the perfect balance of masculinity and femininity. And it had pockets! I wore it to a wedding with loafers and I felt incredible.In the end, I think that dress is my favourite piece from the first collection – a dress I didn’t even think we would have." For the second season, the duo continued to develop the brand’s identity. Do they design with a particular person in mind? "There’s definitely a character there," says Bartley, "a rakish, louche woman". With a portrait of Katharine Hepburn on the cutting room wall, and reference points like Withnail and Lucian Freud, that rakishness is inherent to the Hillier Bartley woman. And the British eccentricity that the pair ooze in person is clearly visible in their designs. The first season was produced entirely in the UK. "But once we started wearing the pieces, we noticed that the tailoring was quite Savile Row, which can be a bit stiff," says Bartley. "Since then we’ve moved production of our jackets to Italy to give them a softer, more feminine feel. It’s still a very masculine silhouette, but it now has a slouchiness that I find more wearable." The business is being developed from each designer’s wealth of experience. They certainly know what they don’t want to do from working in giant corporations turning out six or eight collections per year. They are determined not to undermine the creative side of what they’re trying to achieve, or be swept up in the pace of the fast-fashion industry. "I think if you stick to your design convictions, people either relate to it or they don’t, but you’ll consequently have a much more loyal customer," Bartley adds. "If we try to chase something that we don’t fully believe in, it won’t work. I’m aware we sound rather idealistic. I’m just very happy with the way things are at the moment." The sheer pleasure of the joint project is palpable. They visit the mills and factories they work with and take time with each stage of the design process. "It’s a gift to ourselves that we can do it how we want," says Hillier. "We’re not looking for world domination; we want to do something that makes us feel happy – and we love the product." Bartley adds, "In the future, it might be completely different, but right now there’s an opportunity to do things in a different way. It’s a small, self-funded business, which affords us a lot of freedom." Another thing they share is their dream to open a shop some day. "I want somewhere on Kensington Church Street," says Bartley. "Not a posh megastore, something small. Similar to Mary Quant back in the day where you’d have your workshop upstairs, then bring it downstairs to sell. I want it to feel intimate and handmade."  "And I want a Chiltern Street store," counters Hillier. "That can definitely be done on Chiltern Street…" "But, I’ve got a thing about Kensington Church Street! That’s quite a good ending, isn’t it – 'And then they beat each other up…'" Bartley laughs. Far from having a fight, it is clear that their friendship is key to the brand’s mechanics. "What is nice is that we can back each other up," Bartley says. "It’s incredibly important to know someone’s got your back." She describes it as a process in which the stars aligned. "It’s truly fallen into place. I think that happens when it’s this personal. Nothing’s been difficult. It sounds a bit lovey-dovey, doesn’t it?" Perhaps. But then maybe Hillier Bartley is the antidote that the industry needs to its conventional business model? The duo are building a brand tailored to the demands of the modern woman.  Sandra Choi began working for her uncle Jimmy Choo, then an east London couture shoemaker and fashion editor's secret, when she was a teenager. Born in the UK on the Isle of Wight, she was educated in Hong Kong.  She moved to London to finish her secondary school education and it was during this time that she started to work in the studio where Choo was making shoes for celebrities including Princess Diana.  As Choo's protégé, Choi studied fashion design at Central St Martin's but later abandoned her degree to spend more time designing and managing the operation; eventually she became creative director. Since then, Jimmy Choo has become one of the world's most recognisable luxury shoe brands, creating glamorous designs for women the world over, including Cate Blanchett,  Gwyneth Paltrow and Natalie Portman.  Choi, 43, has two daughters, Phoenix and Cyan, with her husband the fashion-designer-turned-artist Tamburlaine Gorst. She lives in Battersea, London. She shared eight of the treasured personal pieces which inspire her with The Telegraph... Pencils Sketching is my preferred way to work. A pencil stroke is instant, emotional  and intuitive – an uninhibited expression of how I feel. Glass bottle I love to visit vintage markets when I’m travelling, and dainty bottles always find their way home with me. This one came from the south of France.  Watch This vintage Rolex was a Christmas present from my husband. It embodies everything that is important to me: simplicity, character, history and craftsmanship. Photograph This picture of my granny and me was taken in Hong Kong. I lived there from the age of 18 months until I was 13. The city’s culture  and vibrancy still inspire me.  Necklace I found this in Goa, India. I subconsciously seek out jewellery whenever  I travel, so my collection  keeps growing. Shoes This is my all-time favourite pair of shoes.  I designed them in 2005 and have worn them to death. They exude glamour and romance. Dictionaries I used these dictionaries when I was first trying to navigate the English language. When I was a teenager they were constantly by my side. Art book One of my goals is to own a piece of Gerhard Richter’s art. The skill, colour and techniques involved in  his pieces always inspire me.  I find them breathtaking. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Getting the balance between a wedding dress that has enough of a 'wow' factor while not veering too dramatically far from one’s signature style is a challenge all brides face. None more so than Jerry Hall, 59, who married newspaper magnate Rupert Murdoch today knowing that her Vivienne Westwood wedding dress would, quite literally, hold the front page. So it’s perhaps not surprising that Hall chose Westwood to design her dress for the big day. Hall and Dame Vivienne Westwood's personal relationship dates back many years. Hall has walked in several of the designer's catwalk shows and allowed daughter Lizzy to make her catwalk debut in a Westwood show when she was just 14 years old. Hall has also championed Westwood's creations on the red carpet, most recently donning a black, sparkling Westwood gown to attend the Vanity Fair post-Oscars party last week. The first clue that Hall had stayed loyal to her designer friend came yesterday when pictures emerged of a Vivienne Westwood dustbag being carried away from Hall’s home. But where one might have imagined Hall had chosen one of Vivienne Westwood’s classic structured, taffeta dresses or even, a tailored peplum jacket and pencil skirt combination - both silhouettes the supermodel would have pulled off perfectly - the wedding dress she debuted today was a much softer, draped affair.  Hall has known what best complements her long, lean body for decades – form fitting, silky fabrics cut on the bias, almost-flat shoes – and she stayed true to this formula for her big day pairing her Westwood dress with trademark Roger Vivier silver shoes.  So what’s the verdict? “This really is a dress of two halves: the colour is beautiful on her, and I love the neckline and the sleeves. When she’s sitting at lunch during her wedding reception it will look beautiful,’ says The Telegraph’s Fashion Director Lisa Armstrong. “But the transparent fabric around the knees complicates the dress unnecessarily. And the translucent sheen to the tights, perhaps caused by the flash from photographers, is illustrative of a strange, treacherous problems all brides face on their wedding day. It’s always worth getting a friend to take pictures of your potential wedding day look beforehand.” This is, officially speaking, Hall’s first marriage. Despite marrying Rolling Stones rocker Sir Mick Jagger in 1990, he had the Hindu marriage annulled nine years later on the grounds that the ceremony was not legally binding. On that occasion, Hall wore a knee-length, off-the-shoulder creation in white lace commissioned from Antony Price. She sold the dress at auction in 2008, where it was bought for £2,420 by Steven Philip, owner of west London vintage store Rellik. The money was donated to a homeless charity. At the time she said: “For me, this is a time of letting go, simplifying and getting my priorities right. I love it that my dresses can have a new lease of life in someone else's wardrobe. I just thought, 'This is a great way of recycling.' "It's really odd to think that some other woman might wear it at her wedding. I just hope whoever she is has more luck than I did." Hall had four children with Jagger over the two decades that they were together, but ended the relationship after he was repeatedly unfaithful to her. Hall, who walked for all the great fashion houses such as Chanel and Yves Saint Laurent during her catwalk heyday, once said that she would never let her daughters marry like Mick Jagger. She has now found happiness with Murdoch, the billionaire owner of News Corporation. The two met in Australia last year and went public with their relationship at the World Cup final together at Twickenham last October. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Is the second generation supermodel upon us already? Flipping through the latest issue of fashion biannual, LOVE, one might be forgiven for thinking so. Tucked among the fashion stories is a study of Kaia Gerber, daughter of original super Cindy Crawford. Her father, Rande Gerber, is no slouch on the glamour front either. He co-owns the Casamigos tequila company with best friend George Clooney, a friendship recently dubbed ‘Hollywood’s closest Bromance’. Kaia’s startling resemblance to her mother makes her story not so much an issue of nepotism but one of professional inevitability. “There’s something about Cindy and Christy [Turlington] where you can’t quite believe how beautiful she is,” says Love’s Editor in Chief, Katie Grand. “Gisele’s another one. Cindy is so incredibly fit. You look at her and think ‘oh, wow, that gym’s really working for you, isn’t it?’ “You know when you look at Kaia that it’s really going to work for her.” How did Kaia’s mum - also still a working model - feel about her daughter’s ascent into the modelling elite? Grand says she got early signals that Cindy Crawford was fully on board when she offered her home as location. But that left the editor with a quandary - finding a groomer experienced enough to respect Ms Crawford’s hospitality. “All make-up artists leave a trail of cotton buds behind,” she notes. “It always really bothers me. The idea of Cindy kindly lending her house and then somebody leaving a bottle of nail polish remover on a very expensive sofa...” In the end, a solution to everyone’s satisfaction presented itself. “Much to my amusement, I get an email saying ‘are you OK with Cindy doing the hair and makeup?’ To which I yelped around the office.” Because of the lovely thought of a mother offering to make up a face no-one can know more intimately? “I didn’t think of it in that romantic way. I immediately just thought, oh my god, these credits are going to read so well. Hair and Makeup: Cindy Crawford. Styling and photography: Kendall Jenner.” Because, yes, Kaia was shot by her friend, and another of Grand’s protegees, model Kendall Jenner. Grand had spotted three black and white stills by Jenner on Instagram, and emailed her agent immediately to see if she would shoot for Love - he wrote back within two minutes to say ‘yes’. “I emailed back, ‘who would she like to shoot?’ Another two minutes went by and it was ‘oh, she’d love to shoot Kaia’,” says Grand. In 15 years of editing fashion magazines, she says she’s rarely briefed a story as swiftly. Kendall, who Katie brokered out of the world of reality TV and into high fashion at 17, is the daughter of the Kardashians’ ‘momager’, Kris and her former husband Bruce, now Caitlin Jenner. Both Kaia, 15, and Kendall, 20, are possessed of a beauty boon that is seeing the offspring of pivotal fashion figures gently pushing their parents out of the frame. Indeed, they are the latest in a bespoke lineage of fashion children that have appeared in Love since it debuted in 2009. Her last issue featured the first editorial cover story for Lily Rose Depp, the daughter of Johnny and his stunning ex-wife Vanessa Paradis. And if you look closer at the credits of the bumper new issue, the story fleshes out further. “I suppose we do have a few kids of… in this one,” notes Grand. Iris Law, the daughter of Jude and Sadie Frost, is arresting in glitter makeup. Lennon Gallagher, the son of Liam and Patsy Kensit, makes it a triple whammy for debut modelling assignments for second generation superstars in a Moncler Dennis the Menace sweater, sporting his father’s unmissable eyebrow furniture. They are both 15 years old, taking baby steps into rivetingly promising careers. After delighting at the results of shooting Iris Law for the magazine, Grand went on to cast her in the Miu Miu resort collection look-book, with her dad coming along as a very hands-off chaperone. “He sat there all day reading his book and trying not to get in the way. He was really sweet,” says Grand. Like father, like daughter. “She’s got that thing that some kids have. It’s super-infectious because they’re really jolly, really polite, incredibly well brought up and nice to everyone. It does make you think, that expensive education really did work.” Iris is being looked after by the same model agency team that took Georgia May Jagger to worldwide success at the same age. Lennon Gallagher happened after a call from mum. “Patsy phones me every two years and says ‘darling, miss you so much’,” says Grand. “She says, ‘Lennon’s so gorgeous and I’d really like him to do some pictures because he wants to get involved in acting and film. I think it’d be great for him to work with you guys because you’ll really take care of him.’ So I said, ‘OK, I can be on my best behaviour that day’.” Grand has worked closely with the parents of the miracle gene kids – she styled Patsy and Liam for the cover of Arena Homme+ in 1999, and took tickets for Oasis’ Knebworth gigs in exchange for choosing a Ghost slip dress and straw hat for Patsy to wear backstage – so they know what their children will be privy to in her hands. Grand says when she thinks of Patsy, she thinks of “us jumping up and down dancing in my kitchen at five in the morning at my hen night, while Jeremy Healy is DJing”. Patsy must remember, too. “She did say, ‘don’t tell him any of the stories.’” One slipped through, from the make-up artist Miranda Joyce. “She told him this story about being in a car once with Patsy, back when you could drive around Buckingham Palace, with Patsy at the wheel, her leg out of the window resting on the wing mirror, driving in Azzedine Alaia. He was kind of fine about it.” There are more sensitive, hormonal considerations to take into account with a 15 year-old-boy on his first serious fashion shoot. “Lennon was more nervous than Iris, but then there were all the Victoria’s Secrets girls around. We were asking him to dress in front of them, things you do without even thinking about them, and then you find yourself saying oh, hang on, there’s the bathroom to go and put your jumper on to avoid Taylor Hill walking around with her knickers on.” Grand is delighted with all her young charges’ work in the issue. “I love the Kaia pictures,” she says, clearly aware of being at the right side of the curve in the ascension of a blossoming fashion star. “She’s wearing Palace and Richardson, brands that Kendall requested. You can imagine being on that set with them, eating ice cream and being daft.” Kendall Jenner can’t quite believe her luck, either, at her first serious photography commission. Within 24 hours of Kendall posting one of the Kaia images on her Instagram feed, it had 1.4million likes and the stamp of the subject’s approval. “This was so cool for me because it really does come full circle. [Kaia’s] mum was my idol. Now I’m shooting my idol’s daughter.”  See the full shoot in LOVE 16 ‘Fame, Goths & Toffs!’ Autumn/Winter 2016, which goes on newsstands 25 July. thelovemagazine.co.uk Lila Grace Moss-Hack (13) Kate’s daughter is a failsafe future fashion star. Her father, Dazed and Confused publishing impresario Jefferson Hack recently said his offspring considers her parents ‘deeply uncool.’ She scored her magazine cover debut this year for Vogue Italia, cradled into Kate in a touching shot by Mario Sorrenti. Word is that she may be swapping front of camera for the typewriter very soon, before she’s even started studies for her English Literature GCSE. Brains, too! Lourdes Leon (19) Madonna’s very own ray of light. After years of rattling against Catholicism, the Queen of Pop’s firstborn ushered in her mother’s second spiritual tenure: the Kabala years. Lourdes is currently excavating mom’s younger roots at University in Detroit.
