 This past week has seen some major royal style moments. There was Camilla, Duchess of Cornwall's elegant look for her visit to Italy and Austria. Queen Rania of Jordan exuded sophistication in Haider Ackermann as she visited the Trumps at the White House. And here in London, The Duchess of Cambridge dazzled in a full-skirted red dress by Marchesa Notte, a style which is fast becoming her go-to.  But in Japan, Queen Letizia of Spain was offering a lesson in regal dressing to rival all others. From refined daytime tailoring to glittering evening gowns and chic cocktail looks, Letizia - who became Queen following the abdication of her father-in-law King Juan Carlos in 2014 - has nailed the balance of looking contemporary and aspirational whilst also staying true to the unspoken sartorial commandments of the world stage.  Those rules dictate that visitors should consider offering a diplomatic nod or two to their host country. Letizia ticked this box with aplomb in her choice of a velvet Armani Privé dress decorated with patterned silk depicting the cherry blossoms for which Japan is famous, particularly during spring time - it was an adaptation of a look from the Spring 2011 collection inspired by traditional symbols of Japanese culture. She finished that outfit with a pair of ruby and diamond earrings borrowed from the collection of her mother-in law, Queen Sofia.  Another quiet expectation of national figureheads is to wear designers from their country. During her Tokyo trip, Queen Letizia chose several pieces by Felipe Varela, the Spanish couturier who has created many of her go-to outfits over the years. For her first engagement of the tour, she opted for a fitted bright red coat and velvet dress (main picture) by Varela - red is a significant hue in both Japanese and Spanish culture - while for an evening state banquet, she revived a high-octane navy embellished ballgown which had first been created for her by the Madrid-based designer in 2015. Palabras del Rey ante la colectividad española en Japón @EmbajadaTokiohttps://t.co/BNHA2Za9Rv pic.twitter.com/6Q9c3PMe1B Elsewhere during the four-day trip, Queen Letizia, who was a news presenter before marrying the then-Crown Prince Felipe in 2002, wore a polished blouse and pencil skirt look by Hugo Boss, another of her favoured labels and one which offers a subtle reminder of her consciousness for professional dressing.  Then there was an emerald green, floral printed dress by Carolina Herrera, the American doyenne of ladylike power dressing who has dressed women ranging from Hillary Clinton and Michelle Obama to The Duchess of Cambridge and Ivanka Trump, as well as the elite of New York society. Queen Letizia's on-point wardrobe is nothing new; she has been excelling in this game for years, thoughtfully mixing affordable, accessible pieces from the likes of Zara and  Mango with recycled designer buys and dazzling new, and often patriotic, acquisitions. Over the past few years, she has worked with Eva Fernandez , a former fashion editor, who is part of her office of staff but has landed special responsibilities for helping with the Queen's outfits. The pair have often been spotted out shopping together, with Fernandez sticking to a grown-up cool uniform of skinny jeans, cashmere jumpers and artfully nonchalant accessorises. This week's trip to Tokyo proved that Queen Letizia's unerring dedication to a prim and  glossy look has come to epitomise, and the set the bar, for modern royal style.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  How do you inject a brand with personality? How do you articulate fashion in a different way? These are some of the questions that designer Jonathan Anderson posed to himself when he took the reins at Loewe three years ago. He decided the answer was taking the Spanish luxury house into the interiors realm, because "home has never been more important". It’s also a more substantial way of demonstrating a brand’s creative flair, artisanship and know-how – furniture has longevity. Loewe follows in the footsteps of other fashion brands expanding into lifestyle via homeware. And where else do you debut but at Milan design week, an annual event that has been described as the Glastonbury of design – although with twice as many attendees. Modular seating inspired by American minimalism, wool throws knitted into curious male silhouettes, star-spangled rugs, oak pieces hand-carved by Yorkshire furniture-makers; "Loewe: This is Home" draws upon myriad influences and a panoply of textures and techniques. Its eclectic nature is a very personal expression of the craft-obsessed mind behind it – that of creative director Jonathan Anderson.   Irish-born Anderson is full of enthusiasm for his "composite craft landscape". "It’s a collage of different bits of information," he says. "I like the idea that fashion can explode into the household, bringing artisans together to design new physical forms and apply craft in a home."  He references a dizzying range of influences, while explaining the several tableaux that make up the collection. A table composed of a stack  of colourful recycled leather squares nods to minimalist artist Félix González-Torres; a star motif takes its cues from celestial Renaissance ceilings, but it’s also "slightly religious, a little bit like [Eric] Gill woodcuts"; the figurative knitted throws double up as wallhangings, evocative of the Seventies revival of this art form: "you had Peter Collingwood and before that Leger, Picasso and Nicholson…"  Most covetable perhaps is the series of oak items – a ladder, canework screen, candlesticks and bowl – produced in collaboration with Robert "Mouseman" Thompson’s Craftsmen Ltd, a fifth-generation Yorkshire furniture-maker known for the signature mouse carved into every piece it makes. "I have some of his original furniture and wanted to make something more contemporary with them," says Anderson. "I like the idea of a British church furniture revival."  Just half an hour in Anderson’s presence and you begin to understand how, in his dual role overseeing both J.W. Anderson and Loewe, he manages to conceive an entire home collection on top of 12 fashion collections a year. In just three years he’s redefined the Spanish leather brand, reinforcing its reputation for craftsmanship both in and outside the fashion world, exhibiting at the past two Design Miami fairs and showcasing leather marquetry during last year’s Milan design week. Next on the agenda: promoting the work of skilled artisans via the new Loewe Craft Prize.  "When I joined I had this fantasy of building a cultural brand," he says. "I want to articulate fashion in a different way, and I feel the home has never been more important – I like the idea of modular living. It also gives us an outlet to work with more artisans. I want to explore all forms of craft, but in a modern way." loewe.com "Loewe: This Is Home" is on show at the Loewe flagship store, via Montenapoleone 21 , from April 5 until April 9 "Conversation in craft  between Jonathan Anderson and Telegraph Luxury" is at Liberty London on May 4, at the opening event of Loewe: This Is Home; rsvpevents@loewe.es quoting "Craft" to book © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Athleisure has been the fashion industry’s buzzword for the last couple of years – fuelled by either the pursuit of fitness, or at least an illusion of pursuing it: sportswear for beyond gyms and bus stops and yes, trainers you CAN wear to the office. When I mention the phrase to 70-year-old Debbie Moore OBE, the matriarch of Covent Garden’s Pineapple dance empire, she rolls her eyes, and deadpans: “Yeah…”  Next to us lies the yellowed copy of the Evening Standard of November 5 1982, the front page lit up by the seminal picture of Moore – in a mini Lycra ra-ra skirt and sweatshirt – standing on the floor of the Stock Exchange, surrounded by besuited men, as she became the first woman to take her own company public.  Three years earlier, the former model, with the help of a £30,000 bank loan, had opened the doors of Pineapple, which was swiftly followed by an enduring and agenda setting foray into fashion.  Moore started dancing during her modelling days to get fit, when, aged 21, she was diagnosed with an underactive thyroid after her first husband ran off with another woman. Her subsequent weight gain meant her modelling career was in peril. She was also adamant that she wasn’t going to spend the rest of her life medicated on Thyroxine.  She found herself in Arlene Phillips’s Floral Street jazz class. “I used to stand at the back and do all the warm-up, but I could never get the routine right, so I used to leave [at that point].” The benefits of dancing and diet for her, were critical. Within nine months she was off Thyroxine, and back modelling. “Dancing is the finest form of exercise,” she says. “You work every muscle in your body. It’s uplifting because of the music and it’s sociable.” Her well-told tale goes that one Monday morning in 1978, Moore turned up to her dance class to see a closure notice – for that Friday. By the end of the week she’d come up with the concept of Pineapple, as well as made notes of all the teachers’ phone numbers. Seven months later, having secured and renovated the basement and ground floor of a derelict, “rat-infested” old pineapple warehouse (a relic from the relocated fruit, veg and flower market), she opened the doors. “I just had this vision of how it would be, I wanted children to come, everyone from three to 103, all walks of life…”  The creation of “studio to street” clothing came from her admiration of how the dancers customised and layered their workout gear. She also noted the limitations of dancewear – either “shiny nylon Lycra or like school uniform: leotards with high necks and low legs”. She astutely wondered whether Lycra could be combined with cotton to make something less sweaty and better styled. Plie wrap body, in quink ink, £49, Finery x Pineapple Dance Studios The budding entrepreneur contacted the UK arm of DuPont to pitch them the idea. “We got a lot more done in a day then. Make one phone call, make an appointment, done.” They jumped on the idea and developed the fabric for her. Moore hired a pattern cutter who fashioned footless tights and leotards from it; she then had skirts, cardigans and dresses run up in the fabric, intended to be layered on top of each other.  She noticed “everyone” wearing leotards with their jeans – but complaining about the inconvenience. Which led to the concept of poppers on the gusset: problem solved, and “the body” was born. Footless tights became thicker in her cotton Lycra and were re-named “leggings”. She then put proper soles onto ballet shoes so they too could be worn outside.  “Once I’d got the dancers sorted I wanted everyone to be able to have this: they can dress it up to go to lunch, or to the supermarket, or lie on the sofa. It’s this thing of making them feel instantly fit just by wearing it.”  Echappe slip dress in aubergine, £56, Sissone Legging in quink ink, £39, Finery x Pineapple Dance Studios Her 18 years of modelling experience – during which she featured in everything from couture to catalogues – informed her eye for fit and quality. Fast forward 30-odd years and the Athleisure market is worth £7 billion in the UK alone. Unsurprisingly this is the money-spinning arm of Pineapple (there is a stand-alone store on the same street as the studio, a collection with Debenhams and a global wholesale business).  “The whole brand subsidises the studios,” explains Moore. “If I ever sold up, they’d shut the studios. It’s too labour-intensive, the rent, the rates, the maintenance… It’s too hard for the return.”  Arabesque Hoodie Washed Black, £65, Finery x Pineapple Dance Studios Shrewdly, she’s teamed up with Finery for a new collaborative collection, which brings the spirit of Pineapple into the modern sportswear-for-everything mould. Soft black tracksuit bottoms and tops come with velvet ties and rose-gold fastenings; slinky dresses in a rich aubergine are designed to be worn over and under everything, as are the sweetly ruched bodies.  On the day I visit, when I inquire who’s “in”, the receptionist calls out: “Thriller in in the basement, Lion King upstairs”. “It never stops,” says Moore of the studio, which has hosted everything from an Andrex puppy audition (I’m shown pictures of puppies queuing down the street) to a Madonna music video. Chasse ballet wrap in aubergine, £45, Finery x Pineapple Dance Studios Also in today are dancers from ballet’s enfant terrible, the Ukrainian Sergei Polunin's troop, who have just started rehearsals for his Sadler’s Wells production. Moore counts herself as one of Polunin’s benefactors. She’s hosting an upcoming gala fundraiser event, where auction lots include a lunch date with Moore and Arlene Phillips at the Ivy, as well as a bronze sculpture of Polunin’s nude torso by her friend Frances Segelman.  Danka, who has been Moore’s right-hand woman from the earliest inception of the studio, jumps up to show images on her iPhone of the “sculpting party” held at the Hospital Club, where Segelman “live” sculpted a rather game Polunin. “There he is taking his shirt off,” offers Moore. “This is the next Nureyev; this is the beginning of a new era in dance.” Retiring seems very much off the agenda. “I won’t retire. Then what? Take up Italian or piano? No, no. I’ll just drop dead in a studio at 95.” Finery x Pineapple Dance Studios is available from 15th February at Finery and Selfridges     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Before setting out for Calvin Klein’s show on Tuesday evening, I was noodling around on Instagram and clicked into a jolly live video in which 13 year-old Stranger Things star Millie Bobby Brown was interviewing the ultimate American good girl supermodel, Karlie Kloss. It was all sweet and lovely talk about how much they admired each other. ‘See you at the show!’ they signed off. The show, it turned out, comprised a set of dilapidated barns and bulbous factory tubing with a floor ankle-deep in popcorn (the fashion set will be brushing the crumbs off their shoes for days). Raf Simons, now a year on from his first show as chief creative officer at Calvin Klein, has been one of the very few major designers to grapple on such a monumental, emotional scale with social and political commentary. So the juxtaposition of young celebrity and an impending sense of doom did actually make sense, sort of. “It was about heroes…. Like firefighters,” was Simons' pared-back explanation for a collection which addressed unnerving future possibilities  and nostalgia for past triumphs and failures, from the Civil War to the moon landing. With the hand-knitted balaclava as its hero accessory (only a few models, including Kaia Gerber- obviously- were seen without theirs) and a faded hazmat-esque boiler suit as the first look, the show could have been an elaborate vision for the costume design on series two of The Handmaid’s Tale. After Michelle Obama’s official First Lady portrait was unveiled this week, Simons’ patchwork preoccupation, which began in that first collection, gained a renewed cultural currency. Although she wasn’t wearing Calvin, the dress Obama chose for the commission featured a patchwork-print skirt which designer Michelle Smith said had been particularly inspired by the quilts created by the African-American community of Gee’s Bend in Alabama. If that is the ‘now’ status of patchwork, then Simons’ concept for the future was to back it with foil so it that it looked half polite and domesticated, half emergency rescue survival gear. Elsewhere in the collection the practical, dystopian dream wardrobe of survivalists conflated with romance and nostalgia. Swooshing tiered cotton skirts were worn with extra-large tweed coats and elbow length silver gloves of the kind a firefighter might pull on. A silver foil pinafore came with a pretty doily-ish trim and a supple brown leather coat was layered over a trench with fluro orange stripes and worn with a leopard-print hood. There were undoubtedly plenty of pieces which, out of context, will be beautiful in their own right; the voile prairie dresses, tailored tweeds and novelty knitwear. But there was also something disconcerting about evoking desire via looks which communicated pessimism and suffering. Simons’ genius is that he is able to conjure that reality check at all. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Even before her appearance at the Golden Globes tonight, Ruth Negga has been tipped as the break out style star of the 2017 awards season. Nominated for the Best Actress award for her role in Loving, the Ethiopian-Irish rising star has been working with Hollywood super-stylist Karla Welch to hone an experimental yet elegant look which has already won her red carpet plaudits and helped her to bag the cover of January's issue of American Vogue. The Louis Vuitton look which the pair hit on for the Globes, which traditionally kick off the season, has been in the planning ever since November, Welch tells The Telegraph. "It's a custom piece made in the very special atelier in Paris. Nicolas Ghesquiere [Vuitton's creative director] designed the dress for her." The finished creation is "a work of art" Welch adds. "It's a combination of rose gold,  yellow gold and silver paillettes- they were all sewn by hand and it took 120 hours to make." The column silhouette and shimmering finish made for a pristine red carpet look but it's the product of a relaxed attitude to getting Negga's style perfectly on-point. "We just wanted an awesome dress," Welch explains, "what I love about working with Ruth is that we can do a lot of different things but they feel very authentic to who she is. She loves the process but it's actually really easy. It's so good to be a little more free and not get too stressed out." She likens the dress to "armour" which is possibly a very useful feeling for an actress making her first forays into the high octane world of the awards season . After seeing the sketch which Vuitton sent, Welch and Negga "immediately went for it. We love artists - Nicolas is an artist and Ruth is an artist so it felt perfect." Negga is strikingly beautiful with cool cropped hair, a look was kept quite simple by  her hairstylist Vernon Francois “I was inspired by Ruth’s show-stopping dress. My focus was on creating a very elegant look that captured a 1950s feel with an ultra-smooth and luminous finish," says Francois. "I applied a little hairdryer heat and then the rest was all about hand-tailoring the shape with gel and hairspray." And the only jewellery was a vintage 1920s  wrist clasp by Fred Leighton. "We added a beautiful, ethically-sourced 24 carat ruby from Gemfields," Welch says of the precious finishing touch they made.  While the Louis Vuitton is undoubtedly a landmark in Negga's red carpet evolution, every choice carries meaning and excitement for Welch. The week before the Globes is full of parties and warm-up events which have provided an excellent opportunity to showcase an eclectic variety of outfits. The opulent pink and black tea dress by The Vampire's Wife, the label created by Nick Cave's wife and former model Susie Cave, which Welch chose for the BAFTA tea party on Saturday was a case in point. "Well that is the power of Instagram," Welch laughs. "I started following Susie and she started following me. I DM'd her and asked if she'd consider making us a dress- she said she'd love to. I'm so obsessed with it. I love supporting smaller designers. I'm a huge Nick Cave fan and I think Susie Bick (Cave;s maiden name) is amazing and so iconic." It was a special moment for Negga too. "I said to Ruth that Susie Bick is going to make you a dress and she hit the floor. We loved it." Earlier in the week, Negga won praise for an icy blue and pale pink Erdem ensemble at the Variety Creative Impact Awards. "We had a lot of fun with that," remembers Welch. "We're both travelling so much so we meet when we can in New York. We tried that on and loved it and went for it- we loved that it was English and it followed all the Valentino she has been wearing quite nicely." The ladylike mood of the Erdem also presented a clever contrast to last night's armour feel. "We knew we were going to do something hard tonight so I wanted to do a little bit of romance to contrast with the edge of the Vuitton look."  Although it's still early in awards season- the SAGs, the BAFTAS, the Oscars and many more are still to come- Welch's work with Negga over the past few months means there's already a signature emerging. "She can really pull off a lot of things, because she's  a woman not a teenager," reflects Welch. "She has a beautiful confidence with how she carries herself so it's a real pleasure."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Samantha Cameron, wife of Prime Minister David Cameron, isn’t just a spouse to the Most Important Man in the country and a mother to their three children, she’s also a creative consultant at luxury accessories brand Smythson. With this in mind, you’d assume that Cameron would just use her impeccable connections to secure a memorable welcome gift for Peng Liyuan, the First Lady of China, who touched down in the UK with her president husband for an official visit.
 But Cameron is not as predictable as one might imagine; she didn’t pluck one of Smythson’s Nancy, East West or Grosvenor bags off the shelf, but instead opted to champion a creation by young British designer Sophie Hulme. Liyuan was the lucky recipient of London-based Hulme’s classic, square-shaped Albion bag in charcoal. She has the boxy tote in common with Hollywood actress Kate Hudson, who owns the £550 bag in black.
 Kingston University graduate Hulme is obviously thrilled at being associated with the stylish First Lady and singer, who has navigated a week of royal engagements in a number of elegant outfits.
 “We’re absolutely delighted Samantha Cameron chose Sophie Hulme as a gift for First Lady Peng Liyuan, and so pleased we are flying the flag for British Design!” said Hulme in a statement.
 Sophie Hulme bags are presented with quirky additions; brass keyrings which take the form of mini dinosaurs, whistles and robots aren’t uncommon as the designer lives in a converted toy factory and is an avid collector of childhood trinkets. Her covetable bags are stocked at Net-a-Porter, Matches Fashion and Harrods to name but a few luxury outlets.
 Liyuan has been married to Xi Jinping, the President of the people’s Republic of China, for over 20 years and have a 23-year-old daughter together.  Judging by the faces in many of the biggest fashion advertising campaigns and editorials, if you want to become a global supermodel, the fastest way in is to be born into Hollywood dynasty. It seems like every day a new advertising campaign or magazine cover lands in our inbox starring a pretty fresh face with a family tree dotted with famous names. Today's next gen celebrity news is that Maya Hawke, daughter of Uma Thurman and Ethan Hawke, is starring in a campaign film for AllSaints.   Using connections to get ahead in fashion is nothing new of course. Established models like Stella Tennant, Cara Delevingne, Georgia May Jagger, Edie Campbell and Jacquetta Wheeler are all undoubtedly beautiful, but also have surnames and connections powerful and connected enough to open certain doors. As Derek Blasberg once wrote in Vanity Fair, "England is a place where girls from good families apparently become supermodels." The same could be said of Hollywood.  Not all SADs - sons and daughters, that is - should be sniffed at because of the industry's tendencies towards nepotism. While plenty of celebrity offspring are only ever seen in one or two campaigns/ magazine spreads, others work hard to carve out a career that makes them independent of their clickable, bankable surname.  The British Fashion Council has today announced that 39 year-old Stephanie Phair will be its new chair, replacing Dame Natalie Massenet, who stepped down from the role in December. Phair is the youngest person to ever be appointed into the role and, while her name may be not be as immediately familiar as Massenet’s, her influence in the global fashion industry is not to be underestimated. In fact, you could consider her to be a protégé of both the Net-a-Porter founder, and another of fashion’s most powerful businesswomen, US Vogue editor Anna Wintour. Currently the chief strategy officer for Farfetch and an independent board director for Moncler SpA (positions that she will continue to hold alongside her new role) Phair’s experience covers the realms of fashion business, PR, marketing, technology and entrepreneurialism - a potent mix for someone who is set to lead the sector through an era of fluctuating economic situations and Brexit trade negotiations, and one where the internet is changing the way all types of fashion businesses are run. In 1999, Phair graduated from Oxford with a degree in philosophy, politics and economics and, less than a decade later, she was hired by Natalie Massenet at Net-a-Porter to launch its discount site, The Outnet. It’s a jump that might seem big, but by the time she was headhunted by Massenet, Phair had already gained experience with New York PR agency Siren, worked in marketing and brand positioning for Issey Miyake, and handled marketing and public relations for American Vogue.  “What was great about Vogue was that I really saw the fashion business for the first time as a business,” Phair previously told Fashionista. “Back then I think the consumer, in general, saw the fashion business for what the fashion business showed it, which was fashion shows, and designers maybe, and the magazines and the editorials. For me, that perception really changed when I went [to Vogue].” “Anna has always viewed fashion as a business, from how she connects designers to funding, or how she introduces designers to one of the big conglomerates, or how she sees that retail interacts with [Vogue shopping event] Fashion's Night Out, there's a real business goal behind it.” Phair left Vogue in 2005 to join an e-commerce start-up called Portero, the vision for which was to create an ‘Ebay for luxury fashion’.  “A lot of people were like, 'Are you crazy to leave Vogue?'” she said. “I would love to say I was totally a visionary and saw the [rise of internet shopping coming], but I didn't, it was part luck. It happened to be a business that was e-commerce.” Massenet, who was by then already a successful e-commerce entrepreneur with Net-a-Porter, had decided to launch a discount designer fashion website, and hired Phair to plot and run The Outnet in April 2009. It was, coincidentally, only three months after the launch that the UK entered a formal economic recession, and the site thrived to become the leading designer discount site on the internet. “Up until recently, discount luxury fashion was hidden away in out-of-town outlets, but the Internet changed all that,” Phair told Business of Fashion of her vision in November 2010. “It’s now visible and is becoming an accepted form of retail with its own audience and expectations. From day one we wanted to turn discount on its head and offer a luxury experience just like the full price world.” Phair stayed at The Outnet and sat on the Executive Board of the Net-a-Porter Group from 2009-2015. In September 2015, Dame Natalie Massenet left the business that she founded and, by late 2016, rumours began to circulate that she was considering a role with rival digital fashion business, Farfetch. Phair joined Farfetch in November 2016 as chief strategy officer, and Massenet’s appointment as a non-executive co-chair was confirmed in February 2017. The pair have never stated that their appointments were linked, but their relationship has always been an extremely good one, so it would be no surprise if Massenet had chosen to take her with her on her next venture. “I have known and worked with Stephanie for almost a decade [and] her skills bridge the worlds of fashion, business, tech and entrepreneurialism,” Massenet told Business of Fashion of the successor this morning. “I couldn’t be more proud to pass on the baton into Stephanie’s extremely capable hands." The one thing that Phair hasn’t done so much of before is be public-facing to the extent that she will now have to be. While Massenet was an unmissable chair, and a regular at the world's biggest fashion parties with over 170,000 Instagram followers, Phair is extremely private. Being recognised is, in fashion perhaps more than any other industry, something that now comes with her turf as the de facto head of the British industry. Luckily, this is the only, and easiest, C.V. hole for her to fill - a few great street style pictures and we’ll see her on the front row in September. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Lisa Montague is the new CEO of luxury accessories brand Aspinal of London. She was formerly the CEO and  president of Loewe, and before that was CEO of Mulberry. Aspinal is a well-kept secret. It’s a small company with luxury values and products made to a very high standard. It is amazing value for money and that’s really appreciated by its customers. That’s its USP, and it’s not something I’m going to change. I grew up around fashion. My father was a fashion agent in Manchester, and my mother ran lingerie shops. You learn a lot over the dinner table. In the holidays I’d be with my father colour-coding sample swatches, or covering for my mother while she travelled. My family instilled great values: a work ethic and a strong sense of right and wrong. As employers, they always said treat people as you would like to be treated yourself – that wasn’t always the case in retail. I’m still a stickler for right and wrong. Leather mini hat-box bag, £495, Aspinal of London  I don’t take work home with me – I value the separation between my job and my family life. My way of having it all is to make the distinction, so I go into transition mode on the journey and get my head in the right place to be totally ready for the kids [Montague has three children aged from almost four to 14 years old] when I get home. I’ve never thought about sexism in the workplace in Britain. I had a working mother and I was always expected to go into further education and work. But when I went to Spain for Loewe, I expected the conversation to be about me being British and running a Spanish company, but it was more about me being a woman. I realised that America and Britain are much further ahead in this respect. When I went to LVMH, I wasn’t sure I was up to it, and I felt as though someone might uncover the fraud. But I took a lot of deep breaths and ended up loving the experience. I am excited by the breakneck speed of the fashion cycle, but we need both fast and slow. You cannot produce luxury quickly – it takes time to develop quality. There’s a danger of compromising intrinsic design values by trying to go too fast. I’m endlessly positive. Negativity drives me insane. I can be impatient, however, so  I have to stop myself always trying to go bigger, better, faster. I have to remember to take people with me. Aspinal only launched in 2001, it’s  a young business, and it’s punching above its weight. Fifty per cent of sales are online, which means it knows its customer well. We don’t need to build the business in  a traditional way because the market is  shifting, and the opportunity to innovate is  so much greater. The new flagship store in St James’s Market, off Regent Street, which is launching in early November, will be a game changer. At over 3,000sq ft, it’s a big space that will give us a chance to show the whole product line. We’re also aiming to grow the British audience, taking Aspinal out of London, with new stores in Leeds and Edinburgh as well as those in Manchester and Birmingham. Our Michelle Dockery frame bag – now known as the Lady Mary bag – has done really well. It’s a classic British design, but the frame is amazing. Frame bags used to be heavy, but you can manipulate this quite easily. There’s another collaboration for men in the pipeline for spring 2018, which I’m excited about. For spring/summer 2018, in partnership with Murder on the Orient Express [out in November], Aspinal of London has created a capsule collection inspired by the film.  I love the hat box [pictured, above], which is the perfect size and comes in a rainbow of colours – Aspinal does colour so well – and a cream-and-camel two-tone version. Advice? I always horrify everyone when  I give mentoring talks saying maths is the most useful subject. Be open-minded about creativity but also understand the rigour of what it takes to run a business – if you can marry the two, it’s wonderful.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Kate Moss was first spotted in JFK airport in New York when she was 14 by Storm founder Sarah Doukas, and has stayed with the modelling agency ever since. Now, 28 years later, Kate Moss has parted ways with the agency that first launched her career.  "After a successful 28 year relationship, Kate is moving her business in house, and we will continue to maintain an active involvement in our on-going deals for her," the agency told The Telegraph in a statement, confirming the model will now manage her own bookings.  Although Kate's profile has now been removed from the agency's website, Storm insist the decision to split was amicable and the 42-year-old's half-sister Lottie Moss, 18, remains on its books. Lottie was originally scouted when she was a bridesmaid at Kate's wedding to Jamie Hince when she was 13 and then was officially represented by Storm when she reached the age of 16.  In Forbes Magazine's annual 2015 Model Rich List, Moss ranked 12th, but her earnings have dropped. "Kate Moss is a consistent entrant on FORBES' highest-earning models list," they told The Telegraph. "She banked an estimated pre-tax $4.5 million before fees between June 2014 through June 2015 - the scoring period for our most recent ranking -down from $7 million the year prior. Her career earnings approximate $100 million, according to historic FORBES estimates." Cara Delevingne, who was spotted by Doukas when she was a teenager too, also left Storm in last year. The model-turned-actress is now represented by American acting agency, William Morris. Delevingne clarified on Twitter last night that although she is currently focusing on her acting projects, she "never said I was quitting modelling." Instead, she implied she'd stepped back from modelling for personal reasons: "I do not blame the fashion industry for anything. I suffer from depression and was a model during a particularly rough patch of self hatred." Doukas has previously revealed that she took care to protect Moss in the early days of her career. "She was in school, and I don't ever agree with taking anybody out of school," she told Business Insider. "We worked on the holidays and stuttered along for a year. But she wasn't greatly interested in school, and then she left, and then we started. Every day I said, 'I'm going to make you a star.' I didn't know I was going to make her a superstar." Earlier this year we shared Kate Moss' first ever photoshoot which was taken in 1988 shortly after she was scouted by Doukas when returning home from a holiday with her father. "I’ve got this new girl. You’ll love her. She’s just your look," photographer Own Scarbiena remembers being told by Doukas. When Moss turned up on the shoot she was given very specific instructions. "Some girls come with  a ready-made photo pose and you have to work through that. But I just said to Kate, “Pretend you’re bored waiting at the bus stop,” and she  got it."  The Duchess of Cambridge is known for choosing well-known, established designers for her royal engagements, or recycling tried and tested old outfits from her own wardrobe. Today, however, Kate broke with tradition by stepping out in a skirt suit by relatively unknown label Eponine – instantly catapulting the brand’s London-based designer Jet Shenkman, 55, to fashion fame. The Duchess wore a red and white gingham 60s-inspired skirt suit, costing £1,200,  as she accompanied the Duke of Cambridge to the XLP youth mentoring project in Barbican, London.  “Oh my goodness, it’s unbelievably nice,” Shenkman told The Telegraph of how it feels to have Duchess championing her label. The mother-of-four - whose design studio is in her Kensington home - said it remains a mystery how Kate discovered her. But within hours of pictures of the Duchess emerging wearing Eponine, her small firm was inundated with emails and sales enquiries. “I have never experienced anything like this!” she added. Skenkman's small label has been featured in Country & Town House Magazine but relies heavily on word of mouth recommendations. “I don't advertise,” Shenkman says. “It's through prior recommendation - and we quietly worked away and it's sort of worked and that's how I've enjoyed it. It's been a gradual process which I think is the best way to feel your way into it, and then something like this happens and suddenly everything goes mad.” The Duchess’s flattering box pleated skirt and matching structured top are from Eponine’s SS16 ready-to-wear collection. “For me that was a real representation of the 60s mod era,” Shenkman says of the inspiration behind the suit. “One of the details you probably can't see on the photographs is it's got a silver-coloured, sort of, crocodile trim both on the yolk and the insides of the little belts. Those sorts of details are really important, so each piece looks very nice and inside and outside. We use really beautiful linings to give extra weight to the outfit as well.” Shenkman, who was raised in the Netherlands, founded her own label in 2012, having previously worked as a stylist with private clients when her family lived in Japan and Hong Kong. When she moved back to London with her British husband Greg she followed the advice of her friends, and decided to create her own vintage-inspired atelier out of her Kensington home. “My inspiration is the elegance of the 50s and 60s - for women it's not always so easy to try on something that fits them beautifully and at the same time is individual with nice fabric,” she says. While she does create a series of outfits you can buy online such as the Duchess of Cambridges’ suit, the main focus for her label is made-to-measure custom pieces. “I like that with each client you get that very individual collaboration. What we do is pretty unique and every woman is given a lot of attention. We take the finished product so seriously, we really do. If it's not perfect someone has to come back for another fitting,” she says. A mother of four, Shenkman’s studio is in her family home - giving an air of intimacy she thinks her clients like. “It can be a distraction from time to time, but I really enjoy it and am incredibly lucky to have a very supportive family who don't mind loads of women traipsing through the house,” she says of her children, who helped choose the name of her business after their favourite character in Les Miserables. Shenkman also believes that the Duchess of Cambridge may like the fact that Eponine is very much a British brand. All of the fabrics are sourced from a UK-based mill, which also supplies fabrics to a number of Parisian couture houses. “The whole made in Britain aspect is very important to me,” Shenkman explains. “It is so important to support local industry and when you look at my fabrics you immediately understand how beautiful they are.” And true to the so-called Kate effect, although the outfit is not officially for sale, Eponine have already received emails from ardent Duchess fans wanting to get their own version of the £1,200 suit.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This week has been a busy one at the UN in New York for reasons, obviously, entirely unrelated to fashion. Donald Trump has threatened to obliterate North Korea, Theresa May has had an awkward encounter with Boris Johnson in front of the world's cameras and Malala has been whiling away the last days before she starts university meeting with world leaders to encourage them to prioritise education, to name but three of the happenings.  Yet, style-wise, the UN has become a strangely important barometer for the current state of power dressing. You only have to look at the carefully calibrated wardrobe which Amal Clooney put together for her appearences there last year (think: unmissably vibrant Bottega Veneta tailoring and Gucci shift dresses) to see that women who love fashion and understand its semantic possibilities pay particular attention to the UN as a platform.  Last night, Melania Trump gave her first address to a UN luncheon dressed, as one member of The Telegraph fashion team observed, like a 'Barbie Michelin man'. It could not have been a brighter, more visible, more 'HELLO! LOOK AT ME' look unless she had hired a Mr Blobby suit. In fact, her fuchsia coat dress is by Spanish design house Delpozo which is known for its sculptural, bold designs. She even paired the look with her signature deep tan and matching pink Louboutins.  Earlier in the week, the First Lady had taken a wildly different tact when she sat in on her husband's confrontational address to the UN wearing one of her subtlest public appearence looks to date- a double-breasted grey trouser suit with a black blouse.  So what does this all mean? Well in the pink, La Trump was visible, feminine and working the uber-shoulders to take up maximum space, an effect which was only enhanced by the fact that the outfit was mostly photographed from the waist up. It was a big moment for her going it alone- a crucial point- as FLOTUS and she was sure to make a confident splash which also underscored her personal, unashamed love of fashion.  Power connotations were undoubtedly still at play with the tailoring but this was a quieter, more businesslike choice which was perhaps selected to allow the President to take centre stage for his speech and, knowing what he was going to say, keep the spotlight firmly on him- wearing bright pink demi-couture as your husband wields threats of nuclear war would have made the heels-in-a-hurricane, er, storm seem minor by comparison.  Melania talked about kindness and anti-bullying in her pink dress speech, which many have pointed out as ironic given her husband's Twitter tendencies. But if she's letting her clothes do some of the talking this week, then it's clear which outfit, and moment, she wanted us to actually remember.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Pippa Middleton's track record shows a penchant for colourful pieces; very rarely one to step out in head-to-toe black or even monochrome. Today Middleton made the most of the slight raise in temperatures that we've witnessed over the last couple of days and demonstrated that winter doesn't have to herald the absence of colour, by pounding the streets of Chelsea in a burnt orange, collarless number from Zara (this particular style is now sold out, but Jaeger have a similar, albeit more expensive, version).  Middleton paired her punchy coat with a patterned skirt peeking just proud of her orange hem line, opaque tights, ankle boots (Toga do a similar pair) and a black Gucci bag, for a look that appeared relaxed, yet pulled together.  What lessons can we learn from Middleton's bold cover-up? The fact that Middleton's Zara coat is A-line in shape, collarless and equipped with oversized buttons, grants it a certain 60's-esque feel, meaning the coat has context and the zingy colour doesn't look out of place. We suggest layering a black or cream polo neck underneath yours. Not only will this help keep out the cold, but it will also make a bright coat look suitably wintry.  Middleton has hit the nail on the head in teaming her zesty coat with neutral items. Her black tights-skirt-bag combo lets her outerwear do the talking, offset slightly by her monochrome skirt. If you're going to wear a brightly coloured coat, we recommend pairing it with black, cream, navy or grey.  Middleton's tights are to similar effect. They add to the over all 50's feel of the look, while also giving is a cool edge. Wear yours with opaque tights like Middleton, or experiment with patterned or fishnets to rework you coat for evening.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  There are any number of pieces I find myself coveting at the Victoria, Victoria Beckham preview on the last day of London Fashion Week. The dark denim slim jeans that have been fused with felt at the hems? A clever twist on an old formula and a versatile multi-tasker for the woman who wants to look fashionably sleek rather than corporately-smart. The pinstripe shirting dress, similar to one in the current collection, but now with an added ruffle? I’d buy that for the office and as a weekend piece. The ruffle sleeved t-shirts and flared trousers (in forest green, peppermint or black)? The trousers are an excellent cut. VB herself has them in every colour and will wear them with the spongy wool, 60s inspired belted jackets (‘that’s  my equivalent of a twinset”). I’d settle for the forest green, a great in-between shade that slides into the cracks of your wardrobe and goes with everything. But isn’t Victoria, Victoria Beckham meant to be the girlish little sister to the main collection? In which case I shouldn’t be as keen as I am. The VVB collection has had to grow up, Beckham tells me. “She’s having fun, but not too much, fun. She needs clothes for work as well as for evening,” she says. This is the way of the (fashion) world: the constant tilt at youthfulness, even though many customers are older, the same age, perhaps, as 41-year-old Beckham whose ever-evolving closet is a perpetual diversion for millions of women and increasingly, a template for how to look stylish at work. “I think people saw the real me when I came out [at the end of her Victoria Beckham show in New York] in a pair of men’s trousers, a roll-neck and trainers.” For the record (and the minutiae matters) she’s wearing mannish trousers again, plus a navy coat, one front panel of which she artfully pushes aside as she thrusts a hand in her trouser pockets. She’s nothing if not practised in what makes for a photogenic moment, which is just as well, because when I arrive at the store for our meeting, there are a cluster of photographers waiting for her outside on the pavement. This must add complex considerations to her “dressing for work” uniform, but she insists that these days she, and her collections, “are all about making getting dressed easy. And being flattering. Take this sleeveless black dress. We worked hard to get the placing of the ruffle right. You need to be able to wear a bra with it and you don’t want a ruffle that makes you look as though you have four boobs. And you probably want it to make you look as though you have a small waist, even when the cut is oversized.” VB – brand and woman – have loosened up, in every sense. For instance, flats are now part of her uniform. Today it’s a take on Nurse Ratchett white leather loafers. “I just can’t do heels any more. At least not when I’m working,” she says. “I travel a lot.” True. She’s just returned from half term with the children in LA after the New York show, and is off to Hong Kong for the opening of her second store there in three weeks. “Clothes have to be simple and comfortable.” It strikes me listening to Beckham, that after what seems aeons of aping celebrities and playing to the Instagram era with fancy dress, fashion is witnessing a subtle shift towards looking as though you have a proper job and a genuinely busy life. Even dolllygarchs walk around  in tailoring, with their Macbook pros within easy reach (generally inside a croc tote). Certainly there have been far more ideas on the catwalks recently that work for grown-ups. Christopher Kane’s show on Monday is a case of point, as was Victoria Beckham’s main collection, which she showed ten days ago in New York. Will she continue to show there, despite the logistics – and the fact that Anna Wintour says she felt 'let down' by  a 'risk-free' New York Fashion Week? Beckham looks surprised. “Well, she hosted a dinner for us after the show at her house and it  wasn’t boring at all. In fact it was a lot of fun,” she says. “The truth is, New York works for us. We get a great slot on the schedule and it’s important for sales that we get to show early in the calendar.” So this, it seems is how it is to be. Main line showing in New York on the catwalk, one on one personal presentations of the VVB collection in London, which is the way she started out with her main line. London may just have the better deal. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  If you’ve insouciantly shrugged at catwalk trends in favour of a plain cashmere jumper, spent countless minutes/hours/days perfecting your smoky, smudged eyeliner or just bought a tailored black blazer to wear with jeans, then congratulations – you are a signed-up member of the Parisian-chic phenomenon. In recent years, we’ve pored over books that instruct us how to live à la Française. French women, we are told, are happier, sexier and cooler than the rest of us could ever hope to be. And, of course, more stylish. There’s a coterie of French women whose elegant yet effortless look has become something of an obsession, thanks to style blogs and Instagram accounts that dissect their every outift. Think Emmanuelle Alt, the editor-in-chief of French Vogue who sits on the front row at Paris Fashion Week in louche men’s shirts tucked into cropped skinny jeans, with a flash of (always tanned) bare ankle and kitten heels. Then there’s Caroline de Maigret, the 40-year-old Chanel muse and model who is known for her dishevelled hair, biker jackets and nonchalant ways with layering. Top, £199, Sandro Our fascination with the way French women can put a look together has turned into serious business, too. Inès de la Fressange, the chic 58-year-old aristocrat, model and author of Parisian Chic: a Style Guide, and Carine Roitfeld, formerly at French Vogue and with an empire that now includes her own magazine, CR Fashion Book, and a position as global fashion director for Harper’s Bazaar, have both been enlisted by Uniqlo to design collections that bring Gallic style to the global masses. A handful of labels have also imported the exclusive feel of a Parisian boutique and the appeal of timelessly chic clothes to the British high street – helping us to capture that je ne sais quoi for ourselves without forking out for the Eurostar. Dress, £280, Sandro  The headliner among these labels is Sandro, which was started by Evelyne Chétrite and her husband Didier in 1984. For years, their business was wholesale only, but in 2004 the first Sandro store opened in Paris with the aim of bringing cool, luxurious but not ridiculously priced fashion to the market, filling a gap between designer names like Givenchy or Yves Saint Laurent and cheap high-street retailers. Just over 10 years later, its expansion has been exceptional. There are now 480 points of sale worldwide, with 25 in the UK, including 12 stand-alone stores. Last year, SMCP (which comprises Sandro plus sister brands Maje and Claudie Pierlot) reported a 32 per cent rise in sales to €316 million (about £244 million) – enviable numbers for bosses at some of the UK’s struggling high-street retailers. Polo top, £155, Sandro  At the company’s headquarters, situated on the Rue de Turenne in the heart of Paris’s cool Le Marais district, Evelyne is relaxed about the rise and rise of Sandro. It’s a miserable, rainy winter day, but she looks like she could be about to depart for a weekend in Deauville (the seaside destination once beloved of Coco Chanel, who is surely the godmother of the modern French look). Slight and reserved, she’s wearing a striped navy and cream jumper with wide-legged navy sailor trousers and bright white trainers, which, it turns out, are part of her vast Nike Air Max collection. ‘I have so many sneakers!’ she laughs. Jacket, £420, Sandro ‘We didn’t set out to create a brand that was all about French style,’ says Evelyne, now in her 50s, of Sandro’s early days. When she and Didier met, her family were encouraging her to study law. In fact, until the age of 15 she had lived in Rabat, Morocco, and believes that the shock of moving from a small, relatively poor place to the bright lights of Paris enhanced her appreciation of style. ‘When you come from a small town, you absorb culture faster than when you grow up in a big city because you’re more hungry for it,’ she says. Soon she abandoned her studies to join Didier in business. Her instinctive nous for styling paired with his business acumen proved to be a formidable partnership. Coat, £389, Sandro For Evelyne, Paris itself – the architecture, the culture and the way of life – is the biggest influence on the style of the women who live there. It’s not necessarily an essence you’re born with, but ‘a magic that just flows over you’. And one that can’t be taken for granted. To demonstrate, she tells me about a recent text conversation with her daughter who has been studying in New York. She was sending Evelyne links to some clothes she liked and wanted her mum’s opinion. ‘I was surprised because it was all so… American,’ she says, slightly aghast. ‘I told her she really couldn’t buy these things because they are not right, they’re not French.’ Her daughter has clearly been away from the Paris magic for too long. Jacket, £345, Sandro Despite the cool élan of Sandro’s clothes, stores and imagery, there’s still a close-knit family set-up behind the operation. Didier is no longer involved in the business, but after my interview with Evelyne, he’s waiting to meet her at the office. Meanwhile, their son, Ilan, designs the equally successful menswear line, which he launched in 2008, and which has become renowned for cool yet wearable modern classics. Evelyne’s sister, Judith Milgrom, worked at Sandro before launching Maje in 1998, where the aesthetic is less slick and more ‘bobo’ (that’s ‘bourgeois-bohème’). There have been rumours of disagreements between the two sisters, but Sandro’s PR insists that they’re ‘like that’ (crossing her middle finger over the index finger). Weekends are family time, when Evelyne will cook a big Moroccan, Italian or French lunch for everyone – ‘I am the queen of pasta,’ she smiles. From neat leather jackets to tailored culottes, Sandro’s success is also being driven by beautiful cuts and great fabrics that nod to trends but don’t succumb to them. That might seem like an obvious asset when prices can edge up to £800 (although £200 to £400 is the norm), but it’s not necessarily always the way in the ‘affordable luxury’ category. ‘Women notice the love and attention that goes into their clothes,’ says Evelyne. ‘When we first started, I was thinking like a tailor about how each dress would fit each customer,’ she remembers. ‘We still think that way even though we are dressing thousands of people.’ Boots, £315, Sandro In her personal style, Evelyne has that quintessentially Parisian mix of nonchalance and elegance in spades. Her face is bare of make-up apart from kohled eyes and ‘sometimes a little blush’, but her conker-brown mane of hair is bouncily blow-dried.  She ‘adores Pilates’ but stopped doing it for a while and has just started again. She’s used the same Dior Capture Totale skincare range for a few years now. ‘I love sleeping so I can’t afford to take an hour getting ready in the morning,’ she laughs. ‘It’s really about enjoying your life rather than wasting time deciding what to wear.’ THE FIVE RULES OF FRENCH CHIC 1. ‘Never overdress. I would almost never wear stilettos.’ 2. Keep it simple: ‘You should always be cool and modern, but not super-styled, just simple and not too much effort.’ 3. ‘Every woman needs a great jacket, a cashmere jumper and a good shirt or blouse.’ 4. When it comes to trousers, ‘wide legs are always chic’, while ‘skinny pants are rock’n’ roll, and perfect if you’re young, but they look great with a big jumper at any age. You have to work the shape you were born with.’ 5. For an evening look with more Parisian spirit, Evelyne suggests swapping a little black dress for a little lace dress – a current obsession of hers. ‘The lace is very important right now because you can dress it up or down,’ she advises. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Kate Moss is nothing if not game for a laugh, as she proved yesterday on the set of the upcoming Absolutely Fabulous: The Movie. The supermodel was spotted emerging from the murky depths of the Thames wearing a green sequined evening gown with a Champagne glass in hand and a soggy cigarette hanging from her mouth. We can be sure it wasn’t just the aftermath of one of Moss’s legendary nights out as a film crew was present. She was then seen walking along the pebbled riverside arm-in-arm with French fashion designer Jean Paul Gaultier, who was seen carrying a metal detector. Singer Lulu and actress Jane Horrocks, who plays main character Edina Monsoon’s dippy assistant Bubble, were also seen splashing about in the water as they filmed scenes for the big screen adaptation of the comedy favourite. The synopsis for the film, written by Jennifer Saunders, currently explains: Edina and Patsy are still oozing glitz and glamour, living the high life they are accustomed to; shopping, drinking and clubbing their way around London's trendiest hot-spots. Blamed for a major incident at an uber fashionable launch party, they become entangled in a media storm and are relentlessly pursued by the paparazzi. Fleeing penniless to the glamorous playground of the super-rich, the French Riviera, they hatch a plan to make their escape permanent and live the high life forever more! Other pictures from the  set this week showed lead characters Edina and Patsy, played by Saunders and Joanna Lumley, visiting an elaborate riverside shrine to Moss, suggesting that she meets a grisly, water-drenched end in the comedy – likely the ‘major incident’ described above. It’s the second time Moss has appeared in Absolutely Fabulous; she starred as herself in the 2012 Sport Relief special alongside Stella McCartney and model David Gandy. She’s set to be joined in the big screen version by fellow celebs Kim Kardashian and Emma Bunton. The film is due for release next year. Moss is currently fending off rumours that her four-year marriage to The Kills front man Jamie Hince is over. Until now, she has been continuing to wear her wedding ring, though it appeared to be absent on the set of Ab Fab.  You've got to feel for Anne Hathaway and her fellow pregnant Oscar attendees Emily Blunt, Chrissy Teigen and Hannah Bagshawe, Eddie Redmayne's wife. Not only did they have to face the idea of a five-hour Oscar ceremony and then a night of partying without champagne, but a red carpet dress code isn't exactly the easiest thing to pull off when you're pregnant.    Here's how they defied 'maternity wear' in favour of impeccably chic evening gowns at last night's Oscars - and provided inspiration for women with sore, swollen feet but a dress code to live up to.  Note how the jagged gold halterneck on Hannah Bagshawe’s Alexander McQueen gown immediately draws the eye to her chest. Black might seem uninspiring, but when it's a McQueen gown - and one punctuated with dazzling metallic details - it becomes a considered choice. (NB: The gold symmetry between clutch and neckline isn’t coincidence, you know). Expectant mother Anne Hathaway also ran with a black-and-gold colour scheme. Her Naeem Khan dress featured a strapless a black column dress encased in a gold sequined, sleeved overlay. A blooming mass of embellishment, the eyeline eventually settles on her bare décolletage underneath all that high-shine. While Hathaway and Bagshawe enjoyed a looser silhouette, Chrissy Teigen was the poster girl for framing one’s curves. Wearing a nude Marchesa gown covered with beaded burgundy florals and vines, the sheer panels faded into the model’s dewy skin tone. And for that, we salute her.  Emily Blunt's custom-made Prada gown featured delicate silver beading up the torso and straps, but all eyes were on the back, with its glacial train.  It’s ten years today since fashion maverick Isabella Blow passed away, but the impact of both her work and her character are still felt in the industry now. The mother of all future street style peacocks, she was an original, vivid dresser with a penchant for statement hats - and someone who hated the word eccentric. As a fashion editor at Vogue and Tatler, her creative, entertaining work is still referenced by stylists and designers today. On the constant search for new talents- be they models, milliners, or fashion designers- she discovered names like Alexander McQueen and Philip Treacy, as well as models Sophie Dahl and Stella Tennant, describing herself as ‘a pig sniffing out truffles’, when it came to spotting the next big thing and helping them build lasting careers. Here we remember her unique character…  “My career wouldn’t have happened without Isabella Blow,” shares Stella Tennant, the model who has now worked in the industry for over 20 years, working with brands including Chanel and Vogue. “The whole thing started with her putting me in a shoot for British Vogue with photographer Steven Meisel [in 1993]. Joe McKenna styled it, Lee [Alexander] McQueen turned up with a bin liner full of clothes in that he’d whipped up on the kitchen table with a sewing machine and some Copydex the night before. And she was the one bringing all of that talent together. I didn’t know how exceptional it was at the time.”  “Her style was outrageous and fearless, but she had the rare ability to carry it off,” says Tennant. “Her character was absolutely big enough to wear what she wore. I’ll never forget in one of my first seasons [of doing runway shows] I was staying at the Principe in Milan and she came down to breakfast in a transparent black lace dress, Philip Treacy hat and some absolute f*ck off Manolo Blahnik heels, with lots of red lipstick on. It was 8am and she was ready. It made my day.”  Blow became a muse for her protege Philip Treacy, and rarely left the house without a suitably outre headpiece. Some of her most memorable millinery included hats with castles and ships on top, as well as a now-iconic Blow headband. “She understood hats. She loved them,” Treacy remembers. “She was unlike anyone else - a flamboyant dresser and she loved hats. I made so many for her and she wore them all the time, yet treated them terribly. She sat on them, lost them or her dogs chewed them, but she inspired me to make amazing things for her.”  “Everyone who worked in fashion in the Nineties and Noughties has an anecdote about Isabella Blow,” The Telegraph’s Lisa Armstrong wrote in 2013. “Mine is about the time we were both working on a story about a new designer called Bella Freud for British Vogue. Izzie was styling, I was writing. Our editor, Alexandra Shulman, had decreed a naturalistic shoot, "almost reportage-y - the models should be sitting around chatting," instructed Alexandra in her clearest, don't mess-with-me terms. When I turned up to do the interview, Izzie had gone to town with a pot of white clay... They were meant to be statues. There weren't any clothes either.  The famous dress worn by Marilyn Monroe when she sang "happy birthday Mr President" to John F. Kennedy has sold for a world-record price at auction, fetching $4.8 million (£3.87 million). One of the defining dresses of 20th century fashion, the sheer tulle design, scattered with tiny, glimmering crystals, was worn by Monroe on 19th May 1962 as she performed for President Kennedy ahead of his 40th birthday. It was an instant sensation and paved the way for 'naked' dresses, which still spark a furore when worn by the likes of Kim Kardashian and Beyoncé today.  It was bought by Ripley's Believe It Or Not Museum for a total surpassing the previous most expensive dress sold at auction, Monroe's white dress from The Seven Year Itch which went for $4.6 million (£3.7 million) in 2011. Edward Meyer, vice president of Ripley's Believe It Or Not, told the Press Association: "We believe this is the most iconic piece of pop culture that there is. "In the 20th century I cannot think of one single item that tells the story of the 1960s as well as this. It's a new world record for a dress." The auction had long been planned as part of the year that would have seen Monroe celebrating her 90th birthday but this dress was a "last minute addition" from a collector in New York who initially purchased the gown at Christie's historic Monroe auction in 1999 for $1.26 million.  "It's the most historic, important piece of Marilyn Monroe that could ever be offered - it's like the Holy Grail," Darren Julien, President and CEO of Julien's Auctions, tells The Telegraph. "Since then Monroe prices have skyrocketed, so in my opinion our estimate of $2-3 million is actually quite low," Julien said before the auction. "You never know at the end of a day with an auction. You could put  this on display in a museum and people would flock to see it which is what has happened here. "We've had more than 2000 visitors a day wanting to see the dress since it's been on display in our gallery here for the past few days." Julien believes that out of all the Marilyn memorabilia, this dress has particular resonance. "The dress is part of our political history but it's also Hollywood, glamour, fashion. The dress is a work of art in its own right," he explains. "When she walked out onto the stage and took off her fur coat, everyone thought that she was naked and you can hear the gasps in the audience," he laughs. "Marilyn called it 'skin and beans' - she wanted the shock factor and was ahead of her time." The dress cost $12,000 when it was designed by Bob Mackie, who was working at the time in Academy-award winning costume designer Jean Louis's atelier. But whilst it still the dress has added poignancy because it was worn for one of the last public appearances Monroe made before her death in August 1962, it also represents the very beginnings of Bob Mackie's career. "Bob was just  21 years old when he drew the sketch for the dress for  Jean Louis, it was his first job out of college," says Julien of the designer who went on to create dazzling looks for the likes of Cher, Grace Jones, Kylie Minogue and Madonna. "Bob is here in LA for the auction. He is part of its history too, which lots of people are surprised to hear." As well as the 'Happy Birthday' dress, the auction also saw the beaded cocktail dress which Monroe donned in 'Some Like It Hot' go under the hammer, with a buyer snapping it up for $375,000 (£302,000). The delicate black design was said to be so tight that the star had to be lifted on and off the piano which she sat on to perform during filming. "It's one of the most important dresses of her career," emphasises Julien.  Other lots included a 1947 Revlon lipstick with smudges around the rim that was discovered in a secret compartment of one of Monroe's evening bags and some of her favourite costume jewellery pieces. “She actually had very few fine jewellery pieces of her own. For her it was all about the costume jewellery, but obviously when she wore it, it had that wow factor,” Martin Nolan, executive director of Julien's told The Telegraph earlier this year.  A whole section of the auction comes from the personal collection of Lee Strasberg, the Hollywood actor and Marilyn’s acting teacher, who along with his wife Paula, was Monroe’s closest confidante and was left all of her personal effects in her will. "These are items that have never before been seen by the public and which were in Marilyn's possession when she passed away. I think it's really interesting for people to see these items for the first time. It's like they're buying them from Marilyn," says Julien.        © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Christmas at Harrods is serious business. Over 12,000 lights adorn the store over the festive period - 300 of which blow everyday and have to be replaced. But it’s not just lighting that needs constant attention at the iconic store - 100,000 shoppers pass through their doors every day in December. And the peak of frenzy comes on Boxing Day. Over the years, the Harrods legendary Boxing Day sale has featured live reindeers, a garden party and a live performance by Florence Welch. This year the full cast of Elf the Musical are performing. But what’s it like to man the door on the busiest shopping day of the year? ‘Cold,’ laughs Danny Suarez, 57, who has worked at Harrods for over 15 years. ‘But memorable. Where else would you see actual reindeers walking through the door?’ For the past eight years Danny has served as one of the luxury department store’s seven Green Men, who man the doors of the iconic boutique - and, crucially, are in charge of keeping shoppers calm during the sales. When Danny gets to work at 8am to make sure the store is ready for the 10am opening on Boxing Day, he’ll be greeted by some hardcore Harrods fans. ‘Some will have queued for two to three days before,’ he says. ‘They leave their sleeping bags to grab some food, but yes, keenest shoppers are sitting there throughout Christmas Day. The rest start turning up at 2am on Boxing Day morning.’ Many of the Harrods sales shoppers are those who have faithfully returned year in year out, so have perfected their skills. ‘You’ll see people pick a specific door as they know the department they want and the quickest route to get there,’ reveals Danny. Want some of those tips? ‘Door 5 is where the magic happens - the countdown or the parade.. Door 7 is for handbags.’ Danny Suarez escorts singer Florence Welch ahead of the Harrods sale in 2011 ‘There's banter from customers, saying “Can you let me in?”. But no-one gets too pushy,’ Danny says. And no one gets past him until those doors officially open. ‘So far this year I've had two bottles of champagne and an artist couple based in Covent Garden did me a painting of a Green Man,’ Danny says. ‘I get a lot of cards too, and chocolates - people must think we need feeding up.’ But don’t be mistaken into thinking these gifts get you early access to the sales. Even for his favourite customers… ‘A lot of the shoppers we see we are on first-name terms with,’ says Danny. ‘Although, personally, I don’t use their first name. Especially if it’s a lady – I call them ‘young lady’.’ Well, this is Harrods we’re talking about. Sale customers get given Harrods blankets to keep out the cold OK, not exactly news there. But one of the things that most entertains shoppers in the sale queue is taking snaps of the Green Men and their famous uniform. ‘What's the thing with young people having the camera at an angle?’ Danny laughs. ‘I probably get asked about 20-30 times a day. It’s got that knock-on effect… Once someone stops to ask, someone else behind them does the same and that’s how it goes. Sometimes my cheeks ache so much because I haven’t stopped laughing.’ ‘If the temperature gets cold I put another vest on and accept a hug,’ Danny says. But the thing that really keeps him warm on sale day? ‘I might have a full English breakfast up in the staff food hall beforehand.’ But working there is handy for Christmas presents. In fact, Danny’s friends and family practically expect he’ll get them something from the store. ‘That’s fair enough. It’s the thought of not just the gift itself, but that it’s coming in that Harrods green bag.I buy a lot of teddy bears - everyone loves a Harrods teddy bear. And now they do a Green Man one, too.’ But sadly those aren’t in the sale…   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  For her last evening in Bhutan, the Duchess of Cambridge has turned to Beulah London, a label set up by one of her close friends, for one final flashbulb creating evening gown. And, true to style so far on the royal tour, she's using her frock choice to flatter her host nation: wearing a red gown covered in Bhutan's national flower, the poppy.  "That dress was from our Spring Summer 2015 collection, and you can pre-order it again because we only did a limited amount last season," Beulah's co-founder Lady Natasha Rufus Isaacs tells The Telegraph of Kate's dress. "It is one of our classic styles with billowed sleeves and pleats down the front and back, and is in a print that we are known for." Lady Natasha is an old friend of William and Kate's and is married to Rupert Finch, a former boyfriend of the Duchess of Cambridge. Kate has worn Beulah on numerous royal tours, including in Kuala Lumpur and New York, and Lady Natasha says this has understandably had a significant impact on their label. "It's wonderful that she's worn this dress, and worn our dresses before. She's a brilliant ambassador and it's great exposure for us on a global scale. A lot of people go on our site straight after she wears a dress."  It is fitting that the Duchess chose to wear this dress on her royal tour of India and Bhutan, not only because the print incorporates the national flower of Bhutan, but because Lady Natasha Rufus Issacs and Lavinia Brennan, started the brand in India.  "Lavinia and I spent two months working in Delhi with women who had been trafficked," Lady Natasha says of how India is at the heart of their company. "We decided to work in an aftercare home about six, seven years ago, and during the afternoons we worked with the women in a production unit teaching them very basic skills. It was there we witnessed the power of employment that can change people's lives and get them out of poverty, and breaks the cycle of crime." The Kensington-based label this month raised £500,000 in investment, which will see Beulah expand its product offerings. "Currently we sell evening and cocktail dresses," Lady Natasha tells The Telegraph. "But we want to sell a wider range of day wear, such as silk shirts, blouses and separates, and a wider offering of accessories, as well as expanding those products with a social impact." This expansion will benefit their Indian employees. "For Spring Summer, women in Calcutta will be block printing onto the silk of some key pieces of the collection. We set up the label because we saw such power in creating employment opportunities for the women, so we decided we would set up a dress brand in 2011." The Duchess paired her boots with an £89 white linen shirt from Jaeger, her khaki Zara jeans and a khaki leather shooting waistcoat by Really Wild, which is still available for £495.  Keen fashion observers spotted that Kate had first been seen in the boots when she paired them with a tweed country skirt and matching coat for a shoot outside of Blenheim Palace in 2004 - one of the first public photographs of the now Duchess.  “I am delighted to see Kate in the first boots we made for her, over ten years ago,” the footwear designer Chilvers told The Telegraph. “She looks fabulous in them; and the boots look better with age. Penelope Chilvers’ footwear is designed for travel and adventure, so it makes me very happy to see them being worn as they should be as her oldest and dearest wardrobe staples.”  It took the couple three hours to hike up the 11,000 ft cliff to Tiger's Nest, and the Duchess joked that “it’s a great way to burn off the curry.” It's perhaps surprising given the difficult climb and the heat, that the Duchess chose to wear knee-high boots rather than hiking shoes such as the £106 Hillmaster boots she wore when she visited Borneo's jungle, but Chilvers says that her boots are designed for adventures.
