 Belgian fashion designer Raf Simons is departing from the French fashion house Christian Dior after three-and-a-half years at the helm. WWD is reporting that the 47-year-old is leaving the brand “for personal reasons” and that Simons and the storied French fashion house are parting ways amicably.
 The 47-year-old, previously at German fashion house Jil Sander, filled the creative void left after the dismissal of John Galliano, who headed up the label for 15 years. Simons was credited with steering the luxury brand in a more modernist direction and introducing cult items, such as bejewelled sneakers.
 The designer and the brand failed to reach an agreement on a new contract and released the following statement of explanation: “It is after careful and long consideration that I have decided to leave my position as creative director of Christian Dior's women’s collection. It is a decision based entirely and equally on my desire to focus on other interests in my life, including my own brand, and the passions that drive me outside my work. Christian Dior is an extraordinary company, and it has been an immense privilege to write a few pages of this magnificent book. I want to thank Mr. Bernard Arnault for the trust he has put in me, giving me the incredible opportunity to work at this beautiful house surrounded by the most amazing team one could ever dream of. I have also had the chance over the last few years to benefit from the leadership of Sidney Toledano. His thoughtful, heartfelt and inspired management will also remain as one of the most important experiences of my professional career.” Simons was not the most obvious shoo-in for the role after Galliano’s anti-Semitic rant in 2011, which was captured on camera and saw the latter convicted of public insult and quickly lose his job. But Simons' debut, which marked his first ever foray into haute couture, was conceived within just eight weeks of signing his contract and deemed triumphant. It conveyed a subtle nod towards the signatures of the Dior archives and a confident steer away from the flamboyant style of his predecessor. Simons’ first few weeks at the company were the subject of a moving documentary, Dior & I, which laid bare the language barrier between the Belgian and Dior’s French atelier staff; his unconventional way of designing (Simons doesn’t sketch, instead he creates a moodboard for the design team to interpret and draw from) and his first catwalk show, for which hundreds of thousands of fresh flowers were brought in to deck the walls at huge expense. His last ever show was staged earlier this month for spring/summer 2016 and involved a breath-taking pyramid structure of delphiniums within a courtyard of the Louvre museum. But Simons hasn’t just been a master of performance; Dior has enjoyed mounting revenues since his appointment, reporting a 34 per cent rise in profits - to£77 million - this past quarter. Simons started out with his own menswear label in 1995 after studying Industrial Design and Furniture Design at a college in Genk. He was appointed creative director of Jil Sander in 2005 and has continued to juggle menswear collaborations with sportswear brands such as Fred Perry, Adidas and Eastpak. His successor has yet to be announced.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  “I really don’t think we should talk about ageing.” We’re twenty minutes into an otherwise amiable chat, but it seems I have inadvertently pushed one of Helena Christensen’s trigger buttons. Famously one of the most mild-mannered and easy going of the ‘Magnificent Seven’ – a term coined by a New York Times op-ed twenty years ago when she, Linda Evangelista, Christy Turlington, Cindy Crawford, Naomi Campbell, Elle Macpherson and Claudia Schiffer were ruling the catwalk  – Christensen has gone from expansive and jokey to crossing her arms and pursing her lips. She looks both very beautiful and very intimidating, but I push on: because? “Because this is something only women ever have to deal with, not men. Why do men never ever get asked about ageing?” I’m thinking it’s because a certain kind of man would simply shrug and say that they’re maturing like a fine Burgundy, making more money than ever and enjoying late-in-life fatherhood with the 22 year-old lingerie model they’ll trade in some time next year. But this isn’t the moment to be flippant, and in any case the 47 year-old doesn’t seem to expect an answer. If women weren’t reading about the constant pressure of ageing,” she goes on, “it might not be in their heads. And I don’t want any woman to feel that there are any limits imposed by age.” I may have raised her heckles, but Christensen will always remain my favourite supermodel, and this eloquent little eruption – in the midst of calm Danish waters – only makes me like her more. She’s as glorious to look at as ever, a few laughter lines around the eyes, but as hard-bodied as her twenty-something self in a white bustier & Other Stories dress most teenagers would find hard to pull off. I forgive her for her tetchiness around the A word, because she is, after all, at the end of a long day promoting the ‘boyfriend shirts’ she and her business partner Camilla Staerk have designed for Thomson’s five-star Sensatori spa resorts. I even concede that she has a point. We are obsessed with how women age today. Whether this is by nature or media nurture, women are interested in both the process and the implications of ageing. They (and I include myself here) look at someone like Christensen – who doesn’t appear to have had any work done and they want to know their secrets, their ruses, their rules. “Why would there be any rules at all?” she asks, smiling and serene once again. “It’s all about keeping healthy and staying true to yourself and your style. I mean you could be a very unfit 20 year-old and look really dumb in a mini dress, or you could be a super sexy 60 year-old and look great in one. Anyone can wear whatever they want to.”  Even when she was in the thrust of the supermodel madness and writhing around on a beach in the video of Chris Isaak’s Wicked Game, the daughter of a Danish typographer and a Peruvian vintage boutique owner has maintained a detached stance to fashion, celebrity – and tabloid drama. Brought up in suburban Copenhagen, Christensen came to modelling relatively late (having won herself the Miss Denmark title at 18) and with a relaxed, hippy-chick attitude. She eats far more cheese than is decent for any woman with that figure (“but thank goodness journalists have stopped bringing me really smelly ones as gifts”) and has often stated that she “hated the ‘supermodel’ branding.” Her only brush with scandal came at the end of a four-year liaison with Michael Hutchence (when it was wrongly suggested that the singer left her for Paula Yates), and since then she has had a child – 16 year-old Mingus – with American actor Norman Reedus, swapped the catwalk for photography and design, and is now happily ensconced in Manhattan with Interpol singer Paul Banks – as ever living life on her own terms. She describes her current professional balance as being “40% modelling, 40% photography and 20% all kinds of strange, interesting, weird stuff,” and unlike some members of the ‘Magnificent Seven’ her collaborations always have a genuine rather than a ‘big bucks’ feel to them. Which is presumably why after all these decades spent in hotel rooms remains a travelaholic – she has been chosen to design for and spearhead this latest fashion campaign (each of the designs are inspired by a different Caribbean destination). “When I go away I’m so low key that I only bring hand luggage, because the whole airport thing is so frustrating,” she sighs. “So we really wanted to design a shirt with a very casual, loose and deconstructed fit that could double up as a mini dress with a belt and take you from day into night. Because sometimes I’ll get some place and realise I’ve brought too little,” she laughs. “I always run out of underwear, for example, so I’m forever washing it. I’ll literally go on a three-day trip and only bring one pair of underwear. Then I’ll think: ‘what are you going to do now - turn them over or what?’ And by the way,” she she’s quick to point out: “I’ve never done that.” Another – almost equally unpalatable – thing Christensen won’t do is flog herself or her wares on social media. Her instagram account is only two months old and not massively active (“I only caved in because of peer pressure from friends” she quickly explains) and that’s as far as she’ll go in the cyber-sphere. “I’ve always said: ‘whatever’,” she shrugs. “I mean now that I’m on instagram I can see the allure, but there’s something about judging yourself on how many followers you have that could put you in a constant state of anxiety. I would be unable to sleep if I had as many followers as Kim [Kardashian]. It just doesn’t seem natural.” Given how well the likes of the new generation of models, such as Cara Delevigne, Kendall Jenner and Karlie Kloss have utilised social media to increase their profiles, does she never wish she had had access to such a tool when she was starting out? “Oh honestly I feel so grateful that social media wasn’t there before,” she assures me. “I was very happy with just being an elusive, mysterious figure that just appeared in photo shoots. ‘I feel like a lot of my character hopefully came through in the pictures. Because from the start I felt that modelling is like acting in a silent movie – and that was enough for me. I never had the desire to let the world know about the rest of my personality. Just being who I was, am, has always been enough for me.” And although it’s probably easier to be at one with yourself when you’re Helena Christensen, I think to myself as we air-kiss goodbye – all earlier awkwardness forgotten – if banishing all thought of ageing gets you even a sprinkling of her zen, it might be worth a try.  51-year-old co-founder of ethical campaign Fashion Revolution, Carry Somers, is brimming with good ideas to avoid unnecessary purchases, but that doesn't mean she can't invest in pieces she loves. ''Always ask the question: who made my clothes?'' she says. ''Transparency if one of the key issues that we’re addressing, because you can’t begin to tackle environmental exploitation unless you know where your clothes are from.'' And according to Somers, it's not as challenging as you might think to get brands to open up about their production processes.  ''I’m currently sifting through an avalanche of new brands who are starting to publish their factory list, which is really fantastic to see,'' she continues, referring to under-the-radar shoe brand Chie Mihara as one of the labels who were particularly helpful when she queried them via social media about where their shoes are made.  ​Leather shoes, £235​, Chie Mihara; Katie Jones crochet jumper, £995, Selfridges; double-pleat skirt, £89, COS And it's not just little-known brands adhering to demands for accountability. High street giants and well-known designers are also on board. ''I was trying to buy some trainers in Selfridges the other day and the shop assistant produced the Ethical Consumer guide,'' Somers recounts, also naming Rank a Brand and Project Just as very useful when it comes to trying to decipher how sustainable a company is.  As well has doing research Somers has myriad other tricks up her sleeve to help limit her intake of fast fashion, one of the easiest of which is a simple swap. ''I share a lot of clothes with my daughter who’s the same size as me,'' she continues. ''Often I will buy a piece and then she’ll take it to university for a term and then when it comes back to me I fall in love with it all over again.''  Other initiatives adbocated by Fashion Revolution as part of their #Haulternative which encourages refreshing your wardrobe without having to buy new clothes, include hiring clothes, mending pieces, upcycling and even writing a love story to a bits of clothing that mean a lot to you. ''If you invest in something it encourages you to look after it'' says Somers.   Somers also recommends buying vintage, citing both vintage fairs around her home county of Derbyshire and Clerkenwell Vintage Fair in London as treasure troves full of fabulous pre-owned pieces. One of the most eye opening statistics to emerge on the topic of sustainable fashion is that the average piece of clothing in our wardrobes is worn just four times. ''It's really shocking,'' continues Somers. ''I think we forget what we already have, but we should be thinking about how we can work with what's already in our wardrobes and how we cn wear it differently.''  Carry's diverse lifestyle can throw up some some sartorial challenges. ''I was recently speaking in Dublin where it was was cold and wet, and then I had to go straight to Lisbon Fashion Week to sit on a panel full of glamorous people, and I only had hand luggage,'' she says, revealing that her saving grace was her trusty Alexander McQueen dress. ''It goes everywhere with me,'' she says, ''you can just screw it up and take it out again and it still looks amazing - a printed dress is so useful,'' she continues. ''I wore it with some gold heels in Lisbon and then it was fine with some thick tights and boots in Dublin.'' When she's not speaking around the world, Somers is at home in Staffordshire where she resides in Pringle of Scotland dresses and Hunter rain gear: ''A lot of the time I’m working from home, so i’ll be wearing comfortable clothes and something I can climb a five bar gate in follow our new puppy around''. As the founder of sustainable hat brand Pachacuti, if Somers travels anywhere where the sun is shining she looks to a Panama hat top off her outfit. ''Anita Roddick said the best anti-ageing product you can buy is a sun hat, and it’s true,'' she says, citing a pair of gold earrings she got in a house clearance in Hollywood as another one of her fail-safe accessories.   Fashion Revolution Week is 24th-30th April. #whomademyclothes © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Less than seven days ago the Duchess of Sussex turned heads when she arrived at the Victoria Palace Theatre to see a charity performance of Hamilton wearing a short black tuxedo dress by Canadian label Judith & Charles. Gone were the nude tights, the ivory dresses and the perfectly-coiffed waves of late. In their place? Slick court heels, a sharp blazer dress and a nonchalant messy bun.   It was a striking about-turn from the Duchess’s usual fashion formula and harked back to her days as Meghan Markle, Suits actress. Tailoring, mini hemlines and all-black looks were staples in her old wardrobe, and fans of the look, (and those of us who have been secretly hoping she'd up the fashion ante,) will likely be pleased with her latest offering.   The WellChild Awards took place at the Royal Lancaster in London this evening, with the Duke and Duchess attending as guests of honour. The occasion celebrates seriously-ill and inspirational young people and children as young as four years old, and nominations for each of the categories have been open since April.  Meghan continued her slick tailoring theme in a black trouser suit by Altuzarra, which featured flared trousers and a fitted blazer, worn over a silky blouse by Scandinavian label Deitas. It seems the Duchess is following a theme for the new season, and there are four style takeaways we can learn from her swift about-turn...  Over the summer, Meghan showcased a seemingly-endless host of sweet ivory-hued dresses, from a Carolina Herrera number for Trooping The Colour, to a Givenchy shirt dress for Royal Ascot. It's rumoured that the Queen prefers royal women in skirts and dresses, rather than trousers, but the new Duchess, who has so far abided by the unofficial royal style rules sporting flesh-toned tights and below-the-knee hems, took a fashion leap today in a powerful trouser suit. While a bright dress by a new designer may have stolen the show, Meghan ensured all attention was on the young stars being celebrated, opting for a simple, minimal look.  In today's sleek ensemble, Meghan put a stop to any rumours that trouser suits were out of the question for the new Duchess.  The New Zealand-born fashion designer shares the things she'd rather not live without. What’s your definition of luxury? For me, luxury is no longer about how rare your handbag is, how big your yacht is or how hand-made your watch is. It’s about how special you’ve been made to feel. This can be created by the smallest, simplest of things: having your name remembered, being offered a cup of tea, being given time. The times I feel true luxury are when I’m made to feel special and valued.     What are you wearing? I wear my own designs 90 per cent of the time but I like to have sitting alongside them functional and beautifully crafted pieces that are the best examples of their kind, for instance, my Burberry trench coat, my Saint James Breton, my Hermès Carrés silk scarves.   On your feet?  Churches do the best brogues in the world.   Other little luxuries? I fly 250,000km a year and so a few years ago I treated myself to a Louis Vuitton rolling travel bag. No matter where you sit on the plane, travel is draining and it does make you feel better when you have beautifully designed objects to help you on the journey.   Beauty indulgence? Everything by Osmosis Skincare on my skin and Karen Walker Runaway (our latest eau de parfum) on my wrist.   Favourite piece of jewellery? I recently inherited my great-grandmother’s gold pocket watch which I wear on a chain around my neck and it’s my “what would I save if the house was on fire” piece.   On your wrist? I’ve had an Omega Speedmaster Moonwatch for 15 years and I love it.   Dream home? The perfect location for a home would be a cliff top at Te Henga (Bethells Beach) on Auckland's west coast.    Dream drive? I’ve been driving the Lexus RX hybrid for 10 years and can’t think of a better car. Plus, for around town or on fine days, I love my Kalkhoff electric bike.   Private jet or yacht? My city [Auckland] is situated on one of the most perfect harbours in the world - the Waitematā. I don’t get to sail on it very often but when I do, I reminded what a joy and a privilege it is to have this beautiful body of water three minutes from my home.  Sight for sore eyes? Rangitoto and the Hauraki Gulf as viewed from Thorne Bay in Auckland.   Artwork you covet? On First Looking into Chapman’s Homer by Michael Parekowhai. Favourite piece you own? I’m a huge fan of Lee Miller’s photography and writing and I was lucky enough recently to spend the day at Farley Farms in Sussex  where she lived for many years. I have one of her photographs in my collection, of her and Picasso, and, after visiting her home it’s even more special to me than ever.   Collector's item? The paintings of Charles Frederick Goldie.   Ultimate dinner? I would choose Yotam Ottolenghi to make his pearl barley risotto with watercress, asparagus and pecorino. What are you drinking? Two Sisters 2009 Pinot Noir.   Home from home? The Upper House in Hong Kong because the service is the best I’ve ever had, the lighting’s just right and they have yoga in the garden. Also, La Colombe d’Or in the South of France because what’s not to love about staying in a perfect wee inn filled with your favourite artists? Ultimate escape?   A week at Dolphin Island in Fiji.   Design classic you covet?  A Man Ray chess set.   Necessary luxury?  The occasional moment of solitude.   What single thing would make your existence more luxurious?  A month without anyone emailing me.  karenwalker.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Grand and Jenner’s partnerships have been frequent and fruitful since they first met in 2013. Jenner has since gone on to work with brands from Chanel to Estee Lauder, building a modelling career worth millions. On the latter assignment, the duo encouraged fans to apply via social media to be featured, and of the 110,000 applicants, they selected 25 to be photographed by Kendall in Los Angeles last November. "Kendall had come to London for the LOVE 17 launch as she'd photographed the cover stars, and Rankin hadn't shot with her before, and had really wanted to make this video with her,” LOVE editor Katie Grand explained of how the film came to be. “She had the time so we just did it.  It was a super fun day as ever with Kendall."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Just a week after she made her catwalk debut in Kanye West’s New York show, hijab-wearing model Halima Aden is now making waves at Milan Fashion Week. This morning, the 19 year-old  walked at the Max Mara show, while yesterday she appeared alongside supermodel Gigi Hadid at Alberta Ferretti. She tells The Telegraph that she feels “proud” of what she has achieved so far. In the past week,  the fashion industry has welcomed her with open arms, both on the catwalk and with the reveal of her first magazine cover, fronting former French Vogue editor Carine Roitfeld's CR Fashion Book. Roitfeld has become something of a mentor to Aden.  “I felt so powerful in the look that I wore on the runway,” she says of the buzz at Ferretti’s show yesterday. “Gigi is someone I look up to; I had the chance to meet her at the CR Fashion Book shoot and I was star struck.  She was so sweet to take a selfie with me and then she started following me on Instagram. I remember screaming when I saw that she was following me.” The breakthrough star of the season- a Somali-American who was born in a Kenyan refugee camp- was signed by IMG only a few months ago and has been making headlines as a young woman who insists that designers should represent women of all cultures on the catwalk, including those who want to wear modest dress. “Everyone was so welcoming and accepting,” Aden tells us of the reaction she’s received since appearing on Kanye West’s catwalk last week. “I have strict wardrobe requirements based on my religious and cultural upbringing. I haven't received any pressure to be anything other than myself and for that I am so grateful.” “I never knew that a woman wearing a hijab could be a model; it's so exciting,” she says of her goal to encourage more Muslim women and other young women to demand that they are all represented in fashion images. “I never grew up seeing women that looked like me in magazines or on TV and didn't feel like I had a place in the world of fashion. I am honoured to be part of that change.”   Timely, also, is that her first magazine cover is due to hit stands on 2nd March. Roitfeld reached out to Aden after she had seen her model in the Miss Minnesota USA pageant. Wearing a hijab throughout and a burkini during the swimsuit portion of the competition (rather than the usual tiny bikinis) Aden stood out as a young woman who was committed to her beliefs and willing to challenge industry ideals. “My first taste of modeling was the Miss Minnesota USA pageant in late November, not even three months ago,” Aden says. “It's because of that opportunity that so many doors have opened for me.” “Carine Roitfeld's team reached out to me and invited me to New York to shoot for her magazine. They had read about my story in the media and thought I would be a good fit for Issue 10 of the CR Fashion Book. It was my first photo shoot ever!” Having caught the attention of one of fashion’s most powerful stylists, Roitfeld then arranged for Aden to be interviewed by another fashion icon, supermodel Iman. The resulting pictures also show Aden to be a natural in front of photographer Mario Sorrenti’s lense. “I think Mario Sorrenti was shocked to learn at the end of the shoot, that I had never ever done a photo shoot before,” she tells us. “For me, being able to say that my first ever photo shoot was with one of the most legendary fashion photographers in the world is unbelievable.”   After the photoshoot Carine helped Aden to secure her future, encouraging agency IMG Models to sign the star and reportedly setting up the gig with Kanye.   “Carine has told me to continue to stay true to myself,” she says of her mentor’s top advice. “She and her team have become like family to me.” “People seem beyond thrilled that the industry is moving in a direction where beauty of all kinds is represented. The public reaction so far has been overwhelmingly positive.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  There's another supermodel name on the block to add to your Kendalls, Karlies, Gigis and Bellas. 20 year-old Taylor Hill has been modelling since she was 14 and has already amassed an impressive CV of catwalk appearences and campaigns, but her face is about to become much more familiar.  Topshop has cast the Colorado-native as the face of their Autumn collection which means that every time you click for a browse of the 'New In' section or wander into your local Toppers for a browse, it will be Taylor looking back at you for the next few months.  If you're not one of the 4.2 million people who follow Hill on Instagram, then you might not be immediately familiar with the brunette girl whose brows give Cara a run for her money, so allow us to fill you in.  She was discovered on a ranch- where else?- while taking riding lessons when she was just 14 by Jim Jordan, a fashion photographer and agent, who immediately spotted her model potential. Her catwalk debut came when she was 17, in September 2013 when she was cast to walk for the likes of Roksanda Ilincic and Ralph Lauren.  Taylor's career has been all about the slow burn, which is an excellent sign in these days of flash-in-a-pan model moments. A year after her catwalk debut, Victoria's Secret came calling and Hill, a former gymnast, appeared in their 2014 show. In 2015, Victoria's Secret awarded Hill her 'Angel' wings, meaning she joined the exclusive club of toned and tanned supers with the likes of Adriana Lima, Alessandra Ambrosio and Lily Aldridge in their midst.  Cleverly, Hill has kept up with the high fashion side of things too. Last fashion week she walked for Dolce and Gabbana, Fendi and Versace, among others and has also just scooped a spot in Miu Miu's Autumn/Winter ad campaign.  So why now for Hill?  "Taylor is Topshop’s ultimate girl crush" says Kate Phelan, the brand's creative director, “Taylor walked in the February 2016 UNIQUE show – she is a social supermodel and a young woman with style and personality; she is every Topshop girl rolled into one. Whether she is a tomboy in jeans, glamorous in cocktail, or pretty in polka dots." Hill has a sweet, good-girl vibe but can also pull off edginess (see the grungy look she sports in the Topshop pics and her occassional underwear-only Instagrams) which works well in today's all-seeing social media climes . She has said that in her downtime she loves nothing more that snowboarding in Colorado and she appears with her super cute labradoodle Tate in a 'Day in the Life' film for Topshop. Hill also gives good motivational speak: "I would say that anything is possible, because I didn't always think that I was beautiful and I didn't always believe in myself" she told Teen Vogue last year, "people have told me a million things in my life — and especially my career as a model, like, "Oh she's too pretty, she's too tan, she's too short, she's too tall, she's not skinny enough." — and it's crazy! You can't listen to any of it and you have to remember who you are, what you do, and what makes you happy. That's my message: happiness and positivity are such a huge thing for me."    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Film and fashion go together like Breton stripes and denim - two well-loved concepts that, married together, are more than the sum of their parts. They say clothes maketh the man, and it's certainly true that costumes maketh the character. After all, what would Sandy do without her skin-tight leather trousers to fall back on in Grease? More often than not, it's not the finer plot points but the on-screen outfits that linger in our memories - like these, still-iconic fashion moments in film.  Regularly topping polls of most iconic on-screen dresses, Knightley's smouldering impact in this backless satin gown made us all forget that mere mortals can't pull off a slip dress. Especially in that shade of green. It didn't just impress the audience though. Pinned up against the library wall by James McAvoy's Robbie, it also led to one of the most fan-yourself-ladies sex scenes of this millennium. Who can forget Cher Horowitz, the spoiled yet charming California blonde, whose computer-automated wardrobe we're still waiting for to revolutionise our closets twenty years on? An expert in "like, totally important designers" like Azzedine Alaia and Calvin Klein, Cher's signature school girl style of tiny checked mini kilts and knee-high white socks summed up her superficial but somehow utterly winsome naivety, while still making sure she looked like "a total Betty." Alicia Silverstone in Clueless If you think of 80's Madonna, you think of this look, and a flick back through anyone's home photo albums from that decade will unearth a million mini-Madges sporting that perm, that hair bow and that leather jacket. Ostensibly playing "Susan" but really just being herself, Madonna becomes an obsession for a bored and unfulfilled housewife who tracks her down for thrills, and this more-is-more look sums up "free-spirited, mega-magnetic cool girl" in a whirl of bangles, necklaces and curls. Madonna still has a penchant for wearing gloves (fingerless) three decades later.  Alabama seems like just a dumb blonde with a slow toffee drawl, but underneath her bubblegum exterior lies a heart of gold, whose love and loyalty to Elvis fan Clarence (Christian Slater) is unshaken by teeth-clenching violence at the hands of pimps, drug dealers and gun-wielding cops. Her shoulderless top incorporates sugar-sweet chiffon ruffles and kitschy turquoise blue to perfectly symbolise oversaturated Miami style, and no doubt features heavily on Lana del Rey, Ashish and Ryan Lo's moodboards. Her saccharine style shows girliness should not be underestimated - plastic may look fun and a little cheap, but it is surprisingly tough when you need it to be.  The go-to reference for "borrowing from the boys", Keaton's loose-fitting slouchy waistcoat and slacks, polka dot tie and rumpled white shirt has been copied hundreds, if not thousands, of times on catwalks, in editorials, and in every day style. Annie Hall is the effortless, carefree and openhearted counterpart to Woody Allen's neurotic, made all the more apparent by her wide strides and nonchalant take on what, in someone else's hands, would have been boring office wear. No wonder Woody's in love with her when she looks this good. Just as Alex Owens was just a humble steel worker who overcame obstacles to realise her dream of joining a dance company, this could have been just a humble grey sweater, but its slashed neckline made it so much more. Perhaps a pioneer for the oh-so-now loungewear trend, Beals' sweater made even sportswear look sexy by bringing the killer combo of a flash of bare shoulder and soft fleece to the silver screen, and in the process, sparking a wave of dodgy DIY jobs.  Audrey Hepburn's turn as Holly Golightly took two staid classics and made them the pinnacle of chic, teaching us some style lessons we can never ignore. 1) A little black dress, nipped in at the waist, will always look marvellous, and 2) You can spruce that dress up with garlands of pearls for a look fit for a Park Avenue princess.  1988's Heathers, the blueprint for Mean Girls, showed us high school tribal dressing at its finest. To symbolise the Heathers' domination of the school corridors, each gang member wore the same uniform: girlish kilts and novelty hosiery, but with a frankly intimidating edge stemming from bold tartan, double breasting and shoulder pads so wide you wonder how they managed to fit through the door. If ever there was a death knell for androgyny and normcore, Blanchett's glorious wardrobe in Carol would be it. In muted coral silks and warm sables, Carol exudes a commanding yet alluring femininity, her clothes unexpectedly rich, deep, and ultimately breath-taking, just like the romance she has with shop girl Therese. Never has womanhood been so utterly desirable. They're the very first thing you see in the film: a pair of full pink briefs covering a young woman's bottom. The scene's half sexy, down to the sheerness through which you can see the cleft in Johansson's derriere, half innocent, due to the youthful pink colour. It's altogether intimate yet distant, setting the tone for the rest of the Sofia Coppola film, as two lonely Americans (Johansson and Bill Murray) form an ambiguous attachment in the heart of the Tokyo metropolis. While typical homecoming dance scenes involve flashing the flesh and slapping on the lipstick, the teenage Lisbon sisters sport no up-dos and apply no glitter, thanks to their overbearing, repressive parents. In fact their mother is so afraid that they'll risk their virtue she's altered the dresses so they resemble "four identical sacks." The girls appear in matching gowns like children's nighties, with tiny knicker-band frills and a spriggy floral print, yet underneath, we find out the most enchanting sister, Lux (played by Kirsten Dunst), has written her date's name on her underwear, signalling the potent sexuality that lies beneath. We first hear of Mia Wallace when we hear her crime lord boyfriend has demanded John Travolta take her out to dinner. You might expect a gangster's girlfriend to be docile - boring, even - but from the moment you see Mia, you can tell she's nothing of the sort. In a white, long-collared shirt that twists menswear into something ultimately seductive, and a black bob so sharp it could draw blood, Mia Wallace is all surprises. Consider our homebody heroine Dorothy's blue dress and white pinny: so far, so basic. But with her ruby slippers, magicked onto her feet by Glinda the Good Witch, we have sartorial evidence of the magical adventure she's about to undertake. The red glitter shoes turn out to have been Dorothy's ticket back home all along - she just had to show her inner kindness and bravery (and defeat the Wicked Witch of the West) first.  If only we had our very own pair of scarlet sparklers, it'd certainly make our every day life much more exciting. Every time June rolls around, we dream of wearing soft, white, sun-bleached dresses that flutter in the wind just like those Katharine Ross wore to play Etta Place, outlaw beauty and lover of the Sundance Kid. The same Home on the Range romance can be seen in last summer's obsession with Vita Kin's vyshyvankas: flowing Ukrainian peasant dresses that invoke the same prairie spirit - now where can we find a Robert Redford lookalike of our own? Jane Fonda won an Oscar for her performance in Klute, but forget the acting, it's the clothes that have us giving a standing ovation. Fonda's shag hairstyle tops off a wardrobe full of butt-cheek skimming minis, thigh-high boots and bohemian suede waistcoats - she's essentially the celluloid embodiment of the catwalks right now. The showstopping piece? A midnight blue sequinned minidress. Now that's how you do 70s fashion, kids. In a scene so disturbingly powerful it's loved and hated in equal measure, concentration camp prisoner Lucia (played by Charlotte Rampling) performs a striptease for SS guards, bare-breasted and wearing nothing but braces and an officer's hat. It was the inspiration behind Louis Vuitton's AW11 collection, one of Marc Jacobs' most memorable for the French house, and the unsettling mix of sexuality and Nazi fetishism plays with power boundaries, asking "Who is the most powerful? The one who desires or the one who is desired?" by stripping a uniform back to just a naked chest and a peaked cap. The unofficial mascot for Gucci's renaissance in the uber-embellished, bow-festooned hands of Alessandro Michele, Margot Tenenbaum's odd pairing of clothes - a preppy tennis dress and plastic hair barrette alongside the distinguished fur coat, gloves and Hermes bag - is a testament to the multi-faceted nature of womanhood, simultaneously teenage girl and grand old lady. She's a precocious girl playing dress up in a grown-up world and ultimately the coolest Wes Anderson character ever. The opera scene in Pretty Woman is what we secretly hope will happen every time we put on a party dress: that we'll arrive, and suddenly we've left our old shabby no-hope self behind so everyone will see our true radiant beauty. If there's one thing we've learned from the 1990 film, it's to never judge a book by its cover. Unless the book's wearing a red, strapless, velvet column dress and white elbow-length gloves. In that case, it's totally fine. Thelma and Louise (Davies and Sarandon) are tough women who hold their own on a disastrous road trip across America. They don't let themselves become victims of their (admittedly awful) circumstances and don't go down without a fight. For these reasons alone, what better role models could we ask for? And with bad-ass wardrobes like these, replete with true-blue American denim and grungey band tees with the sleeves rolled up just-so, Thelma and Louise have earned style icon credentials as well. We'll have a long hard think about shooting people and driving off a cliff to evade arrest, though. Gwyneth's suitcase in Anthony Minghella's 1999 thriller is full of the kind of clothes that you look good in without even having to try, just like her character Marge Sherwood. She's beautiful in a WASPish, 'proper' way and an heiress with nothing to fret about except which ruched bikini to wear while bronzing on the Amalfi coast. Her loose white cotton blouses, tied at the waist, with full printed skirts like an Italian village girl, are envy-inducing. Not so much the part where an obsessive psycho (Matt Damon) kills her fiancé and steals his identity. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  British Swifties rejoiced when Taylor Swift appeared on a Suffolk beach over the weekend with new makeout partner Tom Hiddleston. Wearing a cream cable-knit jumper, burgundy skinny jeans, wellies and a quilted field jacket, she looked happy and loved up—if mildly bemused by her very British day at the beach. Swift, most at home in coordinated crop top and skirt ensembles, also seemed completely out of her style element. Those wellies may be Le Chameau, with a credible scuff factor, but the field jacket? It’s so oversized that we can only assume Swift borrowed it from the Hiddleston family coat rack. Ditto for the striped, stretched-out pullover she wore for another coastal walk earlier in the visit, back when she thought that sandals might be appropriate beach footwear (ha!). If the Hiddleswift alliance has staying power and Swift spends more time in the UK, she’ll need to make some adaptations to her wardrobe. From one American woman who fell for a British man to another, here are a few pointers for newcomers to British style. Although she’s famously poised and polished, Swift has never made a secret of the effort it takes to maintain her glossy exterior. When in New York, she’s a devotee of modelFIT workouts (she goes with Karlie Kloss), and walks out of every session looking like she had a bevy of stylists tucked into her locker. Her hair? Perfectly blown out. Her lip? Redder than Red, and always applied just-so. Her handbag? Even smaller than the Queen’s. (What? You think she schleps her own tongs and cosmetic bag to the gym?) Step one for Swift’s British style evolution has to be making the whole effect a little less studied. Muss up the hair – losing the Vogue-cover platinum ‘do was a good start. Wear a rumpled parka/your future mother-in-law’s field jacket everywhere, no matter the dress code. And we know you’ve got a driver, but please, please swap out those heels for a pair of scuffed trainers, the Telegraph Fashion team’s shoe of choice with silk slips or tea dresses. The special British-American relationship Swift and Hiddleston have embarked upon is not without precedent: Madonna and Guy, Gwyneth and Chris, Gigi and Zayn – the list of (largely defunct) relationships goes on. Swift already channelled Madonna in her horsey, stately home phase in the Blank Space video, so we doubt she’ll feel the need to go the full Downton Abbey in real life. Instead, she should emulate the style of women like Keira Knightley (in The Edge of Love), Carey Mulligan (circa An Education) and (you knew it was coming) Alexa Chung. It’s no accident that these women all abide by the recommendations in Step One, described above. And Taylor: unlike in sun-worshipping Los Angeles, being pale and interesting is an asset here. Play it up, don't shake it off (sorry). Reformation sundresses may be Swift’s go-to summer garb, but as her trip to Aldeburgh indicated, it’s time to invest in all-weather outerwear. She's already got the right wellies. British heritage brands have plenty of promising options for the rest of her wardrobe. We’d like to see Swift try Hunter or Barbour for a coat, Holland & Holland or Alex Gore Brown for knitwear (so much better than that borrowed pullover), Le Kilt for pleated minis and Penelope Chilvers for Chelsea boots. The latter come in blue velvet, which is essential for that other key characteristic of British dressing: irreverence.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge has carved out a reputation for mastering the art of high/ low dressing, opting for everything from ASOS and Topshop to Alexander McQueen and  Jenny Packham. At the gala concert in Windsor tonight held in celebration of The Queen’s 90th birthday, the Duchess continued to blend budgets, choosing a £3,450 white lace dress by Dolce and Gabbana and a postbox red swing jacket from Zara. The Duchess complemented her designer/ high street mix with diamond drop earrings and a chic low chignon. Priced at a rather affordable £49.99 , Kate’s jacket is described online as “a blazer with back pleat” and at the time of writing was still available to buy in every size apart from small. The dress- made in Italy- is described on Net-a-Porter as a “romantic choice for special events” and comes with a nipped in waist and tiered skirt. Its design is typical of the ladylike signature of Stefano Gabbana and Domenico Dolce who are famed in the fashion world for their celebration of all things Italian; recent themes for their Milan fashion  week shows have included the history of Sicily and the joys of traditional Mediterranean food. At the time of writing, tonight's lace dress cotton dress was sold out or low in stock in all sizes.  The Duchess has long been a fan of Zara. She’s been seen wearing pieces by the Spanish high street behemoth for everything from official engagements and on more casual off-duty days. In fact, it was a cornflower blue Zara dress which the Duchess turned to as she departed for her honeymoon in 2011. It seems that the Duchess has also developed a penchant for the feminine lace dresses which are a mainstay of Dolce and Gabbana's collections. Tonight is third occasion that Kate has worn a similar design by the duo. In November last year, she opted for an elegant black version for the Festival of Remembrance. Kate wasn’t the only resplendently stylish royal at tonight’s concert.  ­­­­It wasn't only the inclusion of Jayden Smith, the 17-year-old son of actor Will Smith in Louis Vuitton’s new ad campaign that has garnered headlines recently, but the casting of a virtual character too. Lightning, the heroic, pink-haired figure in cult game Final Fantasy was given a high-fashion makeover for her first modelling assignment, entering the Louis Vuitton galaxy and blurring the boundaries between reality and make-believe. Vuitton creative director Nicolas Ghesquière rationalised the unusual decision by explaining that the collection that ‘she’ models was predominantly inspired by video games. “Lightning is the perfect avatar for a global, heroic woman and for a world where social networks and communications are now seamlessly woven into our life,” said the Frenchman, adding: “She is also the symbol of new pictorial processes. How can you create an image that goes beyond the classic principles of photography and design? Lightning heralds a new era of expression.” Now Lightning is speaking out about crossing over worlds (stay with us here, there's a Q&A which follows below). Some die-hard Final Fantasy fans may be up in arms that video game publisher Square Enix has allowed its heroine to be modelling for a fashion house, but the character says she 'feels' nothing but pride. In an exclusive Q&A released to The Telegraph by Louis Vuitton, Lightning discusses her new role and her journey of self-discovery. Is it your first campaign? How do you feel to be part of the ‘fashion family’ along with Jennifer Connelly, Michelle Williams, Alicia Vikander?  They are in a completely different world. ­­­­­ As part of the family, but I have so much to learn to catch up to these radiant women who are light years away from where I stand. I hope that one day, we can share the same stage, that different worlds can come together. But who knows? Maybe that’s ambitious, even for me. Fortunately, I’m not one to give up. One of my strengths is “experience.” I’m no stranger to overcoming challenges and finishing what I’ve set out to do. I can face any kind of trial as long as I remember the following words: “It’s not a question of can or can’t. Some things in life you just do.” What do you think about Nicolas Ghesquière’s vision and his collections? Do you recognise yourself in his creations?  Though his style was new to me, the moment I laid eyes on his collection, it was as if I was hit by a bolt of lightning. I knew that with this, people could change. I could change. It turns out I was right. His collection fills me with a sense of serenity and pride. All this time, I thought the only style that suited me was one that mirrored who I was: strong and tough. But I was wrong. He changed the way I see myself. Perhaps I’m finally learning who I truly am. What does it feel like to become a Louis Vuitton ambassador? My clothes were nothing more than armor to stay alive; “dressing up” was a concept I’ve never had. Perhaps that makes me an unseemly choice as ambassador. But this experience has opened my eyes. Fashion isn’t something you’re taught or given, it comes from your own taste and your own choices. It displays the essence of who you are to the people around you. It makes me feel excited, a feeling similar to when I venture to unknown lands. It is a thrill that I, who has faced my share of danger, have never experienced before. LV is a new adventure―a new fantasy―that I will enjoy from the bottom of my heart. What are your upcoming projects? I’m currently winding down after a long journey. My days are peaceful; it’s what I’ve always dreamed of. I hope these days last a long time. But I’m always looking to push myself, to better myself. Sometimes I get the urge to put my life on the line again and test my limits. One day, not so far in the future, I will be out there again, in a world of strife. But I won’t be the same person I was before. I will return to my origins, like a Mobius strip, but it’ll be a new me, one who has evolved. I look forward to the day we meet again. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  As the war correspondent Marie Colvin in A Private War, Rosamund Pike has been majoring on dusty conflict zones recently, wearing a selection of flak jackets and khaki shirts streaked with blood and soaked in sweat. It’s all a very long way from the VIP room of the Armani headquarters in Milan, where Olympic rowers, models, Italian starlets and the fashion label’s top brass were milling around before the autumn/ winter '19 show drinking champagne and not eating canapes. The actor, herself dressed in an impeccable black velvet Armani tux, looked quite at home, though this is the first Giorgio Armani show she’s attended in 10 years. ‘At Armani,’ she says, ‘there’s a way the clothes follow the body that means your true form is revealed. I felt that the first time I ever put on a pair of Armani trousers when I did my Bond film. I thought: “this works for my body”’. Pike’s ice-maiden baddie Miranda Frost in Die Another Day veered between fencing whites and ice blue sparkles so it’s possible that she wouldn’t have found much to her taste on Saturday night's catwalk. Giorgio Armani showed a sombre collection this season, mostly trouser suits with the occasional strapless or one-shouldered column dress in black or very dark navy with the odd touch of indigo. Such light as there was came from the flashbulbs bouncing off navy or black paillettes and sequins embroidered over tops, scarves and dresses. They’ll certainly stand out on an Oscars red carpet awash with sorbet-hued frou-frou. ‘Clothes have their own energy,’ said Pike. ‘They should never feel like costume. You should be able to buy into the energy of a good suit or a wonderful dress. Wearing them should feel effortless.’ This collection certainly packed a punch- anyone dressed in one of these looks would feel invincible, protected by its aura of serious good taste. There was even a knowing wink to other labels’ relentless and shouty branding in a large though subtle dark blue art-deco GA monogram on a black t-shirt.  Today the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge visited street children at New Delhi's main railway station, and Kate wore an Indian-inspired maxi dress by Manchester-based self-proclaimed fast fashion label 'Glamorous.'  The £50 bohemian red dress with lace up details at the chest, long sleeves and a navy trim was on sale earlier this year and has now gone back online following the spike of interest which today's royal outing has attracted. The online retailer reveals that they had no idea that the Duchess had purchased the dress from their Spring/Summer collection, and so it's assumed that the Duchess or her team will have discovered it online or perhaps from one of the high street stores, such as Topshop,  where the brand has a concession. In advance of William and Kate's visit to India, a royal source revealed to The Telegraph that the Duchess looks for many of her tour pieces online: "It's very much a process that she leads, though she does have some help from her staff when it comes to sourcing outfits."  Given how considered The Duchess of Cambridge's fashion choices usually are - wearing a Maple Leaf brooch to touch down in Canada for example - it's perhaps surprising that she choose to wear a dress from a fast-fashion label whilst on tour in India. The country often faces criticism for some of the labour conditions in factories which mass-produce clothes then distributed in the West.  There is no suggestion that Kate's Glamorous dress wasn't ethically produced. "Our factories are all regularly audited and socially compliant - they have to be because of the partners we work with," a representative from Glamorous told us. They tell us that Kate's dress was manufactured in China, although they also manufacture in the UK, the Far East and India. However Glamorous is not signed up to the ETI  (Ethical Trade Initiative), which has become the industry's standard measure of good practice. "If consumers are concerned about ethical standards, most companies will reference on their websites their ethical and sourcing policies in relation to their global supply chains. This doesn't seem to be the case with Glamorous," comments Debbie Coulter, the ETI's head of programmes.  While we have long appreciated the Duchess's clever, down-to-earth mix of designer and high-street labels, it seems a shame she choose a dress manufactured by a Western-based brand to closely resemble traditional Indian print and textiles rather than one by an Indian designer as she did on Sunday with the style she wore by Anita Dongre.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Fast forward to the mid-Noughties, and a model’s popularity is frequently measured by her Instagram following, where she could be making up to $100,000 in sponsorship per post (seriously) thanks to this new-found metric of high visibility. Nowhere was the power of the modern supermodel more evident than yesterday's Miu Miu show. Featuring an all-star line up of models including Kendall Jenner, Gigi and Bella Hadid and Lara Stone and killer accessories like some pearl-encrusted sandals, pictures of the show flooded social media in seconds - closing Fashion Month with a bang. The maestro behind the bringing Miuccia Prada's twinsets and denim maxi skirts to life on the catwalk was Katie Grand, Editor-in-chief of LOVE magazine. "We worked on the clothes along with the looks so it was looking at proportion and what could be new and interesting and real clothing at the same time," Grand told us of reviving her relationship with Mrs Prada. Grand has worked on various Miu Miu advertising campaigns recently but hasn't styled one of the shows since 2005. So how different was the experience almost a decade on? "Not very different, I was still nervous, anxious and thrilled," Grand says.  Her anxiety was unfounded. The collection is already being hailed as one of Miuccia's greats and the catwalk was like a who’s who of modern supermodels: 34-year-old Adriana Lima, best know for her work with lingerie behemoth Victoria’s Secret made a rare catwalk turn, walking alongside models of the moment Kendall Jenner and Gigi Hadid, the latter’s sister Bella and the buxom model-turned-actresss Emily Ratajkowski. Combined, these runway stars boast a combined following over 87 million Instagram followers. So how did Grand pull it off? "We just asked; if you don't ask you don't get!" she told us simply. "The concept was based on unashamed pin-up beauty which we haven't seen since the Eighties, when you see a super beautiful girl walk in to a room and everyone stops. Taylor Hill who opened the show is like a young Brooke Shields."   I spent most of my early Twenties happily foraging for vintage bargains. This was mostly because I was broke and, in the early Noughties, vintage tea dresses, scuffed-up old cowboy boots and geeky glasses were what hipsters wore before anyone thought to turn that phrase into a social movement. But thrifting has come a long way from dingy stores hidden off Brick Lane in east London.  William Banks-Blaney – who opened his chic Marylebone vintage store in 2010 (Victoria Beckham and Amal Clooney are clients) – has just launched his new online proposition; a fine edit of pieces that range from an embroidered waistcoat circa 1775 (styled with jeans, yours for £1,875) and Norman Hartnell Fifties couture to what Banks-Blaney calls his “drunk dresses”. “A drunk dress doesn’t have to have a label,” he says, “they were made to have a good night out in, something that it would be impossible to have a row in.”  Alongside the couture creations are his “great unknowns”, cheerful printed sundresses for less than £300. “While we might do precious things, we’re not precious. We’re not label snobs,” he reassures. “Our entry point is £175 and we go up to anything [he is currently stocking a 1936 Schiaparelli coat for just shy of £10,000]. Our smallest size is a 00 and our largest is a 16 or 18. If a garment still has a story to tell, and is relevant for a woman today, then it will work for us. Vintage is for everyone.” Black and yellow print kaftan circa 1945, £295, William Vintage There are exquisite pieces from Alexander McQueen, Yves Saint Laurent, Halston, Thea Porter… endless wardrobe trophies that offer something completely unique. All pieces are in pristine condition and each one hand-selected by Banks-Blaney, who largely sources from dealers and private sellers.  With vintage there is an extra sense of serendipity – to find something you love, which fits, is rarer than walking into a shop with racks of the same pieces in every size – but that winning feeling is so much greater.  “There’s a different sense of possession,” says Banks-Blaney. “We buy clothes all the time and don’t really think about it. We order stuff online and within a month we’re over it. It’s a different feeling with vintage – it’s something you come back to in your wardrobe because you really love it.”  Ossie Clark safari jacket circa 1968, £385, William Vintage His intention with the website was to create something that would appeal to customers used to the art direction of luxury fashion sites such as Net-A-Porter. “We wanted the site to be very modern and pared-back, so when you look at it you’re just judging the dress. I want you to be able to think, would this work with a pair of gladiators or with a heel?”  Banks-Blaney’s crucial vintage mantra is to keep it relevant – he is not into what he calls “dress up”. “Wear one piece at a time if you don’t want to look like you’ve stepped out of Downton,” he advises. “Don’t overthink it or approach it differently than you would something from a contemporary collection. Simply ask, does it make you happy?”  He doesn’t do vintage shoes or bags: “I love seeing a great vintage piece with contemporary accessories. It’s a much fresher look. I can’t tell you how many red carpets I’ve done where I’ve paired an extraordinarily expensive dress with a pair of shoes from Dune.” 1970's statement collar necklace, £75, Susan Caplan One of the best things about vintage is that the chances of someone turning up to your dinner party or Ascot in the same number are joyfully slim. Plus the opportunity for reinvention, which is no doubt what aficionados of festivals such as the Goodwood Revival feel (attendees often turn up in full Forties vintage regalia). Oxfam recently staged a competition for bloggers who are stylistically devoted to a particular decade, a nifty showcase for their own extensive archive – which is a great place to start for inexpensive fun finds (also available online – Oxfam.org.uk – if you can’t do rummaging). Susan Caplan is a veritable trove of vintage jewellery, too, with very affordable options. There are fabulous gobstopper earrings and stand-out necklaces that will spice up any outfit.  Blush vintage 1960's Norell Tasell NYC dress, £280, Bob by Dop The problem with new fashion now is that it is horribly ubiquitous. In times past, splashing out on an “investment” designer piece assured you some level of exclusivity. But now, with the same luxury fashion collections being sold by every online retailer and shipping to every doorstep in the world, shelling out hundreds of pounds on something so widely available doesn’t bring the same cachet it used to. And let’s not even talk about the same-dress nightmare that getting anything from the high street ensures.    In terms of trends, thanks to Alessandro Michele’s vintage-drenched, kooky eclectic vision for Gucci – we’re all being turned on to maximalism. You can’t afford his £1,000 dresses? Then why not hunt down the original inspiration… Journalist, American ex-pat and Milan resident JJ Martin launched her website, LadoubleJ.com, last year, selling her own sourced vintage from more than 20 years of collecting. “I think luxury is so boring right now, I don’t feel inspired to buy anything,” says Martin on the current state of the fashion industry. “We don’t need to be inundated with product like this. The entire system is on the brink.” “Vintage is having a moment for precisely that reason,” she explains. “Luxury used to be special. It was a way to make people feel distinctive, and like they were expressing their personal style, not that of eight million people. In becoming so quirky and individual, Gucci has really hit the zeitgeist – which is what the vintage customer has always been; a little bit of a magpie, interested in colour, bright patterns and embellishment,” says the self-confessed unashamed maximalist.  Hermès geometric motif dress, 1978, £775 La Double J  For Martin, vintage takes getting dressed back to simply enjoying yourself. “I really don’t take fashion seriously at all. More than ever, you need a wink and a smile in this business. It’s become so bonkers. Digital has turned everything on its head, and there are wonderful outcomes to that, but it’s made me realise that I’m not into the mass game of fashion. If speaking to 10 million viewers means that Kim Kardashian has to like what you’re doing then I’m not remotely interested.”  On her website, you’ll find brilliant bright vintage finds (with prices starting at around £180); from Yves Saint Laurent quilted Seventies jackets to jewellery from legendary fashion editor Anna Piaggi’s private collection. The design is colourful and spirited, with a fun cartoon feel to it. Everything is delivered in colourful, ribbon wrapped boxes with a personalised note (free shipping to the UK).  “We spent a lot of money on fantastic photography so you can see the garments really closely and there are detailed product descriptions” says Martin. Tulipani gospel dress, £420, La Double J Editions She has also launched her own collection of dresses, skirts and shirts (La Double J Editions) taken from the Mantero archive’s vintage prints, one of the oldest silk manufacturers on Lake Como, who work with Dior, Chanel and Pucci amongst others. The prints are tantalisingly loud, but the shapes (“universally flattering on everyone”) T-shirt dresses, classic button-down shirts and tiered maxi skirts are not. “They’re really fun” says Martin, “colour and print really has the power to transform your energy, your mood, your everything.”  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  In the five yeas since Kate Middleton became the Duchess of Cambridge, she has carefully carved out a distinctive style identity, juggling the need to be glamorous but also appropriate, stylish but not a fashion victim while also cleverly making use of clothes and beauty to enhance  her role. There are probably times when a message is construed when there was really no message at all but it’s often irresistible not to read something into a Kate outfit. It might be as simple as ‘today I’m looking at boats, so I am dressed accordingly in nautical white and navy’ through to something a little more nuanced, like the time that she debuted a new Princess Diana-style fringe just days before the announcement that she was pregnant with her first child. These are five classic Kate looks which say the most about her time as Duchess of Cambridge so far… After many month s of feverish speculation about which designer would be chosen to create the most important royal wedding dress in years, a “fashion moment” was immediately declared as Kate stepped out of the Rolls Royce at Westminster Abbey in an Alexander McQueen creation by the label’s creative director Sarah Burton. Created using lace made by the Royal School of Needlework at Hampton Court Palace, the gown incorporated references to the wedding dresses of the Queen, Princess Margaret and Grace Kelly but also had an edge which made it modern. In short, it was just the thing to elegantly transform Kate from commoner to Queen-to-be. Style-wise, Kate took two very different approaches to leaving hospital with her newborns under the gaze of the world’s media. With Prince George, it was all about  blissed-out new mother  mode with a breezy Jenny Packham pale blue  polka dot dress, loose hair tumbling over the shoulders and low wedges (ideal for navigating steps with a future king in arms). The message here was natural and relaxed, let’s not play up too much to the hype thing. With Princess Charlotte almost two years later, the look amped up. This time the hair was carefully tonged into perfect curls and the practical wedges were swapped for heels. Jenny Packham was still the designer of choice for a pretty daffodil print dress but the Duchess won special commendation for her bravery in opting for white. It was about as far from earth mother as you could imagine. In their five years of marriage, the Duke and Duchess have visited all corners of the globe, from the high-octane glamour of Los Angeles to the remote island of Samoa. Kate’s learnt to juggle diplomacy while also pleasing the home crowd. Case in point, this outfit from the couple’s tour of Canada in 2011. The maple leaf hat is an obvious but quite fabulous diplomatic tribute to her hosts, as is the matching brooch, borrowed from the Queen. But the Reiss dress ticks two essential Kate boxes. Firstly, it was the second time she’d worn it- the Duchess has gained quite a reputation for rewearing her outfits. Secondly, people could actually buy it (or something similar). It’s pieces like these which have spurned ‘The Kate Effect’, so-called because if Kate wears it, and it’s available for sale, you can bet it won’t be around for long. A reminder that even Princesses aren’t on permanent primped and preened mode. At the weekend, a trusty Breton top and skinny jeans will do for the Duchess just as they do for the rest of us. Hers are by brands which we are all likely all have in our wardrobes too- Zara, Me + Em and J Crew are a few of Kate’s casual go-tos. Over the past year or two, the Duchess has begun to work closely with Kensington Palace PA Natasha Archer who has been credited for coaxing her into more daring choices, particularly when it comes to the eveningwear. During the recent royal tour of India and Bhutan, Kate chose a glamorous and decorative crop top and maxi skirt ensemble by British designer Alice Temperley. A crop top for a future Queen?  LOVE is renowned for its striking covers and eclectic mix of stars- Cher, Lily Rose Depp, Kendall Jenner, Miley Cyrus and Hari Nef are just a clutch of the characters who have graced the front of the magazine, which is spearheaded by super-stylist Katie Grand.  For the latest 17.5 special issue, Grand has enlisted Alasdair McLellan to select and photograph the girls at the top of their barometer of relevance right now. The resulting title? Quite simply, 'Alasdair's Girls'. Among the stellar young cast is 15 year-old Rowan Blanchard, who is fast gaining a reputation for being as much an activist as an actress; Adwoa Aboah, the preternaturally beautiful model who has walked for Dior, Erdem and Versus Versace and is creating positives from her own mental health struggles with her forum Gurls Talk which encourages women to share their experiences openly; and Slick Woods, the rebel girl model who has been working with Kanye West, Rihanna and Marc Jacobs.  "We just picked girls we liked," shrugs McLellan, explaining the instinctive, zeitgeist-led approach to casting the issue. "They feel so relevant to now. I hate the word 'buzz' but these girls have really got that about them." When they were deciding how to portray these strong, agenda-setting personalities in LOVE's pages, McLellan and Grand struck upon the idea of a pared-back aesthetic. "What was especially nice about this project was that it was in a studio, it was simple," remarks McLellan in his editor's letter.  The idea was based on a book which McLellan had worked on with skateboarding brand Palace, for which he took raw portraits of  the Palace Wayward Boys Choir, the skateboarding collective based at the world famous skate spot on the Southbank. "I really liked that idea of a gang, a mixture of characters aged 16 to 40," he recalls of the project and how it created the inspiration for LOVE.  In the resulting shots, vibrant up-and-coming model Winnie Harlow, who has turned her vitiligo from a condition for which she was bullied to a proud statement of individual beauty, is styled in a bold red Proenza Schouler dress and bucket hat by Stephen Jones for Marc Jacobs and captured mid joyful dance move by McLellan. Slick Woods and Adwoa Aboah take the cover in a a sensitive, tender embrace- both dripping in pieces from Tiffany & co's new Tiffany City Hardwear collection which is celebrated throughout the issue.  In a candidly characterful moment, Edie Campbell and Lily Nova sport rollered hair and plasticised coats from Raf Simons' debut Calvin Klein collection.  Inside, the evocative shots appear alongside interviews and exchanges between the 'Alasdair's Girls' cast.  While the issue might seem like the latest celebration of diversity in the fashion and cultural spheres, McLellan insists that that part comes naturally. "I know people are talking about diversity," he says. "But in the UK, we've been doing it in magazines like Blitz and i-D for 30 or 40 years. When I work with people, I just see their characters." This piece was created in Emilia Wickstead's London atelier, by an all-female team." Emilia Wickstead told The Telegraph this morning that "dressing Emma has been an absolute privilege." She has also been wearing delicate jewellery by relatively affordable labels Catbird and All Blues.  Christian Dior, the fashion designer who gave us the New Look, and the street photographer Richard Avedon were two quite different people, but when they formed a creative partnership the results were magical – and influential It was Carmel Snow, then editor of US Harper’s Bazaar, who introduced Richard Avedon to Christian Dior, shortly after the latter opened his own house in 1946. Although Avedon was a modernist, happiest photographing expensive clothes on the street, and Dior a nostalgic romantic, their work proved highly complementary. Avedon accentuated the bold architecture of Dior’s designs, which in turn brought additional layers of emotion and nuance to Avedon’s bracing streetscapes. Perhaps the happy juxtaposition of their different sensibilities is what Snow intended. She was, in all matters of style, exceptionally perceptive. It was Snow, on seeing those sweeping, full skirts and nipped waists of Dior’s first collection for his own house in February 1947, who dubbed it the New Look. Dior himself, a man who, according to Cecil Beaton, resembled 'a bland country curate made out of pink marzipan’, kept well away from the main action during those shows. He only appeared when it was over, once he had gauged the critical reaction. He could be forgiven his nerves. The storm unleashed on that debut in February 1947 – both positive and negative – created waves far beyond the confines of the fashion world, and placed enormous pressure on Dior to produce collections of cultural as well as aesthetic importance. It was his retro mania that irked the modernists. The post-war aspiration was to look forward – with a degree of pragmatism and frugality. Dior’s New Look, with its yards and yards of costly fabric (Britain was still subject to severe rationing), displayed neither of those qualities. Yet those extravagant, refined silhouettes spoke to something almost atavistic in millions of women around the world. And perhaps there was something a little practical about them. 'Yesterday I stood at Dior for two hours while they moulded me with great wadges of cotton wool and built a coat over the result,’ wrote Nancy Mitford to her sister Diana in September 1947. 'I look exactly like Queen Mary. Think how warm though… All the English newspapers are on to the long skirts and sneer. But all I can think is now one will be able to have knickers over the knee.’ When Dovima – born Dorothy Virginia Margaret Juba in Queens, New York – wore Dior, there was no thought of knickers. The haughtily elegant model could carry off the grandest ballgown with aristocratic disdain. Avedon’s genius was to frame her in a flawless Dior column dress with elephants who were neither fazed by her froideur nor dwarfed by her lofty poise. They are, however, manacled. It’s a poignant symbol of captivity and cannot have been unintended: there is frequently a sly visual aside in Avedon’s fashion photographs – witness the poodle making eye contact with the plumed, jewelled and be-furred woman on a shabby Parisian street. Christian Dior died suddenly in 1957, aged 52. The New Look lasted more than a decade. Audrey Hepburn, a young, exceptionally stylish starlet, photographed in 1959 as a charming gamine in a slimmed-down Dior skirt suit, showed how the brand was adapting under the brief tenure of a relative unknown called Yves Saint Laurent. Later still, under the helm of Marc Bohan, Dior’s still striking, but evolving, silhouettes proved perfect for a new breed of stars, including Barbra Streisand and the model Veruschka. Inevitably the New Look defined – and continues to define – Dior. Women adored it. To them it felt relevant. Avedon made it look relevant. For Christian Dior, it was relevant. 'Everything that goes beyond the simple fact of food, clothing and shelter is a luxury,’ he wrote. 'Our civilisation is a luxury, and that is what we are defending.’ Dior by Avedon (Rizzoli, £115) is available for £99.99 with free p&p from Telegraph Bookshop  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Karlie Kloss is officially taking over the great British high street. If you’ve visited a Topshop store recently, you will have seen the 23-year-old grinning back at you from enormous posters, sporting  relaxed basics embroidered with her name. If you haven’t, then no doubt you’ve caught a glance of a Topshop-clad Miss Kloss on the side of a bus. Now the statuesque beauty is giving us body envy in her new SS16 campaign for Kurt Geiger, the London shoe label that’s gained quite the red carpet following in Hollywood. The sporty theme of the ads sees long-limbed Kloss make looking sweaty appear desirable. Of course, she’s got a ‘fashion sweat’ on (tanned skin that is deliciously dewy and frizzy hair that looks more beachy than chlorine-matted) but the fitness theme marries perfectly with health enthusiast Karlie’s credentials. The Missouri native recently completed a half marathon to get over her hatred of running and is regularly pictured running errands around her adoptive city of Manhattan in leggings and Lycra which suggest she’s fresh from the gym. Kurt Geiger’s emphasis on athleticism for spring was conceived to blur the boundaries between fitness and casualwear as it taps into the trend for all things athleisure. ‘Ditching strict fitness time, bags and shoes are designed to run wild in anytime’ says the brand, hence the ‘run wild’ slip-on sneakers and ankle-tie flip-flops. And its new ambassador reasons: “I've always been a fan of this iconic brand not only for being a perfect red carpet look, but also, now, for every day running from the gym to work and everything in between!” So while we may never look quite as catwalk-ready as Kloss while running from the gym to the office, as least emulating her polished style isn't quite so unobtainable.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We’re used to hearing the last rites being read over bricks-and-mortar stores. But listen carefully and there’s  a cheerful little drumbeat, faint at first, but gathering conviction. It’s the story of imaginative retailing. At the top end, this manifests in boutiques masquerading as homes. Or is it the other way around? Designer Roland Mouret and Jeweller Jessica McCormack began the trend back in 2011 and ’12, when they opened businesses near one another in a magnificent red-brick terrace in Mayfair, once home to well-heeled Victorians. These houses-cum-salons fly in the face of retail orthodoxy: there are no plate-glass windows and the doors are often closed. Sometimes you even have to ring a bell. But the cosy, luxurious and personal service is clearly effective – and the message is spreading. Moda Operandi, which began as an online-only business, now has town houses in Manhattan and Knightsbridge, where clients congregate for styling sessions and  special events. Matchesfashion.com will launch its own town house-headquarters just along from Mouret in  the autumn. Meanwhile, Osman Yousefzada is opening the delightfully quaint sounding House of Osman on Percy Street,  a Georgian nook in Fitzrovia with an   irresistibly racy history. Home to artists, poets, writers and opium dealers, its greatest claim to fame was the restaurant at no 1, which was frequented by George Bernard Shaw, Augustus John and the future Edward VIII. Osman himself attracts his share of artists and artsy women, plus a starry red-carpet following, from Emma Watson to Lupita Nyong’o. Until now, however, he’s never had a shop of his own. Not one to take a run at half tilt, his House spans five elegant, high-ceilinged storeys: workrooms in the basement, retail and kitchens on the ground floor (customers will be offered a menu), design studio on the second. ‘After 10 years in business I finally get a whole world to myself, where I can bring all the projects I love working on together,’ Osman says. That includes art and photographic exhibitions and special events such as a forthcoming ‘perfume performance’ (‘like a cooking lesson but with fragrance,’ he says). If it sounds like a 19th-century salon for 21st-century tastemakers, that’s the idea. Augustus John would be delighted. Designs from Osman's AW18 collection Oh, and the clothes – from bespoke classics to the avant-garde, couture one-offs to T-shirts (albeit £80 ones) and his ever-popular Perfect Five capsule collections of trousers, jackets and knitwear, it will all finally get the space it deserves. He hopes it won’t be intimidating. ‘Yes there’s a doorbell. But we’ll try to make sure the door’s open as much as possible.’  House of Osman is at 32 Percy Street W1 © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
