 Nicola Griffin, a middle-aged single mother from Nottingham, was queuing with her twin daughters at the bank one day when a stranger approached her with a somewhat unlikely question.   The woman was from a hair product company called White Hot Hair. She wanted to know whether Griffin, who then ran a business organising student exchange trips, would be willing to model for their latest campaign. Griffin was sceptical but her daughters, Tabitha and Elly, who were about to start university, urged her to give it a go.  The hair signing quickly led to more modelling jobs, including a skin campaign, lingerie shoot and retirement home brochure. From local model agencies she progressed to London-based Milk Model Management, who had spotted her on Facebook.  Three years after that trip to the bank, at the improbable age of 56 and a buxom size 16, she has just become the latest British pin-up for the Sports Illustrated swimsuit issue, an American institution for more than half a century. This makes her the oldest person to ever appear in the magazine known for skimpy bikinis and doe-eyed youngsters. The shot of a gold bikini-clad ‘real woman’ emerging from the Caribbean Sea has been welcomed as a glorious riposte to body-shamers and ageists who believe quinquagenarians shouldn’t be seen dead in a two-piece. Pigmentation marks, tick. Wobbly thighs, tick. Griffin is refreshingly unapologetic about all of it. “I have a big tummy, but I gave birth to two 7lb babies at the same time,” she says from a hotel in New York. “It is not a flat stomach, it is rounded. This is me. It has not been photoshopped and I have not gone on a diet. This is how a beautiful woman should, can and does look.” She joins the elite ranks of Elle Macpherson, Tyra Banks, Heidi Klum, Irina Shayk and Kate Upton, who have all posed for the publication, and takes her role as ambassador for mature physiques seriously. “I have had wonderful feedback from normal ladies, who are saying this is a breakthrough,” she says. “They think, ‘great, I am not invisible any more. I too can look good - 56, 66, 76, it doesn’t matter.” Not that she’s fashion’s first silver style icon. Griffin, who had never even worn a bikini before the Sports Illustrated shoot, is in fact one of a growing number of mature women upending the industry. Jacky O’Shaughnessy, 64, appeared in a lingerie advert for American Apparel; Balmain recently reunited Naomi Campbell, 45, Cindy Crawford, 49, and Claudia Schiffer, 45, for its spring campaign; Twiggy, 66, is soaring for L’Oreal and M&S, and last year Saint Lauren and Celine both went one better, featuring 80-somethings in their campaigns. Such is the demand for older models that Grey, the UK’s first agency for those aged between 35 and 80, started last summer and has an army of 140 on its books already.  None of this makes Griffin’s late-life career change any easier for her to believe, however. “I keep asking, is this really happening to me?” she says. “Will I wake up and realise I have been having a great big long dream?” If so, it’s a dream that has resulted in her fending off TV and magazine requests, hiding from fans on public transport and acclimatising to autograph requests, online propositions and having her coffee bills paid by obliging gentlemen in cafes. One, from Dubai, asked her to send him a picture of her ears. (She declined.)  Tabitha, 21, who is studying economics at Newcastle University, has had to warn her male friends against requesting her mother as a Facebook friend, something they have taken to of late. Clearly the demand for the mature model is there, then. What’s more suprising, perhaps, is that it took us so long to realise this. So does being (relatively) old in an industry notoriously tough on body-image and self-confidence make it any easier to roll with the punches? “Yes,” says Griffin. “You think, ‘it doesn’t matter. I don’t have anything to prove.’” As for dieting, she is adamant on the subject. “No. Never. What for? Why? I think that is totally, utterly pointless. I’ll still be 56 with two pounds less. I am not competing with anyone. I am just 56 with grey hair and a size 16. End of.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Michelle Obama is never far from our fashion radar. In the eight years that have passed since she took to the stage in a red and black Narciso Rodriguez dress with the newly elected President Barrack Obama, she has consistently dressed the part of First Lady, while staying true to her signature style. Her recent 6-day European tour to highlight the work of Let Girls Learn, a U.S. government initiative she launched with the President in 2015, is the latest proof of her fashion prowess. With royal dinners, tours and public speeches to dress for, the First Lady’s outfit planning must have been a military operation. Outwardly though, Obama was immaculate, traversing each formal occasion with a selection of dresses that were summer-appropriate, culturally aware and flattering. Morocco saw her dabble with scarf prints, but on long-sleeved designs (courtesy of Altuzarra and Etro) that were a departure from the sleeveless styles she favours to show off her toned upper arms. In Spain Obama returned to form, wearing fresh white (sleeveless) creations (from Delpozo and Proenza Schouler) befitting the garden walks she went on with Queen Letizia in Madrid. So, aside from applauding Obama on yet another well-packed suitcase, there are tips we can take from the First Lady’s European tour wardrobe. When dressing for your next formal summer occasion, keep Obama’s failsafe formula in mind. Wandering around the gardens of the Zarzuela palace with Queen Letizia, Obama chose a cotton-blend white midi dress by Madrid-based brand Delpozo (now 60 per cent off at Net-a-Porter). The choice was not just a diplomatic nod to the fashion of the country she was in, but a chic example of a hard-working summer dress that goes the extra mile. Look closely at the fresh white cotton and you’ll see a cape-effect cut-out back that shows off just a little skin, and feminine ties on either side of the nipped-in waist. It’s these details that elevate the dress into a unique one that will stand alone as a modern update on a classic silhouette, or can be dressed up with choice accessories. Note, for example, how Obama has chosen metallic sandals instead of the nude courts favoured by Queen Letizia and the Duchess of Cambridge.  Touching down in Morocco, Obama was photographed wearing a pleated monochrome Proenza Schouler dress, which retails for $1800. Undoubtedly luxe, elegant and interesting, the First Lady fell prey to gusts of wind when embarking the aircraft. To avoid the perils of holding down your own dress hems opt for thick fabrics that will withstand windy spells. Alternatively, wear a close-fitting slip underneath. Practical, but essential when dressing for Britain’s unpredictable weather. Cast your eye along the beautiful, intricate dresses worn by Obama, her daughters Sasha and Malia, and the Moroccan royal family below, and it is the First Lady’s Altuzarra dress that stands out. Its fluttering hemline draws the eye down the leg area, showing off a little more leg than an mid-calf A-line cut would do, and highlights her ankles. The black panels across her torso and arms also highlight the slimmest parts of her body, marking it out as a clever dress indeed. Whether shopping for a skirt or dress for work or play, keep an asymmetric cut in mind for this unfailingly flattering silhouette. Wearing black in summer doesn’t put you in Wednesday Addams’s morbid style camp. In fact, one Telegraph fashion editor maintains that “black and white are your only friends” in summer. All other colours are too high risk and will show sweat patches (not chic). There are certain points to consider when going back-to-black in July, however. As Obama shows, cut is important so that you don’t wash out your frame. Colour, too, should be strong - Obama’s printed Proenza Schouler dress, worn to meet Princess Lalla Salma of Morocco is anything but wishy-washy.   Touching down in Morocco, it was Etro’s swirling prints that Obama greeted waiting photographers in. The paisley scarf motifs could have overwhelmed her slim frame were it not for a black belt sitting neatly on her waist. In a week that has also shown Samantha Cameron relying on a simple belt to break up a patterned dress and frame her figure, we have a new appreciation for the simple accessory. If you don’t own a classic belt (one inch width, in either black, brown or navy), it’s time you got one in your arsenal.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Clare Waight Keller's collections might be of-the-moment, attracting a group of 'It Chloe Girls' including Rosie Huntington-Whiteley and Adele (Chloe dressed the singer for her Glastonbury performance this year), but her aesthetic is anti-bling and timeless. "It's that sense of ease," Waight Keller has previously explained to The Telegraph. "And I try and create that through lightness. That can be hard to do while also remaining modern, as so much in recent fashion has been about bonding, stiffness and structure. So maintaining the core of the house identity, the softness and fluidity, while imposing a sense of modernity is a real challenge. And a lot of it is about the right fabrics."  It’s Fashion Revolution Week, an event designed to mark the anniversary of the Rana Plaza factory disaster and to get us all to question where our clothes actually came from and how they were made. But sustainable style is becoming more than just a short-lived campaign, with some of Hollywood's most famous actresses bringing eco-fashion to the red carpet. Anne Hathaway has spent most of the last month promoting her new film, Colossal, wearing dresses that are either vintage, flea market finds or made from deadstock fabrics, on the red carpet. But for Hathaway, her stylist Penny Lovell says, it wasn’t a difficult, or even a particularly conscious decision to make, as she's addicted to vintage shopping anyway. “Annie wears a lot of vintage fashion in her personal life, really on a day to day basis, so it made total sense to marry this into her work wardrobe” Lovell explains. “She hadn’t done a press tour for a while [Anne has just returned to work after giving birth to her son Jonathan last year] and she just said ‘why don’t we do sustainable this time?’” Hathaway is the second Hollywood actress to ‘go sustainable’ at premieres in recent months, after Emma Watson, who kept a diary of her looks and where they came from on Instagram. Being conscious is now officially cool thanks to these two, which, as cynical as it sounds, could provide the powerful platform that many eco-brands need to step out of the 'niche interest' shadows. “We were both super inspired and impressed with what Emma did,” says Lovell. “We thought it was awesome that she [and Rebecca Corbin-Murray, Watson’s stylist] had commissioned dresses to be made from eco fabrics, but we had a time constraint this time so we decided to start by exploring primarily vintage and archival fashion.” The first sustainable look that Hathaway wore was a Forties-esque chiffon black dress for the Colossal press day, bought for $20 from the Rose Bowl flea market in Los Angeles. “The best thing about that look was that it’s sustainable, it’s affordable, and no one else is going to have that dress because it’s a total chance find,” says Lovell. “Something that Annie also thought was really important was to show young women and girls that you don’t need to spend loads of money to look fantastic. Flea market shopping is so much fun and it's so creative; you can really express yourself and not be worried about cutting things up or customising them.” For their second and third second-hand looks, Hathaway and Lovell approached two bigger designer names, Armani Prive and Vivienne Westwood, and asked to delve into their archives. “I already knew that there are so many pieces that get created that don’t really get worn, so we approached designers to ask if they would loan us some of their archival pieces from old seasons,” Lovell says. “These pieces already exist, they’ve made their environmental footprint.” “Armani gave us the run of the archive. They just said go through the old collections and send us images of things that you like. The dress that she wore was from the second ever Armani Prive collection and it was like a piece of art.” It was the same case with Westwood, who also welcomed the idea with open arms and offered them the chance to borrow anything from her recent collections, leading her to pick a sharp black tuxedo jumpsuit, originally from a 2014 range. “It was so nice to give a design another go-round,” Lovell says. “The logistics have been so much easier too, as there’s no one saying, “oh this sample needs to be with Vogue next week, and we’re not waiting for any production.” Other key looks that the two have sourced together have included a second-hand Givenchy t-shirt, worn for an appearance on the Ellen show, and a 1970s Oscar de la Renta dress, found by chance at the Kit Vintage store in Los Angeles. “It was in such good condition and it was $500, which is amazing for vintage Oscar de la Renta,” says Lovell. “Annie bought it, and we tailored it, but now she has this fun party dress that she’s going to wear to lots more occasions in her personal life, as well as when she did on the red carpet.” As for what the two will do next, Lovell explains that Hathaway is keen to explore and experiment further with the types of sustainable fashion that are available, and may begin to commission more special pieces, like the dress that she asked Adeam designer Hanako Maeda to make from deadstock fabrics, as she gave a speech at the UN. “She’s in an incredible position to raise profiles for different things through her fashion choices - whether that’s by highlighting younger designers, or showing how you can wear vintage pieces. There’s no set plan, we’re just discovering what’s out there at this stage.” “Sustainability seems like the way forward though,” she says, “awareness is growing constantly. It’s been such a good, fun experience for us and I would definitely recommend it to my stylist friends. Neither Annie or I are claiming to be experts, but we’ve become much more aware of it and I don’t think we’re alone in that. Raising awareness, in the end though, will trickle down and create demand.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Cindy Crawford has had a busier fashion month than most but, for once, it hasn’t entirely been her own doing. As the mother of this season’s breakout model star, Kaia Gerber, the tables have been turned somewhat for the supermodelling veteran, as she has chaperoned her 16 year-old daughter through her own first round of catwalk shows. Fear not, though, there have still been plenty major Cindy moments to behold. “I was booked before Kaia - I don’t think Donatella [Versace] even knew that Kaia was doing shows and we had been talking for months about how many of us could get there for that tribute to [her brother] Gianni,” Crawford, 51, tells The Telegraph of how the pair both came to be cast for the same Versace runway show in Milan last month, marking the 20th anniversary of Gianni’s death. Crawford led the finale alongside Naomi Campbell, Claudia Schiffer, Helena Christensen and Carla Bruni, recreating their iconic Nineties catwalk line-up and wearing dresses that looked like liquid gold. “I remember it like it was yesterday,” she says of the first shows the original Supers did together. “I haven’t seen Carla in a long time, but the others - it’s different if you catch up over lunch to standing there on a runway. We all feel part of the Versace family, that brand was such an important part of the beginning of my career.” When her doppelganger daughter was also asked to walk, the family circle was complete. “When Kaia got the part she said, ‘wait, are we going out together?’” Crawford laughs, “I said ‘I hope not, I don’t want to stand next to you, I want to stand with the women my age!’ It was pretty cool, that probably won’t happen again, to be in the same show.” Crawford, who began her modeling career in 1985 and has appeared on around 1,000 magazine covers (Pinterest boasts an edit of her top 500), can afford to be a lot more selective these days about the projects she takes on. This week in Paris, she has celebrated a 20 year-long partnership with Omega; surely the ultimate proof of her staying power? “I’ve been with Omega for such a long time, it’s like we’ve been married longer than I’ve been married to my husband,” she jokes. “Occasionally something new will come up, but it has to tick more boxes off now in order for me to say yes. It’s either a brand I like, or a photographer I like.” It’s easy to understand why 16 year-old Kaia has been influenced by her mother’s glittering success. Crawford says that she would take Kaia out on jobs with her when she was growing up, exposing her to the industry from a young age. “When she was little she liked to play ‘photoshoot’, as she would call it,” she tells us. “She would come onto the shoots with me, so then if she had a friend over I would dress them up in my clothes and I would do hair and makeup, in five minutes. I was stylist, hair and make-up and photographer. We have this entrance to our house that has a bridge and that would be their catwalk.” Crawford has plenty of wisdom to pass on to Kaia, but also more practical advice on things like facial expressions and perfecting a signature walk. “She’s a good student,” Crawford says. “When she decided she wanted to do shows and we agreed, she studied. I told her I’m personally not a fan of the vacant stare and robotic walk - that was not how the models of my generation walked. I said I understand that some designers will tell you ‘don't have an expression’, but my advice is that I think people love seeing personality.” “When you’re walking down the runway you should look like; ‘this is the best dress I’ve ever worn, I feel great in it and don’t you wish you had it’. In the end we’re trying to sell dresses.” The one key difference between her generation of models and their millennial counterparts, she says, is their self, or rather 'selfie', awareness. “All of my daughters friends, they all know their own angles,” she says. “They’re much more sophisticated in that way. I still can’t figure out the selfie thing, maybe that’s because I’m not 16, but I’m like ‘how do you do this?’” Just as any parent would, Crawford speaks with immense pride about her daughter’s achievements so far and also of all the new friends she’s made. “Kaia said, even for the young models, it was super exciting for them to see the supermodel moment,” she says of the gaggle of girls who gathered backstage to watch her, Kaia’s mum, take her turn on the Versace catwalk. “Ten seconds before we [the veterans] were actually nervous! Most of us have kids and we can have a great time being nostalgic about the past, but also catching up about who we all are women that we are today. Everyone’s turned out pretty good.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Cast your eye to the red carpet at most celebrity-filled events and you're most likely to see an elegant Jimmy Choo/ Christian Louboutin/Aquazzura heel. Tasteful and flattering, a spindly-heeled court or elaborately laced sandal has become the natural go-to for offsetting a cocktail dress or couture gown.  But at this week's CFDA Awards, Lena Dunham proposed a new kind of red carpet footwear even more revolutionary than Susan Sarandon's flats at Cannes.  The Girls creator accessorised her monochrome Creatures of the Wind dress with a pair of open-toe pink heels adorned with fluffy rabbits. The $98 'bunny slippers' come courtesy of fledgling New York brand Streetzies, a mother-daughter duo who craft each furry footwear flourish by hand. The business started back in 2004 when artist Pamela Ohlsson made a pair of bunny slippers as a present for her daughter, Copen Aiavolasiti. Ohlsson saw the marketing potential in the eye-catching footwear, which quite clearly chimes with the Playboy Bunny image, and five years later Streetzies was born. On the evening of the CFDAs the company received over 500 emails enquiring about the shoes, according to WWD.  Dunham is not alone in her penchant for what have been dubbed ‘stripper heels.’ Dame Helen Mirren has been using height-boosting Perpex heels as her secret red carpet weapon for years. Back in 2010 she told US chat show host Jay Leno that she used to purchase them in a Hollywood Boulevard stripper shop for $39. She has since told Woman & Home magazine that they she loved them for making her legs "look unbelievably long." Meanwhile, American Vogue recently declared that "boudoir mules" are well and truly back, with their fashion editors fawning over "so-wrong-it’s-got-to-be-good" $34 heels by lingerie website Yandy.  "I love the sassiness of the style—the kitten heel is flirty without being brassy" wrote Marjon Carlos, Vogue's senior fashion writer, "and I can actually walk in the damn things as opposed to their seven-inch sisters...they'll go perfectly with cropped denim and sundresses this summer when I, inevitably, hit the dance floor in them." Stripper heels aside, Dunham’s bunny slippers are only the latest rule-breaking footwear to grace the red carpets this spring. Both Alexa Chung and Cressida Bonas have offset feminine floral dresses with humble black ankle boots. Not embellished heeled styles mind, but unabashedly boyish boots. Why the move towards heavy-duty footwear from a fashion plate who counts ballet flats as her signature style? You only have to gaze at London’s dreary skies to know the method behind Chung’s boot choice.  At the Dior Cruise 2017 show, the 32-year-old teamed her embellished Dior mini dress with patent lace-up boot and a cropped navy peacoat -  weather conscious accessories that lent a hard-edge to her look. At the Royal Academy Summer Exhibition party last night, meanwhile, Cressida Bonas rubbed shoulders with the art crowd in a printed mini, bulky boots and a leather jacket. Her studded and fringed footwear were not only warm and comfy (always important), but added a grungy tilt to her otherwise good girl get-up. In this daring footwear climate, why stop at biker boots and stripper heels? This is what we imagine DJ Cleo Wade to have thought before heading to a Burberry NYC party in a silk slip dress and trainers last night. Yes, trainers! In a move that can only evoke images of Lily Allen circa 2006, Wade threw the rule book well and truly out of the window, and took her adidas Super Stars for a night out with New York’s fashion elite. This is perhaps only one step further away from Julia Roberts and Kristen Stewart at Cannes, who chose to forgo shoes altogether at points on the Cannes red carpet this spring. Whatever next!  Update, on January 5: Photographer Steven Klein has commented on the contentious images of Kylie Jenner for the first time in an interview with W Magazine. Asked if he felt the images were misunderstood, he replied: "People are always going to misunderstand things. It’s human nature. That I accept. It comes with the territory of doing anything of value. In regards to the pictures of Kylie, they are based on pictures I did with Tom Ford a long time ago in W [from the November 2005 issue], where we used very human-like dolls. Kylie and I discussed treating her like a doll. What happened when I shot them for W with Tom was that the dolls were too heavy to carry, so I had to put them in a wheelchair to get them around. I often revisit pictures I’ve done before. Unfortunately, people see things in a personal way, whereas I see things visually. To me, it was just playing with this idea of the pseudo-living doll, the different positions and setups I could do with her. When you do things for magazines, you need to call attention to it somehow so people pay attention to what you’re saying visually, but I never do things for shock value. But what’s interesting is that since then I’ve received a lot of pictures from girls who are in wheelchairs who’ve done their own renditions of the pictures, in a positive way. So maybe for a girl who is in a wheelchair, she might say, ‘Look how beautiful she looks. How great is it that a girl in a wheelchair looks sexy and cool.’ So I always look at the positive aspect of things. You can find negativity in anything.  “I think it can come across as being frivolous, what I do, and what fashion can do for women in a professional capacity,” says Isabel Spearman, picking her words carefully. “But what you wear to work can make a huge difference – not just to how you’re perceived, but to how you feel.” Spearman is a brand and image consultant, advising (mostly female) professionals working at senior levels in the corporate, often unforgiving, world. “They’re at a point in their careers where they need help with image: they’re suddenly doing lots of public facing – speeches, presentations, pitches. My job is to make sure that they feel confident in whatever they’re wearing so they can focus on the work.” First, she interrogates a new client’s working environment: do they travel extensively and, therefore, need a wardrobe that can be thrown in a washing machine, not full of dry-clean only dresses? Or spend most of the time around a meeting room table, where in reality the top half is mostly on display? Then comes an assessment of the client’s existing wardrobe, to test her comfort zone and analyse what works well on her body shape. (Spearman suggests every woman should analyse their own power outfit to assess whether it’s the fit, colour or fabric that makes them veer to that instinctively before a difficult day at work – and then replicate it). Then she puts together suggestions that help to create a wardrobe worthy of a modern, outward-facing career woman. Some might see styling as a depressingly singular place to start for women hoping to boost their careers – but it would be naive to ignore the fact that, given first impressions are made within three seconds of meeting someone, we communicate through our clothes. (And, given the latest Forbes’ Fortune 500 list recognised only 32 female CEOs in America earlier this month, arguably women need all the help they can get navigating the male-dominated corporate world.) “I think what’s important is that clothes empower and reassure you; not to feel – ashamed is too strong a word but –frustrated by putting together an outfit,” is how Spearman puts it, arguing that if you’re not worrying about whether the dress you’re wearing is too short you can focus on the job. But if you are? Well, she’s here to help, with a new weekly column in the Telegraph dissecting workwear dress codes and offering a modern take on power dressing. Spearman is singularly qualified for the job, having started her career at accessory brand Anya Hindmarch and honing her craft in what is quite possibly the most public of arenas: politics. She spent six years working in Downing Street as special adviser to then prime minister David Cameron’s wife, Samantha – a role that saw her overseeing the de facto First Lady’s charity work, foreign trips and media handling, as well as helping put together a wardrobe that was fitting for a global stage. (Sometimes that meant nipping into Zara for some emergency tights; other times coordinating with Michelle Obama’s team on the dress code for a state dinner at The White House.) “I suppose it was creating a brand, the ‘Sam Cam’ brand,” Spearman reflects. “It was taking things I learned from those years in fashion, from a branding perspective, and putting them into action: a lot of what we did with Sam was imaging, and making sure that she came across the way that she wanted to come across.” There’s no denying that thinking through your outfit is important – especially when the whole world is watching. You only have to look at the way people overlaid the Queen’s blue and yellow hat with a pro-Brexit message last week, or the furore caused by those leather trousers worn by Theresa May, to realise the potency – and perils. On the latter, Spearman is sympathetic. “I do think you should make the most of what you’ve got, and May has got fabulous legs,” she laughs. “That’s my take on it! She dresses brilliantly, in a very safe, strong way, which is how she is.” But she also acknowledges that the style challenges facing only our second female prime minister are different from those that David Cameron faced – little more than a jibe about some dodgy beach shorts every summer. “David cared what he wore in the way that it had to be appropriate for the job he was doing, but he wasn’t too fussed about bad press on holiday because he had more important things to think about,” she says. “I think he found it quite entertaining.” Is it right that women in politics are judged by their wardrobes in a way that men aren’t then, I ask her? Spearman is pragmatic: “As long as the tabloids want to write stories about it, I don’t think there’s any way of avoiding it. I think as a woman in the political field you have more choices of what to wear; therefore, you are slightly more newsworthy and you have to be quite careful. No, it’s not fair – but I’m afraid that’s where we are.” It’s a lesson Spearman learnt when she went to work at Downing Street – and found her own wardrobe under scrutiny. “I definitely had to tone it down a little bit,” Spearman says of leaving the fashion world for an environment where wearing lipstick was considered making a statement. “In time, I actually enjoyed dressing in a more corporate way because you could just go to work in a nice dress and heels and not have to worry too much about whether your outfit was in vogue that month.” Still, Spearman says she found finding style advice for working women who wanted to look professional but not dull – not to mention the pieces themselves – was tricky; hence her starting up her consultancy firm. “My clients probably don’t want to wear Celine – they want to wear a really well-cut trouser, dress or suit that will fit in, but that they feel great in.” In her arsenal are a multitude of Joseph blazers, heels you can walk in and well-cut dresses that travel well (though she always has a clothes steamer to hand). As for what a working woman should always keep in her desk drawer? “A spare pair of tights, because there is nothing worse – well, of course there are many more things worse but if you have to go into a big meeting and you have a ladder in your tights… well, that’s a sure-fire way of killing your confidence.” Even in the corporate world, however, Spearman insists there are times when you can up the fashion ante. She recalls a meeting with Carla Bruni, the former French first lady, about a forthcoming trip to Downing Street by Nicolas Sarkozy, the then president. “It was just me and 10 of them. I arrived in an Emilia Wickstead leather full skirt, with black high heels and red lipstick, and I swear, it helped. The French team were equally as groomed – and so I didn’t feel underdressed.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Power dressers of the world unite - and observe a maestro. The Queen has been grappling with this thorniest of dress dilemmas most of her life, and since her coronation in 1953, she has, as subsequent power dressers might put it, “owned” it. A number of her trade secrets are revealed in Fashioning a Reign: 90 Years of  Style From the Queen’s Wardrobe, an intriguing exhibition of 150 of her outfits that opened at Buckingham Palace this weekend - part of a trilogy of exhibitions examining her style. (One opened in April in Holyrood House in Edinburgh; the other will be coming to Windsor in September). The Queen, we are often told, is not much concerned with fashion – although fashion is obsessed with her. Even at 90, with her silk headscarves and box-pleated woollen skirts, she continues to inspire designers – the latest is Gucci’s Alessandro Michele, who explicitly referenced her in a collection he showed in Westminster Abbey in May. But as a woman of opinions she cannot voice aloud, she must surely find the language of clothes both interesting, useful and infinitely flexible. Privately, the clothes she wears are not so different from other upper class 90-year-olds. Publicly – well, how many other 90-year-olds bestride the world’s stage?   The calibrations of every outfit the Queen has ever worn in public – the focus of this exhibition – are so finely deliberated they might have been set out by the Foreign Office. There’s the yellow day dress she wore in Australia, a graceful nod to its national colour and the green gown in Ethiopia, picking out the green of its flag. There is also the sweet joyousness of the Angela Kelly-designed beaded primrose coloured wool crepe coat and dress (with silk-rose adorned hat) that she wore to the wedding of Kate and William in 2011 – on display for the first time. In part, our fascination for the way the Queen dresses has always rested in her uniqueness. How does one dress for one’s role as head of the armed forces? Head of chivalry? Head of the commonwealth? The exhibition has examples of all these, as well as the ATS uniform she wore during the War and some of her ball-gowns. Observing her navigate a path between her personal tastes and her sense of duty, as well as analysing her success at remaining relevant across ten decades (without resorting to wearing hippie beads in the 1970s or athleisure in 2016) are two of the delights of the exhibition. In her youth, both Princess Elizabeth and her younger sister clearly enjoyed fashion. Once Queen however, she had to develop an image of constancy and gravity that transcended fashion – more subtly than that other Queen Elizabeth, with her white face mask, red wigs and jewel encrusted farthingales, but no less effectively. Elizabeth ll’s carapaces, like her Tudor namesake’s, include jewelled gowns and vivid hues. Speaking of the latter – her fear knows no bounds. The eye-socking neon green dress she wore on her official birthday earlier this summer was so bright it saw hashtag #neonat90 trending on social media. A sure sign if one was ever needed that this is a woman who is extremely savvy about the power of clothes. “A very personal dress which had to fulfil a very public occasion,” is how Caroline de Guitaut, the exhibition's curator, describes the unique predicament of Princess Elizabeth’s wedding gown. Norman Hartnell, who had long been entrusted with creating dresses for members of the Royal Family, was a natural choice. “It was 1947 and rationing was still in force and yet after all those dark days of the Second World War, people felt a sense of renewal, a sense of hope and this was embodied in a young beautiful princess and her handsome husband-to-be.”  So how to bring joy to the nation, but also encapsulate the romance of the royal couple, in a dress? Hartnell chose Sandro Botticelli’s Primavera masterpiece as his inspiration. “The cut of the dress is actually very simple but then there’s the embellishment - beautiful embroidered flowers and foliage to evoke Spring. It also has a court train which hangs from the shoulders and is 9ft long, made of silk tulle. It is exactly what Hartnell, in consultation with Princess Elizabeth imagined.” “Britain was becoming very dynamic and strong in the field of design, industry, architecture and fashion; it was a moment of strength in country,” explains de Guitaut of the social backdrop to the Queen’s coronation on 2nd June 1953. Once more, it was the Royal dress which needed to reflect that mood - but there was the added challenge that the coronation service would be televised across the world. “Hartnell realised that the dress would be under international scrutiny so I think that weighed very heavily on his mind,” says de Guitaut.  Hartnell applied his experience of working with film stars like Marlene Dietrich and Vivien Leigh to the task of designing the coronation gown. “I think the most remarkable thing that people don’t realise is that it’s much more colourful than the white and gold you would expect,” de Guitaut says of the bright embroidery which is layered with emblems from across the United Kingdom and the Commonwealth; maple leaves for Canada, wheat sheaves for Pakistan and lotus flowers for South Africa. “All of these contribute colour which I think perhaps people won’t appreciate until they see it in the exhibition.” The Queen has undertaken almost 300 foreign visits during her reign and getting dressed for these trips is no easy feat. Amongst the new exhibits are examples of outfits worn on tours from the 1950s to 1970s and what unites them is a trilogy of considerations. “It’s about understanding the climate, understanding the engagement to be undertaken and weaving in elements of diplomacy,” says De Guitaut. She points to a turquoise Norman Hartnell design which was worn at the Montreal Olympics in 1976 and is embellished with suitably Olympian clusters of rings. There are also numerous examples of The Queen’s outfits being shaped by religious custom. A look created for an engagement in Saudi Arabia in 1979 struck the right balance so as to ensure Her Majesty was as respectfully covered as possible but also clearly visible in the crowds. “This full-length day dress with matching jacket and Frederick Fox turban-hat absolutely covered The Queen, but at the same time because it’s in a beautiful, vivid blue marking her as individual and eye-catching,” de Guitaut remarks. It’s no surprise that a dress made for The Queen to sky-dive out of a helicopter into the 2012 Olympic opening ceremony was thought through. But the most crucial element of the Bond dress might surprise you. “The philosophy behind the design I believe is to have something in a colour that wouldn’t be in any way representative of any of the countries participating” explains de Guitaut. “So that’s why the colour is quite unique; that sort of peachy, coraly, pink.” The dress was designed by Angela Kelly, the Queen’s personal assistant and senior dresser, who has played an integral role in managing Her Majesty’s wardrobe since she took on the role in 2002. Many of her own designs, or ones she has overseen, appear in the exhibition - including that infamous neon green outfit by Stewart Parvin, which sparked a 134% rise in the sales of similar colours on the high street. “I think Kelly has really contributed a great deal, by producing clothes still in these bright fresh colours but slightly adjusting the tailoring and the proportions of The Queen’s clothes, so as to ensure there’s a continuity to her very elegant look,” says de Guitaut.  Goldie Hawn turned 71 yesterday, celebrating in style over the weekend by spending time with family and friends, meditating a lot, and, naturally, having one hell of a girls’ night out. Rounding up friends including Chrome Hearts founder Laurie Lynn Stark, and, of course, her doppelgänger daughter, the 37 year-old actress Kate Hudson, Goldie looked amazing as she hit the town at Los Angeles’ new hotspot, Catch, wearing a tie-front slip dress (arms, legs and cleavage out, of course) with statement earrings , smoky eye makeup and a signature blowdry. Mariah Carey even popped over to sing Happy Birthday. But then, why wouldn’t Goldie celebrate her birthday in this way, posting party pictures on her Instagram page and radiating happiness? She is the champion of eternally great party style, after all. Goldie first began to experiment with her personal party look in the Sixties, when she made the pixie haircut and babydoll silhouette the staples of her boho teen wardrobe. Her look was often mimicked by her on-screen characters and, as she won an Oscar for her role as Toni in 1969’s Cactus Flower and enjoyed all of the party buzz that came with it, American Vogue hailed her to be one of the decade’s greatest It girls. In the Seventies, the newly-made movie star hit Studio 54 with the best of them, her wardrobe of floral dresses and slinky halters moving into the party dressing trends of the disco era. She had her first two children and achieved national treasure status with two TV specials performing show tunes in sequins. It wasn't until the Eighties, however, that she settled on her cocktailwear signatures; textural black fabrics, metallics, big hair, big jewellery and big personality. She’s honed a truly personal style ethos, an ageless formula with plenty of va va voom. Many would say that, at 71, there are dresses that you shouldn’t wear, heels that are too young for you, or bars that you shouldn’t really be going to because you should know better by now. But Hawn has lived a lot, laughed a lot and tried a lot of different party outfits over the years - experience that has only made her party style better now than ever before. So what’s she teaching us? To live life to the fullest and not give a damn what anyone thinks? Yep. To have fun with fashion and ignore all the rules that exist on what is ‘age appropriate’? Certainly. And, perhaps most importantly, whatever your age, there’s always a party worth leaving the house for and you can always find something to wear to it.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  You can’t keep those Jenner sisters down. Kendall and Kylie may have had a tumultuous year – their dad, former Olympian Bruce Jenner, very publicly made the transition to Caitlyn Jenner, and both have found themselves the subject of various scandalous headlines – but that’s not going to stop them rounding it off with a bang. And what better way than a capsule collection for Topshop, one of the world’s most beloved fashion retailers. Following their hugely successful debut collection, which promptly sold out when it was released in June, the sisters have decided to design a Christmas offering for their legions of fans. "We're so excited to be designing another line for Topshop,” say the Jenners. “This collection reflects our favourite holiday fashion. We made sure to include a unique selection of pieces, from glamorous to edgy. Each one is special for the holiday season and captures the perfect party look mixed with effortless LA street style." The girls will be celebrating the festive season with their famous family – they are, of course, the half-sisters Kim, Kourtney and Khloe Kardashian and daughters of Kris Jenner – and are wishing for something money can’t buy under their designer tree: “lots and lots of love for our family, friends and fans!” That’s what they all say when they’ve already got a wardrobe full of Birkins and more Saint Laurent/Celine/Balmain than you can shake a stick at. Not that we’re bitter.  There's a trend emerging in The Duchess of Cambridge's Canadian tour wardrobe. Much like Sophie Gregoire-Trudeau, the wife of Canada's Prime Minister Justin Trudeau who has made it her mission to promote Canadian talent, The Duchess has been favouring the work of British designers so far this week, but in colours which carry that all-important diplomatic message.  For a glittering reception at Government House in Victoria last night, The Duchess added a new designer to her wardrobe, opting for a red dress by British design duo, Preen by Thornton Bregazzi. With its nipped-in waist, draped off-shoulder neckline and full skirt, the dress evoked a chic, mid-century silhouette. The £1000 dress was available in limited sizes on Matchesfashion.com but has already sold out this morning. The style-still available in black- is a commercial piece from Preen's pre-Autumn collection which was inspired by Deborah, Duchess of Devonshire, the last of the Mitford sisters who presided over the grand Chatsworth House and was at the centre of high society throughout the latter half of the 20th century.  One 1952 portrait of Debo, as she was affectionately known, was taken by Norman Parkinson and shows the young Duchess in a sweetheart necklined black gown with the distinctively full skirts of the time. The style worn by The Duchess  of Cambridge 64 years later represents a modern skew on that look.  The dress's red hue was no doubt a nod to Canada's national colours while The Duchess added an extra element of host nation flattery by pinning  The Queen's maple-leaf brooch to the dress.  The brooch was first made in 1939 as a gift from The Queen's father Edward VI to her mother, Queen Elizabeth as they set off on a tour of Canada. Ever since, it has been a mainstay of royal tour wardrobes; The Queen and The Duchess of Cornwall have often worn the sparkling piece and Kate was loaned it for her first tour to Canada in 2011.  Justin Thornton and Thea Bregazzi celebrate the 20th year of their design label this year. The husband and wife hail originally from the Isle of Man, where they met while studying on an art foundation course. In the 90s they opened a popular shop in Notting Hill where Janet Jackson and Kate Moss would come to buy up their pieces (they even created skinny trousers which Moss would buy in bulk).  Preen is now a go-to label for high-profile women wanting to look polished yet interesting. Michelle Obama and Samantha Cameron are both fans of their graphic prints and ultra-flattering cuts. Of seeing Kate wearing their design in Canada, the duo told The Telegraph, “We are absolutely thrilled to see The Duchess of Cambridge wearing our Finella dress. It was a total surprise! The dress is designed to be both classic yet modern, perfect for The Duchess!” Earlier this year, in an interview with The Telegraph , Thronton and Bregazzi discussed the invitation they had received to meet Michelle Obama at The White House. ‘We were allowed two guests, so, of course, we took our mums,’ Thea said. ‘She was saying to each of them, “I bet you’re one proud mom!” and they were like, “Yes, yes, we really are!”’ ‘Sometimes I just think they have no idea what we do,’ said Justin, ‘but when it’s on the cover of the newspaper or a trip like that, they’re really proud.’    No doubt there will be newspaper covers galore for saving today.       © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We may have just reached peak ‘Athleisure’  courtesy of Kendall Jenner. The 20-year-old supermodel sashayed into  LAX airport yesterday wearing a £2,000 tracksuit. Not just any tracksuit, but a luxe retro version first spotted on Edie Campbell on the catwalk at Chloé's SS16 show. The burgundy and camel set features racing stripes down the arms, legs and chest, and is made from (mostly) silk.  The funnel-neck sweater retails for £1,1225, and the wide-legged trousers for £870 on Net-a-Porter, adding up to a cool £2,095. Jenner’s luxe leisurewear follows her stint at Coachella festival wearing wisps of crochet, lace and little else. So, Chloé’s tracksuit must have been the perfect sartorial antidote to a weekend’s worth of scantily clad partying, right? Wrong. Unlike mere mortals who might turn to tracky bottoms in a hungover quest for comfort, Jenner teamed hers with heeled suede pumps and a Givenchy tote. If Victoria Beckham had been cast as Sporty, rather than Posh Spice, we imagine this might have been the end result. Silk tracksuits aside, there’s much to be said for leisurewear when travelling. Smart joggers and sweatshirts are crease-proof, comfortable and can actually look smart. Look for navy, grey and beige separates from the likes of Gap, Uniqlo, Boden and Joseph, and remember to keep the silhouette loose. Athleisure is different to sportswear in that it is cosy and light years away from Lycra legging territory. You're unlikely to catch anyone actually, y'know, working out in it.  How to choose your own luxe tracksuit? Avoid washing out your figure by opting for trousers with elasticated ankles (this will highlight the daintiest part of the leg area). A small, colour-pop cross-body bag will also break up the look, and act as a useful pouch to store travelling essentials in. Take a tip from blogger Alex Steadman and opt for clean plimsolls, rather than Kendall’s preferred choice of heels- much better for negotiating airport escalators. A pair of bright white, or white-soled plimsolls, acts as a punctuation mark and draws the eye down the leg area. So, even if you have opted for wide-strides instead of elasticated joggers, there is an end point to the all that fabric. A word of warning in sweater territory. Zip-up funnel-necks err into 90s trend territory, so if you’re not comfortable emulating Kappa’s old school style, stick to round-neck jumpers with minimal motifs or logos on. Flying long-haul was never more agreeable....  So often older women make that mistake of feeling they need to reach for beige, taupe and any other non-descript hue that will see them blending into the background. Not so for The Queen, who chose a bold neon green outfit by Stewart Parvin for today's milestone Trooping The Colour - celebrating both her 90th birthday and the fact she’s now Britain’s longest serving sovereign. Within minutes of Her Majesty appearing, the choice of colour was being commentated on. Hashtags #neonat90 and  #highvishighness swept social media, as others worked out the exact Pantone she was wearing - #75e41b, for the record. Or, put another way, the exact green used by Apple for the text message iPhone icon. The Queen is wearing #75e41b according to #Chroma, @softpress pic.twitter.com/SwbrZ81qLo But such a millennial-ish reaction perhaps misses the poignancy of The Queen’s outfit choice. "I have to be seen to be believed," she once famously said. And a colourful wardrobe - one that means she can be seen even from the cheap seats - plays a key role in fulfilling this mantra. In 2012 British Vogue magazine published a graphic tracking the bold spectrum of colour the Queen wore across the course of a year. The results were illuminating: 29 per cent blue, 13 per cent pink (a flattering,traditional fairytale colour she chooses for events where she knows she’ll meet children) and 11 per cent green. According to her personal dresser Angela Kelly, The Queen will never wear green if she’s set to be photographed against a lawn or woodland; but it’s the colour she turned to when touching down in Dublin on her landmark visit to Ireland in 2011. That highly logical, very formulaic attitude towards clothes - and the sophisticated understanding of their power - is no doubt what was behind The Queen’s bold block colour today, too. (And, incidentally, one her granddaughter-in-law Kate appears to have learnt from; both women have an exceptionally methodical approach to their outfits which while not necessarily exciting in the truest fashion sense always look impeccable.) It is touching too that on such a momentous occasion The Queen turned to one of her most trusted designers, Stewart Parvin - a British dressmaker who was approached nine years ago to help make the monarch’s wardrobe more modern. "Designing for someone who looks so wonderful in clothes is very easy,” he has said of their partnership. He’s got a point. There aren’t many people - let alone 90-year-olds - who can pull off neon green with such aplomb. As for the rose-pink lipstick - at 90 that's really rather daring and suggests that Her Majesty, often thought to be uninterested in fashion, derives considerable pleasure from shaping her look, and from the pleasure it gives others.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Was there ever a more outstanding look than a scarlet power suit? Amal Clooney made sure that she was visible, nay, impossible to ignore, as she returned to work yesterday, almost four months after giving birth to twins Ella and Alexander, her first children with husband George Clooney. Arriving at the United Nations in New York, the human rights lawyer attended a Security Council meeting where she proposed (and was granted) an investigation into the Islamic State group and the crimes they had committed against the Yazidi people. Clooney has been representing Nadia Murad (a Yazidi human rights activist who was captured and tortured by IS) for over a year now, so this moment was a pivotal one in her case and her career. As such, Clooney made sure that she dressed the part in a skirt suit by Bottega Veneta, accessorising with a Michael Kors work bag and Manolo Blahnik heels. As back-to-work, post-maternity leave looks go, it was perfectly on-point. Clooney often reaches for her boldest suits when she has a key speech to make or a big case to win - last year she wore vivid red, orange and blue Max Mara suits for a series of meetings on behalf of Murad, and she has previously turned to tailored sheath dresses by Gucci and Michael Kors on occasions when she needs to cut a professional, sharp figure on the podium. “The UN has become a strangely important barometer for the current state of power dressing,” The Telegraph’s Bethan Holt reported earlier this week, noting that Theresa May, Malala Yousafzai and more have been out to make sartorial statements alongside their political ones. The strongest takeaway from the week so far is that many seem to believe choosing a popping ‘power hue’ may help their work efforts to pack a greater punch. Like Clooney, Queen Maxima of The Netherlands also opted for top-to-toe red, accessorising her trouser suit with suede heels and a handbag in the same shade as she met with the UN’s Secretary General, while Queen Rania of Jordan looked striking in pure white as she made a speech highlighting the progress that has been made to help prevent poverty around the world. The shoutiest of them all, though, has to have been Melania Trump. In a fuchsia puff-sleeve dress by Spanish label Delpozo, she gave her first ever address to a UN luncheon, encouraging world leaders to think about their children when planning for the future. It was an important moment for Trump in her relatively new role, as the UN is a platform where many First Ladies before her have advanced their ideas and policy agendas, establishing themselves as leaders of change. So returning to our opening query, perhaps we have a new answer; Yes, a dress akin to a pink highlighter pen will make one stand out even more than a scarlet suit. But perhaps Trump needed to throw an even brighter spotlight on her new cause than the established Clooney did, hence why she reached for the neons.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  A model suing Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump's modelling agency will find out later this month if her $225,000 (£158,000) case can proceed. Jamaica-born Alexia Palmer is accusing Trump Model Management - the talent agency founded by the billionaire businessman in Manhattan in 1999 – of racketeering, breach of contract, mail fraud and violating wage laws for immigrants. The lawsuit was originally filed in October 2014; a judge in the U.S District Court has until the end of the month to decide whether a pending motion by Trump’s agency to dismiss the case can go through. If the judge decides that Palmer’s case can proceed, it could put Trump’s immigrant employment practices under an unflattering microscope. Palmer, who was discovered in a Jamaican model agency’s Caribbean Model Search when she was a teenager and became the first Jamaican model to star in Vogue without being signed to an international fashion label, moved to New York in 2011. She claims that Trump’s company lied to the federal government by documenting on her work visa application that she’d be paid a yearly $75,000 salary while living in the US. Instead, Palmer states that she worked exclusively for Trump Model Management from 2011 to 2013 and only received a total of $3,880 in pay over the three years after the agency deducted a 20 percent handling fee and various “insignificant expenses”. Reuters today reports that Trump’s lawyers have called the case "frivolous" and "without merit", with court documents showing that Palmer’s work via the agency only culminated in 10 days of assignments over the three years and that she was more than adequately compensated. “At the end of the day, this model just didn’t have a successful career, and we fully expect to win,” said Lawrence Rosen, a lawyer for Trump Model Management. Palmer's lawyer, Naresh Gehi, says his client was cheated of earnings and seduced by a life of glamour that never materialised. "The visa application the company filed with the government requires that people are paid the full amount," Gehi said. "It’s a requirement.” It is not clear whether Palmer is now represented by a rival agency or still working in the industry. Controversial Republican Trump has pledged a three-point immigration reform plan to ‘make America great again’ if he becomes president. In it he states his mission to put American workers first by hiring them over illegal immigrants, and argues the influx of foreign workers ‘holds down salaries, keeps unemployment high, and makes it difficult for poor and working class American.’ Opponents have already said such a policy is hypocritical, citing reports that suggest Trump’s vast network of hotels across America have favoured foreign workers for menial jobs over US-born residents. Palmer was briefly signed to Models1 in London in 2011 after being discovered. On the agency's blog, she revealed that before she was scouted, she harboured aspirations of being a bank manager: "I love accounting. I’m studying business and accounting at home." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge began her visit to Poland yesterday with a rather blatantly diplomatic fashion gesture, dressing in the white and red colours of the country's flag. But for a party last night hosted by the British ambassador to Poland in celebration of The Queen's birthday, the Duchess opted for a more subtle - but no less striking - nod of fashionable diplomacy.  Kate selected a white midi-length cocktail dress with architectural black detailing by one of Poland's best-known designers, Gosia Baczynska, to wear for the evening's festivities. "Until the last moment, I didn’t know which outfit the Duchess was going to wear," Baczynska exclusively told The Telegraph today, adding that she'd barely slept thanks to her emotionally charged 24 hours. "I had some expectation that she would wear it but I couldn’t be sure so was extremely happy and excited when I saw her in my dress." Unlike many of the designers Kate chooses, Baczynska was - fittingly - present at the reception to which the Duchess wore her dress. "It is an honour and privilege to dress such a style icon," she says. "Moreover, I had a chance to meet Kate and speak to her. It was a privilege to meet and talk to the Duchess." This week's trip is designed to be a masterclass in soft diplomacy, strengthening ties between the UK and Poland ahead of Brexit. So while the dress is an undoubtedly glamorous statement, it is also a symbol of respect and support for the Polish fashion industry from one of the world's most famous women. "I’m really happy and proud that Kate has chosen a Polish brand,"  Baczynska acknowledges. "It means a lot for me and I think for Polish fashion industry as well." The dress is a bold choice from the Duchess who has shown greater willingness to experiment with her style over the past year. The jagged, black-edge pleats on the bottom part of the dress offer a playful contrast to the delicate floral black applique at the waist while the deep v-neckline framed her pearl necklace - debuted during a visit to Paris in March - elegantly.  In his speech The Duke said there is much to celebrate about the warmth of the UK 🇬🇧 Poland 🇵🇱 relationship today. pic.twitter.com/BrPjYBx0lR The dress was a bespoke creation for the Duchess, which Baczynska and her team have been working on for the past four weeks after Natasha Archer, the Duchess's PA and stylist, got in touch asking for a lookbook. "I got excited and started preparing the selected looks. I also knew I should keep this information a secret. I stayed in touch with Kate’s assistant and we were contacting each other about details," she says, clearly mindful of the discreet operations behind Kate's meticulously planned tour-drobes.  "The collection is inspired by myths and legends from Polish culture and folklore,"Baczynska adds. "The dress's folds in particular are made to remind of thistles. The dress was personalized especially for the Duchess after they were interested in this sample from our lookbook." The 51 year-old designer, who says that she prefers to work on a body or mannequin rather than sketching, emphasises that her design approach combines cultural references with what will feel right for her clients. "I was inspired by art, craft and tradition. The most important thing for me is quality which means really good fabric and realisation," she says. "I would like women who wear my outfits to feel special and modern. Classy and a little bit rebellious." Although Baczynska is now well-and-truly Warsaw based and a go-to designer for many of Poland's wealthiest and most famous women, she does have ties to London. Her biography reveals that she gave up studying Fine Arts to move to London in 1991. She then spent time working for a seamstress and honing her dressmaking skills in the city before returning to her hometown of Wroclaw to begin her business.  Baczynska - who also recently dressed Halle Berry in a silver sequinned mini dress - describes on her website how her fashion ethos is a "a revolt against the greyness that surrounded me" in the post-Soviet era. It will surely have impressed the Duchess that Baczynska began her business with very little funding, finding success through hard work and good reputation.  The sophisticated, modern look is one of the Duchess's standout diplomatic fashion choices, pitching perfectly to Baczynska's chic yet slightly rebellious intentions. It rivals the tweed Chanel suit which she selected in Paris in March or the blue and white patterned shift dress by Mumbai-born Naeem Khan which she chose for an historic photograph in front of the Taj Mahal last year. Last night was undoubtedly a royal fashion moment and for Baczynska personally,  it will be an evening to remember forever.       © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The little-known Italian brand Parosh experienced the greatest PR boost in its 25 year history on Monday, when American actress Meghan Markle chose to wear one of its green fitted dresses to announce her engagement to Prince Harry. As thousands of fans tuned in again this morning to see the couple arrive for their first day of duties in Nottingham, many of the world’s designers will have also been on standby again, just in case the royal-to-be has been shopping, incognito, in one of their stores. Almost overnight, a thumbs up from Markle has become the most sought-after endorsement a brand can get and today’s chosen ones included a mix of her go-to American and Canadian labels, with some newly discovered British brands too. The double-breasted military maxi coat by Canadian outerwear label Mackage was an old favourite, worn frequently on cold dashes through Heathrow Airport as she flew in and out to meet with her then-boyfriend. Everything else was new, and British - save for a black, high neck knit by Austrian brand Wolford. Markle’s beige skirt was bought from the cult label Joseph, priced at £595. Sunderland-born creative director Louise Trotter has worked hard to reinvigorate the brand in recent years, bringing it onto the London Fashion Week schedule and making effortlessly cool pieces to covet. “It was a total surprise,” Trotter, fresh off the Eurostar, tells The Telegraph of the spotting. “I’m thrilled that Meghan chose to wear Joseph on her first public official outing with Prince Harry. The skirt is from the autumn 2017 runway collection and is a take on a classic chino military skirt that's sliced, with added pleats and volume.” It is perhaps a conscious choice from Markle to opt for a British brand that the Duchess of Cambridge has rarely worn before (her last appearance in Joseph was in 2013) as headline accusations of a copy-Kate would have been a distraction from the day. Can you even imagine the furore if she had worn, say, a fit-and-flare Alexander McQueen dress?  Similarly, despite a well-documented new-found passion for Somerset-made Mulberry bags, Markle kept things understated by choosing a tote by Edinburgh-based Strathberry. Ironically, Markle's tri-colour design is only sold at the department store Saks on New York’s Fifth Avenue, but the brand has confirmed to The Telegraph that they sent her the style a few weeks ago. With prices starting at £225 for their luxury leather bags, she is perhaps showing an understanding that she needs to give fans a glimpse of something they will be able to buy themselves. That particular colour combination has apparently sold out within 7 minutes, and indeed, Strathberry should now brace itself for bumper sales in the run up to Christmas.  "We are thrilled and honoured to see Meghan Markle carrying our Strathberry Midi Tote," a spokesperson for the brand told us this morning. "It was a fantastic surprise to see that Meghan selected one of our core Strathberry styles to carry on her first royal engagement. We are delighted at the news of her and Harry’s engagement and wish them all the best for this exciting period." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  To say stylist, street style star and co-founder of influencer talent agency Social Zoo Direct, Pernille Teisbaeck, has had a busy 2017 would be an understatement. So far the stylish Scandinavian, who has over 489,000 followers on Instagram, has had a baby, got hitched and published a book (aptly titled Dress Scandinavian: Style Your Life and Wardrobe the Danish Way) and there are still four months of the year to go. ''We're also renovating our house,'' she tells The Telegraph, ''so it's been a crazy year.'' Teisbaeck married partner Philip Lotko in a seaside ceremony on an island off the coast of her native Denmark in as picturesque a setting as you would expect. And the dress, which was a pearl-laden Vera Wang gown, was equally as beautiful. But despite her impeccable taste, she says that choosing a wedding gown wasn't straight forward. ''I was already pregnant last year, so the crazy hormones went into my mind and I couldn’t figure out what I wanted to wear or how I wanted to look,'' she recounts. So how did she eventually land on the dress of her dreams? ''I was looking at all these different blogs and Tumblrs, and I found this dress,'' she remembers. ''I wasn't sure if it was from an old collection, but I found out that it was Vera Wang and current, so I contacted her straight away and asked her to make it.'' Teisbaeck paired the exquisite embellished creation with custom Manolo Blahnik shoes made from the same material as the dress, and wore her hair pulled back into a loose tousled bun at the nape of her neck - emanating the type of nonchalance, typical to Scandi style, that she's known for. On the subject of why she thinks Scandinavian style has gained to much traction in recent years, Teisbaeck accredits an ''effortless chicness'' and to it being ''wearable, comfortable and classic, and not particularly seasonal.'' ''When you look at Italy or Spain for example, women dress themselves in a much more feminine, sexy and colourful way,'' she continues. ''And the way we dress ourselves is slightly more androgynous. There’s something about not showing your boobs or your butt that is kind of appealing because there’s something left to the imagination.'' Teisbaeck, who is often in jeans and an oversize blazer, or a pleated skirt and a chunky knit, has mastered the art of looking simultaneously elegant but comfortable and polished but laid-back. ''For me it’s about feeling super comfortable in what you’re wearing, and then you have that 'glow','' she describes. ''When you put something on and go out the door and you're insecure because the dress is too short or the pants are too tight, you just don't have that same 'glow'.'' What are her top tips for tapping into her strain of Scandi style? ''Less is more,'' she says. ''When I think my outfit has too many things going on, I will look at myself and take something off to make it a little calmer.'' Although that's not to say her ensembles aren't dynamic, with her use of delicate gold jewellery (she's a fan of Copenhagen-based designer Sophie Billie Brah), a chunky gold watch which she inherited, and one of the myriad pair of jazzy earrings she owns pepping up even the simplest of pieces. ''And, go for the basics,'' she continues. ''Even though I wrote a book on this I'm not very good at it,'' she admits. ''You need these basic things in your wardrobe like a white T-shirt or a well-fitted blazer. Nobody wants to buy them because it's boring, but then you end up with a wardrobe where nothing really works together.'' Teisbaeck also adheres to the adage 'quality over quantity', twice a year embarking on ruthless wardrobe clear out that sees the things she hasn't worn in recent months culled.  As a street style star, Teisbaeck is often spotted sporting the latest offerings from her favourite designers, but she's not short of praise for the high street, namely H&M, which she says is brimming with good knitwear and basics. ''Lots of these high street brands do really good quality things,'' she says. ''I love that you can get cashmere and good silks and it doesn’t need to be The Row or Céline.'' The style maven and fashion plate also seeks out second hand bargains. ''Never before in my life have I bought so much second hand clothing,'' she tells The Telegraph. ''I shop for it mainly online from places like Vestiaire Collective - they have amazing pieces that you can spice up with something that's more current, and then add something basic and then you have a good mix of everything.'' She also advocates ''never closing down a trend,'' citing mom jeans as one of things she swore she'd never wear but that is now a key player in her wardrobe. ''Right now I'd say I'd never wear neon, but I've learnt not to shut down a trend, because you will probably end up wearing it at some point.'' © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Iris Apfel became a fashion icon and cover star at the age of 83, when the Metropolitan Museum of Art's Costume Institute presented an exhibition about the New Yorker's vast collection of clothes and accessories.  The 94-year-old has since starred in Kate Spade campaigns alongside Karlie Kloss and Tavi Gevinson, a documentary about her life, Iris, and collaborated with a number of major brands, including & Other Stories, MAC Cosmetics and most recently wearable tech company WiseWear. She started her fashion career after retirement age, but she's the first to call out the fashion industry for being youth obsessed, and ignoring those with spending power.  "The fashion industry doesn't just forget old people, it forgets middle-aged people,"Apfel tells The Telegraph. "The fashion industry is youth obsessed, which is totally insane from a financial point of view so I don't feel sorry for them, they brought it on themselves. Many top designers will make very, very expensive dresses costing many, many thousands of dollars that young people can't afford." She continues: "They make these dresses on 16 year old bodies that can be purchased by women over 65/75 - those are the women in our country anyhow with the spendable income and the time and money to go shopping and they want to buy beautiful things, but it's very hard to find things that are suitable for them. It doesn't make any sense." Apfel has recently entered into the world of wearable tech, collaborating with WiseWear on jewellery that keeps track of your health, sending alerts to your phone via Bluetooth. By simply tapping the bracelet, you can send your emergency contact your exact location.  'I haven't dated in 68 years, but I told them to put down their cell phones' Iris says of her latest project: "I suffer from dehydration and I know what awful things it can do - I've had several people who've come to no good, and fallen, and terrible things have happened and when I heard what they were doing I thought it was wonderful. Everything on the market already was hideous and we needed beautiful things that people could wear to business or to a party." Iris might be entering into the tech world, but don't expect her to set up her own Instagram profile. "I don't use it at all," Iris says of social media to The Telegraph. "I don't look at it or think about what I had for breakfast, it's ridiculous. People seem to live vicariously through other people and other things, and that's why they are all becoming empty shells. You hardly meet anyone with a soul anymore." "I was asked today by some pretty young lady if I'd give them some dating advice," she recalls. "And it's a little difficult for me, as I haven't dated in 68 years, but I told them to put down their cell phones. All they do is press buttons. They go out on dates and they don't talk to each other, and engage with one another, they sit opposite each other pressing buttons. Then they agree with me, and I say 'why do you do it?' and they say 'well everybody does it.' And I say 'that doesn't make it right, and you know it's wrong and you don't like it and you take part in it. You're more responsible than anyone else. Stop it.'" Iris might be a fashion icon, but she quickly shuts down questions of anyone trying to dress like her. "What I think is what I think. If people try to look like me they'll look ridiculous," says the interior designer, known for stacked bangles and her oversized glasses. "They should think about who they are and learn how to think for themselves. Everybody today is like a robot, and I don't want to be part of that. It's about what you like and makes you comfortable. What makes me comfortable, may make you feel very icky so what's the sense of that? If you can't be yourself then just forget it." The straight-talking New Yorker also has a problem with two recent trends, 'normcore' (embracing bland style) and 'twinning' (dressing to match your friend). "If you walk down the street in New York in the winter, all the young ladies look alike," she sighs. "They all have long hair, a black leather bomber jacket and black tights and black boots and they look like they came out of a machine. Particularly today with fast fashion, and stores like H&M, young people who have beautiful figures and can try all these things, they don't need clothes that are magnificently tailored. They could try all the new things."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Jonathan Anderson, the 31-year-old Northern Irish designer set a British Fashion Awards first tonight by winning both the Menswear and Womenswear Designer of the Year awards for his fashion label J.W. Anderson. The unprecedented double victory saw him beat Christopher Kane and Victoria Beckham to the Womenswear prize and Tom Ford and Patrick Grant’s E Tautz in the Menswear category. This is the second time he has been nominated for both awards – last year he took the men’s prize, but not the women’s (which went to Erdem). In previous years he has won New Establishment Designer (2013) and Emerging Womenswear Designer (2012). A graduate of the London College of Fashion, Anderson launched his menswear line in 2008, following with womenswear two years later. He was instantly hailed as a fresh new fashion provocateur, notably for his gender-blending collections, putting men in blouses, tabard tunics and skirts and women in oversize shirting and pyjama styles. At the time, he might have featured in a few mocking sidebars, but in the last few years, these ideas have been picked up and translated over and over again by the mainstream. His two season-spanning Topshop collection (launched in September 2012) was the most successful collaboration the high street behemoth has ever created. Anderson has never been one to rest on an idea though. His show collections have in recent seasons taken abrupt about turns, from structured minimalism to this autumn/winter 2015 blast of 80s lamé fantasia to spring/summer 2016’s softer interpretation featuring attention-garnering giant leg of mutton sleeves and Keith Herring prints which had something of a Princess Di-goes-to-Boombox feel about it. His skill is to crash into the fashion agenda with a new, question-posing skew. Often at an Anderson show there is an awkward, nagging feeling that you're missing a nuanced level of irony, just out of grasp, but this sense of provocation and challenge is something that one imagines Anderson plays on at his own pace.  At his last show in September, the soundtrack was a recording from a documentary of renowned American writer Fran Lebowitz discussing Andy Warhol’s legacy and the idea of fame, before segueing into Rihanna's 'Only Girl In The World' for the finale. The last word on Warhol from Lebowitz: 'it was a joke.' Appointed Creative Director of Spanish LVMH (the fashion conglomerate also took a minority state in Anderson’s own label) owned leather house Loewe in 2013, he spent a year re-working the concept of the brand before unveiling his new agenda setting aesthetic, and has created fashion catnip with his covetable ‘puzzle’ bags and sell out metallic pleated high neck dresses. Crucially, whilst Anderson continues to articulate a transformative and boundary-bashing fashion message he combines this with a retail-winning, keen commercial sense. This essential duality has ensured that as much as he can do cool, his skill and conviction towards brand building means that he can also sell clothes.
