 In what might well have been designed as a pre-Valentine's Day gift, H&M has just released pictures of its latest collaboration with David Beckham. And this time around, the retired footballer and all-round heartthrob is getting in on the athleisure trend. His Bodywear line for the Swedish retailer launches on February 4 and features comfortable sportswear classics, such as sweatshirts and jogging bottoms. There’s not many people who can team grey marl jogging bottoms and a beige jumper and not look like they’re indulging a sick day. But Beckham can. And given that Becks is credited with increasing sales of male underwear by 28 per cent after his last H&M underwear campaign, perhaps you'll soon start seeing your partner lounging around in trackie bums. If so, be heartened by the fact that Becks really does wear this gear to shuffle around his London mansion. “Everything about my Bodywear for H&M has to be authentic. If I wouldn’t wear it then it doesn’t go in the collection!” commented the 40-year-old, who first linked up with H&M four years ago with a collection of briefs. “I’m always trying to evolve the Bodywear collection, and include classic pieces like sweaters and track pants that I would wear out or at home.” Perhaps it was wife Victoria’s own grey tracksuit set which inspired the father-of-four’s latest offering (seriously, we saw it with our own eyes). So, if you're team Beckham over Gandy, get yourself the next best thing this Valentine's Day: Beckham's bottoms.  What better gift could a designer ask for on their birthday, than to have one of the world’s most prominent women appear in their clothes? Better still, when that woman is the outgoing First Lady, Michelle Obama, and the appearance in question is her final hosting of the White House holiday party? That’s exactly what happened to Tanya Taylor on Saturday, the designer’s 31st birthday, when the FLOTUS chose to wear an adapted version of a dress from her winter 2016 collection, striking a masterful balance of festive cheer and sophistication - and all without a sequin in sight. Winter florals are so often overlooked for their Christmas party potential, no doubt out-dazzled by all of the glittery options that flood the high street. But as Mrs Obama proves, the look needn’t be reserved for the boring squib in the corner, and can in fact be a perfect, chic solution for the woman at the heart of the party. The long-sleeved sheath silhouette was a clean-cut choice for Michelle, but the trick was in the placement of its playful embroideries of red and purple poppies. Twining up the dress’ side seams  and under the bust, they outlined the FLOTUS’s incredible figure in a genius, flattering illusion technique.    Cleverly placed florals are fast becoming a signature for this young New York designer, who founded her eponymous label in 2012. Taylor's designs have become a go-to for Obama who has chosen the patterned pieces numerous times during her tenure at the White House, from the fresh blue and white design for a visit to a kids charity in 2014 to the black, cream and green shift she chose for her arrival in India in January 2015.   It’s worth noting Obama's seemingly new-found fact; that winter florals don’t need to be fussy. On the high street, Zara and Topshop have bunches of strategically-placed flower embroideries to choose from (covering everything from dresses to denim), while Warehouse has a sweet-yet-subtle 'English Rose' print, available in half-a-dozen different silhouettes (and currently on a 30% off  promotion). Elsewhere on the catwalk, Miu Miu, Dolce and Gabbana and Erdem led the trend for black and navy-backed florals, proving that their darker canvas only serves to ground the most vivid blooms for a more refined way to wear them until spring comes back around.  Margaret Thatcher's fashion legacy is traditionally thought to consist of pussy-bow blouses, ladylike handbags and pearl necklaces. Yet during this EU referendum campaign, a new cult item once worn by the former prime minister has re-emerged, tapping into a kitsch nostalgia for the last vote on Europe. On the night of Britain's referendum on whether to remain a member of the common market in 1975, Thatcher - then leader of the Conservatives who were in opposition at the time - was given a  jumper emblazoned with the flags of the nine countries who made up the European community at the time. The colourful knit was created by a woollen mill in Scotland and was only worn once by Thatcher as a show of her support for the European trade agreement. help me out twitter where do I buy a Thatcher '75 jumper by Thursday? pic.twitter.com/C6HZvwRu1g #VoteRemain #EUref I'm no fan of thatcher but that is a brilliant jumper. pic.twitter.com/mjYsqGRHSW Fast forward over 40 years and the image of that jumper has resurfaced in recent months as Britain gears up to vote on whether to leave or remain in the European Union. Footage of Thatcher wearing the jumper on Newsnight sparked a national hunt to find out where the original had gone. But frustrated at it being nowhere to be found, the people from underground music community Boiler Room decided to revive Thatcher’s iconic jumper - selling their own version for £45 at a 'new label' they've comically named Common Market.  “The idea started after the vote announcement,” Emma Shore, Boiler Room’s Merchandise Manager tells The Telegraph. “We stumbled across the shots of Thatcher and looked into the history and relevance of the knit. What stood out as opposed to now was the positivity of the campaign – the embrace of a common Europe – and slogans that actually meant something.” we've all just bought that Thatcher jumper, right? Re-launched two weeks ago after some “quick-planning”, the jumper’s revival isn’t just an homage to Thatcher’s famous style nous. “We really liked the strong, simple message and the boldness of literally wearing your heart on your sleeve,” explains Shore. The jumper is also material evidence of a campaign which, according to Common Market, was more positively fought than 2016's referendum battle.  “The sweater plays on one Margaret Thatcher wore on the campaign trail in 1975, when even Tory nationalists espoused closer European integration under the slogan ‘Support Your Local Continent',” they write as a description of the jumper on the page where you can buy it. "The 9 Flags Knit references the positive imagery of the earlier European referendum, when Britain overwhelmingly chose to stay part of Europe.” Shore claims that “the product itself doesn’t have any politics” but does admit that she and her team are in camp Remain. “From a personal perspective we very much support the importance of remaining in a union, and oppose the many outlandish and false statements that have been made. Alongside Wolfgang Tillmans and numerous others we support the importance of engagement and rational debate, also the importance of using your vote. Particularly in this case with the disenfranchisement of so many young people whose future is crucially affected by the outcome,” she tells The Telegraph. With only a few days left before Britain takes to the polls, Shore and her team are under no illusion that their jumper can change the fate of whether we'll remain in the European Union. “We'd  would worry if a jumper could swing an election” she laughs. Still, she hopes it will help make people feel like they are part of something bigger.  “It’s important that people feel like there’s more to this campaign than the economic terms that it’s been fought on - people should be proud to feel part of a wider continent.” One person who's already bought into the 1970's nostalgia? Jeremy Paxman. The newsreader donned a copycat version of the knit, although Common Market wrote on Instagram that “our knit is twice as fine.” By the way Jeremy, if you're reading - they would love to send you one. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Thanks to Carolina Herrera, doyenne of the impeccable, guardian of elegance, grandmother of 12, I am now the owner of a fetching pair of H&M tracksuit bottoms. ‘Ooof, I looove H&M,’ she tells me during our interview, her ruffly South American accent making it sound an exotic treat. She’s also addicted to Midsomer Murders (‘All those killings in such a small place. It’s so fooony’). So I might give that another go too. It should be noted, however, that there’s scant evidence of high-street in the cherry-red cigarette pants, white shirt and red espadrille wedges she’s wearing, all from her diffusion CH Carolina Herrera line. She looks magnificently post-holiday casual, having just flown into Manhattan from Patmos, Greece (which is rapidly becoming ‘Fashion Island’), where she was holidaying with her friend John Stefanidis, the dashing interior designer.  It occurs to me that rather than both heading to New York, we could have met somewhere halfway in Europe. I’m feeling disorientated. She must be destroyed. After all, she is, incredibly, 77. Her eyes sweep from her hands to her tanned feet. No, she is fine. Although not a million blocks from her palatial offices in Manhattan’s Midtown Garment District, in terms of ambience, I’d say the Broadway branch of H&M is several continents away from Herrera HQ, with its family photographs, wrap-around roof terrace, rangy black-clad PR girls and a maid who seems to spend all day making cappuccinos and ‘green teaccinos’ (Herrera’s new passion). I imagine Herrera’s ability to sell anything, including classic glamour to a city that already prided itself on that commodity, was what prompted her friend Diana Vreeland to tell her not to bother becoming a textile designer (‘she said textiles were the most boring thing you could do’) but to go full throttle into fashion. That was over 35 years ago. Despite her lack of formal training, her first show was a huge hit commercially, ‘although not with the press. They thought I was another socialite who’d soon get bored. I’m still here,’ she chuckles. Not just here, but relevant. The company was bought by the Spanish perfume giant Puig in 1995 and Herrera was retained as creative director, a role she still inhabits, as no one else – with the possible exception of her daughter Carolina Herrera Junior – could. The CH line, launched in 2008, designed and produced in Spain, is a repository of snappy chic for women who’d rather look modern and sleek than modern and edgy (the Duchess of Cambridge wore one of its coats on the recent royal visit to Canada). But it’s those phenomenally successful perfumes that pushed turnover in 2015 over $1.6 billion. She’s just launched a new one, in a bottle sculpted in the shape of an improbably high stiletto. Its face is Karlie Kloss. There’s a new expanded Carolina Herrera store in Harrods. Her show in New York last month – crisp, contrasting top-stitched sundresses and denim ballgowns – was a punchy greeting to the traditional Herrera client. This is not a brand sinking into gentle dowagership. There is the main line and wedding collection, the prototypes for which are made in the 16th-floor atelier. Above, in the showroom on the 17th, is her eyrie, a grand yet cosy corner with plush carpets, dark wood, bold stripy upholstery and glamorous photos of the clan. Herrera is remarkably photogenic.  She used to be called Lady of the Sleeves back in the 1980s, because she did things no one else was doing with them. ‘And you know why? Because when you’re sitting at a table and no one can see your skirt, at least you have these fabulous sleeves. They really frame your face.’  Carolina Herrera main line is grand but still contemporary, as evidenced by Michelle Obama’s show-stopping turn in a sky-blue Carolina Herrera ball skirt and black lace top ($12,000, according to guesstimates at the time, and it looked at least that much) at a state dinner in 2014. Then there are Renée Zellweger’s many red-carpet forays in Herrera’s trademark fishtail gowns. Herrera met the actress years ago at a gala. ‘She owned a dog that used to belong to my daughter.’ Of course. The Herrera clan is connected in every direction you look. There was clearly a kindred spark between them because when Zellweger next attended the Oscars, she called Herrera and asked if she could come to the studio. ‘She can stand around being fitted for various outfits for five hours. She knows so much about fashion – and about posing. She was the first to stand with her back to the photographers, with her face three-quarters turned. She’s the only actress I can think of who doesn’t have a stylist.’ Herrera says she herself only wears three or four looks from each main line collection. ‘I don’t design it for myself. Luckily I have clients who have been loyal since the beginning. But I also have 20-year-olds wearing it.’ I never quite get to the bottom of why she restricts herself to three or four looks from the main line. Perhaps she feels it’s too ‘dressy’ for her daily walk through Central Park from her house to the office, whereas CH has more everyday pieces. Yet if anyone exemplifies Upper East Side polish, it’s Herrera, with her patrician Venezuelan credentials and haughty eyebrows. If eyebrows could talk, Herrera’s would say back off, although once you get past those finely arched gatekeepers, she is warm and funny.  I’d imagined that Herrera’s personal style – luxurious yet pared back – is so instinctive that she no longer has to give it much thought. She says she can get ready in 10 minutes, unless she’s going to something mega like the Met Ball, when she pulls out all the stops and gets her hair and make-up done professionally. The rest of the time, she says, all it takes is a slick of red lipstick and a comb through that hair. I’m inclined to accept her word because she’s got that thing – poise, I suppose – that means it doesn’t really matter what else is going on. ‘I’m naturally quite fiery,’ she concedes. ‘But I try always to be positive. I hate negativity. When you have a company that employs hundreds of people, you have to be positive.’ María Carolina Josefina Pacanins y Niño was brought up with dressmakers and riding and ballet lessons – plus a Hungarian governess who, she says, taught her to speak English and French with a strong Eastern European accent.  Her father, Guillermo, an air-force officer, was at one time governor of Caracas. Her mother, María Cristina, and socialite grandmother introduced her to the salons of fashion, taking her to see Balenciaga, Lanvin and Dior. She learnt early on that clothes should fit properly: ‘Even if I buy [high street] I would get it altered. [My childhood] was really quite formal. We would change several times a day.’ For all her innate chic, she’s unexpectedly analytical about how the world currently interprets this trait. She cannot comprehend the criticism meted out to Hillary Clinton for spending money on her suits. ‘This idea that a powerful, successful woman should wear inexpensive clothes is so forced. I think if you are the president and you’re well dressed, it inspires confidence. It’s an advertisement for the country.’ But no, she wouldn’t label herself a feminist. She doesn’t really know what it means, she says. This ought to sound old-fashioned, given that she clearly stands as an alpha-female figure, and it’s not as if there’s a shortage of female role models in her life. Vreeland was one mentor. Another was her mother, who  not only taught her daughters how to look impeccable but coached them in the art of  conversation and used to play an exacting  game with them (they were all called María, incidentally: María Cristina, María Carolina…) that ought to be marketed as an app to the iPad generation. ‘She used to tell us to go into a room and afterwards we’d have to recite everything we could remember seeing. It was an extraordinary training in observation. My eyes learnt early on to look for beauty.’ She was not, however, raised to have a career. She married her first husband when she was 18, had two daughters and was divorced six years later. In 1968 she married Don Reinaldo Herrera Guevara, who had inherited, but appears never to use, the romantic title of 5th Marquis of Torre Casa, seemingly preferring to be known as the long-standing special projects editor of Vanity Fair. Although she dipped a pedicured toe into the world of paid employment as a  PR for Pucci in Caracas in the mid-1960s, she was 40 and living with Reinaldo in New York before she considered the possibility of a career. She was serious about making it a success  from the start. ‘I was not a businesswoman,  but I partnered with people who were. They’re still here.’ If upper-class Caracas in the 1950s wasn’t exactly progressive, it certainly left her with  a core – physically and psychologically – of steel and instilled in her the value of loyalty, particularly where family is concerned. Her three sisters are arriving in New York the day after our interview and although her first  marriage dissolved, her second – to Reinaldo, with whom she had two more daughters – is notably successful. They are a tight clan: her youngest daughter, Patricia, works for the  company in New York. Carolina Herrera Junior directs the fragrance line in Madrid. ‘They came to me because they wanted to,’ she’s quick to point out.  I like the idea of Herrera not being a push-over, yet she never rebelled against her mother, who directed her daughters in most things, behaviour and taste included – it all made  sense to her at the time. She was less strict with her own daughters, although she did try to stage an intervention when Carolina Junior went through a sartorial Madonna stage:  ‘I said, “Darling, not police shoes and a miniskirt.”’ Inevitably, Carolina Junior told her mother, who had dressed most of high society and  numerous first ladies, from Jackie Kennedy to Nancy Reagan, that she didn’t know what she was talking about. Not strict then, ‘but I certainly don’t hold with this idea that you are your children’s best friend. I am their mother. We get along very well, but I don’t want to know something that they might tell their girlfriends.’ One senses discretion may be a cornerstone of Herrera civilisation. ‘Respect and love are key to a happy family,’ she says. She and Reinaldo were – and to an extent still are – stalwarts of New York’s social scene, although in the 1970s they frequented its decadent edges. It’s not that she spent her entire time at Studio 54, but let’s just say there are enough photographs from this period for her to have selected a number of them for a forthcoming pictorial book chronicling her life and glamorous times. Warhol, who became a friend, gave her a portrait of herself in return for the jewelled handbag she was carrying. Her husband thought she was mad – it now hangs in her inner office among the silver-framed family photographs. Nowadays, the Herreras are bastions of uptown society. I think she may miss the frisson of the  old days. ‘In the 1970s and 1980s there was  a very interesting group of people around the world, there were painters, writers, politicians, everything all together! They’d all come together in New York. That doesn’t happen  any more.’    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Awards season is here: today’s Bafta nominations mean that we’re set to see a lot more of the supremely stylish Cate Blanchett ahead of the ceremony on February 14, especially if she wins a Golden Globe this weekend for her performance in Carol. But this time of year always throws up emerging names where acting talent is concerned, too. You may not have heard of half the up-and-coming actress below, but trust us, by the time the year is out you will have most likely watched many of their performances - and admired their style prowess too. Strictly speaking, Saoirse (pronounced Seer-sha, in case you were wondering) is not new to the red carpet; the New York-born, Dublin-based actress has been quietly beavering away on films ever since she got her big break when, aged 12, she starred opposite Keira Knightley in Atonement. Now 21, 2016 is set to be her year after her performance in Brooklyn has seen her nominated for awards at the Golden Globes, Baftas and SAGs. She's enlisted a new stylist and it shows - London-based Elizabeth Slatzman, a contributing editor at Vanity Fair, is also the woman responsible for dressing Gwyneth Paltrow. Ronan and Saltzman are already proving to be a killer combination: Ronan is clearly a young woman who likes to experiment with silhouettes and colourways; she’s worn everyone from Emilia Wickstead to Burberry so far, always with an effortless approach.  Prepare to see a lot more of Larson, for mid-January sees the release of Room, the film in which Larson plays a kidnapped mother. Her performance has earned her an award for a Golden Globe and a SAG Award, meaning she’ll be attending every pre-awards luncheon Hollywood has to offer. For such events the 26-year-old calls upon stylist Christopher Campbell, who helps her secure a wardrobe of skirts and dresses in simple, classic shapes but made modern in bold hues. Fans of TV series Outlander will already have Balfe on their radar. The 36-year-old plays Claire Beauchamp in the hit show, and is looking to add a Golden Globe to her trophy cabinet – not bad for a model-turned-actress.
The Dublin-born beauty used to be a regular on the international catwalks, walking frequently for luxury fashion houses Chanel, Dolce & Gabbana, Givenchy and Louis Vuitton during her twenties. Her model poise certainly stands out on the red carpet: just check out her stance at last year’s SAG Awards in London label Solace. If you’re not already familiar with Vikander, then may we ask under which rock you have been hiding for the past year? The 27-year-old Swede broke out with three films this year (four if you count The Danish Girl, released in the UK on January 1) and picked up a modelling assignment for Louis Vuitton along the way. 2016 will be the year that Vikander goes mainstream. Her performance alongside Eddie Redmayne in The Danish Girl has put her in the running for accolades at the SAG Awards, the Baftas and the Golden Globes. We’re sure she’ll tackle both with just the same amount of Scandi minimalism that has made her such a refreshing fixture on the red carpet so far. After five years and 52 episodes playing maid Anna Bates in Downton Abbey, Joanne Froggatt might just have something to celebrate if her stars align on January 10, when she’ll find out if she’s bagged the Best Supporting Actress role at the Golden Globes. The 35-year-old has recently found her red carpet groove thanks to celebrity stylist Brad Goreski, who works with Jessica Alba and Rashida Jones, and is a co-host on Fashion Police. The difference in her style has been dramatic: instead of blending into the background, she’s embraced flowing gowns and embellished minidresses to make an impact. RIP Mrs Bates.   Her name may mean nothing to you now (aside to its similarities to a certain late, famous Ms Monroe), but a trip to the cinema in 2016 will make Maika Monroe pretty unavoidable: the photogenic blonde is set to star in six films over the next 12 months, including blockbuster Independence Day: Resurgence. The 22-year-old ticks off all the qualities you’d expect in a twenty-something, California-born movie star: pretty, athletic… yet she really does fulfil the latter, as she was on course to become a professional kiteboarder before Hollywood came knocking, even moving to the Dominican Republic in order to train full-time. We think she’s still finding her feet when it comes to narrowing down her signature red carpet look, which will make her ascent in 2016 all the more interesting. Deutch is another relative newcomer who is set to assert herself on the style circuit in 2016, thanks to seven new film releases (catch her first up alongside Zac Efron in Dirty Grandpa). The 21-year-old turned heads in Dior at this year’s Elle Women in Hollywood Awards, and has hit all the right notes in designs by Sportmax and Tanya Taylor at previous industry events.  Given that it's -14 currently in New York it feels apt that Victoria Beckham is offering stealth knitwear solutions for next winter, and debuting them on herself. Backstage before the show, with the model line-up still being tweaked an hour before the unveiling, VB is sporting a cosy pale hued roll neck, loose grey flannel cropped trousers and a pair of bright white Stan Smith trainers (which, unusually, she didn't swap for heels for her post show bow). Having posted a £9 million turnover increase on the previous year's taking in December and with her second store due to open in Hong Kong in three weeks this is a buoyant time for the label, which launched with a collection of 10 dresses in 2008. For AW16 Beckham took the opportunity to take stock. She describes it as “an evolution of my personal style. I looked back at the clothes I've worn and designed and decided to rework key elements.” The central piece was the corset. “I used to wear a lot and it felt very sexy and feminine,” she explained backstage. “I wanted to find a way to bring that back and feel new and fresh.” The key take home in her modern take on the corset is the lack of boning. These are 'easy' pieces, with the fitted basque shape created in knitwear and as bodices on the dresses, but without that forced rigid, constricting structure. The dresses, some knitted in navy, orange and khaki green check, reflect her 'signature silhouette' which is a figure flattering, female friendly one, but updated with a cool, low key attitude, with the sort of understated elegance her customers have come to expect. The shift and move on comes from the elevated techniques used: a heritage houndstooth coat that uses a waxed cord running through it to act as an embroidery took five days to make.   Masculine houndstooth and check fabrics are used to good effect in coats: added design details of knitted cuffs and hems left raw, bringing a neat contrast to the femninine dress shapes. Bold stripes are used to add definition and a keen sense of modernity, and lend that all important “freshness” Mrs Beckham is so keen on.   Skirt lengths are just above midi. Knitted tops, bodices and skirts are layered over each other, or cut to give the illusion of layers. Trousers are knitted and close cut, dresses (some featuring a cute bubble hem) and tops are spliced open gently to reveal slithers of flesh - “something we know our customer loves,” says VB. The pieces are given an added punch a quirk with oversized buttons and silver metallic brooch details. The easiness continues into her footwear, flat pointed monk strap brogues and hefty block heeled ankle boots. For evening and red carpet (perhaps a niche concern) Beckham offers a high waist trouser worn with a cream satin bustier layered under a knitted black top. “It feels like a chic, modern take on red carpet,” she says. It's half term so the Beckham clan were in full effect (next to their usual front row mates Anna Wintour and her daughter Bea) on the front row. Harper sat on her father's lap, doing a military look, with a single breasted gold buttoned navy pea coat with red collar detail and Gucci shoes. Cruz and Romeo were suited and the eldest, Brooklyn was working a T-shirt under his tailoring, his quiff flattened to the side. The children had given their mother “some beautiful flowers” for today's Valentine's Day. She bought them balloons. “We'd spent the whole day with these balloons for the kids and I got out of the car after we'd been working all night, and I said to the driver, ‘Be careful of the balloons!' and he got out the car and said what? And a bunch of them flew up into the air. I was like, no!” A comforting thought that even a Beckham can't have it all run smoothly. It's hard to believe that Victoria Beckham only started showing at New York Fashion Week eight years ago. Her show is now one of the fixtures on the Big Apple's fashion schedule - and not just because it features 4-year-old Harper on the front row. Victoria has managed to turn her clothes into a £34 million business - and her latest collection, happening now at New York Fashion Week - demonstrates why.   Lucas Ossendrijver, the lanky Dutch designer behind Lanvin’s menswear, has an origin myth, but it’s not a very exciting one. Which makes sense when you meet him, and I mean that in a good way. Back when he was an art student in Amsterdam, majoring in fashion design, Ossendrijver was wandering through the open air flea market on the city’s Waterlooplein. He came across an old sports coat, a little on the crummy side and badly out of date. He started examining it more closely. And then he decided to buy it and take it apart, piece by piece. “I thought, okay, how is this thing made?,” recalls Ossendrijver. “I saw all the hand-stitching under the collar, and I took out the lining, just so I could see everything that was inside. For me, that was the first time that I started working with menswear. I thought to myself, if I’m going to design clothes, I have to know how things are made.” See? Not very exciting. But it tells you a lot of what you need to know about Ossendrijver as a designer, and why, after 11 years, he’s still ripping jackets apart and putting them back together in his painstaking way at Lanvin. It is precisely this molecular approach to menswear that has made him among the most influential designers in the business, but even he is a little surprised at the length of his tenure. Eleven years amounts to three lifetimes, he says, if you convert fashion years to human years. “Knowing what the turnover is like at design houses, I never thought I would stay so long.” One way to explain his longevity is the absence of a singular Ossendrijver vision, and I mean that in a good way, too. He’s impossible to pin down. But whatever idea catches his fancy in a particular season, customers can count on meticulous attention to detail, close contact with the latest technical developments on the frontiers of sartorial science and a deep understanding of how clothing feels on the body. The spirit of the origin myth lives on. For Ossendrijver, everything works from the inside out, instead of from the outside in. “I’m not thinking about a person, or about a style, or even about fashion,” he says. “I’m thinking about what clothes are, what they do and how they relate to your body. I’m kind of a nerd that way. Some people work the other way around – they have a theme or they want this or that look. I’m the opposite: it’s all about construction, proportion, fabric. The look on the catwalk at the end – it may be strange to say this – it’s not really that important to me.” You get some idea what he’s talking about by looking at his SS17 collection on the rack at Lanvin’s Paris headquarters on Rue du Faubourg Saint Honoré. If there’s a common thread here, it’s a kind of casual messiness, executed with a watchmaker’s precision. A classic jacket is creased so it looks like it just emerged from the bottom of a suitcase. This is on purpose, mind you. “It looks like life,” he says. Ossendrijver has added reflective strips on the sleeves, borrowed from the hard hats digging across the street from the office tower where you work. The basting stitches that you normally remove from a new garment have been lovingly woven in: do not take them out; they are meant to stay there. Kangaroo-leather jackets have deep folds steamed into them, not out of them. A shirt has been made with an advanced technical fabric from Japan that mixes fibre with metal, all the better to preserve the crinkliness of its wrinkles. For Ossendrijver, these unruly details are precisely what give clothing its clothesiness, and he cherishes them for it. He doesn’t design clothing to look good in a two-dimensional photograph; he wants to engineer something that makes you want to fondle it, to crumple it, to… well, you get the idea. This is not something a designer just starts out doing, of course. You’ve got to follow the rules before you can break them, and Ossendrijver, studious and diligent by temperament, knows the rules better than anyone. He comes from a family of builders in the little country town of Amersfoort, some 30 miles from Amsterdam. There was a woodworking shed beside the house, and it was here young Lucas developed his taste for tinkering. “I was always working with my hands,” he says. “My brother and I loved to make things - rafts or treehouses, stuff like that. I truly think everything comes from there.” After art school, Ossendrijver headed straight for Paris. Amsterdam had no fashion business to speak of, apart from some denim manufacturers, and Belgium, for all its force as a cradle of creativity, just didn’t have the industrial heft he was looking for. “If you really want to do something in fashion, if you really want to know how it’s done, you have to move to Paris.” He started at Kenzo, which schooled him in the hardscrabble world of the business – lessons that young designers, ablaze with creative fervour, too often overlook, says Ossendrijver. “I think a lot of young designers rush off to start their own company and then, after three or four seasons, the company stops,” he says. “You have to learn about pricing, you have to learn about fabrics, you have to learn about manufacturing, you have to learn about the press. Actually, it’s a very complicated business.” Next, Kostas Murkudis, a former assistant to Helmut Lang, took on Ossendrijver to help with his tiny menswear business, which gave him the chance to try his hand at every aspect of the operation. “You had to do everything yourself, which was the opposite of Kenzo. It was very good experience.” This got him to Hedi Slimane, the menswear deity who ruled Dior Homme from 2001 to 2007. “That was my first experience of working with a French couture house,” recalls Ossendrijver. “It was my first taste of real luxury, and it was completely new for me - the way things are done, the kinds of manufacturers you work with, the level of quality. The French call it exigeant, and it means asking for the highest, for the best, with absolutely no compromise. That’s something I hadn’t known about before, and I learnt it there.” In many ways, Slimane is the anti-Ossendrijver, demanding and tempestuous where Ossendrijver is collegial and laid back. Slimane had a look. He had an ideal man - a man who, unlike most guys, could actually button a Dior Homme jacket in his size (I tried this once and failed badly). Slimane imposed his personality on everything that came out of his atelier. When you bought Dior Homme, you knew you were buying into Hediness. (I ended up purchasing the jacket I couldn’t button, with its armholes up around the thorax. It was just so cool and I figured I could eventually get myself down to Slimane proportions. Nope.) “Yes, that’s his way of working,” allows Ossendrijver. “My way of working is different and my personality is different.” In 2005, Ossendrijver wrote to Alber Elbaz, then the much-loved head of design at Lanvin who had breathed new life into its womenswear label. Elbaz was looking for someone who could do the same for Lanvin’s menswear, which was badly out of breath at the time. Ossendrijver got the job, but coming straight from Slimane’s Dior, he worried that he might not have the right make-up to succeed. “I always thought I wouldn’t be suitable as a head designer because I don’t have that personality. I thought you have to have a media presence, you have to go to parties and be photographed with whoever. At Lanvin, I discovered that my personality is my strength. The technicity of what I do is very specific. It sets me apart from other brands and designers. I think people come to Lanvin because they appreciate that kind of elaborate workmanship.” To give me a better idea what he’s talking about, Ossendrijver showed me a sleeve from a suit jacket in the recently finished collection for next winter. Just the sleeve. He comes alive when he starts talking about this stuff. It’s what he loves best. “Here I was interested in making the shoulder as narrow as possible so the shoulder bone sticks out in the sleeve. I started working with the pattern cutter so the whole sleeve is twisted toward the front. We made the sleeve quite large, but then we had to construct a special shoulder pad that went under the sleeve to keep the line very clean and clear. After that we put it on a pressing table to make the sleeve completely flat, like a two-dimensional shape. I always work with opposing volumes, but I also like the idea of starting with something classic - this is basically a double-breasted suit. Then the question becomes, how would I make the suit feel new again? What would I want to wear?” No one could be expected to notice much of this as it flashes past you on the runway. Ossendrijver doesn’t design for first impressions. As he likes to say, this is the work of millimetres. Still, we’re talking about menswear, where tradition and long-standing habit die hard. Ossendrijver often has to battle for every millimetre he alters. “I have to go to the factory, I have to talk to the cutter, I have to talk to the guy who does the fabrics. In order to get them to try something new, you have to know how it’s done yourself, otherwise they don’t take you seriously. You have to constantly convince people to do things differently. Everything is so structured.” This is to say nothing of the guys who buy menswear, who can be every bit as hidebound as the people who make it. He may not have an ideal man in mind as he designs, but he knows men, and he knows they hate change. Ossendrijver adores the rigidly codified vocabulary of menswear – it’s one of the reasons he feels more at ease with it than with womenswear – but he recognises that with those codes come tight limits. “It’s a different way of designing,” he says. “Men are more stubborn in what they wear and what they don’t wear. With women, every season there’s a new look, there’s a new bag. It’s much more decorative. If a guy wears a suit and it fits him, he’ll probably go back to the same suit next season. Once a man finds something that works for him, he sticks to it. I never want to limit myself in the beginning, but then reality kicks in. I have learned over time what I’m not going to be able to sell, what may be too extreme for the brand.” That said, Ossendrijver has become bolder over his years at Lanvin. At the beginning, he was feeling his way somewhat blindly. He had very little to guide him in the way of institutional memory. The company’s founder, Jeanne Lanvin, started by making clothes for her young daughter, then for her daughter’s friends, then for her daughter’s friends’ mothers and so on. Thus, in 1889, started one of the world’s first lifestyle brands, which came to encompass menswear, childrenswear, perfume (remember “Promise her anything, but give her Arpège”?) and even home design (Jeanne Lanvin collaborated with the genius furniture-maker Armand-Albert Rateau). But while Lanvin retained copious archives of its womenswear designs, it had none for menswear. Fortunately, Ossendrijver managed to develop a close working relationship with Alber Elbaz. “I learnt a great deal from him,” he says. “He was involved in menswear, and he appreciated it when I sat in during his womenswear fittings as a second opinion. It’s very rare in fashion to have someone you can exchange ideas with in an open, honest way.” Elbaz got pushed out of Lanvin in 2015 by Shaw-Lan Wang, Lanvin’s owner, but he and Ossendrijver remain close. He won’t get specific about where he might be headed with his next collection, but even his vague hints sound pretty ballsy. He’s noodling with the idea of ugliness, he says. “What makes something ugly? What is bad taste? How do you take something and make it different?” To pull that off, a designer needs a thick hide. Ossendrijver says he’s managed to grow one. “In the beginning, I was crushed by bad reviews,” he says. “Now I read everything. Sometimes I even think, Yes, they’re right. The worst is to hold back and try to please everyone. I’ve learnt the confidence to go for things. Mistakes are good, you know? I like mistakes.” www.lanvin.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Cannes Film Festival came to an end on Sunday evening, and with it ten days of dazzling glamour. While a plethora of actresses and supermodels, from Bella Hadid to Diane Kruger and Nicole Kidman, took their turns on La Croisette's famous red carpet throughout the festival, there was one consistently best-dressed star who, by virtue of her place on the jury, was a constant elegant presence at the premieres, photo calls and parties which punctuate the event. It may come as something of a surprise then to learn that for Jessica Chastain and her stylist Elizabeth Stewart, the fashion element of jury duty  was first and foremost a pragmatic exercise in putting together a wardrobe which would make getting dressed the one effortless element amongst her tightly-packed juror's schedule. After all, as Chastain said in her powerful closing remarks on Sunday (in which she spoke out about the 'disturbing' representation of women in the festival's entries), she had to watch 20 films in 10 days besides attending all those engagements. "She was very concerned with her jury duties so our thoughts were mostly practical," Stewart, who has worked with Chastain for the past six years, explains. "Mostly it was about making getting dressed as easy as possible so as not to distract from the jury responsibilities." Of course, an A-list actress's version of 'easy' is somewhat exceptional. Stewart began to commission custom gowns around a month before proceedings kicked off, turning in large part to designers with whom Chastain already had a long-running and close relationship. "It makes fittings go more smoothly," says Stewart. Her first red carpet look of the festival, a delicately floral and bird embroidered black column dress by Alexander McQueenn, was the result of one such collaboration. "We have a very long history with Sarah," says Stewart of the label's creative director, Sarah Burton. "She made Jessica’s first Oscar dress. She just understands Jessica’s vibe completely." In fact, there were parallels between  that first McQueen dress in 2012 and the Cannes creation- the embroidery against an elegantly simple black dress which looked immaculate with Chastain's red hair and porcelain complexion. One of the standout themes of Chastain's Cannes wardrobe has been the vivid and often unexpected colours which she has worn both on the red carpet and during the day. Her "love of colour" formed a cornerstone of what they were looking for confirms Stewart, nodding to the pumpkin-hued Armani Prive gown worn for the 70th anniversary gala last Tuesday, the lilac Givenchy Haute Couture tasselled dress for the Okja premiere and the scarlett bow-detail Roksanda jumpsuit which was one of the first looks she wore at the very start of the festival. But the colourful look which has been the most praised and discussed of Chastain's choices was actually first intended to seem more pared-back. "We wanted some to be low-key," says Stewart, referring to the grass-green Christian Dior coat dress (top) which they chose for  the premiere of The Meyerowitz Stories. "This was a very simple, almost conservative look, except pumped up by the extraordinary colour!" For all that colour however, there were plenty of doses of powerful simplicity to balance things out. A plain, backless Prada gown worn with a striking cushion-cut red tourmaline Piaget necklace at the amfAR gala was one such moment. "I think Jessica always does very with very simple and classic looks," muses Stewart, emphasising that these choices are a way of harnessing Chastain's inherent ability to transform a piece. "They might not seem like as much on the hanger but she brings them alive." By day, Chastain switched between timelessly elegant looks- like a purple Elie Saab shift dress- and cool, modern  ensembles, like a Stella McCartney checked dress with a slouchy cardigan shoulder robed over the top. "The McQueen coatdress is a dream look for me, just perfection," says Stewart of her favourite daytime look, which Chastain chose to amp up the daytime vibe for a 70th anniversary lunch.  The strategy for this element of Chastain's wardrobe came with a thought process which we can all relate to. "We went for easy as she had so many screenings…pants or simple dresses that we planned on earlier fittings," explains Stewart. "I just lined up in her closet in Cannes so all she has to do was grab and go."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  To Paris Haute Couture Fashion Week, where Kate Moss kicked off the party scene by spinning the decks at Miu Miu’s AW16 presentation. The brand eschewed a traditional catwalk show in favour of an informal salon soirée at the Hôtel de la Païva. Mannequins were artfully dressed in Miu Miu’s ‘Croisière Collection 2017’ of 90s-inspired crop tops, raver platforms, beaded bucket hats and lashings of neon. With club culture and eccentricity at the heart of this zany new fashion offering, there was obviously only one model fit for the job as Miu Miu Club mistress. Moss was captured by Instagram-happy fashionistas crowding around the DJ booth, eager to get a shot of the party girl in action. They didn’t have to crane their necks/phones far, as Kate, cigarette and drink in hand, was throwing shapes and shaking her hair like, well, she just didn’t care. And she looked fabulous. Clad in an LBD comprised of a black bodice with a long-sleeved lace overlay, Moss traversed the gap between demure and revealing with artfully placed heart embroidery. Playfully decadent tassel detailling around the arms, plus a shoulder-robed beige trench coat created a look that was idiosyncratically Moss.  When the Kardashians wear this big knickers + sheer overlay combo they look like, well,  Kardashians. But Kate of course pulled off the whole look with the insouciance and confidence of the preternaturally cool and seasoned LBD wearer that she is- and always has been.  There are some styling nuances a mere mortal can take from Mossy at Miu Miu though. Note how her satin belt and necklace lend jazzy detail to her waist and neckline; this worked for Moss because she spent the night behind the decks, but see her decks are your dinner table. Ankle boots are a more offbeat footwear choice than stilettos, another detail which makes the look more Kate than Kardashian.  Cast your mind back to many of the little black dresses in Kate’s repertoire, and there has always been something unique to every one. The 42-year-old has never just plucked any old plain black frock from a rail, but always favours hard-working designs that boast a little extra something in terms of cut, strap detail, neckline or embellishment. Here are 7 other times that Moss made excellent LBD choices... Back in 2004, Moss made best dressed lists with her feathered form-fitting pencil dress at Coty’s 100th birthday. This off-the-shoulder style would still chime with the current mood for bare shoulders. At the 2007 Met Gala Moss made a case for utterly romantic layered chiffon, showing that LBDs need not always be sleek and elegant.  Diamond-studded Marc Jacobs meant Kate was ready to party in Berlin in 2008. Heavy embellishment on dresses means that few accessories are needed - we’d make like Kate and rock just a heavy kohl eye. Plainer dress cuts require a generous ‘bling’ injection, as proved by Moss in 2009 wearing diamond hoop earrings and some silver wrist candy with a more minimalist LBD. Strapless sweetheart necklines can look a little traditional. But at a 2011 Rimmel party, Kate showed that a diamanté trim, mussed-up hair and slick of red lipstick will soon restore rebel status.  Stella McCartney’s famous silhouette enhancing dresses do the same job as the belt on the Miu Miu dress Kate wore last night. Search out similarly cleverly contoured designs to emulate the effect.  Maxi dresses might evoke thoughts of summer daytime dressing but with asymetric hems and a flash of skin (be that a deep v neckline or ankle-to-thigh split) they make an ideal relaxed spin on the LBD.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  With the world’s eyes on her for every event, it can’t be easy for The Duchess of Cambridge to decide what to wear. So it must be helpful when the theme of the day provides inspiration. Today, the Duchess was in Portsmouth to open the 1851 Trust's Tech Deck sailing education centre with Sir Ben Ainslie at his Land Rover BAR (Ben Ainslie racing) base - and paid tribute to the day’s maritime theme in an Alexander McQueen cream blouse with navy trim and gold buttons and matching navy pencil skirt. The Duchess, who is royal patron of the 1851 Trust, chatted to Savannah Gilaj, India Joly and Ashlyn Collins, all 15 and pupils at Brune Park Community School in Gosport, Hants. Ashlyn said: “She asked us if we had ever been sailing, whether we were going to be sailing, she asked us if we enjoy sport and are we looking forward to it. She said of Kate that she was struck by “how pretty she was,” adding: “It was so amazing. You see her on TV, you kind of don’t don’t think of her as a real person and then to meet her was amazing. “She said she enjoyed sailing and we should definitely have a go.” After touring the centre, the Duchess took to the water with Sir Ben Ainslie. Donning a pair of Adidas trainers and regulation sailing attire including a helmet and lifejacket for the occasion, the Duchess manned an AC45 catamaran and completed an hour-long training circuit of the Solent with the multiple Olympic gold-medal winner, reaching a top speed of 34 knots. The Duchess was seen helping with the rigging and even took control from skipper Sir Ben for part of the trip.  Sir Ben, speaking after the high-speed ride, revealed his team would love to get The Duchess on board for a race. In the world series they are allowed to take a guest. “We would love to get her racing with us as well if we can,” he said. “There’s a lot going on and we will see what the schedule allows.” He also revealed he hopes The Duchess will bring her children - Prince George, two, and Princess Charlotte, one - to the centre, adding: “She is certainly keen to get the Prince and Princess sailing at some time in the future, whether that is down here or elsewhere.” The McQueen outfit is an old favourite of Kate's. She first wore it to open a children's centre to Birmingham in August 2011 but also revived it in June 2014 when she wore it to Bletchley Park. But the look came into its own today as a chic nod to The Duchess’s nautical activities. With its frogging detailing and those gleaming buttons, the blouse and skirt - which are no longer available to buy - channel traditional naval uniforms. Alexander McQueen is, of course, one of the Duchess’s favourite labels. The British design house, whose creative director is Sarah Burton, was responsible for Kate’s wedding dress and has also dressed the Duchess in numerous bespoke and ready-to-wear designs ever since. For important occasions including the christenings of both Prince George and Princess Charlotte, and the Queen’s diamond Jubilee celebrations as well as numerous state banquets, the Duchess has turned to Burton. This also isn't the first time that the Duchess has reflected the theme of her day with her literal fashion choices. In fact, it’s a habit which she's carefully developed during the five years she has been married to Prince William.  Since her marriage, the Duchess has taken on the traditional duty of presenting the soldiers of the Irish guards regiment with a shamrock to celebrate St Patrick’s Day. The Duchess has two coats on rotation for the role; one by Emilia Wickstead and another from Hobbs but both are bottle green in hue as an obvious tribute to the traditional colour of the Emerald Isle. During a tour of Canada in 2011, the Duke and Duchess visited the Calgary stampede and rodeo. Not an obvious royal dressing comfort zone, perhaps. But Kate stepped up to the occasion and went full yee-haw in a stetson hat and appropriately cowgirl-esque Alice Temperley blouse. The Countess of Strathearn - as she’s known north of the border - has been careful to include nod to the north of the border in her looks. She has a Strathearn tartan scarf which she’s been seen in numerous times, once on a visit to Dumfries House. Another of Kate’s favourite McQueen outfits is a tartan dress coat worn on a visit to her old school which is named after Scotland’s patron St Andrew. As a keen tennis fan, the Duchess has been spotted numerous times at Wimbledon and will next year take over as patron of the All England Lawn and Tennis club. In 2012, Kate opted for a knitted cream McQueen dress which was an unmistakable echo of the sporty tennis whites seen on court. In Singapore in 2012, the Duke and Duchess visited an orchid garden where they viewed an orchid named after William’s mother Diana. Kate chose a Jenny Packham dress for the occasion hand painted with - you guessed it - orchids. The day after giving birth to Prince George in 2013, Kate left the Lindo wing and declared the gender of her new baby with a spotted Jenny Packham tea dress in baby blue.  Pippa Middleton and her new husband James Matthews are on their honeymoon in Australia and the Duchess of Cambridge’s sister is trialing all the summer holiday trends at once with her honeymoon wardrobe. Yes, ‘honeymoon wardrobes’ are now a thing, and according to e-tailer Lyst, 60% of 2017 brides are more excited about what they’ll be taking away in their suitcase than they were about their dress on the big day. Destination dressing is booming, and it has become something of a competitive sport - suncream stained cover-ups and battered flip flops will no longer do, as sales of designer espadrilles and status beach bags are surging. Lyst says that an average British bride will spend over £400 on new clothes and accessories to take on her honeymoon, which would likely include a luxe straw hat, metallic espadrilles, a designer beach dress and a decorated wicker basket-bag, according to their data on what customers are buying. Pippa has already ticked three of these ‘boxes’ in the few pictures released of her enjoying a stopover in Sydney during her honeymoon, but, as she certainly wasn’t an average bride, and with her wedding thought to have cost over £730,000, it only seems proportionate that her honeymoon wardrobe has been pricier too. Throughout the trip she has relied on an enormous statement beach bag by Sensi Studio (£317), espadrilles by Castaner (£75) and sunglasses by Persol, as the staples of her outfits. Investing in considered holiday accessories like these is clearly a strategy that pays off, as they are summery neutrals that will go with anything in your case - day or night - with very little styling effort. Pippa has been teaming hers with everything from sweet sundresses to the broderie anglaise Orla Kiely blouse (priced at £210) that she wore yesterday when arriving at Darwin airport. Also in Pippa’s suitcase is a stock pile of summer dresses, mostly by American label Kate Spade. Wearing the brand’s Floral Tiled Mini Dress for dinner last night in Sydney, and a variation of their Ponte Striped Fiorella Dress for a trip to the city’s harbour, she’s sticking to a ladylike, fit ‘n flare silhouette that she knows suits her. Having worn two of their day dresses and another cotton beach style from Kate Spade so far, it seems that this is the label that will ultimately headline her honeymoon wardrobe. And with prices starting at £215 for the dresses, you can bet that others gearing up for their own honeymoons will be quick to follow suit in Spade.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Debbie Harry and Blondie are currently in the middle of a 52-date world tour and, on stage, the 72 year-old is having as much fashion fun as ever. Night after night in Mexico City, Dallas, Austin, Atlanta, Orlando, Philadelphia, New York and Boston (those in just the last 14 days) Harry has brought statement style to her show, pleasing her crowds in embellished capes, extreme ruffles made of recycled ocean plastics, and shouty ‘stop fucking the planet’ slogans. Harry has collaborated with her friends the British design duo Vin and Omi on her tour wardrobe, and together they have brought a futuristic fashion fantasy to life. “We’re very bold designers, our catwalk shows are bold, so we fit very well with her and what she wants to represent on stage,” Vin explains of the partnership, which began for the friends several years ago when they met in New York. “She’s our muse, she’s the main celebrity that we design for and she’s got lots of our different pieces now.” Unlike many stars who will brief designers with a strict, preconceived plan of what they want to wear on stage, Vin says that Harry’s approach is spontaneous and fearless - she will try anything that the duo can dream up, as long as it looks fun and is made of sustainable fabrics. “She’s entertaining on stage but she’s one of the most relaxed performers, she’s not uptight about anything least of all her clothes,” Vin tells us, “Omi, Debbie and I just laugh all the time and that really helps - that’s what show fashion should be about.” The next show that the trio will take on together will be on 11th September; Vin and Omi’s pre-London Fashion Week show at the Andaz Hotel, where Debbie will be making her British catwalk debut. “She’s done New York Fashion Week but she hasn’t walked in London before, so this is a real coup for us,” Vin says. “We’re not into going for the typical model look at all. We get on with 16 year-old models as well as 70 year-old models, but for us casting is really about the vibe of the person.” Indeed, the DJ and television presenter Jo Whiley has walked for them before, alongside her eight year old daughter. Part of the appeal for Harry, though, was to attract attention to a cause she is passionate about. “Debbie is really involved with the Riverkeeper Project in New York, which is about cleaning up the Hudson River as well as others and oceans,” Vin explains. “Our show will be focussed on using fabrics made from recycled ocean and river plastics so she was totally up for walking in it.” Reimagined into puffball bomber jackets and wild ruffles (as is the Vin and Omi way) those wasted and washed up carrier bags will no doubt look revolutionary. “It will be bold,” Vin promises, “and definitely future punk.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Take two supermodels – one of which is a photographer, a suitcase full of clothes and a week on a paradise island. The result is the new Equipment campaign, starring Kate Moss and Daria Werbowy – which feels ever so slightly like rifling through a friend’s private holiday album. Moss, 41, and Werbowy, 32 were left to their own devices by the brand famed for its utterly wearable, masculine shirts when they headed off to Mustique to shoot the label’s spring 2016 campaign. They left behind the team usually required to make a shoot happen: no producer, hair stylist, make-up artist, nail technician,  caterer… no-one tinkering with a wind machine.   Instead they got back to basics on the tropical island, Werbowy armed with her 35mm camera, and became the art directors, subjects and photographer. “Kate trusted Daria completely - it was amazing to watch their process when it came down to execution time and I think it's clear in the intimacy of the pictures how well they worked together” Brett Ramey, vice president of creative at Equipment told The Telegraph. Ramey says: “Kate was the hair, the makeup, the styling, the driver and the production team all in one. Daria was the creative director, art director, the photographer and the visionary. Their dynamic and energy exchange was unlike anything I've ever experienced.” Werbowy, who was born in Poland but raised in Canada, has been responsible for the capturing the last two Equipment ad campaigns, in which she also starred via a series of self-portraits. The brand is celebrating its 40th anniversary this year; it was founded in 1976 by Christian Restoin, partner of renowned stylist and former Vogue Paris editor, Carine Roitfeld.  It was relaunched in 2010 by Serge Azria, the owner of denim label Current/ Elliott. It’s unusual for a brand to hand over creative control to its models, but as Ramey explains: “There is a reason women want to be like, dress like, and act like Daria and Kate. Whatever ‘it’ is, they both have it. Who are we to stand in their way? There is perhaps no greater fashion icon than Kate Moss. Not only is she brilliant but she is hysterically funny and one of the hardest working women I know.”    Ramey told us that she was "blown away" by the images. Elie Saab Couture is the designer of choice for the super rich, as earlier this year  20-year-old bride Khadija Uzhakhova wore a jaw-dropped gown by the house to her '£1 billion wedding' to Russian oligarch Said Gutseriev. With a skirt and four meter tail made of delicate Chantily lace, embellished in a pattern of silk flowers, pearls, clear and mirror crystals and sequins, it was a wedding dress designed to make a make a statement. "I would say that this dress would take 2,000 to 3,000 hours to make, and could have up to 50 people working on it," says Lord of the work that went into this gown. As for the price of a custom couture wedding gown like this one, he reveals: “The most expensive dress I have ever heard of was a Valentino dress costing half a million pounds commissioned by a Russian bride. I would normally say couture gowns by Vivienne Westwood, Elie Saab, Suzie Turner average at around £100,000 depending on the style and materials." Whilst the world of bridal couture is shrouded in secrecy, with fashion houses understandably respecting the privacy of their clients, the output is visible twice a year when the Haute Couture shows in Paris traditionally feature one statement bridal piece.  British couture designers Ralph & Russo’s closed their SS16 show with one of the most spectacular wedding gowns in couture history: a dress with a train so long it required six atelier staff to turn it at the end of the runway. The gown has a total of 826 metres of tulle and 46 metres of organza, with millions of micro-beads, crystals, pearls, delicate shaped organza flowers and three-dimensional petals and leaves hand-embroidered onto the gown. "The embroidery alone for the SS16 bridal gown took over 50 couturiers 6,000 combined hours to create," reveals designer Michael Russo. "We encourage clients to get in touch as soon as possible with bridal requests, and in general advise that six months be given for creation." "Our bridal pieces are extremely intricate and can take over 7,000 hours to make, with up to 24 couturiers working on the gown at any time," Tamara Ralph adds. "The weight of the gown depends on the client’s fabric of choice, but where possible, we do try to reduce this so that the bride is comfortable when walking. We work very closely with every bride to ensure that they are completely happy and confident on their special day." If this seems like a lot of work for a dress that will be worn for less than 24 hours, it’s worth remembering that the traditional white wedding dress is a well-established tradition. Queen Victoria is credited as starting the trend when, in a radical departure of women just wearing their best dresses to get married, she commissioned a white lace gown for her 1840 wedding to Prince Albert. Couturiers noticed that society girls of the time wanted to emulate their Queen and started creating white dresses - a colour that had traditionally been worn when women were presented at court and one which signified wealth because it was difficult to keep pristine. Society brides haven’t always felt the need to walk up the aisle in the most expensive gown their wealthy fathers can buy. In 1919, when industrialist Andrew Carnegie gave away his daughter, 22-year-old Margaret, it was a simple affair, held at the family’s Upper East Side home, with fewer than 100 guests and bagpipers for entertainment. The bride, widely known as “the richest girl in America”, wore a simple white satin dress trimmed with lace. Similarly, when it comes to dressing a royal bride, there are always savings to be made. In April 1923, when Lady Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon, later Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother, married Prince Albert at Westminster Abbey, her silk crepe moire gown followed the fashion for dropped waists, as popularised by Coco Chanel – but she had it run up in house, by a former court dressmaker.  Her daughter, the Queen, famously saved up ration cards to purchase the material needed for her bridal gown, designed by Norman Hartnell, made of ivory duchess satin and decorated with 10,000 white pearls imported from the United States. Her bridal ensemble also included a 15ft patterned full court train attached at the shoulders, and a silk tulle veil held in place by a tiara, lent to the princess by her mother. Ingrid Seward, editor-in-chief of Majesty magazine who has attended many a society wedding, is pleased that brides are reverting back to an “old-fashioned mindset” when it comes to the big day. “The smart thing for a society wedding is to make it very chic and subtle, low key: St Paul’s Knightsbridge, then a reception or a dance at Claridges. If you’re very grand, you have a reception in your own home. You don’t hire a castle.  “There used to be more concentration on the actual symbolism of getting married. Now it seems that brides concentrate on being ostentatious. You can’t get grander than Charles and Diana’s: the emphasis then was very much on the service, not the pomp and circumstance of the wedding. If, like me, you don’t remember much about Jackie O’s or Princess Grace’s wedding apart from the dress, it simply because they weren’t as public or as grand as they are today.”   And couture bridal budgets today are properly eye-watering. One oligarch was rumoured to have touted her £1 million wedding dress budget to her favourite fashion house with the proviso that she got a personal appointment with the designer in question. When he declined, she took her business elsewhere. Whilst European and Hollywood royalty seem to veer towards Italian designer Valentino to create their showstopping dresses - he’s made wedding gowns for everyone heiress Nicky Hilton to Princess Madeleine of Sweden - the Chinese and Russians head to Dior and Elie Saab. The actress Angelababy, known as China’s answer to Kim Kardashian thanks to her 58 million followers on social media, wore both at her £20 million wedding last year. Elie Saab made a wedding dress she wore in her engagement photos and Dior spent 5 months creating her dress for the big day, which saw 170 feet of tulle crafted into seven skirt layers and a 10 foot long train. Because of the workmanship that goes into couture bridal gowns, it's hardly surprising that very few women actually get to wear one of the creations. In 2014 The Telegraph reported that in the three years since Dolce & Gabbana began their Alta Moda collection (Italian for Haute Couture) they sold 15 wedding dresses.  The exclusivity surrounding the couture bridal business explains why other designers are keen to be part of it. Earlier this year Giles announced that he is closing his ready-to-wear line to enter into the world of Haute Couture. He told The Telegraph: "For the last four years we've been quietly developing that side of our business and working with private clients and couture off the back of our fantastic red carpet pieces we've done and had great gals wearing. It seemed like a good growth direction for us and to show it at Paris in Couture is where you show the best of what you can do." Bridal is also part of his business plan, as he said:  "It'd be a logical place for us to go to and also seeing how popular the Bridal collections in New York are and how much they have grown.”  So how does one get to be the type of person who purchases a £100,000 wedding gown? Quintessentially's Lord advises you will need a well-connected wedding planner well versed in the world of bridal couture.  "A planner normally has access and contacts to the Couture fashion houses and works with multiple designers on various commissions. One planner I know is working with Elie Saab on three different gowns commissions at the moment.  If a wedding planner already has worked with the designer, it is easy to commission a custom gown. Brides that commission couture also often already have a relationship with that chosen designer, through buying previous collections." For the rest of us, it's about admiring from afar...  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s the day before the Brexit vote, and I’m on a Paris-bound Eurostar train. I’m en route to spend a few hours in the archives of a French jeweller owned by a Swiss conglomerate whose other holdings include Italian, German, Chinese and American brands. So far, so fashion. This journey, like the fashion world as a whole, is underpinned by an international outlook that seems tinged with premature nostalgia. Today: frictionless movement across the Anglo-French border. From Friday? Potentially, passports, s'il vous plait? Members of the British fashion industry were slow off the mark about intervening in discussions over Brexit. Until the menswear shows in London last week, the highest-profile public statements by industry leaders consisted of Burberry’s Christopher Bailey, Vogue’s Alexandra Shulman and Dame Vivienne Westwood adding their signatures to letters supporting Remain and an i-D magazine shoot of street-cast models wearing photographer Wolfgang Tillmans’ Remain T-shirts. Maybe the sluggish response represented hesitation to take sides in a contentious debate. But as campaigning draws to an end and the referendum result looks increasingly uncertain, the industry has grown increasingly outspoken in favour of the Remain option. Last week the British Fashion Council revealed that 90% of respondents to its Brexit survey said they preferred to remain in Europe, with only 4.3% voting to leave. At the menswear shows, designers Patrick Grant of E. Tautz and Cozette McCreery and Sid Bryan of Sibling took their bows wearing bold ‘IN’ t-shirts. And yesterday, Victoria Beckham declared her support for Remain on Instagram, writing, “I believe in my country, I believe in a future for my children where we are stronger together.” For all its invocations of ‘heritage’ and ‘Britishness’, the UK fashion scene relies on access to European talent and markets. And many fashion insiders are concerned a Leave win will be an harbinger of the end of free trade, bringing with it increased manufacturing costs and a more complicated business environment - leading to higher prices for consumers. "We expect clothing price to increase by 4% because of the tariff and non-tariff barriers that would start applying on imports from the EU," says Swati Dhingra, Assistant Professor Department of Economics and CEP, at the London School of Economics. "Even if Britain puts these import tariffs at zero unilaterally, there would be non-tariff barriers to importing from the EU which would increase clothing prices by 2% on average."  The set-up of established designers demonstrates how complicated Brexit could be practically. Phoebe Philo lives in London and designs for a Parisian house. Stella McCartney, Christopher Kane and Alexander McQueen are British brands part owned by Kering, a French luxury conglomerate whose chief executive resides in London. And it’s no different on the high street. The brilliant Finery - a small British brand that proves it is possible to flourish on the high street here if you get your market right - is backed by a global fashion group based in Berlin and with investment from Stockholm. The other concern is what happens if free movement is restricted, should Britain vote to leave. The 19% of students on the BA fashion design course at Central Saint Martins who hail from European countries are "exceedingly worried," says Willie Walters, course director of BA fashion at CSM, part of the University of the Arts London. "The cross-fertilisation of ideas between students from mainland Europe and Britain is enormous… Brexit would be a huge regression." Many of the most thrilling names on the London design scene have roots elsewhere in Europe. Mary Katrantzou (Greece), Roksanda Ilincic (Serbia), Peter Pilotto (Austria; design partner Christopher de Vos is Belgo-Peruvian), Isa Arfen (Italy), Marques’Almeida (Portugal) and others weren’t born in the UK but chose to build businesses here. "I have lived here 14 years and now have British citizenship" Katrantzou tells The Telegraph, "I employ people from Sweden, Germany, Italy - all over Europe - so we really have that fear of the unkown. Would there be visa issues? How easy would it be? It makes everything very fragile." Katrantzou says that any short term gains which might come from a post-Brexit dip in the pound would pale in significance compared with the long-term effects. "Stores might buy more from us in the immediate future if the pound was weak but there are so many bigger, underlying issues," she says. "All our factories are in Europe so we feel very connected and depend on being able to develop pieces in time for our shows, working to deadlines. In London, the creative industry is a melting pot of people and that is the real core of our business - their perspective and ideas are part of a modern Europe. I want to see my country move forward, not back." But economics aside, is there an emotional side that’s swaying the fashion world towards Remain? Ever since British Vogue surveyed the latest styles from Paris in its inaugural issue in 1916, what happens on the continent has had an outsized influence on British style. Just as our food has improved since we’ve integrated further with Europe, so has our style grown more sophisticated through ease of access to Paris, Milan and Copenhagen. Even the most committed member of the ‘Leave’ camp probably has a stripey (French) top or two and a pair of (German) adidas Stan Smiths nestled in her (Swedish) Ikea wardrobe. Her closet will also feature heavy Spanish representation by way of Zara, which may cease to be quite so cheap or cheerful once duties are added on. And no doubt she'll boast more than a few holiday purchases picked up on European summer breaks. (Side note: how much more satisfying is it finding an item in a Greek market that you know no one else will have?) It’s that merging of cultures that makes British style so unique - and so much more interesting that the homogenized look you see throughout America, for example. Take a tally of where the brands you’re wearing right now originate as an example. See? Europe: It’s a good look on you.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Loyal followers of Victoria Beckham’s style outings will have just one question at the moment: why has she been wearing so many white t-shirts? As she’s dashed between London and New York over the past few weeks, Beckham has been photographed on a near daily basis wearing a slightly slouchy, pristine white tee with a rotating series of jeans or relaxed tailored trousers. It turns out it’s one of her favourite pieces from her new Victoria, Victoria Beckham collection. “I don’t have time to think about I’m wearing. I’m spending so much time focussing on the collection that the last thing I want to think about is what I’m wearing so it’s like a uniform,” the designer clarified last night as she hosted cocktails and canapes on the closing evening of London fashion week at Mayfair’s Mark’s club where she and David love to go when they’re in London. “I thought, let’s do it here and drink some tequila, who doesn’t love a bit of Casamigos? It’s always a bit of joke because everyone knows that I love a little tequila.” Of course, Beckham’s new wardrobe staple isn’t just any t-shirt, but one that she has obsessed over until it meets her exacting standards of sartorial perfection. It comes with her VB initials subtly embroidered in graphic white font on the sleeve. “I hate tees which are droopy around the neck, it needs to be boxy and masculine but not too long in the body. It should be so easy and simple to find but as someone who wanted that, I couldn’t find it.” In a way, the story of the white t-shirt crystallises the Victoria Beckham brand’s raison d’etre: giving women what they want, perhaps even before they know it. For SS18, Beckham has divined that we will need uplifting pastels, preppy tailoring and a few witty motifs in our wardrobes. She took her inspiration from Miami in the 80s; last year she was at Art Basel and fell in love with the city for its “energy, heat and humidity.” “She wants to have fun, she likes prints and she doesn’t want anything overly complicated,” Beckham mused of her ‘woman’ as she flicked through the rails of fuschia and white pleats, zinging Roy Lichtenstein-inspired prints and tangerine silk pyjama co-ords. There’s a dusky pink and white striped suit which Beckham describes as ‘comfortable and effortless’. “I don’t want it to look too try hard so this is such an easy suit to wear with a white tee, a trainer and a heel. You can wear it in the day and in the evening.” Although Beckham built her fashion reputation on her penchant for sleek minimalism, the placing of flamingos on mini dresses and on shirts suggests that she’s relaxing her attitude towards the bright and the bold. “I used to wear a lot of black so I would never understand why certain people used to say ‘you need to wear colour’. I just thought black was great but now I really enjoy wearing colour. When I see pictures of myself in colour it feels fresh and more useful.
