 If you think all fashion heiresses are bubble-headed brats more concerned with tearing through their trust funds than doing something useful, then you’ve not met Leonetta Fendi. The 20-year-old bounds purposefully through the salon at Shoreditch House looking as if she’s just taken a detour from the Women’s March. Dressed like a latter-day Land Girl in a T-shirt tucked into oversized blue workwear trousers, she’s wearing the sturdy boots of someone who prefers to walk rather than Uber it. Her mother is Silvia Venturini Fendi, who heads up the menswear and accessory arms of the Italian luxury house and who, in 1997, created the Fendi Baguette, the little tote that kick-started the It-bag era. Leonetta’s sister, the jeweller  Delfina Delettrez Fendi, also designs accessories for the house. Growing up a Fendi meant growing up at the heart of one of Italy’s most iconic fashion brands. Karl Lagerfeld, who has been designing for Fendi for 52 years, would sketch pictures of her when she was a baby. She has been helping out backstage at her mother’s fashion shows since she was 10, attended her first Dior haute couture show at the age of 12 (‘I was desperate to meet John Galliano’) and can have her pick of glamorous looks from the Fendi archive when the occasion calls. A socialite’s career of front-row photo ops, fabulous furs and expensive friends, with perhaps a little designing on the side, seemed to beckon, but Fendi wants more from life than that. She recently graduated from SOAS, the University of London’s School of Oriental and African Studies, with a degree in politics and development studies, cutting off her waist-length hair in a gesture of freedom to celebrate the end of her exams. ‘I want to go into politics,’ she says, running a dainty hand through her gamine new crop. ‘I want to help people and change things’ – although it’s activism, rather than institutional politics (which she describes as ‘scary’), that interests her most. ‘It’s the small acts, because everything you do is political, even small acts,’ she says. But even those aren’t always enough. ‘All my friends are vegan and I still eat meat, so they’re like, “You’re not that political.” And I say, I still am – in my own way.’ Her own way runs counter to the prescribed route of the fashion It girl. If Leonetta, which means ‘little lion’ in Italian, conforms to any stereotypes, it’s that of the ‘woke’ millennial rather than the spoilt rich girl. Instead of spending school holidays yacht-hopping around Europe, she volunteered in refugee camps in Greece and Athens, ‘giving out clothes and sleeping bags and helping in the kitchens’. She also went to Calais. ‘Four or five times. I was volunteering in the camp. It was hard the first time, especially as you don’t know what to expect. It was crazy – terrible, terrible situations – but I met such great people. ‘I’m still texting them as they move around the world. Some have managed to get into the UK and they’ve claimed asylum and are starting their life slowly.’ It all sounds very worthy, but this bright young Fendi exudes an infectious optimism. Her upbringing had, she says, ‘positives and negatives’. ‘When I was young people would say, “Will you give me a Fendi bag for my birthday?” I started to think, why are they asking me that? That’s not nice. People are going to be friendly with me for that?’ She and all the Fendi cousins went to the same middle school. ‘There were so many of us, we were a clique,’ she says of her clan. ‘That’s when I started to realise what it meant, the family.’ Even so, she didn’t enjoy special fashion privileges. She and her cousins were the last girls in school to get Fendi schoolbags. ‘It was after all the other girls started carrying them,’ she remembers, with amusement more than irritation. For Fendi, like many children born into high-flying families, the challenge is to create an identity for herself. ‘People would say, “But you’re a Fendi – why go to an anti-capitalist march? How can you do that?” People will always judge.’ Her ambition is to work for the UN or an NGO, but she’s not turning her back on fashion and the opportunities a global brand like Fendi offers. ‘Now I’m starting to think of both paths and to aim to combine politics and fashion,’ she says. ‘Fashion is very powerful. It’s one of the most powerful mediums to express yourself in.’ The family specialises in producing unconventional, strong, creative and entrepreneurial women. They have surrounded the young heiress all her life. The brand was founded by Leonetta’s great-grandmother, Adele Casagrande. She opened a fur and leather workshop in Rome in 1918, renaming it Fendi in 1925 after marrying Edoardo Fendi. The business was passed on to their five daughters – Paola, Franca, Carla, Alda and Anna (Leonetta’s grandmother) – who grew up in the atelier, playing with the furs and the bags. With the help of Karl Lagerfeld, who began working for Fendi in 1965, the sisters are credited with transforming the image of fur, from a staple of wealthy women’s wardrobes into a must-have fashion statement. As company president, Carla Fendi, who died in June of this year, introduced the brand to the American market in the late 1960s and masterminded its global expansion in the decades that followed. The Fendis were a rare female fashion dynasty, and as a mark of the sisters’ importance to Italy, they were granted special dispensation by the Italian government to allow their descendants to adopt the maternal surname. In 2001 the sisters sold a majority stake to LVMH. ‘Five sisters was too much,’ Karl Lagerfeld said at the time of the deal, ‘and they were not speaking. The husbands were all happy when they sold.’ After that, most of the Fendi family moved on from the day-to-day running of the business. Only Silvia and Delfina are actively involved today. The expectation is that Leonetta, too, will join them at Fendi, although she insists she won’t be designing. ‘I said no, I don’t know how to draw,’ she admits with a playful shrug. What she excels at is building a bridge between Fendi – where an haute couture coat can cost €1 million – and her own millennial generation, who have a very different attitude to luxury from their predecessors. In terms of shaping the attitudes of the house to appeal to new young customers, she’s Fendi’s secret weapon. To that end, she’s been working with F is For…, the digital platform set up by Fendi in 2016. Produced by and aimed at millennials – the consumer group that all luxury brands are desperate to woo – it showcases live art and DJ experiences on the roof of Fendi’s Rome HQ, as well as profiling young artists, actors and creatives. Fendi – unpretentious, charismatic, warm and confident – is a natural in front of the camera, and stages video takeovers and show coverage on the site as well as scouting for young talent to highlight. Its values of freedom of expression and optimism chime with her. Obsessed with authenticity, plugged into social media (‘I get all my news from Facebook and Instagram’), she says her generation wants to engage with brands that reflect their values. ‘We want to change things for the better and we need everyone’s support. We can’t do it by ourselves. The people that are in power now, we want to have a dialogue with them. We don’t want to wait to be in power to change things. We will make our voices heard.’ Politics was always discussed at home, and she credits her philanthropic Aunt Carla with inspiring her to get more involved with the causes she believed in. She regularly volunteered at Carla’s hospice for children with cancer.   Her interest in politics deepened when she left home at 15 to attend United World Colleges Atlantic, a progressive boarding school in the Vale of Glamorgan, which describes its alumni as ‘agents of positive change.’ Her mother, Silvia, had an unconventional upbringing. Her mother, Anna, was such a dedicated aesthete that she dressed Silvia and her siblings only in black because it was more chic than wearing colour, leading many who met the youngsters to believe they were in constant mourning. Anna art-directed the family’s life to the point that they even ate food dyed to match her favourite shades. ‘There was the blue period, the green period, the black period… All my friends would love to come over because we’d serve blue rice for dinner, up until my mother realised she was poisoning us with chemicals,’ Silvia said in an interview last year. Silvia inherited her mother’s aesthetic sense (although not her culinary tastes), gravitating towards the Fendi ateliers. She began working for the family business as soon as she could. Fendi remembers her mother wasn’t like the other parents at her school in Rome. ‘Like most of the women in my family, she was both the woman and the man,’ she says. She recalls asking her mother to do the school run but Silvia was too busy at work. ‘All the mums would hang out at and come and pick up the kids after school. I would think, why is my mum not doing that?’ While having a mother with a high-powered job might have given her pangs of anxiety as a child, Fendi now has a different take on it. ‘It is good because she is very powerful. She gives me a sense of empowerment. I can do whatever a man can do and do it as well as she could, and I can take care of myself without needing anyone else to look after me.’ As a member of one of Italy’s wealthiest families, Fendi doesn’t try to hide her privilege. Instead, she wears it lightly. During her first year at SOAS she was too embarrassed to invite her university friends over because she was living in her mother’s London house in Knightsbridge. ‘I hated it. I didn’t know where to go for lunch or dinner and all my friends were in east London,’ she says. She moved to Dalston in the second year and spent her time going to marches, lectures and exhibitions, and cycling back and forth to Peckham, where her then-boyfriend lived. ‘I go to Loulou’s [a private members’ club in Mayfair] but also Blues Kitchens or any bar I find. I feel I can adapt to everything,’ she says. After graduation, she took some time out, surfing in Portugal with a group of 30 friends, putting off the tricky business of deciding what to do next and where to call home: Italy, where her teenage bedroom is still plastered with One Direction posters; London, where she’s spent the past three years; or New York. ‘My mum is saying, “Did you find yourself an internship yet?’’’ Whatever she does, we can expect her presence at Fendi to grow. As for fashion, there are plenty of things she would like to change. ‘It’s not enough to put a slogan on a T-shirt – you have to put in place what you talk and advocate for – but it’s a start,’ she says. Sustainability is a big concern for her and her generation, as is exploitation in the supply chain. ‘Fashion has to be conscious about what’s happening around the world. It’s such a massive industry and it also has much potential to reach  the youngest in society. Now, it has to have a positive impact.’ Current and future CEOs take note.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Donatella Versace has always championed youth and talent, but nowadays she’s paying attention to older generations. Her last few shows have featured, if not geriatrics, women in their late 40s and 50s, albeit supermodels.  It’s a loyalty thing. Back in the late 1980s and 1990s, her brother Gianni helped create the cult of the supermodel. He was the first designer to take out exclusive contracts with models that would prevent them walking in any other designer’s show that season. It would cost him – around £60,000 per model for a 15 minute show back in 1993. But it was always worth it in financial terms. Working almost constantly with Richard Avedon, Versace and the supers created some of the most memorable fashion images of the past three decades. The supers are back working, in every sense, for Donatella Versace again. The Icons show a year ago, where she managed to lure Naomi Campbell, Claudia Schiffer, Helena Christensen and Cindy Crawford and her model daughter Kaia Gerber onto one catwalk, was a talking point for months (is it a coincidence that 12 months later the Versace company was bought by Capri Holdings for just over $2 billion?) Late December, behind -the- scenes footage of Shalom Harlow,  the 45 year old 90s super model,  dancing on set of a Versace campaign went viral. “Who says older women are less relevant in fashion? “ says Donatella Versace. The balletically elegant Harlow was in Friday’s show, along with 50 year old Stephanie Seymour, the latter wearing a strappy, skin tight black mesh dress that left onlookers in no doubt that Seymour has a rigorous work-out routine. This is the woman’s whose billionaire husband Peter Brandt had his wife immortalised by the Italian American artist Maurizio Cattelan who created for him a nude sculpture that had half of Seymour’s body jutting out of a wall, in the way that a hunter might display his latest kill. The ultimate trophy in other words. History so far does not record whether Brandt got the joke. While there was much in this collection that represented a departure from Versace’s signature vampiness – clashing colours and textures, fake furs and a slightly kooky, vintage patina to everything – Seymour’s outfit  was quintessential Versace, A version of the safety pinned black dress that Elizabeth Hurley wore to the premier of Four Weddings and A Funeral in 1994. That dress could be said of have launched Hurley’s career, as well as turning the red carpet into the ultimate catwalk. Seymour’s was (marginally )more modest, minus the giant slashes that snaked up the entire length of Hurley’s dress – a nod to changing mores, even in Milan © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Come February 26th, a procession of dreamy dresses will make their way down the red carpet as awards season culminates with its glitziest event: the Oscars. With the Golden Globes and SAG awards over and couture fashion week having taken place in Paris last week, now is the time that actresses and their stylists (some of the most powerful people in Hollywood) will be starting to make decisions about what to wear for the big night although of course, each look remains a closely guarded secret until the moment it is unveiled on the red carpet.  Despite that fact that the dresses are often months in the making, design houses and their clients are well-versed in keeping their Academy Awards dress plans under wraps, with many keeping a few options in mind and sometimes not making a final decision until the day itself. However, given their red carpet CVs and existing alliances with designer labels, it is possible to survey the looks from couture and the Spring/Summer collections to make some educated guesses and predictions ... She's a relative newcomer to the red carpet, but Ruth Negga has proven she has a knack for fashion and a willingness to experiment while her stylist Karla Welch is a pro at coaxing her into bold looks. The Ethiopian-Irish actress has made waves during her promotional tour for Loving in looks by Chanel, Prada, Erdem and Valentino, and for the Globes she served up cool girl style in a sequin zip-up Louis Vuitton gown which took 120 hours to make.  Given her growing contacts book of go-to designers, it's hard to guess where Negga has turned for her Academy Awards look, but we'd love to see her continue her daring streak in something like the sequin gown which Kendall Jenner wore at Chanel's Haute Couture show. We reckon she can carry off the marabou feather trim and would suit an equally vampy beauty look. While for some actresses dressing for the red carpet with a baby bump is a tall order, Natalie Portman does pregnancy style with ease and elegance. So far both Prada and Dior have provided her with awards looks this season, and judging by their minimalist cuts and modest necklines, we assume her Oscars dress will follow a similar formula. Because if it's not broken, why fix it?  As a 'face' of Dior, Portman will likely be contracted to wear one of the house's designs for the Oscars. Portman and her stylist Kate Young have also been paying a fitting tribute to Jackie Kennedy (who Portman stars as in Jackie, the film she is nominated for) so far this awards season so we can expect them to continue to draw inspiration from the former First Lady's simple, elegant look.  With its empire silhouette, this velvet, shooting star print gown could be customised easily for the pregnant star and would look divine on her. So far, Nicole Kidman has gone all out for glitz, glam and sequins on the 2017 awards season circuit. An Alexander McQueen cold shoulder dress with heavy embellishment was an ethereal yet fashion-forward choice for the Globes, while her emerald green Gucci gown, which featured a daringly low neckline and a parrot perching on each shoulder, proved that she's anything but a wallflower. So will she be equally daring for the Oscars, or surprise us with a fashion U-turn? Our bet for Kidman is on an Armani Prive gown. She has a long-standing relationship with the brand and has already worn several of the label's Couture and ready-to-wear designs on her promotional tour for Lion. Plus, she sat front row at the Couture show in Paris earlier this month, suggesting she could have been keeping an eye out for her Oscars gown. We'd love to see her in this flapper style column dress - less glitzy than the rest of her awards wardrobe but an exquisite choice. We imagine the striking orange embellishment would appeal to her inner magpie. Best Actress front-runner Emma Stone has done both girly and sensual so far this season, so which fashion route will she take for the Oscars? She has worn Lanvin, Elie Saab and Giambattista Valli for the Academy Awards in the past, and we'd love to see her in Saab again this year. Might we suggest a custom version of this elegant cornflower blue gown?  Stone's stylist of eight years, Petra Flannery, is know for dressing her clients - who also include Claire Danes and Zoe Saldana - in fashion-forward pieces with a playful edge. We think the cape detail and opportunity to dress up this Saab design with jewellery and accessories would appeal to both Flannery and her client. Moonlight actress Naomie Harris has one of the most colourful style CVs of all the nominees. She mixes up girly looks by younger labels like Rosie Assoulin and Giamba with stalwarts like Armani Prive, and also isn't afraid to wear more experimental pieces by the likes of Rodarte and Gucci. “You need some surprises along the way, then that “wow” moment," Harris's stylist Micaela Erlanger recently told The Telegraph of her red carpet strategy.  We'd love to see the British actress fly the flag for a homegrown label like Christopher Kane. For the most part, her dress choices have bold adornments and form-fitting silhouettes in common, so a floor-length version of this scribble and floral applique gown could be perfect. We don't think the Academy Awards is quite ready for Crocs, however.  Michelle Williams has long been the face of Louis Vuitton's handbag collection , so it's almost certainly inked into her deal that she will be dressed in the label at the Oscars. The 36-year-old has already worn a lace gown and a metallic column dress from Vuitton so far this awards season, with her stylist Kate Young telling Vogue that her SAGs look took months of planning and aimed to be "modern and cool". The Manchester By The Sea actress isn't one for flashing the flesh, so we think this modest yet directional gown featuring the brand's signature checkerboard print is a strong contender to inspire her Oscars look. No doubt Young will add an edgy accessory to the mix. Having graced hundreds of red carpets in her time, Meryl Streep knows what works for her. While relaxed tailoring is her go-to for premieres, awards ceremonies are her time to ramp up the glamour and the sparkles. Perhaps her most iconic look is the gold lame Lanvin gown she wore to the Academy Awards, which coordinated perfectly with her third Academy Award gong, which she scooped for The Iron Lady. While Streep is partial to a form-fitting gown, she chose a floaty white number for the SAGs and it really worked for her, so we're touting this whimsical Valentino Couture gown for her shortlist. With a few tweaks - including a more modest neckline, a slip and sleeves, it would be a breathtaking choice for her. Isabelle Hubert will be making her first appearance at the Oscars. Though make no mistake, she has serious clout in the acting world. Having starred in over 100 movies and known as 'the Meryl Streep of France', she has been nominated for 15 Cesar awards - France's equivalent of the Oscars- and her fashion credentials are equally impressive. Her red carpet style is elegant, structured and usually colourful - she's partial to a bright trouser suit and a bejwelled gown.  Whilst Gucci has dominated the red carpet of late, it would be fascinating to see someone wear this rainbow sequin gown from the brand's Spring/Summer collection. We know Huppert has a weakness for the Italian brand already, as she wore it to the Globes. Failing that, she was also spotted on the Armani Prive front row, so could be eyeing something more minimalist.      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Meghan Markle may have only been propelled to global fame a matter of months ago, when news of her relationship with Prince Harry was revealed, but she has already become catnip for style spotters. So much so, that many have even created businesses from tracking Markle's every style move.  Editors Amanda Dishaw and Christine OBrien-Ross, of Vancouver and Washington D.C. respectively, document and detail every outfit that Meghan Markle wears on their fashion blog Meghan’s Mirror, keeping their dedicated audience up to date on exactly what the actress’s latest look is, where she bought it, and how they can get it for themselves. “When news broke that Prince Harry was dating Meghan, most people’s first reaction was 'Who?' quickly followed by 'Oh, she’s beautiful, and oh my God, I need her coat,'” explains Dishaw of the reason for starting the website. She and OBrein-Ross had already found great success with their first blog What Would Kate Do?, which tracks the Duchess of Cambridge’s style choices, and were predicting that Ms Markle would likely gain a similar following of fashion fans over time. “That was around November 2016, and while we were not surprised that people would be attracted to Meghan’s style, we were surprised with just how much people love her.” That ‘how much’, has translated to an average of 40,000 visitors to the blog (and counting) every month, as the world has been getting to know Markle and her “effortless” approach to dressing. “Our traffic is growing by over 100% month on month,” says Dishaw. “Whenever there is a ‘Meghan sighting’, we see huge spikes in traffic as people are interested in finding out more about what she is wearing and what she’s been up to.” “Any girlfriend of Prince Harry would get a healthy dose of media attention, of course, but Meghan has really [shown that she is not just] a companion – she’s an accomplished actress, a devoted humanitarian and a fabulous fashion icon in her own right.” The most popular post on Meghan’s Mirror to date has been a sighting in Jamaica, when she accompanied the Prince to his friend Tom Inskip’s wedding. “There were many questions about the origins of her Erdem dress - was it bespoke from the designer? Was it customised for Meghan? - as well as the Cartier Love bangle she wore, as it is rumoured to have been a gift from her first husband,” says Dishaw. “We believe it was a hugely popular post because people not only wanted to know what Meghan was wearing, but the world was clamouring over photos of the new couple together for the first time.” Other hits to date have included a February shopping trip that the actress took in Kensington, wearing only British brands, and a sighting of her leaving Heathrow Airport in December, carrying a new Mulberry bag. It’s a style of reporting that requires around-the-clock observations, as the Markle experts monitor news wires and picture agencies, as well as the actress’s Instagram account, for any updates or new images. Getting in first is everything, as fans want to know details of the outfit before it sells out - a reaction akin to the famous “Kate effect” that countless retailers have experienced thanks to the Duchess of Cambridge's style choices. “We constantly monitor for new sightings of Meghan,” explains Dishaw, of the conversations that happen between the editors and their contributors, as they battle to identify, say, those Coach boots from seven years ago, before any other media outlet. “As soon as Meghan has been spotted out and about, the process begins. Emails fly around, text messages buzz back and forth. Meghan is very loyal in her style choices, meaning she often chooses to repeat pieces or brands that she favours. Knowing them can help quickly identify pieces, then we also work with our individual connections – be it with brands, other fashion experts or the wider fashion communities on social media.” If at this point you are still wondering why the fascination, Dishaw explains that Markle’s polished-yet-easy look offers a welcome alternative for those who are sick of seeing inaccessible stars on the red carpet. “As we grew the What Would Kate Do? site, we discovered that women were quite often fed up with the fashion role models offered by celebrity culture,” she says. “They were looking for a source of inspiration for dressing that was different to the alternatives, and in many cases Kate ticked that box.” Markle offers more of the same sophistication, she says, describing her formula as “casual, effortless, on-trend and youthful. Her style manages to both capture new trends while being built around solid classics that she wears time and time again.” While the gorgeous gowns and exotic occasionwear ensembles, of course, make for fantastical viewing, Dishaw says that the looks readers really love from both Kate and Meghan are the ones that they could replicate themselves. “While [Tom Inskip’s wedding] may be our most popular post, Meghan’s most popular looks are 100% her casual styles,” she explains. “We might all like to imagine ourselves attending galas in ballgowns, but the reality is that all of us can see ourselves walking to a yoga class, or grocery shopping in a pair of great jeans. Meghan definitely has the athleisure look down to an art - it’s a chic yet comfortable look, and she looks effortless while doing it.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It is nearly two decades since I first met Karl Lagerfeld, and over the years,  I have come to realise that the only certainty in any conversation with him is that he is likely to avoid the obvious, and there will be many diversions along the way. And so it is that when I meet him in Rome, not long before the Fendi couture show at the Trevi Fountain, the last thing he wants  to talk about is his visionary creative direction for the brand, which he juggles with his role at Chanel (and much else besides). I’ve just seen a preview of the collection, which is in part inspired by the illustrations of the Danish artist Kay Nielsen, whose work included a haunting series of drawings for a collection of occasionally menacing Scandinavian folk tales published in 1914, entitled East of  the Sun and West of the Moon. Quite how this  will relate to the setting of the Trevi Fountain remains unclear to me, at this point. (Later  I remember that Anita Ekberg, who frolicked in the Trevi Fountain in Fellini’s La Dolce Vita, was born and bred in Sweden; hence the possibly tenuous Scandinavian connection?)  As always, Lagerfeld parries any direct questions about the source of his inspiration for  a particular collection. ‘You know, I don’t analyse things that much,’ he says, with a shrug and a hint of a self-deprecating smile. ‘I work with my instinct. My inner voice is the Joan of Arc, you see?’ Out of context, his remark might sound grandiose – but it isn’t. For this is a man who takes his work seriously, while refusing to elevate fashion to the status of art; a designer who has shaped contemporary style for more than half a century, yet always demands more of himself. ‘I’m never pleased with myself,’ he says. ‘I always think I could do better.’  He no longer needs to explain himself; he exists to create anew, rather than look back at his illustrious past. But for the record, he joined Fendi in 1965, Chanel in 1983; he also designs for his eponymous brand, as well as being a  prolific photographer and ardent publisher. ‘My professional life is about forgetting,’ he says, when I ask whether he dreamt this latest Fendi collection (he once told me that he keeps a sketching pad by his bed at night, to be ready to capture the ideas that alight while he sleeps). ‘I make big efforts to forget. Not because I wasn’t happy but because I have to find something else. I cannot stop at what I did.’ This colloquy could be discouraging; and, given that we are in the penthouse of the Fendi boutique in Rome, with a retinue of PRs hovering at a discreet distance, I am aware that the official agenda for our encounter – the celebration of Fendi’s 90th anniversary – is not being adhered to. But Lagerfeld’s conversation tends to be beguiling even when he is opaque. His eyes are hidden behind his trademark dark glasses, his uniform of high white collar, dark jacket and black trousers serving as a customary disguise; but even so, his swift words lead the listener in several intriguing directions.  When I ask about the appeal of Nielsen’s phantasmagorical illustrations, he says, ‘It’s not art deco, it’s very different, it’s much more poetic… Don’t forget, I spent my childhood on the Danish border. I’m a person from the North, and happy to be one; it will never change…’ His reference to his childhood is brief – he will not be drawn on my questions about Hans Christian Andersen and the Brothers Grimm, other than to confirm that he read their stories when he was young. In previous interviews, however, he has told me about his early years in Germany, with a forbidding mother who sounds as if she had something of the archetypal fairytale witch about her. When he played the piano, she slammed the lid on his fingers and said, ‘Draw! It makes less noise.’ When he spoke, she told him to talk faster, as she didn’t have time to listen to his ‘rubbish’. She also told him he had ugly hands (hence he now keeps them covered in gloves); ridiculous hair that stuck out at the sides (thereafter tied back in a severe ponytail); and a fat bottom (subsequently kept in shape by his strict diet). Yet despite these and other cruel jibes (including an unwarranted observation that he had peculiarly large nostrils), Lagerfeld has described his mother as ‘perfect’: because her insults stopped him from becoming egocentric or vain.  But today, there is to be no talk of his upbringing, only of the creative freedom upon which  he thrives. When I ask again whether any specific fables inspired his Fendi couture show – entitled ‘Legends & Fairy Tales’ – he says, ‘I don’t know. I don’t remember. I sketched them without knowing what I was doing and I don’t want to make a fake comment about something  that came quite easily, without too many questions. I’m not a marketing person. 'At work, you know… I never do meetings… I have nothing to do with any of that – it’s just my studio, my pen and that is all.’ The result of his insistence on liberty, rather than corporate control, is a remarkable success story – rising sales at Fendi and Chanel – and, as a consequence, what he describes as ‘a lifelong contract’ at both. ‘My Fendi contract ends in 2045,’ he adds (at which point he will be 112).  ‘Does the contract say, “I can do what I want?”’ I ask. ‘Exactly,’ he says, with a flicker of delight. ‘If not, I would be bored… I don’t want people to interfere or marketing people to make things difficult. I don’t discuss anything with them.’ Instead, he has a friendly, respectful relationship with the owners of Chanel and Fendi (the Wertheimers at the former, Bernard Arnault at the latter), and with Fendi’s dynamic CEO, Pietro Beccari, and Chanel’s equally accomplished president of fashion, Bruno Pavlovsky. If such freedom is an enviable way of working, then it also requires discipline and commitment, which Lagerfeld possesses in abundance (along with  a loyal team, most of whom have been his close collaborators for a decade or more). And while Lagerfeld tends to look ahead, he has a vast knowledge of fashion history and its intersection with wider culture. Here, after all, is a polymath who left Germany to study in Paris, and honed his craft in the houses of Balmain and Patou in the 1950s. It was Lagerfeld, too, who developed ready-to-wear at Chloé in the 1960s, as he proceeded to do at Fendi. The brand was already famed for its superlative furs and leather products, but it took Lagerfeld to add a sense of playful chic and inventiveness, while also enhancing the creativity of the five Fendi sisters, who had inherited the company. (Anna Fendi – whose daughter Silvia is the current creative director for Fendi’s accessories and menswear – says, ‘We always considered Karl a genius. He unites creativity and rationality.’)  At the very least, Lagerfeld has a  notable sense of perspective, and an understanding of the desire fuelling the luxury industry, and the ebb and flow of money that pays for his products. ‘There are many more couture clients than ever before,’ he says. ‘Most of them, you will never see at the shows, because they don’t go to Paris or Rome, they get the collections shipped and shown in their homes on the other side of the world – from China to Japan to Korea and the Middle East. These are new fortunes, you know? They make the rich of the past look poor. In the old days, when an American bought five couture dresses, she was a good client – now,  a client will buy 20 dresses in five minutes. ‘Somebody said to me about a coat in a Fendi collection that cost a million pounds, “Don’t  you think it’s a shame?” I replied, “In your eyes,  perhaps, but for other people, it’s a joy.”’ Yet  he never crosses paths with the new couture clients. ‘We don’t know these people. I don’t know if they see each other, or what their social life is. It’s another world – but don’t compare.  I prefer not to know where it goes…’ He gives me a kiss on my cheek, a kindly gesture to show my time is up, and I leave him to make his final preparations for the show. Could it live up to expectations? Yes, and more: as the sun sets, the models appear to walk on water, gliding along a transparent glass runway across the Trevi Fountain, wearing exquisitely embroidered organza dresses and empire-line gowns embellished with gossamer lace, delicate feathers, ethereal chiffon and the lightest of furs.  Afterwards, as a celebratory dinner takes place in flickering candlelight, within the walled gardens of a Roman villa, I go to congratulate Lagerfeld. ‘Walking on the water of the most famous fountain in the world is quite something,’ he says. ‘It is already a fairytale, no?’ But before I can compliment him on this triumph, he is moving on to the next idea, the following collection. ‘Obviously I could do better, I’m lazy, it’s grotesque,’ he remarks, as if in passing.  ‘That’s your mother speaking,’ I say, emboldened by the darkness, though shocked at the harshness of his judgment on himself. ‘Yes, but I think I’m lucky to be in that position,’ he replies. And so it is that fashion’s reigning emperor remains humble, even as he creates a fantasy in which princesses float across a fountain, and a Northern landscape of snow and ice can be glimpsed, if only for a moment, reflected in the shimmering waters of the Eternal City. Justine Picardie is the editor-in-chief of Harper’s Bazaar and Town & Country    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  How hard is it to run a fashion empire? As Marc Jacobs launches his  latest fashion and beauty collections Victoria Moss visits him in New York to find out.  When I go to meet Marc Jacobs, the designer who turned grunge into a high-fashion statement and photographed Victoria Beckham in a carrier bag, it is exactly five weeks before his next show at New York fashion week. Inside his Soho HQ, there is a feeling of an art class, half-way through. There are colourful scattered remnants of show props gone by, boards covered in collaged collection ideas, tables populated by young, cool-looking New Yorkers, patiently piecing bits of fabric together. Jacobs’s beloved four-year-old bull terrier happily stooges around (“he doesn’t do much any more,” deadpans Jacobs’s PR/Dogstagrammer, who documents Neville’s lackadaisical exploits on Instagram – the dog has 191K followers). The 53-year-old designer looks incredibly good, his taut body apparent beneath his close-fitting T-shirt, with sleeves cut high enough for his cheerily tattooed arms to be on show. On his right arm, among other brightly coloured motifs sits the yellow character of Sponge Bob Square Pants. He lights a cigarette, looks away to the side and sighs: “I’ve had a full on two months.” Helming an empire with estimated revenue of $950 million is clearly no breeze. It’s three years since he left his role as creative director at Louis Vuitton – a seemingly amicable parting – in order to concentrate on his own collections (LVMH also owns a controlling interest in the Marc Jacobs brand). Last year, the diffusion line of his empire, Marc by Marc Jacobs, which had been designed by British duo Luella Bartley and Katie Hillier, was dismantled, with every product now produced under the “Marc Jacobs’ umbrella. For Jacobs this means that, day to day, “I’m much more involved. When Marc by Marc was separate I looked over it and said, 'Yes, I like it, or no, I don’t.’ ” Now, all price points are under one roof – and part of one collection – so those lower-priced jeans, T-shirts and accessories still exist, as do the intricate catwalk pieces.  Jacobs has always had a democratic approach. "It’s important to me that there are things from an evening dress to a T-shirt.” As an extension of this, three years ago, after successful forays into perfume, he launched a beauty line. “I feel like make-up is the final accessory. It’s accessible, regardless of what age or size you are… It reaches a broader group of people, which is exciting,” says Jacobs. The exercise quickly gained traction – when it launched online in 2013, the first five products sold out in hours. The new Air Blush soft glow duo collection, Marc Jacobs Beauty, £28 for each compact, John Lewis Earlier this year, the beauty line made its UK debut in Harrods. Tomorrow, it will expand into John Lewis, with the added temptation of a new blusher, the Air Blush, a jaunty striped dual-colour confection. The products are seriously good. The precision pen black eye-liner is a particular triumph: I think even a toddler could run a straight line with this wand. The Jacobs wit is there, too: the Air Blush comes in colour combinations named Lush & Libido, Lines & Last Night and Flesh & Fantasy – all christened by Jacobs himself.  “I approach it the same way we make a collection. We think about colour, texture, a look and a spirit. Everything is still a design exercise” he explains. Le Marc Lip Crème in Moody Margot, £24, John Lewis The creative process is never a straightforward beast, however, and today Jacobs is distracted. “I apologise,” he says at one point, while reaching for words. “Some days I’m very good at telling a story, other days not, because I’m just somewhere else. Yesterday I had such a creative day. I was very sure of everything we were doing, and I always fear that when I have a day like, the next day is going to be this indecision…” On pulling together a collection, he explains that “it would be nice if there were rules, because it would be much more organised – but then I think we’d all be bored. Sometimes I get frustrated because I’d like to know where the end is, because that would make working on it much more methodical. I think I’d like the relief and maths of that, but it isn’t that way.” His current autumn/winter collection saw him flit from spring’s blue, white and red homage to  Americana to a much darker vision. “It was this idea of the ghosts of New York, and gothic heroes that we’ve liked in the past. We looked at some of the things we’d done, and turned them into different shades of grey, violets and blacks.” There are flashes of Wednesday Addams and Lydia Deetz (Winona Ryder’s character in Beetlejuice), a delicious anti-hero feast for anyone who came of age in the late Eighties and early Nineties, when Jacobs was carving out his career. Jacobs was born and raised in New York, but his early life was not easy. His father died when he was seven and he moved around with his mother until, aged 12, he ended up living with his grandmother on the Upper West Side. He has always had a sharp eye for nailing and troubling the zeitgeist. His grunge collection in 1993 for Perry Ellis conversely saw him fired and won him that year’s CFDA womenswear designer of the year award. His work framed the Nineties, as did his social circle – Kate Moss, Naomi Campbell and Winona Ryder, to name but three. This winter, as Ryder climbs back into our consciousness back on sublime form in Netflix’s Stranger Things, Jacobs has not only referenced her earlier characters but cast her (again, she has appeared previously) in his beauty campaigns. “I never think I’m nostalgic,” says Jacobs. “I’m very much living in this moment, but I’ve been around for 53 years; I’ve certainly retained all of the moments that made me who I am. I don’t question it if, instinctively, something feels right.”  What is it about Ryder, I ask. “It’s everything, every part she’s ever played… She’s a very special, smart person. On a physical level she’s this timeless beauty; we’re drawn to each other because we both have these minds which just don’t shut off.” Jacobs specialises in muses with added attitude – though I’m sure he wouldn’t use the dreaded “muse” word. But his imagery has always been provocative – there are no bland line-ups of faceless models. Beth Ditto and Lady Gaga have both “walked” in recent fashion shows. His current campaign features actresses Sissy Spacek and Susan Sarandon, the rapper Missy Elliot and Courtney Love, as well as the more obvious faces of Kendall Jenner and Cara Delevingne. The women were chosen for their synonymy with the collection. “I thought of Susan Sarandon and the Rocky Horror show, and The Hunger; I thought of Sissy Spacek and Carrie,” says Jacobs. The designer has a Warholian knack of appropriating popular culture and selling it back to us, seamlessly merging high art with arch commerciality. He is the man who put artist Stephen Sprouse’s graffiti work over a classic Louis Vuitton monogrammed handbag and created a cult hit – something coveted as much by a luxury audience as by downtown kids. He is certainly not prone to fashion cliché. When I ask who is the “Marc Jacobs woman”, he exhales his cigarette smoke, looks at me and says: “I don’t know. When I read what other designers say about who their woman is, they use the same three adjectives, 'She’s sexy, modern, and young…’ I mean...” He screws up his face. “I can’t define a person by her age or physical attributes. When anybody can answer that question, I always think it’s a bit of a laugh. I don’t have a formula for people and what they’re attracted to. I also think that as soon as you say, 'Well, that’s not my thing’, you close yourself off from being surprised and delighted.” His clothes run from the everyday with an edge (current collection T-shirts have rough edges and piratical black stripes), to avant garde “fashion” pieces that allow you to adopt a potent character, even if it’s just a heightened way of being yourself. “I’m not like other designers who say, 'Oh, you should wear this, you should wear that…’ I don’t like to impose what I think. Winona is perfect for that, she can come in and choose [herself] a men’s suit and wear it with a blouse… I like people who have a sense of themselves. They might like what we do, but they’re not looking to be told what to do.” I ask if he still finds the fun in what he does. “Yeah, I do. I mean, today…” He laughs. “But I, and everybody here, we love making things. And we really love putting on a show.”  With that, he is off. “I’m going to go back to putting funny graphics on sneakers,” he says with a serious-looking smile, “I think I’ve taken on too much this time, but I always feel that way.” Marc Jacobs Beauty and the new Air Blush launches at John Lewis Oxford Street and John Lewis on 1st September 2016.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Thanks to The Devil Wears Prada, myths abound about the realities of stepping foot inside the hallowed hallways of Vogue. So the prospect of a job interview at one of the world's most famous and respected fashion magazines must bring with it off-the-scale levels of outfit anxiety, right?  As British Vogue celebrates its 100th birthday, we quizzed four Voguettes about how they approached the challenge and gleaned a few of their cool-as-a-cucumber tips along the way. Whether you're hoping that your next career move will take you to the front row, the fashion cupboard or just something with a bigger desk and snazzier lanyard, watch and learn... Julia Hobbs, Fashion News Editor What she wore A lot of black! An H&M lampshade skirt because it’s such a strong, sculptural shape and my version of femininity, an off-shoulder top from Topshop- great for layering- and Nike Air Force 1 hi-tops. Why she wore it It wasn’t too thought out because I always dress instinctively. I’ve always loved the harder side of fashion- there’s a fearlessness to my style. I was never going to walk into the Vogue offices in a mini skirt though! How did the interview go? I was just excited for a chat with Harriet Quick who was fashion features director at the time. In fact, we didn’t talk about anything to do with fashion, instead we discussed M.C. Escher and the art of the impossible. Has her style changed since working at Vogue? I stand out for wearing black in the office so in that respect, not really. At the moment I live in Vetements platforms (I make them comfortable by adding a sheepskin in-sole) and a vinyl trench coat.  Everyone here takes pleasure in dressing up for work but there’s definitely an informality. All my bosses are women so there’s no need to be modest. The work placement assistants who really impress are those who turn up in trainers and just get on with it- there’s no preciousness. The takeaway for non-Voguettes Follow your instincts and don’t think that it’s only designer clothes which will impress. Venetia van Hoorn Alkema, Associate Producer Vogue Video What she wore Black skinny jeans from Topshop which have been washed about 6 million times. A white shirt from T by Alexander Wang, a blazer from Gestuz, a Christopher Kane coat and glittery Prada shoes. Why she wore it I actually had trouble remembering my exact outfit. When I asked my boss, our creative director Jaime Perlman, all she could recall was “something Princess-y, a bit Valentino” about my hair. I’m not sure that I put very much thought into it but the equation seems to have been something smart, something silver and something a bit weird. How did she feel about the interview? I’d never worked at a fashion magazine before but I had interned at Vogue where I would come in every day wearing crazy stuff like my Grandma’s Liberty print dresses. So you could say I’d worked through that fear! Has her style changed since working at Vogue? There are definite trends which happen in the office. You can tell when a certain designer has just done a sample sale because everyone will come in wearing their purchases. It’s wonderful though because when you come in people always say things like ‘you look amazing!’ and discuss what they’re wearing. When Julia Hobbs wrote about the death of skinny jeans earlier in the year, suddenly they disappeared from the office for a while, replaced by the rigid style she’d recommended. The takeaway for non-Voguettes As long as you’re smart, you can get away with something a bit wild.  Violet Henderson, Commissioning Editor What she wore A white silk shirt from Theory, a blazer from Sandro, jeans by Frame and Manolo Blahnik court shoes. Why she wore it I had this strange psychology that as it was Vogue, I shouldn’t dress up too much. I was already working in the same building so had seen all the Vogue girls in the lifts. I decided the best approach was to be simple and classic. I knew that Jo Ellison, features director at the time, was interviewing me and had discovered her penchant for blue jeans which explains those. The jacket was a mistake though- I was absolutely boiling. How did the interview go? We didn’t talk about my clothes at all. In fact, we barely went through any real questions! I think we spent 45 minutes discussing Hilary Mantel. Has her style changed since working at Vogue? I have naturally developed a better eye by being surrounded by all these people with incredible taste. It’s a really funny office because there are no hard and fast rules. The takeaway for non-Voguettes Do your research on your interviewer and dress accordingly. Naomi Smart, Shopping Editor What she wore I had two interviews. You may gasp, but I wore dark turn up Levi’s jeans with an oversized red mohair sweater and Gianvito Rossi black lace up open toed heel booties. To my final interview, I wore an embroidered v-neck sweater, (which I've updated now with the Paco Rabanne one in this picture), an H&M leather pencil skirt and my Proenza Schouler block heels with silver stud hardware. Why she wore it Jeans could be seen as a big interview no-no, but you have to know your audience, after all I was meeting with the fashion director of Vogue, not accounts. Vogue isn’t your everyday working environment; like everything we do, our approach to how women dress at work is more pioneering and not as rigid as other offices. Just like I wore smart jeans four years ago, I could wear a pair of smart tracksuit style trousers with a blazer and heels now. I just chose clothes that I felt comfortable in and that were polished versions of my everyday self. You want the person interviewing you to be able to envision you sat next to them. How did the interview go? The interview was a very friendly download of why I wanted to work at Vogue, of all my interests within fashion and outside and all the usual questions. I knew Vogue and the people who worked for it like the back of my hand - you have to do your research. My interview with Alexandra Shulman, was more formal, but friendly and I tailored my outfit to be smarter to respect the fact that I was interviewing with the editor. Has her style changed since working at Vogue? I’ve stayed true to style, just perhaps more expensive! Quality over quantity - with brands and particular pieces. Office go-tos are still workwear denim, leather, colour and texture mixed with smart silhouettes, and I love a heel as long as I can be running around in it all day.   The takeaway for non-Voguettes Aim to be a more polished version of your everyday self The centenary issue of British Vogue is on sale now. Step inside the Vogue World later this month at the Vogue Festival 2016 in association with Harrods, taking place on 21st and 22nd May at the Royal Geographical Society and Kensington Gardens.  In the world of fashion, having a book documenting your work published by Assouline is the ultimate seal of approval. It’s all a bit of a surprise for Faye McLeod, the Scot who acts as Louis Vuitton’s visual image director. In the six years that she’s worked at the luxury French fashion house McLeod and her team has brought her fantastical imagination to life in the windows of Louis Vuitton stores all over the world; from gilded dinosaur skeletons clutching LV bags, to spookily lifelike waxworks of Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama and giant faux ostrich eggs hatching Vuitton wares. Louis Vuitton Windows is an epic, suitcase-sized tome that celebrates these remarkable feats of creativity in all their glory, detailing the thought and design process behind them via beautiful illustrations and hand-tipped images. Though daunted at first (she couldn’t understand why anyone would want a book of her extraordinary work, but was eventually persuaded by Bergdorf Goodman’s fashion force Linda Fargo), McLeod realised that she wanted people to know her job existed. “I want people to want my job,” she says. “I’m not scared of anybody taking it if they’re really good at it. People don’t know that jobs like this exist in our industry – and the world needs more creative people.” After completing a degree in fashion design McLeod began her career in windows at Selfridges on Oxford Street, before moving on to Topshop, then to Liberty. With those three window-dressing giants under her belt she made the move to New York and eventually ended up at LVMH, the luxury conglomerate that is home to Vuitton, Dior and Celine, to name but a few. Here she found her perfect match in Vuitton. “I think my team and I have been really successful because of the respect for creativity and the freedom they give me to do that. Most [corporations] want to control their creatives but LVMH don’t. With windows they give you room to breath and room to create,” she says. This has allowed McLeod and her team free reign. They search the world for people who can create exactly what they want. “Without Google we would be in trouble,” she jokes. They’ve commissioned, among many other things, a Chinese dinosaur factory (yes, there is such a place) to create gilded dino skeletons, Indian craftsmen to make arrows with just-the-right-colour fletching and UK-based film prop specialists to make incredibly convincing animals including baby deer, giraffes and zebra. She has a particular fondness for animals; her next challenge is to include a pangolin, a scaled anteater she discovered recently while on safari with Kim Jones, Louis Vuitton’s head of menswear. Some of her greatest memories are working with the artist Yayoi Kusama, who collaborated with the brand in 2012. To celebrate, McLeod commissioned a number of extraordinarily convincing waxworks of the 86-year-old to place in Kusama-themed windows. So convincing were they that passers-by were sure it was the actual Kusama partaking in some sort of installation. It is ideas like this that have made Vuitton’s windows perfect Instagram fodder, a true mark of success in this social media-obsessed age. “I’ve worked for so many big companies but I’ve never, ever seen as many people engage with a window as I do at Vuitton. When I started I was like, I’m going to make damn good window so that you’ve got a great background!” says McLeod. She and her team – which includes people from all sorts of disciplines; illustrators, architects, product designers -  also design and create the sets for the always-spectacular Vuitton catwalk shows. Among their accomplishments is the life-size steam train created for the March 2012 show - it was actually made of MDF – and the giant fountain that formed the centrepiece of former Vuitton creative director Marc Jacobs’s final show for the brand. The only idea McLeod’s yet to realise is getting things to float in space. “I’ve not worked that out yet. One day,” she says. We don’t doubt her for a second. Louis Vuitton Windows is available now, published by Assouline © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When this year's theme for the Met Gala was announced as 'Manus x Machina: Fashion in an Age of Technology' even our fashion team struggled with how this would be interpreted on one of the most famous red carpets of all time. Will Kendall and Co be donning futuristic dresses? Or will guests opt for a simple Apple watch to tap into the theme? All will be revealed tonight.  For now, we looked at the 9 times fashion and technology have met; some a fabulous combination of two amazing forces, (Eva Chen x Instagram) some with mind-blowing results, (Kate Moss' hologram courtesy of McQueen) and others raising questions as to whether we've actually benefited from them (that would be a certain Kardashian and her popular video game.) Here's the countdown... When Lucky magazine closed last year, Chen, who was then editor-in-chief at the Conde Nast publication, was quickly snapped up by Instagram as their new head of fashion partnerships. With over 570,000 Instagram followers, Chen was the perfect choice. “Most of the fashion community are already using it,” she says of the popular social media platform. “My job is more about helping people tell their stories in ever more interesting ways.” KT For the few who haven't yet downloaded it, Kim Kardashian Hollywood is a free role-play game which sees Kim's avatar, who wears versions of her own custom Balmain and Givenchy outfits, take users on an adventure to stardom, with 'K Coins' being awarded for users successfully networking their way around Hollywood - they can then use their K Coins to pay for designer clothes and haircuts - all in-app, sadly. Since its launch in 2014, her game has been downloaded worldwide over 40 million times, making the star a hefty 9 figure profit.  KT For ss16, British brand Burberry chose to preview their collection on Snap Chat ahead of their scheduled show at London Fashion Week on September 21st last year. Burberry invited the app's 100 million users to see the finishing touches being made to looks in their studio - the first for a major fashion brand. Even their make-up tests featured in the Snap Chat video. KT In a bid to make Google Glass appealing to fashion-conscious consumers, designer Diane Von Furstenberg created an eyewear line with Google Glass technology. During the SS13 fashion weeks, Google Glass was trending across social media, with DVF models wearing them while walking in her New York catwalk show. KT It was at Alexander McQueen's 2006 Widows of Culloden show, that the ethereal hologram of Kate Moss (an idea of production designer Joseph Bennett) first appeared. McQueen, who was renowned for his love of theatrics and his talent for creating a spectacle on the runway, blew everyone away with this seamless merging of fashion and technology. The hologram was brought back in 2015 for the Savage Beauty exhibition at the V&A, which was a celebration of McQueen's talent. OBS Richard Nicoll's Disney inspired SS15 collection saw a succession of models sashay down the catwalk swathed in soft lilacs, pinks and blues, but it was the technical elements that stole the show. Nicoll's collaboration with London Fashion Laboratory Studio XO resulted in the creation of a dress made from fiber optic fabric, infused with micro LED lights; his take on a modern Tinkerbell. He wowed onlookers by presenting an example of technology and fashion that was deemed actually wearable. OBS  For their AW16 show, French brand Corrèges experimented with the new buy-now-see-now model, but this wasn't the show's most innovative attribute. Design duo Sébastien Meyer and Arnaud Vaillant, with a clear nod to André Courrèges’ space-age ’60s aesthetic, sent a trio of heated coats down the runway with power control buttons on the arm, that triggered a mobile phone-enabled power source. OBS At the time Karl Lagerfeld was expected to be debuting his SS15 collection for Chanel, and Anna Wintour was assumed to be taking her seat in the front row - they were in fact at the launch of the new Apple watch, an event covered by Suzy Menkes. The idea was that Wintour would view the watch, deliver Karl to Paris emporium Colette, and get him to his show on time. A very clever ploy by Apple who in aligning high tech with high fashion, appealed to a far broader spectrum of people. OBS Villoid - a kind of Instagram Pinterest hybrid - launched in September 2015, with Alexa Chung described as "co-founder and secret mastermind" of the anticipated app. Unlike its counterparts, Villoid not only allows you to follow your favourite brands and semi-stalk stylish individuals, creating mood boards and building a profile as you go, but it also offers users a 'buy' button, which directs you to the websites of affiliated sites so you can purchase the pieces youve been oogling. very handy.  “Any Prime Minister, particularly a woman Prime Minister, ought to give a boost to the [fashion] industry,” said Margaret Thatcher in a 1985 interview with British Vogue. “First of all it gives publicity: if people like the clothes you are wearing they might come and buy here.” The duty for a PM — “particularly a woman Prime Minister” — to talk British fashion is a thorny issue for our current leader, Theresa May. With her appearance in American Vogue this month, wearing homegrown brands L.K Bennett and Egg, she’s made a nod to it — but no one would call the piece a fashion interview. In fact, in a sprawling 4000-word feature in the world’s most prominent style magazine, this is all May said on the topic: “Look, throughout my political career, people have commented on what I wear. That’s just something that happens, and you accept that. But it doesn’t stop me from going out and enjoying fashion. And I also think it’s important to be able to show that a woman can do a job like this and still be interested in clothes.” There was no discussion of the industry, no shout-out to favoured British designers; she wore only two outfits in the accompanying Annie Leibovitz photo shoot, and they were decidedly understated. It’s not a leap to assume that a decision was taken beforehand: keep the fashion to a minimum. One can't blame May for that. Only a few months ago, she was widely and voraciously criticised for wearing £995 Amanda Wakeley trousers in a newspaper shoot, with the argument being that the outfit made her look like an insensitive Marie-Antoinette type. Male politicians may wear very expensive suits, but the world doesn't pay much attention; because she's a woman, May's wardrobe has always been a hot topic. In 2014, research by Oxford Economics found that the fashion industry provides 880,000 jobs in the UK. Thatcher was right that any PM has a responsibility to champion it; she herself was photographed four times by British Vogue, and spoke at length on the topic. She explained what her mother, a dressmaker, had taught her; she talked about what she was doing to boost British fashion. In 1985 she outlined, in a rather tactless way, the different kinds of design being done in the UK: “At the reception I gave last year, I noticed that buyers from all over the world were particularly interested in the clothes our young designers were making for young people. If there's a demand for young designers and their work, fine, then we will fill it. I was obviously more interested in the elegant clothes. The publicity was given to the outré, which didn't interest me at all. That didn't matter — the buyers bought them and that helped trade.” Male PMs have also dutifully spoken about clothes, but often in a self-conscious, apologetic way. In 2006, while being shown around the Fashion Retail Academy, then-PM Tony Blair said, “I am not known for my fashion sense. When I wore a particular brand of swimming trunks one year, the sales then collapsed." David Cameron made a slightly more convincing effort in 2013, announcing at the launch of the London menswear shows that "As far as I'm concerned, fashion is not some add on — it is not some accessory to British economic policy. You are absolutely at the heart of the vision that this government has." But for the most part, it was his designer wife, Samantha Cameron, who showed up at fashion receptions and charmed the industry. We are yet to have (or expect) a male PM who could convincingly talk about the clothing business, or wear something that explicitly expressed their style — a Vivienne Westwood tartan suit, say, or red suede Russell & Bromley shoes.  The fact is, 30 years on from Thatcher's comments, the idea endures that a female PM has a special responsibility to reach out to the fashion industry. And while May is plainly interested in what she wears (see her oft-discussed shoes), she doesn't want to be drawn on the subject; perhaps she fears looking trivial. Supporting an industry close to your heart while appearing not to care too much is a difficult balance to strike, particularly when one is appearing in Vogue. On this, May cannot win — but she's not willing to surrender, either.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  She started modelling 20 years ago, has appeared on countless magazine covers, is dating a member of the world’s most famous boyband and was named International Model of the Year at the British Fashion Awards - all by the age of 22. And now Gigi Hadid can add “jewellery designer” to her CV, as she launches a capsule range with French jewellery brand Messika. Hadid, who began her modelling career for Baby Guess when she was just two, is the first official ambassador for the brand, which counts Eva Longoria, Beyonce and Kristen Stewart among its fans. Not content with just having her appear in its advertising campaign (shot by Mert & Marcus), the house also enlisted her to create her own spin on its iconic Move collection, which celebrates its 10th birthday this year. Originally created by Messika’s founder Valerie Messika in 2007 and inspired by childhood memories of her father (a prominent diamond dealer) playing with loose stones, the signature Move collection features three loose diamonds that whizz around within rings, necklaces and bracelets. Since its debut Move has appeared in endless guises: from delicate stacking bangles to chunky chokers and one-off high jewellery pieces. Its latest iteration, entitled Move Addiction, sees the loose diamond suspended within a graphic ‘G’ motif. Minimalistic and strikingly contemporary, the motif appears in white, yellow and rose gold across earrings, rings, bracelets and necklaces which are designed to be stacked, in line with Messika’s ethos of making diamonds wearable every day. And for more special occasions Hadid has also lent the G motif to four one-of-a-kind high jewellery pieces: an ear cuff, a ring, a three-row long necklace and a choker which sees the interconnecting Gs wrapped roughly around the throat. It’s a young, edgy approach to precious jewellery, aimed squarely at the much-coveted millennial market, making Hadid the perfect poster girl. “Gigi is the embodiment of the Messika woman. She is spontaneous, sunny and bright,” says Valerie Messika, who saw something of a kindred spirit in family-focused Hadid. Hadid’s mother, Yolanda, was crucial in her daughter’s rise to prominence, while the model frequently works alongside her sister, fellow model Bella. Messika is also very much a family affair: all of the diamonds are sourced by Valerie’s father, while her cousin Didier Cherqui co-designs the collections. Having previously collaborated with Tommy Hilfiger, for whom she is also an ambassador, on a capsule fashion collection, the model’s previous design experience stood her in good stead. “I loved working with Gigi. Her sense of detail and her discerning eye for fashion completely won me over,” says Messika. “Her unparalleled professionalism and her involvement with the maison throughout the development process deeply inspired me.” In partnering with the Parisian brand, Hadid follows in the footsteps of Rihanna, who earlier this year launched both fine and high jewellery capsule collections with Chopard. Considering the influence of these digital natives - Hadid boasts 35.7 million Instagram followers and counting - we suspect they won’t be the last to add ‘aspiring jeweller’ to their portfolio careers. The Move Addiction collection will be available at Messika and Harrods from September 30     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  ‘Men aren’t really fussing in the morning. They have this uniform, and it means that getting dressed is easy. They get dressed at 6am the same as they would at 9am or noon. They put things in a suitcase, and they don’t seem to be stressed. Women can be a bit erratic in what we buy, and we might end up buying things in sales... I was turning 30, and then I went off to have a baby: I think I just had even less time. I just wanted to be able to get dressed without the bother.” For Alex Eagle, the solution was a uniform for women, and a brand that would keep selling the same staples, rather than pulling the rug out from under shoppers every few months with a brand new silhouette. “I don’t like having something for £500 in my shop, and then suddenly it’s 50% off. The whole idea is it’s not seasonal, so you’re not fooling your customers. If something’s worth £500, it’ll be worth £500 in two, three, four years time.” In 2015, she started with a simple scarf-neck top in black and white silk, with and without sleeves, sold in her eponymous shop in London’s Soho. “My mum has this Piero de Monzi jacket that she spent a whole month’s wages on when she was in her twenties, that we’ve stolen from each other, back and forth. And that was almost the point of the collection - what are the pieces you wear until they’re threadbare?” And so came crisp cotton shirts, easy silk dresses, lightweight knits, with a focus on quality fabrics and timeless cuts. “At the same time, we don’t dress like that. I’m never going to make an orange ribbed rollneck, but we sell them by Courreges, and I love them, I wear them. Isa Arfen makes really lovely dresses: that’s not what the ethos of my collection is, but as a woman, I still want to wear that kind of dress. We try to plug both holes.” As a result, Eagle’s shop itself is an edit of both, the wear-forever and the hot-right-now, plus collectable furniture and artworks - an interest that began when Eagle’s father, now an art dealer, would take her gallery hopping as a child. It’s a one stop shop for the time poor - and, to some extent, cash rich. “I think that’s what luxury is now, it’s saving other peoples time.” This month sees the store round out that uniform with the launch of bespoke suits. “It’s wearing something smart, but you don’t feel trussed up or try hard. After having a baby, when your body changes, and you don’t feel yourself, you can’t slink - I couldn’t, anyway, slink into a little sexy backless dress. I still can’t a year later. That’s been really nice to be able to wear something that fits me, and as I shrink, it can shrink with me. The investment of a blazer that costs £1000, it’s your whole wages in some cases, but it’s pay per wear: buy less and buy better.” Sitting across from me in a busy cafe near the store, Eagle looks at ease. Her trouser suit isn’t the stuff of a fashion peacock, even though the colour, a vivid Yves Klein blue, makes it unusual. But Eagle wasn’t always so restrained in her tastes. “There was a fabric shop on Chiswick High Road where I grew up, and I was crazy about it, I would cut things up with no idea how to sew them together. I’d walk past these shops - Tom Ford was at Gucci at the time, and he’d make these incredible jeans covered in feathers and beads, £700 jeans, and I’d go into VV Rouleaux and spend all my pocket money on all the feathers and all the trimmings, and made a total mess.” Starting her career at fashion magazines Harper’s Bazaar and Tank , she cut her business teeth doing a stint in PR for Joseph before launching Alex Eagle Studio in 2014. The last few years have been busy ones across the board: Eagle’s empire now includes two ‘The Store’ outposts, Soho Farmhouse in Oxfordshire and Soho House Berlin. The latter is owned by her husband Mark Wadhwa, a commercial property developer and keen Soho property mogul who also owns the Vinyl Factory and both Poland street and Brewer Street car parks in London. Eagle’s day to day now centers around 1 year old Jack, as well as her two stepdaughters and husband. “Jack’s the best thing to ever happen to me. But I’m so pleased I waited to have him Some women are obviously superwoman, and hats off to them, but my brain was like baby brain. Still is, a bit.” Eagle’s own mother, a TV and film producer, joined as director of the company two years ago, becoming a driving force in propelling the business forward. “We were washing our own face, but now it’s at another level. She’s used to working with teams, and in TV, if you don’t work to a budget, the show doesn’t get made. Any business that’s run like that can work.” Working with her mother meant meetings could happen at home, or while Eagle breastfed - and it also meant she learned to take a step back and trust that her team, and her mother, could steer the ship. “You know mums are always right. She was always right, my whole life, but it took me until my 30s to think, why don’t I just enjoy that?” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The latest issue of avant-garde fashion publication POP was released today and gracing the cover is Kaia Gerber, the unsurprisingly beautiful 14 year-old daughter of supermodel Cindy Crawford. This is her debut magazine cover and offers final confirmation-if it were needed- that this has has been Gerber's breakthrough summer. The magazine's cover line even asks, "Is this the most beautiful girl in the world?"   The IMG-signed model began the year with her first campaign for under-the radar brand Chrome Hearts but since then, her star status has rocketed. She has starred in multiple photo shoots lensed by some of the world's most famous fashion photographers (hello, Mario Testino), scored a couple of ad campaigns (think Miu Miu and Alexander Wang) and covered magazine covers with her Mum (French Vogue) and now solo for POP, all before many models have even been spotted.  In POP, Kaia is interviewed by fellow 14 year-old Misty Heath, the daughter of POP's editor-in-chief. They discuss everything from Snapchat to their favourite designers, but Gerber also opens up about her long-held modelling ambitions. 'It’s not like I never dreamed it could happen because it’s really all I dreamed about,' she says. 'But I never thought it’d happen this early. It didn’t hit me until Mum and I got the French Vogue cover – even after that I was like, "wait is this really happening?" I’m still kind of shocked.' The images of Gerber- styled by Charlotte Collet and photographed by Charlotte Wales- play on her naturally beautiful look with minimal make-up and loose hair. Wearing pieces from Chanel's AW16 collection, she looks strikingly similar to her Mum in her own early supermodel days with her bold eyebrows and glossy brunette mane. So how does Cindy feel about the young teen following in her footsteps? The original supermodel said to the Evening Standard earlier this year of her daughter's modelling career: "When people ask me about my daughter, I feel like I could guide her in the right direction because I was able to navigate it. You can, it is doable." She added: "These girls, even as they're just beginning, they're not as pigeonholed by how other people see them. Someone like Cara [Delevingne], the reason she is so cool is she gets to be who she is on social media and have that direct relationship with fans." The final model milestone for Gerber to tick off is a catwalk debut which we can surely expect during the forthcoming Spring/Summer 2017 fashion weeks?  Adwoa Aboah has enjoyed a stellar year. She has become a poster girl for the new diverse and outspoken breed of models, walked dozens of catwalks, starred in campaigns for Gap, Versus and H&M, graced the cover of Edward Enninful's debut issue of British Vogue and was named Model of the Year at the recent Fashion Awards.  And now the 25 year-old is capping off 2017 by sneaking in another achievement just before Christmas. Burberry have announced that Aboah will be collaborating with photographer Juergen Teller on a series of images, the first of which are set for release next week, with more to follow in early 2018. The first portfolio of images will launch on Boxing Day, and consists of a series of pictures featuring Aboah posing with her cousins Alfie Husband, George Husband, Richard Theodore-Aboah and Kwame N’Dow, as well as Montell Martin and Mae Muller, along Regent’s Canal in North London.  This initial set of images will introduce Burberry's latest collection, which will be available to buy from Burberry.com on the 26th of December, and sees the familiar Burberry check - which witnessed a significant revival this year - offset by pops of neon and glossy materials. Think laminated trench coats, bright bags and doodle details counterbalanced by neutral hues and classic shapes.  The project was commissioned by Burberry Creative Director Christopher Bailey, who will be stepping down from his role as President and Chief Creative Officer in March after 17 years at the helm of the company. It heralds Aboah and Teller's first collaboration, but also offers a clever stopgap as the house appoints a new creative at its helm. “It has been a huge honour for me to work with Burberry and Juergen Teller on this inspiring project,'' says the Aboah, who couples modelling with her mental health initiative Gurls Talk. ''My role as both model and artistic director is one I have really enjoyed and embraced. Christopher Bailey is an incredible visionary and it has been an amazing experience to work together with him and Juergen to create this series of stories.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It's a holy trinity if ever we saw one; Balmain has reunited three of the original 'Supers' for its latest campaign. Naomi Campbell, 45, Cindy Crawford, 49, and Claudia Schiffer, also 45, star in the black-and-white images, shot by famed photographer Steven Klein, which were revealed via the French fashion house's Instagram account today. The three beauties were selected by 30-year-old creative director Olivier Rousteing, who went some way to explaining the reasoning behind their casting on his personal Instagram account by captioning the images with the following: "U made me love FASHION yesterday , U make me love FASHION today , and U re going to make me Love FASHION in the FUTURE [sic]."
