 A Jackie O-esque, red gingham skirt suit has become the latest outfit to get a second outing  the Duchess of Cambridge. Kate first wore the suit last March, and by wearing it again today - with her Gianvito Rossi suede stilettos and L.K Bennett box clutch - she has cut its cost per wear from £1200 to £600. The skirt and structured top were purchased from London brand Eponine, which specialises in custom-made designs inspired by vintage fashion. Designer Jet Shenkman told The Telegraph last year that she was thrilled to see the pieces joining Kate's wardrobe: “Oh my goodness, it’s unbelievably nice,” she said. It's not the only time that Kate has shopped from Eponine; she also wore a cobalt-blue coat by the brand in January to visit the Anna Freud National Centre for Children and Families. Shenkman thought the Duchess might have been particularly attracted to the brand because of its British background: all the fabrics are sourced from a UK mill. “The whole made-in-Britain aspect is very important to me,” she said. “It is so important to support local industry and when you look at my fabrics you immediately understand how beautiful they are.” The outfit is in keeping with Kate's recent style, which has included several elegant skirt suits, attracting comparisons with famously chic First Lady Jackie Kennedy (portrayed by Natalie Portman in the movie Jackie earlier this year). In Paris at the weekend, the Duchess wore a frock coat by storied French house Chanel which recalled the neat silhouettes which Kennedy made famous. While hers were often licensed Chanel copies, made in America to keep up a patriotic front, the Duchess's made for a diplomatic statement on her first official visit to the French capital.  Kate wore the Eponine suit today to speak at the Royal College for Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, where she was attending a reception for Best Beginnings' Out of the Blue series, a programme of educational films promoting mental health for parents and their infants. She spoke about her own experiences as mother to Prince George and Princess Charlotte, explaining, "Personally, becoming a mother has been such a rewarding and wonderful experience. However, at times it has also been a huge challenge - even for me who has support at home that most mothers do not." "It's right to talk about motherhood as a wonderful thing, but we also need to talk about its stresses and strains.  Cult TV show House of Cards is back – and with it a cold, calculated and meticulous Claire Underwood. Costume designer Kemal Harris tells us how her wardrobe is as razor sharp as her personality – and why it’s inspiring women off screen too… There are a host of reasons Claire Underwood’s character on House of Cards has become so iconic: her resoundingly anti-feminine commitment to Washington’s dirty politics, her cut-throat comments (think: “I am willing to let your child wither and die inside you, if that’s what it takes”) and, undeniably, the fact her immaculate wardrobe generates palpable envy. Featuring slick tailoring and a palette that rarely veers from grey, navy or black, the First Lady’s wardrobe has become a sounding board for working women starved of sartorial inspiration for their 9am-to-9pm routine. And fans are in luck, because Claire’s character, played by actress Robin Wright, is crucial to the new season, which hit Netflix last week. “There was a lot of drama at the end of season three because Claire essentially walks out on Frank,” says Kemal Harris, the costume director responsible for creating Underwood’s look. “Everybody was left wondering what would happen next. Is she still the First Lady? Is she still in the White House? Claire is really front-and-centre in season four.” And that means a newly stocked wardrobe. Wright invited Harris, her personal stylist, to design her on-screen character’s costumes last season. Together, they’ve taken care to reflect Claire’s new status in what she wears. Out of the White House and taking an independent turn, Claire’s character goes back to her roots, literally and metaphorically. With her marriage to Francis hanging by a thread, the First Lady leaves Washington for her wealthy family home in Dallas. As she strips down to get at what Harris dubs “the raw, real Claire”, her outfits riff off a muted colour scheme of nude, beige and cream. The contrasting piping on many of her blazer lapels might seem like a linear flourish, but is, in fact, Harris’s design interpretation of Claire drawing a line in the sand and defining her boundaries to Francis. Harris looked to Lee Miller, the esteemed war photographer, for inspiration. The quiet confidence and independent spirit of Miller, who had been a muse to Man Ray and part of the Surrealist community in the Thirties, chimed with Claire’s own self-reliance. Obsessing over this minutiae is what sets Underwood’s costumes apart from the other working women on screen. “I really nerd out over it,” says Harris, who based her initial costume choices on gut reaction. “I take a quiet moment to read the script, and feed off the emotion I get from Claire’s character.” If an image presents itself, Harris will sketch and design a piece to get the exact fabric, cut and colour. Wright, too, is hands-on. Her role as director of certain episodes means she knows exactly how the light or angle will accentuate her character’s tailoring. For Harris, she can only wish for “more shots of Claire walking down the hallway”, to show off the hours of painstaking pinning and tucking done sometimes just a day before filming. Of Claire’s wardrobe, a third is custom-made, a third comes courtesy of designers and the remaining is bought from high-end department stores, such as Barneys and Bergdorf Goodman. Absolutely everything is tailored to Wright’s frame on a mannequin built to her exact proportions. “I would tailor the shoes if I could!” says Harris. While Harris has no trouble securing high-end brands for the show, she can also be credited for introducing smaller labels to the House of Cards audience. In the series, New York designers favoured by Michelle Obama such as Derek Lam and Joseph Altuzarra sit alongside Dolce & Gabbana, Dior, Armani and Ralph Lauren, who created one of Claire’s most talked-about dresses from the last season: the silver gown she wore when hosting the state dinner for the Russian president. A standout piece from the new season is an archive ivory Ralph Lauren dress with pleat detail around the neckline and full skirt. In episode two, when Claire has to decide between that and a black version for the State of the Union speech, her mother offers some parental advice: “Don’t wear ivory, even with your figure – it will accentuate all the wrong places.” Of course, Claire wears the ivory. Harris credits the ease with which Wright looks so alluringly immaculate as the reason behind the pin-up status of her character’s power wardrobe. “For the average working woman, it is really hard to feel put-together at all times of the day. Everyone is pulled in so many directions, but Claire makes this look so easy,” explains Harris. “What works for Claire is that she knows what makes her feel powerful: a pencil skirt, heels, blazer and a blouse.” So what lessons can women take from Claire Underwood’s style? “Find out what makes you feel strong and adapt it to your environment,” says Harris. “This might be a pair of well-cut trousers and a polo neck, but you can buy the best cashmere polo neck you can afford. By accepting that what you feel strong in is your brand, you won’t be another cookie-cutter person in a suit at work.” Would Claire ever dress to please Frank? “I don’t think anyone can tell Claire to do or change anything,” says Harris. There was, however, a moment in the previous series when Underwood changed her hair back to blonde, after having it dyed chocolate brown, when a poll suggested that voters prefered her with honey-coloured locks. In the end, her ruthless dedication to winning will always triumph. So perhaps, the ultimate lesson from Claire’s power-wardrobe is that old adage: dress for the job you want – not the job you’ve got. And wear Ralph Lauren to get it. A nipped-in waist and asymmetric hemline are universally flattering. Jo Jo drape dress, £150, Whistles Pair with a short-sleeved navy knit for an alternative to dresses. I push past the pain and find love." The Autumn collection includes all of the signatures from the first Ivy Park line, including crop tops, boxy sweatshirts and jumpers and leotards. But oh my is there a back story to every look, and it’s a very expensive a back story too if the New York Post is to be believed The publication uses Amy Adams’s look from the 2015 Golden Globes as a point of reference and breaks it down into dress, hair, make-up, nails and jewellery, speaking to experts in each field. Adams wore a pale blue Versace gown that was almost certainly loaned to her by the Italian fashion house. But don’t mistake a loaned dress as a ‘freebie’. You see, Adams will have employed a stylist to find that dress for her, which will have involved weeks of research. “From talking to designers if you’re doing something custom to getting the samples in and, of course, fittings — it’s crazy,” says Micaela Erlanger, stylist to Lupita Nyong’o. A top stylist like Erlanger will charge a day rate of about $1,500, which means a pay check of around $10,000 by the time their work is done. If the actress they are working with is a nominee, this fee will often be picked up by the film studio. Add to that the cost of the ‘finishing touches’ to the dress, which often involves big fashion houses flying couture-trained tailors to LA, and you add another $2,500 to the bill. The hair is a process too. A hairstylist won’t just turn up and do a ‘do. They will prep a few days before, looking at the gown the actress will be wearing to see what hairstyle will work best. Then, on the day, the hairstylist will spend anywhere from two to five hours perfecting the look. The cost? Well, if you take hairstylist to the stars Chris McMillan, who did Jennifer Aniston and Julianne Moore’s hair at last year’s Globes (he's also responsible for Aniston's iconic 'Rachel' haircut), as an example, the cost is estimated at around $6,000. How? His day rate is $2,000, and then you also need to factor in a couple of days for preparation. Phew. Now to the make-up. A top make-up artist can charge $1,500 for an hour of their time. Some stars will require a dry run a few days before, and also request exclusivity, meaning the artist can’t work with anyone else for that event. This can ramp the cost up to $5,000. Sometimes this will be covered by a brand, like Chanel or L’Oreal for example, in exchange for exclusive use of their products and the subsequent publicity they will receive. Nails are separate to make-up – and many celebs will pay $300 for a house call from a top manicurist. The jewellery is by far the most expensive element, even though it is, once again, loaned to the celebrity. Though there is no purchase cost, there is the cost for security and insurance to consider – you know, those big burly guys you see hovering around Jennifer Lawrence et al when they’re dripping in jewels. A company such as Stone Security Services will typically be employed to guard the jewels not just for the night of the event but for the pre-event fitting too, and the jewels also need to be safely transported in armoured vehicles and appropriately insured. This can amass a cost of $20,000. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  I like to think that I am unshockable when it comes to the level of time and money a woman will invest in her wedding day. In my job as editor of Condé Nast Brides, I’ve seen couples spend five figures on wedding cakes, painstakingly grow their own flowers, and devote days, maybe months, to individually hand painting bespoke invitations. In recent years, though, the number of women choosing to dedicate their efforts and their finances to having a couture wedding dress is on the rise. Brides are looking for gowns that are more outstanding, intricately embellished and, crucially, unique - and they’re willing to pay for it. The dresses created in the couture ateliers of Paris can be limitless when it comes to cost thanks to the hours of handiwork and luxurious materials which go into making them. It's a process befitting of someone in the now-Duchess of Sussex's position. She was to be photographed continuously from all angles as she arrived at St. George’s Chapel, the resulting images effectively becoming an historical documentation of her entrance to the British Royal family. She will have wanted the best of the best.  For other engaged women, the pressures experienced are not dissimilar. It is now a given that guests will post images of the bride on Instagram before she reaches the end of the aisle; why wouldn’t she choose to take total control of her look, and spend money to ensure that she has the outfit she always wanted? It would be all too easy to scoff and dismiss the high cost of a couture gown as frivolous. But consider for a moment the level of skill required to make one. Last year the British designer Phillipa Lepley created a full-skirted dress, covered with heavily embroidered French lace, and set with 100,000 freshwater seed pearls. It cost the bride in question £90,000. ‘You get what you pay for,’ she says. ‘That dress had more than 300 hours of workmanship in it.’ For fashion commentator Camila Carril, who married last year in Florence wearing a dress from Ashi Studio, part of the pleasure came from knowing that she would never wear it, or anything remotely like it, again. An exaggerated princess silhouette with a 2.5 metre train, the dress was so big that her first fitting (couture brides will enjoy multiple private consultations with their designer) had to take place in the garden of her London home because it wouldn’t fit in the living room. ‘It was the dress of my dreams,’ she told me afterwards. “Twenty seamstresses and thirty embroiderers decorated the gown with Swarovski crystals. It took over 290 hours of work over the course of five weeks. Having it designed for me was as close to a fairy tale as I could get.” Last week, images of another such ‘wow’ dress landed on my desk. Luxury brand consultant Rosanna Falconer wore a colourful Matthew Williamson gown as she married George Ryan in Gloucestershire. Work on the dress began nine months before the big day, with a mood board that featured Flora in Botticelli’s Primavera. Every bloom motif was hand painted and embroidered, before being stitched onto Italian lace. Lily of the Valley flowers, cut from Rosanna’s mother’s wedding dress, were added. The result was a truly unique and personal gown - one the bride describes as a ‘cherished best friend’, and her mother believes should be exhibited in the V&A. I have to say, I wholeheartedly agree. Meghan’s Givenchy dress was masterfully cut by designer Clare Waight Keller, its exclusive silk cady fabric developed after extensive research at European mills. Her veil featured embroidered flowers from all 53 countries of the Commonwealth. Its makers had to wash their hands every 30 minutes when making it, to keep it pristine. It will likely end up in a museum, becoming a symbol of the finest design and craftsmanship from this era. Ultimately, what all couture brides want to wear is something that is markedly different to what they have seen before, and they get to challenge a designer to bring that fantasy to life. The client will usually have done a lot of research before arriving at her first appointment with her chosen couturier; she knows the difference between a five-ply silk crepe and a hand embroidered Chantilly lace, she’s looked at runway shows and scoured social media. It’s a creative opportunity like no other as the bride gets to be heavily involved in the design process and she understands why it’s all worth it. This is all research I wish I had done, seventeen years ago when I was about to marry. It makes me wince slightly at the memory of my own wedding gown – bought, as so many are, at an over-crowded sample sale, in a rush and on a budget, backed by no knowledge of the cut and construction of a wedding gown and what it can do for your silhouette and confidence. If only I’d known the job I would go on to do, and the types of dress shopping experiences I would one day be privy to, I’d have waited and done it properly.  Theresa May celebrated the British fashion industry tonight with a reception at 10 Downing Street. Dame Natalie Massenet, Chairman of the British Fashion Council and co-host, said that the party reaffirmed “the message that Britain, and London, is very much open for business.” Falling on the eve of London Fashion Week, the prestigious event was a hot ticket. Designers, fashion editors and retailers  - including Vivienne Westwood (sporting a 'Theresa Talk Vivienne' logo t-shirt) and Samantha Cameron - were invited alongside, for the first time, apprentices working in the industry in an attempt, Massenet said, to “ensure the broadest representatives.” May showed a deft mastery of fashion messaging by eschewing a high-fashion look in favour of a shirt from Palmer// Harding's collaboration with John Lewis. Levi Palmer and Matthew Harding are a young design duo educated at Central St Martin's, one of the UK's best fashion schools. Their designs for John Lewis is part of the Modern Rarity collection and is priced between £100 and £150. The cinched-waist shirt chosen by May originally retailled for £120 but is now sold out, however similar styles are still available. May also wore a slim black trousers by Amanda Wakeley and a favourite pair of lip-printed shoes by Russell and Bromley. The Prime Minister continues in the tradition of both Samantha Cameron and Sarah Brown whose Downing Street parties during fashion weeks became a glamorous date on the calendar and drew a stellar guest list - few people will turn down an invite that gets them through the door of 10 Downing Street. May’s decision to publicly celebrate the industry and particularly its younger workers will have been reassuring for those retailers and designers who have worried about the impact of Brexit on fashion and luxury retailers. Caroline Rush, Chief Executive of the BFC, said May was “a great advocate” of British fashion. “Her dedication to young talent – including welcoming fashion apprentices, scholarship winners and graduate trainees to Number 10 - is a great signal that she is interested in the whole of the industry from young people to global brands,” she told The Telegraph. The Prime Minister’s love of fashion is well known – her flamboyant shoe collection became renowned during her early years as a minister and she chose a subscription to Vogue as her luxury item when she was a guest on Desert Island Discs. Her clothing choices since she took on the top job in June have proven to be a subtle balancing act of style and diplomacy. As the personal appearance of female leaders and the wives of female leaders continue to be dissected more thoroughly than their male counterparts she has clearly decided that it is better to continue dressing in the style she enjoys. While she won’t be seen in wildly directional looks, through her neat uniform of tailoring, often in navy blue, she has nevertheless supported British designers and retailers, including Vivienne Westwood, Amanda Wakeley, LK Bennett and Russell and Bromley. And she hasn’t yet given up her signature leopard print kitten heels. Long may that continue.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  If you missed out on one of Carine Roitfeld’s impeccably-cut coats or signature pencil skirts from her sold-out, debut collection for Uniqlo last year then we have some good news. The stylist, magazine editor and front row stalwart has been beavering away on a second collection with the Japanese retailer - and it's launching very soon.  It's available in selected Uniqlo stores from February 11, 2016 but eager fans can snap it up online from 11pm this evening. And we recommend taking that route, given her first collaboration with the brand sold out within hours. (Also recommended: check out the entire collection now so you know what you want in advance).  This time around, the range is ‘working girl’ themed and this is reflected via performance fabrics (wrinkle-free military jackets feature) and reversible blousons. It is Roitfeld’s schedule - the 61-year-old grandmother splits her time between her native Paris and New York – that informed the hard-working, mix-and-match nature of the collection that forms the ultimate capsule wardrobe. Predictably, the colour scheme is predominantly made up of black stone and khaki, but last season's splash of leopard print has been replaced by a fun, palm-leaf motif. We plan to hold out for the khaki, cotton jacket (especially now that our fashion director confirmed that it is the new camel) with half sleeves (above, £89.90) and the Chester overcoat in black (£129.99), both staples for any wardrobe. Roitfeld, who edited Paris Vogue for 10 years, is photographed at fashion weeks dripping in Givenchy and the like, but thanks to Uniqlo, this range is set to be as affordable as ever. Prices start at £7.90 for lacy tights and jackets range between £49.90 and £149.99. A white T-shirt with an illustration that is ‘quintessentially Carine’, read: sunglasses on, shirt half un-buttoned and tucked into a pencil skirt, talking on the phone, retails for a very reasonable £14.90. Allow us to defer to The Daily Telegraph Fashion Director Lisa Armstrong, who says it's all about the flippy skirt.  "Now that Dry January’s out of the way, my next resolution is to tackle my addiction to trousers, or Leg Shy February," she writes. "Wonderful and varied though trousers are, wearing them every single day is to miss out on an entire category of options. After a while, you lose the knack of wearing skirts and all the paraphernalia (i.e. tights, knee-boots) that goes with, as well as the thought process (which coat works? Is that blazer the right length? are my legs defuzzed?). Just writing all this down makes me realize why I more or less stopped wearing skirts. But think of the pay-offs: flattering, grown- up and sophisticated, assuming you choose the right one. In skirts (and leg-wear) there is none more shrewd than Carine Roitfeld, global fashion director of Harper’s Bazaar. In it I note, are several flip-hemmed skirts. You know the kind of thing – slim fitting but fluted at the bottom, although not exaggeratedly so. We’re not talking mermaids or Torville and Dean. As it happens, I bought a flip-hemmed skirt ten days ago. Mine is midi length, bias cut in black crepe, but flip hem skirts come in various guises. The salient points are that they sit snugly at the waist and hips, before subtly fanning out. This makes them both more flattering and easier to wear than pencil skirts, and more womanly than a full prom style skirt. Sleek, but soft. You must wear them with a heel, but it needn’t cause vertigo. My new discovery is that if a heel is skinny enough, 70 mm can look elegantly high. There’s still the tights issue, but Roitfeld has the solution to that. She’s introduced lacy tights to Uniqlo (a first). And yes she wears them herself to considerable effect. I’m off to get a pair. Meanwhile I also recommend Heist’s smooth opaques – which are lightweight, yet provide full coverage, and seamless so you can wear them with the flippy skirt’s other ally, the platform sandal."  Happy shopping...  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Cecilia Chancellor has a thing about horses. As a child, the model daydreamed of being a mounted policewoman: ‘The only job I could think of that involved horses – I don’t know where the police part came in.’ Whenever she entertains thoughts of moving on from fashion, notions of studying horsemanship in America follow close behind.  Then there was an unforgettable Vogue shoot with photographer Mario Testino in Iceland. ‘The location was across this volcanic landscape and we had a pony to carry all the dresses,’ she recalls. ‘It slipped on something and got spooked – it just took off. You could see these dresses flying in all directions. We had to abandon the shoot for the next five hours, wandering around this lunar landscape, collecting frocks.’ The corners of her eyes crinkle. ‘There were some really good moments like that,’ she says of the early 1990s, when she also travelled to Baja California, Spain, Brazil and Peru with Testino. Not every model would be so willing to trek around the world and chase flying frocks – but Cecilia isn’t just any model.  Now 50, she’s spent three decades in front of the camera. Nearly 6ft tall, with a serene, aristocratic beauty, she’s come to embody more than one fashion moment. Lord Snowdon called her ‘the face of 1985’; nearly a decade later, in 1993, she appeared in the issue of British Vogue that crowned ‘London girls’ the keepers of the new spirit of fashion.  But at the point when many women with her experience might pivot away from the camera, Cecilia is leaning in. And her career is taking flight yet again: magazine covers, shoots with top photographers including Peter Lindbergh, and spots in major campaigns such as Miu Miu. It’s part of a sea change in the fashion industry. After years of signing teenagers to promote their wares, brands are catching on that customers with money to spend – older women – want to see models with life experience in campaigns and editorials.  For Cecilia, the success of 40-, 50- and 60-somethings comes down to the beauty of self-awareness. ‘I definitely feel more comfortable in myself and more appreciative of what I have and what I look like now,’ she says. ‘I wish I hadn’t been as harsh a critic of myself and my appearance as a young woman, but that’s a normal part of growing up, I think – to become more confident. It can only be a good thing that beauty can be represented by all ages and races in fashion, and I do hope that it continues to evolve that way.’ Born in Dorset but first raised in Rome (her father, late magazine editor Alexander Chancellor, was then at Reuters), Cecilia recalls ‘a different kind of childhood’, characterised by rambling. The family spent summers in a derelict Tuscan farmhouse that, despite having no electricity, took her mother’s fancy. ‘We were distraught when we first went there, because you had to cut through undergrowth to get to the front door,’ she says. ‘But then my mother transformed  it. There were these long summers in Tuscany, spending hours in the pool doing synchro routines with my sister.’ They returned to London when Cecilia was seven and she enrolled at St Paul’s Girls’ School. She was a classmate of Camilla Nickerson, now a stylist but then a student-slash-model, who convinced Cecilia to come to a shoot with photographer Perry Ogden. ‘It was a thrilling experience because I took a day off school and made £75 in cash,’ she says.  Next came Snowdon (‘Very civilised and very kind, but I was quite frightened’) and New York. Steven Meisel booked her for Italian Vogue and, after that, everyone wanted to work with her. She went fishing for marlin with Patrick Demarchelier and glimpsed herself on the sides of skyscrapers: ‘Driving from JFK into New York City and seeing some enormous billboard of myself with a Banana Republic raincoat on – that was quite odd.’ One of her repeat bookings was with designer Helmut Lang. Season after season, he featured the same models – Cecilia, Kirsten Owen and Stella Tennant among them – so it felt like a family. ‘The clothes made everyone feel an enhanced version of themselves,’ she says. His was the label she wore most during the ’90s – partly because, she says, he paid her in clothes rather than money, an arrangement Cecilia calls ‘heaven’. (She sold her Lang archive years ago, bar a couple of coats that she still wears today.)  At the height of her success, Cecilia opted out. ‘I needed to regroup, reground and do something else,’ she explains. She completed two art foundation courses and trekked the Himalayas before returning to the swirl of shoots, shows and campaigns. Cecilia took time out again to have her son, Lucas, in 2001, but graced Testino’s 2002 cover for British Vogue that featured 18 models – including Stella Tennant, Naomi Campbell, Kate Moss, Erin O’Connor, Jade Parfitt and Lizzy Jagger – in Union Jack-themed designs. Cecilia held her month-old baby for the shot. ‘He just passed out asleep, he was so overstimulated,’ she says.  Taking years out at a time may seem a career-hindering move, but it’s one of the factors to which Cecilia attributes her longevity: ‘Coming back, you’re refreshed and able to give more, so it’s fun and exhilarating.’ Relationships draw her back in as well. ‘You do develop real attachments and affection for each other.’ And those relationships pay off in surprising ways. After running into Miuccia Prada – who she walked for in the ’90s – at the opening of the National Portrait Gallery’s Vogue 100 exhibition, the designer booked her for Miu Miu’s Resort 2017 campaign. Recently she worked with another name from early in her career, when Peter Lindbergh invited her to France for a shoot that also featured 40-somethings Nadja Auermann and Eva Herzigová. The models’ children created ‘a warm and friendly’ atmosphere. ‘Peter’s such a lovely man,’ Cecilia says. ‘Everything feels easy and very good company.  All the women there love being photographed by him because he looks for the essence of a person. It’s not about how old you are. He lets you be yourself and finds a way of capturing the beauty in that, so he’s a real pleasure to work for, and the results are always lovely. ‘In my eyes, those women only become more beautiful. Life, with all its challenges and triumphs, has made them more beautiful and interesting.’ Stylist: Charlie Harrington. Hair: Roku Roppongi at Saint Luke using Kérastase.   At first glance, the plain white, slightly oversized shirt that Meghan Markle wore to Monday’s Invictus Games appeared unremarkable. Styling it with ripped jeans by Mother Denim and tan leather Sarah Flint flats, the surface message was that she was relaxed, effortless, and had barely given a thought to the fact that images of this particular outfit would soon be immortalised on the internet. As the look she chose to wear on her first public date with boyfriend Prince Harry, this was, after all, one that could find its way into the fashion history books. But all was not as it first seemed. An entire network of Markle style-watchers exists online, addicted to the high of being the first to locate where the could-be-Princess’s new outfit might be from and advising other adoring fans on how to get the look for themselves. The ‘MM’ community quickly found the shirt, by Misha Nonoo, a designer who was once married to Harry’s Eton pal Alexander Gilkes. The plot thickens; the shirt in question was called ‘The Husband’. “Our contributor Laura identified it within minutes of Meghan first appearing,” says Amanda Dishaw, editor of fashion blog Meghan’s Mirror, which chronicles the actress’s every outfit online. She believes that Markle is “keenly aware of the clothing she wears and the messages that she sends”, and notes that she will likely have wanted to throw a spotlight on Everlane, the ethical brand which made her handbag, as well as her friend Nonoo’s small business. “What is often overlooked in the coverage of women in positions like Meghan’s, is how often their clothing selections offer the only chance we get to “hear” from them,” she says. Believe it or not, there are a hundred different ways to communicate through one’s clothing. Perhaps subconsciously, you do it yourself every day, with simple choices like a certain colour to reflect your mood, or a sharply cut pair of trousers that make you stand a little taller in that meeting.  For public figures, the practice can be a little more calculated. The Duchess of Cambridge routinely wears outfits by designers from the nations she is visiting when on tour (coined ‘dressing diplomatically’) or chooses something that literally ties in with the theme of the event she’s attending. A nautical-inspired epaulette-covered Alexander McQueen blouse for the opening of a sailing education centre in Portsmouth, for example, or floral prints at the Chelsea Flower Show. Sometimes the reference is subtle, and sometimes it’s glaringly obvious, but whatever nod the Duchess chooses to give via her clothing tends to go down well with her hosts, as well as giving her public (and we, the waiting fashion press) something new to talk about. “The language of clothes has always been very important to the monarchy, starting with those ermine-trimmed cloaks,” Ingrid Seward, editor-in-chief of Majesty magazine explains. “The Queen has always worn bright colours so she is visible in a crowd - she knows block colours are more flattering in photographs. Diana was the market leader in this way of dressing.”  Markle has clearly been observing and, over the last few months, as her relationship has developed, she has given it a go herself. It started with a tiny necklace back in December. A few weeks after Prince Harry had issued a statement confirming he was dating the American actress, Markle emerged wearing a delicate gold necklace by jeweller Maya Brenner, with each of their initials on it. She had affirmed the relationship to the world, without saying a word. Seward reflects that Lady Diana Spencer did something similar before she got engaged, repeatedly wearing a ‘D’ necklace that Prince Charles had given to her. “Diana loved to play like that,” she says. “Initial chains were very fashionable in the early Eighties. Sarah Ferguson had one too, but hers said ‘GB’ - and none of us could ever work out what that meant!” Another savvy move that Markle has made is to pledge allegiance to the Montreal-born, London-based designer Erdem Moralıoğlu. Canada is Markle’s adopted home nation since she moved to Toronto in 2011 to work on her hit television show Suits and, of course, she is hoping to make some impression on the British fashion scene. Straddling both, Moralıoğlu could well do for her what Alexander McQueen has done for the Duchess, and would be a fine choice of go-to dressmaker given his credentials: Kate and her sister Pippa have both worn Erdem on several occasions, and his latest catwalk collection was inspired by HM the Queen.  Other UK brands have infiltrated Markle’s wardrobe, too. In February, she was spotted wearing a Barbour jacket and Hunter boots as she went shopping on London’s Kensington High Street. She’s added no less than four Mulberry bags to her fashion repertoire, and owns pieces from Burberry and Hobbs. The British designers are, understandably, dying to dress her. Finlay & Co, the West London brand whose sunglasses Markle was pictured in at the Invictus Games, has sold over £20,000 worth of frames this week since the appearance, with their website crashing several times. It is the Kate effect all over again.   “As we start to see more of Meghan in the media, we’ll also start to see more of the pieces Meghan wears sell out even more rapidly,” predicts Dishaw, mirroring “Kate’s ability to ‘make’ a brand [which] is also legendary in the fashion industry. “Should she join the Royal Family, her role would not be as formal as Kate’s, so she will be able to be own this more realistic style,” she continues. “It’s easier to see yourself in a fabulous shirt and great sunglasses than in a formal ball gown.” Just as when the then-Kate Middleton revealed her glamorous new engagement ring in that Issa wrap dress, or when Diana smoldered in her ‘revenge’ dress, Markle’s ‘Husband’ shirt will go down in history the moment Prince Harry gets down on bended knee. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s a truth I hadn’t realised until this year but, like the scent of jasmine emerging in the evening, a classy actress doesn’t come out until Cannes. I’m being outrageously youth-ist here but by classy I mean older, wiser and, to be honest, chicer. I mean the Grande Dames of cinema: the likes of Susan Sarandon, Juliette Binoche, Helen Mirren, Uma Thurman, Julianne Moore, Julia Roberts and yes, even Chloe Sevigny, although it’s hard to believe she’s over 40.   I’m sure these women aren’t actually hibernating through the standard run of awards ceremonies that comes at the start of each year, but it sure can seem that way. In the celebration of youth, pizazz and split-to-the-thigh one-shouldered dresses that parade of red carpets has become, the older women can often take a secondary role. But at the Cannes Film Festival a mature beauty, a woman who has lived and has something to say for herself, comes into her own. The 69th Cannes Film Festival, this year’s fortnight of Riviera-revelling that comes to an end tomorrow, has been a celebration of experience over youth - with the confident and witty approach to appearance that only a life lived and millions of dollars earned can bring. There was Helen Mirren falling down on the red carpet and picking herself up in style. There was Julia Roberts, 48, foregoing shoes as she climbed the steps to promote her new movie Money Monster alongside the impressive Amal Clooney, 38, and Jodie Foster, 53, the film’s director. (Side note: George Clooney was there too). There was Susan Sarandon picking up a Women in Motion award for her role in 1991 film Thelma and Louise and as an ambassador for the beauty brand L’Oreal, after landing the deal at the age of 69. Her truth bombs - that Hollywood has got more sexist not less since Thelma and Louise was hailed as revolutionary for female actresses when it came out 25 years ago - were as daring as her choice of trouser suits and flats. OK, Sarandon did break her leg a few weeks ago, but the mannish look was also worn with panache by Salma Hayek, Jane Birkin, festival juror Vanessa Paradis, Juliette Binoche and Victoria Beckham - a sign that these women have enough fashion nous to eschew the traditional frothy dress. That the festival is an opportunity for women to explore a more relaxed style of dressing is no doubt made easier by the cultural truth that the French do appreciate an older woman. As Carine Roitfeld, the 61-year-old fashion magazine editor who hosted the Amfar Gala party at Hotel du Cap on Thursday night, put it when she spoke to The Telegraph this week: “We’re French, we’re cool about these things. We’re more open-minded. Those older actresses like Susan Sarandon definitely had a moment at Cannes. Julianne Moore in Givenchy was fabulous. It was great to see Julia Roberts there too. I always think she would be amazing to dress.” We’ll gloss over the fact that Roitfeld chose a bevvy of young, lithe, fashion models in barely-there spangly dresses as guests of honour at her party and rather concentrate on the idea that the French do cherish women as they mature. “My style is more simple now - I’ve got to the age now where I know what suits me,” Roitfeld said of her own approach to Cannes red carpet dressing - picking out a lace black dress that was two years old. “You don’t always need a new dress.” Or a hot new face to fawn over. If you’re a star in France, you’re a star forever, a colleague commented. Actresses continue to get good roles in French films, where they – shock, horror - enjoy telling the stories of older woman rather than feeling the need to apologize for them – something clearly noted by Kristen Scott Thomas who continues to act in both theatre and film on the other side of the Channel. Georgina Chapman, the British designer of the luxury fashion label Marchesa (the label most worn at the collective awards ceremonies so far this year) and wife of film executive Harvey Weinstein, disagrees that Cannes celebrates female age more than any other event. “At Cannes you have a lot of movies in competition with each other so you have more actresses than you might see at the Oscars where they are attending mostly because they have a movie that is nominated,” she said on the phone to The Telegraph this week. “At Cannes you also have the jury and people out there for many different reasons so there’s a lot more variety to the guests. I would hate to think Cannes is the only place that celebrates an actress of a certain age.” Of course, the female film stars are there to promote their movies and sell beauty products  as much as they are at the Oscars or any other red carpet event. And it's also the case that some of these mature beauties while avowing the joys of sunblock and serums and the importance of drinking water may also have had work done. But still, older women of achievement are just more joyfully visible in Cannes than at any other time of the movie calendar. As a result famous women appear to relax when they get to the Riviera. And not only in terms of their style but also attitude. With a huge output of interviews over the course of the fortnight, a lot of topics are uncovered and truths emerge – not always palatable. And so this year we have had Susan Sarandon confessing – not without some humour, because as an older actress you get nowhere without one – that she lives in New York and not Hollywood for a reason. “It’s a town where it’s very hard to maintain your confidence because it’s so self-conscious, it’s such a company town,” she told WWD.  “I can just imagine picking up a head of lettuce in a supermarket, running into a producer who then later says: ‘Oh no, I saw her, she is really not looking great these days,’ because you are there without any makeup on or whatever. In New York it’s easier to live.” Chloe Sevigny, who is starring in the Jane Austen adaptation, Love & Friendship, also took the opportunity to remind the world that actresses are still fighting an uphill battle in terms of sexism by talking of the ‘creepy situations’ she has been put in by some directors during her career -  including the one who said, ‘Oh, you should definitely show your body off more before you get too old.” Nice guy, right? But it’s good that Sevigny has the experience and confidence to recount these all too depressing tales.  In Cannes the conversational high heels come off, as it were, and the bare feet emerge. And sometimes they’re not always manicured. Which is more than okay.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The year Queen Elizabeth II was born, 1926, was a pivotal moment in fashion. The shift in how women dress in the 90 years since her birth has been enormous; she was born 14 years before the invention of nylons, 20 years before the emergence of the bikini, 22 years before the launch of hairspray and 38 years before the invention of the mini skirt. "If you think of 1916 and jump forward to 1926, it’s probably the greatest ever change in how women have dressed in such a short space of time," William Banks-Blaney of WilliamVintage tells The Telegraph. "It was following a huge global conflict, but in the middle of the most enormous cultural regrowth the world has ever seen and a big part of that was fashion, so she was born into the height of 1920s glamour." Before you wonder what the DHL Vetements t shirt of 1926 was, 'It items' as we know them didn't exist. "You would never get that scenario ‘who wore it best because everything was one off, everything was custom made," William Banks-Blaney tells The Telegraph. "With Haute Couture now, it is rumoured that there are less than 500 active buyers of Haute Couture in the world and if you back a little earlier to the 70s, 25,000 women were shopping Haute Couture. But in the 1920s pret a porter didn’t exist - it isn’t that they didn’t want to shop it. The idea of getting something off a rail is a very, very modern invention."  "There was a vast difference with what people could spend," Eibhleann McMahon, Head of Creative at Rokit explains. "Couture was highly regarded among the wealthy and prices for a bespoke piece would be equivalent to the vast and varied costs of today. For the average middle class woman, there was an increasing pressure to be on-trend and the concept of shopping as a past time began to take off. Prices varied significantly, depending on fabric and finish and a fashionable dress could cost anything between £2 and £10. An average purse or pair of shoes could be purchased for around £1 - £3 (£30 to £90 in today’s money). The less well off would have to make do with older styles or hand me downs. However, flapper cuts were relatively easy to emulate and cheaper fabrics such as rayon were commonly used to make the styles available in popular pattern books."   "Whether you were shopping in Berlin or Paris or America, the look was coming from Paris and you can’t talk about that look or the period without talking about Chanel," Banks-Blaney reveals. "They really understood women and the change in fashion. As people fled their country, and fled terror, and settled in new locations, it meant that artists, and architects and fashion designers moved countries so it was the first, and at that level really, only time when you have people being transplanted into countries and having a whole new perception on how you should live, dress, and what car you should drive. That’s why a lot of that look is so cohesive. If you look at a flapper dress, a skyscraper and an automobile, they often have the exact same language because fashion at that point was part of a larger message of the newly modern, unlike today when a designer marches to the beat of their own drum. The 1920s was about freedom of movement and women being able to dance, move and dress themselves." "Footwear became increasingly regarded throughout the 1920s as hemlines rose to reveal the shoe," McMahon adds. "The most common styles in 1926 were based around what we may regard as a dance shoe. An elegant T- Bar or Mary Jane, with a almond shaped toe and bow, or ‘Louis’, mid- heel. This basic style was all the more sought- after when adapted with various additions such as inlays, buckles, diamantes or cut outs." Women also wore the cloche hat, which was designed to emphasise the bob, and heavily-beaded or embroidered evening bags. The Great Gatsby was published in 1925, and gives an accurate depiction of the prominence of the 'flapper dress.' "1926 is generally regarded as the year of the flapper and marks a pivotal stage in the life of the hem-line. This was the year where hems were at their shortest, and for the first time in history, women’s knees were on show" says McMahon.  "The desired form was boyish, athletic, slim and ‘flat chested’.  This silhouette emerged in reaction to new found freedoms of the jazz age, where women were able to cast off corseting and favour an outline that challenged norms and rewrote the rules. Tunic style dresses flowed close to, but over the body and often consisted of extra fabric in the skirting to allow for movement and dance. Scalloped, pleated or handkerchief hems were popular in 1926 and favoured fabrics included crepe, rayon, chiffon, satin and silk. There was also a desire to show more flesh, for women’s bodies to be liberated, so sleeveless designs became more commonplace while more daring backless and low cut garments were also available." Although the bias cut is considered a defining style of the 1930s, it was invented in the late 20s. "You go from the cylinder, the column and the drop waist of early to mid 20s to the bias cut, invented in 1927 by Madeleine Vionnet, which changed fashion all over again" Banks-Blaney explains. "A dress that falls against body and curves, and is everything you expect from bias cut." As well as Chanel, another label that was highly influential in Paris in this year was Jean Patou. "He was a man who really understood that sense of freedom," Banks Blaney explains. "In the 1930s he created really sportswear for women, with separates and trousers. He really didn’t see women as being something pretty or put in the corner. In the 1920s his approach was much the same – he and Chanel really dictated taste." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  2016 has undeniably been the year of the social media-made supermodel. Gigi Hadid and Kendall Jenner (not to mention their little sisters Bella and Kylie) have stormed the fashion world thanks to their multimillion-strong Instagram, Facebook and Twitter followings, leaving more established, less tech-savvy models in their wake. It’s no secret that these huge followings win them high-profile jobs – brands are very transparent about the fact that the more followers a model has, the more likely they are to win the big-money jobs because they offer an extra level of exposure. Indeed social media exposure is now written into many contracts. But what we didn’t realise was quite how much these models make via their social media accounts; the figures puts Linda Evangelista’s “We don't wake up for less than $10,000 a day” adage very much in the shade. Ready for it? Kendall Jenner, Cara Delevingne and Gigi Hadid, the three top-ranking models on social media in descending order, are currently valued between $125,000 and $300,000 (about £85,000 to £200,000) for a single post across their social channels. This is according to Frank Spadafora, a former casting director and the founder and CEO of D’Marie Archive, an analytics group that has recently introduced an app and platform to guide agencies through putting a valuation on the social power of a model or influencer. The group has created an algorithm that uses 56 metrics, including post frequency, engagement and click-through rates - to help brands determine how much a from a certain model is worth. Kendall, Cara and Gigi may be the reigning queens but even their lesser-followed colleagues are making a killing.  The likes of Karlie Kloss, Miranda Kerr and Behati Prinsloo can command $25,000 to $50,000 (£17,000 to £34,000) per sponsored post.  Lena Dunham has become the poster girl for body positivity, with her unfiltered Instagram pictures, her naked scenes in Girls and her blanket Photoshop ban. The latest step in her on-going mission to make women feel more comfortable in their own skin is a beautiful, completely unretouched lingerie campaign.  Instead of the usual glossy, seductive advertising we are used to seeing for lingerie, this powerful campaign for New Zealand brand Lonely gives a refreshingly realistic look at women's relationships with wearing lingerie. Dunham is joined in the campaign by her Girls co-star and close friend Jemima Kirke, and they both wear pretty, but wearable, delicate lace underwear sets as they get ready in a New York apartment, which looks it could be a location from Girls. These images are part of an ongoing project called the Lonely Girls Project, which shows women wearing underwear how they do in every day life. The brand says it “aspires to showcase women wearing underwear in a way that we usually don’t see in mainstream advertising and the media.”  The website, which is described as an 'ongoing journal', is filled with candid portraits of women wearing Lonely underwear in their own homes and gardens with absolutely no retouching. “Instead of being objectified, the women who participate in these campaigns – in this case, Lena and Jemima – are empowered and exhibit real beauty that will hopefully help women everywhere feel a little more liberated,” Lonely said of the project. Earlier this year Lena Dunham wrote a powerful piece for her newsletter Lenny declaring that she would never let photographers retouch images of her ever again. "The gap between what I believe and what I allow to be done to my image has to close now," she wrote. "If that means no more fashion-magazine covers, so be it. The 32-year-old model, TV presenter, Vogue contributor and taste-maker unveiled a preview of what’s in store from her collaboration with the 132-year-old retailer. Having delved through the M&S archives located within Leeds University, Chung has put her spin on 31 pieces from yesteryear, adding modern touches and re-thinking them in contemporary fabrics. Last night’s showcase unveiled eight pieces from the range, which it was confirmed will launch on April 13 online and in 66 stores across the country. A spokesperson for the retailer revealed that some 11,000 names had already registered interest on its website.   So what can we expect? Chung, whose personal style is the subject of mass reverence, has veered towards safe, wardrobe classics but with a twist. A pair of wide-leg, canary yellow trousers from 1972 have been re-imagined in navy blue, and a blazer in the same colour circa 1989 for 2016 holds none of the power shoulder connotations; instead, Chung has presented us with a versatile, double-breasted jacket adorned with six gold buttons. The foundations of the ultimate capsule wardrobe can all be found in the selection which has been revealed so far: a stripy tunic shirt that can be styled over skinny trousers or on its own as a dress; a grey, pleated midi school-style shirt and a gingham minidress with puffed sleeves that is begging for a hot summer’s day. Chung attended the party sporting the ‘Frances’ khaki trench coat which was inspired by a hard-wearing, gabardine coat from the 1950s. Underneath she wore a white, ruffled blouse – similar in style to the pink, high-collared version she wore in shots to announce the collaboration. Chung, who lives in New York, explained: “I have always had an affection for Marks & Spencer. I am thrilled to be part of this special and unique project. There was something very touching about looking back through the British fashion and social history for which M&S is synonymous”. Belinda Earl, Marks & Spencer’s style director, added: “It’s really Alexa’s vision and creativity and the combination of the M&S team who from the archive, and the head office, who have made this project come to life.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This week has been undoubtedly about one woman. Four days after Beyoncé sent the internet into meltdown with the surprise release of her visual album, Lemonade, she kicked off her Formation world tour in Miami. She turned to Balmain, Dsquared2, Gucci and Roberto Cavalli for her on-stage wardrobe, which- as we have come to expect from a Beyoncé tour- includes a number of bodysuits and a lot of sparkle. But the key change to her look for this tour, is the addition of Victorian lace sleeves and historical silhouettes, which are also prominent throughout Lemonade. Dan and Dean Caten from Dsquared2 created the dramatic oversized black hat and Victorian-style lace body which she wears to open the show. "Beyoncé wanted to create a historical look, “antebellum” is how she called it," Dean and Dan Caten tell The Telegraph  ("antebellum" refers to the late 1700s and up to the 1860s in the American South) . "A story that could translate into the current climate. She wanted drama, structure and embellishment. Pieces that would be remembered as part of the Beyoncé journey for many years. Our FW16 Women’s show was inspired by the Victorian era, hence why we used elements from the show to create the look." Her Dsquared2 hat is perhaps the most stand-out look of the entire tour, and they explain why it's quite so big. "On stage size, shape and silhouette is everything. They were huge; We only made one sample, 4 times bigger than our regular hat brim. Then they were reproduced by the costume team." The team spent months working on her two tour looks and 20 outfits for her dancers. "Each piece is hand beaded, from corset, to caplet, to body, to gloves, to shoes, including the lace trims which were beaded to add dimension," the designers explain. Of course one of the key considerations is that she is able to dance easily in all of the pieces. "Beyoncé’s shows are very energetic and full of movement," the designers add. "We had to keep this in mind when designing the looks so that her performance was not restricted in any way. The sleeves were attached only at the cup to give her full movement and one zip up the back for the quick change. Every piece was custom made to her full body measurements allowing comfort and ease during her performance." This isn't the first time the designers have worked exclusively with Beyoncé. They created the leather military bodysuit, inspired by the Black Panther Movement, which she wore to perform 'Formation' at this year's Super Bowl. In Beyoncé's album Lemonade she wears dozens of looks, from printed Gucci suits to ruffled Roberto Cavalli dresses, but a central theme running through all of her looks is the Victorian era.  Marni Senofonte, the stylist behind Lemonade, explained to Vogue, "We were going back and forth between the antebellum and Victorian era, and it was before the shows in February. It’s funny because it seems as if [the Victorian trend] is so highly influenced by the last shows. We were kind of laughing because, 'Oh my gosh, we’ve been doing this since November!' But then I was saying, 'All creatives are on some same wavelength I think.'  At the end of January, the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge will undertake a long-anticipated tour of Sweden and Norway - the trip was postponed from November, when the Duchess was in the early stages of her third pregnancy.  Kate is well known for her thoughtful approach to dressing, particularly for international engagements where she is adept at working with her stylist, Natasha Archer, to seek out local design talent as well as flying the flag for British fashion brands. Suggestions of a national palette also provide subtle sartorial nods to her host countries (at her first appearance in Warsaw earlier this year, she wore the colours of the Polish flag) plus she loves to put a twist on local dresses like her Anita Dongre version of the Gulrukh, worn in India back in 2016. Much preparation always goes into planning her wardrobe, but never more so, we imagine, than on this tour, which has two vital considerations. Firstly, the bump (with the Duchess expected to give birth to her third child in April, she will be between six and seven months pregnant) and secondly, the chilly Scandinavian weather, as average temperatures in both countries in late January see sub-zero highs.  We’ve rounded up the labels which might- we hope- appear in her Nordic style arsenal. Preppy dress circa £133 newhouse.se The tour kicks off with two days in the Swedish capital, Stockholm. Alongside their Nordic neighbours, the Swedes are famed stylistas. The buzz around Stockholm Fashion Week (and its counterpart Copenhagen Fashion Week) is feverish, and Scandi influencers are increasingly setting the style barometer for the rest of Europe. Though the slick, minimal aesthetic may be a little edgier than the Duchess’ tried-and-tested, at-home staples, certain labels will tick the royal style boxes. First up, Newhouse, a well-established local favourite with roots back in the 1940s, which delivers classic pieces using beautiful materials. The gold-buttoned classic tweed coat in navy and the Audrey or Preppy dresses, are very much the Duchess’ silhouette. Classic tweed coat circa £330 newhouse.se Siri von Bothmer, fashion editor of Nordic Style Magazine, is an expert in local dress codes. To beat the chill, she says, "layering is key when it comes to Scandi winters. Skirt over jeans, blazer under a leather jacket and a summer dress over a turtleneck." Labels that will help the Duchess on her way include Filippa K, the Stockholm-based designer whose minimal pieces with a sporty edge cater to a well-established international audience, via stockists including Net-a-Porter. Or she could seek out House of Dagmar, a sustainable design studio set up by three sisters - we’ve earmarked the Alicia coat, below, for outside arrangements. Whyred’s high-impact trousers suits would be a bold fashion move, though the label’s printed dresses are more in the Duchess’ comfort zone. Alicia coat, £545, houseofdagmar.com "Minimalism often comes to mind when talking about Nordic style," says von Bothmer of the evolving Scandi aesthetic. "But the winds are changing - we keep the minimalism in our base layers and core, but we’ve seen prints, patterns and colors mixed in quirky ways." For evening occasions, where a little more glamour is required, Par Engsheden is the Swedish royal family’s couturier of choice. The designer of Princess Victoria’s wedding dress has a roster of high-profile clients (the list is a closely-guarded secret). Though his designs are more colourful and outlandish than, say, the UK's Jenny Packham or Roland Mouret, he delivers wow factor and would be a popular local choice. The Duchess might also look to Jennifer Blom, a regular at Stockholm Fashion Week; several Swedish celebrities have been snapped in the designer's head-turning creations and her vivid prints and floaty silhouettes are perfectly suited to bump-dressing. In a Vogue interview earlier this year Christina Exsteen, creative director at By Malene Birger, pointed out that although the style DNA is similar across all Nordic countries, there are notable variations on the theme - where Swedish dressers are very minimal, Norwegians are likely to up the glamour. Cue Veronica B Vallenes for the Oslo chapter of the Duchess's tour - a Norwegian designer with a decidedly Parisian flavour. Her vivid prints, sophisticated tailoring and wrap coats would cause quite a stir - we can see Kate pairing the latter with her signature black tights and long boots. It would be worth the Duchess casting her eye outside of the two countries she’s visiting for wider options to inject Scandi flavour into her tour wardrobe. Denmark, and most specifically, Copenhagen is full of brands that come with serious style credentials. By Malene Birger is a label the Duchess has worn before during her pregnancy with Prince George and the house creates sleek coat dresses, perfect for both icy weather and a burgeoning bump. Perhaps she’ll recycle the navy coat she wore then, or road test something tailor made for the occasion. To really earn her Scandi style stripes, she might opt for a Saks Potts, a brand whose colourful coat styles are guaranteed to work against the sub-zero temperatures. For real fashion kudos, editors will be watching to see whether the Duchess will join the international collective of #GanniGirls. Copenhagen-based Ganni is a favourite with fashion insiders thanks to their quirky, colourful take on the Nordic aesthetic and an outing would earn serious style points for Kate.  It's 14 years since Theresa May stepped into the political - and fashion spotlight - delivering her famous 'nasty party' Tory conference speech, whilst wearing the leopard print L.K Bennett kitten heels that have now become her trademark. Returning to the Tory party conference as Prime Minister this week, May has a lot more than party politics on her hands, namely the small matter of Brexit, keeping the economy on the straight-and-narrow and redefining the centre-ground in UK politics. At the same time, May is also reimagining another area in which she's long been a trailblazer - the thorny issue of female politicians and their fashion choices. Or rather, flying in the face of anyone who says that you can't care as much about fashion as economics.  May set out her stall early on, arriving at her hotel in Birmingham on Saturday - incidentally also the day she celebrated her 60th birthday - in, wait for it, jeans. Proving denim can wore at any age and for any occasion, May kept her jeans skinny in very dark indigo and paired them with a chic cropped tweed jacket. The whole look exuded a kind of assured yet relaxed vibe, which might as well have been saying, "I've got this milestone moment in cementing my leadership so under control that I can afford to stick to the clothes I'd usually wear for weekends mooching around Henley." By Sunday, it was time for full-on back-to-business mode but done in the determinedly stylish way that May has pioneered during her years in politics. For an appearance on Andrew Marr's political chat show, the Prime Minister opted for a pared-back navy skirt suit, accessorised with another pair of old favourite colourful kitten heels by Russell and Bromley and a thin strand of pearls.  Later in the day, a big announcement on how Brexit will unfold coincided with another 'shoe moment' for May. Leopard print had been swapped for an elegant pair of slipper-style loafers, again by Russell and Bromley. Political journalists were quick to jump on the fact the £215 'Charlize' slippers came with steel toe caps, as a sign of May's, er, steely resolve to make Brexit work and steer the transition on her own terms.  But whilst that might have been May's message - she's never been afraid of acknowledging the power of fashion - it's perhaps more likely that she liked the shoes; and didn't care what people would say about them. “She doesn’t mind wearing something people wouldn’t expect her to wear," a friends of the PM's once said. "It’s not an attention-seeking thing, it’s defiant: ‘I know I have a brain and I’m serious so I can wear pretty shoes’.”  'Charlize' slippers, £215, Russell and Bromley The shoes weren't the only noteworthy aspect of May's Brexit announcement ensemble - see also the rainbow-hued bangle, chunky pearl necklace and navy Paule Ka jacket with fluoro belt. This was her first appearence on the conference stage since becoming leader of the party and Prime Minister. By erring more towards the bright, statement-making pieces in her wardrobe, May offered acknowledgement of the moment's significance but in a more playful way than Hillary Clinton's love of a block-colour 'pantsuit'. This is a tactic which she has become well-versed in, knowing when to play to her delight in all thing jewel-hued and when to take a more sombre approach. This morning, it was time for Phillip Hammond to address the party. As May walked with him into the hall, gone were the bright accents of colour which would make you stand out from afar when speaking on a stage. This time, the same ultra-flattering slim black trousers and metal-capped loafers were teamed with an ultra-chic tweed jacket and minimal jewellery - a look which nods to the Christine Lagarde school of political style thought.  May's major conference moment will come on Wednesday when she delivers her big speech of the week - and no doubt another statement style choice which shows serious politics and fashion can happily co-exist.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. At last year's Cannes Film Festival a group of 50-something women were turned away from a screening of Carol because they were wearing flats rather than heels, leading to the controversial 'Heelgate' which became the biggest talking point of the fortnight. So would Stewart wear flats on the Cannes red carpet like Susan Saradon did at last night's Opening Ceremony? "She did wear Converse at the MTV Awards a couple of years ago, but out of necessity because she'd broken her foot," Swennen tells The Telegraph. "When we want to, we make it work. Obviously here at Cannes, we start the night with a heel at least." Kristen Stewart is in Cannes to promote Woody Allen's Cafe Society and Personal Shopper, meaning she has a packed schedule of press conferences, dinners and world premieres. "So far the day stuff has been very casual and simple," Swennen says. "We've done a lot of suiting, very androgynous looks and buttoned up shirts with slacks and great Oxfords and tennis shoes." But that's not to say Stewart can't dress up. For the opening night gala, she wore a Chanel gown with a daring black sheer blouse and a green printed skirt, which was part of the Chanel Resort 2017 collection that was presented only nine days ago in Cuba. "The Opening Ceremony gown was an ode to Woody Allen and the vibe of the movie," Swennen says. "I had just been to Cuba to see Chanel Cruise and picked that straight off the runway because it embodied the essence of the movie." Last month Stewart dyed her hair peroxide blonde - an edgy look that's had a significant impact on her style. "Anytime anyone does a chop or a colour, especially that drastic, it definitely effects the mood and allows me to go in a different direction," she reveals. "Like her hair, the Chanel dress has a cool and edgy vibe even though it's romantic in feel and so that's why we chose it."  Swennen also says it was the white hair that inspired Stewart to wear an all-white Chanel outfit to the Cafe Society photocall. "It adds a different element to the look and and it can work in an entity on its own. I met her when she was 14 and she was blonde originally and I loved it, so I've been begging her to go back ever since so I'm so happy." It is a given that Kristen Stewart will wear Chanel to every major Cannes moment, considering she has starred in numerous campaigns and has even played Coco Chanel in a short Karl Lagerfeld film. But Kristen Stewart isn't the only Chanel face requesting gowns for the Cannes red carpet. Karl Lagerfeld's long-time muse Vanessa Paradis is a juror at this year's festival and also wore a gown from the Chanel Resort 2017 collection that was presented nine days ago in Cuba.  As a result Swennen says she's been preparing Stewart's looks early."We started a while ago because I like to grab stuff from the collection, especially with Chanel, which we do try to wear as much as possible, because there are a few people that are representatives of brand. So we want to make sure we're all sharing the dresses properly."  André Courrèges burst on to the fashion scene in the early 1960s with a radical new way of dressing. His clothes were a riot of bold colours, geometric lines and experimental constructions – an invigorating contrast to the demure silhouettes that had long dominated. ‘Courrèges’ became a byword for modern. His signature use of bright white, stiff fabrics and curved helmets conjured comparisons with the suits worn by the astronauts who were racing to the moon, and so Courrèges became the master of the ‘space age’ look. He made fashion fun with lively presentations and introduced ready-to-wear for a young generation. Women the world over still rely on the simple and elegant miniskirts, tunics and slim-cut trousers that he is credited with introducing, while barely a year goes by without a Miuccia Prada or a Raf Simons referencing Courrèges silhouettes and patterns. Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and Grace Jones were among the designer’s legions of fans in the 1960s and ’70s, and Victoria Beckham, Miley Cyrus and Amal Clooney have all worn vintage Courrèges in recent years – but there was nothing retro about the effect. On January 7 this year, André Courrèges died aged 92 after a long battle with Parkinson’s disease. His label had changed hands several times but hadn’t made any significant noise since the 1990s. In 2011 two advertising executives, Frédéric Torloting and Jacques Bungert, acquired the house and set about preparing for a renaissance. They appointed two young designers, Sébastien Meyer and Arnaud Vaillant, as artistic directors in May 2015. American Vogue hailed their first show at Paris fashion week in September as the ‘runway return of the season’. It is now a grey afternoon in Paris, just a few weeks before show number two, and Vaillant bounds smiling into the open-plan top floor of the Courrèges atelier. It is all gleaming marble, exposed concrete and floor-to-ceiling windows, sparsely furnished with a long Plexiglas table and square white leather stools. If the shiny Mac computers didn’t give it away, then this could still be the futuristic HQ of the 1960s. Meyer is poorly today, but Vaillant is in ebullient mood having just presented the next collection to Torloting and Bungert. ‘This is the best adventure we’ve ever lived,’ he says, beaming. Meyer, 27, and Vaillant, 26, met at the Mod’Art fashion school in Paris eight years ago, but both hail from the South of France. ‘We started working together in a very natural way,’ remembers Vaillant. ‘My Excel files were more beautiful when Sébastien looked at them, and his crazy creativity was more structured when I helped out.’ While Vaillant, the ‘sensible’ one, completed internships at Chanel and Balenciaga, Meyer was more of a free spirit, working on his own projects. One of these was a small collection of clothes that Meyer sewed in their apartment. They showed the pieces to Opening Ceremony, a store renowned for spotting young talent, and it placed an order immediately. Meyer and Vaillant called their fledgling label Coperni Femme and went on to win the ANDAM prize in 2014, a prestigious award whose previous recipients have included Jeremy Scott (now designing up a storm at Moschino), Martin Margiela and Gareth Pugh. Next they were shortlisted for the LVMH Prize, but had to withdraw when the Courrèges offer came up. ‘It was a tough decision to give up Coperni,’ says Vaillant, ‘but it was just too small and Courrèges was too big.’ So how do you set about reviving a label that once defined modernity? ‘We explored the archives a lot in the beginning, but then we stopped,’ recalls Vaillant. ‘We decided that we didn’t want to be stuck in the 1960s so we picked pieces of the DNA, like the construction techniques, the vinyl material and the colours, but adapted it in a current, fresh way.’ For their first show, Vaillant and Meyer chose to reveal only one item at a time. While most designers would put together carefully styled, layered outfits, the models at Courrèges all wore white ribbed body-suits with either a jacket, a skirt, a pair of trousers, a top or a dress. ‘We couldn’t do just a classic show like everyone else, so we decided to focus on the garment,’ Vaillant explains. ‘Fashion goes so fast today, the customer should know immediately what they want from us.’ By showing the items in distinct sections, the collection becomes simple and tick-box shoppable – I’ll take jacket 12 and dress 52, please. In a world where designers tend to content themselves with a sheepish wave once all the models have walked out, the pair surprised watching press and buyers by preceding their show with a speech. ‘Everyone knows Courrèges but there hadn’t been a show for 20 years and we wanted to welcome everyone back,’ Vaillant reasons. ‘The concept was a little different so we explained that. Also, at that time André and Coqueline (Courrèges’s wife and long-time design partner) were both still alive so we wanted to say something to show respect to them.’ It is clear Vaillant feels the weight of the Courrèges heritage on his shoulders. Several times his voice trails off and his eyes widen as he speaks about the house’s history. ‘I think it was the last true revolution in fashion because André and Coqueline almost invented ready-to-wear.’ Courrèges had cut his teeth helping Cristóbal Balenciaga create collections that were beloved of the world’s richest women but inaccessible to most. Along with Coqueline, he sought to democratise fashion, deciding to ‘make garments very fast, easy to wear and quick to produce’ – a process we take for granted today. It seems impossible that a Paris design house might be able to instigate the same kind of change now, but Meyer and Vaillant have a few ideas up their sleeves. One of these is tackling the out-of-sync fashion calendar, which means clothes are beamed across social media six months before they are available to buy. ‘It’s weird and very confusing so we’re thinking about changing the process,’ says Vaillant. Longer term, he suggests vaguely, they have big ambitions about harnessing technology. As fate would have it, Vaillant spent five years working at Balenciaga, with all his spare time dedicated to Coperni Femme. His boss for most of his time there was Nicolas Ghesquière; today Vaillant is wearing the join a weird trip cult T-shirt created by Ghesquière shortly before he left the house. It is a reminder of the sci-fi thread that began with Courrèges and which is still so influential. Vaillant and Meyer are part of a new generation that is making the Paris fashion scene feel exciting once again. ‘Fashion is burning right now; it’s messy,’ says Vaillant, referring to the recent exits of high-profile designer names at big houses – the creative director roles at Lanvin and Dior are both vacant. But at Courrèges, Vaillant and Meyer have found creative freedom, an incomparable archive and a clean slate. The future looks bright.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Taylor Swift has received the ultimate seal of fashion approval; she will co-chair the 2016 Met Gala alongside actor Idris Elba, Apple’s Jonathan Ive and US Vogue editor-in-chief, Anna Wintour. The annual event is considered the Oscars of the fashion world and fetes the opening of the latest major fashion exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute in New York. The gala is themed in accordance with the exhibition and attendees are expected to adhere to a strict dress code specified by Wintour. The 2016 exhibition will be titled Manus x Machina: Fashion in and Age of Technology and will focus on the dichotomy between handmade haute couture and machine-made fashion, reports US Vogue. “Traditionally, the distinction between the haute couture and prêt-à-porter was based on the handmade and the machine-made,” explains Andrew Bolton, curator of the Costume Institute. “But recently this distinction has become increasingly blurred as both disciplines have embraced the practices and techniques of the other.” It will feature more than 100 pieces of fashion as well as ‘in process’ workshops which will showcase technology such as 3D printing. Fittingly, the exhibition will be sponsored by Apple, while Karl Lagerfeld, Nicolas Ghesquière and Miuccia Prada will act as honorary chairs. Hopefully they'll be no bad blood between Swift and Apple - the singer famously caused Apple Music to reverse its payment policy when she refused to allow the company to stream her album, 1989. In an open letter to Apple earlier this year, Swift said she was withholding the record as she was unhappy with the three-month free trial offered to subscribers, causing Apple to take a u-turn and instead pay artists for music streamed during trial periods. For Swift, the announcement comes amid a turbulent week. She and Scottish DJ boyfriend Calvin Harris, with whom she has been in a relationship since March this year, have been forced to deny rumours that they have split up. Harris went so far as to threaten publications with legal action, tweeting “It’s not going to be a ‘happy ending’ for everyone I sue for defamation of character for all these bullshit stories bye bye [sic]”. Swift ‘favourited’ the tweet, putting paid to the rumours that they are no longer together. The couple are yet to make their red carpet debut, but the Met Gala, which will take place next May, should be the perfect occasion. The 25-year-old has seen her fashion star ascend astronomically over the last 12 months, thanks in part to her ‘squad’ of fashionable friends, including models Cara Delevingne, Karlie Kloss, Gigi Hadid, Martha Hunt and Lily Aldridge.
