  The character of Claire Underwood in the cult Netflix series House of Cards has been much lauded as the new measure of style for the powerful female executive: the signature figure contouring shift dresses, the forceful stiletto court shoes, the sharp one sided blonde-bob. All no doubt spotted at an office or high powered garden party near you. But another of the fictional First Lady’s wardrobe trophies has gained almost as much traction and is equally embedded with her character traits: those luxuriant classic-cut silk pyjamas which create the perfect ensemble for late night political scheming. Unsurprisingly the Underwood aesthetic is no accident; it is planned with astute clarity by the actress. “It’s so funny to talk about,” says Robin Wright in that soft, yet precise voice with gentle Texan undertones. “I brought on a stylist [Kemal Harris] that just does Claire’s wardrobe. Cotton is so not Claire. So the silk thing is a no-brainer. They’re made by Christian Dior.” Neatly, for those who can’t quite stretch to Dior prices, Wright has launched her own sleepwear line, Pour Les Femmes – a joint partnership with her friend Karen Fowler. “We met 26 years ago. Karen was a sort of substitute assistant who then ended up hanging on and we’ve been friends since that time,” explains Wright. Fowler, then became a fashion designer with her own label. “We’ve always said we want to build our perfect of idea of a pyjama because we could never find it. And we love being in bed,” Wright continues. Classic pyjama set, £175, make-up bag, £65, both Selfridges The pair have tapped into a burgeoning fashion category. In what is perhaps testament to our spoilt times, pyjamas (for the woman who has bought everything else) have risen up to be a beacon of luxury, rather than a wardrobe basic. At Selfridges, where Pour Les Femmes is being stocked for its second season, there are over 156 pyjama offerings, the store having increased its seasonal buy by 30% after seeing the nightwear category grow 500% from 2009 to 2015. But whilst PLF’s pyjamas are certainly stylish enough to be worn on the school run, for Fowler and Wright there’s a more serious side, too. Since they launched the line a year ago, 50% of PLF’s profits have gone to help Congalese women – a cause Wright has supported for the past eleven years after been introduced to the issue by the American human rights activist (and former special adviser to Bill Clinton) John Prendergast. “A Congalese woman is raped every 48 minutes" says Wright emphatically. "They’ve been so brutally raped that girls crawl on their hands and knees for three days to get to a hospital.” The clothing line helps fund two local charities, Action Kivu and Synergie Les Femmes. “We want to give these women a feeling of comfort and security. That’s what you get when you pull on a pair of pyjamas and get into bed. We feel safe at night and they don’t.” The PLF collection began with their classic pyjama in super soft Indian cotton, white with a pretty faint antique floral print scattered over. “They’re cut a little more femininely than most cotton pyjamas, but it’s the fabric that makes them so sexy. They’re so lightweight,” says Fowler as she flits through the range highlighting the slight translucency of the cotton. There are also very pretty lace trimmed and embroidered camisoles and night dresses – the idea being that these are items you can wear in bed, to the beach or as a top with jeans. Embroidered cotton night dresses (left and right), £165, Butterfly cotton pyjama top (middle), £145, all Selfridges  A lot of it is reminiscent of the sweetest, classic English Victorian nightwear – which is where their inspiration came from. One nightdress is an almost exact replica of one owned by Fowler’s grandmother, others riff off pieces Wright picked up at Portobello market. “You just have to take different lace to make it more modern,” Fowler explains. “We try to find something that’s unique but vintage-inspired.” PLF pieces are the sort you feel like you probably already own, but likely hidden deep and slightly rotten in an old trunk. There is an easy, freshness to the collection. “The fabric was the most important,” says Wright. “We wanted to find the cotton we would want to live in and not take off. It’s stuff we want to wear.” The duo confess to having different taste when it comes to fashion – and the line is born of them meeting in the middle. “I’m more girly,” Fowler explains, before saying to Wright, “but lately you’ve been more girly...” “Yeah I think it’s time” Wright laughs. “Levis and T shirts my whole life. I was tired of being called a boy. They’re like, 'What does he want to drink?’ The short hair...” Wright says pointing to her head. Today in a polka dot Peter Pan collared dress, Wright is a (reassuringly) softer counterpart to her Underwood alter ego. Of the interest in her House of Cards wardrobe, Wright says that “it’s been fascinating to watch it grow. The amount of emails we receive on a daily basis [asking] 'Where can we get that?’ and we have to write back and say 'Well, we designed it.’” Though the on-screen First Lady has worn labels including Derek Lam, Dolce & Gabbana, Dior, Armani and Ralph Lauren, a lot of the pieces Underwood wears are bespoke because they can’t find items with the exacting detail that Underwood requires. For one season, they decided everything would have unfussy 3/4 length sleeves. “We shortened all the blazers, changed the waists, put a button on it, changed the lapel. We always alter, and we have an incredible seamstress who has worked with me for four years, she knows my body, she can do it in her sleep.” The keen point is to “feel lithe and strong” says Wright. And good foundations. “[Joseph] Altuzarra really knows how to make a woman’s dress. Then when you put on a pair of Spanx, nothing is moving, there’s no jiggle. I’m not kidding, there’s a whole body of Spanx under those dresses. You’ve got to tuck in,” she says. Commitment to the Underwood aesthetic is a full-time job. “On vacation, Robin's like “I can’t eat that, I’ve got to get back in those dresses’,” Fowler laughs. “That and a pair of Louboutins or Jimmy Choos...It’s exhausting,” laments Wright. “I will tell you, that’s the hardest part of the job. The heels and standing up so straight all the time. I get a massage twice a week when I’m shooting the show.” It’s no wonder she’d rather be wearing (her own) pyjamas. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Jane Lewis founded her label Goat sixteen years ago, she did so with the intention that women would wear and re-wear the pieces she designed, for years to come, without them ever looking dated. Surely there is no better affirmation that this principle has worked than seeing the Duchess of Cambridge today wearing her Redgrave coat once again, a piece that has been on rotation in her wardrobe since she was pregnant with Prince George back in 2013. “We are delighted that the Duchess of Cambridge continues to wear Goat,” Lewis told The Telegraph today, undoubtedly pleased that the collarless, single-breasted jacket which is now a staple in her collections every season, will see yet another spike in demand from fans. This is the second time in as many weeks that Kate has worn pieces from the London-based line, after buying a new Eloise tunic dress in burgundy to give a speech at the Place2Be forum. Despite the fact that Goat isn’t a maternity fashion line, the Duchess seems to repeatedly turn to Lewis’s designs when she is expecting - its fuss-free lines and quality fabrics presenting easy, failsafe looks for anyone with a changing figure. The Eloise is likely another piece we’ll see her wearing again and again in the future. “I’ve tried very hard to be very discreet,” Lewis told The Telegraph of her approach. Despite dressing Victoria Beckham, Kim Sears, Sienna Miller et al from her boutique on London’s Conduit Street, her label is still very much an in-the-know name. Lewis has said that she has consciously chosen to stay as a small business, not allowing Goat to become over-exposed, or pander to fast fashion trends. “It’s much cooler and more chic to be under the radar,” she said. “We’ve been dressing the great and good for a very long time.” “My motto is style over fashion, because style endures,” Lewis continued. “If you are a stylish person, you are likely to invest in pieces and wear them in your own way.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Gucci, arguably the most famous Italian brand in the world, has revealed exclusively to The Telegraph that the label’s next Cruise show will take place on 2 June in the Cloisters of Westminster Abbey. This will be the first time a fashion house of any nationality has been permitted to show there. The venue, with its stupendous 1,000 year history, represents a personal coup for Alessandro Michele, barely into his second year as Gucci’s creative director, who describes the news, after delicate negotiations with the Abbey, as “magical”. It’s certainly a departure from the more industrially-styled settings he has favoured in Milan. This soaring Gothic (true Gothic, not (19th pastiche) cathedral stands on the site of the abbey where William the Conqueror (another foreigner) was anointed King of England in 1066. Rebuilt in 1245, it is where Geoffrey Chaucer, Isaac Newton, William Wilberforce and Charles Darwin are buried. It is the site of Diana, Princess of Wales’s funeral and of numerous royal weddings. It is one of the most sacred symbols in Britain. No pressure then. None of this will be lost on Michele, who is in many ways the quintessential modern Italian man: fastidiously groomed in his habits, luxurious eclectic in his taste  and a passionate Anglophile, having lived in London for several years when Gucci’s HQ were located in Mayfair during the Tom Ford years. “London is always on my mind and in my memories. I’m obsessed with British culture, past and present. To be able to show the collection inside the Cloisters in Westminster Abbey …” In case purist eyebrows are raised at the notion of this august religious building being given over to fashion, it should be noted that before the 1530s Reformation, when monks were expunged, the Cloisters were used for meditation and exercise. Let’s also not lose sight of the fact that attending Church, particularly weddings (see Victoria Beckham and co at Kate and Will’s weddings) has always been a copper-plated excuse for wearing one’s best.  A thornier issue is cruise collections. Once a bastion of reliably low key wearability, in recent years, they have outgrown their old medium – that of a short, snappy presentation – and glided inexorably towards the full blown show. These require exotic locations, as houses compete with each other to find ever more recherché and prestigious venues. The clothes themselves have become commensurately ornate. Is this a good thing? To be discussed. But in Michele’s case at least, the declamatory exuberance is innate.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Dakota Johnson is doing the red carpet rounds, promoting her new film Fifty Shades Darker in London, Madrid, Hamburg and Los Angeles in the last week alone. And such an intense schedule of high profile appearances, naturally requires a perfectly executed wardrobe of outfits, pitched for each different occasion and audience.   Enter stylist Kate Young, who has worked with the actress for several years now, as well as a whole roster of Hollywood A-listers including Sienna Miller, Natalie Portman and Selena Gomez. Young started her career as the assistant to American Vogue Editor Anna Wintour and has risen through the industry to be crowned the world’s most powerful stylist by The Hollywood Reporter - twice. “I tend to like things that are simple or way over-the-top,” Young reveals of the tactics she’s employed for Dakota’s current tour wardrobe, which has seen her switch pace between minimalist Valentino slip dresses and maximalist, all-frills Gucci in the last few days. “Things in the middle are a little boring to me.” Acknowledging that Gucci is a favourite label in the pair’s repertoire at the moment, Young says she always has to consider whether the label’s never-knowingly-understated aesthetic may be too much for her client, before getting carried away with the dream dresses. “It's so great [that Dakota is a fan of Gucci] because I also love Gucci so much. We just try things and see how they look, it's a balance. Some pieces overwhelm her, but most are great.” Dakota’s look at the London premiere of Fifty Shades Darker last night honoured home-turf designer Alexander McQueen; a tactic that the stylist will frequently employ when embarking on a global press tour. Pacing brands and silhouettes, she says, are an important part of the process, but ultimately knowing what suits her client’s personality and figure is what leads the decision. “Dakota has a great body and she's confident,” she concludes, “so it's always more about her than the dresses.” One thing that the stylist never does though, she says, is allow Dakota’s Fifty Shades character, the protagonist Anastasia Steele, influence the star’s wardrobe in real life. “The Fifty Shades film doesn’t influence our choices,” she says. “The two of us have gotten to know each other better, but she's always kind of had the same style and she knows what works. The goal is to always have Dakota look like Dakota.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. While we will have to not-so-patiently wait to see the collection in full, Alexa has used London Fashion Week as a platform to preview one item that could be this season's version of that ruffled shirt blouse.  At House of Holland and J.W. Anderson today, Alexa Chung wore a black PVC coat from her upcoming collection, which lands in stores on the 1st November. She paired the high-shine coat with blue ankle-grazing jeans, a white t shirt by her friend Tennessee Thomas and chunky black platforms with grey pulled-up socks. After seasons of the front row wearing almost exclusively backless loafers, day two at London Fashion Week saw the return of the platform as the front row at House of Holland saw a line-up of chunky heels.  Alexa Chung's first collection with Marks and Spencer launched in April this year, and the pink ruffled Harry blouse sold out by the end of the first day. While the slip dresses, cardigans and ballet flats were all well-received, the Victorian-collared shirt was certainly the hero item of the first collection. Perhaps the PVC coat's outing at London Fashion Week will secure it the same status when it launches on the 1st November.  Although the PVC coat has competition.  It’s been almost four months since Michelle Obama left The White House but, after laying low for a while and taking a well-deserved holiday in the British Virgin Islands, the former First Lady is back - and making her first public appearances in style. Rediscovering who she is as a private citizen is transition that will take time to navigate and, in Obama’s case, it seems to be extending to her wardrobe choices as well as her career moves. She’s kept on board her acclaimed stylist, Meredith Koop, the woman who helped ensure the First Lady became a global style icon as well as a highly effective ambassador for causes including children’s health and women’s rights during the Obama presidency. "I am impressed by her professionalism, her attention to detail, and her ability to think not only about fashion but also the importance of the moment and the message,” Obama has previously said of her style wing-woman and, as she assesses what exactly her message will be in her new position, that’s a skill she’ll most certainly want at her disposal.   She’s also sticking with tailor Christy Rilling, the woman who makes public figures look not just nice, but incredible, in their clothes and who has been nipping and tweaking her hourglass dresses on every major occasion along the way. But what she is changing is the brands she wears and the message that they project. Now that she’s not on the world stage in quite the same way, Obama can afford to express her personality and leave sartorial political-correctness to her new counterpart Melania Trump.  As such, for Obama's first official engagement at the American Institute of Architects conference in Florida last month, her outfit appeared to be a message that she was feeling relaxed about life beyond Washington. Wearing a subtle colour-blocked dress from under-the-radar New York label, Lafayette 148, she didn’t need to champion a major American designer, and wore a soft, flattering silhouette with bare arms. Obama gave us the clearest indication yet of her post-FLOTUS ethos at Friday’s Partnership for a Healthier America Summit, though, wearing a waterfall shirt by British design duo Levi Palmer and Matthew Harding, drawn in with an Alexander McQueen corset belt and Jimmy Choo court shoes. “When Barack was in office she mostly wore American designers; there weren’t that many outings of British names,” designer Matthew Harding tells The Telegraph. “Now she’s a public citizen, she can wear whatever she wants.” Obama and Koop approached Palmer// Harding for the first time in March, as they began plotting Michelle's new wardrobe to go with her new, post-White House career. “Her stylist got in contact and said Michelle really loves your pieces, we’d like to get some. So we sent her three or four shirts and we wouldn’t let them pay. She’s a really inspiring woman; Michelle Obama is glamorous, but the initiatives she’s started are really important things to stand behind.” Choosing Palmer // Harding’s asymmetric-hem shirt (a bestselling style, priced at £430, that the brand re-imagines every season) was a savvy way of balancing professionalism and personality. Theresa May has also recently turned to the duo for a statement white shirt - a look that was celebrated for its powerful yet creative cut.   “For professional women in the public eye, there’s a lot of history associated with the shirt and you always understand a seriousness and a smartness of wearing one,” Harding says. “But because of the flourish in this design, you cut down a little bit of that barrier and, while people know you’re serious, you’re not too stiff.” Wearing a trio of British labels is something that the First Lady would not previously have entertained either, unless she was engaging in business of some sort with the UK, when she may have seen it fit to dress diplomatically. “Exposing the brand at such important events, including her first visit to London with President Obama, meant a lot to me,” designer Roksanda Ilincic previously told The Telegraph of the times that Obama chose to wear her British label when in office. “I remember feeling incredibly humbled and proud; and that feeling has not faltered each time I see her in one of my designs." Boosting brands around the world is of course an even bigger show of power than to do so in just one country, so perhaps the new MObama strategy is to harness her global appeal. While she was able to use her time as FLOTUS to propel America’s fashion industry and foster the nation's emerging talents. Perhaps now is the era in which we will see Mrs Obama come into her own - wearing, quite simply, the things she truly likes. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  New York Fashion Week can seem to be dominated by 20-something Insta-girls; this week Gigi Hadid collaborated with Tommy Hilfiger, creating a fairground fashion extravaganza while Karlie Kloss and Kendall Jenner have rocked up at too many parties to list. But look a little closer, and it's supermodel and actress Lauren Hutton who is having the most fabulous New York fashion week, attending a series of shows and parties in some seriously brilliant looks. Hutton's fashion week outings kicked off at Tom Ford's glamorous show on Wednesday evening. In a luxurious teal top, Hutton's choice was a precursor to the velvet trend seen at Victoria Beckham's show later in the week. Paired with her sleek pencil skirt, strappy sandals, perfectly-matched berry lipstick and pedicure, Hutton was timelessly elegant in that effortless, ageless way which she has so perfectly mastered.  And it almost goes without saying that the gap-toothed smile which set her apart during her supermodel heyday is still Hutton's best accessory.  At the Fashion Media Awards the following day, Hutton stayed faithful to the slim black skirt plus sandals combination. Your lesson to learn here: once you've found a look that works for you, don't be afraid to wear, wear and wear again. Hutton also trialled the old favourite fashion insider trick of 'shoulder-robing' her tailored white jacket, and there was some flatteringly artful gold embellishment on her white top.  On Sunday, Hutton attended a party to celebrate the 5th anniversary of New York-based label Tome. Designers Ryan Lobo and Ramon Martin's first collection was inspired by Lauren Hutton, so it was only fitting that the woman herself was in attendance to help them celebrate. In a coolly oversized crisp white shirt, casually tied at the waist and worn with slouchy black trousers, Hutton's look was laidback but still modern and polished. No matter what your age, anyone could learn a thing or two from Hutton's style now as much as ever- plenty of us are obsessed with posting throwback pictures of her special way with jackets in jeans from the 70s and 80s. But for  women of her own generation contemplating how to dress, Hutton is definitive poster girl for making your own style rules- want to show off your bronzed decolletage? Go ahead.  Worried you can't do evening glamour while concealing your upper arms? Nonsense.  At 72, Hutton is a NYFW veteran. In 1993, she took to the Calvin Klein catwalk - then in her late 40s, she was proclaimed 'just as good as the current flock of fledglings' by one American newspaper. We say that rings just as true today as it did 23 years ago.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge arrived for her first engagements of the new year this morning, shining a spotlight on vintage-inspired British fashion label Eponine. Visiting  the Anna Freud Centre in Holloway, Kate chose a belted, cobalt blue coat style from the relatively low-key label, which offers a made-to-order service for private clients as well as small seasonal collections that are available to shop online. This is the second time that the Duchess has chosen an outfit from the label that takes its style cue from 1950s and 1960s silhouettes, the first being in March 2016 when she wore a Jackie O-inspired red skirt suit from the brand. Princess Eugenie, too, has since become a fan of the line, wearing one of Eponine’s fit and flare dresses to the Queen’s 90th birthday celebrations. "I am so thrilled to see the Duchess wearing Eponine again,” designer and founder Jet Shenkman tells us. “She looks beautiful as ever." So what of the coat itself? "It is double wool crepe. The first inspiration for the collection was the colours - that came after a visit to Greece. Then based on the classic 50's and 60's shapes we then played with volume and proportions but remained true to the Eponine look," Shenkman reveals. The classic 1950's/1960's shape seems to be one that Kate is favouring, as she ups the glamour in her fifth year as a working royal. She wore a Carolina Herrera red dress coat complete with Peter Pan collar and oversized buttons for a visit to Whitehorse during her visit to Canada in September. And then, a few months later there was another sign that The Duchess of Cambridge and her stylist Natasha Archer might have been pinning images of the timelessly elegant Jacqueline Kennedy to their mood board: the Catherine Walker and co skirt suit Kate wore for a day of soft Brexit diplomacy in the Netherlands. As a fashion strategy, it's a clever one. Jackie O's look is as relevant as ever, especially given next week's release of Jackie - a film where Natalie Portman plays JFK's wife which is tipped for Oscar success.  So who is the woman behind Eponine London, the label helping The Duchess emulate one of the world's most iconic dressers? Former stylist Shenkman founded her business in 2012, naming it after her four children’s favourite character in Les Miserables and setting up a studio in her family home. She regularly posts snapshots from inside her office on the brand’s Instagram account, allowing followers to see garments develop from sketch form to reality. “I like that with each client you get that very individual collaboration,” she previously told us of her bespoke atelier approach. “What we do is pretty unique and every woman is given a lot of attention. We take the finished product so seriously, we really do. If it's not perfect someone has to come back for another fitting.” Shenkman's design studio operates from her Kensington family home. “It can be a distraction from time to time, but I really enjoy it and am incredibly lucky to have a very supportive family who don't mind loads of women traipsing through the house,” she told us. Something else that is likely to have appealed to the Duchess (as well as the fact that she is supporting an up-and-coming UK business) is that Eponine sources all of its fabrics from British mills. “The whole made in Britain aspect is very important to me,” Shenkman told us. “It is so important to support local industry and when you look at my fabrics you immediately understand how beautiful they are.” Kate’s endorsement last year catapulted 56 year-old Shenkman to fashion fame and the designer inevitably found herself inundated with sales enquiries and press requests immediately after the Duchess was spotted in her designs. “I have never experienced anything like this!” she told us at the time. No doubt today’s outing will have the same effect. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This week sees the launch of Rebel x Angels, a plus size fashion line designed by Hollywood star Rebel Wilson. This isn’t her first attempt at fashion design: in 2015 she teamed up with Torrid, one of America's biggest plus-size retailers, on a similar collection but with more of the rock-chick finish which Torrid is known for. I'm surprised that despite rising to stardom as a character called Fat Amy in the Pitch Perfect films and starring as the ultimate fat icon Ursula the Sea Witch in the star-studded Hollywood Bowl live production of The Little Mermaid, Rebel Wilson hasn't become considered a proud, plus-size star. She is rarely mentioned in the same breath as, for example, Beth Ditto or Tess Holliday. In this way, she’s a natural choice for a celebrity clothing line, in that she appeals to someone that knows they deserve to look good, but don’t want to make any big statements with their clothes. Not the wild, out-and-proud attention-grabbing designs of Beth Ditto’s collection, for example, but designed by someone who is undeniably plus size. So, does this new collection have the power to cement Wilson's legacy as a real plus-size star? The range she has designed is not, in its own right, groundbreaking: it meanders between the average and the pleasant. A boxy, bell-sleeve top in a vibrant purple lace is particularly striking, and the Pin Up Super Skinny Jeans look genuinely skinny- something many plus size skinny jeans fail at. Shot on Rebel Wilson herself, who has been styled in a soft-glamour way, all big hair and smouldering eyes, the pieces look great: contemporary, wearable, not discernibly different from clothes marketed at non-plus size women. On Nordstrom’s website- one of the retailers stocking the range and which ships to the UK- however, the items fade away again, back into the identikit fare that generally makes up celebrity plus size lines. Not only do they not really stand out on the collection’s page, they don’t stand distinctly from the other ranges on offer from the retailer. Maybe what we can learn from this is that plus size clothes look better on living, breathing plus size women like Rebel Wilson than they do on static, headless models. What sets this line apart, however, isn’t so much the clothes themselves as the fact the Rebel Wilson line will be ‘updated’ in stores and online every six weeks, responding to trends and customer interest. This long-term strategic approach is new to the plus-size celebrity collaboration space. Some autumn/winter items, such as a faux fur jacket, are already planned for later down the line. It suggests an interesting new way of working, a belief in the future. Keeping these collaborations as an ongoing project rather than a one-off experiment suggests a greater investment in their success. It also gives customers a reason to keep coming back. Seen a cute piece dropped as a teaser on the Rebel x Angels Instagram account? A style-obsessed plus-size shopper will keep coming back to the site, refreshing the page until that piece drops. With the Rebel Wilson collection, this works especially well since she will wear items from her range in Pitch Perfect 3, which comes out in December, and items such as a silver sequinned dress that feature in the film will be available to buy from the release date of the film. While Wilson has created a single collection for release this month, it is clearly not the end of the road- a first in the world of celebrity plus size fashion collaborations. While the initial line Rebel Wilson has produced is safe, and could be said to lack an experimental touch, that experimentation now has room to appear later on. Let’s hope customer demand pushes it towards something bold and inventive.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Ever since Brigitte Macron moved into the Élysée Palace when husband Emmanuel became President in May, her style has come under the microscopic scrutiny which comes with taking a role (albeit very much unofficial, as was confirmed yesterday) on the world stage. Madame Macron's penchant for above-the-knee skirts, skinny jeans and power blazers would have been guaranteed to attract attention no matter what her age, but the fact that she is 64 (and 25 years her husband's senior) means that she has been hailed as a new poster woman for ageless style. So it is little surprise that she has enlisted the services of a stylist to help her to hone her own take on the First Lady look.  Mathieu Barthelat Colin's name was first linked to Madame Macron in June in an article in France's Gala magazine, and his careful tweaks to the look which she had crafted herself, mostly via a close relationship with Louis Vuitton, have been evident throughout the summer. This week, his name has been mentioned again as the row over whether she should be given an official title and office made headlines.  When she greeted Melania Trump in July, Macron wore a white shift dress by Courrèges, the design house which became a byword for futuristic style in the 60s and which has recently been revived by a young design team; it was a considered and clever tribute to a less celebrated part of France's fashion legacy and offered a particularly pertinent contrast to Mrs Trump's classically elegant Dior suit.  Elsewhere, Madame Macron has added several new jackets to her wardrobe by unexpected names such as Alexandre Vauthier and Balmain, more often linked to celebrities like Bella Hadid and Kendall Jenner than first ladies. It's a strategy which shows Macron taking up the mantle of diplomatic dressing in a fresh way.  Although her representatives have refused to comment on Colin's involvement in Macron's wardrobe, it is thought she pays for his services personally rather than using state funds.  So who is Mathieu Barthelat Colin? Rather brilliantly, his other clients include Laure Thilleman, a glamorously sophisticated model and TV presenter who won Miss France 2011. He also has numerous TV styling credits to his name, including dressing contestants on the French versions of The Voice and The Bachelor. The thirty-something became a freelance stylist in 2011 after a stint working for contemporary French label Zadig et Voltaire.  Colin hasn't yet given Mrs Macron a dramatic makeover but his influence is already notable, guiding her away from establishment labels towards younger, cooler brands which she can carries off with her personal brand of edgy chic.  It is not known how long the pair have been working together but Colin posted images from Le Toquet in mid-April when Macron and his wife were also in the area and were pictured walking and cycling together.  Elsewhere on Instagram, Colin often posts selfies showing off his beard and posing with the animals on the farm at his family home. His next task will to help Madame Macron to select looks to placate the public mood after the dramas of this week.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. The furore started when Beyoncé released her explosive visual album Lemonade, which has highly personal lyrics hinting at infidelity within her marriage with Jay Z. “He only want me when I’m not there. He better call Becky with the good hair," she sang, sparking immediate speculation about who she was referring to.  Shortly after Lemonade was released, Roy posted an image on Instagram with the caption: "Good hair don't care but we will take good lighting, for selfies, or self truths, always. Live in the light #nodramaqueens.” via GIPHY Roy was first rumoured to have been involved with Jay-Z in 2014. Gossip site TMZ leaked security camera footage of Jay-Z being kicked and slapped by Solange Knowles in a lift at the Standard Hotel, while Beyoncé stood by silent. Roy, the ex-wife of Jay Z’s former business partner Damon Dash, was swiftly cited as being the reason why Solange attacked her brother-in-law.  The designer's reference to 'Good Hair' reignited these rumours, leading to Beyoncé fans swarming her instagram account with bee and lemon emojis. Whether Roy is the mystery woman or not, the designer faced such abuse she deleted the post and make her Instagram account private. The designer then addressed the speculation directly on Sunday afternoon, calling out fans for "bullying" her. She wrote on Twitter:  “I respect love, marriages, families and strength.  When news broke that Orla Kiely had gone into administration, the collective gasp among the middle classes was palpable. “‘Where will I get my towels now?’ was my first thought,” admits Hannah Rochell, fashion editor, founder of the website En Brogue and Kiely afficianado who, like thousands of others, immediately shared her shock on social media.  The selfie-satisfied, Kardashian cheerleader, Olivier Rousteing, may not seem an obvious champion of the everywoman. But in his own not-so-subtle way, the creative director of Balmain is emerging at the forefront of a refreshing movement to reflect and cater to a wider demographic in fashion – the fortysomethings. In his latest spring/summer campaign, Rousteing has reunited three of the original “supers” – Cindy Crawford (49), Naomi Campbell (45) and Claudia Schiffer (45). Premiering the campaign on his Instagram feed (where else?), he said the trio had made him “love fashion yesterday, made me love fashion today [and you] are going to make me love fashion in the future.”  Calvin Klein’s joyful pictures of mother and daughter Lisa Bonet (48) and Zoe Kravitz (27), all full of beachy abandon, also offer a broader outlook of generation fashion. And on Monday in Paris, Giorgio Armani launched a range of everyday luxury classics called the New Normal with Yasmin Le Bon (51), Nadja Auermann (44), Stella Tennant (45) and Eva Herzigová (42). Armani says the collection reflects a “desire to dress women in their daily lives. It offers garments that maintain the values of elegance and dignity, and at the same time a reflection of modernity.”  A collection of grown-up garments shown on grown-up women should be a no-brainer. But, as we all know, that hasn’t always been the case. Until very recently, the average age of a model in super-expensive clothes was around 18. Then, last year, it was 80-plus, with Saint Laurent and Céline featuring Joni Mitchell and Joan Didion respectively in their campaigns. This was an interesting idea that undoubtedly helped expand the concept of what is cool and who looks great, as well as aligning the labels with zeitgeist heroes, but it was also yet another example of fashion’s obsession with extremes. This shift feels more measured. Ruth Chapman, co-founder of Matchesfashion.com, says that the demographic of 40- and 50-year-olds is “the woman we always consider first. She’s the one who spends the most money on fashion and is most engaged with luxury designer fashion. Social media has been really useful in changing concepts of what and how people want fashion to be seen. If we’re going to be spending a lot of money on something, we don’t want to see it on somebody who’s 17; there’s no correlation between the product and the girl wearing it. Social media has changed the concept of what it means to be beautiful. Long gone is that idea that woman become invisible at a certain age.” While we should be careful to attribute every shift and shake to something that happened on Instagram, what the platform has done is allow women of any age, any size, any look to create their own highly tuned and receptive audiences. Most interestingly, when the audience is put in control, the scope for who can be seen as a model widens. Some of the most popular so-called “street-style stars” on Instagram, are definitely not in the conventional “model” mode. The likes of Eva Chen (35, 528,000 followers), Anna Dello Russo (53, 1 million), Net-A-Porter.com’s Sarah Rutson (44K), Natalie Massenet (50, 142K), Giovanna Battaglia (36, 449K), Inès de la Fressange (58, 106K) and Caroline de Maigret (40, 385K) have gained their fans based on their style (crucially) and personality. They are not the passive blank canvases that models so often represent, but authors of their own extremely successful careers. Not before time, brands have begun courting them, and they’re not simply using these women as clothes horses, but starting to shape collections around them. De Maigret, for instance, stars alongside model Angela Lindvall (37) in Karen Millen’s new campaign. The chain is cleverly capitalising on the fashion kudos it has picked up in recent months through its wearable and well thought-out collections. Gemma Metheringham, chief creative officer, explains that “thirty- and fortysomethings are our heartland customers. Our campaign women resonate with a broad range of women regardless of age. We cast them because we’re inspired by their fashion attitude and personality.” Meanwhile, Maigret’s fellow French style guru, Inès de la Fressange, has just launched her fifth collaboration with Uniqlo – a handy edit of easy-to-wear mix-and-match shirt dresses, serviceable trousers and great knits, all with that crucial Fressangian nonchalance. Ines Milano rib long sleeve jacket, £49.90, uniqlo.com, Bluebelle floral printed crepe top£289, Goat, matchesfashion.com, Rosanne trouser, £89 hobbs.co.uk Other high street brands addressing the fashion savvy but realistic tastes of the 40‑plus market include Jigsaw, which saw a year-on-year increase of 19 per cent over Christmas, Hobbs, 8 per cent growth in both trousers and workwear categories, and Finery, soon to be stocked in John Lewis, a year after launching. Alongside them are a slew of smaller brands that cater to this core market. The Fold, Libby London, Me+Em, Winser London and ethical brand The Acey have forged a strong niche offering great pieces that flatter, ideal for work and events.  Jane Lewis (41), founder of Goat, says designing for “grown-ups” forces a designer to be disciplined, honest and focused. “When you’re dressing women across all ages, there’s a responsibility to design for their needs, their body and their life, so that you’re actually fit for purpose. I think that’s often overlooked. ” Goat offers a considered edit – wide- and slim-leg trousers, dresses with sleeves, blouses that work as well for a wedding as a boardroom, coats that cover knees, in a colour palette from safe to zingy. Button detail A line skirt, £125, karenmillen.com, Leather ankle boots, £135, finery.co.uk, Silk linen detail top, £89, jigsaw-online.com Don’t call this demographic middle-aged, however. Last year, Stella magazine editor Marianne Jones coined the alternative term “Diamond generation”. Jones (50) speaks for many when she says that “for too long fashion has targeted very young girls, ignoring the swathe of older, confident consumers who have a high disposable income and are unsaddled by debt. They are a powerful and stylish army and don’t particularly want to dress in a uniform of wrap dress and nude court shoes.” Increasingly, there’s no shortage of relatable red carpet role models for women over 35. From Amal Clooney to Cate Blanchett, Kate Winslet to Sophie Hunter, Rachel Weisz to Joan Fonda, at 78 rocking, yes, Balmain. Lupe Puerta, Net-A-Porter.com’s global head of client relations, says that “the customers I spend time with love looking at youthful models and seeing what the next generation are getting excited about, because, honestly, they don’t feel any different. But they also want to be represented. This is about inclusion, not exclusion. It’s recognising that there is a place in fashion for everyone. The industry will always be about aspiration and dreams, but we need to reconsider what we aspire to.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Parisian chic and New York cool are two of the most sought-after styling vibes when it comes to modern day dressing. So Zadig and Voltaire’s decision to combine the two by moving its fashion week show to the US in celebration of the label’s 20th anniversary yesterday was something of a no-brainer. At the Skylight Modern gallery in Manhattan’s Chelsea district, Zadig and Voltaire’s artistic director Cecilia Bönström unveiled a collection which paid homage to the effortless yet attitude-laden tropes which have come to define the French label, infused with distinctly New York details. Bella Hadid- Zadig’s current campaign star- opened the show in a look which encapsulated that concoction.  A chunky black knitted jumper came layered over an electric blue polo neck and was teamed with a rocking pair of black, red and blue flared and cropped leather trousers. With her mussed up hair and bold red eyeshadow, Hadid epitomised a hard-edged but relaxed kind of glamour. “I loved the cool, sport-chic way that New Yorkers dress,” observed Bönström  post-show. A former model hailing from Sweden, her own dishevelled blonde bob and choice of  loose knit, roomy tailored trousers and trainers emitted the same effortless vibe which she has become so adept at creating in her Zadig and Voltaire collections. “It was important for me to show in New York to have a big, international visibility,” she added, emphasising the label’s ambitions to bring its version of cool to a far wider audience (they plan to open a slew of new stores in the US). Anyone seeking to define the Zadig and Voltaire look should assess the muses which the brand appoints, says Bönström- there was even a ‘Muse’ slogan knit in the mix on the catwalk. Sasha Pivarova, Jamie Bochert and Josephine  Le Tutour are a few of the names she ticks off as being integral to showing what Zadig and Voltaire stands for. “She has a natural simpleness, she’s nonchalant,” Bönström shrugs, suitably nonchalant herself. Some of the most compelling looks in the show were part of a new experiment with a baggier, layered silhouette which carried the New York influence. “We are famous for lingerie slips, but we pushed the idea further so they were worn over loose trousers,” Bönström explained. Vibrant red chinoserie print trousers were worn with a fuschia silk petticoat dress and an oversized hoodie while another look comprised jeans with puddled on the floor with a leopard printed blue and tangerine slip over the top. The unisex collection also included beanie hats which leant an ease to slick tailoring, grungey camo knits elevated with pin-sharp heels and an off-shoulder cream knit and mannish pants look which nodded to Bönström’s Scandi roots. Ultimately this was a celebration of urban style with attitude and individuality. Bönström explained that the celebratory mood was more important than ever. Asked why she had chosen Bella and her brother Anwar to walk in the show, she said: “I want to have a positive message for the world, it’s so important to have good values- which they do. For me. Bella is everything I admire today.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Gisele Bündchen, 35, stepped out of her New York apartment yesterday wearing a grey crew-neck knit and vinyl trousers. Not cheap leather trousers that happened to look a little shiny, but wet-look, plastic trousers. Yes, plastic! If you’re not familiar with vinyl as a clothing material, let us don our goggles and give you a brief science lesson. Vinyl was first invented around 1920 by chemists eager to create a synthetic material that would make manufacturing everyday products cheaper and more durable. Most commonly used on flooring, and for records, designers have been attracted to the material for its subversive texture and look. It is also incredibly strong, and resistant to humidity and moisture, so, unlike leather trousers, you won’t suffer the dreaded leg sweat. (We have all seen that episode of Friends when Ross, in a sweaty panic, can't get his leather trousers back on in the bathroom). As the world’s highest paid model, it’s fair to say Bündchen manages to pull off the shiny trews with long-limbed ease. But can a mere mortal pull them off? We asked three fashion editors, who are all fans of the trouser style, for their advice.   “I would say vinyl trousers are unforgiving,” confesses editorial director of Lyst, Katherine Ormerod. “But if you're a black skinny jeans fan, they offer a seriously rock n roll upgrade. “Gisele has gone for heels, but I would keep things low key with ankle boots or Converse, plus a band tee and Levi's Trucker jacket. The trousers are enough of a statement on their own, and definitely don't need dressing up.” Vogue fashion news editor Julia Hobbs owns 6 pairs of vinyl trousers, and says that the secret is all in the tailoring. “I have them tailored to fit me on Savile Row, and live in them as though they are jeans with a navy cashmere sweater and beaten up ballet pumps. “My golden rule is never buy leggings,” concedes Hobbs. “Always look for trousers that have have structure and a front zipper, otherwise they can end up looking like a bin liner. The thickness of the vinyl is crucial.” In contrast, French blogger Camille Charrière advocates a more relaxed fit. “Because it's such a sexy texture, I would be more inclined to go with a looser fit, like a high-waisted, wide-legged style, for example.” So, should you ever find yourself near a pair of mirror shine pants, remember: the rest of your look needs to stay pared down, and grungy. Think over-sized tees, boyfriend jumpers and trainers for that I'm-with-the-band-look.  She’s hit the headlines in recent days after being accused of tax evasion in her native Israel, but who is Bar Refaeli? Well, you probably recognise her name; she was catapulted into public consciousness in 2005 when she started a relationship with serial ‘modelizer’ Leonardo DiCaprio. They remained a couple until 2009, briefly reconciled in 2011, then split for good. The relationship undeniably boosted her profile and she soon became Israel’s most famous model export, appearing on the cover of Sports Illustrated and countless other titles. She was born in Hod HaSharon to parents Rafi and Tzipi, a successful model throughout the Seventies whom Bar looks remarkably similar to. She started modelling at eight months old, taking a break form the ages of 12 to 15 because of braces. This latest brush with controversy isn’t her first. She was heavily criticised for evading army service in Israel by marrying a family friend so that she could instead pursue her modelling career. If she had not married she would have had to serve two years of full service in line with Israeli’s conscription laws. She was brazenly unapologetic about the situation, telling GQ: "I really wanted to serve in the IDF [Israel Defence Forces], but I don't regret not enlisting, because it paid off big time. That's just the way it is, celebrities have other needs. I hope my case has influenced the army." She wed billionaire Israeli businessman Adi Ezra in September this year, and once again found herself in the headlines. For the occasion, the couple had requested that the airspace above their wedding venue, the Carmel Forest spa resort hotel near Haifa, be closed to air aircraft except those they had hired for guests and photography purposes – specifically five drones, two helicopters and a hot air balloon. The civil aviation authority initially agreed, but the country’s transport minister made them withdraw the agreement, saying: “The skies belong to the public at large, and exclusivity should not be granted for commercial reasons to relevant organisations.” She wore a custom-made Chloé dress for the occasion. In 2013 Bar was named Israel’s highest-paid model, and currently sits at number 18 on models.com’s list of the most-followed models on social media with almost 6 million followers across Instagram, Facebook and Twitter. While she’s made most of her rumoured $20 million fortune from modelling, she’s also invested in several start-ups, including MyCheck, an app that allows customers to pay from their phones.  From Chloé to Vetements, the SS16 catwalks were full of sports references; some wearable (Alexander Wang's chic black bomber) and others a little trickier (Paco Rabanne silver hoodie, we're looking at you). With a season full of 'marmite' trends like chokers, mules and the It colour, yellow, the comfy casual vibe is very welcome, but does that mean it's as easy to wear as its connotations might suggest? Although it looks simple, such casual pieces require some careful planning to ensure they are sleek enough for work, and chic enough for play. Here is our extensive guide to tackling the sports trend, even if you're usually more of a Louboutin than loungewear girl. If it's good enough for Victoria Beckham, it's good enough for us! Box-fresh white trainers have been hailed the perfect complement to tailored workwear, and are without doubt the easiest way to step into the trend. Already an avid wearer of the classic white trainer style?  Last night, every fashion lover worth her Chloé tracksuit tuned in to the first episode of the BBC’s new fly-on-the-wall documentary on British Vogue. Offering a rare glimpse into the daily routines – and wardrobes – of the women who run the 100-year-old fashion bible, the film showed that Vogue is still full of surprises.  It’s fitting, then, that in the same week, the magazine’s publisher, Condé Nast, has launched a highly-anticipated new venture that’s set to change the way we shop, just like Vogue did. This is Style.com, the company’s first online luxury outlet, and the most closely watched foray into ecommerce in memory.  Not so long ago Style.com was the closest thing the fashion industry had to an encyclopaedia – the website you could count on to publish photos and reviews of every runway show worldwide. In April 2015, Condé Nast closed the site and announced plans to retool it; the new Style.com launched last Friday.  Its Camden office, tucked between a Fitness First and a pub, might have the look of any number of tech start-ups: football table in the kitchen, orderly tanks of colour-coded post-it notes next to jumbo-screen Macs. But the ambition is nothing less than conquering a swathe of the e-comm map currently dominated by the likes of Yoox Net-a-porter Group and Matchesfashion.com.  The site offers wares from more than 120 brands, ranging from leading luxury houses such as Gucci and Valentino to emerging designers like Petar Petrov and Wanda Nylon - and incorporates artificial intelligence to 'learn’ what each shopper wants to see.  “It’s Condé Nast, you know?” says Fashion Director Yasmin Sewell, brown eyes sparkling. “It’s their first owned ecommerce site, so we have to raise the bar on every level. I like the challenge of that.” Fashion Director Yasmin Sewell wears Sharon dress, £896, Preen by Thornton Bregazzi and Lipstick boots, £720, Petar Petrov, both at Style.com The announcement of Sewell’s involvement was, to many people, the first indication of the magnitude of Condé Nast’s commitment to the project. A lanky, tanned Australian with cropped curls and a wicked laugh, Sewell, 40, is a fashion buyer and brand consultant who used to work at Browns and Liberty, and who convinced Jonathan Anderson to design womenswear (he’s the fashion wunderkind who won two prizes at last year’s British Fashion Awards). She possesses a near-magical ability to make anything—a shoe, a tricky trouser shape, a new ecommerce platform—seem desirable as soon as she shrugs it on. Today’s look: an oversized patchworked men’s blazer, a vintage-style white t-shirt and boyfriend jeans, an outfit of which she says, “We’re going to have all of this on Style.com! I didn’t even realise that when I got dressed.”  Editorial Director Melissa Dick wears M.i.h Jeans and Aquazzura sandals, both available or soon to appear on Style.com She’s joined by a fleet of chic collaborators. Along with Style.com President Franck Zayan, formerly of Galeries Lafayette, the director-level team includes Sewell, Head of Innovation Natalie Varma, Creative Director Jane Gorley and Editorial Director Melissa Dick. They’re all applying their self-avowed 'fashion geekiness’ toward the same goal: getting customers to click, dream and buy. “We’re not selling nuts and bolts,” says Dick, 43, previously the editorial director at ASOS and site director for Elleuk.com. “What we’re selling is fashion, and it’s a very emotional thing. Our shopping decisions are quite subconscious and nuanced—often people don’t know what they want until they see it.” Brighton-born Varma, 31, came to Style.com from stints at Net-a-porter, DeepMind (an artificial intelligence-pioneering start-up that was acquired by Google) and Anya Hindmarch; Gorley, 40, brings editorial print and digital design experience (including at The Telegraph) and also worked at DeepMind. She joined before the venture had a name or any inkling that they would be able to use the Style.com URL. “That day we were elated,” she says. Creative Director Jane Gorley wears t-shirt, £222, Sacai; jeans, £1,470, Gucci and Petar Petrov boots, available or soon to appear on Style.com Together the four women make an impressive panel of fashion-tech veterans, though they’re united by more than strong CVs. “Basically we’re all obsessed with shopping online,” Gorley deadpans. Her most recent Style.com purchase was a package of Aurelia beauty products, while Dick’s taste veers toward the edgy (Givenchy and Preen). Aside from the outfits, what sets Style.com apart, Sewell says, is “content, the highest level of tech and the best brands.” Unlike Net-a-porter, Style.com doesn’t hold stock. The site operates a marketplace model in which brands supply their own imagery and handle order fulfilment. So in appearance Style.com shares more with Amazon than most typical luxury fashion e-tailers – but then, Amazon is the world’s most successful online marketplace, so perhaps that’s not a flaw. Sewell says the sales model is an advantage for the breadth and depth of product it enables her to showcase. Retail buyers have to carefully allocate their budgets across pieces they think will sell – usually “the easiest pieces,” she says. Since she doesn’t have to put money behind her picks for the site, she’s free to be more experimental. “I want the site to be very daring, very bold and very fashion forward,” she says. “I think our customer is going to be really into exclusives, quite inspired by street style, trend-led, makes wish lists but isn’t necessarily a follower. What they’ll access will be super-inspiring.” Shopping pages are seeded with galleries and videos. Eventually you’ll be able to shop straight from Vogue and GQ’s websites. Head of Innovation Natalie Varma wears Chloe dress and Gucci heels, available soon on Style.com Nowhere is the team’s shared technological nous more apparent than when Varma starts to talk about the site’s 'human product curators’ and artificial intelligence capabilities. “We’ll be able to provide a much more personalised experience for users,” she says. Sewell likens it to Netflix or Spotify for fashion. “Your homepage will be different to my homepage. Not from day one, because it has to start learning you and that will take time.” It’s an idea that seems likely to have shoppers entering credit-card details before they know it. If they’re a little sensitive about the scrutiny the project has received over its long gestation (Style.com was supposed to launch last September), they’re also focussed on happy customers being the most important indicators of success. “Industry recognition is important for a project that’s been so talked-about. But ultimately success is people buying things and finding great clothes that they like,” Dick says.   The Style.com team is already looking months ahead, when shoppers will find exclusive collaborations from JW Anderson, Vetements (“I can’t say too much but it’s big,” Sewell says), Christopher Kane and Mansur Gavriel. “They’ve created a whole new bag for me, in a fabric that’s not leather, and that’s really, really well-priced,” Sewell says, practically rubbing her hands together in anticipation. “It’s gonna fly.” Natalie Varma Role: Head of Innovation Age: 31 From: Brighton On her wish list: “I'm investing in big sleeves. I’ve got lots of Roksanda on my wishlist.”   Jane Gorley Role: Creative Director Age: 40 From: Toronto, Canada On her wish list: “I’ve got my eye on some silver Proenza boots that are totally impractical but really cool.  Deciding what to wear for work can be difficult enough, but imagine going through the 7.30am trauma of finding a clean, not-too creased blouse when there's the chance that you might bump into Anna Wintour in the lift. Nightmare. Publishing company Condé Nast has introduced a clothes renting system for its United States  employees that will make getting dressed in the morning a little easier. And no, employees haven't been given unlimited access to the legendary Vogue fashion cupboard. The publishing company, which houses Vogue, Glamour, Allure and Teen Vogue, has partnered with clothes lending website Rent the Runway to offer its staff the opportunity to sign up to the program which lets you rent up to three items for an unlimited amount of time. While you might think clothes borrowing websites are used primarily for wedding or prom dresses, this model is starting to be applied to everyday workwear. “The casualization of workwear has really required women to spend a lot more on a monthly basis,” the company's vice president of brand marketing A.J. Nicholas explains to WWD. Rent the Runway claims that 60 percent of professional women spends $3,000 a year on fashion, with 20 percent spending over $6,000, explaining why they have introduced a specific work edit with pieces from DVF, Elizabeth and James, Theory, Preen, Prabal Gurung and more. Employees at Condé Nast will be able to sign up to the Unlimited program for $90 a month, with Condé Nast paying 35% of the subscription. This is Rent the Runway's first corporate partnership, although WWD reports that it is in discussion with other companies. While the Rent the Runway system is currently only available in the United States, Girls Meets Dress is a UK-based clothes lending website with pieces from Victoria Beckham, Stella McCartney and Alexander McQueen. Meanwhile Sweden has introduced a particularly innovative spin on clothes swapping with a project called #Sharewear which allows Instagram users to borrow clothes for no charge. Pictures of clothes are posted on Instagram and the first person to comment underneath the post gets to borrow the item for a week, before passing it onto another user.  Rihanna unveiled her latest Fenty x Puma collection in Paris tonight. Like a rebel tearing up the school rule book, the global superstar brought a booming soundtrack, flashing lights and models stomping on desks to the usually tranquil and studious environs of the Bibliothèque nationale de France. It was a decision which made sense though, as Rihanna riffed on collegiate classics and the tribes of the playground, bringing her signature attitude-laden and sporty spin to designs inspired by the sartorial staples of the classroom. Front-row to watch the spectacle was Cara Delevingne, channelling the perfect just-got-out-bed teen look in an oversized hoodie which she had shrugged over her newly platinum blonde hair. She sat beside Nick and Joe Jonas to complete a suitably on brand millenial front row. While Rihanna and Puma (the collection is named Fenty after the Barbadian singer's surname) might not have the heritage and kudos of the other storied names which show at Paris fashion week, the collaboration brings buzz in spades. The show was livestreamed from Rihanna’s personal Instagram account with as many as 100,000 of her adoring fans tuning it to watch live as she did a final inspection backstage of each look before it took to the catwalk and touched up her make-up before she went out to take her bow. If school was the general theme, then rebels were the heroes of the show. The first look, modelled by a shaven headed cool girl, comprised a padded, floor-length tartan coat worn open so that the model’s (pierced) nipples and silky matching boxer shorts were exposed. High-heeled boots finished the daring, high-octane look. That theme continued in hoods pulled up to cover the eyes, slashed crop tops and trailling long sleeves with which no one could ever hope to hold their fountain pen. It was something of an updated vision of the seminal 1995 film Clueless. Like Cher and Dionne- renowned for their mini kilts and thigh-high socks- the stars of Rihanna’s show had made their uniforms their own. What may once have been a prim cricket jumper was slashed and stretched to become a slouchy mini dress while a varsity knit was shrunken and layered over a high-cut tangerine body suit. There was even a section dedicated to goths, in all their head-to-toe black glory with only acid-hue hair as a pop of colour. Students of Rihanna’s sass-infused personal style will recognise plenty of familiar elements; her beloved thigh-high boots appeared emblazoned with the Puma logo and with trainer-style lacing, oversized sportswear contrasted with slick, sexy pieces in bold shades of apple and sunshine yellow. Many of the models- a pleasingly diverse cast which counted glamazon Joan Smalls and Londoner Adwoa Aboah among their number- wore the same giant hoop earrings as Rihanna herself. When the collection goes on sale in Puma stores and sites around the world in two days time, there will- cleverly- be much to buy, from baseball caps and sports-striped socks to velour tracksuit bottoms and practical duvet coats. No wonder RiRi was rocking down the catwalk as she took her bow.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  For 27 years, Pierre Hardy has designed the men’s and women’s shoes for Hermès – and, since 2001, the jewellery too. It’s fair to say he knows his accessories. Bestriding both the highest level of functional design and the most exquisite materials available,his are collections rich in simplicity. Taking inspiration from geometry and everyday objects, his pieces can be fun and surprising and almost mathematical in their purity: the epitome of modern luxury. ‘When you look at any object of Hermès you have this feeling of truth,’ says Hardy. ‘There is no cheating or pretending. It is anti-gadget.’ And although he was part of the team that designed the Hermès Apple watch, we’ll let him have that. On a sofa at the brand’s Paris headquarters, in his signature black, squarish spectacles, white jeans, black T-shirt and trainers, he is as straightforward as a punctuation mark. American Vogue has called the 61-year-old designer ‘fashion’s favourite brainiac’ and for all the evidence of his creativity – he studied fine art and was a dancer before becoming a designer – Hardy does have something of the scientist about him. Logical and untheatrical, he has a common-sense approach to the often smoke-and-mirrors business of creating luxury fashion. ‘I like to get a lot of things done quickly,’ he says, with a smile that suggests no amount of haste could compromise his precision, ‘so I can go on holiday.’ His name may not have the same recognition factor as Manolo Blahnik or Christian Louboutin, but his designs – whether for Hermès or his eponymous line, now part-owned by Hermès, or for Balenciaga, where he created shoes for Nicolas Ghesquière (including 2007’s memorable robot-style Lego shoe) – boast a fierce quirkiness that has had a great influence on fashion footwear and attracts a passionate following. When he arrived at Hermès in 1990, there was no existing shoe collection to speak of. It’s a testament to his skill that some of the designs he went on to create look like they might have emerged in the 1950s. This season’s Paris loafer, with palladium-plated H buckle, could be an of-the-moment update on an original 1970s design. And the Oran sandal, with its leather upper forming the shape of an H, might have been worn by Jackie Onassis on vacation – except it wasn’t released until she’d been dead for three years. ‘I wanted to make a no-shoe, basically – like walking barefoot,’ says Hardy of the conception of that 20-year-old classic. ‘A very simple sandal that any woman could wear, with a sole and a strap. I was looking at a drawing by an African tribe, a design the women used to paint on the houses, very graphic and beautiful. So we chose to adapt it to the shoe and it made an H. It wasn’t the purpose at all, but when the shoe was done we saw it.’ For the spring/summer 1998 collection, Hardy created the Quick trainer, making Hermès the first luxury brand to design a trainer made entirely of leather, a huge innovation at the time. It’s still going strong. Asked why their appeal has endured, he laughs. ‘Why? I don’t know! There is something that you can’t explain. I’m not a spiritual person at all,I don’t believe in magic. I think it’s just the necessity of the thing. It makes sense and it becomes a shape or a reality.’ But the secret of creating something that becomes a new classic might be found in the way Hardy evokes the past. ‘A lot of the work is based on my memories,’ he says. ‘And a lot of people have an image of Hermès based on their own recollections. Sometimes they’re different to the reality of what the thing was, but that’s OK. What I’m trying to do is to make new memories [for our clients]. So I try to make something better;to give it a new shape and image.’ He says he’s neither nostalgic nor ‘an archeologist’ who is continually diving into the archives. He doesn’t even collect old shoes – something he used to do. ‘Because when I look at some of them, the stitching up is 10 times smaller and the leather of the sole is unbelievably thin– [shoe-making] is not like this any more,’ he says. ‘Nobody can produce this type of object now, so in a way it’s masochistic to even look. Now we have different tools that allow us to do more: unbelievable sneakers, crazy materials. So let’s play with that instead. Each year Hermès introduces a company-wide theme that will be the focus of all its collections. For 2017 that has been ‘le sens de l’objet’, the sense of an object. Hardy has chosen to riff on that in the shoe collection by including styles that feel weighty and solid. ‘I wanted these pieces to be strong or beautiful before being a fashion item –a big sole, beautiful leather, something chunky. Like a beautiful box you look at and feel the reality and density and depth.’ On other pieces he’s taken objects that have been used by Hermès for a long time, ‘like metal rivets and buckles,using them as an ornament to show the beauty in a simple object’. Some themes, he adds, are easier for a footwear designer to work to than others. ‘I remember the year of The Hand...’ Born in Paris, Hardy’s dual passions as a child were dance and drawing. He entered a contemporary dance company but made a choice to leave. ‘Dance is not that open,’ he says. ‘It’s a very “inside world” to focus and work on, and I needed more contact with the outside.’ He taught scenography (the art of creating atmosphere in theatres) for seven years and began illustrating for magazines, such as Vogue Hommes and Italian Vanity Fair. He had no thought of being a designer. ‘It’s different because I’m an old man now, but when I was 18 fashion was couture and I didn’t want to be couture – there were only 10 couturiers in the world. So when I drew it wasn’t as a career, or a project, it was just for fun.’ But back in the 1980s fun could get you somewhere. An acquaintance began working in the Christian Dior studio and asked Hardy to come in and draw the shoe collection. And so began his career in shoes – although again, it didn’t appear that way. ‘There was no pressure, nor mountain of expectation. It was the beginning of the big fashion groups but there was no partition between luxury brands, there was no specification of luxury [as a market]. Even if Dior was the biggest name in fashion it was still quite protected then, quite secretive.’ But accessories were about to become increasingly important to the emerging luxury houses and Hermès saw the man for the job. Three years later he was put in charge of a whole new collection. It would be hard,I say, for anything like this to happen to a young illustrator now. ‘Yes,’ he laughs. ‘Everything is impossible now.’ Perhaps that’s one of the reasons Hardy carried on his teaching at the Duperré fashion school in Paris for so long: to encourage the generations that followed him. ‘Everything can be learnt and taught,’ he says. ‘If you decide to become a painter, a doctor, an architect you have to learn it. I don’t believe in the [idea of] genius. The energy that I put into my job now,I could put into anything else and do [well in] it. You have to learn the rules obviously. I was teaching methodology–creativity is a process in a way, but after that you can play.’ © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. If that’s a look which sounds familiar then that’s because it is. Archer, who is married to Getty’s royal photographer Chris Jackson, has emerged as Kate’s not-so-secret style weapon in recent years.  It’s just over two months since Natalie Massenet resigned from Net-A-Porter, the luxury e-tailer she had set up from her kitchen table in 2000. In a statement she explained that the completion of the company’s recent merger with Yoox Group was “the right time for me to move on to explore new ideas and opportunities.” And it seems she is already doing just that. According to paperwork filed at Companies House, on October 14 Massenet set up a new company called Imaginary Ventures Ltd. A spokesman for the 50-year-old confirmed the new venture but declined to reveal any further information to WWD, who spotted the registration. Massenet is currently subject to a 12-month non-compete agreement, meaning she won’t be able to action her new plans until September 2016. In the meantime she has her role as chairman of the British Fashion Council to keep her busy. Her next project is the British Fashion Awards, which take place on November 23 at the London Coliseum. The night will see Karl Lagerfeld honoured with a Lifetime Achievement Award and Victoria Beckham, J.W.  She's an admirer of Kate Moss in Absolutely Fabulous: The Movie, and now Joanna Lumley's 'fan girl' status has come full circle as she models Moss's collection for Equipment IRL (in real life for those without a copy of the urban dictionary to hand). In New York to do a series of Ab Fab press junkets surrounding the US release date, Lumley modelled one of the silk shirts Moss designed for the French brand, that is famous for shirting and was initially founded by the husband of French fashion doyenne Carine Roitfeld. A lover of bold print and colour, it's no surprise that Lumley should find much to like in Moss's pattern-heavy capsule edit. Though leopard print and lightening bolts both feature, it was the white blouse littered with tiny black stars that caught the actress's eye. For her stint on TV show The View, she tucked the shirt into a pair of slim white trousers and added pristine white plimsolls into the mix. During a week that has already seen Christy Turlington wear white denim and a matching tee, Lumley's white-out proved to be fashion-forward indeed. Of course, Lumley was paying tribute to rock chick Moss, so not everything on the look was perfect 'ivory chic'. She fastened a stud and chain embellished belt around her waist and positioned the shirt's trailing scarf feature down the middle so that it resembled a Rolling Stones-esque skewiff tie. With mussed up hair and a deep red lip, the result was more punk than pristine. Though Jennifer Saunders concocted the Ab Fab plot of accidentally 'killing' Kate Moss, it was her series co-star Lumley that convinced Saunders to pen the script initially. "We've got to make the film, darling," she told Saunders. "Because otherwise we’ll all be dead and we won’t have made the film." Without revealing too much for those who haven't cracked open a bottle of Bolly and watched it yet, Eddie and Patsy are obsessed with Moss in the film. It is then a fitting tribute that Lumley should model Moss for the promo surrounding the release. Moss's Equipment shirts have proved popular with Lumley, 70, Lara Stone, 32, and Laura Bailey, 43,  alike, and thus show the collection has true ageless style appeal. The timeless collection is only the second time Moss has turned her hand to fashion design. Her Kate Moss X Topshop lines were arguably aimed at a much younger audience. Fans of the starry scarf embellished shirt that Lumley was spotted wearing will be sad to know it has sold out on Net-a-Porter, but a similar leopard print shirt with scarf feature is available for £370. Remember though, these shirts need to be styled with sass, as prescribed by Moss and modelled by fan girl Lumley.  Donatella Versace has suggested women are better than men at designing clothes because gay fashion designers  are releasing collections " for the woman they want to be". The Italian fashion designer, vice president and chief designer of the Versace Group, said she believes women understand their bodies better. Her comments in The Times Magazine are likely to raise a few eyebrows among her peers, but she believes female designers have an advantage because they “understand a woman’s body, a woman’s security and a woman’s attitude”. The 61-year-old added: “I love gay people. My friends are all gay. But some of the designers, when they design for a woman, they design for the woman they want to be, you know. They are thinking of themselves. “But themselves and the woman are not the same… I want to design clothes that say, “This is a woman’s clothes.” “Riccardo Tisci is amazing, so many [male] designers are amazing, too – but sometimes there is this little thing where they need to make themselves a little bit behind who they are, and to look at the real woman.” Versace, rumoured to have pop star Lady Gaga play her in a new series of American Crime Story depicting the real life murder of her brother Gianni in 1997, recently told how she wanted to empower women with her latest designs. Some of her latest womenswear collections incorporated a military style, with the inclusion of flat shoes that was seen as radical for the brand. She added: “We are strong. Women are strong… and sexiness does not have to go against power.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
