 You may not know their names, and only vaguely recognise their faces, but make no mistake: these women are changing the way we shop. Known as the ecomm girls, they are the carefully selected models who pose for fashion websites such as Asos, Net-A-Porter and Matchesfashion.com. It’s their flawless figures and girl-next-door charms that coax us into hitting ‘add to basket’. The work may be less glamorous than that of an old-fashioned supermodel, but with online sales now accounting for 20 per cent of all clothing and accessory sales, ecomm models have become vital players in the fashion industry - and can earn thousands of pounds a week.  Internet shopping has transformed the way we choose and consume clothes. Recently we learnt that ‘serial returners’ - customers, typically women, who bulk buy clothes online to try on different sizes and styles and then send them back using free return services - are placing an increasing burden on fashion brands and may even be pushing up prices. Researchers found 56 per cent of people who had bought clothing online in the last six months had sent something back.  For savvy online consumers, the right model can make or break a sale - ecomm modelling is a cut-throat industry. Yet the faces who rule today’s virtual catwalks, and can shift a collection with one perfect set of shots, are sometimes ordinary young women, scouted on the street rather than recruited from modelling agencies.  The work can be grueling. Photographic studios more akin to factories churn out image after image, shooting up to 90 new products a day - a model will pose in each one for various different angles and often then walk in them for a ‘catwalk’ video, as used by sites such as Asos and Net-a-Porter. Still life shots of the garment may be created by literally placing the item on top of the model to give the appearance of shape (which looks better than pieces placed flat on the ground and shot from above) - the model will then be Photoshopped out later.  “It’s really hard work,” says Dominika Grnova, who has modelled for the Asos, Urban Outfitters, Topshop and Forever 21 websites amongst others for two years. “Usually I work 9 to 5. We can do from 30 up to 80 looks per day. It’s change, shoot, video, change, shoot video.” The difference between ecomm models and regular ones is speed - if you can’t move quickly you won’t get asked back. “We move completely differently, we change poses from smiles to moody so quickly,” says Grnova. “I can shoot up to ten brands a day, all with different styles, hair and make-up looks. I can change in ten seconds, even less, if necessary. “Time is money for the clients, so if the model can get through lots of looks per day without looking tired then that’s a bonus.” The appeal is regular work and a good income. “If you do it four or five times a week the money is amazing,” she says. As one of the most popular Asos girls, she has become a star in her own right; she often gets recognised and has 24k Instagram followers. There’s no telling where it will lead: Cara Delevingne started out modelling for Asos before she was spotted by Burberry. Sara-Ella Ozbek, a booker at Next model management, agrees that the key to being a good ecomm model is speed and precision. “It’s probably the hardest work you can do modelling wise,” she says. “The days are busy, there’s a lot of shots to be done and it can be tiring.” There can be a brutal shelf life. Each look will be tracked by the brand and if the clothes don’t sell the model won’t be booked again. An ex-production manager from a major high street online retailer reveals that they used a lot of street cast models – who didn’t have agents – and therefore weren’t wise to the industry regulations. Typically they sign a contract with the retailer and are used until the decision is made to use a different look. Still, the soaring number of online fashion stores has created a huge growth for this strand of modelling.  “Ecomm probably makes up about 40 to 50 per cent of an agency’s work now,” says Karsten Edwards, director at IMM Model Group. “Fees range from £250 up to £1,800 a day, depending on the brand and how popular a model is. If a girl sells well, they’ll keep booking her.”  The biggest retailers often request exclusivity from their most successful ecomm models. “They know they can’t completely ring fence a girl, but they do want to restrict which other brands they can work with.” However, he says some brands use ‘unrecognisable’ models where they’ll chop the head off at the chin – saving money as the model’s fee will be lower and there is no need for hair styling or make-up.  What does it take, then, to be a successful ecomm model? Generally these models have an appealing, approachable and believable quality, more so than models used for catwalk or magazine editorial shoots. They are usually slightly bigger – a size eight rather than a four or six. The onus is on relatability. Different looking models work for different brands – an edgier, pale model will work well for a cool brand like Vetements but for a more mainstream label, shooting swim and summer wear they’ll want a honey toned, healthy looking model. The rise of plus size and petite collections has seen an encouraging influx of different sized models. “A few years ago it was impossible to be 5ft 3 and able to make a living from modelling” says Edwards. Jenny Dickinson, editor of Net-A-Porter’s online magazine The Edit says that when choosing the girl who will sit on the homepage of the site, the biggest concern for her is avoiding a model who is too thin. “I’ve got a 21-year-old daughter and it’s something I’m very conscious of.” She has featured plus size model Ashley Graham on their cover. “That was really important for us. It’s key as a retailer for us to say to all women, you can shop here, these clothes are for you.” Interestingly though, a plus size model may not always technically be ‘plus.’ A representative from one major online retailer, who did not want to be named, told me that size 14 models would be used for size 18+ ranges – given that the camera adds pounds, and women want a level of aspiration. When they used models who were a size 18+ the clothes didn’t sell. Whilst some retailers such as Topshop, ASOS and H&M use a variety of ethnicities to reflect their global customer base, depressingly if you scan through the majority of websites, especially luxury sites, the backdrop is overwhelmingly white. Encouragingly, at Finery, the online high street store launched last year, they are adamant about being inclusive in their casting. Brand director and co-founder Caren Downie says that this was something that “was always very high on our list. We have to cover all ethnicities. We want to appeal to all women, it’s hugely important to us. We’re a London brand and we want to reflect what we look like in our office and what our city is like.” As an online only retailer, image is everything. “A lot of consideration goes into our shoots,” says Downie. “We probably take longer over them than other brands, it’s more considered. If things aren’t selling we will re-shoot it. That’s not necessarily down to the model, it might be the outfit, or the styling…” Given that Finery hit £5million in revenue in their first year, it’s an encouraging success story - and in no small part down to the clever casting of their model ambassadors.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The most significant night in the British fashion industry calendar took place at the Royal Albert Hall tonight with the biggest names in the business in attendance to round off the year in suitably fabulous style. Over 4,000 guests- David Beckham, Naomi Campbell, Kate Moss and Gigi Hadid among them- gathered to toast the rebranded British Fashion Awards - now known simply as 'The Fashion Awards’. The ceremony has now finished, with those who have shaped fashion this year awarded for their contributions.   Read through all the action as it happened in our live feed below...    There was a jovial mood backstage at the 2016 Fashion Awards. Marilyn Manson, the night’s unexpected guest who had presented his friend Demna Gvasalia with the International Urban Luxury Brand award, was busily editing the pictures that had been taken of him. “If I don’t get laid tonight, I’m going to tag you and blame you personally,” he joked, as he poured over pictures of him posing on the red carpet earlier. But for all the hysteria, there was emotion too from the winners of these newly revamped Fashion Awards. “Before the show my dad told me, ‘If you don’t win, you’re still a good designer,’” Simone Rocha admitted. “But I wanted it. I wanted to win.” Rocha celebrated by knocking back a few espresso martinis with friend and fellow winner Molly Goddard, who was so shell-shocked by winning her first ever award she wasn’t even sure what she was going to do with the statuette. “Now I just need a fireplace.” Fellow first-time winner, menswear designer of the year Craig Green was equally blown away. “Oh my god, I probably should have prepared a speech, I probably shouldn’t have worn dirty Converse and a T-shirt,” he faux scolded himself. But it wasn’t just the young British designer who were excited by their acclaim. Legendary photographer Bruce Weber told The Telegraph’s Emily Cronin that he was going to keep his Fashion Award in his oceanfront cabana in Florida - and that it would continue to inspire him. “I’m still a student. I have to work for it everyday just like somebody starting out,” he said. A poignant reminder that humility will always be in style.   The biggest cheer of the night has gone to David Beckham, who took the stage in a velvet jacket to present Ralph Lauren with an Outstanding Achievement award. "I've long been a fan of this man and his extraordinary work," Beckham said of Lauren, before admitting he'd not met him until a chance encounter at Soho Farmhouse earlier this year.  No matter though because Beckham knew Lauren's work. The first American to open a store on Bond Street and, in Beckham's words, the man who made Wimbledon the most stylish sporting event, Lauren has built a globally renowned business around the idea of All-American style.  But even though we knew it was coming Ralph Lauren's lifetime achievement award comes at the end of a particularly momentous year for the 77 year-old designer. Lauren played a fascinating role in the American presidential election, creating a series of suits for self-confessed 'pantsuit aficionado' Hillary Clinton to wear during key moments of her campaign, from the blue look she wore for her opening rally in June 2015 to the purple-edged outfit which nodded to the Suffragettes as she accepted defeat in November. ‘I didn’t know the significance of that colour,’ he admitted to The Telegraph's Lisa Armstrong in an interview to mark his Outstanding Achievement award,  ‘but Hillary’s people did. I just knew it looked beautiful on her.’ Lauren's name is recognised the world over; his Polo t-shirts and jeans have become iconic staples for casual dressing but he also knows how to create impact for formal occassions; he has dressed Michelle Obama and many First Ladies before her as well as Hollywood actresses including Gwyneth Paltrow, Cate Blanchett and Sienna Miller for the most demandingly dressed-up events on the world stage. ‘I don’t know where it came from,’ he says of the instinct for design which came when he began creating ties as a young man, ‘but I knew what I was doing was good because I wanted to wear it.’   It’s clearly Demna Gvasalia’s night as the designer picks up his second award, for his work as Creative Director of Balenciaga. It’s a notable accolade: Gvasalia has been at the helm of the storied Parisian house for barely a year writes The Telegraph's Victoria Moss. Whilst eyebrows may have been raised when his appointment was made to this venerated position: the move has worked. Balenciaga was the king of futuristic, modern fashion, and Gvasalia is exactly that today. He might not have brought tracksuits to the house of Balenciaga - but striped Thai market bags, fluoro leggings and oversized puffa jackets (worn off the shoulder - the christening of perhaps one of the more victim-y and daft street style ‘trends’) have found new fans here. Yet, he has also taken the house codes on and adeptly interpreted them: tweed suits with padded front pockets and prominent shoulders have proved to be a surefire success, and re-established that classic Balenciaga silhouette as relevant once again. All in all, given the extreme heat rising off Gvasalia right now - he is simply the fashion super star du jour.   'Fashion is a beautiful dream and I promise I'll keep dreaming forever,' Alessandro Michele said on stage picking up his award for Accessories Designer of the Year.  Last year he won Designer of the Year, this year Michele has been recognised for the immense service he’s paid to the accessories world, writes The Telegraph's Kate Finnigan. Actually, remind us. Where was the world of accessories before Alessandro Michele? Wearing one minimalist earring, we think. Well, that’s changed. With a single pair of slip on, fur-lined loafers he reinvented shoes. With his blingy grandmother’s attic treasures he coaxed us back into enjoying jewellery - even brooches. With his embroidered colourful bags he has injected joy into arm candy again. And by putting all his models in glasses he made spectacles spectacular. Who’d have thunk. More is more is his mantra and for that accessories do indeed owe him this award. Let’s hope it's multi-coloured and bling-tastic.   In a room full of supermodels (Karlie Kloss at 6 foot 6 and a half in heels towering over them all), the International Model of the Year award was always going to be high octane. So it wasn’t a surprise that Gigi Hadid got weepy on stage collecting her award. Social media also erupted - no doubt in part because of the 26 million followers Gigi has on Instagram alone.  There’s no doubt her social media presence has lent Gigi an appearance of intimacy with her fans which earlier generations of supermodels could never hope to achieve. But to dismiss Gigi’s power as purely a result of the ‘likes’ she can acquire on social media would be unfair. This year alone, she’s showed serious prowess on the catwalk. Walking down the Bottega Veneta catwalk hand in hand with Lauren Hutton was one of the biggest moments of Milan Fashion Week. And Gigi’s see-now-buy-now collection for Tommy Hilfiger, which the model debuted at New York Fashion Week, a massive commercial success. Gigi is a model who has managed to throw off the It girl tag and associations of nepotism (her mum Yolanda van den Herik is a former model, who is herself said to be worth $54 million and is best known as a star of The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills; her dad a wealthy property developer) to forge what’s turning out to be a seriously reputable career in modelling. The only person who might not be so thrilled? Her sister Bella, who was also nominated in the International Model of the Year award but, perhaps forewarned she hadn’t won, was a no show tonight. Still, something tells us the Hadid sisters will dominate these awards - and many more - for a few more years to come.   A pleated skirt may not sound like the most wave-making of garments. But when the pleated skirt in question appears on Jaden Smith, son of Will and Jada Pinkett, in a Louis Vuitton campaign, it’s a tsunami. "He represents a generation that has assimilated the codes of true freedom, one that is free of manifestos and questions about gender,” Vuitton creative director Nicolas Ghesquière said. “Wearing a skirt comes as naturally to him as it would to a woman who, long ago, granted herself permission to wear a man’s trench or a tuxedo…. He’s found an instinctive balance that makes his extraordinary attitude a new norm. That really inspired me in the creative process for this collection.” 2016 was full of gender-bending, groundbreaking fashion moments for Jaden, now 18 years old, and sister Willow, 16, who jointly received the New Fashion Icons trophy at tonight’s Fashion Awards. While Jaden made headlines with his skirted campaign and star turn in The Get Down, Willow joined the ranks of Chanel ambassadors, sitting in the front row and posing for backstage photos with Karl Lagerfeld. “It’s not every day that a 15 year-old black girl with dreads gets elected to be the Chanel ambassador,” she told The Telegraph at Chanel’s autumn 2016 couture show. Overachieving teens, meet your new leaders. That an ‘urban’ luxury brand award even exists is testament to the extraordinary effect the Georgian Demna Gvasalia has had on the fashion industry. Having cut his teeth working at Maison Martin Margiela and Louis Vuitton (under both Marc Jacobs and Nicolas Ghesquiere), Vetements was launched as a ‘design collective’ helmed by Gvasalia but two years ago writes The Telegraph's Victoria Moss. The label was a provocateur from the off - staging its second season show in a sex shop, its third at an out of town Parisian chinese restaurant, it’s fourth, in the American church in Paris (where vaulted stylist Lotta Volkova - and friend of the brand - opened the show in a mini dress approximation of a monk’s habit). The clothes were arch, oversized, streetwear appropriated pieces - the theory being that they were simply making elevated, fashion versions of clothes that they and their friends were already wearing. Cult (and sell out) items swiftly followed: £880 jeans hand stitched together from off cuts; bright yellow DHL t-shirts; ditsy printed midi length tea dresses;Titanic sweatshirts - emblazoned with Leo and Kate in embrace - and worn, with a post-post modern irony by Celine Dion amongst others. At its last show (staged during Haute Couture week in Paris, and in the Galeries Lafayette shopping centre - very meta) Vetements created an epic montage of collaborations - re-anointing Juicy Couture velour tracksuits, Dr Martens boots and Manolo Blahnik kitten heels as It items.   In the midst of this counter cultural take over, Gvasalia was christened by Balenciaga as its new creative director. The move cemented him as an arch arbiter of the current state of fashion, and propelling what  may have passed as a flash in the trend pan into a full blown movement: the reverberations of which are felt clearly by this award.   It’s rare that the men in suits get praise for their contribution to fashion but Marco Bizarri scored a blinder when he hired Alessandro Michele, an unknown member of the creative team, for this very high profile role writes The Telegraph's Kate Finnigan. Part of a business leader’s job is to spot the talent and boy, did he do that. He saw that Michele was the right man to inject the va-va-voom that Gucci had been lacking. He encouraged him to be as creative as he liked. The result has been a huge revival in the 95-year-old Italian label’s fortunes, not because he’s played clever with money or marketing, or played it safe. Far from it. Bizzari allowed creative talent to live large and thereby taught everyone a lesson in how to do fashion.       Alexander McQueen wins the award for British brand, cementing creative director Sarah Burton's seemingly unstoppable ability to create divinely beautiful collections which translate into clothes which women want to buy and wear. This year alone, Burton has whipped up breathtakingly lovely shows inspired by ideas as varied as dreams and sleepwalking and rugged Hebridean adventures. The second-to-last look of her Autumn/Winter show, which took place in London as Burton was to give birth imminently to her third daughter, was a delicate silk eiderdown coat which had attendees enthralled by its beguiling mix of prettiness and comfort. Alongside her ever more artful collections, Burton and her team adeptly re-spin them for modern life. While the Duchess of Cambridge might not be your 'average' woman, she has continued to commission McQueen to create looks which are royal-engagement-worthy and fly the flag for British fashion. Some Telegraph team highlights: the red and white floral patterned dress (taken from the etchings seen on old caravans and canal boats) which the duchess wore on the first day of her tour to Canada, the Paisley-printed, peplum shift which united British and Indian tradition worn in Mumbai and the unusually playfully 'Obsessions' dress debuted at the Wimbledon final. Bravo Sarah Burton and team McQueen!   For those wondering whether people working in fashion eat more than sushi, the answer is a resounding yes. Whilst the awards are happening, those at tables are eating fillets of beef with salt-baked celeriac and English wasabi - and even a side of chips. OK, polenta chips but still…. Meanwhile, for dessert there’s a Christmas vibe going on with mince pies on the menu. As for the drinks? By the end of the night the British Fashion Council estimate the guests will have drunk 700 bottles of Evian and 700 more of Badoit sparkling water. Rock and roll. Don't worry, there were Ciroc Vodka cocktails too.    In a night all about celebrating British design personalities, perhaps it was only appropriate that the 4,000 guests paid special recognition for the magazine that has spent 100 years writing about them. The Editor-in-Chief of UK Vogue Alexandra Shulman was presented with an award to celebrate the title’s centenary by Mario Testino - the photographer who has become a household name and an A-list favourite thanks to the images he’s shot for the magazine. It rounds off a stellar year for Shulman, who marked Vogue’s centenary by doing what Vogue does best: pulling in exclusives that keep the industry talking. That certainly happened when Shulman managed to persuade the Duchess of Cambridge to make her first appearance on the cover of a magazine - and hiding the coup from the BBC cameras who had spent 10 months in Vogue’s offices trailing the team for a documentary about their centenary. “That girl next door is just shtick,” Vogue’s Fashion Director Lucinda Chambers told The Telegraph of styling the astute Duchess in Burberry and a Beyond Retro vintage hat. Someone else who isn’t exactly as you’d expect is Vogue’s editor herself. Whilst some thought Shulman came across quite austere on the BBC’s documentary, her own diary of Vogue’s 100th year presents a very different view - and one that most people within the industry recognise. Talking of her fear of flying and always having the wrong underwear, Shulman told The Telegraph earlier this year that her biggest responsibility - and the thing that really kept her awake at night - was making her magazine excellent month in month out. Perhaps tonight’s industry recognition might help ease her concerns.   "Three men have changed how I see America: Mark Twain, Walt Disney and Bruce" says Bailey.  So who is Weber, the man honoured with tonight's award in memory of the legendary fashion stylist Isabella Blow, who nurtured the likes of John Galliano and Alexander McQueen? Remember those steamy Calvin Klein and Abercrombie & Fitch campaigns from the 1990s? Of course you do - the tanned, muscular men in the photos were always going to make for indelible images, writes The Telegraph's Emily Cronin. They’re only part of the reason that Bruce Weber, the photographer behind those campaigns and countless other memorable photographs, wins the Fashion Creator award this evening, a prize five decades in the making. "Bruce’s endurance is testament to his pure talent, his undeniable creativity and his singular warmth and generosity," says the British Fashion Council's chairman, Dame Natalie Massenet. "His expansive body of work in photography and film is iconic, and he himself is rightly an icon of the creative fashion community. He is one of the foremost photographers and creative talents of our age who has helped shape the fashion industry we know today and I have a great deal of admiration for him.”   She scooped the New Establishment award two years ago and now Simone Rocha has scooped the big one. Congratulations, Ms Rocha! There’s really no stopping this designer, who recently turned 30 and celebrated the first birthday of her daughter, Valentine. Rocha’s hybrid aesthetic of Japanese avant-garde and Victoriana, using experimental fabrics and off-centre silhouettes, is unique in womenswear and gave her brand an immediately indentifiable look when she launched 8 years ago. She continues to conjure up one stellar collection after another and a growing collection of accessories and jewellery. With the most prestigious international stockists, from Dover Street Market to Colette, she opened her first London shop a year ago. A second is on its way for New York. “I’ve always made clothes for many different kinds of women,” she told The Telegraph in her melodious Dublin brogue earlier this year. “And now I physically see them coming into my store – older women, mothers and daughters,  students, people who are obsessed with fashion and some who aren’t really that interested. And I get good insights from them. The other day Lynn Yaeger [a renowned New York fashion journalist] was saying, “They’re so comfortable, did you know that?” And I was like, “Erm, yes, it’s on purpose, Lynn! I spend a lot of time making the clothes comfortable so that every­one can wear them."   When Craig Green launched his showstopping catwalk collections, he had to contend with a great of tabloid tittering from the sniping ‘who would actually wear this?’ brigade, writes The Telegraph's Stephen Doig. Granted, wooden planks across the face, tent structures aloft around men’s shoulders and a smashed up collage of cardboard boxes around the heads of his models were a tough sell, but served to put his shows, and the burgeoning London Collections Men showcase as it then was, on the map. Skip to the Fashion Awards this evening and it’s clear that anyone who wrote Green off as a one-hit catwalk theatrics wonder did so at their peril. As proved when the designer won the GQ Fashion Fund earlier this year, Green’s aesthetic might be one of haute-conceptualism, but his brand is grounded in reality - gauzy tops and neat jackets make up the core product that sell in their droves, away from the more hifalutin pieces. Taking his cue from the codes of uniform - workwear, school attire, even monastic robes - Green’s served to push the boundaries of London menswear and remind the press that so oft overlook the city why it’s such a talent treasure trove.   The editor of Italian Vogue has been honoured with the Swarovski award for Positive Change . Accompanied by the British Fashion Council's CEO, Caroline Rush, and Nadja Swarovski the trio mark a glamorous start to the ceremony that's been rebranded this year.  The intention is to turn the 2016 Awards - which are sponsored by Swarovski - into an international showcase, with ambitions to rival the starry, Anna Wintour-run annual Met Gala in aid of the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute in New York.  As such, they have worked hard to attract A-list heavyweights to the event, including Bella and Gigi Hadid, the supermodel sisters who are up against each other in the Model of the Year category.  But while the supermodel pair might have dominated the news agenda thus far, they were but twinkles in their parents' eyes when the very first British Fashion Awards took place in 1989. Naturally, it was a glamorous affair from the off. Princess Diana was guest of honour, presenting Hardy Amies with the British Fashion Council's Hall of Fame award. The evening saw the debut of what became known as Diana's 'Elvis' outfit- a white strapless dress which came with a matching bolero jacket with a collar resembling the raised styles once made famous by Presley himself. It was created by Catherine Walker, the British designer who Diana relied upon from as early as 1981 for appropriate yet glamorous looks for her public engagements. With her slicked-back hair, Diana was working the on the-cusp-of-the-90s looks to perfection. There were just 7 awards presented at that first ceremony, versus the 14 we're expecting tonight. Some things never change though; Naomi Campbell was pictured smiling with designer Rifat Ozbek and posing in a Lakers cap at those first awards.  The Duchess of Cambridge has become remarkably adept at bringing a mixture of labels to her royal wardrobe; one week it's a £22 pair of trousers from Gap, the next it's a bespoke designer piece. It's a strategy which is masterful in its execution, one moment giving an impression of complete accessibility, the next adding a soupçon of aspiration (think the L.K Bennett dresses she has favoured this summer) and then introducing a look into the mix which serves as a reminder of The Duchess's dazzlingly glamorous royal credentials. For her first day of engagements on this trip to Canada, The Duchess was emphasising the I'll-be Queen-one-day factor in a bespoke dress by her favourite design house, Alexander McQueen. Landing in a rather rainy Vancouver, Kate immediately drew comments of approval from Twitter-watchers, commending her for an experimental start to the tour.  The Duchess's chosen dress comes from a look in Alexander McQueen's Resort 2017 collection. Designer Sarah Burton has discussed the collection's romantic references, saying she was inspired by the intricately beautiful floral patterns seen painted on gypsy caravans and canal barges in the British countryside. The dress, which won't be available to buy until later this year, comes in a mini length with dramatic voluminous layered sleeves and includes a delicate handpainted floral motif.  Needless to say, the version worn by The Duchess today had been somewhat altered; the sleeves took on the guise of a shirt with their slim fit and white cuffs meanwhile the skirt had been lengthened but retained the tiered, gypsy-influenced silhouette. Kate also kept the original buttoned-up feel with a mandarin collar fastened tightly around her neck.  The Duchess of Cambridge is widely expected to nod to local, Canadian designers at some point during her eight-day trip, but today's look was all about showcasing the best of British design. There was, however, a respectful nod to her hosts with the red and white colour palette of the design echoing Canada's national colours.  Alexander McQueen is the British fashion label most closely associated with The Duchess of Cambridge. Creative director Sarah Burton, appointed following the death of Alexander McQueen in 2010, was chosen to design both the gowns worn by The Duchess on the day of her wedding to Prince William, bringing the exquisite skill for which McQueen is known to unprecedented attention on the world stage. Ever since, The Duchess has leaned on Burton, who has recently given birth to a third daughter, to create bespoke pieces for important occassions, such as the christenings of George and Charlotte. Kate is also a fan of ready-to-wear McQueen pieces; at this year's Wimbledon final, she wore an unusually decorative 'Obsessions' dress by the label, in a print depicting an array of shells, charms and jewels. Instead of her beloved nude court shoes- always a chic but ultimately safe choice- The Duchess picked out the red hues of the dress with a co-ordinating £640 Miu Miu clutch bag and Russell and Bromley's £165 Pinpoint court shoes. During today's visit, William and Kate will visit Sheway, a charity helping young mothers, the Immigrant Services Society where they will have the chance to speak with people who have moved to British Columbia before finishing the day by meeting some young Canadians of a similar age to them and then finally, calling in on a coastguard station. One thing's for sure; that Alexander McQueen dress will lend a suitably regal and glamorous presence to proceedings.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Remarkably for an industry which thrives on the shock of the new, progress in fashion often feels - to paraphrase a catchy Eighties hit by Paula Abdul - like taking two steps forward and three steps back. The 29 year old, size 18 model Ashley Graham features on two British magazine covers this month: Cosmopolitan and Vogue, which in theory should be a goal scored for those who would rather see a variety of female shapes sell them clothing. But, Vogue's, editor-in-chief Alexandra Shulman has divulged that many designers weren’t just reticent about dressing the (non sample size) model, they point blank refused. Only the American label Coach, led by British designer Stuart Vevers, accommodated the magazine by producing special pieces which she could wear. In the rest of the shoot she wears a mixture of vintage, Isabel Marant, Giorgio Armani, Jil Sander, J Brand, Rodarte, Burberry and Rag and Bone. Ashley Graham wearing a Coach jacket on the cover of British Vogue's January edition.  Whilst the visibility of different sized models is - largely thanks to social media (Ashley Graham has 2.7million Instagram followers) - gaining pace, as much as these models insist that they are now a bona fide part of the fashion industry, the truth is that mainstream designer brands do not touch them. There are designers who feature bigger models in their shows  - in New York this season, Tome and Sophie Theallat both cast ‘plus’ models - but as encouraging as this is, these are hardly household names. Ashley Graham wearing a vintage jumpsuit in British Vogue. Typically, when curvier models are used in fashion magazines, their shape is fetishised. One particularly encouraging aspect of Graham’s Vogue shoot was that she was dressed in boiler suits and trousers - this wasn’t the tits and arse approach that most take. In contrast, this is exactly the tack that Cosmopolitan took with their Graham shoot - which features her on the cover in a black bodysuit. Yes, she has a lingerie line to promote, but wouldn’t it be more encouraging for her to be used as any other model? Say, wearing some clothes? If in shooting a bigger model an editor is wanting to appeal to a wider demographic of readers wouldn’t it be more useful to show them wearing outfits that women in real life would wear? The hysterical backslapping that occurs in magazines when using a bigger model is patronising, it must never pass without comment: readers are going to know that this model is larger, because we’re going to show as much of her flesh as possible! How progressive.   Ashley Graham wearing a bodysuit by Ashley Stewart on the cover of Cosmopolitan's January issue. Diversity in fashion might be something consumers are now calling for, but for the most part the industry is as sizeist as it ever was - and even a Vogue cover shoot isn’t going to change that. Many designers are pathetically precious about who they would ideally have in their clothes. In the same way that they don’t want to lend to whom they consider to be unsavoury celebrities, nor do they want their clothes sullied by larger sized women. When interviewing some, they’ve rolled their eyes and mock-shuddered when we’ve discussed the merits and pitfalls of spotting real women on the street in their creations. One story doing the rounds at fashion week was in regards to the horrified designer - who has dressed the Duchess of Cambridge - recoiling in disbelief when one fashion editor had the audacity to order a piece from his collection in a size 14. But sizeism, or lack of thought regarding different sized women daring to show an interest in buying new clothes extends beyond pretentious designers, stuck up in their ivory towers of emaciated perfection. Attempting to shop in any designer boutique - or even some high street ones - when one is more than a size 12 can feel like an uphill struggle. Online, the bigger sizes generally sell out first, more frustrating however is when some brands don’t even deign to create pieces in larger sizes than a 12.   In up market stores most display a single (smallest) size of any designs, which means that in order to try anything different to the shop floor stock, one has to wait for a shop assistant to fetch it from the stockroom. At the sixth request for a different size  - especially when they have come back empty handed as fewer pieces are bought in larger sizes - it becomes a little dull. Recently, whilst browsing in a posh Knightsbridge boutique, I asked for a dress in a 14 - the one on display was a size 8. I also explained to the sales assistant that I am pregnant (the dress was oversize), so would be after the biggest size possible. She returned about ten minutes later to inform me that the store had only bought the dress in  a size 8 but perhaps I'd like to try it on anyway? What to do in the face of such moronic service, but roll one’s eyes and walk out. Is anyone catering to the median demographic in this country of the 5’3, size 16 woman? Democratically, the high street, and particularly online retailers have a far more acute focus on the reality of women’s dressing requirements - shrewd considering the plus size market is predicted to be valued at £7.9billion. Evans, Dorothy Perkins, H&M, ASOS Curve, Mango, Boohoo.com, Missguided.com, Phase Eight, New Look, Forever 21 and Simply Be all sell trend-led fashion for women over a size 16 (as well as for petite sizes, too). What if you want to drop some serious cash, and buy into better made, better cut, clothes created to last? Your options are still frustratingly slim. Ridiculously, while the luxury fashion market falters, it still steadfastly refuses to acknowledge that by servicing all women who might like to wear their clothes they could perhaps up their declining sales. For all the lip service paid to diversity in fashion, and the so-called opening up of a snobbish, closed industry by the influx of social media, out there on the shop floor nothing has changed.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Throughout the summer, Rio has drawn all eyes. The Olympics brought with them the dazzling Usain Bolt, the awe-inspiring Simone Biles, and Nick Skelton, aged 58, triumphing over a broken neck to bring yet another gold home for Team GB. But for those of us who were there,  it felt as if the Games could have been in Vladivostok or Timbuktu or on the moon. Competitors and spectators were bussed from stadium to track, never seeing the extraordinary beauty and wildness of the city, aware only of the traffic that snarled roads into a hooting, beeping cacophony. Laura Trott, our most garlanded woman Olympian, told me she hadn’t been outside the Olympic Village. She never got so much as a sniff of Ipanema beach. Earlier in the summer, however, another circus had come rolling in, this time a high-fashion one: Louis Vuitton, one of the world’s most valuable luxury brands, chose the Brazilian party town for its cruise collection. The entwined VL on a buckle or suitcase are a globally recognised symbol of wealth and status – as familiar as the five linked rings of the Olympics. Yet, when Vuitton touched down, in all the pomp of its $10 billion annual revenues, the aim was not to impose the French maison on Rio. Rather it was all about exploring the culture, life and colour of this most vibrant city. ‘It’s exciting to be abroad with a collection,’ Nicolas Ghesquière, the creative director of the brand, told me in the cream and marble glamour of his suite at the Copacabana Palace Hotel. ‘To travel with a collection and do something exotic is a very Louis Vuitton idea. The image of the house is all about the luxury of travel, so what could be more symbolic?’  Indeed, Louis Vuitton’s first innovation, in 1854, was a rectangular trunk that could be stored easily. Just the thing to take on a trip to South America. And it’s true that the 45-year-old Ghesquière himself, in clumpy boots and black knee-length shorts, looked ready to thwack his way through a rainforest, machete in hand. There was something a little piratical about his black beard and his slim physique, honed by years of horse riding and fencing. Cruise or resort collections are an increasingly important part of the international fashion calendar. Most people are familiar with  the idea of spring/summer or autumn/winter shows in the world’s fashion capitals of New York, London, Milan and Paris, during which designers display their clothes in a 10-minute runway show in March or September, six months before they appear in store. But the cruise show is a completely different beast. ‘I don’t know if the people who buy fashion really have an idea of what cruise is,’ admitted Ghesquière. ‘It’s the creator’s opportunity to mix things up. We’ve got the exoticism of clothes for the privileged traveller [these arrive in shops in the cold months, ready to be snapped up by anyone who prefers to escape to the heat], but it’s the collection that stays in store the longest, so it has to be right for every season. Showing in Paris is amazing, but it’s very challenging and there’s all this competition. Here, it’s challenging, too, but all you need is one theme and you can go anywhere in the world.’  Brazil was, in fact, an inspired choice. When design houses do a cruise show they have days in which to show off their inspirations and their power to a captive audience of celebrities, photographers, writers and bloggers. Vuitton took its guests helicoptering over the improbable curves of the Sugarloaf Mountain, whose cable car’s moment of glory was James Bond and Jaws’ 1970s fight scene in Moonraker. The brand closed off Corcovado mountain, so that invited guests could post Instagram snaps with the huge art deco statue of Christ the Redeemer without having to fight through mobs of crazed tourists brandishing selfie sticks. Cocktails one evening were enlivened by Alessandra Ambrosio, the local supermodel, cavorting (it’s the only appropriate word) in a very skimpy bikini at the shallow end of a rooftop pool, with a photographer wading thigh-deep in combat pants to capture her best angle. But the most impressive element of Vuitton’s brief, though passionate, fling with Rio was its choice of the Niteroi Contemporary Art Museum as the location for the catwalk show, which was the highlight of all the fun and games.  ‘It all happened because of the Niteroi Museum,’ recalled Ghesquière. This 1996 circular flying saucer of a building was designed by Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer and is perched on a rocky outcrop outside the city. It is perfect for a fashion show because it has got a ready-made runway: a red-painted concrete walkway that spools out of the opening and loops its way down to the ground. It’s a building that looks like it’s going places, especially since Michael Burke, CEO of Louis Vuitton, authorised a complete restoration of the museum in time for the crucial evening. No hint of things not being ready on time here… luxury brands are much better organised than Olympic committees. Burke and Ghesquière share a love of architecture – the last cruise show, in Palm Springs, was at Bob Hope’s old house, which, designed by John Lautner, was eerily similar in its circular shape and dramatic setting. ‘I was keen to carry on this exploration of architecture,’ said Ghesquière. ‘Buildings are symbolic and Niteroi represents Brazil in the world.’ ‘Nicolas and I are obsessed with this building, and we’ve taken a year to restore it,’ Burke told me, standing on that red aerial runway after the show, while the cheers of a huge crowd of Brazilians, desperate to catch a glimpse of local celebrities and international stars, wafted on the warm night breeze. ‘It has a positivity and an optimism. It’s like it is telling us the world could be a much better place.’ And so, in truth, could Rio. ‘Yes,’ he admits. ‘It’s a terrible time here in terms of politics and economics. It’s a democracy, so it’s messy. But I’ve been coming for 25 years and I love its colour, the people, the positive mentality in the face of adversity.’ Was Zika a factor in their calculations, I wondered. ‘Zika?’ he laughed. ‘Have you seen a problem? I haven’t. It’s geographical naivety to think it’s an issue here.’ As for the show itself, it was as riotous and exciting as the setting. There were zips and studs, ruffles and dramatic cut-outs. There was a nod to football – the national obsession – in the prints, and bags that looked like beatboxes celebrated the music of Copacabana Beach. There was turquoise and fuchsia, emerald, hot orange and yellow. It was at once sexy, sporty and futuristic. ‘I was inspired by two things in opposition,’ said Ghesquière. ‘Rio is tropical and exotic, yet very urban. Nature is explosive here but you’ve also got this amazing architecture. It’s a beautiful chaos. And here I am, a Frenchman, presenting an idea of French luxury. It’s a great contrast. France is cold, Brazil is hot, and I’m trying to match the coolness and heat, and show them my point of view.’ For a venerable and world-famous name in leather goods, Louis Vuitton is quite new to fashion. ‘Marc [Jacobs] developed the fashion,’ agreed Ghesquière, ‘and was the founder of our prêt-à-porter, so it’s recent. Vuitton has a beautiful history and a wonderful archive but we’re in a new phase.’ Central to Ghesquière’s influence on the label are the women he has brought on board. They range from Catherine Deneuve, who was in Rio to see the cruise show, to Michelle Williams. How does he choose them? It is, he says, ‘a mutual recognition. They choose me and I choose them to be on Team Vuitton. They want to wear the clothes, I want them to be part of my close circle that includes Charlotte Gainsbourg, Jennifer Connelly, Michelle, Selena Gomez. She reflects this generation: she’s full of energy and very popular. I make them a lot of special clothes. For Alicia [Vikander], I’ve made maybe 17 dresses for ceremonies. But you take her to the Oscars and she wins, and it’s magnificent timing.’  With Gomez and Jaden Smith, Will Smith’s digital-savvy son, on board, Ghesquière is clearly courting a Millennial customer: ‘You have to be fresh,’ he agreed. ‘But fast fashion is dangerous. Some things take time to make, but people see images of pieces they want and don’t understand why it takes so long to get them. They are confused by the immediacy of desire and the wait. It’s complicated. But if you have a real desire for something, you can wait.’ Ghesquière himself always had a passion for design. The son of a golf-course owner, he decided he wanted to work in fashion aged 12. ‘Everyone understood, though they’re not a fashion family at all,’ he told me. ‘But French TV talked a lot about fashion and I’d watch  Jean Paul Gaultier, and I was fascinated by how fashion works with other elements of culture.’ His first big role was with Balenciaga, which, he said, ‘was a beautiful period – but to keep it a beautiful period I had to leave’. His tenure ended messily, with a lawsuit, as such roles sometimes do. Then Bernard Arnault, chairman and CEO of LVMH, which owns Louis Vuitton, came calling.  ‘It all happened very fast,’ he told me. We spoke at a time when it seemed no creative director could stomach the relentless digital demands of the job, with label after label resorting to in-house designers as big names stepped out of the limelight. Not Ghesquière: ‘I am less and less private,’ he said. ‘I’ve learnt to share a bit more and give a bit more. The position with Louis Vuitton has taught me that things are very friendly online. No one thought fashion would be so huge. Even if all they can do is follow you on Instagram, everyone still wants a part of it. And this is a point in my life when I’m happy to share things. It isn’t forced. There’s a lot of pressure, but I wanted it. Sometimes I wonder if I am a bit lost, then I think, “No, it’s OK.”’ So how does he relax? ‘By working. Being a creator is a lifestyle, a vortex; you’re always absorbing, then you re-express it with fashion…’ and start dreaming about where to hold the next cruise show.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Model Leomie Anderson has throughout her career used her position within the fashion industry to speak candidly about issues facing young women. Anderson, who has walked for the likes of Victoria's Secret and Moschino, has spoken out about everything from how black models are unfairly treated backstage at fashion week to the pressure on young girls to send sexual images to men. And so it is fitting that she has created her own fashion line, which combines her sporty street style with her commitment to empowering women. Today Leomie Anderson is launching her brand Lapp, which includes a collection of cool pieces with empowering feminist messages, as well as a blog where she will publish stories from women from all backgrounds. "With Lapp I will create clothing pieces which have a message that relate back to women's issues," Leomie tells The Telegraph. "The first collection is called the 'consent collection' which is inspired by my blog post about peer pressure for young girls and there are three t-shirts with phrases women can say to say no in situations." The brand is launching with a capsule collection of three vintage-style American ringer tees. "The t-shirts are colourful and cute and fashionable. I worked hard to make them so that when you look at them you won't think 'oh my god this is a serious message, I could only wear this to a feminist ball'" explains Anderson. "I want it to be a fashion statement too because I have always used fashion as a way to express myself and make a statement - whether a serious one or to show my personality. I want people to want to wear it, rather than feel like they should wear it because of the message." As for the slogans, Anderson reveals: "One of them says 'LOL Nah', one of them says 'error.jpg' which is for young girls to do with sending naked pictures and the other one says 'you tried.' "I want to see women and girls hash-tagging the brand, and see them reclaiming 'no' by wearing a t-shirt and making it cool to say no. There are so many negative labels for women who choose to say no, so I wanted to make something that is positive." The brand Lapp isn't just about consent, as the next collection, which the model is currently designing, will focus on body ideals.  Fashion can be sneered at, but Anderson has experienced first-hand how it is an industry which can play a significant part of conversations. "Fashion blends in with art and politics and is reflective of the time, and I have built a name for myself in fashion, so why not use what I have built to do something positive?" says Anderson.  On the Lapp blog readers will have the opportunity to contribute their own stories and pieces. "So many girls have something to say but think there is no point saying it as think 'I don't have a following, and will probably only get 10 readers'. But that's not an excuse for you to not say what you want to say, so I am using my following as a platform for these women. People know me for speaking out on issues, so I felt like I had a responsibility," she explains. Models have traditionally been viewed as 'blank canvases,' but young models are increasingly seeing being a role model as part of their job. "I don't think a lot of models are doing enough with their reach," Anderson adds. "Some think putting hashtag 'free the nipple' is enough to be a voice for women, and I don't think it's enough. I don't think every celebrity should support a cause, but as models we go through so much as young girls and know what it's like to be alone in a different country, and we know what it's like to need to speak to someone. We have such young girls that follow us, we have a duty to do something positive for them."    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Until recently, Isabella Rossellini only wore black. “I belong to that New York fashion generation of the 80s and 90s when we were always wearing black. It’s so easy to wear,” she laughs over the phone from L.A. But then the legendary actress and model met Sander Lak, the designer behind the label Sies Marjan which is shaking up the NY fashion scene with its vibrant colour palettes and modern cuts. “When I saw Sander’s collections, there were exactly the colours for someone used to wearing a lot of black. There is a real statement of joyfulness and wanting colour back,” she observes. “Now, I put an incredibly bright pink sweater with black pants.” After being introduced to 65 year-old Rossellini through a friend, Lak was- unsurprisingly- charmed so decided to ask her to star in his autumn/ winter 2017 advertising campaign which was to be photographed by Bruce Weber. “The first person I kept thinking of was Isabella Rossellini. Bruce Weber and Isabella have such an amazing history together and it was my dream to revive that,” says Lak of the duo, who created pared-back yet spirited photographs together during the 80s and 90s. Sies Marjan FW17 Campaign by Bruce Weber from Sies Marjan on Vimeo. The result- seen for the first time today- is a refreshingly happy set of images, akin to a modern spin on Benetton’s 90s ads.  Rossellini, whose gamine beauty is as radiant as ever, stars alongside a brilliantly varied cast of faces which includes her son Roberto, Russian supermodel Sasha Pivovarova and her five year-old daughter Mia, model Lexi Boling and her boyfriend Ben Allen. Their delicious combinations of fuschia, peppermint and Cadbury purple are enough to persuade anyone wedded to their black staples to experiment with a blast of colour. Rossellini says that it was an “instant yes” when she was asked to do the campaign. The Sies Marjan images offer an alternative interpretation of the diversity which has, to varying extents, been embraced by the industry of late. “It has been the quest for many people in fashion, how to include everybody?” she says. “Sometimes it can be seen as a political statement which is a bit of a turn-off. But Bruce’s artistry and Sander’s joyfulness in fashion and colour made the campaign and photos feel right; they’re joyful, glamorous and attractive.” “The pleasure of working with Sander is that he is defining himself right now as a young person,” Rossellini, who is the daughter of director Roberto Rossellini and actress Ingrid Bergman, enthuses. “He understands the definition of male and female is blurred. Age? He doesn’t care. And race, he doesn’t even see it.” It is rather a different proposition to her work with Lancome. Famously, Rossellini became the highest paid model in the world when she was signed to the beauty giant in 1982 but was rather unceremoniously fired in 1996 because she was feared to be too old to be able to sell customers the beauty dream. When she was rehired last year, it was the most potent signal yet that big brands understood customers wanted to see positive and inspirational examples of women who were aging, yes, but looking good with it. “They haven’t put me in an advertisement campaign but I think the will is there,” Rossellini says of her work with Lancome now, acknowledging that a company steeped in heritage cannot be quite so nimble as the start-up set-up enjoyed by Lak. “There must be a reason but I’m not an executive, I don’t see the market research. There is a real discussion about it but there is also a tradition.” For Lak, the Sies Marjan campaign- which includes pieces from his debut menswear capsule collection, set to hit Matchesfashion.com in November- had a purposefully relaxed feel. “Fashion is a serious business and a lot of the time it can get quite heavy, especially these days, but I never forget the joy that it brings to me and the people around me,” he says. “The campaign is a bit of this celebration of the joy that fashion can be, and should be! Let’s not forget it's just clothes, and I see that as a beautiful thing, it's the reason why I do what I do, the clothes!” The inclusion of so many models of different ages and looks is worn lightly and naturally. “It's not so much a consideration as it is a reality of the world. Our customers are female, male, young, old, small, big, every color skin tone existing and of so many nationalities - it would be a shame to not find a way to represent that.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
