 I want the magazine to be a love letter to Arabia,” asserts the newly appointed editor-in-chief of Vogue Arabia, Deena Aljuhani Abdulaziz. “I want to give the reader aspirational images, fashion criticism, beauty, wellbeing and lifestyle. The world is saturated with information and publishing is weaker because of that but what’s missing is the dream. Even advertising campaigns used to be so well done, I would cut and pin them. There needs to be distinction. I want the glamour back!” Abdulaziz, seated in the restaurant at The Mark Hotel on the upper east side of Manhattan and sipping an iced black coffee, is the picture of edgy glamour. The 41-year-old mother of three wears her hair in an Eighties New Wave style undercut at the sides, and the multiple piercings in her ears are pinned with small glittering studs by Sophie Bille Brahe and Monique Péan. She is striking with her dark almond eyes, her aquiline nose and tapered red fingernails. Back in her native Saudi she favours “suitable clothing worn in a super-stylish way”, (the modesty-protecting abaya and hijab are law for women in public), but outside Saudi she goes for architectural pieces with a clean, distinctive silhouette and flattering heels by Aquazzura and Manolo Blahnik. Today she’s wearing a baby blue piqué trapeze-line dress with a crochet flounce by Ukrainian designer Vika Gazinskaya.     The girlish innocence of the dress is in sharp contrast to her voice which swerves between gravelly, worldly-wise New Yorker and theatrical old-school fashion maven. She is colourful, exclamatory and caveats her anecdotes with lines like, “I’ve told this story so many times, I hope I’m not going to bore you…” Yet there is nothing dull about Abdulaziz, who married into the Saudi Royal Family (to Sultan bin Fahad bin Nasser in 1998), grew up in Riyadh on a diet of Western fashion magazines, MTV and a mountain of fashion books and who, for the past 10 years, has been working in luxury retail as the co-founder and buyer of a fashion concept store in Riyadh called D’NA.  Right now, Abdulaziz is assembling her team and meeting with power players in the industry before she takes her annual family summer vacation in America. “The Arab world has 250 million women. There are certain things that unify the Arab experience and there are differences throughout the region but I know those, and there are certain parameters that make sense culturally. Nudity is offensive as is religious symbolism. It’s common sense really.” Fear of flying, the wrong underwear, a rogue documentary maker and John Kerry all play a role in the frenetic life of Alexandra Shulman, editor of British Vogue. As she celebrates the style bibles 100th anniversary, here is an extract from her private diary of a momentous year at the magazine.
 _By Alexandra Shulman, Friday 14 October 2016_
**September 1, 2015**
Three nights ago, in a restaurant by the sea, just off a coastal road in Puglia, some children at the long family tables next to ours were playing with their pencil cases, lining up the coloured felt tips in order. Today, back in London, it is like the first day of term, and I wish I had a new box of coloured pens that I could bring into work with me, shiny and neat and full of promise. Though of what, I couldnt say.
September 1 was my fathers birthday. If he were still alive, he would be 102 today. Instead his ashes were shot into the sky 11 years ago in a rocket my brother, Jason, made from Evening Standards, the newspaper where my father \([Milton Shulman](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1462636/Milton\-Shulman.html)\) worked for more than 40 years. He loved being a journalist, having a soapbox and a public voice, whether that be theatre criticism or politics or anything, really just so long as he was heard. I dont feel that way about editing Vogue. Its Vogues voice, not mine.
Although I do, of course, have a choice in what that voice says. After three weeks on holiday, I feel disengaged and not sure whether I have any\-thing to say on any subject relevant to the magazine. It will take a few days to reimmerse. I put on a striped shirt from Zara that I bought before the holiday. Its refreshing to wear something new ammunition for the day ahead. A shirt feels as if it has a clarity of purpose, which will be helpful.
 Even so, its strange: a costume rather than the holiday clothes of the past days. Before leaving for the office, I go to Gails bakery down the road and buy croissants and a Chelsea bun for my son, Sam, whose flight home from New York is scheduled to arrive this morning. Hes been away for nine weeks. Im so excited to see him. Tonight Ill roast a chicken for us. I wont relax until I get the text saying hes landed.
**September 7**
Ive returned to work with five big projects to achieve: a centenary issue, [a big party to celebrate our 100 years](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/events/vogue\-100\-best\-dressed\-kim\-kardashians\-opts\-for\-sheer\-dress\-for/), the 2016 Vogue Festival, the filming of a BBC Two documentary about the magazine, and the successful installation of an exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery. When I consider them all, I want to go back on holiday.
**September 14**
The garden at home never looks lovelier than when Im about to get on a plane. Yesterday morning the figs had finally ripened enough to eat, and the sun was shining on the [new autumn colours](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/style/shopping\-on\-mount\-street/autumn\-fashion\-trends\-you\-need\-to\-know/) that are peeping through all the dusty green.
  As I left for Heathrow I felt sick, and waiting for the flight to New York I was feeling so bad that I nearly cancelled the trip. Ive hated flying since I was 19, and the degree of my terror waxes and wanes. Once weve landed, Im excited to look out of the window at the tarmac. If you believe youre bound not to survive a flight, arriving intact is hugely pleasing. [Diane von Furstenberg](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/new\-york\-fashion\-week/diane\-von\-furstenberg\-gets\-modernised\-jonathan\-saunders\-on\-raisi/) was my first show \(at New York fashion week\) and I went there straight from the airport.
  At the end, in true showman style, she appeared, fiery\-maned and running down the catwalk with her still\-incredible legs on display, shaking hands and locking eyes with the audience, reminding me of Bill Clinton. New York collections are often a commercial version of what Europe provides for the previous season. Its what America does so well: the designers turn someone elses idea into something that makes money.
 > "Ive made a massive error here and this film is simply going to be incredibly trashy and simplistic"
 Even on the first day, I could see the huge [Cline](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/cline\-introduces\-us\-to\-faye\-wong\-chinese\-pop\-sensation\-\-and\-your/) influence in the longer lengths, the silhouette, the heavy, clumpy shoes that everyone loves. When Phoebe Philo arrived at Cline in 2008, she seemed to tap straight into a style vein that so many women relate to. Unsurprisingly, the American designers hate the notion of copycatting, even more than their stereotype as successful sportswear designers.
However, commercially theyve had the last word, and over the past 40 years, the American market has been the primary powerhouse of the industry. Its changing now, though: China and other Far Eastern countries are becoming the leading players.
Nowhere is it clearer that we are in the last days of the American empire than in the fashion industry. Fabrics and designs are being tailored to the requirements of the Eastern market. The big brands are spending fortunes expanding there, and although many Middle Eastern women are hidden behind burkas, their wardrobes contain some of the most ravishing Western fashion.
  
 
 **September 19**
Last night was the London Fashion Week party I hosted with the \[US\] ambassador and his wife, Matthew and Brooke Barzun. It was heavenly, and I went to bed happy. I arrived at the neo\-Palladian Winfield House in Regents Park 15 minutes before kick\-off, to be prevented from entering by the massive security detail outside the gates, heightened because of John Kerrys stay.
But eventually I was led past the childrens skateboard slope the Barzuns had erected outside the front door, and into the house. Victoria Beckham arrived to the usual accompaniment of flashbulbs, but in terms of celeb power she was upstaged a few minutes later by John Kerry.
I imagine that he could have slipped in through a back door and headed to bed, or at least for a private drink upstairs, but he gamely confronted a heaving room of partying guests. Victoria was introduced to him almost immediately, and stayed talking to him for so long that I thought he might never meet anyone else, but he hung out at the party for well over the half\-hour I had been told he might be there.
  Hes so tall that eye contact is almost impossible if youre my height, and in a noisy room, ear contact is not that easy either. The social temperature of the room soared when news of his being here spread; he was the real stardust that transformed the party.
Later, I found Victoria on the terrace with her shoes kicked off. I asked her what she had talked to Kerry about. He said hed seen me at the UN, she answered, referring to a speech she had delivered earlier in the year, and he said, We gotta talk about Syria. Her look showed she found that suggestion as surprising as I did.
**November 10**
At dinner last night David \(Jenkins, Shulmans partner\) asked whether I knew that he liked endives. Endives? Yes, endives. You had them in the salad the other night. Are there any in this one? He poked around fruitlessly at the endive\-free plate. It reminded me of the newly married butler, Carson, finding fault with his poor wifes cooking at their marital dining table in Downton Abbey.
 Breakfast yesterday with Nicholas Coleridge, who runs the UK company. We both ordered mashed avocado with chilli flakes and lime, and poached eggs no toast. What have we come to? Are we simply fashion\-lifestyle victims?
Nicholas had a scribbled list of issues to talk to me about, which included the idea of an African Vogue supplement, and who I was planning to invite to the centenary dinner. George Osborne? Ed Vaizey? I answered that I was planning to ask Jeremy Corbyn, and Id see if Emily Sheffield, m[y deputy editor](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/what\-do\-you\-wear\-to\-a\-job\-interview\-at\-vogue\-four\-editors\-share/), could exert some influence on her brother\-in\-law, David Cameron. Theres only room for 300 guests and, given the number of big beasts in fashion, its going to be tricky to get the right balance for the guest list.
**January 3, 2016**
After 10 days break, I woke up this morning and went to the farmers market in the pouring rain. I stewed some apples with cinnamon, put on a stock to simmer, and wondered whether it would be possible to have a life of just reading all the books Ive now got piled up on the big table in the bedroom, and do very little work. I could run every day, make vegetable soups, let my hair go grey and And then what? Would I be content? David, who had just woken up, said that thousands of years of philosophers have pondered this same question.
**January 30**
Im 37,000ft above the ground and travelling at 560 miles per hour, or so it says on the map in front of me on this flight to Milan. Im also feeling thoroughly queasy, which is partly my flying anxiety and partly my total stupidity in waking up with a hangover from dinner last night.
David and I went to my friend Flora Frasers, and I was so gripped by the conversation between fellow guests Charles Saatchi and former Lib Dem cabinet minister [Chris Huhne](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/uknews/crime/11386970/Disgraced\-former\-cabinet\-minister\-Chris\-Huhne\-returns\-to\-Parliament.html) that I drank way too much wine. Charles, whether genuinely or simply to be controversial, described both Putin and Trump as magnificent, in his flat London accent.
 > "Victoria Beckham arrived to the usual accompaniment of flashbulbs, but she was upstaged by John Kerry"
 Chris is a passionate Europhile, and is looking extremely well in the aftermath of his jail experience. He didnt appear remotely rattled and was keen to hammer home his pro\-Europe stance. We left at the same time as Charles and his new girlfriend, Trinny Woodall.
Just before he left, as we stood in the hallway, he grabbed me and pulled me under one of the overhead spotlights and peered behind my ears. You havent changed, he said, explaining that he was checking to see whether Id had work done. Weird, undoubtedly.
  **February 4**
I must buy some new clothes. I have weeks of events and fashion shows coming up and nothing to wear. Clearly nothing is a relative term as I have two cupboards full of clothes, but nothing I have is new, and Im meant to look like somebody who has new clothes.
**February 17**
Last week ended well, so this week Im certain that something difficult will happen as a reproach to me for feeling too relaxed. Organising all the different strands of [the Centenary](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/understated\-glamour\-the\-duchess\-of\-cambridges\-first\-vogue\-cover/) is emotionally exhausting. One thing goes well; another veers into difficulties. Mario Testinos Decades shoot arrives and is luscious. But we still have the final Tim Walker portraits to nail: Tracey Emin has twice cancelled even as he arrived at her house.
 > "I wondered whether it would be possible to have a life of just reading all the books Ive now got piled up on the big table in the bedroom, and do very little work"
 Tim is getting a bit fed up. David Beckhams people want a number of different concepts to propose to David, if he is to agree to be included. I know that Tim wants to shoot him on a football pitch, kicking a crown into the air, which would be wonderful. But I have a feeling David might not think so. My fashion director, Lucinda \([Chambers](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/style\-lessons\-to\-learn\-from\-vogues\-lucinda\-chambers\-whatever\-you/)\), walks into my office saying she had a great meeting with \([David](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/david\-bailey\-jack\-nicholson\-turned\-me\-on\-to\-viagra\-very\-young/)\) Bailey about the [Ab Fab](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/events/everything\-we\-know\-about\-absolutely\-fabulous\-the\-movie/) shoot.
They havent worked together for many years, and I was worried about how they would get on. He told her he liked the energy of the unexpected and asked her why she hadnt had Botox. We have our monthly circulation meeting and start making plans for what we hope will be a high\-June centenary\-issue sale. The circulation team are projecting about a 25 per cent rise in year\-on\-year news\-stand sales, which is a big ask. I always feel maddened when I see someone reading Vogue at the hairdressers. Why dont you buy your own copy? I want to say, as I glower at them from my hideously unflattering gown.
The film crew have practically disappeared from the office and my staff keep asking me what I think [the documentary](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/people/alexa\-chung\-vogue\-documentary\-the\-future\-of\-fashion/) will be like. They are suspicious of director Richard Macers hapless approach and feel theyre being tricked in some way. I trust him about 70 per cent, but in the end I have no idea what will emerge. What on earth made me think it was a good idea to do it all those months back?
  **April 15**
Last night I took part in a discussion in the NPG theatre, focusing on changes in the fashion world since I first started my editorship. The audience asked good questions. One young woman had spotted that the [cover line](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/fashion/style/look\-back\-at\-100\-years\-of\-vogue\-covers\-as\-the\-magazine\-celebrate/) on my first issue, April 1992, had read, Do we still need feminism? and asked me if I considered myself a feminist.
I know I should unhesitatingly say yes. But, if Im honest, feminism is something I have rarely considered in a personal sense as opposed to the theoretical. If youve been brought up in a household of journalists, where it was always expected that as a woman you would work and be as successful as a man, it doesnt have the kind of emotional resonance it might for women coming from a different background or working in a different world.
But then, my father often shouted at me that no man would marry me if I didnt lose weight, or if I continued to argue so much. It didnt matter, though, since his love for me was never in doubt.
Last night, for the first time in years, I woke in the night and really wanted to see him walk through the door of the flat where we lived, put his trilby hat down on the hall table and come into the study where we ate dinner, with all the bustle and purpose and, it has to be said, self\-absorption he carried with him.
Id be able to smell the sweet scent of his skin that had always been the same from when we were tiny and crawled into our parents bed in the morning, and he would make a tent of the sheets with his legs in the air, which we could huddle under.
  
 
 **May 17**
I have my final dress fitting for the centenary dinner, and run into Erdems shop in South Audley Street with a variety of bras and knickers to try with it. The dress is hanging in the dressing room, a little like a child waiting to be collected from school.
I try it on with a pair of fine\-gauge Lycra cycling\-style knickers and a new bra, and it fits perfectly, though the shorts make me feel horrible. The lace embroidery now snakes across the sequins, and the boat neck is wide enough. Erdem stands back to survey his work and says, Its great. Really nipped and wicked, as he looks at me with those sloe eyes, adjusting the neckline to lie flat across my collarbone.
 > "I feel maddened when I see someone reading Vogue at the hairdressers. Why dont you buy your own copy? I want to say"
 He leaves the dressing room for a moment and I remove the shorts, which are clinging to my hips. I cant bear to wear such hideous underwear, even if it does give me a better shape. Standing in front of him in the shop we look at me again together in the mirror and he photographs me from the back and the front.
I ask him if he can see any difference from moments before, and he says perhaps the waistband is sitting a little better now the neckline is adjusted. I tell him about the removal of the shorts and hes polite enough to say that it looks better without, though I immediately feel Ive loaded him with too much information on the underpinnings of a 58\-year\-old woman.
   **June 11**
Yesterday Richard filmed me for the last time. He had wanted me to think of something that had some personal relevance, so I suggested we visit a huge old horse\-chestnut tree in Hyde Park, which I remembered playing under when I was very young.
After the filming he travelled with me in a car to the office and we joked a bit about this being the last time he would be filming me in a car. Then he leant forwards to fiddle with his camera and said, Theres something I want to tell you about the documentary. Kind of what were doing? Aha. Whats that? Well, you know I said I didnt want to use a voiceover narrator, that it was a bit tacky and overdone? Yes. I remember.
Id thought what a relief it would be not to have that clichd narrator. Well, weve had to change it a bit. And now, well, there is one. Or a kind of one. You know how usually theyre narrated by an actor? Well, we arent doing that. At this point I was becoming concerned by what he was about to say.
Um... Its going to be me. You know, not a huge amount of it. But its kind of about how a man who knows nothing about any of it goes into Vogue. My mind went into split screen one half thinking, Keep calm, theres nothing you can do about this and maybe itll be OK, the other thinking, Ive made a massive error here and this film is simply going to be incredibly trashy and simplistic. I couldnt believe Id allowed it to happen. Our one shot after so many years of refusing to let cameras into Vogue and Id blown it. This was now going to be a mocking Ladybird guide to the fashion world. What do you think? he asked.
  
 **June 23**
As I took my seat in a small room in Soho to view the documentary, the nerves took hold. Watching yourself in something like this is the most curious activity. I kept wondering what I was going to say, rather as if it hadnt been me sitting there, in far too many endless car shots staring crossly out of a rainy window.
Richard sitting behind me was still and serious as we watched his vision of Vogue for two hours. Through telling the story of a number of our shoots and the plans for the centenary issue, he certainly succeeded in getting across how much we all cared about what we did and, also, showed the hard work that goes into each issue.
Was it the film that I would love to have made about Vogue? No. I dont think it conveys how wide Vogue is nowadays, the influence it bears, the number of areas we are involved with, the fantastic journalism we include. Am I happy with how Im portrayed? Not particularly I seem very depressed through much of it, and prefer to think of myself as a funnier, lighter person than I seem on screen.
   I also dislike how I look most of the time, and cant understand why Im wearing the same blue top throughout most of the first programme. People will say, There she is, editor of Vogue and all. Youd think she could change her shirt.
Are there moments I really hate? Yes. The whole saga of the swapping of the Rihanna cover with the previous issue because of American Vogue jumping ahead of us is given a ludicrous weight, and when Richard says to camera that I rang threatening to pull the whole film if he talked to Anna Wintour about it, I felt misrepresented.
It was the one really devious thing he did. Of course, in the documentary when Anna is filmed she is hugely complimentary, which makes me look even sillier. I dont know what the rest of the office will think.
**[Inside Vogue: A Diary of My 100th Year](http://books.telegraph.co.uk/Product/Alexandra\-Shulman/Inside\-Vogue\-\-A\-Diary\-of\-My\-100th\-Year/19349052) \(Fig Tree, 16.99\), by Alexandra Shulman, out on October 26, will be available for 14.99 from the Telegraph Bookshop \(0844\-871 1514; [books.telegraph.co.uk](http://books.telegraph.co.uk/)\)**
    But for a publishing house whose empire was built around the empowerment of women, how complicated are those differences to reconcile? “In whatever market or region Vogue is published, the brand has to take into account the country’s cultural sensibilities,” says chairman and chief executive at Condé Nast International, Jonathan Newhouse. “We rely on an editor who understands these sensibilities and how to navigate them.” Abdulaziz is highly connected, international, fashion obsessed, opinionated, fun – and business savvy. When Newhouse started the search for that editor, she cleared the field. Yet, launching another Vogue (the 22nd edition) into an already mature glossy market (Elle Oriental, Marie Claire and Harper’s Bazaar Arabia are well established) and navigating the cultural diversity of the target MENA region (Middle East and North Africa) is a big remit. Condé Nast has partnered with Dubai-based media company Nervora, and Vogue Arabia will debut in digital form this autumn, taking over the existing Style.com/arabia site (in both Arabic and English) and roll out into print in March 2017. “There has been a growing demand for Vogue in the Arab world for a while, and now the time has come to make it a reality,” says Newhouse. The region’s style commentators are full of praise for the new girl. “Deena is a unique individual, not just here in the Middle East, but abroad as well. Her love for fashion stretches far beyond simply cloaking herself with the latest trends or collections. She has a vast in-depth knowledge of the history of fashion. For her, it’s not just about trends. She truly understands context, past and present, as well as across borders, which is one of the many reasons why she will be particularly great at the helm of Vogue Arabia. The Middle East has a new but burgeoning fashion scene, and it’s important for intellect to be injected into it from the get-go,” says Anum Bashir, a Qatari-based creative consultant and blogger behind desertmannequin.com. “Deena has pioneered this role for a very long time by not only wearing regional designers like Nathalie Trad and Reem Al Kanhal, but by also lending her expertise to them, connecting them to other industry influencers,” add Bashir.  In fashion, points of view matter. Back in the 1990s, Vogue editors were considered the elite – among a handful of arbiters of style.  Now, with the digital and blogging revolution the old hierarchy has been broken down with thousands of ‘new’ style pundits entering the field. To be heard and seen takes a big personality. Abdulaziz has been effectively ‘nurturing’ her fashion personality from an early age. She first discovered style through a copy of Tatler and later, as a teenager, got hooked on Vogue. “That changed my life – literally and figuratively. I realised there were other people who like what I liked. I brought back every single issue of US Vogue to Riyadh,” she says. A full-blown obsession quickly emerged. “I studied it cover to cover and even read the credits. What I was interested in most was the process – how did these people come up with these ideas? There was no Google. I would go to bookstores and use my ‘book’ allowance to purchase all the fashion and art books that were referenced in the magazine. Most of my friends did not necessarily want to talk about Nan Kempner or Christian Lacroix and I stood out as being different.” Crushes on Madonna (she used to buy fingerless lace gloves from Harrods) and the New Romantics followed. “Miss Selfridge was epic for me, as was Boy London and the King’s Road. I followed music via Smash Hits – Mel and Kim, Eighth Wonder, Depeche Mode – and I was crazy about Sade! I was going for something glamorous – not the imagery of a teenage magazine – and Vogue made you dream. That’s what I say to my daughter but she does not understand,” says Abdulaziz, throwing up her hands. Her style spurs were also sharpened via her mother. “She looks like Anouk Aimée and is the quintessential 1970s Yves Saint Laurent woman. We used to go to the couture shows, to Valentino and Chanel,” says Abdulaziz.  Her father, realising her degree in translation was not going to turn into a career, decided to fund the start up of her own boutique – quite a statement in a country where only 15 per cent of women are employed outside the home. She already had great contacts including Azzedine Alaïa (she is a regular client) and Sheikh Majed Al Sabah, the influential Kuwaiti retailer also known as “the Sheikh of Chic”, and they helped open brand doors. The D’NA boutique was conceived as a members’ only club, with statement pieces from designers including Alaïa, and then newcomers like Mary Katrantzou and Jason Wu. “Remember Voyage?” says Abdulaziz, referring to the much hyped boho store and label in London that exercised a members’ policy in the late 1990s. “That was the closest thing. The reason we did it is because Saudi is a conservative country. How can I do the interiors and play the movies I like without interference? That was the question. We did not do it to be snobs. In fact, it was free but the club idea created a buzz.” Abdulaziz’s theatrical leanings and instinctive taste made for an immersive type of luxury that customers wanted to be a part of.  “Deena is one of those truly inspiring women that you meet once in a while, who empowers you with her presence,” says Mary Katrantzou. “She has incredible innate style, and I always think of her as the archetypal woman of modern times when I’m designing.” In July, Abdulaziz resigned from D’NA and sold her shares to her partner. Being an editor-in-chief does not marry well with another day job. She needs to make Vogue Arabia work as a ‘brand’ and deliver beyond the page, into social media (her Instagram account, @deenathe1st, has 48k followers) and into real lives in the form of high-cachet events and awards, which will include the DDFC (Dubai Design and Fashion Council) fashion prize for emerging talent. A retail background differentiates Abdulaziz from her fellow Vogue editors. It’s given her a great grounding in guiding the aspirations of women. “At a fashion party you would be surprised how sophisticated it is, yet the Gulf is really big and people tend to generalise. In Saudi, women are either highly sophisticated or not at all – there is nothing in between. Saudis and Kuwaitis are the oldest in terms of exposure to fashion but I think the new generation has lost that elegance.” Abdulaziz skirts politely and niftily away from political issues (Saudi Arabia was ranked 134 out of 145 countries in the 2015 Global Gender Gap Index) and indeed the subject of the Saudi Royal Family. She tries not to use the ‘princess’ moniker. “There are 10,000 Saudi Royals so I’m not royal by birth and it’s not my place to represent the family. I was a commoner before I became a Highness. I want to be known for what I do, not a title,” she says. Her husband first spied her in the Food Hall at Harrods. “He found out who I was through mutual friends, and a courtship began. In Saudi, you have to have a chaperone if you are courting. If he dumps you, the whole city knows about it! “We knew it was right. It was my father who was hesitant – he did not want me to become a socialite or trophy wife. But when he met the Prince [who works in the Saudi Arabian ministry of culture], he knew it was a good match,” she says. She married in Alaïa couture and the couple have been together for 18 years. “He’s my best friend and biggest supporter. I am ‘a lot’ as a personality – I’m opinionated. For any man to be comfortable with that says something,” she laughs. One conjures up images from Sex and The City 2, which sees the gang jet off on holiday to Abu Dhabi to discover abaya-wearing women sporting catwalk ensembles beneath their modest layers. Abdulaziz is keen to demystify dress codes. “Abayas are long robe-like things – it looks strange to wear a short dress with that. What works well is palazzo pants or a long dress. Our erogenous zones are also different to what people think – we are not are not afraid of wearing slit skirts or open backs. We do dress for other women and when there are events with men present, of course you will wear something more conservative. It’s about your comfort level and context,” says. “There are just some things you do and don’t do, in the same way that you would wear tights to Buckingham Palace.” The personal luxury goods market in MENA is estimated at $9billion dollars. In the context of the slowdown in the Russian and Chinese economies, it is an attractive market for advertisers. “Vogue Arabia is going to have a strong voice. I want it to be intriguing enough for non-Arab women to pick up,” says Abdulaziz. It will stand for glamour but not the big, lacquered hair, bejewelled robes, crocodile attaché cases and ginormous gems of the oil boom. Abdulaziz, in that little blue dress and punkish earrings, with a wardrobe full of Margiela, Haider Ackermann and Alaïa, intends to extinguish that cliché. “It’s scary and thrilling and my life will change being an editor. Maybe I can’t go to so many parties. Maybe it’s more about private dinners. It is a huge responsibility but Vogue Arabia  – it will be gorgeous.”    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The fashion designer Azzedine Alaia, known as the 'King of Cling', has died aged 77. Born to wheat farmers in Tunisia, Alaia became one of the greats of Parisian fashion with a glamorous, sculptural aesthetic which was more concerned with flattering and celebrating women than presenting new ideas simply for new ideas' sake. Although  he never courted fame and celebrity, Alaia's body conscious, exquisitely tailored designs were worn by some of the world's most famous- and best dressed- women. Michelle Obama made a rare concession to wearing a non-American designer when she chose his neat fit-and-flare knitted dresses while she was First Lady. Gwyneth Paltrow, Rihanna, Madonna, Tina Turner and Victoria Beckham have also worn his designs.  Naomi Campbell considered Alaia to be her 'papa' after he took her under his wing when she first began modelling aged 16. She would stay with him whenever she was working in Paris and he would fetch her home if she sneaked out to night clubs. "He really taught me everything about the business," she has said. When Alaia's work was snubbed by the Metropolitan Museum in 2009, Campbell refused to attend the annual Met Gala- fashion's Oscars- in solidarity.  A quiet rebel of the industry, Alaia eschewed hurrying to finish collections in time to show on the official fashion show schedules, he would say: 'it's ready when it's ready'. When it was, fashion editors, buyers and clients would flock back to Paris especially. He called the working conditions demanded by many major design houses 'inhumane'.  His final show was held in July this year, although there was no suggestion then that it would be his last. He posed cheerfully alongside Karlie Kloss and Naomi Campbell- the diminutive 5ft 3in designer towered over by the supermodels he adored.  Raised in Tunis by his maternal grandparents, Alaia found a mentor in fashion-loving local midwife Madame Pineau whom he would assist with her deliveries. In turn, she introduced him to the fashion magazines which would inspire his future career. He moved to Paris in 1957, where he worked for Christian Dior, Guy Laroche and Thierry Mugler.  Between jobs, he made ends meet as a housekeeper. While caring for the children of Comtesse Nicole de Blegiers, he was introduced to Cecile de Rothschild and Greta Garbo, through whom he created a network of loyal private clients which has continued to grow ever since. In 1980, he presented his first ready-to-wear collection.  Alaia had a famously strict approach to his work, often staying up all night to pin and drape but also insisted that everything stop in his studio for long, convivial lunches. British Vogue editor Edward Enninful paid tribute to Alaia, calling him "a true visionary... the generosity of his spirit and the genius of designs will never be forgotten." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Cindy Crawford’s marriage to Richard Gere was during a bygone era when the private lives of celebrities was far more, well, private, thanks mainly to the lack of social media. As such, not a huge amount is known about the former couple, and Crawford has never been too keen to divulge information about the four-year marriage, which took place when she was just 23 and he was 40. But, with a book celebrating her career in modelling due out, the 49-year-old has been feeling a bit more open. Speaking with Fern Mallis, the executive director of the Council of Fashion Designers of America, Crawford revealed what her first wedding was like – and it sounds decidedly less glamorous then we’d expected. "I was a Midwest girl who had watched a lot of movies and I dreamed of getting married in this big fairytale wedding,” she said. “We had been dating a couple years and I kept asking when we could get married and finally he was like 'okay we're going to Vegas tonight.' It was The Little Chapel of The West. Herb Ritts was my bridesmaid and photographer, actually. Richard was trying to give me what I wanted…I wore an Armani suit but I didn't dream of getting married in a navy suit. And I didn't even have a blowout! I had a ring that was made out of tinfoil because it was so last minute." No big white dress, no ring and not even a hairdo. Sigh. Perhaps that was a sign of things to come: the couple split four years later. "There wasn't a good power balance there and that was my fault because I gave all my power away to him,” she explained. “I was also just too young and still a kid, I don't think I was the adult version of myself yet, I was 23 years old and I thought I was an adult because I had some success and money…He was in a different chapter of his life." Thankfully she is now happily married to former model and businessman Rande Gerber, with whom she has two children, Kaia, 14, and Presley, 16. The couple wed in the Bahamas in 1998, and Crawford wore off-the-rack John Galliano. She also spoke briefly about her friendship with Amal Clooney – her husband Rande co-owns Casamigos Tequila with George Clooney. "Amal is smart, she is obviously beautiful, but the thing that impressed me the most about her is that she's not only completely interesting but she's also interested—she's always asking you questions, she has asked me questions about the fashion world—it's easy to be friends with someone like that who is very interested."  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge arrived for a gala dinner at the National Portrait Gallery this evening, choosing a bespoke, forest green lace gown by Temperley London for her latest red carpet appearance. Attending the 2017 Portrait Gala, Kate met with a room full of artists and fashion insiders - It girl Alexa Chung was among those in attendance, in a voluminous off-shoulder dress. But by choosing a subtle, classically stylish gown, Kate held her own in the crowd. The Duchess did, however, up the ante when it came to her accessories debuting a bold new pair of earrings from one of her favourite jewellery designers, Kiki McDonough, for the occasion. A version of her candy pink tourmaline and green amethyst earrings are outlined with diamonds, and are currently in the sale on the brand’s website, reduced from £8,900 to £5,340 - a spokesperson for the brand confirming that Kate's actual ones were a special commission, made from even larger stones. Showing her loyalty to Temperley, which is of course another British brand, is also clearly an important point for the Duchess. This is the fifth time Kate has turned to Temperley London, the label founded by Alice Temperley in 2000, in the last year, and cements the brand’s status as a leader in her wardrobe. For those keeping score, the Duchess has contrastingly tallied four appearances in Jenny Packham and two in Erdem over the same period, eclipsed only by her other firm favourite Alexander McQueen, which she has worn on seven recent occasions. Tonight’s gown also holds a striking resemblance to another red carpet gown made by Temperley, and worn by Kate to the 2012 premiere of War Horse. The silhouette (high lace neckline, long sleeves, slight flare at the hem) is evidently a tried-and-tested favourite for Kate, who has never been afraid to repeat an outfit if she knows it works for her. Other appearances in the label, which is also a favourite for stylish Sloanes like Poppy Delevingne and Kate’s sister, Pippa Middleton, have included two hits on her trip to India last year, when the Duchess commissioned some beautifully embroidered pieces from the designer. While tracking the Duchess’s fashion credits may sound like an arduous task to some, her endorsement and the subsequent ‘Kate effect’ on sales can offer tremendous boost to fashion brands. London design duo Brett Tyne and Lucy Lyons will no doubt be celebrating this evening, as Kate teamed a gold clutch bag from their niche label Wilbur & Gussie with the Temperley gown. Their ‘Charlie’ gold glitter clutch is made in the UK and priced at £195 - meaning that they are the ones who will likely experience the greatest surge in interest overnight, from fans who want to copy Kate's look.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  For managing to keep a secret as huge as designing a Duchess' wedding dress under wraps for months, British designer Clare Waight Keller most definitely deserved a prize. The designer, who is currently at the helm of Parisian luxury house Givenchy, was named as The 2018 Fashion Awards British Designer of the Year Womenswear, an award presented to her by actress Rosamund Pike, and the Duchess of Sussex herself, who made a surprise appearance for the special occasion. Some 4,000 guests descended upon the Royal Albert Hall for the ceremony, which saw Waight Keller, who bagged the fashion commission of the year designing the Duchess of Sussex' bateau-necked wedding gown for her ceremony back in May, receive her award.  It's notable that she wasn't the only designer that took home an award complete with a royal seal of approval. British designer Richard Quinn won the Emerging Talent Womenswear accolade, presented to him by Karen Elson and Michael Healy. You may remember Quinn hosted a surprise special guest of honour at his AW18 show back in February: the Queen, no less, sat front row atop a plush blue cushion as she took in Quinn's bright autumn/winter collection, after making her way around the designers' showrooms at 180 The Strand.  Alongside them, Valentino's Pierpaolo Piccioli was awarded Designer of the Year, while Miuccia Prada was presented with an Outstanding Achievement award.   The category that always sets social media alight is Model of The Year, with the accolade aiming to celebrate the 'global impact of a model, who over the last 12 months has dominated the industry, with an influence that transcends the catwalk,' according to the British Fashion Council. The award was scooped up by Kaia Gerber who, in her debut season this time last year, secured a plethora of major bookings, and since, there has been no sign of her schedule easing up. The fact that the young model also has over four million Instagram followers will no doubt have been taken into account.  17 year old Gerber beat stiff competition in her category to come up trumps. She was accompanied by Adwoa Aboah who won the award last year and had made appearances on a tonne of shows in her winning year. As well as this, the British model was making a waves with her charity and campaign work for mental health issues, and with her own incredible online side hustle, Gurls Talk, a digital community for young women. Adut Akech, a model raised in a Kenyan refugee camp, was also a finalist for the award alongside Bella Hadid. Gerber, who was a finalist last year, ultimately won however and British singer, Rita Ora who wore a printed coord and Mary Jane heels presented her the award. The glamorous evening celebrated 15 awards, with a host of stars in attendance. Neelam Gill, Alek Wek and Winnie Harlow were among the models in attendance, and were joined on the red carpet by the likes of Naomi Watts, Poppy Delevingne and David and Victoria Beckham, who arrived hand in hand.  Demna Gvasalia beat both Alessandro Michele at Gucci and Jonathan Anderson at Loewe to win Accessories Designer of the Year for his work at Balenciaga. Gucci's neverending reign wasn't unnoticed however, and the label was awarded Brand of the Year, presented by singer Lana Del Rey.  Alexa Chung and Penelope Cruz at the 2018 Fashion Awards Jerry Hall presented Dame Vivienne Westwood with the Swarovski Award for Positive Change, an award which celebrates 'individuals who have made a positive impact on society, the environment or both, and forms part of Swarovski’s efforts to promote a more sustainable future for us all.' The outspoken Westwood has long been a campaigner for climate change awareness, British civil rights and PETA among others.   The celebrations continue following the show, with Fat Tony set to DJ, following a finale performance by Ellie Goulding singing an Aretha Franklin rendition and a dedicated tribute to Judy Blame and Michael Howells by Boy George.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  You’d be forgiven for wondering why I’m talking about tomatoes when I’m writing about clothes, but let me share something my friend told me recently. ‘This is going to sound weird, but when I used to go to the supermarket with my mum, she’d choose tomatoes and I’d feel sad for the ones we left behind. I secretly apologised to them.’ To most people, clothes are commodities, but to others, such as Jo Wood, they are alive. (For the record, I don’t know how she feels about tomatoes.) Animistic feelings such as these can cause problems – I once read about a woman who bought a load of dolls on QVC because nobody was bidding on them and she felt sorry for them. In Jo’s case, it manifests itself in a bulging wardrobe  – stuffed with decades of memories. On the day that I meet them (her clothes), I had planned to be home for school pick-up (a perk of being a self-employed stylist). My brief from Jo was simple: to help her clear out her old clothes.  I usually spend three to four hours going through a client’s wardrobe, but as I look around me at all these garments crammed on to rails, piled  on sofas, spilling out of bags and baskets in her Primrose Hill home, I realise this is no ordinary wardrobe edit. And by the way, I am not even in her wardrobe, I’m in her lounge. We haven’t got to the wardrobe yet, which I’m soon to discover is also full to the brim. Apparently, if you can’t list every item in your wardrobe, you’ve got too many clothes – and you don’t need the ones that you can’t recall, so you just get rid of those.  Not my theory, but tempting under the circumstances. What does Jo think of that? ‘Oh, my God,’ she bursts into laughter, looking around the room. ‘I know. It’s crazy. All these clothes. I’ve been paying to keep this lot in storage for years. It’s madness.’  It was a visit to the storage unit with her boyfriend, Paul Scarborough, that prompted the cull. He couldn’t believe what he saw and questioned what she was keeping it all for. Jo says she had once hoped her daughter Leah might like them, or her granddaughter (Leah’s daughter Maggie), but that wasn’t to be. So the storage unit was emptied – into her lounge. ‘I thought if they were in my way I’d be motivated to get rid of them,’ she reasons.  People have different motivations for getting rid of old clothes, whether it’s a change in body shape, job, lifestyle or relationship. For Jo, it was also a feeling  of suffocation, of having too much. The accumulation over the years had become overwhelming. She wants to live with less.  ‘I moved on [emotionally] a long time ago,’ says Jo, ‘and I don’t need this stuff any more.’ She points to the clothes and her wedding dress from the day she became Mrs Ronnie Wood. I ask her if she’s really getting rid of it? ‘Yes, do you want it? Are you getting married?’ She thrusts it at me and laughs. I admit, Jo seems ready for The Big Clear-Out, but no matter how ready someone is, the physical act of letting go can be hard. For most people, it comes down to money or memories. I’ve heard all kinds of reasons why someone can’t possibly part with something. With Jo, it’s ‘we were on [a Stones] tour in Shanghai and I had nothing to wear so I bought this,’ she says, showing me a gold-patterned silk gown with a wow factor that’s off the charts. I pick up a fabulous, grey, washed and worn shirt. ‘Johnny Depp gave me this. We were at a party and I said I loved his shirt. He asked me if I wanted it and when I said yes,  he took it off and gave it to me.’  As we go through the clothes, I am aware that my mouth is wide open and I have goosebumps. Here, among the Gucci, Pucci and Hulanicki, I feel like I am living these memories, too. It’s a privilege, not only to find such an amazing fashion archive but  to hear where the clothes have been and what they’ve seen. I know why she treats them as old friends. Luckily, Jo isn’t attached to anything because of its price tag, whereas many women insist on keeping something because of how much it cost. To get them to see it for what it is, I remove the item’s value. It can be as easy as asking, ‘Would you buy it, right now, at a car boot sale, for £5?’ Cue look of horror and the realisation that they wouldn’t. Nor does Jo fight me on the things that are too small for her, which can happen. ‘My body changed after I had kids. Even my ribs are bigger. I loved being thin but I’m not now and that’s just how it is. You have to adjust.’ I pick up an Alaïa skirt that looks too small for my seven-year-old daughter. It’s tiny. ‘Can you believe I used to wear that?’ she says, reading my mind. ‘I didn’t eat – none  of us did,’ she says, then winks at me and gestures to her nose as she sniffs. If the rock’n’roll lifestyle has affected her, it doesn’t show. Today, Jo is vivacious and bouncy in her athletic gear and cute schoolgirl plaits, having come back from a boxing class to shoot an ad for her organic skincare line. There’s a pile of Natural Health magazines in the corner, opera coming through her Sonos, and the only addiction she has is to Ancient Aliens, a TV show on the History Channel she watches on repeat. Given her personality, it’s no surprise Jo has many looks. One minute she’s floating in chiffon, the next, fierce in hardcore Balmain. People call me to help them look current, but Jo could not care less about the look of the season or what other people think, so when it comes to deciding which clothes will take pride of place in her newly streamlined closet, we break all the rules. Regardless of when she last wore something or what she’s got to wear with it – if she loves it, it stays. There’s diversity in what she keeps, but consistency in what we get rid of. One shape that keeps cropping up is a skater-style dress that doesn’t suit her. I’m wondering why she has so many, until  I spot an old black-and-white phototograph on the mantelpiece where she’s dressed in that exact style, as a little girl. She tells me that her mother (a seamstress and maker of elaborate dolls’ clothes, now passed away) made the dress for her and it was her favourite. The penny drops. There’s always a moment like this with a client, when both of us realise the roots of certain clothing choices. It’s by understanding these choices that the impetus for change can come. I think it’s true of life – it’s only through feeling and understanding that we can put things to bed. Jo looks nostalgic for a moment and then puts the dresses on the reject pile.  She doesn’t need to replicate that moment from her childhood, just to remember it. Johnny Depp’s shirt gets to stay, and who am I to blame her? There’s another T-shirt given to her by Slash from Guns N’ Roses that he wore on stage. ‘I sound like a crazy collector of clothes from famous people,’  she says, laughing, putting on a top hat and playing air guitar. We look at the mountain of clothes that she will get rid of and she has a moment of ‘What on earth am I going to wear?’ panic. We both laugh. There are easily 50 jackets and 100 dresses still in this wardrobe and they’re all amazing. Often there are gaps that need to be filled but in Jo’s case she just needs to wear the clothes she has. I order a couple of things to refresh her look and mix in with the other clothes – a Haider Ackermann white shirt (she doesn’t own a white shirt) and a pair of Robert Clergerie white lace-up boots, like posh Dr Martens. Just two new purchases will replace the thousand-plus items we are getting rid of. We decide to hold a sale, so Jo’s amazing clothes can find new homes and have another life. It’s clear she wants them to keep on living. She’ll donate some of the proceeds to Apne Aap, a charity that works to put an end to child trafficking, and the simple suits, skirts and dresses to Smart Works, a charity that dresses women for job interviews, to help get them back on their feet. I remind her that even though she’s getting rid of the clothes, she gets to keep the memories. ‘Great!’ she says, upbeat.  She disappears to take a call. When she returns some time later, she asks, ‘How are you, girls?’ ‘Fine, thank you,’ my assistant and I reply. It turns out she’s talking to the clothes. I think she’s going to miss them. Jo Wood’s clothes will be on sale in London this Thursday, 21 September. Space is limited.  If a red carpet is an invitation to go all out, then the annual Cannes Film Festival is a 12-day challenge – an ultramarathon of style, if you will. But in among the diamonds and wedding dresses worn as ball gowns this week (yes, truly), there’s also been a surprising trend on the ascendant: the rebels who have been rewriting the dress code. While Jessica Chastain in Alexander McQueen and Elle Fanning wearing Vivienne Westwood Couture might have stuck to the traditional route, the Grande Dames of Cannes proved that with age comes the confidence to wear things your own way. A bold, head-to-toe print could be overwhelming, but Salma Hayek dressed hers down with flatform brogues, while Juliette Binoche eschewed ballgowns for a jewel-coloured trouser suit. So why not ditch the “age-appropriate frock” and agonising heels you had earmarked for the summer wedding season, in favour of your own Cannes-approved style rebellion. The premise seems simple. Ask yourself two questions: do you love it? And are you comfortable? If not, here’s how to break the rules. First on any rebel’s shopping list? Leather. Leading the charge was Susan Sarandon; the 70-year-old actress and activist chose to forgo safer (read boring) options in favour of a floor-length black leather skirt. It’s a bit ooo-err, a bit risqué, and really rather good. Add to that a pair of black, slingback kitten heels and Sarandon’s signature black sunglasses and you’re on to a winner. If a leather skirt sounds like too much chafing for you, then why not swap your regular cover-up for a leather jacket? Uma Thurman used her black leather biker to balance out her uber-feminine, floor-length satin skirt, but if black feels too heavy, try coloured leather instead. Emma Thompson’s highlighter-yellow leather jacket is a great summer party staple. Topshop Unique have a good version for £400, or head to Zara for cheap and cheerful faux leather at £29.99. The second step towards style subversion? Denim – or more specifically, jeans, so long as the rest of your outfit is smart enough to balance out the casual wear connotations. Case in point: Isabelle Huppert in high-waisted Chloe jeans, offset by a slinky silk shirt and high-heeled sandals. Maybe you won’t follow suit and wear jeans to your cousin’s church wedding, but for a summer cocktail party? These are just the thing. One final act of red carpet rebellion we can all take happy note of is a simple one: flats. Aymeline Valade’s patent black leather brogues looked refreshingly modern with her jewel-toned trouser suit, but 80-year-old actress Vanessa Redgrave went one better in box-fresh white Converse that tied in perfectly with her monochrome tailoring. Well, in a sea of women in pinching stilettos, don’t you want to be the one still dancing when they turn the lights up?   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We all turn into our mothers eventually, or so they say. Terrifying as it may be to think of ourselves developing the habits that we found so annoying as children, when it comes to fashion, a few style lessons from someone older and wiser can be a valuable gift - particularly if your mother happens to be a renowned style icon. So what have our favourite stylish celebrities learnt from their mums - and is there something in it for us?  Fashion powerhouse Anna Wintour may be intimately familiar with all the trends of each season, but her wardrobe rarely reflects it: year after year, she sticks to neat, patterned dresses, chunky necklaces, big black sunglasses and the occasional fur wrap. Her 29-year-old daughter Bee Shaffer takes a similarly conservative approach, in a wardrobe made up predominantly of pretty floral frocks. Experimental it is not, but why mess with a winning formula? Carine Roitfeld, former Vogue Paris editor and now the editor of the eponymously named CR Fashion Book, has one of the fashion industry's most instantly recognisable aesthetics. Unapologetically sexy and very French, Roitfeld's wardrobe is predominantly black with plenty of pencil skirts, stilettos and flashes of leopard print (and it's no big deal to see her bra on show too). Her daughter Julia's style is a little more varied - she wore a grey sweater and white tulle skirt to the recent Dior show - but tight, black and sexy is definitely her comfort zone. "Style really reflects who you are and I like people to take me seriously; I think that’s something I learned from my mum," Tali Lennox once told Matchesfashion.com. Her mother Annie Lennox is the 80s pop star whose tough, androgynous style remains iconic: a lesson in not following the crowd.  Far from understated, supermodel Jerry Hall was the ultimate 1970s and 1980s glamazon: a cloud of blonde hair, a huge smile and a wardrobe of slinky and metallic gowns. Her brand of glamour was always at top volume, and you can see her influence - as well as her genes - in her vamp-ish model daughters.  Madonna has always been queen of the eff-you fashion statement; even at her early concerts in 1984, she was pairing handfuls of crucifix pendants with an exposed lacy bra. It's this rebel spirit that she's passed on to daughter Lourdes Leon, who favours pink hair, fishnet tights - and of course this Mawi bag, with 'DEALER' emblazoned in diamante. Actresses Goldie Hawn and Kate Hudson aren't fashion twins: Hawn loves a girlish mini-skirt, while Hudson's look tends to feel more sophisticated. But they have an attitude in common: when Hudson was once asked for her mother's top fashion tip, she said "There's no outfit in the world that will be more head-turning than a woman who walks into a room with great energy." They both look like they're having the time of their lives. For years now, Emma Thompson has been arriving at premieres with her daughter Gaia Wise on her arm and a look on her face that says, "I may actually burst with pride." The pair often co-ordinate their outfits, with 17-year-old Gaia usually opting for jumpsuits in colours that complement her mother's tailored separates. No bum-skimming dresses for this teenage plus-one: both mother and daughter are pure class. Doppelgangers Cindy Crawford and Kaia Gerber are usually seen with high-waisted jeans, long tumbling hair and immaculate make-up. The effect is the kind of breezy, all-American beauty the rest of us can only dream of. Former First Lady Michelle Obama has flair when it comes to what you might call 'the power dress': short sleeves, bright colours and prints, and clean lines. Her daughters Sasha and Malia, now 15 and 18, are similarly fond of a smart mini-dress - though you'll also find them in the usual teen fare of grungy hoodies and jeans. From that famous trench coat in Kramer Vs Kramer to the belted black and white Lanvin gown she wore for the 2014 Oscars, Meryl Streep has always looked her best in pieces that nip in at the waist. Her daughter and fellow actress Mamie Gummer favours the same hourglass silhouette. Leaving aside the confusing fact that Lisa Bonet could be Zoe Kravitz's sister, not her mother - the two are strikingly alike in their personal style. Kravitz has picked up her mother's bohemian taste, from the floor-skimming dresses to the long braids and liberal use of jewellery : cool, sultry and (apparently) effortless.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  After successful partnerships with the beauty giant Estée Lauder and the American superstore Target, Victoria Beckham has announced a new collaboration with Reebok. The Reebok x Victoria Beckham collection is slated for late 2018, and will form a part of the sportswear giant’s Innovation Collective, with next autumn’s range expected to be the first in a long-term partnership. So is the idea that Victoria Beckham might be able to do for Reebok what, say, Stella McCartney has done for Adidas? Since Stella began collaborating with Adidas twelve years ago, her collections have, yes, consistently encouraged sales, but perhaps more importantly, she’s helped to make the Adidas brand a key part of the fashion conversation. Personalities like singer Ariana Grande, model Gigi Hadid, actress Teyana Taylor and gymnast Aly Raisman already have partnerships with Reebok that help to make the brand relevant to their respective young and cool fan groups, but the brand hadn’t got a Stella in their arsenal; a woman in her forties who loves to exercise and look great while doing so, who just so happens to be a design leader and global trendsetter, too. Both Beckham and McCartney have great, grown-up taste, and Beckham will undoubtedly aim to develop functional but flattering high-performance clothing. Beyond that, though there will be a greater expectation for sophisticated ‘athleisure’ pieces. As the lines between our work-out gear and our leisure wardrobes have become increasingly blurred, there’s a prime opportunity for someone like Beckham to design sports-influenced clothes that could easily be worn with, say, the day-to-day pieces she makes at her eponymous label. “I have long incorporated sportswear into my wardrobe and daily life and I am thrilled to be coming together with Reebok on such a dynamic proposition," Beckham said yesterday as she arrived at the Reebok headquarters in Boston for her first day at work. She was practising what she preached immediately, wearing a pair of Reebok’s understated Club C trainers with a pair of easy black trousers and a t-shirt from her main fashion line. “To have the opportunity to challenge the traditional notions of fitness wear within a fashion context is something I have always wanted to do.” Puma enlisted Rihanna just over a year ago to help them push design boundaries with her Fenty collections, and reach new audiences via shows at Paris Fashion Week. Kanye West, too, routinely presents his Yeezy at Adidas collections on the New York Fashion Week schedule. But there was previously no rival to McCartney when it came to wearable sportswear for grown-up women. Reebok declared their new collaboration to be ‘a pivotal moment in the worlds of fitness and fashion’. Hyperbole? A bit. But a partnership to be genuinely excited about, for sure.

 It's no secret that here at Telegraph Fashion we can't help but eyeroll whenever we hear the term 'festival fashion.' But at Glastonbury this weekend the likes of Alexa Chung, Cressida Bonas and Suki Waterhouse undid some of the damage done by years of fringing, flower crowns or tiered maxi dresses, introducing us to a set of cooler, modern pieces which work for festival dressing now.  If you are set on avoiding the boho festival uniform this summer- a move we strongly encourage- here are some looks spotted in the Glastonbury mud which are practical (hallelujah!) and stylish, but most importantly give the impression that you're there to get down-and-dirty with the music rather than just achieve a perfectly choreographed Instagram shot.  This year Alexa Chung centred her Glastonbury wardrobe around a pair of skinny, high-shine vinyl trousers instead of jeans or denim cut-off shorts. The key to wearing vinyl trousers is to keep the rest simple, as shown by Chung who paired hers with a white tee and pink cable knit cardigan by Ganni for their first outing, and then a navy jumper and her trusty Barbour jacket.  If you are considering investing in a pair of vinyls, Vogue fashion news editor Julia Hobbs owns six pairs, and says that the secret is all in the tailoring. “I have them tailored to fit me on Savile Row, and live in them as though they are jeans with a navy cashmere sweater and beaten up ballet pumps." “My golden rule is never buy leggings,” concedes Hobbs. “Always look for trousers that have have structure and a front zipper, otherwise they can end up looking like a bin liner. The thickness of the vinyl is crucial.” Warning: we are yet to test the intricacies of pulling on vinyls in a two-man tent, but if you've tried it please do let us know how  you got on.  Mango, vinyl trousers, £24.99 The hoodie has made a grand return to fashion this year thanks to Vetements' cult oversized sportswear sweaters- one sold-out hoodie was emblazoned with the faces of Leo and Kate in Titanic. But at Glastonbury we also saw the return of the humble, simple zip-up jersey hoodie. Alexa Chung and Poppy Delevingne proved that there's a very specific way of styling said-hoodies; layered under a bomber or denim jacket, with the hood pulled half over your hair- a useful way to tackle the third or fourth day without a hair wash too.  Uniqlo, hoodie, £19.90 Grimes' approach to her stage look was surprisingly Sloaney. She wore an XXL rugby shirt with a large white collar and crest at the chest. Her spin was to wear it as a dress with a belt and black tights. Time to raid your boyfriend/ husband/ brother/ Dad's wardrobe.  Let's face it, this athleisure trend is going nowhere any time soon. Suki Waterhouse wore classic burgundy shiny jogging bottoms with a white stripe down the trouser leg. Instead of wearing a full red tracksuit as seen on the catwalk at Chloe this season, she mixed her trackies with a leather jacket and band t-shirt. Chloe's tracksuit 'Cady' pants, £1,271 Cressida Bonas stuck to her tried-and-tested Glastonbury uniform, wearing short denim dungarees by Zara (they've now sold out) with Hunter Original classic boots. She also makes a strong case for wearing a fisherman's yellow jacket- not only very stylish but will also make you much easier to spot in the crowds.  Topshop, Denim dungarees, £39 Floral embroidery is a pillar of boho festival fashion, but Suki Waterhouse showed that an embroidered leather biker (her's is by Etro) is a tougher, cooler spin on the trend. An investment piece that will work just as well in the city as in a swampy campsite.   Christopher Kane, embroidered leather jacket, £1,410 Alexa Chung stayed cosy in a pink cable knit cardigan with classic wooden buttons by Ganni. Sadly it's from the AW16 collection, so you'll have to wait until September if, like us, you want to buy it immediately.  Waterproofs are a reality of British festivals, but there's a new generation of cagoules which are much chicer than your standard raincoat. Make your waterproof jacket sheer and colourful, like Suki Waterhouse, Lottie Moss and Natalie Dormer who all wore Hunter's £140 sheer smocks. Hunter Original smock, £140 Edie Campbell looked seriously cool in a buttery tan shearling jacket by Coach, which she paired with a white slogan tee, black rolled up jeans and rose-tinted shades. Shearling is poised to be a key style for AW16- it was on the catwalk at Chloe, Topshop, Carven, Coach and many more- so there's no shame in investing in time for Wilderness then bringing it out again for autumn.  Coach, Shearling vest, £995 OK, this one is something of a long-shot for non It girls but how warm do Cara Delevingne, Suki Waterhouse, Poppy Jamie and Clara Paget look in their hi-vis?  They were by far the most practical VIPs in bright orange oversized air-traffic-control style coats, complete with reflective silver strips. Don't worry, they hadn't stolen them from the backs of Glasto's car park staff but were wearing personalised jackets by Anya Hindmarch.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  In a week's time the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge will be heading to India and Bhutan on their next royal tour, so as you'd expect from one of the world's most scrutinised women in the world Kate has been busy preparing an appropriate wardrobe.  The Telegraph has learned that the Duchess will take 12-15 outfits for the six days of official visits but that alongside daytime dresses and evening gowns, they'll be a surprising addition: a pair of hiking boots.  Whilst the Royal couple are in Bhutan they'll go on a six-hour trek to Tiger's Nest monastery said to require peak physical fitness and hiking gear, likely to be the £106 Hillmaster boots the Duchess last wore when she visited Borneo's jungle.   The official tour starts in Mumbai on April 10, and the Duke and Duchess will travel to New Delhi, the Kaziranga National Park and Thimphu, capital of the Himalayan kingdom of Bhutan, and the Taj Mahal. A small team have made a rehearsal trip to India and Bhutan, on which Kate's private secretary Rebecca Deacon made notes on factors to consider about the locations the Duchess will visit, so that she has an idea of what outfits will and won't work. The team took a photograph of every place the Duchess will visit, so that she can use these images as a guide to determine how formal she needs to dress and what colours will look best against the backdrops.  "She is in charge of it herself and takes an interest in paying tribute to the host country with nods to their culture and local style on at least a few of the engagements," a royal source told The Telegraph. "The important factor on this tour is the heat, so that's an issue that plays a big part in the choice of outfits." On previous royal tours Kate has made a point of dressing diplomatically - wearing a dress by Canadian born designer Erdem Moralioglu to touch down in Montreal, for example. She wore a dress by Australian label Zimmermann whilst on Oz's Manley Beach, and on her three-day trip to New York in 2014 she wore two pieces from American designers, a Tory Burch coat and J. Crew jeans.  Just a few days after it was announced the Duke and Duchess would be travelling to India, Kate wore a dress by Indian designer Saloni for a function in London - hinting perhaps that she'll also rely on the designer's print and colour filled collection for the upcoming tour.  The Duchess of Cambridge often opts for bright colours while on royal visits, which is a trick she has picked up from the Queen. “She may subconsciously be following the Queen’s style,” explains Ingrid Seward, author of The Queen’s Speech, of the Duchess of Cambridge selecting stand-out colours. “The Queen has always worn bright colours so she is visible in a crowd. She also knows block colours are more flattering in photographs.” But whilst the Duchess is likely to have spent months talking with designers about commissioning pieces which nod to the host nations, she will also have shopped for pieces online. "It's very much a process that she leads, though she does have some help from her staff when it comes to sourcing outfits," the royal source added. The Duchess' personal assistant, Natasha Archer, will accompany her on the royal tour, as will her hairdresser Amanda Cook Tucker. Although Kensington Palace have never confirmed whether Archer acts as an official stylist to the Duchess, speculation over her role mounted when she was photographed entering the Lindo Wing after the birth of Prince George holding a clothing bag. It's now said that Archer is responsible for helping Kate become more experimental with her choices and ordering much of Kate's online shopping.  Together, the Duchesses trousseu will no doubt be impressive. It was estimated that the Duchess of Cambridges' wardrobe for her Australia tour in 2014 cost £38,000 in total, with pieces designed by the likes of Roksanda Illincic, Alexander McQueen, Catherine Walker and Jenny Packham.       © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We now have sartorial proof that autumn is in the air courtesy of The Duchess of Cambridge, who switched from the pastel hues we saw her in earlier this week to a decidedly cosier choice for a visit to Manchester today. Kate wrapped up against the chill in a coat by Erdem for a packed programme which included visits to the city's Football Museum,  Manchester Cenotaph, the 'home of Graphene' at Manchester University and Francis House Children's Hospice.  The coat is based on a look from Erdem's Resort 2016 collection which was debuted in June 2015 and would have been available to purchase at the end of the year. With its oversized grey, pink, blue and black check print, the design has a distinctly British and wintery feel  with just enough pops of colour to ensure the crowds could spot the Duchess at a distance. Kate finished the ensemble with a simple pair of navy Rupert Sanderson heels, Oscar de la Renta gold and faux pearl earrings (not the first time she's worn pearls this week) and low pony tail which she later took out, finishing the day with her hair loose around her shoulders. The collection which the coat forms a part of was based on the idea of splicing Victorian and 60s influences, a reference which is reflected in the prim, below-the-knee silhouette.  Erdem Moralioglu is one of the most anticipated names on the London Fashion Week schedule, and has become much-loved for his romantic, intricately crafted and historically-inspired designs; his most recent show blended the adventures of Queen Henrietta Maria, wife of Charles I, and the nautical glamour of 1930s Deauville, the French town where Coco Chanel had a home.  Notably, Moralioglu was born to an English mother and a Turkish father in Montreal, Canada so this coat might have initially been ordered with September's royal tour to British Columbia and the Yukon in mind. On The Duchess's last tour to Canada in 2011, she chose a navy lace Erdem shift dress to step off the plane and wore another blue style during the tour. Since then, Erdem's feminine designs have become go-tos for Kate. In October last year, she opted for a dark floral printed silk gown to attend a Women In Hedgefunds gala dinner and in 2012, it was a pale blue embroidered dress from the London-based label for the Trooping the Colour ceremony.  The Duchess has also developed a penchant for Erdem's elegantly striking coats. In March this year, she attended the Commonwealth Service in another knee-length cover-up, this time in grey with overlaid black lace while in 2014, she wore  a green Erdem coat in New Zealand which she has also worn since. The final stop of the day for The Duke and Duchess in Manchester is @FrancisHouseCH, which Princess Diana officially opened in 1991 pic.twitter.com/mf2riRzat6 The last stop on today's full schedule was Francis House Children's Hospice which was officially opened by Princess Diana in 1991. Kensington Palace tweeted an image of Prince William's late mother at the opening which showed her wearing a jacket with a checked pattern which echoed  that of Kate's Erdem style- a respectfully subtle tribute perhaps?       © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  British supermodel Kate Moss has a 368-page coffee table book devoted to her 25-year-plus career, and next week a dozen of the model's favourite photographs of herself will be exhibited in the UK for the first time. The Photographers 2015 is a major photographic event opening at the Beetles+Huxley and Osborne Samuel galleries in London, and the Kate Moss Portfolio forms part of it. The selection was produced by Danziger Projects to spotlight one of the most photographed women in the world, and the leading names who have worked with her. 41-year-old Moss has worked with some of the greatest fashion photographers of all time since being scouted in an airport aged 14, and many of these names are referenced in her edit: Mario Testino, Annie Leibovitz, Juergen Teller and Bruce Weber. Photographs from the mid-Nineties right through to the late Noughties have made the cut; an iconic nude picture of her taken by then-boyfriend Mario Sorrenti features. She was 19 when the picture was taken for Calvin Klein’s Obsession fragrance. Photos from her turns in the British and Paris editions of Vogue also feature, as does a lesser-known image of her sleeping on a pavement taken by Terry Richardson. Despite having starred on hundreds of magazine covers and in numerous advertising campaigns, Moss recently revealed that she sometimes still has a “Ooh, look, there’s me!” moment when she sees herself in public. She is currently the face of Rimmel, Mango, Etro, Balenciaga, David Yurman and the My Burberry fragrance, and is also a contributing fashion editor at British Vogue. Photographs by world-renowned photographers Richard Avedon, Henri Cartier-Bresson and Erwin Blumenfeld will be exhibited as part of The Photographers 2015, which will be staged from November 25 to December 23 at the Beetles+Huxley and Osborne Samuel Galleries in Mayfair, London.

 The Topshop Unique London Fashion Week show has a long-held reputation for sparking a Kate Moss related moment (think that 2007 show when the supermodel basically single-handedly made flare jeans relevant again). But though Kate wasn't at today's Topshop AW16 collection (she's hurt her foot in a skiing accident), her sister Lottie was representing the family on the front row.  Fittingly, Lottie told us that it was Kate who first introduced her to the high street store. "I think it's a dress my sister gave me from one of her collections," Lottie told The Telegraph of her first Topshop piece. "The Kate Moss collection for Topshop - it was a sparkly sequin minidress and I remember that so clearly. I was probably 12 or something, and I still have it." Kate did eight collections for Topshop and her sister says she still wears pieces from the range. "I've got another thing from her collection - like a summer dress and that's really cute. That's probably from like, 4 years ago and I still wear it now," she added.  Lottie, who made her fashion week debut at the Topshop Unique show in 2014 with her big sister Kate, went on to admit there are advantages of being a supermodel's sibling: regular cast offs. "Yeah when I go round there she's like, 'Here you go!' with all sorts of stuff that doesn't fit her anymore," she told us. And her favourite Kate Moss hand-me-down? "I've got this fur coat that's mink and it's so nice." If Lottie likes her supermodel sister's 60's aesthetic, she was in luck - because Topshop Unique's latest collection felt at times like an homage to the fashionable era. Leopard print sweaters, gingham mini skirts and smudged eyeliner were all in abundance - a rock-chick look that you could imagine both Moss's buying into.  Some on the front row had even bought into the look in advance. Supermodel Lara Stone sat front row wearing double leopard print - a blouse and coat - paired with a peach leather skirt. She was one of a number of big models watching the show, alongside Karlie Kloss, Jourdan Dunn and king of the male modelling world Lucky Blue Smith - who told us he wasn't a fan of Zoolander II.  The front row stars were all wearing Topshop, of course. Karlie Kloss paired her black jumpsuit with tight french pigtails and pink lipstick, whilst Erin O'Connor wore jeans a huge pink fluffy coat and black fluffy Topshop Unique sandals as they no doubt made a fresh shopping list from the AW16 show.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
