 And each of her black patent ‘work shoes’ has an added insole for comfort. And dress hems fall below her knee and are weighted to avoid any Marilyn moments. It was during the Royal Tour of Canada in 1970, when young Royal dressmaker Ian Thomas made her a matte-silk trouser suit in a bid to modernise her look. Her preferred styles are the Royale and the black patent Traviata (23cm x 20cm x 10cm). The bag has a longer handle to ease the process of handshaking. Since 1947 glove maker Cornelia James Ltd has provided HM with dozens of pairs a year. She has an extensive collection of the square versions. She’s worn the ornate State Diadem - which was made in 1820 for George IV’s Coronation - for every state opening of Parliament since 1952. The Queen relies on transparent umbrellas from the British company Fulton, with a trim that is colour co-ordinated to her outfit.  Rachel Trevor-Morgan is her favourite milliner. She's also briefed to ensure that the hat isn't so tall The Queen can't get out of a car easily. Plain white with a Royal motif for daytime occasions. A tartan number for the country. So there's no chance of them trailing in soup.  Given HM often has a series of outfit changes every day, it's essential clothes can be changed easily and quickly.  The Queen's dressing team make sure they know exactly what was worn when so that they're not in danger of repetition.  As well as creating flashing platform shoes and a hair accessory that juxtaposed a crucifix with a banana, Dolce & Gabbana had another tactic designed to get the millennials interested in their show at Milan Fashion Week this weekend - a front row packed with the latest batch of social media sensations.  One of their guests was Sarah Synder - a 21-year-old model who's already been tipped by Vogue as 'the downtown cool kids' version of Kim Kardashian West' thanks, in part, to her 900,000+ followers on Instagram.  So who is she? Smith has starred in campaigns for Chanel and Louis Vuitton and Synder has fronted a campaign for Uniqlo and appeared in Forever 21's product shots.  But Snyder's style that marks her out as one to watch. With a Lily Rose Depp-esque blonde neat bob, sulky doe eyes and a heavy reliance on cult label Vetements, she's got the insouciance that seems to appeal to millennials these days.  She religiously documents her outfits on Instagram, posting daily outfit shots, and a quick scroll unearths slogan tees, creepers, chokers and full tracksuits by the likes of Vetements, Opening Ceremony and V Files. The model was falsely accused of stealing a Hermes Birkin bag, and wrote a powerful account of her experience of being arrested for Harper's Bazaar.  For most designers, dressing a First Lady would be a dream come true. Indeed, many have seen their businesses boom thanks to their dresses take a starring role on the world stage during the Michelle Obama years thanks to her relentless stream of joyful, wearable wardrobe choices. The fashion world has delighted in this close relationship with politics but is all that set to stop when Melania Trump becomes FLOTUS in January? For Sophie Theallet - one of Obama's favourite designers - the answer is a resounding yes. French-born, New York-based Theallet is the first fashion designer to come out publicly saying that she won't be dressing Melania Trump. “As one who celebrates and strives for diversity, individual freedom, and respect for all lifestyles, I will not participate in dressing or associating in any way with the next First Lady," she wrote in an open letter on Twitter. "The rhetoric of racism, sexism, and xenophobia unleashed by her husband’s presidential campaign are incompatible with the shared values we live by.” Open letter | Sophie Theallet | November 17th, 2016 pic.twitter.com/g1hIAyBmdF In some ways, Theallet's sentiments aren't entirely surprising. The fashion world is liberal, open-minded and Left-leaning (Hillary Clinton received overwhelming backing from the industry) so the election of a Republican President was always going to present an awkward moment, particularly when that President is Trump with his divisive policies. Designers have already made their reticence about Melania clear by their attitude to seeing her wear their clothes on the campaign trail - conspicuous silence. When she wore pieces she'd bought at Net-A-Porter from Gucci, Ralph Lauren, Roksanda and Emilia Wickstead for key moments in the campaign, the usual statements of being 'honoured and delighted' which are so often forthcoming from designers' press offices did not emerge. Instead, many designers have been engaged in private discussions about how to deal with 'The Melania Problem' when requests from her team have come in to borrow their samples - that problem being as much about aesthetics as politics. Because with her poker-straight bronde hair, love of Louboutins, lashings of lip gloss, permatan and "done" face (yes, of course, she has denied ever having had surgery or Botox), Melania's glamazon vibe is the antithesis of many designers' ideal - and the natural, accessible look which has made Obama so appealing.  It's a similar story amongst fashion writers and publications who, having spent years covering Obama's style religiously (and fruitfully), are now pondering how to tackle covering Melania. (One US company have apparently decided non of their publications will write about her style). And yet, is all this angst rather pointless, not to mention veering on snobbery? After all, it's patently impossible to ban anyone from wearing your designs if you sell them in shops where they are readily available to buy. In fact, one can almost imagine Melania vindictively ordering a batch of Theallet dresses as a two-fingers to her public statement. She does have good form with seemingly perceptive outfit choices after all; she made a speech wearing a dress by Roksanda Ilincic, a designer who also hails from the former Yugoslavia and she wore a Gucci pussy bow blouse in the wake of Trump's pussy grabbing scandal.  The irony is that as a former model Trump knows how to wear clothes - and to many women she will represent the epitome of aspirational polish. Indeed, that Gucci shirt sold out on Net-A-Porter within hours of Trump being seen wearing it. And no doubt we will see a similar phenomenon happen to the tightly fitted sheath dresses, power coats and waist-cinching silhouettes she'll bring to the White House from January.  Perhaps that's why for all the Theallet-style sentiment, there are designers who are being more measured in their approach to Melania. "I’m going to give Melania the benefit of the doubt,” Moschino creative director Jeremy Scott told Vanity Fair this week. “She looks good in clothes. She wears them well, she’s got a good figure... Obviously [Melania] looks great, but I can’t divorce it from who she is. I don’t know Melania. We don’t know Melania.” Joseph Altuzarra was equally tentative, telling the New York Times, "I don't want to not dress people I disagree with." In fact, some designers believe that by boycotting Trump, they could be going against the very values which they claim to be defending. "It would be hypocritical to say no to dressing a Trump," Marcus Wainwright of Rag & Bone has said. "If we say we are about inclusivity and making American manufacturing great again, then we have to put that before personal political beliefs."  But perhaps the final word should go to Carolina Herrera, a stalwart of American elegance who has dressed numerous First Ladies. After all, she has the air of someone used to dust settling after a drama.  "You'll see everyone dressing Melania. She's representing the United States," she told Business of Fashion.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s been six months since Kate Moss launched her eponymous modelling agency, vowing to take all that she’s learned in her almost 30-year career, and impart some wisdom onto the next generation of stars. In the April issue of British Vogue, she’s revealing the fruits of her work so far. Explaining her approach to her new role, Moss says that she feels a ‘maternal’ instinct to look after her young charges, perhaps even more so because she has experienced the harshness of the industry for herself. “I don’t want a young girl to feel bad if she has to wait around,” she says of her openness, and the fact that she shares personal stories from her career with the models in her care. “I was that person with Steven Meisel, even though I was the face of CK [Calvin Klein] at the time. I had to sit around for days. It can be really hard. I’m maternal; I don’t want the girls to feel insecure.” Moss's comments come at a time when the modelling industry is under a harsher spotlight than ever before. Last week, furore overshadowed Paris fashion week when casting director James Scully wrote a scathing post which accused  Balenciaga's then-casting directors of locking 150 models in a stairwell, labelling them "sadistic and cruel".   "It's inconceivable to me that people have no regard for human decency or the lives and feelings of these girls," he added. It seems that Moss is also sensitive to the extreme demands which models often face as part of their work. “As a model I am prepared to stand in a bikini at the end of an ice glacier when it’s minus 30, because that is what the client has booked me to do and that’s the job,” she tells Vogue. “So, as I get older, it seemed like the natural thing to do was to take responsibility for my choices both as a model and with the branding I put my name to.” Moss signed her first female model back in October; 16 year-old Elfie Reigate, who happens to have been a bridesmaid at her 2011 wedding to Jamie Hince, and is the daughter of supermodel Rosemary Ferguson and artist Barry Reigate. Reigate made her catwalk debut last season securing an exclusive booking with Alexander McQueen, and this season she walked exclusively for Burberry and fronts the brand’s new advertising campaign. Moss, evidently is an agent who values the quality of her protegees’ gigs over the quantity. As a Vogue Contributing Fashion Editor, Kate also styles Reigate and her first male signing Louis Baines for a shoot in the issue, photographed by her boyfriend, Nikolai von Bismarck. It is Moss herself, however, who graces the cover and is photographed by Mert Alas and Marcus Piggott. In the cover image, we see a grown-up vision of the supermodel. Aside from her bold red lips, the 43 year-old looks pared-back with the faintest of fine lines and freckles evident- a subtle indicator perhaps that this is Kate Moss 2.0, model agent and fashion editor before us.  In the accompanying interview she talks candidly about her attitude to the paparazzi, as well as a rare encounter with London’s Tube network. “We went on the Tube the other day,” she says. “I hadn’t been on one for a long time, although when I started modelling it’s how I went to all my go-sees.  House of Cards is back. We repeat back! The fourth season of the sitcom, celebrated for its dirty politics and loaded dialogue, is about to hit Netflix. Fans are expecting answers to the big question: will Claire really walk away from President Francis Underwood? And, if so, what (immaculate and stylish) shoes will the First Lady be wearing as she does so?   Stylist Kemal Harris, who took over styling Claire Underwood last season, has posted a picture of the moodboard that has inspired her new season costumes. Featuring photographer Lee Miller’s portraits and the Dior archive shots, we can surmise that Claire's wardrobe will follow the same ‘timeless, decisive and feminine’ mantra her stylists have carefully created across three season.  Tom Broecker was Underwood's first costume designer - winning two nominations at the 2013 Costume Designers Guild Awards for his work creating the ultimate on-screen power wardrobe.  "With her character we really wanted to have this armoured, tailored, right, nothing out of place feel," he's previously told Elle of working on House of Cards set.  The result was a host of outfits from Prada, L'Wren Scott, Armani and Theory that looked polished and barely veered from a simple palette of black, grey and white.  Harris kept the same aesthetic last season but introduced some new designers to the First Lady's White House wardrobe.  Alexander McQueen, Altuzurra and Proenza Schouler were featured on screen and Harris also custom made clothes for actress Robin Wright to wear - some of which seemly inspired real life First Lady Michelle Obama.  So what secrets can we learn about dressing for the job you want from the ultimate ice queen in Manolo shoes Claire Underwood? Here's four tips to take away: Thanks to a quality seamstress, Underwood’s clothes fit her like a glove. Harris has previously revealed that almost every piece is altered to suit Wright’s shape, but that fittings are done on a mannequin (an exact replica of Wright) to save the actress countless hours of pinning and tucking. Made-to-measure services might seem like a costly habit to get into, but focus on tailoring to get the best results. A blazer that hugs your shoulders rather than swamps them is a powerful garment to own. Claire’s careful edit of accessories - a Cartier watch and Saint Laurent Sac du Jour - spell out power. They are considered, practical and, most importantly, timeless. Even her spectacles - medium tortoiseshell rims - toe the line between functional and fashionable. Frivolous is not a word that can be associated with the First Lady. Would Claire be seen dead in denim? What do you think? The closest Underwood gets to ‘off-duty’ is her slick black running gear and a pair of silk pyjamas for the bedroom. If you want to emulate power, you have to be committed to a seriously slick silhouette. Harris has previously referenced Lauren Bacall and Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy as her costume muses for Claire, and both women read from the same classic book of fashion. Underwood’s wardrobe riffs off a strictly clean colour scheme. Think block coloured garments in beige, grey, navy, black and burgundy. This might seem safe, but feminine prints risk looking fussy next to her suit-clad male counterparts. Note the neckline on Underwood’s dresses. With her cropped hair cut, the scooped neckline always reveals enough of her honey-coloured skin to look tantalising, but not sexy. This truly is an art. We advise steering clear of push-up bras to achieve the same aesthetic. Designers known for their classic workwear - Ralph Lauren, Derek Lam, Jason Wu - are also a safe bet, as they will stick to the demure lines they are famed for. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  In a recent interview with American Vogue Theresa May highlighted the fact that, while journalists are quick to emphasise that she has ''recycled'' a piece of clothing, ''there aren't many people who buy things only to wear once.'' The Prime Minister has a valid point. But like it or not, an item worn twice or more to a key public event, is indication that May is a fan of the brand she's wearing. Whether her almost unwavering loyalty to British brands  is evidence of patriotic dressing or is simply because she likes them, as she suggested in her Vogue interview, May has repeatedly looked to L.K.Bennett, Russell & Bromley and Amanda Wakeley, among others, for the sleek tailoring and pops of colour she favours.  Here's our round up of the Prime Minister' best-loved fashion brands... Theresa May was recently photographed by Annie Leibovtiz  for American Vogue, while wearing a blue L.K.Bennett coat and dress. But the British high street stalwart has long been one of the Prime Minister's go-to brands for clothes and accessories. This is hardly surprising given that L.K. Bennett caters for smart, professional woman who don't want to rule out bright colours or print, nor skimp on shape and cut.  Be it a tailored jacket, a structured dress or kitten heels; Theresa May has looked to L.K. Bennett on numerous occasions to provide her with flattering pieces that are, while suitable, far from boring. Cropped jacket, £275, L.K. Bennett  Although May refuted the notion in her recent Vogue interview that the Vivienne Westwood tartan suit she has worn on a number of key occasions (including to deliver a key Brexit speech in January of this year and at a Conservative conference in 2013) is her lucky suit, we can at the very least deduce from the suit's multiple outings that the Prime Minister is fond of the British prints and tailoring which Westwood is famed for. May also wore the thigh-high boots for her Vogue shoot, nodding to their longevity as a firm favourite. Over-the-knee boots, £455, Russell & Bromley In keeping with May's penchant for smart pieces with a twist is London-based designer Daniel Blake, whose coat the Prime Minister has stepped out in a number of times.  Most fashion fans scrolling through Instagram for the first time on Boxing Day probably expected photographs of illuminated Christmas trees and piles of presents to dominate their feeds. Instead, they found tribute after tribute to George Michael, who died on Christmas Day.  The pop superstar and prolific songwriter was behind many of the anthems of the 1980s and '90s- and his videos were the crossroads for the worlds of fashion and music. Nowhere was this more true than in 'Freedom! '90'. The video starred the five leading supermodels of the day - Linda Evangelista, Naomi Campbell, Christy Turlington, Cindy Crawford and Tatjana Patitz- lip-syncing to Michael's lyrics.  The video was inspired by photographer Peter Lindbergh's January 1990 cover of British Vogue which showed models in a refreshingly honest way - a revolutionary move after the gloss and glamour of the previous decade. "They were the kind of models who were really independent, joyful and sporty, but – most importantly – they were strong in themselves. I thought that should be the future," Lindbergh recently told The Telegraph of that era-defining image.  By this morning, those models were among the dozens of fashion insiders sharing their memories of Michael, 53, on the social network. Evangelista posted a photo of herself with Turlington and Michael, writing:  am beyond heartbroken and devastated by another tragic loss. R.I.P. dearest Georgy. #GeorgeMichael # ripgeorgemichael" "It's a blue Christmas without you #GeorgeMichael Thank you for your soulful music and open heart ," read Turlington's caption to an image of her face from Freedom.  Campbell posted two pictures: one from the 1991 Versace show in which she, Evangelista, Crawford and Turlington walked the runway arm in arm, mouthing the lyrics from Freedom, and another of Michael's face.   Crawford posted a video clip from an awards ceremony, and wrote, 'Feeling very honored to have been part of #GeorgeMichael's #Freedom90  video. His bravery inspired all of us. RIP George.'   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  After the much lauded cover choices for this season’s September issues (which featured Beyoncé, Rihanna, Ruth Negga, Zendaya, Lupita Nyong'o and Tracee Ellis Ross among others) the question of diversity in fashion has reached a tipping point - is this a mere flash in the pan trend, or something more lasting?  It will take time to see if there is indeed a marked shift in how women and men are represented in the industry, but it’s useful to take a reading of how things are looking now that the first round of fashion shows have come to a close.  Historically, New York has perhaps made greater strides than others in showing different, interesting and varied women on its catwalks. This season, it didn’t feel like a stunt. At Ralph Lauren’s glorious 50th anniversary show, everyone from grandparents to grandchildren were represented. For Calvin Klein and Michael Kors, the brief that women of a cross section of ages and sizes shop these collections was well met - Yasmin Le Bon (53) and Stella Tennant (47) were in the former, Ashley Graham, Karen Elson, Angolan model Blesnya Minher, Alyssa Traore, Martiniques’s Karly Loyve, Lineisy Montero and the Hadid sisters walked for Kors in show castings that truly covered a full spectrum of ethnicity. Whilst  Rihanna showcased her latest Fenty for Adidas collection on a heavily pregnant Slick Woods.  Equally a wider question  is starting to circulate - what is diversity exactly? There is certainly progress when it comes to seeing women of colour and varied ethnicity, see the Crazy Rich Asians effect - perhaps money-makers have finally cottoned on to the fact that there is huge scope for profits in appealing to broader communities (duh). But it was at the Opening Ceremony show where the biggest strides were taken in terms of really opening up a fashion show to all who want to partake in the industry.  It wasn’t even really a fashion show. Co-curated with renowned drag artist Sasha Velour (who won the brilliantly addictive cult programme RuPaul’s Drag Race last year) the collection was given over to 40 LGBTQ models, performers and artists to produce a riotous experience which unlike most fashion week events was raucously enjoyable - and everyone stayed for the after-party. The audience whooped and cheered, laughed and clapped. Velour compered whilst her drag-queen compadres performed in inimitable style. Some had even created their own performance pieces from the fabrics on offer from the Opening Ceremony spring collection.  The unique event was created as part of Mercedes Benz Fashion’s #WeWonder Manifesto project which is an initiative through which the car manufacturer supports provocative artists, collaborating with them to produce experiences which explore their ideas about how the future might look. Having recently worked with Solange Knowles and Slick Woods, the co-creative directors of Opening Ceremony,  Humberto Leon and Carol Lim (who founded the brand in 2002) were enlisted as the latest impressive talents in the series.   After the show, they took part in a panel discussion and explained how they had embarked on exploring the theme of their own personal and professional journey's for the production, and what this had meant for them, and their label going forward - questioning the traditional format of a fashion show, and whether this is remains the best way to communicate a message.  For Leon, this was a very personal contribution, having come out around age 19, he has always striven to represent different voices within the industry and offer something which they could find themselves reflected in. For many of the performers - who were each inspired to explore their own life "journey" in the show, this was an emotional gathering, to find so many LGBTQ artists pulled together was something unique. One thing that the experience caused Leon to ponder was how it “was interesting to think about what the models actually wanted to wear, and letting them choose, so they could feel truly themselves.”  Lim offered that the clothes here “were secondary to the event, it’s about the idea of the experience in the room. [At a normal runway show] no one's looking at the clothes anyway they’re all on their phones”. Clothes, she reasoned, can be shown anywhere, anytime- this was about using their platform to offer something different and truly inclusive which the pair are passionate about. “Fashion, surprisingly, seems to be an industry where there is a 'norm',” considered Leon, “we love this world but we want to do something different. To follow suit is the easy route.” Velour made a poignant point that as a lover of fashion and after winning series 9 of the widely watched Ru Paul’s Drag Race, last year she enquired about being able to attend some of the New York shows. She received a defeaning silence and no invites, this season ,however, she was running her own show. It does make an interesting point, the fashion industry is heavily populated by the LGBTQ community, but still largely persists in presenting a neat, conservative stand point excluding their own. For Leon, this is merely “a starting point to doing more things like this.”  They’re certainly not lacking in high profile support. Watching  - and whooping - from the front row were Whoopi Goldberg, Nicki Minaj, Crazy Rich Asian’s Awkwafina, Kelly Rowland, Slick Woods and Baz Luhrmann. After teasing the audience throughout with cardboard cut outs, for the finale, out popped Christina Aguilera to round off proceedings in her defiantly diva style. As Lim, who alongside Leon, watched the whole thing unfold as part of the audience enthused, it was “an uplifting and incredible night.” Which surely, is what fashion should always be.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Sir Mick Jagger - rock legend and style icon, has weighed in on the state of style today in a new interview. The 72-year-old rocker and his band The Rolling Stones are the theme of men's style bible Another Man's latest issue, and Jagger stars in a vast, 40-page shoot alongside weird and wonderful artefacts from his wardrobe. "I don't mind digging up old clothes and wearing them... but digging up old stories is a bore" he tells the London-based magazine. He goes on: "People just don't dress up like they used to... When people went to the theatre everyone dressed up. I don't really miss that. But do you like going to the theatre and seeing a bloke with not very nice legs in shorts and flip-flops?" Just last week the Rolling Stones completed their America Latina Ole Tour of South America, playing across Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Peru, Colombia and finishing in Mexico. Jagger explained how venue sizes impact on his choice of clothing: "If you're playing in a 1000-seater, people can see you more, but playing in a 15,000-seater arena, you have to cut more of a dash. You have to have a silhouette and a colour, and some kind of item that's going to get noticed and followed, whether it's a scarf or a hat." The Latina Ole Tour saw Jagger don a variety of bright, embellished jackets; in the pages of Another Man, a double-breasted, pale pink suit by Cortlands which he wore on Top of Pops in 1971 has been photographed in bandmate Keith Richards' leopard lined tour trunk. But even after 50 years on stage, Jagger is still on the hunt for the most practical pair of shoes. “On a big stage, you've got lots of surfaces. You've got wood and you've got metal, and you've got stairs, lots of stuff to negotiate, and sometimes it's a bit wet and slippery. So shoes are a very practical thing. I'm always trying to find sneakers that are going to give you support so you don't twist your ankle."  Is Princess Diana Victoria Beckham’s new fashion muse? Admittedly, this is a question I never thought I’d ask, but then again, who could blame Beckham if she has been taking sartorial notes- conscious or otherwise- from one of the twentieth century’s greatest style icons. In the past few months, there has been a renewed focus on Diana thanks to the 20th anniversary of her death and the new exhibition about her style- Diana: Her Fashion Story- which opened at her former Kensington Palace home in February. Judging by some of the looks which Beckham has worn in New York while she’s been there for work over the past couple of weeks and a detail or two in her latest collection, it seems that even she was not immune from the influence of a foray into the Princess’s style archive. Clearly, VB has not abandoned all her modern minimalist principles in favour of colour-pop 80s skirt suits and taffeta gowns but she has undeniably been peppering some key Diana pieces into her repertoire. Let’s examine the evidence… As she spent the week in NY preparing for her SS18 show, Beckham adopted a simple and easy uniform consisting of high-waisted, dark indigo jeans and a white t-shirt. In itself, that’s a classic 90s Diana ensemble, but the designer made the reference unequivocal when she added a chic lilac blazer to her utilitarian outfit for a post-show dinner with her family. It was date night with David on Monday so Victoria plucked one of the most romantic new pieces from her latest collection for the occasion- a pie-crust collar blouse. Breezy riffs on the ultimate 80s top were also a standout piece at Sunday’s show where they were worn untucked with relaxed flares and slouchy trouser suits. The similarity was unmistakable, even if Diana wore hers more regally,  primly tucked into ladylike skirts. Princess Diana was a stickler for the matchy-matchy look, so often her outfits for public engagements would be accessorised with a bright pair of heels, sometimes with added sparkle. The lilac, cornflower blue and mint green heels which appeared on sunday’s catwalk- and which VB has been wearing herself- wouldn’t have looked out of place in Diana’s own formal wardrobe, while the glittery heels in the collection would have been ideal for state banquets and film premieres. Perhaps one of the best known images of the late Princess is the picture taken when she was working as a nursery school teacher before her marriage, with the sun shining through her delicate summer skirt giving it a translucent look. Earlier in september, Beckham gave the look a power dressing spin by teaming a similarly diaphanous style with a matching blouse and heels. They do say imitation is the sincerest form of flattery.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s safe to say that journalist turned designer JJ Martin is not one for the minimalist, pared-back look. ‘I’ve always been a printaholic, super-pattern-loving maximalist,’ she declares, clad in a floor-length vintage dress and coat that neatly prove her point. ‘You know that moment around 2010 when everyone went minimal with Céline? I didn’t get on that particular train.’ Martin is the exuberant personality behind La DoubleJ, a fashion and lifestyle brand that she launched in 2015 as an online shop, selling vintage clothes and jewellery. Quickly realising that selling vintage is ‘trickier than one would like’, she designed a simple dress in six different vintage prints that she unearthed at the Mantero silk archive in Como, Italy. This capsule collection soon expanded to include skirts, shirts, sweatshirts and outerwear. Most recently, she has added plates and table linens, all emblazoned with vibrant patterns that can be mixed and matched.   She is in London to launch a La DoubleJ pop-up shop at Liberty, which will run until the end of this month, but home is in Milan. Born and brought up in LA, she relocated to Italy in 2001 ‘for love, the biggest cliché’, moving in with her then boyfriend (now husband) Andrea, in his bachelor pad, where they stayed for the next eight years before finding their current apartment. ‘It’s not like New York or London where the market is always moving,’ she says. ‘Great homes in Milan have been in the same family for 300 years, and they’re not selling them. It took forever to find something that would work for us.’ Sixteen years of living in Italy have shaped both Martin’s interior style and her work. ‘I really received my education in furniture and design since living here,’ she says. Her experience as a contributing editor for Harper’s Bazaar and *Wallpaper has also had an impact. Her task with La DoubleJ is to discover the Italian brands that are ‘really deserving and spectacular, but not very well known’ and shine a spotlight on their work. Along with Mantero, she also works with the textile producer, Mascioni and the ceramic company, Bitossi. ‘We’re not a traditional fashion company, and I don’t consider myself a fashion designer. I see myself as more of an editor of the project,’ she says. She is also a scrupulous editor of her home. Maximalist it may be, but cluttered it is not. Everything is carefully chosen, meticulously arranged and regularly reviewed. It took Martin five attempts to decide on the colour of the hallway and office alone: they were chocolate-brown, black, aubergine and suede-lined before she settled on their current incarnation, which she describes as ‘the colour of the sea around the island of Panarea’.  ‘Italians don’t have colour cards,’ she notes, ‘and they don’t follow budgets, schedules or timetables. This was my first experience of relaxing in the creative process. I feel like I learnt.’ The search for furniture, most of which came from flea markets, junk shops and the odd antiques shop, was another learning experience. ‘I had four or five favourite dealers in Milan, and  would visit them on rotation every weekend,’ Martin recalls. ‘I would say,  “I want these chairs. What should I  do with them?” They all had amazing  taste and gave me so many ideas, which  I would go home and put into practice.’ David Hicks prints cover a couple of antique chairs; a pair of colourful paintings by her great-grandmother hang on an equally brightly papered wall, and  a baroque mirror above Martin’s vintage walnut desk is surrounded by simple  drawings, paintings and prints. ‘It’s not  a big, show-offy apartment, but every corner of it is curated,’ says Martin.  Her favourite space, however, is the terrace, which she had restructured three years ago, and which has since been ‘spruced up’ by her old friends, design duo Emiliano Salci and Britt Moran of Dimore Studio. Lined with blue-glass tiles and abundant with jasmine and wisteria, it is a serene, restful space with spectacular views over the city. ‘Milan doesn’t have parks or green spaces, so I really missed the feeling of being in contact with nature,’ says Martin. ‘Creating this space in our own home has changed our lives; I go out there every morning to meditate and do yoga.’  The terrace is also the scene of twice-weekly drinks parties in the summer, while in the winter, they move indoors. Martin will be hosting her customary Thanksgiving dinner for 60 in a couple of weeks’ time. ‘Even if we’re only having eight people over, the mood is always boisterous, vivacious and Italian,’ she says. ‘I prefer that kind of environment.’  ladoublej.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Fashion designer Karl Lagerfeld is suspected of having hidden more than 20 million euros (approximately £15m) from French tax authorities using complex transactions between various companies, L'Express weekly reported Wednesday. French authorities declined to comment citing the privacy of tax affairs. A spokesman for Lagerfeld, who is creative director for French fashion house Chanel and Italian brand Fendi as well as having his own label, also declined to comment when contacted by AFP. French tax authorities "suspect that in the space of six years the man with the ever-present black sunglasses omitted to declare 20 million euros" in France, wrote L'Express. An investigation is allegedly focusing on the 7L bookshop in Paris, which Lagerfeld founded in 1999. According to L'Express, the bookstore houses a photo studio owned by a British-based company, which takes in the revenue from Lagerfeld's photography work. The investigation is allegedly looking at whether the bookstore loses money and thus does not pay taxes. The 82-year-old designer frequently captures the advertising campaigns for both Chanel and Fendi as well as designing the brand’s collections. In 2013 he staged an exhibition of his work in Paris, displaying a broad range of screen prints, digital prints and Polaroid transfers.   The news weekly said French tax authorities suspect the foreign transactions allowed the "concealing of the undeclared professional activity" of Lagerfeld as a photographer. French authorities are also said to be interested in the activities of two property investment companies and a tax adjustment Lagerfeld received in the 1990s. Last year, Lagerfeld revealed that his beloved cat, Choupette, had made 3 million euros through modelling assignments. Lagerfeld isn’t the only designer to have his finances probed: Italian designers Stefano Gabbana and Domenico Dolce were cleared of tax evasion charges in 2014 after a lengthy courtroom battle. They were convicted in June 2013 on charges of having failed to file tax declarations for a Luxembourg-based company that, according to prosecutors, was meant to evade taxes that the company should have paid in Italy.  Following Saturday's news that the Duchess of Cambridge would appear on the cover of British Vogue's centenary issue, today sees the magazine go on sale in selected newsagents.  As well as three additional portraits by British photographer Josh Olins, the feature includes an account of how the shoot and cover came together as a collaboration with the National Portrait Gallery (of which the Duchess is a patron) from British Vogue editor, Alexandra Shulman.  Here's what we learnt. "She didn't want to dressed as a fashion plate and was not keen to be shot in gala gowns and tiaras," writes Shulman of the Duchess's stipulations for the shoot to be understated. Instead the mood was to be relaxed and focused on the countryside-loving, private-side of the Duchess and her life in Norfolk.  We already knew that the Duchess's signature high/low mix of labels was a theme which ran into the Vogue shoot; in one of the shots released already she wears a striped Petit Bateau top while in another it's a Burberry trench. But the mix becomes even more intriguing in the rest of the images thanks to Vogue's fashion director Lucinda Chambers. A shirt by traditionally British brand Cabbages and Roses is worn with a skirt by up-and-coming London Fashion Week label, Le Kilt. The Duchess wore a Le Kilt skirt to an engagement in February, so might have decided to incorporate designer Samantha McCoach's work into her wardrobe after the Vogue shoot.  Shulman writes that the wardrobe gathered for the shoot was very much inspired by what the Duchess "likes to wear when she is off-duty- jeans, shirts, t-shirts. The same as the rest of us." We wonder though whether flared dungarees are really part of the Duchess's everyday repertoire? In one image she wears a pair of indigo overalls by AG Jeans - the same denim brand which last year collaborated with Alexa Chung - which are currently on sale for £312.38. Given that her work is often seen on shoots for avant-garde titles such as Dazed or with youth brands like Calvin Klein Jeans, Branka was a clever choice - getting across The Duchess's freshness with lighter than usual eyeliner and blusher. If Vogue were able to tempt the Duchess into experimenting with make-up, her hair remained in the hands of Amanda Tucker, the Duchess's personal hairdresser. Kate arrived on the shoot wearing a parka, with her hair already in rollers. Shulman explains that despite this being her first magazine shoot, the Duchess "scarcely" checked herself in the mirror and expressed no concerns about her appearance.  It's perhaps proof of her bona fide royal status after five years of marriage to Prince William that the Duchess has no need of a phone like the rest of us. "While everyone else constantly checked their phones she never brought hers out, not once." All of which means the Duchess will have missed the frenzied reaction online to her newfound status as Vogue cover girl.  Leave the “I voted” stickers and candidate badges to the amateurs. When the most committed Hillary Clinton supporters head to the polls to vote in the US presidential election today, you will know them by their pantsuits. Early Tuesday morning, American women began sharing photos of themselves (and their daughters) wearing pantsuits on the way to the voting booths. It’s likely that many of them are members of Pantsuit Nation, a ‘secret,’ invitation-only Facebook group that has attracted more than 2.5 million members in under three weeks. “Wear a pantsuit on November 8. You know why,” the group tagline reads. OFFICIAL "PANTSUIT POWER" FLASH MOB FOR HILLARY from Celia & Mia for HRC on Vimeo. Or perhaps their outfits were inspired by Pantsuit Power, a video of a jubilant flash mob of 200 dancers in New York’s Union Square. The dancers wore (surprise, surprise) pantsuits, some of which were furnished by Topshop. Even naked-dress devotee Beyonce has embraced the style. The singer wore a Givenchy by Riccardo Tisci pantsuit to perform at a pro-Clinton concert on Friday night. Her backup dancers donned simpler MObama-blue suits, worn over custom “I’m with her” t-shirts. It’s not just a case of women rummaging through the backs of their wardrobes, either. Searches for women’s pantsuits on shopping site Lyst have risen by 460% since January - a “massive resurgence” that has “confounded expectations”, says Lyst Editorial Director Katherine Ormerod, particularly since many shoppers have searched for pantsuits in unseasonal white. (Many viewed Clinton's choice of a white pantsuit to accept her nomination as a subtle tribute to the Suffragettes.) Not so recently, trouser suits were easy to write off as sartorial crutches for female heads of state and executives keen to broadcast their ability to compete in a man’s world. But in an election in which the fashion statements could have started and ended with Trump's obnoxious "make America great again" trucker hats, pantsuits have come to symbolise alignment with a whole spectrum of feminist and pro-Clinton values. Part of the rise of the pantsuit comes down to comparison. Nothing could be farther from the kept-woman associations of Melania Trump’s nipped, tucked, hobbling dresses than a suit cut to let its wearer stride across a rally stage. And no doubt Clinton is aware of pantsuits’ legacy as a uniform for women’s liberation. In 1910, the American Ladies’ Tailors’ Association created what it called the “suffragette suit”: a blouse, jacket and ankle-length divided skirt that permitted the wearer to take long, forceful strides on the road to voting rights. Long after women gained the right to vote (in 1920), they were still required to wear dresses or skirts on the floor of the US Senate. That rule stood until 1993, when Senators Barbara Mikulski and Carol Moseley Braun led a “pantsuit rebellion” that brought about amendments to the official dress code. Clinton, of course, would have watched that rebellion from the White House. Since then she has embraced and encouraged her association with the once-derided style. The candidate’s first Instagram post, from June 2015, featured a rail of red, white and blue pantsuits, captioned with “Hard choices” (also the title of her bestselling memoir). Her Twitter bio reads, “Wife, mom, grandma, women+kids advocate, FLOTUS, Senator, SecState, hair icon, pantsuit aficionado, 2016 presidential candidate.” She has worn Ralph Lauren Collection pantsuits for key campaign events, and an official campaign t-shirt featuring a rainbow of pantsuits sold out before election day. An Instagram account, @hillarystreetstyle, juxtaposes selections from Clinton’s vast archive of pantsuit photos with images of celebrities - David Bowie, Amal Clooney, Gigi Hadid - in similar designs. With the tenor of public debate about this election reaching ever more rancorous, hostile lows, it’s no wonder Clinton would seek to let her clothes do at least some of the talking. If election-day Instagramming is any barometer, American women hear her, loud and clear.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Phoebe Philo, the designer who has arguably redefined how women dress in the past decade, is departing the French fashion house Celine after months of speculation that her resignation was imminent.  From streamlined, architectural handbags to minimalist tailoring and ugly-chic shoes, Philo's artfully modern influence made fashion grow up and speak to grown-ups. If you have taken to wearing trainers for anything other than the gym, reframed Birkenstocks as an acceptable summer staple or  lusted after a navy-only wardrobe, then it is Philo you have to thank. Her decision to cast then 80 year-old author Joan Didion as the face of  Celine's Spring 2015 campaign was instrumental in ushering in a new era of appreciation for older women and their style in the fashion industry.  Philo's pared-back personal style and cool demeanour created a cult following which meant the bows she took at the end of her shows were as highly anticipated as the collections themselves. When she wore a pair of Adidas Stan Smith trainers at the end of the Spring Summer 2011 show, they became a fashion must-have within months. To this day, they endure as a quiet statement of thoughtful style. Subtle style ticks beloved of a certain tribe of fashionable women, like tucking hair into polo necks, originated with Philo. As Victoria Beckham evolved her design label from its initial tight edit of bodycon dresses, her collections frequently nodded to the Celine look with critics drawing comparisons between her designs and Celine's streamlined blazers, wide-legged trousers and relaxed silk shirts. Beckham has also been a regular advocate of the hair tucking thing.  Bags are the lifeblood of any design house and Philo succeeded in introducing several styles which were catnip to Celine acolytes. The small cross-body Trio is a sleek new classic beloved of women who might usually reject the notion of an It bag while the wing-sided Phantom is devoid of overt branding but has become instantly recognisable.  Celine in the Philo era has been as expensive as it looked- prices rarely dipped below £1000 and a good coat could cost upwards of £3000. But there were plenty of ways to 'get the look' on the high street. Intepretations of Celine catwalk pieces, from abstract-print dresses to high-vamp heels, would appear in Zara or Topshop within weeks of appearing on the catwalk while the likes of Cos and Joseph offered the same luxuriously simple look at a fraction of the cost.  Beyond her covetable designs and personal aesthetic, Philo represented a new era of the female designer- a woman designing for women, and placing her role as mother as highly as that of creative director. Her contract at Celine was negotiated to allow her to spend time with her children and the Autumn 2012 show was cancelled to relieve pressure when she was expecting her third child.  “Working with Céline has been an exceptional experience for me these last 10 years," Philo said in a statement seen by WWD.  "I am grateful to have worked with an incredibly talented and committed team and I would like to thank everyone along the way who has been part of the collaborations and conversations… it’s been amazing.” She will show her last collection at Paris fashion week in March. The fashion industry rumour mill has pointed to 44-year-old Philo as a likely successor to Christopher Bailey at Burberry but, according to WWD, she 'will not work for another label in the near future'. That may not rule her out at Burberry though, as Bailey is set to continue working with the company in some capacity until the end of 2018.  When Philo, whose star had risen during her five-years creative director at Chloe between 2001 and 2006, was appointed to revive Celine in 2008, the house had barely been a presence on the fashion scene since Michael Kors' tenure in the Nineties. LVMH, the conglomerate which owns the house, transformed working practices and moved the atelier to from Paris to London to accommodate Philo's desire to be based with her family.  Although financial results for Celine alone are not available, Philo is thought to have helped fuel a rise in sales from €200 million to more than €700 million. According to insiders, Philo has been less present at Celine's headquarters over the past year, allowing her design team to take a more prominent role. Whether they will continue to design in her spirit or be led by a new tastemaking personality remains to be seen. But Philo will be hard to beat.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Another day, another fashion expert who is keen to make clear exactly how they feel about Melania Trump’s style. But this time it’s not another designer who is keen to state whether or not they will be hoping to dress the new First Lady. Today’s opinions come from André Leon Talley, American Vogue’s outspoken Contributing Editor, one of the stars of The September Issue and the man who accompanied Melania to Paris on a shopping trip to the couture shows to find her wedding dress for a 2005 Vogue feature. “Get ready for super-cinched waists, hourglass silhouettes and pencil skirts,” he told the New York Times. “She is already into one-shoulder, which Jackie Kennedy wore by Oleg Cassini. Melania likes monotone matching coats and beige dresses, but that hair will always be flying once she goes down the stairs of Air Force One.” “She has those impossibly high four-inch, towering stilettos,” he continued. “Clearly, her clothes will cling in the right places, accentuate her figure and her model-style long tresses.” Leon Talley then went on to accuse the new first lady of “trying too hard” when she chose to wear a Ralph Lauren jumpsuit on election night and suggesting that her hair needs an “upgrade”. “[She] opted at 3 a.m. for a palazzo jumpsuit, with one arm exposed and a flounce over the other — it seemed to me too Mar-a-Lago, a huge, full-volume jumpsuit. Trying too hard,” he said. “And I am so tired of the long hair falling on both sides of her face. She has to upgrade her coiffure.” The 67 year-old esteemed fashion editor’s opinions may seem cutting, but taking guidance from his influential voice could actually be a wise move for Melania. Leon Talley’s career began in 1974 when he worked for $50 a week at Andy Warhol’s Interview magazine, and he subsequently rose through the ranks at trade bible Women’s Wear Daily and W magazine, before landing at American Vogue in 1983. In 2008, alongside his work for the magazine, he became a fashion advisor to Michelle Obama and introduced her to the young New York designer Jason Wu, who she went on to buy dozens of dresses from during her husband’s administration, including her inauguration ball gown. By arranging this kind of exposure for Wu, whose work was a relatively unknown before his hit at the inauguration, Leon Talley has undoubtedly had a hand in launching the then-26-year-old’s fashion empire, now reportedly worth $10million. Likewise, by setting up a relationship between Mrs Obama and a hot new name on the scene, André also upped the style credentials of the new First Lady and paved the way for the myriad of fashion hits to come. Michelle has, as we all know, been one of the most stylish FLOTUSes in history, wearing labels from Preen to Versace. So does he want to do the same for Melania Trump? André’s friends, the designers Tom Ford and Marc Jacobs, have already refused to dress her because of her husband’s principles and policies, so surely he would have his work cut out if he wanted to get some good brands on side? He knew Melania well before her husband ran for president but realised how divisive it could be to say that he found her “a wonderful person to be with” when he gave a comment to a tabloid reporter, and several friends and colleagues got in contact to swear at him for supporting the “Evil Empire”. “She’s a nice person. I do not endorse Trumpism on any level,” he explains of the comments in this interview. “So why can’t one be positive and want her to shine? I mean, it’s good she cares about napkins, crystal, dinner plates with gilded edges to the point of over the top, and abundant flower arrangements.” “In the end, why pick on her when they should be picking on her husband’s billionaire cabinet and his seeming readiness to turn the country back towards oppression, anti-Semitism, anti-culturalism, etc.” “She’s very private… I don’t think that she would try to change the White House in any way. I don’t think that’s what she’s interested in.” American Vogue officially endorsed Hillary Clinton during her campaign (the first time in history that the magazine has ever backed a candidate) and Leon Talley’s boss Anna Wintour furiously raised funds for the Democrat, who she called “optimistic, forward-looking, and modern” in her editor’s letter. But Vogue is now having to come to terms with the Trump result and just last week Anna was spotted meeting with her old friend Donald at Trump Tower, perhaps attempting to build some bridges. “As for Anna Wintour going to Mr. Trump, she’s a powerful woman, she’s running an empire, she’s the editorial director of Condé Nast,” Leon Talley said of the Vogue editor. “We can’t judge her for going to a meeting. She’s a professional, powerful woman. That’s all I have to say.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  News that Burberry is to replace its outgoing Chief Design Officer Christopher Bailey with Riccardo Tisci broke while a large group of fashion journalists were on the Eurostar to Paris on Thursday to see the shows there. A deep pall of gloom descended on the carriage. It’s not that the 43 year old Tisci isn’t talented – some of his collections at Givenchy, where he reigned for 12 years were beautiful. But his aesthetic – extremely etiolated models draped in fabulously expensive neo-Goth outfits à la Lisbeth Salander in The Girl with The Dragon Tattoo – is hardly inclusive. At least not in the way that fashion is now beginning to talk about inclusivity – in terms of making clothes for women of all shapes and sizes. Nor could it be further in spirit  from the soft, Modern British Heritage tradition that fuelled Burberry’s tremendous renaissance over the 17 years that Bailey was in charge. In fairness, Tisci, who in person is smart and charming, may be capable of a much richer, broader purview than the one he repeatedly rehearsed at Givenchy. In the past, he has lived in the UK (working for Monsoon) so understands at least some of its foibles. He was also an early champion of gender diversity, championing the transgender model Lea T. It’s worth remembering too, that while he was at Givenchy he transformed a small, ailing house – albeit one with a famous name – into a thriving concern. Much of its income was derived from sales of t-shirts and collaborations with sneakers brands such as Nike, but what else was Tisci to do. “When I first arrived at Givenchy, there was barely a working photocopier” he once told me. He left there last year amid expectation that he would take over at Versace, whose rock-and-raunchy sensibility seemed a natural fit with his own (he is best friends with Kim Kardashian West and Kanye West) and where Donatella Versace had always been a loyal supporter. But they couldn’t agree terms and that deal fizzled. So now Burberry… where he could do wonderful things with the trench coat, which has always been Burberry’s central pillar. His cutting, tailoring and know-how with leather is impressive. He can also do wonderfully filmy, delicate chiffon blouses and dresses when he turns his mind to it. And while he was at Givenchy, there were a couple of years when its Antigona bag was a must-have – the kind of outcome for which all fashion brands, including Burberry, pray, but rarely achieve. The £719-million-a-year Burberry, whose sales are down, could really do with some hit accessories. But does it need Tisci? The industry had been hoping for Phoebe Philo. The Brit turned Celine into a powerhouse – and the label to which women of all budgets looked for inspiring clothes they could also wear. Even if they couldn’t afford Celine’s stratospheric prices, they knew the high street would produce myriad copies: Philo has been one of the most influential designers of the past decade but announced her departure from Celine last December. With Marco Gobbetti, Celine’s former CEO now in charge at Burberry, it was assumed Philo would follow him. But fashion CEOs work in mysterious ways. Gobbetti looked even further back in his career to the time he presided over Givenchy, between 2004 and 2008. So, Tisci it is. It will be an interesting ride. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  From Eva Hertzigova’s traffic stopping ‘Hello Boys’ Wonderbra campaign in 1994, to Kylie Minogue's banned bucking bronco Agent Provocateur ad in 2001, the world of lingerie modelling isn’t without controversy. Which is perhaps why the Victoria & Albert museum landed on the idea for their latest exhibition: Undressed: A Brief History of Underwear. Opening on 16 April, the V&A exhibit promises to explore our own personal relationships with underwear, as well as the huge impact lingerie has had on culture - from sex and gender, to fashion design and fabrication. And no doubt gather huge crowds in the process. But what’s it actually like for a working day to involve reclining in your knickers and getting paid upwards of £10,000 a day? Meet Montreal-born, Hoxton-dwelling Michea Crawford (30) who has worked as a lingerie model for the past eight years. With her 34DD chest and 24 inch waist, Crawford segued organically from fashion, to sportswear, to swimwear and finally underwear modelling. “There just kept being less and less clothes on every shoot I did,” Crawford jokes. Currently at Premier Model Management, and a regular for brands such as ASOS, Agent Provocateaur, Melissa Odabash and Figleaves, Crawford assures us there is a very unglamorous side to the lingerie industry. Firstly, go sees: where models are sent to meet and impress prospective clients. While fashion models can turn up in some unbearably cool ‘model off duty’ leather biker jacket, slub t-shirt and acne boot combination, Crawford’s only sartorial necessity is an impossibly small nude g-string: “If you’re the last girl in a line of eight to try on the sample lingerie set, you don’t want to be caught short without your own pants to wear discreetly underneath,” she explains. Body hair also becomes something of a daily concern. “When girls turn up for a shoot with ingrown hairs or an unkempt bikini line it can really slow things down as the make up artist will have to work on covering up any blemishes. So, you’ve really got to be on top of your grooming game in that area.” You’ve also got to set any personal space boundaries aside as make up artists dab concealer and brush bronzer “in places you never imagined you would need them.” Last minute bookings are a regular occurrence, so keeping in shape is also a prerequisite. Despite working out twice a day and sticking to a healthy diet during her busy periods, a certain amount of pre-shoot anxiety is unavoidable - and there are no shortcuts to getting in shape fast. The desperate pre-shoot regimes employed in the fitness modelling industry (such as downing shots of whiskey to dehydrate the body, or dodging liquids altogether on shoot day), to quickly enhance definition have been well documented, but lingerie models can’t use these tactics. “Once, a fellow model told me to drink gallons of green tea and four shots of vodka the night before a shoot, then drink nothing all day to flatten my stomach, but my face ended up looking dehydrated and tired too. Lingerie models needs to look healthy and pretty as well as fit, so now I just make sure I’m really hydrated the day before, and sip little bits of water on the shoot.” Fashion models may end up wearing some questionable ensembles on shoots, but could anything really compare to nipple tassles and a full chainmail bodysuit? “Weirdly, I feel more exposed in S&M kit than I do when I’m completely naked. I’ve done nude ads for body lotions where I don’t feel self-conscious in the least, but once you’re in a harness and suspenders you feel like there’s a neon sign above your head saying: ‘Look, she’s practically in the buff!’” Playful kink aside, the risk of getting arrested is very real. “We were on location in a very small, affluent town in France and the locals kept calling the police because they thought I was just walking around exposing myself. Every time we saw a squad car, I’d have to throw a t-shirt on and pretend it was a fashion shoot.” Other occupational obstacles include mother nature's insistence in making constant changes to our breast size. Reportedly, they change every six months, but Crawford has missed out on jobs when her breasts have suddenly grown because of hormonal or dietary changes. Her innately adventurous-but-accident-prone persona has also thwarted a few big booking: “I am in and out of bandages almost as often as underwear. I recently broke my foot on a fitness holiday in Thailand and had to cancel a big job back in London because there is no photoshopping that out.” On her days off, Crawford admits she’ll happily chuck on a pair of Primark, white cotton bikini briefs and go about her day. She reserves thongs for the gym, but if she leaves the house, she always packs a nice French knicker just in case her agent calls her in for an impromptu casting. “I’m like keys, check, wallet, check, lace panties, check.”

 Hillary Clinton made history yesterday when she accepted the Democratic presidential nomination. While this moment was about so much more than what she was wearing, Clinton knows that everything down to the colour of her jacket has significance and is an important branding tool to communicate key messages regarding her campaign.  Clinton stepped away from Democrat blue and patriotic red pantsuits that she has favoured throughout the campaign so far, and instead opted for a sharp White-House white suit. It was elegant, sleek and polished, making her look presidential, but the simple white cut and matching top also didn't distract from the thing she wanted the world to focus on: her powerful speech.  She might have opted for white to stand out against the shower of red and blue balloons, knowing that this contrast of colour would give the most impact in the photographs printed in newspapers throughout the globe. However it has also been suggested that the colour white was a nod to her making history as a woman, and getting one step closer to being the first female President of the United States. "What an incredible honor that you have given me, and I can't believe we just put the biggest crack in that glass ceiling yet," Clinton said at the Democratic National Convention in Philadelphia this week. A number of people on Twitter noted that her white pant suit can also be seen as a classic symbol of feminism. The British and American women in the Suffragette movement, who often wore smart outfits in purple, white and green when protesting, used fashion to create a clear, recognisable political identity and to further their cause. White was worn by the Suffragettes to signify purity.  Clinton, as the first major party female nominee, is wearing white, the color of suffragettes. As did Gerry Ferraro in VP speech in 1984. She’s wearing white. #DemsInPhilly pic.twitter.com/qEB9hJqpgZ Whether she intended to reference the Suffragettes or not, there is certainly a marketing strategy to every outfit Hillary Clinton wears during her campaign, devised by the very best in the industry. According to Business of Fashion one of the advisors in camp Clinton orchestrating her image for these key moments is Editor in Chief of American Vogue, Anna Wintour. "On certain occasions, Wintour has approached designers to procure outfits for Clinton, who has settled into a uniform of brightly coloured pantsuits and jackets by US designers. Unlike many celebrities, who are often lent or gifted fashion items, Clinton’s campaign pays for her clothes," reports BoF. She also hired Michelle Obama’s former aide Kristina Schake to help shape her style and image. Hillary Clinton has created a consistent political uniform, wearing block colour trouser suits throughout her presidential campaign. "Far from making her seem trivial, Clinton’s subsequent detours, albeit succinct, into fashion chit-chat have helped her seem more rounded, less touchy," The Telegraph's Fashion Director Lisa Armstrong has argued previously about why we need to accept that what Hillary Clinton wears does matter. "But authentic? Owning her inner bitch ? (Are we really ready to reclaim that word by the way and what would it look like – Cruella de Vil?) Surely for most of us finding a workable mode of power-dressing (and we all need outfits that make us look as though we know what we’re doing) is about accepting that sleight of hand is involved. It’s a question of fixing on an image that looks right and accustomising ourselves to it until it feels right." One woman trying to make a point that we can notice- and comment on- Hillary Clinton's outfit is the owner of the Instagram account @hillarystreetstyle. The Instagrammer, who has chosen to remain anonymous, has poured through the archives to find pictures of Clinton dressed like style icons on the red carpet, including Angelina Jolie, Victoria Beckham, Grace Kelly and more. The Instagrammer explained to Vanity Fair that she hopes that fashion can become an accepted part of our dialogue about politics: “I think hopefully, particularly if she has a second term, maybe she can just wear what she wants for once.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  A model has written an open letter on Facebook after apparently being told by a modelling agency that she was "too big". Charli Howard's response to being pressured by the agency became an online hit, with thousands of people offering their support. Howard, 23, who has modelled for Harper's Bazaar and photographer Rankin, claimed she was told she was "out of shape", despite the fact that she is size 6-8. The agency, which she did not name, apparently suggested she could lose "an inch off [her] hips". WEDDING Howard wrote that the way models are forced to become thinner is making young girls ill. “Here’s a big ---- YOU to my (now ex) model agency, for saying that at 5’ 8” tall and a UK size 6-8 (naturally), I’m ‘too big’ and ‘out of shape’ to work in the fashion industry. I will no longer allow you to dictate to me what’s wrong with my looks and what I need to change in order to be ‘beautiful’ (like losing one ----ing inch off my hips), in the hope it might force you to find me work. “I refuse to feel ashamed and upset on a daily basis for not meeting your ridiculous, unobtainable beauty standards, whilst you sit at a desk all day, shovelling cakes and biscuits down your throats and slagging me and my friends off about our appearance. https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=y6Sxv-sUYtM “The more you force us to lose weight and be small, the more designers have to make clothes to fit our sizes, and the more young girls are being made ill. It’s no longer an image I choose to represent. I cannot miraculously shave my hip bones down. Let’s face the facts: when I was 7 and a half stone, I still wasn’t thin enough for you. When I went to the gym 5 hours a week, you still weren’t finding me work. I can’t win.” Howard later wrote that she had been "blown away by the support and, needless to say, I am slightly overwhelmed by it all". Last month Australian model Rosie Nelson, who is also 23, said that she was told by an agency that she needed to “get down to the bone”. She launched a Government petition that has already got 90,000 signatures to protect vulnerable young men and women in the industry. "I’m a 23-year-old model and I’m a size 8, weighing just 55kg," said Nelson. "But when I walked into one of the UK’s biggest model agencies last year they told me I ticked all the boxes except one - I needed to lose weight. "At the time I just accepted what they said because I’d been modelling for a while and I knew the standard was that we needed to be thin."  We are used to seeing pictures of immaculately dressed people hanging around at fashion week, captured 'waiting for an Uber' or 'rushing into a show', but the street style game at Seoul Fashion Week last week was a little different. The meticulously organised outfits are the same, and the subjects still have the same act-like-you're-not-being-photographed attitude, but in Seoul those being photographed aren't old enough to tie the shoelaces on their Instagrammable trainers.  Clicking on the hashtag #SeoulFashionWeek on Instagram unlocks hundreds of adorable pictures of toddlers in matching outfits outside the shows. Caroline Issa, fashion editor of Tank Magazine, says that they were the main attraction of the week. "It really was those kids who stole the limelight. There are certainly a lot of very very fashion forward little children being dressed up by the mums and thrust into the spotlight outside the shows," she told The Telegraph of one of her instagram posts which got almost 2,000 likes. But just like grown up street style, the pictures aren't as authentic as they may seem. These aren't just children of editors or designers doing a Harper Beckham for the day; many of them are planted outside the shows by brands as part of an Instagram-led marketing strategy.  'A lot of the kids are wearing matching brands when they first come out and then will change after an hour to another brand' "There are definitely more this year," says street style photographer Alex Finch, who has covered the Seoul shows for years. "I think they know that people will take their picture and seeing as most of them are wearing items from local online kids stores, it's a good way for them to get promotion for the brands, as well as the 'models' themselves." It's no coincidence that so many of the children were wearing New Balance trainers, sporty bombers and baseball caps. "There were plenty of mothers there but the show is definitely run by the online shopping mall photographers and stylists," Finch explains. "The brand, 'MLB' [which sells baseball merchandise] had a special team of brand marketers accompany two of the children as they were promoting the brand specifically. Everything is planned before they come out. A lot of the kids are wearing matching brands when they first come out and then will change after an hour into another brand." British fashion blogger Susie Lau, who was also at Seoul Fashion Week this season, felt uncomfortable witnessing the toddler street style scene. "It was so weird because they'd be like quite normally dressed parents (not that trendy looking), bringing their kids trussed up in these uber trendy, super co-ordinated outfits," she tells The Telegraph. "And they'd be telling their kids to do cute things like pose, eat potato chips or play with their toys and generally play up to the cameras." Lau says the children would be surrounded by anywhere up to 30 photographers at one time. "There was one point where there'd be five or six of them all lined up against the concrete ramp and the photographers would just go along and shoot them all like a red carpet line-up step and repeat," she recalls. "I found it a bit disturbing to be honest." Caroline Issa thought Seoul's toddlers were more cute than cringe, but agreed that after a while the pint-size fashion week peacocking lost it's appeal. "These kids were adorable and seemed used to the spotlight, but I think even with adults, after a while of getting photographed you get bored and  the kids seemed more interested in playing on the sidewalks."  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  On Wednesday evening, Jasmine Tookes will take to the Victoria's Secret catwalk in Paris wearing the $3million Fantasy bra which forms the pinnacle of the annual underwear spectacular. In previous years, the honour has fallen to the likes of British model Lily Aldridge and Brazillian supers Gisele Bunchden, Adriana Lima and Alessandra Ambrosio. Tookes is, of course, as toned and gorgeous as her preternaturally sleek predecessors, but her appointment as this year's Fantasy bra wearer has marked a change in message of glitz, glamour and perfection that has long become associated with the Victoria's Secret Angels.  When  the brand unveiled Tookes as the wearer of the Fantasy bra, images from the photo shoot showed her posing on a luscious velvet sofa in knickers and said bra - which is crafted from 9000 gemstones and is so heavy it has required her to do specific back-strengthening exercises. So far, so your-average-underwear-shoot. But from some angles, the images revealed faint stretch marks on Tookes' upper thighs. While neither Tookes or Victoria's Secret made any public statement, the images seemed to be a tacit recognition that, yes, even supermodels aren't entirely perfect and a nod, maybe, to the body positive, anti-Photoshop movement which has taken hold over the past few years.  Tookes is also the first black woman to be chosen to model the bra in nine years after Selita Ebanks and Tyra Banks (who Tookes cites as an inspiration) were chosen in the earlier years of the show. "I feel like it's such a milestone for Victoria's Secret to have a woman of colour wearing the fantasy bra, because there's only been two in the past," Tookes told Fashionista in October. "It's major, and I think it's awesome I get to represent that." This weekend, Tookes - who has African, European, Brazilian and West Indian roots -  was also forced to defend herself on Instagram and Twitter after she was accused of bleaching her skin. “First of all. Lighting is everything and not to mention I’m way darker in the summer and much lighter towards the winter my skin tone changes all the time just like everyone else,” Tookes wrote. On Twitter, she added "Just CRAZY!!! I love my skin! It’s my favorite thing about myself ❤️." Born in Huntington Beach, California, Tookes was first discovered when she accompanied her mother - the celebrity stylist Cary Robinson - on a photo shoot. She has walked in shows for Burberry, Stella McCartney, Yves Saint Laurent and Prada (among many more) and has been part of the Victoria's Secret line-up since 2012. The 25 year-old has also starred in campaigns for Jimmy Choo, Ralph Lauren and DKNY, recently appearing with her 7 year-old sister in J.Crew's seasonal catalogue.  While Tookes might not be quite as well known as some of her Fantasy bra-wearing predecessors - despite her 1.4 million Instagram followers - it seems that she may, unwittingly perhaps, have the power to use her Victoria's Secret role to break down preconceptions and add a dose of reality to a show which can sometimes seem to be all about impossible-to-achieve perfection. The Victoria's Secret models are all open about the level of training which they embrace to hone their show-ready bodies, another aspect of the role which Tookes is proud to talk about; "I love being able to share with people how to be healthy and take care of their bodies," she said to Fashionista. "A lot of my fans will say, 'Thank you so much, I got into working out because of you,' and I love that because I love being able to motivate people."  Tookes grew up playing volleyball and softball, and spent ten years practising gymnastics but in an early interview in her career, from 2011, she was vague about her commitments to healthy living, just saying that 'yoga could possibly be in my future'. She also shrugged off any notions of a healthy diet, telling The Cut: "I hate to say this, but I'm one of those people with an extremely fast metabolism.  I eat, eat, eat, and yet I can’t seem to gain any weight.   Lobster and crabs are favorites. Also, I LOVE pizza … I think I could eat pizza every day." A clue as to how she'll be celebrating after the VS show finale?   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Christmas jumpers tend to be novelty kitsch items, rather than something you'd like to wear when you don't have a mince pie in your hand; but this year a host of models have made it their mission to give Christmas jumpers a stylish makeover. For Save the Children's annual Christmas Jumper Day the charity has teamed up with a number of fashion faces and the label Selfish Mother, founded by blogger Molly Gunn, to create festive knitwear with a contemporary edge. Rather than nostalgic intarsia jumpers, these are minimal sweatshirts in black, grey and navy with tongue in cheek metallic slogans on the front. Models Poppy Delevingne, David Gandy, Jon Kortajarena, Karen Elson, Laura Bailey, Erin O'Connor and Immy Waterhouse have each worked on designing their own sweatshirt and, of course, have all been photographed in the jumpers, proving these are pieces you'll want to wear come December. Poppy Delevingne's slogan is 'Cracker,' Immy Waterhouse's is 'Baubles', Erin O'Connor's is 'Off Duty Elf', Karen Elson's is 'Sparkle' and David Gandy's - the cheekiest of all - is 'Nutcracker'. When paired with a pleated skirt or worn over a ruffled high collar shirt, these jumpers wouldn't look out of place at any Christmas party.  This year Christmas Jumper is on 16th December, but the sweatshirts have just gone on sale on Selfish Mother's website. The unisex jumpers are £45 and the children's versions are £20, and 50% from each sweatshirt will be donated to Save the Children.  That money will help Save The Children in a number of ways. "Money raised from the sale of the sweaters could help Save the Children give children living in a refugee camp clothes to keep them warm through winter or buy nutritious food for their entire family," says the charity's Head of PR, Helena Wiltshire. "It could also help us to bring essentials like healthcare, education, protection and food to the millions of children around the world who are missing out on the most basic support. All this, just by wearing a sweater – it’s a very silly way to solve some very serious problems!" This isn't the first time that Save the Children has tried to give Christmas Jumper Day a fashionable slant. Last year the charity teamed up with a host of fashion personalities including Kate Moss, Bella Freud, Erin O’Connor and Henry Holland to create chic festive jumpers.
