 Welcome to the first edition of our new She Wears It Well feature: a regular dose of inspiration devoted to our favourite stylish women. We'll discover how they make their look work, and what the rest of us can learn from their stylish approaches. We’re kicking off with four women from very different professions, who reveal how they master a 12-hour working wardrobe.  47-year-old Clare Hornby,  founder of clothing brand Me+Em, gets through her working week by steering clear of heels and investing in flattering trousers.  Wool stripe jumper, £119, Me+Em;  jersey layering shirt, £79, Me+Em; leather wide leg pant, £399, Me+Em; reversible strap saddle bag, £269, Me + Em; Shoes, Clare’s own 1. Always ask yourself ''is a trend flattering?'' The side stripe trouser trend is good because they slim your legs. I can't stand things that don't make you taller, slimmer, longer.  2. Look for brands that invest in fabric and cut and for pieces that are both functional and comfortable, that move with the body rather than against it. If these pieces are machine washable, even better. 3. If you like colour, wear a bright shade away from your face by layering it over a blouse with a high collar. You'll find you can wear tones you have previously ruled out. The Me+Em layering shirt is good for this.  4. Employ little twists that keep your look contemporary. A smart white trainer and a wide leg trousers are perfect for this, without making you feel as though you've over done it. 5. Sometimes a slightly trendier bag worn with a classic suit will give your outfit that edge you're looking for.  44-year-old Vice President of Marketing for jewellery brand Pandora and mum of two, Jo Glynn-smith, has one key rule when it comes to workwear: be yourself.  Electra cotton blouse, £380, Anna Mason; Carmen cotton skirt £380, Anna Mason; sterling silver birthstone ring stack, £40 each, Pandora; sterling silver blue & turquoise enamel ring stack, £55 each, Pandora; grey boots, Jimmy Choo (Jo's own) 1. People get very flustered about workwear. It’s a bit like going to a wedding and overthinking it so much that you end up looking like someone else’s mum. You should just be yourself. 2. Nike Courtez are my go-to, I have three pairs of the same black and white style. 4. Amy Schumer settles into Wintour's pristine office in One Trade Centre, wearing her signature Vogue uniform- a floral fitted dress, black-out sunglasses, a pearl necklace and a coffee cup bigger than her head. She might have the Wintour wardrobe down, but Schumer finds selecting pieces from the clothes rail and eating a green leaf for lunch much harder than she anticipated. In an unlikely twist however, it turns out that Anna Wintour is a stand-up pro, as there is the sound of canned laughter when she asks the audience at an open mic night: "Is anybody here on a first date? Last date?" She also manages to squeeze in a Game of Thrones joke as she exclaims "Wintour is coming" before doing a dramatic mic drop.  For Amy Schumer's cover of the July issue she is photographed by Annie Leibovitz in a red off-the-shoulder Dolce and Gabbana gown. The actress might be on the cover of the most prestigious glossy fashion magazine, but in her accompanying interview she maintains that she has very little interest in the industry. “I don’t think it’s stupid; there’s no moral reasoning,” she says. “It’s just not my thing … I just have this sense of entitlement that I should be able to feel comfortable at all times, like I could go to bed at any moment in what I’m wearing.” But it's not all jokes, as the star also reveals her vulnerable side opening up about how she copes with the enormous personal criticism she receives online. "Some days there will be a bunch of websites dedicated to trying to get me to just shut my mouth, or I’ll walk into a greenroom and someone had a caricature artist draw me and it’s with a martini glass, looking like a linebacker with Jay Leno’s chin," she tells the magazine. "That can get to me. I’m not without that vulnerability.” "I’m so sorry to disappoint anyone who thinks I walk around at all times with a margarita in one hand and a dildo in the other," she continues.  To have one designer leave a major house in a week is unfortunate. To have two up sticks…Six days after Raf Simons and Dior announced that they would be parting company, the announcement came from Alber Elbaz that he was leaving Lanvin. Inevitably the rumour mill has clicked into overtime since the news was made official on Wednesday evening. Was Elbaz leaving for Dior? Perhaps. Creatively he is certainly capable of doing the job. Even though Lanvin’s profile has dipped slightly in the past two or three years, it’s worth recalling that when Elbaz joined it in 2001, the house was, as he later put it “a sleeping beauty”. That was stating the situation kindly. As a fashion house, Lanvin was almost moribund, having been owned previously by L’Oréal, which understands how to sell perfumes, but not how to make clothes that induce women to spend thousands of pounds. Elbaz, intelligent, witty, thoughtful, laconic, gifted, did. Within a year the Israeli designer had transformed Lanvin into the hottest name in fashion– inventing a new sartorial language for it and in the process, turning it into a cynosure for all that was most desirable, elegant and modern in clothing. His speciality was making clothes fluid and comfortable yet graceful – and reviving the dress. Bypassing sketches, he worked directly on the body, folding and draping onto his mannequins, but mainly eliminating. Seams, restrictive internal construction, extraneous darts, even conventional finishes (he is master of the raw edge) were methodically subtracted in the quest a refined, polished yet subtly disheveled ease– a fashion paradox that proved irresistible and one which Phoebe Philo would, in her own way, explore when she arrived at Céline in 2008. If Céline has been the aspirational guide for stylish women over the past five years, Lanvin occupied that role for the best part of 10 years - as evinced by H&M inviting the label to collaborate with it in 2010. It may still be size XS next to Dior, with annual revenues recently estimated by Women’s Wear Daily at £250 million compared with Dior’s most recent haul of £1.9 billion, but like Céline, Lanvin has been hugely influential. Also like Céline, it charges more than you ever thought conceivable for ready-to-wear. As Elbaz explained to me recently “a lot of labels now don’t have in-house ateliers, so they’ll do a sketch and send it off somewhere in the world to be made and they don’t have much control. For months and months, we sit in front of the mirror and we find that volume. Then we shorten it. We lengthen it...in that sense the ready-to-wear is like a couture collection. That’s what we do at Lanvin. We do couture at ready-to-wear prices. If there’s a red coat, and I do it in black, we have to change the whole thing otherwise it doesn’t work.” Not that he was complaining. As he wrote in his recently published Manifest, a book of his musings, “I prefer evolution, things move gradually”.  Note that word evolution. In the contexts of his and Simons’ retreat from two major houses, it is explosive, for evolution is precisely not what designers are allowed to engage in these days. With a minimum of six collections a year (two ready to wear, two couture, two “pre”) and all their accessory lines, they have become conveyor belts of design sound-bites. The relentless hunger for (perceived) newness that consumes almost all of us means the gestation period once allowed for new ideas has evaporated. The medium (be it Instagram, Snapchat, Periscope) is more important than the message, which is merely a means to selling more accessories. “Oh those ***** bags,” lamented one designer to me recently, driven to distraction by the demands of his shareholders. And the industry wonders why so little of what appears on the catwalk is wearable or even desirable. Ever since John Galliano’s meltdown and subsequent firing from Dior in 2011 and Marc Jacobs departure from Louis Vuitton in 2013 there have been periodic rumblings that the top jobs are becoming untenable. Do other major industries have such a speedily revolving door where their chief creative are involved? The last time I interviewed Elbaz – earlier this year, when we met to discuss the history of Lanvin exhibition he curated in Paris - he seemed a little weary of the reductive interpolations of some retailers. It’s not that he doesn’t appreciate that fashion is a business – he cut his teeth working in New York’s Garment District – but he hates it when merchants use previous numbers to (under) estimate what women will want. The truth is, no one ever knows what’s going to sell, he told me. “So when the merchants say they want pink for Dallas, red for New York, black for Paris,” he ignores them. “I recently designed some dresses that were so floaty and voluminous I almost didn’t bother to show them. I thought no one would order them. They sold out”. What differentiates Simons’ and Elbaz’s respective departures however is the expression of the rupture. Whereas Simons and Dior were at pains to define the decision as mutual – they had “failed” to reach agreement on a new contract - Elbaz made it clear, in the communication he sent out on Wednesday evening, that he had been let go. “At this time of my departure from Lanvin at the decision of the company’s majority shareholder,” he wrote, “I would like to express my gratitude and warm thoughts to all who have worked with me passionately on the revival of Lanvin over the last fourteen years”. That majority shareholder would be Mrs Shaw-Lan Wang, the Taiwanese magnate who first appointed him. So, to return to that original question? Are Simons’ and Elbaz’s exits connected? There’s no doubt Elbaz, who was briefly creative director at YSL and before that worked for seven years for the exacting Geoffrey Beene, could do it. His is not the only name in the ring though. Phoebe Philo has inevitably been suggested – although it seems highly unlikely that she would trade her role at Céline and a work-life balance that enables to spend a chunk of her time in Somerset, for the pressures of the top job at Dior. For that matter, would 54-year-old Elbaz want it?  He doesn’t have his own label to fall back on, unlike Simons. But even so – would he welcome the pressure, or see it as an invigorating challenge? The bigger question perhaps, is why would there be any doubt? The Dior job is the biggest and arguably one of the most prestigious, in fashion. The fact that anyone might not want it - or any of the other stellar positions that come up - suggests something may be rotten in the state of fashion.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  16 year-old Kim Turnbull has signed with respected London modelling agency Select Model Management, making her the latest teenager to join the new-generation London Fashion Week set. It’s thought that the signing was made primarily off the back of Turnbull’s Instagram pictures (gone are the days when a model’s only chance of getting scouted was to hang around nonchalantly at a shopping centre) and also following a series of starter shoots with Illustrated People (an of-the-moment streetwear brand based in East London), Puma and i-D magazine. Turnbull, whose streetwise sense of personal style has already attracted over 5,000 followers to her Instagram page, is believed to be dating Rocco Ritchie, the 16 year-old son of Guy Ritchie and Madonna, after he made a permanent move to London in the summer following a lengthy custody battle between his parents. In the last week, Kim has shared several pictures of herself, Rocco, Madonna and his siblings skiing in Verbier, and she has previously been spotted by overzealous paparazzi going for coffee with Ritchie and his best friend Brooklyn Beckham on many occasions. The couple have also, however, been savvy networkers attending several high profile fashion parties together last season, including a LOVE Magazine and Marc Jacobs-hosted bash, and a Dazed & Confused party in association with Calvin Klein, giving them the opportunity to meet influential editors like LOVE’s Katie Grand. We’ll expect to see Turnbull following in the footsteps of Cara Delevingne, Kendall Jenner and Kaia Gerber in becoming Grand’s next model protegee, then? Kim’s own family tree is full of creatives too; her grandfather was the lauded Scottish sculptor William Turnball and her grandmother was Kim Lim, the Singaporean artist, after whom she is named. Her father and uncle, Johnny and Alex Turnbull, were in the post-punk band 23 Skidoo, and Johnny produced the 2011 documentary about his father’s work, Beyond Time, which Jude Law narrated. Kim has already made her runway debut, walking in the Maharishi show at the London Collections: Men last January. But after signing with Select, which also manages the careers of Daisy Lowe, Sam Rollinson and Amanda De Cadenet, it’s likely that she’ll make an exclusive appearance for a major designer at the upcoming fashion weeks in February, no doubt leading to a subsequent lucrative campaign deal. Select’s strategic handling of their new client Sofia Richie, daughter of Lionel Richie, for example, saw her shoot from relative obscurity to become an Instagram star with over 1.8 million followers, making her catwalk debut at Chanel, all in the last six months. Dolce and Gabbana, too, released their SS17 campaign imagery yesterday starring 20 year-old actress and social media sensation Zendaya, as well as half a dozen other teenagers with celebrity parents and freshly-inked modelling contracts, including Presley Gerber (son of Cindy Crawford and Randy Gerber) plus Rafferty Law (son of Jude Law and Sadie Frost). Over the next few years some will no doubt break off to become actors, designers, photographers and more, but one thing is for sure right now; the next fashion generation is coming of age - and 2017 is their breakthrough moment.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  While it has become as much the norm for pageboys and bridesmaids to be dressed down in linen shirts and Converse trainers in recent years, Pippa Middleton opted for very traditional outfits for the gorgeous gaggle of children who acted as her attendants for her wedding to James Matthews on Saturday.  The wedding party, which included Countess Philippa Hoyos, Lily French, Avia Horner and Princess Charlotte as bridesmaids and Casimir Tatos, Edward Sebire, William Ward and Prince George as pageboys all wore bespoke outfits by Pepa & Co.  Pepa Gonzalez, the founder and designer of the childrenswear label which is renowned for its classic designs, created a series of ivory and gold looks.  The boys were dressed in classic gold knickerbockers with cummerbunds and double-breasted shirts while the girls wore full-skirted dresses complete with sash and bow with frill detailling at the collar and sleeves.  All the children wore pale shoes and white socks or tights. They carried baskets filled with petals and floral rings while the little girls wore floral head dresses.   "It was such an honour for me to be part of it all," Gonzalez said on Instagram. "I will always have fond memories of this project, and feel so lucky to have designed these outfits for the most adorable and sweet group of children." Savvily, Gonzalez has now launched a collection of pageboy and bridesmaid looks which are remarkably similar to the looks made for Middleton's wedding. The line- released just hours after the adorable pictures of George, Charlotte and co were beamed around the world- includes £94 silk knickerbockers and £280 sash dresses, along with all the hairbands, tights and shoes to match.  In fact, a full pageboy look comes in at £374 while a full flower girl look can be achieved for £448. It is likely that Pepa and co. was chosen because of the close ties which the label already has with with the Cambridge family, as George and Charlotte have already worn numerous pieces from the collections; for his third birthday portraits George wore a whale-motif jumper by the brand while Princess Charlotte was dressed in a smock detail dress for the children's tea party which she attended during the royal tour of Canada last year.  "It's such a pretty theme," comments Rachel Riley, another childrenswear designer who has also dressed Prince George and Princess Charlotte. "It's not unexpected from a very traditional family, but the effect is understated and beautiful." Riley adds that the sage green, champagne and subtle copper tones which were incorporated into the bridesmaid and pageboy looks "fit perfectly for a country wedding, the colours are warm and pretty. It creates a perfect harmony." "We believe Pepa & Co is appealing because Spanish childrenswear is slightly more formal yet timeless in design," Gonzalez has previously told The Telegraph. "In Spain, the style is much more classic for children; Peter Pan collar shirts, soft colours, floral prints. But it is funny how we actually follow English styles in Spain." It is thought that The Duchess of Cambridge was introduced to the Spanish childrenswear labels which she dresses her toddlers in by Maria Borallo, their nanny. "At Pepa & Co, we keep the essence of timeless clothing for children and enjoy seeing our children look like children," Gonzalez added. "The classic clothing I design for Pepa & Co is inspired by the clothing from past decades that we and our parents once wore as children." No doubt the adorably traditional looks which Prince George and Princess Charlotte were seen in today will spark a renewed trend for classic bridesmaid and pageboy looks at weddings across the world, in keeping with the trends which the royal toddlers have already set: the pieces they wear regularly sell out and it has been estimated that Princess Charlotte could be worth £3.2 billion to the UK economy during her lifetime.   "Demand has not only been created in England for this traditional Spanish style but around the world too," Gonzalez recently told The Telegraph. "I receive orders daily from around the globe from as far as Korea, Brazil and the United States."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge joined senior royals including the Queen, Prince Philip and Princess Anne at an Easter service in Windsor this morning, with all family members showing up in their Sunday best. Almost everyone in attendance at St. George's Chapel chose an off-white or in-season pastel colour for the church service, which allowed the Queen to stand out in her vibrant turquoise dress coat by Angela Kelly. Her Majesty's look was punctuated by a cluster of pink spring blossoms on her hat and completed by her signature black handbag and block-heeled shoes. The Duchess of Cambridge, meanwhile, wore a bespoke coat by Catherine Walker; one of the go-to British names in her style repertoire. It was a piece that she had been seen in before, on her royal tour of Canada last October, and it received a great response from fashion critics on its debut. With its Peter Pan collar and piped edges, it is a decidedly more youthful piece than many of the dress coats that she has chosen for other recent church services and weddings and, as such, it still feels like a fresh look on her today. Fans on Twitter described her accessories as nods to the late Jackie Kennedy's style, most evident in the type of pillbox hat she chose, worn with a coordinating up-do hairstyle. The Duchess finished her look with a cream envelope clutch bag and her signature nude court shoes, once again proving their versatility and ability to solve any occasionwear dilemma that spring might throw her way. Princesses Beatrice and Eugenie both followed a similar styling cue to Kate, wearing spring-like colours and small, but embellished, pillbox hats. Beatrice opted for a pale lilac lace dress, set off by a plum clutch bag and velvet heels, while Eugenie chose a double-breasted dress that looked like a twist on a classic British trench coat. Between them the royal family offered an excellent dose of inspiration for those currently hunting in the bank holiday sales for occasionwear looks; soft spring colours, elegant lace and floral details will see you through the season in style.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It was the summer of 1988 when  the photographer Owen Scarbiena took some test shots of an unknown 14-year-old on the tennis courts  at Battersea Park. The girl was Kate Moss and this was her first photo shoot at the start of a career that would see her go on to become the most famous model of our time. Moss had very recently been discovered by Storm Models’ talent scout Sarah Doukas, at New York’s JFK airport as the teenager was returning from holiday with her father. When Doukas landed back in the UK she called Scarbiena. ‘I’ve got this new girl,’ she told him. ‘You’ll love her. She’s just your look.’  ‘I was very minimal,’ Scarbiena  says. ‘I shot with a wide aperture, no lights, no make-up.’ And no clue of what Moss was to become either, although he could see she was a natural. ‘Some girls come with  a ready-made photo pose and you have to work through that. But I just said to Kate, “Pretend you’re bored waiting at the bus stop,” and she  got it.’ One might say it has been her signature expression ever since.  The photographs, which have never been seen before, will be exhibited at Zebra One Gallery in north London later this month.  Would Scarbiena like to shoot the supermodel again? Of course he would. ‘It would be great to see how we’ve both changed in 28 years,’  he says.  'The Kate Effect' is the well-recognised phenomenon of The Duchess of Cambridge's ability to make the clothes she wears sell-out and propel labels to new levels of recognition. Now, that frenzy has reached one of Canada's most promising up-and-coming luxury brands.  Yesterday, The Duchess made a quick change from a Jackie O-style red coat by Carolina Herrera into a grey wrap coat by SENTALER, an outerwear label founded by Belgrade-born, Toronto-based Bojana Sentaler. The £707 coat has now sold out on Sentaler's website but is available to pre-order for delivery in February 2017.  "As a designer, it is a dream come true for The Duchess to wear a piece from my collection," Sentaler told The Telegraph hours after Kate was pictured painting totem poles, touring a steam train and observing extreme mountain biking in the label's pale grey coat with signature ribbed sleeve design. Sentaler said that she already knew that Kate had the coat but was unsure when it might make an appearance. "Her stylist discovered SENTALER and reached out to us directly. The entire relationship is very organic," she explains. The Duchess's stylist is Natasha Archer, who began working as a PA at Kensington Palace but whose role has segued into guiding The Duchess in creating a confident, glamorous and - crucially - regal look over the past couple of years.  "I did not know if and when The Duchess would wear a SENTALER coat, but I am ecstatic that she chose to wear it on the Royal Canadian tour," Sentaler continues. "She looked so gracious and elegant in SENTALER and I honestly couldn’t be happier. She is very feminine and her style is composed of minimalistic silhouettes with the perfect fit, which is also what SENTALER stands for." Although it has only been a few hours since The Duchess was seen in SENTALER, the effect has been immediate. "I can tell you that the coat she wore was sold out within a few hours and is now on back-order," the designer explains. "The same coat is selling fast in all the colors we offer on our online shop. We have witnessed an instant impact internationally as soon as The Duchess appeared in the SENTALER coat." While The Duchess of Cambridge undoubtedly brings awareness of SENTALER to a new international audience, the label already knows what it's like to be the subject of a frenzy after being worn by a VIP. Sophie Gregoire-Trudeau, the stylish wife of Canada's Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, has worn SENTALER on several occasions.  "When Sophie Gregoire-Trudeau wore the various coats from the SENTALER FW15 collection, specifically the white surialpaca coat during Canada’s Prime Minister’s swearing in ceremony, our company started receiving instant media interest and sales inquiries," Sentaler remembers. "We were receiving orders from across the country including remote places where we would not be able to reach our clients otherwise." With the forensic attention which is paid to the fashion choices of women in the public eye, comes great power. Jessica Mulroney, friend and style advisor to Sophie Gregoire-Trudeau told The Telegraph last week about the moment when she and the Prime Minister's wife understood the support they could offer to the fashion industry. “She wore a coat by SENTALER and  people went crazy for it, we had created this media frenzy, like you see with Kate," she explained. "Then we realised we had a responsibility to create more moments like that to give designers an international platform.” Ever since the pair has highlighted Canadian design talent during Gregoire-Trudeau's public engagements. By choosing to wear SENTALER, The Duchess of Cambridge indicates that she is also conscious of this power, as well as carrying out an act of cleverly subtle diplomacy.  "Being in the business of fashion, especially in Canada, I can tell you that it is challenging to build international awareness in such a competitive market place," Sentaler admits. "The Duchess and Sophie are both the epitome of influence and can excel the growth of a brand exponentially by simply wearing a piece from their collection." Sentaler was inspired to begin her business after meeting Karl Lagerfeld in 2008. "I had a chance meeting with him in Dubai in 2008. His words of wisdom encouraged me to follow my dream and pursue my career in fashion. Shortly after my encounter with him, I started thinking about launching my own fashion line." Her coats are created from a luxurious alpaca wool which she discovered while travelling in Peru. "It is lightweight but warm, with a sensual feel and beautiful drape," says Sentaler of the qualities which are clear to see in the images of Kate wrapped up in her coat yesterday. Sentaler employs families in Peru to produce the coats, an initiative which brings support to local communities. Next on Sentaler's agenda is expansion to "all major fashion cities in the world like London, Paris, Shanghai and Dubai." Thanks to The Duchess of Cambridge, that ambition may now be a step closer.      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When 69-year-old actress Susan Sarandon took to the SAG awards red carpet in a white Max Mara suit with a black bra earlier this year, Piers Morgan spearheaded a body-bashing  campaign, claiming it was "tacky" of the Hollywood star to reveal so much skin at an awards show. Her hair is slicked back and she's shot in a darkly lit studio.  Marc Jacobs revealed the campaign on his Instagram, writing one of his characteristically long captions about why he selected her. "Like so many teenagers, I spent countless Friday and Saturday nights at midnight screenings of The Rocky Horror Picture Show at the 8th Street Playhouse (which is still standing!) and the Festival Theatre on 57th Street (which has long since closed). TRHPS was a coming of age and right of passage. It became an invitation (or excuse) to dress up and express oneself fearlessly. The cult classic made it cool for boys to wear sequins, satin and fishnets." He continues: "I fell in love with Susan Sarandon’s onscreen portrayal of Janet during her “loss of innocence” scene by way of a crossdressing alien and her giddy, ecstatic rendition of, “touch-a, touch-a, touch me…” There was a subtle rebellious quality that I found in Susan with how she chose to play Janet and perhaps (as I now look back on it) her decision as a young actor to take a role in a film that challenged the notion of gender roles.  In the hyper-stylized, gothic film, The Hunger, Susan’s portrayal as the lesbian love interest of vampire Catherine Deneuve was yet another progressive challenging of normal and a testament to Susan’s artistic exploration of boundaries." Each face is introduced on Marc Jacobs' own Instagram account with an essay about why he asked them to join the group and what they mean to him.  'London is so full of memories.’ Rosita Missoni, the octogenarian matriarch of the Italian fashion house, is standing in the living room of her daughter, Angela’s, home. Though it has recently snowed, the sun is burning through the clouds, bathing Lake Varese and the Alps in hazy light. Rosita is wielding a souvenir tray decorated with pictures of the capital’s tourist traps, with the statue of Eros in Piccadilly Circus at its centre. It is a reminder that London is where she met her late husband, Ottavio, the brand’s co-founder, who died three years ago at the age of 92.  It was on a summer-long sojourn with her convent-school classmates that the 16-year-old Rosita attended the 1948 London Olympics, nuns in tow. ‘I noticed an Italian preparing to run in the 400m hurdles,’ she recalls. ‘He had the style of a Grecian athlete. He was very handsome.’ Rosita willed him to win – and he did. After a chance introduction, they arranged a rendezvous under the statue of Eros. Within five years they were married. She shows me the winged figure on a necklace that she has worn since losing her husband. ‘Otto, my great-grandson, calls it “Cuuppidooo”,’ she says fondly.  It is appropriate, then, that London is hosting Missoni Art Colour, an exhibition at the Fashion and Textile Museum exploring the artistic origins of the brand’s founders. It is  a celebration of a 60-year partnership that spawned one of fashion’s most powerful dynasties. What started in 1953  as a knitwear workshop in the basement of their home in Gallarate, Lombardy, has become a byword for breezy affluence. After unearthing a batch of 1930s space-dyed yarns in her family’s factory, where embroidery and kimonos had been made for generations, Rosita discovered knitting machines that allowed the use of an endless variety of shades: the colour-clashing striated Missoni knit was born. The timing was impeccable. Missoni rode the wave of the ready-to-wear revolution, and was a catalyst for fashion’s shift from Florence to Milan. By the late 1960s, the couple were the bright young things of New York, thanks largely to US Vogue editor Diana Vreeland (a fan of Missoni vests).  In the age of the fashion conglomerate, it is impressive that Missoni, whose revenue for 2013 was €170 million, remains both profitable and resolutely a family affair. ‘I have the memories and knowledge of someone much older,’ says Angela, the creative director behind its runway collections since 1997, when her mother officially stepped down. ‘As a young girl I met  everyone from the president of Neiman Marcus to Joan Burstein, who opened Browns with Missoni inside. I always preferred spending time with my parents’ friends to time with my companions in school.’  The factory that Rosita and Ottavio built in 1968 – which remains the company’s only one – was her playground, though she insists that her taking the helm was not a foregone conclusion. ‘I wasn’t seeing that as my future. I always knew I would work for a living – there had already been four generations of working Missoni women. But I’d thought about being a vet or a psychologist. I was in and out of the business for pocket money, but it was my parents’ work.’  Seeing Rosita and Angela side by side in Angela’s modernist home is fascinating. Rosita looks on benevolently as her daughter halts the photo shoot to swap a vase of pink roses for sunflowers. She reties Angela’s belt as Angela flips her head to tousle her long waves of dark hair. Wordless approval passes between them. How have they made working together a success where others have failed? ‘I don’t know any other story,’ Angela says. ‘My parents were very liberal. I never felt pressure from them. I never felt judged. We are all different – and fashion comes down to the female genes in the family.’ As the linchpin of fashion’s most familial empire, does Angela ever get a moment to herself? ‘Not much,’ she says, sighing. ‘At work  I’m always providing solutions. And I’m still  a constant point of reference for the children.’ Her daughter Margherita, 33, who runs the Margherita Kids label, is building a house 10 minutes away. Margherita’s siblings, Francesco, 31, and Teresa, 27, currently working on a plus-size clothing range independent from Missoni, both keep their wardrobes at Angela’s house. ‘I’ve already spoken to Margherita twice and Teresa once today,’ Angela says. Not long after, her phone trills – it is her son. Three years ago, Angela’s brother Vittorio, the brand’s chief executive, went missing in a small plane off Venezuela. It took months for the wreckage to be found, and the family dynamic was altered indelibly. ‘Now, also for my brother’s children, this has become the family house as much as my mum’s place,’ Angela says.  The warmth of Angela’s home is a reflection of her often irreverent spirit. When we touch on her mother’s abiding sense of style, she tells me it is something that Margherita has inherited, but that she feels has passed her by. ‘That’s a perfection I never reached,’ Angela says, not unhappily. ‘I’m a bit more wild.’ On cue, Rosita sweeps in to taste-check her outfit – a Missoni tunic worn over a black top, black trousers and antique Lanvin earrings – with her daughter. ‘Perfetto,’ Angela says, before rolling her eyes affectionately and adding, ‘What can I say? I told you!’ Many artworks the family has long held  dear are on display at the Fashion and Textile Museum. In the exhibition, first shown at the MA*GA museum in Gallarate, are paintings  by stars of 20th-century Italian art, such as  the luminous graphics of Luigi Veronesi, and works by the female face of the 1960s avant-garde, Dadamaino.  The canvases of Ottavio Missoni stand out – he could have become a painter. His paintings are shown alongside a series of his epic textural  tapestries, which cover a wall in the main gallery. There is room for fashion, too: about 100 archival Missoni ready-to-wear pieces selected for their tone and texture are on display.  ‘It’s not a fashion retrospective. It’s a whole art-and-craft experience,’ Rosita says of the show, designed by her surviving son, Luca. ‘Art has always been our biggest source of inspiration.’ She speaks effusively of the abstract artist Sonia Delaunay, whose pattern book she found at a flea market in Paris and hurried back to show her husband – and whose inclusion here is a huge draw. ‘To me she was a goddess. She had this idea of playing with patterns beyond the clothes, to the house, to the car. We too had this notion of creating a world of pattern.’  Now 84, Rosita still spends her days at the  factory, working on the Missoni Home collection. ‘It’s one thing to sketch and choose a cloth, and another to keep working on creating fabrics and textures,’ she says when I ask what marks out Missoni after all these years. ‘If I want to  see a stripe I can get it made in a few hours. This is a craft that distinguishes us from the other fashion houses – that, and the fact that [the  family] are all cast from one knit.’  Missoni Art Colour is at the Fashion and Textile Museum, London SE1, until  September 4, supported by MA*GA and the Woolmark Company (ftmlondon.org) © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Each year Town and Country 's September issue - named The Modern Swan issue - is graced by a fresh class of society debutantes. This year's heiress in the spotlight is Princess Olympia of Greece whose life resembles the most fantastical episode of Gossip Girl. The 20-year-old London-raised society girl is the daughter of Pavlos, Crown Prince of Greece and Prince of Denmark and Crown Princess Marie-Chantal Miller, and is currently a student at the Parsons School of Design in New York. But judging by her Instagram, she's more likely to be seen on the front row at Paris Haute Couture Fashion Week than drinking cider at a student union.  Although Olympia now resides in New York - when she's not jetting between Paris and the Greek Islands - she was raised in London from the age of seven. The Greek monarchy's reign ended in 1973 but the family still keep their titles and certainly still move in European royal circles (Prince Charles is her godfather). For her 20th birthday last month Olympia and a group of friends flew to Mykonos for a Hello! Magazine- worthy celebration. Among the tanned, impeccably dressed guests was her cousin Talita Von Furstenberg, the granddaughter of New York fashion designer Diane Von Furstenberg. It's not just the circles she moves in that makes her comparable to a real-life Blair Waldorf or Serena Van Der Woodsen, but her high fashion wardrobe too. A quick scroll through her Instagram feed unearths plenty of Valentino, Michael Kors, Balmain and Louis Vuitton, with an anti-Paris Hilton heiress look that has landed her features in Teen Vogue, Vanity Fair and Tatler.  Olympia might be a student, but she attends a number of the most exclusive events on the fashion calendar. She did a three week work experience stint in the couture department of the Dior atelier, but unlike your average work experience alumni, she has a guaranteed front row seat at every Dior show, where she perches alongside guests including Emma Watson.  Fashion is in her royal blood. In 2000 her mother launched her own successful luxury childrenswear label, Marie-Chantal, and she has boutiques in Chelsea and Notting Hill. Marie Chantal's 1995 wedding shows just how much she cares about high fashion, as she wore a spectacular silk wedding dress by Valentino and the atelier also made 62 outfits for the wedding party, dressing a number of royal guests including Queen Sofia of Spain. Princess Olympia recalls the best fashion advice she has ever received to Town and Country : "From my grandmother to my mother to me: "It is always better to be overdressed than underdressed, as you never know whom you may come across on the street." From my father: "Please, Olympia, wear shoes you can last the night in."  Kendall and Gigi wear matching ones, Sienna Miller throws hers on post-gym, and Kate Moss relies on her satin number to pay tribute to David Bowie. In short, the bomber jacket is the cover-up worth relegating your winter coats into storage for.   The classic streetwear piece has seen a resurge of popularity thanks to cult brand Vetements, headed up by Demna Gvasalia, who has also taken the helm at Balenciaga after the departure of Alexander Wang. Bombers in khaki, orange and black (often with luminous inner linings) are the label’s bread-and-butter, along with other voluminous, structured outerwear. On the other side of the pond in New York, bombers have long been the uniform of rapper-come-designer Kanye West, who had Alpha Industries jackets printed with ‘Yeezus tour’ for his 2014 show dates. Said jackets were passed onto his Kardashian family members, and what Kendall Jenner wears, many are eager to pick up on. Jenner and model friend Gigi Hadid have been spotted ‘twinning’ around New York, as they nip from the gym to model castings and lunch in matching black and khaki bombers, respectively. Model Miranda Kerr, meanwhile, relies on hers for that all-important exit from LAX airport in front of waiting paps. Perched delicately on her shoulders, the cocoon-shape provides the perfect frame for her svelte frame and the skin-tight clothes hugging it. Elsewhere, the SS16 catwalks were awash with bombers as Elie Saab, Loewe and Emilio Pucci dabbled in the athleisure trend, and streetwear veterans Alexander Wang and Rag & Bone continued to revamp the classic. Stella McCartney and Tommy Hilfiger were also on hand to tick the preppy box. Such an influx of designers has meant that new faces, and not only models, have been experimenting with the transitional cover-up. Actresses Lily Collins and Liberty Ross toted embroidered bombers to Stella McCartney’s Fall 2016 presentation, and designer Jasmine Guinness was spotted wearing a fetching silk red one during the LC:M presentations.  As a public figure who embodied glamour, intrigue, duty and mystery, Diana, Princess of Wales's wardrobe was one of her most powerful means of communication throughout her 16 years in the public eye. Although she died when she was just 36, the world had seen Diana transform from a shy, demure teenager to a sophisticated international celebrity. The fact that the Princess owned just a handful of her own clothes when she was flatsharing in London working as a nursery school teacher seems baffling when you think that one of the projects which occupied most of her time in what would turn out to be the final year of her life was deciding which of the countless couture gowns overspilling from her wardrobe room at Kensington Palace to sell for a charity auction at Christie's.  "It's interesting to see how her style, thank god, changed," quipped Joan Rivers to the New York Times as she toured the Christie's exhibition of pieces to be sold. In the end, it was the velvet off-shoulder number by Victor Edelstein that Diana wore to dance with John Travolta at the White House in 1985 which fetched the most, $325,000, proving how  an outfit can become so symbolic and evocative of the moment for which it is worn. It's little wonder then that Diana came to epitomise late 20th century fashion- from polka dots and ruffled blouses to LBDs and power tailoring- her style choices came to speak of different chapters in both her personal life and the evolution of fashion. The bling, jewel colours and exaggerated silhouettes of the 80s suited the striking, regal image she was projecting as one of the most senior member of the royal family while the pared-back, simple aesthetic of the 90s was ideal for her new phase where she could blend the businesslike and the daringly independent- think shorter lengths and casually elegant jeans and tailoring.  "She was an expert in the language of clothes," Eleri Lynn, curator of 'Diana: Her Fashion Story' told The Telegraph earlier this year. Anna Harvey, the former deputy editor of Vogue and Diana's stylist, confirms that the Princess was acutely aware of the messages her style would project. "She was always very thoughtful about how her clothes would be interpreted, it was something that really mattered to her."  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Annabelle Neilson, the fashion muse, reality television star and Primrose Hill set socialite, passed away on Thursday 12th July, police have confirmed. Neilson, who was 49, described Kate Moss as a ‘sister’ and became a fixture on the London fashion scene in the early Noughties, partying with Moss, Naomi Campbell and the designer Lee Alexander McQueen, for whom the trio of women served as muses. Describing McQueen as her best friend, Neilson was the last to see him alive before his suicide in 2010. Born in March 1969, Neilson grew up between West London and Oxfordshire - her grandmother was a second cousin of the late Queen Mother. Neilson attended a private school, but was bullied because she was severely dyslexic and left education at 16 with no qualifications. She moved to Perth, Australia and was the victim of a horrific assault which she would later say changed her life. Tied to a tree, she was attacked by a man - who was later convicted of killing three women - and beaten for hours, leaving her in need of reconstructive surgery. “I managed to escape with my life but I needed reconstructive surgery because my face was so disfigured,” she would share years later. “After that, I fell into a serious depression and became a heroin addict because it provided an escape bubble and was the only way I could cope. In a way, heroin saved me because otherwise I would have killed myself.”  Neilson had struggled with drug addiction in her later teens, but it is understood that she became sober in her twenties and stayed sober for the rest of her life.  She married millionaire banker Nat Rothschild in 1994 after eloping to Las Vegas, and the couple divorced in 1997. Neilson enjoyed a career as a model and muse in the early Noughties alongside McQueen and Moss, and made occasional catwalk appearances with her friends at fundraising events. She starred in two seasons of Bravo's reality TV series Ladies of London from 2014 to 2015 and became one of the most popular women on the show, which followed the lives of eight British socialites.  According to her Instagram page, the last event Neilson attended was the wedding of Edward Spencer Churchill, the Duke of Marlborough's half-brother, and her ex-boyfriend, on 8th July. She was pictured wearing feathers and sequins with friends Poppy Delevingne, Kimi Hammerstroem and Kate Moss.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  “It’s taken a lot of hard work to get here, you really have to earn your stripes on this street. Or, should I say, pinstripes,” says Kathryn Sargent. It’s an appropriate analogy; this week the 41-year-old from Yorkshire made history as the first woman to open her own namesake store on Savile Row. The fact that this is an area defined by a patrician sense of heritage and tradition, where tailors’ shops evoke the feel of a gentleman’s club, makes Sargent’s achievement all the more remarkable.  Savile Row isn’t famed for its acceptance of change. When tailor Tommy Nutter opened his boutique in the 1960s he caused outcry by breaking with the tradition of velvet curtains shielding the shop inside, and placing mannequins wearing the clothes on display in the windows. When Ozwald Boateng and Richard James came to Savile Row in the 1990s, their defiant, apparently unseemly act of opening their stores on the weekend caused many a colonel to choke on his kippers.  So how has the world reacted to the first woman opening up shop on London’s most traditional street? “Yes, it’s quite surreal," she admits. “There’s an incredibly long history to Savile Row. But I have been trained here and I’ve been part of this tailoring community my whole working life. If I hadn’t had that background, opening a shop with a woman’s name above the door might not have been as warmly received as it has.”   It’s true that women have always played an integral, if discreet, behind-the-scenes role in Savile Row’s story; nipping, pinning, cutting and sculpting the suits that have made this street the pinnacle of tailoring. “I trained as an apprentice at Gieves & Hawkes for five years, and had two amazing women who looked after me. One was a military tailor who did all the lacing on military uniforms, the other was a finisher who did all the lining and buttonholes, and they really ran the show. They ruled the roost and showed me that there were strong women within these teams, despite being outnumbered.”  Such formidable presences helped give Sargent the confidence to shatter what she terms the “windowpane check ceiling.”  “Have I felt like a woman in a man’s world? Initially yes, but nowadays I realise that I’m a woman in a diverse world,” she says diplomatically. “Traditionally there’s been an expectation that if you went to see your tailor, he’d be an older gentleman in a suit, but you soon realise that what matters is being able to communicate with the client and developing your expertise. Having said that, my father wouldn’t ever let me measure him!”  The handsome, panelled environs of her emporium at 22 Savile Row are a long way from Leeds, where Sargent grew up, but it was another pioneering Yorkshire woman who prompted her to attend fashion school at Epsom college. “I always thought that Vivienne Westwood was wonderful, I really wanted to follow in her footsteps,” she says.  Yet while Westwood’s fashion identity is defined by a renegade sense of experimentalism, for Sargent the draw was technique and tradition. “I was obsessed with construction and would buy old Burberry suits in charity shops just so I could take them apart and put them back together again, to see how they were made,” she explains.  Years of training in how to make the cut, so to speak, followed before Sargent started picking up accolades for her work. In 2000 she won the esteemed Golden Shears Award, a hallmark of excellence awarded to newcomers in the industry. And two years ago she launched a bespoke tailoring service in Mayfair, which proved so successful she felt the time was right to launch into “the Row” with a standalone store.  “There really is no quick fix in this line of work,” she says of an industry where every stitch of the needle is measured, every cuff sleeve considered, and apprentices can train for years before being deemed to have reached a standard sufficient to be let loose on a customer’s cloth. “There’s no one person on this street who knows everything, you’re constantly learning.”  Sargent, herself sharply attired in an impeccable black suit with crimson neck scarf, believes part of her success is due to the fact that it’s no longer just men who want to shop on Savile Row. “I work a great deal with global business leaders and CEOs, and they are women as well as men. I cater to women who have worked hard to get to where they are and need high performance tailoring to help them look professional. My clothes aren’t fashion pieces, they are there to do a job. A suit can do a huge amount for a man or a woman.”  Top divorce barrister Baroness Fiona Shackleton is know for buying her suits on Savile Row but, of course, Sargent is far too discreet to name her clients. Instead, she cites the Queen and the Prince of Wales as prime examples of elegance and masters of the art of looking appropriate, alongside Sean Connery’s Bond and Fred Astaire. “He’s one of the most enigmatic suit wearers of all time,” she says of the latter. “He showed how you can move in a suit, and of course he had most of them made on the Row”.  For anyone else seeking to join the esteemed ranks of gentlemanly outfitters on this most revered street in men’s style, Sargent has only one piece of advice: “Find out as much as you can, seek advice and be patient. Don’t expect it to happen overnight.”  Watching her guide clients through cloth swatches and sweep through the heavy curtains to her fitting rooms, it’s clear that Sargent’s patience has most certainly paid off.  "A good tailored jacket should frame the face, if it doesn’t fit properly there it won’t anywhere else." "See what the cloth does for your complexion. If you opt for a bold statement shade or check, think about how it will fit in your wardrobe day to day." "Consider the shirt you’re going to wear with it, whether a single or double cuff, and allow for that in the length."  "If you’re having something made bespoke, it must have longevity." "The suit itself should always err on the side of classic." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This week, British Vogue editor Alexandra Shulman went on the record to say that she “absolutely strongly believes" that the use of extremely skinny models on the catwalk does not give girls body issues. True or not, our new contributor, plus-size model Bree Warren, argues that surely, it is time that we had a high visibility of different body shapes to reflect all women in society. Bree Warren is a UK size 14 Australian model living in Brooklyn, New York. She was scouted twice as a teenager but only seriously considered modelling while she was at university, studying journalism and business management, after seeing the success of plus-size model Robyn Lawley. While many argue that plus-size equals unhealthy, conversely, Bree is the beautiful image of radiant health, with a naturally curvy physique more familiar to ordinary women the world over. Represented by Models 1 and booked by e-tailer as ASOS to be its first ever Curve model. Bree is a surfing fanatic, who blogs about her travels at thewaveprovocateur.com. Regardless of where you are on the size spectrum, no topic can divide a dinner table faster than the term ‘plus size’. Interesting? Maybe. But ground-breaking? No. Ironic isn’t it? After decades of curvaceous triumphs from the likes of Crystal Renn, Tara Lynn and Candice Huffine, the most polarising fashion conversation is still a model’s size. To me, the whole idea of labelling models based on size is so passé. I may not be old enough to remember the ’80s supermodels, but I’ve seen hundreds of pictures of their strong, physiques; what’s odd is that we as a population are growing taller and larger yet our models, public figures and media personalities have shrunk. I get that plus-size models are perplexing. Plus-size women buy plus-size brands who use plus-size models to sell plus-size clothes they don’t fit into. Confused? I don’t blame you. I concede it’s confusing but I don’t understand why plus-size has to be so controversial. To me, the whole plus-size debate is simple. It’s not about being underweight or overweight, it’s about acknowledging differences. There need to be more shapes and sizes in fashion, not just one. We need diversity. We need artistic, creative and fashion-forward diversity. The talent is out there - we just need to use it. The #droptheplus social media campaign launched earlier this year called for labels to be removed to describe models by their size, and encouraged retailers to be more inclusive in their design range and size. Yet at the same time, I’ve witnessed complaints levelled at models - such as Robyn Lawley and Myla Dalbeiso - for not being plus enough. My own body has been debated in my Instagram comments more times than I care to think about; the whole thing casually menaces the industry, flaring up from time to time. Yet, changing the name or dropping the “plus” tag will not eliminate the problem. To clarify, anyone over a UK size 10 is considered plus-size and that’s where the confusion lies. I am not talking about being obese. Most agency curve boards represent size 10 to 18. Most girls are over 5’9” and most of the work is for UK 14 to 16. This is a normal, healthy weight range and some of them are in such incredible shape, it is hard to match up. Plus-size shapes and sizes are all so incredibly different for both the models and the women who are buying. To me, that’s what makes it interesting. We need diversity that is universally promoted and accepted. It’s good for us as women. It’s good for us as a society. It’s good for our children and yes, it’s good for our wellbeing. I believe that seeing more realistic body types in the media will help to end the cycle of body image issues, food abuse and shocking self-esteem. As a teenager, I saw only one body type in fashion and I want to change that for the next generation. For a long time, I avoided the “what do you do?” question. In bars, eating at restaurants, waiting at airports my lies were airtight. If I told the truth, I would watch strangers size me up and launch into a charged discussion. See, that’s the thing about fashion; everyone has an opinion and I wanted no part of it. But then something happened. I changed. I realised that there’s a bigger issue at play here. If I am going to do a job, I want to do it well. My story is different. I never tried to be a mainstream model. I never went to extreme lengths to change my body to fulfill a dream. Quite simply, I was made this way. I am tall with broad shoulders, big feet and wide hips. I could never be a sample size so I never tried. Give or take some unnecessary wining and dining, my body has stayed the same since I was 18. For the most part, the fashion industry as a whole has welcomed me. My agents, clients and teams have been exceptional. While there still may be only one size on the runway, the landscape is shifting. There’s a new wave of plus size models carving out a middle ground that’s attainable and relatable, bridging the gap between what has been and what I hope will be. These days with social media, you can see what we really look like, you can see where we go and what we do every day. The archetypal fashion walls have fallen. I read an article that discussed the digitisation of fashion and it said, “If everyone’s invited, will anyone want to come?” My answer is “yes!” It’s a new game and we are all players. Fashion is participatory, fast, downloadable and deletable. For years, fashion has banked on exclusivity as its currency, but for the first time, we have the power. We have the power to build each other up. We have the power to change fashion. You can’t ignore the masses. Women have money to burn and we want to see a range of body types, not just one.  It’s a situation which many women will relate to: you meet a stylish friend and admire a sparkling piece of jewellery they are wearing, realising that it would look so much better with your outfit than your current adornment.  Few friends, however, are generous enough to offer you the item on long-term loan. But it has emerged that this was how a diamond brooch which Margaret Thatcher wore for some of the most memorable moments of her time in Downing Street came into her possession. The provenance of the Cartier brooch- a geometric chevron design from 1937- has come to light after its owner, who wishes to remain anonymous, offered it for auction at Sotheby’s Fine Jewels sale which will take place on 7th June. It is estimated to fetch £25,000- £30,000 “The seller and Mrs Thatcher were very good friends,” explains Jessica Wyndham, head of Sotheby’s London jewellery department. “They were together one day and discussing how Mrs Thatcher’s own brooch didn’t quite match what she was wearing so the seller said ‘why don’t you borrow mine?’” Renowned for her elegant personal style, Thatcher pinned the brooch to her right shoulder on the day that she offered her resignation to The Queen and for a meeting with Ronald and Nancy Reagan at Claridge’s in 1990, as well as numerous other international occassions.  Thatcher is said to have been captivated by the deeper meaning which the dazzling Art Deco piece might signify. “She remarked that she liked the idea it resembled  an arrowhead, as arrows were symbolic of so many happenings in our history,” explains Wyndham. Mrs Thatcher was known for her love of jewellery and especially brooches. In a sale of her possessions at Christie's auction house two years ago, a diamond flower brooch dating from the start of the 19th century sold for £158,500  The sale is something of a full circle moment, as the brooch was first purchased by the seller in 1986 after she popped into Sotheby’s on her lunch break after receiving a bonus. The proceeds from the sale will be donated the Endeavour Fund which supports the recovery of wounded and sick servicemen and women.  “This was a particularly dear piece to the seller because Mrs Thatcher was such a close friend,” adds Wyndham. “She needed some time to enjoy it following Thatcher’s death but wanted to raise funds now for a charity which is close to her heart.” The sale also comes at a moment when brooches are becoming increasingly popular. "Buyers realise how the brooch is one of the most versatile jewels to wear," says Wyndham. "Many designers today have been exploring the endless possibilities of the brooch; no longer constricted to the lapel on a jacket, they’re styling them into the hair, on the sides and backs of dresses and on accessories such as gloves and bags." The brooch's estimate is "akin to other diamond jewels by Cartier from the same period" but it is difficult to predict whether The Thatcher effect will inflate its eventual selling price. "As jewellery is such a personal means of adornment, provenance of a well-known figure will always create more interest but that interest is never quantifiable," Wyndham explains. "It is very exciting for someone to own that little slice of history, especially one that’s been photographed and documented on so many important historical occasion." Sotheby's Fine Jewels sale takes place on 7th June   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It takes a truly creative mind to successfully fuse fashion with diamante sparkles and make something worthy of a $1000-plus price tag. Such was Judith Leiber’s skill. The creator of the fashion industry’s favorite clutch bags and accessories passed away this weekend in Long Island, New York, aged 97. Ms Leiber’s husband and long-term collaborator Gerson Leiber passed away only a few hours before the designer and according to reports, both died of natural causes. “I consider her to be a genius, absolutely without a doubt,” Mr Leiber told the crowd at the 2017 opening of 'Judith Leiber: Crafting a New York Story' at the Museum of Art and Design. He added that his wife was “the greatest pathfinder for women. She broke through the glass ceiling so many years ago.” Ms. Leiber’s hugely successful business was largely built on the minaudières she created- small accessories holding no more than a lipstick and keys, things of gaudy, gorgeous beauty. Traditionally shaped crystal-covered boxes with jeweled fastening clips gave way to wild variations; a bejeweled pineapple or a pavé  diamond rose perhaps? Why not. Hillary Clinton received a crystal covered evening version of Socks the cat when she entered the White House, following a tradition that started with Nancy Reagan. However, it was the sparkle-coated cupcake in the first Sex and the City film that really brought Ms. Leiber’s outrageously extravagant work into the spotlight.   It was a style that grew with the designer herself. After meeting American soldier Gerson ‘Gus’ Leiber on a street in her native Budapest during World War II, the young woman waiting out the war as an apprentice in a handbag factory fell in love. The couple married and moved to New York City shortly after the war ended and Ms. Leiber went to work honing her craft in the showrooms of Seventh Avenue. Mr Leiber focused on art, becoming a modernist painter with work exhibited at the Met and Smithsonian, among others.  Starting out with her first line in 1963, Ms. Leiber’s early designs were simple, leather classics, “decidedly understated” to quote Women's Wear Daily. The disco era of the 1970s brought a change in fashion’s outlook and Ms. Leiber, who had been experimenting with new shapes, was already onto a winner with her crystals, a detail that Mr Leiber said came about by accident. A design called the Chatelaine was a gold, metal purse on a sparkly chain created by Ms. Leiber in 1967 but when the couple took the first delivery in New York, they were forced to make fashion lemonade. “The bags were unsaleable,” Mr Leiber told the New York Post in 2017, “the electroplating wasn’t even and there were pockmarks all over. It was Judy’s idea to add crystals. It started a whole new career!” The Leibers lived in Brooklyn for the first few years of their marriage before moving out to Springs, near East Hampton, Long Island permanently by the end of the 1950s. The couple opened The Leiber Museum in their home, where many of their works and inspirational pieces recreated their imaginative world for the public. As artist and designer, the Leibers were the perfect match. Already collector’s items, now would be a good time to pick up a minaudière by the winner of the CFDA’s Lifetime Achievement Award in 1994, just one of many prizes awarded to Leiber over her career. It would be well worth tracking down a souvenir by one of fashion’s greatest, yet lesser-known names.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Emma Watson took to the red carpet in LA last night on the latest leg of her Beauty and the Beast promotional tour. The actress became the latest star to wear a look from the debut collection from Oscar de la Renta's new creative directors Laura Kim and Fernando Garcia. Her sleekly tailored jumpsuit offered a sharp contrast to the fairytale, caped gown which she wore for the London premiere last week which was a bespoke creation by Emilia Wickstead. Last night's ensemble had a glamorous yet minimalist feel thanks to its pointed-V shaped bustier and single rose gold brooch adornment at the hip. She paired the jumpsuit with the black pointed stilettos by Burberry, which she has been wearing throughout the promotional tour as part of her support of the '30 wears' initiative which is spearheaded by Eco Age, the London-based sustainable fashion consultancy. The simple premise is that we should only buy something if we can be sure we'll wear it 30 times. This isn't the first outfit de la Renta's new team have created for Watson's Beauty and the Beast appearances. In Paris two weeks ago, she opted for a richly embellished bustier with vibrant red sash detail and black cigarette trousers also from Kim and Garcia's New York fashion week show, which took place in February.  Their modern, polished spin on the Park Avenue Princess look for which the label is renowned has been a resounding hit on the red carpets. At the Oscars, last years' best actress winner Brie Larson topped best-dressed lists in her black, velvet ruffled gown which came with the same pointed version of the sweetheart neckline as Watson's jumpsuit last night. Later on Oscars night, best actress nominee Ruth Negga graced the after-party circuit in a strapless, cream, bell-skirt gown with flashes of brightly-coloured sequins.  Watson is documenting all of her looks on a dedicated Instagram account - @the_press_tour - where each outfit's sustainable credentials are meticulously described. "She is truly an inspiration; so passionate about important issues and I have so much admiration for her," the designer Emilia Wickstead told The Telegraph last week. "I love that Emma feels comfortable in her own skin, that she is humble and real to work with and that she goes out of her way to empower women and for what she believes in. She is bright and brilliant to be around - it's an honour to have dressed such a strong, young female role model and hero of today in one of my designs. Women for women!" Watson's premiere appearance came in the wake of a row which erupted earlier this week when images were released from a shoot which she appears in in the latest Vanity Fair. The star is shown wearing just a rope capelet by Burberry, prompting some to accuse her of hypocrisy by posing 'topless' in spite of her feminist principles. She hasn't commented on the row, but plenty came to her defence, arguing that women have the right to wear whatever they like. Choosing the most modern of necklines for last night's appearance may even have been a defiant yet elegant retort.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When H&M shared a picture on Instagram last week of their latest swimwear model- 60-year-old Scottish stylist Gillean McLeod - the portrait received over 100,000 likes, hundreds of comments and quickly became a news story around the world.  One person who doesn’t quite understand all of this fuss over a picture of a woman with grey hair in a plain black swimsuit is Gillean herself. During a phonecall with the California-based model she keeps steering conversation back to the same question: "but, what do you think is the fascination with this swimsuit thing?" McLeod might struggle to understand why a picture of her in her swimwear is quite so remarkable, but to the rest of us who are used to seeing swimwear campaigns on rakish 19-year-olds, it’s a refreshingly postive image which is highly deserving of every single ‘like’ it gets. Gillean started her modelling career when she was 53, despite turning down offers when she was younger. “When I lived in London in my early 20s, I used to get stopped in the street and asked to model, but I was really shy, and had bad acne as a teenager and it really affected my self esteem,” McLeod tells The Telegraph. “I never thought that could be me and so I'd always say 'no, no, not me'. I never wanted to be on camera.” McLeod spent 25 years working backstage on fashion shoots as a stylist, but when she was 53 a photographer friend convinced her to let him shoot her portfolio. Within days, she had a modelling agent and the jobs began to roll in. “It wasn't easy when I was 53 doing it for the first time, I almost had a panic attack on my first commercial, but I talked myself out of it and it has become easier, and easier,” McLeod says of suddenly finding herself in front of the camera. “I didn't think I'd go for swimsuit modelling, that's for sure,” McLeod adds.   Her first photoshoot might have almost triggered a panic attack, but modelling has made her feel more confident about her looks. Suprisingly, it isn’t the campaigns she has landed that have made her feel beautiful (H&M, Uniqlo and an upcoming shoot with a supermodel for an American designer), but the ones where she got turned away. “I have been to hundreds and hundreds of castings where I never made it to callbacks and didn't get the jobs,” McLeod explains. “At first I took it personally, and then I realised you're just not the person they are looking for today. You are either it, or you aren't, and that's the end of the story and it has nothing to do with you. The more I was turned away, the more comfortable I became because I realised you are either it or not it, and it has made me much more confident.” There was an added twist to the now-famous H&M swimwear shoot. Not only was she in a swimsuit but she also wasn't wearing a scrap of makeup either. “It was a little bit of a strange thing because usually when I go for a job there is hair and makeup, but the photographer didn't want me to have any hair or makeup," she recalls. "I had literally nothing; not even moisturiser on my face. I was so surprised when he was like 'no we're just going to shoot now.'” As for how she found the confidence to do a barefaced swimsuit ad in her sixties, McLeod says that swimming is her secret. “I have always been a swimmer. I grew up in Malaysia and Scotland, and living in the tropics, I always swam so for my whole life I have always been comfortable in a bathing suit. I swim 2,500 meters, four times a week, and it's something I've always done and it does keep you in fabulous shape.” It seems that McLeod is part of a growing movement of women showing that bikini wearing isn't just for size 6, 16 year-olds. Earlier this year, an image of 90 year-old Irene Carney wearing a bikini went viral while this month 21 year-old Lesley Miller shared her uplifting story of wearing a bikini for the first time after a lifetime of body image struggles. It's understandable then that McLeod is all for more diversity when it comes to swimwear imagery. “I think that people should just get over how we are supposed to look,” McLeod says. “We are inundated with these images of scrawny women in their suits, and they are very young. Every single person is very different and we need to learn to become really comfortable with ourselves, and that's something that happens with age. You just have to give up with these things; and put on your suit. You have to talk yourself out of it, because imagine if you didn't go swimming that day, or wear your bikini that day and you miss out on time at the beach with your family or something.” Within days of McLeod’s swimsuit picture being shared on Instagram, women were turning to her for advice. ‘How does she stay in shape’ (Pilates, swimming and hiking). Botox? ("Right now I’m not doing anything to my face"). And the most-frequent question of all, ‘how does she have such great hair?’ (no dyeing, no blow drying and no product except coconut oil). Eager question-askers will be pleased to  hear that McLeod is currently working on launching her own blog, with photoshoots and advice for women her age. Meanwhile, her very stylish Instagram page should become your new go-to inspiration for outfit ideas. “My mother was very elegant, and quite wealthy, so she loved to wear YSL,” the Scottish model says about her style. “I always looked up to her with these simple, elegant clothes, but mine is more eclectic. I love to wear Comme des Garcons or Junya Watanabe, and bits and pieces from Dries Van Noten, Marni and Vivienne Westwood. I don't buy a lot of clothes, but less and spend more. I have Commes Des Garcons skirts from 12 years ago I still wear every day.” As bikini season approaches, it's all about being a bit more McLeod.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Here they are, mother and daughter, the supermodel Cindy Crawford and Kaia Gerber, hanging out at the Coachella music festival. This is not something you would have seen much a decade ago, but these days it’s routine. Your mother used to be a social liability, never mind in the context of a music festival: now she probably saw Guns N’ Roses back in the Nineties; she may well have a nifty technique for getting past security backstage; she almost certainly has clothes you want to borrow, even though she’s 50 and you are 14. And this is how the rules get blurred and we end up in a slightly undignified “shorts off”, with Cindy winning by an itsy-bitsy margin. There are rules governing mother-and-daughter dressing which are a lot clearer than the “Am I Too Old For” rules and it’s crucial that the mother (stepmother in my case) grasps them because no daughter/stepdaughter can easily say: “Please Don’t Be Doing The Same Stuff As Me.” It’s not that Kaia will be thinking, “Oh God, mum looks better than me”. She definitely won’t. But what she might be thinking is, “What Can I Wear That Is Only For Young People and Never for Moms, However Fit They Might Be?” It’s so obvious what’s happened here. Rande Gerber has said to Cindy, last time they were at the beach house: “Babe, you look SO HOT in those shorts.” Cindy (who has just turned 50, the point at which all women experience a late rush of denial and confidence which may or may not result in a radical haircut/affair/purchase of an insanely provocative bikini) will have thought DAMN RIGHT. I HAVE SO STILL GOT IT. I’M GONNA WEAR THESE BABIES OUT! And there you have it. Rule one of the mother-daughter dressing pact – Steer Clear of Her Territory, even if it feels like a matter of minutes since it was very much your territory – up in smoke. You may think, “Come on, it’s Cindy Crawford! She has got damn good legs.” But legs are not the issue here. The issue is the No Compete Clause. No muscling in on the kid’s territory. Concede the ground. Pass the baton. Back Off and let the juniors claim what is rightfully theirs. There is not much room for experimentation if your mother is matching you, shorts for micro denim cut-offs. And, let’s face it, those denim shorts would give you pause if your teenager was wearing them. There’s another thing, too: I know from personal experience (ahem) that older women have a cooling effect on clothes from younger women’s perspective. If they did have their eye on something, you have the ability to make it seem lame in a nanosecond. You are not just competing, you are killing it dead for them, forever. So when they say, “I love that suede mini skirt”, be the mum who says, “Oh! It’s very short”. Not, “Ooooh me, too: do you think they do it in my size?” That’s uncool.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  American socialite-turned-fashion blogger, Olivia Palermo, might plan her Paris Fashion Week outfits to the letter, but her luxe looks all have something in common: a humble belt, or scarf. It might not sound like rocket science, but Palermo proves that the simplest of accessories can become the linchpin to pull entire outfits together. Let us take you through her Paris wardrobe to show how the fashion maths works. Without a flash of metallic around the waist, this cosy look would run the risk of washing out Palermo’s figure. Note how the New Yorker has not traditionally belted her sweater around her torso either. By folding the knitwear neatly over one side, only a small section of the belt is visible, yet the eye is immediately drawn there due to the metallic buckle. What a clever clogs. This Kim Shui coat boasts two-tone snakeskin sleeves, fur panels, fur pockets and yellow piping. In short, there is a lot going on. Rather than let the bulky materials swamp her petite frame, Palermo employed a belt to cinch in her figure and pull the whole look together. Kapow! Electric blue leather was certainly a zany colour choice at the Blumarine store opening. Not for Palermo, who paired the punchy piece with her arsenal of muted knitwear. Where does your eye settle on this vibrant look? The belt! Yet another leather win for the street style star, who let the skirt bunch over the belt for a casual look. Quite clearly Palermo was not going to belt up her leather dungarees, which, she reports on her blog, were a total steal on her last trip to Japan. #Annoying. To divert attention from all that black leather, the savvy dresser tied a patterned silk scarf around her neck. Hers might be from Hermès, but there are a host of purse-friendly scarves on the high street too. So, next time you’re craving some retail therapy, take a look at your existing wardrobe. Add a belt, buckle up and watch outfits enjoy a new lease of life. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
