 Kate Middleton does a sterling job representing UK Inc. abroadbut apart from her shoes – always a bit of a weak spot - she has played an especial blinder in India: pretty but understated, reliably glamorous, never knowingly over-done. Yes she has help. She always did, but for some reason the Palace now feels more comfortable admitting the glaringly obvious fact that state dressing requires state aid. Currently it comes from her PA turned stylist Natasha Archer, who did a clever job adapting that flow-y, ankle length kaftan by Indian designer Anita Dongre into a more conventional-Kate-friendly dress. The Palace’s obsession with presenting the younger royals as exactly like the rest of us when they self-evidently are not, adds an extra layer of complications to Royal Tour Dressing. In 1938, when Elizabeth, the current Queen’s late mother, prepared for a State Visit to Paris, there was no question that she would slip in the odd bargain outfit. Norman Hartnell was designer designate for the entire tour. Not that anyone envied him particularly, the Queen having a reputation at that point, for frumpiness. The French press sharpened their quills. Unperturbed, Hartnell, in a flash of genius, designed an all white wardrobe (Elizabeth was in  mourning for her mother) of frothy gauze that emphasized her blue-blooded fairy tale background and very British  - and un-Wallis Simpson - virtues of modesty and charm. The world swooned, the Queen became an object of adoration and the Anglo-Franco relationship was re-enforced at a critical moment in history.  Even in 1961, when the Kennedys visited De Gaulle in Paris, Jackie Kennedy couldn’t wait to glide into her couture Givenchy and Balmain. The French loved her impeccable and evident appreciation of French style and the fact that the American First Lady so evidently appreciated – and knew how to wear – French fashion. Jackie also used the tour to promote the work of Oleg Cassini, her favourite, naturalised American designer – to such widespread approval that JFK remarked in a speech in Paris: “I am the man who accompanied Jacqueline Kennedy to Paris, and I have enjoyed it”. At a time when America’s fashion industry felt inferior to Europe’s the First Lady’s patronage and international fame was a hugely helpful vote of confidence.   The Duchess of Cambridge’s wardrobe must do a more nuanced job – presenting the Royals as polished, but in touch, modern yet traditional. It should promote British designers while demonstrating a down to earth knack for thriftiness while excluding anything that might possibly have been produced in a sweatshop. And that’s where the Duchess’s sure and stately progress sometimes runs aground. Yesterday’s decision to wear a £50 made-in-China dress from Glamourous, a Manchester based label was definitely a misstep. No one is suggesting Glamourous manufacturers in sweatshops. However it hasn’t signed up to the Ethical Trading Initiative. If you’re going to wear high street as a Royal, these moral wrinkles need to be ironed out.  On the other hand, she’s probably wise not to dress like a dollygarch who’s just been on a  spending spree. Especially when visiting street children - although it’s entirely possibly they would have appreciated something a little more princesssy... complicated isn’t it?   Carla Bruni-Sarkozy, dressed head to toe in couture Dior when she and her husband visited London in 2008, was more regal than The Queen. The male section of the media salivated at the time - especially over one picture that framed her bottom in a Pippa Middletonian halo. But in retrospect Carla’s swanky outfits and professional model-grade posing came to be viewed as the beginning of the end for President Bling Bling.   That’s the other thing about state dressing - it must withstand not only instant scrutiny, but the merciless gaze of hindsight. Poor Carla, who probably thought she was merely doing her best to promote one of France’s main artistic and economic endeavours, and therefore didn’t even try to wear anything British on that trip.    Which brings us to frockery: the art of using frocks to flatter nations. Michelle Obama set the bar high, wearing Roksanda (Serbian based Brit) and Christopher Kane (Scottish) to London and Azzedine Alaia (Tunisian born) to Paris. But it’s complicated, as the Duchess knows, after a previous tour when she wore what she believed to be a locally designed dress to a dinner in the Solomon Islands, only to discover it came from the Cook Islands. Frockery requires rigorous research and tact. It must pay subtle yet unmistakable homage of to the traditions and crafts of the host country without laying itself open to accusations of cultural appropriation. The salwar kameezes and saris donned, respectively, by the late Princess of Wales (in 1996 at a London Cancer Benefit co-hosted by Imran Khan) and Cherie Blair (pick any  year between 1998 and now: Mrs B loves Indian robes) would invite turbulent Twitter commentary these days from those who enjoy being offended, but interestingly, the host nations themselves always seem to enjoy being flattered.   If all that weren’t sufficiently demanding of a frock, it must withstand the withering assault of a thousand mega-powered, fish-eyed, cruelly distorting lenses and the gazes of a gazillion fashion police. It must not turn transparent under flashlight, gust upwards even in a hurricane, crease, sag or droop. Underwear must never show (as far as State Tours are concerned, the age of Madonna never happened); sweat is categorically not tolerated. Is there a department in the Royal Household dedicated to deodorant testing? And if not, might this be a job creation scheme for Prince Andrew?     The Mint Velvet/Monsoon (both brands are currently taking credit) wedges are an odd yet endearingly Kate choice, and those £99 wedges have become a trademark, just as Launer bags are The Queen’s, and upturned brims and coats-and-matching-dresses were the Queen Mother’s. The dress, niftily adapted from an ankle length kaftan by Natasha Archer, the Duchess’s PA turned stylist, has a boho elegance to it reminiscent of Isabel Marant – who probably got her inspiration from India. It is essence of Yummy Mummy, ideal for almost every eventuality, even wicket-work and will be the most sought after and copied look of the entire tour. Wouldn’t it have looked cute - and occasion appropriate - if she’d slipped on a pair of plimsoles?   At a Garden Party in Delhi to celebrate the Queen’s 90th birthday, the Duchess turned to one of her favourite party designers, Alice Temperley. A two-piece (£995 and £1995) from the spring summer collection, featuring Indian motifs and lattice embroidery, it’s quintessential Kate– modest but feminine. Black and white is quite a harsh look to pull off in real life, despite fashion’s obsession with it. But the gauze adds some softness. Note the raised waist – a tried and trusted optical tactic the Duchess deploys to make her legs look longer. The earrings are an uncontrived ethnic touch. The loose hair – some up, some down – is more youthful than her swept back chignon. Brownie points to Royal coiffeur Amanda Cook for avoiding frizz in the 66 per cent humidity.       While this couldn’t be described as a youthful look by contemporary standards , this striking cobalt beaded (in India) Jenny Packham dress works perfectly on the Duchess. These pictures will hold up well in years to come. The complementing earrings by Jaipur based Amrapali, are a clever touch – some serious statements were required to offset that rather mature updo, however chandelier earrings would have been distracting given the sparkly bodice. A shawl in matching fabric is another idea to borrow: it looks as if it’s part of the dress, providing cover and warmth in the air conditioning, without falling into dread pashmina territory (although India is home to exquisite pashminas).  Strong make-up works with the hair: she looks stunning.       The tear drop motif may have originated in Kashmir in the 11th century, but it was the Scottish town that gave Paisley its name after the East India Tea Company introduced it to Scotland in the C17th. Who better to pull it all together than Sarah Burton of Alexander McQueen who adapted a look from the current pre-fall collection for the Duchess. Arguably wearing Accessorize earrings when everyone knows you have access to ravishing jewellery is a frugal step too far, particularly when visiting a country with centuries of exquisite jewellery making expertise. Black court shoes might have been a chicer choice, but the £195 leg-lengthening LK Bennett nudes suggest the duchess, as ever, was dressing to ensure her figure looked its best no matter what angle the lenses were coming from.   Given her exemplary attention to detail, it seems out of character for the Duchess not to have referred to the Royal Hand Book and had some weights sewn into the hem of this cream Emilia Wickstead dress to prevent it blowing up around her thighs. On the other hand, given how otherwise safe the dress is, it would be nice to see this as a small act of mischief. Clock those killer Rupert Sanderson heels.   This high neck Temperley London Edwardian-esque dress with pretty pleated darts in the skirt (plus chignon) is reminiscent of Princess Anne in the 1970s  - no bad thing – but also nods to current fashion trends du jour – that pretty green, and the sheer lace yoke and sleeves give her a modern edge (ish). Her green amethyst and tourmaline earrings are by Kiki McDonough and were specially made for her to celebrate the birth of Princess Charlotte.  By day three (one imagines the Royal advisors reasoning), the Republicans will be carping about the cost of all of this, so crack out something cheap and cheerful. This £50 number from Glamorous, a high street online brand (also sold at Topshop) again nods to India. She doesn’t often do a maxi, but it suits her. She’s also wearing flats (£175 by Russell & Bromley) which adds a pleasingly casual air. Last night’s final look, this pretty, colourful number from US designer Anna Sui, fits her printed  tour theme – she’s not pulling out any surprises here. But she is tentatively buttering the Anglo-American relationship and has debuted a new pair of her beloved wedge shoe in black. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  'Do you read Very British Problems?’ asks Alexa Chung, apropos of nothing and referring to the Twitter account, turned book, turned television series, that mocks our national hopelessness. ‘The other day, they were pointing out how every time a British person goes towards Customs they’re sure they’ve suddenly stashed grams of coke in their case. 'At City Airport the other day I got pulled into a room before I even checked in. They went through everything. Then I got through the other side and they checked everything again. Then, when I got to America, they pulled me aside. I was like: “What’s going on today? What are they looking for?”’ She puts on an American accent and a sideways look. ‘“Got any loafers in here, Chung?”’ I have no idea why we’re talking about this, or even why it’s entertaining, but Alexa’s Very British Goofiness, swiped with a bit of rock ’n’ roll and a knowing wink at her own image, is essentially the recipe of her success. The 32-year-old is famous as a clothes horse, but her sharp wit and talent for observation are what made her so eminently employable as a TV presenter when she started out back in 2006, and what make her valuable as a trendspotter and designer for J Crew’s Madewell, AG Jeans, and currently Marks & Spencer. It’s refreshing, in an industry that can have plenty of style and no sense, that Alexa talks pertinently and entertainingly for donkies – she’d blow away the competition on Radio 4’s Just A Minute. So if fashion doesn’t work out for her… But it is, which is why we are sitting in a nature reserve in the middle of two reservoirs in Stoke Newington, north London. When I looked at the location on Google Maps I thought Alexa really must be aching for privacy, but it turns out that Lizzy, her best friend from school, has just opened a café here in what used to be a coal shed. Delicious smells emanate from the kitchen while pretty women hang mobiles of hand-drawn bats from the ceiling. It’s all so wholesomely hip.   Alexa orders a smashed sweetcorn concoction, sourdough toast and coffee. As we breakfast al fresco, the sun lights up her cream Carven blazer (worn over a black T-shirt and high-waisted Levis, fashion fans). Lizzy’s café reminds her of the Comic Relief Great British Bake Off she did in 2015. She skips into an anecdote about how she was flying in from LA and Lizzy had to liaise with her TV agent about what she was going to make, then quickly teach Alexa the day before. While, sadly, the lime and courgette cake didn’t earn her any gushing compliments, she did come first in the technical challenge. ‘It was crumpets and I won because in my head, I was like: “What does Gill Chung do?” [Gill being her mother]. I always see her put a wet tea towel over stuff and I absolutely smashed it.’  Mary Berry, she says, is a canny fashionista and asked if her boots were by Penelope Chilvers. ‘I was like: “Yeah, they are, Mary.” And they have these hyper-coloured celebrity eyes, Mary and Paul Hollywood. You know, when famous people have shiny eyes?’ Yes, I say, avoiding hers. ‘Paul’s eyes are crystal clear. Celebrity eyes.’ Quite frankly, it’s a relief to have someone who chats instead of postures. We may be forbidden to discuss her hot alleged boyfriend, Scandinavian actor Alexander Skarsgård (he, Tarzan), but after purring romantically about Arctic Monkey’s front man Alex Turner all those years ago, I bet she’ll never spill on her love life again. She will, however, speak effusively about… books. (She was going to study English literature at King’s College London, but then was signed as a model). Her current read is Nora Ephron’s Heartburn, which is a corker. ‘It’s so funny. She does a really good introduction where she says: “They call this a thinly disguised novel, which they never say about men who have drawn from their real-life experience.”’ The Girls, however, the supposed big book of the summer, she condemns as ‘annoying’ and recommends instead the memoir Walking Through Clear Water in a Pool Painted Black, by Cookie Mueller, the American artist, writer and John Waters actress, who was apparently one hell of a woman.   Left: The inspiration - This gold blouse was a bestseller in the early 1980s Right: The new collection - Aire blouse, £39.50 I’ve read that there are 42,000 Google searches every year relating to Alexa’s ethnicity. So if you’re one of the inquiring ones, here’s her story. She was born on Bonfire Night 1983 to a Chinese father, Phillip, and Gillian, an English graphic designer, and is one of four siblings. She grew up in Hampshire and was spotted by Storm Model Management when she was 16, then modelled for four years before starting as a TV presenter on Channel 4. As the host of shows, she started to be admired for her model looks and quirky style. Designers began throwing clothes at her, Mulberry named a bag after her, and other retailers lined up to collaborate.   Which leads us to the topic of the day: M&S. Her second and final collection for Marks & Spencer lands in just over a week. Like the first one she did for spring, it has seen her rifling through the retailer’s labyrinthine archive in Leeds, finding forgotten garments from the 1940s, the 1980s or whatever decade her magic (celebrity) eye thinks she can turn into show-stopping must-haves. And so she has come up with another high-necked shirt, this time in blue (the pink one was the hit of the last collection) and as high-necked shirts were all over the catwalks for next season, that will be one of the best things to buy. Like a fashion soothsayer Alexa has also picked out a shiny black trench coat, also a sure hit – you couldn’t throw a stone at the Paris spring 2017 shows without hitting a similar style. A black square-necked velvet dress is her version of a grown-up party frock, a navy blue velvet tuxedo is excellent. The leopard midi dress feels very 1970s, and a men’s coat from the 1940s that she has tweaked for women has had her friends believing it’s Prada. She says the white, hooded faux-fur jacket – which she calls ‘The Queen’ and is in her opinion ‘mega’ – will be brilliant for New York winters. A tiny, stretchy, crushed blue velvet dress, which could only ever look good on Alexa herself, we’ll leave to one side.   Left: The inspiration - Faux fur jacket from 1981.  M&S has been selling them  since the 1970s Right: The new collection - Crown faux-fur jacket, £99 ‘For this collection, I was thinking: what happens after dark? I wanted to make a tuxedo, I wanted 1970s disco, Studio 54. Fabric-wise, I thought it could be a bit more shiny. Synthetic, but in a good way. And I was thinking of photographers and imagery that I like, Guy Bourdin or Bryan Ferry. It’s kind of Roxy Music – a bit slinkier, a bit edgier. Marks & Spencer definitely has that in the archive: the ability to be a bit more sexy. There’s an Abigail’s Party weirdness going on.’ She felt more confident when working on the collection this time around. ‘There was no pre-thought on the first one; I was so stuck on provenance and making sure that the pieces were exact replicas of the originals,’ she explains. ‘This time, I was less afraid to tinker with things and make it slightly more appropriate for now.’ Working for M&S has made Alexa feel like people know what she actually does for a living. ‘Now, in my corner shop, it’s the first time anyone there has any idea who I am or what I do. People like it. So it’s made taxi rides and talking to my grandma easier.’ Until I told her, she didn’t know about Alison Stankard, the woman who wrote a public letter to M&S earlier this year to say she didn’t think Alexa was representative of its customer and that she, as a mother-of-three and a blogger, was a better choice. ‘I think they have that audience down, no?’ she sniffs. ‘I don’t think the objective was to cater to everyone. That might be narcissistic of me to think it was my view… but it was meant to be through my lens, to bring a different kind of customer in, I think. I don’t know.’  Does she worry about whether her collections are successful? ‘Yes, I worry. It’s just a blanket worry I have in life. Not necessarily about approval. I’m kind of a Girl Guide, so I don’t want to let anyone down – especially not the brand that has brought me in to give them my opinions. But, really, I just want my friends to like it and people that I know. When I’m making something, I always have someone in mind. For the navy blue suit, I was like, “Oh, my friend Gillian would love that.” Or the trench for Tenessee. They’re my muses.’ This is all leading up to the launch of the Alexa Chung fashion brand next May, which, sadly, is another verboten topic, probably because of all the many publications how are hankering to be the first to reveal The Truth about Alexa’s label. Left: The inspiration - The print for these pumps is taken from this 1930s dressing gown Right: The new collection: York shoe, £39.50 ‘That Certain Thing That I Can’t Talk About is what I think about all the time,’ she says. ‘I’m working really hard. It’s why I’m braindead at the moment. I haven’t slept for a while. I do the 3am to 6am shift, which is lovely. If anyone’s got some spare kids they need me to look after, I’m available.’ The week after we meet, she will be flying back to New York. ‘New York’s so easy-peasy. You can just be a teenager forever.’ She likes coming back to London because it’s ‘a bit more domesticated. My friends are all in couples, all thinking about babies, weddings, dog care. Whereas in New York, I have friends who are older, younger, whatever, and everyone seems to be at the same stage of Peter Pan. It’s Peter Pan City. I guess there people focus more on their careers, and there’s not the space to have dinner parties. No one asks if you want to come round for tea. But here, it’s teapot o’clock all the time.’  The Archive by Alexa Collection for Marks & Spencer is available from 1 November in store and at marksandspencer.com   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The New York-based handbag designer, founder of Edie Parker and known for her boldly coloured acrylic clutch bags, shares the things she'd rather not live without. What’s your definition of luxury?   Not worrying about anything.   What are you wearing? It changes every season. Right now I love Prada, Haider Ackermann, re/done jeans and vintage robes and dresses from New York vintage.   On your feet? Gianvito Rossi, Paul Andrew and Adidas.   Other little luxuries you love? Expensive t-shirts. Mostly by Isabel Marant, Current Elliot and the Row. I have purchased expensive underwear in my life but really the brand Commando is unbeatable.   Beauty indulgence?  Botox, balayage, perfume by Frederic Malle.   Ultimate wristwatch?  A vintage Cadenas by Van Cleef & Arpels. Most treasured piece of jewellery? A Georgian heart-shaped rose-cut ring crowned with three additional rose cuts. My husband knows I love hearts and bought it for me after the birth of our third child. It’s dreamy, cool, unique and sentimental. I never take it off.   Dream drive? Secretly I want a green Rolls-Royce Corniche II convertible with tan interior for the country. In my real life in the country, I drive a Chevy.   Private jet or yacht?   In my fantasy life, I’d have both. If I fell on hard times, I would give up my yacht. Begrudgingly.     Dream home? Gloria Vanderbilt’s house in New York for my home base, Gio Ponti’s Villa Planchart because its spectacular, and John Stefanidis’ house in Greece for the summer.   Sight for sore eyes? I love a mountain, and you cannot beat the Rockies.    Artwork you covet? The list is long. I would really love a little Modigliani nude.   Favourite piece you own? A polaroid of Dolly Parton by Andy Warhol. What would you most like to amass a collection of?   Compliments. And jewellery by Suzanne Belperron.   Death-row meal? A well-toasted whole-wheat everything bagel with plain cream cheese, smoked salmon, tomato, onion, capers and a few slices of cucumber.   What are you drinking?  Less of everything. But either Blanco tequila or good vodka. On ice with lime. Home from home? Hotel Esencia in the Mayan Riviera. My best friend got married there and I really love guacamole.     Ultimate escape? Again, the list is long. Places I have never been but dream of going: Mozambique, the Seychelles, the Maldives, Bora Bora, Tahiti, the Galapagos Islands. I could go on…   Necessary luxuries? Time with my children. And fancy face creams.   What single thing would make your existence more luxurious?  Sleep. However, when the Japanese designer Tomo Koizumi made his debut on Friday night, it certainly ticked all the “pinch-me-is-this-real?” boxes. His credit sheet read like a fantasy wish list; think styling by Katie Grand, make-up by Pat McGrath, Guido Palau on hair and shoes by Tabitha Simmons.  One of the original supermodels, Cindy Crawford, has announced that she's done with the modelling world.  Crawford, who turns 50 this month, has hinted to Rhapsody Magazine that she's marking her big birthday by retiring. "I'm sure I'll have my picture taken for 10 more years, but not as a model anymore," she said. "And that's OK. I've done it. I've worked with all these incredible photographers. What else do I need to do? I can't keep reinventing myself. I shouldn't have to keep proving myself. I don't want to." It's perhaps fitting then that her last modelling job before retirement was one of the most talked about campaigns of the year. She fronted Balmain's SS16 ad alongside supermodels Naomi Campbell and Claudia Schiffer - a decision designer Olivier Rousteing made to pay tribute to the golden age of modelling. "U made me love FASHION yesterday , U make me love FASHION today, and U re going to make me Love FASHION in the FUTURE [sic]," he wrote on Instagram at the time about his casting choice. In a way, Cindy's decision to retire comes at an unusual time. Until very recently, the average age of a model in super-expensive clothes was around 18. But just last week Armani launched a campaign featuring Yasmin Le Bon, Eva Herzigova, Nadja Auermann and Stella Tennant that proved that 40 somethings are now calling the shots in the fashion world. As Ruth Chapman, co-founder of Matchesfashion.com, put it at the time:  "the demographic of 40- and 50-year-olds is the woman we always consider first. She’s the one who spends the most money on fashion and is most engaged with luxury designer fashion. If we’re going to be spending a lot of money on something, we don’t want to see it on somebody who’s 17; there’s no correlation between the product and the girl wearing it. Long gone is that idea that woman become invisible at a certain age.” Still, before you start mourning the loss of Cindy's genes she's handing on the modelling mantel to her two children, Kaia and Presley Gerber. Kaia is signed to IMG Models and has featured in the pages of Vogue Italia, while Presley is in the latest issue of CR Fashion Book.  "When people ask me about my daughter, I feel like I could guide her in the right direction because I was able to navigate it," Cindy told the Evening Standard about allowing her daughter to follow her path into modelling. "You can, it is doable. "These girls, even as they're just beginning, they're not as pigeonholed by how other people see them. Someone like Cara [Delevingne], the reason she is so cool is she gets to be who she is on social media and have that direct relationship with fans."     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.   Daisy Ridley is proving to be a powerful role model when it comes to body image.  The Star Warsactress has written a refreshingly honest message about the pressures on women to appear perfect, reminding us that we shouldn't take those perfectly-filtered Instagrams, and well-lit pictures on the red carpet too seriously. Ridley posted an obviously filtered selfie in which she has expertly defined brows, masterly applied smokey eyes and a flawless complexion, and wrote over the top 'I woke up like this #nofilter #nomakeup.' Ridley wrote alongside the image: "3 of these statements aren't true... Social media is great but also a bit scary cause what people post is the most filtered, most carefully chosen and cleverly edited moments of their lives. And self esteem is a huge issue for people around the world." She then says about her own approach to body image: "My skin isn't great so I don't post no make up selfies, much as I'd like to; I have a trainer urging me on in workouts and don't include all the times I say 'I can't do it' and I don't smile all the time but I like to share the pictures where I am. But I actually do love myself, I try to think good thoughts always and am surrounded by the most wonderful people, so I'm keeping it balanced (like the Force, obvs). Just thought I'd say :)." This isn't the first time the 24-year-old British actress has spoken honestly about the pressures on women to fit into one beauty ideal. "'Real women' are all shapes and sizes, all ethnicities, all levels of brave, have families, don't have families," she wrote in response to body-shamers. "I am a 'real woman' like every other woman in this world."    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  If, like us, broderie anglaise dresses sing of romantic summer memories, let Kirsten Dunst provide some light relief. The star, who is notably selective of her party appearances, chose a black embroidered Marc Jacobs gown for Elle's Women in Television dinner, and looked positively bewitching in the new darker take on the needlework pattern. The stitch appeal? The black eyelets looked almost faded when sitting over the lighter underlay, creating a dress that looked worn, loved and not just loaned for an event. Ruffled strap Olgana Paris sandals also brought the actress’s look bang up-to-date with spring’s New Romantics trend, where frills and lace are positively encouraged. Let’s not forget the event was a glossy LA one, and Dunst was surrounded by many polished personalities. A smattering of Fred Leighton jewels and baby pink lipstick ensured the actress held her own against her contemporaries, while her side swept hair chimed with the interesting dress choice.  We all know the power of a great outfit to make you feel ready for anything, but clothes can also be used to conjure up a bewitchingly terrifying atmosphere, even without Friday 13th/Hannibal Lecter-esque face masks. Speaking to The Telegraph, veteran costume designer Kate Hawley revealed the secrets of creating a spine-tingling film world through costume on the set of Crimson Peak, the 2015 gothic noir from feted Spanish director Guillermo del Toro, starring Mia Wasikowska, Tom Hiddleston and Jessica Chastain. Crimson Peak has gained a dedicated cult following among horror connoisseurs for its sumptuous visuals, so we asked Hawley: “Just how can clothes make a film scarier than ever?” Crimson Peak felt like “an opera in two parts,” Hawley says, talking about the visual dualism that runs through the film. Mia Wasikowska’s character is transplanted from wealthy Buffalo, in America - “[a place] suffused with soft tobaccos and golds” - to the dark decaying Allerdale estate in England, where the colour palette was heavily blue-toned. The high contrast of Mia’s golden dress with the dark house in one of the key scenes suggested a sense of vulnerability and warning, like “a canary in the coal mine. We did lots of camera tests for that colour too, because it’s quite a tricky colour!” Kate adds. Crimson Peakincludes many healthy doses of blood and gore, so the costume team needed to have a lot of duplicate wardrobes “in varying states of decay,” says Kate. “[There are] a lot of repeats needed as well for a Guillermo del Toro film. You finish making one dress in a week, and then he goes ‘I need ten of them!’ and you just think, ‘Oh my god!’” The team also had to maintain the high production values without “running amok” with the budget, so a lot of the pieces were adaptable and detachable. Kate revealed “We’d have so many bodices made, but the skirts we’d make more of, and those skirts had so many levels to them that we could hook and unhook them and replace the bottom tier if it all got too much with the blood and the snow [on set].” Certain parts of the costumes were incredibly labour intensive, with one highly detailed leaf motif on Jessica Chastain’s black and blue dress taking a team of eight people weeks to make. “We justified that on one level because it got a lot of screen time, but really we couldn’t start doing 10 versions of that. So we used a technique where it was lightly stitched on, and we took the whole thing off and transfer to the next dress." Essential costume items might come from rather unexpected sources: "Standing next to an over six foot tall Tom Hiddleston, Jessica [Chastain] wanted to gain height. You never think of her as being on the shorter side - Whenever I think of her on film she seems very statuesque - but she is! We had to get stripper shoes for her to wear - we got them from the porn shop down the road from the studio. I was slightly crying inside because everything was so carefully made with 'period' in mind, and then underneath she had these plastic stripper shoes on so we had to cover them up and Photoshop them out." "[The actors' bodies are] modern bodies, which are very different from the period body," Kate explains,  adding that for Jessica Chastain, "the weight of her wig plus the constriction of her corset actually caused her a lot of pain. Wearing these things for hours every day [is tough], and a heavy wig pressing on your forehead and can cause headaches. We’d try to relieve that pressure, of course, but Jessica was amazing - she used that discomfort for her performance in character as well." "Usually I’d draw [all the costume sketches] from the front, but everyone was going “Can you give us the back?' [Lots of the key scenes were] all about people disappearing down corridors, so the back was quite important!" “Guillermo himself told me to add another 20% on [when creating things for maximum impact] because things always get reduced," Kate says. "There was a lot of costume experimentation and prototyping that went on, [the question being] "When does a sleeve get too big?” "We had to build furniture of different sizes - like Goldilocks and the three bears - so that everything in the Sharpe family's house made Jessica and Tom look stronger, and made Mia look smaller, showing her weakening and declining. And we did that with the costumes too, so the sleeves became smaller to show her fragility. If you look at her nightdresses - we made many, many nightdresses - sometimes the sleeves are big, sometimes the sleeves are small. We'd have to sit [Mia] in the [scale-altered] chair and we’d work out the right size of sleeves to make her seem really small." "I’ve never done as many nighties as I’ve done on this film. [The team] would ask 'Can we get another nightdress?' and I’d be thinking 'How many ways can I do a nightdress?' I feel like I’ve done my nightdress quota for a while," Kate laughs. A large proportion of your budget as a costume designer on a period drama piece will go on the items you won't even really see: the underwear. "When you’re working on a modern piece you list for your budget breakdown 'Oh, hat, bag, shoes,'" Kate says, "but for a period piece, it’s like “And there’s corsets, then there’s stockings, then there’s another petticoat here, and we need three petticoats to do that dress because of the silhouette," and all of it has to be made - with [a period drama like Crimson Peak], everything has to be made. There’s no shop to which you can go to buy all of that stuff." Original vintage pieces were an excellent starting point but they did not end up being used, Kate said. "As we developed a more and more symbolic world, [the original pieces] weren't lending themselves to that." Instead, the period pieces were heightened with a few nifty tricks: "We took liberties with [the costumes], it wasn’t exact [period wear] by any means. Some people said 'Oh, it looks very real,' and I’d think, 'Actually when you see the reality, it’s not!' We kept to the silhouette and things like that, but in some moments, you want [the costumes] to exaggerate a feeling, so you need three extra metres of fabric to create movement [that wouldn't strictly be there]."  Let’s face it, How To Be Single was never going to be a career-defining film for Dakota Johnson. But if the actress and her co-stars have not been taking the promo tour seriously, Johnson has certainly been making thoughtful style choices. The Texas native took on London's rainy West End in a custom-made gold Marc Jacobs gown that was in keeping with SS16's trend for slip dresses, pairing it with jewels by Messika. Her own high-shine slip boasted ruffle detailing that extended down from the shoulders into an open-back feature that attracted exactly the right kind of attention.  Johnson then did what every 26-year-old would do and hotfooted it towards the trendiest party of the night. Hanging on the arm of journalist friend, and full-time socialite, Derek Blasberg, Dakota took her agold Jacobs to the Vogue 100: A Century of Style opening reception. It was there that she gave top models Lara Stone, Erin O'Connor and Karlie Kloss compeition in the glamour stakes. It's the first time Dakota's worn Marc Jacobs on the How To Be Single tour, but it's another example of her bold, fashion choices for the series of red carpets. The long-time fan of Gucci has had designer Alessandro Michele on speed dial, frequently calling upon him for her turns in the spotlight. A stint on Good Morning America saw the star step out in Gucci’s heeled clogs. Yes, clogs. No mean feat for a woman trying to cut her teeth as a serious fashion follower. Gucci’s clogs, however, come with an ankle-stabilising strap (crucial to avoid stomping and looking clunky) and neat Horsebit detail. Johnson might have been wearing a high-shine pleated skirt and furry J.Mendel coat, but all eyes were on her platforms. High five, DJ! The NYC premiere, meanwhile, saw her plump for a nude, flowing Saint Laurent gown with voluminous sleeves and a smattering of sequinned stars. Look closely, and you can see that the actres is wearing an eclectic selection of rings on her fingers - another styling tip learnt from Michele at Gucci. Though the conservative silhouette would not look out of place on seasoned red carpet pro Keira Knightley, it is difficult to imagine other actresses looking so at home in this nude colouring.  Peachy hues, ugly shoes and lamé gold lengths? We doff our caps to Dakota.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Lately, the romance between fashion and art seems to be taking a more serious turn.  Earlier this year Christopher Bailey’s exhibition in Burberry’s pop-up Maker’s House immersed us – and his latest collection – in the art and studio of Henry Moore, with the help of major sculptures, maquettes and personal ephemera loaned  from the Henry Moore Foundation. Then last summer there was Duro Olowou’s  memorable curated show revolving around art, textiles and much more at Camden Art Centre.  Now the latest fashion designer to turn curator is JW Anderson, whose  Disobedient Bodies, opened at Hepworth Wakefield last week and runs until June 18. The show consists of a rich and wonderfully idiosyncratic selection both from the Wakefield’s Modern British holdings as well as Anderson’s own extensive collections of art, fashion and design– along with some eclectic outside loans. The exhibits range from  sculptures by Henry Moore, Barbara Hepworth and recent Turner nominee Anthea Hamilton through bulbous contemporary ceramics by Magdalene Odundo to vintage couture by Christian Dior and Madame Grés. There are also  conceptual classics by Yohji Yamamoto and Comme des Garcons, chairs by Gaetano Pesce and Gerrit Rietveld and a film of Martha Graham performing her 1935 Lamentation, in which she creates shapes from inside a tube of fabric.   But the starting point for Anderson was the outrageously radical reinterpretations of the human form in the early works of Moore and Hepworth. “I was struck by how rebellious they were, and how shocking it must have been, ” Anderson says. He has put gender subversion at the centre of his work and also owns work by Ben Nicholson and Keith Vaughan as well as a major collection of studio ceramics. “In my own work I try and look at how ugliness could be new and how to work through that.” Certainly there are many unexpected conversations, as well as some surprising connections in the bodily investigations running through this most gregarious of exhibitions.  It has been deliberately devised by Anderson (in association with the firm 6a architects) to give the feeling of “an intimate social gathering in someone’s home,” with the Hepworth’s Galleries divided into a series of  columns and  chambers using curtains of pleated white muslin and fabric from Anderson’s archive. Here, encounters include some of Anderson’s vividly androgynous knits holding hands across from Sarah Lucas’s languid looping bunnies and a Comme des Garçons Monster cardigan tying itself in knots before a particularly kinky Hans Bellmer doll.  In another space the thrust of a Dior dress echoes the bump of a Jean Arp marble, and Albert Giacometti’s Standing Woman and totemic bronzes by Hepworth and Louise Bourgeois loom before a wall of dangling Helmut Lang harnesses.  And it’s not just the art world that has been invited to this party. In an inspired variant on the usually tokenistic (and tedious) institutional education projects, kids from local schools have been invited to dress up in in some of the most precious pieces of couture. The pictures of the little darlings resplendent in vintage Comme, Issey Miyake and Elisabeth de Senneville taken by leading fashion photographer and long-term Anderson collaborator Jamie Hawkesworth form an intrinsic part of the show.  Throughout and where possible, in homage to Hepworth’s desire that visitors experience her sculpture with their hands as well as their eyes, visitors of all ages are  encouraged to physically engage with many of the exhibits. We are invited to sit on several of the classic chairs by Eileen Gray, Gerrit Rietveld and Gaetano Pesce and to get up close and personal with the forest of giant dangling JW Anderson jumpers which hang in the same room as the photographs of the children. “Ultimately clothing is to be worn, there is a physicality to it and that’s what I want people to feel – the colour and the motion.” says Anderson, who also stresses that  “I’m not here to give anyone a history lesson… these are just objects that send me crazy.”   Disobedient Bodies: JW Anderson curates the Hepworth Wakefield is on at The Hepworth Wakefield, Gallery Walk Wakefield, West Yorkshire WF1 5AW until June 18   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  'I love denim,' says Julie de Libran, artistic director of Sonia Rykiel. 'It’s workwear for me.  You can get things done with it.’ We are in the St Germain headquarters of the famous and  fun fashion house, which helped to establish the Left Bank as the hip heart of Parisian chic when it was established in 1968.  It’s the day before the Sonia Rykiel autumn/winter 2016 show during Paris Fashion Week, and de Libran is showing me a piece from her current collection – what  I thought was a luxurious bouclé wool coat, but which turns out to be made of denim. 'It’s all cut-into, sliced and then washed so that you create this texture almost like tweed. It was a lot of work, but even on  the inside it’s so beautiful. There’s just so much you can do with denim.’  De Libran, who was formerly Marc Jacobs’ right-hand woman at Louis Vuitton and before that design director at Prada, has been at Rykiel for two years. She’s French but spent her teens in California and is a die-hard jeans addict. Ask her how many pairs she has and she pulls an anguished face. 'Seriously, every time I go somewhere I try on so many... I don’t know how many I have, but there’s a whole closet full of them. I divide them by colour – all my white jeans, my blue, my black...’ She’s not wearing them today – she’s in a miniskirt, tights and long boots – but normally you’ll find her in jeans, she explains. 'When you’re a working mum  [she has a 10-year-old son] they’re easy. You just pull them on and I know I can get a lot done – from my morning through my working day and into the night.’ Interestingly, while a lot of us think of jeans as something low-maintenance to wear, de Libran has a different, and dare I say it, more Parisian attitude to the garment: it keeps her in check. 'I like discipline and, just as I think heels can give you discipline, so does denim.’ Say, what? 'The fit of your denim – isn’t that the most important test you have? If your jeans aren’t fitting, that’s when you have to be careful the next day [with what you eat]. Luckily, we have  larger cuts and stretch denim, straight denim, but the fit is a kind of test for me every morning.’ For this spring, Sonia Rykiel’s denim comes frayed and embellished, as drop-hemmed swinging jeans and denim flares. The tweedy denim coat and jacket with a matchy skirt are a cute take on a classic two-piece. There are no skinny styles – so is de Libran of the camp that believes that the skinny jean is over? 'No, I still wear skinny. I have skinny jeans that are also stretchy, which are for my days on the couch at the weekend. I put those on in the morning and a big sweater and great heels and I can get things done. I still like the silhouette. It depends on the woman, on your body – but I know that I still like them because I can show my legs and sometimes I need to cover my tummy.’  Being a denim aficionado, though, she doesn’t confine herself to one style, cut or shape. 'All different shapes work. You can alternate, depending on your mood. Yesterday, I had huge wide denim trousers on with a small sweater, but another day I might wear a tight legging jean.’ De Libran moved to America in the 1980s when denim became a status symbol. 'It was all about Levi’s, they were idolised,’ she recalls. 'We wore Levi’s to school all the time. Denim was so important then: the fit, the wash. I’d cut them, customise them. But it was hard denim, you had to wash them before you wore them. I think I probably did that thing of getting in the bath wearing them [shrink-to-fit]. Every time I go to America, I still try on all the jeans.’ She’s also a fan of Japanese denim, which is very trendy right now, acknowledged as the best quality and used in the Sonia Rykiel collection. 'I was in Japan in the summer and bought so many jeans,’ she says. 'I love the look, the hems, the weave.’ For autumn/winter, it’s an upscale ’70s denim look at Rykiel: wide-legged jeans and jackets, black and blue panels in different washes, patched with brown suede on the waist, cuffs and pockets, plus a prairie-style ruffled dress (left) that looks as though it’s made of denim but is a blue-washed Tencel fabric and as light as a feather. Denim that looks like wool, man-made fabrics that look like denim… it’s not a fabric, or a look, that’s going away. De Libran nods, 'Yes, it’s a good time for denim.’ ￼  All soniarykiel.com   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Arriving at LAX airport on Friday, Amber Heard was probably unaware that she was making a major fashion statement. One that would hush a multitude of style diktats which usually tell us that it’s not acceptable to wear double denim.   Heard, 30, paired her high-waisted jeans with a grey tee and denim utility jacket, of the same hue as her trousers. Her stone-washed get-up was punctuated with black mules, a black wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses. With two worn-in tote bags perched on each shoulder, crumpling the jacket and throwing it off-centre, the actress looked unconsidered, practical yet super cool and anything but a cliché. In the past, double denim, or the ‘Canadian tuxedo’, has suffered a bad reputation, due to misguided patchwork outfits worn by pop stars (we’re looking at your Britney - below). Cast your mind back to the 1950s though, and double denim was a Hollywood favourite worn by screen icons Marilyn Monroe (The Misfits), James Dean (Rebel Without a Cause) and Marlon Brando (The Wild One). No longer considered functional workwear, the utility fabric made its way from the American West to the youths of America, who wore it as a symbol of defiant, non-conformity and a badge of casual ease.  Heard is not only a stylish example of how double denim went from cowboys to catwalks, but how to wear it this season. Her over-sized, boxy jacket cut nods to the resurgence of workaday, or ‘chore’ jackets. This mannish style pairs well with jeans as it sits loosely on the silhouette, rather than cutting the torso in half as shorter, traditional styles tend to. Note how The Danish Girl star has left her jacket undone, so that her t-shirt breaks up the look. Tucking it into the high-waisted jeans also elongates the legs, highlighted even more by her low-block mules. A quick word on shading, too. Go for matching, or similar, denim shades to avoid breaking up the outfit and looking disjointed (remember patchwork Britney). Though she has added a wide-brimmed hat and shades for company (most probably in an attempt to go incognito amongst the airport paps), we’d advise keeping everything else on your outfit to a minimum. Double denim is about looking street-wise, rather than calculated, so enjoy the freedom of this minimal weekend wear.  J Brand Lacy denim jacket, £330, Net-a-Porter Madewell denim jacket, £140, Net-a-Porter   Great The Shirt denim jacket, £350, Net-a-Porter © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The breathless BBC drama The Night Manager, which cost £3 million per episode to make, might have documented the undoing of illegal arms magnate Richard Roper (Hugh Laurie), but it was his trophy girlfriend, Jed (Elizabeth Debicki), that piqued our interest. Jed's excellent collection of kaftans and maxi-dresses brought a touch of glamour to Sunday night television.  And last night, the actress Elizabeth Debicki reminded us just how much we're missing her statuesque glamour, by appearing on the red carpet in a Vionnet dress to mark the show's premiere in the USA. The netted maxi dress, embellished with green flowers, was typical of Debicki's bold style - and proof that she's one of the freshest style inspirations off screen as well as on.  The maxi dress showed off Debicki's height, all 6 foot, 2 inches of it - something that meant The Night Manager costume director Signe Sejlund had to commission bespoke pieces for the drama. Sejlund deliberately sought out unusual labels to get across the fact that Jed was a complex love interest - aloof and vulnerable, yet willowy and achingly beautiful. "I liked the idea of Jed being one button or a zip away from being completely naked. The blue dress Jed discards to go swimming naked in the sea was specially designed to slip off," Sejlund has said of the maxi she commissioned YDE Copenhagen designer to Ole Yde to create for the show.  “Jed has a ‘secret’ child and a past, she wasn’t born into money,” Debicki told The Telegraph of her now iconic TV role. “She tries to fit in but doesn’t quite succeed, partly because deep down does she really want conform.” Debicki assumed she would conform, herself, to the family tradition of becoming a dancer. But as she grew taller - at 6 ft 2" she’s a match for the towering Laurie - it became clear that acting rather than dance was what really appealed. After drama school she began what she assumed would be the inevitable round of auditions and rejections. But on just her third outing she did a remote screen test for the Australian director Baz Luhrmann who was casting The Great Gatsby. He was so impressed that he immediately flew her out to LA. If Debicki was overshadowed by Carey Mulligan during the 2013 Gatsby press circuit, she has certainly not gone unnoticed during the media red carpet tour of The Night Manager. Her lithe frame and short, slick hair style give her an air akin to Tilda Swinton, which is no mean thing. Her brief turns in the spotlight alongside co-stars Hugh Laurie, Tom Hiddleston and Olivia Coleman have seen her dabble with gun metal lamé Armani Privé, head-to-toe sequinned Prada and dramatic caped dresses. Her fashion prowess comes courtesy of stylist Annabelle Harron, who also advises Jaime King and Patricia Arquette. And the pair will soon have more red carpet looks to plan. The Paris-born, Australia-based actress is rumoured to be playing the sultry Mistress Death in the second installment of the Marvel franchise Guardians Of The Galaxy, which is slated for release in April 2017. Until then, here's hoping she'll continue a sting of effortless off-duty looks.  Burberry is well-known for its love of up-and-coming British talents. To date, it has kick-started the careers of models including Rosie Huntington-Whiteley and Cara Delevingne, and musicians including James Bay and Tom Odell. The brand’s latest campaign is no different. It sees a cast entirely made up of bright young things – one of whom is Bella Yentob, the 21-year-old daughter of BBC creative director Alan Yentob and documentary maker Philippa Walker. Bella made an under-the-radar Burberry debut in September when she walked in the brand's spring/summer 2016 show at London Fashion Week. It’s an experience she remembers as “terrifying but really, really fun and a great thing to be part of,” she told The Telegraph over the phone. Strikingly pretty with enviably long, wavy chestnut hair, she’s modelled a little over the past few years for publications like i-D and for brands including Supremebeing and Alexander Lewis, but this is her first appearance in a campaign. “I’m no one special so I don’t really know [why they chose me],” she says self-deprecatingly, “but I suppose we got on quite well.” On the campaign shoot  she relished the opportunity to work with Mario Testino and Christopher Bailey, Burberry’s CEO and chief creative officer, both of whom she calls “ wonderful and talented men”. “I don’t wear make-up and this was all au naturel. No make-up, no hair and that’s what I do normally so that was really nice,” she adds. “I’ve done a bit of modelling, but I’ve never been that comfortable in front of the camera, so it was nice that there was no make-up and also nice that my first campaign was with Burberry, a brand that I really respect.” Yentob has no aspirations to become a full-time model but says she couldn’t pass up this opportunity. “I do love fashion but it’s not really my thing - but I think Burberry is great, especially because I don’t adhere to the idea that anything can really be in or out of fashion; if a piece of clothing is really nice it should be timeless and I think that’s what Christopher is about; timelessness and timeless style,” she explains. Her personal style is what she describes as eclectic, she shops mostly at markets and she looks to her friends and mother for inspiration. At the moment she’s studying English Literature with Creative Writing at the University of Manchester and has recently been trying out her skills as a poetry writer (she offers Paul Muldoon, C.K. Williams and Tom Pickard as her current poets of choice). Her future most likely lies in this creative direction, though she’s not sure exactly where yet. “I want to make things and make things better in some way but I’m not sure exactly what or how yet but I enjoy acting writing and photographing, just life. Enjoying the view!” Joining Bella in the all-new British cast are Dylan Brosnan (son of Pierce), sisters Ruth and May Bell, Hayett Belarbi McCarthy, Eliza Fairbanks, Misha Hart, Liam Gardner, Sol Goss, Ben Gregory and Louie Johnson.  Aside from the aforementioned bright young things, the star of the campaign is Burberry’s new rucksack, the break-out accessory from the SS16 collection. They sold out immediately when made available straight from the catwalk in September. Customers wanting to bag one now can do so via burberry.com, with delivery by the end of the year.  The campaign was shot aside Burberry’s ground-breaking Snapchat campaign earlier this year, when a series of dedicated images and accompanying videos were released live on the Burberry Snapchat platform in October. The Snapchat Campaign was live for just 24 hours, before disappearing making Burberry the first brand to shoot and publish its advertising campaign, live as it happened through the platform. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  A return to elegance is the big news during July Couture Week in Paris. Nowhere is this more apparent than at Dior, where designer Maria Grazia Chiuri makes a two-finger salute to the nauseating theatrics and bad-taste selfies of Instagram. Opening the show is Ruth Bell, the 22-year-old face of Dior, wearing a midi-length cape dress and beret - the first in a line of models dressed in fit'n'flare silhouettes in an exquisitely restrained palette.  Beyoncé is unveiling a new campaign for her activewear label Ivy Park today, but the star of the show is not, in fact, the pop powerhouse herself. Instead the singer asked her Los Angeles-based, sexegenarian choreographer, Karen McDonald, to front the images, modeling logo-emblazoned leggings, hoodies and vests from the line alongside actress Laverne Cox and model Grace Bol. “I got a phone call from her camp to tell me that she would very much like for me to be a representative of my age group in the new fashion campaign,” McDonald tells The Telegraph. “I was of course delighted and said yes.” Beyoncé describes McDonald, who has taught dance for over 40 years and still teaches and takes classes every day, as an inspiration, and McDonald believes that the star felt it was important to reach new audiences with her clothing line, which had previously been targeted at younger fashion fans with campaigns fronted by models like 18 year-old Selah Marley. “I think that fashion is a part of her art and she realised how important it is to reach all age groups within this era of female empowerment,” McDonald says. “When you see someone who is very powerful extending themselves, you feel inclined to [want to] be a part of that.” Working out so regularly, McDonald acknowledges, is not a priority for everyone in their sixties, but she says that getting the right kit can help anyone to start making a confident effort. Indeed, when the singer launched Ivy Park back in March 2016, she did so with the intention of encouraging women all over the world, of all ages, to exercise more and to look and feel great while doing so. “Of course I want to wear different things when I exercise now to when I was 20,” she considers. “I like things that are trendy, but also classic. Sometimes I want to wear baggy clothes, but most days I like sleek ones that show my lines. I like things that show my body off, because dancers work hard to keep in shape.” McDonald has worked with Beyoncé for several years now, including on performances for the Grammys, around her hit album Lemonade and on television commercials. She had previously worked with Michael Jackson on his Thriller video, as well as extensively on Broadway, which she describes as a real passion. “They all have one thing in common; a sense of discipline and greatness for their art,” she says of what the performers she has worked with are like in real life. “Beyoncé is a force. She’s energetic, so powerful, when she walks into the room it’s like she expands as she’s walking towards you. "She’s the best, and she wants everyone around her to give their best. I love Beyoncé because she’s studied all styles of dance and she’s really worked hard. Is her talent natural? Absolutely it is, but you have to have that work ethic to be truly that great. As soon as you think you know who she is, she shakes it up and comes out with something completely different, and that takes real work.” As for Beyoncé’s own workout style, McDonald doesn’t exactly dispel the rumours that the icon (slash bionic woman) can dance all day in heels pain-free. “It depends on what day it is,” she says carefully. “She’s the kind of person who gets down dirty when she works out, so it depends what type of rehearsal it is and how long it lasts. She does have a look, and expresses her own sense of style when she's exercising. "But in a six hour dance rehearsal you might start in trainers and then work it up to translate into heels and gowns and sequins as the practices go on, to reflect what you might actually do in the performance.” In Ivy Park, it seems, both dancer and choreographer have found something practical and personal to wear and feel great in. “I always like to be fashionable, even at a dance class, it’s just a part of the dance culture,” McDonald says. “A lot of things that dancers have worn over the years, designers have copied and brought them into the fashion world because dancers have always had a good sense of style. "My only rule is to have as much fun as possible.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Cast your mind back to what you wore in your teens. If you were a product of the Eighties, chances are combat trousers, handkerchief tops, chokers and unabashed flashes of diamante were involved. No such humorous faux pas’ have been the case for Bristol-born actress Maisie Williams, who has spent her entire teenage years in the media spotlight owing to her role in epic medieval fantasy series Game of Thrones. As headstrong tomboy Arya Stark she is sword-wielding, scruffy and often mistaken to be male. And in the new series of Doctor Who, she's set to play a Viking maiden alongside Jenna Coleman. But as a young starlet in real life, navigating press junkets, awards ceremonies and premieres the difference couldn’t be more dramatic. With stylist Harriet Byczok by her side, Williams, now 18, has posed for paps in hip labels Sandro, Self-Portrait and Markus Lupfer, while also staying true to the high street budget of her peers. Peppered amongst her red carpet looks are gems from Topshop, ASOS and Lavish Alice, while her Instagram gives away that she enjoys sprees in Miss Selfridge. Though many have been quick to compare Williams to young, polished American actress Kiernan Shipka, who has also grown-up in the scrutiny of the Mad Men limelight, it is her down-to-earth sensibilities that have garnered more coverage than her gowns. Take her initial audition for Game of Thrones, for example, which she almost missed because it clashed with a school trip to the local pig farm. Worried that her class crush might end up getting friendly with another girl, Williams made the tough call to choose Hollywood over hogs. Since then, she has used her public voice to speak out about the issues surrounding first world feminism – “there are women in the rest of the world who have it far worse” – and promoted the issues surrounding online bullying in BBC drama Cyber Bully. Perhaps, then, a better comparison than Shipka would be Emma Watson, who graduated from Harry Potter fame to a HeForShe campaigner, promoting gender equality. Williams was unfortunately misquoted as saying she was “impatient” with Watson’s take on feminism in her UN speech, however the two have reconciled any misunderstandings and the annoyance has spurred Williams on to campaign further. Her strong-mindedness caught the eye of pop culture provocateur Dazed & Confuzed, who put Williams on the cover of the SS16 issue along with the title ‘Maisie Williams: absolutely lawless’. Teen Vogue also came knocking with a punk makeover and slot in 2014’s Young Hollywood shoot. In between sword-wielding, shoots and socialism, it’s reassuring she still finds time to be a normal teen, eating pizza with pals and posting selfies.  Pierre Bergé, the business partner of the late Yves Saint Laurent, has died aged 86 at his home in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, southern France after a long illness. While Bergé may not have put his name to the Yves Saint Laurent empire, he was the maison's co-founder and the business mind behind its success. Bergé and Saint Laurent went into business together in 1960 after the designer had left Dior following a series of controversial collections.  La Fondation PB-YSL et la Fondation Jardin Majorelle ont l’immense tristesse d’annoncer le décès de Pierre Bergé.https://t.co/LA1JSaXMiv pic.twitter.com/TciJS94iHD Saint Laurent's eponymous label became a renegade presence in the fashion industry thanks to a series of bold design offerings from 1966's Le Smoking to the Mondrian-influenced collection of 1965.   "You can't separate them out, but his male suits that he dressed women in were revolutionary,”  Bergé  told The Telegraph last year as he launched two museums dedicated to Saint Laurent's legacy.  "It is the one piece of clothing that is 100 per cent masculine, so to get a woman to wear it was quite something. At the same time, if a woman is to wear a masculine piece of clothing, she has to develop her femininity and her weapons of seduction.” Bergé remained dedicated to the business until his departure in 1999 and has been a fierce protector of the designer's memory since his death in 2008- the couple were joined in a civil union shortly before Saint Laurent succumbed to cancer.   "We are the only ones to have such a collection; neither Balenciaga, nor Dior nor Chanel can claim this, because they didn't keep the original outfits, only the customers' models," Bergé said of the enormous archive which he had meticulously preserved of Saint Laurent's work, said to contain 5,000 Haute Couture garments and 15,000 accessories."During each collection, he'd say, 'that will go in the museum',” Bergé remembered. "He was aware, and he was right, that he was the last of the great couturiers." In recent years, the art collector and gay rights campaigner, has been outspoken on the state of the fashion industry and the direction of the Yves Saint Laurent label today. Despite widespread controversy about the designer Hedi Slimane's overhaul of the house in 2012,  Bergé was unafraid to praise his collections. "I adored it; it's exactly what needed to be done," Bergé said of Slimane's debut. "It’s very moving for me, because it’s the spirit of Saint Laurent, but revisited with Hedi’s enormous talent." The rest of the industry, however, was not met with such high praise. "Today, the fashion houses supposedly continue to turn out haute couture but they don't have customers, because I don't call Russian prostitutes customers," he said in last year's interview with The Telegraph. "They continue to offer it in the belief it will sell ties and perfume - that's their right but I don't believe it and think it is condemned to die out.”     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Today the Spice Girl turned fashion designer, who shows at New York Fashion Week, has launched a T-shirt and keyring to raise funds for initiatives and charities supported by UNAIDS.
 The crisp white top, which features an exclusive World AIDS Day artwork of a handrawn heart with the logo’s red ribbon for eyes, is priced at £90. The keyring, also adorned with a red ribbon costs £165 and both will be sold in Beckham’s Dover Street store in London’s Mayfair, and on victoriabeckham.com.
 “The world has committed to end the AIDS epidemic as part of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and I truly believe this is a real possibility” she commented today. She added: “We have come such a long way in the fight against AIDS. Huge global efforts have created proven results, and more and more people are accessing treatment and prevention services. But we are not there yet. There are still people being left behind due to gender inequalities, stigma and discrimination and lack of resources.” Beckham visited Ethiopia in October as part of her philanthropic duties, where she held a jewellery-making class to men and women in order of AIDS prevention care and education.   She explained that as part of her role, she is “proud to take a stand, speaking up for change and pushing on towards our common goal of ending AIDS”.
 Beckham is keen to use fashion to raise money and awareness for those in need; earlier this year she donated designer outfits outgrown by her four-year-old daughter Harper to Mary Portas’ charity shop to aid Save the Children.  Whether she's lighting up the red carpet in a glamorous floor-length number at The Golden Globes, or in an effortlessly chic casual outfit at a Cannes Film Festival photocall, the German actress Diane Kruger offers a brave and stylish outlook on dressing for both day and evening.  As she celebrates her 41st birthday, we look at her most fabulous looks since she hit the spotlight in 2004 and the sartorial lessons we've since learnt from her... Kruger’s sweet pinstripe crop top could look a tad young if paired with skinny jeans and trainers, but her high-waisted trousers and strappy heels ensure her look is evening-appropriate and stylish.  A point of interest is always a good idea when pulling together an outfit, particularly when it comes to occasionwear. An LBD could easily fade into the background if it’s too simple, and Kruger’s mesh sleeves and lace detailing are the answer to this. Think less Strictly Come Dancing, and more Dolce & Gabbana SS17 and you’re onto a winner. Sequins are perfect partywear when the silhouettes are kept long and loose. Note Kruger’s slick and simple black accessories, too.   A print as an accent adds a punch to a simple look, but a few prints together make for a statement outfit. Kruger’s striped skirt works perfectly over her printed shirt dress. Stick to the same colours or a similar print to ensure you still appear polished and pulled together. Her buttercup yellow heels are the perfect punctuation mark. Kruger’s shirt and bow tie were a welcome breath of fresh air on the red carpet in 2009. The masculine vibes were counteracted perfectly by her pretty makeup look and high heels. Make this work for you every day by wearing printed platforms with a trouser suit, or a cami dress with trainers. An LBD is classic and fabulous, but a bold red dress is a surefire way to make a stylish statement. If you opt for a plain colourblock style, you can switch up your accessories each time you wear it to keep the look fresh. A printed silk pyjama top is our go-to for effortless chic day-to-day, and look just as great with straight leg jeans and strappy flats as they do with a pleated skirt and heels for evening occasions. Ignore all Angelina at the 2012 Oscars memes - a thigh split can look great when worn correctly. It breaks up a long black bottom half easily, and looks best with a simple shoe and an otherwise modest dress. Stick to a just-above-the-knee split to keep it chic. If you don’t want to leave your boho roots behind when heading to an elegant event, just look to Kruger for a great example. Her chiffon dress and beachy locks wouldn’t look out of place with wellies and a leather jacket at Glastonbury, but overall her polished look deems it red-carpet appropriate. A jumpsuit, particularly in slinky or structured fabrics, in jewel colours or with some embellishment or beading, is just as evening-appropriate as a dress, and a lot more practical. Wear statement earrings with a strapless style, and bright accessories with black options It’s annoying when our sartorial choices don’t marry up with the day's weather, so it’s always worth bringing a cover-up along in case the weather takes a turn for the worst. If we’re honest, a pashmina wouldn’t be our first port-of-call - we’re partial to a fitted blazer or printed kimono which both look great dressed up or down.   It’s easy to assume shorter hair isn’t as versatile as longer locks but Kruger’s choppy curly bob proves otherwise. After she chopped off her mid-length hair, she wore an array for styles from a mini top knot to a sleek straight ‘do. Although ‘shoulder-robing’ is a popular choice among fashion types to showcase an outfit to its full potential, there’s a lot to be said for the humble cape, which does the same job without the inevitable tricky balancing one must have to navigate when wearing a coat on their shoulders. Kruger has the right idea keeping her statement number buttoned up, but it would look equally great open to show off a printed top. Pink was all over the SS17 and AW17 catwalks and if you want to get in on the act, you’ll need to find the shade that works for you. Blush pinks suit fairer skin tones, and the brighter hues suit olive and darker complexions. Go for a tonal look or use your pink piece as a summery accent with monochrome looks.   Kruger proves that staple denim cut offs can be worn away from a sandy beach in the Caribbean. Pair with a floaty top and barely there makeup to ensure you look more Kate Moss than Love Island. Sandals or espadrilles are best, but a heel can work if it’s tan and with a chunky block heel. Some pieces are just worth investing in. They’re classics that hold their value, go with everything and make any outfit look chic and a bit more expensive. We’re not saying head out and buy a Burberry trench and a Chanel handbag, but just look at the stylish edge they give Kruger’s simple outfit. What quicker way to fast track your style to French chic heights than with a white beret? Kruger pairs hers with a smokey eye and matching white dress. If you’re wary of such a statement hue, a black option is just as sweet.   Who says a fitted gown is the only way to go for dressy occasions? A full skirt is classic, stylish and ultimately more comfortable to wear. Pair with a fitted top to balance your proportions and always wear with a heel.   You never know how important they are until you need one, or your current one lets you down when you most need its support, so it’s worth investing in a strapless bra to meet your needs and ensure you’re not limited in outfit choices this summer. Thankfully, we did all the hard work and road tested tons of them to find the best to buy now. Not only is it thicker and warmer, but the sumptuous texture of velvet means it looks especially good in jewel tones like violet, turquoise and burgundy. If you’re not heading anywhere this summer that requires a floor-length gown, why not opt for a velvet kimono, or belted blazer over a midi dress? This sweetheart neckline gown with billowy sleeves is the best of both worlds; Kruger’s dress is perfect for the red carpet, flashes her decolletage (and more importantly, ensures all attention is on those diamonds) and keeps her arms warm while she poses for pictures. Kruger’s lightweight checked trench is ideal for spring transitioning and although it looks particularly great with denim and black courts, it will ultimately work with everything in her wardrobe. The oversized style means it will be good over chunky knits come winter, too. Naturally when one thinks of a cut out dress, images of supermodels in bodycon minis spring to mind, but Kruger proves they can look mature, stylish and flattering in her strappy dress with pleated skirt. Note her hemline is kept long and loose.   In recent seasons, a single dangly earring has been the accessory du jour, but Kruger’s stud option makes a great statement too, particularly for those with shorter hair or if you’re opting for an updo. A cuff is also a sweet option if you don’t have pierced ears. Especially while the evenings are warmer, it’s worth investing in a flattering cami dress that can be worn with a blazer and metallic accessories. We especially like how Kruger has toughened hers up with a smokey eye, thin choker and strappy heels. Wear yours over a t-shirt and with flats when the weather cools down, and then with statement earrings come party season. High-waist wide leg trousers are flattering and ideal for warmer days. Pair with a white blouse or blue shirt for the office and go for tan accessories which are arguably more summery than their black counterparts, and your go-to office summer look is complete. Although not an obvious pairing, there’s no denying that wearing both a dress and trousers will make for a warmer choice. If you have a great embellished dress and chic trousers, who’s to say you need to pick between them? The trick with vinyl trousers is to not overthink them. Kruger expertly partners hers with a white vest and strappy heels, as if they were replacing her ordinary blue jeans. Go casual and pair yours with Converse trainers and a denim shirt or make them evening-appropriate and wear with court heels and a printed blouse. Kruger knows that the power of a smart-casual outfit lies in the accessories. Her simple Breton and cropped kickflare jeans are perfectly paired with a leopard shoe, metallic sunglasses and that pink neckerchief, tied artfully around her neck. It would look equally stylish on her wrist, handbag or tied round her belt loops. Upgrade your off-duty look with a splash of checks a la Kruger. Her denim jacket and printed shirt dress is ideal a casual day out. Heeled boots and a ladylike tote keep her outfit looking grown-up. Kruger’s printed silk tunic and matching trousers cut out the ‘what-top-goes-with-these-trousers’ dilemma we’re so used to on a Monday morning. All they need is sleek black accessories to ensure they steer clear of pyjama territory. The rule is, if you’re wearing a skirt or dress of a shorter length, keep your top half covered up. Kruger sensibly obeys this rule and looks chic in her long-sleeved sequin number. Trouser suits have been in fashion’s eye of affection of late and if you’ve got in on the act and invested in a coloured one, why not step it up a notch and try a printed version? Kruger’s Miu Miu set is smart and pretty - think of the mileage you’ll get from them as separates, too. With a nude court heel and metallic clutch bag, Kruger’s duck egg dress would have been especially princess-y. Not one to confirm to the obvious, she pairs it with a black leather and socks and heeled sandals. Where you’d be right in thinking ticking too many trend boxes would be deemed a little try hard, there are times when it can look both stylish and daring. Case in point, Kruger and her embellished plunge-neck dress with floral skater skirt, off-the-shoulder cream knit, patent ankle boots, round sunglasses and red bag.     While the top half of Kruger’s outfit looks like it’s ready to run errands on a Sunday afternoon, the bottom half wouldn’t look out of place at a fashionable bar. Together, they counteract each other and sit in harmony. As separates, they’re probably the hardest working prints in many wardrobes, and if you haven’t been wearing them together, you’ve been missing out on fashion’s favourite clash. Wear your Breton top with leopard flats and loose denim and you’ll see what we mean. The 60s called, and they’ve said we can keep Kruger’s double denim look as she looks uber-stylish. The oversized jacket and straight jeans are the perfect pairing and her Breton top and fresh white sneakers only add to her casual look. Although an old tracksuit or jeans and a sweatshirt are perfectly comfortable for flying, there’s nothing particularly stylish or ‘fashion’ about them. Enter Kruger and her gingham skirt and denim shirt combo. The print of her skirt means seatbelt creases aren’t noticeable, and her lightweight but cosy roomy shirt are perfect for enthusiastic plane air-conditioning. Black accessories and a sunhat are ideal partners. In previous years, matchy matchy looks have been seen as contrived and boring, but neither can be used to describe Kruger’s fun orange pumps and matching pout. Granted, if her nails and bag had also been the same shade of peach then it may have been a step too far. You needn’t feel trapped when it comes to evening-appropriate shoes as increasingly flats are becoming more jazzy. Kruger’s studded ballerina flats are an excellent complement to her pretty dress - they’re edgy, chic and most of all, comfortable.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
