 When you’re Donatella Versace and you’re the first show to start the SS16 Haute Couture season, you don’t mess around. The Italian designer signed up some of the world’s hottest models to star in her Paris show - including Lara Stone, Irina Shayk, Stella Maxwell, Rosie Huntington Whiteley, Joan Smalls, Natasha Poly and, of course, Gigi Hadid. Wearing goddess-style gowns and trouser suits constructed with rope and featuring extensive cutaways, the collection was classic Versace: strong and unashamedly sexy. "Versace has its own tradition: barely there dresses that defy gravity and every other known force field. Can’t work out how it’s staying on, other than the wearer’s will power? This is Versace’s favourite kind of outfit," says The Telegraph Fashion Director Lisa Armstrong of the collection on our sister site Telegraph Luxury. "But if the ambition was familiar, the execution was radical. Leather backed velvets were cut into panels using water jets. A multi-segment dress that took a month to crochet was held together with ropes of Swarovski crystals fused to look like the shoe laces." READ MORE: Lisa Armstrong on  defying gravity at Atelier Versace It wasn’t exactly a surprise that Versace’s Artistic Director Donatella pulled off a model army for the show. This is the brand that launched the supermodels back in the 1990's, after all. And the latest Versace campaign features Natasha Poly, Raquel Zimmerman and Gigi Hadid lounging against the stark backdrop of the California salt flats. But it’s a savvy move, guaranteeing that the Versace brand remains relevant to fashion fans around the world who now watch fashion shows by refreshing instagram and twitter. Just as Donatella used a picture of herself and Gigi to launch her instagram account last year, so getting her to close the Couture show suddenly makes that million dollar collection (yes, really) relevant to the masses. Few people other than the high-flying couture customers in attendance - and Rita Ora, who’d already scored a couture look to wear on the front row - will be able to secure one of this show’s catwalk creations. But Gigi’s pre-show attire - think skintight leggings with a waistband featuring the classic Versace insignia - might just see a surge in searches of vintage Versace on eBay. Such is the power of the insta-model.  Jonathan Anderson is a busy man. He runs his eponymous brand, J  W Anderson, from a studio in east London three days a week, commuting to Paris to spend the other two as creative director at Loewe, plus paying a visit to the Spanish’s brand Madrid HQ once a month. Each brand shows both womenswear and menswear at their respective fashion weeks twice a year – so four catwalk shows in all. This year, he added a collaboration with high street giant Uniqlo for good measure – its sell-out success will be followed by a second, due in 2018. The upward shift in pace – and in Anderson’s career trajectory – began when the world’s largest luxury goods conglomerate LVMH acquired a minor stake in J W Anderson in 2013, simultaneously announcing his ascension to the top at Loewe. It makes for a mammoth workload, though if Anderson is overwhelmed, he hides it very well indeed. “I just work quite fast,” he says in a Northern Irish accent softened somewhat by years spent in London. He carves out half an hour from work to catch up over the phone, just three days before he will win dual prizes at the Fashion Awards – though he doesn’t know it yet. “I like to keep things moving. I can’t do meetings that lag on and I can’t deal with bulls---. People have to come very prepared, to already have worked it out. They need to make sure what they’re asking is important, not not important. It’s about efficiency, really.” It appears to be working. At the Fashion Awards, held in London’s Royal Albert Hall on Monday night, Anderson received two awards – for J W Anderson, British womenswear designer of the year, for Loewe, accessories designer of the year. Having both brands honoured suggests that he is yet to let either ball drop, though Anderson is used to juggling – in 2015, J W Anderson won both the womenswear and menswear categories. The accessories category is newer to Anderson, and perhaps the sweeter for being so hard-fought. “When I first joined Loewe, I put this massive wager on my own head that I had to come up with a bag. Because I had never designed one, I felt like I had to own it. I remember seeing different components from different menswear bags, and clipping them all together, changing the access point to the top, from the side, to the top of it adding a strap. And I knew the minute it was sitting on my table.” Anderson’s Puzzle bag has become a bestseller for Loewe – one of its pillars, as he calls them. “I think it was unique – I’ve never seen a bag that looks like that. It’s an incredibly difficult bag to copy: time-consuming to make, made up of multiple pieces.” Not, of course, that that will stop the high street trying. Fast fashion labels like Zara and Mango are quick to take “inspiration” from the catwalks, and with their speeded-up production, often have their versions (with the required points of difference to avoid lawsuits) on sale months before the designer originals. Loewe’s accessories, which so often become cult buys of the season, have become favourites for these copycat brands. “It’s kind of flattering. I don’t think it really matters – you’re going to be able to tell the difference. Ultimately, these things happen; we live in a post-modern world, and it doesn’t really get me riled up,” he laughs. “Because it’s sort of part of the process – it means that it’s working!” At 33, Anderson is the youngest in a generation of young British designers that includes Erdem Moralioğlu, Christopher Kane, Jonathan Saunders and Roksanda Ilinčić. But while the others are often photographed arm in arm at fashion parties, Anderson has always stood slightly apart from that set. “I don’t know if I see myself as an outsider; I just feel like I’m an individual. It’s not about holding them at arm’s length. I love when people do good collections – I don’t need to know that person. I just want to understand the clothing, the work. Because then I can use it to say, I need to push myself more, or am I being lazy, am I doing enough? “When you work in a business, it’s like sport somehow,” he says – a mentality no doubt inherited from his father, Ireland international rugby player turned coach Willie Anderson. But it’s an attitude echoed in fashion, too. “I remember Karl Lagerfeld once telling me ‘look, competition is good’. And I believe that, because it makes you think. It makes you push yourself to become better.” Lagerfeld may have distanced himself from his contemporaries – he famously feuded with the late designer Yves Saint Laurent (though that centred around a man) and, like Anderson, has chosen to take on more than most, designing across Chanel, Fendi, and his eponymous label, but his career speaks for itself. “In America, arrogance is treated in a completely different context than how we deal with arrogance in Britain. Ambition is sometimes mistaken as arrogance. Or responsibility. I have a responsibility. When you employ people – every single one of my collections, I am nervous about. Because I need it to work. I need it to sell so that I have an office to go to. “People might read me being my own self as arrogance. I don’t really care. But what I do care about is that people see that I love the work. And that I’m doing the work.” At the pace Anderson’s setting, I don’t think anyone could argue with that. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Is it any coincidence that the Scandinavian feelgood hygge storm hit at precisely the same moment that the cyclone of political turbulence swept us up and knocked us off our feet? I think not. Whatever hygge really means – a debate that I’ll avoid – there is no doubt that in this climate, both figurative and literal, I want to stay inside, comfort eat and hang out with loved ones more than ever. I want to invest in quality, in things that I know the creators care about making. It’s time to discover the zen, quiet labels who imbue calm in both the clothes and the wearer. Cue two designers creating thoughtful womenswear. The first is a new voice who is reacting against the high turnover of designs and ideas that she was required to produce while consulting for high-street labels; the second is a man who creates pieces to be layered and worn every day, replete with details that shout quality and care. Hockin Charlotte Hockin is obsessed with construction, a preoccupation that materialises in her designs. With over a decade spent in the industry working as consultant designer, in 2015 Hockin decided to launch her own brand, realising that she'd always regret it if she didn't make the leap. Her pieces feel built: precision-cut, sink-stitched and overlocked in extremis; for Hockin the inside of a trenchcoat or skirt is as important as its outside. Long gilets with overlocked patch pockets are layered on top of reversible knits, and on tops and skirts the double-faced fabric leaves a trace of high-contrast colour down the exposed central seams. Hockin’s subdued and grown-up colour palettes make me want to collect and layer up each piece, keeping me warm without looking frumpy. Don’t call it minimal; these are thoughtful and tranquil clothes whose making is manifest. hockin.co Maison Rabih Kayrouz It wouldn’t surprise me if under the Webster’s Dictionary definition for “warm” the synonym Rabih Kayrouz appeared. The Lebanese designer has a personality, brand and spirit of generosity that sets a very high benchmark in the fashion world. His shows in Paris are stuff of legend (last season the prima ballerina Marie-Agnès Gillot danced her way through the show to a standing ovation) and this January during couture week, he threw out the fashion calendar to present his ready-to-wear collection months early. He showed beautifully cut cream cashmere coats, tailoring in salmon pink and khakis with flats – all so easy and breezy and chic. Ruffled dresses worn atop pressed trousers, thick sapphire corduroy suits with matching coats, silken striped palazzo pants in citrus and nude. This is comfort dressing at its most elegant and well-cut. Available at matchesfashion.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Since launching lifestyle site Goop in 2008, Gwyneth Paltrow has tantalised readers with a stream of occasionally beguiling but more often bemusing glimpses into her life. The site has featured recipes for homemade pumpkin-seed milk and Paltrow’s favourite “elevating adaptogenic latte” alongside recommendations for vagina-steaming and aerial yoga – to hilarity among Gwynnie-watchers. And now – far from the erroneous rumours earlier this year that she was walking away from her site – the Oscarwinning actress is betting that women will want to refresh their wardrobe alongside their next gut-cleanse kit. So this week she introduced Goop Label, a line of “carefully crafted essentials” based on pieces from the 43-year-old working mum’s personal wardrobe. Think low-key basics that give the appearance of working-on-anyone, but probably work best on a gym-honed, edamame-fed Paltrow, to be fair. “I wanted to create product that is incredibly high quality and delivered at a great value,” Paltrow said, adding in typical gobbledy, er, goop: “I think there’s a huge white space in the market for luxurious ready-to-wear at a direct-to-consumer price.” Goop started as a newsletter in which she could share personal travel tips, recipes and shopping finds – anything that would “nourish the inner aspect”, as the tagline promised. Her informal style and unparalleled access proved compulsive, and it now has over three million subscribers. Never afraid of featuring something polarising (a $15,000 vibrator?), it’s always clickable. It has helped that, over time, many of Paltrow’s more fringeyseeming recommendations – juicing, cupping, cleanses – have entered the mainstream. So what can we expect of her sartorial offering? The Pattner Peak Lapel Blazer and coordinating Eliza Wide Leg Culotte from the new Goop Label collection Her latest charge to Gwynethise the masses will see a very limited number of pieces land on goop.com every month. The first “drop” of items are typical of her laidback-luxe style: a grey tweed blazer with matching wide-leg culottes, for instance, and a chambray denim button-down shirt. The idea is that each piece comes with a back story (presumably because shopping is also to be seen as a journey to inner nourishment). The Pattner Peak Lapel Blazer, $695 (£524), is a belted, singlebreasted grey tweed blazer with flap pockets and subtle epaulets. It’s named after Goop’s head of collaborations and based on the design of one of Paltrow’s favourite jackets. She wears it with the coordinating Eliza Wide Leg Culotte ($325/£246), and in her “design inspiration notes” says: “I’m a real suit girl, and September, to me, connotes getting back to work and buckling down... I was very inspired by English schoolboy grey flannel suits – but with a feminine spin.” The Elise Chambray Button Down shirt and Classic G. Tote from Goop Label All Goop Label items are produced in Italian factories used by brands including Azzedine Alaïa and Proenza Schouler. They are ordered by the dozens rather than the thousands, and once the pieces are gone, they won’t be restocked. “It’s a clever way to launch,” says Emily Gordon-Smith, head of fashion at Stylus, the innovation research and advisory firm. “The limited drops and the idea that it’s focused on key items that are going to work really hard for you are going to be big news.” And, so far, it seems to be succeeding. The Elise Chambray Button Down shirt, admittedly the cheapest design of the bunch at $195 (£147), sold out less than 24 hours after it went online. It proves that while it’s easy to ridicule Gwyneth’s “working mum” goopisms, an army of women out there want to look like Paltrow at any price. And in a way, it makes sense. Her stockpiles of denim cut-offs, blazers and simple dresses help create the kind of easy wardrobe most busy women hanker after. Similar styles from the British high street (L-R): Horatia tweed blazer, £159, Joules; Brennan tweed textured trousers, £175, Whistles; classic chambray shirt, £39.50, Boden; Banks bonded leather tote bag, £125, Jaeger at John Lewis “The chambray shirt is precisely what I want to see from Goop’s fashion line,” says Sarah Bailey, editor-in-chief of Red magazine. “That American laid-back luxe is exactly what you want from her.” “It’s easy to forget what a savvy business woman she is,” Bailey added. “I actually spoke to her about her plans to launch apparel at the beginning of the year. ‘Sell the way that women want to shop,’ were her words to me. ‘When it's July and I am buying a really thick cashmere sweater that kind of takes the fun out of it.’ How true.” How Paltrow will fare against other celebrities who have moved into creating fashion lines is anyone’s guess. Victoria Beckham, who has just shown her latest collection at New York fashion week, has certainly made a success of it. “There’s always room for celebrity collections,” says Gordon-Smith. “From what we’ve seen, this product seems to have been put together with integrity. There’s definitely going to be a market.” Goop Label isn’t available outside the US yet, but if you like these pieces, watch this space. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Victoria Beckham collected her OBE for services to fashion and charity work from the Duke of Cambridge this afternoon, wearing a loose-fitting black jersey dress from her eponymous fashion line. She also chose to eschew a hat.  The subject of what the designer, who celebrated her 43rd birthday on Monday, might wear for the occasion has been a topic of hot discussion amongst fashion pundits since her award was announced in December, and today’s look proved to be a clear milestone in the evolution of her personal style. Of course, Victoria has experience in matters of dressing for royal occasions, having accompanied her husband David when he received his OBE for services to football 14 years ago. Back then, though, Victoria was a rather different woman. Wearing a spiky fascinator, with poker straight hair, and a matching ensemble of a black brocade dress and jacket, her look was symbolic of her vision of Noughties glamour. Embellished and taut, it was a nervous Holly Golightly-take on doing ‘posh occasionwear’, rather than seeming like something she felt comfortable in. Now though, Victoria is a globally renowned designer, and the mother of four has developed a far more understated, yet polished, sense of style. Today’s Posh-does-not-so-posh look was surely a prime example of this, as the choice to wear relaxed jersey, with simple burgundy court shoes and an undone, low bun hairstyle, is a complete contrast to the aforementioned all-done-up outfit. In fact, swap the heels for her beloved Adidas Stan Smith trainers, and the look could work for casual engagements, too.  Her decision to not wear a hat as many recipients do (though hats and gloves are “not required" in the Buckingham Palace dress code) shows further confidence in her signature look, as well as a possible familiarity with the Duke of Cambridge, whose wedding she attended in 2011. If you type ‘What to wear to meet the Queen’ into Google, over 41,000,000 results emerge. Beckham could have taken to scrolling through Pinterest to see what other public figures have worn to collect their honours – actress Naomie Harris’s elegant Mary Katrantzou dress surely provides a fabulous recent example, also without a hat. Instead, though, Beckham stuck to her sartorial guns and deserves props for not diverting from her principles just because of the situation’s gravitas. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  "It all started with a pair of earrings Poppy bought in St Tropez," explains Edgrado Osorio, founder and creative director of Aquazzura, the 'It' shoe label of the moment. The elaborate drop earrings, one a gem-covered sun and the other a moon, sparked the inspiration for the duo's new collaboration, which goes on sale on December 10. The British model and socialite has teamed up the Colombian cobbler behind the brand for a nine-piece range that includes the designer’s signature lace-up flats embellished with moons and stars, as well as espadrilles and lace-up heels. "Women like Poppy are global nomads; a girl that travels around the world needs something for every sort of occasion," he adds in this exclusive behind-the-scenes video of the pair working in Osorio's studio. Poppy adds that every girl needs a pair of boots, heels and flats (to dance the night away in, of course). The friends have also been inspired by Delevingne's memories of her Moroccan wedding last year. The 29-year-old officially married her husband in a central London ceremony on May 16, 2014, to which she wore Chanel couture, but followed it up with a second, weekend-long ceremony at Marrakech's five-star La Mamounia hotel a few weeks later. To this celebration she wore a spectacular custom-made Pucci gown by Peter Dundas. The full-length, white Seventies-inspired gown included blouson sleeves and was peppered with pretty pastel-coloured flowers, and had a suitably bohemian vibe to go with the hippy-chic event.  Alexa Chung began the publicity drive for her new fashion brand earlier this week, when she launched a new website and teased a video showing just three pieces from her upcoming collection. But now she’s in Vogue, specifically fronting the British edition of the magazine’s June issue, and she’s giving fans a better look at the long-awaited collection, which will be unveiled in its entirety on 30th May. Styled by the magazine’s fashion director, Lucinda Chambers, and photographed by Mario Testino, Alexa wears a Breton top and a gold sequinned beret by other designers on the cover. Inside though, she models pieces from her new eponymous label, including a crochet tank top layered over a sequin tulle maxi dress, styled in a mash up by Chambers with pieces from Chanel, Prada, Dolce and Gabbana and Diane von Furstenberg, as well as vintage finds from London emporium Beyond Retro and lingerie by Agent Provocateur. Throughout the story titled The Things You Do, Sam McKnight styles Alexa’s hair, while Val Garland does her makeup, creating sultry and textural looks, set in the bathroom of a suite at London’s Dorchester hotel. Accompanying the cover story, Chung’s collection gets more focus in a second shoot for the issue, lensed by Oliver Hadlee Pearch and styled by Verity Parker. Pixie Geldof, for example, debuts a multicoloured crepe dress and leather heels from the Alexachung collection - pieces that will now undoubtedly be populating fans’ shopping lists, as they gear up and save up for the launch at the end of the month. Chung, 33, a contributing editor at the magazine describes launching the collection as “just the start”, offering that she’d “love to open a shop” within her first five years in business. “This is a moment in my life where I felt I could dedicate all my attention in one direction,” she says in the accompanying interview. “Age has something to do with it … I’m young enough and excited enough to start something new, but old enough to think I could pull it off.” Available from May 31 at Alexachung.com and Style.com.  Coachella, the Met Gala, the Grammys... Rihanna has been a staple of the international party scene for so long that it comes as a surprise to learn that this year is the first time she's appeared at the Cannes Film Festival, surely the most glamorous affair of all. So to what does La Croisette owe this pleasure? The superstar was hosting a dinner to launch the latest High Jewellery collection by Chopard, the Swiss brand which has been the official partner of the Festival since 1998. But unlike her contemporaries who also showcase hundreds of carats worth of jewels over the course of Cannes, Rihanna was enlisted not just to wear the pieces, but played a big role in their design. The Rihanna Loves Chopard collection officially launches in June and consists of a range of everyday stacking jewels, a reincarnation of Chopard's "Ice Cube" design from 2000, that start at £1,070, alongside one-off, High Jewellery pieces with price tags of five or six figures.  It was the latter that Rihanna, alongside Chopard's co-president and artistic director Caroline Scheufele, celebrated in Cannes on Thursday 18th May. Guests including Julianne Moore, Petra Nemcova and Winnie Harlow attended an exclusive dinner held at the Chopard rooftop, which was decorated with a lavish display of multicoloured flowers, echoing pieces in the collection which pay homage to Rihanna's Barbadian roots. The range includes a mismatching pair of earrings with floral designs picked out in tourmalines, tsavorites, rubellites and diamonds - an exuberant ode to the Carnival - which Rihanna first wore at the Grammys in February. While other pieces are similarly vibrant - there's also a Barbados-inspired necklace and an anklet inspired by peacock feathers with over 6,000 gemstones - at last night's launch the singer opted for a more pared-back palette of solely white diamonds which she paired with a black Ralph & Russo gown. Pared back doesn't mean traditional though: she wore a thin choker consisting of a row of white diamonds adorned with a diamond flower - in total 69.55 carats of diamonds - along with statement earrings which saw 21.77 carats of round, pear, oval and marquise-cut diamonds crawling up her ear lobes, each finished with a single pear-cut stone to dangle elegantly below. The "less is more" rule doesn't apply in Cannes, so she also modelled a jewelled watch set with 31.76 carats of diamonds, and two rings: one with a marquise-cut stone and the other featuring brown diamonds and rock crystal quartz.  The following day (Friday May 19), Rihanna showcased more pieces from the range on the Cannes red carpet. At the premiere of Okja she wore a white diamond floral cuff on one arm and a black nephrite and diamond cuff on the other, adorned with a 31.95-carat cushion-shaped emerald. She finished the look with a pair of emerald, diamond and rock crystal quartz earrings and no fewer than three rings from the High Jewellery collection. It's a strikingly modern approach to the rarefied world of Haute Joillerie, one which signals Chopard's intention to woo a younger consumer. After all, the days of asking one's husband for a diamond parure to wear to a gala dinner are on the way out, and the women who wear High Jewellery today are just as likely to pair their statement cuff with jeans and a t-shirt as with their haute couture. And who could be a better poster girl for the modern take on diamonds than Rihanna, whose Instagram images of her at Cannes garner "likes" in their hundreds of thousands? “I have always been in love with Chopard’s exquisite jewellery, so to actually design collections with them is something I still can't believe… to reveal the new pieces in Cannes is pretty amazing,” said Rihanna in a statement. “It was a really incredible process and I learned so much! I can't wait for everyone to see them.” “Rihanna and I collaborated closely on these creations," commented Caroline Scheufele. "With her unique style, she redefines the way people see and wear jewellery. I am thrilled to welcome Rihanna in Cannes; the Festival is very special to Chopard and to me. To see Rihanna walk the red carpet wearing our co-designed creations was a unique moment; the pinnacle of glamour and creativity.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.   It's not often that an outfit first worn at a glittering  London party would also work for an engagement in the rural depths of the Norfolk. But on this balmy summer's evening, the Duchess of Cambridge was attending a fundraising gala for East Anglia Children's Hospices (EACH), one of the charities of which she is royal patron. Hosted at Houghton Hall- the grand stately home of the Duke and Duchess's friends, the Marquess and Marchioness of Cholmondely- prices for tickets to the gala evening began at £6,000 with funds going towards the Nook appeal to build a new hospice in the county.  And so it seemed only fitting that the Duchess would reach for one of the most glitzy gowns in her wardrobe, a pale pink, sequinned-scattered dress with fluttering cap sleeves by British designer Jenny Packham. The delicate tulle dress was first worn by Kate in 2011, shortly after her wedding to Prince William, for another fundraising dinner in London to support ARK (Absolute Return for Kids). At the time, the glamorous dress retailled for around $5015, according to the website What Kate Wore. Kate accessorised the glimmering gown with a Prada clutch bag, chandelier diamond earrings and a bracelet which was originally a choker belonging to Queen Mary. There was one subtle difference to the Duchess's look tonight, compared to 2011. Whereas four years ago, a bouncy blow dry was Kate's hairstyle of choice which gave the look a romantically fresh feel, this evening she opted for a chic, low chignon up-do creating a more polished, grown-up spin on the outfit- befitting perhaps given that the Duchess has matured in her role as a senior member of the royal family, as well as become a mother during that time. Sometimes it's the granular details which speak the most. Jenny Packham has become one of the Duchess's most trusted and often-worn designers and has been commisioned to create looks for some key moments in Kate's life. It was Packham's feminine and classic aesthetic which won over the Duchess for the outfits she wore to present Prince George and Princess Charlotte to the world. When the Duke and Duchess left the Lindo wing with George in 2013, Kate wore a simple, pale blue, polka-dotted empire line dress. Just hours after Charlotte's birth in 2015, it was a white and yellow floral dress by Packham which the Duchess opted for to make the journey home. Packham's designs have also become solid red carpet favourites. From a sequinned column dress worn to the TUSK awards in 2013 to a bespoke sea-blue gown with lace detailling chosen for an  Olympics concert and a dramatic black off-shoulder dress for a hedge fund dinner, Packham's creations pack a fashion punch without veering from the perfectly-pitched levels of appropriate  which the future Queen's role demands. "Most of our customers want something glamorous," Packham told Observer.com in 2014, "they want to be looked at, but not for the wrong reasons. It’s based off of feminine elegance."  Earlier this year, William and Kate celebrated five years of marriage. From a fashion perspective that of course means that the Duchess has now worn rather a lot of outfits. So many, in fact, that it's even proving tricky for Kensington Palace to keep up. This evening, the palace told reporters that the Duchess was wearing a dress first worn in LA to a BAFTA event. It was down to the devoted online community of Kate style enthusiasts to provide a correction.          © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Think Chanel advert and visions of otherworldly romance and glamour with a soupçon of Parisian spirit likely come to mind. Enter Kristen Stewart, Hollywood actress with rebel attitude, to redefine that perception with a just-released film as part of her starring role in the campaign to launch Chanel's latest bag innovation, The Gabrielle (Gabrielle was the real name of Coco Chanel).  In the film, Stewart is seen dancing and running through an abandoned warehouse space, with brief snapshots of faded grandeur evident in the background, a smashed chandelier here or an elegant sofa pushed up against a concrete  wall there. Filming took place before Stewart shaved her hair off and she is seen with a disheveled bun and wearing her signature off duty uniform of a white tee, black skinny jeans and trainers, with a classic Chanel tweed jacket thrown nonchalantly over the top for good measure.   Eventually Stewart's energetic routine finds her beside a cream version of the  bag laying on a dressing table, grabbing it then leads her to a dusty window where 'Gabrielle' is scribbled in the dust of a window. "We landed on a search for Gabrielle's spirit," Stewart explains in a behind-the-scenes glimpse of the film, which was directed by Daniel Askill. "There's something eerie about it, but also quite exuberant.... It represents the first glimpse which Gabrielle is allowing you to have of her." Stewart has enjoyed a four-year long relationship with Chanel, becoming one of Lagerfeld's treasured clutch of A-list muses who also include Lily-Rose Depp, Lottie Moss, Cara Delevingne and Lily Allen. ‘I’ve gotten to know him,’ Stewart told The Telegraph earlier this year. ‘As an outsider I thought, “He’s a character, he’s a fashion designer, he’s probably insanely pretentious.” But the guy ended up being the total opposite of that.’ For her part, Stewart has developed a reputation for showcasing Chanel in a refreshingly offbeat way. At last year's Cannes film festival, the Cafe Society star made headlines for wearing a Chanel t-shirt which she and her stylist had customised themselves, an act which few might dare to commit but which added a spirited twist to the look. "We cut it that morning," her stylist Tara Swennen told The Telegraph at the time. "I would easily say about seven or eight inches. It always makes me cringe a little bit, like is Karl going to come kill me at some point. But it's a T-shirt, it wasn't that bad. We had a sweater option and it wasn't right with the weather, so we just decided to slash a shirt. It's very Kristen."  As the Gabrielle bag film confirms, Stewart's coolly relaxed interpretation of Chanel designs is here to stay.      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Dig out your slip dress and prepare to smudge your lipstick because singer and grunge style maven Courtney Love is teaming up with US e-tailer Nasty Gal for a collaboration. Details about the partnership are scarce but the news was announced via the company’s Instagram account with the nugget that it would be ‘coming soon’ (and the lure of a competition to win entry to the launch party in Los Angeles). But if details are thin on the ground, the idea's got us excited. Think of Love and you probably immediately picture of her in bias-cut slip dresses, ripped tights or sporting lashings of colour – accessorised with a guitar. And whilst there's bound to be some of that aesthetic featured, perhaps there'll also be a nod to the fact that these days Love's style is more sophisticated. “It took me a long time to pay attention to fashion, but now I'm at a pretty conservative point in how I dress,” the 51-year-old recently told Harper’s Bazaar. “I'm into ladylike clothes, like Victoria Beckham's—her dresses are flawless on me.” Back in 2012, Love launched her own collection, Never the Bride, a grunge-meets-Victoriana range made from repurposed vintage clothing. This label seems to have quietly slipped from the radar, but perhaps the proposed link-up with Nasty Gal makes more sense - and will help Love's aesthetic reach a new audience. The site is aimed at style-savvy millennials and stocks a plentiful supply of own-label and branded designs which cater to a variety of budgets. In 2014, Nasty Gal teamed up with writer Lena Dunham to dress her for her book tour, as she and the site’s founder, Sophia Amoruso, are friends. Amoruso became something of an accidental entrepreneur when she began selling vintage clothing on eBay from her bedroom 10 years ago. Her knack for presenting stock in a desirable way and making pieces inspired by her vintage finds resulted in Nasty Gal, a dot com success story that employs over 400 people in Los Angeles and has become a go-to site for Americans. Aged just 30, in 2014 she released  #GirlBoss, a business-focused book with the aim of empowering other women to get into business. Now, the question you've been pondering throughout: will you be able to get the collaboration shipped here? The short answer is yes you can order Nasty Gal online for delivery to the UK but a word of warning, you might incur some customs charges at the Post Office. So don't get too excited about their value-for-money deals.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Oscars wasn't the only glitzy event taking place in America on Sunday night. As Hollywood's finest took to the red carpet on the West Coast, First Lady Melania Trump was hosting her debut Governor's Ball in Washington DC. Bringing together 46 Governors for a 'dazzling, sensorial experience', Melania was out to woo at the first event she has personally organised as First Lady. She chose ‘Spring’s Renewal’ as the theme for the evening, and stated that "the scents of jasmine and roses [will] fill the air as we give thanks for this great nation and the glory of renewal.” As such, she debuted a fresh, blunt haircut and a softer makeup look, but has seemingly decided to only release shots taken above shoulder height after the event, concealing whatever dress she was wearing on the night. Perhaps Melania feels that her clothes have taken too much of the limelight in recent weeks and that posing for a full length picture would detract from the message that she was trying to offer up last night. She’s recently made the headlines any time that she has chosen to wear a designer label that isn’t American (thus going against her husband’s “America first” directive) and has also been accused of relying too heavily on a Jackie Kennedy-inspired look that isn’t her own. Ahead of the inauguration, she also found herself at the middle of a fashion boycott, as several major names, including Marc Jacobs and Tom Ford, spoke out to say that they would never want to dress the new First Lady. All that said, the pressure on Melania had been easing up a little last week, as she wore pieces by American labels including Carolina Herrera and Ralph Lauren, and found a new style trick to add to her repertoire; wearing Republican red to show us her colours. Her little black number from last night seems subtle enough, so surely it wouldn’t have caused too much controversy to reveal? Another theory, of course, is that the new FLOTUS didn't want to appear to be in competition with the Oscars. On the other side of the country, hundreds of the world's most glamorous actresses were being photographed in their finery and so any picture of Melania in a gown that would have emerged last night would have been lost in the white noise on Twitter. Asked in the week whether the scheduling of the Governor's Ball and the Oscars on the same night was a deliberate calendar conflict the White House's press secretary Sean Spicer simply said that the President and First Lady had no concerns about missing the Hollywood ceremony on TV, and that all of their focus would likely be on welcoming the Governors to the capital on Sunday night.  First Daughter Ivanka Trump, meanwhile, was possibly less concerned about media attention, as she posted a picture of her and her husband Jared Kushner on Instagram before they left the house. Ivanka wore a navy column gown by New York label J. Mendel with a polka dot panel draped into the bodice. J. Mendel is a name that Ivanka has been a fan of for some time, sitting front row at designer Gilles Mendel’s New York Fashion Week shows and wearing pieces from his collections on numerous occasions. Interestingly, she teamed the dress with a pair of sandals from her eponymous fashion line, which has been struggling in recent weeks after Ivanka distanced herself from the company due to conflicts of interest with her new political position, and several prominent US department stores dropped it. The social media attention that Ivanka might attract for those shoes could well provide a welcome boost to sales at Ivanka Trump HQ, while, at her first social gathering, Melania Trump has chosen to leave her legions of social media fans eagerly waiting to see what she actually wore. Two very different tactical plays from two very different members of the new First Family. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This week the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge are on a two-day tour of Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly. The whistle stop visit began today with engagements at Truro Cathedral, a cider farm and the beach in Newquay. We may be ushering in the autumn season, but the Duchess was resolutely sticking to a summery look for her varied schedule. She opted for a classic pastel pink dress with short sleeves, a fitted bodice with body contouring seams and a gently fluted skirt by American designer Lela Rose. The blush dress is still available to purchase on Rose's own website, reduced from $1295 to $777. This is a look which fits seamlessly with the Duchess of Cambridge's simple yet elegant style signature.  She paired the dress with old favourite nude-hued accessories; a pair of espadrille wedges and L.K Bennett clutch bag.  Double faced blush pink dress, $777, Lela Rose  The Duchess usually leans on British designers for official visits of this nature, to show support for the nation's fashion industry. So her choice of a dress by Lela Rose, a New York-based designer, is a rare exception.  Lela Rose launched her own collection in 1996, and although she specialises in bridalwear, her ready-to-wear pieces have been worn by the likes of Ashley Olsen, Jessica Alba and Selma Blair. The Duchess of Cambridge has worn Lela Rose once before, selecting an ivory cocktail dress with white circle lace sleeves and a peplum panel over the skirt to wear to an evening reception during her and William's tour of Australia in 2014. "I woke up to dozens of pictures on my Instagram feed of the Duchess in my dress. I can’t tell you how much fun it is to wake up seeing this and it just makes your day" Rose told The Telegraph. "She has worn my designs before but it just never gets old. It is always a thrill!"  When The Duchess first wore Rose's dress in Australia it was seen as an unlikely move to select an American designer when she usually dresses so diplomatically on royal tours, wearing pieces by designers from the host nation or from the UK. In fact, Rose knows a thing or two about designing for state events and so her appropriate yet feminine aesthetic is actually a logical addition to the Duchess's wardrobe. "I believe that if you look good, you feel good and that is the goal for every piece that I design" Rose explains. "It’s somewhat simple in theory but there are many components that go into that goal. I like to use fabrics that are comfortable, luxurious, and feel great on. The colour palette needs to be sophisticated yet fun, and the details whimsical yet more like a surprise rather than overbearing. The cut of the pieces are very flattering on and work for a range of sizes with seaming that is not only interesting but really flatters the figure." Lela Rose is proof that a high profile client, such as the Duchess of Cambridge, can transform a label into an established, go-to brand. The designer's reputation took off when she created outfits for Jenna and Barbara Bush to wear to their father George Bush's inauguration in 2001. Lela Rose continued to work closely with the first family, designing 14 bridesmaid and maid of honour dresses for Jenna Bush's wedding in 2008. Rose added that "the impact [of The Duchess wearing one of my designs] is enormous in terms of having a wider-and global- audience seeing our brand. It is also a personal high for me- I am a big fan of her." The appeal of Rose's designs is demonstrated in the dress chosen by the Duchess today which would be as ideal for work as for a wedding or, indeed, for a day of royal engagements.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  From its inception in 1878 as a small family saddle-maker Connolly went on to become the leather supplier to Ferrari, Rolls-Royce and the Royal coronation coaches. Its latest incarnation is the work of Isabel Ettedgui, wife of the late founder of Joseph (the seminal eponymous boutique). Together they took over Connolly in 1999. When her husband passed away in 2010, Isabel shuttered the original Mayfair store, but late last year she quietly relaunched it from a Georgian townhouse on Clifford Street. This new shop is the home of Ettedgui’s very personal vision: a treasure trove of Connolly clothing, leather goods and homeware, alongside things she loves – be it a Charvet scarf, vintage Cartier box or sculptural wooden vessel from a designer sourced through Instagram.  What drove you to relaunch Connolly?  I’ve always believed in the brand. I’d been involved with Connolly since the 1990s and I wasn’t ready to let it go. The combination of its history and heritage is unique. At its core, it’s about things that are well conceived and well crafted; it’s really not about fashion. I think there is a need today for a new form of luxury. I’m not saying I’ve found the solution, but I think people have been missing that sense  of ownership and discovery. Do you see Connolly as a leather goods brand, a lifestyle brand or a clothing brand?  It really all starts from the leather. Connolly is all about leather, but it’s also about the design, quality and simplicity of the product, too: it’s not about having 500 bags, it’s about having just two or three. That said, I do see Connolly  as a lifestyle brand because it’s such a personal project for me, full of things I like. The first rack you see in the store is hard to tell if it’s womenswear or menswear…  The idea is to overturn the notion that the man goes downstairs and the woman goes upstairs to browse. Here, you go shopping together and buy the same coat and shirt! I used to wear my husband’s clothes; they were always handmade and beautifully detailed. Most women need a great blazer, two pairs of trousers, a good coat, and beautiful knitwear: all silhouettes borrowed from menswear. I think a man’s shirt on a woman is the sexiest thing in the world. What makes Connolly different from your previous retail experiences? I want to sell clothes that a woman really  wants, things I really want. Joe taught me  that Connolly could be a fashion brand, when  I didn’t necessarily think it could be. But I also really wanted to do something with homeware and furniture. I wanted to live in the brand a bit, to give it life and I think you can only do that by absolutely immersing yourself in it. Because it is small and personal, people also feel they own a part of the brand. What are you most excited about in Connolly’s future?  Part of me just picked up from where I left off, especially working with old friends. But the exciting bit is what I can do with the brand and how far I can take my idea of modern luxury. How can it sustain itself, and what makes it work? Connolly is a great name with a great history and I’d like to keep it going for as long as I possibly can. My biggest joy is going to the knitwear factories, I just love it. Seeing people produce and craft beautiful things is extraordinary and such a joy. 4 Clifford Street, London W1; connollyengland.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  As she launches her first fragrance with Comme des Garcons, the former model and creative-director-at-large of American Vogue shares a few of her favourite things. What’s your definition of luxury? Something I can’t afford. Your style? My signature is my hair and usually head-to-toe black. What are you wearing? A large portion of Céline and Prada. My new favourite piece is my Céline shearling coat. Must-have accessories? I love my Louis Vuitton handbags – of which I have many – and a huge selection of earrings. Beauty indulgence? My new perfume, Grace by Grace Coddington! Precious pieces? A little vintage diamond cat given to me by the stylist Joe McKenna. It has a ball which is a pearl. Joe gave it to me for my 70th birthday. The other thing I love is my diamond tennis bracelet and eternity ring from Tiffany that my partner Didier gave me. Timepiece? I’m not crazy about watches, but I do wear a Rolex. Dream home? Maybe a small cottage in Cornwall or Devon or a house in Jamaica. Most coveted artwork? I would love a Matisse. Favourite piece you own? A vintage Edward Weston print of a cat, also from Didier. What do you collect? Steiff cats – all cat paraphernalia – and photographs. What’s cooking? David Chang – at my house, I would leave it up to him. What are you drinking? Coca-Cola. Favourite hotel? The Draycott, they always make me feel at home. Sight for sore eyes? A view of the sea. Ultimate escape? A trip through Antarctica on the Lindberg Silver Explorer. Dream drive? I have always been partial to the old Thunderbird. I remember seeing one driving up and down King’s Road in London when I was a teenager and I always fantasised about owning it. I eventually got one but sold it because it kept breaking down. Luxurious necessity? First class travel. What would make your existence more luxurious? An extra couple rooms in my apartment and an extra couple of cats!  Design classic? I want a mid-century shearling chair. I love everything in my house, particularly my George Sherlock – a very comfortable sofa! © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It’s not just the oodles of wavy silvery hair. Winks, a six year old miniature poodle with impeccable genealogy, is, like his mistress, Linda Rodin, innately stylish with seemingly minimal effort. True, Winks once had a $500 Dogue-cut, but that, intones Rodin in her Long Island twang, was a mistake. “I was recommended this dog-clipper who turned out to be a celebrity dog clipper…” she trails off, one arched brow hovering questioningly above her trademark cat eye glasses. These days Winks makes do with what his mistress calls “the garden variety clip”. Not that this dents his swagger. Winks is a style star and so much a part of Team Rodin, that they share top billing on her Instagram feed (@lindaandwinks, 96,000 followers and counting). Team Rodin is small, but growing. The beauty company she started from her kitchen (truly) in New York’s Chelsea in 2008, was acquired by Estee Lauder two years ago and now has more than 100 stockists. She has moved from kitchen to swish  downtown offices, but home is clearly still where she is happiest. “A new friend recently came round to my apartment and said, 'Now I know why you don’t go to parties. All your friends are here.’” She was talking about the bits and bobs, the lovingly nurtured plants (like Prince Charles she conducts lengthy conversations with them) and the extensive wardrobe, cultivated, but rarely culled, over decades. Rodin oozes what used to be called good taste, but is more often described now as Having An Eye. She can walk into a scrappy flea market, which she does most weekends, and find the item – be it cardigan or couch – that looks a million dollars. She is far happier bartering on 26th and Broadway (home of one of New York’s last great vintage lot) than she is in a chi-chic boutique. “Who pays those prices?” she asks of designer collections. Er, hello? Isn’t she wearing an embroidered cardigan from Gucci? “30 bucks from a stall,” she replies. One or two key pieces - mixed in with her beloved jeans, simple checked shirts and delicate jewellry, customized with charms - is her general rule.  Her mother Billie, was a looker, who never had to try that hard. Her aunt, who had a nose job in the 1920s (“It was terrible, but a nose job, in the 20s, that was something”) was the one with the style. “She was quite plain but she was wearing turbans, kaftans and false eyelashes when she was 94.” Rodin, an angular beauty, is a combination of the two. As for those finds, she lovingly chronicles them along with portraits of Winks, 1950s snaps of her mother and favourite beauty products on her Instagram account. It’s a captivating, personal window on a certain kind of world, one inhabited with style rather than wads of cash and freebies. Despite her large following, she says designers rarely gift her. “I’m too elderly,” she laughs. In the old days, she would have been at the helm of a glossy magazine, fashioned in her likeness. She has worked as a stylist for American Harper’s Bazaar, Vogue, Revlon and Victoria’s Secret (“all those busty models, but that was fun. And they were so nice.”)  Now she communicates through social media – and has 20-year-olds stopping her in the street to take a selfie with her. “I think they like the fact that I’m older,” she muses. “They’d like their mothers or grandmothers to dress a bit more boldly.” Courage has never been lacking from the Rodin repertoire. “Sometimes I’m too blunt,” she says. Get her on American politics, the gentrification of New York, (“the city’s finished. No one can afford to live here. Every time I go away, another neighbourhood service shop gets turned into a Starbucks,”) or “helpful” cab drivers (“I hate it when they try to lift me out of the car. I’m 67, not an invalid”) and there’s no shortage of opinion. As she says, “wishy washy, I am not.” “It wasn’t deliberate,” she says of her second – or is it third, given she originally studied photography - career in the beauty world. “I was happy styling. I would mix up oils for my own dry skin – Jojoba or apricot oils as the carrier, neroli and jasmine because I adore the scent and calendula, arnica and evening primrose oil because they worked. Then friends began asking about them, so I would give them as gifts, like you would bake cakes if you were a cook.” Her nephew, a wiz in finance caught her at it one day, mixing up batches in coffee cups in her bathroom and asked her how much she was selling them for. When she broke the news, he read her a few financial facts of life, ordered some measuring beakers and persuaded her, finally, to write down the formulae. Before long Rodin’s Luxury Face Oil became one of those insider tips, discriminately shared around the industry. Until she finally found a factory in New Jersey to do it for her, she was mixing up 4-500 bottles every weekend. Within months, facial oils became all the rage, although few smell as good as Rodin’s. Her products (there are now hand creams, body oils and soaps) are remarkably good. Her perfume, Linda Rodin Bis, is a delicious blend of anise flower, bergamot, rose de mai, jasmine, musk, with a wonderful powdery base that gives it an almost 1950s elegance. Inspired by her mother, it’s much more sophisticated than the synthetic smelling compounds pumped out by many, larger brands. She has also just launched a collection of lipsticks in searingly chic, trademark shades. Long lasting,  intensely pigmented and super moisturizing, they too are outstanding.  Disarmingly, she makes no great claims for her products, although others do. “There’s so much bull****  talked about beauty,” she says. “But this makes you feel good and that’s the root of looking good.” That and a daily bath.  Her low maintenance approach speaks of old-fashioned values, albeit in a strikingly modern package. Not that she’s immune to contemporary neuroses. When a Californian friend who hadn’t seen her in a while asked why she hadn’t had a face- lift, she had a wobble, albeit brief. “I never had a problem when I went grey at 35,” she says. “I never felt I looked old until I hit 60… but it’s hard sometimes in this youth fixated culture, to resist the tide.” Luckily she was born with independence of mind. Her father, “the only poor Jewish dentist on Long Island,” was an artist manqué and her mother was also “very creative.” It was sunny, suburban 1950s America. There were animals galore – chickens hatching in the cellar, her brother’s pet snakes, dogs, rescued birds. At 16 she was in a serious car crash. At 17 she used the $1000 compensation to go to Italy – a big deal for a young American girl in the 1960s. She never married, or had children and never regretted it. She’s close to her nieces and nephews and was very attached to her late sister, Christine, a “hippy who wasn’t remotely impressed by fashion labels.” And now she’s having the biggest renaissance of her life. “Me, a Luddite. Isn’t it ironic? There are young women who know me from social media.” She pauses to take in the wonder. “At my age that’s quite something - especially as some of them have never heard of Madonna”.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When it comes to dressing for the office in the summer, it can be tricky to find the balance between looking appropriately chic and but also keeping cool. This morning, the Duchess of Cambridge showed us a winning workwear combination which will take you from meetings in the chilly air conditioning  to the sticky commute home in style. The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge and Prince Harry were out this morning launching their Heads Together campaign, which aims to break the stigma surrounding mental health, at the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in East London. The Duchess proves that when it comes to summer workwear you can't go wrong with a crisp white blouse and a boldly printed skirt. The Duchess's slim-fit cream blouse with full sleeves and an elegant round neck is by British label Goat and is available online for £290. An elegant ivory shirt is a simple way of achieving a pulled-together look in the heat. If the famous 'Kate Effect' is anything to go by, the Duchess's blouse is likely to have sold out by the time you read this, but never fear- we've already created a guide to the best white shirts which will help you to achieve the look.   The Duchess paired her blouse with a navy,  teal and white geometric print a-line skirt by Gap's big sister label, Banana Republic. Although this style is no longer available on Banana Republic's own website, it is currently available to buy at Zalando for £105.  According to our calculations, this is the first time that the Duchess has worn the American high street label famed for its workwear classics. The brand has however already benefited from the retail magic which Kate's endorsement brings; in a savvy marketing move in 2013, Banana Republic reissued the sold-out Issa wrap dress which she wore in her official engagement photographs in 2010, as part of a collaboration with the London-based brand founded by Daniella Helayel. Banana Republic might be a new high street find for the Duchess of Cambridge, but she is already a fan of British label Goat, which specialises in luxury cashmere. The Duchess of Cambridge has previously worn several shift dresses and cashmere coats from the label, which was founded by Jane Lewis in 2001 and is known for its classic tailoring and luxury staples. She particularly favoured Lewis's designs as alternatives to traditional maternity wear, choosing a cream 'Redgrave' style while she was expecting Prince George and chic 60s-inspired black coat with cream trim on a visit to New York shortly after her pregnancy with Princess Charlotte was announced.  The Duchess of Cambridge is praised for mixing affordable high street pieces with high end designer labels, and just last night she mastered this high-low style perfectly at the Queen's 90th birthday gala where she wore a £3,450 white lace Dolce & Gabbana dress with a £49.99 red jacket from Zara.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Cara Delevingne made the move from runway model to blockbuster movie star, an essential part of that transition was finding a styling team who could give her Hollywood polish, while still looking like the girl from London in her animal onesies and cartoon tees. Delevingne turned to Rob Zangardi and Mariel Haenn, who also work with Jennifer Lopez, Gwen Stefani and Rachel McAdams, to dress her for her promotional commitments for her first film, Paper Towns. Now with Suicide Squad about to hit cinemas, Delevingne is back on the red carpet again and is making more waves with her fearless fashion choices.  In a landscape where adventurous style usually means an everyone-can-see-your-knickers sheer skirt, Delevingne is carving a position for herself as the one actress who will wear what she wants, how she wants. While promoting the blockbuster Suicide Squad this month Delevingne has made haute couture look like it was made for a comic book convention, in cartoonish belts, over-the-knee fantasy boots, 90s raver top knots and gothic black lace. It's like something dreamed up by The OC's Seth Cohen.  "Not only were we inspired by fashion in different eras for this promo tour - 60s mod, 70s punk - but there was always an element of an elevated, chic superhero in each look," explains Rob Zangardi of the comic book mood board for these looks, "everything from mesh to a thigh high boot to a camo print." At last night's London premiere, Cara Delevingne summed up this punk attitude in an Alexander McQueen biker jacket, a black lace slip dress, thigh-high boots and black leather Camden Market-style cuffs clamped to each wrist. The comic book theme does of course lend itself to more adventurous dressing, as Zangardi points out: " With something like Suicide Squad, it’s even more fun because the film is such a good time. It’s an action, comedy, fantasy blockbuster all at once. It’s meant to be this epic experience. That lends itself to creating more avant-garde looks and incorporating more punk, rebellious, and high fashion elements into the ensembles."  "Cara is a risk taker," adds Mariel Haenn. "Her style is always evolving because she, as a person, is always trying new things. As a supermodel, she can take on different characters and concepts and pull them off effortlessly and make them her own." While most actresses might give their stylists a side-eye if they suggested wearing a Wednesday Addams style mini-dress with sheer thigh high socks, thanks to her years of modelling, Cara Delevingne is willing to experiment. "She also has the foresight to know that even when something looks super unappealing on a hanger, it might be a total showstopper on," adds Haenn. "All of that put together creates this great balance of knowing what she wants, but willing to be flexible with new ideas." Dressing to the theme of your movie could run the risk of looking formulaic, but Delevingne's promo tour wardrobe has had a consistent thread with each look adding something unexpected. One fixture in almost every one of her Suicide Squad ensembles however is her over-the-knee black leather Christian Louboutin boots, with intimidatingly high, sharp stilettos. "Cara is tall and athletic, she has legs for days - she’s an absolute dream to dress," says Rob Zangardi. "The over the knee boots really highlight those features and add sexiness, while staying true to Cara’s tomboy personality." Cara Delevingne built a huge loyal fan base largely down to her infectious, and refreshingly open, personality. And her stylists say working with Cara is just as fun as you'd imagine from looking at her goofy Instagram page. "Fittings with Cara are a blast," says Mariel Haenn. "She’s professional but still a totally hilarious, positive energy. That’s true for when we actually run through the looks. We never try just one style or one type of look. With Cara, we always know we can go so many different directions and she will be open-minded." Beauty has been just as much of a focus for the adventurous Suicide Squad look, with Cara sporting electric blue eyeliner, intricate braids and dark smokey eyes. Her stylists have worked closely with her hair stylist Jen Atkin so that the looks are in sync. "We’ve known Jen Atkin for years so it’s a very easy, organic back and forth on creating the look from head to toe," adds Mariel Haenn. "Jen has fantastic taste and knows exactly what to do. We’ll talk about the look and then get out of her way. She’s a hair genius."   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  ''When it comes to fashion, for me, less is always more,'' 38-year-old nutritional therapist, Eve Kalinik, tells The Telegraph. ''There's never a formula per se - I always get up and put on what feels right.'' Evidently Kalinik, who made the move from fashion PR to nutritional therapy a few years ago, takes the same positive approach to clothes as she does to food. ''I like to wear an outfit that reflects my personality, especially for therapeutic sessions, because it relaxes my clients,'' Kalinik continues, claiming a pair of pom-pom-laden shoes by Malone Souliers actually have the power to make people smile. ''I just think that when you're having a conversation with someone about an issue that's very personal and perhaps something they've been dealing with for years, it's nice not to look too formulaic and serious.'' Satin jacket, £510, Acne Studios; No. 21 silk shirt, £409, Matchesfashion.com; No. 21 silk trousers, £375, Matchesfashion.com; Golden Goose Deluxe trainers, £310, Matchesfashion.com  When she's not in one-to-one meetings with patients, Kalinik is often hosting a workshop or speaking about her view  on nutrition (which includes avoiding quick fixes and fads, and encouraging people to eat for the soul and connect with their food as well as being concerned with what is on their plate) in front of a room full of people. ''That's when I think you need a statement piece,'' she says, citing a patterned Stella McCartney jumpsuit as something she might wear for a day when she's required to take centre stage. ''A good blow-dry and a pair of heels are also essential if I'm doing a presentation, both immediately make me feel empowered,'' she continues. ''Although, only if I'm standing still - I can't walk in heels!'' But surely she needs to wear something a little more practical while experimenting with new recipes in the kitchen? ''Yes, if I'm cooking I always wear my red leather Malle W. Trousseau apron. It was an investment and I absolutely love it - it inspires me to cook!'' Between client consultations, writing a columns for both Matchesfashion.com and Psychologies Magazine and concocting bowls of goodness that are almost too perfect-looking to eat, when does she find time to go shopping? ''I like to shop little and often,'' says Kalinik, ''I'm quite an impulsive buyer. If I see something and fall in love with, I buy it, because I know I'm going to wear it. I don't sit and ponder it for ages.'' Kalinik's secret to Wearing It Well is being in tune what types of clothes makes her feel good - something, she says, is an extension of exploring what her body needs nutrition-wise. Eve’s book ‘Be Good To Your Gut’ is available to pre-order at amazon.co.uk © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We hear regularly of how the Duchess of Cambridge, Queen Letizia of Spain, and other key European royals may or may not have changed the face of regal fashion in the last few decades, but there is another ‘Queen of style’ who perhaps deserves more airtime for her sartorial efforts; Queen Rania Al Abdullah of Jordan, who turned 47 yesterday. Since marrying Prince Abdullah in 1993, Rania has embraced her nation’s dress codes and traditions like the best of them, but she has put her own fashion-forward spin on things too. Rania had mastered the art of public dressing long before our beloved Kate was even on the scene - championing the same royal dressing formula nude courts, form-fitting dresses and smart dress coats that the Duchess turns to for daytime occasions since the early 00s. Her favourite labels include major European houses (Valentino, Dior, Armani) as well as cool, unconventional choices for a royal (Victoria Beckham) and, diplomatically, plenty of Middle Eastern names, too. Perhaps what is most refreshing of all about this royal, however, is that you can follow her every fashion move on Instagram. While Kate, Letizia and others choose to only share certain elements of their life on very public occasions, @QueenRania updates her 3.6million followers on a weekly basis, sharing new pictures and ‘throwbacks’ of her four children, Crown Prince Hussein, 23, Princess Iman, 20, Princess Salma, 16 and Prince Hashem, 12, as well as highlighting her work on key projects to improve Jordan’s education and healthcare offerings. Peppered in, naturally, are hundreds of glorious outfit photos, each attracting up to 150,000 ‘likes’ on average from her adoring online community of fans. It’s a strategy akin to the one employed by another 47 year-old, the American First Lady Melania Trump and, as an image-building tool, it’s a savvy way for Rania to connect with her people and offer an insight into her life and style. In fact, when the two met back in April they each posted a picture of themselves together, clocking up over 500,000 likes. In having a voice and showcasing her style as she does, Rania has arguably crafted her royal fashion icon status entirely. With a bigger audience and greater influence than many of the most prolific fashion bloggers and reporters out there, it’s no wonder that the designers are falling over themselves to dress her. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It didn’t take long for the world to realise just how much of a style-setter Princess Charlotte would prove to be. Within minutes of the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge appearing on the steps of the Lindo Wing with their 10-hour-old daughter a year ago tomorrow, the makers of the £68 shawl she was draped in were flooded with requests from parents eager to purchase a similar style. “It was within a few minutes we noticed on our website that the shawl was starting to sell," Gillian Taylor, director at the Nottingham-based company G.H. Hurt & Sons recalls of that iconic day, which saw 100,000 people visit their website from over 183 countries. “We sold a lot initially in America, Australia, Canada and are still selling some now.” Although we have only seen the Princess a handful of times since in carefully stage-managed official portraits, each has provoked a similar reaction amongst retailers. Such is the so-called ‘Princess Charlotte effect’ that experts at Brand Finance have predicted that she’ll be worth more than £3 billion to the UK economy across her lifetime. For the brands the Duchess of Cambridge chooses to dress her little girl in the impact is immediate and tangible. “Princess Charlotte wearing two of our floral dresses has had a huge impact on our brand,” Margarita Pato, who started Spanish childrenswear label M&H with her mother and brother tells The Telegraph. “It’s especially important for medium sized brands like us - we only have five stores in Spain.” Whilst the dresses Charlotte appeared in were already sold out when the pictures broke (“we only offer ten per store of each dress otherwise all the girls will be in the same outfit”), the halo effect has left the brand planning to launch an ecommerce site which will ship to the UK, Europe and the USA. Kate is clearly at pains to minimise the frenzy that surrounds each picture of Princess Charlotte. She’s dressed her daughter in near-identical outfits - those M&H floral dresses with pink cardigans - in three of the seven times she’s been seen. But a poll released last week claimed that 1 in every 5 parents say they consider Princess Charlotte to be a major style icon for their children - and the shopping statistics back it up. After the image of Princess Charlotte wearing pink booties on a family skiing holiday was released in March, kids retailer My1styears.com experienced a 97% increase in sales of a similar style. “Demand for items Princess Charlotte wears will surge massively on our site,” explains a representative from online childrenswear shop Alex and Alexa. “We saw an increase in customers searching for pale pink cardigans and floral dresses after the first shots of Princess Charlotte were released last year and this grew again after the release this month of the adorable shot of The Queen with her grandchildren.” In the last public photograph of Princess Charlotte ahead of her first birthday - sitting on the knee of Great Granny to celebrate The Queen’s own special birthday - it’s telling that she paired her M&H dress with a cardigan by another Spanish label, Pepa & Co. "We had a huge uplift in traffic to our website following the release of the Royal portraits and we have almost sold out of this particular style from that season," explains founder of Pepa & Co, Pepa Gonzalez. "The royals have not only created demand in England for this traditional Spanish style, but around the world. I have received an order from South Korea!" Prince George and his famous sister have been dressed in predominantly Spanish childrenswear labels, including Amaia Kids and Fina Ejerique. Although this has largely been credited to the fact the children's nanny Turrion Borrallo is from Palencia in Northern Spain, it’s perhaps also because the classic Spanish childrenswear aesthetic suits the Royal family. “Culturally the Spanish have always dressed children up at the weekends in a very classical fashion; traditional Sunday best styles and beautiful fabrics without a hint of fad or trend,” editor-in-chief of Smallish Magazine Estelle Lee says of the newfound interest in Spanish childrenswear amongst the UK’s elite parents. “Here, there seems to be a backlash against the vulgarity of dressing children as mini-mes, in eye-watering designer wear that can only be dry cleaned. So recently there has been an influx of brands importing the Spanish aesthetic: tasteful, keeping childrenswear simple and age appropriate. Parents want to keep their children looking as though they've just tumbled out of Enid Blytons faraway tree. Which is exactly as it should be.” Gonzalez - who started a South Kensington based kidswear boutique specialising in Spanish labels - agrees. “We believe the Duchess of Cambridge is drawn to Spanish childrenswear because of their elegant and slightly more formal yet timeless design," she tells The Telegraph. "The style is much more classic for children with peter Pan collar shirts, soft colours, floral prints. We keep the essence of timeless clothing for children and enjoy seeing our children look like children." Spanish childrenswear also tends to be more affordable than designer kidswear labels, which is likely an important factor for the Duchess of Cambridge who has been careful to wear attainable, high street brands. The most expensive dress at M&H is a purse-friendly £22. And whilst some might feel the Spanish retro style is making the little Royals appear old-fashioned, British luxury childrenswear designer Rachel Riley explains it’s more about an appropriate formality. “In the stamp portrait the Queen is wearing a formal dress and Charles and William are wearing suits, so it’s appropriate for Prince George, even though he’s two, to wear a formal outfit,” she says. “Shorts and a shirt is appropriate for his age - he wouldn’t wear a mini suit and he wouldn’t wear anything too casual because everyone else is looking formal.” So if we had to make a prediction about what Princess Charlotte will be wearing in the official portrait of her released tomorrow on her first birthday? Something Spanish, retro in feel - and guaranteed to sell-out. 1.     Mayoral Majoral is a hugely popular Spanish childrenswear label, loved for its Sunday-best dresses and floral prints. Childrenswear store Alex and Alexa note: “This is one of our most popular brands, as the price points are really competitive.” 2.     Torres Torres creates vintage-inspired formalwear, with traditional princess silhouettes and plenty of bow and floral flourishes. 3.     Pretty Ballerinas Pretty Ballerinas have been making their signature ballet pumps in a Menorcan village by the same family since 1918. A chic option for little feet. 4.  Pepa & Co Princess Charlotte wore  a pretty pink cardigan from Pepa & Co in the official photographs to celebrate the Queen’s 90th birthday. The  London-based boutique offers timeless pieces in muted tones and prints, made 100% in Spain. 5.   La Coqueta La Coqueta might be based in North London, but all of the pieces are “proudly made in Spain.” Head here for printed floral dresses, buttoned up cardigans and sensible t-bar shoes. 6.  Nanos Nanos is one of the ultimate go-to labels in the Spanish childrenswear world, and was founded in 1963. Its short dresses with matching bloomers are still popular today.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Brigitte Macron is French Elle’s new cover star, appearing in jeans and one of her signature tailored power jackets. In the accompanying 10-page feature, Madame Macron opens up about everything from her relationship with her husband to her views on the controversy surrounding their 25 year age gap, but also reveals a lot about her much-talked-about sense of style. The Telegraph spoke to French Elle's fashion director, Brune de Margerie, who styled Brigitte for the shoot at the Palais de l'Elysée just a few weeks ago, to get the inside fashion story... Photographed at the Élysée Palace, 64 year-old Macron wears a cream tailored jacket by Dior with a white T-shirt and jeans by Saint Laurent on the cover of the magazine. The look echoes that which she wore to meet Rihanna last month and is perhaps a go-to for occasions when she doesn’t want to come across as a 'stuffy politician'. "We did want to do a 'fashion statement', but wanted something timeless and modern," de Margerie tells The Telegraph. "And we loved the idea of mixing jeans, jacket and a T-shirt, which is very French. It's classic and chic."  Macron has forever been a fan of shorter hemlines even before she became a public figure, but has come under fire from critics who have suggested that she is ‘too old’ to wear them. “I wear above-the-knee, not minis!” she tells Elle, putting the record straight. “Although I loved to wear minis when I was younger, we would hide them in our bags when we went out…. and we’d slip bloomers on underneath to dance to rock ‘n’ roll. We went from very short to very long — that was until my grandmother spotted me in one and exclaimed, “My goodness, you look like a frumpy old granny.’ Never again!”” Macron has championed Parisian labels since entering the public eye but in her Elle interview, she reveals that she counts designers including Karl Lagerfeld and Nicolas Ghesquière as not just acquaintances but friends, too.    "Her only request was to wear Louis Vuitton because she is close to Nicolas Ghesquière," de Margerie reveals. "And Elle proposed to her Dior, Yves Saint Laurent and Azzedine Alaia."    And they are, perhaps unsurprisingly, all French. “Why not, if it does some good for the French fashion industry,” she responds when asked if it bothers her that people continuously comment on her clothes. “I’m really into fashion, and there’s this fascination the world over around this idea of the French woman.” Balmain’s Olivier Rousteing, Alexandre Vauthier and Azzedine Alaïa are all namechecked, and in the photoshoot, she wears a tailored red jacket by the latter. “I have always put a lot of effort into the way I present myself, just ask my children or students!” Macron says in the interview. “I would never leave the house before choosing an outfit and doing my hair — the results may vary, but I cannot do otherwise.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
