 If Rihanna wants to wear something within hours of it debuting on the catwalks in Milan and Paris, she can. The singer is the face of Dior, has a collaboration with Manolo Blahnik and has relationships with every major designer. But the singer also uses her huge star power to spotlight the work of a number of emerging British designers, likely aware of the huge impact she can have on under-the-radar labels.  Yesterday the singer was spotted in New York in an acid green tutu from British designer Molly Goddard's SS16 collection. It's quite the endorsement for the 27-year-old Central Saint Martins graduate, who has only had four presentations at London Fashion Week, and is an industry name.  Parking the question for a second of how Rihanna managed to pull off doing a coffee run in green ruffles, how did Rihanna come to be wearing Goddard's £1,250 'Sophie' dress?  "Rihanna bought the dress from Browns in London," Goddard tells The Telegraph. "With so many endorsements and loans it’s great to know she bought it - that shows real support."   Rihanna didn't hold back on the accessories either, wearing Aquazzura rainbow pom pom sandals, a silver cracked leather Dior Diorever bag and $50,000 worth of diamonds, with bracelets and chokers from Le Vian and Hearts On Fire. She also did the noughties trick, as often employed by Paris Hilton, of making her Venti Starbucks a crucial part of her look. Goddard says of Rihanna's styling: "I love seeing how everyone wears my collections so differently, its about being comfortable and confident. She looks amazing. The dress is made from panels of smocked tulle, it has over 20 meters of fabric in it." Handmade nostalgic chiffon dresses are Goddard's signature and she has had a fascination with Sunday-best princess smocks ever since her mother made them for her as a child. "I was still trying to squeeze into the old ones from when I was little when I was 15," Goddard has previously said of the frilly frocks.  Only two years ago the Central Saint Martins graduate pulled together her first collection in just six weeks, which showed off the official schedule at London Fashion Week, with models wearing her smocks layered over their own clothes. Now sponsored by Newgen, Molly Goddard's presentations have become an editor's choice thanks to their fantastical set ups. For AW15 she set up a life drawing class and for SS16 models were part of a make-believe sandwich factory. Rihanna has a history of championing new or unknown talent - at the 2015 Met Gala she was one of the only stars to wear a look by a Chinese designer, Guo Pei.  As the man behind Michelle Obama’s finest fashion moments, Jason Wu is on a mission to prove professional clothes can be pretty. Jane Mulkerrins meets him New York On the second floor of an ornate five-storey townhouse on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, Jason Wu is perching on a sleek grey sofa.  ‘I had fun decorating this house,’ grins the Taiwanese-born, Canadian-raised, New York-dwelling fashion designer. There are vast gilt mirrors and claw-foot baths, juxtaposed with minimalist chaise longues. ‘It’s my fantasy house,’ he enthuses. In truth, the androgynous 33-year-old, in white trainers and skinny black jeans, the sleeves of his jacket rolled up, looks barely old enough to have a mortgage. And while he is doing very well for himself, with a successful eponymous label almost a decade old – its reputation boosted in no small measure by the two inauguration gowns he designed for Michelle Obama – whether even he could afford this property remains to be seen.  The house has actually been hired for the day, by Hugo Boss, for whom Wu has acted as artistic director of womenswear since 2013, and which, this week, is launching Boss The Scent for Her.  Wu’s signature style and that of the German fashion house might not seem the most obvious bedfellows; Wu is renowned for indulgently feminine, frothy frocks, while Boss has a reputation for clean, masculine lines. ‘We’ve softened her up, she’s become more feminine,’ he says of his collections for the Boss woman. ‘The straight lines have become more curved, the tailoring has become softer.’ With his own label, Jason Wu, and his work for Boss, Wu oversees a demanding 12 collections a year. ‘I love getting my hands dirty, and I don’t mind working crazy-long hours and weekends,’ he says.  Born in Taipei, Wu had only a few select words in English when his mother moved the family to Vancouver, Canada. ‘She wanted my brother and me to have opportunities other than those that were available growing up in Taiwan in the 1980s,’ he says. ‘It was much less acceptable there for a boy to be interested in anything that might be seen as feminine.’   Wu began reading fashion magazines, with a dictionary beside him. ‘That’s really how I learnt English,’ he remembers. ‘And it was when I got bitten by the fashion bug.’ At 10 years old, he begged his mother to buy him a sewing machine. She not only obliged but also hired her son a sewing teacher.  ‘The deal was that if I had a “proper” education before I focused completely on fashion, then I could do whatever I wanted in college,’ he says. Wu was sent to two very traditional, straight-laced, preppy boarding schools, in Massachusetts and Connecticut. Which, for a gay teenager with a strong interest in fashion, was ‘super-difficult’. ‘I was not 100 per cent comfortable with myself. I felt like an outsider. But that was part of what made me strong, and who I am today.’  From his dorm room, aged just 16, the already industrious Wu launched his first company, designing clothes for dolls. ‘I was much more courageous when I was younger,’ he says. ‘I’d never been to New York before, and I took a train, by myself, from Connecticut, and went to have a meeting with Integrity Toys.  ‘When I talk about it now, it doesn’t seem believable, but that’s how I started,’ he laughs. ‘My friends were working as baristas and I was going off to China to look at production.’  He studied fashion at the prestigious Parsons School of Design in New York, but dropped out with just six months to go to launch his own label in 2007. ‘But I’d barely got my foothold when the financial crisis hit, and stores began reducing my orders,’ he recalls. ‘We were left with all this inventory, it was really tough.’ Fortunately, help soon arrived – in the glamorous form of the new First Lady. Wu, still only 26 years old, was commissioned to design a gown for Barack Obama’s historic inauguration ceremony in January 2009. ‘I was scared out of my wits,’ he admits.  ‘But I just went with my gut, and that’s how I’ve been in my entire career.’ He delivered the white, floor-length chiffon gown to Washington, DC personally, but was not told in advance whether Michelle would definitely be wearing his dress.  ‘It was all so secretive,’ he says. ‘I was watching on TV, just like everyone else, to see what she was going to wear.’ When he saw her in his design, he burst into tears.  ‘As a designer, you want to be in fashion magazines, you want to have great shows,’ he explains. ‘But to be a part of history, and that particular moment, that was a once in a lifetime.’ The gown now hangs in the American History Museum in DC. ‘That the work will outlive me in a way that’s culturally significant is so incredibly special for me.’ Michelle Obama has since worn Wu for numerous high-profile appearances, including the second inauguration ball in early 2013 and on the cover of US Vogue. He must have a fairly close relationship with the first family now, I suggest. ‘It’s… yeah… I mean… it’s very continuous now,’ he says, coyly. ‘In fashion, the best you can hope for is to have returning clients.’  Michelle Obama has helped encourage a softer, more stylish approach to dressing in places like Washington, DC, according to Wu. ‘It used to be that women in “men’s worlds”, especially in a political environment, were afraid to express their femininity in case they risked not being taken seriously, or not looking professional,’ he says. ‘What Michelle’s brought to the political field is that you can wear something that’s feminine, a little bit sexy, but not compromise your power or your intelligence.’   Queen Letizia of Spain is another who gets that right. ‘She wears Boss so much,’ he says. What about Claire Underwood, aka Robin Wright, in House of Cards, television’s most stylish fictitious First Lady? ‘She also wears Boss,’ he nods, then beams. ‘And Jason Wu. She wears a lot of both.’  In the fourth season, Kevin Spacey, as the machinating, murderous President Frank Underwood, was dressed in Boss Made to Measure, Wu reveals. ‘I think I have a knack for the political figure,’ he smiles.  In April this year, Wu married his boyfriend, Gustavo Rangel, in Tulum, Mexico. It was a black-tie affair, featuring an al-fresco dinner and a DJ set by Wu himself. The couple met a decade ago, at a New Year’s Eve party. ‘Seriously, it’s like one of those movies; who meets at a New Year’s Eve party?’ he laughs.  Wu was still a fashion student at the time, and Rangel worked in the department store Saks. These days, Rangal is chief financial officer for Jason Wu.  What are they like at separating work and home life? ‘Terrible. The worst,’ Wu admits. ‘But it is what it is.’ ‘My parents moved us here so that I could have a career in something creative – in art, or in fashion,’ he reasons. ‘So all of this, it feels like my own American dream.’  Boss The Scent for Her is available from 20 August, £44 for 30ml © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The general concensus on Kim Kardashian's 'exiting the Air B'n'B apartment to leave for the airport' outfit is that her idiosyncratic combination of items is downright 'bizarre'. Here on The Telegraph's Fashion desk, our thoughts are a little more nuanced. We're not generally ones for analysing Kim's every outfit- generally they blend into a sea of somewhat predicatable black and beige body-con dresses  and leggings- however, this get-up piqued our interest- and not for all the wrong reasons.  When its component parts are listed- cycling shorts/ Spanx, a transparent bra, furry sandals and an oversized silk robe- Kardashian's late-summer concoction sounds like the stuff of worst-dressed list nightmares but with her slicked back wet-look hair and careful proportion play there's something clever going on here. Of course, it's part of Kardashian's carefully curated and ongoing fashion evolution. In recent weeks, she's asked fans: 'Doesn't my waist look photoshopped?' as she posed in one of those aforementioned skintight dresses with matching over-the-knee boots, appeared at the VMAs in a see-through vintage LBD by former Dior designer John Galliano and thrown a curveball in a slinky silk maxi skirt, although admittedly it came split to the thigh. The common thread? Each look is distinctively 'Kim' with a thoughtfully Fashion (capital letter intended) nod.   There's a reason why plenty of women will relate to Kim's latest experimental ensembles. Since giving birth to her second child, Saint West, last December she has documented her struggle to return to a body which she is happy with. “It isn’t easy to just bounce back,” she said in a post on her app earlier in August. “I was so jealous of women who had these cute little baby bellies and would gain 25 pounds — and then, a few weeks after giving birth, somehow look exactly like they did before they were pregnant … That’s not me." As September's merry-go-round of fashion weeks approaches, expect plenty more thought-provoking looks from the reality star. In the meantime, here's how she made yesterday's outfit look not quite as bizarre as you might expect... It's hardly shocking that Kim Kardashian would opt for a nipple-exposing bra (her's is by La Perla) and wear nothing over it, but her choice of corset to complete the look is actually very of-the-moment. The corset is making a comeback, largely thanks to Victoria Beckham and Prada who both showed the waist cinching accessories in almost every look of their respective AW16 shows. When Prada's loose corsetry landed on Net-a-Porter last month, they sold out almost immediately. Paired with that sheer bra, Kim conveys a masterful balance of personal branding versus fashion nous. When your image depends on highlighting your tiny waist-meets-voluptuous hip proportions at every possible moment, ingenious body-con become necessary. So you can see how the idea to introduce cycling shorts into her repertoire entered Kim's mind. How does she make them work? The longer length which hits just above the knee and hip-grazing corset length create an ultra-flattering silhouette.  They might recall Dad-at-the-beach sandals, but the last couple of summers have seen the humble pool slider become the ultimate luxe laidback fashion shoe. In no form is this better exemplified than in Givenchy's £385 mink sandals. Similar styles are also available for £15 at Sports Direct, with no fur included.  Every new Mum develops a sartorial fallback or two- an item which she knows she can always rely on to make her feel polished in five seconds. Softly tailored duster coats became Kim's version of this, but with her bomber jacket/ kimono silk hybrid she ups the ante without sacrificing that cocoon-like feel. It adds a relaxed kind of drama to the look. While sheer bras and fur shoes aren't items any of us will be rushing to emulate any time soon (although, be our guest) a breezy cover-up is a piece we can all get on board with.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  In the high stakes, high finance world of the male modelling elite, industry truth can often be stranger than fiction. “There was the model that we took to a shoot in the Mojave Desert,” says one menswear stylist, who would rather not be named. “He was an absolute monster. Most boys can joke it off if you want to put them in an Astrid Anderson power-thong but some have problems with it.” Finally the stylist realised the problem. A call was put into the model’s agency back in London and his Ritalin prescription procured. “It calmed him down and we got the pictures. I always say, if you take a teenager from the middle of nowhere and plonk them on a fashion shoot with all these massive personalities around them, problems will arise. When they start, a lot of them literally haven’t ever spoken to a black person, let alone met a real-life homosexual.” Ben Stiller’s Zoolander film franchise has taken some of the fictional sheen off women in the fashion industry, parodied mercilessly in Absolutely Fabulous and The Devil Wears Prada, and given it a fresh shot of testosterone. At multiplexes around the country this weekend, it is the boys who are stepping up for their close-up as Zoolander 2 goes on general release (read Telegraph fashion director Lisa Armstrong's review here). If the tittle-tattle shared backstage at shows, castings and on shoots is anything to go by, Stiller’s source material potential from the real world of male models ranges from the sublime through the ridiculous. One fashion editor described a young male model that has had a splendid first 12 months in the business as “basically a beautiful brain-dead moron.” He paused. “It probably won’t do him any harm in the long-run.” “It doesn’t tend to be a diva thing with the boys,” says another stylist who would also sooner keep his industry tales strictly entre-nous. “There’s a naivety which can translate as stupid model stories.” He relates the episode of a boy he’d worked with on several advertising campaigns and whose regular modus operandi was to arrive to meetings carrying a skateboard. Spotting the model’s rising and impressive Instagram following, a big money fashion brand decided to stage an event with the boy. “They fly him in from America to Britain and build, at huge expense, this great skateboard ramp for him to use. He stands there and says ‘oh, what’s the ramp for?’ They say ‘it’s for you’ and he takes me aside and is like ‘but I can’t skate.’ So he’s been carrying this prop around with him forever, for no reason. The client has flown him in Business class from New York, built him this incredible skating apparatus and he can’t use any of it. I said ‘look, you’re going to have to get on it and push yourself up and down somehow.’” So far, so Zoolander. But one thing the film doesn’t get right, is the presentation of main character Derek’s life as a jobbing male model being a constant whirlwind of glamour, such as hobnobbing with Penelope Cruz on the cover of US Vogue, or dating Cara Delevingne (albeit for three hours). “It does sound awful, but these models are really are like objects at the end of the day,” says a casting agent. “They can be treated like bits of meat and some of the boys really struggle with that. It’s a little like prostitution in a way.” He mentions the male model who had earned a reputation amongst stylists for being spectacularly well-endowed and was advised to turn up to an underwear casting pretending to have forgotten to wear pants. “So they ask him to take his trousers down and he does and just stands there.” He got the job. “Also, like prostitution, modelling is one of the only jobs in the world where women are paid twice as much as men,” adds the agent. He says that routinely male models are offered a flat half rate for the same job as their female counterparts. “They’re just not taken as seriously as the girls in the bigger industry picture. A high fashion brand can name what they want to pay the boys. It’d maybe be £10,000 a day for a job for a pretty, muscly boy whereas the girls would get £50,000 for essentially the same work.” These sums can do things to a boys’ ego. The bravado starts to emerge. “When they start out, for boys modelling can be thought of as quite jokey,” says the casting agent. “They’ll come to the party after a show and get drunk and hang out, whereas the girls tend to be a lot more mature. They know what they’re doing is potentially big business.” There are of course exceptions to the rule. The astonishing ascending star of a male model like Lucky Blue, the young Texan who trades off his Zoolander-ish pout and smoulder and is making a fortune from the reach of his social media profiles, draws parallels with the career trajectory of a young pop dynamite like One Direction or Justin Bieber. “Oh absolutely,” says one stylist. “He’s at the stage now that Cara Delevingne was at the start of her career. He’s getting mobbed before shows. He’s gone global, talking directly to followers in China and Asia.” On the other side of the spectrum are the male models who are in it for the perks. “There’s that whole London scene of cool, skinny kids who do one Saint Laurent show, get to meet a couple of older supermodels and a load of young girls and all of a sudden one of them’s going out with a pop star’s daughter,” says another stylist. “They’re the hot young fodder for these single women with incredibly glamorous connections.”    It’s certainly true that when the dividends pay off, if the boys are good with clients and on catwalks and super professional about their work, ample rewards will be reaped. The raw power of a particularly striking male model at a snazzy LA party is still a sight to behold. “Famous women do literally throw themselves at them," says one stylist. "In a sense, they’re the perfect trophy to remind everyone they’re still virile while retaining control and knowing they won’t answer back.” Not that they can always share these stories with mates back home. Often the children of famous, monied parents will bring along Non-Disclosure Agreements for their beau to sign on a first date. “If she’s a famous person’s daughter she wants to protect the family, make sure they’re not going to talk about this, that and the other. You can see why. I’ve heard of one model having to sign an NDA to say they wouldn’t disclose that they’d signed an NDA.” Oh Stiller, where art thou? White Hot Hair specialises in products for grey hair, and Griffin was signed up to model its products. Griffin said that she was “very honoured” to be the oldest person to feature in the magazine, but rightly added: “‘old’ to me means when you’re 100.” This casting adds to a deeper shift within the fashion industry:  a slow but confident embrace of 40-plus models. It makes perfect sense for brands wanting to capture the attention of consumers who will naturally respond to imagery of aspirational women who are similar in age. That doesn’t mean that teenage models will find themselves out of work, but personalities with a rich story and life experience are being cast more frequently. And Griffin has mounds of that.  Olivier Rousteing, the 31-year-old Creative Director of French fashion house Balmain, could hardly be more L.A. He is often seen with a Kardashian on his arm or sandwiched in the middle of his #BalmainArmy of golden supermodels (Rosie Huntington-Whiteley, Cindy Crawford and Doutzen Kroes amongst them), all of them wearing his signature crystal studded mini dresses or sequinned jumpsuits. So it's appropriate that he is on the phone to The Telegraph from Balmain's first LA store where he is hosting an opening party and celebrating the launch of his collaboration with Beats by Dr. Dre, for which he has created two custom designs of wireless headphones. "I’m so happy to be under be under the sun in LA,'' he laughs. ''A lot of things are happening, you know, it’s a dream come true.'' Rousteing took the helm at Balmain in 2011; at the tender age of 24, he was the youngest creative director in Paris since Yves Saint Laurent. Since then, he has reinvigorated the house with an unashamedly bling aesthetic which has made the label catnip to glamorous celebrities and socialites in need of glitzy good-time attire.   ''Music has always been part of my life and has always been inspiring to me - I could never create without music so it felt very natural,'' he explains of his decision to partner with the audio brand founded by Dr.Dre and Jimmy Lovine in 2006 and which was subsequently snapped up by Apple in 2014. Besides, a pair of the khaki and gold headphones seem like the most modern of finishing touches to a classic, dazzling Balmain creation.  Rousteing admits that his own musical tastes are rather varied. He wakes up to Michael Jackson ''They Don’t Care About Us'' every morning, and is currently obsessed with Ed Sheeran ''Shape Of You'' and Rihanna's latest chart topper, ''Wild Thoughts''.  For the last six years, Rousteing has been forthright in his demand for greater diversity on the catwalk and in his campaigns, casting models of all ethnicitities to represent Balmain. But he has also spoken about his reluctance to acknowledge colour in any capacity - something that stemmed from his growing up in an adoptive family whose skin tone was different to his own.  "It’s all about diversity,'' he enthuses in his dulcet Bordeaux tones Given the reputation Rousteing has for his mastery of Insta-friendly glamour, it would be remiss not to quiz him for his thoughts on super-quick ways to look put-together. He barely hesitates before replying, ''Oh, I think the most important thing that a woman has to wear for glamour is the lipstick. I’m a designer and I would love to say it’s about the clothes, but no matter if a woman is in a T-shirt or a bodycon dress,  it’s all about the lipstick.'' ''You can wear a white T-shirt if you have the red lipstick and it feels like Femme Fatale,'' he continues, before citing Brigitte Bardot in Saint-Tropez in the '70s as a source of fabulous summer inspiration: ''I mean to me, this is the best.'' So where will the designer-cum-Instagram-sensation be heading on holiday after his L.A pitstop? ''I'm going to Mykonos - I've been going there for seven years - the island feels like home,'' he says. ''Summer for me is different than it is for other people because I have a fashion show in September,'' he adds, ''so I try not to travel too much so I can focus when I come back and not be jet-lagged. When I get back when I need so much energy.'' Something tells us he'll still squeeze in a party or two.  Balmain x Beats headphones are available at Apple.com, Balmain.com and Harrods.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Alexa Chung says that the inspiration for the second collection from her eponymous fashion label was somewhat unconventional; awkward American prom photos, with silhouettes borrowed from both the Fifties and the Eighties. “They're actually style wise probably two of my least favourite decades, but in my mind funny prom photos featuring couples with listless expressions are always from those eras,” she tells The Telegraph of her Alexachung autumn range. “I became drawn to the stiff cakey dresses of the Fifties and that teddy boy look that was then regurgitated in the Eighties, but through a posh girl, Tatler rave lens. I just wanted it to be fun.” Fun fashion is something that the television presenter-turned fashion designer undoubtedly specialises in. The reigning queen of the London party scene, Chung has launched (and relaunched) a thousand street style trends since she first appeared on our screens in Popworld in 2006, from denim shorts with tights to tousled bob haircuts. After years of collaborations, dabbling with capsule collections for brands from AG Jeans to Marks and Spencer, she finally put her own brand on the map back in May and is now establishing her design handwriting. Alexachung is preppy, girly, masculine and cool - all at once. “I hope like most things we make to be wearing them forever,” she tells us of her favourite piece from season two, a “blue and white floaty long gingham dress”. The prom photos on her moodboard, she says, led to a look at new ways of merging traditional menswear and womenswear silhouettes. “It originally started as a way to divide the collection in to masculine and feminine looks and to spark the design process from that distinctive viewpoint,” she notes. “Literally girls on one side boys on the other because tailoring and tomboyishness is as much a part of this brand as the ultra girly dresses.” “I had a leavers ball I attended once sixth form ended,” Chung says of the closest thing she ever got to actually going to a prom herself. The critical question; what did she wear? “I made a skirt out of black taffeta fabric that I half stapled and half sewed myself into,” she says. “On top I had a backless pink sequin top. It was weird but I think I thought I was like Sarah Jessica Parker or something.” In terms of her party style now, Chung has come a long way, but she’s still just as willing to bend the rules and throw, say, an oversized tuxedo jacket over a dainty ballgown, or a natty jumper over a silk dress. Her essential, though? “Probably red lipstick,” she says. “I'm not particularly experimental when it comes to makeup so if I have a red lip on it usually means I'm ready to party.”   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Annie Pollet, 46, is co-founder of fashion boutique Iris. She lives in London with her husband Adam and their five children, aged two to 18. She takes us through her busy day... The division of labour between my husband Adam and I is complicated, but it works. While I’m creative director of Iris, he runs a pizzeria, which means his routine is more flexible for the children: I have 18-year-old twins, Felix and Lola; Adam has two daughters Antonia, 18, and Daisy, 16; and we have Clementine, who is two. Just before 7am, I put the kettle on and have some porridge, put Clementine in front of Peppa Pig while I sort myself out, then scream my teenagers out of bed. I get to the Iris offices in Kensington at about 9.30am after the nursery run. It’s a fashion studio so there’s no need for a suit; I might wear cosy cashmere tracksuit bottoms or dungarees, usually with trainers. Though if I have an appointment with, say, Harrods, I’ll up the ante and wear a pretty dress, boots and a masculine blazer. I leave the office on the dot at 5.10pm to avoid the traffic, then put Clementine to bed by 7.30pm. Afterwards, we relax, have family dinners and more adult conversations. Adam does the cooking; usually lasagne or curries, which are popular with the teenagers. We ban phones at mealtimes, but often I will still need to deal with some work emails, so I sometimes spend 15 minutes after dinner checking what I’ve missed. We always watch TV but often only for 30 minutes, otherwise we fall asleep. Having a baby when you’re a bit older and have grown-up children, isn’t the same as when it’s your first baby. We’re exhausted by the evening. We love her, of course, but it’s different and I haven’t embraced the ‘making friends with other mums’ thing this time. She fits in with everything else that’s going on in our lives – I often find her in my son’s bedroom with loud grime music on. I don’t get much calm time for myself, probably because I’m not a late-night person and can’t stay awake beyond 10.30pm. But I’ll read the newspaper or a book in bed – then it’s up to do it all again.      Veja Nova trainers: Recently I’ve been permanently in Vejas. They are the perfect fashion trainer.  No sooner had oohs been aahed over those pictures of a tousle-haired Prince George arriving for his first day at the Westacre Montessori School in Norfolk, last week, than online parenting forums were filled with mums trying to get their hands on his natty navy jacket. Swiftly pinpointed as a smart but comfortable quilted number from his mother’s favourite store, John Lewis, the high street stalwart - long the go-to destination for good value back-to-school clothing - was duly inundated with enquiries.  And while customers were disappointed to find that George’s particular style, complete with corduroy elbow patches, hasn’t been available since 2013, an almost-identical coat has already had to be restocked several times. “Within the first two days we saw a 447 per cent increase in enquiries for our Children’s Quilted Hooded Jacket in Navy,” says a John Lewis spokesman. “And that’s increased 100 per cent again this week.” If the fashion world has always worshipped at the altar of youth, it now seems to be in the grip of a toddler fashion boom, led by the pint-size Prince - dubbed “the world’s most influential toddler” by Forbes magazine. Though the outfits may be tiny, the figures are anything but: the UK childrenswear market is now worth £5.6bn, according to Euromonitor, with a retail value estimated to rise to £5.9bn by 2017 and only get bigger from there; Mintel expects it to hit £7.8 billion by 2019.  Infantswear (for 0- 3-year-olds) grew by 25 per cent between 2009 and 2014 – nearly triple that of the nine per cent birthrate – thought to be due to strong “gifting” market. Think babyboomer grandparents with disposable income to lavish on their adored grandchildren, not to mention a rise in older mums, who tend to be more financially secure. Retailers are responding in kind. In 2013, Harrods expanded its childrenswear department to 66,000 square foot. Net-a-Porter provisionally registered the name Petite a Porter back in 2009, while Alex and Alexa, a sleek online kids boutique selling 9,000 lines of children’s designer clothing, is enjoying such success that it recently added a ‘Luxury Ski Store’, with items such as a William Sharpe Grey Swarovski Epaulettes Tracksuit selling for an eye-popping £464.  Surpisingly (or worryingly, depending on how you see things), some of the under-threes at the front of the fashion pack are even dressing themselves.  “When it comes to toddlerwear, children are developing a sense of style and often outfit choices will be a combination of the parents and the child’s choice,” says Jenny Slungaard, PR Manager for Alex and Alexa, which was set up seven years ago by parents-of-five, Alex and Alexa Theophanous. “With the rise of social media, particularly Instagram, parents are becoming a lot more conscious about what their children wear - as are the kids themselves.  For Alex and Alexa, (former toddler) Harper Beckham remains the site’s “key trend driver”, with that floppy Chloe hat sending it into meltdown. “She wears so many of the pieces we stock and we always see sales increase as soon as she’s been photographed in them,” says Slungaard.  But across the board, no toddler drives more sales than George: from the Start-Rite shoes he wore in his first Christmas snaps, to the nautical style Crocs he was spotted playing in at the Polo last year. His trend-setting quilted jacket, however, suggests the little prince has been kitted out in the most affordable toddler gear of all - a hand me down. William’s stepsister Laura Lopes (daughter of Camilla Parker Bowles) whose twin boys, Gus and Louis, would have been wearing size 2-3 year old clothes when the jacket was onsale back in 2013, is an obvious contender for purchasing the original.  But even in this Prince George is ahead of the fashion curve – because hand-me-down, or second-hand, kids’ clothing is suddenly big business, too. Spanish company Percentile and US model ThredUP pay for ‘nearly-new’ kids clothing from families before selling through an online store, even arranging collection from sellers. European store Vintykids.com does the same but will only hand over the money to the original owner once the sale is completed.  In the UK, Vestiaire Collective, which allows sellers to list pre-owned designer fashion on its online boutique has introduced a Kids section selling luxury labels like Bonpoint and Baby Dior (“Dior red evening dress, in perfect condition, worn once, size 3 years, £275”). Aside from the eco credentials, the benefits are obvious - stretching that clothing allowance, without compromising on quality or style. Newest to the resale market is Little Circle, launched in the UK by former Tatler Fashion Director, Anna Browmilow and former Morgan Stanley Executive Director, Lisa Picardo, which encourages buyers to re-sell to the site, as soon as their little ones have outgrown their purchases. Dresses from niche chic luxury European labels - “quirky and chic” Belgian brand Maan, “Parisian chic” label Noro, “sophisticated but gently retro” London label Hucklebones - sell from £60, while the Costumes And Party section features a £97 pink velvet “fantasy cape”. One mini fashionista more likely to be spotted in couture than cast-offs is Kim Kardashian and Kanye West’s daughter, North. Her wardrobe reads like a who’s who of 21st century fashion; Balmain, Givenchy, Celine, Balenciaga. Last year, she caused a Kardashian-esque uproar of her own when she was spotted stepping out in a $3500 real fur coat, leggings and Doc Martens boots on her way from Daddy’s Adidas fashion show in New York.  Although elements of North’s style may not be attainable (let alone desireable) for most parents, Slungaard notes her overall aesthetic still boosts sales: weekly snaps of her en-route to ballet classes prompted the site to invest in “the biggest range of tutus ever in our history” to meet search demand.  Soon, of course, North West won’t the only little lady giving George competition in the fashion stakes; after pictures of Princess Charlotte were released in November, Alex and Alexa reported “an explosion” of customers searching for identikit ‘pale pink cardigans’ and ‘floral dresses’. Fashion watchers - and retailers - must be counting down the days to her nursery debut, in September 2018. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When Ivanka Trump became one of the most prominent first daughters in history, her initial strategy for dressing in her unusual role could hardly have been more traditional. For the Inauguration Ball in January, she opted for a sequinned gold tulle gown by American designer Carolina Herrera- it was a classic, referential to first lady history and, well, safe. It was her stepmother Melania Trump who took the far bolder step of collaborating with unknown designer Herve Pierre on a simple, modern column design.  For a while, she stuck with heritage US names such as Oscar de la Renta (or her eponymous label) and very grown-up silhouettes. But in recent weeks, an intriguing new strategy has emerged from the first daughter which has seen her develop a more relatable style which taps into the mores of millennials. Whether it's under-the-radar names, ultra-affordable, trend-led brands or the buzzworthy labels which prompt some to part with a month's rent for a pair of shoes, Ivanka has- curiously- been trying them all.  Earlier this week, Ivanka arrived for a meeting on tax reform wearing a pink polo neck top with clashing red trumpet sleeves. Bravo to Ivanka for defying stuffy dress codes and all, but the top came from Staud, the L.A cool girl label which has become catnip for the street style crowd and Insta-influencers over the past year or two. She has also been seen wearing a velvet turtle neck top by Tibi, a label whose shows have fast become the most anticipated of New York fashion week thanks to its understated yet interesting pieces.  Like any self-respecting millennial (at 35, she is just on the cusp of being part of the social group), Ivanka has, seemingly out of the blue, developed a serious Zara habit. Just today, she left  her Washington home wearing a checked trouser suit by the Spanish brand which has made Amancio Ortega the world's richest man. Earlier in October, she also wore a pencil skirt and sweater from Zara, amongst numerous other pieces which pepper her recent outfits.  The first hint that a first daughter wardrobe transformation was afoot came over the summer when Ivanka wore two dresses by Reformation, another L.A-born label which creates sustainable but on-trend summer and party dresses which are also beloved of Karlie Kloss, Emily Ratajkowski and Taylor Swift- not exactly the Washington elite demographic. Wearing a breezy white cotton design to board Air Force One, Ivanka would not have looked out of place sipping green juice in Echo Park.  So what's behind Ivanka's wardrobe switch-up? Perhaps it's simply that she's loosened up since those uncertain first months in the White House when it might have seemed more sensible to Washington-ify her image than experiment too much. She has also sought to distance herself from her personal brand which frees her up to try different designers at similar price points. This could also be the scheme of Cat Williams, the stylist who Ivanka is said to have enlisted to dress her while she advises her father. Although she's not a first lady, Ivanka will be conscious of the impact which women in similar positions to her have had over the years- so why not make her mark by bringing millennial favourites to the corridors of power, perhaps she even hopes to win some over in the process? That's a tall order, but as soon as we see her wearing Supreme, we'll know she's serious.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Is there anything more joyous than the international sartorial judgement that we are allowed to indulge in during Olympic Opening and Closing ceremonies?  Everyone claims to have a phobia these days – whether it’s of heights, confined spaces, or the current favourite, gluten – but jewellery designer Delfina Delettrez’s entomophobia is genuine. Her new Insectmania collection for Dover Street Market, launched last week to coincide with Photo London, consists of three unique brooches, each housing a real taxidermy insect from the Rome-based designer’s personal collection, and it’s part art, part therapy. “I am currently between desire and repulsion when it comes to insects,” explains Delettrez, who initially couldn’t even be in the same room as the bugs, instead directing her team via video. “I am of the belief that what repels us is truly what attracts us in the end. Making the Insect brooches has really helped with my phobia. For the Insectmania collection I did all of the dissection myself, studying the anatomy of the insects as I went along. The designs have moved on as I let my fears go, and I am not afraid to let the insects go." Intriguingly displayed under super-strength microscopic lenses at Dover Street Market, the brooches are made in Delettrez’s Roman atelier from either rose, white, or blackened silver, each hyper-realistic bug spanning over 16cm long, and clutching its prize of a baroque pearl, a watery-green quartz, or a darker green tourmaline in its jaws. The actual taxidermy insects are suspended in resin inside the abdomen, like creepy unborn babies. But there’s real beauty in these pieces, evocative of the surreal – think Isabella Blow in her Philip Treacy lobster hat, or Schiaparelli’s enormous embroidered insects. They could look incredible as a scuttling trio on the lapels of a black smoking jacket, or perched on the rim of a little felt hat. A limited edition range of earrings, a pendant, and a brooch in the same collection sees insects with fantastically elongated, kinetic legs, the necklace on a chain of freshwater pearls set in blackened silver.  'I remember my sister calling me and saying, “I’ve just found out I have breast cancer.” It was as though she was going to the drug store,’ recalls swimwear designer Melissa Odabash of her older sister Jamie breaking the news of her impending treatment and mastectomy. ‘She said, “I will be in and out. And I’ll have a reconstruction.” Then she just kept saying, “I’ll be fine, I’ll be fine.”’ It has been more than 10 years since Jamie was given the all-clear, but today Melissa is speaking at the launch of a range  of swimwear she has designed for women who have had mastectomies, in tribute to her sister’s survival. It is a collaboration with online retailers Amoena, which specialises in post-mastectomy designs. Former model Melissa has scores of A-list fans, including Rihanna and Gwyneth Paltrow. She is the swimwear designer of choice for the Duchess of Cambridge and was chosen by Pippa Middleton to create her honeymoon bikini. (Melissa remains respectfully tight-lipped on her royal connections but has previously said Pippa would be her ideal bikini model on account of her curves.) But despite her glamorous career highlights, she regards her mastectomy collection as her greatest achievement. ‘Helping women who have had cancer and boosting their confidence is the best thing I have ever done,’ she says. Jamie is the second oldest of Melissa’s four siblings and was just 38, with a three-year-old daughter and a seven-year-old son, when she was diagnosed. American-born Melissa, who now lives in London with her husband and two daughters, 18 and 14, was based in Italy at the time.  ‘It happened eight months after my father died suddenly from a heart attack at 62,’ Melissa recalls. ‘My mother was getting over the loss of her husband – they had been married for over 40 years – and dealing with a daughter with breast cancer too. It was full on. But Jamie is the most positive woman. She never complained, but I’m sure it was worse than she let on.’ That gritty attitude, Melissa says, is  a family trait. ‘We are not complainers. When my mum had a mini stroke, she went home and blow-dried her hair before driving herself to the hospital.’  Even though she was not in the ‘at risk’ age group, Jamie went for annual breast exams, and it was after one of these that she was given the shocking news that she had breast cancer. Thankfully, it was still stage one, which meant the tumour was small and had not yet spread.  Reflecting on her ordeal, Jamie  says, ‘I was so lucky that they found it early as I didn’t feel a lump or any symptoms.’ The tumour was in her left breast, and her doctor advised that she could either have a lumpectomy and radiotherapy or a mastectomy. ‘I opted for a total mastectomy because at the time I had young children and did not want to commit to prolonged and uncertain radiation treatment,’ she explains in her no-nonsense manner. ‘I am a hiker, I like the outdoors, I had young children and I was working in real estate at the time. I just wanted to deal with it and move on.’ It was only as she was preparing for this interview that she allowed herself to think back. ‘I don’t see myself as a cancer survivor but when I started to write notes for this, I got weepy for the first time,’ she says. ‘It was more difficult than I wanted to admit back then. At the time, I went on automatic pilot – I don’t do drama. Now, I look back and am more reflective and very grateful.’  While Jamie’s approach powered her through her mastectomy, the reconstruction surgery was far more complicated, and involved several operations. Despite having a successful reconstruction (which involved inserting a saline implant to stretch the skin then replacing  it with gel), Jamie, who has always loved the beach, went from feeling comfortable with her body to being self-conscious in a swimsuit. ‘There was a swim club we used to go to where we would meet friends and hang out on the weekend, but after the operation I didn’t go into the water for about two years and always wore cover-ups,’ she admits.  Melissa sent Jamie dozens of her designs to try, but regular swimwear often didn’t have the support Jamie was after or cover the scars from her operation. ‘Thick seams used in the cups are uncomfortable against the sensitive scar area,’ she explains. ‘Implants, either gel or saline, are heavier than normal breast tissue so need more support, and the added weight makes the scar tissue extra sensitive.  ‘There is a mental and emotional element as well. You are self-conscious as your body image has changed, but you are still the same person and I think feeling confident in swimwear is a major hurdle. It is more difficult than any other article of clothing because you’re vulnerable and exposed.’ It was during a holiday with her sister in Florida that Melissa came up with  the idea of designing a range of swimwear for women who have fought the disease. ‘My sister has a great body and has always been fit, but I noticed she was not feeling herself on the beach,’ remembers Melissa. She set about designing a range for women who’d had mastectomies – many of whom have not had reconstructions. Her first line, in collaboration with the Future Dreams breast-cancer charity, was for Net-A-Porter. The collection was chic and sexy, but also practical. The designs had pockets to fit a prosthesis or artificial breast form for women who hadn’t had reconstruction and featured higher arm openings and wider coverage to hide scars. The fabric was strong but soft, to give support for heavy implants yet still feel gentle on sensitive scar tissue. ‘It sold out within six weeks. I don’t sell out my regular collection in that time!’ says Melissa. ‘The demand is incredible because breast cancer hits so many people.’ In fact, it is estimated that one in eight women will be diagnosed with the disease in their lifetimes. Her second mastectomy line, the first with Amoena, again sees all Melissa’s profits going to Future Dreams. The range has been modelled by the Sky News sports presenter Jacquie Beltrao, who had a mastectomy three years ago, and includes strapless one-pieces and bikinis with on-trend zip-up tops. Melissa fine-tuned her designs with a panel of four women who had been through the illness. ‘They came to a workshop and  I said, “Ladies, let’s get naked so I can see.” They tried on everything and weren’t the least bit embarrassed, especially as I told them I have seen about a billion ladies naked. I kept tweaking the design and sending them back and forth to my muses and to the factory until they were right.’ Jamie says, ‘Melissa is committed to the cause, not because of me, but because breast cancer affects so many women. When we were young our parents would take us to  the beach for our holiday. I think a lot of families feel at their happiest on the beach. So of all the things Melissa could have done, I am so pleased it is this.’  amoena.com/uk-en; futuredreams.org.uk   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Cool California girl Kirsten Dunst was always going to be one-to-watch during Cannes Film Festival. Her stint as juror kicked off last night at an opening drinks reception, and her outfit did not disappoint. Dunst, 34, supped champagne alongside fellow jury members Vanessa Paradis and Valeria Golino in a barely-there pink dress embellished with chantilly lace and miniature pompoms. The ‘Puzzle’ gown comes courtesy of Aouadi Paris, the eponymous, under-the-radar brand of Marseille native Yacine Aoudai. Though his “urban-classy” label is only two collections old, Aoudai has an impeccable fashion CV. He left Balmain, where he worked as a designer alongside Christophe Decarnin and Olivier Rousteing, to form his own studio and create couture designs, many of which would make perfect alternative bridal choices as well modern eveningwear.  With its intricate beading, organza panels and body-skimming silhouette, Dunst's gown is a prime example of his signature.  If Dunst brought effortless elegance to the opening night, Vanessa Paradis was a vision of classic French chic. The actress kept it low-key in a monochrome pussy-bow blouse and mannish blazer which had a cool Helmut Newton vibe. She kept things casual in a pair of skinny jeans which would make  Kate Moss would be proud. and slim-fit jeans. A pair of fuschia pink round-toe pumps were the only flash of colour on her beatnik look.  Paradis is long-time ambassador and muse of Chanel so we expect to see her dressed in looks designed by Karl Lagerfeld during the festival. The French fashion house has recently extended the baton to Paradis’s daughter, Lily-Rose Depp. The doe-eyed 15-year-old has attended many of Chanel’s recent shows and parties, though a modelling contract has yet to be decided upon. Paradis, herself, has enjoyed a relationship with the Chanel brand since she was a teenager, famously swinging across a giant birdcage for a TV fragrance ad when she was 20 years old. If this was a stylish case of things to come, we can expect Dunst and Paradis to play the perfect high-low duo throughout Cannes.  If you dream of dressing just like Kate Moss, there are a number of key building blocks that you'll need in your wardrobe to make it happen. Grey skinny jeans, a Bella Freud jumper, a leopard-print coat and a tailored jacket are all essentials in building an authentic Moss look. Recently, a new item has been added to that line-up in the form of a pair of  classic Repetto pumps.  The latest item that Kate Moss has been wearing on loop is a pair of patent-leather Repetto Rose Mary Janes, with a 3cm block heel and a delicate buttoned strap. The supermodel is in Toronto this week for the launch of Cosme Decorté at luxury department store Saks Fifth Avenue, and she wore the £215 patent pumps to both the evening and the day events. For her first engagement, the supermodel wore the shiny shoes with a little black wrap dress with gold beading detailing on the shoulders and fishnet tights. Then the next day she chose the same pair for an in-store event with a monochrome printed shift dress with a roll neck and long sleeves. Moss proves that these Mary Janes aren't just a throwback childhood style, but are a chic grown-up option for work or evening occasions. Whether you're sick of court shoes, done with ballerinas or can't bear the thought of another night out in stilettos, Moss gives us the green-light to go for sensible cross-bar block heels instead.  Over the past 20 years Kate Moss has become an unofficial ambassador for Repetto. When she was photographed in the classic black ballet pumps in 2003 they quickly became the It shoe of the decade. The French label has a history of celebrity endorsements. Founder Rose Repetto started creating ballet shoes to take you beyond the barre in 1956 when Brigitte Bardot, a former ballerina, asked for a pair of 'outdoor ballet pumps' in red that she could wear for her role in the film And God Created Woman. Shortly after this Repetto created the 'Cendrillon' ballet flat, which is now available in a rainbow of colours and is still hugely popular.  Although the ballet flat has been overshadowed thanks to the huge popularity of the horsebit loafer, the old favourite pump is slowly making a comeback. Miuccia Prada showcased ballet flats (with added ribbons and buckles) on the SS16 Miu Miu catwalk, and Alexa Chung has started re-wearing her black ballet pumps, also thought to be by Repetto.  READ: How ballet pumps have had a makeover © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Earlier this week, images of Laura Haddock gracing the red carpet for the London premiere of Transformers: The Last Knight in a candyfloss pink gown were beamed around the world, and it felt like a new style starlet was born.  Haddock's own numerous Instagram posts, showing the dress in all its glory from countless striking angles, confirmed that it had been a moment for her as well. "Huge thank you to the wonderful @emiliawickstead for putting so much love and care and time in to designing and making this dress for me. a moment I will never forget.. x" she wrote.  Although Haddock's name and face will be familiar- she has been in Luther, The Inbetweeners and Guardians of the Galaxy- her star role in Transformers: The Last Knight  is propelling her to a new level of fame, a fact acknowledged by the hashtag #MyFirstTour which she has been using to document her whistlestop global journey from China to Chicago promoting the film, released yesterday in the UK. Her wardrobe for the multiple-stop publicity tour has had all the gloss and poise of a seasoned actress with a very precise sense of her own 'look'. "Laura has such exquisite day-to-day style - she's totally chic and feminine," says Aimee Croysdill, the British stylist who has been helping Haddock with her style choices  for nearly four years. "I amped everything up and translated this natural elegance to a red carpet setting," she explains of the simple yet clever strategy which she employed for this latest round of looks.  "We've done lots of red carpets, but this time Laura is the leading lady so we pumped up the volume – quite literally – the dresses got bigger!" The tour set the bar high early at the Guangzhou premiere with a "really special couture moment" in the form of  a blush pink and silver dotted tulle creation by Giambattista Valli which would give Carrie Bradshaw's mille feuille dress a run for its money.  The fairytale theme continued with that fabulous Emilia Wickstead concoction in London. "Laura has worn Emilia many times, she's a particularly special designer for us because Laura wore an Emilia dress when she was nominated for a Critics Choice awards which was the first time she stepped out in public after having her baby," Croysdill explains of the special relationship they have forged with one of London's best loved designers. "As soon as we had the premiere dates we knew Emilia had to be a part of the moment," she continues. "Laura loves a low-back, criss-cross dress so we pitched that to Emilia, she took the idea, ran with it and sent us a sketch which totally brought the idea to life. It was a one sketch wonder. Emilia was in every fitting and she made the whole experience so special. The tailor, Brigetta, looked after every minute detail, she really has magic fingers." Haddock's trio of dreamy, pink dresses was completed with a soft rose Miu Miu gown with a dramatic train and delicate spaghetti straps, the modern princess effect enhanced with a tulle hair bow and a glittering of Piaget jewellery. "We had a lovely breakfast with Miu Miu at the beginning of this year to discuss having a moment on this tour," Croysdill remembers. "This particular gown was shown to us only a few weeks before the premiere. As soon as we saw the photos we knew we were going to love it, but in real life it completely blew us all away." For the photocalls and interviews peppered between the premieres, Croysdill retained the pretty, polished message- a cool contrast to Haddock's practical professor look in the film- of those ballgowns. "We've had some very hot days so the weather has had to be a major consideration. Luckily Laura loves delicate light fabrics; we chose ones in a pastel nude tones to create lots of feminine soft moments," she says of a Kelly Simpkin lace-hemmed slip dress and a Natasha Zinko green and purple, off-shoulder 1950s look. All these looks may be pristinely elegant, but Croysdill insists that behind the English rose exterior, there is also a very British sense of normality to the way she and Haddock, who is married to fellow actor Sam Claflin, work together. "We have so much fun doing it. We have friends pop in and out of the fittings to have a cup of tea, some times a G&T! It's a true family and friends affair. Our favourite fitting pal is her little boy." © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.   The rise and rise of Hope Hicks may be one of the defining sub-narratives in the age of Trump. Last week, the 28 year-old was named interim White House communications director, becoming the fourth member of staff to hold the post in the past eight months. If Ivanka Trump's tweet in reaction to the announcement is anything to go by, then we can soon expect Hicks to be confirmed permanently in the position.  Congratulations to my talented friend & colleague Hope Hicks on being named WH Communications Director. I know she will do an amazing job! That Ivanka Trump is a cheerleader for Hicks- who has become one of the President's most trusted aides- shows the depth of trust which Hicks has fostered since she was introduced to the Trump family fold in 2012. First, whilst working for PR firm Hiltzik Strategies and soon after, when she was brought in-house and worked on PR for Ivanka's fashion collection as well as some of the Trump hotels. Now that the First Daughter's influence is winning out at the White House- it has been reported that chief strategist Steve Bannon was ousted in part by her and husband Jared Kusher- it is hardly surprising that Hicks is becoming a more powerful figure than ever.  "They're such a wonderful family, it's an honour to serve them in these different ways," Hicks said in a video for Forbes, filmed shortly after the election. It is one of just a handful of occasions that her voice has been heard in public or that she has been quoted on the record. Hicks' penchant for discretion had stood in her good stead though; during the presidential campaign, she was the gatekeeper to Donald Trump. All media and interview requests were passed through her and it is thought that he would dictate his infamously prolific tweets to her. Even now, she is often the only advisor in the room when Trump is giving interviews or taking important meetings. He calls her 'Hopester' and once described her as 'really shy but really talented' as he introduced her at a campaign rally. The pair seem to have forged a relationship as solid as  that of Hillary Clinton and Huma Abedin.  If Hicks has been reluctant to take the limelight, then her personal style speaks volumes about her way of working. Her remarkable ascension takes cues from the Ivanka Trump modus operandi with her polished look and quietly professional and cheery way of working, helping her to stand her ground amongst the more outspoken figures who have surrounded Trump so far- Sean Spicer, Anthony Scaramucci , Steve Bannon  et al- and fallen by the wayside. Having modelled for Ralph Lauren  during her teens, Hope Hicks still subscribes wholeheartedly to the ultra-groomed, All-American style. Her everywoman way of dressing comprises the classic 'power arm' shift dress in pretty prints or bright block colours.  “Dresses are easiest for me, especially on the road," Hicks said in a blog post on Ivanka Trump's website in 2015 when she was working at the Trump Organisation. "I don’t have to think about pulling together an outfit. It’s one piece to put on, and then I’m out the door." A perfectly on-message statement for Ivanka's Women Who Work philosophy. While Kellyanne Conway, another woman who has survived as a trusted member of Trump's team, opted for headline-grabbing red, white and blue Gucci at January's Inauguration, Hicks kept things classic in a black coat with a fur collar; glamorous but firmly non-shouty. She tends to carry either a black leather tote bag or a Louis Vuitton Neverfull. Ray Ban aviators are her sunglasses of choice. It is with her grooming that Hicks underscores her position in the Trump administration. Like Ivanka and Melania, she is never seen without a pristine blowdry and a perfectly made-up face. Her shiny brunette hair means she has drawn comparisions with Bee Shaffer, daughter of American Vogue editor Anna Wintour, and model Hilary Rhoda. She favours a slick of bright lipstick, whether it's pearly pink or deep, dark red. The only beauty detail which sometimes belies the hard work and long hours which she is putting into her role working with the most powerful man in the world, is the top knot which she is sometime spotted wearing as she exits Air Force One with the First Family.  If the style of Sarah Huckabee Sanders -the new White House press secretary- has been summed up as 'relatable' (thanks to her love of pearls, flat shoes and simple dresses) then Hicks creates the link between that and the Trump women's ultra-glossy look. It's an attitude which balances getting on with the job and looking the part, an exact towing of the line set down by Trump when he decreed that his female staff should 'dress like women.' When she was asked by Forbes if working as an adviser to the President was part of her plan, Hicks was honest: "I knew very little about politics and I wasn't expecting to take part in this and certainly not to play the part that I have." Yet, somehow she has now emerged as one of Trump's inner circle. How long things stay that way remains to be seen, but the rise of Hope Hicks is not over yet.          © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Victoria Beckham has received one of fashion’s highest accolades: a nomination for the prestigious Womenswear Designer of the Year award at the British Fashion Awards, which are dubbed the Oscars of the fashion world. The former Spice Girl will battle it out with J.W. Anderson and Christopher Kane to win the accolade, the most sought-after of the event. If she triumphs, she will join an impressive roster of designers to have scooped the title, including Alexander McQueen and Phoebe Philo for Céline. Last year Beckham picked up the Brand of the Year award for her eponymous fashion label, which despite only being seven years old, boasts annual sales of well over £30 million. After six years of showing at New York fashion week, she opened her first store on London’s Dover Street in 2014. Other design talents to be recognised on the shortlist include Alexander McQueen, Anya Hindmarch, Burberry and Stella McCartney for Brand of the Year; Faustine Steinmetz, Molly Goddard and Thomas Tait for Emerging Womenswear Designer; and Georgia May Jagger, Jourdan Dunn and Malaika Firth for Model of the Year.  "In our house it's Halloween all year round," Heidi Klum once told People. With an Oscar-winning make-up artist and prosthetics whizzes on speed dial, the mother-of-four means serious business when it comes to her spine-chilling fancy dress costumes. This year was no exception for the supermodel. She promised fans her outfit would be one of her "most intense" costumes to date and she didn't disappoint. Here's a look back at her some of her most frightful and dramatic personas from years gone by - from a robot, to Jessica Rabbit, to a wrinkle-covered granny... The model and television personality went with a Shrek theme this year. While she looked a spitting image of Princess Fiona, her boyfriend was transformed into Shrek for her 19th annual Halloween party at Lavo New York on Wednesday. Fictional character Jessica Rabbit was Klum's muse for the 2015 holiday. To get the voluptuous figure the model spent days prior to the party in a prosthetics lab, leading her Instagram following to suspect she might be dressing up as curvaceous Kim Kardashian. In 2014 the supermodel transformed into a butterfly - a gigantic one, incorporating huge rainbow-hued wings and mesmerising bug eyes. For her make-under Klum was blessed with grey hair, lashings of wrinkles and pigmented skin. The German model, who hosted her annual bash at New York's Marquee nightclub, topped off her look with a bouclé skirt suit, pearls and a walking stick.  Klum's costume plans were thwarted in 2012 when Hurricane Sandy hit America's East Coast. Instead of letting her Cleopatra-inspired costume go to waste, the model changed the date to December 1 and had an extra month to perfect her look. Oscar and Emmy-winning make-up artist, Bill Corso, transformed the model's face with hundreds of carefully placed crystals, highlighting her cheeks, lips and the bridge of her nose. Talk about razzle dazzle. Covered head-to-toe in simian-like hair, Klum even secured a pair of prosthetic monkey breasts for her ape evolution in 2011. Heidi's husband of seven years, Seal, made for a menacing beau by her side. There's nothing more eerie than wheeling into your own Halloween party on an autopsy table. With two blood-splattered doctors in tow, Klum told the MailOnline of her look: "It's kind of like a dead body with the first layer of skin ripped off. It's basically like me naked." Klum's naked self was achieved by much airbrushing on top of a basic map of a dead body, drawn upon her skin and the skull cap atop her head. Add some red contact lenses and rotting teeth and bingo! Dead as a doornail. All Hallow's Eve 2010 saw Klum transform herself rather literally into a Transformer. The mother-of-four chose red and purple as her superhero colours and danced the night away (or not) in a pair of hydraulic crane shoes. In contrast to his 8ft alien transformer wife, Seal played the silver-enrobed muscle man. Of their matching costumes, Klum promised to recreate the looks for their children, who love superheroes, at a later date. Reflecting on her crow costume, Klum revealed that the beak was actually rather cumbersome and made drinking most difficult. The wings also caused the 41-year-old and then-partner, Seal, problems in the car en route to the party venue. Picture Hindu goddess Kali and you'll probably recall her multiple colourful arms. You probably won't envisage a bonus arm belt with bloody hands hanging off it, or a couple of decapitated heads clasped in her finger tips. Such was a blue-dipped Klum's interpretation of Kali in 2008. You can't blame the Halloween enthusiast for donning a catsuit once in her costume career. Good old Klum eschewed the sexy Catwoman vibe in favour of a velveteen kitty, complete with collar, whiskers and subtle feline fangs. Costume collaborator Martin Izquierdo recalls that the 2006 sinful apple was the most taxing costume of Klum's to create. Why? Because the German beauty was heavily pregnant at the time.  The nation’s hearts collectively broke with the announcement that Mary Berry would no longer be judging The Great British Bake Off, the highlight of our television viewing year -  some even said it would never recover. How we were wrong. Enter Prue Leith; restaurateur, author and OBE. Even after 2017’s seemingly unforgivable blunder, (Leith tweeted the winner hours early) she is now firmly into her second year as the new Mary.   Any true cookery show fan would recognise Prue from her eleven year judging stint on Great British Menu and as she continues into her much anticipated second season, Prue, alongside fellow new additions Sandy Toksvig and Noel Fielding, has been welcomed into the fold. The highlight of a Tuesday night, Bake Off 2018 has had its fair share of surprises and delights. With Paul Hollywood dishing out handshakes like they’re breath mints, and Rahul, Bake Off’s shyest but arguably most-talented contestant, consistently presenting incredible show stoppers, this year’s six million viewers have had a lot to get excited about.  Aside from all the cake-making, it’s once again become impossible to ignore the sartorial aptitude of the our favourite TV judge (sorry Paul) and her apparent taste for bold, fun dressing. Not one to be outdone by Noel’s penchant for a jazzy shirt or the occasional lamé trouser, Prue holds her own in the style stakes. While Mary Berry was responsible for the immediate sell out of a Zara bomber jacket, it’s possible that after this season of GBBO is over, Prue’s selling power won’t be far behind. Here’s what we’ll be buying after taking fashion advice from Prue Leith: A necklace connoisseur, Prue is never seen without a statement piece of costume jewellery  and they are too good to go unnoticed. She's proud of her love for necklaces, speaking out about it on her blog, ‘there’s something wonderful about choosing the right necklace - or necklaces, plural, to add a dash of élan to an ordinary outfit.’ Just this year, Prue’s necklaces have been compared to the children’s game Kerplunk, a tribute to Mondrian and some slightly less, er, savoury items usually found behind a red velvet curtain. She has even been approached to create her own necklace line, so watch this space. Wearing bright colours is not for the faint of heart, but with a show like Bake Off it’s only right to spend your day tasting the contestants culinery masterpieces with a wardrobe full of sunshine shades. Forget about an accent bright colour to lift an outfit, Prue isn’t afraid to do block colour using primary shades alongside jewel-toned brights to create a look. She’s going against every rule we’ve ever been told but her pairings of emerald and fuschia, or bright blue with lemon yellow, are enough to make you throw out the rulebook altogether. Rather than choosing neutral, nondescript glasses, Leith lets her face furniture take centre stage, always sporting multicoloured or purple frames.  Statement glasses aren't for everyone, we grant you, but if your specs are a key part of your 'look' and you're keen to expand your eyewear horizons, let Leith lead the way.  Finding a tunic that errs on the right side of traveler-chic and working out how to style it isn't easy. Invest in the wrong shape and you could end up looking like an overgrown gap year student. But done right, a tunic that hits you somewhere between the upper thigh and a couple of inches above your knee, worn over slightly cropped trousers, makes for a stylish ensemble. Case in point is Leith, who pairs hers with a longline waistcoat and orange mules to excellent effect.  That’s right, you heard correctly - no longer banished to the annals of the early 2000s (and favourite of fellow new national treasure Doria Ragland - see her patterned one at The Duchess of Sussex’s cookbook launch) - Prue Leith rocks a pashmina. Used alongside her signature necklaces to add yet more colour to her look and presumably stay warm in the Bake Off tent, Leith could be responsible for making us rummage through the backs of our wardrobes for our once discarded shawls.  Jurassic World star Bryce Dallas Howard won over the red carpet at the Golden Globes earlier this month when she revealed she had bought her Jenny Packham gown herself at a department store. As a size 6 (UK size 10), she revealed that she can’t borrow gowns from designers as easily as other size 0 or size 2 actresses. Last night at the Critics' Choice Awards Bryce once again went without a Hollywood stylist and bought her own Balmain gown online, taking advantage of the wonders of next-day delivery. She bought her black Balmain gown with a plunging neckline and silver star detailing on the hip from Elyse Walker for £909.79 - a good price if you consider that a top red carpet stylist can charge around £1,500 a day for their services. She paired it with t-bar peep-toe black heels and an Edie Parker black box 'Fiona' clutch with pearl detailing.  Dallas Howard explained why she often buys her own gowns on the Critics Choice Awards red carpet: 'I’ve alluded to this a little bit before, but when you’re not a sample size or if you don’t have a direct relationship with a designer or if you don’t have a lot of notice - those size six dresses aren’t available.’ She added: ‘'What I’ve found is, if something is last minute, I go to Neimans or I get something online... I’m really taped and I’m touching my breasts a lot, making sure that the tape is still sticking. I hope it’s not awkward for anyone.'  While buying your own awards season gown might seem like an alien concept to many, Bryce laughed off the suggestion that she was amazing for wearing off-the-rack. She said to E!: ‘No I’m not amazing, these are expensive dresses!’ I think it would have been better if it wasn’t a typical fancy dress. The people I’m so obsessed by are able to go to a store and get something vintage that’s under $7 and they make this beautiful gown – I’m not that person.’ Celebrity stylist Manny, who works with Jourdan Dunn and Lottie Moss, talked The Telegraph through the reality of red carpet sample sizes: ‘In Paris generally sample size is a 6-8 [UK size] and if you are busty it’s near impossible to fit into a sample. For celebrities larger than a sample size often a brand would let you pull from store stock, but then it means you can’t make alterations as it needs to go back.  There’s no denying that Karl Lagerfeld is abnormal. At 82 years old he helms three international fashion brands; Chanel, Fendi and Karl Lagerfeld. For Chanel alone he designs seven collections annually – two ready-to-wear (the latest of which will show at Paris Fashion Week today), two haute couture, one pre-fall, one resort and one Metiers d’Art. Not to mention shooting the corresponding campaigns himself. While most his age are enjoying retirement, and most likely suffering from age-related ailments, Lagerfeld is jetting around the world as the most in-demand and influential man in fashion. Not surprising, then, that scientists want to test his DNA – after all, his genes appear to contain the elixir to eternal youth, if not aesthetically then mentally and physically. "I was asked by somebody to do this. Because they think I’m not normal,” he tells the November issue of British Vogue. “But I flatly refused. Unique pieces are unique pieces. But I think very flattering, huh? And also I was asked for skincare for men because they think I am remade. But I am not remade. I am all fake but not remade.” He shows no signs of slowing down as his age increases; he's tied in to contracts with Fendi and Chanel until he dies (or perhaps we should say, if he dies). “I think I’m pretty lucky that I can do what I like best in perfect conditions. I don’t have to fight with anybody. You know my contracts with Fendi and Chanel are for life? And I don’t feel tired at all. I hate slow people. Horrible." Even being alone – he has never married and does not have children, though does have a beloved pet cat called Choupette – doesn’t phase him. “If you are sick and old with no money then it must be hard, but in my case it is the height of luxury to be alone,” he says. While the prospect of a fashion world without Lagerfeld is certainly a far less entertaining one, we expect death is far too boring for him and he'll no doubt find some way around the inconvenience.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Theresa May brought a soupçon of French chic to the floor of the House of Commons this afternoon as she took part in PMQs wearing an Hermès scarf elegantly layered underneath her navy suit. Although the exact white and blue style May is wearing today is no longer available, similar designs in the same Carré size begin at around £295.  Given her imminent plan to trigger Article 50 and begin the UK's exit from the European Union, the Prime Minister's choice to accessorise with an iconic design by a heritage French brand might be interpreted as a smart act of diplomacy - or just another example of her famed fashion nous. May is a known Hermès  scarf aficionado. Long before she moved into Number 10 she was seen enlivening sleek tailoring with the silk foulards and she has been frequently been seen with one knotted around her shoulders or tucked into her jacket since becoming PM.  In 2013, she was gifted a £280 Hermès scarf by her then-counterpart, French interior minister Manuel Valls. Home Office records show that May made a payment, which meant she could keep the gift. May's successor as Home Secretary, Amber Rudd, was also given an Hermes scarf by Bernard Cazeneuve last year. Like May, she opted to keep hers too.  It's not just Theresa May who has used an Hermès scarf as a tool for political dressing. Christine Lagarde, the Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund who frequently makes best-dressed lists for her personal brand of sophisticated professional style, is also a fan of their classic ability to add a dash of colour and elegance to pared-back suits.  In fact, Lagarde has defiantly continued to wear her Hermès despite being criticised for her love of designer clothes. The Leftist French newspaper Libération  once described her as "an upper-class woman cut off from common people and more preoccupied with her look than their welfare, the way such elegant, chic people are."  First introduced in 1937, the Hermès silk scarf is steeped in tradition, taking up to 18 months to complete. Designs have been created by artists from around the world with more than 1200 now in the archive. Two collections are issued every years, each comprising twelve styles, 6 of which are re-issues of vintage prints. Given an Hermès scarf is sold every 25 seconds somewhere in the world, the Prime Minister is not alone in her appreciation of this timeless accessory.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
