 Victoria Beckham is one savvy marketeer. It’s just days before her SS17 New York fashion show, and, as usual, the designer is teasing out what we can assume are designs from the new collection. Heading from hotel-to-studio to make final preparations, Beckham has used the brief moments between hotel lobby and taxi as her very own catwalk. Here’s what we have learnt from her savvy strutting. VB’s trousers have been veering into ‘wide stride’ territory for some time, but now they run the risk of slipping off her hips too. Her new cropped pants, with two hip pockets and six front buttons, draw the eye immediately to the crotch area, which is elongated more than any other trouser Beckham has worn previously. And against all odds, the mother-of-four pulls off the drop crotch trews. With a black silk shirt tucked in and her dainty ankles framed by chunky gladiator sandals, there is nothing ‘skater’ about the star’s look. Tip to take: The key to looking pulled together while wearing such a relaxed look is to add luxe-looking accessories into the mix. Beckham’s gold watch, top visor sunglasses (£295 at victoriabeckham.com) and rings all paint a picture of a sophisticated woman who knows entirely how to style herself, and has not, in fact, purchased the wrong size trousers. The former Spice Girl is fond of an artfully placed hip bag. While us mortals struggle to find a practical balance, Beckham manages to sashay with her belongings perched neatly on her left side. Thankfully, the design she is carrying looks closer to a tote bag than a clutch and can be carried by holding the straps as usual when you actually have iPads, wet wipes, wallets, bottles of water etc to cart around. Tip to take:If you can’t quite fathom Beckham’s ‘tote on hip’ styling flourish, simply swap your cross-body bags for a pochette, and carry on your hip instead of under your arm. Fashion editors favour the slim clutch style during fashion week, as it houses show tickets perfectly. The famous VB statement - “I can’t concentrate in flats” - seems like a distant memory, as the star has been happily stepping out in adidas Stan Smiths and point-toe brogues for seasons past. Next on her footwear repertoire journey is chunky sandals, which hint at a classic gladiator style owing to the cross-strap feature. Long may this practical side of Beckham reign! Tip to take:Wear chunky sandals through September with long, wide-legged trousers, so that just a little of the shoe is visible. This is how Céline styles the shoe style season after season. A crisp white button-down is an invaluable tool to keep you looking polished. Beckham has had a collarless, classic and tuxedo bib shirt on rotation this week, and all have looked utterly sleek tucked in her trousers. Tip to take: Instead of rushing to buy the latest autumn trend pieces, take a look at your basics. Investing in two quality shirts will have far greater longevity than that leopard print top you’ve been eyeing up on the high street.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  A major exhibition of the late Azzedine Alaïa’s work will open in London in spring 2018, the Design Museum announced on Wednesday. Azzedine Alaïa: The Couturier, set for a five-month run from 10th May, will showcase more than 60 examples of Alaïa’s couture pieces - from impeccable tailoring to the spray-on-tight dresses that were synonymous with his name. Before his death in November, Alaïa collaborated with guest curator Mark Wilson to personally select works from his archive for display - a factor that will likely motivate thousands of international visitors, keen to see one of the designer's final projects. Alaïa apparently also spent time documenting his creative process for the museum, meaning the exhibition will be a must-see for fashion students too. ‘Following his untimely passing on 18 November 2017, the Design Museum will now present this unique exhibition planned by Alaïa himself exploring his passion and energy for fashion as he himself intended it to be seen,’ a spokesperson for the museum said in a statement. ‘Azzedine Alaïa was recognised throughout his life as a master couturier who expressed the timeless beauty of the female form in the most refined degree of haute couture.’ This public tribute follows one made last week at the British Fashion Council’s annual Fashion Awards, which saw Naomi Campbell, Stephanie Seymour, Veronica Webb and more of the designer’s supermodel friends and muses speak about his impact and legacy on stage in front of an audience of industry figureheads. “Everyone in this room knows that Azzedine was able to transform a woman’s body into something special; make you look great and still like a woman,” Campbell said. “He captured the essence of femininity. But beyond his work as a designer, from the second day I met him, he became my papa.” © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.    This article was originally written and published in November 2011 but has been republished to coincide with the 2015 Victoria's Secret Show. Most models would have you believe they eat whatever they like - "I eat burgers and French fries!" they protest, as if they fall out of bed every day looking like a magazine advertisement. Industry people know that's not true, and so does supermodel Adriana Lima. Lima is disarmingly frank about what it takes to prepare for the Victoria's Secret fashion show - watched by eight million people, reportedly - in which the world's highest-paid models wear barely-there lingerie as part of a production that costs $10 million. So here's what it really takes to be an Angel: Lima, 30, has been working out every day with a personal trainer since August. For the last three weeks, she's been working out twice a day. "It is really intense, it's not really the amount of time you spend working out, it's the intensity: I jump rope, I do boxing, I lift weights, but I get bored doing that. If I am not moving I get bored very easily." She sees a nutritionist, who has measured her body's muscle mass, fat ratio and levels of water retention. He prescribes protein shakes, vitamins and supplements to keep Lima's energy levels up during this training period. Lima drinks a gallon of water a day. For nine days before the show, she will drink only protein shakes - "no solids". The concoctions include powdered egg. Two days before the show, she will abstain from the daily gallon of water, and "just drink normally". Then, 12 hours before the show, she will stop drinking entirely. "No liquids at all so you dry out, sometimes you can lose up to eight pounds just from that," she says. "It's like they're training for a marathon," says Sophia Neophitou, the British fashion editor who is chief stylist for this year's show. "Adriana works really hard at it. It's the same as if you were a long-distance runner. They are athletes in this environment - it's harder to be a Victoria's Secret model because no one can just chuck an outfit on you, and hide your lumps and bumps." The body type they are looking for when casting for the show harks back to the Eighties, says Neophitou, to the golden age of the original supers: Linda, Christy, Cindy, Elle and Naomi. "It isn't about being a waif, it was about being empowered and you can achieve that," Neophitou says. Lima has been an Angel since 2000. She has since had a baby. Two of her fellow Angels walking the runway this year, Doutzen Kroes and Miranda Kerr, have each recently given birth, too. The preparation is all worth it, says Lima, because the show is the highlight of her year. "Actually, the Victoria's Secret show is the highlight of my life. Becoming an Angel, once I achieved that, it was a dream come true for me. And I know that after all this is done, when I sit down with my daughter one day, we are going to look back and it's going to be very special." What does being hand-picked to represent the brand do for a model's career (not to mention her income)? "It opens up so many doors, everyone knows your name, the whole world knows you now," she says. "Any model in this world would love to be an Angel."  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When tickets to Beyoncé and Jay Z's On The Run II tour sold out globally in under 15 minutes earlier this year, those of us who managed to bag one (I'm not smug at all) knew we'd be in for a treat come June. Last night, the UK leg kicked off at Cardiff's Principality Stadium, and the couple didn't disappoint. As megastar performers,  fashion is a vital part of the spectacle and as the couple performed solo and joint hits that date as far back as 2003, it was clear that Beyoncé's fashion prowess is as on point as ever.  She emerged in a sheer studded blazer with a matching bodysuit and bejewelled face mask, all custom pieces by American designer LaQuan Smith. The 29 year old designer is known for his provocative outfits, with Rihanna, Cardi B and Kim Kardashian among the stars who sing his praise. Her bejewelled, semi-sheer look is an example of Beyoncé's strategy of regularly championing up-and-coming labels. For her 2016 Formation tour, she enlisted lingerie brand Nubian Skin - a label dedicated to creating nude underwear for women of colour - to provide underwear for all of her dancers. For the Formation video, she wore an array of heavily embellished chokers by New York brand Dylanex which had launched two years prior. Since, it has been worn by Kendall Jenner, Rihanna and Katy Perry.  While glittering leotards are a given at a Beyoncé concert, there is always a frisson of something offbeat. Last night, that came in the form of a custom Gucci outfit (she regularly works with the label on outfits for events or just Instagram moments). The look featured the label's collaboration with artist Dapper Dan and included an oversized hoodie and thigh-high boots with Gucci's signature double G logo emblazoned all over them; an OTT streetwear-inspired costume finished off with one of the gimp masks which designer Alessandro Michele likes to  add to his catwalk looks. Rihanna has also been partial to this look in recent years and it's become the ultimate superstar style power move- who else could pull one off, after all? In her 20 years as a global star, the singer has proven she isn't one to shy away from using her platform as a voice for her audience; be it with politically-charged lyrics, songs about female empowerment or with references to black culture. These statements are often reflected in her style choices, many of which enhance and add to her message. Here are five times Beyoncé 's look transcended the simple stage costume... Beyoncé used her headline set at Coachella earlier this year, which had been delayed for a year following the announcement of her second pregnancy, to showcase a host of bespoke outfits by French fashion house, Balmain. Beyoncé's stylist, Marni Senofonte enlisted Balmain's Olivier Rousteing to create five meticulously crafted looks for her two-hour performance. Her first look, and the centrepiece of the five, was about honoring black culture as she channelled Nefertiti, with a tall headdress said to be similar to the one found on the bust of the Egyptian Queen in 1912. Her dancers flanked in catsuits with sphinx symbols, and the singer thanked her audience for allowing her to be "the first black woman to headline the festival".  While her looks wouldn't be deemed typical daywear, global fashion search engine Lyst noted that in the 24 hours following Beyonce's string of heavily-embellished looks at Coachella, searches for Balmain increased by 22%.  The surprise release of Beyoncé's 2016 single, Formation, came after a string of police brutality reports across America. The singer didn't shy away from referencing them, with lyrics containing strong political and social criticism and owning her heritage as an African-American woman from the South. The politically-charged video included references to both the New Orleans' Katrina disaster and the Black Lives Matter movement.  In it, she wears and references a string of high fashion designers, including luxury fashion house, Givenchy. She wears a cream lace Alessandra Rich gown and several dresses by Gucci as she stands on cars amidst a flooded town- it's a visual which blends her humble beginnings and status as one of the world's most famous and successful performers.  The accompanying video to Queen Bey's 2008 hit, Single Ladies, featured the star alongside two dancers, performing an impeccably choreographed routine that would go on to spur hundreds of spoof videos. While we'd typically expect such a minimal set (the backdrop for the video was grey, and featured just a few dancing blocks) to allow for a fabulously glamorous outfit to take centre-stage, instead, Beyoncé and the dancers wore simple one-shouldered black bodysuits ensuring all attention was on the lyrics and the routine, proving that sometimes less is more.  Beyoncé's pregnancy reveal outfits are at either end of the fashion spectrum. She famously announced her first pregnancy on stage following a live performance at the MTV Awards in 2011 wearing a sleek Dolce and Gabbana sequin tuxedo jacket and smart black trousers. As an encore erupted, the singer pulled her blazer back to reveal a small bump beneath her white shirt. A clever blend of reveal and conceal. However, it was her second pregnancy announcement last year featuring a more eclectic look that went viral and sparked thousands of comment pieces. The image of the singer in a burgundy lace bra, blue shorts and a mint green veil with a floral backdrop debuted her twin bump in a goddess-y, mother nature fashion which spoke to modern obsessions with fertility and motherhood. The image has since garnered 11.2 million likes; the fourth most-liked picture on Instagram ever.  In the nineties and early noughties, Destiny's Child were at the height of their success. Beyonce and her former bandmates, Kelly Rowland and Michelle Williams, were infamous for their matching looks, which were often handmade by Beyonce's own mother, Tina Lawson. The R&B groups coordinating costumes symbolised their solidarity as a trio and made a statement on the red carpet. It also made for memorable music videos; most notably, the band's 2001 hit Survivor, in which they they all wore different camouflage pieces throughout. If they weren't wearing the exact same look, you could bet they'd be wearing the same material and colour in different cuts. Nowadays, it's hard to imagine Bey deigning to go matchy-matchy with anyone other than her husband or children.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We are now just weeks away from the 2016 Olympic and Paralympic games, and so naturally a number of carefully timed sportswear collections are dropping ahead of the Opening Ceremony on 5th August. Today H&M has released an inspiring collection called Every Victory, with the face of H&M Sport Caitlyn Jenner fronting the launch.  Jenner, who won the gold in the decathlon in 1976 in Montreal, narrates the short film which celebrates 'personal victories' and talks about her struggles with gender identity and the power of sport. "I felt like I couldn't do it alone, or with the entire world watching my every step," Jenner says. "I fought to belong, and for my right to be different. I felt trapped by my body and by what others expected of me." She continues: "I had to find strength within me that I didn't know I had. I questioned whether it was really worth it, nothing came easy. But nothing truly important ever does. To keep going no matter what the obstacles is, is what victory looks like. Whether you are representing your country, or yourself." As she speaks, the short film shows a number of inspiring athletes training, including Chelsea Werner- the gymnast with Down's syndrome- Namibia Flores - Cuba's only female boxer who has fought against prejudice to reach the top of her game- and the surfer Mike Coots who lost his leg in a shark attack.  As for their kit, the collection is affordable, with £24.99 graphic leggings, £14.99 sports bras and sports jackets all under £40. Despite the low prices it is also technical sportswear, as H&M developed the line in collaboration with the Swedish Olympic team. The high street chain has also designed the uniforms for the Olympic and Paralymic teams for Rio 2016. In a highly personal interview to coincide with the launch of the collection Jenner opens up about the role sport has played in her life. She says that she now keeps her Olympic gold medal in her drawer with her nail varnishes and says, "you know what the medal is great for? Show and tell with the kids." Being able to be honest with somebody about who you are.”  She also discusses having low self esteem at school: “I thought everyone was smarter than me and better students than me.  The year is 1986. Eight-year-old Gary McQueen poses by a backstreet wall outside his nan’s house in Stratford, East London. Dressed in a New Romantic scarf and blazer, big enough to fall off his shoulders, the 18-year-old boy taking the photo on his Instamatic camera would go on not only to change fashion, but make their shared surname synonymous with it. The boy in question was Gary’s uncle, Alexander McQueen. Meeting Gary James McQueen, now 37, you are struck by his eyes: dark blue with a cheeky twinkle when he laughs. “My uncle used to style me up. He tried to do something with my hair then eventually he’d give up and go, ‘It’s a birds nest.’” The family resemblance is strong. Not just that he talks with the same dropped aitches that locate his birthplace east of the Bow Bells. As he shows me the collection of men’s silk scarves he has created with Anderson and Sheppard, the Savile Row tailors where Lee, as McQueen was known, trained, it is clear that Gary’s aesthetics are a chip off the old block. Death and Re-birth are the main themes, with birds, bones, skulls and insects (locusts, mostly) in shades of grey, black and red. McQueen was the cheeky working-class cockney sparrow taken under the wing of aristocratic fashion stylist Isabella Blow both as protégé and power tool. Within the rarefied fashion world, McQueen stood out in every way. The son of a London black cab driver, his talent would transcend any limitations of the British class system. Legend has it that, while training at Anderson and Sheppard, he stitched an obscenity into the lining of a suit destined for the Prince of Wales. McQueen brought danger to London fashion in the mid-Nineties with his theatrical shows that explored sexuality and other taboos. He made British fashion cool and gave it the super-league status it had long lacked. Like his uncle, Gary is the son of a black cab driver. Indeed, it was because Gary’s mother, Janet, Lee’s elder sister, was out driving her cab, that uncle Lee (Blow was the one who suggested he took his second name, Alexander, for his label) would babysit and fashion photo shoots would be top of the agenda. “We’d be at nan’s house in Biggerstaff Road, where Lee lived. When mum was out working, he’d let us watch horror films like Hellraiser.” Gary believes this sparked his own love of character creation: “The way my uncle approached art was through storytelling. He designed for characters, not people. That’s what I love to do.” Despite the 10-year age gap, this understanding became a bond. When Gary was 12, his mother remarried and re-located the family to the German town of Luelsdorf, near Bonn. Gary remembers hearing about Lee through family talk. “Nobody thought he was going to make it that big. He was quirky. I loved him for that. Mum openly admits to feeling embarrassed and protective. She worried that his shows were too ‘out there’.” Lee and his big sister were extremely close. Kim Blake, the fashion PR who represented the designer, recalls how his shows were always delayed “to wait for Janet”, who would be battling her way through fashion-show crowds. Lee’s mother, Joyce, would be backstage helping, “but it was Janet he wanted front row”. Gary had returned to London to study graphic design when a position came up at McQueen for a textile designer. He “jumped” at it, not least because his dreams of becoming a fine artist were not working out. He had taken a job with the council, having become a father to two small children, Zara, who is now 16, and Mason, now 10. His youngest daughter, Violet, now four, was not yet born. At 25, Gary remembers how Lee informally introduced him to the menswear team in the Clerkenwell studio. “It was a sweat box, basically – just chaos. For two months, no one really knew who I was. They probably thought I was one of Lee’s boyfriends,” he laughs. Gary kept his head down. He recognised the “grey area” of being the boss’s nephew. Handily, his talent for printed textiles, his training in (then new) computer technology and having a stepfather as a printmaker helped. As did his fashionable looks. At our meeting in an art studio in Dalston, Gary wears a tight black cashmere sweater showing off a toned torso, with trendy brown drainpipes “bought on the high street”, with expensive Alexander McQueen snaffle loafers. Reminiscing about life working at McQueen, Gary explains that “everything was urgent”. He added: “People would rush around like headless chickens when Lee was in the building. “First you’d smell his cigarette smoke, then hear his psychotic laughter. Everyone liked to please him. He would ask people to do the impossible. “For Lee, nothing was impossible. Everything could be done if you tried hard enough. And for him, you always did. He had such high expectations. I’d get the sharp side of his tongue, then the next day he’d pat me on the back.” At the time of McQueen’s death in 2010, Gary had been working for his uncle for five years. “We worked weekends, and late nights closer to the show – not ideal when you’re a dad. Lee had a bad lifestyle. I was not close to his friends. He kept his life private. After work, I’d go home to my family and Jane [his partner, who was then a banker].” Gary thinks his uncle started to get “more down” after Blow’s suicide in 2007. He recalls his last conversation the day before his uncle took his own life: “We had discussed a memorial statue for my nan [Lee’s mother, who had died a week earlier]. He liked the design of an angel, but wanted the hands to face upwards. I’d been concerned [about him], but that day he seemed optimistic. He looked bad, but was in good spirits. I don’t know what people could have done – he’d made his decision.” Gary continued to work for the Alexander McQueen label after Sarah Burton (another of Lee’s protégés) took over as creative director. In 2011, she famously created the Duchess of Cambridge’s wedding dress, propelling the McQueen name to even greater global recognition. “Sarah is such a nice person, so genuine,” said Gary. “She genuinely wanted the best for Lee and really made me feel comfortable.” But, thanks to the confidence his late uncle had instilled in him, Gary left the label in 2012 to set up on his own. “My uncle will always be with me, but I want to be my own person and, at the same time, carrying his spirit forward. Scarves are a way of paying tribute to my uncle, and a starting point for me.”     Gary has also created cards for Chasing the Stigma, a men’s mental health charity. “A lot of things happened in Lee’s life which made him the person he was, made him the great person he was but also caused a lot of his demons.” He is reluctant to be called a ‘fashion designer’ box preferring ‘multi-tasking artist’. You may find him working on a 3d sculpture or 2d print. Or picking blood from the bones of a rotting boar’s jaw to come up with an accessory for a photo shoot. He is particularly proud of a digitally engineered print for a women’s scarf inspired by moonlight on moving bodies (these are available from his website). “Its got that feeling Lee would loved.”  Gary McQueen's scarves are available to buy at GaryJamesMcQueen.com  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This year has been the death knell for skinny jeans. Fashion has moved on. They’re over: too ubiquitous and potentially unflattering. Whenever the fashion world twigs that something it’s previously been obsessed with, hits a level of mainstream mundanity it does a sharp, snobbish about turn. And yet - for most retailers - skinny jeans still make up the bulk of their denim sales. In March, the trend forecasting agency WGSN declared that skinnies constituted 54% of the denim business in most stores. So in spite of the proliferation of designers, fashion writers, bloggers and ‘influencers’ banging on about wider silhouettes and rigid denim styles, most women haven’t budged an iota from their skinny affection. If you walk down any street they’re wearing clinging, skinny jeans - if they’re under 25 they’re probably also sporting some serious rips across their legs. And most of these women don’t look very much like the models who are traditionally shot wearing sample size denim. One reason behind this is that like most things in modern fashion, there is no one definitive anything. There is no one heel height that gains traction over others, skirts can be happily mini or midi depending on your preference. And perhaps one day you feel like slouching around in a looser boyfriend style jeans, and on others you pick out your favourite skinnies. But there’s also another rather basic reason which fashion has a tedious habit of overlooking. Sizeism is a real issue in  the industry: a story that was doing the rounds at fashion week featured a famous designer being aghast that an editor had the audacity to order a piece from his collection in a size 14 (she’s slim but tall). Yet, the average dress size of women in this country is a size 16 (in America, it’s a 20). The largest size most denim brands go up to is a 32 (which is a 14/16). These women couldn’t winch their way into a rigid pair of denims if their life depended on it. One - the sizes don’t go up that far, and two anyone - regardless of size - who has wider hips or a curvy posterior needs a little stretch to get those denims up. The key reason why skinny jeans - or simply those that contain 1-2% stretch - will always win out over rigid, stiff denim - is that most women don’t have a chance of actually getting into anything else. Yet, bizarrely given that the denim market is worth an estimated $108 billion, most denim brands don’t seem to have cottoned on (sorry) to this simple fact. Until now. And it’s taken a Kardashian to do it. Good American launched this week. In a market seemingly saturated with premium, and not so premium denim brands, you’d have thought that the last thing that the world needed was one more. And yet, this label - the brain-child of Brit Emma Grede (who serves as CEO of Good American) and Khloe Kardashian (of the Kardashian family inc) is doing something that no other denim brand has ever done. Good American is making jeans that women keenly want to wear, and strikingly, showing them what they will actually look like in the jeans - rather than pushing a sample size model at them and hoping that their powers of imagination are strong enough to picture themselves wearing the style in four sizes larger than the projected image. The collection is broken down into three styles of jeans: ‘Good legs’, ‘Good cuts’ and ‘Good waist’  - all have a high waist, and are a variant on the classic skinny jean - from slim fit straight leg to super skinny. The stretch fabric is geared towards dressing women with shape - the waistband is reinforced to be ‘gap proof’ - so no more of that annoying gaping at the back for those with a much smaller waist to their hips. The jeans run from a size 0 to a 24, and on the website, there are three size variants of models for each style - a 2, 10 and 14 - so you can see how they fit different shaped women. But this isn’t simply another celebrity fashion line, there is serious credibility here. The brand is based in LA - the mothership of innovative denim, but more interestingly, Grede is married to Jens Grede - one half of the incredibly successful denim and lifestyle brand Frame - and both he and his business partner Erik Torstensson (also partner to British Fashion Council Chairman, Dame Natalie Massenet) are investors in the project. Speaking about the collection to ELLE.com, Kardashian explained that “For me, the biggest thing was the range in sizes. We're about to provide this really fabulous denim line that's really trendy and cool for a great, diverse range of women.It's about women of individuality and diversity, but also about being comfortable in yourself. That's what we're trying to promote. It's not about fitting into a size two. I just want people to be healthy and love who they are and be in control of your life. But that doesn't mean you have to be a size six.” Grede adds that “the reality of the fashion industry is that it's stuck in this idea of only providing sample sizes [and] this idea of when you're in a department store you can't actually go onto the designer denim floor and find anything above a 10 (a UK size 14). And 10 is relatively small. It's ridiculous. So this feels revolutionary because it kind of is. We hope other brands follow suit and it becomes the norm. That's why we keep talking about a "denim revolution." Having [sizes] 0 to 24 is not a weird thing. The average size woman in America is a size 16 (UK size 20). She should be able to go in her local store and find a beautiful pair of designer jeans.” The collection sits in the ‘premium’ denim space - with prices running from £130 to around £160 - the site is US based but ships to the UK. The shift in fashion towards us so-called ‘real’ women is happening, slowly but surely. It will be interesting to see how many other brands follow Good American’s simple yet strikingly smart approach. Fashion that all women can wear? Now that really is ground-breaking.  There has been much talk about the death of the skinny jean of late. There’s no doubt that the classic rigid cut has surpassed it in terms of fashion clout, but can we really wave goodbye to such a weekend wardrobe staple? Let Sienna Miller offer some sartorial guidance. The actress took to New York streets in a pair of stonewashed grey Frame skinnies yesterday, but managed to make the style, which is neither the colour or shape du jour, still relevant. A certain amount of fashion maths is involved when attempting such an apparently effortless off-duty look. Note how Miller has paired her skinnies with a billowing, oversized shirt which she's casually half-tucked .  The open-neck of the shirt also acts as a focal point away from the form-fitting denim. Next, cast your eyes down to Miller's ankles. She's rolled up the hem so that at least two inches of her ankles are showing. That flash of skin is all-important for getting a flattering spring effect. Two more styling tips to bring your skinnies bang up-to-date. Snip the hems to give a frayed finish (trust us it’s what all the fashion insiders are doing). And wear with white trainers, à la Sienna. The actress’s pumps are the trusty Supergas that you probably wore in our teens, proving that it’s still OK to wear plimsolls and skinnies in your mid-thirties (the mother-of-one is 34). Just do your fashion maths first. The style worn by Sienna - Frame's Le Luxe Noir style has a cashmere feel, which is not only ultra comfortable, but makes the edges easier to fray than rigid denim.  She’s got a British fiancé, adores La Moss and is designing for one of our heritage brands, Belstaff. Now, this New York girl is moving to London. Jane Mulkerrins meets Liv Tyler By anyone’s standards, Liv Tyler has wasted very little time over the past couple of years. When I first met the actress and model back in April 2014, she was deep in the filming of her first television role, as Meg, a young woman markedly altered by grief, in the HBO series The Leftovers.  Liv – star of big-screen hits including Stealing Beauty, Armageddon and The Lord of the Rings – was then 36, single and a divorced mother-of-one; her son Milo was nine. Having grown up as an only child herself, she would ‘definitely’ like to have more children, she’d told me, over oysters and craft ale at a gastropub near her home in Manhattan’s West Village. ‘I’m 100 per cent planning on it, but the clock is ticking,’ she said. ‘If the stork could just drop it off on my roof, I’d be so happy – I’d have, like, 20.’ Fast-forward to today and Liv’s domestic set-up looks dramatically different. Her second son, Sailor, is now 18 months old, and she has a daughter, Lula, too, born in early July. Liv, now 39, is engaged to their father, David Gardner, a British football agent and David Beckham’s best friend, who also has a nine year-old son, Grey, from his previous marriage to the ex-Hollyoaks actress Davinia Taylor. ‘I know, wow, so much has changed,’ gasps Liv. ‘And none of it was planned at all.’  Planned or not, her swiftly expanded brood fulfils a long-held ambition. ‘I can remember being six and I had all these dolls – I’d always take care of them and tell everyone I was going to have a big family some day. Then, at one point, I thought maybe I wasn’t going to…’ She pauses, and sighs happily. ‘And now it’s my whole world. Yesterday, I was sitting in my pyjamas holding Lula, and Sailor and Grey and Milo were all running around and playing. It was the most beautiful morning, and I just had to pinch myself.’  On the day we speak, three weeks after Lula’s birth, Liv is at a holiday house on Long Island, enjoying a break at the beach, with David, the four children, and two nannies. She admits: ‘That feels a little ridiculous, but it definitely takes a village.’ And if the addition of three new children and a fiancé were not sufficient, further change is afoot. Two weeks after we speak, Liv, along with Milo, now 11, Sailor and Lula, will be relocating to London’s Primrose Hill. Gardner has made attempts to move to New York with Grey, ‘but it wasn’t an option because of custody reasons,’ explains Liv. ‘I’m definitely a New Yorker through and through, but for our family right now, England is going to be wonderful. It’s a little more kid-friendly, with all the space and parks. David and Grey are so used to grass that they can play football on, and New York really is the concrete jungle.’  In between giving birth, twice, and planning a transatlantic move, Liv has also designed a capsule collection for the British heritage brand Belstaff. The 12 autumn/winter pieces, which have just gone on sale, include a military-style pea coat with leather trim and gold buttons, two leather jackets, a cape with a leather collar, a pussy-bow blouse, slim-fit trousers and a pair of riding boots. Along with designing the range, Liv stars in a three-minute film for the brand, Falling Up, in which she plays a female aviator. Both the film and the collection itself pay homage to the 1920s pilot Amelia Earheart, the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic – dressed by Belstaff.   The collection is, Liv says in her distinctive breathy, honeyed tones, ‘a celebration of the feminine and masculine rolled into one,’ inspired by classic pieces from her own wardrobe, and that of her fiancé.   ‘David has the best fashion sense ever, and we’re pretty much the same size, so I borrow his clothes all the time,’ she admits. ‘His feet are bigger than mine, so I can’t wear his shoes, but I borrow his jackets, blazers, coats and shirts. He steals my pyjamas too. He loves wearing them.’ Her second collection, to launch in 2017, will be more overtly feminine. ‘I had seen a picture of Katharine Hepburn in this black-and-white polka-dot blouse and trousers, and it’s something I always wanted,’ she says, dreamily. ‘It was a great inspiration to make our own version of it.’   The daughter of model and groupie Bebe Buell, Liv famously only discovered at the age of eight that Steven Tyler of Aerosmith was her father, after meeting him at a gig and noticing a resemblance between herself and Tyler’s daughter, Mia. Until then, she had believed her father to be Buell’s on-off, long-term partner Todd Rundgren, also a musician. She spent much of her childhood moving between Maine and Virginia, where her grandmother, Dorothea Johnson, taught etiquette to the children of diplomats, before Buell moved to New York when Liv was 12.  But despite her all-American upbringing, it should come as no surprise that Liv is so thrilled to be moving to London. From designing for Belstaff to choosing fathers for her children (Milo’s father is Royston Langdon of the British band Spacehog), she’s taken Anglophilia to a whole new level. ‘When I was growing up in New York City in the ’90s, there was a big group of English people who influenced me,’ she says. ‘Lucie de la Falaise [the model niece of Yves Saint Laurent muse Loulou de la Falaise] was my first girlfriend in New York. She was a little older than me, and she and Marlon [Lucie’s husband, who is the son of the Rolling Stones’ Keith Richards and Anita Pallenberg] and I met at the same time.’  If that sounds like the most fashionable group, there’s more. ‘Then, I was 15 when I met Kate Moss, and Lucie and Kate made the biggest impact on me,’ says Liv. ‘There was something unique about them – I was completely in love with them. I learnt so much from them and their style.’  There is, she believes, a different sensibility among Britons. ‘You guys definitely have more fun; you’re much better at letting your hair down. There’s something very playful and magical about the way all my English friends see everything. You love to dress up and go for adventures. You make going for a walk in the garden and having a cup of tea sound and feel like the most exciting thing in the world.’ It was Moss [Grey’s godmother; Beckham is his godfather] who introduced her to Gardner. ‘He’s a really manly man,’ she gushes, when I ask her about their relationship. ‘A Manchester man. It takes me a minute to understand everything. I need translations all the time.’ Gardner became best friends with Beckham at 14, when the pair were both members of the Manchester United youth team, along with Ryan Giggs, with whom Gardner is still close. ‘He’s very masculine, but tender and loving, and very hands-on with the kids,’ says Liv. ‘He’s definitely juggling a lot, with working and being Daddy to so many, but he is very good at being there for the things that are important.’ Will they get married? ‘I’m sure we will,’ enthuses Liv. ‘It’s something we talk about and we’re planning on, but right now we’re just enjoying every second of where we are.’ Liv began working in fashion at 14, putting her huge blue eyes and unfeasibly pouty, pillowy lips inherited from her father to use as a model. But she soon changed her focus to acting, starring in independent films including Empire Records and That Thing You Do!, before Bertolucci’s dreamily evocative coming-of-age story Stealing Beauty made her a star. In her 20s, she played Arwen, the elf maiden in the The Lord of the Rings trilogy, and starred in other big-budget smashes such as Armageddon and The Incredible Hulk.  She married Langdon at 25, and gave birth to Milo a year later. Then, in her 30s, she stepped back from films to concentrate on raising her son, along with his father, from whom she was divorced amicably in 2008. ‘From a young age, I had this idea that if you are very successful in your career and you’re giving all your attention to that, the life of your family possibly won’t flourish as it might,’ she says. ‘I can live with the career part not going so well, but I don’t think I could live with my family not being happy.’ These days, she appears to have found a healthy balance. She had recently given birth to Sailor when David Beckham was designing his own capsule collection for Belstaff, and taking on his first acting role – in the accompanying short film, Outlaws. ‘Because of the connection through my David, they were asking me about the script, and casting – and then they just asked me if I’d like to produce it,’ she says. ‘I’d always wanted to, but never had the chance, and it seemed a great opportunity to get a feel for it.’ She has since co-produced the feature film Wildling with Trudie Styler. ‘I would love to create a story and produce and direct a film. Getting the chance to execute an idea, like with Outlaws, gave me an appetite to want to take it further.’  More immediately, though, a week after landing in the UK, Liv will be on a plane to Australia, to film her last scenes for the third and final season of The Leftovers. After that, she’s fully available for hire. ‘I’m really excited to move to London with a clean slate, and just say, “Hey, I need a job.” I’m excited for a whole new adventure in my life right now.’    The Liv Tyler x Belstaff collection is available now © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Could the Hermès Kelly actually overtake the Birkin in the popularity stakes? For many, it’s the most trivial question you’ll consider today, but for handbag feinds and luxury collectors, it’s one that could inform an upcoming investment, or at least prompt a dreamy new Pinterest wish list. According to Jérome Lalande, a leather goods expert at Collector Square who has collaborated with Hermès for twenty years to help locate rare pieces, new data shows that the Kelly is having a comeback, with prices up 350% in the last decade and popularity surging in the last year. “The Birkin bag was the most in-demand Hermès bag, but the past year has shown a reversal of the trend, putting the Kelly bag in the spotlight,” he explains. Kellies accounted for 24% of all Hermès bags sold at auctions in the last decade, while Birkins fell slightly behind at 20%, according to Collector Square’s LuxPrice-Index. It’s the story that’s selling it, according to the experts. The bag’s design was originally inspired by the saddle bags created for horse riders in the 1880s before Hermés revamped it as the Sac à Courroies in the 1930s. The actress Grace Kelly was first associated with the style after she was spotted carrying one on the set of To Catch a Thief in 1954. Two years later, though, she sealed its status as an icon (and its name) when she used one to shield her pregnant stomach from the paparazzi as she announced her engagement to Prince Rainier of Monaco. Hermés made the name change official in 1977, and the Sac à Courroies became the Kelly forevermore. Hermes Kelly 40 cm handbag in grey togo leather, £8,080, collectorsquare.com  When the Birkin, inspired by Jane Birkin, came along in 1985, though, the Kelly had competition. "At the beginning the [Birkin] bag was not a success,” Lalande told The Telegraph. “When it was first produced 1985 it wasn't really in demand and not that many people knew about it. Then everyone was still asking about the Kelly.” "The craziness about the Birkin began in the mid 90s. It's like the Rolex watch, we don't know exactly why it became just so popular. I think when people started to be interested in buying Birkin bags, Hermes limited the production which increased the demand even more." Celebrities have, however, expressed a heightened interest in Birkins over the last decade. The Birkin has become a status symbol, with stars from Victoria Beckham to Kim Kardashian boasting big collections of both new and vintage bags. New Kellys, meanwhile, currently have a waiting list of over a year - perhaps they are now seen as the more exclusive, lesser-spotted choice? "[Both] bags are very expensive, but people purchase them as both a pleasure and investment, they are looking for the best value for money - and that comes from Hermes first and foremost," says Lalande of the fact that both the Kelly and the Birkin have consistently appreciated in value in the last decade, unlike most other luxury goods. Instagram audiences have now shared and tagged over 3.4million pictures of the #HermesKelly on the social media site, only 200,000 behind the #HermesBirkin. Many of those images shared are the now-vintage snaps of the bag’s original champion, Grace Kelly, wearing hers with white driving gloves, giant sunglasses and an enormous coat draped over her shoulders. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Scrolling through Instagram last week, I came across a picture of someone who looked so, well, nice, that I felt compelled to buy the Warehouse dress off their back. The person who posted the picture was the celebrity stylist Angie Smith, taken of her client, the daytime television presenter Holly Willoughby. In certain high fashion circles, this confession could be deemed career suicide. But after a month of catwalk shows, watching anonymous models parading next season's collections, I looked at this picture of Willoughby and simply thought; I can see here what that dress might look like on me.   Willoughby has been consciously and quietly upping her fashion credentials since hiring Smith last January, selecting pieces from both the high street and the high end that are stylish but not scary. The pair have been sharing daily snaps of Willoughby’s outfits over the last few months, with interest in her style peaking in the five weeks since she returned to work on This Morning after her summer holidays. Since 4th September, her looks have racked up more than three million ‘likes’ and plenty, besides me, are even saying yes to the Will-you-buy effect. Fashion search engine Lyst tells The Telegraph that an L.K. Bennett skirt worn by Willoughby, which attracted more than 167,000 people to press ‘like’ on Instagram, also prompted more than 3,000 to then search for the skirt on their website in the two hours after Willoughby posted the image on 21st September. Searches for the brand L.K. Bennett, also increased by 30% on Google on the same day. Willoughby’s other recent hits have included pieces by Massimo Dutti, Very and River Island, all of which have experienced similar spikes after Willoughby has revealed that she is wearing pieces by them on her page. Lyst searches for Hobbs dresses rocketed by 132% on the day that she wore one, while Whistles skirts received a 33% boost. The greatest success story so far, though, was a rainbow striped, sequin dress by the London Fashion Week-showing designer Ashish. More than 300,000 people ‘liked’ Willoughby’s picture of the dress she was going to wear on The Jonathan Ross Show, prompting a 300% surge in UK Google searches for the designer. Despite its £1,408 price tag, the dress promptly sold out on both Net-a-Porter.com and MatchesFashion.com. Woman wears dress, dress sells out. 'What’s all the fuss about?', you might currently still be asking yourself. The appeal of the first lady of daytime television seems to actually be pretty simple; she looks like any one of us. Her style is polished and glamorous, but with elements that we could all so easily pull off for ourselves. Willoughby’s stylist, Angie Smith, previously told me that the presenter thinks carefully about what she chooses to wear on air, knowing that women around the UK might be influenced by her look, but also that television cameras can be very unforgiving when you get it wrong. “Dressing for TV is trickier than the red carpet because you’re going to be shot from so many different angles and depending on the show you might be moving around a lot and sitting down,” Smith told us of the considerations. “We work with a seamstress who will alter things until they fit perfectly.” “We don’t tend to chose things from the catwalks for This Morning because we’re really keen, and I know Holly’s really keen, that she’s not wearing things that are ridiculously expensive,” she added. “We want viewers to see something that’s a great look and think ‘I could get a lot of wear out of that’.” She's right, and I will. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  If the Duchess of Cambridge’s wardrobe choices for the first day of her India and Bhutan tour are anything to go by, then royal style enthusiasts are in for a week of her now signature deft balance of diplomacy, ease and classic glamour. Following in the footsteps of the Queen and Princess Diana, the Duchess’s three outfits each showed a respectful consideration for her host country, resulting in some beautifully bold colour choices, but also represented some of the best of British fashion. For a wreath laying ceremony at The Taj Hotel, Kate opted for a vibrant red shift dress with peplum detail by Alexander McQueen, the British fashion house which is perhaps most closely associated with the Duchess. Creative director Sarah Burton designed the Duchess’s wedding dress and has been called upon on numerous occasions since then. The dress chosen yesterday is adapted from Burton’s Pre-Fall collection. Its decorative paisley print proved to be a masterful detail, subtly nodding to both Asian and British textile tradition. The teardrop pattern was originally woven in the Kashmir region in the 11th century, eventually arriving in the United Kingdom via the East India Company in the 1700s. It became known as Paisley after the Scottish town which later began to produce sought-after scarves and fabrics in the swirling prints. The duchess accessorised the look with L.K Bennett’s £175 Floret court shoes in her favourite nude shade, and a high-street pair of earrings from Accessorize.  For a cricket match and tour of Mumbai’s most-deprived areas, Kate changed into a breezy, delicately printed dress by Mumbai-born designer, Anita Dongre. This first outfit by an Indian label proved cool enough for being caught at mid-on by Sachin Tendulkar and a game of football. Dongre- who works with specialist artisans to preserve traditional skills- is advertising the “Gulrukh” dress for $236 (around £167) on her website. It did, however, seem slightly absurd to be running around in front of the cameras in a pair of £99 cream wedges by high-street brand Mint Velvet, but it’s not the first time Kate has teetered on heels when flats would have been perfectly acceptable.   Kate enlisted another trusted British designer, Jenny Packham, to create a bespoke cobalt sari-like dress and shawl for the evening gala but care was taken to incorporate Indian elements; the intricate beading on the bodice and shawl was done in India while opulent blue earrings by Jaipur-based jewellers Amrapali finished the ensemble.  Baz Luhrmann's Netflix series The Get Down, which charts the very beginnings of hip hop in the late 1970s, not only has an epic soundtrack, but a carefully curated wardrobe built specifically for each character. To understand the style in the emerging hip hop clubs in the burning South Bronx, Baz Luhrmann and his executive producer Catherine Martin, who is also his wife, pored over images of teenagers from the time. And there was one photographer who was so influential for the costume department, that Baz Luhrmann made him a character in the Netflix show. "The internet allows you to discover elements of social history that aren’t classically stored," Catherine Martin explains to The Telegraph. "Joe Conzo is considered the first photographer of hip hop and photographed the Cold Crush brothers when they were still at high school. Out of that came an enormous wealth of street style photographs from the late 70s because those kids processed their own photographs and those photos document the period perfectly." "Joe Conzo has photos of himself in high school sat with all his classmates," adds Martin. "Baz would go through the photos and say ‘I want the classroom to look like Joe Conzo’s, I want a kid in the class to have the same hairstyle as Joe Conzo's." And there was no shortage of images for The Get Down team to work through; Conzo's archive includes over 10,000 images of every aspect of teenage life in these early years of hip hop. "I am considered by The New York Times the man who took hip hop's baby pictures," says Conzo. "I was a chubby little kid with a big Angela Davis afro and I wasn’t that athletic and I wasn’t a DJ or an MC. My parents gave me a point and shoot in the 70s, and I was one of the only kids walking around with a camera. I was the odd one out doing photography." Although these pictures from his little point and shoot now serve as a rare authentic archive of street style at the time, back then he was just taking pictures of his friends with no idea that hip hop would become a significant cultural movement outside of his neighbourhood. "I went to school with some of the pioneers of hip hop, like Easy A.D. and Tony Tone of the Cold Crush brothers, and they invited me to take pictures at their first jams," explains Conzo. "I became the Cold Crush brother's official photographer and through them I met Afrika Bambaataa, Kool Herc, Treacherous 3 and all the pioneers of hip hop." 'I wasn’t sent down from Uptown to the Bronx to photograph the little blacks spinning on their heads or writing on the wall' "I wasn’t sent down from Uptown to the Bronx to photograph the little blacks spinning on their heads or writing on the wall," he says. "What separates me from the other photographers, is that I was part of the culture too and was one of the kids I was photographing. I was capturing my friends in the neighbourhood I grew up in, not knowing I’d be capturing a time capsule and documenting a period piece with no foresight that the images would be important 40 years later. I was just photographing my friends because it made me popular." They might have been pictures of his friends hanging out in the graffiti-splattered South Bronx, but now they are considered bona fide early New York street style images. Even though these teenagers had very little, what they wore was a crucial part of their identities. "We took fashion very seriously and it is a very important part of hip hop culture," says Conzo. "You wanted to dress to impress, always, always, always. Knowing that you didn’t have much to show, but you made the best of it and built on what we had." As for how they 'built on' their limited belongings, Conzo explains some of their customising tricks: "We would sew a crease down the middle of our Lee jeans so they looked like they had a permanent line. Sneakers don't last that long and our sneakers were hand me downs so we used to clean them with toothpaste to keep them fresh, iron the laces and paint them. We wore them every single day, but we took care of them." It wasn't just the trainers that they made their own. The boys would graffiti their clothes, in the same way they did subway and derelict buildings. "Our graffiti friends used to paint our Levis jackets for us and we used to graffiti our jeans also," he adds. "Anything that separated us from the norm." In the same way that their music was highly revolutionary, Conzo and his friends would also spearhead trends. "Before Run DMC made Adidas famous, we were wearing them," says Conzo. "You would look at your favourite MC or DJ and see what they were wearing and try to emulate them. I wore bell bottom jeans - they could never be straight jeans - with one leg rolled up and a sweatshirt with sleeves cut off. If I was lucky I would iron on letters, spelling my name on the back." When watching The Get Down you won't just see the street style that Conzo captured mirrored in every single character, but if you look carefully you'll also spot an actor dressed just like him taking pictures in the background.  The Get Down will be available on Netflix on 12th August   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. "If you met her and you didn't know who she was or what she did, it would be inconceivable to you that she was Beyoncé. Some really famous people, even when they're off-duty, have this energy that is sort of overpowering. She does not have that," says Paltrow. "She is so dialed down. She's the sweetest mother. She's very shy. You would not believe she is Beyoncé Knowles. You would be like, "No, that was not her." And that's why when I see her perform, I'm like, 'Oh, shit, I forgot.'" Although there is one concession to Bey's normality- "She doesn't make grilled cheese. Definitely not. I make the grilled cheese."  The fashion designer Hubert de Givenchy has died, aged 91.  The French aristocrat, whose full name was Count Hubert James Marcel Taffin de Givenchy, was one of the best known fashion names of the twentieth century. He developed a refined and elegant signature which was apparent from his first collection in 1952 ('a star is born' declared New York Magazine at the time) until his eventual retirement in 1995.  "The House of Givenchy is sad to report the passing of its founder Hubert de Givenchy, a major personality of the world of French Haute Couture and a gentleman who symbolised Parisian chic and elegance for more than half a century," a spokesperson for Givenchy said this afternoon. "He will be greatly missed." Hubert de Givenchy's most famous client was undoubtedly Audrey Hepburn, who wore one of his designs to accept her Academy Award for Roman Holiday in 1954. He went on to design her costumes for the films Sabrina and Breakfast at Tiffany's including the now-iconic little black dress worn by Hepburn's character Holly Golightly in the latter and, quite perfectly, he also received an Oscar nomination for his work on her costumes in Funny Face. “It was a kind of marriage,” Givenchy told The Telegraph of his relationship with the actress in 2015. Although he worked with other actresses, none came close to the friendship and respect which Hepburn and Givenchy developed for one another. “Little by little, our friendship grew and with it a confidence in each other,” he said. “There [was never] any criticism of the other person, no upsets.” "It was... an enormous help to know that I looked the part," Hepburn once said of the designer. "Then the rest wasn't so tough anymore. Givenchy's lovely simple clothes [gave me] the feeling of being whoever I played."   It was perhaps their mutual appreciation of a pared-back look which made the pair's relationship more profound than  merely one of a client and a designer. “I always respected Audrey’s taste. She was not like other movie stars in that she liked simplicity,” he added.  Others on Givenchy's star-studded client list included Wallis Simpson, Duchess of Windsor, Princess Grace of Monaco and Jackie Kennedy Onassis. For every woman, whether she commissioned a gown, or daywear, the Givenchy experience was one of dazzling elegance. British Vogue commented in the Sixties: “A Givenchy coat would be most women’s ideal of the perfect way to look in daytime.” His collections of separates in the Fifties, and inventions like the shirt dress in 1957, transformed the possibilities of luxury daywear for women.  In 1988, Givenchy sold his company to LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton for $45 million, although he remained as creative director until his retirement in 1995. Since then, the Givenchy label has continued to help set the fashion agenda with designers including Julien MacDonald, John Galliano and Alexander McQueen at its helm.  The longest-serving creative director, other than the man himself, was Riccardo Tisci who was named artistic director of womenswear in 2005 and brought the brand into the modern red carpet era, with stars from Beyonce to Kim Kardashian becoming fans. Tisci departed in February 2017 and, after a year out of the spotlight, will join British brand Burberry this September. "Hubert de Givenchy’s confident style has always been an inspiration and I am very grateful for the opportunity to be a part of this legendary House’s history," said Tisci's successor, the current creative director Clare Waight Keller, when she was appointed at the house just a year ago. "I look forward to working with the teams and writing a new chapter in this beautiful story." Speaking to The Telegraph in 2015,  Givenchy described the ways that he has seen the fashion industry evolve in the almost-70 years since he founded his label. “I have an enormous interest in everything, but I am just sad about fashion now because the epoch is sad,” he considered, describing the loss of original couturiers Cristóbal Balenciaga and Madame Grès as a great sadness for the fashion world.  Of his ilk - Yves Saint Laurent, Christian Dior and the other great mid-twentieth century phenomenons - Givenchy was perhaps the last living legend. His legacy is a name and a design handwriting which undoubtedly be referred to by generations to come - and in Waight Keller's hands, for now at least, it seems to be protected. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  "My designs are a full expression of my feelings,"  says Sara Battaglia. Judging by her playful collections, we must therefore assume that the designer oozes joy, fun and glamour. As part of such a creative family – her sister Giovanna is a fashion stylist, brothers Antonio and Luigi are art dealer and designer respectively, and her parents are artists – it was no surprise when Sara launched a handbag line in 2010. In 2016 she collaborated on a collection of bags with Salvatore Ferragamo. And now this spring sees Battaglia launch her debut clothing range of chic and colourful daywear. When did you decide you wanted to be  a designer?  It was making clothes for my Barbie as a child  – such a cliché, but true. I remember stealing a piece of fabric from my mother to make my first handbag when I was six. She was very upset... You  started as a handbag designer – what  made you want to branch out into clothing?  It’s funny because the clothes have been in my mind since I was a child. But like other brands, such as Gucci or Louis Vuitton, that launched with shoes or bags, I wanted to start my label with accessories. Eventually, my clients started asking me when I was going to launch a ready-to-wear line, so it happened organically. It became very important for me in terms of growing my business, which is my passion.  How do your clothes and bags relate? The two are very connected – in fact, so far,  the pieces most directly related to my bags have been the most popular. The rainbow-striped leather work, or the leather flower net  – where I applied techniques from my bags to clothing – have been creating the most buzz. My bestselling bag is plissé leather, so the first ready-to-wear piece that I designed was a plissé top with a matching trouser. It was very difficult to get the technique right on the clothes because of the different scale. Translating my flower net bag into a dress took a lot of experimentation and hours at the factories to figure out how to attach one flower to another on a moving silhouette, but we got there in the end. How do you put your look together? The bag is actually the most important for me, so I start with that. I tend to choose the most colourful one – say bright red – then I’ll match the bag to my trousers and then to my heels.  How are your clothes designed to be worn?  The idea is daywear – but not everyday wear. I wanted to create a line to take a woman from morning to cocktail hour. She might be going to a business meeting on a Friday then flying off to St Tropez for the weekend, but she’s wearing the same outfit throughout. I’m focused on the needs of the modern woman, and want to offer her something simple but beautiful, special and different.  What are your top tips for effortless style? I always say invest in basics that have interesting detail, and a lot of accessories. Obviously handbags and shoes, but then headbands, hats and sunglasses, too. When  you’re in a rush, you can throw on flats, add a simple dress with great accessories and a  bit of lipstick and you’re ready to go.  Sara Battaglia is available at boutique1.com; matchesfashion.com; net-a-porter.com  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Olivier Rousteing has brought a magic touch to Balmain with his #Balmainarmy of supermodels and launched a sell-out capsule collection for H&M  last year. The race to buy Balmain at high street prices brought new meaning to the idea of chaos, with a spokesman for H&M confirming it was their fastest-selling collaboration to date. Given Olivier Rousteing's proven ability to turn his colossal social media following (3.2 million Instagram followers and counting) into sales, it's not surprising that he has been enlisted as the latest designer to collaborate with NikeLab on a sportswear collection. Rousteing has brought his glamazon warrior aesthetic (think the Jenners and Kardashians in power mini dresses)  to sportswear, with his signature metallic detailing running through the collection. The 'Football Nouveau' offering features gold Nike swooshes, leggings with decorative gold zippers, cropped hooded tanks, body-con dresses, gold piping and gold trainers that are a play on football boots. Basically, a LOT of gold.  "My inspiration was building a new glamour that is still effortless and connected to football," Rousteing says to The Telegraph of the embellished sportswear. "You can find all the gold details and embroideries that I’m used to and love, but I wanted to tone down because I want to respect Nike's price range. It inspired by champions and the gold trophy and the feeling that you can get on field." As for the decision to focus on football, Rousteing explains: "In a few weeks it is the Euro Cup so it is perfect timing. Soccer has always been a part of my life - I have been played football from the age 10 to 15. I played football to please my Dad and I loved the team spirit which was new to me because I’m an only child and adopted. I learned the importance of sharing and team spirit, and sharing with a team the same goal.  It taught me so many things that today are part of my work – team spirit is very important in fashion and the competition to achieve a goal, which football taught me." The flashy sportswear looks like it was made for the Christiano Ronaldos of this world, so it's fitting that the footballer was enlisted into Rousteing's #BalmainArmy for the campaign. In fact the footballer was the first person to see Rousteing's work for Nike. "He saw it first because I trust him as  a friend, and as the man who will wear those clothes," the Paris-based designer explains. "It was important he liked it because he has a great style. Christiano Ronaldo is a great soccer player, but he is also global and followed by everyone. Footballers are the new icons." But it was important that the collection also works for his muses, as well as for footballers. "I am inspired by women like Jourdan Dunn or Alessandra Ambrosio or Rihanna in it because bit of pop factor – you can find the glamour of the bodycon dresses in the collection," Rousteing adds.  Rousteing has built a "crowd" of supermodels and singers who wear his clothes from Kim Kardashian to Cindy Crawford, but if he could hire one more recruit it would be the President of the United States, Barack Obama. "I would love to see Barack Obama wearing my collection," Rousteing tells The Telegraph. "I think it would be a huge honour and someone I would love to meet. He is on the top of my wishlist for my crowd." Instagram has been key to Rousteing's strategy at Balmain, and the designer explains that he uses Instagram comments to influence his work. "I love my comments on Instagram because I try to understand where it comes from and some of the comments are really smart, and sometimes the critics are good and haters are fun." Rousteing wants some people to hate his designs, because he thinks a mixed reaction is a sign of success. "The more haters you have, the more lovers you will have. If you don’t have hate, you don’t have love, the more people love something the more people will hate it – you need balance." Rousteing's collaboration with H&M was the fastest selling designer collaboration to date, but it was unexpected for him. "I was really surprised, but pleased with success of H&M," the designer adds. "I didn’t expect it to be as much as it was, but with collaborations you challenge yourself as a designer because you are working for someone else and you try to keep your aesthetic and vision, but adapt it. Nike was a revolution in my mind, because I was challenged as a designer to work for a different crowd that may not be able to afford my work with Balmain. It's an honour to work with such an institution at just 30 years old." Stylish sportswear is now big business, and the phrase 'athleisure' was even added to the Merriam-Webster dictionary earlier this year. Morgan Stanley estimated that the activewear market will be worth $82 billion in sales globally by the end of 2020. The CEO of Nike, Mark Parker, claimed in 2014 that 'leggings are the new denim'.  Host Gigi Hadid switched her outfit not one, but six times during the American Music Awards last night, providing something of a masterclass in how to do a costume quick-change, and giving music’s biggest divas a run for their money, by putting on a show with her fashion choices. The AMAs is the one stage on which it has become a custom for the host to change multiple times throughout the night. Last year’s compère, Jennifer Lopez, remains the record holder, after she worked her way through an outstanding effort of fifteen couture ensembles during the two hour-long broadcast. ‘We did our research and J.Lo's team told us to do less changes,’ Gigi said on the red carpet before the ceremony, conceding that, despite her catwalk experience, there was no way she could out-do Lopez who 25 years of experience in swift backstage changes. ‘I'm going with about half, but they're great looks and they're going to get a good amount of time.’ Gigi’s arrival look was a white lace Roberto Cavalli gown, no doubt selected by the supermodel’s stylist, Monica Rose, for its flattering off-the-shoulder proportions and its nod to the wider gypsy trend. To open the show, she chose a spliced red dress from Atelier Versace, her boyfriend Zayn Malik also wearing a look from the label as he collected the Best New Artist award. Next, the supermodel- who also used her AMAs appearence to perform an impersonation of Melania Trump- went with two looks by British designer Julien MacDonald, adapting a short suit and a crocodile-textured gown from his spring 2017 collection, which will arrive in stores in February. Finally, it was a black keyhole dress and a sheer sparkly jumpsuit with athleisure-trend touches - a drawstring waist and ribbed cuffs - before she changed back into her camel-coloured cashmere jumper and jogging bottoms to go home. Speaking exclusively to The Telegraph, MacDonald revealed how the collaboration came to be. 'We work closely with Gigi and her stylist Monica Rose to secure the right looks for her at events and often work together on custom looks,' he said. 'This is a great creative process where we send sketches to Gigi and her team and work together to create the perfect look.' 'Firstly, she wore a sharp tailored white jacket, heavily embellished with Swarvoski crystals and metal chain fringes from my SS17 collection. Her nude cocktail dress was custom made, a reptile-inspired enamel cutaway dress, creating the effect of a second skin.' 'She is one of [my] favourite supermodels in the world,' MacDonald added. She has effortless style whether during the day or on the red carpet.' There’s more to the fashion performance, however, than just popping on a few statement outfits to try and make the next morning’s headlines. The AMAs are the kick-off to awards season and are therefore a chance to showcase what fresh-off-the-catwalk looks your stylist was able to commandeer before any other star got a whiff. For a star carving their image, it's an ideal opportunity to align yourself with a key new fashion house, or even just an on-trend silhouette that you want to become your signature for the season ahead. Note Lady Gaga’s choice of power pantsuit (an unmistakably political nod that we should expect to see more of) or Zoe Saldana’s championing of blazing hot new label Monse.  It’s also a star’s first chance to stake a claim to being the setter of one of the bigger red carpet trends that we might expect to develop on the road to the Golden Globes, the Oscars and so on. In that case, as Gigi knows, it’s a very good time to hedge your bets.     © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  There is a giant roll of orange furry fabric sitting on the desk of the designer Sander Lak. Discovered in an antiques shop on a recent trip to upstate New York, it sums up the playful approach of the 33-year-old who’s creating just the right blend of slouchy-yet-sumptuous clothes that women want to wear right now. "I’m figuring out whether to reupholster one of my chairs in the office, cover a sofa at home or just make a coat from it," says the creative director of Sies Marjan (a composite of Lak’s parents’ names), the cult line of cocooning knits, Fortuny fabrics, silk roll-necks and cargo pants in a zingy palette that staged its first show to much furore at New York Fashion Week in February. "It happens all the time – I’ll find a fabric and then it just starts living its life however it’s meant to be." It’s this kind of idiosyncratic thinking that has come to define Lak’s career. He first found fashion as a film-obsessed teenager with ambitions of being a director: "I would draw fictional film posters," he explains in his pan-European accent. "There was a clear moment when I became preoccupied with making the clothes look as real as possible, thinking about the shape of the pocket and how the fabric falls and drapes." After studying menswear at Central Saint Martins under the late Louise Wilson (he counts Mary Katrantzou, Mark Fast and Christopher Shannon among his fellow alumni), Lak worked at Phillip Lim and Balmain, before becoming head designer at Dries Van Noten. It was the American investors Howard and Nancy Marks who enlisted him to create a new brand out of the former atelier of Chado Ralph Rucci Collection – and less than two years later, Sies Marjan was born. Lak has led a remarkably nomadic life. Born in Borneo, he grew up between Gabon, Scotland, Malaysia and his mother’s native Holland. "My late father worked on the Shell oil platforms so we moved every four years," he says from his Midtown studio, which, like his apartment, is decorated with midcentury modern furnishings and objects collected along the way (he counts his African masks, Hans J Wegner chairs, Brunei ceramics and a table picked up by his mother at a Scottish aristocrat’s house sale among his favourites). "Whether it’s on your body, in your house or on your bookshelf, the stuff we surround ourselves with is such an important part of who we are," says Lak, who has curated a series of objects from the online auction house, 1stdibs.com, to sit alongside his clothing collection in stores. "To build a brand today you have to tell a story beyond the clothes."  While their aesthetics are radically different, Lak is aligned with the Alessandro Micheles and Demna Gvasalias (with whom he shares the Vetements stylist Lotta Volkova) of this world, who have been pushed into the spotlight after years of working behind the scenes. Lak’s is an understated vision of luxury that’s rooted in reality. The Sies Marjan debut was peppered with high-low references from floral shower curtains to scenes from Nineties club culture (recreated in jacquard). "My generation approaches women in a much more human way," says the designer, whose "Girlfriends" campaign features real-life pals (including Trish Goff) rather than an anonymous army of models – "No one wants to be a fashion automaton any more."  His creative process is unusually methodical and deadline-driven. Colour comes first, then fabrication and gradually the garments and "the story" evolves. But out of precision, magic happens. "We spend a lot of time just looking at what people are actually wearing on the street. We really use that and play around with it. That’s all that’s left for designers. We’re not going to reinvent the wheel. It’s about playing with those codes. That’s what I love doing," he says, adding mischievously: "If that stops and I get bored, I’ll just start making films."  Sies Marjan is available at matchesfashion.com   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  One of the most influential fashion designers of the Swinging Sixties has passed away aged 92. André Courrèges was known for his futuristic designs and in particular his Space Age collection from 1964, which made him one of the most exciting designers of the moment. The late designer’s family confirmed to French press that Courrèges passed away at home in Neuilly-sur-Seine, a suburb to the west of Paris, on January 7. Courrèges was an avant-gardist who put a geometric and often outré twist on micro-mini skirts and dresses. He made streamlined clothes his signature, and became known for his little white dresses and trouser suits. Brigitte Bardot, Jackie Kennedy, Françoise Hardy and Romy Schneider were all fans. There is a debate over who invented the miniskirt  - was it Courrèges or was it Mary Quant? Either way, both designers had their finger on the pulse when it came to pioneering a whole new way of dressing for a generation so eager to embrace it. But Courrèges' career could have turned out so differently. He trained as a civil engineer until the age of 25, and then headed to Paris where he joined the legendary fashion house founded by Cristobal Balenciaga. He was employed a pattern cutter for 10 years before deciding to set up his own label in 1961. The influences of his first line of work – references to architecture and technology - were clear to see in his collections. On the Courrèges website he is quoted as saying: “If my subject happens to be a woman, maybe I’d make her a dress. But sometimes a dress isn’t able to communicate all the emotions that I wish to convey. So I try to express my ideas through other mediums, like architecture.” Born in the Pyrenees, Courrèges created a futuristic atelier in his hometown of Pau, which was renovated three years ago and used a centre for producing the label’s prototypes. Although Courrèges retired in 1994, the brand has since existed by way of perfumes through licensing agreements. The high-fashion arm of the business was relaunched in 2014, with two young Frenchmen, Arnaud Vaillant and Sébastien Meyer at the helm. France's president, François Hollande, was one of the first to pay tribute to André Courrèges on social media, writing: "A revolutionary designer, using new materials and geometric shapes, André Courrèges leaves behind a footprint in the world of high fashion."
