 “I wanted people to take my brand seriously,” said Alexa Chung backstage after her debut catwalk show at London Fashion Week this morning, “and to understand that I have aspirations for longevity… it’s not another collaboration that will disappear”.  Breaking with the public perception of what Alexa Chung is has been a challenge, but one that Chung is keen to meet head on. But that doesn’t mean necessarily breaking with the perception of what Alexa Chung wears. Her ability to identify product that will sell - for M&S, Superga, AG Jeans - is a strength in building her own brand. If those collaborations - and the smaller presentations Chung has held in lieu of catwalk shows so far - were dress rehearsals, then here was the opening night. Chung hasn’t tried to erase what came before - like the black PVC coat, an iteration of which could be seen in that M&S collaboration and in this latest collection - but she’s fine tuned her offering. Yes, you could imagine Chung herself wearing these clothes - but Chung’s ability to influence trends was what gave her fashion credibility in the first place. Fittingly, the show centered around transitions - the kind seen at the airport, allowing Chung to layer and clash her style references. Against a wood panelled maze of airport corridors there were slim fitting jumpsuits, pyjamas for outdoor wear (in case there was any doubt that Chung’s women were turning left once on the plane), stretch-knit sundresses worn with jelly shoes and brown suede coats. One look might be worn by a woman “from Dublin, but going on a Roman university excavation trip.” A trip to Margate trawling vintage shops for inspiration is borne out by looks that dipped between decades- a 1930s mustard silk evening dress one moment, a 1990s black silk slip dress the next, and multiple references to the 1970s, like a safari suit inspired by a found reference of Bianca Jagger “in her PJs. And I’m always stalking any of those rock stars from the 70s.” Considering it was her first catwalk, Chung didn’t make it easy on herself. “All of it was quite a challenge - not necessarily the collection but the moving parts of putting on an actual fashion show. We wanted to do something that wasn’t a conventional runway, so we came up with the maze - great idea, but also quite challenging for the models to navigate,” so, she laughs - “we put arrows on the floor.” This addition to the London Fashion Week schedule is a natural one, especially as there is a Britishness that underlies all of Chung’s designs. The appearance of so many coats in a spring summer collection- many with hoods - might seem incongruous to some, but not to anyone familiar with British summertime. The ‘destination’ scarf print looks, at first glance, to be printed with little Eiffel towers, a nod to previous ALEXACHUNG presentations held in Paris - but actually, it nods to Brighton Pier and Bognor Regis, she laughed backstage.  Brigitte Trogneux’s style has piqued interest the world over in the past month or so, with her penchant with skinny jeans, sharp tailoring and mini skirts signalling a refreshingly risqué rewriting of the rules of political style.  For her husband Emmanuel Macron’s Inauguration as French President this morning, Trogneux opted for a powder blue dress and jacket by Louis Vuitton, which she accessorised with pale beige high heels and a neatly elegant top handle Capucines bag, also by Louis Vuitton.  Although the cigarette-slim leather trousers and New Balance trainers which Trogneux has worn on the campaign trail suggested a woman who would coin a new spin on political dressing, there were some of indicators that she, and Louis Vuitton’s artistic director Nicolas Ghesquiere, had looked to tradition in their choice of look for today’s ceremony.   On social media, immediate comparisons were drawn with the Ralph Lauren skirt suit which Melania Trump wore on Inauguration Day in January which was in turn said to have been inspired by Jackie Kennedy’s 1961 look.  There were also similarities with Princess Diana in her post-divorce years, when she favoured polished tailoring but with skirts in more daring lengths than she had been able to experiment with as a royal.  Brigitte Trogneux is wearing the same color as Melania. While Trogneux’s outfit suggested a respect for the tropes of world stage dressing, other details- like the military button detailling of the jacket and above-the-knee length of the dress- confirmed that she will nevertheless continue carving out a First Lady look which is all her own.  The French media has praised Trogneux for her "cool attitude" and "wonderwoman" style. She is also the latest incarnation of the insouciant French look which has become shorthand for aspirational dressing around the world.  Trogneux’s take swaps the messy bed hair for a defiantly glossy blow dry and slouchy silhouettes for figure-enhancing cuts, but the message is still ageless and unashamedly- yet modernly- sexy.  It was unsurprising that 64 year-old Trogneux- who will work as an unpaid advisor to her husband, concentrating on education reform- turned to Louis Vuitton for her most important outfit on the public stage to date. After meeting Delphine Arnault- Executive Vice President of Louis Vuitton -  in 2014, Trogneux developed a close relationship with the house which means they now loan her looks for many of her public appearences. It’s a policy which has created some controversy in France, and the moment that her husband entered the Elysee Palace could have marked a turning point for Trogneux. But she has clearly decided that the Vuitton partnership will remain.  Indeed, when it come to diplomacy and patriotism, Vuitton is the smart choice. As the jewel in the crown of LVMH, one of France’s most prestigious and successful business conglomerates, Trogneux’s choice of designer projects all the right messages.  Vuitton is also less well-associated with dressing high profile public figures, with Chanel and Dior having historically held the monopoly in this area.  Although, Chanel’s Karl Lagerfeld is said to know the Macron- Trogneuxs and submitted a sketch to WWD for the Inauguration look, so we can no doubt expect to see her wearing the label at some point.  And one can imagine that Maria Grazia Chiuri, Dior’s recently installed creative director who has made feminism and women’s rights a mainstay of her design message, will have plenty of ideas for dressing a Presidential wife with a difference.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This year marks 100 years since the beginning of British Vogue, and what better way to celebrate than to feature a model the same age as the magazine itself? Harvey Nichols have stepped in to do the honours, casting centenarian Majorie Gilbert, known as Bo, in an exclusive campaign for the May issue. Bo, who has lived alone in a supportive housing facility in Birmingham for the past 26 years, has never modelled before but was discovered by Harvey Nichols' advertising agency Adam and Eve on Google, after an article celebrating her 100th birthday appeared in her local paper, the Evesham Journal. She becomes the oldest model to feature in Vogue. "I was shocked really,” Bo said today,“just unbelievable. Something that you would never dream of thinking about or doing, it was quite an honour to be asked.” In the campaign shots, she dons a designer outfit which any woman - no matter what her age - would likely love to wear; a bright fuschia coat by Dries van Noten, a Victoria Beckham black top, tailored trousers by The Row and shoes by Celine. The look is accessorised with a Lanvin necklace and bespoke Valentino glasses - and of course, Bo’s fabulous mane of silver hair. The documentary video accompanying the campaign points out that the average age of a model is between 16 and 25, before cutting to a shot of 100 year-old Bo sitting on her sofa sipping a cup of tea with her birthday card from the Queen and few choice chintzy ornaments on her mantelpiece.  Bo was born in the midst of the first world war  on January 12th 1916 and has always loved fashion. “I dress for myself, I never dress up for boys.” A woman after our own hearts. Yet, for Bo fashion has always been more of a hobby than a full-time occupation. "I love wearing nice things it’s always appealed and still does." She moved to Birmingham from Aberdare in Wales at the age of 11, then started working at a cardboacd box manufacturing company called Bostons as a teenager. She stayed working there for 47 years, keeping the factory going during the second world war and eventually becoming a director. She met her husband Dennis at a dance and they had a daughter, Stephanie. They have both since died but Stephanie's husband Peter still visits often. Bo still stays true to her Welsh roots, often baking her speciality - a traditional fruit cake called Teisen Lap. She says that she always  admired the style of Audrey Hepburn ("she showed herself off beautifully") and  believes it’s important to “keep standards up.” Her dabblings with fashion go back as far as her teenage years, when her talented dressmaker mother would create outfits she called “a bit more fashionable than otherwise we could have afforded.” She said she now chooses “nice cardigans” and trousers, which she finds “easier than wearing a skirt.” As you might expect, Bo has seen plenty of fashions come and go during her lifetime. “I remember  the  first time I saw a lady in a trouser suit, I’d never seen anything like that before it really caught my eye,” she recalls. Bo is still dedicated to looking glamorous every day, always applying make-up, wearing heels and ensuring her hair is done. She hints that she might like to see people today make more of an effort; “now you never see anyone in a hat,” she comments. “It was a privilege to work with Bo,” says Shadi Halliwell, creative and marketing director at Harvey Nichols. “She is a fabulous, independent lady who epitomises timeless style.” Brittany Lippett, account director at Adam and Eve, said it was an “utter joy” for the team to work with “this lovely 100-year-old”, adding: “She has such a wonderful personality and was keeping everyone entertained.”  Although Bo doesn’t give away any secrets about how she’s stayed so fit and healthy for 100 years, it’s clear that her no-nonsense approach probably has something to do with it. “I do things a lot of people wouldn’t do at my age,”  she says. Like starring in a Vogue campaign.

 If 'diplomatic dressing' is the trendiest thing that a European royal can do right now, then the Duchess of Cambridge is the one to beat at it. This Scandinavian trip has been no exception and every day since the Duchess touched down in Stockholm with her husband, the Duke of Cambridge, she has been deftly infusing her wardrobe with Scandi style influences. Outdoor wear by Fjallraven and a coat by Ida Sjöstedt have both made appearances, alongside a balance of her British favourites; Erdem, Catherine Walker, Alexander McQueen and Burberry. The sustainable approach is a cause close to the Duchess of Cambridge’s own heart. Last week she wore a printed scarf by London-based label Beulah, a brand created to ‘support and empower vulnerable women’. Her future sister-in-law, Meghan Markle, has also supported brands with responsible concerns, including Stella McCartney, DeMellier London and Welsh denim label, Hiut.  At Dolce & Gabbana's SS17 show during Milan Fashion Week in September it was clear the Italian house was shifting its focus towards a new fashion generation. The front row was comprised of YouTubers, famous people's teen offspring and Instagram stars (christened 'The Millennial Generation’ by Dolce), all with a legion of followers obsessing over their every move - never have so many squealing teenage girls swarmed the entrance to a Milan showspace. It is now clear this wasn't just a one-time invite, as Dolce & Gabbana has today released its new advertising campaign, showing that the brand is rethinking its marketing strategy to court and target the Instagram set. The SS17 images, which are named #DGMillennials, were shot in Capri, Italy back in October and have a bright-eyed cast with a total follower count of  over 50 million. Twenty one year-old internet star Cameron Dallas, who has 16.1 million followers on Instagram and 5 million subscribers on YouTube , caused a frenzy at the SS17 show, and is starring in the campaign alongside a number of other internet stars, including teenage model and social sensation Luka Sabbat. Another key ingredient for a perfect 'internet fashion storm' in 2017 is celebrity offspring models, and so it's no great surprise to see that Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber, Daniel Day Lewis's son Gabriel Kane, Jude Law and Sadie Frost's son Rafferty Law and Pamela Anderson's son Brandon Thomas Lee are all in the line up as well.  The women's campaign, has equal viral potential, with singer Zendaya (33.2 million followers) and Brooklyn Beckham's ex-girlfriend Sonia Ben Ammar among the stars. Model Thylane Blondeau, who caused a controversy when she modelled in a grown-up editorial for Vogue Paris at the age of 10, is also one of the millennial faces. Traditionally campaign castings are kept a highly confidential secret, only revealed when glossy magazines hit newsstands or a press release is circulated months after being shot, but in keeping with the spirit of the project, the cast were encouraged to share pictures from the set on all social media platforms with the hashtag months ago. Cameron Dallas, for example, shared a picture of him arriving in Capri back in October, and it gained 879k likes and almost 8,000 comments less than 24 hours after being posted.  What is unclear is whether these millions of likes and hysterical comments will ever translate into sales; luxury brands aren't designed for a mass audience, and existing shoppers may not want to be dressed in the things being coveted by their teenage children. But perhaps Dolce is playing the long game here to get ahead and foster its next wave of customers.  Those following the Dolce & Gabbana hashtag are predominantly students without the money for a £2,000 bag, but by speaking to them now, arguably the Italian house is creating an appetite for luxury shopping within this demographic ready for when they have more than just pocket money to spend on a Dolce & Gabbana lipstick.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  London is melting. It’s the hottest day of the year, and outside Giles Deacon’s Brick Lane studio, the youth of Shoreditch are wilting in their rompers and crop tops. Inside, we’re above it all in the couture zone – a place of custom-woven double jacquards and hand-painted gold feathers, of gowns so lavish, so transporting and so expensive, they may well come equipped with their own weather systems. Behind a closed door, Deacon is directing Gwendoline Christie (the Game of Thrones and Star Wars star who happens to be his partner) as she swishes through a series of looks from his first couture collection. At 6ft 3in and with a regal confidence befitting the only actress ever to portray both a Shakespearean queen and a Stormtrooper commander, Christie seems born for gowns, particularly those with Deacon-esque heights of verve and individuality. She wears a silk gown printed with bird eggs of the British Isles with the same confidence and ease that most women would bring to their favourite jeans. ‘Giles has long been one of my favourite designers,’ Christie says via email later. ‘He has two of my favourite attributes in artists: wild imagination and technical rigour. [His designs] can be practical, otherworldly, sculptural and mind-bending, but you always feel celebrated as a woman when you wear them… Their confidence somehow increases yours. It’s quite a power for a designer to have. His clothes have personalities.’ Christie and Deacon, a couple for nearly four years, have collaborated on designs for some of Christie’s biggest red-carpet moments (the black ostrich-feather embellished column gown she wore to the London premiere of Star Wars: The Force Awakens included). ‘It’s a pleasure to work with your partner,’ Deacon says, sitting at the studio table. ‘She’s a fantastic muse. She’s a character herself, and her trail of various characters is brilliant – she’s pretty transformative, which is always an interesting thing from a designer’s point of view.’  Christie, similarly, is fascinated by character within costume. ‘It’s a wonderful experience to inhabit different forms for my work ,’ she says. ‘I have recently worn costumes made from armour and their structure fascinates me as much as a couture dress.’ In January, Deacon suspended activity on his ready-to-wear line to focus on couture. He’s fresh from presenting his first couture collection in Paris and still seems dazed and delighted by the ‘rapturous, really wonderful reviews’. He was already the most couture-like of London designers, with rich, dramatic designs and shows that had more in common with performance art than standard runways. Deacon supported his main line with a string of collaborations (Ann Summers apparel, an LG washing machine) and a small but strong roster of private clients. The latter made the official switch to couture less a leap than a pivot. ‘What I really love doing,’ he says, ‘and what people really love from us is beautiful, crafted dresses.’   Deacondrew inspiration from Lady Ottoline Morrell, the Bloomsbury Set patron whose affairs were as legendary as her parties (she counted philosopher Bertrand Russell and artist Dora Carrington among her partners). The looks he created for one of her imagined gatherings include an emerald silk jacquard gown with tonal crystal panels, a frond-printed pink satin gown with embellished corset and a razor-sharp silver silk jacquard dress with a smocked velvet capelet. Deacon designed many of the ensembles with specific clients in mind. His ‘25 to 30’ worldwide clients include women ranging in age from 25 to 70. They find him through word of mouth, and what mouths they are. ‘I am very good friends with a Saudi princess who has been great about introducing me to a number of her friends.’ Bespoke day dresses start at £8,000; the mid-tier eveningwear looks come in at about £24,000, and prices can spiral to £120,000 for extravagant wedding gowns. Part of the value lies in the understanding that Deacon won’t produce more than one version of each look per territory. ‘My clients all want something that’s beautifully made and considered for them, and they’re willing to pay for that.’  Unlike ready-to-wear fashion, which typically operates on a six-month lead-time, Deacon’s atelier can fulfil couture orders in three months. Deacon’s studio team creates digital avatars for each client – they can send 3D renderings of bespoke designs for a  client to swipe through from her yacht or ski chalet. So it is that couture, the most hallowed and esoteric corner of fashion, remains modern and relevant. ‘I like to keep things as controlled as possible and the lovely thing about making couture pieces is that you can do that,’ Deacon says. ‘I want the label to be a very advanced couture house for the 21st century.’ © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. Over this, Perry wore a delicately embroidered red silk tulle veil and an elaborate chrome headpiece, finishing the ensemble with a red Japanese Tabi boots.  Perry- who is renowned for her peacocking style choices- quickly sparked speculation that she may even have shaved her head in order to fully commit to Galliano's vision, although it soon became clear that her blonde crop was simply smoothed down underneath the sweeping veil.  Brooklyn Beckham is fast becoming a red carpet fixture. Now 16, the teen is au fait with the ins and outs of posing, pouting and, now, presenting at awards ceremonies. Last night he accompanied his fashion designer mum to the US Glamour Women of the Year Awards in New York, where she was presented with an award that recognised her not only as a ‘fashion force’ - she's a major player on the New York Fashion Week schedule - but also her philanthropic efforts as an international goodwill ambassador for UNAIDS. Looking smart in a slim cut suit, Brooklyn took to the stage to tell his famous mum how much he loved her before handing her the award – but not before the rest of the family had also professed their admiration via a pre-recorded video message. "You're my mummy of the year: not just this year but every year!" said 10-year-old Cruz, while Burberry model Romeo, 13, added, "Congratulations, Mummy. You definitely deserve this award. Oh, one more thing: Can you please make kids' clothes?" "We're all so proud of you, and I'm so excited to be with you tonight to present you with this award," said Brooklyn to the audience. "I love you." Victoria then gave a short speech, which included an uncharacteristic smile and even a peace sign, a throwback salute from her days as a Spice Girl. "I love what I do and I feel blessed to be given the chance to pursue and fulfill my career ambitions,” she said. “It started with the Spice Girls and girl power and now I'm channeling that same message to women through my collection. I want to support, empower and really make women feel like the best version of themselves." Earlier in the day the mother-of-four appeared on Good Morning America where she spoke about the challenges of being a working mother and how fellow designer Diane von Furstenberg had helped her come to terms with the pressures. "For me, I was having dinner with Diane von Furstenberg a few months ago and she's a woman I have an enormous amount of respect and admiration for," she said. "I said to her, 'Diane, when your children were younger and you were working, did you feel guilty?' And she said, 'Absolutely not. It's a waste of time, a waste of energy, it's ageing. "That was great advice because I'm sure there are lots of women right now who are thinking, 'I feel guilty. I've got kids and I'm going to work.'  It was one of her first key solo engagements since accepting role as an official advisor to her father, President Donald Trump, so Ivanka Trump will have known that all eyes would be on her as she spoke at the W20 international women’s summit in Berlin today. The First Daughter's decision on what to wear for the occasion will have been almost as carefully plotted as what she would say, and White House style watchers have been speculating on social media as to whether she would opt for one of her signature power sheath dresses when meeting German Chancellor Angela Merkel, or soften things up a little. Ivanka chose to fly the flag for American brands on this global stage, wearing a dress from New York designer Michael Kors’s spring 2017 collection, covered in Fifties florals. Indeed when Kors first presented the dress on the catwalk back in September, he did so with Judy Garland’s Get Happy as his backing music - a reference that, at the time, was supposed to remind his audience to forget about the then-impending US election for a moment, and just focus on the fun of fashion. Of course, Donald Trump won, and fashion and politics have mixed plenty of times since in the last six months, so the meaning has altered a lot now that we see the dress on Ivanka the First Daughter. Kors, for the record, was not one of the New York names to shun the Trumps, but equally he hasn't embraced dressing them in bespoke looks either, instead leaving them to shop for off-the-rack looks in his stores. "Mrs. Trump has been a longtime client at our New York boutique," Kors said when the First Lady wore one of his suits to a speech given by the President. "She has a keen understanding of what works best for her and her lifestyle.”  If Ivanka had considered the idea that florals and their springlike sentiments may give her a boost when tackling the special relationship her way, then she wasn’t the only one to harness their appeal. Queen Maxima of the Netherlands also wore bloom prints as she joined the panel, which included other notable female leaders and politicians including Canada's Foreign Minister Chrystia Freeland and International Monetary Fund Managing Director Christine Lagarde. While she may have supported another designer via her choice of dress, Ivanka did also wear pieces from her eponymous fine jewellery brand (the Patras Octagonal earrings and ring) which may anger her critics. The First Daughter came under fire when wearing a bangle from her collection for an appearance with her father on TV show 60 Minutes, as Twitter users accused her of profiting from the presidency by promoting her own products. Ivanka is in Berlin for a few more days to work on the 'special relationship' between the US and Germany, offering plenty of further opportunities to make an impact with her take on power dressing. With a somewhat softer, yet equally impactful approach than the one her father took when he met Merkel back in March, it will be interesting to see whose strategy is most effective.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  With a moniker such as his, Manolo Blahnik was never going to be a bank manager, a teacher  or an accountant. No: Manolo Blahnik was destined to make shoes. His name sounds like an an exotic dish featuring truffle, its cadence pleasing to enunciate. Where are your shoes from? ‘Manolo Blahnik.’  Although, in truth, the ‘Blahnik’ was dropped years ago, its owner belonging  to that elite coterie of designers so famous that no surname is required. Blogs, songs and Facebook pages have been penned  to ‘My Manolos’, while in Sex and the City, Carrie Bradshaw pleaded with a New York mugger, ‘You can take my Fendi baguette, you can take my ring and my watch, but please don’t take my Manolo Blahniks.’ A Manolo is many things – light, elegant, tasteful – but what it definitely isn’t is a Loub. The world is divided into two sorts  of shoe-lover: the Manolos and the Louboutins, and never the twain shall meet. If the red-soled, sexed-up Loub is adored by women who consider a platform heel the best way to achieve extra stature, the spindly, waifish Manolo is its alter ego,  worn by women who perhaps don’t need shoes to enhance their stature. Anna Wintour is a lifelong fan, famously buying several identical pairs of beige mules every season. She is also a lifelong friend. ‘I have no words to express my desperate affection for her,’ says Blahnik. ‘She’s a divine woman. So normal and loyal. We went to the movies together all the time in New York, because we loved movies. So we went at 9 o’clock in the morning. This was before she was at Vogue. No time now, poor thing.’ There are many paeans to stylish women in Blahnik’s book Fleeting Gestures and Obsessions, a coffee-table book so heavy you may require a new, reinforced coffee table to hold it (at 488 pages, it weighs more than a small child), but none is quite so heartfelt as the one to Anna Wintour. Also lauded in Blahnik’s book are Cecil Beaton, Gore Vidal, Marie Antoinette, Anna Piaggi, Irving Penn and Mary Beard, the 60-year-old classicist with whom Blahnik bonded over a shared love of Ancient cultures. ‘Oh my God, Mary! Mary is the love of my life now,’ he exclaims. ‘I went to see her [debate with Boris Johnson]. Oh! She killed him! She really destroyed him! They were debating Roman versus Hellenistic cultures.  I went mad!’ Blahnik exclaims a lot. In fact, most of his utterances are exclamations, apart from those he feels a little sheepish about, which are murmured inaudibly. He is a glorious interviewee, though you suspect he was an even more glorious one 10 years ago, in the days when it wasn’t quite so incumbent on a designer to stay powerfully on-message. He has the air  of a man who once got into trouble for something that he said, and is trying – to his chagrin – not to repeat the error.   This is possibly why two audio recorders sit on the large, polished boardroom table between us: mine, and the one placed there by his PR. Blahnik thinks both are mine until the end of the interview. ‘It’s not yours? Well, whose is it?’ he cries. ‘You taped this?’ he scolds his PR.  Manners maketh Manolo, a man so delightfully old school that he greets me in a lilac double-breasted linen suit, hands stained with ink, apologising for a lack of bow tie, the absence of which he will hide with his hand when I ask for the obligatory selfie at the end of our interview. Even as an infant, one imagines him as well-mannered.    Born in 1942 and raised in Santa Cruz de la Palma in the Canary Islands, his Spanish mother’s family owned a banana plantation, while his Czech father’s family owned a pharmaceutical company in Prague. He was home-schooled before attending university in Geneva, after which he enrolled  at the Ecole de Beaux-Arts in Paris. He arrived in London in 1968, prompting a love affair with England that endures (he lives in Bath). It was Diana Vreeland, then-editor of US Vogue, who encouraged him to start making shoes after seeing one of his sketches; by 1972, he was collaborating with Ossie Clark. In 1973, he borrowed £2,000 to open a boutique on Old Church Street in Chelsea, London, where his store remains to this day. The fact that only now, some 43 years later, is Blahnik opening his second standalone store in London, might be seen as remiss, until you consider the not-insignificant detail that his business remains independent. Given that the entire luxury goods market is controlled by a very small – some might say too small – number of players, this is a huge achievement. ‘Everybody’s been bought by somebody,’ Blahnik agrees. ‘I don’t want all that. As long as I am able to pay my rent on my building, and my rates and things, I’m OK.’ Besides, there are advantages to being independent. ‘I’ve reached a point in my life where I’m totally free. The tyranny of public opinion doesn’t really bother me any more. People say, “How do you last so long?  Forty-five years is a very long time!” – you know why? Because I never compromised too much. I am the “no” man.’ And it’s true: he is the ‘no’ man, rejecting trends and fads with unusual self-belief.  He said ‘no’ when everyone else was doing platform shoes. (‘Wonderful that it [the trend] has gone, because it destroyed so many beautiful legs. Even a small girl in platforms looks smaller and ridiculous.’) And he said ‘no’ when everyone else was doing trainers. ‘I have now a trainer, but it’s like a boring old shoe because I don’t like all this chains and gold and things that all my colleagues are doing. I hate them. This bling nonsense is gone, gone, gone to me for a long time. I don’t want to see that again. A trainer is a trainer.’ He says the industry has changed ‘totally’ since he started out, ‘Simply because designers don’t even go to the factories any more. They send the things on the computer, most of them. I just tell you that it’s sad. I’m old-fashioned. I still cling my nails to tradition. I have to touch, see, balance.’ His customers have also changed. ‘You have a new public which is not exactly… ’  he tails off, desperately trying not to offend anyone. ‘Maybe they have taste, or this mania for names or whatever it is, but it’s not the same public as before. Before, it would be decisive women. Now we have the Chinese. “Do you have that one in five colours?”  ‘This is why it has changed now. Not [buying for] the love of things. Buying for the sake of buying. But you understand. They’re a new country coming up. The Russians have good taste – some have fantastic taste. ‘Others have… I won’t say anything, because they’ll take it badly. They love to be seen with something that has been seen somewhere else. English women used to be incredibly “someone has it –  I don’t want it. I will have another one.”’ He says he doesn’t go to fashion shows any more.  ‘I find it tedious now, because I’m old.’ Then, wickedly adds, ‘That’s not true, because  I could fly tomorrow morning to see Azzedine [Alaïa]. But there are not many Azzedines around. He is the last one.’ There has been much debate recently about the increasingly fast pace of fashion, what with John Galliano and Raf Simons both exiting Dior. Does he feel affected by this? ‘No. John Galliano is still the master.’ I’m not sure whether he has deliberately misunderstood me, so I repeat the question. ‘Azzedine and John are the last two true designers, and let me tell you, I went to Milan last week, and when I was there,  I passed through Maison Margiela [John Galliano’s new home] and saw two dresses that if I was a woman I would have snapped up in seconds – beautifully made, beautifully cut.’ Certainly, Blahnik isn’t the only septuagenarian to be wistful for a bygone era, but the reverence with which he speaks of Ossie, Zandra, John and Azzedine, and of the models and muses from his halcyon days, implies that he finds the modern world lacking in some fundamental beauty. Many of the women he eulogises in his book – Naomi Campbell, Lucy Birley, Amanda Harlech, Julie Christie, Kate Moss – are British. ‘I love British women!  I adore the way they move. The people  I mention in my book, they’re not necessarily very beautiful, but they move in some way that I find captivating.’  Has he seen Kate Moss recently?  ‘I wish, but I don’t have the time and now she’s got another boyfriend. The last time we had lunch was after her wedding, but her wedding was 100 years ago. I don’t see Kate but I love her still. That boy [Jamie Hince] was great for her. And they adored each other. But things don’t last too long.’ I tell him I’ve been wondering whether every era gets the muse that it deserves. ‘I guess so,’ he says. It depresses me that Kim Kardashian is… ‘Is that a muse?’ he shrieks, interrupting. For some people, I say.  ‘Vile, vile,’ he says, more despairingly than meanly. ‘Jean Shrimpton, Twiggy…  these kind of girls were idols. I don’t even know who is what any more. And there are so many. So famous. Celebrities – I hate that word “celebrity” – because in my time, people did things. They used to be copied because they were doing something.’ He sighs. ‘We are being invaded by American culture, and there’s nothing we can do. Someone recently asked me, “What does your brand stand for?” I don’t even know what my brand stands for!  ‘My brand stand for someone who… I like shoes, that’s all. And I do the kind of shoes that I like. But I cannot define myself.’  Mr Blahnik, there is no need. Your shoes say more than mere words ever could.   Manolo Blahnik at the Burlington Arcade in Piccadilly, London, opens on Feb 4th © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  While many (we're looking at you Blake Lively) use the Cannes Film Festival as an opportunity to wear feathers, sequins and mountains of tulle, Lily Rose Depp is playing it a little more casual. This morning she brought a little teen spirit to proceedings, wearing a relaxed hoodie to the photo call of The Dancer. Of course, this wasn't just any hoodie. Depp opted for a sporty purple, red and blue knitted style which- with its matching short shorts- formed a very haute kind of tracksuit. The 16-year-old daughter of Cannes juror Vanessa Paradis and Johnny Depp is breaking into acting, and has a number of projects listed in 'post-production' section on her IMBD page. Today, she attended one of her first ever film promotional duties,  as expected the Chanel ambassador turned to Karl Lagerfeld for her moment on La Croisette.  It's a look that only a teenager (with the keys to the Chanel sample room) can pull off. While you might expect her to wear a pair of trainers with such a sporty look (perhaps Chanel's light-up sneakers from the SS16 collection), Depp wore red strappy Chanel stilettos with an ankle strap covered in the house's key emblem, the camellia to elevate her sporty get-up. There has been much discussion about the supposed flat shoes ban on the Cannes red carpet this year, with Julia Roberts going barefoot on the red carpet last night and Kristen Stewart wearing trainers to a Cannes Gala dinner. “Things have to change immediately,” Stewart said of Cannes's wardrobe rules. “It has become really obvious that if [a man and I] were walking the red carpet together and someone stopped me and said, ‘Excuse me, young lady, you’re not wearing heels. You cannot come in.’ Then [I’m going to say], ‘Neither is my friend. Does he have to wear heels?’ It can work both ways. It’s just like you simply cannot ask me to do something that you are not asking him. I get the black-tie thing but you should be able to do either version—flats or heels.” Depp- who is the face of Chanel's eyewear collection- has only made a handful of red carpet appearances, but she is already carving a signature laid back approach to formal dressing. At the Met Gala earlier this month, the teenager wore a white heavily embellished Chanel Haute Couture Spring 2016 halterneck gown, with a matching bomber slung off her shoulders. She clearly inherited her mother's Gallic nonchalance.  Depp seems to be learning from the Victoria Beckham school of posing, always favouring an intense pout with attitude over a toothy grin. She responded to the suggestion that she looked 'moody' on the Met Gala red carpet, by posting a headshot from the red carpet where she had a deadpan expression, and added the caption:  "Y'all said She'd look good if she were smiling." There's bona fide fashion justification for Lily Rose Depp wearing a hoodie to the Cannes Film Festival.  Hooded sweatshirts are making a comeback this season.  Azzedine Alaïa and curator Mark Wilson were “90% of the way through” their plans for a new blockbuster exhibition of the Tunisian couturier’s work, when Alaïa passed away on 18th November 2017. “There was no question that it would still go ahead,” Wilson tells The Telegraph of the decision to continue with the project, which will open to the public at London’s Design Museum on thursday. “I spoke with Maison Alaïa, the museum and Carla [Sozzani, a friend a contributor to the project] about three weeks after his passing, and they all agreed, it is what he would want.” Entering Azzedine Alaïa: The Couturier, visitors are greeted with a line-up of some of Alaïa’s most recent works, including a gown modelled on the catwalk by Naomi Campbell at his final ever couture show, held in Paris last July. “It has become a celebration, in it’s own way,” Wilson says of the tribute. “I was really adamant that we shouldn’t change anything about the way he had planned it and the finished show, I think, is Alaïa’s temple.” Here, Wilson explains what to expect... “Azzedine was a perfectionist, he would not release any design unless he was satisfied with it, so there are no deconstructed pieces on show here, only the finished works,” Wilson explains. “But you don’t need to see his pieces split open to appreciate the work that went into them. He worked like a sculptor and made everything himself. Every dress started with pinning fabric on the models, then he cut his own patterns - that’s something that most designers never do themselves. Fitting fabric to the form of the body is the technique at the centre of every one of his designs, and you can tell that from pictures on the red carpet or wherever, but in person you can understand and see that construction.”    Outfits worn by Tina Turner, Grace Jones and Naomi Campbell are amongst the 60-piece display, which spans from the early 1980s to his final creations.  “He and I talked a lot about whether to theme things and the result feels quite grouped by technique,” Wilson explains. “There’s the series of famous bandage dresses, there are versions of the flamenco dress that are embroidered in metallics, and there are pieces that show his use of rivets, or exotic skins. But then in amongst them there is the Grace Jones dress, the Tina Turner dress - those pieces that have now become classics.” “Every gown on show was recut and made by Azzedine specifically for the exhibitions,” Wilson explains. “He’s done a special elongated silhouette for the mannequins which looks so much more effective and glamorous than what you get when you sometimes see clothes in exhibitions. He always understood display - 22 years ago he built a mannequin to Naomi’s [Campbell’s] body measurements because he was so conscious of presenting a great silhouette.” “I told Azzedine that I didn’t think it would be a good idea to build walls within the space - it’s 850 square metres, but you don’t want to make things look small. I gave him the option to create screens and he agreed immediately. We asked several of his friends, like Marc Newson and Kris Ruhs, to create these backdrops, and the results are like 10 metre high art works - really fitting for the Design Museum. It’s entirely personal, though, these are all people who were important to him." “One thing that I hope people will take away from their visit is the timelessness of Azzedine’s work,” says Wilson. “They could have been made 30 years ago, or tomorrow, you cannot date any of these items. Unlike most designers, he didn’t pick a new theme each season to inspire him, he was always doing his own, unique thing. He was always reworking, and working towards perfection and that makes him unique. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  France has been without a First Lady ever since Valérie Trierweiler walked out on François Hollande in 2014. To be fair, the country had enjoyed a rather chic time of it until then. There was Carla Bruni-Sarkozy whose years in the Élysée Palace were defined by her transformation from sultry chanteuse to impeccable political wife, wearing prim skirt suits, shift dresses and formal coats with dainty ballerina flats and kitten heels (nothing higher, for fear of overtowering her husband). Then came Trierweiler whose style was more relaxed but possibly truer to the quintessential Parisenne look; slightly dishevelled-but-perfect-in-its-own-way blowdry, sleek tailoring and the odd pair of towering heels. She looked like she dressed for herself, and was bothered about looking good but not so much so that she'd waste too much time on the matter; let's call it polished nonchalance.  Yesterday, Emmanuel Macron- formerly of Hollande's Socialist party and now leading his own 'En Marche' movement- took the lead after the first round of voting in the Presidential election. He'll now face Marine Le Pen in the final round but looks set to become France's new President once votes are cast on May 7th; he's aleady being hailed as France's 'JFK'. One element of Macron's CV which has added extra frisson to his campaign is his wife Brigitte Trogneux. At 64, she is 25 years his senior and epitomises a new spin of French  style which is at once soignée and glamorous. Trogneux and Macron met when she was his literature teacher at a private school in Amiens. They developed a close relationship and stayed in touch after Macron left, eventually marrying and moving in together along with Trogneux's three children.   With her ultra slim frame and long legs (which French tabloids regularly salivate over), Trogneux looks more like a former model than a former teacher and dresses accordingly. Images of the couple together during their recent years in the limelight reveal her penchant for mini-length dresses, skinny jeans and luxe accessrories. Her interpretation of French style doesn't conform to the super relaxed, low maintenance vibes of many  Parisian It girls but one imagines that former French Vogue editor Carine Roitfeld is her high-priestess of style inspiration: it's all about opting for the most figure-flattering looks and looking sensually and agelessly sexy without straying into Trump-level glossy territory. The French media has praised Trogneux for her "cool attitude" and "wonderwoman" look.  Beauty-wise, Trogneux is a peroxide and tan devotee- the former definitely requires regular upkeep from her hairdresser but her bronzed skin suggests  regular sun worshipping with a little subtle help from a St Tropez bottle here and there.  After meeting Delphine Arnault- Executive Vice President of Louis Vuitton -  in 2014, Trogneux developed a relationship with the house which means they now loan her looks for many of her public appearences; a rarity for anyone other than A-list celebrities. She has also sat front row at Vuitton and Christian Dior shows, proof- if it were needed- of her natural love for fashion.  In some scenarios - such as a debate between the Presidential candidates at the beginning of April - Trogneux has shown a mastery for brave but also effortless styling which, should she eventually become First Lady, would make her a new kind of political dressing fashion plate for women the world over. You might think that such an important event in the campaign would call for something pulled-together and elegant but instead Trogneux arrived in distressed skinny jeans and a luxe knit, anchoring the look with snakeskin kitten heels and a mannish blazer. 'Laidback, quietly confident styling = laidback quietly confident candidate' was the political message. A taste of things to come?   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Melania Trump opted to channel Jacqueline Kennedy for her daytime look as she accompanied her husband now-President Donald Trump to his inauguration which took place this afternoon. The couple attended St John’s church in Washington early this morning and then went on to meet with Barack and Michelle Obama at the White House before the Inauguration ceremony. Melania's pale blue suit was created for her by Ralph Lauren, America’s most famous and prolific living designer. “With the historic swearing-in of her husband, Donald J. Trump, as the 45th President of the United States, the First Lady-elect will become America’s new First Lady wearing an American designer who transformed American fashion, Ralph Lauren,” a spokesperson for Trump announced this morning. "It was important to us to uphold the tradition of creating iconic American style for this moment," Ralph Lauren said in a statement to the New York Times.  With its demure knee-length skirt and bracelet-length sleeves, the ensemble immediately recalled the ladylike yet simple look which was coined and made famous by former First Lady Jacqueline Kennedy. In fact, the suit seemed to have taken direct inspiration from the Oleg Cassini design which Kennedy wore for John F Kennedy’s daytime Inauguration ceremony 56 years ago in January 1961. Lauren and Trump had, however, added some more modern elements to give Trump’s look a more updated feel. The double-faced cashmere jacket came with a raised shawl collar and cropped, wrap effect, serving the double purpose of shielding Trump from the 5 degree temperatures and adding a distinctive edge to an otherwise pared-back silhouette. Melania accessorised today's suit with elbow length leather gloves and suede stilettos in a matching shade of icy blue while her hair was swept up into a chic up-do. The pastel tone of the suit provided a sophisticated contrast to Donald Trump's vividly red tie.  Ralph Lauren had been mooted earlier this week as the designer who was creating Melania Trump’s Inauguration wardrobe. While his designs are now considered to be American classics, the 77 year-old who was born in The Bronx, New York has spent his career pioneering a distinctive preppy, easy and elegant style. His $6 billion company has outposts across the world while the Polo horse emblem is globally recognisable.  During his Inauguration address this afternoon, Donald Trump announced that his adminstration would encourage everyone to "buy American and hire American", another hint that his wife will be supporting the American fashion industry during her time as First Lady.  During the Presidential campaign, Lauren became closely associated with Trump’s rival Hillary Clinton, creating a series of bespoke pantsuits for the Democrat candidate. Clinton also turned to Lauren for the beige pantsuit which she wore to today's Inauguration. Yet, Melania - who has historically favoured European designers like Chanel and Gucci - was already courting Lauren by choosing his ready-to-wear pieces which she purchased in store. For the third Presidential debate, Trump chose a black Ralph Lauren jumpsuit and for her husband’s victory speech, Melania turned to another jumpsuit, this time white, from his collection. Yesterday, Melania kicked off her Inauguration looks with a military-inspired black coat by New York designer Norisol Ferrari, this was followed by a glittering gold evening gown courtesy of another New York name- Reem Acra. The trio adds up to suggest that Trump will be adhering to the glamorous  but covered up look which she displayed throughout the campaign while tweaking her designer choices to present a patriotic roster.  Given Jacqueline Kennedy’s profound fashion legacy and the clever blueprint she created for modern First Lady dressing, Melania’s decision to echo her style in today’s look seems a fitting homage. And a sign that Melania Trump will be using her clothes to send subtle messages in the way so many of her predecessors have.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  It would be in the realm of Howard Hughes megalomania only to employ staff whose hair colour matches the brand livery, yet, in the case of Nadège Vanhee-Cybulski, her auburn mane must seem a lovely added extra to the creative talents that she is bringing to Hermès, with its trademark zesty orange packaging. In the environment of the Hermès Maison, a Hugh Casson-designed interior on the corner of Bond and Bruton Streets, Vanhee-Cybulski, with her luminous pale skin and freckles and wearing a man’s Hermès silk twill shirt and casual trousers, complements the polished wood, leather panelled walls and brass fittings. It’s early June and the creative director is in London to talk me through her AW16 collection for the house. The palette of salmon pink, saffron, navy and port wine brings an assured sense of the taste that Hermès, founded in 1837 as a saddler, is known for.  While some designers, notably Tom Ford and Pierpaolo Piccioli at Valentino, prefer to halo their creative work in a seductive cloud of references and witticisms, Vanhee-Cybulski introduces each piece of the collection like a scientist displaying an invention: “This model is wearing a cape-jacket with intricate work in double-face cashmere and leather. It’s almost like peeling a part of the double face and sliding in the leather,” she says, indicating a virtuoso graphic pattern of the supplest leather and finest cashmere. “What is great is that inside it is totally flush. The leather is just four millimetres thick, almost like paper,” she adds in her gentle-toned voice. The cape-jacket in question boasts seamless sides and gently domed shoulders, and falls to mid-thigh. It is both a piece of armour and a cocoon and this “touch me, touch me not” sartorial language might be just right for our highly social and yet deeply private times. “It’s important to work with a woman’s body and reveal her silhouette,” says Vanhee-Cybulski, of an aesthetic that seems to fuse sensuality with modesty. There are hand-loomed double-cashmere knits; sweeping godet skirts; a selection of suede tunics, slim midi-skirts and jackets pierced with delicate palladium studs; glorious oversize “twillaine” silk-knit pullovers and a zip-up-and-go silk bomber jacket featuring the Hermès Palmes Royales scarf print in different scales. “In the collection, I want to sustain our equestrian roots,” says Vanhee-Cybulski of her mission. “By that I mean the sophistication and aesthetics of the saddle, the leather goods and the story of know-how – it is interesting to bring that into the ready-to-wear world, which is more about cuts and silhouette.  I don’t want to cut and paste the equestrian world but I want to find a transformation.” During Paris Haute Couture Fashion Week in July, Hermès showed its first standalone Resort collection, which will sit alongside the main women’s and men’s collections in stores in a bid to attract transeasonal custom and satiate our demand for newness. Not that Hermès likes to dabble in novelty or folly – the house’s modus operandi is to deliver a timeless sense of beauty that befits the hefty price tags and superlative quality. The research and development in fabrics, cut and techniques and in even the smallest closure mechanism demands deep pockets and, above all, time. The new bag, the “Baton de Craie,” for example, features a semi-precious stone clasp – in the shape of “craie” or piece of chalk. Vanhee-Cybulski also works with an accessories team and shoe designer, Pierre Hardy, on developing new styles. Yet that investment in quality and “know-how” is what distinguishes Hermès products from luxury parvenus. Items, whether a grained goatskin perfecto jacket, herringbone linen safari suit or slouchy chevron wool trouser, are designed to weather climatic extremes, social fads and status anxieties to become a part of one’s life for the long haul. For an artistic or creative director, the role requires patience, vision and an ability to work with the atelier team to translate the house codes and expertise into wearable, desirable and high-function clothes. Vanhee-Cybulski, now 38, came to Hermès in 2014 with a strong track record in womenswear and a deep knowledge of, and obsession with, menswear.  She previously worked for the Olsen sisters in New York on their pared-back, ultra-luxe label The Row, in London for Céline and prior to that, at Maison Margiela. All three brands have garnered a cult following and strong commercial sales with their distinctive, thoughtful, grown up collections that steer away from the clichés of femininity and the traps of trend to create a real wardrobe. This is a school of purist fashion based on a sense of complicity and a love of the garment over and above style. In her role, Vanhee-Cybulski now joins a peer group of taste-making female creatives including Stella McCartney, Phoebe Philo, Julie de Libran at Sonia Rykiel, and relative newcomers Gabriela Hearst and Rosetta Getty, who are driving the business of fashion forward. While their visions are distinct, what they do share is a hands-on work ethic and humility. “I remember after the interview it was, ‘See you tomorrow’ I didn’t know what it meant. My husband told me, ‘You have the job!’ For me, it was surreal but it was an offer that I could not refuse,” says Vanhee-Cybulski, on being interviewed by artistic director Pierre-Alexis Dumas, and his cousin, CEO Axel Dumas – both great-great-great-grandsons of the founder, Thierry Hermès (the family still owns a majority share of the company). “I did not have any prejudices, or preconceived ideas – I thought, let’s meet the team, let’s meet the atelier and build from there,” she says. “The conversation was very natural. I’ve always seen Hermès as a brand with integrity and with soul – you feel the imprint of the hand. I don’t want to sound spiritual, but you feel that a man or a woman has shaped that object and you see how impeccable – uncompromising – the quality is, using natural fibres and materials, turning that into something very civilised.” The womenswear creative director role was previously occupied by Christophe Lemaire and prior to that Jean Paul Gaultier, who followed Martin Margiela. The contracts tend to run for five to 10 years and Hermès likes to stick to that tenure and make sure any changeover is cordial, fruitful. With the rapid turnover of talent at power-house brands, often accompanied by dramatic statements and lawsuits, Hermès tries to steer a steady course. The creative directors in the team work in the service of the house rather than as rock-star appendages. Hermès does not want to witness risk swerves and U-turns – the transitions are as smooth and precisely engineered as the leather on the much-loved Kelly and Birkin handbags. “I don’t really struggle – it’s very free,” says the seemingly unflappable designer whose daily uniform is trousers, sneakers and a shirt. “It is really about not imposing or crushing but about being sensitive to the house and the techniques they use. It’s about appropriating, shifting, and continually balancing heritage and modernity,” she says. Whereas many designers come to fashion via a love of street and club culture, or via an obsession with the fantasy of glamour, Vanhee-Cybulski’s fascination has always been more anthropological.  She was born and raised in Lille in Northern France and describes herself as Flemish. As a young girl, she became mesmerised by the stories garments tell not only about their owners but also about social history. “I think about clothes as thoughtful objects – that is how I have always understood them from opening my mother’s wardrobe, to finding a naval jacket or a shirt in a secondhand store,” says the designer, who over the years has amassed a vast collection of shirts. “Some are bespoke, others vintage and in many different materials from silk twill, to poplin and flannel. They are like characters to me, they all have their personalities,” says Vanhee-Cybulski, who possesses a tender, discerning eye. In that carefully preserved, semi-autobiographical collection, she also has tour T-shirts from Massive Attack and Portishead as well as personal favourites from Margiela, Céline and The Row. She studied fashion at the renowned Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp, which has nurtured extraordinary talents including Margiela, Raf Simons and Demna Gvasalia, the much-lauded founder of Vetements and now creative director of Balenciaga.  “What’s unique in Antwerp is that the teachers are also fashion designers and curators. They force you to develop your own language and express where you’re from. These were the formative years. The first piece I made was an experimental skirt – it was pleated and also sculpted,” she says, of an endeavour that fused the tidy and conservative and shape-shifting possibilities of fashion. At Hermès, you can witness that sensitivity to line and nuance at play in an intricately embroidered gold silk-satin dress, a flared-sleeve double-faced cashmere edge-to-edge coat in buttermilk or the chevron-panelled silk twillaine maxi dresses and skirts. “As a young woman, I used to collect Hermès leather bracelets, they were the epitome of the house. I was interested in the mechanism – we have an atelier that just works on clasps. My other Hermès pieces were silk scarves – such strong colours and distinct equestrian iconography. It’s as if Hermès took the role of narrator, telling stories through the prints. I always love that angle of the house,” she says. Vanhee-Cybulski seems very content in her role as narrator, weaving together new and old stories to tell in her collections. She does not clamour for social-media attention or podium positioning, nor does she care for posing for portraits. She lives in the Pigalle area of Paris with two Jack Russells and her English gallerist husband, whom she met while working for Céline in London. Their two professional spheres (he is opening a gallery in the Marais later this month) chime even if their priorities and tastes in décor sometimes do not. “He is British, I am French – you are talking about the coffee table versus the dining table. When I moved into his apartment, he had a nice coffee table and the dining table was a small square in the kitchen. This is not possible – we need to have space to dine, I want to have good lunches and dinners! With Britain, it’s more about tea and cocktails. I always joke about it,” says the designer. She exercises the same measured calm in her personal life as she does in the nomenclature of clothes. She rarely wears make-up, save for red lipstick, and her choice of exercise is boxing. For the record, her dream dinner guests would be Cecil Beaton and Irving Penn. She is particularly fond of Penn’s “portrait series” of cigarette butts. “To be able to see such beauty in a cigarette butt! They must have had to pick up so many, it must have been like a casting,” she smiles. Finding character and beauty in the smallest of stitches, the turn of a cuff or the infinite variations of the grain of leather is a sign of true talent. “I love the language of clothes. My job is to enhance the personality of the wearer. I adore it when a woman takes a piece from a catwalk look and puts it with a T-shirt or jeans – that says so much more about her,” says Vanhee-Cybulski. The designer pops on a reversible edge-to-edge coat and bids me goodbye to head back to Paris – in time for a civilised dinner, one presumes. hermes.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Amal Clooney gave an impassioned speech at the UN last week as part of her defence of Iraq's Yazidi people and ongoing campaign to stop ISIS from committing further brutality.  "Justice is what the victims want," Clooney said, "but justice will be forever out of reach if we allow the evidence to disappear, if mass graves are not protected, if medical evidence is lost, if witnesses can no longer be traced." She happened to deliver this impassioned speech in a bright yellow dress and matching coat from Bottega Veneta - one of a series £20,000+ designer looks she wore during her trip to New York.  As you might expect from today's 24/7 media, the press coverage of Clooney's New York business trip has ranged from forensic detailing and scrutiny of the £168,000 designer "maternity wardrobe" she has showcased over the past few weeks to outrage that anyone should dare to notice or comment upon her clothes when she's working on such highbrow human rights issues.  But whilst of course it's utterly unnecessary to talk of women "flaunting" their baby bumps or question whether Clooney should be wearing 4 and a half inch heels at 6 months pregnant (short answer: there's no medical reason why not), it's surely unhelpful to have such a dichotomy of opinions.  After all, Clooney herself has not only mastered the alchemy of fashion and campaigning since she became George Clooney's wife in 2014, but recognises the power that her public image can bring to her professional work. "If there are more people who now understand what is happening with the Yazidis and ISIS and if there can be some action which results from that... then I think it's a really good thing to give that case the extra publicity that it may get," Clooney told the BBC last week of making peace with the scrutiny she now faces as a celebrity and working woman.  As such, we're missing the point if we don't recognise that Clooney might well be using her public image - and fashion as part of that - as a potent weapon to raise awareness of global human rights abuses, especially among people who might not otherwise hear them. You may think that's a sad truth, but it's one Clooney is toying with masterfully - rather than choosing to ignore. She proves herself to be infinitely smarter than anyone who worries that clothes and harrowing cases of human rights abuses can't be talked about in the same paragraph, because what she wears is a tool for widening the scope of interest in what she does. The choice of a vintage Dior skirt suit or a Gucci dress might be the hook in but while we're there looking at that picture, we'll learn about the plight of those victims she's passionately defending. Besides, what if Clooney happens to be a woman who both appreciates the bold statement-making abilities of a daffodil-yellow Bottega Veneta dress and coat but is also professionally and personally concerned about the plight of young women like Nadia Murad, the Yazidi woman she represents captured and raped by Isil in Iraq in 2014? The two interests are not mutually exclusive. And to suggest they are isn't just sexist - it's undermining an industry that brings in £28 billion a year to the UK economy alone.  That's a sentiment that led to British Vogue’s editor Alexandra Shulman commissioning the Real Issue of Vogue - an issue free of models. “I feel strongly that women who are in positions of authority or power, or who work in professions should be able to indulge their interest in clothes and fashion without it seeming frivolous or that they don't care about their jobs enough,” she told The Telegraph  at the time. "In this country there is still a stigma attached to clearly enjoying how you look and experimenting with it if you are a woman in the public eye and not in the fashion or entertainment business.” Of course, Clooney is much more than a fashion plate (breaking news: all women who love fashion are) but let's not dismiss the immense influence of her personal brand of power dressing. She knows what she's doing as she strides to speak to ambassadors in a pair of £780 heels; let's not patronize her by pretending otherwise.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Identical twins are a rare and celebrated commodity in fashion, as the teenage Bell sisters found when they started their career three years ago. But what happened when one of them shaved off all her hair?  Sisters Ruth and May Bell were just regular jobbing models until Ruth shaved her head.  The identical twins were having dinner in London one evening in June this year when Ruth went outside to take a call from their management agency, Elite. When she returned, she told her sister, 'They want me to do an Alexander McQueen campaign.’  'I said, “That’s brilliant,’’’ remembers May, who is immediately identifiable as the more sanguine of the two 19-year-olds. 'And then she said, “They want me to shave my head.’’’ In December the Bell sisters will have been modelling together for three years. Slender, fair and blond, with eyes that can look as curious as sea creatures within the delicate structures of their pale faces, they were spotted, aged 16, at Lakeside shopping centre in Essex by a scout from Elite.  Twin beauties are a find in fashion. Pretty times two, those shared genes can lend a powerful beauty or eeriness to a photograph.  But when Elite entered the twins into its 2013 national modelling competition to see how they would fare, it was May alone who scooped the top prize, securing her the nomenclature 'Baby Kate Moss’ from the blog The Fashion Spot, and a two-week trip to China. 'May’s better at walking than me,’ explains Ruth cheerfully, as the two sit alongside each other amid the minimalist gloss of their agency boardroom. 'I tended to fall over then.’ May wears dresses; Ruth wears jeans. On the face of it, at least, May comes across as the grown-up –thoughtful, considered. Ruth is the guileless tomboy – 'or actually, just a boy’ as she puts it. Born in Dover, Kent, they live down the coast now in Deal, with their father, an accountant, and mother, a civil servant. 'We’ve never lived so far from the sea that we can’t walk to it,’ says May.  They have a 21-year-old sister, who has just graduated in physics from Durham. 'She is the clever one,’ Ruth adds. At the time of the competition they were still doing their A-levels, so they modelled occasionally, 'for pocket money’. Ruth began modelling full- time last September, while May embarked on a short-lived university course in paramedic science. 'I was too young,’ she says. 'I saw a lot. Now when I’m on a job and it’s a long day, I always think, it could be worse, I could be on an ambulance.’ Between them they began clocking up a nice portfolio. Ellen von Unwerth shot them as pastoral Geminis for Italian Vogue; they scored big campaigns for Topshop and Urban Outfitters.  Catwalk jobs, May says, were more difficult. 'It’s very specific to have two people looking the same in one show. It can be something that people play on in photographs, but during fashion week if [casting agents] couldn’t pick both of us I think they thought, oh, we feel mean, so we won’t have either.’  That problem disappeared less than 48 hours after Ruth took the phone call and decided to comply with the photographer David Sims’s wishes and have her hair shaved to the bone. 'I wanted to do it.  I wanted to do the McQueen campaign. I wanted to work with David Sims and [the stylist] Joe McKenna. And I wanted a new haircut anyway,’ she says.  When you trade on your looks, shaving off your long blond assets is a big deal. Not only for the individual model, but also for their agency. 'Yes, it’s a conversation,’ says Vanessa Emilien, head of  special talent and PR at Elite. 'The company has to think about what the impact is going to be on the girl’s future work.’ There was also May to consider. 'She told me not to do it,’ Ruth says. 'No!’ counters May. 'I said, personally I wouldn’t do it. And I mean, it could have gone one of two ways, couldn’t it?’ It took 15 minutes for the hairdresser Paul Hanlon to plait Ruth’s hair and cut through the thick rope of it. Her agent was crying. 'She was panicking that she’d ruined my career,’ says Ruth.  She donated her old hair to the Prince’s Trust, to make wigs for children going through cancer treatment. May had done this previously when her hair was cut from hip to shoulder length. 'I thought that I could do something more useful than selling it for extensions,’ she says. Sims’s blurry, romantic Alexander McQueen autumn/winter 2015 campaign, with its shy, shorn Ruth, came out in August. The impact on its star was instant. 'I think I worked for two weeks straight, then I had a day off, and then I worked a bit more,’ she says.  Ruth went to New York Fashion Week but didn’t walk a single show as she had to keep flying off on one brilliant job after another, including a shoot for a Saint Laurent advertising campaign.  Her shaved head and small cherubic face made her 'unmissable’, as models.com pointed out, on the catwalks of Milan and Paris. She did Gucci and Versace and opened the shows at Iris van Herpen and Lanvin, where she set a different tone for the house, speeding down the runway in a white shirt and black trousers. 'Alber [Elbaz] called me Mini-Me because I was dressed like him,’ she says.  Meanwhile, May, although still working hard, (she’s starring in The Kooples’ autumn/winter campaign) didn’t do the international fashion weeks. What impact has Ruth’s haircut had on her? 'It has affected my work as well,’ she says. 'We don’t get as many twin things any more; I’ve lost that.
