 It is quite wonderful that the name of  a fashion label as steeped in luxury as Bottega Veneta translates simply to ‘Venetian shop’. In a world beset with brands clamouring for attention, it’s worth remembering that not everything needs bells and whistles swinging from its fasten-ings. For those happier to stroll confidently into  a room than to stand at the door waiting for  a red carpet to appear, the stealth luxury of Bottega Veneta – worn by Julia Roberts, Salma Hayek and Rose Byrne – is worth exploring. This year marks the 50th anniversary of  the brand, which began life in Vicenza, Italy, founded by Michele Taddei and Renzo Zengiaro with the simple remit to produce exquisitely made leather goods by skilled artisans. The  signature intrecciato, an intricate process whereby strips of leather are handwoven together, was developed at the label’s inception and is still in use today. It delivers a subtle form of branding as far away from logo-mania as it is possible to get. This has always been Bottega’s USP – in the 1970s its advertising coined the phrase, ‘When your own initials are enough’  – and the focus on pristine craft and quietly beautiful design has remained. Also celebrating this year is Tomas Maier, the German-born designer who has helmed the brand for 15 years. Maier was recruited by Tom Ford when Ford was creative director of the Gucci Group (now Kering), his precise eye and minimal approach an ideal match for Bottega. It has grown into a serious lifestyle contender (reaching €1 billion in sales in 2013), with fragrance, fine jewellery, luggage, eyewear and furniture, as well as men’s and women’s ready-to-wear collections, all under Maier’s aegis. In person, Maier is as understated as his work, dressed down in dark slacks and a long-sleeved top when we meet at the new Bottega Veneta Maison, a two-storey bleached-wood haven  featuring every element of the brand’s offering  on Rodeo Drive in LA. He is perhaps a little at odds with the Beverly Hills women swarming the store on its first day open: there were queues outside earlier, and at the cocktail party that launched the Maison, attendees were actively shopping, pulling woven bags off the shelves – not something I’ve witnessed at any other store launch, but then this is Rodeo Drive… After stints at Sonia Rykiel, Guy Laroche  and Hermès, and having started his own  eponymous line in 1997, Maier took on the  creative director role at Bottega in 2001, lured by the calibre of the workshops and the  promise of complete creative control. ‘This came to me when I was 43,’ he tells me. ‘It felt like the right time. I said to myself, “This is an opportunity that probably won’t come again in life.” The potential for the company was in the workshops – it’s all about the product and the way it is made. I saw the potential.’ His outlook on fashion is refreshingly straightforward. ‘I think on every level – clothes, leather goods, shoes – all these things are never meant to be for the moment,’ he says. ‘They’re meant to be products that last; that  you probably use for a certain time and then  put to rest for a while, and then you bring them back out and they’re even better because they’re no longer attainable – it makes them more desirable.’ It is this philosophy of timelessness that makes Maier’s work covetable for anyone sensible enough to want an investment of hundreds, if not thousands of pounds to promise longevity. Natalie Kingham, buying director at matchesfashion.com, attests that ‘the aesthetic appeals to a woman whose style is minimal and polished, who favours quality fabric and the best cuts. Loyal customers return for luxe wardrobe staples that they can wear off-duty and to the office.’ Maier reels off the practical details that ensure this. ‘I’m very concerned with the weight of something,’ he says. ‘If I don’t need  a lining, I will never use a lining. To line  something, for me, is very old-fashioned; I like products that have a single layer.  ‘I like pockets for women, always. A woman should never be without a pocket – even in  an evening dress. It’s a horror,’ he adds, his expression slightly aghast. ‘I like clothes that work for you, and that you can manipulate.’ For a designer, he has a hearteningly practical attitude to getting dressed – essentially the end point of all fashion, and yet so often not treated as such. ‘The most important thing  a woman needs to know about herself is  proportion. There’s a question of proportion and colour. One has to figure out what colour one feels good in, and what colour is better to stay away from. With proportion – what works for me and makes me feel good, and what doesn’t look right.’  Maier believes the crux of style is cracking your individual codes – ‘Do I look better in  trousers? All women who went down in history with great style were women who figured out what worked for them. I think this is how you come over as a great [dresser], when you stick to it. I love that more than anything, when you’ve figured out your hairstyle and then have that style all your life. Women who have a precise look feel more authentic.’ His eye was honed early. Born in 1957 in Pforzheim to creative parents – his father was an architect – Maier attended a Waldorf school, where imagination was particularly valued, throughout his childhood. ‘It was pretty clear when I was a kid that I liked design and being in the environment of my father’s [work],’  he says. Wanting to move on from small-town life, he was attracted to fashion as an escape route. He studied at the prestigious Chambre Syndicale de la Haute Couture in Paris, where he stayed to live and work for 25 years. His robust approach to fashion is suited to his now somewhat peripatetic lifestyle. While he is effectively based in the unlikely style centre of Florida, he travels extensively. ‘I have three studios,’ he explains, ‘in Milan, New York and Florida. Six months of the year I’m based in Palm Beach, Florida; for the other six months I’m travelling between Italy and New York. I’m always somewhere else.  ‘It suits me – I set it up like that. I like to be  in different places. I get tired of a place after  a while – it’s too much of a routine. I move on, go to another place, and it’s a different life.’ The appeal of Florida, where he resides with his partner, Andrew Preston, and their two pet chihuahuas, is ‘being outdoors, it’s very quiet. It’s good for working, it’s very concentrated.  I like that when I stop working I can be outside. I’m not locked up.’ With his design team in Milan, he is, he thinks, ‘pretty cool as a boss. I give people a lot of time.’ Affording a glimpse of his exacting nature, he explains, ‘When we work it’s very intense and you better be listening, as there’s  a lot going on. There’s a lot of information in  a very short time. Then I don’t see people for two or four weeks, so there’s a lot of time to process what has been talked about.’ In the autumn/winter 2016 collection, the idea behind Bottega Veneta is clear: the pieces form a perfect ode to simple yet striking clothing. Beautifully tailored black cashmere coats worn with elegantly loose black slacks and knitwear; heritage tweed and full skirts; splashes of leopard print and cool cream  trouser suits, offer something for the grown- up style connoisseur. ‘I’m not talking to a girl who’s 16 or 18, so let’s try to make clothes for the women who buy them. It’s probably more like 30 onwards,’ he muses of the women who wear his work. ‘It’s a serious luxury customer.’ Of the collection, he says, ‘I always like sweaters and skirts. I always love dresses for women. You know, us men, we’re so jealous that women can just dress with one single garment. It  seems like a dream. We have to club together all this stuff. [A dress] is so minimalist – I like single items.’ The Bottega Veneta anniversary show at last month’s Milan Fashion Week was a tribute to the house and its craftspeople, who were invited into the new, grand show venue,  the Accademia di Belle Arti di Brera, where models snaked through hallways lined with classical artworks. In a sign that even this  most traditional label is moving with the  times, Maier combined his men’s and women’s collections in this show – instead of showing  a separate collection during the city’s men’s fashion week. ‘The whole thing about shows,’ he explains, shaking his head, ‘it’s too much. Maybe it’s nice to have [only] two shows a  year. I don’t need all these shows, and I don’t think anybody needs too many shows. It’s  a bore. Too much in your face,’ he continues, showing pragmatism from which other designers could learn. And while the expansion of the brand continues, with another Maison to follow in New York next year, in the same vein as the new LA base, it will remain reassuringly expensive and exclusive. Maier believes the luxury feeding frenzy that seems to have taken over the world is ‘an overdose. They will look back at this period, the late 1990s and the 2000s, and will realise that this frenzy of opening stores  corresponded to a time. People were overly ambitious. It’s not the right approach. We have 240-plus stores. That’s plenty.’ He knows that there is nothing special and rarefied about  having your product hawked on every street corner in every town. This isn’t just any old Venetian shop, after all.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge is now, we can all agree, a pro in the royal dressing stakes. For her increasingly regular royal engagements, she strikes a careful balance between introducing new pieces, whether by designers she's never worn before or old faithfuls like Alexander McQueen or L.K Bennett, and reviving favourite looks from past appearances. This means that she has become both famously 'thrifty' but also noted for her glamour and support of British design names. But there are other more subtle elements which signify the Duchess's style prowess. Today, Kate visited two Action for Children projects in Wales where she learnt about the support the charity - of which she has recently become patron - offers young people in need. She opted for a neat burgundy skirt suit by Paule Ka. She first wore the look by the French ready-to-wear label back in 2012 and today paired it with black tights and knee-high boots.  But it's the Duchess's black polo neck jumper which she layered underneath the nipped-waist jacket that was today's most noteworthy outfit addition. It marks the third time this year alone that Kate has worn this staple piece for a public engagement. Just last week, on Valentine's Day, she visited RAF Wittering to spend the day with air cadets and wore black skinny jeans, a military-look red blazer by Philosophy di Lorenzo Serafini and a black polo neck while on a chilly January Sunday morning she wrapped up warm in a puffa jacket from ski brand Perfect Moment and, you guessed it, a black rollneck.  Kate's nifty use of the black turtleneck goes back even further though. On Christmas Day, she layered her burgundy Hobbs trench coat over one; and for a visit to a women's project in Gloucester late in 2016, she paired a tweed Dolce and Gabbana skirt with one.  Why does a polo neck make such a useful addition to Kate's royal wardrobe? It's brilliant for keeping warm during chilly walkabouts without the need to resort to a scarf which may not look as good in photographs. The sleek silhouette keeps things uncomplicated so is an excellent foil to bright colours or statement pieces. A polo neck also feels elegant but serious, which is just the mood to strike when you're one of the most glamorous women in the world visiting a place where the atmosphere needs to stay sobre, hence its usefulness for charity and church-related outings.  Much of the above also applies to those of us more likely to be contemplating dressing for the office than for a royal engagement. A good stock of polo necks, be they in black or other colours, will become your saviours on a chilly day for layering underneath shirts or jumpers, while they also look excellent underneath dresses. Top tip: give your summery numbers longevity into autumn or from spring-time by wearing a white polo neck underneath.  For such a useful and seemingly simple piece, the polo neck has a rather illustrious history. Its beginnings were humble, being used mostly as a practical cover-up. But during the 20th century it became a favourite of the intellectual elite. The French philosopher Michel Foucault was renowned for his love of a white jersey version. In the 1960s, the Beatnik look spawned a generation of black polo neck fans with everyone from The Beatles to Audrey Hepburn lending them iconic status. The most recent proponent of the black polo neck was Apple's Steve Jobs who was never seen in anything other than his custom-made Issey Miyake turtlenecks and jeans.  While the Duchess's black polo neck is as yet unidentified - in a way, part of the beauty of it - there are a few key brands which you should turn to build up your arsenal. At the affordable end of the market, ASOS often do excellent multi-packs of polo necks and always have well-fitting, refined versions like this £18 style in stock. Uniqlo though really should be your one-stop polo neck shop. Their Heattech range offers fine but cosy options such as this - currently on sale for £9.90 - while in-store their merino offering comes in an array of great neutrals. For something a little slouchier, head to Marks and Spencer's menswear department for cashmere and merino styles which are well-cut and brilliantly made. Wolford's Colorado polo neck bodysuits are the ultimate for seamless layering. And if you can afford to invest then Balenciaga, The Row and ACNE are all renowned for their mastery of the turtle neck.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  A feminist sweatshirt worn and subsequently manufactured by model-turned-actress Cara Delevingne is causing a copyright furore online. The minimalist design, which bears the slogan ‘The Future is Female’, is being sold by the 23-year-old for $40 via represent.com and is a carbon copy of a top recently bought by Delevingne’s girlfriend, singer Annie Clark. Clark bought two slogan tops – one for herself and one for Cara - from a Los Angeles-based design studio and feminist community centre called Otherwild. Otherwild co-founder Rachel Berks got the inspiration for the top after seeing a photo from 1975 of Alix Dobkin wearing a t-shirt bearing the slogan on the lesbian feminist Instagram account @h_e_r_s_t_o_r_y. The photo was taken by Dobkin’s then-girlfriend, photographer Liza Cowan. The t-shirt was made to raise funds for Labyris Books, the first women's bookshop in New York City, which opened in 1972. Otherwild’s Berks obtained permission to recreate the t-shirt and was delighted to sell one to Clark; demand for the top reached fever pitch when Delevingne was photographed proudly wearing hers. Articles in the New York Times and i-D magazine ensued, spotlighting the frenzy. But Berks has called out Delevingne on Instagram for copying her design, branding the move “indefensible”. She wrote: “Otherwild's redesign and reissue of the FIF tees and buttons is protected under copyright law, which mandates that any reproduction of an existing known public work must be altered at least 20% from the original.” Berks explains how Delevingne could have chosen to wholesale her tops, of which she donates 25 per cent of the proceeds to US charity Planned Parenthood. She adds: “Delevingne could also choose not to wholesale from Otherwild and create her own design of the slogan on clothing to sell. But Delevingne's choice to lift and manufacture Otherwild's design, claiming it as her own to sell with an undisclosed charitable offering, is indefensible.” Delevingne announced her move to sell her own slogan tops to her 23.5 million Instagram followers on December 7 with the message: “A lot of you have been asking for one of these – so I decided to put them up for sale, with proceeds going to Girl Up !” She has sold over 1,200 so far and is donating an unspecified amount from sales to Girl Up, the United Nations Foundation’s adolescent girl campaign, which promotes the health, safety, and education of girls in developing countries. Delevingne clearly states that the design is: “A recreation of the original shirt worn by Alix Dobkin in 1975 in a photograph by Liza Cowan” but omits any mention of Otherwild. Her post on the social networking site has garnered almost 7,000 comments, ranging from many users calling for the British model to collaborate with Otherwild, to others stating their neither Delevingne nor Otherwild own the rights to the slogan. She responded to the comments by writing: “I did not steal anything, they did not create the slogan.” Berks is clearly miffed at the timing and similarities between hers and Delevingne’s design. “Her actions ironically counter the very message of the slogan ‘The Future Is Female’, and it's confounding that she would do this to a small queer feminist-owned business after purchasing the product from us just a few weeks ago,” she wrote on the Otherwild Instagram account. Representatives for Delevingne have been contacted for comment.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  "There’s no doubt that Ms. Trump has a second job right now,"  U.S District judge Katherine Forrest said on Tuesday, her words laced with understatement. Forrest was referring to the ongoing federal court case between Marc Fisher Holdings LLC, the company Ivanka Trump partnered with to launch her eponymous shoe collection, and Aquazzura Italia SRL, the Italian shoe company which has accused Trump of copying its designs.   In the latest twist to the ongoing saga, the First Daughter’s lawyer Darren Saunders has claimed that "she was not involved in the design, promotion or sale of the shoe" and therefore cannot be made to testify in the copying case.   The row centres around Aquazurra’s £490 ‘Wild Thing’ sandals with their pin-thin heels, fringed detailing and pom-pom finished laces and Ivanka Trump’s $87 Hettie designs - with their pin-thin heels, fringed detailing and pom-pom finished laces. According to Bloomberg, Aquazzura lawyer John Margiotta complained that: "We are having trouble scheduling Ivanka Trump’s deposition. On Friday, we were notified that they are not in fact willing to produce Ms. Trump at all." Of course, since Donald Trump became President, Ivanka Trump the brand and Ivanka Trump the person have become, in theory, two entirely different things. Whereas Ivanka once made her life as a working mother and businesswoman part of the inspirational messaging of her own label, using Instagram- and the hashtag #womenwhowork- to show herself wearing her designs while juggling the demands of work and home, she has had to distance herself from being so forthright about that connection since her father took political office, and she herself became an adviser and moved to Washington. She handed over the running of the business to its president, Abigail Klem, and its financial matters are in a trust which is under the management of her husband Jared Kushner’s relatives. And yet, 35 year-old Trump has still been proudly wearing pieces from her eponymous collection during the numerous tours and engagements which she has appeared at during her time as First Daughter. Just this week, she carried her own label ‘Greenwich’ bag as she accompanied her father to Wisconsin, she frequently wears Ivanka Trump strappy sandals or simple pumps with statement dresses and in Israel in May, she finished off the black and navy look which she wore to visit Jerusalem’s West Wall with jewellery from her collection. It all adds up to a suggestion that Ivanka Trump is still very much an unofficial ambassador. Recently, she has also taken time out of her political schedule to promote her book, Women Who Work, which may not necessarily be linked directly to her fashion collection but nevertheless amps up her public image even more. So how does all this relate to the Aquazurra case? Back to Saunders’ claim that Ivanka wasn’t involved in the "design, promotion or sale of the shoe". Before November last year, Trump claimed to be dedicated to every aspect of her brand and has proven her loyalty by continuing to wear (and effectively promote) her label’s designs at a time when she is one of the most famous and photographed women in the world. Now she is expecting to be seen as removed from the brand's interests. But whether the legal system allows her to get away with that remains to be seen.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  As a fashion journalist, I find there is nothing more satisfying than a reliably well-dressed celebrity - and Gwyneth Paltrow, who turns 45 today, is one of them.  Save for a temporary blip some years ago (more on that later), the actress has maintained a stellar red carpet record throughout her career. Remarkably, even looking back at her first public appearances in the mid-Nineties (when she was engaged to Brad Pitt) throws up some fashion gems - namely a red velvet Gucci trouser suit worn to the 1996 MTV Awards that would look just as good today as it did then. Sure, with a body honed by Tracey Anderson and years of following a macrobiotic diet (nope, still don't know what that really means...), crystal clear Hollywood skin and blonde locks that never look less than glossy, it would be easy to assume that she'd look good in sack. And she probably would. But she looks better than good - she looks amazing. So, what's her secret? Paltrow has benefited enormously from the era of the ‘uber stylist’; stylists that have become well-known in their own right for dressing the great and good of Hollywood. She began working with Elizabeth Saltzman, a former Fashion Editor for Vanity Fair and US Vogue, in 2007, after a run of ill-received outfits. “Two that come to mind are looks I wore to the Oscars in 2000 and 2002,” she reminisced via her lifestyle site Goop in 2013. “The first is the Calvin Klein. It’s an okay dress but not Oscars material. I chose it because I wanted to disappear that year. Also, the goth Alexander McQueen I wore a few years later. There were a few issues; I still love the dress itself but I should have worn a bra and I should have just had simple beachy hair and less makeup. Then, it would have worked as I wanted it to - a little bit of punk at the Oscars.” She’d lost her fashion mojo and Saltzman helped her rediscover it. Both looks were a fall from fashion grace after the much-lauded, now-iconic candyfloss pink Ralph Lauren gown she had worn to the 1999 ceremony, where she picked up the Best Actress Oscar for her role in Shakespeare In Love. That dress had secured her a permanent place in the countless ‘Greatest Oscars Dresses Of All Time’ lists that populate the internet each year ahead of the annual event. But thirteen years later, and with Saltzman in her corner, she was back and secured another spot on those same charts thanks to a white caped Tom Ford gown. “Knowing what a risk that was – it didn’t have a sequin or a pouf, it had a cape – I wrote all the worst headlines that could possibly come,” Saltzman told The Telegraph in April this year. “I didn’t have a back-up dress, there was no other fitting. But that’s been remembered every year since; every Oscars, I turn on to watch E! while we’re getting everyone else ready, and it always comes up.” The duo did it again at this year's Met Gala. They commissioned a simple white sequined sheath dress by Calvin Klein that echoed one of Paltrow's earliest fashion triumphs - a silk slip dress by the same designer, worn to the same event in 1995. It was a fitting full circle moment that saw the actress outshine many of the 25-years-younger attendees.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  We now have proof that Kate Moss has always had supermodel star power, as a set of rare early photos that have recently gone on sale serve to reveal. The images, by fine art and portrait photographer Stephanie Pfrieder Stylander, star a then 18-year old Moss in her very first US fashion editorial back in 1992. Then a relative unknown, Moss’s now-iconic waifish features are in full display in the shoot for Harper’s Bazaar Italy, as she plays one half of a couple in love on a New York tourist trip, her beau played by Swedish model Marcus Schenkenberg (he of the chiselled jaw and Calvin Klein ads fame). Against a backdrop of famous New York sights, including the city skyline, the subway and the back seat of a yellow taxi, the rookie Kate Moss poses in a selection of outfits that foreshadow her ascent to style icon status, with a glossy pair of black sunglasses and a leopard print mac, both eerily reminiscent of the supermodel’s future fashion picks. The photographs, on sale at Pfriender Stylander's website, range in price from $1,250 to $5,000 for the predominantly black and white prints, some of which have been treated with dots and colour for a pop-art feel, as in the original editorial. While Pfriender Stylander and Moss’s model agent clearly saw something in the Croydon-born beauty, they couldn’t possibly have predicted how big she would become.  "In our house it's Halloween all year round," Heidi Klum once told People. With an Oscar-winning make-up artist and prosthetics whizzes on speed dial, the mother-of-four means serious business when it comes to her spine-chilling fancy dress costumes. This year was no exception for the supermodel. She promised fans her outfit would be one of her "most intense" costumes to date and she didn't disappoint. Here's a look back at her some of her most frightful and dramatic personas from years gone by - from a robot, to Jessica Rabbit, to a wrinkle-covered granny... The model and television personality went with a Shrek theme this year. While she looked a spitting image of Princess Fiona, her boyfriend was transformed into Shrek for her 19th annual Halloween party at Lavo New York on Wednesday. Fictional character Jessica Rabbit was Klum's muse for the 2015 holiday. To get the voluptuous figure the model spent days prior to the party in a prosthetics lab, leading her Instagram following to suspect she might be dressing up as curvaceous Kim Kardashian. In 2014 the supermodel transformed into a butterfly - a gigantic one, incorporating huge rainbow-hued wings and mesmerising bug eyes. For her make-under Klum was blessed with grey hair, lashings of wrinkles and pigmented skin. The German model, who hosted her annual bash at New York's Marquee nightclub, topped off her look with a bouclé skirt suit, pearls and a walking stick.  Klum's costume plans were thwarted in 2012 when Hurricane Sandy hit America's East Coast. Instead of letting her Cleopatra-inspired costume go to waste, the model changed the date to December 1 and had an extra month to perfect her look. Oscar and Emmy-winning make-up artist, Bill Corso, transformed the model's face with hundreds of carefully placed crystals, highlighting her cheeks, lips and the bridge of her nose. Talk about razzle dazzle. Covered head-to-toe in simian-like hair, Klum even secured a pair of prosthetic monkey breasts for her ape evolution in 2011. Heidi's husband of seven years, Seal, made for a menacing beau by her side. There's nothing more eerie than wheeling into your own Halloween party on an autopsy table. With two blood-splattered doctors in tow, Klum told the MailOnline of her look: "It's kind of like a dead body with the first layer of skin ripped off. It's basically like me naked." Klum's naked self was achieved by much airbrushing on top of a basic map of a dead body, drawn upon her skin and the skull cap atop her head. Add some red contact lenses and rotting teeth and bingo! Dead as a doornail. All Hallow's Eve 2010 saw Klum transform herself rather literally into a Transformer. The mother-of-four chose red and purple as her superhero colours and danced the night away (or not) in a pair of hydraulic crane shoes. In contrast to his 8ft alien transformer wife, Seal played the silver-enrobed muscle man. Of their matching costumes, Klum promised to recreate the looks for their children, who love superheroes, at a later date. Reflecting on her crow costume, Klum revealed that the beak was actually rather cumbersome and made drinking most difficult. The wings also caused the 41-year-old and then-partner, Seal, problems in the car en route to the party venue. Picture Hindu goddess Kali and you'll probably recall her multiple colourful arms. You probably won't envisage a bonus arm belt with bloody hands hanging off it, or a couple of decapitated heads clasped in her finger tips. Such was a blue-dipped Klum's interpretation of Kali in 2008. You can't blame the Halloween enthusiast for donning a catsuit once in her costume career. Good old Klum eschewed the sexy Catwoman vibe in favour of a velveteen kitty, complete with collar, whiskers and subtle feline fangs. Costume collaborator Martin Izquierdo recalls that the 2006 sinful apple was the most taxing costume of Klum's to create. Why? Because the German beauty was heavily pregnant at the time. Accompanying the bulbous, bloody apple - plus snake - to the spooky shindig was Seal, moonlighting as a buxom, blond Eve. Who knew vampires enjoyed burlesque fashion? With a bleeding heart pinned like a rosette on her corset and a cobweb cape trailing behind her, an ultra-curly Klum put other revellers to shame. Heidi's date for Halloween in 2004 was a, erm, skeleton, which enjoyed a piggy-back on the model for the duration of the evening. The model, herself, chose a red witch as her guise and navigated her way around the soirée with a mammoth wooden broom to keep her patent heeled boots steady. Touching down at the 2003 haunted Halloween bash was a gold space alien with metallic armour and thick braids bursting out of her golden helmet. By golly, doesn't Betty Boop look ferocious! Bedecked in blingtastic fake jewels, Heidi vamped up the poor caricature of a Jazz Age flapper to within an inch of her flapper life. Klum kicked off her infamous Halloween career with a bang as a bloodied version of 11th-century Anglo-Saxon noblewoman, Lady Godiva. Rocking up to the 2001 party on horseback, in a latex catsuit and luminous, lengthy white wig, Klum stamped herself a serious spooky contender. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. The park became a state of mind. The park became my strength. The park is what made me who I am. Where's your park?" "When I'm working and rehearsing I live in my work out clothes but I didn't feel there was an athletic brand that spoke to me," Beyoncé said in a release. "My goal with Ivy Park is to push the boundaries of athletic wear to support and inspire women who understand that beauty is more than your physical appearance. True beauty is in the health of our minds, hearts and bodies. I know that when I feel physically strong, I am mentally strong and I wanted to create a brand that made other women fel the same way." Now we can get even more of Beyoncé on Instagram, as she has set up a new designated profile for her label, @weareivypark.  So Alexandra Shulman is resigning from her role as Editor-in-chief of British Vogue and while tributes have been paid to her agenda-setting editorship, thoughts are inevitably turning to the top job which she now leaves vacant and who might move into her pristine white office at Vogue House. Shulman's departure will certainly cause seismic change. Her resignation is a turning point for the publication as it faces a chance to carve out a new direction in an ever-changing fashion magazine environment so it's understandable that there was little chance of any other topic being the subject of insider water cooler chatter today. Just a few of the questions in the new editor's in-tray: How do you continue to attract younger readers to buy the magazine when they've grown up more inclined to head online? How does the website relate to the magazine- and what should its identity be? Who are the people and what is the look which will define a new generation of Vogue? Is Kate Moss still your go-to cover woman?  It's a job which countless girls might dream of- as the Devil Wears Prada myth goes- but there's really only a small group of editors and insiders with the credentials to take on the task.   WWD, one of the fashion industry's most-trusted news sources, is already tipping Katie Grand as a favourite to take over from Shulman. Grand founded LOVE - a magazine which expertly blends the mainstream with the avant-garde- in 2009 and has seen it grow into the kind of publication which regularly creates headlines with its covers, whether that's by showing Cara Delevingne and Kendall Jenner locked in an embrace or Kate Moss in the bath.  Grand's knack for capturing (and, arguably, creating) the zeitgeist has proven digital impact too. Her LOVE Advent calendar initiative attracted 84 millions page views to the magazine's website last December, with the likes of Bella Hadid, Emily Ratajkowski and Kim Kardashian starring in videos which were catnip to their vast social media audiences.   Alongside her work at LOVE, Grand styles shows for designers including Louis Vuitton, Gucci and Prada. While those close relationships with major brands could prove fruitful in an ever-more competitive commercial environment, WWD's Samantha Conti points out that this could be a stumbling block to Grand's appointment. "Condé famously frowns on outside, commercial freelance work, and especially by the editor of such a high-profile title," Conti says. "The question remains whether Grand would even want to relinquish her lucrative fashion gigs for the Vogue one." Another fashion pioneer who could breathe new ideas into Vogue is Dame Natalie Massenet, the outgoing chairman of the British Fashion Council and founder of online designer shopping mecca Net-a-Porter. She began her career in glossy magazines, but a sixth sense that we'd soon all be clamouring to buy our Jimmy Choos from the convenience of our sofas or offices led her to found the shopping destination which she eventually sold, netting a $111 million fortune in the process.   Massenet would undoubtedly have plenty of ideas for diversifying Vogue- as Shulman did with her Vogue Festival- and last year's launch of Style.com is proof that Conde Nast wants to compete in the online commerce market of which Massenet is the fairy Godmother. She has long been mooted as a successor to US Vogue's Anna Wintour but might she keep the British Vogue seat warm for a few years first?  There's also a coterie of Vogue insiders who could take on the challenge, having witnessed Shulman doing it first hand. Chief among them is  deputy editor Emily Sheffield will have been working at the publication for over 11 years when the Editor-in-chief position opens in June. Sheffield has also proven herself to be unafraid of speaking out so could happily pick up the mantle of calling the fashion industry to account over issues like diversity and sizing, as Shulman has done.  Last July, she wrote an impassioned defence of her brother-in-law, David Cameron after his post-Brexit resignation, while her Twitter feed shows that she's just as keen to offer up opinions on politics as kitten heels.  Another similarity with Shulman is Sheffield's very British network of connections (her sister is Samantha Cameron) which would give her the nous to continue the magazine's distinct identity within the global portfolio of Vogue publications. The recent Vogue documentary did, however, suggest that Shulman and Sheffield are by no means peas in a pod; some scenes showed the two disagreeing about which cover options they preferred.  Meanwhile, Lucy Yeomans (ultra glossy editor of Porter magazine), Nicola Jeal ( the powerhouse editor whose CV includes Elle, The Observer and The Times),  Justine Picardie (editor of rival publication Harper's Bazaar) and Lisa Armstrong (The Telegraph's very own fashion director) have also been mentioned among the names which might be on Conde Nast's list.  Who might present a more controversial choice? There's Eva Chen, the Head of Fashion at Instagram who was a rising editor star before that at Lucky and Teen Vogue and has done wonders to make fashion more accessible thanks to her social media prowess. She's married to an Englishman so a move to London wouldn't be such a ridiculous thought. But rumours that Anna Wintour might make a return to the UK are about as fanciful as fleeces making a fashion comeback.         © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The Duchess of Cambridge has earned herself a reputation for being unafraid to recycle her favourite looks, often bringing back favourite pieces from outfits gone by and staying true to beloved staples like her black skinny jeans and L.K Bennett accessories. But today, the Duchess confirmed that she's still committed to keeping the looks that work by wearing one of her oldest 'public role' outfits, a red Luisa Spagnoli suit which was first seen in February 2011 when the then-Kate Middleton and Prince William visited St Andrew's University (the place where they met) just months before their wedding.  Almost six years on, the two-piece looked as elegant as ever as the Duchess kicked off Children's Mental Health Week by giving a speech during assembly at Mitchell Brook Primary School in London this morning. With its ladylike peplum waist and round collar detail, the suit has a timeless Jackie Kennedy quality which means it looks just as right now as it did in the pre-Duchess days. For the suit's first outing, Kate paired it with knee-high-suede boots by Aquatalia, black tights and a polo neck jumper- a practical combination which perhaps lacked the polish which she has since mastered. For today's take, the Duchess opted for a glossy blow-dry, nude tights and black suede heels. All the occasions when Kate has worn the red suit The suit, which originally cost £465, hasn't been hiding away in the Duchess's wardrobe for the past six years though. She is said to have chosen it for that particular occassion because there had been an earthquake in New Zealand around the same time she had first worn the ensemble and it fittingly also reflected the colours of the district of Canterbury, the South Island region which the royal couple were visiting- a signature diplomatic dressing move. The third time that Kate was seen in her Luisa Spagnoli was in a portrait to mark her becoming patron of the Air Cadets in December 2015.  It's buys like these which we can likely expect to see the Duchess wearing on-and-off for years to come. It will be some time before we know whether Kate will keep such a long-running archive of outfits, but her carefully classic style indicates that she purchases with longevity in mind. We know that she customised a dress by Anita Dongre which she wore to play cricket during a tour of India last year by chopping a few inches off the hem. Similarly, it seems like the Duchess and her PA and wardrobe adviser Natasha Archer may have altered the Luisa Spagnoli suit as the pencil skirt appears to be a couple of inches longer than when it was first seen in 2011, perhaps updating it to be more suitable for royal engagements.  The Duchess is known to create 'the Kate effect' with any brand which she patronises, but today's look proves that the phenomenon could also be a powerful reminder to make considered investments which can be worn years after they are first purchased.       © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  The festive novelty sweater is a style-free zone, right? Not this year. In the true spirit of Christmas, five top models and designers have paired up to create covetable designs to raise money for Save the Children. In a vast, whitewashed studio in north-west London, model Poppy Delevingne works through her poses for the photographer. Click, click, click. Doing dressed-down chic in dungarees over a sequinned black jumper, her platinum-blonde hair and berry-red lips make for megawatt glamour. But she’s not the only star of the show. Everywhere I look in the room there’s a famous fashion face. Dree Hemingway, great-granddaughter of Ernest, slouches on a sofa; Karen Elson sits having her make-up done, her russet hair in granny curlers; Henry Holland hangs out in a silk YSL shirt. Considering the levels of supermodel-dom in the room, I expected everyone to be rather more keyed up, but the atmosphere couldn’t be more laid-back. So there’s a slight delay, that’s fine; Dree is happy to kill the time dancing in unselfconscious circles to the pumping music… The reason for this calm? For all the fashion talent on show, this gathering has nothing to do with the exclusive world of catwalk shows and edgy haute couture. It’s about a charity – Save the Children – and it’s about Christmas jumpers. Hang on, fashion and Christmas jumpers don’t exactly go together. But as it turns out, they do. For this project, Save the Children and luxury online retailer Matches Fashion have brought together five of the world’s top models and five of its most celebrated designers to create a range of luxurious, desirable cashmere jumpers. Kate Moss and Bella Freud’s bears the slogan ‘Fairytale of New York’, referencing the bitter-sweet Christmas anthem by The Pogues. Poppy Delevingne and Christopher Kane’s black showstopper glitters with outsize sequins, like snowflakes falling in the dark. Meanwhile, Giles Deacon and Erin O’Connor’s brings a gothic edge to a demure, ladylike cut, and Henry Holland captures Dree Hemingway’s jeans-and-sneakers slacker cool with his ‘Jolly’ design. Finally, shoe designer Charlotte Dellal, of Charlotte Olympia, and Karen Elson have fun with a motif of a panther chewing savagely on a red stiletto heel. Each of the designs is clever, beautifully finished and, above all, highly wearable. All of the proceeds from sales of the jumpers, which cost £365 each, will go towards Save the Children’s ongoing projects to alleviate child poverty in Britain and across the globe, and to the charity’s current Child Refugee Crisis Appeal. ‘Given what’s going on at the moment and what happened tragically with the little [Syrian] boy [found drowned on a Turkish beach], it’s become even more important that we recognise children suffering in the world,’ says Natalie Kingham, buying director at Matches Fashion. Helena Wiltshire of Save the Children adds, ‘Our emergency work is constant. You can never predict these things, but you can pretty much predict there’s going to be something somewhere, so we are always ready.’ All of the models and designers involved talk about the fun they had working on their Christmas jumpers, but also with passion for the seriousness of the cause and the importance of the fashion world taking a stand. ‘Fashion is sometimes treated as being the tinsel on the top of the Christmas tree,’ says Karen Elson. ‘It can appear that we in fashion don’t give a damn about anything that is happening in the world, but I would beg to differ. The people I work with are all compassionate and really want to make a difference. People in the business, particularly the models, come from various different places in the world. So I think it’s really wonderful that Save the Children is trying to engage the fashion industry. If you can reach the kids who are into fashion and have them understand the situations that are happening in the world, then I think we’re doing a good job. So that’s what we’re trying to do.’ Kate Moss The iconic model has been at the heart of British fashion for almost 30 years. But her influence doesn’t end with glossy ads and fashion spreads; her signature rock-chick style has shaped the way we dress for over two decades. Kate says: ‘Bella is an incredible designer, and a dear friend, so it was fun creating a festive jumper with her. The fact that Save the Children helps children around the world is amazing and, with the other models and designers, we’re proving that fashion really can save lives.’ Bella Freud Bella launched her label in 1990 and has collaborated with some of the biggest names in fashion, including Biba, Jaeger and Barbour. Bella says: ‘I was trying to think of a good word or phrase to put on a Christmas jumper. But that made my mind go blank. And Kate said, “What about ‘Fairytale of New York?’” And that was instantly it. It’s such a poetic title, it’s romantic – andthen there’s Shane MacGowan, who is a great friend ours. It was typical of Kate to come up with the most brilliant phrase.’ Erin O’Connor Stalwart of the runways, Erin has modelled for everyone from Valentino to Versace, and Vivienne Westwood. She has a one-year-old son and is an ambassador for Save the Children. Erin says: ‘We were absolutely Christmas mad in our household. I have two sisters, and we have a huge Irish family, so we got lots of hilarious, itchy, wool jumpers sent over from Ireland. Now it’s become a tradition in our house: it’s illegal to appear on Christmas Day without your jumper. My dad looks just like Father Christmas. It’s too good. I’m normally an elf, and my son Albert has about three changes a day. ‘I loved working with Giles. For our jumper we took inspiration from his previous collection, so there are some cool gothic undertones going on, yet it still encompasses the spirit of Christmas. It’s quite romantic in a way. ‘Each trip I’ve made as a Save the Children ambassador has had a forceful impact; it stays with you forever. That’s why by doing something like this, we share the message so that everybody who sees it can help. It takes away that overwhelming, daunting feeling of thinking that you can’t do anything to help.’ Giles Deacon The designer has worked with Bottega Veneta and Gucci, among other labels, and in 2003 founded his own label, Giles. He recently launched a debut line for Debenhams, Giles/Edition. Giles says: ‘Erin is like the most extraordinary couture model that you could ever imagine, but with this fantastic Brummie sensibility and down-to-earthness. The combination makes her extraordinary and infectious. We didn’t want our jumper to be too Christmas. We’d just finished the autumn/winter collections and we’d done lots of crochet and embellishments, so it seemed a really good idea to put those on to the collar and cuffs. Erin came up with the colour combo, and it came out great. ‘When I was growing up, my family always had hilariously decorated Christmas socks. We’d all put tinsel and baubles on them. I think my mother will have some terrifying photos somewhere, which I should make sure she takes to the end of the garden and burns.’ Dree Hemingway Actress and model Dree is the great-granddaughter of Ernest and daughter of the actress Mariel Hemingway. She is the face of Chloé fragrance, and recently appeared in the film While We’re Young with Ben Stiller and Naomi Watts. Dree says: ‘I became involved with Save the Children because it’s vital to give kids a childhood, and I think a lot of kids are born into this world without that option. Henry really has fun with what he does, which is why I wanted to work with him. This jumper was about being simple and not too loud. We wanted something you could throw on every day.’ Henry Holland Henry launched his label in 2008. He now designs both women’s and men’s collections. He also presents Channel 4’s The Changing Room. Henry says: ‘Dree’s got a great sense of humour. She’s a ball of energy. In many ways she’s a bit anti-fashion and follows her own rules. We always used to wear our new pyjamas on Christmas Day and only take them off to get dressed for dinner.’ Poppy Delevingne Older sister of Cara, Poppy is a model and actress. She has been the face of Louis Vuitton and worked with Burberry and Chanel. She has just finished filming Knights of the Round Table: King Arthur, directed by Guy Ritchie, with Jude Law and David Beckham. Poppy says: ‘Christmas was always a big deal in the Delevingne household. There’d always be a ton of us and it would be mayhem. Me and my husband [James Cook] are very close to our families, but it does mean that we spend a lot of the year with them. When I was growing up, we were always wearing really weird things throughout the year. My sisters Cara, Chloe and I were allowed to wear what we wanted, and we’d definitely come up with some really bizarre outfit choices. Our design is kooky and cosy. It’s the perfect jumper to wear to the pub or a wine bar, but it’s also a showstopper. Cara and I are both now working in film. The charity wants to create an environment where all children have a shot at life, a shot at education and have their basic rights taken care of.’ Charlotte Dellal Charlotte launched her footwear and accessories label Charlotte Olympia in 2008.  The fashion world has been paying tribute Barry Kamen, the former model and stylist at the forefront of the Eighties Buffalo scene who died earlier this week at the age of 52. Alongside late stylist Ray Petri, and photographers Mark Lebon, Jamie Morgan, Roger Charity and Cameron McVey, Barry and his Levi’s model brother Nick helped define the look of the pioneering youth culture movement that changed the face of fashion. Barry and Nick became muses for Petri after meeting him in a clothes shop and the pair’s mixed heritage (Burmese, Dutch, Irish and English) – and unquestionable beauty – made them the poster boys for a generation tired of commercial fashion. “He [Petri] took these kids off the street and put them in front of the camera for the first time,” Kamen said of how he found fame. “A mixed-race boy is now the normal, quintessential, good-looking boy, but at the time it was shocking.” The “rude boys and rebels” style Petri created - perhaps best defined by oversize tailoring mixed with sportswear, and the nylon MA1 army surplus flight jacket and Levi’s 501s look - defined a decade, eventually filtering back into mainstream fashion, and is still much in evidence today. Kamen went on to become a stylist himself, collaborating with Vivienne Westwood and a pre-supermodel 14-year-old Naomi Campbell, and contributing regularly to The Face, Arena and i-D magazines. In later life he became an artist. As news of his untimely death spread this week, the fashion world payed tribute to Kamen on social media.  There's a certain irony that Amal Clooney - the human rights lawyer who would rather we all cared about the abuses going on in the Maldives more than her clothes - has become a pin-up for a modern working woman. But someone has to. Because aside from the fictional Alicia Florrick in The Good Wife and Scandal's Olivia Pope, there aren't many women in the public eye making work wear look appropriate yet interesting. So how does Amal achieve that classic, professional look - one that's unwavered by trends, but still manages to look fresh?  Amal knows that tailoring is key. It doesn’t matter whether Amal’s blazer is from Topshop or Dolce & Gabbana, it looks expensive because it fits her well. When buying a new jacket make sure it fits neatly on your shoulders (without pulling across the back) and narrows in on your actual waist. A local tailor (most dry cleaners offer alteration services) will be able to adjust styles that are slightly too large. A suit and open-neck blouse runs the risk of looking tired and one can easily feel uninspired by submitting to such a common work ‘look’. Try swapping your button-ups for a high-neck blouse, a tip employed by Amal to make her pinstripe suit look less corporate than it might do with a starched white shirt. Polka dots or florals might seem a little outré for male dominated work spaces, but in timeless hues they can still look right. When attempting a pattern, pare down all other accents on your outfit. Amal’s dotty dress works because her black shoes, tote and sunglasses fade into the background, rather than compete with the busy dress. The plum-shaped buttons on Amal’s bold red midi transform the dress into a statement piece. Remember the gold brooches the lawyer peppered her plain black coat with this winter too? Focusing on the smallest of outfit accents pays off and marks her out as a considered office dresser willing to go the extra mile to achieve a killer look. Nude shoes quite rightly make many a woman recoil. But done well, a skin-coloured heel can elongate the leg area and go perfectly with all skirts and dresses. Amal opts for a sandy suede pump, which does not pretend to be nude and relies on texture as its defining feature. A particularly feminine suit or dress cut can benefit from an edgy undercurrent. Check out Amal’s choice of nail colour with the below red suit. Near-black, a lacquer choice we would never guess for the prim and proper lawyer. Sometimes it pays to gently surprise. Hand’s up if your summer work wardrobe consists of the same suits worn without a blazer or sans tights? Amal’s pale suiting makes a case for smart seasonal ensembles that come into their own once the sun comes out and navy no longer looks on-point.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Attention everyone: a Grace Coddington film is on its way to the big screen. After her standout appearance in seminal fashion documentary The September Issue in 2011, a biopic of the flame-haired fashion insider’s life is in the works. The 74-year-old confirmed to Fashionista that the rights to her best-selling memoir, Grace, have been acquired by A24, the production company behind The Bling Ring, Ex Machina and Obvious Child. As the long-standing creative director of US Vogue, Coddington has set the tone for the evolution of fashion editorial, working with the biggest names in photography including Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, Norman Parkinson and Annie Leibovitz, but it was her surprise smash hit in The September Issue that launched her into the public consciousness. The fly-on-the-wall documentary delved into the arduous process behind the September issue of US Vogue, traditionally the most important of the year because of its vast number of pages. While it was expected that Anna Wintour would play a starring role, it was her right-hand woman who caught the camera’s eye, stealing the show by daring to stay true to her own vision in the face of commercial pressure, and answering back to the famously formidable editor-in-chief. The documentary transported Coddington from behind-the-scenes maestro to household name. In Grace, the Vogue head honcho recounts how people would stop her in the street, even mouthing “I love your work!” at her through the window of her nail salon when she was mid-manicure. Her striking look comprising an all-black outfit in contravention of Wintour’s ban on head-to-toe black, and a shock of flaming red hair, undimmed despite her advanced years, has even made her appearance a popular fashion Halloween costume - a mark of icon status if ever there was one. Soon after the film’s release came the publication of her memoirs that recount her journey from a rural upbringing on the tiny island of Anglesey, through a glamorous modelling career and two marriages, to obtaining one of the most influential positions in global fashion. After a slew of recent stunning fashion documentaries including Dior and I (2015) and Iris (2015) have whet the appetite for inside scoops on the industry, all we can do is await the cast announcements with bated breath.

The dress is not a new design from Emilia Wickstead, but one of her classic 100% wool day dresses. When the couple arrived in New Dehli they lay a wreath at the India Gate memorial in honour of the 70,000 Indian soldiers who died in World War One. Here the Duchess struggled with her Emilia Wickstead dress, which lifted in a gust of wind. Members of the royal family often have lead weights sewn into the hem of their skirts to prevent such a wardrobe malfunction. Stewart Parvin, who designs outfits for the Queen, has previously said of this trick: "I just pop a couple of weights into the hemline of her dresses and coats and it makes them hang beautifully. If there is a flap in the coat then I will sew in one on each side of the split to even it up. And sometimes if she is wearing a lightweight chiffon skirt I will sew in a smaller lead weight the size of a pea or even a length of chain." Central Saint Martins graduate Wickstead made a name for herself by making chic made-to-measure clothing for personal clients. “I saw a niche in the market where made-to-measure wasn’t being done in a modern, fresh way or in a short period of time,” she told The Telegraph. “Traditionally, bespoke orders take a very long time, but  I thought, ‘Here we are with all these fashion-forward ideas – why not?’ I did  it backwards.” As a fan of the 32-year-old New Zealand-born designer, Kate is in good company.  Samantha Cameron wore an Emilia Wickstead dress on the day her husband was elected PM, and Academy Award nominees Saoirse Ronan and Brie Larson  have both stepped out in her feminine looks. Wickstead, herself, describes her designs as ‘Classic with a twist. Like Martini with a twist.’ It is this timeless aesthetic that no doubt attracted the Duchess, and we wouldn't be surprised to see the designer’s dresses make another appearance on the 2016 royal tour.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Chiara Ferragni doesn’t do things by halves. She does them by the million. She has over 5 million Instagram followers, over 1 million Facebook ‘likes’. Her blog-turned-lifestyle website, The Blonde Salad, boasts 6 million monthly page views. Her revenue projection for 2015 is $9 million (about £6 million). Not bad for a 28-year-old fashion blogger. She started The Blonde Salad in 2009 (the moniker is courtesy of her hair colour and mixed-bag of interests) on the back of her significant Flickr following – she had been using the image-hosting site since 2007 to post her daily outfits. She, with the help of then-boyfriend Riccardo Pozzoli, found her footing in the then-relatively-unpopulated style blogging arena quickly and lucrative offers to partner with fashion brands such as Dior and Louis Vuitton soon began to flood in. Four years into studying - and three exams away from completing - an International Law degree at Milan’s Bocconi University, Ferragni decided to put all her focus onto the blossoming venture. It was worth it. The Blonde Salad is no longer an outfit-tracking, day-to-day log of her life, it’s a full-blown lifestyle site with its own editorial team. Ferragni herself is now considered one of the most influential figures in the industry, commanding thousands in appearance fees, never wearing the same outfit twice (yes, never) and constantly being photographed as she jets around the world. She’s no longer ‘just’ a blogger, she’s a digital entrepreneur. But it is a side-project that has seen her financial worth rocket; the Chiara Ferragni Collection shoe line. Started two-and-a-half years ago by Ferragni, Lorenzo Barindelli and Paolo Barletta, the range incorporates styles including glitter-caked skate shoes, to velvet smoking slippers emblazoned with emojis and biker boots. “When we started it was just a game,” Ferragni admits when we meet in London, where she is feting the brand’s first pop-up shop in Selfridges. “They were the shoes I wanted to create but there was no real idea behind it.” They’re much more than that now. Last year they accounted for 70 per cent of the reported £5 million revenue generated by Ferragni. The remaining 30 per cent came from The Blonde Salad website, its advertising and corresponding brand tie-ups. It is this impressive statistic that has cemented the willowy Italian as arguably the world’s most successful fashion blogger, and certainly the only one who has managed to translate a blog into a global, money-making brand. Now more of an artfully highlighted Uptown ‘bronde’ than a blonde, Ferragni resides in Los Angeles. She boasts a staff – or TBS Crew as she lovingly calls them - of 18, made up mostly of personal friends (despite breaking up in 2013, Pozzoli still runs the business side of things and the pair are still great friends). It is this, she says, that has allowed her to surpass her blogosphere colleagues. “I could have been like so many other bloggers or ‘influencers’ who just have their agent and are more like celebrities, but I’ve never wanted it to be only like that,” she says. “Of course, I still want that part in my life but I also wanted to create a brand.” In case you need further proof that she’s done just that, consider this. In last 12 months she’s become the first blogger to score a coveted Vogue cover, been the subject of a Harvard Business School case study, and been crowned one of the 30 most influential people under 30 by Forbes. She’s completely unphased by the recent ‘blogger backlash’ that’s’ swept the internet. When Australian blogger Essena O’Neill recently denounced not only her own social media presence as wholly false and incredibly misleading but those of many others, the blogger bubble looked frighteningly close to bursting. It’s all “part of the game”, says Ferragni. And it’s a game she’s winning, perhaps because of her so-positive-it-hurts mentality. “Of course, you decide which story you want to tell,” she says, “for me it’s been very authentic so sometimes I’m super happy and I post four pictures one after the other, sometimes I’m busy and I don’t, sometimes I’m sad and I post a sad picture.” In fact, she finds the less frequently she posts on social media, the more interested her followers are when she does. “I mean, maybe [the bubble will burst] but there will be something else,” she ponders. “As long as you’re ahead of a trend I think you’re going to be fine. You really have to have a multitasking mind that can switch form one thing to the other easily without too much focus on ‘oh I’m going to Instagram my life’. In a few years we might not still be into Instagram, but hopefully I’ll be into the next thing and have fun do it.” Indeed, she got into blogging long before it became oversaturated and when she started out Instagram didn’t even exist, so she knows how quickly things can change. The photo-sharing app has started a new breed of ‘social influencers’, she says, who have superseded bloggers, one of whom is her younger sister, 22-year-old Valentina. “She started an Instagram two years ago and she almost has 1 million followers and she doesn’t have a website or blog,” she explains. “She posts similar to what I post and she’s started getting her own projects because people like her style and like following her. So I think there is room for everyone as long as you have an alternative voice and you have something to say to the people.” This new kind of competitor doesn’t bother her though. “It gives you so much motivation, at least for me. Where other people can get jealous I feel like it’s amazing to see other people succeed as long as you want to do better,” she says with the confidence of someone who has, so far, bettered everyone in her field. It’s a confidence that has certainly come with success, but it's also thanks to a mini-epiphany she had three years ago. “I woke up one day and was like ‘I love what I’m doing and I’m super proud of what I’ve done so far’. I don’t want to care anymore, I just want to do it my way and people are probably going to be fine with that. Since that moment, since you really don’t care so much about what other people think, you are just so relieved and everything is just so much easier,” she says, again with only the gusto that someone who’s successfully achieved such a thing can. At 28 she’s accomplished more than she could have ever imagined and she wants to share her message: anything is possible. “Of course, you’re always going have people against you but sometimes it’s part of the game ... I don’t want to inspire people just to be bloggers, it can be in any area. As long as you want to take risks and are very passionate. I’ve always been very passionate about what I do, and I think it shows in what I do.” It certainly does. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  What to wear to hang out with a Prince for a few days in front of the world's media? It's not a style dilemma which many of us will ever have to face but should the occassion ever arise, we can now look to Rihanna for a masterclass.  This week, Prince Harry was joined on his tour of the Caribbean by the Bajan star who managed to achieve that trickiest of conundrums- staying true to one's personal style whilst also playing to the unspoken rules of the occassion. Rihanna  is renowned for her avant-garde style, unafraid to step out wearing just an baggy hoodie (by Vetements, of course), a lime green blazer or furry knee-high boots. All that means she's become a flag bearer for younger designers, often choosing to support emerging names by commissioning them to make clothes for her, although she's equally at home in established labels like Dior, Dolce and Gabbana and Gucci too.  When it came to spending a couple of days in the company of Harry, RiRi's looks were all cleverly very much 'her' but with a more grown-up, polished feel than many of her usual ensembles.  For her first encounter with the man now known as the boyfriend of Meghan Markle, Rihanna turned to Matthew Adams Dolan, a Massachusetts-born young designer whose oversized denim pieces she's worn numerous times before. She was meeting Harry at an event to mark 50 years since Barbados's independence but the dress-code was still low-key. Instead of opting for one of Dolan's more challenging silhouettes, Rihanna and stylist Jahleel Weaver settled on an asymetric chambray design with extra-long sleeves and a ruched waist which was appropriate but still had sufficient cool factor.  That evening Rihanna and Harry sat next to each other at a concert to celebrate the anniversary. While the Prince kept things smart but predictable in burgundy corduroys and a navy shirt, RiRi threw a perfectly judged curveball in a fabulously maximalist flowing patterned dress by Marni - the Italian brand which makes the conceptual, wearable. With its pleated skirt and balloon sleeves, it was an elevated version of just the sort of thing any stylish woman would want to waft around in when temperatures are hovering around 30 degrees. Rihanna paired hers with the strappy yet simple black heels which she so often favours but it would have looked just as good with easygoing flats. The next day, the pop star and the Prince joined forces to mark World Aids Day by sitting next to one another to take tests for HIV. It's a process which Harry has been through in public before, in a bid to raise awareness of the quick and simple procedure required. Rihanna opted for an idiosyncratic take on pulled-together daywear for the engagement, choosing a cotton shirt and high-waisted, wide-legged trousers by French designer Jacquemus. Suitably serious yet with no personal style sacrifice.  Jacquemus is one of the most exciting young designers working in Paris now and has become a fashion editor favourite of late, thanks to his clever cotton creations which are interesting but flattering- those trousers offer a modern spin on classic French elegance which has ageless appeal. Simon Jacquemus is also your man for shirts which don't scream 'this-is-for-the-office-and-nothing-else'. But it is notoriously difficult for designers to make it from promising-among-insiders to internationally known, which is why Rihanna's choice to wear pieces from his SS17 Provence-themed collection is an important one.  "It's so beneficial to have that kind of support" Craig Green, another emerging name, told The Telegraph earlier this year when Rihanna commissioned him to create a look for her Anti world tour. "It means that my work reaches a different audience- plus my Mum and my sister actually know who Rihanna is, so it really means something to them." With the added star quality of a Prince in tow, Rihanna's looks from the past few days are bound to have an impact.                      © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Who runs the world? They do. From politics and business to fashion and culture, these women don’t just shape the times we live in – they style them as well. This is how... Catherine, Duchess of Cambridge
How to be a modern-day future Queen? Kate’s considered image makes the most of the message-giving power of clothes, without turning her into a fashion plate. The buttercup-print Jenny Packham shift she wore just hours after giving birth to Princess Charlotte showed she’s tough as nuts, and she’s a champion of British designers such as Jonathan Saunders. But her love of high-street labels like LK Bennett and Hobbs and tendency to 're-wear’ show a common touch. Victoria Beckham
Since launching her eponymous label in 2008, Victoria Beckham has transformed her image from glamorous pop star to uber-chic designer. Pairing luxurious pieces from Saint Laurent and Céline with her own minimalist designs, Beckham has seduced the fashion industry, while cultivating a way of dressing, to which women the world over aspire.  Hikari Yokoyama
Yokoyama is making a name as a stylish player on the art scene, consulting for auction site Paddle8 and acting as a trustee for the charity Women For Women. The Chicago native, who is engaged to White Cube founder Jay Jopling, favours eclectic pieces by Christopher Kane and Miu Miu, as well as insider favourite Misha Nonoo.  Natalie Massenet
Although she left Net-a-Porter this September on the eve of its merger deal with Yoox, Massenet is probably the site’s best advert. Also Chairman of the British Fashion Council, her American roots and French upbringing play out in her impeccably put-together outfits and polished grooming. She embraces femininity with floral dresses by Erdem or lace creations by Alessandra Rich, and can be counted on to give of-the-moment young designers a sophisticated spin.  Anna Wintour
The legendary US Vogue editor has a code of dressing which, one imagines, saves precious time during her carefully timetabled routine. Her signature bob is always immaculately blow-dried and she rarely veers from custom-made Manolo Blahnik slingbacks, which the designer has been making for her since 1994 (in two bespoke shades of nude created to match her skin tone). Dresses are usually by Prada or Chanel, and almost always sleeveless to show off tennis-toned triceps. The final Wintour touch? Those famous dark glasses.  Christine Lagarde
Lagarde is the managing director of the International Monetary Fund. She’s French, so is genetically wired to look great, but there are some key components to her brand of elegance. First, there’s the silver-grey crop and tanned skin. Then there are the scarves that she apparently unwinds from around her neck and throws across her shoulder to move negotiations forward. And it must help to have a direct line to a 'darling woman’ at Chanel…  Rihanna
Chameleonic Rihanna is calculated in her approach to event dressing, using her clothes to push boundaries and make statements. At the China-themed Met Gala this May, she eschewed oriental-imitations worn by other guests and chose designer Guo Pei to create a magnificent, authentically modern take on Chinese fashion. Then, there was the 'So Naked’ gown which Mel Ottenberg and Adam Selman dreamt up for the 2014 CFDA Awards; shocking but history-making.  Sheikha Mozah bint Nasser Al Missned 
Unusually for a female Qatari royal, Sheikha Mozah bint Al Missned has created a prominent international profile. Her love of fashion is clear from the perfectly coordinated Valentino and Chanel couture looks that make up her wardrobe. Her biggest impact has been showing how high fashion can be adapted to adhere to strict Islamic dress codes – whether you cover your head for religious reasons or not, she makes you want to wear a turban.  Marissa Mayer
Yahoo’s chief executive has made headlines with her minimal maternity leaves and stringent workplace policies, but finds time to enjoy great fashion. She once paid $60,000 at a charity auction to have lunch with the designer Oscar de la Renta and collects the house’s cashmere cardigans. She has spoken openly about her love for shoes and prefers bright colours and art-printed dresses to a lacklustre corporate uniform.  Samantha Cameron
It’s little wonder Samantha Cameron is so deft at pushing boundaries (yet staying appropriate) in her role as Prime Minister’s wife; until 2010 she was creative director at leather-goods brand Smythson. In her time at Downing Street, she’s promoted British fashion, been admired for her relatable yet elegant looks (favourites include Roksanda Ilincic and Jonathan Saunders) and paid sartorial tribute to Margaret Thatcher by wearing a pussy-bow blouse to the former PM’s funeral. Folorunsho Alakija 
One of Africa’s richest women came to the UK to study fashion in the early ’80s, when London’s creative scene was characterised by an experimental attitude. Who knows if the experience stayed with her, but she’s been brilliantly bold in her style choices ever since. The tycoon often wears one-off traditional headdresses in a zinging palette of lime, purple and magenta, teaming them with exquisitely embroidered and printed dresses.  Queen Rania of Jordan
Queen Rania has assumed a major role on the world stage, dressing in a clever mix of high-fashion and Eastern designers. Chloé, Miu Miu and Alexander McQueen are among her most-worn labels, plus edgier pieces by Peter Pilotto and Jordanian favourite Areej Al-Qudah. Queen Rania posts her looks on Instagram, along with updates on her charity projects for her 990,000 followers – it’s an adroit method for drawing attention to her causes.  Peng Liyuan 
If Taylor Swift were to marry the US President, the fame level would be off the scale. This is the position that folk singer and wife of China’s President Xi Jinping, Peng Liyuan, holds – and her wardrobe reflects her different roles. There are ostentatious stage costumes in eye-catching fuchsia and scarlet, which have made her an icon in her own right. For political engagements such as her recent visit to the UK, Peng opts for sleek suits, or pieces that nod to Chinese culture with Mandarin-collar details. Her secret weapon is Ma Ke, a Chinese couturier whose looks for Peng have won plaudits. The Queen
In the earlier years of her reign, the Queen kept up with trends, trying out Christian Dior’s divine New Look and the graphic shorter lengths of the ’60s. But in the past 30 years, she has developed a formula of bright, block-coloured coats with matching hats, plus her faithful Launer handbag and Rayne heels. Most of her wardrobe is custom-made by dressmaker Angela Kelly and the priority is that Her Majesty should always stand out in a crowd.  Angelina Jolie
Persuading global policy makers to take you seriously can’t be an easy task for a Hollywood actress, so a diplomatic wardrobe is a necessity. Sharp suiting has emerged as a staple look for Jolie. She opted for a demure ivory skirted version by Ralph & Russo to receive her honorary damehood last year, while Michael Kors and Saint Laurent are also favourites.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
