 What does a fashion stylist actually do? There is a moment, somewhat stagey, in The Editor’s Eye, the 2012 documentary about American Vogue’s senior stylists, when the creatives in question, tasked with this question, are each lost for words. Four years on, with time to reflect, and a book of her pictures from American Vogue to publicise, it seems a good opportunity to ask Phyllis Posnick to tackle the question again, especially given the narrative nature of her pictures. “I suppose the Phyllis component part of the picture is the way the woman in it actually looks, and the casting of the model,” she begins thoughtfully. Phyllis Posnick,  New York 2016, Annie Leibowitz 'I’ve often ended up in fights with photographers, but Annie is the one where I came closest to thinking, “That’s it, she’s never going to work with me again.” In fact, we didn’t’ work together again for more than a year. She feels the clothes get in the way. Sometimes I go very quiet, because you can’t fight in front of the subject. It’s stressful. Everyone wants to create the best picture, but sometimes, even with the best preparation in the world, what you get on the day isn’t what you signed up for.’ “Sometimes the photographer may have the final say on casting but I’ll make the initial selection. The hair, the make-up… if there are clothes as well, then I select them and they determine the direction of the shoot. If the clothes aren’t very good then the pictures aren’t good.” There often aren’t clothes, because Posnick is the executive Vogue editor responsible for the arresting images that punctuate the magazine’s beauty and health pages. Often charged with illuminating the banal sounding (a feature about mascaras) or impossible (a story about moisturising creams for extreme temperatures, the challenge being that the creams were all invisible on the skin), Posnick and her collaborators have invariably mined artistic gold, sans clothes. They’ve had to. Whereas her Vogue colleagues might have 10 or 12 magazine pages to tell their story, Posnick generally gets one. It has honed both her technique and her argument, turning her single image into a sensational, occasionally sensationalist visual statement that more often than not constitutes highly glamourised social commentary. 'ADHD’, New York 2011, Steven Klein 'Karlie Kloss is one of my favourite models for her balletic grace and incredible body. My role in this? Casting and explaining the initial idea to the photographer and helping to channel their ideas into something that will work for the magazine.’ Hence the book’s title: Stoppers. There is the 2008 picture of the model Guinevere Van Seenus wearing grotesquely large wax lips, overseen by a highly sexualised nurse (inspired by the nurses Posnick had seen in the Marc Jacobs for Louis Vuitton show, which in turn had been inspired by the artist Richard Prince), to accompany a piece on cosmetic surgery that goes wrong. And a prescient-looking Kristen McMenamy, in 1995, being pushed in what looks like a hi‑tech S&M wheelchair by a semi-naked, armour-clad robo-model to demonstrate our growing obsessions with gadget-dominated exercise. Or a headless model in a genuine medieval metal chastity belt alongside a 2002 article on birth control. Her collaborators read like a Who’s Who of 21st- (and 20th-) century photography: Steven Klein (“the only photographer I know who can turn a child’s inflatable pool toy into a sexual predator,” she writes in Stoppers); Helmut Newton (“He’d tell me my ideas were dumb, and then incorporate bits of them into the shoot”): the British Tim Walker, who will happily turn down a job if it doesn’t feel right; Bruce Weber (who asked Posnick why she had to make everything so difficult); and the late Irving Penn, with whom she began working in 1987 and who wasn’t averse to making things difficult himself. 'Cult Creams’,  New York 1996, Irving Penn 'We found a dairy in upstate New York that made very rich, thick double cream. We had two models sitting in a tub taking it in turns while an assistant threw buckets of cream at them. Both models knew what they were letting themselves in for.’ He once agreed to do a “natural light” story with her, but only if she could find the original Parisian studio where he’d shot a previous “natural light” story decades before. That studio no longer existed, but the Vogue scout found one in the same street, “complete with the same dirty windows and the same light”. Why does she make everything difficult, I ask? She smiles. “I’ve been accused of being meticulous, maybe that’s part of it.” Commenting on a Posnick/Penn picture that co-starred a glossy pair of red lips and a live bee, Hamish Bowles, a fellow Voguette, said “Phyllis would have trawled every apiary in America in the casting of that bee”. Her father was punctiliously punctual at picking her up from school every day. “My mother was neat and always on time. I’m from Austrian stock…” 'Yves Saint Laurent blouse’, New York 2005, Irving Penn 'This was built around the mask, which was made by the make-up artist Peter Phillips. We knew the model needed to be very pale and the lips very dark, so Peter white-washed her body and her hair was sprayed white. Penn wanted to shoot her in an old-fashioned negligée, so I found dozens and brought a rack of clothes to the studio. Penn liked just one…’ And she enjoys a challenge. One senses that she still regrets choosing to study business at Syracuse University when she was 18, rather than art or fashion. “I did it because I thought it would be easy. It was.” It was also her route out of a happy, but circumscribed upbringing in a small town on Long Island. “My parents were very watchful and I wasn’t exposed to much, except through books or films. I couldn’t wait to get away.” She married the minute she left Syracuse, an art director who gave her her surname (she was born Phyllis Werther). They moved to London for his work and she landed an assistant’s role at British Vogue, “a dream job that growing up, I never imagined would come to pass”. I estimate this would have been the very late Sixties or early Seventies – Posnick is as economical with dates as she is with biographical details. The internet is no help on this: how she has managed to stay beneath its radar is a near miracle. Even her clothes are the (fashion editor’s) version of anonymous: head to toe navy or black, generally from Céline, and, inevitably, almost no visible signs of make-up. 'Mascara Wars’, New York 2001, Irving Penn 'When we shot this, the big beauty companies were engaged in a kind of mascara wars.Penn wanted to shoot with the model’s eyes closed in extreme close-up. He’d been pushing and prodding the brushes around her lashes. At the end of the day when she opened her eyes, this was how she looked, so he shot it spontaneously. I don’t know whether it was infection or irritation.’ Her pictures are her chosen platform of expression and they are often as subversive and confrontational as Posnick, in person, is self-effacing. Was she was quietly naughty at her strict school? “Not naughty enough,” she counters. “But I was and am very curious.” She is still surprised when people accuse her of deliberate provocation and was taken aback when a gallerista described some of her work as grotesque. “To me, they’re funny. There’s always a sense of playfulness.” I wonder whether the models she casts always feel that playful. There was the duo who spent all day in a tub having buckets of thick dairy cream thrown at them. Another had her eye so prodded by mascara wands that, when she finally opened her lids at the end of the day, the whites of her eyes looked like a constellation of blood streaks. “I always tell everyone exactly what is entailed,” says Posnick. “I never want anyone to feel they’ve been ambushed.” She clearly respects the great models. “People sometimes ask me what the model actually does in my pictures, because often they’re obscured. We had one model hide her face completely behind a soccer ball for a picture. But her neck was so elegant and the way she tilted her head so coquettish that it brought a lightful touch to an otherwise quite menacing shoot. Another model we used to go with a piece about obesity was genuinely large, but Penn picked her from my selection because she was so comfortable naked and so graceful.” 'Honey-Do’, March 2013, Tim Walker 'Persuading Tim to do a picture is a process – sometimes short, other times not – which can be challenging. That’s a good thing, because it takes us away… to somewhere more creative and original. He knows what’s necessary – props, set design location. If he doesn’t get them, he could change his mind and refuse to do the shoot.’ But the commonality of beauty is not her concern. She is not after pretty imagery or universal tropes, but a kind of truth that she hopes stands the test of time. What is the power of her pictures, beyond the decorative? “I think in this era of instant everything, when people get so much information on social media, they’re evidence of the importance of studied preparation. When they’re good, they get people talking… and, actually, they look good small, too, when they’re reproduced on Instagram.” She attributes Irving Penn, to whom Stoppers is dedicated, “with teaching me to see and to think laterally. Everything is questioned,” she says. It sounds exhausting. “Well, occasionally there are sleepless nights if an idea won’t come. But I’m not this exacting at home,” she says. Or rather, at the two homes she shares with her second husband, the rare book and antiques map dealer Paul Cohen – the “one on Fifth Avenue with extraordinary light, white walls, wood floors, and the one upstate which is more colourful”. Both, she maintains are cosy, relaxing and conducive to her passion of cooking, and if the art in them is slightly unsettling – prints of her Vogue work – that is in the eye of the beholder.  Stoppers: Photographs from My Life at Vogue by Phyllis Posnick, published by Abrams (£45) Selected images will be auctioned at Phillips London om the 3rd November.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Gucci's creative director Alessandro Michele is an Anglophile, demonstrated in his Cruise 2017 collection which was a “love letter to England.” Models walked through the Cloisters at Westminster Abbey (the first time a fashion show has ever been permitted to take place there) in Union Jack jumpers, headscarves and tartan kilts, which riffed off the Queen's Balmoral look. It is perhaps not surprising then that instead of casting a Hadid or a 'somebody on Instagram' for the campaign, he picked the queen of British theatre, Vanessa Redgrave, to wear his re-imagined regal uniform. The 79-year-old actress shot her first campaign with photographer Glen Luchford at Chatsworth House, the grand sixteenth century home of the Duke and Duchess of Devonshire in Derbyshire. Ms Redgrave had a spectacular Gucci-over, wearing a union jack jumper, cricket whites-inspired robe and floral dress and skirt as she poses in the stately grounds. Vanessa Redgrave landed her first role in 1957, and has appeared in more than 70 films, won an Oscar, Tony, Bafta Golden Globe, and SAG award, and was described as the "greatest actress of our time" by Tennessee Williams. She is the  perfect person to wear Gucci's very British collection not only because she is a national treasure, but because she also has her own history with the fashion house. In the 1966 film Blow-Up her character Jane carries a small Gucci handbag with a bamboo top handle - a style which was later revived by Frida Giannini, the former creative director at Gucci.  The Italian designer fell for London when he worked at Gucci's previous head offices in Mayfair for a number of years during Tom Ford's tenure. “London is always on my mind and in my memories," Michele explained to The Telegraph the impact this had on his eccentric design aesthetic. "I’m obsessed with British culture, past and present. To be able to show the collection inside the Cloisters in Westminster Abbey is magical." Chatsworth House isn't just a location for the campaign, as Gucci has announced it is also partnering with the estate for three years, in which the house will support activities and events, including an upcoming style exhibition. Alessandro Michele met the current Duchess of Devonshire by chance, and after bonding over their mutual love of art, history and culture they decided to collaborate.  While teenagers might still be still be sweeping up some of the biggest campaigns in the industry - 16-year-old Lily Rose Depp and 15-year-old Willow Smith have appeared in recent Chanel ads and 14-year-old Kaia Gerber has just been named as the face of Miu Miu - there is a growing number of brands casting older women and catering to a wider demographic. Joan Didion, 80, has modeled for Celine and Joni Mitchell, 72, fronted an ad for Saint Laurent. 100-year-old Bo Gilbert, who lives in a supportive housing facility, also made her modelling debut this year for Harvey Nichols in the pages of British Vogue.  © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Last weekend we were all agog at the young Prince George greeting President Obama in a personalised bath robe. This week it is the turn of his mother, smiling, relaxed and understated, on the cover of the most famous fashion magazine of them all. Since her engagement to Prince William, the Duchess has barely put a foot wrong with her style (well, perhaps a foot - not everyone is won over by her signature wedge shoes). The diplomacy she displays in her choice of glamorous but not showy garments is quite something, and she hasn’t dropped the ball on this important occasion. The brown suede coat and white shirt she wears in the cover shot are made by Burberry, Britain’s biggest luxury fashion label which has a deeply populist appeal together with a strong heritage and a Royal Warrant - the perfect choice for a woman who will one day be Queen. In fact, it’s surprising she doesn’t wear the label more often - she’s rarely been seen in it until now. Burberry is also a brand that’s able to translate her love of the countryside, an effect she adds to with a dark green hat, not dissimilar to the kind she’s often been seen to wear on off-duty weekends, but here sourced from the vintage shop Beyond Retro. This appears to be the first time she has worn a vintage piece - aside from Royal diamonds and an upcycled dress of her mother’s. It suggests a thriftiness that The Duchess likes to display, and wins her style points - mixing luxury with vintage is the sign of a woman comfortable with her own taste and not afraid to experiment. The rich earthy colours and soft tactile fabrics of these garments lend a kind of 1970s’ Ali Mcgraw style to the shoot, enhanced by the honeyed glow of the light and complimenting the Duchess’s brown hair and eyes. Kate has a love of strong eyeliner, famously doing her own for her wedding. This time, the make-up artist Sally Branka, who has previously worked with Emma Watson on a Vogue cover, has given her heavier eyebrows, a healthy peachiness and a softer line on the eyes.   Deciding to work with Josh Olins - at 36, a relatively young British photographer - is a refreshing choice. Olins shoots for Vogue and its international editions and has done advertising campaigns for luxury labels such as Louis Vuitton and Stella McCartney. But he has also shot David Beckham in his underwear for the high street brand H&M and Victoria Beckham, winking on the cover of the style magazine, i-D.   Whether his subject is a model or a celebrity, Olins is able to capture not only their self-possession and poise but also their warmth and personality. He’s the perfect photographer to bring out the Duchess’s beauty and likeable nature in these informally styled images. All the clothes the Duchess wears are by Burberry, which could do wonders for the mammoth brand that has struggled over the last year, apart from the vintage hat and the rusty coloured striped t-shirt by the French high street brand Petit Bateau, whose clothes for children and striped t-shirts for women are beloved by yummy-mummies everywhere. Again, a canny choice for a Royal and, at £35, one that will no doubt prompt a rush on the retailer’s stores and website. What’s fascinating is that this is a shoot for a fashion magazine by a fashion photographer with a major fashion brand that does as much as it can not to appear fashionable.  And yet when we look back on the series we will find that the Duchess’s clothes and make-up, the setting and the mood, perfectly captures something of Britain in the Spring of 2016. Two of the portraits of HRH The Duchess of Cambridge shot by Josh Olins will be available for public view in Vogue 100: A Century of Style at the National Portrait Gallery from Sunday 1st May.  There was a lot riding on what the Duchess of Cambridge might choose to wear for a Friday night in the city of chic. After all,  Paris is a byword for a very particular breed of effortless elegance; perfectly put together but never de trop.  In the end, Kate pulled a blinder in a black tweed dress hitting just above the ankle, cinched at the waist with a leather belt and accessorised with a co-ordinating set of pearl jewellery for this evening's reception at the British Ambassador's residence, expertly ticking off the requisite tropes of classic Paris style.  The black dress was by Alexander McQueen, the fashion house to which the Duchess frequently turns, especially for these high-octane outings. Creative director Sarah Burton famously designed Kate's wedding dress in 2011 while before tonight's look, she had most recently created the floral-printed, off-shoulder evening gown which she wore to the BAFTAs in February. This weekend's visit to France has been billed as a 'charm offensive' for the young royals as the UK prepares to trigger Article 50 and begin Brexit negotiations with the EU. While that might all seem very much political rather than fashion territory, the Duchess's choice of a McQueen design underlines the cultural and business ties between Britain and France. McQueen is a British label at its core; founded by Lee McQueen, son of a Black Cab driver, in the Nineties and now under the creative directorship of Macclesfield-born Sarah Burton. It is owned though by Kering, the international luxury conglomerate founded by French businessman, François Pinault. Alexander McQueen shows its collections at Paris fashion week twice a year.  The look was dazzling in a manner which the Duchess rarely toys with, imbuing an air of  sophistication without being an obvious statement showstopper. "One is never over-dressed or under-dressed with a Little Black Dress," Karl Lagerfeld, longtime creative director of Chanel once said, echoing the unfussy style philosophy set out by the label's founder Gabrielle Chanel in a 1926 illustration published in American Vogue which compared the usefulness of the Little Black Dress she had designed to a Ford car. If confirmation were needed that a LBD was the logical style solution of the evening, the French wife of the British ambassador, Lady Llewellyn was also wearing one. The Duchess's pearl jewellery- a gobstopper ring, bauble necklace and Balenciaga earrings- was also a nod to classic Gallic style and added interest to an otherwise pared-back look- a key consideration when impact is required for those pictures which will be beamed around the world. The Duchess has often referenced the Sixties look of Jackie Kennedy- most notably during another recent diplomatic mission to the Netherlands- so her jewellery choice also plays to that strategy; "Pearls are always appropriate," is one of Kennedy's best known style mantras.  The striking simplicity of the LBD was harnessed by Princess Diana, who was the first member of the royal family to wear the non-colour for anything other than funerals. In 1994, she famously picked a Christina Stambolian above-the-knee look for the Serpentine Summer Party which was also the night when the interview in which Prince Charles confessed to infidelity was broadcast. It was a sexy look which exhibited defiant nonchalance, marking her out as a woman who was powerful rather than pitiable. The message behind the Duchess's dress tonight? A respectfully diplomatic study in Parisian chic.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  In the all-pink backstage area at last month’s Victoria’s Secret fashion show, Brazilian model Adriana Lima had expressed the pride that she felt at being cast as an ‘Angel’ for the 18th year in a row. “I do feel just as excited as the first time,” she told The Telegraph. “1999 was my first show for the brand, and it was on Wall Street. It was the first time a fashion show was streamed live on the internet and I was so nervous to be next to Stephanie Seymour, Heidi Klum and the supermodels. I never thought that I would achieve as much as this in a modeling career.” Now, it seems, Lima has had a change of heart. Less than a month after the spectacle in Shanghai, the 36 year-old has taken to Instagram to declare that she will no longer take her clothes off ‘for an empty cause’ - a statement that has prompted both praise and a backlash from her fans. Describing a recent scenario in which an unnamed brand asked her to pose in a ‘sexy video’ for social media, Lima explains that she made a snap decision to turn her back on projects that promote unrealistic body types, as it came days after a friend had opened up to her about her own body insecurities. ‘Even though I have done many [projects] of this type, something had changed in me,’ she wrote of the epiphany. ‘When a friend approached me to share that she was unhappy with her body, then it made me think.... that everyday in my life, I wake up thinking, how do I look? Was I going to be accepted in my job?’ To get into the shape required for the Victoria’s Secret show and other lingerie modelling jobs, it’s widely known (and wrongly accepted) that models go to extreme lengths to achieve the ‘right’ kind of figure. The hashtag #TrainLikeAnAngel is routinely used by models to show how heavily they exercise in the months leading up to the show, with one trainer previously telling The Telegraph that he advises his charges to "visualise ice cream but drink water. It's the best thing for you post workout." Lima, who has two daughters Valentina, 8, and Sienna, 5, with her ex-husband Marko Jarić, described the ‘physically and mentally unhealthy’ image that the fashion industry as a whole projects to women and stated that she hopes to change that image in her work from now on. “In that moment I realized that majority of woman probably wake up every morning trying to fit in a stereotype that society/social media /fashion etc imposed [sic],” she wrote. “I thought that’s not a way of living and beyond that, that’s not physically and mentally healthy, so I decided to make that change. I will not take of my clothes anymore for a empty cause [sic].” “I am tired of the impositions,” she shared, “we 'as woman' can't be continuing living in a world with such superficial values, it's not fair for us. I want to change it.” Lima has more than 11.5 million followers on Instagram, and for every fan expressing their delight at the possible end to the era of thin being in, there were several there to criticise Lima for waiting so long to make the declaration after years of benefitting from these projects which have helped her to become a household name. “She’s on her way out from VS now that she’s approaching 40 and is scrambling to reinvent herself,’ wrote one critic in the comments box. ‘She’s finally having this epiphany after 18 years of making millions and her career is ending. If she had pulled this stunt a decade ago, it would have actually held some weight.” Others were more forgiving, with many suggesting that it was ‘groundbreaking’ to hear an established name turning against the enormous brand and that things need to change across the industry to prevent a singular body type from dominating in fashion imagery. In September, Lima had told People that she intended to stay a Victoria’s Secret for ‘as long as my body allows me, at least until I am 40,’ but the post indicates that she may be hanging up her wings with immediate effect. Lima ‘unfollowed’ several of the company’s most influential executives, including show head Ed Razek and a number of the models she once called ‘family’. Fellow Brazilian Alessandra Ambrosio, also 36, formally announced her ‘retirement’ from the Victoria’s Secret immediately after the show last month, after 17 consecutive years of appearances. Her departure was somewhat less explosive. “Words cannot describe how grateful I am to have been working for this amazing brand that inspires me and women all over the world,” she said at the time. “Last night was so emotional to say goodbye to my #angel sisters but we put on the biggest and best show ever.” Unlike Lima, it is assumed that she wants to keep in touch.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Melania Trump has added a perhaps-unlikely new label to her style repertoire; the British start-up Cefinn, founded this year by Samantha Cameron. On a visit to discuss an ongoing drug addiction epidemic in West Virginia yesterday, Trump forwent her typical ‘America first’ policy (usually we see her in Michael Kors, Ralph Lauren and other big New York names) instead choosing Cameron’s vivid green ‘belted muslin shirt dress’ design, with signature Christian Louboutin snakeskin heels. Priced at £295, the dress is still available to buy in sizes 6-14 from Cefinn's website and at Net-a-Porter.com. It is understood that the current US First Lady and the former British Prime Minister’s wife don’t personally know each other - indeed their times in office didn’t overlap, meaning that they would never have crossed paths on diplomatic tours, or at official events for heads of states. The two undoubtedly have a lot in common, though, in that they both understand the demanding role of 'First Spouse', as well as the unique set of wardrobe requirements and pressures that come with it. Whatever Cameron chose to wear during her husband’s time in office was heavily scrutinised, whether for its appropriateness for the occasion (remember how the tabloids lashed at her for not wearing a hat to the Royal Wedding in 2011?) or the unspoken messages she may be trying to convey through her clothing (one must always represent British brands when abroad, of course). It's a territory that Trump has also had to navigate with care since entering The White House on 4th January. When she founded Cefinn back in February, Cameron outlined the gap that she had spotted in the market, catering for stylish, professional women in need of sophisticated workwear. ‘There’s definitely a market for sleek, fashion-conscious affordable office wear,” she previously told The Telegraph of the balance she hoped to strike with her quality fabrics and flattering cuts for women of all ages. She noted, however, that these were also the sartorial solutions that she hadn’t been able to easily find for herself while her husband was in office, thus rendering Cefinn an ideal place for any woman hoping to look polished in the public eye to hit.  Belted muslin shirt dress, £295, Cefinn at Net-a-Porter.com  “I remember the first couple of party conferences looking really odd because I had to borrow things,” she said of the challenges she faced at Number 10. “I’d turn up and [the special advisers] would say, “What are you going to wear?” I’d show them all these things I thought were really nice, but they’d all be grey or black. You realise quite quickly that you have to put in a bit of time and effort. When I see the Duchess of Cambridge or Michelle Obama, I know that getting it that right, which they do, takes a lot of time.” While Cameron may not know Mrs Trump, she did get to know Mrs Obama very well and has expressed great admiration for her former American counterpart. “Michelle Obama and I would compliment each other privately,” Cameron told The Telegraph. “She was so good at supporting British designers if she was coming to Downing Street or if we were going to Washington, we would check with her team, so that we didn’t turn up in anything too similar. Yes, I’d love to have her wear my label, but I haven’t asked her.” Putting party politics aside, it's likely that Samantha Cameron will still be chuffed to see Obama's replacement, Mrs Trump, wearing her designs this morning. She of all people knows the stakes - anything that she, or Obama wore during their time in office was almost guaranteed to sell out, as the media beamed their pictures around the world. Obama is widely credited with launching the career of now-established New York name Jason Wu, while Cameron championed London's Roksanda Ilincic, Christopher Kane and Preen during her tenure. Endorsement from a First Lady on either side of the pond is exposure that, particularly for a new brand, money simply can't buy. Cameron might even be grateful that, after all her years launching other people's fashion businesses, someone has finally returned the favour. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  When I stop to think about it, or when my friends remind me, I realise that my life is somewhat strange.  I get paid to walk up and down catwalks across the fashion capital cities; I get photographed wearing designer clothes, looking dreamy, zany or girl-next-door-y. I’m often made to look older or more beautiful than I really am or just completely different – the  pictures are someone else’s vision of me. I’m only part-time, though. Most of the time I’m a human-sciences student at University College London and devote my days to writing essays on ‘The spectrum of ambiguous genitalia in male sex reversal’  or ‘Whether finding crude oil inadvertently represses women’. On days like these, when I’m sitting in  the library, I start to appreciate my dual lifestyle.  I think in truth my two worlds, each of which is slightly suspicious of the other, complement each other nicely.  Friends often ask me about the fashion world and about my modelling. Is it glamorous? Have I met Kendall Jenner? Perhaps it would be better to ask my older sister, Edie, a veteran of the modelling world and, in every way, the real deal. Hard-working and a true co-creator of the photos she stars  in, she deserves her profile.  Sometimes, people ask more provocative questions. How does it feel to work in an industry that promotes unrealistic body ideals, or hires underweight girls? This is hard to answer. To feel socially responsible for a huge multi-national industry is perhaps unrealistic. On an individual level, I do not feel like I represent anything unrealistic, nor am I underweight. From personal experience I only know what it’s like for the models. When a 24-year-old model is told to lose weight so that she can be as small as all the 16-year-old girls just starting out, it’s as exasperating as it is sad, especially when  her career may depend on it. For some though, it’s simply a sacrifice that comes with the job.  To some of my friends, the fashion world is  a bit silly – closed, incestuous, narcissistic – and models plain uninteresting. A lot of people think of themselves as above fashion and don’t care about clothes – as if that is all fashion  is about. One of the problems I have with these conversations is coping with people’s urge to  generalise. Is fashion serious or unserious?  Is it political or apolitical? Is it or isn’t it art? Well… The truth is you can’t really gener- alise about fashion. Fashion combines design,  photography, personalities, video, sound  and more; it’s an industry full of paradoxes.  It’s commercial and corporate at the same  time as being niche and underground. It  combines subcultures with mass consumption. It can be an art but it lines the shelves of  high-street shops. It can have, and not have,  an opinion. Another problem is that everything is changing. We, as models, are now hired not just for the way we look but also for the way we think and live – or rather, the way we appear to. People want to know who the women are who sell them their clothes, and clients as well as consumers want girls with a strong following or whose personal ethos seems close to that of the brand. This means having a strong online presence (via Instagram, Twitter or both), which in turn means posting a lot of selfies, bikini shots on the French Riviera and bowls of acai berries – the healthier and more sun-kissed the photos, the better. So, what kind of issues does this throw up? Answer: an awful lot that have to do with beauty, identity and female empowerment. What does a world obsessed with appearance, and the female body, mean for feminism? What does it mean for the countless young girls who look at these photos on Instagram and wonder why they don’t look like that and think  that’s what they should aspire to be? These photos are a million miles away from the styled, fantasy world of magazines. These photos  supposedly represent a real world – no matter how unreal, in truth – and thus, the message they send is all the more poignant.  I’m not saying that I disapprove of any  particular lifestyle. Nor do I disapprove of  self-promotion for profit. If you are your own  business, how you promote yourself is key. However, fashion is part of popular culture  and it’s popular culture that spreads the messages of movements like feminism. It’s popular culture that will, I hope, progress feminism to the point where the stigma of the word falls away and I will stop hearing, ‘Hang on a minute, do you actually call yourself a feminist?’  The fashion world that I have come to know is one that loves, needs, understands, employs and empowers women, as few industries  do. Victoria’s Secret girls aren’t just models: they’re role models. They’re promoted as women with ambition who’ve worked extremely hard and been successful: women who are professionally, socially, physically and sexually empowered. But the Victoria’s Secret Angel’s path to empowerment is reserved for the minority with the right look, body and lifestyle. Also, fashion is a business and the majority of women are simply consumers. There is nothing feminist in meeting your sales targets by playing on women’s perceived insecurities. The same goes for ‘inspiring’ women to get fit by constantly reminding them how very far removed they are from their dream selves.  A number of individual models are also turning feminist on social-media websites. Cara Delevingne is a familiar example. More current is Emily Ratajkowski. Made famous  by her role in Robin Thicke’s Blurred Lines music video, she now models for high-fashion brands. However, she got more media attention for a topless selfie with Kim Kardashian. A lot of her images are seen as pornographic – but that, she says, doesn’t mean they’re exploitative: first, because they’re genuine expressions of her sexuality, and secondly, because she’s in charge of when and how she does them. All of this is fine and you cannot impinge on her freedom to post these photos, but how many women, of whatever shape, would feel the same if they did the same?  While Emily Ratajkowski’s control of the situation and message ring true, there are only so many times you can slap a pseudo-feminist sentence on to an Instagram picture before the commercial narcissism shines through. Consistently reducing feminism to the naked female body begins to be regressive.  The relationship between fashion and feminism is complex, problematic and still evolving. If it’s to continue its journey into the mainstream, feminism needs the fashion world: needs its support and needs the girls who represent it. On the other hand, it’s a relationship fraught with ambiguities and contradictions, not the least of which is that ‘feminist fashion’ encourages feminist debate to focus disproportionately on the female body, at the expense of issues such as the wage gap, and potentially imprisons it there.  Debates and problems like these produce the pleasure of being able to slink back into my  student life where ‘ambiguous genitalia’  surprisingly becomes the more straight- forward subject. © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  On Monday night at the Met Gala, Madonna did what Madonna does best: created controversy by flashing her bottom in a Givenchy lace ensemble. Now, the 57-year-old has responded to those who immediately took to social media saying that a woman her age should 'put it away,' by claiming that her outfit was actually a political statement about how society wants older women to be invisible.  Within minutes of Madonna stepping on the red carpet Twitter was flooded with comments criticising the singer for showing so much skin. Piers Morgan tweeted 'put it away,' and another user wrote 'You need people in your life who will tell you the truth, otherwise you'll end up like Madonna.' But ever the professional when it comes to owning her controversial statements, Madonna has fought back, saying the reaction has been "proof that we still live in an ageist and sexist society." "We have fought and continue to fight for civil rights and gay rights around the world," she wrote on Instagram. "When it comes to women's rights we are still in the dark ages. My dress at the Met Ball was a political statement as well as a fashion statement." 'If you have a problem with the way I dress it is simply a reflection of your prejudice' She goes on to say that society is still afraid of older women embracing their bodies - and refusing to be invisible.  "The fact that people actually believe a woman is not allowed to express her sexuality and be adventurous past a certain age is proof that we still live in an age-ist and sexist society. I have never thought in a limited way and I'm not going to start. We cannot effect change unless we are willing to take risks." As such, Madonna believes that Riccardo Tisci's dress has the ability advance the feminist cause. "By being fearless and by taking the road less traveled by. That's how we change history," she continued. "If you have a problem with the way I dress it is simply a reflection of your prejudice. I'm not afraid to pave the way for all the girls behind me‼️ As Nina Simone once said, the definition of freedom is being fearless." Madonna isn't the only star taking to their own social media accounts to counter criticism of their red carpet looks. Sarah Jessica Parker was so irritated by one blogger's suggestion she didn't stick to the tech white tie dress code with her tracksuit and tails look, she decided to take him on. Albeit in a slightly tamer way than Madonna.  “I’m a stickler for the theme and pay close attention to what it means. . .[e]very year with great consideration, research and conviction," the actress explained underneath his instagram post criticising the star. "The understanding of man and machine, how they intersect, when and why is what we considered. Perhaps you weren’t aware of the technology used in the details and embellishments of the design. "Or perhaps you simple didn’t like that I wore which is completely fine but you can’t accuse me of not paying close attention and adhering to the theme. With respect and warmest regards, SJ.” Will the A-lister backlash against critical red carpet watchers, mean an end to the worst dressed lists? Unlikely. The concept was invented way in 1964 by designer Richard Blackwell as an alternative to publicist Eleanor Lambert's  International Best Dressed List and a way to promote his own label. The late designer would invite reporters to a breakfast at his Hollywood home on the second Tuesday in January, and would reveal the 10 celebrities who made it onto his list with remarks such as “she looks like a masculine Bride of Frankenstein”; “she looks like a gypsy abandoned by a caravan” and “an over-the-hill Cruella DeVille.” Wonder what Madonna would make of that? © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism. "I was at the Oscars, waiting to hear if my name was called, and I kept thinking, Cakewalk, cakewalk, cakewalk. "And then, as I started to walk up the stairs and the fabric from my dress tucked under my feet, I realized my stylist had told me, 'Kick, walk, kick, walk.' You are supposed to kick the dress out while you walk, and I totally forgot because I was thinking about cake! And that's why I fell." The following year, at the 2014 Oscars, she again fell over, this time on the red carpet. The culprit this time?  Marilyn Monroe famously sang that diamonds are a girl’s best friend, but if she were performing today, those words might go a little differently. Something like: ‘Pavé diamonds set in gold-vermeil sterling silver are a girl’s best friend.’ Admittedly it doesn’t have quite the same ring to it, but it does describe a modern attitude that has transformed our relationship with jewellery in recent years.  Monica Vinader, who celebrates a decade in business this autumn, has been at the forefront of this ‘sweet spot’ jewellery revolution. She has hit on a new formula that has taken her from making pieces as a hobby to being a name who hundreds of thousands of women around the world have in their newly transformed jewellery boxes. Her brand appeals to everyone, from you and me to the Duchess of Cambridge, who has mixed her Cartier, Garrard and treasures borrowed from the Queen with Vinader’s more relatable green-onyx Siren earrings or the Riva diamond cluster drop earrings for numerous royal engagements. Kate Winslet, Naomi Watts, Bella Hadid, Eleanor Tomlinson and Rita Ora are just a few more of the celebrities who adore Monica’s ‘accessible luxury’ designs. Even Gareth Southgate isn’t immune to a little piece of Monica; he accessorised his now-iconic waistcoat with a Monica Vinader men’s friendship bracelet during one of England’s World Cup matches earlier this summer.  It’s no surprise, then, that in the past three years, turnover at Monica Vinader has trebled to reach £35.8 million, with that figure expected to climb to £50 million next year. At her offices in Norfolk, London, New York and Hong Kong, Vinader now employs 220 people. Between January and July this year, 150,000 friendship bracelets, one of her signature designs, were sold – that’s more than 5,000 a week.  F‘I definitely think jewellery and diamonds have been demystified in the past 10 years,’ says the designer from her studio on the Holkham Estate in Norfolk. ‘When we started this, I don’t think there were as many brands that catered to women’s self-purchasing. The desire was always there but the product itself wasn’t.’ Vinader’s first inkling that luxurious need not mean astronomically expensive came growing up in San Sebastian in Spain with her antique dealer parents. ‘My mother would always talk to me about this French technique called vermeil. Later, I started playing around with it and seeing how I could get it to do what I wanted it to,’ she remembers of the process that has now helped to make her into a household name. Vermeil is the term used for silver, or sometimes bronze, that has been gilded in gold, so you get that precious effect, but at a more affordable price.  Nura necklace, £295, Monica Vinader After studying fine and decorative art at the City & Guilds of London Art School and working for luxury jeweller Tateossian for three years, Monica moved to Patagonia and then Mexico with her husband Nick. While there she carried on experimenting with jewellery, making it as a hobby while they ran fishing and shooting lodges. When she moved back to the UK and had her daughter Scarlett, now 11, Vinader persuaded her business-minded little sister Gabriela, who had been working for Amazon, to come on board. ‘I realised there was a gap between fine and fashion jewellery. It had to be something that resonated with me, my friends and peers, and what we wanted to wear, but also with people older and younger than me.’  Though she had belief in her business model, they were starting out in the middle of the financial crisis. ‘Everyone was talking about the end of the world, so no one was interested in investing, she says. ‘We went to friends and family because we were looking for very small amounts of seed money, but 2008 was not a good year to do that. We mortgaged our family house to get through Christmas. It was risky, but also one of the best things we did – we needed to give it all we had.’ Clockwise from top left: Riva wave ring, £250; Siren wire earrings, £135; Riva diamond hoop earrings, £325; Siren cluster cocktail ring, £175 A decade and several rounds of investment later (including £20 million from private equity house Piper in 2016) and Vinader’s designs, which are made in India, have become cult purchases. Monica, who is so glamorous and gregarious that she immediately makes you feel like an old friend, cites stacking and personalisation as two concepts central to her success. At the time of writing, there were 127 stacking rings available on monicavinader.com, ranging in price from £55 for a slim, organically-formed silver and white topaz band to £650 for a 0.35-carat pavé-diamond disc.  Grown-up friendship bracelets, which combine elegant, engravable plates of metal with sleek, colourful plaited bands, are another key creation in the range – the Fiji was the original, introduced in 2009, but now there are 108 variations in the collection, including the Havana and the Nura.  ‘We have 18-year-olds and 70-year-olds wearing the same piece. Someone might buy a £200 bracelet as an aspirational thing, and someone else might buy 20 in a year and gift or stack them,’ Vinader says. Last year, fashion search platform Lyst found that 78 per cent of jewellery purchases are now made by women; Monica’s success is testament to that. So when she was looking for charities to partner with, Women for Women International UK was a natural choice. This year she has become an ambassador for the organisation, which works with women in countries affected by conflict. Fifty per cent of proceeds from the Nura friendship bracelet range will be donated to the charity – Princess Beatrice has already shown her support for the initiative by wearing hers.  This has been a summer of celebration for Vinader, who marked her 50th birthday with a big party at the Norfolk home she and Nick have lovingly renovated. ‘I danced the night away, which was exactly how I wanted to celebrate,’ she says.  ‘We believe we have the makings of a big company with a long way to go. The next 10 years are about us growing even more,’ she enthuses. Clearly her sweet-spot jewellery mission has only just begun.    © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  From delicate gold jewellery to the new breed of kaftans, let Kate Bosworth and Cindy Crawford help you stay chic on the beach...  Kate Bosworth hit Hawaii with just her trusty frayed denim shorts for company on the beach. Paired with a tomato red string bikini, the stonewashed denim let the hot-hued top sing. Rely on classics that you feel comfortable on holiday, you never wear half the emergency beachwear you buy pre-holiday, after all.  Where to shop: Topshop’s denim shorts selection is as reliable as the retailer’s catalogue of jeans. Bag yourself a pair of worn-in Levis at your local vintage shop, or for a slightly higher price on Farfetch.com. Remember to stick to a light wash, and keep rips to a minimum, to let your top half take centre stage. Left to right: Eres Gigri Le 7 bikini top, £165, Net-a-Porter, and MOTO vintage Ashley shorts, £28, Topshop; Kiini Yaz crochet-trim bikini, £225, Matches Fashion, and Levis shorts, £88, Farfetch Brands such as Mes Demoiselles, Vita Kin and Talitha have caused premium beachwear to rocket in popularity. Forget sarongs, plain kaftans and roomy t-shirt dresses, you need at least one chic kaftan in your arsenal. And if the word ‘kaftan’ fills you with dread, opt for a fluid shirt dress, like Cindy Crawford’s patterned piece from Le Tartes Swimwear. Think of Tilda Swinton in A Bigger Splash as your beach muse. Where to shop:Use MATCHESFASHION.COM as your portal for beachwear brands about to hit the mainstream. Le Sirenuse, Positano is our current obsession. Left to right: Le Sirenuse, Positano Brenda Morocco-print cotton kafta, £195, Matches Fashion; Daft Farrah Fawcett embroidered-cotton kaftan, £305, Matches Fashion For your own dose of Riviera chic a wide-brimmed straw hat is a necessity. Stick to lightweight, camel styles for a classic beach accessory that will never date. Fresh white brims, like model Bella Hadid’s (below), really pop against a sun tan though. Where to shop:Every high street retailer will stock at least one straw hat for summer.  Victoria Beckham approaches airport corridors with the same level of perfectionism as her fashion week catwalk show, so it's not surprising that she has won an award for what she wears in and out of Heathrow. Victoria Beckham is regularly photographed on the commute between London, Los Angeles and New York, and has savvily captialised on the phenomenon as an opportunity to showcase her label. Instead of wearing jogging bottoms and a blanket scarf like your average flyer, Beckham strolls fresh off ten-hour flights tailored tuxedo jackets, coats and pencil dresses with her signature towering heels.  All those years of wearing Louboutins through airport security has paid off, as British Airways have announced the designer as their 'World's Best Dressed Traveller,' followed by Amal Clooney in second place and Kendall Jenner in third position. Hollywood stylist Elizabeth Saltzman, who works with Gwyneth Paltrow and Uma Thurman, said: “Victoria Beckham always gets it right when flying and it’s so impressive. Usually there is a menswear element to her travel wardrobe, it’s chic and sophisticated but still classic and comfortable." She adds: “The women on this list are all powerful examples of the modern world. Their style is classic with a personal twist. This is about the power of women and being able to balance it all.” But don't be fooled, travelling when Victoria Beckham-style means private jets, first class cabins and trollies transporting you straight from check-in to your gate, instead of the mere mortal's reality of Easyjet, indirect flights and constant queuing. Thanks to Instagram we know that Victoria Beckham is just like us when she is up in the air and away from the cameras, as she kicks off her heels and dons the complimentary slippers.  She might have her airport dressing equation down pat now but there have been times when Victoria Beckham hasn't always got it quite so right. In 2009, she took airport dressing a little too literally, dressing like she was ready to take control of a Boeing 777 in a grey Captain's hat and matching coat.  Two words to avoid in conversation with Dree Hemingway on the brisk LA morning on which we meet are ‘coffee’ and ‘socialite’. ‘Coffee’ because she’s on a juice cleanse in desperate need of a caffeine fix, and ‘socialite’ because despite and throughout her various incarnations as a professional ballerina, model and actress, she has occasionally been branded one. “It drives me crazy!” she shudders, frail, translucent-skinned and coddling a fresh mint tea in a West Hollywood café. “To me it means that you’re not doing anything – that you’re only known for showing up to a party. And nobody ever calls a man a socialite, do they?” She’s right. Although any man with a lineage like hers might run the risk of being reduced to an ‘It Boy’. Because 28-year-old Hemingway isn’t just an up and coming independent movie star (with two films, Live Cargo and Love After Love to be released next year), top model and the new face of Jaeger’s spring/summer 2016 campaign, but the great granddaughter of Ernest, daughter of Oscar-nominated actress, Mariel, and niece of the late, great 70s supermodel, Margaux. A heritage she has embraced to the point of adopting her mother’s surname in her early twenties. “I’m really proud of the Hemingway name,” she explains.  “And although there was a delicate moment when I didn’t want my father [director Stephen Crisman] to feel that I was pushing him away, he completely understood. It definitely opened doors faster - I’m not in denial about that. But I think it also made people scrutinize me under a microscope to see if I was worthy of this lineage.”  Hemingway’s desire to prove herself worthy is conspicuous when glancing over her CV. Ten years at the New York City Ballet School, followed by a stint at RADA at 17 and a subsequent move into modelling (“although acting has always been what I want to do, I didn’t feel ready”) doesn’t smack of lazy entitlement. There’s also a reverence when she talks of modelling that’s rare in anyone who has successfully made the transition to acting. But Hemingway has never felt the need to disparage or break away from one profession in order to succeed at the next. “I hope I’ll always model, no matter how well the acting goes. It irritates me when actresses are ashamed of ever having modelled. I’ve learned more doing this than anything else." Shooting the Jaeger campaign with the talented fashion photographer Boo George she says was just as rewarding as shooting a film. "When you’re modeling but you’re creating a short movie that’s captured in stills, almost harder than straightforward acting.” If the campaign images released this week are anything to go by, Jaeger may finally have found the face that fits (and more importantly sells) in the way that M&S have with Rosie Huntington-Whiteley. Founded in 1884 and once on a par with luxury giant Burberry, Jaeger has been forced to reinvent itself in the face of its ‘disposable fashion’ high street competitors, but Hemingway believes that “by exploring more of a street-wear realm, with pieces that are both for day and night” the British brand is moving in the right direction. “I love the simplicity of the designs it’s got a real Celine feel to it. And I like women being able to express their femininity and sexuality in a non-fluffy way.” Hemingway’s Instagram followers will be familiar with the model’s tomboyish style – inspired by the Katharine Hepburn films she would watch as a child. But on the whole she is not a fan of social media. “Before, it was all about talent, and sometimes when you see the girls who are hired now, I don’t think it is about that anymore - it’s about how many followers they have, how much money they can scrape  out of people and how quickly.” What Margaux Hemingway would have thought of the workings of the industry today, she can only imagine. Only eight when her charismatic, six-foot aunt committed suicide in 1996 - the day before the anniversary of Ernest’s own suicide - she nevertheless retains strong memories of the first supermodel to sign a million dollar contract. “She was such a hick! Nothing cute or sexy about her!” she laughs. “All this foul stuff would come out of her mouth, but she had this amazing energy about her. It was so powerful. And I just remember feeling so infatuated by her.”  Growing up in Idaho, Hemingway and her younger sister Langley Fox were more interested in their aunt and mother’s colourful careers than the writings of their great grandfather. “Of course he was a presence in our lives, but it was never a big deal back then.” When she was given The Old Man and The Sea to read as a teenager at school, she found it “dry and very much driven towards male readers. Also I was expected to like it and I was a stubborn teenager.” Declaring – in an interview years later – that her favourite writer was F Scott Fitzgerald was an act of youthful rebellion, she admits. “People got so mad at me,” Hemingway laughs. “It was when Twitter first started and I got so scared I cancelled my Twitter account. I really didn’t want to be thought of as ungrateful.” Dree Hemingway wears striped top, £60 and wide leg trousers, £150 both by Jaeger Since then Hemingway has learned a little diplomacy, choosing her words carefully when I raise the subject of her mother’s 2013 documentary, Running From Crazy – which charted the family’s history of mental illness (not only did Ernest kill himself in 1961, but his father Clarence and siblings Ursula and Leicester also chose what became known as “the family exit”). “I still haven’t seen it,” she frowns. “And I was opposed to my mother making that film, but I now think it has helped a lot of people which is great.” Does she believe that depression is genetic? “I don’t know… I’ve gone through some depressing moments but never in my entire life would I want to commit suicide. I grew up with so much knowledge and awareness of it [mental illness], and my mother’s reaction was to be very, very healthy – but almost too strict with things when we were growing up. So I decided to try and find my own balance and I think I’ve done that. I don’t believe in the ‘Hemingway curse’ because it’s such a sad concept and the implication is that I don’t have a choice.”  She may have chosen to distance herself from the tragic element of her heritage, but ever since reading Paula McLain’s fictional account of her great grandfather’s love affair with his wife Hadley, she maintains she has felt closer to him than ever before. “When I recently read The Paris Wife, I felt such an affinity with Ernest – his love of the outdoors, the sea, and talking to strangers – and that book launched me into wanting to read all the rest.” Coincidentally, she has also started writing herself. “I started writing poetry last year, but I haven’t shown it to anyone. I’m too shy. One thing I’ve always said,” she smiles, getting up to go, “is that I’m not a writer.” From left to right: Tangerine dress, £250; Slouchy cream jumper, £125; Resin and metal bangle, £35; Denim shirt dress, £120; Khaki jumpsuit, £199 all by Jaeger   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  This picture was taken at a party thrown for me in Paris in 1985. I’m with Sibylle de Saint Phalle, who was my assistant and muse. She was my friend’s girlfriend who had come from Paris  to England looking for work. I thought she was fabulous so I offered her a job. I didn’t have a clue at the time but she was fashion royalty, the niece of both artist Niki de Saint Phalle and the fashion designer Madame Grès. I loved her Parisian-ness. To somebody like me who’d come from Liverpool, she was as exotic as it got.  Back then, and this was before the Channel Tunnel, Paris seemed very far from London – philosophically, mentally, socially. I’d already had a shop in London for five years by the time this photo was taken, but the party marked my entry into Paris, which was, and still is, the centre of the fashion world.  I’d just started designing for Jean Paul Gaultier. He’d seen me a few years earlier in the video for Culture Club’s Do You Really Want To Hurt Me? wearing a three-piece suit and a fez that I’d bought from Flip in Long Acre, Covent Garden. He asked me to model in his first menswear show – he was doing a 1940s Casablanca look – but I’d broken my ankle so I couldn’t. We met the next time I was in Paris and he asked if I was interested in working with him. Of course I said yes, and he said, ‘I’m going out for lunch for an hour. Do some sketches around the fez idea and I’ll see them when I come back.’ So I went to a bookshop and bought some Basildon Bond notepaper, the kind you used to write your thank-you letters on at Christmastime, and sketched on that. And he went through them all saying, ‘Yes, no, yes, no…’ And then he said, ‘My assistants will be in touch in a week’s time and tell you the quantities.’  With hindsight, the party was the beginning of something – Gaultier was there and Thierry Mugler, but at the time I was just thinking, this is an exciting new world and I don’t speak French well enough! I didn’t have two pennies to rub together, either.  I didn’t have a credit card so I didn’t know if I’d be able to pay my hotel bill. There were no cashpoints, only five bureaux de change in the whole of Paris, where they stamped your passport to say how much money you’d withdrawn because of the exchange controls.  But I think the interesting thing about this picture is that it was taken by the paparazzi. I was a 27-year-old milliner from England having a small fashion party in Paris and all these photographers turned up. In the early 1980s there had been this sudden explosion of visual media – the new MTV channel, style magazines like i-D and The Face. Until then, Tatler had party pages but they were filled with photographs of the aristocracy, not fashion people. Suddenly people were interested in us. And how we looked was just as important as what we did. stephenjonesmillinery.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Griping about unimaginative Oscar dresses has become an annual ritual among fashion watchers (myself included). The list of “atrocities” regularly committed by attendees of the Academy Awards includes hogging the middle of the road, navigating the red carpet while under the influence of beige, and failure to wear any neckline that isn’t strapless. So while reporting on the Haute Couture shows for The Telegraph in Paris, I mentally put myself in the celebrity stylist’s shoes. Actually, since most celebrity stylists don’t attend couture, being otherwise engaged answering the multiple sartorial demands of their charges, this was better than being in their shoes. This was like being on stilts, standing in front of them. I was ringside at the greatest fashion show on Earth. How hard could it be to pick out a dozen or so ravishing frocks? Um, where to start? The first issue is that dressing an actress for the biggest night of her career is no longer where many couture houses direct their main energies. At the Couture shows, it was notable how many maisons have largely turned their backs on safe Oscar-appropriate styles in favour of appealing to their (paying) clients or to prestigious editorial in fashion magazines. Dolce & Gabbana actively discourage its appearance on the red carpet, knowing their customers prefer exclusivity. On the couture catwalks, spectacularly lavish ball-dresses and embroidered tunics popular at Middle Eastern weddings, or “avant garde” barely-there experiments that might work for a Rihanna video, but would set off every pace-maker at the Academy Awards, now outnumber generic red carpet dresses. “The problem is, the Oscars aren’t regarded as fashion any more,” says Fiona Golfar, editor-at-large of British Vogue. Golfar has attended the Oscars with her husband, the producer Robert Fox, and dressed actresses for them. “It’s surprisingly tough getting hold of decent dresses for them,” she adds. “For one thing, there’s a strict pecking order, both among actresses and designers. You can have a great actress who might score an A among her peers, but only rate a B or C in the fashion world, because she isn’t considered to wear clothes well.” Or she might be the wrong age. When Golfar dressed Dame Maggie Smith the year she was nominated for Gosford Park, she was informed by one house “that they weren’t interested in dressing a woman in her mid-sixties”. The hierarchy cuts both ways. Actresses want to be seen in labels of commensurate status, or above. Labels tend to feel the same. Double As include Julianne Moore (“despite her age,” as one Hollywood insider put it), Jennifer Lawrence (“she can even make falling over look good,” said the same insider), Tilda Swinton, Cate Blanchett, Rooney Mara and, suddenly, Alicia Vikander. Acute status-awareness leads to a degree of unseemly horse-trading behind the scenes, with some stylists stockpiling dresses they have no intention of putting on their clients simply to prevent other stylists having them, or reduced to promising designers they’ll put an A-lister into their dress, provided that designer agrees to dress their other, less exalted clients. It sounds like a bear pit, but then stakes are high. The right look (hair and make-up are also key) can make casting agents reassess their preconceptions about an actress’s bankability. If she’s just played a dowdy frump or had a run of period parts, the Oscars are her chance to demonstrate that she’s a bankable sex-pot. The perfect dress isn’t one that’s merely flattering. It should position you on the map as a potential fashion muse, which means you can begin collecting fees for wearing certain labels on the red carpet. Not all fashion houses pay actresses by any means, however many jewellery companies do. One Hollywood agent told me that an Oscar nominee can charge up to £200,000 an outing - though it's more usually jewellery rather than fashion houses which pay. The Holy Grail of red carpet dressing – apart, possibly from winning an award for your acting – is a contract with one of the big European fashion names. These are even more rare than Oscars however. Cate Blanchett has Armani; Jennifer Lawrence, Marion Cotillard, Charlize Theron and Natalie Portman have Dior, Alicia Vikander and Michelle Williams are signed up to Louis Vuitton; Kristen Stewart, Keira Knightley and Julianne Moore have affiliations with Chanel. Depending on their deals, actresses are obliged to wear these brands at a certain number of key events, appear in advertising campaigns (generally shot by top fashion photographers and therefore considerably more beneficial than the average cheesy, heavily-air-brushed beauty ads they also star in) and make occasional appearances on the front row. The money is the big draw. “Many Hollywood actresses earn less than the public imagines,” says Anna Bingemann, who has styled Rachel Weisz, Naomi Watts and Uma Thurman. “Most films are pretty low budget these days. Many indie films pay actors less than they’re paying their nannies, and there’s no back-end.” A financial association with a prestigious fashion house can be a career life line. Brands like to lock their mascots in for several years, not least because it allows them to build a creative relationship based on trust. Too many of them have been burned by actresses and stylists demanding five enormously expensive options, only to ditch all of them at the last moment, while somehow failing to return any of them. The twinkling Armani Privé ballgown Cate Blanchett collected her Oscar in two years ago showed what happens when an actress and a designer hit the sweet spot, creatively. But these exclusive arrangements also means there are fewer dresses to go round those actresses outside the magic circle. Another chink in the system, says Bingemann, is that there are now so many noteworthy awards. “In the old days, no one in America really watched the Baftas. You had the Globes and the Oscars. Now you have the Sag Awards, the Baftas, the Independent Spirit Awards, the Emmys…no one ever cared about the Emmys. But now that television is sexy, everyone watches those too. You’re talking months of awards.” Campaign trails can start back in September with the Venice film festival. That’s a huge number of dresses. “The sensible strategy,” says Bingemann, “ would be to hold back the best dresses until the Oscars, but it doesn’t work like that.” So to my Oscar picks from Couture. Hmm. All I can say is that compromises were made. I’ve omitted sheer, although in real life, designers could probably be coaxed into adding linings and I’ve bypassed anything that won’t play well in Milwaukee. I had a hard time finding much colour – then again, given the controversy surrounding this year’s nominations and the sobering situation in Syria, monochrome might be the order of the evening. I thought hard about weaning Kate Winslet out of her habitual stiff columns and into something floaty and about trying to make Rachel McAdams look a bit more left of field. But Winslet’s stiff columns work for her and left of field might look all wrong on McAdams. And what do you do about Charlotte? Once she was a Double A – 69, but a hot fashion property because, hell, she’s Charlotte Rampling and innately stylish. Then came the race row. Now some designers may feel cautious about dressing her… this Oscar dressing business is not as easy as it looks.   A striking colour and a touch of Gothic drama, this has Rooney Mara’s (Best Supporting Actress nomination) name on it. Widely expected to wear a Saint Laurent-style Le Smoking, Charlotte Rampling (Best Actress nomination) could still surprise in something softer but still quintessentially French. Plus Karl Lagerfeld won’t give a damn about her controversial remarks on the Oscars race row. Best Actress nominee, Saoirse Ronan’s stylist has gradually been coaxing her into more daring choices. Ronan, who says she stipulated no flowers or pastels, has worn both to great effect. This metallic floral lace is youthful but Oscar worthy. Admittedly the neckline’s quite a statement, but nothing Jennifer Lawrence (Best Actress nomination) can’t handle.  She’d look amazing with bright red lips and minimalist make up too. Less for her to trip up in too. This flattering combination of classic and interesting, would considerably up the fashion ante for Rachel McAdams (Best Supporting Actress Nomination) without alienating her fans. Your classic girl next door (if you live in Hollywood). Brie Larsson’s (Best Actress nomination) style credentials are untested. Lavender Schiaparelli, with strong hair and make‑up would mark her card as a potential fashion player. Undoubtedly a great actress, Jennifer Jason Leigh (Best Supporting Actress nominee) is Hollywood’s odd-ball. Versace would be an unexpected curve-ball for her. This Versace also happens to look quite edgy, yet sexy. After the taupe ballgown she wore to collect her last Oscar, Cate Blanchett (Best Actress nomination) may want a colourful column. Look no further.   © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Entrepreneur and investor Carmen Busquets was nominated by Caroline Issa for her mindful approach to business Venezuelan entrepreneur Carmen Busquets was among the first professional investors to see the value in fashion e-commerce when, back in 1997, she became a co-founder and major investor in Net-a-Porter.com. Since then Busquets has gone on to invest a total of $50 million in a number of fashion tech giants in the UK and United States, including Moda Operandi, Lyst, Business of Fashion, Farfetch and more recently, start-up bespoke knitwear company Unmade. An early investor in New Age pioneer Deepak Chopra in the 1980s, she credits her success in business to her mindful approach. We say: Everyone knows about her investment prowess, but Busquets’ latest mission is to weave mindfulness and sustainability into the fabric of the fashion industry in a meaningful way. She says: "People tend to focus on my success, but they don’t talk about the mistakes I’ve made or the difficulties I’ve had to overcome; the fact that I’m deaf, or that I found out aged 40 that I am dyslexic, which explains why previously I couldn’t communicate my ideas the way I can now. "Both my parents meditated, so I grew up with the discipline of spiritual teacher George Gurdjieff, who advocated awareness through mind and body. Sometimes I see things too early. But when you are mindful, you tend to be more connected to whatever the universe has to say. "It’s important to have great partners, and investors who think like me. I choose carefully who I want to invest in and work with. I work with those who add value, and those I can learn from while they learn from me. It’s never one way; the teacher should learn as much as the pupil. That takes the arrogance out of the equation… It’s never too late for people to learn."  Look out for: Integrating mindfulness and meditation into business, Busquets is inviting CEOs in her portfolio to a series of retreats to encourage them to do the same – the first one taking place in Bhutan later this spring. This ripple effect of positivity in the workplace will also be one of the topics up for discussion when Busquets presents  her approach to mindfulness in business at the House of Lords in May. carmenbusquets.com © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.  Stella McCartney has once again teamed up with Adidas to create kits for over 600 athletes for the 2016 Olympic Games, creating performance wear that is both technical and will hopefully make British athletes stand out on the global stage.  Rather than a minimal approach, McCartney's aesthetic this year is busy with a focus on bold logos and patriotic emblems. As expected there is a strictly red, white and blue colour palette, with loud letterbox red Boost trainers and matching socks. Although the kit is designed for over 600 athletes across the Olympic and Paralympic Games and a number of disciplines, the kits are all closely interlinked thanks to a splattering of logos, letterman-style GB embroidery and a specially commissioned coat of arms. Adidas commissioned the College of Arms to design a new coat of arms for Rio 2016, which will be used on almost everything, from Jessica Ennis Hill's crop top to the cycling Lycra suits. The highly patriotic coat of arms incorporates the floral emblems of the four Home Nations (a rose, thistle, leek and flax) and at the top sees a lion resting on a crown made of gold, silver and bronze medals. The Latin banner on the crest means "conjoined in one", representing all of the sports unified together. Although the design team considered using a fox, they decided to stay with the oh-so British lion, which is also a symbol of strength and athleticism. Adidas have got the technology covered as fabrics are 10% lighter than in London 2012, which can help to bring athletes closer to standing on the medals podium. Tom Daley said of the technology at the grand kit reveal at Seymour Leisure Centre:  "My trunks are quite small! But overall the kit is 10% lighter so for track and field and cycling it helps you go faster. We'll be ready for it." "I feel pride when I put on the GB kit and the crest brings us all together," Olympic winning athlete Jessica Ennis-Hill said of the kits at this morning's launch. "It's an opportunity to come together as a team and with kit we feel like a huge team together." On Twitter there have been mixed reactions to the design, with most of the conversation focusing on how small Tom Daley's swimming trunks are.  Excuse us for a moment while we marvel at the impossible smallness of Tom Daley's trunks. It's all part of Stella McCartney's efforts to make Team GB's Rio 2016 kit 10% lighter than before; the technical prowess here is really something to behold.  To the rest of the 600-strong team's Olympic wardrobe, and we were surprised to see things had taken a turn for the vintage. McCartney's motif of choice was not a graphically deconstructed and modern Union Jack along the lines of 2012 but a nostalgic coat of arms with a lion at its beating heart and references to a thistle, rose, leek and flax to represent each of the countries which come together under the GB umbrella. Adidas called it a "a traditional symbol" to contrast with the "21st century look and feel of the kit". You could read all sorts of things into the subliminal messaging behind this use of heraldry. Does it nod to Great Britain's assertion of its heritage as the country which gave the world Queen Elizabeth, National Trust properties and Harry Potter? And the British Lions, of course.  There could be a more fashionable explanation. Mythical creature references are very of-the moment thanks to Gucci, where designer Alessandro Michele has employed serpents, panthers and birds of paradise in his recent must-have collections. Rather than forking out £2660 for a snake embellished bag, Team GB get the look with a lion emblazoned crop top instead. The drawstring waist jackets, logo leggings and sleek boxy cut sweatshirts have all drawn admiring coos from the fashion desk, and will look elegant and refined among the cacophony of kit variations which the Olympics always brings. But when you see McCartney herself with a lipstick red coat draped over her shoulders among the athletes on stage, it makes you think that a little more scarlet might have packed a mightier punch. But perhaps McCartney's leaving that job to the athletes themselves.  View latest offers from Adidas © Telegraph Media Group Limited 2019 We rely on advertising to help fund our award-winning journalism.
